Dans la Suret\`ep, les insectes constituent une menace permanente, en raison notamment de la grosse rétention de mati\`e dans l'habitat sous forme de graines, decelles de plantes cultivées comme le Phaseolus. La maîtrise entomologique est indispensable pour éliminer les végétaux sous forme de graines et pour empêcher la propagation d'insectes dans l'agriculture. Le projet de maîtrise entomologique a été mené au sein de cinq équipes de Jeunes Professionnels de la Sureté du Mali (JPSM) dans le district de Kayes. Le triaje au cri, le panage au pain et l'insecticide avec des grains de riz ont été utilisés comme instruments techniques. Le travail a commencé en mai 2018 et a été poursuivi jusqu'à la mi-décembre 2018. Nous avons répertorié 150 tétes d'ouvriers eupelmidés sur un total de 9,5hectares le long de la rive droite du fleuve Niger dans le district de Kayes. Aucun assaisonnement d'Eupelmus orientalis Crawford n'a pu être repéré. Nous nous poseons maintenant la question de savoir si cette sélectivité a atteint son objectif, en respectant les différents critères retenus dans la directive européenne 2013/30/EG et ce, sans mettre en danger la population de paysans résidant dans ce district qui ne sont pas touchés par cette épineuse.

Doubly-charged scalars have been proposed as a dark matter candidate and to explain the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. These particles can also be produced at colliders and, if they decay into standard model (SM) particles, may give signatures with large multi-lepton invariant masses. In this paper, we show that LHC Run II data for production of pairs of doubly-charged scalars can be used to place the strongest direct collider constraints to date on the parameter space of such a model. We also consider a specific two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) as an example, and show that after correcting for effects from oblique electroweak corrections, this model is disfavored with respect to the observed Higgs signal strengths. We then update our previous analysis of this model, including constraints from LHC Run II data for multi-lepton plus MET signals. We show that, in this case, 2HDM models with explicit flavor symmetries remain consistent with all data.

Heterogeneous materials are comprised of many types of constituents that interact with one another in complex ways. Examples of such materials abound in nature, from soils to tooth enamel to vegetation canopies to spider silks to human bone. The structural organization of these materials gives rise to a broad spectrum of spatial and temporal heterogeneities, or patterns, that can profoundly affect their mechanical and physical behavior. Over the past few decades, a theoretical framework known as heterogeneous materials theory has been developed to describe and model these complex, structured materials. In this series of three papers, we provide an overview of some of the fundamental concepts of heterogeneous materials theory. In particular, we discuss the emergence of structure in these complex, structured materials and introduce two primary concepts that are central to this field: heterogeneities and length scales of organization. We also introduce some of the basic organizing principles of spatial heterogeneity and describe how such principles can be incorporated into a formal heterogeneous materials theory. We then describe the general methodology of two-point correlation function modeling and present a collection of illustrative examples that can be used to develop an intuitive understanding of this approach. We also demonstrate how two-point correlation function modeling can be used to make quantitative predictions regarding mechanical behavior. We conclude the review by outlining some of the key open questions in this field and identifying some areas for future research.

Using high-resolution (0.1”x0.1”=1-2 pc) imaging polarimetry of the hot, obscuring circumnuclear dust in a sample of 31 FR I radio galaxies from the Archive of Chandra Survey (ACSW) we characterize the strength, structure, and position angle of the optical nuclei. Nuclear polarizations of ≥5% are observed in 19% of the galaxies, with a weak trend for decreasing polarization with increasing distance from the radio core. Polarizations are observed to change sign between inner and outer regions (within 0.1-3.0 arcsec), ranging from -2 to 5% in seven sources, with no obvious relation to host galaxy properties. Polarization position angles (measured near the 50% level) are generally broad, ranging from 0°-90° (with a mean of 60°) and do not align with the radio structures or kpc-scale dust disks seen in high-resolution (sub-pc) imaging. We argue that the observed nuclear polarizations are not produced by scattering on aligned dust grains, but likely arise from dichroic absorption within small (<50 nm) aggregates of aligned, non-spherical silicate or graphite particles. This conclusion is supported by the observed variations in the polarimetric properties of the dust as a function of distance from the nucleus and the requirement that the scattering phase function be substantially forward-peaked. Our results suggest that the central parsecs of radio galaxies are regions of active, small-scale structure with highly irregular (possibly transient) magnetic field configurations, large populations of aligned dust particles, and likely sources of significant obscuration for ionizing active galactic nuclei.

R Leo is a semiregular variable star with a spectral type M7.5 III, which means it is a red giant. Red giants are cool, outer most layers of stars which have recently went through a red giant star phase. Red giant stars have bloated stellar shapes with extended outer shells, and have cooling bright cores. R Leo is one of the most massive red giants, and is almost as bright a star as the entire region of the Milky Way galaxy. R Leo is a semiregular variable star. This means that its photosphere varies in size and heat capacity, which causes variations in apparent brightness. R Leo's apparent magnitude varies between 3.8 and 4.2 over a span of 4 days. Maser emission from the SiO molecule has been detected from R Leo before, but its exact location was not known. The new data presented here localize the masing gas to a region approximately 30% of the star's radius from the photosphere. This suggests that the masing gas is much closer to the photosphere than previously thought, perhaps even in the stellar wind. This relatively close proximity make these SiO molecules very susceptible to decay by photodissociation. Silicon monoxide, SiO, is a monoxide molecule with a light silicon atom. It is the most abundant molecule after H2O in the atmospheres of late type stars. Maser emission from SiO has been detected from many cool stars including red giants. Masing gas has been assumed to be near the photosphere for decades, but these data indicate that the gas may be much closer to the stellar surface than previously thought. This could have large implications for theories of how masing regions evolve over time. This paper presents new data that localize the masing gas to a region approximately 30% of the star's radius from the photosphere. The new data suggest that the masing gas is closer to the photosphere than previously thought, perhaps even in the stellar wind. This could have implications for how masing regions evolve over time.

NAND formula, also known as N-ary NOR function, is a compact representation of a relation between a large number of binary variables. NAND formula consists of a few burden hard-coded gates, and some sum and product variables. Modern NAND circuits contain tens of millions of such variables. It is crucial to develop efficient circuit simulation algorithms for profit analysis, design validation and hardware/software co-design. We present a compilation flow for NAND formula evaluators with a small number of burden gates. The main idea is to do peephole optimization and bit-level rewriting to gradually simplify the NAND formula. This technique can greatly reduce the number of sum and product variables. We applied our technique to two widely used NAND models and achieved over 90% reduction in the number of sum and product variables. Our techniques can be readily applied to other complex circuits with a small number of burden gates.

The recent observation of gamma-rays from blazars by the Fermi and HESS telescopes has lead to a revision of our understanding of the properties of the extragalactic background light (EBL). Models of galaxy formation now suggest that gamma-ray absorption by the EBL is significant enough to prevent detection of distant blazars. Additionally, the spectral measurements of these sources are best explained by an exponential cut off in the EBL spectrum at energies above 80 GeV. This phenomena is known as the Fermi-2, Fermi-1 and HESS spectrum conflict. New EBL observations with future telescopes, like the EBLacker, the Simons Observatory and the Dark-Star survey, could confirm or refute these model predictions. This work proposes a model in which gamma-rays are deflected by Galactic Dark Matter (DM) and Galactic Center Excess (GCE) emission to explain the spectrum conflict. These models can fit the current GLAST and HESS observations and predict the emission expected from future instruments like the EBLacker and Simons Observatory.

Cooperation is an important factor of evolution and one of the defining features of human societies. While individual rationality requires each player to maximize their own profits, cooperative behavior is often at odds with individual interests. In this paper, we consider a multi-agent system that incorporates a reward mechanism to promote cooperative behavior. In particular, we consider the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma and each player has an individual payoff based on a fixed probability to cooperate or defect. Each player not only observes their direct neighbors, but also learns from the global density of cooperators. We find that the interactions between players promote the emergence of cooperation. In particular, whenever cooperators emerge, players are progressively rewarded for their local contributions and the overall cooperation level increases steadily over time. In the limit, players approach a completely cooperative state, while defectors become extremely rare. We also observe that the final level of cooperation is robust against various distributions of player qualities and natural fluctuations.

We present a direct measurement of the spatial curvature of our universe combining the information from distant supernovae Ia with the local gravity environment of the Sloan Great Wall galaxy cluster. The combined data set yields a value for curvature of −0.006 ± 0.008 (1σ), corresponding to a flat universe with 96% confidence. This measurement is consistent with a curvature of 0, as expected for a universe described by general relativity with a cosmological constant. However, we also find a significant statistical correction to the measured value of the cosmological constant of ΔΛ = −0.054 ± 0.032 (1σ), corresponding to an open universe with 99.99994% confidence. This correction, which we find to be consistent with statistical fluctuations expected from measurement uncertainties, provides a robust determination of the universe's spatial curvature. The spatial curvature of our universe has significant implications for the laws of gravity. The spatial curvature is proportional to the density of matter and hence a detection of curvature rules out large-scale matter distributions required to explain the observed acceleration. We suggest that this detection, in conjunction with previous observations of an accelerating universe from supernovae and the cosmic microwave background, necessitates the introduction of novel forms of energy with negative equations of state, such as dark energy.

Beta-dystroglycan is a Schwann cell membrane receptor for laminin found in the basal lamina that surrounds neurons. In the peripheral nervous system (PNS), dystroglycan functions to connect the extracellular matrix with the actin cytoskeleton, thus enabling Schwann cells to adhere to, and organize their cellular processes on, the axonal surface. In central nervous system (CNS), similar function of dystroglycan has been suggested, but the evidence is less robust. Mutations in the dystroglycan gene (DAG1) cause a congenital muscular dystrophy known as dystroglycanopathy. Using the mouse Model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (MDX), we found that utrophin, a functionally homologous protein of dystrogin, is upregulated at the membrane of Schwann cells. A search for the responsible mRNA transcript identified dystrobrevin-2 as a likely binding partner of utrophin. By co-immunoprecipitation experiments, we demonstrate that dystrobrevin-2 is part of the same complex as utrophin in Schwann cells. Furthermore, using RNA-Seq and qRT-PCR analysis, we report changes in beta-dystroglycan processing in the MDX Schwann cells: in the axonal surface of Schwann cells, the beta-dystroglycan transcript is reduced by half, and this reduction is statistically significant. In the cytoplasmic pool of Schwann cells, we found the full-length beta-dystroglycan transcript was dramatically reduced with no significant change in transcript splicing. Furthermore, this reduction is statistically significant. These significant changes in the level of the full-length and cleavage transcripts of the beta-dystroglycan gene correspond with a redistribution of the protein from the axonal surface to the cell membrane. In the axonal surface, there is no reduction in beta-dystroglycan protein. These results suggest a novel role for beta-dystroglycan in Schwann cells: that of anchoring the membrane to the extracellular matrix via utrophin in the axonal surface membrane and dystrobrevin-2 in the cell membrane. In addition, the reduction in full-length and cleavage transcripts of beta-dystroglycan in the Schwann cell cytoplasmic pool suggests another role for beta-dystroglycan in Schwann cells: that of sending a signal to the nucleus. The role of utrophin in Schwann cells has not been previously examined. We hypothesized that utrophin, a functionally homologous protein of dystrogin, might compensate for the lack of dystroglycan by forming a complex with dystrobrevin-2 in the Schwann cell membrane, thus anchoring the membrane to the extracellular matrix via dystroglycan. Our findings reveal a novel function for beta-dystroglycan in Schwann cells: the anchoring of the membrane to the extracellular matrix via utrophin

Cosmic rays in clusters of galaxies exert multiple ionizing and heating impacts. First, the high energy particles escape from clusters and accumulate in large amounts around the cluster cool core. The combined effect of several Coulomb scatterings and Inverse Compton scattering results in a huge radial pile up of thermal energy that in many cases is sufficient to offset cooling rates. Second, the extremely high energy secondary particles produced by hadronic interactions between cosmic rays and atoms in the cluster atmosphere can penetrate deep into the cluster and heat the thermal electrons through adiabatic expansion losses. Third, the flux of very high energy gamma rays, possibly generated by the decay of pions produced in interactions between cosmic rays and cluster gas, can be very high and may extend to large cluster-centric distances. A positive feedback loop is then established in which the acceleration of cosmic rays is sustained by the heat generated by these various impacts. The feedback process is inherently self-regulated. Cosmic rays eventually get fully accelerated but then the same process leads to the "blowing away" of the heat accumulated in the cluster core by a very powerful convection flow. Clusters without a strong enough heat source may therefore live shorter lives. However, some clusters may be caught in a metastable state with abalance between positive and negative impacts. The paper is based on a very large, new Monte Carlo simulations of the heating and cooling of the ICM by cosmic rays in galaxy clusters.

The long-wavelength (low-frequency) dynamics of liquids, such as water, appear to be well described by the Stokes equation. In this limit, the viscosity conveys a local divergence of velocity field. Incompressibility of the liquid implies a divergence of stress tensor as well. In turn, the force balance between stress and elastic forces leaves an intrinsic shear wave whose amplitude decays as the inverse square of the distance from the forcing point. These few simple assumptions are enough to account for most of the complex non-equilibrium phenomena in the low-frequency rheology of Newtonian fluids. However, in practice most real-world liquids have non-Newtonian properties. This is particularly evident in the limit of long wavelengths, such that the elastic forces become negligible as compared to the viscous forces. In this limit, the only mechanism of forcing is viscosity. It remains to be seen if this simple model is capable of accounting for the low-frequency rheology of such fluids.

The magnetorotational instability (MRI) is a key process in astrophysics and fluid dynamics that has been studied in rotating systems for decades [1]. Recently it has been realised that the MRI can occur in a shearing box that mimics the differential rotation that is present in the atmosphere of a galaxy or a accretion disc into which gas can fall. Since the first simulations of this instability [2], it has been shown that this mode of instability requires a sufficiently uniform shearing box in order to develop. For a shearing box with a zero net shearing rate, the MRI is only driven by magnetic field fluctuations, and consequently only becomes unstable when the magnetic Reynolds number is sufficiently high (so that the magnetic energy can be replenished by diffusion). In this paper, we perform the first simulations of the MRI in a shearing box with a zero net shearing rate, and show that the magnetic Reynolds number must be increased by at least two orders of magnitude in order for the MRI to become significantly nonlinear. We analyse the sources of error in our simulations, and argue that the basic instability appears to be damped by numerical viscosity. When we increase the resolution of our runs by a factor of two, we see some of the fine features of the instability, but overall the growth rate of the most unstable modes is reduced. We argue that the most likely resolution to accurately capture the full dynamics of the MRI in this setup is achieved when the effective Reynolds number and the magnetic Prandtl number are both equal to $10^4$.

In this paper we establish the anabelian geometry of the moduli stack of curves, M_{g}, in positive characteristic. We do this by passing from M_{g} to its profinite completion, Mink(g) of M_{g}, together with the corresponding continuous automorphisms, Γ(Mink(g)). Using the theory of complex analytic rigid spaces we can then construct an anabelian structure on the corresponding analytic space, Mink(g). We use this to prove a structure theorem for the pro-abelian fundamental group of M_{g}, describing it in terms of fundamental groups of modular curves and the Teichmüller tower. As a corollary, we show that the natural map from the abelain fundamental group of M_{g} to the absolute pro-abelian fundamental group is an isomorphism. Our main new technical result is a description of the local pro-abelian deformation rings for general points of Mink(g) (see Theorem 1.1). As an application, we deduce that every local deformation problem for general points of Mink(g) has smooth moduli. As an additional corollary we deduce that the formal deformations of a general point of Mink(g) form an abelian scheme. We then study M_{g}(C), the moduli stack of stable curves of genus g over a curve C, and its relation to Mink(g). We prove that the natural map from M_{g}(C) to Mink(g) is proper with generic fiber isomorphic to the moduli of P GL(2)-bundles on C (see Theorem 2.5). As a corollary we deduce that the absolute anabelian geometry of M_{g} is determined by theétale anabelian geometry of M_{g}(C). Using the structure theorem for the pro-abelian fundamental group of M_{g}, we deduce in particular that the absolute anabelian fundamental group of M_{g} is independent of the choice of characteristic (see Corollary 4.2). Using the results of [8], we then deduce that M_{g}(C) is anabelian whenever C is affine (see Corollary 4.3). The main results of this paper, namely the structure theorem for the pro-abelian fundamental group of M_{g}, as well as the anabelian properties of the stacks M_{g}(C) for affine C, have both been announced before. We include here complete proofs.

A dramatic variability of X-ray absorption lines in the black hole candidate Cygnus X-1 is reported. The source was observed by satellite-based X-ray telescopes during a state transition of the source: from the bright soft state to the faint soft state and back. A highly variable absorption line profile was observed only in the soft state. In particular, the deepest absorption features are observed only in the soft state, indicating an origin in the inner region of the accretion disk. The variability pattern is inconsistent with the absorption produced by a distant, neutral, static absorber such as the interstellar medium or a distant, gravitationally-lensing galaxy. Instead, the observed variability pattern is consistent with an origin in an outflowing, ionized absorber, such as an accretion disk wind. The variability amplitude and profile are consistent with those expected from the response of the absorber to changes in the continuum. These results suggest that the origin of the absorber may respond to changes in the source luminosity, providing a potential new method to investigate the structure and dynamics of the absorber.

Mass-loss events in the later evolutionary stages of stars are critical for the understanding of the final fates of stars. Radial velocity curves of typical stars with radiative outer envelopes can be accurately modeled using theories of mass-loss processes. However, the processes that drive the dramatic mass-loss events observed in some supergiants are not so well understood. Of particular interest are the events that drive the rapid mass-loss exhibited by many of the Luminous Blue Variables (LBVs) and the Quasi-periodic Modulations (QPMs) of the radio signatures of several supernova explosions. Recent results on the rapid mass-loss of LBVs have greatly increased the number of known examples and provided a framework for explaining some of the more extreme events observed. In some cases, the observed mass-loss is well described by relatively simple, magnetohydrodynamically-driven stellar winds. In other cases, the mass-loss is more consistent with radiatively-driven winds. This might indicate that multiple mass-loss mechanisms are at work in these objects, or that more complex processes, such as clumping or substantial rotation, are involved. The QPMs observed in the radio signatures of several supernova explosions also continue for many years after the explosion. These modulations are usually well described by simple harmonic functions with frequencies near 0.25, 0.6, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.5 cycles per year. The 0.6 cycle per year frequency has also been found to decrease with time as the supernova evolves. This seems to indicate that the process that produces the modulations has memory. In most models, this requires a binary companion or another form of internal resonance. A variety of observational and theoretical approaches have been used to study these dramatic mass-loss events. Recent modeling has benefited greatly from the theoretical advancements made in the areas of hydrodynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, and nuclear reaction networks. Future work will likely benefit from the continued study of individual objects and also from coordinated monitoring programs designed to detect the onset of such rapid mass-loss.

E. Convery, S. Dolan, J. Horner, T. J. Jones, V. E. McBride, K. O. Morgan, J. Murphy, H. Pan, M. A. Price, N. J. Wagner, M. A. Wood, and J. Zhu Black Hole Accretion in Low States: Electron Heating. From the central engine of a low-mass black hole (MBH) X-ray binary, multiple flares of hard radiation are observed from radio waves to gamma rays. During the flares, the accreting material is observed to harden significantly, likely due to the effect of electron heating. Using three MBH X-ray binary observations performed with the Chandra X-Ray Telescope, this effect is modeled and a correlation between the variability in the different energy bands is found. From this correlation, it is estimated that electron heating is the most likely cause of the variability in the lowest energy bands (soft X-rays and far UV).

Dew Point Depression Observations A 630-meter sloping path across the western United States was instrumented to measure the downwind saturation at a number of representative hillslope positions. Hill slope saturation differences correlated linearly with the measured dew point depression, with a strong negative slope indicating that as saturation decreased, dew point depression increased. The plot of dew point depression vs. hill slope saturation difference is shown as an example of a continuous piecewise linear relationship with two linear regions. The two regions have significantly different slopes, with the upper saturation difference region having a negative slope similar to the lower region. The estimated dew point depression at saturation difference of zero (i.e., at an isothermal line) was around -75.6° C. The warm wet storage product with temperature around -75° C can be generated by quickly increasing the saturation difference from near zero to around 0.5. The estimated saturation difference at -75.6° C dew point depression was around 0.5.

We consider the most general gravity action with abelian gauge fields in three dimensions with a Chern-Simons (CS) term. The corresponding equations of motion following from this action are analyzed. It is shown that in the presence of an AdS-type matter source, the solution to the equations of motion may have torsion. CFT dual of this theory in the weak-field approximation is presented. For simplicity we consider the case of a vanishing torsion potential. The corresponding equation of motion is a generalized Maxwell equation with an additional nonmetricity tensor. In order to illustrate the main ideas we present the corresponding classical solution. At large values of the radial coordinate the metric of the black hole resembles the well-known solution in General Relativity with an AdS-type source. At the same time, the nonmetricity and the curvature of the connection depend only on the radial coordinate and do not depend on the transverse directions. We conclude that the three-dimensional gravity with torsion is the corresponding CFT dual to the theory of gravity with abelian gauge fields described above.

A Branch and Cut algorithm for the Halfspace Depth problem is proposed. The problem is known to be strongly NP-hard. The proposed algorithm first generates a set of bounding boxes for the input space. Then, it solves a series of strongly reduced instances by a branch and cut approach. In order to speed-up the solving process, the intermediate solutions are cached. In order to guarantee the optimality of the found solution, a cutting plane based approach is used. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated on two large scale aircraft landing problem instances from the CUT willingness to pay dataset. The obtained results are compared to the best-known solutions obtained from the CUT automated optimisation tool as well as two existing cutting plane based algorithms.' Reference: Z. Du, Z. Hu, W. Yang, and J. Cheng. A Branch and Cut Algorithm for the Halfspace Depth Problem. arXiv:1901.02347, Jan. 2019.

In this paper we propose a quantum algorithm for the classical approach to the graph isomorphism problem using a quantum walk. This approach, due to Hell and Neubauer, is based on a classical algorithm due to Bron and Kerbosch that constructs an explicit mapping between the vertices of the two graphs, using a combination of depth-first search and transitive closure. We describe the quantum algorithm in detail and provide an experimental quantum implementation on small test graphs. The obtained results indicate that our approach is promising from the perspective of the application of quantum computing to computational problems. The astronomical community regularly holds discussions on proposals for new telescopes, and this cycle has now been going on for more than a decade without a new large optical telescope being funded. This lack of new facilities is the result of a misguided approach to proposal evaluation that does not accurately represent the cost of new construction projects, does not fully account for the risk of cost overruns, and ultimately does not reflect the needs of the astronomical community. We propose a different approach that better represents the costs of projects and places greater emphasis on the benefits of new facilities, including the opportunities for international collaboration and improved technical capabilities. We hope that the astronomical community will embrace this new and more appropriate process for future construction projects, and that established telescopes will be expanded to meet the growing needs of the astronomical community. Since 2006, proposals for new telescopes have been submitted to the astronomy community for evaluation. These proposals cover a broad range of cost and technical specifications, and the Evaluation Board for New Telescopes (EBT) has evaluated each proposal based on an evaluation template that has remained essentially the same since 2005. The evaluation process includes several key areas for consideration, including cost, technical design, and management. The cost component is broken down into two main areas: 1) the cost of the initial capital outlay for the facility, and 2) ongoing operating expenses, including operations and maintenance, maintenance, and personnel costs. The technical evaluation focuses on the design and capability of the telescope, with the submission assessed on its ability to achieve its science goals. The management evaluation looks at the management, including board and committee structures, and compliance with the Open Periodic Table (OPT) principles. The EBT has published evaluation templates for each of these areas, and each submission is evaluated based on the availability of relevant skills and facilities, the likelihood of cost and technical success, and other administrative considerations. Although there are some improvements to the evaluation process in the Proposal Revision 1.0 document, there are some aspects of the proposal evaluation that should be reconsidered to better represent the actual costs of new projects and account for risk. First, the cost evaluation does not adequately represent the cost of projects, as it does not include inflation adjustments, allow for useful contingency periods, or reflect changes in the purchase price of capital equipment over time. These errors can lead to an overall overestimation of costs, as projects often require additional time to perform system or equipment design reviews, detailed construction drawings, or other activities that drive up the cost. In addition, inflation can significantly impact project costs, and similar projects completed at different times will often have different costs due to the inclusion of updated prices and shipping delays. Second, the evaluation does not adequately account for risk and cost overruns. The prompt emission of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) is usually attributed to synchrotron emission of highly relativistic jets. However, the exact emission mechanism is still unknown. While the broadband afterglow phase typically extends to IR or Optical frequencies, the prompt phase usually peaks in the gamma-ray band. It is therefore important to study prompt emission separately from afterglow emission. Here, we report the broadband afterglow and prompt emission of the bright burst GRB 061121. The afterglow phase covers the optical, UV and X-ray bands and can be well described with a single power-law. In the gamma-ray band, the prompt emission can be well described by the Band function. The low and high frequency plateaus, which are hallmarks of the Band function, coincide with the optical and X-ray decay phases, respectively. This implies a physical association between the prompt and the afterglow emission. We discuss implications of this result for the emission mechanism of the prompt phase.

Using an asymmetric beam splitter and sending only a small portion of the incoming atoms through one arm of the interferometer, we enhance the tunneling probability through the potential barrier relative to the classical limit. For small splitter asymmetry and assuming that all other parameters are fixed, we derive an expression for the enhancement factor that increases quadratically with the nonlinearity coefficient. For reasonable values of the nonlinearity coefficient in an ensemble of hyperfine states of cesium atoms, we obtain a 100-fold enhancement of the tunneling probability. Our approach can be readily implemented in existing matter-wave interferometry setups and can be of use, for example, for measuring small deviations from classical gravity or high-accuracy inertial sensors. The authors are Dmitry Budker, Andrey Derevianko, and Yi-Pei Chen In this paper, we propose using a nonlinearity-assisted quantum tunneling in a matter-wave interferometer for high-accuracy inertial sensors and small deviations from classical gravity. We describe an approach to enhancing the tunneling probability through a potential barrier by sending only a small portion of the incoming atoms through one arm of the interferometer. Assuming that all other parameters are fixed, we derive an expression for the enhancement factor that increases quadratically with the nonlinearity coefficient. For reasonable values of the nonlinearity coefficient in an ensemble of hyperfine states of cesium atoms, we obtain a 100-fold enhancement of the tunneling probability. This approach can be readily implemented in existing matter-wave interferometry setups and can be of use, for example, for measuring small deviations from classical gravity or high-accuracy inertial sensors.

In this paper the longitudinal impedance of an XFEL undulator is calculated for operation in current-enhanced SASE (Self-Amplified Spontaneous Emission) schemes. The undulator radiation impedance is derived from the wake fields and is used to study the reflections from the input ZLWstairs filter for several current-enhanced SASE setups. The performance of the setup based on seven cells of [1] is discussed in detail. It is shown that more than 90% of the input power can be reflected with only 10% loss, which is considered very good for a proof-of-principle study. The presented results show that the presented setup is very promising for reaching the originally proposed performance target of current-enhanced SASE mode at XFEL. [1] Schulz, T., et al. To understand the gas dynamics of galaxies, trace the plasma processes, and diagnose the high-energy astrophysical emission, there is an increasing need for a model gas phase abundance analysis of He-like ions. We present a new method for the He-like iron K-shell spectral region that has significant advantages over existing techniques. This new technique uses a modified combination of light-atom approximation and multiple scattering theory to model the X-ray attenuation through a gas cloud. It is capable of determining both gas density and elemental abundance with high precision, over a large dynamic range, for a large number of species, i.e. up to 28, while traditional methods can only determine the density or the element abundance. We validate the new technique with three sets of plasma test results and find that our method has ~40% higher precision and can detect density changes of ~30% with similar precision as the traditional methods. For example, the new technique can detect He-like Fe XXIII at an electron density of 10^{10} cm^{-3} for an observed flux of 10% that of the He-like Fe XXVI line, while the traditional method only can detect the He-like Fe XXVI line for a signal to noise of 5. This technique could provide a powerful tool for future X-ray missions, like the International X-ray Observatory (IXO) and the Adversary Probe, which will have unprecedented spectral resolution for investigating physical conditions of gas clouds in the Universe.

In this paper we study gradient RG flows of the worldsheet sigma model for targets that are not flat. Such flows arise in situations when the target space is curved but admits a Killing vector field. The worldsheet metric becomes dynamical and isFlows of the worldsheet sigma model for targets that are not flat. Such flows arise in situations when the target space is curved but admits a Killing vector field. The worldsheet metric becomes dynamical and evolves according to the Ricci flow. In particular, we consider the WZNW model at the critical level with this background metric. We construct and study a family of exact solutions to the relevant flow equations. The solution describes the running background metric, the regular mode of the quantum sigma model fields, and their flow. The metric, the quantum fields and their flow interpolate between two neighboring vacua of the initial (flat space) WZNW model, which correspond to an AdS and a dS geometry in the space of coupling constants. We give an exact description of this interpolation using the quantum KdV equation. The constructed metric flow interpolates between the AdS and dS critical points of the $ g_{\text{ str }} = 0 $ Argyres-Douglas electrodynamics.

In the study of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), it is well known that the log-log correlation between gamma-ray fluence and GRB duration has a break at the shortest duration seen from Swift, about 2 s. The correlation between the fluence in two different energy bands and the break time is also non-linear. This has been explained by assuming that the observed energy bands sample different regions of the GRB relativistic jet, with higher energy bands sampling regions of faster-moving baryons. A physical origin for this break time has been missing, until now. It is demonstrated that the break time in the observed correlation is the result of a competition between the variability time scales of the engine that powers the burst and the resolution time scale of the detectors. The origin of this variability time scale is not a priori known, but is likely associated with internal gravity waves in the plasma outflow produced during the jet acceleration. A physical origin for the break time is demonstrated to be impossible. Thus, the previously-observed high-energy correlation between Swift GRBs no longer holds. A complete catalog of Swift GRB spectral parameters is presented. The catalog can be accessed online at https://observatory.gsfc.nasa.gov/ estimations/UXT11Y

Recent infrared observations with the Spitzer Space Telescope have revealed the presence of warm dust around several accreting low-mass stars in the cores of star clusters. This dust, likely produced in the stellar jets, is associated with dense, optically thick disks orbiting within 0.5 au of the central stars. The disks have masses of 10−7 to 10−5 M⊕ and radii of 100 to 1000 au, similar to those of transitional disks around T Tauri stars. The Spitzer observations have found no evidence for dusty disks orbiting the brown dwarf binary 2MASS J04231426+3203266, perhaps because this system lacks a jet-driven wind or because the separation of the binary is sufficiently large to prevent disk orbital resonance. The occurrence of disks around accreting low-mass stars in star clusters but not around accreting brown dwarfs in the same star clusters suggests that disk formation is contingent on processes independent of, but not incompatible with, core accretion.

The longitudinal atom scattering spin-channel and the pariteat-breaking Berry phases in atoms The scientific work presents a theoretical approach of the longitudinal atom scattering spin-channel and the Berry phases which break the symmetry between fermions. The possible observation of these phases requires neutral atoms with a high gyromagnetic ratio. The quantum state of the atom in the free space can be approximated by a linear combination of the magnetic substates with a high Lande factor. We consider a combination of three non-degenerate sublevels of the ground state. The atomic sample is located in the far-off resonant optical longitudinal magnetic field. This field acts on the total atomic angular momentum, which allows to consider the magnetic sublevels as the two-level atoms. The interaction of the atom with the field can be expressed by the Hamiltonian which corresponds to the Dicke model. The solution of the Schrödingier equation for the field parameters shows that the time evolution of the system creates two independent subsystems: the even and the odd states. The former is similar to the Hamiltonian describing non-interacting atoms. The latter has the form of the Hamiltonian describing interacting atoms. The nonzero mean value of the even state is determined by the structure of the odd state. The difference between the mean values of the even and odd states is the quantum observable. In the first approximation in the dipole-dipole interaction constant the quantum dynamics of this observable is found. The differences between the mean values of the atomic spins and the even and odd states are the pariteat-breaking Berry phases which break the symmetry between fermions.

We have studied the prompt emission of the optically dark gamma-ray burst (GRB) 051028 with the Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) and the Konus-*Wind* spacecraft of the Russian gamma-ray space telescope. We present a multi-band study of this GRB, which lasted longer than the observations of any other gamma-ray burst detector. During the initial phase, the lightcurve exhibits a shallow decay and a 2.3 s bump on a time scale of 0.1 s, which could be an example of a third phenomenon. Hadronization in semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering on nuclei has been studied using the statistical hadronization model (SHM). The model was found to describe the experimental data well, with both the shape and normalization of the transverse momentum distributions of pions and kaons being reproduced well. The excitation functions of both the p/d and K/pi ratio for several values of the atomic number of the nucleus have been computed, and good agreement with the available data has been obtained. The nuclear modifications of these ratios, defined as the ratios for nuclei over that for protons, have also been computed. While the p/d ratio is essentially unchanged by the presence of the nucleus, the K/pi ratio is significantly decreased, which is due to the increased contribution from decays of weakly excited resonances in the nuclear environment. The nuclear modification ratios are also compared with those computed from a theoretical model based on energy-loss photoproduction of jets in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Good agreement between the two is found. The data described above were taken with the HERMES and COMPASS experiments at DESY, CERN, and LMSL.

In electron-nucleus quasielastic scattering, the transferred four-momentum squared, |{q}|^{2}= (|{{q} }_0|, |{{q} }| cos {\phi }_{{q} }), is small but not infinitesimal, as required by standard treatments. In the range 0.1< |{q}|^{2}< 0.5 (GeV/c)2, the differential cross section can vary by several orders of magnitude, even for a given target nucleus. This fact, combined with the relatively high cross sections, makes quasielastic scattering an excellent means of studying the Nuclear Medium Modification of hadrons. In this paper, the scaling of the differential cross section with the fourth power of the nuclear mass is shown to be a natural consequence of the eikonal approximation, valid for low inelasticities. This scaling is illustrated in quasielastic scattering from nuclei and is shown to provide a remarkably good agreement with experimental data from a variety of nuclei. The proposed scaling has two important applications. First, it allows for extraction of cross sections for elementary scattering processes from measurements of the average nuclear cross section. Second, it allows for predictions of quasielastic scattering amplitudes from structures inferred from other types of scattering. These applications are illustrated using examples from the field of Neutron Scattering.

In this paper, we present an experimental test of non-local realism (NLR), a variant of Bell's theorem with the same underlying assumptions, but with stronger conclusions. The assumptions of NLR are that, for any given pair of space-like separated events, the results of local measurements on one can't be predicted by localhidden variables (LHVs) on the other, except with some probability, depending on the settings of the local measurements and the setup of the experiment. In our test, we set up a modified version of the CHSH scenario with bit-flip errors, which simulate the behaviour of the local measurements in the sense of NLR. We show that the violation of the modified CHSH inequality with experimental data is in agreement with the disturbance caused by bit-flip errors within the margin of error, ruling out the possibility of classical explanations. The result stands against a wide range of local realistic models, and is a strong violation of NLR.

Astrometry with "Carte du Ciel" plates, San Fernando zone. I. Digitization and measurement using a flatbed scanner. By scanning a subset of the "Carte du Ciel" plates, collected between 1914 and 1976 in the San Fernando zone (latitude 40° 30' to 41° 15' South and longitude 71° 30' to 72° 30' West) of the French Empire, with a flatbed scanner, we obtain astrometric data for several hundred thousand stars. These data are presented and used to assess the global robustness of the star positions measured on the "Carte du Ciel" plates. In addition, we present new measurements of the plate scale and show that it has not varied significantly over the period of the scanned plates. We also estimate the global proper motions of the detected stars, and show that they are not significantly different from zero. The comparison with published proper motions taken from the Berkeley Later Type Stars (BLE) survey and other sources shows that the dispersion of the differences is largely due to systematic errors in the "Carte du Ciel" proper motions. The dispersion of the differences, as well as the direction of the differences for certain stars, indicates that systematic errors also affect the "Carte du Ciel" proper motions. We finally present new measurements of the photographic scale error, which is used to determine the absolute star positions on the plates.

Two new basaltic asteroids, 2020 BP59 and 2023 BP33, have been discovered in the near-Earth asteroid (3547) entity group. These two new asteroids are the largest members of this group and have estimated diameters of 44 and 40 km, respectively. The new asteroids are both about 3.5 x 2.0 km in size and have estimated masses of approximately 7.7 x 10^{19} and 1.1 x 10^{20} kg, respectively. These make them among the most massive bodies in the main-belt. We determine their orbits using multi-integrations and based on osculating orbit analysis. Our dynamical results show that both asteroids have low perihelion distances of 0.96 and 0.88 au, respectively. The large size of these two asteroids and their low perihelion distances suggest that they may have significant amounts of heat energy due to collisions in their early histories. We determine their orbital evolution based on chaotic asteroid dynamics. Both asteroids are subject to significant collisonal hazards over the next 200 Myrs.

The discovery of two extremely low luminosity Milky Way globular clusters has substantial implications for the formation and evolution of the Galaxy. These clusters, described in detail in this paper, were originally selected from the data from the Dark Energy Survey. Radial velocities and other data are presented here for the first time. The minimum luminosity of these clusters is 6.9×10^−7 L⊙, more than 1,000 times fainter than anything previously discovered in the Milky Way. They have very little individual stars and are heavily disrupted. They are probably most similar to extremely low luminosity satellite galaxies of other galaxies, such as Segue 1, Willman 1, and Coma Berenices. A comparison with models of the Galaxy suggests these clusters must be 10-12 billion years old. Their density and orbits suggest they were probably accreted as a group. Similar associations may have been the building blocks of larger galaxies such as the Milky Way.

Today marks one year since the first identification of a potential major merger between the Milky Way and M31. This milestone was observed from a distance of about 320,000 ly, the closest approach of the pair since their most recent merger some eleven billion years ago. The merging pair are now locked in a hard-core collision course and will collide in five billion years. During the collision, a fantastic array of interesting phenomena are expected to occur. Active galactic nuclei in both galaxies will likely experience periods of significant accretion of matter and gas, resulting in the production of luminous jets, gamma-ray flares, and perhaps even observable effects at other wavelengths. The disc of stars in the central regions of each galaxy will violently interact, producing spectacular star-forming regions and maybe even new modes of star formation. The masses of the galaxies are nearly equal, making them the second most massive binary system known. The event is of exceptional interest to astronomy as a whole, and significant observing campaigns have been organized with instruments such as the Hubble Space Telescope and the Plateau de Bure interferometer.

Resolved stellar populations are critical probes of star formation histories and dynamical histories of galaxies. The Orion Nebula Cluster (ONC) provides an important benchmark for testing and developing techniques for interpreting observations of resolved stellar populations, owing to its proximity, well-determined position, luminosity, and age. Several studies have characterized the ONC with deep near-IR and HST data; however, their results are at odds regarding both the presence and nature of a Plummer-like IMF and the actual extinction toward the ONC. In this study, we use X-ray data from the Chandra Orion Ultradev deep survey to study the resolved stellar population in RCW49, a small local galaxy infalling into the Milky Way. We compare our results with the recent study of the ONC and discuss the impact of physical and observational parameters on the derived parameters. We also briefly discuss the possibility of comparing resolved stellar populations seen in different wavelength bands and the potential pitfalls.

Commençons par dire que des performances à objectivement sur les bases de données sont souvent accessibles via une API client implemented dans plusieurs langages (Java, Python, C, etc.). Dans cette lettre, nous proposons une alternative pour mettre en place un système dynamique pouvant aider aujourd'hui standardiser cette API et permettre la prise en compte des performances liées au volume d'étapes (exploration) pendant l'evaluation. L'approche dynamique utilise une plate-forme de simulation de données libre (Spark) et un workflow mapping équivalent à ce qui peut être exécuté sur une machine plus classique. Des travaux similaires concernant les performances dans le domaine des données notamment pour les applications spécialisées sont discutés.

We present the results of a search for diffuse optical streams in a sample of 71 low-redshift ($z < 0.2$) groups and clusters of galaxies. We used deep imaging of a 1.7 square degree field around the south Galactic pole with the GRavitational lOng Survey Telescope Array (GRAvaroo), which is composed of five small optical telescopes. After careful application of various data quality filters, we identify three candidate systems with coherent, faint, linear streams of stars consistent with a stream-like configuration of the disrupted satellite galaxies. The brightest of these three candidates, with a heliocentric recessional velocity of 14,200 km/s, is consistent with other confirmed satellites of the Milky Way at lower heliocentric velocities, supporting its identification as a dark-matter-dominated stream. The other two candidates, with heliocentric recessional velocities of 24,300 km/s and 32,300 km/s, have very low satellite galaxy contamination and can each be plausibly associated with an identified accretion event in the fossil record, suggesting that the streams have physical properties similar to those of previously-observed cosmological streams. If confirmed, these systems would represent the lowest-redshift galaxies containing streams of stars arising from the disruption of satellite galaxies and would represent a record of some of the most massive accretion events in the local volume. These results suggest that wide, faint, linear features may be a common property of galaxy groups and clusters at low redshift, even in the absence of massive central galaxies, and that these systems may represent important constituents of the overall cosmological stream population.

L-Alanine zwitterion, a new molecule with a formula of C((O)HNCH(CH(NH3)2)COOH)2NH4+, is reported. The zwitterion has a positive charge on the imine nitrogen and two hydrochloride salt forms in aqueous solution (HCl and NH4Cl) and in the crystalline state (NH4Cl). In the crystalline state, the zwitterion adopts a hydrogen-bonded dimer structure. In addition to the vibrational spectra of the zwitterion in the solid state, both the zwitterion and the two chloride salts are successfully modeled. The modeled zwitterion structure and vibrational spectra agree with the experimental results. The experimentally determined hydrogen-bonded dimer structure is also found in the modeled zwitterion structure. The aqueous and crystalline forms of L-alanine zwitterion were characterized using a combination of experimental and computational techniques. The abstract is very long because it also includes a background on the topic and general comments on the paper. neutron star is the term used to describe a celestial object made almost entirely of neutron, the subatomic particles with the atomic number of indivdual nuclei. Neutron stars are incredibly dense objects, with more mass than that of the Sun packed into a volume of about a cubic kilometer or more. Neutron stars are formed as the result of the supernova explosion that occurs when approximately 99% of a star's mass has been condensed into its core. Such extreme densities are reached because neutrons are so much more dense than normal atoms, and the strong force that binds nuclei together weakens as you get closer to the core. When the core has reached approximately 2-3 solar masses, there is not enough mass to support the core against its own gravity. The excess energy is released as a supernova explosion, also known as a neutron star formation. Most neutron stars are found in close binary systems with another neutron star or, more rarely, a black hole. These systems are known as low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs). LMXBs are interesting systems to study because they allow us to study neutron stars from two perspectives. The first is " quiescent " (also known as "inactive" or "non-pulsing") in which the neutron star orbits a more compact companion and is not emitting X-rays. The second is when the neutron star "transientsly" (for a time) increases its X-ray emission, called an "outburst". When an LMXB transits from one to the other state, it is interesting to study the differences between the two states. For example, we have recently shown that transientsly brighter outbursts are associated with an increase of the neutron star's spin period. Conversely, when the neutron star is quiescent, but its X-ray emission is somewhat brighter than normal, its spin period is found to be larger than when the source is significantly fainter. These differences in behavior have suggested a "two-states" model for the behavior of LMXBs. In this model, there are two types of accretion regimes onto the neutron star, with the differences between them explained by different ways in which the captured material is deposited onto the neutron star surface. The first is called "Spoon-fed" in which the capture material, mostly protons, sticks to the neutron star surface, forming a "spoon" shaped structure. Such transients are found to be brighter when the neutron star has a higher spin rate. The second is "Indirect" in which the capture material, mostly electrons and protons, forms a "cloud" around the neutron star.
