A new methodology is presented to put constraints on warm dark matter (WDM) particle masses by using QSO lensing statistics. This is achieved by constructing the halo mass function for different WDM models and combining this with the observed surface density of strongly lensed QSOs. The change in the QSO lensing rate caused by WDM is calculated as a function of WDM particle mass, and using recent observational constraints on the density of matter in the universe this allows us to place limits on the WDM particle mass. Current limits from this work and previous studies using galaxy lensing are in good agreement, giving a joint WDM particle mass limit of 800–900 keV. This is the most stringent limit from a single galaxy survey using lensing tomography and the first study to place a limit using strong lensing alone. Future surveys with the Euclid and WFIRST missions should be able to probe WDM particle masses as low as 200 keV using the same method. This technique can also be used to study other forms of hot dark matter, such as axion-like particles, at small masses using similar statistics from future surveys.

Using data from the AmerenCup experiment, we present a search for high-energy (30 MeV – 300 GeV) neutrino emission from sixteen gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) detected by the AMANDA telescope between 2000 and 2006. We find no evidence for emission above background in any of the bursts, and place 90% confidence level limits on gamma-ray burst neutrino rates that are more than an order of magnitude more restrictive than previous studies. This work extends the published analysis by including events in which the highest-energy cascade photon emitted by a parent muon neutrino was not detected. We find no evidence for emission above the diffuse atmospheric background in four of the bursts. For the remaining twelve bursts, we set a limit on the flux of muon neutrinos of 0.8–2.9 times the flux predicted by the simple, parameterized emission model of Waxman & Bahcall (1997). The diffuse neutrino flux predicted by this model is quite low, and is not strongly constrained by our limits. However, the fluxes from individual bursts may be much higher, and thus capable of testing this model of gamma-ray burst outflows. The most stringent limits are a factor of approximately three lower than the models of Dermer et al. (2002), which predict neutrino emission from many gamma-ray bursts. — http://arxiv.org/abs/1511.08208

HD97048 is a A3V star situated approximately 15.7 light years from the Earth. This star has a planetary system made of one gas giant in orbit around it. In addition, this star is known to have at least five exoplanets. The fifth planet, HD97048 e, was detected with the aid of the instrument HARPS, which is installed at the ESO 3.6 meter telescope at La Silla. This planet is in orbit around its parent star in less than one day. In this article, we take a closer look at the exoplanet HD97048 e, whose characteristics make it very interesting for the search of life elsewhere in the universe. It has a mass similar to that of Mars and an orbital radius of 0.1275 astronomical units. This is an orbit almost within the star's atmosphere. Since the beginning of the year 2005, the planet's eccentricity has been increasing, which could make the conditions for life difficult to sustain. This increase could also explain the observed brightenings of the planet, since gas and dust will be more abundantly expelled from the vicinity of the planet, thus approaching Earth like levels.

We consider a system of semiconductor superlattices with a tilted magnetic field. We study the stability of the basic states of this system, which correspond to different distributions of charge between the wells and barriers. We found that the system demonstrates a complex behavior in a wide range of the parameters of the system. For some parameters of the system, the system has up to 5 different basic states. In the area of linear stability of some of these basic states, we found a twist-scroll bifurcation, which corresponds to the birth of two-dimensional stable scroll wave patterns. We have also found a region of chaos, where the nonlinear dynamics of the system becomes unpredictable. We have calculated the directions of the Lyapunov exponents for this region, and found that two of these exponents are negative, which indicates the presence of stochastic dynamics in this area. *Robert Ashcroft* March 2019 The system we study in this paper is called a "semiconductor superlattice" (SSL). SSLs are made of two different materials -- a well material and a barrier material -- that are periodically repeated along one or two directions. The period in these directions is called the "superlattice period". The charge distribution in SSLs determines their optical and electronic properties. In this paper we study how the distribution of charge in SSLs changes when the parameters of the system, which correspond to physical properties of the materials, are varied. We study the changes in the charge distribution using the method of Maximally Stable Sets (Mermin). This method assigns to each distribution of charge in the SSLs a set of parameters of the system which will keep this charge distribution stable. We also use methods from dynamical systems theory to find the sets of parameters which correspond to changes in the charge distribution leading to bifurcations, where two different distributions of charge change their stability. We find that the system we study in this paper has a complex behaviour in a large range of the parameters. For some of these parameters we found two different types of bifurcations: twist-scroll and Neimark-Sacker. The first type of bifurcation was birth of two-dimensional scroll wave patterns, while the second type was the birth of regions of chaotic dynamics. We calculated the directions of the Lyapunov exponents for these regions, and found that two of these exponents were negative, which indicates the presence of stochastic dynamics in these areas.

The presence of pre-galactic ionized regions - referred to as proto-clusters - surrounding early structures is suggested by the large-scale over-density in the abundance of low-mass galaxy halos at high redshift. Such regions would have processed and enriched the inter-galactic medium (IGM) prior to the formation of reionized galaxies, and so might be detectable in the observed Ly-alpha forest (LAF) at low redshift. Here we present a search for highly ionized proto-cluster regions at $2.2<z<3.5$ using two sets of data: a 17-cycle (7.5 hours) WET exposure of the Boötes void and three new fields along the cosmic web at similar redshifts, combined with the SDSS DR7 spectroscopic sample. This data set completely lacking any large regions devoid of galaxies, we set 95% confidence upper limits of $\Delta z=0.04$ on the fraction of the IGM ionized by such a cluster. These limits are independent of the assumed geometry, scale size and ionization state of the proto-cluster, and imply that the number of such regions in the history of the universe is $<0.5$% of the total volume of the LAF absorbers at these redshifts. If such regions were, for example, preferentially ionization "voids" of radius $30h^{-1}$ Mpc at $z>2.2$, then the upper limits indicate that less than 0.2% of the LAF volume has been ionized by these regions. This is the first robust, model-independent limit on the abundance of proto-cluster regions that could have been responsible for reionization.

In this paper we establish a precise link between two objects that are seemingly very different, the quantum cohomology ring of certain G/P and the homology of the affine Grassmannian. We achieve this by constructing, for each Weyl group element w, a perverse sheaf, denoted ws, whose constructural homology is equal to (ws)QH(wP/wP). This allows us to give a purely combinatorial description of the cohomology ring. As a first application we show that certain rational polylogarithm functions are special values of classical ${\mathfrak{p}}$-adic Whittaker functions. We then deduce a closed formula for the character of induced representations for generic levels, in terms of classical ${\mathfrak{p}}$-adic Whittaker functions. As a further application, we show that certain periods of intermediate cohomology of a minuscule Springer resolution are equal to classical ${\mathfrak{p}}$-adic Whittaker functions.

We present near-infrared spectroscopic observations of the host galaxies of a sample of nine luminous QSOs at z<0.5 selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). These observations were designed to search for evidence of strong CaII systems, which are good potential signatures of very distant galaxies. We find two previously unknown examples of strong CaII systems at low redshift, and we discuss the implications of our findings for the redshift distribution of strong CaII absorbers. We find no strong evolution in the frequency of strong CaII systems from z=0.5 to 0, but we argue that this may simply be a consequence of small number statistics. We compare the properties of the QSOs in our sample with those of similarly luminous radio-quiet QSOs from the SDSS, and we find that the two samples are similar in black hole mass, accretion rate, and environment, although the strong CaII QSOs tend to have larger host galaxies. This implies that the hosts of strong CaII QSOs do not contain unusual amounts of dark matter. We find marginal evidence that the strong CaII QSOs reside in higher-redshift L* galaxies compared to the SDSS comparison sample, but we argue that this may simply be a consequence of the small number of strong CaII systems with known host galaxy redshifts. We conclude that the high incidence of strong CaII absorbers at low redshift and the similarity of these systems to high-redshift QSOs suggest that strong CaII absorbers predominantly occur in highly clustered environments at all redshifts. This suggests that the systems producing strong CaII absorbers may play an important role in galaxy formation, perhaps by triggering the rapid formation of dense virialized structures at late times.

Optimal occulters are designed for a given set of parameters, to minimize the time required to complete an imaging survey of a given volume of space, while maximizing the number of planets detected. We present a method of calculating the optimal density and size of massive exoplanet-finding occulters based on knowledge of the properties of the system, such as the size of the optics and the properties of the planet to be found. We focus on the scenario where imaging optics with diameters of 10 cm and 30 cm are used to find Earth-like planets. In this scenario, we demonstrate that the optimal occulter has a core density of 19.5 g/cm3 and consists of a shell with a thickness of 5.7 g/cm3 surrounding this core. The outer radius of the occulter is approximately 0.26 times the radius of the imaging telescope and the total mass of the occulter is 16.7% of the total telescope mass. We also perform the calculations for the case of 30 cm optics and find that the optimal occulter for this scenario is similar to the 10 cm optics occulter with the same density core/shell structure, but with a thinner shell. Finally, we present the results of simulations showing the number of planets detectable within a 3 days survey for the optimal occulters and for a set of less optimal configurations. We find that the optimal configuration can detect 99.7% of the planets within the given volume and survey time and the simulations demonstrate that reducing the density of the occulter by a factor of two and increasing the total mass of the occulter by a factor of two would result in a 55% decrease in planet detection rate for this scenario. We show that our results can be generalized to other scenarios with different imaging telescopes and properties of planets to be found. We demonstrate that the methodology presented in this paper can be used to efficiently design massive planet-finding occulters, find the optimal parameters of the occulter, and identify unoptimal configurations which could decrease the total number of planets detected without significantly increasing the survey time.

The terminal decline in oil production is widely perceived as an important factor likely responsible for recent and projected global economic instability. In the short term, the surge in oil prices caused by declines in global oil production may provide a welcome boost to the world economy. However, the long-term environmental and economic implications of such a rapid expansion of the fossil fuel industry are significant. Ultimately, the extraction and consumption of oil for fuel will diminish the quality of the available carbon-based energy resource, the fossil fuel supply, by requiring higher carbon-intensity extraction and combustion processes. Furthermore, given that the majority of the known fossil fuel reserves must be burned if the use of these reserves continues to grow at past rates, the amount of global CO2 emissions will increase dramatically in the future. This has potentially dangerous long-term implications for climate stability and poses significant risks to long-term economic growth because many economists forecast that the rapid expansion of the global oil industry over the next several decades will be driven primarily by policy, rather than the actual productivity or reserves of fossil fuel fields.

A series of spinel oxides MgAl2O4 with a wide range of stoichiometry was synthesized by conventional solid-state techniques and their crystal structure was refined by X-ray diffraction method. Among these, Mg0.7Cr0.3Al2O4 has a novel [Cr3+]2+ (3+):[Al3+]3:O4^4- substitutional disorder which was confirmed by successful refinement using FullProf and direct methods of Rietveld analysis. This is the first report on the substitutional disorder of trivalent Cr in spinel structure. The 3+ ion has a distorted octahedral environment of 6 oxygen anions and a nearly square-planar geometry of 4 remaining anions. The extent of disorder increases with increasing substitution ofCr3+ (3+) for Mg2+ (2+) cations, leading to the stabilization of the crystal structure as confirmed by relative density and PXRD data. The study of electrical conductivity using Seebeck coefficient shows a decrease with increasing substitution of Cr3+ (3+) for Mg2+ (2+), which can be explained on the basis of band structure modification due to presence of Cr3+ (3+):[Al3+]3:O4^4- substitutional disorder.

Recent experimental studies have revealed striking inhomogeneous properties in high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Specifically, nanoscale electronic structures have been revealed with (1) quasiparticle interference patterns with a fourfold period corresponding to the underlying CuO2 bunkravitic lattice, and (2) bososcillation patterns with a fourfold symmetry reflecting the bunkravitic lattice and also the presence of biO eerald crystals. Superconductivity emerges on the biO planes, which exhibit a charge-transfer (CDW) insulating property above a CDW transition temperature Tcdw. The superconductivity on the CuO2 planes, however, exhibits an unusual competition between the bunkravitic CDW order and electronic inhomogeneities arising from, for example, disorder and stripes, leading to the strong pseudogap phase above Tc. We argue that this phase is best described as a bunkravitic superspin liquid with fluctuating electronic inhomogeneities. The theoretical scenario is supported by recent STM imaging and spectroscopic studies as well as the observed bunkravitic, electronic, and superconducting correlation patterns. Notably, this new paradigm reconciles the long-standing enigma of the bunkravitic CDW order in the high-temperature superconductors with their anomalous electronic properties, while opening a promising avenue to search for its experimental signatures.

The notion of holomorphic bundle was introduced by Ehresmann in his fundamental paper describing connections in fibre bundles. The modern definition follows naturally from the analogous definition in complex analysis. A holomorphic bundle is a pair (E, p), consisting of a complex vector bundle E on a complex manifold M, and a holomorphic structure on E, that is, a compatibility between the complex structure on M and the smooth structure on E, such that p is a holomorphic map. As with complex vector bundles, one can ask for E to be endowed with a Hermitian fibre metric and a orthogonal geometry; the orthogonal geometry in this context means that the connexion should preserve the holomorphic structure. The theory of holomorphic bundles is very rich, with connections providing the links with many areas of mathematics and physics, ranging from complex geometry to physics to equivariant complex geometry. The present article reviews some of these links. I. Shestakov and U. Unitonn, “Holomorphic parakinetic bundles”, J. Math. Sci. (New York) 211 (1), (Feb. 2014), 314-333. <http://arxiv.org/pdf/1308.2516v1.pdf>

Entanglement is a crucial resource for many quantum information processing tasks, from quantum key distribution to quantum computational algorithms. While the generation of Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen entanglement between spatially separated parties is usually simple via local interactions between separable states, doing the same for Gaussian states of light is a much harder task. Gaussian states, which include laser modes and many other optical systems, are completely defined by their first and second moments (means and covariances), whose dynamics are non-linear and cannot be inverted freely. This prevents Gaussian states from being separable under any product classical-quantum (PQC) map, even though local Gaussian operations and classical communication (LOCC) may generate Gaussian states that are not fully separable. As a consequence, the simulation of Gaussian distributed random variables is not possible with a separable state, and thus entanglement distillation among Gaussian states, crucial for quantum information network security, is not possible without the help of non-Gaussian operations. Here we show that local Gaussian operations and the simultaneous application of local Gaussian unitaries to each mode—entangling Gaussian states that are otherwise fully separable—are sufficient to accomplish entanglement generation between any number of parties, with a scaling linear in the number of modes. This allows for the simulation of Gaussian random variables with Gaussian states, distillation of Gaussian entanglement with local Gaussian operations, and the experimental implementation of quantum information tasks requiring Gaussian states, with experimental certification a important goal of the field.

Distortion Minimization in Gaussian Layered Broadcast Coding with Successive Refinement Xiaoqiang Xia, Lihua Xie, and Shih-Fu Chang IEEE Transactions on Communications, Vol. 67, No. 5, pp. 3728-3741, May 2019 Gaussian layered broadcast coding with successive refinement was proposed in the seminal work by Koetter and Hoeky (KD III). The idea is to partition the source message into layers, and encode the layers with a long block length assuming perfect knowledge of the headers of the lower layers. The headers are further encoded with shorter length assuming imperfect knowledge of the lower layer headers. The resulting coding rate can be conveniently optimized over the Gaussian distribution, leading to an optimal layered coding strategy that is able to approach the capacity of the underlying multi-user discrete memoryless channel (DMMC) within 1 bit per channel use for many channels of interest. Successive refinement, however, typically incurs an accumulated distortion that increases with the length of the encoding block. In particular, for a DMMC with memory size K, when the encoding block length is no greater than (the so-called max-delay), the distortion can be shown to increase linearly with the block length. When the block length exceeds (the so-called delay-limited regime), the distortion can be shown to increase at most linearly with the block length. The exact slope in the delay-limited regime, which we refer to as the delay-regime slope, has been identified for only a few DMMC examples. In this work, we provide a general result for the delay-limited regime slope, which is shown to coincide with the latest know result for several specific examples, including the Hyperlabel Broadcast Channel (HLC) and the Gaussian Multi-Unicast with Successive Refinement (MUSIC).

In this work we study the onset and dynamical evolution of the low T/|W| bar-mode instability of non-rotating neutron stars. We simulate the unstable non-spherical instability using a multi-fluid formalism that treats both the bulk and vortical motions of all the fluids. Our main results can be summarized as follows. (1) We find that the instability is most easily excited in the context of pure gravity modes. This is due to the fact that the unstable mode corresponds to a bar-mode, and the rapid radial flow of matter in the unstable configuration facilitates the excitation of gravity modes. The growth rate of the instability decreases with the increasing pressure support. (2) We study in detail the instability development in different physical regimes, including weak, intermediate and strong pressure support. (3) We determine that a large portion of the nascent neutron stars are likely to develop torus-like structures as a result of the instability.

Magnetic multilayers comprising a Ni80Fe20 layer pair separated by a Nb spacer layer show promising applications as magnetic sensors due to their high magnetic anisotropic energy. A larger out-of-plane magnetic moment in Ni80Fe20 is observed in trilayer samples compared to bilayers, suggesting an enhanced degree of magnetic interlayer coupling. Here, we report a stray-fields-based magnetoresistance (MR) mechanism in Ni80Fe20-Nb-Ni80Fe20 trilayers. Specifically, a magnetic stray field from the Ni80Fe20 spacer layer induces a first set of out-of-plane stray-fields in the Ni80Fe20 layer. As the applied magnetic field is increased, these out-of-plane stray-fields propagate into the Nb spacer layer, where a second set of out-of-plane stray-fields is generated. Since the Nb spacer layer has a substantially higher magnetic anisotropy energy than the Ni80Fe20 layers, the total stray-fields in the Nb spacer layer are reduced compared to the applied field, leading to an enhanced MR ratio. We measure a five-fold increase in MR ratio at 10 kOe for trilayers with Nb spacer thicknesses ranging from 0 to 40 nm, as compared to a two-fold increase in MR ratio for bilayers with the same Nb spacer thicknesses. The stray-fields-based MR mechanism is likely responsible for the enhanced out-of-plane magnetic moment and MR ratio in trilayers, and we demonstrate that by appropriately adjusting the thickness of the Nb spacer layer, this MR mechanism can be employed to optimize the performance of Ni80Fe20-based magnetic sensors.

Exoplanets are of great interest to scientists, not only due to the scientific value of the information that can be obtained about their physical and orbital properties, but also due to the possibility of finding life-hosting planets. Planets with surface temperatures compatible with the existence of life on Earth, known as habitable planets, can be discovered around the most abundant stars in the galaxy. A particularly attractive group of such planets are those with shorter periods of time between two successive transits across the face of their host star. Such planets are known as "hot Jupiters". The existence of such planets in the habitable zones of their host stars offers the possibility of rapid atmospheric studies using the methods of dynamical atmospheric spectrometry. The atmospheric composition can differ significantly from the composition of the planet's surface due to intense heat and pressure from the sun's light. Knowledge of the surface gravity is thus essential in order to correctly interpret the results of such studies. In this paper, we present a novel technique to accurately determine the surface gravity of transiting extrasolar planets by measuring the duration of the planet's ingress and egress with respect to its host star. We show that the surface gravity of the transiting planet can be determined with an error of less than 2% when the orbital period of the planet and the period of the host star are similar. In the case when the period of the star is half the period of the planet, the error in the surface gravity determination can be as high as 6%, but is always less than 13%. The most important factor influencing the determination of surface gravity is the ratio of the planet's orbital radius to the radius of the star.

Trapping and guiding single atoms and ions in three dimensions is a crucial technique for sensitive metrology and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics. We demonstrate the precision control of collisions between a single ytterbium ($^{171}$Yb) ion and a single atom and of neutral atom-ion pairs. We load a single ytterbium ion and a single ultracold rubidium atom into separate U-shaped magnetic traps created by current-carrying wires. We then move the ion trap down and to the right, and lower the ion trap potential such that the center of the ion approaches the center of the atom trap. In this crossed, harmonically confining potential, we observe coherent quantum collisions, evidenced by sequential trap periods in which both the ion and the atom remain intact. We also observe an exponential decay of the atom-ion and ion-ion complexes, consistent with radio-frequency-driven sympathetic cooling. Our results illustrate the ability to precisely control both the position and strength of atom-ion and ion-ion potentials, with potential applications to quantum simulation, sensing and metrology.

The NUGA galaxy survey is an integral field spectroscopy survey of 32 early-type galaxies, undertaken using the SSO Telescope. Here we present the data and analysis for the sole spiral galaxy in the sample, NGC4569. We find that the majority of the molecular gas in NGC4569 resides in a large-scale bar. This is shown to be driving a two-sided slow-rotating wave in the potential, funneling gas inwards. The molecular gas in this bar is compact, having a deconvolved size of approximately 1.1 kpc. Using a simple rotating bar model, we show that this observed size is consistent with that expected for the bar strength. We detect molecular hydrogen in two secondary resonances, providing further evidence for the existence of a massive bar in the centre of NGC4569. This is the first molecular hydrogen observations of a large scale bar in a spiral galaxy. The presence of a bar in the centre of NGC4569 and its relation to the molecular gas observed are discussed.

NGC 1904 is a globular cluster in the Milky Way located approximately 18,000 light years from the Earth. While it has been studied in multiple passbands in previous works, this is the first comprehensive study of the entire cluster in the blue and green part of the spectrum. The cluster turn out to be slightly brighter and larger than previous studies in the blue indicated, with the brightest stars reaching up to Visual magnitude 8.5. The brightest stars are also shown to have a Blue Straggler Branch, characteristic of stars evolving off the main sequence. The mass function for the bright stars is fitted to a Kroupa profile, showing a deviation from a normal profile, which the authors attribute to the mass segregation effects. The radial profile of the cluster is studied in the core, intermediate and outer regions. While the density of stars decreases monotonically with the distance from the cluster center in the inner regions, the profile flattens in the intermediate region, showing a clear separation in the sub-structures. The velocity dispersion is studied in the core, intermediate and outer regions, and is shown to increase with radius in the intermediate region and decrease in the outer regions, showing a clear separation between the core and the halo.

In this paper, we consider hypersurfaces in $\bR^3$ of the form $F(x, y, z) = 0$, where $F(x, y, z)$ is a function of continuously differentiable class. We assume that the one form $\omega = F_z \ dz + F_y \ dy + F_x \ dx$ is non-vanishing on the support of the hypersurface. Under these assumptions, we prove that the associated maximal operators are of weak type $(1, 1)$ when $p > 2.$, where $1. = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{p}$. This generalizes a result of Pipher, Tang, and Yan to a more general class of hypersurfaces. Our proof follows the same method as in Maggi's treatise, with some extra arguments needed for the hypersurface case. We give the full details in this paper because this is a new result and the method is of independent interest.

The giant Ly-alpha nebulae associated with three radio galaxies at z~2.5 (1+z=2.5) were imaged with the VLT/VIMOS integral field spectrograph in the 911.3-970.4 Å wavelength range. The spectra were visually classified as type 1 (high excitation), type 2 (low excitation) or unclassifiable based on equivalent width measurements. The relative proportions of the different types were found to be independent of radio galaxy luminosity (represented by rest frame 75 μm radio power). When combined with recent optical narrowband imaging, the VIMOS data are used to assemble spatially-resolved spectroscopic energy distributions (SEDs). The radiation field is dominated by starlight at the peaks of the radio emission, but there is also significant evidence for dust heating in many of the radio galaxies. Type 1 spectra are ubiquitous and found in all three radio galaxies, suggesting that the ionizing sources are young, photo-ionized regions illuminated by the active galactic nucleus (AGN). A minority (~10%) of the spectra are type 2, and may represent regions at different evolutionary stages, excited by a distributed older radio source. Unclassifiable spectra are likely to be lower-excitation regions excited by shocks, although some may represent areas of active star formation.

Recent studies in evolutionary and molecular biology have shed new light on the molecular basis of organismal complexity and fitness. Most notably, these studies have demonstrated that the genetic material of living organisms, DNA, is virtually always transcribed into RNA, which, in turn, serves as a blueprint for producing the vast array of protein molecules that orchestrate nearly all cellular functions. Proteins carry out most biochemical processes, and a protein's structure encodes its function. However, the evolutionary tuning of protein structure and function toward optimal function and stability is limited by a cost grounded in structural complexity. Accordingly, virtually all molecular evolution—the contingent tuning of protein structure—occurs at the expense of functional stability. These and other lines of evidence suggest that organismal complexity and molecular evolution are fundamentally bounded by the thermodynamic stability of protein structure. This analysis suggests a unifying principle of biological organization: Complexity and stability are coupled processes, such that increases in one entail increases in the other to a point, after which further increases in one passively destabilize the other. By this analysis, organismal complexity and molecular evolution are bounded by the intrinsic costs of protein stability. This principle extends beyond the molecular and biochemical levels to inform broader questions about the organizational capabilities of life. What limits, then, on evolution can a complex living system as large as human civilization achieve? The answer to this question provides novel insight into the observed pace of molecular evolution. Most notably, rapid protein sequence evolution is insufficient to overcome the thermodynamic costs of protein stability. This in turn suggests a mechanism by which natural selection might cease to operate on genetic material, thereby frustrating natural selection and potentially leading to the extinction of a species. At the same time, this analysis suggests that a powerful, new engineering principle is within reach: the evolvability of protein structure and function could be vastly expanded through targeted mutations to the structural components of protein heteromers. The ability to decouple functional stability from structural complexity would allow natural selection to continue to operate on protein sequence, potentially leading to dramatically accelerated rates of molecular evolution and thereby the biological elaboration of artificial life. In summary, the thermodynamic costs of protein stability define a fundamental limit on organismal complexity and molecular evolution. At the same time, this limit represents a novel and powerful engineering principle, through which a union of biological and artificial life may be realized. Classical T Tauri stars (cTTSs) are low mass pre-main sequence stars surrounded by substantial magnetospheres generated by strong, previously-unknown magnetic fields. These fields are moderate in strength, with surface flux densities ranging from a few hundred to several thousand gauss. The topology of the fields is not well understood, but their dipoles are nearly aligned with the rotational axes of the stars. We have used the Hubble Space Telescope to study cTTSs in several young clusters and associations with a range of ages (1-10 million years). We have detected strong, previously-unknown magnetic fields in approximately half of the cTTSs that we study. The strong, poloidal components of the fields are typically oriented parallel to the rotational axes of the stars, with typical surface flux densities of a few hundred gauss. The fields are not well described by simple, dipolar models, and often have significant toroidal components. The field detection fraction depends on the age of the associated cluster, with a low of 50% in the youngest clusters and associations, to a high of 100% in older clusters. These results suggest that the strong, previously-unknown fields are generated near the stars and are magnetically capped, with only a small fraction of the magnetic energy able to drive stellar winds. We speculate on the origins of the fields and their relation to the evolution of the associated stars. The strong, previously-unknown fields may inhibit the evolution to main sequence stars, perhaps by channeling electron heat into slow modes that disrupt the inner regions of the stellar magnetospheres.

Cooperative Action in Eukaryotic Gene Regulation: Physical Properties of a Viral Example Richard A. Lenski, Jeffrey M. Feldmann, and Craig M. Perez arXiv.org eprint arXiv:1603.00711 [ physics.gen-ph, March 14, 2016] In this paper we discuss a conceptually simple, well-controlled, and quantitative approach to modeling gene regulation in a eukaryotic organism. The regulatory region of the copy number control region of Viral DNA is described by a mathematically idealized one-dimensional single-link chain polymer. Individual viral genomes occupy sites on this one-dimensional chain and exert a positional effect on the rate of transcription initiation by the host RNA polymerase II enzyme. As described by a rate equation, the general behavior of this gene regulation system can be understood by considering the probability of a polymerase binding to a particular site. For an appropriate choice of physically based parameters, we show that this system exhibits cooperative behavior -- an increased probability of binding at nearby sites relative to a simple addition of independent probabilities. The relative probability of cooperative binding depends on chain length, valence (number of neighboring sites bound with probability increased by interactions), and temperature. We discuss implications of our observations for biological systems. In summary, we present a physically based model for eukaryotic gene regulation in which binding cooperativity plays a central role. This physical concept, which has long been of interest in other biological systems, here reveals its importance in eukaryotic gene regulation. Our model is distinguished from others by its clear physical basis and a quantitative description of its behavior. It makes specific predictions about the effect of chain length, valence, temperature, and sequence on the probability of cooperative binding. These predictions can be directly tested against existing data and against results from alternative models. Our model also suggests testable experimental protocols for exploring the role of cooperative binding in eukaryotic gene regulation. Our results demonstrate that cooperative binding is an important physical basis for understanding gene regulation in eukaryotic organisms and is likely to play an analogous role in other biological systems. Model Source: Richard A. Lenski, Jeffrey M. Feldmann, and Craig M. Introduction Gene expression is central to biology. Eukaryotic organisms use DNA as a blueprint for making proteins. A protein-coding gene is transcribed into an RNA molecule, which then carries the information-containing sequence of nucleotides, known as the DNA “message”, to the ribosomes, where it is translated into a protein. Gene expression is inherently stochastic, and gene regulation focuses on altering this stochasticity to achieve a desired outcome. Gene expression is the target of an intense field

Femtosecond laser pulses pass through anatomic resolution pinholes in a thin metallic film. They form a tightly focused beam, with a transverse intensity distribution like a cusp. This structure is designed to confine spin-polarized fermions to a one-dimensional potential. They interact via a potential that tends to make them parallel, and attract or repel them based on their relative spin. We observe that the fermions remain stable in this one-dimensional potential. They oscillate about the center of the trap, but never spread out and escape. They even display what appears to be tunneling to a region of slightly lower potential. This is in marked contrast to the behavior of non-fermi gases, which rapidly decay into an impenetrable Bose-Einstein condensate. Our results may be explained by a simple, empirical model based on the s-wave scattering length, and support recent speculations that atoms may be able to simulate models of one-dimensional condensed matter systems.

The discovery and characterization of new nearby white dwarf (WD) systems is important for many fields of astronomy. The minimum mass of each WD orbiting a solar-type star, the binaries are called white dwarf binaries (WDBs). The frequency of WDBs is a critical input to tests of planet formation and for determining the distribution of stellar mass in binaries. Furthermore, WDBs have cooling times that span many Gyr, and by studying their orbital parameters and spectra, one can learn about WD physics, evolution, and asteroseismology. In this paper we report the discovery and parameters for 33 new WDBs, increasing the total to 90. We characterize each system using archival data from a wide variety of sources, and where possible we present new optical or NIR spectroscopy to measure the surface gravities of the WDs. We measure an average mass for the systems of 0.55±0.02M⊕, which we compare with predictions from binary evolution models. In particular, we find that models with strong wind losses, such as those that employ a momentum-driven winds, are not able to match the observations. We also find that accretion models with stable hydrogen-rich envelopes are preferred, although this may require fine-tuning of the initial-to-final mass relation and mass loss. We summarize the results in a catalog available on the website accompanying this paper.

A previous paper reported on molecular dynamics simulations of a silica melt, which were performed using a specialized weak thermal coupling algorithm that mitigated speedup bottlenecks and achieved best-in-class efficiency on a hybrid cpu-gpu platform. Here, we report on new calculations using the same codebase but with five to seven times longer simulation lengths, in order to better characterize the slow dynamics of the system. Our new results support the hypothesis that one of the most important slow modes involves rearrangement of the corner network of silica. We also found that the mean-squared displacement of silica particles is non-diffusive at long time scales, in contrast with a previously published analysis that was based on a shorter trajectory. We provide a possible explanation for this discrepancy and demonstrate that the diffusive behavior of silica at long time scales can be well-approximated by a double-exponential decay. Journal reference: Computational Materials Science (CM synthesis)

The paper examines the characteristics of the nonstationary complex networks, which includes but not limited to the time-varying network and unsynchronizable networks. The nonstationarity originates from the rapid changing of the network structure and/or nodes’ dynamics. Since the network is nonstationary, the conventional network measures cannot fully reflect the network characteristics. To this end, the theory of recurrence plot is adopted to characterizing the network dynamics, and the method to quantify the nonstationarity is proposed accordingly. The analysis on the generated model and empirical data shows that the nonstationary complex networks are very common in real-world networks, such as the dynamic network and brain network. The further investigation on the biological network reveals the functionality difference between the stable and nonstationary complex networks. The nonstationary complex networks have broad implications in the real-world networks. For example, the brain network and large biological network are usually modeled as stationary networks, where the complex dynamics cannot be captured. On the contrary, the nonstationary complex networks reveal the underlying nonstationary dynamical behaviors, and thus can be used to achieve more accurate results for some applications, such as the network disease and dynamic forecasting.

LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 is a dense, low-temperature, magnetic material used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The favorable properties of LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 arise from its fully spin-polarized ground state, although this property is only stable at low temperatures, and above a certain concentration of yttrium. Here we present a comprehensive thermodynamic and transport study of LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 over a wide temperature and composition range. We find that the material exhibits three distinct phases as a function of temperature and yttrium concentration, in agreement with previous studies. At low temperatures and high yttrium concentrations, LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 exhibits a gas-like behavior with classical ferromagnetic order, and we determine the expected phase diagram in this region. At intermediate temperatures and low yttrium concentrations, we find evidence of a novel magnetic quantum critical point, but the low-temperature behavior remains to be characterized. Finally, at high temperatures and low yttrium concentrations, LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 undergoes a spin glass transition. We present a unified theory that describes the three phases in this region of the phase diagram, and we show that the spin glass transition is in the droplet relaxationalglass universality class. Our study of LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 provides a complete description of the phase diagram in this classical ferromagnetic system. Such a phase diagram is crucial for the development of an understanding of the properties of LiHo_xY_{1-x}F_4 and for the optimization of its performance for use in MRI machines.

A general central limit theorem is proved for the information-theoretic statistics of Gram random matrices with a given variance profile. The result applies, in particular, to the standard parametric and nonparametric estimation of the scalar variance and the mean of a multivariate normal distribution. In the former case, the scalar variance is always estimated unbiasedly while the mean is estimated unbiasedly only when all the variances are estimated to be 1. The Gaussian variance profile models are carefully compared to the Laplace and the double-factor models. Numerical experiments on practical classification problems consistently confirm the superior performance of the variance profile estimation over the conventional mean estimation, which justifies the recently gained popularity of the information-theoretic criterion in machine learning and statistics. The result is a direct corollary of a more general uniform distributional convergence in the large Gram matrix size limit, which is of independent interest and may have other applications.

The MadGraph team is pleased to announce the latest major version upgrade of MadGraph, v4. MRELEASE is an important milestone for MadGraph, marking a significant evolution from early series-based simulation approaches to the modern runtime-based simulation paradigm, with unprecedented numerical precision and accuracy. MadGraph v4 boasts numerous other improvements, notably in the form of a robust and well-established Web front-end, a myriad of new out-of-the-box analysis capabilities, and improved support for LHCRun 2 and IceCube configuration. We encourage all users of MadGraph to update their codes to the latest release. MRELEASE Highlights - MadGraph has been upgraded to v4, featuring a robust and well-established Web front-end. - MadGraph is now based on the modern runtime-based simulation paradigm, with unprecedented numerical precision and accuracy. - Numerous improvements have been made to MadGraph’s core functionality, including the addition of new out-of-the-box analysis capabilities and improved support for LHC Run 2 and IceCube configuration. Web data is increasingly accumulating in databases, cloud storage, and file systems. These collections of data typically require a data analyst to first extract the data into an intermediate system such as a spreadsheet, before performing data science techniques such as machine learning on the data. Scientific workflows provide a native framework for data analysts and data scientists to collaboratively analyze and store data, by warehousing data in a database table and applying data science techniques at the database level. In this paper, we present Warehousing Workflow (WhWorkflow), a scientific workflow management system that facilitates collaborative data warehousing over web data in a database table. WhWorkflow provides a generic data discovery layer, connectors to common data storage systems, and workflows to collaboratively extract data, cleanse it, and load it into the target database table. We demonstrate the effectiveness of WhWorkflow through two case studies: collaborative spam detection on email data and collaborative pharmacovigilance data analysis on drug trials data.

In computer science, type theory, a universal model for type checking, provides a mathematically precise framework for reasoning about programming language syntax and semantics. Typeclasses form the foundation of Martin-Löf type theory, and are used to impose a mathematical structure of categories on types. Typeclasses allow for a concise and modularized description of syntactic abstractions; however, the use of typeclasses to model computation requires global inductive hypotheses about the structure of effects, and thus cannot capture local relationships between program entities. Game semantics, on the other hand, provides a locally inductive and compositional account of effects, and can be used to faithfully model the interaction of program entities; however, typeclasses can no longer be used to express local relationships between program entities. In this work, we demonstrate how to reconcile these two perspectives, by providing a Curry-style open type functor semantics that generalizes the open game and the open monad, and relates them by deriving a closed transformation between them. We show that the transformation relates well-typed programs under a closed game semantics with open games, and under a closed monad semantics with open monads. Our results enable applications of type theory in areas such as typechecking, program verification, dependently typed programming, and distributed computing.

SCF methods, also known as self-consistent-field methods, are an important class of techniques in quantum chemistry for solving the electronic structure problem. The Hartree-Fock method, proposed by Paul Hartree and Robert F. Service [1] and later developed by Robert Marshak [2], was the first SCF method and remains widely used. In this technique, the system is approximated as a collection of non-interacting electrons, or, more accurately, a set of orthogonal orbitals, called Slater determinants, that describe the system. TheHartree-Fock equation, wherein the energy of the system is expressed as a functional of the orbitals, is then iterated to self-consistency, that is, to a solution in which the orbitals do not change between iterations. Several generalizations of the Hartree-Fock method have since been developed. The coupled perturbed Hartree-Fock (CPHF) method, proposed by Gilbert [3] and developed by Freeman and Subbaswamy [4], is one such generalization. In this approach, the orbitals are allowed to change between iterations, and the energy is still expressed as a functional of the orbitals. However, the functional is approximated by the sum of the Hartree energy and a Fock energy expressed as a functional of the orbitals. Variational iterated perturbation theory (VIPT) is a similar generalization, proposed by Edward [5] and developed by Hyberts and Wood [6]. VIPT also represents the energy as a functional of the orbitals, but differs from CPHF in the manner by which the functional is approximated. The energy is expressed as a sum of a Hartree energy and a "free-energy" functional, which involves only perturbation theory within a given order. Variational perturbation theory (VPT) is another generalization of the Hartree-Fock method. It is based on a similar functional, but the functional is minimized with respect to the orbitals, as opposed to being treated as a fixed parameter. All of these generalizations of the Hartree-Fock method share the feature that the energy of the system is expressed as a functional of the orbitals. This review focuses on the development of the Hartree-Fock SCF method, as well as some of its generalizations, over the past few decades. We begin with a detailed description of the original method, outlining the various approximations that underlie its derivation. Next, several variants of the method are described. We then move on to describe the development of related ideas. For example, the CPHF method and its generalizations are described, and connections between these methods and Hartree-Fock are established. Finally, some challenges for the Hartree-Fock SCF method and its generalizations are discussed, including the need to develop efficient parallel algorithms. For the problem of weighted matching in general (arboreal) graphs, we show that the continuous relaxation of the linear programming (LP) dual (which is often used in practice) is equivalent to solving a max-product algorithm. We then generalize this result to graphs that contain a tree-subgraph, which covers a large class of arboreal networks. In particular, this covers all graphs that can be matched with a polynomial-time algorithm when all edge weights are 1. For such graphs, we also show that the continuous relaxation is in strong duality with the original discrete optimization problem, and provide a primal feasibility guarantee. Finally, we present some empirical evidence that the max-product algorithm performs better than the LP relaxation on arboreal instances. In a quantum auction, a seller can allow the buyer to make queries with potential rewards according to a price schedule. The buyer can also make a final bid which is binding. We characterize the optimal behavior of the buyer and the seller for two different scenarios. In the full information scenario, the seller reveals the entire price schedule to the buyer before the auction starts. In the second scenario, the seller only reveals the current lowest price and the buyer has to guess the future prices based on previous experience. We call this the historical bidding. We present algorithms for the buyer and the seller which take these scenarios into account. For the full information scenario, we give a two-stage optimization algorithm for the buyer. In the first stage, the buyer adapts a linear program to the history to find an upper bound on the optimal strategy. In the second stage, the buyer solves the linear program optimally. We show that this is a valid algorithm and that it computes the optimal strategy in strongly polynomial time. We also give a lower bound and show that it is tight. For the historical bidding scenario, we give a simple algorithm for the seller. We show that for a range of price functions this is an optimal strategy and that it is truthful.

In the standard model (SM), flavor changing neutral currents (FCNCs) are forbidden at the Lagrangian level, but occur at the tree level via the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix in processes such as $b \to s\ell^+\ell^-$ or $B_{s,d} \to \pi\pi,\pi K, KK$. Such FCNC processes provide promising channels to search for signals of new particles and interactions. We perform a global fit to the latest available data on $B_{s,d} \to \pi\pi, \pi K, KK$ with the objective of extracting information on new physics (NP). We consider a generic NP model which contains four-quark operators and impose constraints from lepton flavor universality, $\Delta F=2$ processes, global fit to the CKM matrix, as well as direct searches for heavy leptons and $Z'$ bosons. We find that consistent fits to the data are only possible for masses of new vector-like fermions at the 10 to 100 TeV scale. Such heavy degrees of freedom could account for the recently discovered $B$ and $K$ anomalies. The outcome of our fit has important implications for the future of $B$ factories and the LHCb experiment. If NP exists, it likely has large interactions with theStandard Model(SM) through the $b$ quark. Consequently, direct searches for new heavy particles such as vector-like quarks at the LHC, and probes of $b$ FCNC processes at the next generation of $B$ factories and the LHC will be crucial in further elucidating the mysterious $B$ meson decays.

Recent high-resolution imaging and reconnaissance spacecraft surveys have shown that about 20-30% of sun-like stars are in multiple systems. The mutual gravitation between components in multiple systems may have profound effects on the overall system dynamics and therefore the evolution of planetary systems. The higherorder multiplets are usually hierarchical with short-period orbits. It has been shown that even second-order perturbations from outer planets can drive the inner planets on chaotic orbits on very short time scales. In this work, I examine the dynamical interactions between two planets in the general three-body problem with one primary and two equal-mass companions. I demonstrate that apart from the widely studied Hill stability boundary and corotation resonances, the 3:2 mean-motion resonance is also a stable region for coplanar non-resonant two-planet configurations. In addition, I present that eccentricities of stable two-planet systems could be extremely high, up to 0.95, and still be stable. I also provide detailed numerical calculations of the restricted three-body problem with two additional planets using a Chebyshev-Fourier spectral method. Both two-planet and three-planet systems exhibit similar phase space structures. I illustrate the key role of secular chaos in driving the systems to extremely high-eccentricity orbits. I also present that there are significant differences between coplanar and inclined cases in the Hill stability boundary, corotation resonances and secular resonances.

Nanotechnologies offer a unique opportunity to control morphology, structure and phase of individual nanotubes. In this study, we demonstrate that dielectric, metal and semiconducting single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) can be used to engineer the system’s response. Using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and Raman spectroscopy, we identify CNTs in heterostructures as the major light emitter. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that, in fact, CNTs acting as a recombination centers significantly contribute to the total light generation. While semiconductor CNTs significantly boost light emission in the visible range, silver and copper nanotubes enriched with plasmonic effect boost light in the near-infrared and terahertz regions, respectively. The proposed CNT heterostructures reveal tunable emission across the whole spectral range and offer perspectives for technological applications in photonic devices. The growth of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has attracted significant interest over the past decade owing to their unusual chemical and physical properties, and their potential for a broad range of applications. The optical properties of CNTs have been demonstrated to vary widely, ranging from strong light absorbers to strong light emitters.[1, 2] These properties arise from the unique structure and composition of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs), which include a 1 nm diameter tube with either a zigzag or armchair circumference.[3] The electronic structure of the SWCNT can be either semiconducting, semimetallic or conducting, depending on the diameter and helicity of the tube.[4, 5] A large variety of materials and their combinations can be combined with SWCNTs to engineer their optical response.[6–11] Such sophisticated control over optical response is crucial for improving the performance of a wide range of applications, ranging from photonics and optoelectronics to biological imaging and detection. In this work, we examine two different types of SWCNTs – semiconductor and metallic – and their combinations. We demonstrate that dielectric, metal and semiconducting CNTs can be used to engineer the system’s response. The numerical simulations reveal that CNTs acting as a recombination centers significantly contribute to the total light generation. While semiconductor CNTs significantly boost light emission in the visible range, silver and copper nanotubes enriched with plasmonic effect boost light in the near-infrared and terahertz regions, respectively. Such heterostructures may have promising applications for terahertz and infrared optoelectronics and telecommunications.

Using data from the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) on the Hubble Space Telescope, we present the first far-infrared/submillimeter spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of a sample of distant star-forming galaxies at ~z > 0.7. We find that the galaxies have total infrared (TIR) emission between 1 and 1000 μm similar to that of localstar-forming galaxies, but their TIR/Eddington ratio is enhanced by a factor of ~3-30 compared to lower-redshift galaxies of the same far-infrared/submillimeter luminosity. These observations indicate that SFRs in these galaxies are enhanced by similar factors, although the intense starbursts may not be as confined to the central regions as in local counterparts. A fraction of these galaxies have buried quasars with 2 μm rest-frame dust absorption break larger than 1000 μm. We argue that the intensestarbursts in these galaxies are facilitated by the abundant cool gas available due to rapid galaxy growth at high redshift. The observed enhancement of the TIR/Eddington ratio implies that these galaxies have much higher gas accretion rates onto their black holes than their low-redshift counterparts with similar Eddington ratios. These high accretion rates may be facilitated by the deeper potential wells, higher merger rates, or higher gas fractions at high redshift. The inferredhigh gas accretion rates onto supermassive black holes at high redshift imply that these systems may become extremely powerful quasars at high redshifts, similar to the population of large red quasars at high redshifts.

The light curve can be roughly divided into three segments: a shallow decay segment (SDS), a normal decay segment (NDS), and a sharp decay segment (SDS). The SDS can be naturally interpreted as the early super Eddington light from the tidal disruption event (TDE) with a circumbinary planet (CBP). We carefully study the properties of the SDS using both the simple one-zone reprocessing model and more complex multi-zone reprocessing model. We find that the following physical processes are required to reproduce the observed behavior of the light curve: (1) the stellar debris absorbed energy via internal shock in the SDS; (2) the wind from the accretion disk heated the CBP; (3) the tidal disruption flare (TDF) from the CBP illuminated the CBP; (4) the interaction between the debris and the CBP, and between the debris and the disk contributed to the late-time light excess; (5) continuous energy injection from the central SMBH. We also compare the expected reflection signature from the CBP with the data and put constraints on the distance between the CBP and the black hole (BH). We also compare the expected reflection signature from the CBP with the data and put constraints on the distance between the CBP and the BH.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) is a valuable experimental technique for the study of molecular structure and dynamics. In common experiments, such as sensitivity-enhanced nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, a high-energy signal is generated that activates all spins in the laboratory frame. This high-energy signal attempts to orient the nuclear spins, but because the nuclear spin system is comprised of many coupled spins, this often leads to rapid relaxation towards an incoherent mixture of states. This effect, called dephasing, is understood as arising from environmental interactions between the nuclear spins, and is a limiting factor in most experimental situations. Recently, there has been interest in the possibility of engineering particular quantum dynamical processes that can inhibit or even reverse dephasing, opening the door to new applications for NMR and extending its range of applicability. This report provides an overview of the subject, starting with the simplest cases of coupled spin pairs, working through selected applications to larger quantum registers, and outlining current research directions. Dephasing is typically caused by environmental interactions that act to randomly orient the nuclear spins. For coupled spin pairs, the most basic system, this leads to a statistical mixture of state vectors, each corresponding to a particular combination of oriented nuclear spins. This report begins by considering the simplest case of two coupled spin-1/2 nuclei, for which analytical solutions exist. The collective dephasing behavior of large quantum registers is then described, with applications to liquid state spectroscopy and sensing, and current research directions are outlined. A second section describes the analogous problem of environmental noise acting to destroy quantum coherence, resulting in a dynamical quantum phase transition where the evolution of the system becomes completely random. This process is often called quantum decoherence, and the effects are similar, but quite different. Decoherence is particularly a problem for large registers of nuclear spins, for which analytical solutions are not known, while dynamical phase transitions are still relatively unexplored. These effects are illustrated for coupled spin triplets and nontransition metal alkalis.
