Two mechanisms have been proposed to account for the anomalous temperature dependence of the Debye frequency in glasses. The first one, based on a vibrational instability due to the difference between the phonon and dielectric relaxation times, was originally proposed by Alexander and Mills [1]. Later it was shown that it could also lead to a Boson peak in the glass specific heat [2,3]. The second one, which focuses on the occurrence of multilevel systems in the excitation spectrum [4-6] and was developed by several groups, attributes the anomalous behaviour of the Debye frequency to the presence of two-level systems. Both mechanisms have been observed in experiments [7-10] and discussed in recent reviews [11,12]. Here we present an unified interpretation of both anomalies in terms of vibrational instability. The occurrence of multilevel systems results from a dynamical tuning of the interlevel distances to the phonon periods. In contrast to the established view the two phenomena are interrelated: the dynamical tuning occurring at large amplitudes of the instability is also necessary for the Boson peak to occur. The Boson peak stems from quasiparticle excitations related to the instability and thus also reflects the dynamical nature of the instability.

Supernova 1987A was one of the closest and best observed supernova in decades. Fifteen years after the explosion, observations at radio wavelengths still play an important role in our understanding of this object. In this paper, we present high-resolution images of SN 1987A at 14 different radio frequencies between 76 MHz and 14.5 GHz. We use data from the Multibeam Observing System on the Australia Telescope Compact Array, the Jansky Very Large Array, the LOw Frequency ARray, the Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope, and the Pinwheel Radio Telescope to produce the highest-resolution (between 3.4 and 22 AU at different frequencies) and most completely sampled (every two hours for 15 years) images of SN 1987A to date. We discuss our findings in the context of current three-dimensional models of the SN and conclude with a summary of the remarkable legacy of SN 1987A.

Aperture efficiency is one of the most important parameters of a radio telescope, since it is directly related to the telescope’s ability to capture electromagnetic radiation. In this work, we present a detailed ray-tracing and physical-optics analysis of the aperture efficiency of the Whittle-Bergemann antenna, a Vivaldi antenna with a synthetic aperture designed to improve its low cross-polarization levels. This analysis takes into account diffraction effects from the aperture stop, as well as antenna outside surface, and it is done for both the electric and magnetic field. We conclude that the aperture efficiency of this antenna, as calculated by physical optics, is around 65%, which is in good agreement with the ray-tracing simulations that we have done, that predict an efficiency of around 65% as well. This article extends the analysis presented in [1], which analyzed only the electric field aperture efficiency. This work also improves the analysis of the magnetic field aperture efficiency, that was not calculated in [1]. This is of particular interest for the Vivaldi antennas, that have been designed to improve the low cross-polarization levels, which is currently an important issue in radio-astronomical instrumentation. The Whittle-Bergemann antenna is based on a Vivaldi antenna with a synthetic aperture, which is placed close to the feed of the antenna, in order to improve the low cross-polarization levels. This antenna has been introduced in [2]. It has a synthetic aperture that wraps around a hyperbolic surface, which improves its performance. The analysis of the aperture efficiency of the Whittle-Bergemann antenna presented in this article can be of particular interest to people interested in radio astronomy, since it describes its performance, by calculating the aperture efficiency from both the electric and magnetic field. We have also performed a detailed ray-tracing and physical-optics analysis of this antenna, which was not presented in [1] and [2], where only the electric field aperture efficiency was calculated. In addition to diffraction effects from the aperture stop, we have also considered the effects of diffraction from the antenna outside surface, which is especially important for radio telescopes. The analysis presented in this article is done by considering the aperture efficiency for both the electric and magnetic field, as calculated by physical optics. We conclude that the aperture efficiency of the Whittle-Bergemann antenna, as calculated by physical optics, is around 65%. This is in good agreement with the ray-tracing simulations, that predict an efficiency of around 65%. This article is written in Layman's terms. The purpose of this article is to make antennas and radio telescopes accessible to a larger audience, by simplifying the concepts and jargon used in radio astronomy, so that more people can enjoy this interesting and exciting science.

Grassmann algebra is an algebra constructed on a vector space with a property that it's subspaces form a right ideal. In this paper, first we introduce the concept of skew derivation, which is an anti-linear map that satisfies the Leibniz rule and derivation property. Then by defining the kernel of a skew mapping we generalize the concept of orthogonal vectors to arbitrary vectors and derive basic properties of skew inner products. Finally, as an application, we give an alternative proof of the associativity of Grassmann algebras. The concept of skew derivation was introduced for the first time by E. C. getto in 1965. Later in 1972, A. M. Bin Oljoin and M. B. Semenov gave another definition of skew derivation and applied it to different fields of mathematics. In this paper, we give a detailed study of skew derivations and skew derivable mappings, and apply it to Grassmann algebras.

We present high-resolution 8.4GHz VLBI observations of the type-Ia supernova 2004et in the local galaxy NGC6946. We detect the supernova at day 9.5 after the optical maximum, finding a positionally-unresolved source with a size of 0.07 parsecs, indicating that the expanding supernova blast wave was successfully slowed down by the interaction with the dense interstellar medium in the host galaxy. We discuss various interpretations of this result with respect to the high optical luminosity and inferred low-opacity explosion of SN2004et and the properties of the local interstellar medium. The full text of this paper is available from https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07786 SN2004et was a type Ia supernova, one of the best-understood class of stellar explosion. From the early times after the explosion, SN2004et showed remarkable high optical luminosity, making it one of the brightest supernovae ever observed. This significant optical luminosity implies very low opacity of the ejecta, in agreement with typical characteristics of type Ia supernova. The inferred low opacity enabled us to study the early phase of the blast wave interaction with the local environment. Here we present VLBI observations of the type Ia supernova 2004et at 8.4GHz, approximately 80 days after the explosion. The observations show a positionally-unresolved source with a size of 0.07 parsecs, suggesting that the interaction between the supernova blast wave and the dense interstellar medium in the local environment was successful. We discuss various interpretations of this result with respect to the high optical luminosity and inferred low-opacity explosion of SN2004et and the properties of the local interstellar medium. One possible explanation is that the supernova exploded in a region with very low density of free electrons, i.e. with nearly full transparency of the supernova ejecta. Such regions are commonly observed in the local environment of other type Ia supernova and called cavities. Another possible explanation is the presence of very dense but magnetized clouds in the local environment, which would lead to significant amplification and refraction of the shockwave. Further VLBI monitoring of a larger sample of type Ia supernova at early times after the explosion would allow us to infer general characteristics of the environment around these powerful stellar explosions.

A large effort has been devoted to the construction of surrogate models of black hole (BH) signals in data analysis of Advanced LIGO (aLIGO). Among the wide array of methods developed, Matched Filtering (MF) remains the most widely used technique for BH signal detection from aLIGO’s measurement data. Yet, despite being decades old, the MF technique has never been challenged on aBH data. In this Letter, we implement and test the MF technique on two recently published numerical relativity (NR) BH merger simulations: the Effective One Body (EOB) model and the Spectral Einstein Code (SpEC) spectral code. For each simulation, we construct the corresponding “template” BH signal in the frequency domain and filter it with a bank of NR waveforms from GCN numerical relativity catalogs. We find that in both the low and high frequency regions, the detection efficiencies of the NR waveforms are far below 100%, even for high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) sources. By contrast, the MF technique is 100% efficient in both regions. We also test the MF technique on simulated Gaussian white noise and show that the detection efficiencies are 100% for all SNRs. These results show that NR waveforms are not suitable for aLIGO data analysis. Furthermore, the low detection efficiencies of NR waveforms cast doubt on aLIGO’s claim that it has observed gravitational waves from two merging black holes.

Longitudinal data are frequently encountered in social, psychological, and economic research. The analysis of such data is complicated by the fact that the response variable is measured repeatedly over time on the same individuals. In this setting, it is often of interest to understand the effect of a treatment on an individual's response, while controlling for within-individual changes over time. This leads to the problem of individual heterogeneity, where unobservable time-invariant individual differences may affect both the response variable and the treatment variable. In this paper, we develop semiparametric methods for causal inference about the average treatment effect among individuals with different characteristics, while controlling for the effect of time-invariant individual characteristics. We develop a new class of efficient and adaptive estimator, and establish statistical and strong empirical validity for the proposed method. We then illustrate the use of the proposed method with an educational data set on individual student performance.

A very large magnetic flux rope erupted from the active region (AR) NOAA 11429 on the Sun on 2017 November 7. The eruption was observed by a number of satellite observations. It was also associated with a filament eruption and a B9.7 class flare. The pre-eruption structure of the flux rope is a crucial factor that determines the eruption behavior. If the flux rope is strongly twisted, the outer boundary of the flux rope can become unstable and rupture due to the kink instability. If the magnetic tension is less effective compared with the twist, the flux rope can erupt without magnetic instability. In the presented paper, we investigate the formation and evolution of the flux rope and the associated solar wind depending on the stability of the outer boundary and magnetic reconnection underneath the flux rope. About 22 minutes prior to the eruption, the twist (torsional strain) of the flux rope sharply increased. Then the outer boundary of the flux rope became unstable and ruptured. Around 19:20 UT, an erupting jet, consisting of the prominence and the twisted magnetic structure, was observed by the HiRISE camera on board the Mars Exploration Rover Spirit. Approximately one minute later, the flux rope erupted and caused an intense negative sunspot with a dark coronal mass ejection (CME) and a solar wind. Observations of the post-eruption solar wind indicate the formation of a magnetic flux rope. The flux rope was erupting with a speed of more than 3000 km/s and a height of 14 R~sun. It also shows clear signatures of magnetic reconnection underneath. The speed of the post-eruption solar wind decreased with height, which might be explained by the conservation of the flux. In the presented paper, we investigate the formation of the flux rope, the acceleration of the erupted jet and the magnetic reconnection underneath the flux rope based on data from several instruments onboard the Solar Dynamic Observatory, the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory, the Mars Exploration Rover Spirit and the Interplanetary Mission Division of the NASA. The presented paper is interesting to read for a general audience. It also provides insights into the pre-eruption structure, the formation and the evolution of the flux rope and the underlay magnetic reconnection during the eruptive process.

A unique spectrum of the Tycho supernova remnant (SNR) has been discovered with the Subaru HDS spectrograph. The emission line spectra of the SNR exhibit clear Balmer emission features from hydrogen through to the IRT band at 7471 Å. This is unusual as the expected cooling frequency for such a young SNR has previously only been observed in the radio regime. The HDS spectrum is the highest resolution optical spectrum of the SNR to date and shows that the spatial distribution of hydrogen emission is distinctly non-uniform with the higher spatial resolution afforded by the HDS data. The Balmer decrement in Tycho is consistent with an equilibrium ionization mixture of oxygen, neon and nitrogen (OYeah) within a non-equilibrium ionization mixture of hydrogen. These findings suggest that Tycho's shock is predominantly hydrogen-rich and collisionally ionized. This is surprising given the long duration (over 15000 years) and the proximity of the SN event that formed the remnant. This implies that the swept-up circumstellar material (CSM) has undergone significant processing at the hands of the shock front.

The superconducting state in doped copper oxides is often separated into two categories, high-temperature superconductivity (above ~100 K) and low temperature superconductivity (T_c<10 K). The former emerges from poorly understood fermiology, but the origin of the latter has been more clearly established as strong electron-electron interactions. Superconductivity in the underdoped regime of copper oxides is an exception, where strong antiferromagnetic fluctuations have been suggested to suppress the formation of the fermiology needed for superconductivity, leading to a competing state of asob phases. Here we report inelastic neutron scattering measurements of magnetic fluctuations in n-type Ca(Fe(1-x)Co_x)_2As_2, an isoelectronically substituted superconductor with T_c of 10 K that has been suggested to exhibit fermiology-driven superconductivity. We find that the doping evolution of the low-energy resonance peak reflects that of the superconductivity, rather than that of the antiferromagnetism. The results suggest a competition between fermiology-driven superconductivity and asob phases is preempted by a competing state of incommensurate magnetic fluctuations, and raise the possibility that asob phases is the competing state of copper oxides above the pseudogap temperature T^*.

Three different procedures to assemble model cohesive powders in three dimensions were studied. The assembling procedure had no influence on the final microstructure for the studied powders with different diameters but had an influence on the total simulation time. The number of simulation steps to achieve a certain displacement of the bottom plate was lowest for a powder with different diameter per unit length. The impact of the assembling procedure on the results of the simulation needs to be considered for comparison of simulation results with experimental data. The contact law is also of importance for the outcome of the simulation, here, four different laws were studied. In case of Hertz’ law, the influence of the powder contact geometry on the contact behavior needs to be considered, too. Using the Hertz-Hertzian contact law, a brittle behavior was observed for two of the three studied assembling procedures. For the third procedure, a plastic deformation was achieved with Hertz-Hertzian contact law. This could be related to a geometrically induced sub-surface plastic layer at the interface between the two powders, which is influenced by the assembling procedure.

The metallicity gradient of a galaxy is one of its most basic structural characteristics. Chemical abundances of HII regions in M 33, the third brightest visual galaxy in the Local Group, are used to study its metallicity gradient. The obtained results show that the outer regions of the galaxy have lower metallicity than the inner ones. The derived slope is almost flat within the limits of the uncertainties. This means that at the average, the metallicity of the gas does not change significantly from the center to the edge of the galaxy. The possible reason of such a weak gradient is the lack of important episodes of star formation in the outer regions of the galaxy, which consume the enriched gas. The author(s) of the paper above used spectral data of HII regions in M 33 to determine the galaxy's metallicity gradient. The obtained results showed that the average metallicity of the gas does not change significantly across the radius of the galaxy. It means that there is no significant radial flow of enriched gas towards the outer regions of the galaxy. The most plausible explanation of this result is the lack of significant star formation in the outer parts of M 33. The research was conducted by V. A. Klypin, S. A. Koposov, and J. S. Bullock.

The IDV source J1128+5925, a new candidate for annual modulation? Annihilation of Wimps? Ali YS, Hirvonen J, Päske J, van Vliet R, Allaert N, EHT Collaboration (arXiv:2004.08711v1 [hep-ex]) - Submitted for publication - April 2023 Since the first claims of the detection of megavolts of energetic electrons from distant blazar PKS 1441-19 in 2015, extensive multi-messenger follow-up of this and other potential IDV sources has been performed. No IDV was detected from PKS 1441-19 in the 2022-2023 observational season. However, a new candidate for IDV, J1128+5925, was detected during that period. While prior detections of this source as a highly variable TeV gamma-ray emitter argued against it being a strong IDV candidate, its large flux and short-time scale variations argued for further follow-up. Using data from multiple instruments, spanning over four years, and separating the orbital and superorbital variability with statistical significance, we report the strongest evidence to date for annual modulation in this source. While there are several astrophysical explanations for the observed variability, our analysis favours that IDV is a real phenomenon and that J1128+5925 is a new candidate. Evidence for annual modulation in J1128+5925, as shown in Figure 1, is significant at the 8.3 sigma level. While uncertainties in the superorbital period make it difficult to distinguish between this and a constant hypothesis, annual modulation at the 9.4 sigma level is highly unlikely to have arisen by chance. Furthermore, no evidence for a decrease in the integrated flux between 2022 and 2023 is seen, as would be expected for IDV. We conclude that this is evidence for annual modulation in J1128+5925, which can be explained by annihilating WIMPS with a mass of 20 to 30 GeV being present in the galaxy halo.

Exoplanets are discovered around every new star that is being studied. Given that there are many more stars in globular clusters than there are in the field, it is reasonable to assume that many planets should be found around globular cluster stars. Indeed, some globular clusters do appear to have a high fraction of planet-hosting stars. This paper will evaluate the number of planets that could be found around globular cluster stars with current detection techniques. The analysis will consider both the detection efficiency of current techniques and the properties of planets around globular cluster stars to determine if there is an observable difference between planet frequency in globular clusters and the field. I will show that current planet detection techniques should be capable of identifying planets around cluster stars at the same rate as in the field. Therefore, no statistically significant difference between the frequency of planets in globular clusters and the field is supported by the current data.

In full counting statistics, the moments of the transferred charge take on different values than those of a Gaussian distribution if the detector has a finite resistance. The third cumulant is positive for any value of the counting field if the environment's resistance is larger than a certain threshold. In this case, for long times after the QM system has reached its steady state, its dynamics is that of an inverted harmonic oscillator. We study experimentally the counting statistics of charge transfer in a quantum point contact (QPC) as a function of the environment's resistance R. By applying a suitable voltage bias to the outside World, we can change the environment's impedance and, thus, the threshold for non-Gaussian behavior. For small enough resistance, we observe that the third cumulant is always positive. This result is in quantitative agreement with the prediction of a rate equation model based on a full quantum description of the dissipative QPC, both for negative and positive values of the counting field. Our work provides the first direct experimental access to the full counting statistics of a microscopic quantum system coupled to an external system with arbitrary spectral density.

Recent progress in the understanding of the properties of diffusive SNS junctions has been achieved by investigating their transport properties as a function of the nature and the position within the junction of the involved interfaces and by considering the limit of strong spin-orbit coupling. In this paper, we present an analytical treatment of the non-equilibrium properties of such diffusive SNS junctions. In particular, we focus on the supercurrent flowing in the junction, which is generated by a non-equilibrium pairing mechanism. We discuss the dependence of the resulting supercurrent on the interfaces, and in particular we focus on the effect of nonideal interfaces, scattering at impurities and potential fluctuations at the interface. We find that for realistic interface conditions and spin-orbit coupling strengths, the induced supercurrent is of the order of 1% of the equilibrium critical current, and that a reduction of the induced supercurrent due to the scattering at impurities or potential fluctuations at the interface can be partially compensated by tuning the shape of the order parameter interface profile.

Astronomers using the Chandra X-ray observatory have carried out the deepest ever survey of the universe in the X-ray band. In the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), they have detected 740 sources, of which 122 are X-ray emitting Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs). Deep spectroscopy has shown that roughly half of the X-ray emitting AGNs in the CDF-S are completely absorbed in the visible band, and are only observable in X-rays. This has allowed us to study the average obscuration properties of the universe in the distant, early stages of galaxy evolution, which are crucial for understanding how galaxies grow. At $z=2-4$, the CDF-S contains the largest uniformly-selected sample of distant, obscured AGNs known. These are responsible for most of the metals in the early universe, and so are vital for understanding the re-ionization of the universe. The total amount of matter obscured by gas in the CDF-S is estimated to be around four times the mass of the Milky Way, with individual masses reaching up to 1022 M⊙. If the mean molecular weight of the gas is assumed to be around 0.5, this corresponds to a total of around ten trillion Solar masses of matter, concentrated in just these few sources. As we approach the peak of galaxy assembly in the early universe, these sources are ideal laboratories for studying the evolution of gas and dust throughout the universe.

A soft X-ray study of Type I AGN observed with Chandra has shown that: - The standard model of accretion onto a black hole includes two regions: an inner, optically thick, geometrically thin disk and an outer, funnel-like flow which includes the wind and from which most of the radiatively inefficient accretion power is released. - The mass outflow rate in the wind, calculated from the rate at which relativistic particles are detected, is a significant fraction of the mass flux carried by the flow. - The two-phase nature of the flow, as indicated by the detection of high-ionization lines and the presence of a two-component X-ray absorber, is apparently a general property of Type I AGN. - The principal source of seed photons for Comptonization is likely the cyclo-synchrotron emission from the population of high-energy electrons in the flow.

The scaling relations of incompressible MHD turbulence are well studied and accepted (see Heyer & Brunt, 2004 for a review). On the other hand, the characterization of compressible MHD (CMHD) turbulence and its scaling relations are less understood. Compressibility can have a significant impact on the nature of MHD turbulence. For example, numerical studies suggest that Alfvénic-wave cascades are modified to compressive cascade in the presence of background compression, i.e., negative cross helicity (H incarcerons). An important challenge in characterizing compressible MHD turbulence is the extra degree of freedom, density, which generally leads to non-linear interactions between different wave-numbers. How the interactions and anisotropy affect the scaling of the most energetic structures in CMHD turbulence is unknown. Using high resolution, idealized, compressible MHD simulations, we examine how the energy spectrum and the third-order structure functions of density depends on the energy injection scale, spatial resolution and spectral resolution. We find that while the inertial range scaling in CMHD is similar to incompressible MHD, the energy distribution at very small length scales is significantly different. For injection scales smaller than the proton collisional length, the energy spectrum is well fitted by a Burgers scaling $E_k \propto k^{-3/2}$, which is consistent with the prediction of CMHD phenomenology. For larger injection scales, the energy spectrum follows a $-5/3$ Kolmogorov scaling. Furthermore, the structure functions show multiscaling behavior, which is again different from incompressible MHD. The scaling exponents are dependent on both the energy injection scale and the spatial resolution. The spectral scaling exponents can also be different from the classical Kolmogorov $\xi^{-5/3}$ scaling. We also explore the effects of numerical artifacts by changing the variables and symmetry used in our analyses. The effects are generally small and cannot explain the complex multiscaling behavior observed. This study provides numerical evidence for the modified scaling relations of compressible MHD turbulence. The scaling exponents depend on the injection scale, numerical resolution and on how the data is analyzed. This paper has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Computational Physics. Please cite the published version if possible.

In this letter we investigate the possibility that the four-dimensional (4D) gravity could arise as a warped metric on a five-dimensional (5D) Anti-de-Sitter (AdS) space in a supersymmetric braneworld model. In this scenario, the observable universe is viewed as a three-brane that is a domain wall living in the AdS space. In order to have an exit from the domain wall curvature instabilities, a bulk scalar field is introduced. This field, called the chameleon field, couples to the world volume of the brane via the Israel coupling, where the coupling strength is related to the brane tension. By analyzing the equations of motion we obtain the conditions on the brane tension and bulk potential such that the theory acquires a healthy stable 4D gravity at low energy. By using these conditions we show that the mass of the Planck particle can be naturally generated. We also study the possibility that the supersymmetry is broken on the brane. To that end we introduce explicit (F) and soft (D) breaking terms to the brane supergravity Lagrangian. We show that without the explicit breaking, all the scalar masses are determined only by the brane tension and the gravitino mass, and thus are naturally of order of the gravitino mass. With explicit breaking, the scalar masses can be naturally of order one, if some conditions are satisfied on the soft parameters. Our results suggest that in order to explain the 4D gravity we live in from the 5D fundamental theory, the theory might be supersymmetric on the brane. Supersymmetry breaking on the brane naturally explains the hierarchy between the Planck and the Electroweak scales without postulating large extra dimensions, and thus provides a rationale for low fundamental gravity scale.

Here we present a zoom-in cosmological simulation of structure formation, called Project ECHO, whose spatial resolution and dynamic range is sufficient to study the formation of individual galaxies and the circumgalactic medium (CGM). We find that the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) in our galaxies forms at z = 2.5–2.0 due to the slow ejection of metal-rich gas from metal-poor galaxies by galactic outflows. The ejected metals are heated and lose their ability to form new stars clusters in the CGM, resulting in a shallower MZR. Observational evidence for such galactic outflows has been found in the escape velocity of high-redshift galaxies and the offset in the distributions of reionization emission and the Lyα forest. Finally, we find that the scatter in the MZR increases with decreasing oxygen abundance, which can be used to place constraints on the simulations and potentially identify residual problems with galactic outflow implementations.

Two efficient QMC estimators of the spherically and system-averaged pair density, which are both variance-zero and bias-zero for equal-sized simulation cells, are proposed and studied. These estimators, which utilize a particle-number projected (PNP) trial wave function, are constructed by applying an arbitrary positive-definite one-body operator to each simulation cell and then taking a symmetrically constrained average. The resulting estimators are both spherically symmetric and system-size independent, and converge with resolution to the pair density of a spatially and system-averaged density matrix of the underlying wave function. Both the one-body and two-body terms of the projected wave functions contribute to the pair density, with the two-body contribution falling off exponentially with inter-particle distance. The variance of this projected-wave-function estimator is analyzed via a positive-definiteness argument, and shown to be identical to the universal upper bound on the variance of any unbiased QMC estimator of the pair density. Numerical simulations confirm the efficacy of this estimator for a broad class of Hamiltonians, including some that exhibit strong correlations. Finally, we introduce a symmetric two-body estimator derived from the same PNP wave function, and show that it is unbiased with variance identical to the projected-wave-function estimator.

Virialization is the process by which galaxies and large scale structure form from cosmic matter density perturbations. Early simulations of structure formation assuming pressureless dark matter (CDM) predicted a nearly coincident timing for the buildup of the massive galaxies we see around us and the termination of the process of structure formation. Recent cosmological N-body simulations suggest a strong evolution in the structure of dark matter (DM) halos with mass. Simulations of small systems like galactic satellites suggest these evolve toward the center of their host halos while preserving their individual identity, however large galaxy halos like the Milky Way appear to be nearly universal density distributions with a shallow inner core. In this paper, we compare these recent results to the long-standing suggestion of universal density profiles at virialization first proposed by Zel’dovich and Bertchastovich and observed numerically by Doro et al. in 1998. Using a sample of $\sim$300zoomed DM simulations from the Horizon-AGN suite, we measure the halo density profile and assembly time for a wide range of halo masses. We measure a universal profile at virialization with a shallow inner core consistent with the prediction of Zel’dovich and Bertchastovich, with departures from this profile driven by accretion and minor merger events.

The chemical composition of the Type II Cepheids is relevant for understanding their evolution, dynamics and pulsation. For the first time, we report the abundances of thirteen chemical elements for the BL Her and W Vir variables. The Type II Cepheids are pulsating stars in the Cepheid instability strip of the H-R diagram and they are primary distance indicators. The knowledge of the chemical compositions of these variables is of great importance for further refinement of the P-L relationship based on the physical parameters derived from their spectra. It is also very useful to study their evolution and dynamics. Our abundance analysis was based on the integral field spectroscopy (IFS) data. In total, 56 individual spectra of 14 BL Her variables and 7 W Vir variables were used for the analysis. We employed the elemental abundance analysis technique called the spectral differential imaging (SDI). We applied a very accurate and robust analytic method of SDI which we have developed recently. We achieved an uncertainty of 0.2 dex for chemical abundances determined from individual spectra.

Black holes (BHs) are one of the most remarkable objects in the universe. Masses of these super dense objects can be determined by studying the motion of gas and light around them. The gravitational force exerted by BHs can be calculated by the motion of surrounding matter. Since, for a Schwarzschild black hole, the mass can be estimated by the following relation: M=Mass of Object/ (Gmm/r^2) where, G is the gravitational constant and r is the distance between the object and the center of the black hole, it is necessary to know the exact distance between the object and the center of the black hole to determine the mass. It is generally not possible to measure the distance between the object and the center of the black hole directly, so it is necessary to estimate it. The exact orbit of particles around black holes can be calculated by the laws of physics. According to the theory of relativity, the equations of motion are modified and the higher the energy of a particle, the greater the effect of this modification becomes. As a result, the energy of a particle has an effect on its orbit. The amount of this effect can be determined from the spectrum of the black hole. Since, according to the quantum theory, electrons are particles that emit radiation, the spectrum of the black hole also has a high-energy component that exponentially decreases with increasing energy. The amount of this decrease can be used to calculate the distance between the electron and the center of the black hole. It is observed that for large black holes, the deviation of the motion of particles from the normal trajectory becomes significant for high energy particles and the spectrum becomes exponential. For this reason, an exponential component is observed in the spectrum of large black holes. In this work, soft X-ray spectra of 13 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) are studied. The mass of the central super massive black holes (SMBH) in these AGNs are estimated by considering the soft X-ray spectrum as an exponential component. Estimates are compared with the actually observed masses and it is observed that there is a high correlation between them. It is shown that in some cases, the deviation of the actual from the estimated mass can be large but it still is in agreement with the estimated value within the error.

High order convergent multigrid methods on domains containing holes are presented for solving the constraint equations of black hole initial data. The domain at hand may contain nontrivial topology and have arbitrary algebraic shape. The constraint solver is based on a certain combination of a least-squares finite element discretization and a discrete version of the conformal method for the boundary problem. To construct the multigrid method, nested patches of coordinate patches are used to cover the hole. The coarsest grid contains only one patch and each subsequent grid successively splits the domain into two parts, one of which is covered by a neighboring patch. The method is shown to converge of order at least 2, which is better than the polynomial convergence of standard conforming methods. Finally, three numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the method's capabilities. The present work is a follow-up to a previous arXiv publication (arXiv:1901.09671), where similar methods were presented for polyhedral domains. In the present work, the methods are developed for domains with holes and are demonstrated on several examples including the black hole initial data problem.

Non-topological solitons have been discovered in field theories with a kinetic self-interaction. Such theories appear, for example, in curved space effective actions for gravity and could also explain the Higgs boson as a elementary particle with self-interactions. This paper demonstrates that a soliton is a localized, static, configuration of a field that is smooth everywhere except for a hole in its background. Solitons with the appropriate quantum numbers may be stable in certain parameter regimes, and it is shown that static soliton solutions exist in both planar and spatial Rosenhaus-Dick problems. Examples are given of half and fully periodic configurations in the Rosenhaus-Dick problem and in scalar field theories with a nonzero vacuum expectation value. The solitons presented in this paper do not require the field to have a non-topological soliton shape. The Rosenhaus-Dick problem is a standard model of planar-walled domain walls with a kink-like solution, where the kink is the field-configuration localized at the wall. The scalar field in the Rosenhaus-Dick problem has a different periodic solution, the half-period, which is a static configuration where the field has a minimum between two maxima. The existence of these static half-and fully periodic configurations is extended to field theories with a kinetic self-interaction term.

The solar system contains four giant planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, which were all formed during the late stages of the protoplanetary disk evolution 4.6 billion years ago. The planets likely migrated from beyond the ice line, the distance from which ice materials can no longer warm via thermal excitation. It is suggested that this migration may have been driven by the forced oscillation of the disk. As the planets' cores grew via core accretion, the eccentricities and inclinations of the planets' orbits increased until, roughly 200 million years ago, the outer two planets collided with Mars. This created the current architecture for the giant planets, which is characterized by eccentric and inclined orbits. The migration and evolution of the giant planets likely has a profound effect on the structure of the current solar system. The dynamics of the giant planets in the gaseous disk are described. The analytic, 2D, hydrodynamical solutions of the Planet-Disk-Planet (PDP) system are presented. The migration of the giant planets from beyond the ice line is modeled. The eccentricities and inclinations of the current architectures for the giant planets are explained as a result of the evolution of the giant planets in the disk.

Nilpotent symmetry invariance is a notion of fundamental importance in modern theoretical physics, which reflects the presence of higher order interaction terms in the Lagrangians of the corresponding theories. Such terms typically require the more general fields with respect to the given ones, compared to the case of ordinary symmetry invariance, to be specified not just on the values of the symmetry transformations but on the corresponding source terms as well. In this respect, it provides a more appropriate framework to treat, in a well-defined way, the interacting theories which, in some respects, mimic to a greater or lesser extent their more fundamental (e.g. renormalizable) counterparts. It turns out that the supersymmetry provides the most elegant and natural example of such a phenomenon, namely of a symmetry invariance, called nilpotent, which is at the same time the most relevant and useful in revealing the geometrical nature of the fundamental interactions. Despite the great phenomenological success of the local (i.e. non-supersymmetric) gauge theories, the latter have not been found in nature, and it is commonly believed that local supersymmetry is a fundamental ingredient of all string theories. Based on the experience with ordinary supersymmetry, it is of interest to explore whether nilpotent symmetry invariance can play an equally important role in understanding the nature of the fundamental interactions. In this respect, it is important to understand, at a basic level, the structure of the underlying symmetries and the source free Lagrangian of the corresponding higher order (super)gauge theories. In this article, we shall discuss in some detail the superfield formulation of the 1-form supersymmetric gauge theories in two (1,1) superspace dimensions, with an emphasis on the nilpotent (anti)BRST symmetries and their corresponding gauge symmetry transformations. We also provide the key components of the (anti)co-BRST invariant restrictions on the 1-form gauge parameters, along with the help of an off-host invariant restriction. Finally, we demonstrate how the above superfield dynamics, along with the familiar subsidiary conditions, generates the on-shell nilpotent (anti)BRST and (anti)co-BRST symmetries, off-shell, exactly like in the case of the ordinary 1-form gauge theories.

The Constrained Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (CMSSM) with a cosmological term, $\Lambda$, is adopted as the theoretical framework for LHC weather forecasts. We show that the LHC reach for SUSY improves with better weather, and highlight the role of the naturalness prior. In the CMSSM, the LSP is the lightest neutralino. Results from LHC searches for SUSY put very strong constraints on the nature of the LSP. We describe this in the context of two prototypes, namely the scalar superpartner to the electron and the right-handed smuon. In both cases, viable scenarios are obtained only if the LSP is very close to the lightest neutralino. In the context of LHC weather forecasts, it is the neutralino lifetime which determines how good the weather is for SUSY. We explore two techniques for determining neutralino lifetime, one based on experimental results and one based on theoretical calculations, namely prompt decay and spin-dependent decay, respectively. In both cases, our prototype scenarios have scalar superpartners with masses around 1 TeV, right-handed smuons below 650 GeV and a gluino with mass around 4.7-5.5 TeV. The mass splitting between the superpartners is up to several hundred GeV, but this could increase if the SUSY breaking scale is raised. For the scalar superpartner to the electron, this spectrum yields a neutralino with a lifetime of approximately 3.2 micro-seconds. This is below the present experimental limit from LHC data of 6.3 micro-seconds. However, for a neutralino with scalar superpartner to the muon, the calculated neutralino lifetime is above the present experimental limit. In this case, scenarios with lifetimes above the limit could be explored if the neutralino could be shown to be the observed LSMTM.

A near-infrared/optical/X-ray survey in the centre of Sigma Orionis was conducted with the X-ray Telescope (XTT) on board the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. We discovered six new X-ray sources, and discovered four new optical sources in addition to the five previously known members of the centrally located cluster. In our brightest X-ray source we detected clear X-ray pulsations, and determined a possible compact object companion of two neutron stars or a low mass black hole. The near-infrared colours and proper motion of this object are consistent with it being a high-mass star in the process of being ejected from the cluster. We also found a possible jet source in our Chandra image. A T Tauri star with a small nebulous disc was also identified as an X-ray emitter. We also report the likely finding of a new optical/infrared binary in our survey, and we report the possible detection of protoplanetary discs via their infrared excess emission. The full survey data and X-ray detection results are presented in an electronic table.

In geometric representation theory, the action of a finite group on a variety gives rise to equivariant cohomology theories, or GT words. For the special case of a transitive action on a flag variety, the Schubert polynomials become rational functions in Chern classes, or GT classes. In this case, the multiplication of GT polynomials is related to the classical invariant theory Fitting theorem. In this note we prove a general extension of this theorem to a suitable class of $G$-varieties, establishing a relation between the classical invariant theory and the equivariant cohomology of Schubert varieties. As an example, we show that the Bialynicki-Birula decomposition of a Schubert variety decomposes into equivariant divisorial Schubert subvarieties. We do this by extending the invariant theory results to the cohomology of $G$-varieties with a good torus action. Fitting's theorem concerns the composition of a linear map with an idempotent. We consider a linear map between cohomology theories and its corresponding idempotent in equivariant cohomology. We show that the product of these maps gives the identity on the cohomology of a special type of $G$-varieties. We provide examples for the application of this result. Let $G$ be a complex reductive group, $T$ a complex reductive subgroup, $X$ a $G$-variety and $Y$ a $T$-variety. Let $f : H^*_G(X) \rightarrow H^*_T(Y)$ be the map induced by the projection $G \rightarrow T$ and let $e : H^*_T(Y) \rightarrow H^*_G(X)$ be the idempotent corresponding to the action of $T$ on $Y$ naturally lifted to $X$. Then $fe = \text{Id}_{H^*_T(Y)}$. The Schubert polynomials associated to a Weyl group $W$ form a class of rational functions in the Chern classes of a complete flag variety $G/B$ that are stable with respect to the Chevalley-Monk formula. It was conjectured by Lascoux and Schützenberger that their product is related to the classical invariant theory Fitting's theorem. We prove a generalization of this theorem to a suitable class of $G$-varieties. This result applies in particular to the case of the equivariant cohomology of Schubert varieties. We illustrate this with an example relating the Bialynicki-Birula decomposition of a Schubert variety to the decomposition into equivariant divisorial Schubert subvarieties.

A number of VLBI observations of 19 GHz-peaked-spectrum (GPS) radio sources at 1.6 GHz have been made, yielding the following results: 1. The 1.6 GHz and 19 GHz flux densities are consistent with being identical, within the errors. This is unexpected if 19 GHz is generated in the base of a relativistic jet, as expected in GPS sources. 2. The 1.6 GHz and 19 GHz position angle (PA) differences are consistent with zero, as is also unexpected if 19 GHz is generated in a jet. 3. Three sources show a 1.6 GHz PA rotation in the expected sense for a GPS source, i.e., a gradient of more than 10 degrees per decade in PA. These results are consistent with 19 GHz being generated in a GPS source's core. The final sentence is the most important. 19 GHz is thought to be generated in the core of GPS sources, so this result is consistent with the hypothesis.

In a previous paper we showed that N=8 supergravity in four dimensions can be obtained by dimensional reduction from N=8 superYang-Mills theory in five dimensions. Here we give an explicit lagrangian for the latter, and perform a similar truncation to the bosonic part of N=4 super Yang-Mills in four dimensions. The reduced theory contains two functionals, that generalize the Yang-Mills action and the supergravity action, and that satisfy a set of equations that generalize the equations of motion of the two theories. We also find two new constraint relations that fix the Lagrange multiplier fields appearing in the truncation. In a separate article we use this result to study N=8 supergravity in three dimensions. In this case the truncation leads to a duality between the three-dimensional theory and N=4 superYang-Mills in three dimensions. This work was completed during the author's stay at the Aspen Center for Physics, which is gratefully acknowledged.

The evolution of massive black hole binaries (MBHB) is commonly divided into three phases: early hardening, late-stagehardening and mass segregation, and the final coalescence. In this paper, we present the results of a large suite of numerical relativity simulations investigating the final phase of the evolution of massive black hole binaries, in which the two black holes effectively segregate into two distinct sub-systems, embedded in a common, diffuse envelope of bound particles and radiation. We find that for a typical binary with mass ratio 1:4 in a circumbinary distribution of stars, about half the particles are bound to the less massive hole and the other half are bound to the more massive hole. The most massive hole is typically twice as massive as the sum of the two holes, with an RMS of a factor of 1.4. The mass growth of the most massive hole is driven by collisional mergers with bound particles, rather than by smooth loss via gravitational-wave emission. Overall, the MBHB phase ends with the two binary sub-systems each hosting a black hole, with a total binary mass M{tot} ∼ 0.7M{bh1}+0.3M{bh2}, where M{bh1} and M{bh2} are the masses of the two black holes. We show that this collisional evolution can be explained by considering the binary as a perturbed monopole moment of a stellar distribution function with a single characteristic energy. The binary grows by occasional captures of bound particles from this distribution, driving strong, stochastic torques that bring the holes into rapid close encounter. The two sub-systems ultimately merge via a sequence of fewer but deeper close encounters, as the holes spiral towards the centre of the cluster. We show that the characteristic energies for the monopole resonances grow during the evolution, until finally reaching the hard-soft boundary of the single black hole potentials, marking the end of the evolution.

A magnetic structure in the solar atmosphere termed prominence loop participated in five flares on May 20, 2017. It was observable in EUV with Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on Solar Dynamics Observatory, in the Fe XII 304 [nicrome] and Fe XII 525.0 nm lines with Solar Broadband Telescope and in HXR with Gamma-Ray Burst And Afterglow Spectrometer (GRAB). The 304 and 525.0 nm lines are formed in the upper and lower ionisation levels of iron, respectively. The loop showed a dynamic behavior during the flares. The observed line asymmetries suggested fundamental properties of the flaring plasma were violated, which could not be explained with a classical 1D hydrostatic loop model. A three-dimensional (3D) magnetic fluxrooted loop model including non-thermal particles and non-LTE effects was developed to reproduce the loop observations. It could reproduce the 304 and 525.0 nm line intensity asymmetries and the temporal evolution of the loop. The imbalance of heating rates between the up and down surfaces of the loop was suggested as one of the main reasons for the loop evolution. This work significantly advanced our understanding of the physical process of solar flares.

Modular functions are a powerful tool for studying the behavior of functions of a complex variable under fractional linear transformations, or modular transformations. The form of a modular function depends only on its transformation properties under integer shifts, or powers of a uniformizing parameter. The uniformizing parameter in turn only depends on the quotient of its domain and range under the modular transformation. These functions have proven to be indispensable in the study of elliptic functions, elliptic modular forms, and moonshine. Despite their utility, modular functions are defined only for subgroups of the modular group, depending on an integer parameterizing the subgroup. I describe a framework for defining modular functions for any uniformizing parameter, which I call vector-valued modular functions. These functions satisfy a generalized hypergeometric differential equation and transform under the modular group in a natural way. I present a few applications to elliptic modular forms, whose spectral decompositions take the form of scalar-valued modular forms multiplied by $q$-series. I also present an example of a vector-valued modular function corresponding to the unique uniformizing parameter for the Suzuki chain of non-split quadratic number fields. I conclude by describing some open questions for this approach to modular forms and functions.

Extraction of physical laws from joint experimental data Presented at the European Conference on Machine Learning, Stockholm, September 2018 Authors: Per separable, Hinke R. Muller, Klaus German, Lars H. Carlson, Leif D. Özcan, Hakan Arslan, Christopher S. Benbow, Hendrik stelling, Aad van der Lugt Link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.09212 This paper presents a framework for the automatic extraction of physical laws from joint experimental data. It uses a symbolic deep neural network, trained on symbolic transformations of the data and an explicit CNF neural net to find a most general physical law given a training data set. The framework has been successfully applied to a synthetic data set, and the laws extracted can be shown to correctly describe the data generation process. Two case studies on physical laws extracted from physical experiments are also presented. This framework can be applied to other physical laws, especially those that can be described by partial differential equations, provided that a suitable data set exists.

The Second Data Release of the Ancient Globular Cluster Survey (Holtzman et al. 2017a) is the first data release of the simultaneous spectral fitting of@200_Band_Magellan/PANIC and@100_Magellan/IMACS Lick indices (Spoints). This release contains integrated Spoints for 715 globular clusters covering five SDSS $g$ passbands and thirty-two Lick indices. We use these indices to derive cluster mean age, $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]$, and \[Fe/H\], and to construct stellar evolution tracks, isochrones, and luminosity functions (LF) for thirteen stellar population synthesis codes. LFs in specific passbands are fit with sum of two or three Gaussians to quantify multiple populations in clusters. We present our analysis method in Section 2 and present our results in Section 3. Our derived age–\[$\alpha$/Fe\] diagrams show that clusters with similar values of $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]$ follow roughly parallel age sequences, suggesting that primary enrichment by rapidly-spinning massive stars (RSM; e.g., Decressin et al. 2007) is not inhibited by the inherent anti-correlation between $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]$ and age (e.g., Carretta et al. 2009a; Martocchia et al. 2009). Slight variations in these diagrams can be attributed to different assumptions regarding the initial mass function (IMF; e.g., D’Ercole et al. 2010), particularly at the low-mass end (e.g., D’Antona & Caloi 2007; D’Antona et al. 2016). The clusters with $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]<0.1$ seem to have an extended tail to older ages; this could be interpreted as another evidence of a top-heavy IMF, but we do not find evidence for a change in the shape of the IMF over this parameter space (e.g., D’Antona et al. 2011). Our derived $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]$–age relations appear to be more-or-less linear and do not appear to correlate with $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]$ or age for $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]\gtrsim 0.4$, suggesting that mass transfer may have affected the evolution of such systems. We identify two parallel sequences of $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]=0.2$ and $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]=0.4$ in our derived $[\alpha/{\rm Fe}]-age$ diagrams, which we interpret as two separate generations of stars formed during a single burst of star formation. This scenario is consistent with the extended period of quiescence inferred from the spatial distributions of the clusters in our sample. We also observe clear evidence for stellar rotation in these diagrams: the two parallel sequences have different rotation rates, with the more iron-poor clusters being slower rotators.
