The Colour Reconnection (CR) algorithm aims at solving the principal problem of hadronization by merging in optimal way the short-living colour octets into singlets. The CR scheme is implemented in the HERWIG event generator, which was used at LEP for precision electroweak measurements. The present note describes an analysis of colour reconnection effects in the decay WW -> llll with the DELPHI detector at LEP-2. The data sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1186 pb-1 collected by the DELPHI experiment at centre-of-mass energies of 130 GeV and 136 GeV has been analysed. The comparison of experimental observations with the expectations from standard model event generator HERWIG demonstrates that the CR scheme works similarly good at 130 and at 136 GeV. The measured WW annihilation cross sections and the W-boson polarization parameters have been determined separately for four mutually excluding phase space regions and no significant differences with the standard model predictions have been found. The implications of the experimental findings for the CR parameter space are discussed.

The Millennium Galaxy Catalogue (MGC) is a wide-field imaging survey designed to sample the galaxy population within the virial radius of the Local Group. The catalogue contains detailed data for nearly 10,000 galaxies, which allows us to probe the relationship between supermassive black holes and their host galaxies in great detail. We present the full table of black hole masses for MGC-DR2, the second data release of the survey. We find that the local supermassive black hole mass function is consistent with that of a similarly characterised local inactive galaxy population. Contrary to previous studies, we do not find any dependence of supermassive black hole mass on properties such as the mass or velocity dispersion of the host galaxy. We also consider the role of environment in explaining these trends, and find that different galaxy populations inhabit distinct regions of the supermassive black hole mass– host galaxy property space. We therefore conclude that the growth of supermassive black holes and their hosts is independent across the full range of observed properties, and that local dynamics do not fully explain the bimodality of local galaxy population into early- and late-type systems.

Solar coronal holes (SCHs), dark regions in the Sun's corona, are sources of fast, diffuse, and inhomogeneously propagating shock waves called surges. The surges erupt from active regions into the low solar corona and can propagate as far away as the Heliospheric current sheet (HCS). Here we study the propagation of magneto-frictional waves in the vicinity of a coronal hole SOHO 15 next Resolution of heliospheric current sheet. The waves, observed in the longitudinal magnetic field, are of small-amplitude and low to middle frequencies and travel as divergence waves or torsional waves. Both the linear and nonlinear stages of the waves' propagation are affected by the coronal hole. The attenuation rates of the longitudinal magnetic field and the computed fast magneto-sonic speed are higher in the coronal hole than in the neighboring regions. The higher attenuation in the coronal hole is likely caused by the shock-accelerated particles that propagate along the coronal hole boundaries. These results may affect interpretation of helioseismic and coronal hole parameters deduced from remote sensing data.

In astrophysics and cosmology, the evolution of gas in gravitational fields is governed by the equations of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), which are well-suited to large-scale systems but can be challenging to solve on small spatial and temporal scales such as those found in the cores of galaxies and galaxy clusters. When the equations are extended to includeGeneral relativity, strong magnetic fields, and a variable rather than constant adiabatic index, we show that they are dramatically simpler. In particular, we find exact, steady-state, self-similar solutions with no analytic continuations that connect to the subsonic, transonic, and supersonic solutions with constant adiabatic index. The exact solutions are in excellent agreement with numerical solutions of the full MHD equations. These results suggest that MHD with a variable rather than constant adiabatic index may provide an acceptable approximation on both large and small spatial and temporal scales in a range of astrophysical and cosmological systems.

The production of Tsallis entropy in the limit of weak chaos and a new indicator of chaoticity Xuanyu You, Junliang Lin, Lei Zhang, Xiangfu Wang 2016 Jul 10; 57(14): 4833-4840 https://arxiv.org/pdf/1607.05534.pdf In the Tsallis formalism, Shannon entropy and Tsallis entropy are related by a normalized factor, which is called Tsallis index. The Tsallis index is a new indicator of chaoticity. If the Tsallis index diverges, the system reaches the limit of weak chaos. Here we study a new indicator of chaoticity based on Tsallis entropy production. In a system with many degrees of freedom, the differential of Tsallis entropy production may diverge at the limit of weak chaos. Using the Cauchy point and the logarithmic point methods, we give the conditions for the divergence of the differential of Tsallis entropy production and the condition for the system to reach the limit of weak chaos. The divergence of the differential of Tsallis entropy production is a new indicator of chaoticity. At the same time, it is an efficient indicator for the rapid determination of the limit of weak chaos. In particular, our method is a simple method to determine the divergence of the differential of the Riemann zeta function at a trivial zero. Applying the method to some cases with many degrees of freedom, we find that the divergence of the differential of Tsallis entropy production has some connection with the Lyapunov exponent and the largest eigenvalue of the iteration matrix.

The gamma-ray binary LS I +61 303 is composed of a compact object, most likely a black hole, accreting from the gas captured by the companion star. The companion is a main sequence star of spectral type O9.5V, located at a distance of 2.4 kpc. The orbit of the binary is highly eccentric, with a period of 12.8 years and an apastron of 5.5 A.U. The detection of eclipses and dips, highly polarized gamma-ray emission, as well as the detection of a collimated jet, suggest that the compact object is hidden for most of the time, with occasional brief appearances as it spirals towards the star. The system's dynamic nature has been a matter of debate, with some studies supporting a scenario involving the existence of a third body, while others advocate for the colliding-winds model. In this scenario, the stellar wind from the companion sweeps up and compresses a dense circumbinary disk around the black hole. This disk produces the majority of the observed gamma-ray emission. In this paper, we assess these two models using a combination of numerical simulations and analytic arguments. The main result of this assessment is that the accretion model, though less elegant and more complex, is more successful at reproducing the multiwavelength data. The accretion model for LS I +61 303 relies on the existence of an accretion disk, fed by material captured from the stellar companion. The matter is likely channeled towards the black hole through a hot, relatively poorly ionized magnetospheric outflow. The rate of capture is highly eccentric with respect to the black hole's orbital plane, allowing for a persistent but irregular supply of material to the disk. Thermal coupling between the disk and the magnetic field of the black hole prevents the formation of an externally thin disk, and allows for efficient high-energy emission via synchrotron or magnetically confined jet models. In contrast, colliding-winds models posit that the compact object is a Wolf-Rayet star, composed of a fast-moving WR wind blowing over a dense, slow-moving O-star wind. The system is highly eccentric, with the periastron being the site of the colliding winds. These two winds slow down and collide, producing a complex, partially ionized, region of shocked gas and emission. Although the existence of colliding winds has been demonstrated in the case of massive stars, we demonstrate that colliding winds can also apply to relatively low-mass companion stars, producing observable emission. Furthermore, the emitting region in colliding winds is small and localized, whereas the large orbit of LS I +61 303 requires a distributed emission region. Through a combination of 1-D and 3-D simulations, we show that a colliding winds scenario cannot reproduce the multiwavelength spectral energy distribution of LS I +61 303, and predict that the system should be relatively radio-quiet.

A singly negatively charged self-assembled InGaAs quantum dot with a effective Landé g factor of -0.44 was studied in a noncollinear magnetic field. By using optically detected electron spin resonance, we measured electron and hole spin relaxation times exceeding 4.5 μs and 0.7 ms, respectively. The long hole spin relaxation time greatly exceeded the values predicted by the Fermi’s golden rule and the Hölder inequality, and was consistent with the best theoretical estimates for GaAs with conduction band effective mass. We argue that the unexpectedly long hole spin relaxation time is the result of the suppression of electron-hole correlation-induced transitions between the heavy-hole valence band and the split-off conduction band induced by the strong quantum dot vertical confinement. The authors would like to thank Dr. Roman Skrotski for fruitful discussions and providing experimental data. This work was supported by the Foundation for Polish Science (FNP).

Systems with a large number of degrees of freedom, such as living organisms, mechanical devices, financial markets, or social systems, are often regarded as complex. However, whether a system is complex or not has been debated, and many approaches to measuring complexity are ad-hoc, lacking a solid theoretical underpinning. Here, we propose an approach to the measurement of complexity based on self-organization and emergence. We illustrate our approach with three case studies: protein folding, the bacterial flagellum, and stock market returns. Our analysis indicates that complexity, as we define it, underlies these and other phenomena. Moreover, the proposed approach to complexity measurement may facilitate the discovery of new principles of simplicity underlying phenomena that have been regarded as complex. We argue that a complex system must exhibit self-organization and emergent properties. The proposed approach to complexity is based on this theoretical framework and on three case studies: protein folding, the bacterial flagellum, and stock market returns. We use a combination of algorithms and statistical analysis to demonstrate that these systems exhibit self-organization and emergent behavior, as we define it. First, we show that these systems have "negative coupling": changes in one parameter affect other parameters in the system, but in a direction that reduces the overall complexity of the system. Second, we show that these systems have "cross-scale interactions": lower-level interactions give rise to higher-level dynamics. Third, we demonstrate that these systems have "multiple stable states": multiple configurations are accessible to the system, some of which are more stable than others. These three aspects of self-organization and emergence are central to our proposed approach to complexity, and we illustrate our approach with three case studies: protein folding, the bacterial flagellum, and stock market returns. Our approach to measuring complexity is based on three case studies: protein folding, the bacterial flagellum, and stock market returns. For each system, we quantify the complexity of each of three case studies: protein folding, the bacterial flagellum, and stock market returns. For each system, we calculate a complexity metric that is based on our proposed approach. We illustrate our approach with three case studies: protein folding, the bacterial flagellum, and stock market returns. Our analysis indicates that complexity, as we define it, underlies these and other phenomena. Moreover, the proposed approach to complexity measurement may facilitate the discovery of new principles of simplicity underlying phenomena that have been regarded as complex.

Star clusters are important tools for studying a range of astrophysical phenomena, such as star formation, stellar feedback, and gravitational dynamics. These compact groups of stars are often found to contain a vast range of properties; while some clusters are simple populations of coeval stars, many are created through dynamical processes that assemble groups of previously unrelated stars with similar ages and chemical compositions. The diversity seen in these star cluster systems hints at a complex evolutionary history, but direct observational evidence has been difficult to obtain due to the crowding and dimness of clusters in distant galaxies. Here we use archived Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph data to identify and characterize the spatial distribution of star clusters in the grand design spiral galaxy M51. The full spectrum of environments cluster (FCOE) catalog contains 122,695 individual star cluster candidates, identified from archival Hubble Space Telescope data by machine learning algorithms trained on high-contrast imaging from the Advanced Camera for Surveys. We estimate cluster ages from the strength of the hydrogen Brackett Jump at 2.166 microns, and demonstrate that there is an approximately log-normal distribution of ages with a peak at log(age/years) ≃ 7.6 and a standard deviation of 0.4. We determine the systemic velocities of clusters via cross-correlation with a library of model spectra and find that this clusters have a nearly Gaussian velocity distribution with a peak of v ≃ 265 km/s and a standard deviation of 39 km/s. Lastly, we show that clusters exhibit two distinct distributions in projection on the major axis of M51, with more than 60% located within 2.5 kpc of the galactic midplane.

A model multicellular organism resembling the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum can be self assembled in a Petri dish from a single uniform cell suspension in the presence of bacteria. The resulting colonies exhibit a morphology reminiscent of social amoebae, including separation of multiple independent, isolated domains that resemble mature differentiated cells. The cells in the domains consume the bacteria local to the domain and this localized consumption supports the observed morphogenesis. The resulting organism exhibits molecular and phenotypic characteristics of differentiated cells as well as the ability to respond to environmental signals by differentiation, proliferation and migration. The observed ability to undergo multistage differentiation similar to multicellular organisms suggests that this approach may provide a useful platform for the discovery and study of novel biologically active molecules and for development of next generation therapies. The model multicellular organism described here exhibits a morphology reminiscent of social amoebae including isolated domains that exhibit differentiated cellular characteristics. This organism can undergo multistage differentiation similar to multicellular organisms. Thus this model organism may provide a useful platform for discovery and study of novel biologically active molecules and for development of next generation therapies.

The magnetic fields of isolated neutron stars are very weak, but the magnetic fields of pulsars are some of the strongest magnetic fields in the Universe. The origin of these fields is a longstanding mystery, and recent studies have suggested that the fields are generated through a process known as quantum confinement, in which the inner region of the neutron star forms a torus due to the rotation of the fluid inside of it. Recently, a very strong magnetic field was detected emanating from the surface of the sun. The field is organized into arc-shaped structures that extend tens of thousands of kilometers from the surface of the sun, and these structures have been observed to rotate with the sun. If the structure is a magnetic field, it would be one of the largest magnetic fields detected in the universe. If it is generated by the sun, this would suggest that incredibly strong fields can be generated at diverse locations in the universe, and that these fields can interact over extremely large distances.

In two dimensional electron gas (2DEG) with spin-orbit coupling, a conserved spin Hall conductance can exist in the absence of a net spin polarization. In this work, we report that the spin Hall conductance is still conserved even when a net spin polarization does exist. We show that the spin Hall conductance is related to the Berry curvature of the dressed electronic states and is therefore time-reversal invariant. The conserved spin Hall conductance is then shown to lead to a dissipationless charge spin current even in the presence of a nonzero magnetization current. We calculate this spin current within a self-consistent Born approximation and find that it is linear in the magnetization current, in agreement with the Kubo formula for the spin Hall conductivity. Finally, we discuss experimental implications of our results. We construct a low energy effective theory for the 2DEG with Rashba spin-orbit coupling in a perpendicular magnetic field. By performing a functional derivative, we derive the effective action in terms of fermions with four-component spinor notation. By making a Schrieffer-Wolff transformation and linearizing the dispersion around the Dirac points, we obtain the low energy effective Hamiltonian. It contains four pair of Weyl fermions with opposite chirality. The pairing between the Weyl fermions with opposite chiralities is controlled by the inter-valley (spin) coupling, which is generated by a quantum correction to the gauge field. This spin coupling term is odd under time-reversal and enforces a conserved spin Hall conductance in the system. We then consider a setup with an applied electric field in the direction transverse to the 2DEG plane and spin-dependent magnetic fields in the plane. In the presence of these, there will be a charge and spin current. While the charge current is accompanied by a voltage drop in the magnetic leads, the spin current is not. It is instead associated with a dissipationless transverse spin magnetization, which is independent of the voltage applied to the leads. The origin of the dissipationless transverse spin magnetization is the spin coupling term generated by the quantum corrections to the gauge field, which enforces a conserved spin Hall conductance in the system.

Zakharov simulation study of spectral features of on-demand Langmuir turbulence in an inhomogeneous plasma. The paper is of interest to space physics specialists due to the use of Plasma Physics equations to describe transport and evolution of plasma components in the solar wind. The performed simulations demonstrate that the spectrum of plasma dispersion fluctuations produced by on-demand Langmuir turbulence in an inhomogeneous plasma has a form of a number of discrete spectral lines. The lines shape and their number depend on the parameters of an initial perturbation and on the level of inhomogeneity of a plasma background. The simulated lines can be used to extract information about the initial perturbation and about plasma inhomogeneity. The performed simulations can be easily reproduced using publicly available code. Inhomogeneity of a plasma background can be introduced by a wave excitation scheme that employs a movingLangmuir trap with an inhomogeneous density profile. A solution of the Plasma Physics equations that describe transport and evolution of plasma components in the solar wind is used as a background model. The turbulence is generated by moving the trap section that contains plasma at a speed that corresponds to the phase velocity of an ion plasma period at the wave number corresponding to the trap oscillation frequency. The spectrum of plasma dispersion fluctuations produced by on-demand Langmuir turbulence in an inhomogeneous plasma has a form of a number of discrete spectral lines. The lines shape and their number depend on the parameters of an initial perturbation and on the level of inhomogeneity of a plasma background. The simulated lines can be used to extract information about the initial perturbation and about plasma inhomogeneity. The performed simulations can be easily reproduced using publicly available code.

The nature of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) remains one of the most intriguing issues in contemporary high-energy astrophysics. Although numerous observations and arguments strongly suggest that most GRBs are associated with the death of massive stars, the progenitor system of GRBs remains mysterious. In this paper, we report on a long-lived optical counterpart of the bright GRB 031203. The peak luminosity of the optical counterpart was less than 10% of that of the gamma-rays. The optical light curve is very smooth, without a precursor, signature of chromatic light effects or other typical features of a collapsar model. We propose that GRB 031203 belongs to the long-GRB population, whose progenitor is a massive star with low-energy jets. This low-energy jet interpretation is also supported by the unusual X-ray and gamma-ray absorption column densities. The optical and X-ray observations of this GRB favor a prolonged activity of the central engine. We suggest that the activity lasted longer than that of typical long-GRBs but less than that of typical short-GRBs.

The open cluster NGC 1883 is located in the anticenter of the Milky Way and presents one of the highest known concentrations of stars per cubic parsec. The age, distance and radial velocity, metallicities and spatial distribution of its members have been studied here for the first time. The turn-off region of the main sequence is clearly seen in the color-magnitude diagram, indicating an age of about 1.2 million years. The distance is derived as 19.6 ± 1.2 kpc, which corresponds to 2.3 ± 0.2 × 10⁶ pc3. The radial velocity is −22.3 ± 1.2 km/s, corresponding to a heliocentric distance of 13.2 kpc. The metallicity is estimated at [Fe/H] = −0.07 ± 0.03, which is equivalent to approximately one-tenth of the solar metallicity. The spatial distribution of the cluster members shows a relatively uniform distribution without any significant signs of disruption, with a slight overdensity around the center of the cluster.

Landau \(\Gamma\) and \(\chi\) automorphic functions on \(\mathbb{C}^n\) of magnitude \(\nu\) are defined and studied. \(\nu^{-n}\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}_n\), where \(\mathbb{H}_n\) is n-dimensional upper-half space, is identified as their native space. For such an n-tuple \((m_1,\ldots,m_n)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^n\), the quotient \(\Gamma(m_1,\ldots,m_n)\), where \(\Gamma(m_1,\ldots,m_n)=\{A\in\SL_n(\mathbb{C}): \text{abs}(A-I_n)\leq m_1,\ldots,\text{abs}(A-I_n)\leq m_n\}\), plays the role of domain. Eigenfunctions of the induced Laplace operator on such domains are studied using the method of stationary phase. Some properties of Landau \(\Gamma\) and \(\chi\) functions are obtained and their application to study subspaces of rational functions are also suggested.

A novel z' gauge symmetry based on string theory is proposed. This z' is anomaly free, has a stable proton, and contains light neutrinos that may explain the short baseline neutrino anomalies. An R-parity breaking term is introduced to account for the observed baryon asymmetry of the Universe. The z' symmetry is used to explain the muon - muonCollider compatible neutrino parameters. We consider here a simple extension of the Standard Model (SM) with a gauge symmetry $SU(3)_C\times SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y\times z'$ where the prime denotes the symmetry is new. The introduction of a $z'$ symmetry stabilizes the proton and makes the light neutrinos, which can explain the short baseline neutrino anomalies, naturally a mixture of a light active neutrino and a light sterile neutrino. The active-sterile mixing is constrained by a zero reactor angle and the lower bound on the effective number of neutrinos $\Neff$. The $z'$ model can also explain the observed baryon asymmetry of the Universe via leptogenesis and the required leptogenesis hierarchy can be generated via renormalization group running. The $z'$ model contains a R-parity breaking term which could explain the dark matter. The lightest $z'$ particle is a good candidate for dark matter.

Quark-lepton complementarity (QLC) was proposed to account for the wide success of the standard model (SM) throughout the spectroscopy of particles up to the TeV scale. We argue that this success also implies the validity of QLC for low energy phenomena. We make a set of predictions that can be tested at current and near future experiments. First, the existence of a light isodoublet of scalars with different CP parities is a generic prediction of QLC. Second, lepton number is violated in the low energy lepton doublet and the stability of the lightest charged particle (LCP) is connected to the assignments of color and weak iso-spin. The presence of the LCP and its stability bound the mass of the isodoublet scalars. Third, baryon number is violated at low energies via instanton interactions. This leads to a suppression of the proton decay rate relative to the standard model. Finally, we show that the dark matter is most likely a complex fermion that interacts via the weak force.

Earthquake excitation is one of the important hazards which may cause enormous loss of human life and significant amount of damage to property and environment.In this work, we propose a system to predict structural response for a specific period of time after an earthquake has occurred. For this, we first model the ground motion using proper ground motion models. The ground motion is then converted to structural response using software FRED. We train a feed-forward artificial neural network using earthquake response data from 9 stations of Indian Seismic Network which are close to the expected site of an hypothetical earthquake and have similar geology. The predicted structural response is then compared to observed structural response using mean absolute error as metric. We perform our analysis for different network sizes and number of neurons in the hidden layer and find that our model can accurately predict structural response up to 4 seconds after the earthquake has occurred. Authors: Ritabrata Mohapatra With an intent to generate few slides for my seminar, I tried my best to keep the content relevant. This is definitely a good start which can be developed upon, a dedicated model for earthquake response prediction can be developed using proper hyperparameter tuning and data from various networks across the globe can be combined and trained on a single model.

Integral formulas for the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) are obtained by using the Schütz formula for tagged particles. We begin with a review of this process and the symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP). Then we state the main results for ASEP and outline the proof. This proof is based on showing that the density matrix satisfies a quantum version of the Klimontovich equation, which is then used to define quantum many-body Hamiltonian. This Hamiltonian is then diagonalized in a suitable complete set of functions. Terms in the resulting formula are expressed using orthogonal polynomials and can be evaluated explicitly. In particular, as an illustration, a very simple expression for the current is obtained. The current through a filled chemical bond in a one-dimensional lattice is also studied. Keywords: asymmetric simple exclusion process, quantum many-body system, orthogonal polynomials Reference: [Integral Formulas for the Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process] Nejat Avlos and Younghan Jeon arXiv.org arXiv:1905.02748 [math.PR] May 2019 The asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) is a one-dimensional quantum many-body system. This paper gives an integral formula for the ASEP, the generator of the time evolution for theExpectation[f, z, {0, W}] where z is the coordinate of the initial particle and W is the width of the system. The formula is expressed using a kernel given in terms of orthogonal polynomials. The kernel can be used to find an explicit expression for the current across a bond that contains a fixed number of particles. A simple formula for this current is also obtained.

The gas and dust around the young star beta Pictoris is mostly located in a disk around the star, but there is also some material located in a bipolar nebula surrounding the star in the sky. The dust and gas is mostly composed of sand and small rocks and follows the same shape as the material of the star itself. Theories to explain the shape of the star and the surrounding material include models that include collisions between asteroids, gas being pulled from the star, or comets from another star passing close to beta Pictoris. The observations were taken using the Herschel Space Observatory and the Spitzer Space Telescope. More information on this and other stars look at https://www.space.com/starchild. This paper describes the dust and gas around beta Pictoris from 600 astronomical units (au) to 40000 au from the star. Download the full paper (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epsl.2018.10.004).

A relatively nearby elliptical galaxy Leo elliptical NGC 3379 hosts a low-mass satellite galaxy Leo IV. Spectroscopy of its satellites’ stars reveals that this satellite had a higher star formation rate in the past and had a more eccentric orbit than it has today. Simulations show that the growth of the main galaxy NGC 3379 can transform a low-mass satellite galaxy into a faint dwarf like Leo IV. This discovery demonstrates that even the low-mass satellite galaxies in massive halos can undergo transformation by their host galaxies, and a diffuse matter in the form of neutral hydrogen was found around this satellite galaxy with a highly eccentric orbit, which is an excellent example of the transformation of low-mass systems through interaction with their host. Leo elliptical NGC 3379 is a massive elliptical galaxy located at a distance of approximately 30 million light years from the Earth. It is a relatively nearby galaxy and its properties were well-studied. One of its satellites, Leo IV, was discovered using the Sloan Sky Digital Survey in 2015 and observations of its stars revealed that it had a more eccentric orbit and had a higher star formation rate in the past. Simulations showed that NGC 3379 can transform the properties of this low-mass satellite through interaction with it. In particular, Leo IV can evolve from a faint dwarf to a more massive system. This is evident by the detection of a large amount of neutral hydrogen around this satellite, which was also observed for the first time in 2015. This discovery demonstrates that even the low-mass satellite galaxies in massive halos can undergo transformation by their host galaxies.

Zero-point radiation (ZPR) is one of the least understood concepts in quantum mechanics, and has been subject to numerous speculations and misinterpretations. The vacuum of the quantum field theory, being a completely undefined, random and incomplete state, possesses a random energy density. If this energy was partitioned into finite volumes, the associated random fields would fall below the zero-point energy, and thus have a positive energy. Such a vacuum fluctuation could perhaps be described as a "spontaneous creation of particles and antiparticles", but such a description would be entirely conventional and lack any evident symmetry requirements. A more accurate, though still inexact, description would be that of a "zero-point field" or "zero-point radiation". The latter term has been informally used to describe an essentially unlimited number of vacuum fluctuations of any kind, both positive and negative, per given volume or domain. Here we present a rigorous calculation of the energy density of the quantum vacuum in the paradigmatic cosmological model, the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) spacetime. We demonstrate that, for extremely large spatial domains, the vacuum energy density, as calculated by the corresponding Hamiltonian, converges to a finite non-zero limit, equal to a quarter of the total zero-point energy. The latter quantity corresponds to the lower limit on the energy density that is possible in Einstein's theory of gravity. The result can be interpreted as the manifestation of the Zero-Point Energy Hypothesis in the most extreme domain accessible to our calculations and assumptions. The predicted density of vacuum energy, equal to approximately 5.8 x 10−30 J/m3, is 38 orders of magnitude smaller than the critical density of the universe, and might therefore have been the dominant factor in the early evolution of the universe, leading to its observed inflationary state. The presented calculation is carried out in the framework of the corresponding Hamiltonian operator in quantum cosmology, and the lower limit on the density of the vacuum energy is inferred from the fact that the total zero-point energy can not be lower than the energy of the universe, estimated at approximately 2.2 x 10−8 J. The demonstrated relation is reproduced within the relative error of approximately 4.3 x 10−30. In order to achieve such a high precision, a whole range of possible short-comings and assumptions, both mathematical and physical, is carefully examined and found to be in conformity with the demonstrated relation. The most significant shortcoming, regarding the notion of vacuum energy, is that it is commonly accepted to be a single number, whereas in fact it is a range of distributions. In the presented theory, these distributions are assigned covariant forms. Such a form of representation is also employed in the calculation of the total energy of the universe, which extends the applicability of the presented theory to the gravitational field. Thus, the Zero-Point Energy Hypothesis is tested and confirmed in the very extreme domain

Galactic nuclei harbor supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in their centers, which may be growing via accretion from cold gas. SMBH binaries grow over timescales of hundreds of millions of years, interacting strongly with the surrounding gas and stars. We report that in three nuclei with multiple galactic disks, circumnuclear gas displays orbital patterns and kinematic gradients consistent with a recent, rapid triggering of SMBH binary evolution. The SMBHs are separated by tens to hundreds of parsecs, with large-scale gas and stars on Keplerian orbits about each black hole. The black holes coevolve by radiating gravitational waves and aligning their spins with their orbital angular momenta. The mass ratios of the stellar to supermassive black hole are consistent with predictions of galaxy mergers, and their projected separations imply characteristic timescales for nuclear gas torques and binary evolution of <100 million years. This study demonstrates that SMBH binaries can grow via gas torques and demonstrate that in three nuclei with multiple galactic disks, circumnuclear gas displays orbital patterns and kinematic gradients consistent with a recent, rapid triggering of SMBH binary evolution.

One of the most plausible origins of narrow emission lines in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) is gas in motion towards the nucleus, typically referred to as a “receding” gas supply. By using simultaneous spectral modeling of gas dynamics and ionization, we show that for a subset of 65 AGN with both optical spectroscopy and X-shooting, the vast majority of galaxies have double-sinusoidal receding profiles, with two distinct minima: one indicating motion out of the nucleus, and one indicating motion into the nucleus. These data suggest that the distribution of accretion rates onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in AGN host galaxies may not follow a single decreasing function, but rather may consist of a double-peaked distribution. The physical mechanism that could give rise to this distribution remains unknown, but the observed bimodality indicates the possibility that “two-mode” feedback may be an important component in AGN-host galaxy coevolution.

In a previous paper we introduced the notion of branched covered cylinders and showed that several symplectic fixed point theories (with moment maps given by branched covers) may be obtained by Hamiltonian reduction with respect to a branched covered circle action. In this paper we generalize our method to obtain fixed point theories corresponding to branched coverings with totally ramified cyclic branched covers over the circle. In particular, we construct a Hamiltonian reduction from a three-dimensional symplectic action with a Hamiltonian which is a degenerate double-well potential with two wells of depth one (i.e. with two dividing curves) and obtain the corresponding moment map image by solving a certain system of two coupled PDEs. We illustrate how our results apply to compute the reduced symplectic actions corresponding to the double cover of the sphere with three or with four punctures, as well as to an Enriques surface with its usual involution. The reduction process of a Hamiltonian action on a symplectic manifold with a Hamiltonian whose level sets are pre-quantizable (i.e. given by branched coverings with totally ramified branched covers over a circle) is studied. A two dimensional reduction is performed where the circle acts on the target of the covering in a Hamiltonian fashion. The symplectic fixed point manifold is described in terms of solutions to a system of two coupled PDEs.

Graphene has attracted tremendous research interests in recent years due to its outstanding physical properties and potential applications in many fields such as electronics, energy, and sensors. The most common synthesis method of graphene is the mechanical cleavage of highly pure graphite. However, this method is not suitable for large-area production, and it typically produces graphene samples with a considerable amount of contaminants. Epitaxial graphene, i.e. graphene grown directly on a SiC substrate, is a promising approach to large-area production and purification. In this work, we review the epitaxial graphene synthesis methods and their applications. Graphene is widely considered the most valuable graphite form. Monolayer graphene is a two-dimensional (2D) material with a carbon-atom lattice. It has unique properties such as extremely high electrical and thermal conductivities, and extremely high specific surface areas. Due to these excellent physical properties, graphene has numerous potential applications in different fields. Graphene synthesis typically requires high temperature and vacuum conditions. Furthermore, the synthesis is time-consuming and inefficient. Recently, epitaxial graphene, i.e. graphene grown directly on a SiC substrate, has been developed to solve these problems. SiC is a robust material with many excellent properties such as high thermal stability and high electrical conductivity. The epitaxial graphene grown on SiC substrates has high quality with few defects such as wrinkles and vacancies. The review presents the epitaxial graphene synthesis methods and their applications. First, we discuss the synthesis methods and related requirements for different substrates. Next, the experimental results of epitaxial graphene synthesis are summarized. Then, we discuss the applications of epitaxial graphene in electronics, sensors and energy. In the last part, the future research directions for epitaxial graphene are discussed.

Using the Mileura Widefield Array low frequency demonstrator field prototype system, we report on observations of the crab giant pulses (GCTs). The Mileura field is located at ~1260 km distance from the mooncenter and exhibits highFaraday rotation. We recorded 20 hrs of observations in 2016, during which we detected 5 GCTs and determined Faraday rotation measures (RM) following each pulse. We also triggered simultaneosly 1.2 MHz of recording modes at two adjacent north-south locations in the array. In this band we detected two GCTs but only with sub-meter accuracy due to the long field of view of the array. We estimate the distance to the GCTs based on the dispersion measure (DM) and the RM, and constrain their sizes to be ~1 mas. We detect DM and RM vectors typically aligned with the center of the GCT peaks, consistent with the extreme magneto-ionic conditions in the crab pulsar magnetosphere. The results presented here demonstrate that the Mileura Widefield Array has the sensitivity to detect the GCTs with DMs up to ~15 pc/cm^3 and demonstrate its ability to perform multi-frequency searches for DM and RM variations across GCT pulses. Such observations can potentially detect the earth rotation relative to the rotating neutron star magnetosphere.

Modern wireless networks exhibit an ever-increasing demand for higher data rates. To meet this demand, wireless communication systems must leverage multi-antenna technology, which provides the potential for significant increase in spectral efficiency through spatial multiplexing. However, the practical implementation of such technology poses several significant challenges. Chief among these challenges is the understanding of the fundamental limits of such systems in the large-system limit. In this work, we derive such limits for a popular transmission scheme known as spatial multiplexing with tabular channel statistics. In particular, we characterize the diversity-multiplexing tradeoff for the case where the number of antennas at the transmitter and receiver grow large, but the ratio between them is constrained. We further characterize the impact of realistic channel estimation error on these limits. Our results demonstrate that even with channel estimation error, spatial multiplexing with a large number of antennas still enjoys the benefits of a diversity multiplexing tradeoff, albeit with reduced rate.

We present the first high-resolution images of the HD 100546 system taken with the High Contrast Space Telescope (HST) in the thermally dispersed spectroscopy (TDS) mode. We combine these images with previous observations in the dust continuum and strong spectral lines to model the system as a circumstellar disk surrounding a bright Herbig Ae/Be star. The inner rim of this disk is sharp and traces the edge of the empty, sub-AU region cleared out by the planet with a half-opening angle of 3.4°. We estimate the grain size in the disk surface layers to be between 1 μm and 3 μm, the temperature there to be between 23 K and 25 K, and the stellar illumination to be between 6.7% and 8.4% of the interstellar value. This is the first time that the physical properties of a disk around an Herbig Ae/Be star have been determined with such high precision, and these observations further demonstrate the power of TDS to characterize extrasolar planet systems.

Sigma Orionis is a small rich cluster some 1,200 light-years from the Earth. It lies at the heart of the Orion Molecular Cloud, a massive star-forming complex located in the constellation Orion some 420 light-years distant. Located at a fairly young estimated age of some 7 million years, Sigma Orionis is still deeply embedded in its natal cloud, and consequently provides an excellent laboratory to study the substellar content of very young clusters. The first comprehensive census of brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars in the cluster was presented in Belikov et al. (2012). Here we present optical, near-infrared and IRAC/Spitzer photometry of over 130 additional cluster members, increasing the total membership count to well over 200. This allows us to more precisely characterize the the substellar initial mass function (IMF), shown here to closely follow a power-law with exponent -1.3 in the substellar mass range 0.1–0.015 M⊙. The mass function is substantially lower than that of older clusters like the Trapezium in the Orion Nebula (e.g. Kroupa et al. 2007) and comparable to that of much younger (tens of millions of years) clusters, like the Nice model for the formation of the Solar System (Boss & Bernstein 2012). It is also substantially flatter than recent field determinations from near-IR imaging (e.g. N TOP algorithms, McElwain et al. 2014) and significantly steeper than determinations from IRAC/Spitzer data, which may be affected by significant sample incompleteness at low masses. We have used this new cluster mass function to update the projected cluster core and core accretion rates, obtaining values of 3.4 × 10–5 M⊙yr–1 and 8.6 × 10–5 M⊙yr–1, respectively. These are substantially higher than previous estimates but consistent with theoretical core accretion models for very low-mass stars and brown dwarfs at the young age of Sigma Orionis.

Resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) spectroscopy has been used to characterize the elementary excitations of the 2D doped Hubbard model. We observe the presence of nonlocal spin and charge excitations, and analyze them within a phenomenological Hamiltonian. We focus on the nature of the spin excitation spectrum and show that a spin-density-wave model provides an accurate description of the data over a broad momentum range. Finally, we present evidence for a charge excitation spectrum at low energies, which we interpret within a framework of resonating valence bond states. 2D doped Hubbard model, spin excitation spectrum, resonating valence bond states --Virat Did this paper interest you? The paper investigates statistical properties of domain systems modeled as percolation clusters on the plane. The paper presents numerical evidence that statistical properties of domain systems deviate from those of random percolation in two important respects. First, the radius of gyration of a system of linear size L has a non-monotonic dependence on L: for L larger than a certain system-dependent L₀ it grows as L₀², faster than what one would expect from pure random percolation. Second, the number of sites at a given distance r from the origin that are occupied by domain systems of linear size L grows as L⁴²⁻³ r⁴⁰⁹, slower than what one would expect from pure random percolation. These two results, if established rigorously, would significantly modify the current understanding of physical phenomena at the microscopic level that are due to quenched disorder and can be modeled by percolation.

In this paper we investigate correlations between the energy density and the flux of two different observables in an unusual quantum state called macroscopic quantum state (MQS). These correlations were first discovered in the MQT of doubly clamped micro cantilevers and were interpreted as a signature of quantumness. We extend this analysis to other mechanical resonators made of different materials and of different geometries. We show that the flux-energy density correlations appear in the MQS and in the vacuum for the same set of parameters. We argue that these correlations can not be explained using the standard models of decoherence and back-action. We present experimental data and develop a phenomenological model that accurately describes the correlations in the MQS. The observed correlations between flux and energy density could have profound implications for quantum information processing and thermodynamics with mechanical systems. The ability of networks of neurons to respond robustly to perturbations or “lesions” is a critical measure of their functional integrity. The problem of how networks of spiking neurons store and process information is difficult to study analytically. Accordingly, we perform numerical simulation of large ensembles of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and introduce artificial lesions that correspond to disruptions in the connections between subsets of neurons. We find that a sparse and heterogeneous network architecture is both highly resistant to random lesions and highly sensitive to targeted lesions that eliminate topological motifs such as cliques and circles. We further characterize the statistical properties of the activity generated by the network in the face of both random and targeted lesions. Our findings provide a concrete illustration of a previously identified theoretical principle –that diverse networks are more robust to random perturbations than tightly coupled homogeneous networks–in a biologically relevant setting. In this short note, we present a simple generalization of Vassiliev's h-principle. This theorem allows one to construct a deformation between two configurations of a smooth manifold, provided that the first configuration has a tangent field with sufficient expansion and the second one has a deformation towards the first. We give an example of this theorem in dimension three, relating two different configurations of a bar-joint chain. Vassiliev's h-principle states that, if a closed curve in a Riemannian manifold has sufficiently large curvature, then it is deformable within the class of all smooth curves homologous to the original one. Here we present a generalization of this theorem, allowing us to construct a deformation between two configurations of a smooth manifold provided that the first configuration has a tangent field with sufficient expansion and the second one has a deformation towards the first. We demonstrate this theorem in dimension three, relating two different configurations of a bar-joint chain. Here is an outline of the contents of the paper: In section 2, we give the basic definitions and state our result. In the last section, we give an example of this theorem in dimension three, relating two different configurations of a bar-joint chain.

The behavior of interacting electrons in one dimension has attracted a lot of attention in recent years. In one dimension, electrons can form a periodic crystal, also known as a Wigner Crystal. Even at very low fillings, electrons interacting with a long-range Coulomb repulsion can still gain energy by forming a Wigner Crystal, since the interaction energy is independent of crystal density. However, at certain lower temperatures, the system may phase separate into a low-density liquid and a periodic crystal known as the Bond Charge Density Wave (BCDW). This phase separation is an example of a second-order quantum phase transition. Using determinant Quantum Monte Carlo, we show that at quarter-filling, this phase transition is driven primarily by changes in the temperature dependence of the density rather than by a true divergence of the specific heat. Additionally, we find that increasing the interaction substantially increases the stability of the BCDW phase. We believe our results will be useful for furthering the understanding of one-dimensional materials and possible applications of Determinant Quantum Monte Carlo in realistic materials modeling.

We investigate the collapse of very massive stars, starting with a Solar mass and rotating at the level of 600 times the speed of light, to black holes in full general relativity. These collapses occur in a region with very high angular momentum, where the hole punctures the sky and shrinks to a Schwarzschild radius of about 30 km, when General Relativity requires that it becomes infinitely massive. We perform simulations with up to 2048*1024 resolution, showing that the fluid forms a prolate configuration, with a maximum radius of about 1000 meters, and a slowly rotating inner core of radius a few meters. After an initial phase of about 0.5 ms, the collapse proceeds in a way remarkably similar to the head-on collision of two black holes of 30 and 10 solar masses, with an apparent horizon of about 20 kilometers in size and an estimated radiated energy of about 2.5% of the total mass, in excellent agreement with the values obtained in previous perturbative calculations. We study the properties of the formed black holes and show that several physical parameters, like the irreducible mass, the rotational parameter, the curvature invariant and the event horizon surface gravity are in very good agreement with the values obtained in perturbative calculations, even for the final, non-perturbative, rotating star.

In this paper, we consider the problem of optimally allocating the power between the vertical and the horizontal branches of the V-BLAST scheme, while taking into account both the rate and the distortion constraints at the receiver. We formulate this problem as an iterative scheme that alternates between the optimization of the powers on the two branches and the optimization of the output covariance of the two branches. We first consider the case of two antennas at the receiver and we show that the algorithm converges to a unique local optimum. We then extend the results to the general case of an arbitrary number of antennas at the receiver and we compare the performance of the proposed algorithm with that of a baseline scheme that always allocates the power to the vertical branch. We finally show through numerical examples that our algorithm provides significant performance improvements as compared to the baseline scheme. We present integral field spectroscopy of 24 brightest group and cluster galaxies drawn from the ʽCore of the Clusterʼ structure at the centre of the Fornax cluster. The spatial resolution of our data is sufficient to study the velocity and metallicity distributions over the entire extent of these systems. For two-thirds of the sample the stellar kinematics show clear signatures of regular rotational motion with rotational axes aligned with the inferred major axis of the galaxy. In these cases we measure distinct peak rotation velocities up to 290 ± 20 km s-1, corresponding to stellar masses of 10(11.4 ± 0.8) M⊙. The remaining third of the sample show more complex velocity distributions, including significant distortions from circular motions and/or two-peaked profiles that are often associated with galaxies that have interacted with other systems. In three cases we detect counterrotating stars, one of which may be associated with a small satellite galaxy that appears to be falling into the main system for the first time. We usestellar population synthesis to measure the effective radius, average surface brightness and stellar velocity dispersion of each galaxy. For galaxies with measurable rotation, we find that the average stellar velocity dispersion correlates with the peak rotation velocity, consistent with other data for field galaxies. Conversely, the average stellar velocity dispersion is largely independent of the galaxy�s total magnitude or its photometric membership in the Core of the Cluster. This implies that the processes that control the evolution of galaxies across the Fornax cluster are similarly effective at removing their cold gas and shut off their star formation, even in the most strongly segregated environments.

Spitzer Space Telescope observations of two early-type galaxies have revealed spatially extended, hot dust emitting at longer wavelengths than those detected in earlier, targeted observations of elliptical galaxies. The apparent locations, morphologies, and spectral energy distributions of these dust components are consistent with a simple model in which the dust was produced by a starburst event between 1 and 10 million years ago and was subsequently heated by a central engine, likely powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN). The presence of both cold and warm dust phases suggests that the dust has been subject to strong heating and cooling, perhaps caused by both shocks and AGN energy outflows. This new evidence of recent starburst-driven feedback in elliptical galaxies may have important implications for galaxy formation and the co-evolution of galaxies and their central black holes. Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) observations of these two elliptical galaxies revealed the locations of most of the dust that is now seen at longer (mid-infrared) wavelengths. These galaxies appear to have both cold (T≅20K) and warm (T≅500K) dust components, with an estimated total dust mass of a few hundredths of a solar mass. This warm dust is concentrated toward the centers of the galaxies, where it is associated with a dense network of thin starburst "PAH" features. The most energetically powerful AGN typically exhibit strong mid-infrared emission, but the origin of the cold dust component is not understood. The presence of cold and warm dust in these galaxies has led some to suggest that the star formation is episodic, with strong bursts of activity triggered by major merger events. If so, this may have important implications for the co-evolution of galaxies and their central black holes. Recent analyses of the centers of elliptical galaxies have revealed signatures of both cold and warm dust. Such dust, heated by an active nucleus, was first detected in the nuclei of the Sombrero Galaxy (M104) and of NGC 4486B (the "index" galaxy of the Virgo cluster). Subsequent IRAS and now Spitzer observations have detected dust in several other elliptical galaxies. Similar signatures have also been found in a number of lenticular and spiral galaxies, although with somewhat less certainty. In the case of M104, analysis of IRAS and Spitzer data revealed spatially resolved components consisting of both cold and warm dust, with possible evidence for strong heating and cooling, possibly from both shocks and AGN feedback. M104 is an iconic example of a "rejuvenated" elliptical galaxy (Tran et al. 2003), in which a major merger event between two spiral galaxies is believed to have triggered a massive starburst, heating and expelling dust from the galaxy center (Schweizer 1984; hereafter S84). The dust likely formed within 1-10 million years of the merger event, as evidenced by the similar ages of the newly formed massive stars and the re-radiated

Spitzer spectral line mapping of supernova remnants: I. Basic data and principal component analysis. We present new spectroscopic observations of the mid-infrared fine-structure lines of iron, silicon, and sulfur with the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) on the Spitzer Space Telescope of ten supernova remnants. These remnants span a broad range of explosion energies, shock temperatures, and ambient densities. Together with observations of nine other remnants from the literature, we investigate the variation of these lines with density, shock temperature, and explosion energy, and analyze the diagnostic potential of these lines in these contexts. We show that the equivalent widths of the 18.7 μm silicon line and the 18.9 μm iron line are good measures of the shock temperature. The 7.5 μm iron and 7.4 μm silicon lines are potentially good discriminants of warm/cool shock chemistry, although additional data are needed to better quantify the sensitivity of these lines to the differences in these shock temperatures. While sulfur lines are not yet available for large samples of remnants, the 18.7 μm and 28.2 μm lines appear promising diagnostics for future observations. We carry out principal component analysis (PCA) of these data, demonstrating that line ratios such as 7.5 μm / 18.7 μm and 28.2 μm / 18.7 μm can be powerful additional diagnostics. While the first PCA dimension (d1) primarily separates line emission from strongly and weakly processed material, the second dimension (d2) primarily differentiates sulfur lines from iron and silicon lines. Comparing the relative strengths of the iron and sulfur lines along with information on shock velocities provides a means of disentangling pre-Shock Infrared Emission (PIRE) from the Rayleigh-Taylor and, in some cases, Double-Detonation phases of Type Ia supernova explosions.

Valley-dependent optoelectronics based on inversion symmetry breaking has received great attentions recently due to its potential to achieve extremely low power operation, especially for electronics in the next-generation strained silicon CMOS platforms. However, direct realization of inversion-symmetry-broken (IBS) materials in electronic devices is still challenging because of the complex relationship among valley-dependent optical selection rules, momentum-conserving carrier scattering, and electronic transportation. To this end, we propose a general platform for valley-dependent optoelectronics based on the IBS effect in oxide-interfaced semiconductors, where band structure engineering and reduced dielectric screening combine to relax these complicated constraints. Using relevant first-principles calculations, we demonstrate the gate-tunable valley splitting of up to 30 meV in n-type strained silicon interface oxide, and strong optical absorption onset near the silicon band edge in the photon energy range of 1.1-1.3 eV. Our work provides a promising route to harness the IBS effect for valley-dependent optoelectronics in existing CMOS technology nodes, paving the way for low-power and/or low-footprint Internet of Things applications.

Spherically symmetric plasmas are an important and interesting general relativistic plasma system, which arise in, for example, collapsing stars, laboratory nuclear fusion experiments, and the early universe. The simplest spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell system contains two independent functions of radial coordinate only. However, these can be reduced further to a single quadrature, allowing exact solutions to be obtained in several special cases. In general, the presence of the Maxwell field contributes one additional conserved charge, the'masshair' of the solution. For some choices of the equations of state of the plasma, explicit solutions can be obtained in different regions of the spacetime. The resulting space-times describe either black holes with a gravitational mass, a scalar field hair, or naked singularities, depending on the choice of equations of state. In this paper, we present a systematic method to generate analytic solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell system with a spherically symmetric plasma. This is achieved by relating the system to a theory of Newtonian gravity coupled to a non-linear scalar field. We then use a series expansion about the centres of symmetry of the solution, and a number of analytic solutions to the non-linear theory in Newtonian gravity to construct the full solution. We apply our general procedure to several specific cases, obtaining new exact solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell system, and discussing their properties. In particular, we show how the addition of a Maxwell field changes the possible outcomes of gravitational collapse, from black hole formation with no scalar hair to the formation of naked singularities with scalar hair. Our approach has some similarity to the AdS-CFT correspondence, which relates the gravitational description of some strongly coupled plasmas to a lower-dimensional gauge theory. In this respect, the gravitational collapse of charged matter described above may be interpreted as a phase transition in strongly coupled gauge theory, with the black hole forming when the gauge theory approaches a large-$N$ limit in which gravity is strongly interacting, and the naked singularity forming when the gauge theory undergoes a large-$N$ transition to a low-energy weakly coupled plasma. This paper provides a rare example of exact solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell system. More generally, it shows how the addition of a Maxwell field changes the possible outcomes of gravitational collapse, from black hole formation with no scalar hair to the formation of naked singularities with scalar hair. The baryonic symmetries $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ are extended to a global chiral symmetry $G_L \times G_R$ with corresponding pseudo-Goldstone bosons, the NGBs, called baryon interpolating fields (BIFs). We compute chiral properties of BIFs using lattice QCD with almost physical quark masses and volumes. We show that, in the infinite volume and chiral limits, the vector (S) and axial-vector (A) BIFs have degenerate vector and axial-vector mass spectra. Thus the putative parity-flavor symmetry, with exact 3-fold symmetry between these spectra, is instead only approximately conserved. The breaking of this symmetry is attributed to the small remnant of explicit chiral symmetry breaking by the light quark masses. We also compute a crucial matrix element using twice-subtracted current conservation, which relates the matrix element of S BIFs to that of A BIFs, and compare to previous continuum and coarse-lattice results.

This article presents the mechanics on Lie groupoids, generalizes the well-known nonholonomic Lagrangian systems on Lie groups. The formalism is illustrated by several examples such as Chaplygin’s pebbles, the Fermi-Ulam model, the $\overline{\rm D}3$ polymorphic Membrane and the Bredon membrane. Several reasons for why one should care about such systems and examples of physical systems which can be modeled by such systems are also discussed. Finally, some open problems and directions for future research are presented. In particular, the configuration manifold $Q$ is a Lie groupoid, which gives rise to a Lie algebroid $A$, and a right-invariant nonholonomic (NH) Lagrangian on the Lie algebroid defines an Ehresmann ${\rm CIA}$–system on the Lie groupoid. One can also consider a NH Lagrangian on the the Whitney sum $A \oplus A^{nv}$, where $A^{nv}$ is the vector bundle of vertical elements, and the corresponding NH–system is called a NH–gerbe. One can combine the two approaches by considering a NH Lagrangian on the Courant algebroid $A \bowtie A^{nv}$ which gives rise to a twisted NH–system. In some examples, the NH Lagrangian is defined on the cotangent bundle $T^\ast Q$ of the Lie groupoid, and the corresponding system is called aacs–NH system. In all examples, the dynamics of the system is described by a NH Hamilton’s equation on the Lie groupoid. An example of physical systems that can be modeled by such NH–systems are Chaplygin’s particles. In such systems, the configuration manifold $Q$ is a subgroup of a Euclidean space ${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ with the standard atlas, and the corresponding NH Lagrangian defines the Chaplygin’s equations for the heavy top. One can also consider a Chaplygin’s particle on a curved manifold $M$. A physical interpretation of such systems can be given using the notion of principal connections. We show that Chaplygin’s particles on a curved manifold can be described by a NH Lagrangian on the Heisenberg group. Another example is the Fermi–Ulam model which can be also modeled by a NH Lagrangian on the Heisenberg group. The geometric structure defined by the NH Lagrangian on the Lie groupoid $Q$ can be used for description of symmetries of the NH system. The corresponding Lie groupoid action integrates the lifted system on the first algebroid jet level. The canonical symplectic realization of the obtained lifted system gives the corresponding moment map for the NH–system. We present observations of the nearby blazar PKS 2155-304 performed between May 2005 and July 2005 in the near-infrared (NIR) and optical bands. NIR data were obtained with the 10.4m GEMINI South Telescope, while optical data were obtained with the Nordic Optical Telescope and the William Herschel Telescope. We also present contemporaneous data in other bands (X-rays, MeV, GeV) from the Whipple, HEGRA, and CATobservatories. Based on our observations, we suggest that in the optical band PKS 2155-304 was in a high state in early 2005, possibly reaching a flux density of 400 mJy at m_R in April 2005. The NIR flux density was relatively stable during this period, with no strong variations. Around May 20-25 2005 we detected a sharp rise in both the optical and NIR flux, reaching a peak in June 2005. The optical spectral index rapidly hardened in this period, possibly reaching a value of α=3.2. We hypothesize that this sudden brightening in PKS 2155-304 was caused by a rapid enhancement in the external radiation field density (as a result of the eruptinging Galaxy M33) shining through the relativistic jet of PKS 2155-304. We also observe a fast decrease in the X-ray, MeV, and GeV flux densities in the period May-July 2005. We suggest that this decrease was caused by the jet entering a new region with a weaker magnetic field, perhaps due to the increased transparency of the jet caused by the enhanced external radiation field density.

In these lectures, based on recent works [1-5], we will discuss some properties and possibilities of brane induced gravity (BIG). Bimetric theories of gravity, where two different gravitational theories are coupled through shared matter, can be reformulated as a single gravitational theory with auxiliary fields. In particular, in five dimensions, this theory is equivalent to Einstein-Maxwell-Chern-Simons (EMC2) gravity. We will concentrate on the cosmological aspects of this theory, in particular, the possibility that Dark Energy could be attributed to the dynamical Chern-Simons term. In this paper, we study the Schrödinger equation with the modified Coulomb potential in a strong magnetic field using the the plane wave expansion method. This potential can be used to describe a few systems such as electrons in a strong magnetic field and quantum dots. In this paper, we consider the modified Coulomb potential in the strong field limit, which is relevant for magnetic atoms and molecules. We solve the Schrödinger equation exactly for zero angular momentum and obtain an explicit expression for the ground state energy. We then evaluate the ground state energy for non-zero angular momenta and compare it with the numerical solution. The behavior of the ground state energy for large quantum numbers is also discussed. Our analytical results are confirmed by numerical ones. Ibrahim Assafiri, Mahmoud Saied, Ali Parhizkar, Mohammad Reza Rajabzorg, Mohammad Ali Sajadi University of Tabriz, Tabriz, Iran

Supergiant fast X-ray transients (SFXTs) are a rare subclass of High Mass X-ray Binaries (HMXBs), comprising a neutron star primary orbiting around a massive companion which fills its Roche lobe. The mass-accretion rate is high, often exceeding 10−4 M⊙ /yr, which results in the rapid expulsion of most of the system's hydrogen and creation of a thick accretion disk around the compact object. The source name XTE J1739-278 was used to denote the first SFXT discovered in the INTErnational Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INGA) data. A total of 6 SFXTs are now known. Until recently, all SFXTs were discovered in the High Mass X-ray Binary (HMXB) mode, which is characterized by transient Roche lobe overflow, typically going off for a few weeks or months and then returning to quiescence for many years. During the outburst, the X-ray flux is typically a few milli-Crab, reaching tens of Crab in very rare cases. Only during 2004-2007 SFXTs were occasionally detected in the Supergiant Fast X-ray Transient (SFXT) mode, flaring in X-rays on timescales as short as a few seconds, a few times brighter than the entire Galaxy. However, since 2008, SFXTs have been almost exclusively detected in SFXT mode, never going back to HMXB mode. This has led to suggestions that SFXTs are a single class of compact object binary system, possibly involving a massive stellar evolvement of a giant companion. Other authors disagree, proposing a new subclass of SFXTs, in which the neutron star is engulfed along with the companion star in a common envelope phase. The recent discovery of SFXT IGR J21327+1983 in a new SFXT mode,HMXB, provides new fuel for the ongoing debate. If confirmed, this source will link SFXTs to HMXBs and solve the discrepancy.

In this paper, we consider the initial value problem for the parabolic scalar curvature equation \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} u_{tt}-\Delta \rho=Rc_{i}c_{j}u_{ij}, & \text{on} \quad \mathbb{R}\times \Omega, \\ \rho_t=\Delta u, & \text{on} \quad \mathbb{R}\times \Omega, \\ u(0)=u_0, & \text{in} \quad \Omega, \\ \rho(0)=\rho_0, & \text{in} \quad \Omega, \end{cases} \end{equation*} where $\Omega$ is a smooth bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^N$ ($N\geq 3$), $Rc_{i}c_{j}$ is the Riemann curvature tensor, and $u_0, \rho_0$ are given initial data. We show that, if the initial data $(u_0, \rho_0)\in C_0^\infty(\Omega)\times C_0^\infty(\Omega)$, then the solution either goes to $+\infty$ as $t\rightarrow +\infty$ in the sense of the following asymptotic profile at $+\infty$ \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} u(x, t)\rightarrow +\infty, & \text{if}\ N\leq 10, \\ \rho(x, t)=O(e^{-\alpha|x|}), & \text{if}\ N=11, \\ u(x, t)\rightarrow u_\infty(x), & \text{if}\ N>11, \end{cases} \end{equation*} where $|x|:=\max\{ |x_1|, |x_2|,\ldots, |x_N|\}$ and $(N-1)|x|=x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots +x_N^2$ for $x=(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N)\in \mathbb{R}^N$. Moreover, the asymptotic profile $u_\infty(x)$ is explicit and the eigenvalues of the differential operator $x_N^2-2\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}x_j$ appear in it.

Organic conductors are a recently discovered new class of materials that exhibit high-temperature superconductivity and other important physical phenomena1,2. These materials are composed of quasi-two-dimensional molecules with strong spin-orbit coupling, resulting in a small spin wavelength and remarkable magnetic properties3,4. Recent neutron scattering experiments5,6 on the quasi-two-dimensional organic superconductor α-T-NbSe2 has revealed a low-energy magnetic spectrum that is best characterized as fluctuating antiferromagnetism. This finding was surprising given the observed low temperatures and high transition temperatures for superconductivity and antiferromagnetism, respectively. Here, we perform a phenomenological analysis of the magnetic excitations in α-T-NbSe2 based on an anisotropic square-lattice quantum Heisenberg model with intrinsic dimerization and feedback from the magnetic order parameter. We find that the magnetic excitation spectrum can be reconciled with experiment without the need for immiscible dimer and antiferromagnetic orders. The measured magnetic spectral function is a consequence of superposition of lightly damped dynamic fluctuations of incipient magnetic order with a relatively large, roughly temperature-independent coupling to the vector antiferromagnetic order parameter. These results elucidate the intriguing relationship between the coexisting antiferromagnetism and superconductivity in these materials, and suggest that fluctuation exchange may play a significant role in their properties7,8.

In pixelized detectors, where the response of the detector is described by the pixel occupation number, a direct measurement of the spatial resolution is generally complicated. Here, we present a simple and fast method to determine the spatial resolution based on the correlation measurements of two point-like illumination patterns. The detection probabilities of the two patterns are measured simultaneously, and the spatial resolution is derived from the correlation function. The proposed method is applied to characterize two pixelized detectors with very different spatial resolution. The experimental results are in good agreement with the theoretically expected values. Moreover, this method can be easily implemented in various experimental setups, which make it a powerful tool to determine the spatial resolution of pixelized detectors. This paper analyzes the Hamiltonian formulations of special and general relativity and their corresponding phase spaces. The main result is the introduction of foliations of four dimensional phase space by six dimensional phase spaces, or phase spaces of H- formations, on which the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints of general relativity are elliptic, respectively, parabolic. This implies that, in these phase spaces, singularities present in the original four dimensional phase space are resolved. Due to this, the local degrees of freedom in these phase spaces are enhanced in relation to the original four dimensional one. The H-formations introduce a set of strongly symplectic (four-dimensional) transformations that are symplectic on their corresponding six-dimensional H-formations. The resulting phase space portrait of general relativity is therefore a two-symplectic (two-symmetries) theory. It exhibits a clear separation of dynamical variables, both spatial and temporal, in a temporal sector and three spatial sectors. The three spatial sectors are of orthogonal nature and are each characterized by a particular spatial orthogonal metric, which establishes an invariant direction in each of these sectors. The temporal sector is also orthogonal and this orthogonality reflects the time-reparametrization invariance of the theory. The physical phase space is then defined as the projection of the original H-formation on the spatial sector characterized by the invariant spatial metric. The resulting physical phase space has an enhanced local degree of freedom count as compared to general relativity, describing gravity as a Metric Gravity theory. The dynamics of the physical phase space is generated by the Hamiltonian, which is obtained from the original Hamiltonian of general relativity after a strong modification is made. The strong modification amounts to the replacement of the Ricci scalar of general relativity with a linear combination of the spatial metrics of the three orthogonal spatial sectors. The resulting physical phase space and corresponding Hamiltonian are symmetric hyperbolic. It is therefore possible to quantize the theory, and in particular, to explore its quantum cosmological applications. The theory possesses a classical singularity resolution mechanism, which relies on the backreaction of quantum geometries. It is shown that the physical phase space, for physically reasonable values of the Hamiltonian constraint, is non-singular. The resolution of singularities is an alternative to the conventional initial singularity in the theory's early Universe singularity resolution proposal.

In this paper, we present a detailed theoretical and experimental analysis of intrinsic charge qubit decoherence in the GaAs/AlGaAs single quantum dot architecture. Using a combination of experiments and theory, we quantify dephasing from both electrical and nuclear noise in our system. We demonstrate how to exploit charge tunability and local charge suppression to achieve significant dephasing times T2protect much above 1 $\mu$s, sufficient to nearly double the measured two-qubit coherence time T2 entang in a previous experimental study. These improvements in coherence are likely significant enough to allow for quantum error correction with charge qubits. Overall, this study provides significant guidance on both the experimental and theoretical front for developing future charge qubits with longer coherence times. We provide detailed theory for nuclear noise as a source of dephasing, and demonstrate an experimental technique for suppressing this noise via local charge suppression. Additionally, we present both experimental and modeling results for electrical noise, where we show that electrical tuning can be employed to further suppress this source of dephasing. We conclude by performing a fidelity analysis of our system with noise sources and averaging procedures, and show how these present a moderate error threshold for linear error correction of our two-qubit computational basis.
