Galaxy evolution in the infra-red: comparison of a hierarchical galaxy formation model with SPITZER data. In a hierarchical model of structure formation, galaxies form by the coagulation of lower mass systems. The process is modelled using the semi-analytic code [galform]{} which follows the formation and merger histories of dark matter haloes and subhaloes. The model generates realistic present-day galaxy populations in both field and group environments and successfully reproduces the basic demographics of galaxies in several classes, including spheroids, disks and active galactic nuclei (AGN). In this work, we test the model against Herschel/SPIRE observations of the infra-red galaxy population, using far-infrared and submillimetre wavelengths as a measure of the star-formation rate (SFR). We find that the model is able to reproduce the SPIRE counts and the distribution of fluxes with surface density at bright flux levels, but overpredicts the number of bright sources at low surface density. At intermediate flux densities, the model does a good job of reproducing the shape of the distribution but underpredicts the number of sources by a factor of 2-3. We explore several potential causes of this discrepancy, but find that most of them are insufficient to explain the factor of 2-3 difference in flux density. A plausible cause we suggest is the inclusion in the code of spheroids but not of starbursts in the cool core/mantle of cluster galaxies; this neglect was motivated by a lack of observational evidence at the time. Including starbursts in the model but not in the luminosity function leads to a very good match to the observations. The code [galform]{} is available in its current form from http://galform.mpastorff.de.

Comet Hale-Bopp was a remarkable visitor to Earth in 1996. It was visible in the morning twilight for several weeks, captured the interest of the public and press, and was the subject of a large number of studies in all wavelength regions. In this paper we present the results of our study of Hale-Bopp in the mid-infrared. We observed Hale-Bopp with the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) and the Copernicus Space Observatory in April, May, and June 1996. In these data we see evidence of polarized light from Hale-Bopp for the first time. Our observations suggest that Hale-Bopp was composed of numerous thin, strongly elongated grains of ice which were aligned nearly perpendicular to the orbital plane of Hale-Bopp and its parent nucleus. These results may be explained if the asymmetric ejection of material from Hale-Bopp's nucleus was the source of Hale-Bopp's rotation and orbital angular momentum. We also examine Hale-Bopp's dust coma and calculate its minimum orbit intersection distance (MOID). We find that the MOID of Hale-Bopp at the time of our observations was approximately 3.2 Earth radii, a value similar to the observed coma size. We consider implications of our results for models of the formation of Hale-Bopp and its parent nucleus and for future cometary missions.

A microscopic analysis of the water dynamic condensation at the surface of a fused silica glass induced by a standard optical crack tip test suggests a possible microscopic mechanism that could explain the dynamic water condensation at the crack tip which has been recently observed and reported. The surface topography and the dynamic water condensation at the crack tip, depending on the mode of the mechanical stress applied, could change in real time. Therefore, the optical crack tip test could be used to capture these time dependent phenomena that could provide useful information to improve the understanding of the dynamic water condensation process. This work is of particular relevance for the optical fiber communication industry, where the light is strongly focused at the tip of the optical fiber which could increase the local temperature and thus the dynamic water condensation at the fiber tip. Furthermore, the dynamic water condensation could also have a great impact on the sensing industry. The light scattering generated by the dynamic water droplets could be used to detect the mechanical stress in the surrounding medium.

Epsilon Aurigae (ι Aur) is an α2 CVn binary system with an F3 IV primary component and an K0 IV secondary component. Epsilon Aurigae is the second brightest star in the northern hemisphere sky, and it is almost always visible to the naked eye. The primary component is surrounded by a thick, hydrogen-filled envelope that causes it to be much cooler and less luminous than the Sun. As a result, Epsilon Aurigae has an unusual evolution on the H-R diagram - it is almost stationary along the main sequence but becomes a giant many centuries into the future. Historical estimates of the star's distance have varied considerably, from under 4 pc to over 14 pc, and recent high-precision parallax measurements from the Hipparcos satellite gave a distance of 11.65 pc. IUE spectra of the Epsilon Aurigae system showed Balmer emission from the primary star, although its spectrum was dominated by that of the secondary. The IUE data showed the presence of a thin cirrus-like hydrogen envelope around the primary star, at least 20 times less dense than the extended thick wind of the same star. The relative strength of the emission lines in the primary's spectrum varied periodically, with a period of 14.4 days - the rotation period of the primary star. Analysis of ultraviolet observations obtained with the Solar Mass Spectrometer on the Ulysses spacecraft suggested that Epsilon Aurigae was losing mass at a rate of about 10-9 to 10-8 kg s-1. In this work, recent UBVJH photometry of Epsilon Aurigae is presented. The variation in temperature of the primary star as a function of wavelength is discussed, as are the H Lambda emission line profiles. The overall brightness of the system is estimated using simple models for the primary and secondary stars. Finally, implications for the current mass-loss rate of the primary star and the evolutionary state of the system are discussed.

Galactic plane SNRs (supernova remnants) are powerful consumers of interstellar gas and dust, as evidenced by their interaction with the ISM in the form of shell-like remnants, and by the detection of bright, warm emission from some SNR shells (known as SNRs). More than 200 such remnants have been detected. Theories of SNR evolution predict that some remnants, such as plerions, will produce relativistic jets. The detection of such jets from a number of SNRs (see below) provides support for this theory. On the other hand, the non-detection of such jets from a number of young SNRs (e.g., 0509-67.5, 1572, Cas A) suggests that some, or even most, SNRs do not produce relativistic jets. Other proposed explanations for the non-detection of relativistic jets from some young SNRs are (1) an intrinsic lack of power in the supernova explosion, (2) acceleration of particles to non-relativistic speeds in the SNR shell, (3) that most remnants have their jets obscured by surrounding dense material, or (4) that the jets disappear from sight after a few hundred years. The gamma-ray satellite GLAST, with an estimated on-orbit sensitivity 5 times better than that of EGRET, should be able to detect gamma-rays from many SNRs. Detections of such gamma-rays would be strong evidence for the theory of remnant evolution and for the production of relativistic jets from some SNRs. On the other hand, non-detections would provide interesting new information about the nature of these remnants. The theoretical rate of bright gamma-ray SNRs should be approximately the same as the observable rate of young Galactic SNRs. Therefore, detections of gamma-rays from many young SNRs within the first few years of GLAST's operations will give us a clear indication of the efficacy of this technique for studying SNRs.

The uncertainty in the chemical composition of the Sun has significant implications on the dynamics of the climate system, which can be studied using low degree oscillations (LDo). In this work, a sensitivity analysis is performed to investigate the impact of the change in the solar abundances on the low degree modes, using an inverse approach. It is observed that the low-degree modes are most impacted by the changes in the abundances of CNO elements in the solar plasma. Changes in the abundances of elements other than CNO does not have significant impact on the low-degree modes. The sensitivity of low-degree modes to the change in solar abundances can have severe implications on the prediction of solar activity, and hence on the climate predictions. bibliography: https://arxiv.org/src/2004.08422/anc/abundance_sensitivity.bib Authors: D. In this paper, we study the representability of convex sets by positive semidefinite matrices. We show that every closed, convex set can be represented as the intersection of a hierarchy of cones, where each consecutive pair of cones has dual distance 2. The representation is positive semidefinite if and only if the set is full-dimensional. We show that the set of covariance matrices of finite-energy signals can be represented as a nonnegative semidefinite program, and that this representation is optimal. These results generalize previous positive results on symmetric representability. We also show that for every symmetric cone, there exists a representation with symmetric cones, in which every cone is pointed and has minimal generating set consisting of maximally oxidative vectors. The proof relies on a result of Veinoglou and Ho demann on sums of squares decompositions with specified support. Resonant X-ray scattering (RXS) studies of a wide range of materials have revealed that the structure of insulators can have a direct impact on their electronic properties. In particular, recent RXS measurements on a series of La_xCa_1-xMnO3 (LCMO) ordered perovskites have revealed a close connection between the static distortion of the oxygen octahedra and the underlying electronic properties, in that the electronic and magnetic phase diagrams of these materials may be mapped directly onto the structural phase diagram. RXS measurements on a second series of LCMO compositions (x = 0.33, 0.50, 0.67) have shown a divergence of the ground state structure from the phase diagram determined from other studies on the (x = 0.50, 0.67) compositions. We use LDA and perturbative RXS calculations to show that this divergence is associated with a change in the fundamental building block from the typical square-planar MnO_4 arrangement seen in the x = 0.50 and 0.67 compositions to a more distorted (MnO_3)J-lattice arrangement present in the x = 0.33 composition. We use density functional theory in combination with the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method to determine the ground state crystal structure and the associated structural distortions for all compositions. Using the information on the J-lattice, as determined from our analysis, we identify the key parameters of a minimal model describing the electronic and magnetic properties of La_xCa_1-xMnO_3.

We present a near-infrared survey of star-formation in M33 using the Infrared Array Camera on board the Spitzer Space Telescope. This survey, covering an area of 22.5 sq. degrees, identified 56 individual HII regions and 10 compact clusters of young stars. The physical properties of the HII regions (size, electron density, mass, and luminosity), were derived by modelling their integrated nebular spectra using the code CLOUDY. From the spatial distribution of the young stellar population, we find evidence for hierarchical star-formation in M33, with individual regions forming within clusters, and clusters forming within larger complexes. The complexes themselves may represent the earliest stages in the evolution of more extended, grand-design spiral galaxies. The authors would like to thank the referee for their helpful comments. This research has made use of the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, which is operated by the JPL, under contract with NASA.

Spiral arms are long filamentary structures in galaxy discs, supporting bright spiral arms, and forming stars over time. Sellwood & Carlberg (1994) found that over time, spiral patterns in stellar discs in galaxies such as M51 become mildly oval. This is because new stars are formed along spiral patterns, trailing the pattern rotation, while the old stars in the spiral arms rotate with the pattern. This trailing rotation creates a net circular streaming in the plane of the disc. This circular streaming may be observed in the form of a net Doppler shift of the line-of-sight (LOS) velocities of stars in the disc. Here we present the results of an analysis of the detailed LOS velocity field of M51 using integral field spectroscopy, obtained with the WIYN 3.5-m telescope and OHB, that resolves the circular streaming kinematics in the plane of the disc. We find that the circular streaming has a pitch angle of 20-30 degrees, and at large radii in M51 the streaming orbits may be approximated as logarithmic spirals.

Galactic super star clusters (SSCs) are small ( approximately 2pc in size), dense (approximately 10,000 members/Spc3), very young (a few million years old) systems which are observed in the centers of many galaxies. Super star clusters form through either the direct collapse of giant molecular clouds or through coalescence of smaller clusters. Despite their abundance, properties of SSCs have not been studied in great detail due to their spatial resolution limitations in external galaxies. This has recently changed with the launch of the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) which has allowed the discovery of much fainter SSCs in the centers of nearby galaxies. We present the results of hydrodynamic calculations on super star clusters with a strong second collapse in both gas and stars. The second collapse forms a second population of stars that can significantly impact the global properties of the SSC. We present an approximate analytic technique for determining the impact of the second collapse on SSC properties, and apply it to super star clusters with a bimodal (collapse) initial density distribution. We show that the ratio of first to second collapse regions in SSCs is strongly correlated with global SSC properties. In particular, SSCs with a strongly peaked initial conditions, such as those formed in cuspy dark matter profiles, have a significantly higher ratio of first to second collapse than those formed in flat or cored profiles. This leads to SSCs with cuspy profiles having a higher median age and lower median stellar mass than those formed in cuspy profiles. This provides a solution to the "core catastrophe" problem, which describes the apparent discrepancy between observations and numerical simulations of cuspy dark matter profiles that suggest SSCs should not be able to form. We present typical SSC properties as a function of both halo profile and initial conditions, and discuss the implications for hierarchical structure formation theories.

Gamma-ray production around supermassive black holes was first proposed more than three decades ago [1]. To date, searches for gamma-ray emission from supermassive black holes have been unsuccessful, with the most probable way to reject the gamma-ray emission from these systems being due to the presence of a strong stellar gravitational field. Recently, however, it has been suggested that supermassive black holes may accelerate particles to very high energy levels, where interaction with background radiation can result in the production of gamma rays [2]. In this work, we report the detection of gamma rays with energies of approximately 620 GeV - 1 TeV from the vicinity of the supermassive black hole in the giant radiogalaxy M87. These gamma rays are best described by a power-law spectral shape with an exponential cut-off at a energy of approximately 740 GeV. We propose that these gamma rays were produced by the interaction of the ambient radiation field with very high energy protons in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole in M87.

In this note we present a method to determine the anomalies in large-angle anisotropy (T, E, B) maps, derived from the WMAP data. We found that the T anomalies (in Galactic plane) show significant patterns, which are correlated with the large-scale structures. The correlations are expected, since the magnetic field is likely to be correlated with the large-scale structures. However, it is remarkable that the E-type anomalies (in the Galactic equator), and the B-type anomalies (in the Galactic poles) also show such correlations. The pattern in E-type anomalies are very similar with the T anomalies, while the pattern in B-type anomalies are opposite to T and E anomalies. Such patterns, which can not be explained by the Galactic magnetic field, can not be explained by the primordial magnetic field, and are very interesting for the further study.

In this Letter, we propose and demonstrate a method to entangle independent photons by time measurement. This method takes advantage of the spectral and spatial individually addressable nature of photon pairs and the spectral crosscorrelation between the down-conversion and the reference photons. The spectral crosscorrelation operates like a speedometer, measuring the frequency difference between the paired photons and revealing the entanglement between them. The pair entanglement is proven by violation of a modified Franson inequality. The technique is implemented by simultaneously addressing the spectral and spatial modes of the paired photons, and a two-photon six-dimensional entangled state is generated and revealed by this method. The method is robust to a certain extent against the diurnal cycle, allowing for significant increase in the chance of generating the entangled state. It is fully compatible with present photon pair source and has a high potential in scaling up. Our work paves the way towards on-demand high-dimensional entangled states and mature foundation for secure quantum communication.

In the standard model of cosmology, the Universe is spatially flat and its expansion is driven by a cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, which leads to a solution to the horizon, flatness, and cosmological constant problems. An alternative model with a nonzero vacuum energy density is described by the $\Lambda$ term in the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric, which leads to a solution of the horizon, flatness, and cosmological constant problems. In this paper, we test this model using data from the 5th data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-III DR5), covering 10,240 square degrees in the southern galactic cap. We use the distance modulus, $m-M=29.39\pm0.16$, from the surface brightness fluctuation method to measure the absolute magnitude, $M_{B_j}$, of the characteristic surface brightness, $\mu_B^*$, of each galaxy in the sample, and then infer its angular diameter distance using $\mu_B^* = 5\log(d_A) +25$, where $d_A$ is the angular diameter distance. Assuming a cosmological model with a nonzero cosmological constant, we calculate the likelihood as a function of the vacuum energy density, $\Omega_{\Lambda}$, and compare this likelihood to that of a spatially flat FLRW universe. We find that the data are consistent with both models, but that $\Lambda$ leads to a better fit with $\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.788\pm0.031$ (68% confidence level), in excellent agreement with the current best estimate from the WMAP satellite of $\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.761\pm0.023$ (68% confidence level). We perform a likelihood ratio test to quantify the statistical significance of the results, finding that the data are inconsistent with the null hypothesis that $\Lambda =0$ at a $>99.9999$% confidence level.

Galaxies are surrounded by large scale structures: the halos in which they form, and the filaments and sheets in which they are embedded. Mergers between galaxies are important for galaxy evolution, because they can bring in new material, angular momentum, and, perhaps, new satellite galaxies. Observational searches for satellites have traditionally been difficult, because they are easily disrupted or removed by the galactic environment. N-body simulations have proved to be a powerful tool for predicting the frequency and properties of satellite galaxies, but predictions still require observationally-informed scaling with the underlying dark matter halos. Recently, satellite galaxies have been identified in cosmological dark matter simulations, without including the baryonic physics that would likely disrupt them. In this work we use a set of zoomed-in, high-resolution cosmological simulations to examine the relation between mergers and the formation of satellite galaxies. We find a strong dependence of the survival of satellite galaxies on the relative masses of the satellite and its host, and on their orbital parameters. Satellite galaxies that are on highly eccentric orbits are much more likely to survive for several crossing times than those on more circular orbits. Satellites on prograde orbits around their host are more likely to survive than those on retrograde orbits, and satellites on highly radial orbits are more likely to survive than those on low-radius orbits. Satellite galaxies that form near the center of their host are more likely to survive than those that form far from the center. We also find that the internal structures of galaxies, as measured by their phase-space structure, are a better predictor of the fate of satellites than their dark matter halos. In particular, satellites that are either on radial orbits or on highly eccentric orbits will have large amounts of stars stripped from their outer parts. The time until all of the satellite’s stars are removed depends on its orbit, with radial orbits being more unstable than more circular orbits. Overall, we find that merging plays a large role in shaping the satellite galaxies we see in the universe today.

Exoplanets have been discovered around a multitude of host stars. Planet detection is affected by the location of the host star within the galaxy, the stability of the planet, the longevity of the observations, and the characterization techniques available. HD 100777, HD 190647, and HD 221287 are three late-type stars that harbor Exoplanets which are being monitored by the HARPS search for southern extra-solar planets. The detection of these Exoplanets is noteworthy as the parent stars are close to the start of the main sequence and therefore are relatively rapid rotators. The planet around HD 100777 is the closest orbiting planet around a rapid rotator, with an orbital period of 2.39 days. The detection of such an orbit around a rapid rotator is remarkable as rapid rotation can induce spin-orbit coupling that modifies the planet's orbit. Planets around rapid rotators may have undergone so-called de-coupling and may behave differently to planets around non-rotating or very slowly rotating parent stars. HD 100777 b is an extraordinary planet as it is a "hot Jupiter" with a mass of 0.68 M⊕ and a radius of 1.35 R⊕, suggesting a very thin hydrogen layer. The detection of such a low mass hydrogen layer is surprising as HD 100777 is a rapid rotator. The implications of these results are discussed.

Recent observations suggest that the solar orbit around the center of the Galaxy may be spatially displaced with respect to the galactic disk. I present Bayesian estimates of the kinematic parameters of the solar motion based on a sample of highly probable stream stars with proper motions measured by the PPMX and SPM4 projects, as well as on a larger sample of probable stream stars from the GSC 2.2 and PPMX-PT projects. I find that the Sun’s moving with a 220 km/s velocity towards (galactic longitude, galactic latitude) = (305.9°, −2.4°) ± (3.6°, 2.4°) at a rate of −2.2 ± 0.2 km/s/kpc. Assuming a distance of the Sun from the galactic center of 8.5 kpc, this displacement implies a spatial half-thickness of the solar disk of 14 pc. The estimated Sun’s velocity is in agreement with previous results, while the spatial offset is less than previously believed.

Non-abelian Yang-Mills theories have two different formulations called the first and second quantizations. Both formulations have their advantages and shortcomings. One of the advantages of the first quantization is that it is easy to write down classical equations of motion. Unfortunately, this formulation is not very good for numerical simulations. One of the advantages of the second quantization is that it produces the correct quantum behavior in the limit of small lattice spacing. Unfortunately, this formulation is very complicated and it is difficult to get meaningful results from Monte-Carlo simulations. In this paper, we introduce a new formulation of non-abelian gauge theories in the first quantization. This new formulation has the correct classical limit, and it is very simple to perform Monte-Carlo simulations on the lattice. We also introduce a novel lattice discretization of the second quantization formulation that reduces the cost of Monte-Carlo simulations to near the continuum limit. In this new formulation, we call the resulting theory dual (or adjoint) representation. The coupling that controls the strength of non-abelian interaction is exactly the same as in the second quantization, but the path integral localizes to the dual representation, which is formally equivalent to the first quantization. This duality allows us to simulate the second quantization with only first quantization simulations, which should be much more efficient.

In this paper, we consider the problem of determining the minimal probability of ruin for a jump-diffusion risk model. We provide a characterization of the minimal probability of ruin via a convex game that consists of a stopping game and a control game. At each horizon, the player has to choose between playing the risk process until the time of ruin and terminating the play with some safe liquidation wealth level. The control game is then played with the strategy chosen by the first player determining the time and the level of the jump process. By applying an extended version of Sion's theorem to this game, we are able to characterize the value function of the stopping game as the unique classical solution to a degenerate elliptic partial differential equation. Finally, we prove that this value function is both the minimal probability of ruin and the unique maximum probability of survival. This work is of interest to risk managers, researchers, and students who are interested in problems related to determining the minimal probability of ruin for a jump-diffusion risk model.

Noise-induced resonance and frequency locking in a spatially extended phytoplankton-zooplankton system with linear coupling and nonlinear inhibitor terms. We consider a system of PDEs describing the spatio-temporal dynamics of density of phytoplankton (x), zooplankton (y), and the proportion of resources available to phytoplankton carried by zooplankton (s), (1) (2) where u, v, w, and q represent the corresponding spatial and temporal derivatives, x0, y0, and s0 are the mean concentrations, and F is an advection term and nonlinear terms describing the grazing of phytoplankton by zooplankton and competition for shared resources. In this system, resonance and frequency locking can arise due to spatial variation in parameters and noise-induced entrainment of the fast and slow dynamical modes. We study these phenomena via a linear stability analysis of the system's uniform solutions and via numerical simulations of the stochastic system. We use the latter to demonstrate that, for a certain range of parameter values, frequency locking occurs even for moderate values of additive noise.

PopIII stars are the first generation of stars in the Universe. We carry out a computational zoom simulation of the reionization epoch and identify the first PopIII star halos and their hosts. We find that the most massive PopIII stars form in the most massive dark matter halos with a bias factor of 5-6. The bright quasars at redshifts z = 6-7 reside in the most massive halos with M p ≈ 10(12) solar masses, which contain the most-massive PopIII stars. By using advanced simulation techniques that model the first stars directly, we found no significant variability in the PopIII star formation rates and showed that PopIII star forming regions had Jeans masses of a few 10{7} M⊙, which were understable by standard PopIIIMassive, metal-enriched gas condensation models. These first PopIII stars likely had initial masses between 100 and 400 M⊙ and formed early in the Universe at redshifts z ≳ 20. Our results emphasize the high mass end of the PopIII star initial mass function, with the most-massive PopIII stars residing in the most-massive dark matter halos.

In this work, we present a novel algorithm to solve the equations of general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics and magnetodynamics, called ECHO. This is an Eulerian conservative high-order scheme, which uses operators to approximately solve the divergenceless constraints, and keeps exact conservation of momentum, angular momentum, and energy. This method satisfies the super divergence-free constraint, and does not require a Powell correction to capture shocks. The adjustable maximal Lagrangian-Eulerian position error controls the Lagrangian Canalization phenomenon. In this work, we implement this scheme in a newton-krylov-division iterative framework to solve the constrained equations efficiently. The results of various tests show that the ECHO method is accurate, efficient, and has strong robustness. In particular, it can capture the dynamics of MRI in complex systems, and has better convergence and stability than traditional high-order schemes.

In this paper, we study online scheduling with deadline constraints. The input jobs may have arbitrary duration, but we are only allowed to schedule one job at a time, and once a job starts, it must finish by its deadline. We model this as a non-preemptive retrial algorithm, where the job that is running at time t is simply continued by a new job that starts at time t+w, where w is the maximum job duration and is some large value. We call this the restart scheme. We analyze the expected total time w until all jobs have finished, when each job i has its deadline Di. We find that this expected total time is surprisingly large when D1+D2+...+Dn < Di, even though each individual instance is trivial. In particular, it can be linear in w and n, even when all jobs have the same duration w and all jobs have deadlines that are pairwise different.

In recent years, there has been an increasing interest in studying the effects of non-trivial boundaries on quantum field theory (QFT), leading to the concept of “edge physics”. In particular, for systems with appropriate properties, the presence of boundaries or defects can give rise to localized states with interesting physical properties, such as edge modes, which are protected by symmetry and can exist even in the presence of bulk interactions. One particular aspect that has received considerable attention in recent years is the effects of boundaries or defects in a relativistic QFT, described by a quantum field theory in $(1 + 3)$-dimensional Minkowski space. In this case, the effects of the boundaries or defects can be captured by a particular type of gauge transformations, namely, “gauged Wick rotations”. In this work, we consider a quantum scalar field in two dimensions, defined on a circle, and coupled to a temporally varying electromagnetic field with zero magnetic field and non-zero electric field. The electric field induces a non-trivial background for the scalar field, which in turn modifies the dynamics of the electromagnetic field through the “gauged Wick rotation” transformation. We study the evolution of the electromagnetic field from an initial time-dependent state, and calculate the Wightman functions corresponding to the charged components of the electromagnetic field. We show that, even though the initial state is time-dependent, the corresponding Wightman functions become time-independent at late times, depending only on the difference between the two times. We further study the associated two-point function and show that it reduces to a Fourier expansion in the late time limit. Finally, we examine the consequences of this late-time behavior on quantum field theory, in particular, the effective energy density stored in the electromagnetic field. We find, surprisingly, that this energy density becomes time-independent in the late time limit. We interpret this result as an effective vacuum energy density arising from the nontrivial dynamics of the electromagnetic field, induced by the temporal variation of the scalar field. We examine the implications of this result on quantum vacuum processes, in particular, on photon production in a time-dependent electric field. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this approach to studying phenomenological effects of “hot edges” in thermal field theories.

In high-energy heavy-ion collisions, particle production is strongly influenced by the path length dependence of the initial spatial anisotropyparticipating in the reaction. Rapidity dependent Hanbury-Brown-Twiss (HBT) interferometry measurements can provide constraints on the spatial extent and the strength of the reaction initial pressure gradient. Supported by an anisotropic flow calculation, two quantitative methods are proposed to determine the electric charge correlations in the phase space of the produced particles around mid-rapidity. Applying these methods to the published Bose-Einstein correlations data obtained by the NA49 and the CERES collaborations at the SPS, the electric charge correlations are determined as a function of rapidity and energy. It is shown that at all energies and rapidities the strength of the charge correlations is maximal for like charges and decreases with the opposite charge correlations. The rapidity dependence of the correlations strength shows a minimum at about 3.2 times the pion chemical potential and increases at larger longitudinal distances from the mid-rapidity.

X-ray bursting magnetar XTE J1810-197 was observed with the *Chandra X-ray Observatory during an X-ray active phase in 2013. The source was seen to turn off at lower energies, with only a soft X-ray component remaining after extrapolation. The spectrum could be well-fitted by a power-law with a photon index of −0.8, similarly common for other quiescent neutron stars. However, an Fe Kα line was present at 6.4 keV with an equivalent width of 50-100 eV, much higher than seen in other quiescent neutron stars. The line was strongly Doppler shifted to ~0.8 keV, with an inferred black hole spin of up to ~0.87. The source underwent an X-ray outburst in 2019, and a subsequent Swift observation confirmed the presence of a soft X-ray component with a power-law shape like before, but with an apparent increase in photon index to ~1.4. The discovery of such a soft X-ray power-law component from a quiescent neutron star provides the first direct evidence for large changes in the neutron star surface temperature corresponding to changes in the mass accretion rate.

The epoch of the ionizing UV radiation from young stars, known as the reionization epoch, is one of the most significant and intriguing transitions in the early Universe. This transition has direct implications for the temperature and polarization power spectra of the cosmic microwave background, as well as the abundance of low-mass dark matter halos. While observations of high-redshift galaxy spectra are consistent with the Thomson limit (the extent of this transition), the opacity of the baryons to the Thomson scattering coupling prevents the reionization of structures smaller than $M \sim 3 \times 10^9 M_\odot$ from fully satisfying observational constraints. Local groups thus represent a powerful substructure test of reionization, in which a patch of sufficiently small volume can remain ionized even after the larger cosmic neighborhood has been reionized. Using the McDonald Observatory's Faint Object Spectrograph, we have obtained new, deep spectroscopy of the stellar populations of five proximate dwarf spheroidal galaxies and use these data to measure the volume-averaged neutral fraction as a function of cosmic time. We find that the median neutral fraction increases from $x_e \sim 0.2$ at $z \sim 7$ to $x_e \sim 0.8$ at $z \sim 3$, with large and rapid fluctuations on scales of $\Delta x_e \sim 0.5$. This evolution is consistent with the rapid growth of a Pop II central galaxy in the lowest-mass dark matter halo in our Local Group, the Virgo cluster dwarf galaxy M86, whose luminosity-averaged escape fraction is estimated at $f_{esc} \sim 0.3$%. Our results suggest that reionization was fully completed by $z \sim 3$, in conflict with previous estimates based on the larger-volume statistics of high-redshift observations. The minimum halo mass responsible for this effect is $M \sim 10^9 M_\odot$, which is approximately the minimum halo mass at which the central galaxy of the Local Group would have sufficiently high luminosity to reionize the IGM. We highlight the sensitivity of this method and discuss observational strategies to refine our measurement of the local ionizing emissivity and thus of the timing and completion of reionization.

In this paper we present rotational widths for 102 galaxies, measured from our opticalintegral field spectroscopic sample of spiral galaxies. We combine these widths with new optical photometryfrom the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 12, improved distances from the Surface Brightness FluctuationSpite Plate Method, and a dynamical Tully-Fisher relation to produce a comprehensive model forthe full rotation width - luminosity relationship. We find that the residuals in the rotation widthsfor a particular galaxy are strongly correlated with the surface brightness of that galaxy. This result isconfirmed by an investigation into the cause of the residuals - seeing-related errors. Using a dynamicalTully-Fisher relation which is robust against seeing-related errors, we find that the residuals in theTully-Fisher relation are entirely attributable to the surface brightness of the galaxy. Therefore, we presenta method for predicting the rotational width of a galaxy from its optical luminosity, using only redshiftand surface brightness observations. We apply this relation to an external dataset of 31 galaxies with known optical luminosities androtation widths, and find that the predicted rotational widths are on average 12.2% larger thanthe observed rotational widths. While this offset is significant, it is considerably smaller than theseeing-related errors found in the above analysis. Therefore, we conclude that our new, surfacebrightness-sensitive rotational width measures are an improvement on those presented in our previous paper. Wehope that this new version will be of use to scientists working with optical rotation widths but havingsubstantial concerns about the seeing-related errors in the published Tully-Fisher relation.'

The low carbon abundance of I Zw 18 has been a puzzle for decades. Using the SWIFT X-ray Telescope, we measure the gas phase oxygen abundance in the interstellar medium of I Zw 18. We find 12 + log(O/H) = 7.95 ± 0.07, 1σ, significantly lower than the inferred oxygen abundance in its large-scale interstellar medium hydrogen envelope (22.78 ± 0.15), and much lower than the average 12 + log(O/H) for star-forming galaxies. The discrepancy could be due to recent chemical enrichment, abnormal nucleosynthetic origins for some elements, or unusual dust depletion patterns, but we consider an alternative explanation that some of the standard assumption for TSV models are not applicable to I Zw 18. This research was presented in a paper titled "SWIFT X-ray Telescope Detection of Oxygen in the Interstellar Medium of I Zw 18" by J. Brinkerink et al., which can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.00069

Ensembles of magnetic monopoles have been widely studied in the literature due to their potential relevance in quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the underlying theory of the strong interaction. These ensembles provide a framework to explore non-perturbative aspects of QCD that cannot be studied via Monte Carlo techniques. In this work, we confine such an ensemble using magnetic monopole solutions of the Bogomolnyi equation. These magnetic monopoles are point particles with both electric and magnetic charges. They couple via the magnetic dipole moment. We use a modified Powell scheme to solve the resulting non-linear equation and generate ensembles of monopole solutions. The confining strength of the ensemble is controlled by varying the 't Hooft coupling constant, a parameter of the theory that governs the magnetic monopole's self-interactions. We characterize this ensemble via several order parameters and observe that the system exhibits deconfinement, a phenomenon in which the magnetic charges freely move in the Euclidean spacetime. This Letter describes an initial investigation into the confining properties of such an ensemble and the order parameters that characterize it.

Recent observational campaigns have discovered a widespread, but inhomogenous, CIV galactic wind from starbursting galaxies at high redshift, identified through characteristic blueshifted CIV absorption associated with the outflowing wind. We use hydrodynamical simulations to investigate the wind properties around galaxies at redshifts z = 3-5, when the typical escape velocities of z = 3-5 galaxies are of order 200 km/s. The fraction of baryons in stars of these galaxies at high-redshift is typically 80%, and thus likely progenitors of local ellipticals. We identify four primary wind signatures, which can be distinguished by detailed spectra and spatial resolved observations: a broad component from winds driven by SNe and stellar winds from aged stellar populations, a dense shell around the shocked interstellar and intergalactic medium, and gas temperature and ionization state driven winds from young massive star populations. The combined effects of these diverse wind signatures leave characteristic imprints in the CIV equivalent width and spatial profile, which can be used to distinguish galactic winds around high-redshift galaxies from other sources of CIV in the IGM.

In this paper, we propose a novel Memory Network (MemNN) architecture that unifies and extends three key functions - temporal memory, sequence memory, and co-occurrence memory. The MemNN architecture uses memory units that operate on different time scales, allowing the model to remember past events in chronological order, as well as important patterns across a sequence of events. We also present a simple method for parameter sharing across memory units, which substantially reduces the number of model parameters. The MemNN architecture is trained end-to-end on a large scale image classification task using stochastic gradient descent, and we demonstrate the competitiveness of our model on ImageNet. In our Cifar setup, using only 3.6M parameters, our MemNN model outperforms all published ImageNet results using the same architecture, with a top-1 accuracy of 57.9%, which is 2.5% higher than the previous state-of-the-art. The MemNN model also substantially reduces the test error compared to all previous published image classification results.

We present observations of M87 in the mid-infrared from 1 to 10 $\mu$m obtained with the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF). The M87 nucleus is detected at 2.3, 3.8, 4.8, 5.8, 8.0, and 10.3 $\mu$m. Modeling of the emission from the nucleus shows that it is well described by a single-temperature thermal composite model component with a dust temperature of T = 160 $\pm$ 20 K. For the first time, the nucleus is resolved at 8.0 and 10.3 $\mu$m. The 8.0 $\mu$m image shows a dominant extended component in addition to a warm component associated with the nucleus. The 10.3 $\mu$m image shows two compact sources, one coincident with the 8.0 $\mu$m source and a second source offset by 2.2 $\pm$ 0.4 pc from the nucleus. The combined 25.6ks IRTF observations were repeated on M87 on 2019 Jan 12.1. Contour plots of the combined observations, and the individual visits, reveal that the 8.0 $\mu$m source has exhibited flux variability by up to 80% over time. We also show that the spectrum of the nucleus has not changed between the 2004 and 2019 epochs. The 8.0 $\mu$m variability, combined with the near- and mid-infrared detection, suggests that M87 has a compact hot inner engine. The 8.0 $\mu$m variability may be due to changes in the structure or temperature of the hot inner engine or changes in the distribution or temperature of the circum-engine dust.

In fluorescence microscopy, energy transfer between two fluorophores can be utilized to detect molecular interactions (e.g. protein-protein interactions). This technique is especially valuable for biological systems, where simultaneous excitation of both partners is often not feasible. For the interaction to occur, the molecules must be in close proximity. Therefore, the Forster energy transfer mechanism was utilized to study the average distance between freely diffusing, membrane-bound dyes in a live cell membrane model. The fluorophores were excited using a 405 nm laser and the emission was recorded using a photomultiplier tube. The steady-state fluorescence quenching from the donors was modeled using the Stern-Volmer equation with multiple quencher concentrations and presented as an average distance between the dyes as a function of time. The model was validated using a known adjacent dye pair. The Forster energy transfer model was utilized to measure the average distance between membrane-bound, freely diffusing dyes over time. Based on the energy transfer results, a vesicle membrane was created in silico using COMSOL Multiphysics 5.2, and the average distance between the dyes was calculated for a simulated, live cell membrane. The membrane contains lipids and membrane proteins, and therefore may represent a live cell membrane. The results showed that the membrane thickness influences the average distance between the dyes, as well as the average distance between the dyes and membrane proteins. This suggests that the average distance between membrane-bound dyes may be altered by membrane proteins.

We present HST/WFC3 ultraviolet space Telescope observations of the young massive cluster (age $\sim$ 2 Myr) in the nucleus of the nearby SBb spiral galaxy M33. The HST observations allow us to measure the distribution of young, extremely massive stars in this system for the first time. Our results show that: 1) the young, most massive stars are heavily concentrated toward the center of the cluster; 2) a significant fraction of these stars are in binaries; and 3) the most massive young stars are widely distributed across the inner region of the cluster, with no discernible spatial structure. These observations reveal the on-going disruption of young massive star clusters in the era of HST and pose challenges to current theories of cluster formation and evolution. The nucleus of M33 hosts a remarkable massive young star cluster (age $\sim$ 2 Myr), which has provided an excellent laboratory to study the early evolution of massive stars and their role in cluster evolution. Young massive star clusters (YMSCs, age $<$ 2 Myr) are the most massive and densest stellar systems in the Universe. They play a critical role in the feedback of both energy and metal-rich stellar winds into the interstellar medium (ISM) of their host galaxies, as well as the establishment of chemical enrichment patterns in the early Universe. They are also test beds for theories of massive star evolution. Despite their importance, relatively few YMCs have been identified in nearby galaxies with sufficient resolution and depth to permit such studies, especially at intermediate and high redshifts. In order to provide a comprehensive test of theories of massive star cluster evolution at intermediate and high redshifts, we have begun a survey of nearby galaxies with the HST/WFC3 to identify YMCs. This survey, coupled with follow-up studies at other wavelengths, is enabling us to test our understanding of the initial conditions for star cluster formation and the processes that shape their subsequent evolution. This paper presents ultraviolet space Telescope observations of the young massive cluster in the nucleus of the nearby SBb spiral galaxy M33. These observations reveal the disruption of the cluster, already evident in the spatial distribution of the most massive young stars (age $\sim$ 1 Myr), and show for the first time that a significant fraction of these stars are in binaries. In addition, we present analysis of this cluster's properties based on earlier Hubble Space Telescope observations (Östlin et al. 2014) and conclude that this cluster has a mass of approximately $10^5$ M$_{\odot}$, a half-light radius of $\sim$ 30 pc and is comparable in size and mass to some of the most massive known clusters in the LMC (age $\sim$ 5-7 Myr). These observations pose challenges to current theories of cluster formation and evolution.

In recent years, the landscape of string theory moduli has become much richer due to the development of many new techniques for constructing vacua. In particular, a class of strong-weak coupling dualities has been developed which maps a large subset of such vacua to weakly coupled configurations of branes and fluxes. These techniques have been successfully applied to stabilize moduli, and at the same time generate realistic particle physics spectra and detectable signals at LHC. Such effective field theories often involve the enhanced global symmetries of certain supergravity configurations (localized stabilized moduli, axions, et. al.) and in turn, these symmetries often admit non-abelian global symmetries. In this paper we discuss various techniques for exploiting these global symmetries in order to simplify the construction of realistic models along the lines of holographic supergravities, and in particular those of minimal de Sitter and no-scale form. We discuss general global symmetries, their embedding in non-abelian group structures and show how the associated non-abelian gauge symmetries naturally act as a gauge symmetry for the (U(1)R) symmetry present in such theories. As a simple class of examples we demonstrate how certain models of gauged supergravities with non-abelian global symmetry subgroups can be simplified to no-scale models. In addition to these symmetries, we also discuss generalized structure compactifications and their relation to the recently proposed integrable systems and their exact solutions.

Wright's constants in graph enumeration relate to the first four moments of the area under a Brownian excursion. An excursion is a Brownian path away from zero, and so its area under these paths is the sum of zero-mean squares, or Brownian areas. The constant for a certain degree of graph enumeration is the expected number of brownian areas of a specified size. These moments are calculated using the pragmatic method of analytic combinatorics. In addition to exact values for small values of the degree, good upper and lower bounds are also provided. Atomic electric dipole moments (EDMs) violate both spatial and temporal symmetries and therefore require an explicit or spontaneous violation of either parity (P) or time reversal (T) symmetry. The most general P, T-invariant Hamiltonian that can lead to a non-vanishing atomic EDM contains electric dipole (E1) and magnetic dipole (M1) transitions between atomic states. For neutral atoms, the Schiff theorem states that the contribution to the atomic EDM from E1/M1 transitions is proportional to the nuclear electric dipole moment (edm). The Schiff theorem has been proven for zero nuclear edm, and so a limit on the electron EDM effectively limits the nuclear edm. In 2004, an experiment searching for a nuclear edm resulted in a null measurement with a 90% confidence level constraint of d_n < 0.87\times 10^{-26} e cm, which can be converted to an electron edm limit of d_e < 8.7\times 10^{-28} e cm at 90% confidence. In 2009, the CODATA redefinition of the electron radius increased this limit to d_e < 1.7\times 10^{-27} e cm. In 2019, a new experiment using a cold gas of Rb atoms measured d_e < 1.1\times 10^{-29} e cm, resulting in a new limit of d_n < 0.29\times 10^{-28} e cm (90% C.L.) which, when combined with the 2004 limit, d_e < 0.88\times 10^{-27} e cm. The difference between these two limits, d_n = 1.1(3.4)\times 10^{-28} e cm, is the most stringent test of the Schiff theorem to date. The theoretical explanation for this discrepancy remains an area of active research.

J 0903+0357 is a nearby L dwarf observed by the Gaia satellite in the preliminary data release. It has a radial velocity and two new optical spectra, one from GTC and one from LBT. J 0903+0357 is one of the most distant and faintest L dwarfs yet observed. J 0903+0357's radial velocity is 22.2 km/s, indicating it is a low-mass member of the local solar neighborhood. The spectra are consistent with L dwarf characteristics, but the JHK colors are unusual for L dwarfs, especially its red color. This color cannot be explained by the late-M spectral classification, so it may be a binary or a very low surface gravity object. If it is a binary, it would be the most distant and most tightly bound system of any L dwarf. Alternatively, a late-L companion to a mid-M dwarf could explain the red color. It will be important to observe J 0903+0357 over multiple epochs to determine which of these scenarios is correct.

Due to their active galactic nuclei (AGN) black holes can now be observed across almost the entire range of cosmic times. These energetic outflows have a profound impact on the growth and evolution of their host galaxies, which can be classified into two modes: suppression and activation. In the first mode, the energetic outburst of the AGN can heat and expel the interstellar medium (ISM) of the host galaxy, effectively shutting down star formation and quelling the growth of its potential descendents. This mode of AGN feedback is most effective at high redshifts, prior to the epoch of reionization (EoR), where the host galaxy’s ISM can only survive in highly ionized pockets within the larger universe. In the second mode, the black hole gradually emits, in slow trickles, energy that is sufficient to prevent the cooling of the hot ISM, thereby allowing star formation to resume. Observationally, this second mode of AGN feedback is most prevalent at low redshifts, where the galaxy is able to cool through collisional processes. Despite the importance of these modes, they are not well understood and are implemented in galaxy formation simulations using sub-grid models with substantial free parameters that affect the efficiency and mode of AGN feedback. To address this, we present a physically motivated model for the energetic feedback of AGN within the cosmological evolution of dark matter, gas and star particles. By considering the radiative and mechanical energy outputs of each black hole over a large time-step, we capture the gradual mode of AGN feedback and its effects on the evolution of the ISM within galaxies, allowing more effective interactions between black holes and their hosts. Within the simulations presented here, we compare the evolution of galaxy groups and clusters, finding that the model presented here with black holes radiating for a fixed length of time is sufficient to reproduce the observed scaling relations. Additionally, we find that this mode of feedback suppresses star formation within the central galaxy in groups and clusters, lowering its specific star formation rate in good agreement with observations. We provide model configurations that match a range of scaling relations for groups and clusters across a broad range of mass. We also consider an example implementation of this model for the EAGLE simulation, providing a realistic description of the hot gas properties within galaxies and the population of black holes. Overall, our model provides a unifying description of AGN feedback, emulating its observed phenomenology across cosmic time whilst offering a more physical approach that may allow improved constraints on the co-evolution of galaxies and their central black holes.

The transit of an Earth-sized planet in front of its star occurs when the projected separation of the planet and star is small. At such times, the size of the planet, expressed here as a percentage of the host star's radius, reduces the stellar photometric signal by a detectable amount. While radial velocity (RV) measurements of the host star are not affected by the transiting planet, they are affected by other noise sources with a correlated nature, such as the reflex motion of the host star induced by the transiting planet. We have developed an analytic formalism that incorporates correlated noise in a Bayesian framework to infer the properties of exoplanets in transiting configurations, such as the planet's radius, period, and position relative to the star. We validate our formalism with numerical simulations and apply it to the detection of a simulated transiting hot Jupiter in the K2 dataset. We place 95% confidence on a 5% radius measurement of the planet in transiting configuration for K2 data, and demonstrate the capability to detect and characterize transiting hot Jupiter planets with radii greater than 4% using data from the TESS mission. Finally, we show that future space-based transit surveys, such as PLATO and the proposed DARWIN mission, should be able to detect transiting super Earths (with radii between 2% and 4%) and characterize their atmosphere for a statistically significant sample of planets.

Recent deep, wide area surveys have discovered faint, extended radio emission on angular scales of 8arcmin to 3arcmin. These previously unrecognized structures may be filaments of the Warm Hot Intergalactic Medium (WHIM), shock-heated gas in the accretion filaments of galaxies, or cosmological filaments produced during the epoch of recombination. If the latter, their low surface brightnesses would require significant amplification by the residual cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies. We report the discovery of such radio emission in the Coma cluster field, and use it to infer a large (0.2-0.5keV) component of hot, shock-heated intergalactic gas. Such a component, if pre-heating of the intergalactic medium (IGM) was sufficient to reduce the residual entropy of the IGM by a factor of 8-30 at mean density (as expected from cosmological simulations), would have evaporated the vast majority of the gaseous halo around each cluster member. This would have enriched the intracluster medium (ICM) in low-entropy gas and prevented the ongoing growth of the BCG’s cool X-ray halo. Furthermore, based on their offset locations from the brightest X-ray peaks, the radio structures appear to connect clusters on the 100-1000kpc scale, suggesting the presence of intercluster shocks with 130-1300km s-1 bulk velocities, in agreement with numerical simulations. Finally, we find that the VLA radio flux densities of six projected radio galaxies are dominated by lobes and substantial bridges of (narrow-band selected) optical emission-line plasma, with total projected physical extents of order 1-3 Mpc. If this emission-line plasma is not substantially debiased, then its energetics (a few 10$^{56-57}$ erg) and large-scale distribution on the Mpc scale (tens of kpc-scale filaments interspersed with tens of kpc-scale walls and blobs) strongly suggest that these radio sources inflated bubbles in the ICM, perhaps through low-level turbulently driven heating.

Mo is a relatively heavy transition element and at standard pressure it exists in the stable hexagonal crystal structure (h-Mo). It's melting point is 1315 °C. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) is a powerful method for studying the behavior of materials over a long period of time. Recently, AIMD has been applied to study the melting point of Mo. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first melting curve of Mo calculated by the phase coexistence method. The results show that the melting point of Mo computed by AIMD is 1413 °C, which is 3.2 °C higher than the experiments. The melting curve of Mo has been studied by several experiments and simulations. The melting point of Mo computed by the nudged cell framework (NCF) is 1273.7 °C, which is 7.8 °C lower than the experiments. According to the previous phase coexistence method, we can predict the melting point of Mo by calculating the coexistence curve of h-Mo and its non-hexagonal structures such as γ-Mo and δ-Mo. The melting point of Mo predicted by our calculation is 1413.4 °C, which is 3.2 °C higher than the experiments. The main difference between our calculation and the previous phase coexistence method is the use of the non-hexagonal structures in the phase coexistence calculation. We think the previous phase coexistence method did not consider the instability of these non-hexagonal structures. According to the calculations of the formation enthalpy, the enthalpies of these non-hexagonal structures are higher than h-Mo. The formation enthalpy of δ-Mo is equal to that of h-Mo, but the enthalpy of γ-Mo is higher than h-Mo. Therefore, the melting point of Mo calculated by our method is higher than that calculated by the previous phase coexistence method.

Preferential attachment models are commonly used to describe the evolution of networks. These models assume that new nodes connect to existing ones according to some local attribute which increases with connectivity, typically the degree. One such model, the scale-free network was found to have a degree distribution that follows a power law. Numerous other models have since been proposed to explain the diverse range of observed network attributes. These models are typically simplified stochastic processes, which can be simulated to produce network realizations. This paper considers a related question to that of network formation, namely how network structure impacts the growth of new nodes. These new nodes can be source nodes, which initiate connections to target nodes, with the number of connections dependent on the degree of the source and the rank of the target. This yields a differential equation which can be solved to yield the degree distribution of the resulting network. For the simplest case of binary connection assignment, the degree distribution follows a bipower law, with one exponent for the low degree nodes and a second for the high degree nodes. It is argued that this captures the variation in network attributes common to models of network growth.

Heterogeneity and increasing returns may drive socio-economic transitions. Industrialization often begins in the periphery of a system, where diseconomies of scale are present, but centralize when innovations enable improvements in scale efficiency. Increasing returns may drive centralization. An example is the Industrial Revolution, where major innovations included the steam engine and factory production, combining heterogeneous components. Concurrently, emerging market indicators point to increasing returns in several sectors, including transportation, finance, and waste management. These increasing returns may reflect granular heterogeneities, e.g. in the transportation system, where shorter distances and broader networks of roads and airports may present increasing returns. These heterogeneities may interact with innovations, as improved transport and communications reduce the costs of scale improvements. These interactions may lead to systemic transitions. Applying these ideas to historical systems, this paper suggests that the Industrial Revolution began in the periphery of Europe, with significant improvements in transport and communication that enabled the adoption of the steam engine and factory production. Conversely, emerging market transitions often begin in the interior, where innovations appear local, but are generalizable across the system. These interior transitions present increasing returns, but eventually lead to system-wide adoption. These ideas may also explain the challenges of incumbent economic sectors. After significant improvements in scale efficiency, heterogeneities may increase returns in the centralizing forces of increasing returns, until the sector is unable to defend its entrenched position. This dynamic may explain the successes and failures of incumbent companies, as their focus on incumbent improvement delays but does not prevent systemic transitions.

Complex dynamical systems such as the climate or the brain are composed of many interacting parts. For example, the atmosphere is linked to the ocean, and the ocean is linked to the land surface, all of which affect the climate. Similarly, the human body is linked to the brain, which affects how we think and feel. Despite their ubiquity, complex dynamical systems composed of many interacting parts are challenging to study due to their complexity. Analytical solutions are often not available, and large-scale simulations are prohibitively expensive. Computational scientists have developed algorithms to study such complex dynamical systems by splitting them into subsystems that are simpler to analyze, and connecting the subsystems with computer models of integration. This approach has been particularly fruitful in modeling the climate, where coupled atmosphere-ocean and land-atmosphere models have been instrumental in understanding the atmosphere's role in warming and ocean's role in cooling the global temperature.

In general, enforcing that a formula of first-order logic is consistent is undecidable. However, various consistency proof techniques have been developed forspecific fragment of first-order logic, such as propositional dynamic logics (PDLs) and monadic second-order logic (MSOL). Furthermore, a number of algorithmic and complexity results have been developed for quantifier elimination, consistency, and model checking for these fragments. In this paper, we develop meta-theoretic methods to strengthen these results to fragments of first-order logic that allow arbitrary quantified constraints (formulas with universally and existentially quantified variables). Our main technical result is a strengthened version of Skolemization, which allows us to encode a quantified constraint in an MSOL formula with a constant number of extra variables. Furthermore, we develop a method for encoding quantified constraints into monadic second-order logic such that consistency can be decided and model checking for quantified constraints can be reduced to consistency for MSOL with a strengthened version of Skolemization. We demonstrate the application of these methods to prove various consistency and model checking results for fragments of first-order logic with quantified constraints.

A global Wolf-Rayet content of 12% was derived for the nearby NGC300 galaxy, significantly higher than the current estimates of 7% (Schaerer & Vacca 2010). This high value might be explained by the recent star formation episode implied by the detection of an ULX in the outskirts of the galaxy (Israel et al. 2014). However, a closer inspection of the archival data indicates that the upper limit on the global WR content of NGC300 is in fact 7%. Furthermore, the upper limit WR contribution to the U-band magnitude of the whole galaxy is 2.2%, in contrast to the 8.3% derived from the global Wolf-Rayet content. This apparent discrepancy can be explained by the late-type stellar content of the galaxy. Late-type stars dominate the light at optical wavelengths, and given the age-metallicity relation, they will exhibit a high fraction of early-type Wolf-Rayet stars. Indeed, a KS test on the observed and modeled optical colors of the galaxy yields a low probability (P < 0.001) that the two samples were extracted from the same population. We estimate the global WR contribution to the U-band magnitude of the galaxy to be 1.2%, in agreement with the observed upper limit.

A braid group is a group consisting of loops in three-dimensional space that are linked together by taking one loop, passing it through another loop coming from the first, and returning the first loop to its original position. In the paper, the authors analyze the set of all possible linking patterns among multiple loops and show that this set is isomorphic to a permutation group. This implies that every loop in a braid group can be linked with every other loop in a countable infinity of ways. The paper also presents a cycling operation that performs a specific linking pattern in a braid group. Summary A braid group, exemplified by the well-known example of the three-strand braid, is a group of loops in three-dimensional space that are linked together by taking one loop, passing it through another loop, and returning the first loop to its original position. In previous works, it has been shown that every loop in a braid group can be linked with every other loop in an uncountable infinity of ways, but the authors present a linking pattern that is not considered in previous works: the pattern is invariant under a permutation of the loops. This linking pattern allows the authors to demonstrate that every linking pattern in a braid group is obtained by performing the cycling operation.

Dangling bonds at the amorphous semiconductor/oxide interface can mediate magnetic interactions between localized electrons. These interactions lead to magnetic coherence, reflected in the coherent spin relaxation observed in dangling-bond magnetic transistors. Here we develop a theoretical model of dangling-bond spin relaxation, and use it to analyze experimental data on this relaxation process. We find that coherent spin dynamics on dangling bonds at the amorphous semiconductor/oxide interface can account for the 1/f spectral density of dangling-bond spin relaxivity observed in recent experiments. The theoretical model describes the spin relaxation as a combination of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck stochastic processes, with the correlation time determined by the spin-orbit scattering rate. The theory also accounts for the observed magnetic field and gate dependence of the correlation time, as well as the insensitivity of the 1/f spin relaxivity to small variations in the local symmetry and bond length of the dangling bonds. We further use the theory to develop a new method for the independent measurement of the spin-orbit scattering rate based on dangling-bond spin relaxometry. The developed theory provides a general framework for understanding the coherent spin dynamics in complex, disordered systems, and may be extended to describe other phenomena involving spin transport and relaxation mediated by local disorder.

Bacterial chemotaxis is a navigation system used by microorganisms to detect chemical gradients in the environment and initiate adaptive responses. Bacteria in the same chemical environment show variability in their behavioral responses, from no response to sharp persistent direction changes. To date, the variability in bacterial responses have been linked to mutations in individual cells or even whole bacterial populations, but not to emergent behaviors at the level of the individual cell. Here, by combining microfluidics with high-throughput imaging, we show that variations in the temporal dynamics of individual cells under the same chemical stimulus are sufficient to explain differences in the population level behavioral variability. We demonstrate that the dynamics of bacterial polar deployment, which is correlated with persistence in responding to a chemical gradient, are encoded in the timescale of the polar rotation. Our work provides a fundamental link between individual cell behavior and emergent population level phenomena, and has implications for understanding complexity in bacterial physiology and infectious disease.

A strong emission line from the CN radical, whose restframe wavelength is 98 meters, was detected in the infrared spectrum of the Cloverleaf quasar at a redshift of 2.56. This is the highest redshift at which this emission has been detected. The large observed equivalent width of this line and its non-detection in archival observations of the same quasar taken between 2001 and 2013 indicate that the line has increased in flux by a factor of ~30% in less than nine years. The large amplitude of this change, along with the high space density of galaxies at this redshift, make it likely that the line is associated with star formation, possibly triggered by the merger leading to the Cloverleaf quasar's broad absorption line wind. The CN radical is an important trace species in the interstellar medium of galaxies and is a prominent component of the molecular universe. It is one of the most symmetric organic molecules, with a minimum of 44 nuclei. Its most stable form is the linear molecule hydrogen cyanide (HCN), whose inversion (the molecule's base is on top) suggests a lower energy state (longer wavelength) in the molecule's electromagnetic spectrum. This so-called Lambda-doublet at 12CH+ and 15N36 isotope of the CN radical has been observed in absorption in the nuclei of galaxies, at low redshift (z < 0.4). The equivalent width of this Lambda-doublet is used as a powerful diagnostic of the star formation rate (SFR) in galaxies, since the UV light from young, massive stars produces a photodissociation region (PDR) around their birthplaces, with subsequent conversion of molecular hydrogen to HCN via reactions with other hydrogen-bearing molecules. Detection of emission from the CN radical at high redshift, z = 2.56, is surprising. The large observed equivalent width of this line and its non-detection in archival observations of the same quasar taken between 2001 and 2013 indicate that the line has increased in flux by a factor of ~30%. The large amplitude of this change, along with the high space density of galaxies at this redshift, make it likely that the line is associated with star formation, possibly triggered by the merger leading to the Cloverleaf quasar's broad absorption line wind.
