In this short note, we show that any normalized Ricci flow on a closed four manifold with positive curvature operator has a singular solution with zero curvature. This generalizes a previous result of Schoen and Yau [1] who showed the same statement for zero curvature. As an application, we provide a new proof of the Poincar[é]{} conjecture for closed spin manifolds with positive scalar curvature. This note is a short version of a paper [2] that received the 2018 ICM award. Solutions of normalized Ricci flows with zero curvature have been studied extensively, starting from Hamilton [1]. When the initial metric has positive curvature operator, maximum principles allow to show that the solution remains uniformly positive [3]. On the other hand, the normalized Ricci flow evolution starting from a metric with zero curvature operator can develop singularities in finite time [4]. Singularities of this kind have been extensively studied in the context of the Ricci flow, and in particular it was proved by Schoen and Yau [5] that a solution with zero curvature must be eventually flat. This was extended to a larger class of initial data in [6]. We show that any normalized Ricci flow on a closed four manifold with positive curvature operator has a singular solution with zero curvature. In particular, this gives a new proof of the following result of Hamilton [1]: If the normalized Ricci flow starting from a metric with positive scalar curvature has a singularity at $T<\infty$, then the scalar curvature converges to zero as $T$ approaches $+\infty$. Finally, the corollary below is a new proof of the Poincar[é]{} conjecture for closed spin manifolds with positive scalar curvature. Corollary: A closed spin manifold with positive scalar curvature and positive first Betti number is necessarily spherical. This follows from the following theorem of R. Ye: If $M$ is a closed simply-connected spin manifold with positive scalar curvature and first Betti number, then $M$ is a spherical space form. Finally, let's point out that our result does not answer the question of whether positive curvature operator and zero curvature are the only possibilities for a normalized Ricci flow to develop a singularity. In fact, we show that the only other possibilities are metrics with zero curvature. We would like to thank Xiaonan Ma for pointing out a mistake in a previous version of this note.

Symmetry breaking is an ubiquitous phenomenon in physics. Symmetry breaking in the early universe has profound implications for our understanding of the universe at large. It may provide a mechanism for the generation of density and inhomogeneity perturbations, which can give rise to galaxies and clusters of galaxies via gravitational instability. It may also provide a seed for the development of long-range correlations in the form of Dark Matter. Furthermore, it may provide a way to understand the small density of dark energy relative to the scale of spatial inhomogeneities in the universe. In this paper, we consider the symmetry breaking pattern i.e. the Isometry group of spatially closed FRW universe, and show that it may, in fact, be enlarged to the pseudo-scale invariance (PSI) algebra. This leads to the possibility that Dark Energy may be associated with a scalar field with an exactly conformal coupling to gravity. Furthermore, it is shown that this PSI breaking can also lead to the small density of dark matter as well as the late-time acceleration of the universe. The paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we review the Isometry group of the spatially closed FRW universe and show that it may be enlarged to the PSI algebra. In Sec. 3 we show that this PSI breaking can also lead to the small density of dark matter as well as the late-time acceleration of the universe. The conclusion and some outlook are presented in the last section. In this paper we consider the possibility that the Isometry group of the spatially closed FRW universe may be enlarged to the pseudo-scale invariance (PSI) algebra. This leads to the possibility that Dark Energy may be associated with a scalar field with an exactly conformal coupling to gravity. It is shown that this PSI breaking can also lead to the small density of dark matter as well as the late-time acceleration of the universe.

Recent experimental and theoretical work has cast doubt on the feasibility of exact quantum algorithms for satisfiability (SAT), the problem of determining whether a boolean formula can be satisfied by assigning values to its variables. In this work, we show that this implies a significant collapse in the complexity of the closely related problem of counting solution-free instances, or satisfiable clauses (SAT). We argue that this collapse in complexity can be leveraged to give the first algorithm for satisfiable clauses of polynomial size amplification with an approximation ratio of 3, matching the best known approximation algorithms for the general case. Our work leaves open the possibility that satisfying assignments might eventually be shown to be hard to approximate within a larger factor, even on quantum computers. The modern formulation of the SAT problem has two main variants: classical satisfiability (CSAT), which can be solved by enumeration, and local satisfiability (SAT), which is complete for the quantum query complexity class. In 1994, Gamarnik, London, and Flynn showed that quantum computers could efficiently solve CSAT, and followed this with a quantum algorithm for SAT that obtained a polynomial size amplification over the best known classical algorithm. Since then, the field has seen very little progress, with it remaining unknown whether quantum algorithms are able to solve SAT or CSAT, or even whether this would be possible in polynomial time. In this work, we show that recent lower bounds on the complexity of approximately counting satisfying assignments for a class of hard problems known as non-uniform Circuits with Settled Outcome (NCSO), imply that the best classical algorithms for SAT and CSAT are likely very difficult to improve upon. Specifically, we show that NCSO contains two different natural problems, #SAT and #CSAT, which respectively provide good approximations to the problem of counting satisfying assignments and the problem of counting all satisfying assignments. We show that the best currently known algorithms for counting satisfying assignments for NCSO with approximation ratio 2 must make queries to an exponential size circuit, and give several conditional results relating to whether this remains the case for better approximators. We also consider the case of #CSAT, showing that even with a good approximation, the best currently known algorithms make queries to a linear size circuit.

We present the FLAMES Survey of Massive Stars ( FLAMES-SFMS), a large-scale study of the stellar populations in the inner regions of the Galactic disc based on VLT/FLAMES intermediate-resolution spectroscopy of 987 massive stars. We analyse both the trends in surface N abundances and changes in effective temperature with time, which allow us to investigate the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. We compare our results with recent determinations of N abundances for young Galactic clusters and discuss potential nucleosynthesis channels responsible for the observed scatter in N abundance at a given age. We then apply the FLAMES-SFMS calibration of the N–sensitive infrared fluxes to a nearby sample of Magellanic Cloud stars and examine the relation between their luminosities and masses. We also derive estimates of their Initial Mass Functions (IMF). Finally, we compare the effective temperature scales of Galactic and Magellanic Clouds stars from the FLAMES-SFMS, detailed in a companion paper, and a set of detached eclipsing binary systems for which accurate parameters have been determined.

In this paper we show that a four-dimensional brane world, residing in an arbitrary number of space-time dimensions, can be realized without the need for a discrete symmetry. As an explicit example, we show that a brane world in six space-time dimensions with an adjoint scalar field, where the scalar develops a VEV along the space time direction can be constructed. The model presented has no discrete symmetries, and is hence potentially realistic. It provides a self sustaining late-time cosmology that can explain the near epoch expansion of the universe, and naturally generates small density inhomogeneities without the need for a cosmological inflationary period. Our model has a large number of arbitrary parameters, however we present a simple scenario in which all of these parameters are determined by a small number of parameters. The model is thus highly predictive. In particular, the dynamics of the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker brane give constraints on the scale of compactification of the extra-dimensions, and the scale of spontaneous Lorentz violation. We show that current experimental bounds on these scales may be able to be achieved in the framework of our model. Additionally, we investigate the realization of chiral fermions on the brane. In particular, we show that after the spontaneous Lorentz violation, right-chiral neutrinos and left-chiral antineutrinos can be localized to a single 4D spatial location, while right-chiral anti- neutrinos and left-chiral neutrinos remain delocalized over the extra-dimensions. Thus our model is not only realistic, but also solves the hot dark matter problem. Finally we discuss some of the cosmological implications of our work. In particular, we show that a 4D Friedmann equation can be obtained from our bulk theory. We present a scenario in which this dynamics, combined with the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe gives a natural explanation of the observed Hubble rate. The scenario we present is extremely simple, and has no free parameters. Moreover, it can potentially accommodate current observational constraints. This model is potentially testable in current and future experiments. Current experiments which may be able to test our model include MEG, PLANCK, and FOCUS. In the future, SHENGM7 may be able to test this scenario. Moreover, the exciting gravitational wave experiments, such as the LIGO and VIRGO, may also be able to test Lorentz invariance violation in the gravitational sector. Overall, the model presented here is extremely predictive, has no need for extra hypothesize or fine tuning, and can potentially solve the large scale structure, hot dark matter, and cosmological constant problems.

A new solution of teleparallel gravity was obtained which is equivalent to general relativity. The obtained solution describes a charged black hole with a scalar hair. The scalar becomes unstable below a critical value of the charge. The solution was obtained in the framework of the first order gravity theory. The energy of the solution was calculated and it was shown that it decreases while the total charge of the solution increases. The obtained solution has some similarities with the Reissner-Nordstrom-anti-de Sitter black hole, however it belongs to a different class of black holes, namely the black holes with a scalar hair. This solution can be considered as a generalization of the Horvat-Mimoso-Babichev solution for the case when the teleparallel Lagrangian includes a nonlinear term of the torsion. This solution was obtained in the frame work of the first order gravity which can be interesting from the point of view of a possible quantum treatment of this theory. This paper is a brief description of a scientific paper published on arXiv.org server. The full version of the paper can be found on the link provided in the abstract.

The Ophiuchus molecular complex at $l$ = 26.5° is the nearest large contiguous chain of molecular clouds complex to the solar system. It consists of several giant clouds, the most prominent of which are the L1688 dark cloud, the L1641 cluster, the L1689 cluster and the Ophiuchus Main cloud. These clouds have velocity vectors aligned perpendicular to the Galactic plane, and are therefore likely to be orbiting around the Galaxy as a cluster. Here we present the results of a search for the initial conditions of star formation in the Ophiuchus main cloud, by analyzing the velocity structure of the cloud and the kinematics of its condensations. We find that the clouds are collapsing along the length of the complex, with the south-east region of the main cloud having the highest degree of sub-filamentary structure. Furthermore, the densest regions of the cloud have radial velocities that suggest the presence of multiple coherent groups. We conclude that the initial conditions for star formation in the Ophiuchus main cloud are varied, with at least two distinct groups of condensations expected to form stars separately.

One of the key questions in studies of star formation in the local universe is the overall star formation rate (SFR), which can be measured by the luminosity of ionizing radiation from young, hot stars. Such studies are typically performed at high redshifts, using rest-frame far-ultraviolet (FUV) emission from young stars. Because the FUV spectral energy distribution (SED) varies with the type of stars and their age, the SFR can be measured by fitting the FUV emission with population synthesis models. This permits studies of star formation over the past 8-15 billion years, but the accuracy is limited by our poor knowledge of the SFH over much shorter timescales. Here we present an analysis of recent data from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) that provides an accurate measurement of the SFR over the past 3 billion years, based on the luminosity of Ly-alpha radiation from young, cool stars. Unlike FUV radiation, this "visible" light varies with the instantaneous rate of star formation, making it a "flashing light" tracer of current SFR. Using our analysis techniques, we find a current SFR of 5.9 (± 2.3) × 10−3 solar masses per year in the local universe, 90% of which occurred in the past 3 Gyr. By comparing this with an older (13.7 billion year) estimate based on the evolution of the solar system's gold content, we conclude that the current SFR in the local universe is comparable to that of the last several billion years. These results provide crucial new constraints for models of star and galaxy formation in the universe.

The Casimir force is a long-range force arising from fluctuations in the quantum electromagnetic field that is caused by the boundary conditions. The Casimir force is important in microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and has been applied in nanotechnology to manipulate and stabilize nanomechanical systems. The origin of the Casimir force is the excitation of electromagnetic modes between the closely spaced boundaries. Therefore, changing the boundary conditions by the varying optical properties would change the Casimir force. In this work, the experimental approaches are demonstrated to change the Casimir force through the varying optical properties. Experimentally, the force is measured by using an atomic force microscope setup with a sphere and a plate as sample bodies. The sphere is composed of two layers of different materials and the plate is covered with distributed Bragg reflectors with different grating periods. The experimental data are compared with theoretical predictions and good agreements are obtained. Therefore, the experimental approaches presented in this work are feasible for varying the Casimir force by the varying optical properties and could be useful in the Casimir and many other applications.

The acceleration of the universe seems to be due to a mysterious force called dark energy, responsible for 70% of the universe. Dark energy has a unique property called gravity, which causes things to accelerate toward it. However, dark energy is supposed to be a constant, and this leads to a problem known as the cosmic coincidence problem. People think that this constant should not be sensitive to the local geometry and composition. However, recent work shows that if bubbles of false vacuum exist, then the gravity on them can change the acceleration of the universe locally, solving the coincidence problem. False vacuum bubbles are allowed by current theories, and are consistent with supernova data. This local change in the acceleration solves the cosmic coincidence problem. The detection of local acceleration change would confirm the theory of bubble-based dark energy, and this would be an exciting development for cosmology. The linearization of the Painleve' III-VI equations and the reductions of the three-wave resonant system are described. The Lax pair of the linearized Painleve' V equation is obtained. The additional symmetry and constraint conditions for the parameters of the reduced equations are obtained. The classical R- matrix for the reductions of the three-wave resonant system are constructed. use over 400 words. This quest to understand development has led to a great progress in modern stem cell research and a plethora of potential treatments for various medical conditions. A common goal of many of these treatments is to drive differentiation to form specialized cell types. In this work we present an alternative approach to cell differentiation using an electric field. We find that A253, a photoreceptor-inducing cell line derived from mouse embryonic stem cells, will adopt neuronal morphologies when exposed to an electric field in a consistent, predictable and scalable manner. Furthermore, we find that the neuronal cells exhibit sodium, potassium and calcium currents, supporting the idea that these cells are, in fact, neuronal. Finally, we validate that the exposed cells are capable of contributing to functional retinal tissue in vitro. This could have great implications for treating conditions like retinitis pigmentosa and bringing new therapies to patients through novel, scalable and inexpensive methods of differentiation.

In this paper we study the abstract functional analysis problem of whether a given multi-variable operator matrix is Schur. In particular, we give a characterization of Schurness for a set of multi-variable operator matrices which we call the Schur generalizations of the Schur class (SGS). We also study transfer function realization of the Schur generalized constant-Kirchhoff model (SGCK) and obtain a new, equivalent characterization of Schurness for this class of models. Our main tool is operator matrix intertwinning, which allows us to reduce many questions about operator matrices to questions about contraction semigroups. This is because, in our setting, operator matrix intertwinning is just matrix multiplication; and questions about contraction semigroups are classical and well-understood. We also make use of several classical results on the Schur class, particularly those of Bognár and Tropp.

In this paper we study a random splitting tree, that is a random tree where the vertices split their incident edges according to a random procedure. Such a random tree can be thought of as a growth model, where each vertex, upon growing, independently decides, according to a probability distribution, to split its incident edge in two. The contour of such a splitting tree is the shape that the tree has after growing to infinity. We are interested in the asymptotic shape of splitting trees, that is the limit of a random Galton-Watson tree conditioned on having a large number of vertices. We prove that the contour of such a conditioned tree is a Lévy process. We also give various recursive formulas for the expected height, width and volume of the contour, as well as various functional central limit theorems. Finally, we apply these results to the asymptotic shape of splitting trees with finite size conditioned on having a large number of vertices.

The shape of dark matter (DM) halos is a fundamental property, reflecting the complex process of DM aggregation and the effects of astrophysical processes such as hierarchical structure formation and feedback. The evolution of DM halos is simulated using a variety of numerical methods, making it possible to predict DM halo shape as a function of halo and orbital parameters. In this work, we present the first measurement of the effect of orbital parameters and chaos in DM halo structure. We find that orbits with similar properties to that of our local group result in triaxial, highly prolate halos, with degree 2 rotation – contrary to observations which imply spherical, axisymmetric halos in such configurations. Halos in more chaotic orbital scenarios are less well-aligned with observations: they are either nearly spherical, but with significant triaxiality, or are extremely prolate, but with lower degree of rotation. The evolution of DM halos in a given cosmological simulation is also often described using cosmological Principal Component Analysis. We show that the first two components of this multivariate distribution of halo properties are well-correlated with halo orbital anisotropy and chaos, providing a practical means of predicting the shape of DM halos in cosmological simulations.

The spin of carriers in semiconductor structures has recently attracted a lot of interest due to the possibility to generate and manipulate spin-polarized currents with the use of either magnetic or non-magnetic structures. The low-dimensionality of semiconductor systems, such as two-dimensional electron and hole gases (2DEG and 2DHG, respectively), plays a crucial role in spin-related phenomena. Despite many achievements in the study of electron systems, the role of the Luttinger term in the Kane model of the 2DHG has not been fully explored. We present a theoretical study of the resonant spin polarization in a 2DHG with the Luttinger term, structural inversion asymmetry and Zeeman splitting. We show that the resonant spin polarization excited by circularly polarized light depends on the light frequency and has multiple peaks, which are related to the light-induced modification of the Luttinger term. The presented results could be useful for the further experimental studies of spin-related phenomena in 2DHG systems.

A semi-detached configuration is an hierarchical multiple system in which a star is orbiting a more massive companion (the white dwarf or subdwarf core) in a close, circularized orbit. These systems are of particular interest in astrophysics, being among the lowest-mass binary stars. SS Leporis is a semi-detached binary system whose components are respectively a late-type (mainly K) star and a white dwarf. Such a system is spatially resolved for the first time with the VLTI instrument VINCI at sub-mas resolution, and its integrated diameter has been measured for the first time. The resulting value of the binary system is dSi=3.35±0.14 mas, corresponding to a projected physical separation of 2.65±0.13 × 10-4 solar radii. The measured value is in very good agreement with theoretical predictions (2.94 solar radii).

In this study, we have identified mitochondrial colorectal tumor (MCT) peptides that inhibit cancer cell proliferation. MCT1-5 were discovered using a functional genomics approach. MCT1-3 areSSL/CBM domains, a structural motif that is found in numerous protein families, including the ubiquitin-like Nedd8, autophagy-related MAP1-LC3, and rRNA-processing Lsg1/Rat8 families. The antiproliferative MCR peptides bind the insulin receptor (INSR) and inhibit the formation of the insulin-INSR complex, leading to dephosphorylation of RB, inhibition of cell cycle progression, and consequent antiproliferative effect. Cancer cells rely on the phospho-RB pathway to grow, so the MCRs represent a novel class of antiproliferative agents. Further characterization of MCR structures and functions may lead to new anticancer drugs. Gene names, MCT1, MCT2 and MCT3, refer to mitochondrial colorectal tumor genes 1, 2 and 3, respectively. These genes were discovered using a functional genomics approach. The antiproliferative MCR peptides bind the insulin receptor (INSR) and inhibit the formation of the insulin-INSR complex, leading to dephosphorylation of RB, inhibition of cell cycle progression, and consequent antiproliferative effect. Cancer cells rely on the phospho-RB pathway to grow, so the MCRs represent a novel class of antiproliferative agents. Further characterization of MCR structures and functions may lead to new anticancer drugs. Insulin and INSR are proteins that are involved in regulating human growth and development. MCRs, also called INSR/Ins peptide complexes, are able to bind insulin and prevent it from binding and activating its receptor, leading to reduced INSR tyrosine kinase activity and inhibition of insulin-dependent processes. One of the main physiological functions of insulin is cell proliferation. By blocking the binding of insulin to its receptor, MCRs inhibit cancer cell proliferation. The insulin-INSR complex is composed of two INSR polypeptides and two insulin molecules. The INSR proteins consist of an extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, and an intracellular domain that includes the tyrosine kinase domain. The INSR extracellular domain binds insulin and INSR transmembrane domain transmits the signal from the INSR cell membrane to the intracellular domain, leading to INSR tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation and downstream signaling. The antiproliferative effect of MCRs may be explained by dephosphorylation of RB. This inhibition is caused by the absence of the insulin-INSR complex and decreased INSR tyrosine kinase activity. Without tyrosine kinase activity, RB is dephosphorylated and cannot block cell cycle progression.

Exoplanet population studies suggest that around 10% of exoplanets have a substellar companion. If these substellar companions exist in close orbits around their stars, they can interact with their companion planets and induce stable long-period oscillations in the exoplanets' orbits. In this Letter, I use the induced long-period oscillations to prospect for these substellar companions with a next generation TESS mission. Assuming TESS observes a transiting planet around a G-type star every 2 weeks, I show I can detect nearby substellar companions with radii R≤0.35R⊕, where R⊕ is the Sun's radius, out to 10-20AU with a statistical significance of 6σ. These substellar companions can have a wide range of masses, from less than the Jupiter mass up to ten times the Earth mass. These prospects suggest that a TESS mission can test a significant population of substellar companions around transiting exoplanet host stars, and can serve as a precursor mission for future exploration of these systems with next-generation telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Extremely Large Telescope.

High Metallicity of the X-Ray Gas up to the Virial Radius of a Binary Cluster of Galaxies: Evidence of Galactic Superwinds at High-Redshift arXiv.org, @2017arXiv170701598M Measurements of the chemical composition of the high-redshift Universe are restricted to the locations of bright lensed galaxies and quasars, where the density of the intergalactic medium (IGM) is high enough to allow for the detection of metal lines. The gas in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of galaxies, on the other hand, is typically less dense and the metallicity of its chemical constituents is potentially severely diluted. We present X-ray absorption spectroscopy of the O VII edge of a cluster of galaxies at a redshift of z = 0.194, obtained with the Reflection Grating Spectrometer (RGS) on board XMM-Newton. We detect strong O VII absorption lines up to a radius of 2.1 Mpc from the cluster center. The high metallcities, as derived from the line measurements, of up to 7% solar indicate the presence of enriched gas outflows from the clusters galaxies with very low volume filling factor and high Mach number. Such winds are typically observed in local clusters, but not before z = 0.194. The low volume filling factor and the high velocity of the gas clouds imply substantial kinetic energy and mass outflow rates, of the order of 1042 erg s−1 and 1003 M⊙ year−1, respectively. The energy and mass loading factors are comparable to those found in local superwinds and quasar feedback. The discovery of superwinds at high-redshift demonstrates the importance of these processes in the evolution of the cosmic environment and the growth of structure.

We present the third and final paper in a series studying the Homunculus on the Eta Carinae star. The Homunculus is a strong, bipolar shock-generated optical nebula encircling the stellar core and formed in a major outburst about a century ago. In the first paper, we described how previous studies had shown the Homunculus to be most clearly represented as an oblate spheroid, with a major axis of 17 – 20 and a flattening of 0.33 – 0.4. In this third paper, we investigate the dynamical structure of the Homunculus by modeling it as a rotating gas torus, i.e. a donut. The Homunculus has been known to be highly asymmetric since its discovery, with a prominent hourglass-shaped front and a wide, wavering, bipolar back. These latter two features suggest that the Homunculus has a bipolar outflow along its axis of symmetry. By modeling the Homunculus as a donut and assuming that the equator rotates much faster than the poles, we have found that such a bipolar outflow can naturally produce the hourglass shape and wavering width seen in the Homunculus. In fact, our models with fast equator rotation (approximately 250 km s-1) very closely reproduce both the Homunculus shape and wavering width. We thus conclude that the Homunculus must have a fast, bipolar outflow along the rotation axis, likely resulting from the main outburst some hundred years ago.

In this paper we report the first Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) calculation of the groundstate of positronium. Using the multiscale method we solve the relativistic Schroedinger equation for positronium including the first relativistic corrections, i.e., 1S-2S splitting, Bethe logarithm and annihilation correction. We obtain the 1S-2S spacing of 2.75(5) eV which is in agreement with the recent experimental value of 2.75(5) eV. We predict the 1S groundstate energy as 2.57(3) eV which is in agreement with the most accurate experimental value, 2.54(3) eV. Additionally, we compute the positronium groundstate charge radius which is in excellent agreement with the most accurate experimental measurement, 0.77(8) fm. Furthermore, we provide the first non-perturbative QED prediction for the groundstate total lepton pair transition charge radius of 0.80(3) fm.

In this article we present a rigorous mapping between the Ising spin glass models and the Ising models in the long temperature range, where the former only exhibit disordered behavior. The proof is based on the so-calledyss Hamiltonian decomposition, which allows one to write the partition function of the spin glass model as a product of simpler terms, each corresponding to a particular configuration of frozen spins. The nature of the frozen spins implies that the couplings between corresponding terms in the Ising and spin glass models are positive, and thus the whole product has to be positive, allowing us to restrict the consideration to positive Boltzmann weights, which greatly simplifies the analysis. The mapping is carried out for general graphs, meaning that the underlying lattice structure is not specified. We expect the following direct implications of the presented results: 1. The existence of a zero temperature phase transition in the Ising and spin glass models with proper choice of parameters is equivalent. 2. The critical behavior at the zero temperature phase transition of the Ising and spin glass models is identical. 3. The dynamical behavior of the systems at low temperature is related in the following way: The dynamical behavior of the corresponding Ising models at low temperature regime is characterized by a spontaneous breaking of the global $Z_2$ symmetry (spin inversion). However, for spin glasses, this global $Z_2$ symmetry is broken at any finite temperature due to the presence of frozen spins. The spontaneous breaking of the $Z_2$ symmetry at finite temperature indicates the lack of rigidity of the frozen spins, namely the de Almeida-Thouless (AT) line of the phase transition in the dynamical behavior of the spin glasses. We also provide a number of technical results, such as the explicit freezing probability bounds, which are likely to be useful for further studies.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are powered by black holes in their nuclei, whose masses are inferred from the velocity width of their broad emission lines. A method to substantially increase the distance precision of these lines is to consider them as part of an ensemble of supermassive black holes with a single parameter, the Eigenvector 1. The Eigenvector 1 is a dimensionless principal axis vector that aggregates information about the orientation and strength of various observable properties of an AGN. One of these properties is the width of the C IV emission line, which is in turn related to the velocity width of the broad emission line region. It is shown that if the width of the C IV emission line is included as a parameter, the Eigenvector 1 can account for 99.7% of the variation in the full set of Eigenvector 1 parameters. Therefore, this suggests that C IV emission line widths may be an accurate way to estimate the masses of supermassive black holes in AGN, with a relative distance precision of 4.2%. The Eigenvector 1 also predicts a tight relationship between the width of C IV and the width of H$\beta$, and this is also observed. Finally, this paper presents a new Eigenvector 1 quasar catalog, which includes 9948 quasars from the 5月新版 AGN Eigenvector 1 parameters and accurate relative distance estimates, and is available at https://wac.asna.org/code/new/civ.php.

Nonlinear oscillators based on semiconductor microcavities provide an excellent testbed for studying chaos, bifurcations, and non-linear effects1-3. An external periodic force, which can be applied either optically or electrically, can induce complicated and interesting behaviors4-7. In this Letter, we report a dynamics-controlled truncation scheme to find high-dimensional chaotic attractors in the semiconductor laser with a saturable absorber. By introducing a dynamics-dependent truncation procedure, long transient chaotic orbits are truncated by chaotic solutions of low-dimensional truncation systems. With this truncation scheme, we are able to observe novel dynamical behaviors in semiconductor laser with a saturable absorber, such as intermittency and bifurcations from torus to strange attractor. Our method can also be applied to any high-dimensional nonlinear system. We study the semiconductor laser with saturable absorber and external periodic force (SA+EFP). The laser dynamics can be described by the following equations7: +j0=σ(I+Iref)−(1−σ)I−j(γ+β|A|2)|A|^2+η(t); [1] where A is the complex field, and Iref, γ, β, σ, and η(t) are the reference current, gain loss, feedback gain, feedback loss, and time dependent perturbation, respectively. |A| is the magnitude of |A| and is proportional to the intensity of the optical field. By setting the external pump at the desired frequency, the laser dynamics can be reduced to a one dimensional map (1DMA), which is composed of two terms. The first term describes the phase dynamics, while the second term describes the intensity dynamics. In our simulation, we choose the parameters γ = 2 and β = 4, and the saturable loss coefficient σ = 0.8. By setting the modulation of external periodic force to be a limit-cycle oscillation, a chaotic attractor in 1DMA can be obtained. If the dynamics of the full model is truncated at a particular dimension, it is possible to observe long transient chaotic orbits in 1DMA. In addition, we can still observe the existence of limit-cycle oscillation in the truncated system. However, the truncation dimension controls the transient time of the chaotic orbit. If the truncation dimension is high, the transient chaotic orbit is long. If the transient chaotic orbit is long, we are able to observe more interesting dynamical behaviors. For example, if the transient chaotic orbit is long enough, it is possible to observe intermittency and bifurcations from torus to strange attractor. In contrast, if the transient chaotic orbit is too short, the dynamical behavior of the laser can not be observed.

Massive young stellar objects (MYSOs) are among the most luminous and turbulent objects in the interstellar medium, yet their complex structures and transition to rich stellar clusters makes them challenging to study. In this letter, we present a multi-epoch high-frequency radio continuum study of a sample of 38 MYSOs. These sources were chosen to be strong water masers, potential signposts of high-mass star formation. We find a high incidence of positive spectral index gradients (approximately half the sample), which are often large and exhibit variability on timescales of weeks. We interpret this as variability of the free-free emission primarily arising from shocks excited by protostellar outflows and jets, in agreement with recent findings at lower frequencies. We also find a large population of sources with negative spectral index gradients, likely arising from free-free emission from ionized accreting material. The infrared luminosity, inferred mass accretion rate, and spectral gradient characteristics of this sample suggest that many of these sources may be in the process of transitioning from MYSO to either evolved star with an ionized inner disk, or to a less massive star with a circumstellar disk.

Recent years have seen an explosion of data describing three-dimensional (3D) chromatin folding in the human genome. The consequences of this folding on the human genome function and its regulation are only beginning to be understood. We performed a broad analysis of chromatin folding with respect to a number of the key features of the human genome including gene density, repeat content, CpG island location, and replication timing, with the goal of identifying any potentially interesting patterns or relationships. We found that chromatin folding is positively correlated with gene density and negatively correlated with repeat content. Additionally, folding over genic regions is enriched in active histone modifications, particularly those related to transcription initiation, but depleted of repressive histone modifications. Folding over CpG islands is depleted of both activating and repressive histone modifications but is depleted of nucleosomes. Finally, the early- replicating regions of the human genome exhibit depleted 3D folding. Together, these data suggest that chromatin folding is permissive for the underlying genomic function but also facilitates some level of localized regulation.

Puncturing is a simple technique to improve the performance of turbo coding. It has been known for a long time that one can construct a simple systematic single parity check (SPCH) code that can approach the Shannon limit. However, constructing good random puncturing patterns is a difficult problem. In this paper, a pseudo-random puncturing pattern is proposed. The performance of turbo coding with this pattern is compared to conventional turbo coding with fixed puncturing patterns. It is shown that the new puncturing pattern significantly reduces the error floor without causing any noticeable performance degradation. This work was done at ETRI. Reference: 1. A. G. i. A. Almansoori, A. Al-Shater, and D. D. Falconer, "Pseudo-random Puncturing: A Technique to Lower the Error Floor of Turbo Codes," IEEE Communications Letters, vol. 17, no. 8, pp. 934-937, Aug. 2013.

Recent years have witnessed a significant surge of research activities in the area of quantum many-body systems. Particularly, the theoretical understanding of quantum phase transitions in such systems has significantly improved. In this work, we study a two-channel Kondo necklace model, describing a system of interacting magnetic atoms locally threaded by a magnetic flux. We employ an extended dynamical mean field theory framework to obtain the phase diagram and the thermodynamic properties of this model. We observe a quantum phase transition from a flux-free non-Kondo (NCK) phase to a Kondo necklace (KN) phase with increasing hybridization strength. Interestingly, the NCK phase is also a quantum-flux insulator, where magnetic flux insertion results in a discontinuous quantum phase transition to the KN phase. We compute and discuss the temperature-dependent electrical and thermoelectric conductivities across different phases of the model. We find that, at zero magnetic flux insertion, while the KN phase exhibits an anomalous vanishing thermopower, NCK exhibits a sharp, non-monotonic behavior with a peak at a finite temperature which signals a first-order quantum phase transition to the KN phase.

In this paper, we report on the performances of the MEGAPIE target, which is a central design for the GS2040E case (2 MW net power output). A substantial neutronics study was carried out for the first time for such a high temperature reactor configuration. Results were also compared with the simulations made for the actual design. Neutronic performances of the MEGAPIE target were found in good agreement with the actual design, with a DSA of 4.1% and a 3% level averagedteam pair space and momentum divergence. In addition, results showed that the hydrogen control rod have a strong impact on the reactivity and neutron economy of the core. The optimized configuration of the MEGAPIE target, called MEGAPIE+ is finally proposed. The MEGAPIE+ core configuration has been shown to perform close to the optimal one in terms of thermal efficiency, while improving the neutronics performances, thus leading to a significant reduction of the weight and the DSA.

Uranium is a heavy metal, which makes it potentially interesting as a coating material for electromagnetic components. Its major drawback is that it is toxic. This paper presents the results of an investigation into multilayer coatings based on uranium. The first stage of the study, fabrication and structural characterisation, is addressed in this paper. Coatings were fabricated by a wet method, and their structure was characterised using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. It was shown that the obtained coatings had cubic structure and contained uranium in the form of Cerenkov radiation. The proposed coating structure was shown to have good corrosion resistance. This work was carried out within the scope of the "Regional Initiative of Excellence", research project number 4-0192/2016/RRC of Rosario University. I. Fabrication and structural characterisation

This paper presents an analysis of the stability of parallel kinematic machine tools, and introduces the kinetostatic performance criteria as a way to design such machine tools to have improved stability. The kinematic equations for a serial machine and a parallel machine are modified to include inertia terms, and the resulting set of equations is called the kinematically coupled equations. The stability of a serial machine and a parallel machine are analyzed in terms of the eigenvalues of the kinematically coupled equations at a singular point, and it is shown that if the inertia values are chosen such that the secant and tangent stiffnesses are the same for both machines, then the parallel machine will be more stable. Using this criterion, a set of machine parameters is chosen for a particular machine tool design, and the resulting machine is shown to have improved stability over the machine designed using traditional criteria. The kinematically coupled equations presented in this paper may also be used to design other machine tools, such as those with flexible joints, where the inertia values can be assigned judiciously to achieve the same.

Cosmic rays are ionizing particles from the universe. They are mainly generated by explosive events such as supernova explosions or active galaxies. Their energy spectrum, measured at the Earth, exhibits a steep energy dependence with a power-law index of about -3. With the help of the analyzed data from the Fermi LAT detector, it was possible to determine the energy spectra of 12 different supernova remnants. The obtained spectra are in accordance with the predicted spectrum of particles, which is formed due to nuclear collisions of cosmic-ray nuclei in the interstellar medium. The presented results also serve as a basis for the discussion of the mechanisms of acceleration of cosmic rays on the galactic scale and for establishing correlations between the spectra of various cosmic-ray sources and the distribution of different gas clouds in the universe. In August 2015, the LAT (Large Area Telescope) on board the Fermi gamma-ray space telescope had detected gamma rays from 12 regions of the sky, corresponding to several supernova remnants (SNRs). From this data, the authors were able to deduce the energy spectrum of these particles. The spectrum they observed is in good agreement with the spectrum that is expected from nuclear collisions of cosmic-ray particles in the interstellar medium. The results also show that the spectrum of these particles can be used to study the mechanisms of acceleration of these particles on a galactic scale and for establishing correlations between the spectra of various cosmic-ray sources and the distribution of different gas clouds in the universe. Since their discovery in 1954, the energy spectrum of cosmic rays has been extensively studied. It is known to have a sharp increase in energy, with a power-law index of around -3. Through various research methods, scientists have identified many sources that generate these particles, including supernova explosions and active galaxies. These particles affect the biosphere and the environment in which they land, and have long been believed to play a fundamental role in the formation of planets and stars. With the Fermi gamma-ray space telescope, it was possible to detect gamma rays from 12 regions of the sky corresponding to several supernova remnants. By modeling these gamma-ray signals, the spectrum of these particles could be deduced for the first time on a regional scale. The results show that the spectrum of these particles exhibits a great variation over space: while in some cases the spectrum can be fitted with a single power law, in other cases multiple power laws were found to be necessary to fit the data. Moreover, the spectrum of some remnants exhibited a high-energy cutoff, which is generally believed to be evidence of acceleration of these particles in the galaxy. Using these data, the energy spectrum of these particles could be deduced for the first time on a regional scale. The spectrum of these particles exhibits a steep energy dependence with a power law index of -3. In this paper, we study a hybrid cellular automaton (CA) model of cell colony growth. The model is a combination of a classical CA model for self-organized aggregation process and a Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piscounov (FKPP) type reaction-diffusion equation for pattern formation. The model exhibits two distinct dynamic behaviors: a stable pattern and a wave-fragile pattern, depending on the values of model parameters. In the former case, the model shows a usual aggregative behavior: a stable pattern is formed by the local cell-cell collision-driven aggregation process and remains stable against small perturbations. In the latter case, however, the system shows a wave-fragile pattern: a stable pattern is formed by the local aggregation process but is spontaneously broken into small clusters via a (directed) wave propagation. The model parameters corresponding to the wave-fragile pattern are very sensitive to small changes. We conduct a linear stability analysis of both patterns and clarify the condition of each pattern's stability.

There has been debate over the formation pathway of S0 galaxies, with most models favouring their formation from spirals following a merger. This presents a challenge, as mergers are rare. An alternative formation pathway is for S0s to be stripped of their gas and stars as they wander through cosmological environments. In this model, S0s form from spiral galaxies, but the stars remain in their globular clusters after the process of stripping. Here we present evidence for this model, as we detect stellar populations in the globular clusters of three S0 galaxies, each with many globular clusters that are spatially distinct from their spiral galaxy hosts. We also compare the metallicities of the globular clusters in the three galaxies to that of their spiral galaxy host. The metallicities of the globular clusters in the S0s are consistent with those of the spirals, and suggest that the formation of S0 galaxies did not solely occur through merger events. We propose that the S0s in our sample were formed through stripping of their globular clusters.

In recent years, a number of high precision numerical simulations of the early universe have been performed, generating large datasets describing the spatio-temporal structure of the initially small density fluctuations. Whilst these datasets have proven valuable in themselves for understanding the evolution of the early universe, it has become increasingly clear that fully interpreting them in the light of modern observational cosmology requires comparison with the large body of observational data which is also becoming available. To this end, it has been proposed to gather these simulation datasets from across the entire community in order that they can be organized, classified, marked up with defining metadata and made available for statistical analysis; this has come to be known as the Cosmic Code Comparison Project. The proposal to set up such a collaboration has been adopted by the international community in the form of the Cowboy 2015 cosmology simulation challenge, which will provide a simulated dataset (as well as associated metadata) to participants of the C3 project. In this paper, we describe the motivation, planning and implementation of this ambitious international collaboration.

Modules with a finite number of composition factors are called finitely determined. In this paper we characterize regular modules of the form R(a,b) for rational numbers a,b. It turns out that a regular R(a,b)-module is finite unless a is an integer and b is a positive integer multiple of ap-1 for some positive integer p. A module is regular if every cyclic submodule is generated by a single element. Every finitely generated regular (a,b)-module is a shift of a module R(p,b) for some integer p. As an application, we show that if a is not an integer and R(a,b) is a semisimple module, then b is a positive integer multiple of a(p−1) for some integer p. mawr In this paper we characterize regular modules of the form R(a,b) for rational numbers a,b. There has been a growing consensus that active galactic nuclei (AGN) can be spatially and spectrally variable on many different time scales, from years to decades. Such long-term variability is believed to be caused by structural changes in the nucleus, such as moving clouds around a supermassive black hole (SMBH) or changes in the scale height of the accretion disk. Here, we report on the results of a systematic statistical analysis of long-term variability of AGN at cm radio frequencies. We have assembled a large sample of 22 AGN observed with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) at 8.4 GHz, which is composed of 14 BL Lac objects, seven quasars, and one blazar of unknown classification. The total observing time spanned by our data set is 18,642 hours, and the time resolution is 62.5 minutes. We tested for intraday variability (IDV) in the form of changes in flux density on time scales of minutes to hours. We found no evidence of IDV in any of the 22 objects during our monitoring, with the most stringent upper limits for 13 of the objects at the 2σ level. To search for longer-term variations, we also examined the entire 18,642-hour dataset using a continuous wavelet transform. We found statistically significant variability on time scales of days to months in 14 of the 22 objects. We interpret this variability as being due to structural changes in the accretion disk and/or close to the SMBH. For comparison, we also analyzed archival data from VLBI observations of 22 AGN at 5 GHz and found variability on time scales of days to decades in 20 of the objects. Our work suggests that AGN exhibit more pronounced long-term variability at cm than at cm radio frequencies. We speculate that this may be caused by synchrotron self-absorption becoming more important at lower frequencies.

A clustering algorithm based on soft-constraint affinity propagation is proposed. Unlike most existing algorithms that optimize a binary objective function, it solves an initial problem by partitioning the vertices of a soft affinity graph and uses a continuous optimization framework to further refine the partitions. In this framework, the similarity between vertices is modeled by a soft affinity and used to measure the quality of partitions. An affinity propagation based approach is employed to optimize the similarity by allowing a vertex to move along its soft neighborhood's similarity gradient. It has been applied to several real-world data sets, where it is shown to perform favorably compared with other state-of-the-art algorithms. gain, the algorithm can also be applied to data with discrete attributes, as long as the attributes are encoded as vertices in a graph, and can be effectively clustered using traditional algorithms. put, the presented algorithm has a good performance and easy to be implemented.

We present the results of timing observations of the ultra-compact X-ray binary 1A 1246-588 performed with the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories in 2012-2013. We detect a 1258 Hz high-amplitude kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) in the timing spectra. The QPO has a peak amplitude of 40% in the 10-1000 Hz frequency range and a centroid frequency of 1258 Hz. These results suggest that 1A 1246-588 contains a neutron star with a rotational period of approximately 690 msec. eferences 1. The astrophysical S-factor for the 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be reaction has been measured via prompt and delayed gamma detection down to the 0.862 MeV gamma energy (T = 0.28 KeV) of the 7Be ground state, for neutron energies between E_n = 20 and 1000 keV. The combined sensitivity and precision of the present measurement is uniquely capable of testing current three-body models of nova reaction rates. This benchmark measurement of the 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be S-factor will also significantly impact future nova nucleosynthesis simulations. The 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be reaction is important in the r-process nucleosynthesis pathway. Specifically, the 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be reaction is one of only two nuclear reactions that directly link protons toneutrons in the nucleus chart, and thus its rate strongly impacts the expected abundance of lead in the universe. The 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be S-factor has been the subject of many past experiments, but the majority of past measurements were made at higher neutron energies, thus missing the 0.862 MeV gamma of the 7Be ground state. The results presented here represent the most sensitive and precise measurement of the 3He(alpha,gamma)7Be S-factor to date, with an estimated total experimental uncertainty of less than 25%.

In the past few years, some discrepancies between the Standard Model (SM) predictions and the $B \to K \pi$ observables have been observed, such as the tree-levelatively large $K^* \pi$ mode fraction in $B \to K^* \pi \pi$ and the sizable $ K \pi$ mode fraction in $B \to K \pi$. These observations have led to extensive discussions about potential new physics (NP) contributions to such decay modes. In this paper, we provide a systematic and model-independent analysis on these two important processes, $B \to K^* \rho$ and $B \to K \pi$, within and beyond the SM. First, we show that within the large recoil region, $B \to K^* \rho$ can also receive sizable NP contributions. If one combines it with $B \to K \pi$, a NP scenario with sizable contributions to both $B \to K \pi$ and $B \to K^* \rho$ is favored by the present data. We then provide such a scenario, which involves tensor operators and a CP-violating phase, and is also compatible with the current $B \to K \pi$ data. In order to further confirm this scenario or to probe new physics scenarios beyond it, more precise measurements of $B \to K \pi$ are needed, such as the ones from LHCb, Belle II and super B factories.

Hypre and PETSc are popular packages for large linear system solution. BLOPEX is a new algorithm for solving locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problem, which is efficiently implemented in hypre and PETSc. BLOPEX preconditioned conjugate gradient (CG) is the best-scored method on the partition of local problems on all tested distributed cluster systems. BLOPEX also exhibits good performance on hypre CG with optimal preconditioner and multigrid preconditioned Krylov solver. A thorough performance study using both synthetic and real matrices shows that BLOPEX is the state-of-the-art solver for partitioned locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problems. BLOPEX solves locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problems using the conjugate gradient method. The search direction is obtained by preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) with a (locally) optimal preconditioner. The proposed BLOPEX algorithm is implemented in two popular software packages, hypre and PETSc. BLOPEX is tested on both synthetic and real matrices and it is shown that BLOPEX is the state-of-the-art solver for partitioned locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problems. In this paper, we present a detailed performance study of BLOPEX using both synthetic and real matrices. We show that BLOPEX is the fastest solver for many problems. This makes BLOPEX the state-of-the-art solver for partitioned locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problems. In particular, BLOPEX is shown to be highly scalable, being the best-scored method on partitioned locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problems on all tested distributed cluster systems. It exhibits good performance on both hypre CG with optimal preconditioner and multigrid preconditioned Krylov solver. A thorough performance study using both synthetic and real matrices shows that BLOPEX is the state-of-the-art solver for partitioned locally optimal preconditioned eigenvalue problems. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we give the problem formulation and a brief overview of existing preconditioned eigenvalue solvers. In section 3, we describe our BLOPEX algorithm in detail. In section 4, we present the numerical results. Finally, we give a short summary in section 5.

M82F is an extremely young, massive cluster associated with the starburst galaxy M82. It was identified in archival data from the Digitized Sky Survey (DSS) and subsequently observed with the ACS and WFPC2 instruments on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). The high spatial resolution and sensitivity of these observations have allowed for the measurement of multiple structural and star-formation parameters of M82F, which have not been well constrained in previous studies. We find that M82F is a very compact ($r_{1/2}\approx11$ pc), highly prolate ($\epsilon=1.5$), and super star cluster in formation with an estimated current stellar mass of $M\sim3\times10^5 M_\odot$ and an estimated age of $\tau\sim2.2$ Myr. We also detect evidence of two older ($>2$ Myr) populations of stars in the form of spatially distinct populations (SDPs). The younger SDPs are concentrated within a central $r\lesssim3$ pc, whereas the older SDPs are more extended and roughly follow the overall light profile of M82F. The two-aged structure has not been observed in previous massive clusters, and it is likely the result of the elevated star formation rates in M82. We suggest that the presence of two populations of stars is the likely cause for the unusually blue colors of M82F. The combination of its prolate morphology and two-aged structure suggest that M82F may have recently undergone a merger event, which could have triggered intense nuclear star formation.

Modern techniques have been used to calculate the electronic properties of carbon nanotubes (CNTs). These techniques include the density functional theory (DFT) as implemented in the SIESTA code and the empirical pi-Bond model. The properties calculated include the band structure, work function, the adsorption and dispersion energies, charge density analyses, and the eigenfunctions of the isolated nanotube, which is used to calculate the Zitterbewegung oscillations. The calculated properties are compared with available experimental data and other theories. The merits and deficiencies of the different techniques are discussed. The DFT-based pi-Bond model gives a good description of the electronic structure of carbon nanotubes. One of the most critical phase transitions in the history of the universe was the so-called reionization of the universe. While the Gunn-Peterson trough in the spectrum of luminous objects indicates that the Epoch of Reionization (EoR) was likely complete by a redshift of 8-10, its exact timing and extent remain uncertain. Here we present constraints on the timing and topology of ionized regions across the entire volume of the early universe, derived from the large-scale structure of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), independently of any model for the ionization process. Using the South Pole Telescope, Advanced 148-Reuons Telescope, Atacama Cosmology Telescope,QUIJOTE Telescope and the Polarbear Telescope, we detect large-angle polarization on angular scales of 5 x 10 arcminutes, corresponding to a physical scale of 1.5 x 10 (14/H) centimeters at z = 8-10. By modeling these signal foregrounds, we place 95% confidence level upper limits on large-angle intrinsic CMB polarization of P = 2.3 x 10(-5) on scales of 30 arcminutes and P = 2.0 x 10(-4) on scales of 5 x 10 arcminutes. We show that the latter limit, derived from the recently reported detection of large-angle CMB polarization, already places the strongest independent constraints on EoR duration and topology to date, equivalent to only a 1% ionized fraction on small scales and 50% ionization at large scales. By comparing this limit with predictions from cosmological radiative transfer simulations, we estimate that the EoR was likely completed by a redshift of z > 9.5 (95% confidence), lying somewhere between 9 and 10, with a large island of partial reionization likely present by z = 10.5. In addition, this limit provides the most stringent constraints to date on the duration and topology of EoR ionization on small scales. Future improvements in sensitivity from next-generation CMB observatories, such as the Simons Observatory and the Probe satellite, will improve these constraints by an order of magnitude, providing powerful new probes of early structure and new contraints on EoR models.

We study chaotic behavior in classical solutions of string cosmology. In the light of string theory, the early universe is regarded as a four-dimensional transient region of a higher-dimensional universe. Hence, there is a potential for chaotic behavior in the string frame. We find, for a wide range of initial conditions, that the string frame solution exhibits exponential divergence from the initial conditions. However, this is not sufficient to show chaos, since the physical frame solutions can converge exponentially to themselves. We give a detailed example of this behavior, using a new self-similar solution of the string frame equations. We also discuss the phenomenon of symmetry breaking in the classical solutions of string cosmology. In the light of string theory, the early universe is regarded as a four-dimensional transient region of a higher-dimensional universe. Hence, we expect that the four-dimensional geometry of the universe will exhibit both explicit and spontaneous symmetries. Classical solutions exhibit both trivial and non-trivial isometries, and for non-trivial isometries, we can distinguish between exact and spontaneously broken symmetries. Exact symmetries form a group, and the order of this group is an important issue for cosmology. We find that in the case of the self-similar solution described above, the group of exact isometries is $SL(2,\mathbb{R})\times SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ (in two different vector representations), and that the order of the corresponding Lie group is eight. This means that the solution exhibits explicit symmetry breaking. On the other hand, the spontaneously broken gauge symmetries are $U(1)\times U(1)$, and we argue that this is the correct group structure for the early universe in string cosmology. Finally, we use the string frame self-similar solution to estimate the fate of the chaotic behavior in string cosmology. In particular, we study the time evolution of the Weyl scalar curvature, which plays an important role in studying chaos in string cosmology. When the Weyl curvature is small, the string frame solution exhibits exponential divergence. However, for realistic models of the early universe, this Weyl curvature becomes large. If the Weyl curvature is large at late times, then we can use the Friedmann equations to show that the density of string frame radiation and matter is exponentially small in the future. Hence, chaotic behavior in string cosmology is transient, and in the presence of realistic sources, chaotic behavior will ultimately be diluted away.

We present narrow-band imaging and Keck spectra of the nuclei of three low-redshift active galaxies with central surface brightnesses lower than ~28 mag arcsec−2, selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). All three galaxies contain massive (~4–7 × 1010 M ☉ ) young (<1 Myr) starbursts, with typical mass fractions of ~5%, concentrated in the central 500–1000 pc. These are among the most intense (in terms of spatial density) and young starburst regions identified in local galaxies, and may represent the nuclear super-star clusters (SCCs) of "transition type" galaxies (see, e.g., Dowsett et al. 2011). The masses and compact sizes of these starbursts are strongly reminiscent of those in local galaxies that are undergoing or have recently undergone a major merger event. The star formation rates (SFRs) of these starbursts are consistent with those expected from the global Schmidt laws of their host galaxies, assuming a typical gas density and depletion time at the centers of galaxies.

Baumslag-Solitar groups are a generalization of a well-known quotient of the free group. In this paper, we present a duality approach to study representations of Baumslag-Solitar groups. More precisely, we prove that for any positive integer m, every representation of the one-relator group with m relation is dual to a (possibly different) representation of the abelianization of the group. Using this duality, we recover some well-known results about one-relator groups with integer relations as particular cases. We also deduce some stability results for representations of Baumslag-Solitar groups. We use our duality to study a question on hereditarily just-infinite groups. A group G is called hereditarily just-infinite if every subgroup of G is either just-infinite or finite. Hereditarily just-infinite groups are a generalisation of just-infinite groups. We prove that if a one-relator group with torsion is hereditarily just-infinite, then its abelianization is an elementary amenable group, which is a direct generalisation of a classical theorem of Mal’cev.

Nuclear fragmentation has been studied extensively over many decades, both experimentally and theoretically. The basic premise is that a nuclei breaks up into pieces in a process known as nuclear fragmentation. Both strong and electromagnetic interactions are involved, depending on the mass and charge of the nucleus. Many particles and fragments are created and each of these particles or fragments carry a certain amount of the original nuclei's kinetic energy, which can be expressed as a magnitude of kinetic energy per nucleon. This article presents a study of nuclear fragmentation patterns of $^{9}$Be, $^{14}$N, $^{7}$Be, and $^{8}$B nuclei as recorded in their alpha decay. It has been observed that $^9$Be, $^{14}$N, $^{7}$Be, and $^{8}$B alpha decay nuclei tend to break up into groups of three particles, with the third particle being the lightest of the four. In the case of $^9$Be and $^{14}$N, two of these three fragments have nearly the same mass, with the third fragment being lighter. In the case of $^{7}$Be and $^{8}$B, the two nearly equal mass particles are always the two lightest particles, while the third particle is typically either lighter or of an intermediate mass. This phenomenon is not fully understood, but is a subject of this study.

In this paper, we discuss the microscopic origin of non-isotropic dissipation in the surface layers of mesoscopic superconductors. The anisotropy stems from the structure of the spectrum of surface electrons and manifests itself in a non-isotropic thermal decay of quasiparticles excited by external forces in the surface layers. We argue that the anisotropy of the electron scattering in the surface layers of superconductors with an effective (Mg,Ti)B2 structure results from the variation of the interatomic distance in the perpendicular to the surface layers. We show that in the framework of the developed model it is possible to describe the main experimental data on non-isotropic thermal decay of quasiparticles in Nb and Al thin films with a good accuracy. The proposed microscopic mechanism of the non-isotropic quasiparticle decay in superconductors with an effective (Mg,Ti)B2 structure can be applied to the analysis of a wide range of physical effects in these materials, including the physics of superconducting current distribution over the surface and spontaneous magnetic field generation.

In this paper, we argue that the geometry of musical distances—the patterns in which musical distances vary across a composition—reflects fundamental aspects of the composition. We develop a method for quantifying these distances using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), and show that the resulting distance matrices carry interpretable structure that reflects musical meaning. We apply this method to representative samples of classical, jazz, and rock music, and find that different genres are characterized by distinct distances, and that these distances are robust to time period, composer, and world region. We also find that musical distances are stable over time for the same musical compositions, and that they are correlated with a variety of extrinsic musical variables, including sheet music duration, recording technology, and awards won. Finally, we demonstrate that these distances cluster together in distinct groups that correspond to genre, and show that this classification is superior to that produced by traditional music theory classification. Overall, we provide evidence that the geometry of musical distances provides information about musical meaning that is not fully captured by existing metrics of musical similarity, and that this information can be applied to large corpora of musical compositions.

In this work we study a particular stochastic process associated to a convex function of the entropy for a class of Markov chains. The associated flow of probability measures satisfies a partial differential equation, where the gradient is represented by an entropy-entropy dominated dynamics. We prove that the correlation decay exponentially fast provided the corresponding logarithmic Sobolev Inequality is satisfied. This work extends a previous result by Menottini and Oliveira, who considered the particular case in which the dynamics are driven by the Kullback-Leibler distance. The entropy-entropy dominated dynamics, or Fokker-Planck equation in weak form, appears in a natural way in the calculus of variations problem associated to the entropy. This kind of dynamics has been used to describe the evolution of probability measures, corresponding to a dynamical system involving a large number of particles. In this framework, an important case of entropy-entropy dominated dynamics corresponds to the Kullback-Leibler dynamics, which was already analyzed in the one-dimensional case in a series of papers by Rössler and Kurtz. In this work we consider the more general case of the convex function of the entropy, and the multidimensional case. We also include a detailed proof of exponential correlation decay. The result that we present here can be seen as an extension of a previous result by Menottini and Oliveira (2014), who considered the particular case in which the dynamics are driven by the Kullback-Leibler distance. Cosmic rays interact with gas to produce a range of chemical products. In this work we show that this process also modifies the elemental composition of the gas. We apply our model to the gas observed in the prsent day universe and show that, although the Xelement enhancement is typically much lower than in high-z systems, it is able to reproduce the general trend. Finally we show that the evolution of the enhancement depends strongly on the shape of the cosmic ray spectrum at low energy. We apply our model to a broad range of spectra and show that different spectra lead to Xelement enhancements at the level of $10^{-3} - 1$ solar values at $z = 0$ for different metallicities at $10^{-4}$ solar values. This wide range of possible enhancements highlights the importance of experimental studies of the early evolution of the Universe. We describe an effect whereby the interactions between cosmic rays and the primordial gas influence both the gas phase and the element abundances. This has important implications for the potentiality of the gas to form structures and for the evolution of the heavy element abundance with time. We apply our model to the gas observed in the present-day Universe and show that although the general trend of the Xelement enhancement is lower than in high-redshift systems, it is still sufficient to reproduce the general trend. We also show that the evolution of the enhancement strongly depends on the shape of the cosmic ray spectrum at low energy. Our work highlights the importance of experimental studies of the early evolution of the Universe and the need to obtain a better understanding of processes occurring at low energies, such as the interaction between cosmic rays and the gas in the early universe. We provide a formalism for computing the evolution of the chemical abundances, including the element abundance enhancement, starting from a given ionisation and chemical networks and a given spectrum of cosmic rays. The results of the calculations are self-consistent as they can be fed back into the ionisation and chemical networks. The new networks have to be specified in terms of the twelve essential reactions needed to generate the sixteen molecules containing a significant fraction of the enhanced elements and a full network for eleven further elements (B, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, K, Ca, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, Mo, Ta, W, Re, Ru, Os, Hg, Tl, Pb, Bi, and Po). The updated chemical composition can strongly impact the cooling/heating rates of the gas, the star formation, and the gravitational collapse and further enrichment of the gas. The effects described in this work are not restricted to the epoch of reionization but extend to any time in the history of the gas, until the gas is removed from the simulation by some feedback mechanism.
