Kagome lattice has attracted much interest recently due to its exotic properties, such as spin liquids and superconductivity. However, the effects of the spin chiral order, which is prevalent in Kagome materials with half-filled spin-1/2 f electron, have been rarely explored. In this work, we demonstrate that the spin-chiral ferromagnetic order, which breaks time reversal symmetry, can induce finite orbital magnetization. We perform systematic electronic structure calculations on a minimal model of the ferromagnetic Kagome lattice, and find that the orbital magnetization in this model is large and grows significantly as the stability of the spin-chiral ferromagnetic order is enhanced. We demonstrate the robustness of the orbital magnetization by explicitly including charge fluctuations and the effects of spin-orbit coupling. We further show that the orbital magnetization is nearly isotropic and nonzero for all in-plane directions, in contrast to the chiral spin structure, which has strong direction dependence. Our findings suggest that the Kagome lattice with spin-chiral ferromagnetic order is a promising material for observing the orbital magnetization.

The character ring of a finite group is the space of all class functions on the group. This ring has a natural structure as a commutative, associative algebra under pointwise multiplication. The group algebra is the special case where the group is assumed to be abelian. Hopf algebras are non-commutative generalizations of commutative algebras, and the character ring is a Hopf algebra. In this paper we determine the Hopf algebra structure of the character ring of classical groups. In particular, we show that it is a cocommutative coradical graded Hopf algebra, and compute the structure of its coradical ideal. As an application, we use these results to determine the character of the baby monster group. The character ring of a finite group has a natural structure as a commutative associative algebra under pointwise multiplication. This ring is referred to as the character ring of the group. A character of a group is a class function on the group that takes the value 1 on the identity element. The character ring has been studied for a long time, and is of interest in its own right because of its applications to combinatorics, number theory, and representation theory. As an algebra, it can be defined for any finite group. The group algebra is the special case where the group is abelian. The character ring has a natural structure as a Hopf algebra, with product given by pointwise multiplication and antipode given by inversion. In this paper, we study the Hopf algebra structure of the character ring of classical groups. In particular, we show that it is a cocommutative coradical graded Hopf algebra, and compute the structure of its coradical ideal. We also determine the character of the baby monster group. The character ring of a classical group can be defined using a basis of elementary characters. We show that the character ring is a cocommutative coradical graded Hopf algebra. The coradical is the maximal nilpotent ideal, and is generated by elementary characters. We explicitly compute the elementary characters of the symmetric, alternating, and general linear groups. We then determine the Hopf algebra structure of the character ring of the orthogonal, symplectic, and unitary groups. We also determine the Hopf algebra structure of the character ring of the finite general linear groups and the special linear groups. We give a complete description of the Hopf algebra structure of the character ring of the Baby Monster group. I would like to thank Prof. S. Carnahan at the University of Virginia for helpful discussions and guidance. To model the effect of electromagnetic barriers (barriers between materials of different indices of refraction) and tunneling barriers (barriers that allow tunneling through them), we derive general constraints on the thicknesses, refractive indices, and densities of states of dielectric multilayers and potential barrier stepwise heights. These constraints are applied to dielectric/dielectric and dielectric/potential barrier multilayer structures to determine the ranges of acceptable parameters for electromagnetic and tunneling barriers, respectively. For each type of barrier, we find that the transmission, dispersion (wavelength shift), and density of states are inversely proportional to the fourth power of the ratio of the barrier height to the incident wavelength. By setting these parameters for known barriers, we demonstrate that it is impossible to construct a stepwise potential barrier with arbitrary layer arrangement that transmits less than 10-8, disperses less than 10-9, or has a density of states less than about 10-4 states/eV/nm2/Ci. Likewise, it is impossible to construct an electromagnetic barrier with a refractive-index difference between the layers greater than about 5.8×10-3 for completely reflecting barriers and greater than 2.2×10-2 for barriers with less than 90% transmittance. These constraints can aid in the optimization of future electromagnetic and tunneling barrier designs and in the development of practical implementations of these effects.

The optical and electrical properties of diarylethenes (DAs) can be reversibly switched between two stable states by different wavelength light. This property has been employed to design optical and photo-switchable molecular devices, ranging from photorefractive media to optical data storage and molecular devices. Recently, molecular devices based on diarylethenes have been developed, exhibiting photochromism, i.e. the ability to switch between two different states, one stable in the dark and the other in light. In this study, we present a theoretical investigation on diarylethene-based molecular junctions. The current-voltage (I-V) characteristics reveal that the DA molecular junctions exhibit reversible and cyclable switching effects via light illumination with two different wavelengths, indicating the application potential of DA molecules in optical and photo-switchable molecular devices. Generally, the photochromic diarylethene derivatives are regarded as the light-driven switching element and its associated molecular device is constructed by introduction of different electrodes. Based on this mechanism, the current-voltage (I-V) characteristics reveal that the DA molecular junctions exhibit reversible and cyclable switching effects via light illumination with two different wavelengths, indicating the application potential of DA molecules in optical and photo-switchable molecular devices. VCS 0413-647, also known as 3C 49, BL Lac, and TNuna, is a well-known compact steep spectrum radio source (CSS). Over the years, VCS 0413-647 has displayed a relatively constant intemperal brightness, yet various studies have shown it to be variable at all wavelengths. Here, we present the results of a large multi-wavelength observing campaign on VCS 0413-647 in 2017. Optical and near-infrared observations were obtained with the Keck II telescope and the Very Large Telescope (VLT), respectively. X-ray and gamma-ray observations were obtained with the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and the Large Array, respectively. Radio observations were obtained with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array, the Australia Telescope Compact Array, the phased VLA, and the Molonglo Observatory. We present the results of our milliarcsecond-scale radio imaging study of VCS 0413-647. Our observations showed a core-jet structure with an angular separation of 0.15 mas (or ~8.6 light-years at the redshift of the source, z = 0.0812) between two blobs aligned with the jet. This structure, along with changes in total flux density, brightness temperature, polarization, and morphology, confirm the variability seen at all wavelengths. We interpret the variability as a possible change in Doppler factor, θD, caused by apparent superluminal motion of the blobs at ~0.15c.

The Gamma-Ray Imager (GRI) is a gamma-ray astronomical mission that was selected for implementation by ESA as a European Space Agency (ESA) Technology Development Program (TDP) initiative. The GRI technology demonstrator was successfully launched by a Pegasus 2 rocket on 5 January 2021, from Space Coast, Florida, USA. GRI is the first Small Bodies Participating Module (SB PM) of the larger Artemis program. GRI is a compact and lightweight gamma-ray astronomy mission for detecting and characterising gamma-ray emissions from solar system objects. It will be installed on the moon with a suite of experiments for studying the gamma-ray emissions of the lunar surface, the Earth-Moon system, and the sun. The gamma-ray astronomy instrument consists of a soft gamma-ray detector and a neutron detector. The gamma-ray detector is based on the Compton imaging technique, which combines data from incoming gamma-ray photons and Compton scatter events to form two-dimensional images of regional gamma-ray distributions. These images will provide information about the chemical composition, internal structures, and spatial distributions of targets within the fields of view. The neutron detector measures neutrons released by binding energy interactions between gamma-rays and materials. GRI will provide critical information to understand high-energy emissions from a variety of celestial bodies, including their composition, structure, and dynamics. GRI also has the potential to provide new scientific knowledge about the lunar environment, while allowing for characterization of potentialemisissions into the lunar gamma-ray environment.

Post-CCSD(T) molecular atomization energies (i.e., atomization energies after correction for single and double excitations, but before frozen pair.) are typically computed on a smaller basis set than coupled cluster doubles (CCD) energies, though there is no rigorous rationale for this. Here, we demonstrate that basis set convergence for atomization energies can be rationalized with the pair natural orbital partial correction (PNOC), which captures the importance of dynamic correlation in the post-CCSD energy. Using explicit correlation as a metric, we show that PNOC energies converge more rapidly than CCD energies with basis set size. This rationalization allows us to predict that atomization energies computed with the CBS-QB3 method, which combines dynamic correlation through the CBS connection cost with a reasonably accurate semi-local exchange-correlation functional, will converge substantially more rapidly than CCSD(T) atomization energies on a basis set consistent with the quality of the CBS-QB3 geometry. We test this hypothesis for ten systems with experimental atomization energies and CCSD(T) geometries, and find that CBS-QB3 atomization energies converge to within 1 kcal/mol on a 6-31G** basis, in good agreement with the CBS-QB3 CBS (6-31G(d,p) + CBS-QB3) equilibrium geometries. These results demonstrate that CBS-QB3 can be an efficient method for predicting atomization energies and that post-CCSD(T) energies are sufficient to rationalize basis set convergence.

Theory of anomalous diffusive reaction rates on realistic self-affine fractals. Using the fractal formulation of diffusion, we introduce a general theoretical framework for anomalous reaction kinetics on statistically self-similar processes. This general theory is illustrated by a first-passage-time (FPT) problem with explicit analytical solution, which allows us to calculate reaction rates in arbitrary spatial dimensions. In one dimension, this general theory reduces to a previous theory for anomalous reaction kinetics on Lévy flights, with additional quantitative comparisons that validate the theory. In higher dimensions, the anomalous reaction rates can be organized in a hierarchical expansion in spatial dimensions, where the first term is the well-known Wiener process and the second term is a novel type of diffusion with spatial power-law dependence. The theory is applied to anomalous reaction rates for noninstantaneous and non-Markovian single-molecule reactions on realistic fractals. The theory accurately captures anomalous reaction rates for a range of spatial dimensions and reaction mechanisms, and offers a universal platform for reaction dynamics that complements existing theory for Markovian reactions.

The photon box was proposed as a thought experiment to illustrate one of the fundamental aspects of quantum mechanics, complementarity. In its most basic form, the idea is as follows. A quantum system, in this case a photon, is placed in a box with fully reflective walls. The photon in this case acts as a wave, and can traverse the box in an infinite number of different paths. A strong light source, such as a laser, is pointed at the box so that the photon may react with the walls. The reaction would be manifested as a shift in the light reflected from the walls. The photon would be observed as being either reflected or not reflected from the walls depending on whether a measurement is performed immediately after the photon has had time to interact with the walls or after a delay. The principle behind this experiment is that wave-like properties, such as the photon's ability to traverse the box in an infinite number of different paths, are observed to function independent of whether or not an instantaneous measurement is performed. On the other hand, particle-like properties, such as the photon's interaction with the walls, are only observable if an instantaneous measurement is performed. The two types of measurement conflict with one another and so can neither be simultaneously true nor false. The conflict is described by the word complementarity. The photon box has been performed in a laboratory setting several times. The most famous case is the Delay Phased Arrays (DPA) Experiment, performed at NIST in Boulder, CO, USA, which produced the first conclusive evidence of complementarity in the photon box. The principle behind DPA is nearly identical to that of the original thought experiment. However, instead of using a laser to point at the box, DPA used a monochromatic beam of light from a helium-neon laser. Since the laser is not a strong light source, the photon's wave-like properties are not significantly affected by the interaction with the walls. In this case, the measurement of the reflected light can be performed with a photodiode with a significant degree of confidence. The Delay Phased Arrays Experiment was a success, but it does not fully realize the potential of the photon box. The original thought experiment as proposed by Einstein and Bohr could be significantly improved. Einstein and Bohr assumed that the photons would interact with all of the walls simultaneously. In this case, the reflected light would become more of a wave than a particle. The conflict between these properties would once again lead to complementarity. However, the Delay Phased Arrays Experiment only fully realizes half of the photon box. The other half is the degree of uncertainty that Einstein had predicted for the photon's momentum. In this case, the conflict between the particle-like nature of the reflected light and the wave-like nature of the photon's momentum would lead to another form of complementarity, which has come to be known as the uncertainity principle. Theory of nonlinear frame transforms allows one to consider new general relativity (GR) theories with nonintegrable metrics and different scenario for the gravity equations’ solution. The frame approach is used to derive new class of exact solutions in 4D and 3D metrics with nontrivial parallelizations of theender Spaces (3D and 2D) and induced torsion. The gravitational field equations in this theory are written in the form of nonlinear partial differential equations for the components of the Riemann-Cartan geometry, which after some nonholonomic constraints and double Sideway-mirroring transform to the system of ordinary differential equations. Such new solutions can be parameterized in terms of two-parametric family of exact solutions with nontrivial torsion and nontrivial spin interaction terms, which effectively modifies the initial (in General relativity) absence of spin in equations of motion and interactions. Such kind of nonlinear interactions between spin and torsion are appeared to be very important for solving the long-standing problems of modern fundamental interactions physics, including the origin of masses, hierarchy problem, dark energy and dark matter.

A species, the parasitic wasp, Monoksa dorsiplana, has been successfully reared in laboratory conditions to provide pupal parasitoids for release in Brazil to suppress the onion thrips, Thrips tabaci. This was achieved by using the larval diet of Centruroides elegans (Chilopoda: Scutarcidae), a common scolytid pest found throughout South America. The successful rearing of M. dorsiplana, a gregarious larval endoparasitoid of T. tabaci, has significant potential to support augmentative biological control programs in South America. These findings will be of benefit to the international effort to suppress T. tabaci throughout the Americas. Superconductivity was observed in the newly discovered oxide YBa_2Cu_3O_7 in 1997. Since then, this material has received substantial attention, and many unusual properties have been observed, including non-monotonic temperature dependence of the transition width and a small high-temperature_"normal"_ phase below 100K. Despite this attention, the nature of the superconducting state in this material remains a topic of active investigation. Here we report results of a comprehensive study of the stability of the superconducting state in YBa_2Cu_3O_7 performed using magnetic and electric field modulations of the transition temperature, with resulting change in critical temperature `dT/Adep`. We find the upper critical magnetic field to vary by approximately 25% over the range 0-9 T, with no evidence for compensation by the lower critical magnetic field. Field modulation of the critical temperature was observed up to 9 T, with a magnitude that decreases approximately linearly with field strength. We propose that inhomogeneities in the crystal structure or impurities may give rise to an orbital effect in this material, leading to an increased sensitivity of the superconducting state to spatial variations in external fields. The observation of non-monotonic temperature dependence of the transition width in YBa_2Cu_3O_7 has also been the subject of recent theoretical interest. It has been proposed that the non-monotonic behaviour may be related to the presence of an additional "normal" phase at low temperature. Our study of the stability of the superconducting state in this material also provides evidence of the presence of this low-temperature phase, with a critical temperature of approximately 4K. We suggest that non-monotonic temperature dependence of the transition width may be related to thermal fluctuations near the normal-to-superconducting phase boundary. Our study provides clear evidence for the presence of fluctuations in the YBa_2Cu_3O_7 material that are unusually sensitive to both magnetic fields and temperature. We suggest that these fluctuations may play a key role in determining the unusual properties of this material, including the non-monotonic temperature dependence of the transition width and the presence of a low-temperature phase.

In the standard model (SM) with its minimal particle content, the electroweak chiral Lagrangian (EWCLL) is the appropriate low-energy effective field theory (LEFT) to describe the strong interactions of the weak bosons. By construction, the precision tests of the EWCLL allow to put strong constraints on new physics (NP) scenarios. Here, we use the latest precision measurements from the LHC and electroweak observables to put strong constraints on a generic Higgs-portal type model. We find that the model is strongly constrained for a large range of the model parameter space. In particular, the model predicts charged scalar boson with a mass below 530 GeV at the 95% CL, and the invisible decay width of the Z boson is expected to be larger than 0.2 MeV at the 95% CL. These bounds could be further improved by using the current and future precise data of the electroweak observables.

The worm-like chain (WLC) theory has been the canonical model for describing the bending stiffness of biopolymers such as DNA, RNA, and proteins. This model assumes that the biopolymer is a homogeneous chain of classical links connected by non-classical rigid bonds. Despite its wide use, the WLC model does not consider the effect of the chain’s innate heterogeneity and bonds that may be prone to partial breakage. To address this deficiency, several modifications to the WLC model have been proposed. In this paper, we present an alternative theory based on the worm-like chain with breakable bonds (WLCBB). The proposed chain has several bending degrees of freedom and an additional linear stiffness resulting from the breaking and reformation of bonds. The exact solution is obtained by mapping the problem to a classical intersection problem in plane. The theory is used to study the mechanics of a short DNA fragment with two rigid obstacles located at both ends. The obtained results show that the theory can explain the DNA’s flexibility without the need to consider excluded volume effects. The theory also predicts that with the decreasing of the DNA fragment’s length, its flexibility will increase until a critical point, and then decrease after that. This paper is a revised and extended version of [1].

The electromagnetic response of high-Tc superconductors is investigated within the framework of the slave-boson and doped-carrier theories. In the slave-boson theory, the pairing force is expressed in terms of Bose fields. The magnetic and electric susceptibilities are calculated by introducing into the theory a static Coulomb interaction and applying a fluctuation exchange approximation. The magnetic susceptibility is positive for all dopings and is in satisfactory agreement with the neutron scattering experiments on YBa2Cu3O6. The electric susceptibility is positive for small dopings and becomes negative for larger dopings. The onset of negative susceptibility at some critical doping suggests the possibility of a macroscopic electric polarization at low temperatures. The onset of negative susceptibility is consistent with the onset of static charges reported by photoemission experiments. The doped-carrier theory identifies the electromagnetic excitations with holes in the CuO2 layers. This approach accounts for the magnetic susceptibility and the neutron scattering results on YBa2Cu3O6, but is unable to account for the onset of negative electric susceptibility at small dopings. The single-particle excitation spectra obtained by the two theories have important implications for the superconductor-metal transition in high-Tc superconductors.

Recent opacities have been released for low-mass metal-poor AGB stars undergoing the Third Dredge Up, that include the newly available Al3+ and Zn2+ opacities. The effect of these opacities on the nucleosynthesis and chemical yields in these stars is studied. The nucleosynthesis from both the quiescent and thermal pulses is altered by the inclusion of these metals. The included studies also includes the effect of using these opacities on the predicted pulsation periods of these stars. This work is relevant for those studying a diverse array of topics in astronomy, including nucleosynthesis, stellar pulsation, and Galactic chemical evolution. The detection of gravitational waves (GWs) and the derivation of their detailed properties have been accomplished over the last several years using a number of detector configurations. The most recent of these coincided in frequency with the estimated chirp mass of the system, determining an accurate sky location for the source. No electromagnetic (EM) counterparts were detected by any current alliance, leading to the assumption that the compact object coalesced from a white dwarf. While a neutron star (NS) – neutron star merger provides an excellent description of the observed signal, the weak observational evidence leads to the possibility that the event may have been a double white dwarf collision. In this case, the estimated parameters of the coalescing compact objects are quite different. While the physics of double white dwarf collisions is quite plausible, the uncertainties in the astrophysics and observation process result in a ~30% probability that a detection of the same signal was incorrectly attributed to NS – neutron star merger, resulting in a poorly characterized source and an incomplete observation of the gravitational-wave universe.

Depending on the coupling constants, the system may also support symmetry-breaking moving Bright and Vakhitov-Shazki pseudoelectric solitons. As mentioned in the title, this work considers both symmetric and asymmetric (i.e., isotropic vs. anisotropic) nonlinearities in Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) systems with linear coupling. Randomness is an essential element in the financial markets. Although traditionally randomness has been associated with the quantum world, increasingly more evidence is showing that classical randomness, i.e. from random number generators, is a key factor in financial markets. In this paper we review some of this evidence and then present our own work that shows that not only is classical randomness important, but that it plays a central role in how market participants react to new information. We also present some new methods that can detect and quantify classical randomness in financial data. The increasing importance of classical randomness in financial markets. Traditionally, the term 'financial markets' has been associated with the quantum world, and indeed quantum mechanics has had a major impact in the development of mathematical finance. One central tenet of quantum mechanics is that decisions cannot be based on incomplete information. In other words, investors and traders have to have perfect information in order to be able to forecast future events. Classical randomness is an important underpinning of this unpredictability. While quantum mechanics has been incredibly successful in describing the behaviour of atoms and other particles, its application in the financial markets has so far been limited to randomness arising from the quantum world. We will present empirical evidence that shows that classical randomness, i.e. from random number generators, is an essential part of financial markets. In particular, we will present evidence that: 1. The market reacts to classical randomness 2. Market participants take advantage of classical randomness 3. Quantifying classical randomness in financial data It is now well-known that the integrity of the stock market can be seriously compromised by insider trading. Most people assume that insider trading is based on confidential, or 'dark', information. This is not the case. There is a lot of public, or 'white', information out there and much of it is random in nature. As we will show, much of the randomness in financial data can be accounted for using simple, well-known random number generators. Finally, we will present a number of new and original methods for detecting and quantifying classical randomness in financial data. Some of these methods are based on wavelets. We also develop a new technique, based on the Earth Mover's Distance, that can be used to quantify the distance between different random processes. Using these new methods we can show that the market is reacting to classical randomness, that market participants are taking advantage of classical randomness, and that this classical randomness is a key factor in explaining market behaviour. *Note: This paper was originally published in the Financial Review. The connection between host galaxies and their central supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remains a subject of intense scrutiny. One of the most distinctive characteristics of this link is the so-called “ fundamental plane of black hole activity” (Reines et al. 2013), according to which the optical/UV luminosity of the host galaxy is statistically correlated with some BH-related property. Very few observational evidences have directly associated the presence of the central SMBHs with the specific character of the host galaxy stellar population. Here, we report on the study of the surface brightness profiles of early-type galaxies hosting active nuclei, aiming at a possible evidence of the influence of the central supermassive black hole on their global properties. From Hubble Space Telescope optical imaging, we measure the surface brightness profiles of 35 early-type galaxies hosting Seyfert nuclei, and compare them with those of a matched control sample of 35 early-type galaxies with no sign of active nuclear species. At large radii, where the stellar distribution dominates, the two samples are indistinguishable. At small radii, where the SMBH sphere of influence is expected to imbue the galaxy potential, the radial brightness profiles of the Seyfert hosts deviate from those of the matched control sample, becoming progressively deeper with increasing radius. These results provide the first evidence that the global properties of early-type galaxies are influenced by the presence of central supermassive black holes at the centers of their host galaxies.

Using data from Advanced LIGO’s first two observing runs (O1 and O2), we search for signals from intermediate mass ratio inspirals (S2 IMSs). Such signals would carry unique imprints about the dense stellar cores of their hosts, enabling us to uniquely determine the stellar structure and distance. We place upper limits on the rate of such signals as a function of mass and strain. We further place lower bounds on the radius and distance to the putative host stars. We discuss the implications for the radius problem and the implications for planetary systems around intermediate mass stars. We use data from Advanced LIGO’s first two observing runs (O1 and O2) to search for signals from intermediate mass ratio inspirals (S2 IMSs). Intermediate mass ratio inspirals are a distant population of stars whose signals would carry unique imprints about the dense stellar cores of their hosts. Using these signals to measure the structure of the host stars and their distances would enable us to answer longstanding questions about the radius problem and the existence of planets orbiting intermediate mass stars. We place upper limits on the rate of such signals as a function of mass and strain, and we discuss the implications for the radius problem and the existence of planets around such stars. We searched for signals from S2 IMSs, with a modelled expectation of 1 S2 IMS per 4-6 weeks at distances of 15-45 parsecs. We placed 95% confidence level upper limits on the rate of these signals as a function of mass and strain. Assuming a population of IMSs with uniform distribution in logarithm of mass, we can use these rates to derive lower bounds on the radii of the putative hosts. We discuss the implications for the radius problem and the existence of planets around intermediate mass stars. For example, at a distance of 15 parsecs, we can place a lower bound on the radius of the host star of roughly 4.2 R⊕ for a 1.4 M⊕ S2 IMS and 6.3 R⊕ for a 1.4 M⊕ S2 IMS. Assuming a log-uniform distribution of IMSs, we can use these rates to derive upper bounds on the number of planets with a radius of R⊕ orbiting intermediate mass stars. We also search for signals from systems with nearly equal mass companions. These can be used to measure the spin of the companion star and thus test general relativity. We discuss the implications of these results for the radius problem and the existence of planets around intermediate mass stars, and we show how these results can be used to test general relativity and determine the spin of companion stars.

Burnt-bridge models (BBMs) are a simple artificial network motif that exhibits a sharp transition between the unburnt and burnt state that has been used to study systems ranging from bio-inspired computing, to chemical systems and soft-condensed matter systems. The bio-inspired field of molecular motors has recently begun to exploit BBMs as a means to explore the relationship between structure and function, where dynamics of molecular motors interacting with BBMs have been identified as a potential design variable. In this work, we introduce a simple two-state BBM that exhibits a locked-in state that is dependent on the dynamics of the molecular motors. Using a simplified two-state BBM, we are able to qualitatively reproduce the locking phenomenon observed in the more complex BBMs. Further, by adding discrete rotational dynamics to the motor, we are able to reproduce the observed locking behavior using a one-dimensional BBM. Our findings suggest that the locking phenomenon observed in more detailed BBMs is a result of the coupling between continuous rotational dynamics of the molecular motor and the BBM’s structural dynamics.

Planets are discovered around other stars by three distinct methods: direct detection, where planets are observed through the wobble they induce in their star's motion; transit, where planets are inferred from the dimming effect they cause as they pass in front of their star; and astrometry, where the planet's movement is measured by the change in position of its star relative to nearby stars. Recently, three teams have announced the discovery of planets around faint red dwarf stars using data from the MACHO survey. This method makes use of transit observations alone, without the need for additional detections. Such planets could be very Earth-like and might be particularly abundant around smaller red dwarfs. Here we report our analysis of the MACHO observations, and conclude that only two of the announced planet candidates are likely to be genuine planets. We suggest reasons for the discrepancy between the MACHO data and the published Planet Recovery Efficiency estimates for five of the candidates, and we conclude that a likely explanation is that observational artefacts are confusing the data for these five candidates. Further observations are required to confirm the existence of the MACHO planets.

Single sting theories in AdS_2 have an AdS_2 x S2 description in which the string spins in the ${\bf R}^3$ of AdS_2. At strong coupling, the string dynamics are described by M-theory on AdS_3 x S3. I propose that the high energy limit of this M-theory string is a quantum Lifshitz sigma model on AdS_2 x S2. The metric and the three form of the Lifshitz sigma model are computed. The CFT calculation of string scattering in theLifshitz sigma model is reviewed. Anomaly Ward identities for the symmetry algebra of the Lifshitz sigma model are written down and compared to the CFT calculation. This proposal for strongly coupled string theory in AdS_2 agrees with the M-theory description at strong coupling and with the sigma model description at weak coupling. The proposed string theory has a unique expansion in string coupling and ’hole’ amounts, where the ’hole’ amounts are closed superstring momenta. In particular, the string tension is positive and there are no tachyon condensation leading singularities.

A fundamental issue in many experiments on Deeply Quenched Liquid (DQL) systems is the stability of the interface between the DQL and the Gas ( vapour) phase. In order to evaluate the stability of the interface, and consequently the robustness of the DQL system, it is necessary to determine the equilibrium interface width. In this work we show how the interface width can be calculated from the grand canonical thermodynamic potential using a volume integration method and show the interface width dependence on the Hamaker constant and the Bond number. We show that in order to maintain a stable interface, a minimum value for the Hamaker constant must be satisfied. We demonstrate this by comparing the grand canonical thermodynamic potential calculated for a DQL system with that of an equivalent vapour system and show that the interface is stable when the Hamaker constant is less than this minimum value. For the Bond number we show that as the interface becomes increasingly slender (Bond number increases) the Hamaker constant must increase in order to maintain the stability of the interface. We discuss the range of Hamaker constants that satisfy these stability criteria and show that it is likely that most experimental systems do not satisfy these stability requirements for calculating the thermodynamic properties of the DQL system. We describe a method to stabilise the interface between the DQL and Gas phases that satisfies these stability requirements and provide example calculation of thermodynamic properties of a DQL system using this interface stabilised method.

The recent remarkable progress in the numerical simulations of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at high temperatures and baryon densities make it possible to study the QCD phase diagram in the vicinity of the quantum chromodynamics critical point (CP). One of the main goals of ultrarelativistic nuclear collisions is to create and study the properties of the matter under extreme conditions. The predicted phase structure is such that at high temperatures and low baryon densities, matter is described by QCD in the limit of heavy quarks mass $m_Q \rightarrow \infty$ (known as Quark-Gluon Plasma or QGP). In contrast, at low temperatures and high baryon densities, the matter is expected to be in the color superconducting state - the so called Color Superconductor (CS). The QCD phase diagram in the plane of temperature vs baryon chemical potential (or, equivalently, the pressure) is unclear. Experimental investigations of the QCD phase structure and the search for the QCD critical point are among the main tasks of the heavy-ion collision experiments at the high-energy accelerators. In this article, we consider an hydrodynamic description of QCD equations of state at various values of the baryon chemical potential $\mu_B$ and the temperature $T$. We compare the results of our calculations with the lattice QCD predictions and the recent thermal models predictions. We demonstrate that the latter are not reliable at small $\mu_B$. We also discuss the applicability of these equations of state in the context of the relativistic heavy-ion collisions. We show that the viscosity to entropy density ratio $\eta/s$ as a function of temperature for different equations of state dramatically increases at small baryon chemical potential. In this region, the Boltzmann approximation does not apply and effective kinetic theory description must be used. The last part of the article is devoted to the analysis of the critical endpoint, which location depends on the equation of state and is expected to be near the baryon chemical potential of about $\mu_B \sim 400-500$ MeV at zero temperature. Our results show that the critical endpoint is likely to be far from the region of heavy-ion collision experiments at the top beam energy (about 200 MeV per colliding nuclei) but could be reached at low beam energies (about 50 MeV per colliding nuclei) within the next few years.

Bond formation and slow heterogeneous dynamics in adhesive spheres with long--ranged repulsion: Quantitative test of Mode Coupling Theory Xiaowei Zhu, Haotian Wang, Bingnan Zhang, and Changsong Zou Adhesionmolecules play a critical role in various technological and biological processes. For example, many marine species rely on adhesion to anchor themselves to the sea bed; geckos can stick to smooth surfaces with a grip hundreds of times stronger than that of a conventional adhesive; and some plants use water as a locomotion mechanism by capably spreading water droplets in the forms of adhesive structures called hydrogels. Despite their ubiquity in Nature, the microscopic mechanism of how adhesion molecules self-assemble into highly ordered structures is still not well understood. Previous computational studies have explored the role of intermolecular interactions in the self-assembly of adhesion molecules. For example, adhesion was observed to increase with increasing range of the interaction potential, but the physical mechanism for this effect remains elusive. Recently, multi-scale modeling frameworks, such as Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) and mesoscale modeling, have been used to gain new insights into the interplay among long-range repulsion, short-range attraction, and thermal fluctuations in the self-assembly of adhesive spheres. These studies have shown that adhesive spheres with short-range attraction but long-range repulsion (“repulsive spheres”) may form disordered cluster crystals, termed “colloidal glasses,” in high dilution. However, it is not clear if these attractive interactions, typically modeled using a parabolic potential, can lead to ordered phases, nor has the dynamics of these systems been studied. We perform extensive Molecular Dynamics (MD) and Coarse-grained MD simulations of monodisperse attractive and repulsive spheres to study the phase behavior and the dynamics of cluster glass formation. We find that, in the highly dilute regime, repulsion prevents the formation of well-ordered crystals but promotes the formation of a disordered cluster glass. Using a combination of multi-structure analysis, Voronoi construction, and centroid shift identification, we demonstrate that clusters in the cluster glass exhibit slow dynamics. We perform finite-size scaling and demonstrate that the four point correlation length, the dynamical length scale characterizing the slow dynamics, diverges at the Mode Coupling Theory (MCT) critical point, providing strong evidence that the system is in a slow glassy state. Our work provides a framework for future studies of glass formation in systems with a broad spectrum of long-range interaction potentials. Three-dimensional (3D) unstructured oceanographic data sets are large and complex, often including multiple data types at different spatial and temporal resolutions. The large size and heterogeneity of these datasets can make it difficult to perform analysis or discovery on the data. In this paper, we present a set of diagnostic tools to summarize and explore 3D unstructured oceanographic data. The summary tools provide a global overview of the data volume, composition, and geometry, as well as a local view of each data set’s features. The exploration tools allow users to search and browse the datasets based on metadata and features, and to apply spatial and temporal filters to identify subsets of the data. We demonstrate the usefulness of these tools with several examples of analysis and discovery on 3D unstructured oceanographic data. The summary tools provide a global overview of the data volume, composition, and geometry, as well as a local view of each data set’s features. The exploration tools allow users to search and browse the datasets based on metadata and features, and to apply spatial and temporal filters to identify subsets of the data. We demonstrate the usefulness of these tools with several examples of analysis and discovery on 3D unstructured oceanographic data. Our data products include three-dimensional oceanographic and hydrologic data from IMaG, a provider of 3D ocean surface data (https://imag.ifremer.com/). The data are organized in 4 packages, each corresponding to a different domain of ocean study: ocean surface currents, bathymetry, hydrography, and aerosol. Each product includes files in NetCDF, DSD, and ASCII formats, as well as an SQL database that allows for fast data retrieval and automated processing. The IMaG data sets typically cover large spatial extents ( thousands of kilometers) and vary in both time and space. The resolution and extent of the data vary with the domain and product, but are typically varying from a few meters to several tens of kilometers and from a few hours to several months, respectively. The data volumes are substantial, ranging from tens of gigabytes to terabytes and often including multiple formats and resolutions. While the data are often well documented, a few key concepts, such as data depth and time coverage, can be challenging to understand. Additionally, the sheer size and complexity of the datasets can make it difficult to perform analysis or discovery on the data. In this paper, we present a set of diagnostic tools to summarize and explore these large, heterogeneous data sets. The summary tools provide a global overview of the data volume, composition, and geometry, as well as a local view of each data set’s features. The exploration tools allow users to search and browse the datasets based on metadata and features, and to apply spatial and temporal filters to identify subsets of the data. We demonstrate the usefulness of these tools with several examples of analysis and discovery on 3D unstructured oceanographic data.

A coupled-channel model of the $\pi N$ system can provide a powerful means of analyzing photoproduction and hadronic interactions at low energies. The model parameters may be determined from scattering data in the s-waves, where effective interactions exist, or from the reproduction of the experimental data in the partial wave expansion. The dynamical coupled-channel model applied to the $\pi N$ system, when extended to the W $\leq$ 2 GeV resonance region, describes the mass and width spectra of the resonances very well. The model parameters are determined by a nonlinear least-squares fit to the experimental data in 1724 total degrees of freedom. The model may be used to predict the properties of these resonances in the W $\leq$ 2 GeV resonance region and to estimate the production mechanisms for these resonances in high-energy hadronic reactions. A weakly anisotropic inhomogeneous medium may, in general, support three mutually orthogonal polarization modes. Assuming that these modes are non-dispersive, the dielectric function of the medium can be written as a sum of tensor contributions, each of which is a function of only one polarization direction. The evolution equation for the Stokes vector, which comprises the components of the incident light's Stokes vectors after scattering in the medium, may then be represented as a coupled set of linear differential equations. Assuming that the contrast of the medium's anisotropy is small, the coupled system may be reduced to a pair of scalar evolution equations for the scalar quantities I, Q and U, where I is the total intensity, and Q and U are the degree of linear polarization orthogonal and parallel to the medium's anisotropy axis. This system of coupled evolution equations may then be solved in the case of an incident light beam whose intensity and polarization are uniform in all three spatial dimensions. The resulting expressions for I, Q and U as a function of radius are displayed as intensity diagrams for various values of the anisotropy and linear birefringence parameters. The similarity between the behavior of these diagrams and that of the top-hat transform of the Pskelly-Nepvel distribution is noted. The ability of such an approach to reproduce experimental results for a number of cases is also discussed.

In this paper we analyze the influence of an external magnetic field on the decoherence of a central spin coupled to an antiferromagnetic environment. The central spin and environment form a closed system, which we analyze within a reduced density matrix approach. In particular, we focus on the case of longitudinal relaxation, considering a constant magnetic field in the z direction. In this case, the corresponding decoherence rate is shown to exhibit resonant behavior as a function of the magnitude of the magnetic field, with a maximum corresponding to the critical field h = J, where J is the exchange coupling between the central spin and the environment. We discuss the physical implications of this result and its experimental implications, suggesting the possibility of exploring this phenomenon in spin glasses. We study the influence of a magnetic field h in the z direction on the decoherence of a central spin S, coupled to an antiferromagnetic environment formed by N spins. In particular, we are interested in the case of longitudinal relaxation, which can be described by a rate equation for the reduced density matrix of the central spin. We adopt a mean-field approach, considering an effective single-spin Hamiltonian and solving the associated quantum master equation. We focus on the case of a constant magnetic field, with magnitude J, and we analyze the corresponding resonant behavior, with a maximum corresponding to the critical field h = J. We discuss the physical implications of this result and its experimental implications, suggesting the possibility of exploring this phenomenon in spin glasses.

The recent discovery of the Schrödinger Greene method (SGM) for calculating holographic entanglement entropy (EE) in vacuum gravity backgrounds has led to the formulation of a covariant holographic entanglement entropy proposal (CHSMEE). This proposal states that the quantum extremal surface (QES) EE is given by the (covariant) Donaldson-Schreiber (DS) gauge theory action evaluated on a relevant configuration, where the relevant configuration is defined as the boundary value of a gauge field on the interior of a globally minimal area deformation of the projected QES onto the surface. Assuming that the proposal holds for general vacuum gravity backgrounds, CHSMEE reduces to a prescription for calculating EE for asymptotically AdS geometries. The proposal is applicable to holographic theories with a Lagrangian description, and, at least in minimal surfaces examples, yields results that agree with direct calculations of EE from QES wavefunctions. The proposal also possesses a consistency requirement that the EE found this way is a property of the CFTstate and is independent of how the QES is constructed. In this paper we apply the proposal to various examples, including a toy model, and find that in all cases the proposal yields results that agree with direct calculations from QES wavefunctions. Furthermore, the proposal appears to be extensible to higher dimensions, at least for minimal surfaces examples. Finally, we discuss how the proposal can be extended to EE of covariant flux operators and propose tests of the proposal for such operators.

Type Ia supernovae are the best distance indicators available today, being standardizable candles with the advantage of their high luminosity being directly linked to the amount of Chandrasekhar mass exploded in a white-dwarf system. The progenitor system of these double-degenerate systems is believed to consist of a carbon-oxygen white dwarf, accreted material from a non-degenerate companion and most likely a neutron star (or black hole), which eventually reaches enough masses together with gravity to detonate as a type Ia supernova. We present near-infrared and optical observations of the type Ia supernova 2001el obtained with the Very Large Telescope (VLT) and the European Southern Observatory's New Technology Telescope. The peak of the light curve of 2001el was observed at approximately 120 days after the fitted explosion date and the spectrum is very similar to what is observed in typical type Ia supernovae one month after maximum brightness. We investigate possible causes for the late-time light curve break observed in 2001el, comparing it with normal type Ia supernovae and with other type Ia supernova ejections observed in a different cosmological context (SNe 2002bo, 2003hv, 2003bb and 2003ee). Our results favour a Chandrasekhar-mass white-dwarf model for 2001el, even though we cannot completely rule out the presence of a non-degenerate companion, nor a helium-rich composition for the progenitor. Late-time observations of more type Ia supernovae are crucial for reaching a better understanding of the degenerate binary scenario and of the role of possible explosion variations.

The Coma cluster is the first single-instance cluster detected in X-rays by the Rosat satellite. Its impressive morphology has been confirmed by all high-resolution X-ray instruments with the exception of the Chandra and XMM-Newton telescopes, whose observations revealed the existence of a large-scale peripheral component associated with the cluster. This component is aligned with the Coma center and connects it with the cluster Abell 1367, situated at the South-West direction. We report the detection of a south-west extension of the Coma cluster, discovered in the Chandra observation. It has a size of approximately 2 Mpc, amplitude of 7500 km/s, a position angle of 90 degrees, and covers the front of the main cluster component. The position of the sub-cluster coincides with the emission peak of the thermal cluster gas and the brightest galaxy members. The existence of the sub-cluster supports a scenario in which Coma is the result of a merger with another galaxy group, which led to the observed cD galaxy being left behind.

Mass and motion in the Local Volume ========================== Using a novel large scale structure analysis algorithm, constrained N-body simulations of the Local Volume (covering a 6 Mpc radius sphere around the MW galaxy) have been performed. We quantify the total mass distribution in this volume using three sets of simulations: one with constrained initial conditions (CC), one with self-consistent initial conditions (SC), and one run with fully unconstrained initial conditions (UC). We find that in the CC and SC simulations, dark matter accounts for approximately 16% and 13%, respectively, of the total volume mass in the Local Volume. The total mass distribution in the UC simulation is much more variable, ranging from as little as 3% in small high density regions to over 50% in the densest regions. We estimate the total mass of the Local Volume assuming the galaxies are contained withinbound clusters, finding it to be (6.1 ± 1.7) x 10^12 M_{\odot}. In our constrained simulations, the stellar component of galaxies accounts for approximately 0.5% of the Local Volume mass. We estimate the gravitational force generated by the Local Volume dark matter and galaxies, and find that it is capable of exerting a torque on our MW galaxy of magnitude (2.5 ± 0.5) x 10^18 gravitational units (GU). This is approximately 5% of the MW's total rotational support, and is approximately equally split between gravitational forces due to dark matter and those due to galaxies. In summary, our results show that the Local Volume is not merely a passive dark matterhalo, but that the mass distribution is significantly altered by the baryonic matter in the galaxies and dark matterhalos. We calculate the velocities of individual particles in our simulations, and identify the virialized structures in each. We find one bound galaxy cluster, the Local Group, and two distinct streams of galaxies. The SC and UC simulations contain a similar number of bound clusters, while the CC simulation contains significantly fewer. The streams in the UC and SC simulations each merge with our Local Group at different angles; the SC simulation contains one bound system only if one excludes the main halo of the MW itself. The Local Volume is therefore not a smoothly rotating structure, but instead contains several relatively unbound structures in a complex web. This work is based on results from the LDDE: DARK simulation suite, which was selected for presentation at Cosmology2014. LDDE: DARK is a high-resolution extension of the Delucia-Villa & Fry ([@delucia_villa]) massive galaxy formation simulation. The Local Volume simulations presented here were performed with the VAsync: LVL1 code, modified to include a novel large-scale structure analysis algorithm (Spandspen et al., [@Spandspen]). The lens-redshift test is an astronomical observation method which can be used to test cosmological models and study the evolution of galaxies. This method makes use of the fact that distant galaxies are strongly magnified by foreground clusters of galaxies, and can be used to place strong constraints on these two parameters. In this work, we study the extent to which these constraints are robust to uncertainties in the mean projected mass distribution of the cluster and in the strength of galaxy evolution. We find that the precision with which cosmological models or the evolution of galaxies can be tested is quite robust, except in the case of models with a strong variation in galaxy evolution with halo mass, or an exotic source population with a strong redshift evolution. For these cases, the lens-redshift test is insensitive to model parameters, and we are only able to place upper limits on the uncertainty introduced by the simplifying assumptions we have made. This work may help guide the choice of observable parameters which can provide the most robust constraints for testing cosmological models or studying galaxy evolution using the lens-redshift test.

The deuteron electrodisintegration threshold cross section is one of the main doorway to study the interaction between the electromagnetic and the nuclear field. This process has been studied in the past at low and intermediate energies with various models and limited precision. In recent years the availability of powerful numerical methods to solve relativistic quantum mechanical problems allowed for the first time to perform calculations at higher energies, approaching the deuteron breakup threshold. We present here a simple approach to the calculation of the process at relativistic energies based on a distorted wave Born approximation. The formalism is applied to study the process at a laboratory energy of 1.2 GeV, which is relevant for the creation of hot dense matter in current and future accelerator facilities. We find good agreement with previous results from optical models and the expected deviation from them at backward angles. The manuscript is partly based on a talk presented at the INT workshop “Electroweak Astrophysics and Fundamental Interactions” (September 2024).

The space of quantum theory representation of natural numbers, integers, and rational numbers, i.e. {0, 1, 2,...}, {0, 1}, {0, 1/2, 1/3,...}, and {0, 1/2, 1/3,...}, is a topological space. In the space of quantum theory representations, the operations of addition and multiplication by natural numbers are continuous maps. The space of quantum theory representations of natural numbers, integers, and rational numbers is completely regular, separately compact, and metrizable. The Banach-Alaoglu-Thuente theorem guarantees that this space is compact with respect to the bounded convergence topology. Dirichlet and Potts are two related but different algorithms used for labeling a given set of data points. In this work, we build a large dataset ofLabeledMedicalImages obtained using both the Potts and Dirichlet algorithm and show that these two approaches give very similar labels. We then use the Jaccard similarity coefficient to compare these two sets of labels and show that the pairwise similarity between the Potts and Dirichlet labels is very high (≃0.9). We finally propose a simple adversarial attack that fool both the Potts and Dirichlet algorithms and show how this similarity in error leads to the same incorrect labels. Our code and dataset are available at : https://github.com/aewalters/potts-vs-dirichlet Comments and suggestions are most welcome!
