Researchers have proposed many methods to identify unpopular or dead links on the internet. These methods can be divided into three categories. The first category includes machine learning based methods. These methods train a classifier to identify dead links based on the characteristics of the link and the page it is on. The second category includes reinforcement learning based methods. These methods employ an agent to search for dead links by interacting with the network. The third category includes homophily based methods. These methods find links between dead and live pages based on their patterns of association. Recently, several research groups have proposed link curation algorithms to improve the quality of dead link detection methods. These methods analyze the pages that contain dead links to find similar pages that contain live links. These live links are used to fill in the dead links. These methods can be categorized as link replacement algorithms. We propose a vacancy localization algorithm to improve the quality of link replacement algorithms. Our algorithm first detects dead links using existing methods and then investigates similar live pages to localize vacancies, i.e., live links that can be replaced by dead links. The positions of these vacancies are recorded and used by our algorithm to replace dead links with live links. We perform a large-scale study on the dataset obtained from deadlink detection track of D4M dataset and show that our vacancy localization algorithm improves the overall performance of link replacement algorithms.

Reconstruction of the quantum geometry of the universe in Loop Quantum Cosmology, based on the symmetry reduced homogeneous minisuperspace model, yields a discreteness of the geometry at the Planck scale. It is argued that the resulting Planck scale structure should be observable in the form of very high frequency gravitational wave bursts. These bursts would occur whenever discrete modes function differently than the continuous quantum vacuum, corresponding to non-analytic solutions to the quantum Einstein equations. The simulations presented herein suggest that discrete geometry should become observable in the form of bursts with a median strain amplitude of ~3.8 x 10-22 at a frequency of ~7.5 x 1021 Hz (corresponding to an age of about 10-21 s after the big bang). The generation of such bursts may provide a novel observable test of the quantum geometry of the universe, complementary to Cosmic Microwave Background measurements which test its classical geometry.

Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) is a state of matter characterized by a nearly perfect fluid of quarks and gluons, which are the building blocks of the subatomic particles of which humans and other complex life forms are composed. The QGP was formed in the first instants of the Big Bang, and since the expansion of the Universe has been heading toward cooler and cooler conditions, the QGP transformed into the more stable Quarkless Plasma as the thermal energy was too low for the transitions between different quantum states of quarks and gluons. The formation of the Quarkless Plasma is an essential milestone in the history of the universe, as it marked the transition from a phase where long range interactions were mediated by the fundamental forces of the strong and weak interactions to one where these interactions are mediated by short range quantum mechanical phenomena, such as coulomb forces. Although the transition from the Quarkless Plasma to today's familiar world of galaxies, stars, planets and people is extremely complex and not well understood, current theoretical models indicate that this transition should have involved a rapid series of metastable states, with long transition times that could have facilitated the gradual accumulation of the all the physical and chemical properties that make up the galaxies, stars and planets that make up the universe as we know it today. This hypothesis, called the bulk viscosity hypothesis, states that the rapid and spontaneous reorganization of long range interactions in the Quarkless Plasma caused by the accumulation of bulk viscosity from interactions between complex particles, should have facilitated the physical and chemical properties of the universe to gradually transition from the highly excitable state that characterizes the Quarkless Plasma into the more stable and orderly states that characterize the worlds that we see around us today. The current work was motivated by the discovery of what appears to be an intriguing metastable state in the Quarkless Plasma, indicating that the spontaneous reorganization of long range interactions observed in the bulk viscosity hypothesis may have occurred more gradually than originally believed. Additional motivation for this research is the observed discrepancy between the theoretically predicted viscosity of the Quarkless Plasma and the empirically observed viscosity of the Quarkless Plasma, indicating that although the spontaneous reorganization of long range interactions appears to have occurred more gradually than originally believed, it appears to have occurred in a manner that is still not well understood.

The accretion of planetesimals is one of the key processes in the planet formation. The growth of planets larger than Mars' mass depends critically on the growth of their residual core, which can only be established through a continuous supply of solid material coupled with the core contraction. In this work, we perform a series of formation and evolution simulations for a sample of cores, with different accretion histories, and compare their outcome compositions with the observed ones for super-earth and hot-super-Earth exoplanets. We find that the cores of super-earth and hot-super-Earth planets tend to have negative and positive accretion histories, respectively. More specifically, during the giant planet formation, the super-earth cores can only accrete 10-30% of its final mass while the hot-super-Earth cores can accumulate up to 70-90% of its final mass through planetesimal accretion. Furthermore, the increase of planetesimal accretion impacts the core’s composition. The super-earth cores tend to have higher average amounts of iron-group elements and lower amounts of light elements compared to those without planetesimal accretion. By contrast, the hot-super-Earth cores have higher enrichments of light elements than those with no planetesimal accretion. These features in core compositions can be verified by the observed super-earth and hot-super-Earth planets. Note: please avoid fancy language and neologisms. Simple English and clear scientific expressions are expected.

A quantitative analysis is given for the separability and entanglement of quantum states in $(2\times{D})$- and $(3\times{D})$-dimensional systems by single-qubit and single-qutrit unitary transformations. For a two-qubit state $\rho$, it is shown that its concurrence $\mathcal{C}(\rho)$ and $\alpha$-uncertainty $\Delta_\alpha(\rho)$ are good measures of its separability and entanglement, respectively, where $\alpha$ is a proper threshold value. It is also shown that the state is separable iff its reduced two-qutrit state is (i) fully entangled (NE), (ii) fully disentangled (product state), or (iii) biseparable but not fully entangled. It is further shown that the amount of entanglement in a $(3\times{D})$-dimensional system is upper bounded by the corresponding concurrence of the reduced $2\times{D}$-dimensional state. Finally, as examples, the results are illustrated for several two-qubit and two-qutrit states of various dimensions, including Werner and isotropic states, and the Horodecki states.' Keywords: Quantum information; Quantum entanglement; Unitary transformation; Entropy; Coefficient of variation PACS numbers: 04.60.Nc, 02.60. Os, 03.65. Yz

A 3-stranded quantum algorithm for the Jones polynomial is presented. The Jones polynomial is a function from oriented links in 3-space to complex numbers, and is an important invariant in the study of knots and links. The Jones polynomial has numerous applications in low-dimensional topology, and has found uses in bioinformatics, coding theory, chemistry, and physics. The Jones polynomial has a particularly nice mathematical property in that it is a polynomial in the normalized Jones function, V(x) = tr( x )[Jones polynomial]/(q−q') where x is a specialized variable related to the form of the link, and q and q' are standard quantum parameters. In this algorithm, the Jones polynomial is calculated using O(n) quantum gates, where n is the number of strands in the link, in contrast to existing quantum algorithms for the Jones polynomial, which have runtime dependence on the number of components in the link.

Wireless networks are formed with nodes that can wirelessly communicate with each other. In an IEEE 802.11 wireless network, nodes can communicate in the 2.4 GHz frequency band and can form the wireless network with other networks. The nodes have limited power and data rates, so they have to choose how many nodes to connect with and form a network. In this paper, the authors use a many-to-one function to calculate the many-to-one throughput capacity of an IEEE 802.11 wireless network. A many-to-one function is a model which shows the amount of information a node can transfer to another node before running out of energy. Through this many-to-one function the authors can calculate the maximum number of nodes that can communicate with each other in an IEEE 802.11 wireless network. The many-to-one function is used to give network architects a tool to decide on how many nodes to connect in an IEEE 802.11 wireless network and how large the network should be.

On 2005 December 28.36 UT, a Type Ib supernova (SN Ib) was discovered in the nearby galaxy M74 (NGC 6503). Soon thereafter, observations by the Swift X-Ray Telescope detected a source (Swift J2058.4+0547) undergoing very rapid X-ray variability, possibly indicative of a highly relativistic jet. If this is associated with the SN Ib, it would make it one of the fastest-evolving supernovae for which such a connection has been detected. SN 2005bf is the first observed example of a Type Ib supernova at nebular phases, when the star had a detectable hydrogen envelope and produced significant amounts of heavy elements. This raises the possibility that the rapid neutron star (RNPS) produced by the explosion may have gone through a magnetar phase, powered by spin-down torque, and that the circumstellar material (CSM) from this phase may have contributed to its late-time X-ray emission. The estimated dipole field strength of the neutron star implied by this fit is B ~ 4.7 × 10^{12} G, one of the largest fields ever observed in a neutron star. This extreme field is likely the result of the efficient extraction of rotational energy by the magnetar. It is thus possible that the energetic explosion of a core-collapse supernova was, in this case, propelled by a strongly magnetized neutron star. This unique event may thus have significance for not only the study of these interesting populations of neutron stars, but also the broader field of high-energy astrophysics and cosmology.

A peculiar structure was identified in the galaxy NGC 1275 (CENTAURUS A): a “hole” with an estimated mass of approximately 1042±409 solar masses, located some 55 million light-years from Earth and about 18,000 light-years in diameter. This object has been called an “Egg” by some, and a “Hen” by others, and still others have regarded it as an intriguing phenomenon in its own right, devoid of taxonomic classification. To date, no evident cause for the creation of this “ Hole within a galaxy ” has been identified. We argue that this structure is most likely the result of the recent violent merging of two galaxies, whose nuclei have fallen inside each other’s gravitational sphere of influence, forming a core-filled nucleus that resembles an Egg. A galaxy merger can also account for the the steeper than expected velocity dispersion of the stars in the core of the Egg, compared to that of the stars in the surrounding region, as predicted by numerical simulations of this kind of events. This and the Egg’s small projected mass make it very likely that it has already fallen completely through its merging progenitors, and will continue to do so in the future. In this sense, we consider the Egg to be a transient structure, of a similar nature to Galactic Hotspots, whose name it loosely resembles, although their origins are clearly unrelated.

Cosmic rays (CRs) are energetic particles in the space, mostly beyond our solar system. Their origin and propagation are key to understanding the fundamental physical processes in the universe. We present a global model of the propagation of CRs, which describes the sources, interactions andObserved signals in a comprehensive way. We apply this model to the data from AMS-02, the first spectrometry of CRs in the cosmic radiation, in the energy range from 0.5 GeV/n to 500 GeV/n. The model parameters are fitted to the measurements, and the goodness of the fit is excellent. We determine the spatial and energy distributions of the sources, and the propagation parameters. In the energy range considered, the sources are predominantly local with contributions from the Solar System, the local galaxy and extragalactic sources. The local contribution is constrained as function of rigidity and latitude. Propagation parameters show strong dependency on rigidity, and consistent with a Kolmogorov spectrum in the interstellar medium, with a spectral break at about 4 times the radius of the solar system.

Reinforcement learning (RL) and evolutionary computation (EC) are powerful and popular techniques that are broadly used to address complex optimization problems. Although traditionally thought of as distinct approaches, in this work we show that by carefully blending them, both global convergence speed and practicality can be greatly improved. More specifically, we develop a novel hybridization called evolutionary reinforcement learning (ERL), which seamlessly integrates the key ideas behind RL and EC, leading to accelerated convergence, and better stability and diversity of the obtained solutions. Our approach is general and can be applied to a broad spectrum of problems that are difficult to solve by conventional techniques. We demonstrate this on several benchmark problems, including classical problem instances from the literature as well as new ones designed to highlight the versatility of the approach. Finally, we also test our approach on complex network dynamics problems, and show that it is highly effective in helping the system converge to better solutions with a much lower computation cost.

An interesting property of the electromagnetic field is birefringence: the plane of polarization of a light wave rotates when traveling through a magnetic field. Over the past century, many observations of the magnetic fields of stars and planets have suggested the presence of a light dilaton or axion, two hypothetical particles that might couple to the electromagnetic field and cause birefringence. To date, these particles have not been observed, and limits on their presence have been published in several steps over the past several decades. This paper presents new limits on the strength of the dilaton and axion coupled to the electromagnetic field, using data from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO). No evidence for these particles was found, imposing limits beyond existing constraints. These results suggest that the coupling between the electromagnetic and dilaton or axion fields must be extremely weak, and therefore further research to observe such a coupling is unlikely to be successful.

Recent spectropolarimetric observations of Balmer-dominated shocks have revealed the presence of a so-called transition zone with characteristics in-between the pre-shock and post-shock regions. The characteristics of this zone are dependent on the properties of the incoming flow, such as the Mach number and the pre-shock magnetic field strength, as well as on the shock strength. In this paper, we present the results of 1D numerical simulations of Balmer-dominated shocks in the strong shock limit, which enable us to characterize the nature of the transition zone and to compute its physical properties as a function of the shock parameters. We find that in strong shock limit, the width of the transition zone scales as the distance between the centers of the pre-shock and shock zone, while its temperature and velocity dispersion scale as the square root of the corresponding pre-shock values. Furthermore, we find that the fractional abundance of ionized carbon decreases exponentially from the pre-shock value to nearly zero across the shock front. We provide scaling relations which can be used to approximate the physical properties of the transition zone in between the pre-shock and post-shock regions, on the basis of the knowledge of the physical parameters of the incoming flow and of the shock.

Spheroidal and torsional modes of shear oscillations were studied in the solid globe models of nuclear physics and pulsar astrophysics. Oscillation equations in the form of ten coupled generalized Sturm-Liouville equations for the radial and tangential displacement components as functions of the longitude and colatitude coordinates are derived and solved. For a spheroidal geometry of the fluid layer, i.e. for an interior equilibrium model of a neutron star with a plane symmetry, the spectrum of eigenfrequencies is obtained in the explicit analytical form. It consists of discrete spheroidal and torsional branches with different properties. The spheroidal eigenfrequencies are determined by the multipole indices n, l and m. The torsional eigenfrequencies are determined by the indices k and m. The spectrum of eigenfrequencies is continuous for l = |n| + 1 and k = |n| + 2, and it contains the two branches with negative square of eigenfrequencies (imaginary eigenfrequencies). The spectra of eigenfrequencies are depicted as functions of the Lamé and Love parameters for some values of the multipole indices n and k. The obtained results are discussed in the context of neutron star seismology.

Heavy-quark fragmentation is a vital process in the characterization of heavy hadrons. It has been shown previously that the nonperturbative heavy-quark decay constant and the distribution of light quarks in the hadron play a significant role in the phenomenological description of hadron fragmentation. In this paper, we analyze the fragmentation process in the framework of perturbative QCD by means of factorization. We demonstrate that the previous conclusion still holds true with the fragmentation function being replaced by the generalizedfragmentation function. Moreover, we propose to use generalized parton correlation functions to parameterize the generalizedfragmentation functions. Numerical calculations show that the distribution functions obtained from the fragmentation and generalizedfragmentation functions are consistent with each other, and the physical predictions are also provided. Our study can be easily extended to the quarkonium hadroproduction, and its results will provide a useful framework for probing the mechanisms of nonperturbative processes in heavy-ion collisions.

Recently, the Higgs sectors of the MSSM and the next-to-MSSM (NMSSM) have been studied in the light of experimental results from the LHC. Light neutral CP-even Higgs bosons can be realised in the large tan_beta region only if the lighter stau is lighter than the lightest supersymmetric particle (LSP) and, in the MSSM, the lighter stop is also lighter than the LSP. However, in the NMSSM this is not necessary, and the lightest CP-even Higgs boson can be light even if both stops are considerably heavier than the LSP. In this case, the Higgs bosons may be pair-produced at the LHC, and at the same time the LSP is weakly interacting and thus escape detection. We study this novel scenario, obtaining explicit examples that satisfy all experimental constraints. We compute the production cross sections of this SUSY Higgs boson pair at the LHC, showing that it can be substantially larger than the corresponding production cross section in the MSSM, and discuss the observability of this scenario with the HL-LHC.

The energy cost of wireless communication has become a major concern for the proliferation of broadband services. In the future, it is expected that wireless systems will be exposed to multiple simultaneous wireless traffic types and will be required to support high spectral efficiency, large number of devices, and coverage of complex terrain. To meet these demands, next generation wireless networks will need to be energy efficient, while maintaining high data transfer rates for each link. This becomes a significant challenge for current CDMA systems, since wireless channel characteristics are highly time variant due to both fast fading and large scale multi-path effects. Traditionally, this issue has been handled through the use of sophisticated receivers that are able to rapidly detect the channel, and adapt transmit power accordingly. However, the rapid changes in channel characteristics require the design of very complicated and energy intensive receivers, which cannot be practically deployed. In this paper, we analyze a more energy efficient approach that adapts the transmitter to the current channel state, allowing the transmitter to adjust its transmit waveform in such a way that reduces the average transmit energy per bit, independent of the receiver. This is accomplished by careful control of the waveform’s peak power, while ensuring that the signal satisfies the average power requirements of the system. Our main result is a general lower bound on the energy per bit as a function of the peak and average power constraints. Based on this lower bound, we construct a waveform that converges to the bound with high probability, under the assumption that the channel is known at the transmitter. Our analysis provides insight into the role of the system parameters, such as the bandwidth and number of paths, on the energy efficiency of the waveform. We also propose a low-complexity receiver that is able to track the waveform with high probability, and thus, track the energy efficiency of the waveform. Numerical results show that our waveform significantly outperforms existing transmission techniques in terms of average energy per bit, while guaranteeing reliable communication across time-varying fading channels.

Cesium vapour offers many advantages as a candidate medium for magneto-optical resonators. The large Landé g-factor, $g_{F} = 7/2$, of the 7D$_{3/2}$ state makes the D lines particularly suitable for optical investigation of magnetic responses. These resonances are very narrow (a few Hz), and their sensitivity to temperature and pressure, both of which affect the Cesium density, makes stability requirements moderate. We have studied the D$_2$ line at 795 nm in an extremely thin cell, with a Cs layer only 9 pm thick. Feshbach resonances in this system lead to narrow and highly sensitive absorption lines that should make the cell suitable for active optical magnetometry. We observed robust magneto-optical resonances that were highly linear with applied field, with a sensitivity of 8 mG / (Hz cm$^2$). We believe that the narrow linewidths and simple setup make this a promising candidate medium for optical magnetometry with minimal additional hardware.

This paper investigates the networked dynamic behavior of interconnected systems. For this purpose, based on the passivity theory, a sufficient condition for stability of interconnected systems is presented in terms of a quadratic matrix inequality (QMI). Unlike the existing results, the considered system is composed of interconnected subsystems, and the subsystem input includes control input and input from other subsystems. Due to the coupling between the subsystems, the presented stability criterion can be applied to the interconnected systems with delays and component mismatches. Several examples are given to illustrate the effectiveness of the developed results. In a networked system, multiple subsystems are often interrelated. For example, in a biological network, each biological process is influenced by other biological processes. Therefore, a desirable stability criterion for a networked system should consider the effect of network connections on stability of the subsystems. The stability criteria presented in this paper allow us to consider such coupling effects.

A dense reservoir of gas and dust surrounds young stars, but the process by which stars acquire the materials needed to form remains a mystery. Observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Very Large Array (VLA) have provided evidence that mass may be transferred from larger to smaller scales via gravitational fragmentation and stellar accretion. Here, we present a class of hydrodynamical and non-hydrodynamical models of gravitational fragmentation in massive protostellar disks that focus on the role of line emission from the disks' component molecules in coupling the disk properties to ALMA and the EVLA resolutions. We find that, for an ALMA survey of 16 sources that uniformly samples parameter space over three star-forming regions, a statistical detection of line emission can provide constraints on the gas masses in the innermost few hundred au, including the transition from gravitational instability to vertically integrated Toomre's Q≈1.0 at a radius of ≲100 au, the location where material is first funnelled toward the central protostar on ≲1-10 yrs. Line emission can also provide constraints on the infall rates of ≲3×10−6M⊙yr-1, independent of the mass of the central star. For a VLA survey of nine sources that uniformly samples parameter space over the Cygnus X star-forming region, we find that the infall rate can be determined to within a factor of 2.5, with an average uncertainty of 40%. While models with Keplerian rotation profiles around the central star are ideal laboratories for predicting emission line profiles and strengths, likely ALMA survey lengths are too short to conclusively determine the rotation profiles. However, given the existence of anomalous velocity wings in observed line profiles from disks around young stars, we predict that future ALMA and VLA observations with higher spectral and angular resolutions may be able to discern a diversity of rotation profiles even for a single source, including radially declining rotation and local enhancements in the rotation profile.

English syntax evolved rapidly in the last millennium. A prime example are cases, which shifted from syntactic roles (direct objects, indirect objects, etc.) to a more categorical structure. As this transition happened in the dialects of distinct (Southern) English regions, it's tempting to speculate about differences in "localness" or other compositional factors. This paper presents a network-theoretic investigation of early Modern English syntax, from a corpus of quotations from Robert Lowth's 1762/3 Introduction to English Grammar. It finds four distinct syntactic roles (NP, VP, CP, and wh- word, which are the subject of this paper), and these seem to have co-existed alongside of a basic case system (N, V, C) since at least the 13th century. Beyond these core findings, the paper presents a methodological contribution to computational syntax by presenting network-theoretic analyses of English syntax for the first time. The corpus is available under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license, and the LaTeX source document is available at https://github.com/matteocastelli/EarlyModernEnglishSyntax.

Late-type red supergiants (LTRSGs) are evolved stars that are the immediate precursors of massive Wolf–Rayet stars and cannot be observed in the local group of galaxies. This includes the Milky Way (MW), the Local Group (LG) and the satellite galaxies of the MW, such as the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC, respectively). They are of particular interest due to their importance as both the upper end of the initial mass function (IMF) and as possible progenitors for compact binaries, such as gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and potential gravitational wave sources. Despite the proximity of the LMC and SMC, and their extensive observational studies, only a small number of LTRSGs have been identified. This may be due to LTRSGs being evolved stars and so relatively faint, or due to them not existing in these galaxies, for example due to their high luminosity requirements. To test this hypothesis, I searched for LTRSGs in two satellite galaxies of the MW, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. I used deep, high-resolution imaging from the 6.5 meter Magellan telescopes and the wide-field Pan-STARRS1 (PS1) Survey to identify candidates and extract photometric information. Two bona fide LTRSGs were identified in the SMC, but not in the LMC. This suggests that although LTRSGs do not appear in the LG, they may exist in small satellite galaxies such as the LMC.

Recent advances in graphene electronics and informatics have spurred development of various graphene based electronic devices. In this work, we propose a graphene spin transistor that harnesses the spin degree of freedom of electrons for functionality. We evaluate our proposed device using quantum transport techniques and demonstrate that the on-state current through the device can be modulated by applying a gate voltage, enabling us to operate the device as a logical switch. Our study provides a platform for exploring various device designs and functionalities based on the spin degree of freedom of electrons in graphene. This work was performed at Argonne National Laboratory, using facilities supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Office of Basic Energy Sciences, under contract No. DE-AC02-06CH11357. Graphene, a two-dimensional atomic crystal, has remarkable electronic and mechanical properties1-4. In particular, its charge carriers behave like Dirac fermions, where the linear dispersion and the associated near-light velocities make graphene a potentially promising material for high-speed electronic applications5,6. Graphene exhibits spin-orbit coupling arising from its particular structure, which gives rise to spin-dependent contributions to the electronic band structure7. Moreover, its high strength of Coulomb interaction can lead to the fractionalization of electrons into spin and charge degrees of freedom8. These properties of graphene offer the exciting prospect of manipulating the spin degree of freedom of electrons in a graphene device for spintronics applications. Exciting recent progress in the development of low-dimensional materials has enabled experimental exploration of intriguing physical phenomena arising from the spin degree of freedom9-19. Spin-orbit interaction in two-dimensional systems, such as the dirac surface states in topological insulators, can give rise to a number of intriguing phenomena, including the spin hall effect20, magnetic anomalous Hall effect21, and the intrinsic spin Seebeck effect22. Graphene has been shown to exhibit magnetotransport phenomena related to the spin degree of freedom, such as the anomalous and conventional Hall effects23,24, and the spin Seebeck effect25. The spin hall and spin Seebeck effects in graphene arise due to the existence of an energy gap in the spin-up and spin-down conduction bands, which generates an intrinsic spin field9,10,11. These properties have inspired proposals for graphene-based devices that exploit the spin degree of freedom for functionality. For example, an electric field induced spin splitting in a graphene electron gas channel has been proposed for use in spintronic devices26. However, further development of graphene devices for practical applications requires an understanding of fundamental device operation principles, as well as a comprehensive design space exploration. In this work, we propose and analyze a graphene spin transistor that operates through the manipulation of the spin degree of freedom in electrons. Similar to the gating effects that modulate electronic transport through traditional field effect transistors, we demonstrate that an applied gate voltage can modulate the spin transport

A quantum key distribution (QKD) system is developed using superconducting single photon detectors (SSPDs). QKD systems using semiconductor detectors are vulnerable to channel noise, which causes detection errors due to light emitted by the scintillators in the detectors. However, the SSPDs used in this work have no detection noise due to room temperature operation, enabling high bitrates and secure key generation over channels with high levels of channel noise. A key generation rate of ~1 Mbit/s over a channel with 40 dB of losses is achieved, along with proof of detection, identification, and accidental coincidence rejection. These results represent the first high speed, high volume QKD system using SSPDs and demonstrate the viability of this technology for future high capacity, low cost quantum networks. The application of SSPDs to QKD allows the development of systems with high bitrates and secure key generation over channels with high levels of channel noise. As a proof of principle, a QKD system using SSPDs achieves key generation at ~1Mbits/s over a 40 dB loss channel. This is the first QKD system to achieve high speed operation with SSPDs and the first to demonstrate securekey generation over a high loss channel.

A rigorous time-domain analysis of full-wave electromagnetic cloaking is presented, which demonstrates the possibility of invisibility in electromagnetic waves for the first time. The proposed solution to the electromagnetic cloak problem is to change the behavior of the electromagnetic wave on the outer surface of the cloak, such that the wave changes its phase while traveling around the cloak, such that the wave is canceled out when it exits the cloak. This is in direct contrast to solutions presented in the past which changed the electromagnetic wave's amplitude while traveling around the cloak. By establishing this phase change as the governing mechanism of invisibility, it is shown that a virtual image can be formed anywhere along the route of the electromagnetic wave, even if the cloak is rotated or extended. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this phenomenon is not limited to spherical cloaks, but can be extended to non-spherical cloaks, which greatly increases the functionality of the cloak. Finally, an assessment of the applicability of this phenomenon to biological imaging systems is provided, in which it is demonstrated that the proposed cloak is able to function in the radio frequency spectrum, where conventional electromagnetic cloaking is not possible.

Using data from the INTErnational Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL), we have studied the gamma-ray emission from the Galactic Centre region. The region is of interest due to its proximity and high concentration of massive black holes and pulsars. We performed a detailed spatial and spectral analysis of the 18 months of public observations covering the region. We find significant emission arising from the central 6 parsec, with spatial structures and spectral variations on both long and short time-scales. In particular, we identify a newly discovered MeV gamma-ray halo surrounding the central core. We investigate the possible origins of the emission, and find that both leptonic and hadronic processes are necessary to explain the data. In the former scenario, we consider both broad-line and narrow-line regions, and find that a combination of simple one-zone models are insufficient to explain the data. In the latter scenario, we consider the possibility of a population of fast transient sources. We find that a physical model in which distant supernova remnants collide with molecular clouds is consistent with the data, and require a dense wind of material from the central supermassive black hole to explain the gamma-ray halo. We discuss the testable implications of this model, and suggest future gamma-ray observations which may distinguish between the two scenarios.

Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPO) in the X-ray flux from some compact objects have been discovered over the past three decades. Two distinct families of QPO have been identified; the lower-frequency (LF) QPOs (0.001–30 Hz) and the upper-frequency (HF) QPOs (0.03–300 Hz). The HF QPOs are particularly intriguing, as several sources have more than one distinct HF QPO peak, indicating that these objects are rotating near to some stable self-frequency. The distinct frequencies of the HF QPO peaks, their clustering around some values and their occasional stability over long time periods, are best explained if the peaks are produced by fluid moving in circular geodetic orbits in a compact object such as a neutron star or a black hole. The gravitomagnetic effects produced by the fluid could be responsible for the modulation of the orbital periods, causing the distinct HF QPO peaks. In this way, the gravitomagnetic effects could act as a unifying mechanism for several existing models of compact objects.

Astronomers presented high-precision astrometry on the VLT/FORS1 at time scales of few days for the first time. Based on images obtained in five intermediate bands between 450 and 930 nm and collected over a baseline of 2-3 days, the proper motions of various objects were determined with precisions down to 12.8±4.9 km/s, corresponding to acceleration figures of up to 8.2 m/s2. While this result can be achieved for individual objects, the most exciting results were obtained for fields containing clusters of stars. In the old open cluster NGC 7142, a group of 22 probable cluster members was identified whose kinematics suggest they are most likely associated with the cluster. An acceleration of up to 5.2 m/s2 was determined for one of these stars, the most significant measurement of its kind to date. In addition, the proper motion of another open cluster, NGC 1976, was measured for the first time, revealing an acceleration of 1.2 m/s2. The results presented here demonstrate the capabilities of modern large telescopes to measure accelerations using astrometry in multiple bands over short time baselines and therefore have important implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of stars and their environments.

In this paper, we perform a detailed comparison between several low-temperature and high-temperature approximation schemes for the stationary solution of the Ornstein-Zernike equation involving friction and hard-sphere interaction. We compare these schemes with numerical solutions of the corresponding integral equation and with Monte Carlo simulations of an effective hard-sphere (H Obamacare) model. We also show that our results can be used to obtain low- and high-temperature approximations for the solution of the Lado-Swift-Hohenberg equation, which is widely used to study patterns formation in evaporating drops and films. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In the next section, we present the main equations and approximation schemes. The results of the comparison between these schemes and numerical solutions of the integral equations as well as with Monte Carlo simulations are presented and discussed in section 3. We conclude the paper with a brief summary of the main results in section 4.

Magnetic, magneto-thermal and magneto-transport properties in SmMn2Si2-xGex compounds were investigated. All samples were synthesized by high-pressure high-temperature method. The SmMn2Si2 compound has a substitution-independent short-range ordered (SRO) MnSi-type structure with the D4h point group symmetry. Inverse compensation between the large positive temperature coefficient of the specific magnetic heat coefficient and the negative temperature coefficient of the total magnetic entropy suggests the presence of local magnetic order in this compound. Some of the samples were substituted with Ge up to x = 0.18. With Ge substitution, the SRO phase is stable up to only x = 0.12. For higher Ge concentrations, a structurally unrelated disordered phase with A2-like structure emerges. This phase is characterized by negative temperature coefficient of the total magnetic entropy and weak positive temperature coefficient of the specific magnetic heat coefficient. Surprisingly, in the disordered phase, a gradual increase of the Mn local magnetic moments by Ge substitution was observed. Additionally, the magnetization curve at low temperatures for Sm0.82Ge0.18Mn2.62Si2 compound exhibits a rapid increase below 2 K, most likely due to a reduction of magnetic interactions between Mn local moments via Ge substitution. The transport measurements revealed semiconductor-type behavior for all samples with the exception of the disordered phase of Sm0.82Ge0.18Mn2.62Si2 compound, which exhibits a weakly-conducting behavior. These results indicate on the presence of competing short-range and long-range orders in SmMn2Si2-xGex compounds and a tendency of the system to phase separation with the formation of separate Ge-rich regions with a weak conducting antiferromagnetic (AFM) long-range order and relatively Mn-rich regions with a short-range ordering. The latter exhibits a gradually decreasing Mn local moments with Ge substitution and, hence, a gradual changing from the AFM to weak ferromagnetic (WF) state. The presented study sheds light on the mechanisms of magnetism and electrical transport in these materials and their evolution with Ge substitution.

A new "diamond-ring" star has been discovered in the galactic centre. The unusual morphology is characterised by a "cross" structure composed of two opposite "arms" which present a different brightness and are connected by a "bridge" region. The "diamond-ring" system appears to be relatively young, less than 200 thousand years old, and its formation has been triggered by the strong gravitational interaction with the compact radio source Sgr A*. Numerical simulations showed that the "diamond-ring" system may have been disturbed by strong gas flows produced by the radio source. The discovery of this "diamond-ring" system, which may also be considered a "disrupted system", represents an important step forward in our understanding of the formation process of multiple systems. In particular, it seems that the development of multiple systems does not depend only on the properties of the formed objects, but also on the influence of their neighbours.

Personal archives (PAs) are frequently used to record and preserve personal information and data over time. Internet browsing activities are typically considered personal information that should be stored in a PA. However, personal archives may consume significant storage resources and curation resources. The current research focuses on methods and systems to evaluate different personal archiving strategies for Internet browsing activities. Three evaluation dimensions are proposed: storage resource consumption, curation cost, and retention utility. Four browsing scenarios are evaluated using a search engine as the retrieval method. The results indicate that automatically-generated short-term PAs are the most storage-efficient strategy for frequent browsing activities. For infrequent browsing activities, gold-based PAs provide the best overall storage-efficiency and retention utility tradeoff. Keywords: Personal Archives, Internet Browsing Activity, Short-term PA, Gold-based PA, Retention Utility, Search Engine

We report the detection of six magnetically-driven explosions of rapidly-rotating white dwarfs (WDs) following accretion-induced collapse. The survey was conducted using the ASAS-SN virtual telescope, which monitors the entire visible sky every few hours. Such explosions had not been observed from these objects before as all previously-known examples were from low-mass WDs. These explosions are characterized by a rapidly- rising brightness in the days leading up to the explosion, followed by a plateau, and ultimately a decay in magnitude. The plateau is caused by the ongoing collapse of the rotating WD to a neutron star or black hole. The explosion is confirmed by the presence of an underlying plateau in the subsequent light curve, which is not seen in cases of stable nuclear burning on the WD surface. The plateau duration and luminosity are consistent with the expected range for the amount of ejected material. We compare the observations to 1D hydrodynamical simulations of accretion-induced collapse with and without the inclusion of powerful magnetic fields, and find that the emission can best reproduced by simulations that include magnetic fields. We calculate the magnetic fields required to drive the explosions are approximately 100MG, which is within the capability of future megnetore facilities such as the Exawatt center for Plasma research in the EU and NASA's Long duration balloon program. Here we report on the detection of six exploding WDs, all of which had been observed by ASAS-SN previously. Of the six, four showed plateau-like light curves with distinct decreases in magnitude in the days leading up to the explosion, consistent with previous reports of magnetically-driven explosions from low-mass WDs. Two additional objects, namely SDSS J0804+2052 and SDSS J2315+1855, showed distinct plateau-like decreases in magnitude without the preceding increase in brightness, consistent with the scenario for magnetically-driven explosions from rapidly-rotating WDs for the first time. We compared the observed plateau durations and luminosities to simulations that included and excluded magnetic fields, and found that the emission from both simulations was best reproduced by simulations that included magnetic fields. Using our measured plateau durations and luminosities, we calculated the corresponding ejected material masses for each event, and found that these were within the expected range for material ejected in such explosions. We also determined the probable locations of the progenitor stars by cross-referencing our sample to Gaia Data Release 2 and found that four of the exploding WDs had most likely been observed in the field of view of their respective host galaxies. This is consistent with the idea that explosions from rapidly-rotating WDs are more likely to be detectable from their host galaxies than explosions from low-mass WDs. Our findings demonstrate that magnetic fields have a critical impact on the explosion mechanisms and outcomes from this astrophysical scenario and that such explosions are a promising avenue for the retention of mass in rapidly-rotating WDs. The epoch of reionization (EoR) was the last phase of the evolution of the neutral intergalactic medium (IGM), during which the ionizing background from the first galaxies was able to globally reionize the IGM. Early simulations of this epoch tended to overpredict the depth of the EoR, suggesting that sources were too rare or of lower luminosity than expected. Subsequent modeling improved the likelihood of detection and reducing the magnitude of the ionizing sources necessary. Here we present the results of an ensemble of twelve 50-hr zoomed simulations of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR) undertaken with the zoominitial conditions (ZIC) method. Our largest simulation (B2) has a boxsize of 20h$^{-1}$Mpc and a mass resolution of 1.4$\times$10$^{10}$M$_{\odot}$ per spatial pixel. Each simulation fully incorporates baryonic physics (including treatment of metal diffusion and updated versions of the TreeSPH code), a suitable model for the initial density field, and a battery of different radiative transfer post-processing to capture the patchiness of the EoR. The duration of this sequence of simulations varies from $0 \leq z \leq 15$, with redshift bins uniformly sampled in time and space and a maximum comoving spatial resolution of 1.5$\times$10$^{-3}$h$^{-1}$Mpc. We analyze the EoR signal in the light of ionizing UV photons as deduced from our ensemble, finding good agreement between the mean intensity of UV photons and the volume-weighted global Thomson scattering optical depth. Simulated sightlines also exhibit an extended tail of high optical depth that agrees well with high-redshift galaxy observations. However, our simulation suite contains a sufficient number of low-density, high-redshift systems to reproduce the observed mean intensity at the $\lesssim$20% level, even in the lowest-resolution simulation. We also examine the spatial distribution of EoR structures in our highest-redshift simulations and find good agreement with results from higher-resolution simulations. Our work presents twelve 50-hr zoomed simulations of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR) with sufficient resolution to capture the prominent features of the EoR and provides a valuable tool for subsequent tests of proposed EoR models and statistical analysis of the volume of the Early Universe simulated to date.

We show that the Bohmian mechanics of a quantum system whose wavefunction is entangled admits local de Broglie-Bohm trajectories in the limit of an infinitesimal wavelength. More precisely, we show that the Bohmian position of a test particle is a local constant of the motion for any wavefunction that is a nontrivial entangled discrete or continuous superposition of product states. We give an explicit formula for this local de Broglie-Bohm wave in terms of the original wavefunction, and we apply our result to delocalized solutions of the one-dimensional quantum many-body dynamical Yang-Lee model, which includes the 1D Bose gas, the 1D hard-core gas, and the spin 1/2 XX model. We establish this result by first considering a discretized version of the original wavefunction, in which the original wavefunction is a nontrivial entangled superposition of product states. We then show that a similar result holds for the continuous limit of this discretized wavefunction. The proof proceeds by showing that the Bohmian position is a constant of the motion for any wavefunction that is a product state of the original wavefunction and its complex conjugate. We show that the real and imaginary parts of the continuous limit of the discretized wavefunction each have this property, and then prove the result by proving that the real and imaginary parts of the original wavefunction satisfy this property separately. We also show that the continuous limit of the discretized wavefunction converges to the original wavefunction in the limit of an infinitesimal wavepacket. The proof also gives us an explicit formula for the local de Broglie-Bohm wave in terms of the original wavefunction. We demonstrate the versatility of this formula by applying it to localize delocalized solutions of the dynamical Yang-Lee model. Our result generalizes a recent proof of the existence of local de Broglie-Bohm trajectories for single qubits that are in a product state of eigenstates of the z-axis component of the spin operator and its adjoint operator. We show that this result extends to the full quantum many-body dynamical Yang-Lee model, which cannot be solved by existing numerical techniques. Our result has implications for experiments with quantum systems. For example, we show that it may be possible to measure local de Broglie-Bohm trajectories for entangled many-body quantum systems using imaging techniques such as electron microscopy and light microscopy in combination with conventional Bohmian quantum mechanics experiments. We also suggest an application to quantum magnetometry. We show that the spatial structure of the Bohmian local de Broglie-Bohm wave reveals information about the local values of the angle of the total spin in the dynamical Yang-Lee model, which may be used to image this angle. Atomic data from the Iron Project (IP) have been made available via the internet for use in stellar and plasma physics, quantum chemistry, nuclear physics, materials science, and atomic science. The IP has been a long-term collaborative effort among many institutions to collect and organize accurate, robust, and well-vetted atomic data for all elements with masses between He and copper. The data has been organized in easily browsable databases with custom HTTP and HTTPS endpoints. We provide here data for radiative transition rates and collision strengths for Ca II. The data have been checked for reliability and consistency against other sources and our previous data for similar elements. Where data were not available elsewhere we have provided our own calculations and estimates of the uncertainty to allow for modeling and analysis by others. The full details of the data and its organization, including references to the original sources, can be found at https://doi.org/10.26208/data.0000002329.

Pulsars are known to emit radio pulses with an approximate periodic shape. The emission is from the magnetic poles of the neutron star and the direction of the magnetic axis is almost always perpendicular to the magnetic axis. The intensity of the pulse varies according to a predictable pattern. The variation is divided into manycomponents or subpulses, which are approximately 1/percent of the pulse period. Previous work has shown that the subpulse modulation properties of pulsars at 92 cm can be used to determine some of the pulsar's physical characteristics, including the magnetic field strength and the angle between the magnetic and rotational axes. Here we show that the subpulse modulation properties of a pulsar at 92 cm also depend on the frequency of the emitted radio pulses. Specifically, the widths of the subpulse modulation profiles widen with increasing frequency. This is consistent with a model in which the subpulse modulation is caused by a interference pattern between two components of the radio emission, which are emitted with different frequencies.

Nucleosomes are the fundamental unit of chromatin. The structure of chromatin is formed by nucleosomes and linker DNAs that are wrapped around histone proteins in regular patterns. These patterns determine its higher-order structure and lead to the formation of chromosomal domains with different structural and functional properties. One of the critical parameters determining the higher-order structure of chromatin is the diameter of its fiber. It has been recently shown that small fluctuations in the diameter of chromatin fibers may have a large impact on the organization of DNA in chromatin. The influence of the diameter of the nucleosome core was proven to be significant, whereas the influence of the histone H1 was not confirmed. To explain the obtained experimental results, it was proposed that another factor, i.e., the cylindrical shape of the nucleosome and the histone H1, may also have a significant effect on the structure and organization of chromatin. These factors may affect the effective diameter of the fiber and, thus, the structure and properties of chromatin. A quantitative analysis of the proposed model will be presented here. The parameters of the model were obtained from the analysis of experimental data on the average diameter of chromatin fibers and the average diameter of the nucleosome and the histone H1. Using this model, we have calculated the effective diameter of the fiber and the average probability of the formation of defects in histone H1. The latter was estimated from experimental data on the frequency of occurrence of histone H1 defects. The comparison of the model predictions with the experimental data has shown that taking into account the cylindrical shape of the nucleosome and histone H1 leads to a satisfactory agreement between the experimental and theoretical results. This supports the proposed hypothesis on the effect of the cylindrical shape of nucleosomes and histone H1 on the structure and organization of chromatin.

Fusion energy is an emerging technologies with great potential to alleviate the world energy crisis. However, widespread applications of fusion energy are currently limited by high costs associated with currently employed reactor designs. As an emerging technology, heavy water reactor is used as a baseline design for the ITER project which will achieve commercial fusion reactors in the 2030s. The fusion energy benefit will be realised once ITER is successfully upgraded to DEMO in the 2040s. There is, therefore, an urgency to reduce the cost of fusion reactor development by developing an inexpensive baseline reactor design. In this work, we present a hybrid model for fusion at deep sub-barrier energies. The model combines quantum mechanics molecular dynamics which solves the time dependent Schrödinger equation to compute electronic structure with a force field to compute the nuclear part. We validate the model by reproducing the survival rate and released energy of 53 experiments performed at the Royal Holloway, University of London. The model is then applied to the case study of an ohmic heating in hydrogen gas. The proposed hybrid fusion model can be directly used to simulate the design and operation of ITER DEMO reactor. The model could also be applied to optimize other fusion reactor designs such as MIST.

A long electromagnetic afterglow of a gamma-ray burst (GRB) is conventionally expected to generate a two-shock structure: an reverse shock propagating into the circum-burst environment and a forward shock propagating into the ejecta. In this work, we report the discovery of a rebrightening feature in the X-ray light curves of 11Swift GRB afterglows. We demonstrate that this rebrightening can be well explained by a jet-break model, in which the jet opening angle increases suddenly at a break time (t_b) after the prompt emission. We measure the typical values of t_b and the post-break slopes, which are comparable to the results from synchrotron-self-Compton (SSC) model prediction for some theoretical setups. We suggest that the break time t_b may be used as a new diagnostic for different theoretical models, and put constraints on the circumburst medium density and the initial radius of the shell. The original research is published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, Vol. 875, L27 ( March 2019).(1)

He-4 is the most abundant element in the universe, and its prevalence in galaxy clusters and the Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect have been well established. However, the gas fraction of galaxy clusters is not large enough for all the helium to be neutral, and recent claims of non-negligible gaseous helium in massive galaxy clusters have thus far been contested. Using high-quality data from the South Pole Telescope, we conclusively rule out this possibility at the 3σ level. In the last decade, new X-ray astronomy facilities and innovative analyses have allowed the detection of the SZ effect to clusters of galaxies, proving the existence of faint, ubiquitous cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons scattered by the electrons in the hotter regions of the clusters. The thermal SZ effect is specific to each cluster, and its spectral signature can be used to estimate the total thermal energy, the Hubble constant, and the gas mass fraction of the cluster. The non-thermal (or SZ Pauli) effect, discovered a decade ago, has a spatial structure that depends on the particles' distribution and can be used to probe the interaction of the clusters' contents with the energetic particles of the large-scale structure. In this work, we present and analyse X-ray and SZ observations of the galaxy cluster ZwCl 2764. We measure the gas fraction of the cluster and its ICM temperature and density. We also use the SZ observations of the cluster to constrain the Hubble constant. We find a best-fitting cosmological parameters of H0 = 68.2±1.5 km/s/Mpc, which is in agreement with the results obtained from other cosmological probes.

In the nuclei of active galaxies, a supermassive black hole and an accretion disk are frequently observed. The former is fundamental to determining the central mass, while the latter is the most efficient means of extracting energy from it. Thus, measurement of the mass of the central black hole is one of the most direct ways of assessing the activity of a galaxy. Since the Fe Kα emission line is among the most significant spectral features of the putative accretion disks in active galaxies, it is a viable method of measuring the mass of the central black hole. To this end, we analyzed an archival Suzaku observation of the nucleus of the radio-loud active galaxy Centaurus A. No significant line features were found, and we set a 90% confidence limit on the line normalization of 6.4%, which is the most stringent limit to date for this source. This lack of detection can be explained by a variety of means. If the emission region is neutral, it may be consistent with the stellar velocity dispersion of the central cusp, and this is also viable in terms of the reflection model. Additionally, there is evidence for a Compton thick absorber in the X-ray spectrum, which could be obscuring the nuclear region. Furthermore, there are known issues with the previously employed data analysis methodology, and it is possible that a systematic error in that work is responsible. In short, a positive detection of the Fe Kα line provides a strong case for the presence of an accretion disk, while a lack of such a detection does not rule out the presence of an accretion disk.

In this paper, we consider a one-dimensional damped wave equation in a square. We show that the longitudinal strain energy density, which is the metric in elasticity theory, is a geometrical quantity that satisfies the damped wave equation. The longitudinal strain energy density has been used to characterize the mode I and mode II transversal vibration of a plate. We find the formulas to compute the longitudinal strain energy density at a point in the square based on the value at neighboring points. The solution of the damped wave equation indicates that the longitudinal strain energy density decreases in time like an exponential. We also show that the area strain energy density, which is the metric in Fluid theory, is a geometrical quantity that satisfies the damped wave equation. The area strain energy density has been used to describe the irrotational flow of a fluid. We also find the solution of the damped wave equation and find that the area strain energy density decreases in time like an exponential.

A combination of experimental and computational techniques is used to characterize the mechanical response of keratin fibres at the molecular level. We probe the secondary structure of purified chicken feathers by Raman spectroscopy and find that the alpha helix structure dominates the starting material but that it gradually transforms into a mixed beta sheet/random coil structure as water is removed. We model this alpha helix -> beta sheet transition using all-atom molecular dynamics simulations and show that this transformation is primarily driven by the loss of alpha helix structure and the corresponding increase in sheet structure. We use nano-indentation to probe the structure-property relationship in these feathers and use complementary atomistic/mesoscale modelling to correlate the mechanical response with specific structural features. We find that local chain bend structure (as opposed to overall crystallinity) governs the mechanical stiffness of the feather, with this stiffness decreasing dramatically once the feather transitions from an alpha helix to a random coil structure. We further explore the role of hydration, and find that while bulk properties (modelled by Brownian dynamics) are independent of hydration, local chain bend structure is dramatically influenced by the presence of water, particularly at intermediate time scales. Overall, our results demonstrate that the nanomechanical response of keratin is governed by both local chain bend structure and hydration effects, and that nano-indentation can be an effective technique for probing keratin structure at the molecular level.

Interstellar ices may provide the only reservoir of organics in the Galaxy, and thus their chemical compositions and structures are crucial to our understanding of how life originated on Earth. The simplest possible organic molecule, HCOOH, was recently detected in the interstellar medium (ISM) through its infrared vibration-rotation band at 3735 cm−1. Infrared spectroscopy of this band has now been performed for a series of solid HCOOH analogues, grown in an interstellar ice analog consisting of amorphous solid water deposited on a metal surface. The results provide strong evidence that the 3735 cm−1 band arises from quantum mechanical tunneling between local energy minima on an asymmetric double-well potential energy surface. This information will be of value in understanding the origin and evolution of carbon on Earth and other planets. Ice analogues of HCOOH have been grown in an interstellar ice analog consisting of amorphous solid water deposited on a metal surface. High-resolution infrared spectroscopy has been performed on the 3735 cm−1 vibration-rotation band of the HCOOH molecule. These data provide strong evidence that the 3735 cm−1 band arises from quantum mechanical tunneling between local energy minima on an asymmetric double-well potential energy surface. These results provide crucial information about the chemistry and physics of interstellar ices, which are vital to understanding how life originated on Earth.

Graphene, a monolayer of carbon atoms with a remarkable atomic structure, has attracted immense interest recently because of its diverse extraordinary properties, such as extremely high carrier mobility, which leads to the achievement of the record high carrier mobility of ~26,000 cm2 V-1 s-1 in monolayer graphene. One major drawback in the practical applications of graphene is the lack of band gap, which severely restricts its utilization in energy related devices. Traditionally, semiconductors are utilized to manufacture electronic devices such as transistors, solar cells, and LEDs due to the abundance of silicon and the highly effective crystalline structure of silicon based semiconductors. The lack of band gap in graphene has led to investigations into several methods to introduce a band gap in graphene. Recently, it has been theoretically shown that an alternative approach to introduce a band gap in graphene, which is without the need for any external constraint or reagents, is to introduce a periodic potential through modulating the potential landscape on the surface of graphene with an external gate electrode. One such method is to introduce a periodic electric field, which can be achieved through Coulomb drag, where one layer of charge carriers is subjected to an electric field and a second layer of charge carriers is polarized in the opposite direction of the first layer. Coulomb drag has been observed in two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in semiconductor systems with the presence of a high concentration of electrons and holes in a material with a band gap, such as GaAs, InAs, or GaN. Therefore, Coulomb drag is a viable approach to introduce a band gap in graphene. In this work, we observe Coulomb Drag in graphene, the first observation of Coulomb Drag in a 2D material system. By growing a thin layer of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) on top of a synthesized graphene monolayer, we can isolate and control the charge carriers in one layer from the other via structural electric field screening. An electric field is then applied between the separated layers and is observed to produce charge separation in the layer subjected to the electric field. This charge separation induces a static polarisation in the other layer via the Kapitza-Dirac effect. The induced static polarisation is observed via capacitance measurements on the separated layers. We observe positive drag, where the charge carrier layer with applied electric field has a higher charge density and negative drag, where the charge carrier layer with polarisation has a lower charge density. Coulomb Drag in graphene is successfully observed for the first time and opens the door to study a material with unique properties such as graphene in a fully tunable bandgap environment, h-BN.

Multicritical behavior of the gonihedric model is analyzed. This theory is a 3+1-dimensional generalizations of multicritical Ising model with dynamical critical exponent z=3. We show that this model exhibits multicritical point with (3,2) Lifshitz point symmetry. We exactly solve the model using loop series method and show that the model has second-order critical lines that connect three tricritical points with (1,1), (2,1) and (1,2) Lifshitz points. These critical lines meet at multicritical point that satisfy (d,m)=(3,2) Lifshitz point symmetry. We find that model has sixth-order phase transitions along the first-order lines that separate phases with different realizations of (d,m) Lifshitz points. The Lifshitz point with (3,2) symmetry was first described in the framework of Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson theory with (d,m)=(3,2) symmetry breaking term in the Hamiltonian but it was later shown that this behavior is not stable, the true Lifshitz point with (d,m)=(3,2) symmetry exists and it can be realized in the gonihedric model. We also describe how to extract numerical values of the critical exponents and construct phase diagrams for various values of dynamical critical exponent z.

We present deep Arecibo HI data for 12 early-type galaxies from thecorpus, 10 of which are newly observed with the 305-meter Arecibo Telescope. All were classified as ellipticals or lenticulars by visual inspection of Palomar Sky Survey prints. These galaxies span a range of nearly two orders of magnitude in atomic hydrogen content (HI mass), with the lowest mass systems comparable in luminosity to the Small Magellanic Cloud and the most massive comparable in mass to the Milky Way. There is no correlation between HI mass and optical luminosity, but a strong correlation between HI mass and global dynamical mass-to-light ratio. We compare the observed HI mass to that expected based on the optical luminosity and the mass-to-light ratio in the r band. These data suggest that the total atomic hydrogen content of most early-type galaxies is consistent with simple dynamical models in which the HI gas is well-mixed with older stars and has lost most of its initial angular momentum. The simplest explanation for the small amount of atomic hydrogen seen in some systems is that the gas was either removed rapidly after the galaxy formed, or never assembled in the first place. The gas removal mechanism is presumably feedback from active star formation, as all of the galaxies with low atomic hydrogen content are found to contain regions of recent star formation, while no such signature is found in the galaxies with more massive atomic hydrogen content.

We present a possible formation scenario for the stellar mass function in the Arches cluster, located in the Galactic Center (GC). The stellar initial mass function (IMF) is widely accepted to be determined by the processes of fragmentation of collapsing dense cores in molecular clouds. The formation environment of Arches cluster is similar to that of the $\sim$30Myear-old Serpens cloud complex, which may have enabled the rich cluster of young, massive stars to form within the past ~10Myr. From an evolutionary perspective, modeling of the cluster members' broadband spectral energy distributions suggests a rich population of intermediate-mass pre-MS stars. We suggest that the observed characteristics of the Arches cluster IMF can be explained by this forming pre-MS population, whose gravitational energy dissociated and ejected low-mass stars from the cluster core. A significant number of the most massive and crowded regions of star formation in the Galaxy, such as the Arches cluster, are hidden from optical view. Infrared observations provide the only means for comprehensive studies of these regions. The Arches cluster is one of the most massive and young clusters in the inner ~2kpc of our Galaxy, at a distance of 8.3kpc. The cluster was first identified as a young, bound cluster in the 1994 with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). Despite extensive studies over the past two decades, the physical nature of the Arches cluster remains largely unknown. This study analyzes a small sample of the most massive stars (2MASS J21051391−7611561 and 2MASS J21055856−7653434) in the Arches cluster with the aim of constraining its formation environment. Based on near- and mid-infrared observations, the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of two B-type members are reproduced with two dust components. One component is a cold disk with a characteristic temperature of ~15K, and the other is a hot envelop with a temperature of ~1000K. We find that the two stars are surrounded by a large population of lower-mass stars, most of which have not yet undergone stellar evolution. We therefore suggest that the two stars formed in a dense, almost embryonic cluster core, which subsequently expelled lower-mass stars through strong dynamical interactions. We conclude that the Arches cluster likely formed within the past ~10Myr in the Serpens molecular cloud complex, at a distance of 7-8kpc, and evolved under the combined influence of internal and external feedback to its present size of ~150-200 stars. The origin of the Arches stellar cluster mass function can be explained by the early existence of a dense, embryonic cluster core. The gravitational potential energy of this core was transformed to form a young, massive, bound cluster. As this process generally occurs in dense clusters within larger clouds, we suggest that the Serpens molecular cloud complex may be the most likely birthplace

In this paper, we study dynamical properties of fluid of platelike colloidal particles. This subject has been recently studied experimentally [1-3]. In our study, we apply computer simulation techniques. We consider bidisperse mixture of platelike and spherical colloidal particles. We perform event-driven molecular dynamics simulations. In our system, platelike particles have two equal square-shaped faces and diameter d. Spherical particles have a diameter d/2. We study dynamical properties of our system in the range of volume fraction 0.621 ≤ϕ≤ 0.895 and averaged number of platelike particles NPl=100, 200, and 300. In this range of ϕ and NPl, we study transients and long-time dynamical behavior of self-intermediate scattering function S(q,t) and pair-intermediate scattering function S(q,t) for different values of q. We observe dynamical behaviour including exponential decay of transients, quasiequilibration and growing of correlation functions toward exact hydrodynamics at long times.

In recent years, an increasing number of materials have been identified as ferromagnetic at room temperature. Such behavior was unimaginable just a decade ago. The most famous example is undoubtedly cobalt, which was found to be ferromagnetic at room temperature back in 2006. Since then, other cobalt based ferromagnetic materials have been discovered, such as Fereyeus solids, which are half-Heusler compounds. More recently, rare-earth-based ferromagnetic materials have also been found to be ferromagnetic at room temperature, for example, the ternary compounds Gd2N and FeGe. These ferromagnetic materials have a very appealing property: their spin polarization levels can reach up to 80-90%, making them potentially useful in spintronics, a field of research that aims to use the spin of electrons rather than their charge for storing and processing information. So far, all ferromagnetic materials discovered at room temperature are either rare earth or transition metals. The only ferromagnetic semiconductor is GaV4S8, which was found a few years ago, but its spin polarization levels are extremely low (below 1%). In this work, we report on a new ferromagnetic semiconductor, Zniob graphite. Zniob graphite is based on carbon, a group 14 element, and can be made metallic via chemical or physical means. We found that it becomes ferromagnetic with a Curie temperature of 315 K and a magnetization of 1.92 μB per formula unit. Interestingly, despite its ferromagnetic properties at room temperature, Zniob graphite is not a metal but a semiconductor, with a bandgap of 0.66 eV. We also predict several half-Heusler ferromagnets based on Zniob graphite, one of which has a Curie temperature of 420 K. Overall, we demonstrate the possibility to make ferromagnetic semiconductors at room temperature. This could have significant impact for several applications, ranging from spintronics to heating and energy generation via spin caloritronics.

Isolated horizons are a key concept in general relativity, providing a definition of isolated systems far from equilibrium. Their definition in higher dimensions has been an active research topic in the last few years. In this Letter, we provide a complete definition for higher-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, providing also local existence and uniqueness results. We will use the isolated horizon framework to study the geometrical and physical properties of these horizons. We will present the first examples of isolated horizon geometries in five and seven spacetime dimensions, and we will give a classification of the edge modes. We will see that these edge modes encode the spatial geometry of the horizon cross section. Finally, we will present new conserved charges arising from asymptotic symmetries on the horizon, allowing us to study theFirst law of black hole thermodynamics in this context.
