In this paper, we present a communication model for adaptive service provisioning in hybrid wireless networks that consist of both licensed and unlicensed spectrum bands. We consider a communication-enabled wireless network where wireless services are hosted by servers and the hosts can be connected to the wireless networks through access points (APs). The AP access information (licensed or unlicensed) is dynamically shared with the servers using a reverse proxy which we call the spectrum guardian (SG). The SG then adapts its behavior to provide the services either over licensed or unlicensed spectrum bands. We formulate the problem of adaptive spectrum band selection for delivering services over air as a coupled multi-agent coordination and spectrum band selection optimization problem. We employ game-theoretic techniques to solve the formulated problem. We provide a rigorous performance analysis for the proposed spectrum band selection algorithm. We also evaluate the performance of the formulated problem using extensive simulations and demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed spectrum guardian algorithm.' We perform simulations to study the performance of the SG in various network settings with different number of spectrum guardians and servers. We also consider different spectrum management policies and evaluate their performance under the SG framework. We show that by using the SG, the AP access information can be shared with servers in a decentralized and privacy-preserving manner, thereby enabling flexible spectrum management while ensuring an efficient use of the spectrum bands.' Our proposed SG spectrum band selection algorithm can adapt to various network and spectrum management policies and can ensure a minimum performance under any network setting. This enables our SG to efficiently exploit the benefits of both licensed and unlicensed spectrum bands for delivering wireless services to the servers.' Our proposed SG not only helps the spectrum managers in efficiently utilizing the licensed and unlicensed spectrum bands but also enables the servers to seamlessly enjoy the benefits of both licensed and unlicensed spectrum bands for delivering their services to the end-users.' We also study the performance of the SG in a cache-aided network setting with different cache strategies. We show that by properly using the cache, the SG can greatly improve the system performance under both uncached and highly dynamic network settings. We provide a performance bound for the SG with optimal cache usage and demonstrate its performance close to the bound.' author: - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

Alkanols, or alkyl alcohols, are common components of fuels and industrial chemicals. Due to their hydrophobicity, these compounds are particularly abundant at the oil-water interface. Here, we report molecular-scale observations of alkanols at the water-air interface, showing that alkanols vaporize and condense as mixed layers on the water surface. Despite their thermodynamic stability in the vapor phase, alkanols self-assemble into nanoscale multilayers, consistent with an unusual condensation mechanism. Our findings illustrate a complex interplay between submicrometer scale intermolecular forces and macroscopic phase behavior and have implications for both atmospheric and oceanic phenomena. Our findings illustrate a complex interplay between submicrometer scale intermolecular forces and macroscopic phase behavior and have implications for both atmospheric and oceanic phenomena. Alkanols, or alkyl alcohols, are common components of fuels and industrial chemicals. Due to their hydrophobicity, these compounds are particularly abundant at the oil-water interface. Astronomers using the HATNet visual surveys have discovered an eclipsing binary, HAT-TR-205-013, that consists of a star with a massive dark companion. High-precision radial velocity measurements confirm that the companion is a dark star and not a stellar or substellar object. The minimum companion mass is determined to be 65 M$_{JUP}$ and the radius of the companion is 7.2 R$_{JUP}$. The density of the companion is 6.7 x 10^{5} kg/m^{3}. The existence of dark stars with such low densities make it possible for them to be stable against nuclear reactions. The HATNet team has located eight additional systems with similar dark companions. These “HAT-P-27” systems will be presented in a future paper. This work was presented in a preliminary form at the Conference on Lasers Astrophysics and Technology (New Mexico, USA; 13-17 March 2013) and at the IAU General Assembly in Moscow (Russia; 20 September 2013).

A data warehouse engineering (DWE) benchmark designed to assist data warehouse architects and implementation teams with understanding and evaluating competing data warehouse products. The benchmark measures coverage of data warehouse best practices as well as the implementation complexity of 12 primitive operations performed upon a common data model. The resulting metrics can be used by data warehouse architects to guide their evaluation process as well as by data warehouse implementers to assist in choice of technology platform and help stakeholders make better-informed choices with respect to data warehouse investments. The benchmark is extensible and new primitive operations and data model anomalies can be easily added, thus growing the suite of metrics and enabling data warehouse professionals to track the ongoing evolution of data warehouse architecture and best practices. The design and development of the benchmark is described in this paper. Benchmark results for seven data warehouses, developed using three widely-different technologies, are also provided. The DWEB benchmarking suite measures the coverage of data warehouse best practices as well as the implementation complexity of 12 primitive operations performed upon a common data model. The data model is implemented as a dimensional data model withSQL/Transact-SQL and child-parent relationship description using nested sequences. The primitive operations are materialized as procedures in the DWEB implementation repository, which is a GitHub organization. The coverage of data warehouse best practices is assessed via a questionnaire which is filled out by an independent party. The implementation complexity of the operations is measured using several measurements including: lines of code (LOC), modules, and the average number of revisions per line of code, module, and overall implementation. The resulting DWEB metrics can be used by data warehouse architects to guide their evaluation process by allowing them to compare competing data warehouse product offerings with respect to best-practice implementation and coding practices, as well as with respect to the amount of resources and time needed to build and maintain the data warehouse. In addition, the metrics can be used by data warehouse implementers to assist in choice of technology platform by providing a "Facts Check" on underlying architectural trade-offs such as ease of implementation, governance, and performance, which often drive a data warehouse's architectural choice. The DWEB benchmark development effort was conducted as an open-source project within the GitHub organization Data WAREHOUSE ENGINEERING STANDARDS (DWEBS). All relevant source code, design documents, and test procedures for the benchmark development are hosted on GitHub along with a detailed methodology for participating in the benchmark development and for the evaluation of completed benchmarks. The DWEB benchmark is designed to be extensible by addition of new primitive operations and anomaly assessment for deviations from best practices. As new best practices and architectural trade-offs become known, these can be easily added to the benchmark suite by the data warehouse community as an extension. This will allow the benchmark to evolve to keep pace with the ongoing evolution of data warehouse best practices and architectural choices. The first version of the DWE

Titan is the only celestial body other than Earth with a substantial atmosphere and an environmental composition similar to that of early terrestrial atmosphere. Titan's atmosphere contains abundant molecular nitrogen, argon, and methane. Titan's atmosphere also hosts nitrogen-ice clouds, the only such clouds in the solar system. It has been proposed that nitrogen could be photolyzed into nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and other oxides at altitudes as high as 50 km, with subsequent reactions leading to the formation of sulfuric acid particles and complex organic molecules. In this work, we investigate in situ sampling of aerosols generated in the mesosphere and thermosphere of Titan using the NASA ICESat-1 laser altimeter. The observed composition does not support the proposed photolytic theory. Instead, we identify two origins for the aerosols: (1) saltation of cometary debris from the historical C Rings and (2) global sulfuric acid rain induced by ultraviolet outgasing from organic hazes in the Titan atmosphere. These aerosols provide insights into the history of Titan's atmosphere and the sources of physical and chemical processes on Titan.

Nuclear matter with different contents of isospin asymmetric charges experiences different degrees of attractions. In nuclear interactions, as a rule, particles of opposite isospins attract each other, and the total isospin is a good quantum number. Therefore, nuclear matter with different degrees of isospin asymmetry can be achieved by adjusting the content of the asymmetric charges. The common way is to change the number of protons and neutrons. However, the corresponding equation of state (EOS) often has relatively large uncertainties, because the parameters in nuclear many-body theories are not sufficiently constrained. In contrast, although the density and isospin dependence of the nuclear interaction are more complicated in real world, the EOS of isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter in the cold nuclear matter approximation can be predicted by effective field theories such as chiral effective theory, due to the involved strong interactions at low energies. In this work, based on a well-constrained contact interaction at relatively high energies, we obtain the EOS of isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter at zero temperature in a relativistic mean-field model with the nonlinear Walecka model as the chiral limit. The resulting EOSs satisfy the required conditions of neutrons and protons almost equally and present relatively stiff symmetry energy. The differences among different models, such as the interactions beyond the Walecka model, can be understood as the uncertainties of the EOSs. The characteristic properties of the EOSs are presented through the corresponding phase diagrams.

Recent high-throughput protein structure prediction methods generate large numbers of protein structure models, from which some may be wrong or poorly predicted. We study whether structural motifs – short recurring networks of local contacts in proteins – can explain some of the model inaccuracies. We show that the 20-node contact networks of protein structures frequently match local subnetworks of protein–protein interaction networks. By comparing model predictions to these interaction networks, we can systematically analyze which subnetworks are frequently mistaken, and therefore could be targets for further protein structure prediction. We find that frequently mistaken networks with high centrality often correspond to low-complexity regions in the structure and share sequence similarity with closely related proteins. By using a large repository of protein structures, we provide case studies showing how this network analysis can be used to improve existing protein structure prediction methods. This paper studies the structural underpinnings of protein model inaccuracies. Recent high-throughput structure prediction methods generate large numbers of protein models. While some of these models may be low-accuracy predictions, others may be entirely incorrect. The Structural Biological Model (SMo per) corpus contains hundreds of millions of models and will soon contain billions. Understanding the structural underpinnings of model inaccuracy can help to improve the accuracy of structure prediction for new proteins and may also guide efforts to distinguish predictions that are incorrect versus predictions that are merely low-accuracy. We use graph-theoretic methods to identify local networks of contacts in protein structure that match local networks of contacts in protein–protein interaction networks. These local networks of contacts often correspond to small and simple regions in the protein structure that share high sequence similarity with other proteins. These match networks can be used as targets for further protein structure prediction or as filters to remove false predictions from related proteins. Our main contributions are: 1. A method to identify local networks of contacts in protein structure that match local networks of contacts in protein–protein interaction networks. 2. Case studies showing how this analysis can be used to improve protein structure prediction methods.

Currently favored candidates for dark matter are weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPS). The nature of WIMP interactions with Standard Model particles is an open question, but WIMPS could naturally interact via gravity. Direct detection experiments search for nuclear recoil caused by WIMPS scattering off the nuclei of experimental detectors. The elastic cross section required to detect WIMPS by this method is model dependent, but Direct Detection experiments place strong constraints on the possible values of this cross section. The recent gravitational N-body simulations of the merging galaxy cluster 1E 0657-5 determine a cross section less than about 6 pb at the 90% confidence level. This result places the first strong direct experimental constraint on the self-interaction cross section of dark matter, an important property for WIMPS. The ability of WIMPS to interact self-interaction cross section must be much less than the the core cross section of typical WIMP candidates, which is of the order of 10 - 40 pb.

Longintitual dynamics describes the motion of particles in a given system. In the context of celestial mechanics, the motion of planets in the solar system is described by the Newton's laws of motion. The same is true for the spacecrafts in space, which is influenced by the Sun and other planets, but also by much smaller irregularities in the spacecraft itself and in the Space environment. These deviations from a straight line motion are called perturbers. In this work, we consider a very small, orbiting irregularity in the solar system, namely the asteroid 2005 US10. We perform a numerical integration of the equations of motion of the perturber, considering a wide range of initial conditions. We verify that the evolution of the spacecraft follows a unique pattern, in which the osculating orbit of the asteroid slowly precesses around the Keplerian orbit of the spacecraft. We calculate the time scale of this evolution, and we show that it depends mainly on the parameter called dynamical friction, which is closely related to the viscosity of the gas surrounding the perturber. In the end, we discuss the applicability of our results to the Asteroid capture mission, which is a proposed future manned mission to a minor body in the Solar system.

Interstellar dust is composed of a wide variety of submicron sized carbonaceous and siliceous grains arising from different types of parent bodies with a composite size distribution. The smallest observed interstellar grains, with a minimum size of 4.6 angstroms, are most likely arising from low temperature carbonaceous asteroids. The majority of interstellar grains, with a radius of 0.1-0.3 μm, have most likely sporadic formation from carbon rich gas clouds or volatilized polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). While the sizes of the majority of the observed interstellar grains range from 0.1 to 0.3 μm, they appear to have an arbitrary cut off around 1 μm, with a probable aggregate of denser aggregates. The characteristic sizes of these aggregrates ranges from 0.3 to 1 μm. It is not clear if these aggregates form through agglomeration or some other process. In addition, the surfaces of these aggregates are coated with a thin layer of polar non-volatile material that provides a second cross-section of hydrogen bonding sites. It is believed that this layer of non-volatile material provides the cementing mechanism for the aggregates, binding them into larger structures. The typical size of these structures ranges from 0.5 to 5 μm with a preferred size of 2 μm. The dominant composition of these larger interstellar grains is likely going from silicate cores to graphite overlayers as this provides a high transparency to infrared radiation.

Delta Scuti stars (DSCTs) are often found in open clusters. The origin of these clusters is not clear yet. It has been proposed that DSCTs could have been formed through dynamical interactions in clusters. In this context, the variability of the fundamental mode amplitude could be used to trace the dynamical history of DSCTs in clusters. However, a comprehensive study of the fundamental mode amplitude variability of DSCTs is missing and could bring new constraints on the cluster dynamical history. We have carried out a comprehensive study of the amplitude variability of the fundamental mode of 33 DSCTs in open clusters and we compare it to existing stability criteria. Our study shows that the observed variability of the fundamental mode amplitude in DSCTs cannot be simply explained by classical linear calculations. A physical mechanism for non-linear amplitude variations has to be taken into account. We performed numerical simulations of non-linear radial oscillations of DSCTs with a new version of the F stars integrator of the [arepo]{} code. This new version solves the linearized Euler equations with a high order Godunov scheme. The comparison of these non-linear simulations to our observed DSCTs properties shows that temporal temperature differences in the atmospheres of DSCTs induce non-linear radial pulsations that could explain the variability of the fundamental mode amplitude observed in DSCTs.

Astronomers have long known that the universe is full of small particles of radiation known as cosmic microwave background radiation. This radiation is of immense scientific value as it was the last light that was emitted at the Big Bang, and thus can be used to probe the state of the early universe. Recently, scientists have developed a model of how this background radiation may be generated by quantum mechanical effects within the universe. The model describes the universe as a sea of zero-point fluctuations, with particles taking on every imaginable (virtual) position in this sea. As the universe expands and its temperature drops, these virtual particles have an increased tendency to settle into the lowest-energy positions, leading to a background of virtual radiation. This model has one key flaw: it does not describe the universe as a collection of particles, but rather a collection of waves. This is analogous to modeling the ocean as a collection of sticks floating on top of a boiling pot of water. The waves are the waves of the ocean, and the sticks are the particles of the boiling pot of water. The particles of the model, the waves of the universe, have not been observed. In this model, the particles of the boiling pot of water are the photons of the cosmic microwave background radiation. As the universe cools, the photons have an increased tendency to assume the lowest-energy positions, that of equilibrium with the cold universe. When the temperature of the universe drops below 3000 K, the photons are no longer in equilibrium with the quantum fluctuations of the radiation, and thus begin to free-stream, moving away from regions of high density and toward regions of lower density. This is analogous to a water bottle left out in the cold. As the bottle cools, water molecules begin to move toward the bottom of the bottle, leaving a region of space with lower density than the surrounding air. In this work, we consider a modified model of this phenomenon, in which the particles (photons) do not move, but the background radiation does. The universe, in this case, has a "frozen sea" where the particles settle at the bottom of the sea but the radiation waves continue to wave throughout the universe. In this model, as the universe cools, the radiation waves continue to wave throughout the universe but the particles have settled at the bottom of the sea, leaving regions of higher and lower density. This provides a mechanism by which the universe can undergo a phase transition from a state of thermal equilibrium to a state of nonequilibrium, or a cooling dominated phase transition.

We present the discovery of a new low surface brightness galaxy (LSBG) SDSS J121811.0+465501.2. It is located at a distance of 97.1 megaparsecs (Mpc) from the Earth, corresponding to a spatial scale of 3.24 kpc/arcsec. J121811.0+465501.2 has the optical dimensions of 14 kpc x 7 kpc and aLSB disk size of 9.5 kpc. The absolute luminosity is estimated to be 2.65 x 1038 erg/s, which means that it would have been undetectable without the Subaru Telescope's Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) deep imaging data. With a measured heliocentric radial velocity of -290 km/s, the new LSBG is a good candidate for being a member of the local group of galaxies.

The magnetar CXOU J164710.2-455216 was identified in the well-known supernova remnant Westerlund 1 using data from the Chandra X-ray observatory. Emission from the magnetar likely originated from interactions between the star's magnetic field and the nebula's gas anddust. The emission originated from a cloud of dense, cool materialthat extends several hundred light-years around the magnetar. Thecloud has a higher-than-normal density, which could be caused by the materialbeing propelled away from the magnetar at a rate of tens of thousands of milesper second. The cloud's high density and motion with respect to thenebulosity suggest that it was expelled from the system as a result of ahypothetical companion star to the progenitor of the compact object. Ifthis is the case, the expulsion of this cloud could have a significantimpact on the system, such as temporarily brightening the magnetar'sx-ray emission.

We report on the discovery of 87 regions of distinct inter-network patterns of emission at millimetre wavelengths in aligned filter scans of the Sun made with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). These regions, which represent a persistent coronal mass ejection (CME) that occurred from the same active region during the course of the observations, occupy 2.5% of the solar disk and are observed to travel at speeds of up to 1400 km/s. They are closely aligned with each other and with the inter-network pattern of dark regions, and form a coronal mass ejection belt that is wider than either the inter-network pattern or dark region patterns. Cosmological N-body simulations that included aTreatment of dark matter as collisionless particles revealed that approximately 70% of the total matter in the Universe is in the form of dark matter halos. There is an emerging view that galaxy clusters, which are the largest collapsed structures in the universe, are surrounded by enormous dark matter halos. In this sense, galaxy clusters can be seen as galaxy clusters, not as individual galaxies. In this paper we explore the possibility that a significant fraction of the dark matter in galaxy clusters is in the form of Warm Dark Matter (WDM). Warm Dark Matter particles have a finite temperature, and were relatively more abundant during structure formation. We show that if the warm dark matter particle mass is in the range of 10-15 keV, galaxy clusters such as the Shapley Supercluster and the Sloan Great Wall can act as magnifying glasses and produce cosmic rays with the right properties to account for the observed flux of electrons and Positrons. This provides a novel method to detect WDM, and may also explain the recently observed flux of Electron-Positron pairs.

A large number of planet search programs have been undertaken to detect planets orbiting other stars. The physical characteristics of such planets, e.g., mass, radius, orbital distance are essential clues for understanding their formation and evolution. The planet population synthesis theory has predicted the occurrence of super-Earths and Neptune-mass planets around M dwarfs (0.1-0.3 solar mass). Planets around M dwarfs may have higher occurrence rates than those around F, G, and K type stars due to enhanced migration rate and upsurge of core accretion in warmer host star conditions. However, current transit surveys for planet candidates are mostly biased against the very low-luminosity, low-mass M dwarfs, which limits the statistical interpretation of the exoplanet population around these stars. To address this, we have conducted an imaging survey for planet candidates orbiting 45 nearby low-mass (M dwarf) stars using the SPHERE/VLT and MMT/Hectospec instruments. The survey is also intended to detect any evidence of substellar companions around these targets by taking spectra for faint companion candidates with Hectospec. We have so far identified three new planet candidates around M dwarfs, including two super-Earths and one Neptune-mass planet, and excluded the possibility of planets around eight host stars with sufficient high confidence levels. This result, combined with radial velocity and other planet detection surveys, suggests that super-Earths are the most frequent type of planets among the recently found exoplanet population around M dwarfs. In this paper, we present the survey design and preliminary results from the first year of observations.

Using a compilation of 185 type Ia supernova peak-magnitude versus rise time measurements, we present a systematic analysis of the diversity among these supernovae in relation to their decline rate-corrected rise times (sink times). We show that a physical model with a single rise time distribution cannot describe the data. A two-component decay model, with a small fraction (~15%) of supernovae exhibiting fast rise times (rise time < 15 days) and the majority (~85%) of supernovae exhibiting rise times in the range 15 - 40 days, is preferred over a single-component model at a significance of 4.3 standard deviations. The fast-rise-time supernovae have more negative peak magnitudes, slower decline rates, and longer rise times than those with normal rise times, indicating that the fast-rise-time supernovae are an intrinsically different subset of supernovae. These results suggest that variations in the physical properties of type Ia supernovae are evident even at the earliest stages of their explosion.

Ionization fraction of the intergalactic medium (IGM) increases with increasing redshift during the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). Simulations suggest that ionized regions grow via self-regulation by conductive and ram pressure gas dynamics. The fastest growing modes in these ionization fronts are advection dominated, and thus the Eulerian weighted average, or WENO, scheme is appropriate for accurate capturing of these dynamics. We implement a WENO scheme for a finite volume, dynamic adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) code and show improved convergence and conservation properties of various diagnostics when compared to the Van Leer Limited Volume (LLL) scheme. In this simulation, we explore the growth of a single ionized region in a periodic box over 20 Million years, showing good convergence and conservation of the ionized fraction and temperature. use 200-400 words Ionization fraction of the intergalactic medium (IGM) increases with increasing redshift during the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). Interaction between proteins is crucial for the stability and function of a protein. Networks provide a valuable tool to understand the interrelationships between proteins and how these interactions impact the function of the protein. Clustering coefficient, which measures the degree to which a node is a part of a local network of interconnected clusters, has been found to be a key property of complex networks with applications in network robustness, dynamics and heterogeneity. In this study, we have calculated clustering coefficients for a number of protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks. Results show that clustering coefficients of PPI networks are generally low compared with those of corresponding random networks. Furthermore, we have observed that the degree distribution of PPI networks follows a power law, which may explain low clustering coefficients of the networks. Our findings could be helpful for a better understanding of the architecture of PPI networks and related biological implications. Zhang, W., Chen, M., Zhang, L. & Wang, J. (2017). Clustering Coefficients of Protein-Protein Interaction Networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.04288.

3C 66A, formally named ApJ 253. 1001, is a quasar located at a distance of around 170- 320 million light years from Earth, depending on the assumptions made about its redshift. In the optical band, it exhibits characteristic flat spectrum, which changes to a negative one in the radio band. Variability at these two wavelengths occurs on a timescale of hours to decades, respectively. In this work, we model the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) of 3C 66A using astronomical observations of synchrotron emission, thermal dust emission, and starlight. We combine these models with radiative transfer in a spherical geometry to account for the variability observed in the source. We find that a spherical torus, or doughnut, geometry with inner and outer radii of 500 and 3000 Schwarzschild radii, respectively, and half-opening angle of 20 deg captures the broadband SED of 3C 66A and its variability observed in the infrared to radio bands during the WEBT campaign of 2003 -- 2004. We discuss the implications of our model and the constraints it puts on the torus properties.

We develop a systematic expansion of the Chern-Simons modified gravity theory in terms of the parameter α, which provides a measure of the gravity modifications. This expansion is obtained by solving the field equations order-by-order in α. We work out the leading-order and next-to-leading-order terms and show that they correspond to the parametrized post-Newtonian (PPN) approximation. Finally, we apply our formalism to the analysis of some recent gravitational wave experiments and parameter estimation analysis to test the theory of general relativity. We find that current tests of general relativity are not sensitive enough to probe α, and future experiments may constrain α to be much less than 1%. In this paper, we first give two results on homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomials. A homogeneous polynomial is called Hessian nilpotent if its gradient field at every point of $\mathbb{C}$ is nilpotent. The first result is that any homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomial in two variables of degree at least four is a sum of squares of polynomials. The second result is that any homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomial in three variables of degree three is a sum of squares of linear polynomials. These two results extend some known results in the literature and are interesting in their own right. The first result on two variables has been conjectured by McKay and Robb and confirmed for all but one degree four case. The first result on three variables has been conjectured by Zubor and confirmed for all but one case. These two results establish a connection between homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomials and sums of squares of polynomials. This connection will be useful in understanding homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomials, which have applications in optimization and control. The first result is obtained by applying the Hodge decomposition to the associated homogeneous polynomial ideal. The Hodge decomposition says that any homogeneous polynomial ideal in two variables of degree at least four is the difference of the gradient ideal and the image of the partial derivation, i.e., the ideal is the sum of the gradient ideal and the image of the partial differentiation. The second result is obtained by applying the Ohsawa-Takegoshi theorem to the homogeneous polynomial ideal generated by the given polynomial and the square of its derivative. The Ohsawa-Takegoshi theorem says that any homogeneous polynomial ideal in three variables of degree three is the difference of the linear ideal and the image of the partial differentiation. These two results suggest the following problem, which will be interesting. Given a homogeneous polynomial in more than two variables, how to characterize its summands? In other words, what is the relation between the homogeneous polynomial and its derivatives? We hope this work can shed some lights on this problem. There are two related works which are closely related to the results in this paper. The first work on two variables extends the result on all but one degree four case of the first result. The second work on three variables gives a complete characterization of homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomials in three variables of degree three. There are some related works that are not covered by this paper. In particular, we would like to mention the article by Viro and Guletskii that characterizes forms defined by four homogeneous polynomial equations in three variables. This work is jointly completed by Jingjun Han and Yuming Zhao.

Central schemes are powerful numerical methods for computing approximate solutions to conservation laws with source terms. In this work, we prove several stability and monotonicity results for central schemes, which enable us to construct high-order and robust central schemes for a wide class of hyperbolic conservation laws with source terms. Specifically, we show that any central scheme with at least second-order accuracy in space and time satisfies the discrete maximum principle, and that any linear central scheme with at least third-order accuracy is monotone increasing in the following sense: if we denote the numerical solution at time step n by Xn and the corresponding exact solution at time tn by φ, then Xn+1 ≥ φ for all Kn→∞, where Kn is the maximum width of the cell intervals over which the numerical solution is computed. We also present a variety of examples to which our theory can be applied. These include the 1D quadratic nonlinear Euler equations, the 2D isentropic gas dynamics equations with generalized bow shocks, and the 3D isentropic gas dynamics equations with self-organized shock waves. Finally, we present several numerical examples to validate the theory and the efficiency of the proposed central schemes.

Many biophysical and biochemical studies have underlined the crucial influence of carbohydrates in living cells. Indeed, carbohydrates seem to be essential for various life processes, such as cell recognition, structural integrity, energy storage or as transmitters of chemical signals. Thus, the effect of carbohydrates on the structure and dynamical properties of proteins of interest has received great interest in recent years. In this study, we focus on the effects of three commonly occurring carbohydrates, trehalose, maltose and sucrose, on the dynamical and structural properties of hen egg-white lysozyme by means of Molecular Dynamics simulations. We find that these three carbohydrates influence the protein dynamics, as well as its secondary and tertiary structure. In addition, we find that maltose has a more pronounced stabilizing effect on the protein structure than trehalose and sucrose. Further, the dynamical quantities are found to be related to the protein-carbohydrate interaction strengths.

Recent observations of distant galaxies have revealed the existence of an "unknown force" which shapes the universe. The existence of this force, known as dark energy, is confirmed by the observed accelerated expansion of the universe. This 'dark energy' is thought to permeate all of space and essentially make up 68% of the energy budget of the universe. According to general relativity, the 'dark energy' should cause gravity to become stronger with distance, leading to more rapid increases in velocity when observed approaching the center of a galaxy. Galaxy rotation curves have proven to be more shallow than this, possibly signaling the presence of 'dark matter', with which 'dark energy' interacts to produce the observed gravitational force. This 'dark matter' is thought to make up 26% of the energy budget of the universe. It is possible that the observed 'dark matter' and 'dark energy' interact only on large scales, allowing for the possibility of 'dark matter' on galactic scales but only 'dark energy' beyond this. This 'brane theory' has the same weak gravitational force on small scales as general relativity but different forces on large scales. Recent experiments have shown that the universe may in fact be four dimensional with matter existing on a three dimensional brane. This 'brane theory' can explain both the 'dark matter' and 'dark energy' interactions necessary to explain galaxy rotation curves.

Lattices have been widely used in various disciplines including computer science, statistics, and even social sciences to better represent the underlying structures. For example, the protein structure can be thought as a three-dimensional lattice, where each element in the lattice corresponds to a particular protein atom, and the distance between any two atoms indicates the shortest path through chemical bonds and other interactions between them in the protein structure. In this way, the protein structure can be simplified as a Boolean lattice, where each lattice point is either “1” or “0”, representing the existence or nonexistence of a chemical bond between the corresponding atoms. Similar lattice concept has also been used in social sciences to model social ties in terms of close friends and distant friends. In this way, social networks can be viewed as a special kind of graph with vertices representing individuals and edges indicating the strength of ties between corresponding individuals, which can also be conveniently represented as Boolean lattices. Therefore, by looking at graph structures in various applications in a lattice-aware manner, we can potentially detect underlying patterns and structures that are otherwise hidden due to the insufficient modeling capabilities in the existing approaches.

Interlacement is a way to measure the path-wise intersection of one-dimensional random process. It was introduced by S. interlacements and I. Melbourne in 2010. In this paper, I study the vacant set of random interlacements. I prove that when interlacement varies sufficiently slow, almost surely, the vacant set is empty. When interlacement is quick, I prove that the vacant set has full intensity. I use these results and coupling to prove that when interlacement percolates, it connects for almost sure. We present the first high-accuracy, high-reliability effective-one-body (EOB) binary waveforms for nonspinning, equal-mass, black-hole (BH) coalescences with mass ratios as low as q = 0.2. Such waveforms, which are restricted to the small mass-ratio limit of general relativity, are essential for the rigorous and accurate computation of emitted radiation and the estimation of Source Terms in computational EM and GW astronomy. We demonstrate that, with a single adjustment for the mass ratio, our waveform family, dubbed DECOULper waveform approximates the analytic solution of the effective one body (EOB) equations to < 10^{-4} over the full spectrum of two compact object systems. We show that our DECOULper waveforms, which are computed in close parallel with the effective one body (EOB) equations, are well-suited for use in hybrid waveforms, where radiation from a numerical relativity simulation is infused with the DECOULper waveform at key stages of the evolution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our waveforms using several approaches. First, we show that our waveforms predict the radiation in tests in which we waveform a single, isolated BH. Next, we show that when using high-precision numerical-relativity waveforms for binary black-hole mergers as an initial condition, our DECOULper waveforms accurately predict the radiation produced in the subsequent dynamical evolution. Lastly, we show that our waveforms can be easily and efficiently used within the Grandchallenge surrogate modeling approach, where they provide accurate Source Terms for radiation from BH-BH mergers, despite being computed for equal-mass systems.

The nearby QSO I Zw 1 is identified as a radio source by optical observers since 1898. I Zw 1 is classified as an Narrow Line Seyfert 1 galaxy. I Zw 1 is associated with a giant molecular cloud. Distance measurements give a range of 28-40 Mpc, which makes I Zw 1 one of the closest active galaxies. Emission lines are redshifted into the optical spectrum of I Zw 1 and reveal the presence of a massive black hole of approximately 10^7 M_{\sun}$ at its nucleus. The large luminosity and brightness of I Zw 1 are produced by the inner regions of this black hole. The presence of a molecular cloud so close to the nucleus of I Zw 1 is interesting, since molecular gas is typically only found near the nuclei of normal galaxies, and not in the bulges of active galaxies such as I Zw 1. One possibility is that the molecular cloud is being disrupted by the jet generated by I Zw 1. Alternatively, there could be a dynamical interaction between the radio source and the cloud, possibly caused by the radio source expanding into the cloud. I Zw 1 may also have triggered star formation in the molecular cloud, as revealed by optical emission from massive stars.

Relativistic charged particles moving with non-zero velocity experience radiative reaction, a phenomena whereby the particle loses energy in the form of electromagnetic radiation. This effect can have profound implications for the survival of charged particles produced in high energy collisions. Surprisingly, even a slowly moving charged particle can undergo electromagnetic radiation over a long time period, reducing its energy without ever reaching zero energy. In this paper, we develop a classical relativistic theory of the radiation reaction due to absorption and emission of electromagnetic radiation for an arbitrary charged particle. We consider both the case of a particle moving non-relativistically and that of a highly relativistic particle. In the latter case, we derive an approximate relativistic form of the classical electromagnetic Lagrangian and Hamiltonian, valid in the limit of high particle velocity and weak radiative reaction. We show that the equations of motion of the relativistic charged particle derived from the relativistic Lagrangian and Hamiltonian are equivalent to those of non-relativistic motion of a particle with a modified effective potential. We perform a parameter study of the relative strengths of radiative reaction and non-relativistic motion, showing that the most likely scenarios for survival of a charged particle moving with non-zero velocity are those in which the particle is either very weakly charged or moving with very low velocity. We conclude with a discussion of our results and suggestions for future work.

Stochastic fluctuations are ubiquitous in biochemical networks. While often being detrimental, they can also improve the robustness of biological systems to external and internal fluctuations in parameter values. Here, we investigate the contribution of these fluctuations to the overall noise in pathways through a coarse-grained model for glycolysis. We show that the fluctuations in the concentrations of the enzymes and substrate particles give rise to a rich variety of statistical behaviours. Three main regimes can be identified, which depend on the intensity of the fluctuations relative to the mean concentrations: a non-linear regime where the noise increases the pathway flux, a linear regime where the noise increases only the randomness in the pathway flux, and a saturation regime where the noise becomes deleterious. We also investigate the effect of the fluctuations on the efficiency of the pathway and show that, in general, efficiency is maximized when the fluctuations are largest. Overall, our results demonstrate that fluctuations play an important role in shaping pathway performance and that an understanding of their effect is necessary to predict the efficiency of biological pathways.

The Wide Field Surveys have been an important part of the modern astronomical landscape for over a decade. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), which was carried out between 2000 and 2010, was the most ambitious of these projects. Since the inception of the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), a state-of-the-art dark-time camera installed on the Blanco Telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile, another wide field survey, Legacy ExtraGalactic Dataset (LEGED) Survey, has been executed. This article aims to give an overview of the key aspects of each of these surveys and of DECam in particular, highlighting their scientific impacts. In particular, it will describe how the combination of these surveys has helped to shed light on some of the biggest unknowns in modern astronomy, including Dark Matter and the accelerating rate of expansion of the Universe. These surveys canvassed an area of the sky 8 times larger than that of SDSS, enabling the detection of much deeper and more unusual astronomical phenomena. For example, over 400 million previously unknown galaxies have been identified, providing a fundamental re-analysis point of view in galaxy evolution, structure and formation. In addition, they have allowed the detection of thousands of new solar systems, shedding light on the existence of these objects and helping to chart the Milky Way’s nearby stellar population. In terms of new observational methods, these surveys made use of many novel techniques to analyse these datasets, including asteroid detection from image time-streams, recognition of variable stars, the computation of the baryon acoustic oscillation scale in images, and the automated identification and characterisation of supernovae and other transient phenomena. DECam is also unique in its ability to image in three separate bands in parallel over a field of view of 1 degree squared in just 15 minutes. In addition to the large increase in the amount of light that can be collected from each object, this allows for the ability to conduct multi-wavelength observations of the same field. This is vital for understanding the physical processes that occur in them, and DECam has already contributed to the discovery of many gravitational lenses and of large numbers of gamma-ray bursts. The deployment of DECam on the Blanco Telescope represents the first of a new generation of large-aperture telescopes whose construction will continue to provide crucial data for the major current astronomical projects in the years to come.

Game theory has been applied to modeling dynamic spectrum sharing in wireless networks, however, most existing works either assume that QoS requirements of delay and loss are satisfied simultaneously, or rely on dynamic programming to solve the original complicated resource management optimization problems. In this paper, we consider the problem of joint energy-efficient modulation and spectrum sharing under the latency and loss QoS constraints in the downlink of cellular networks. Specifically, we formulate this spectrum and energy efficient modulation problem into a classical Markov decision process (MDP) and propose a deep learning based solution, i.e., using deep Q-learning, to cope with the complex non-linear characteristics of the proposed problem. Compared to the existing works, our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We establish the connection between the optimization of CDMA network and deep Q-learning, which greatly reduces the search space of the efficient spectrum and energy allocation. 2. Instead of using the conservative heuristic methods in the existing works, we leverage the learning capabilities of deep Q-learning to search for the efficient solution. 3. We consider the latency and loss QoS constraints of downlink data transmission in the network, which has not been well taken into consideration in the existing works. Our simulation results show that our deep learning based approach can achieve significant energy saving, while satisfying the latency and loss QoS constraints, comparing with the existing heuristic methods. This work was initially submitted to arXiv on October 18, 2019, and has been updated on January 10, 2020.

Composite fermions, best viewed as electrons dressed with one flux quantum, are quite different from ordinary electrons. Rather than being particles of charge 1/2, they are quantum particles of charge 0 and might even be thought of as fermions of zero spin. When confined to ordinary three-dimensional liquids, composite fermions take on even more peculiar properties. Their true low-energy behavior is a chiral,logarithmic conformal field theory (CFT). In this paper, we present a path-integral derivation of the CFT description of composite fermions. We show how to represent composite fermions as conformal blocks of a chiral CFT, resulting in a wave function defined on any Riemann surface. We illustrate our results by explicitly computing the wave function for the ground state of the first excited state of the Laughlin quantum Hall state at fill factor \(\nu =1/(2q+1)\). Though related to CFTs, wave functions obtained by this approach do not correspond to the states normally studied in CFT, but rather describe a particular excited state. This wave function construction provides a robust approach to modeling composite fermion systems and may be extended to study more general excited states.

Recent experimental observation of stimulated Brillouin backscattering (SBS) in plasma-based accelerators [1–3] has created considerable interest in applying this technique to inertial confinement fusion (ICF). Current kinetic-ion simulations of SBS in ICF conditions cannot replicate these reflectivities, and previous comparisons to experiments have relied on simplified models that may not fully capture the complex plasma environment. Here, we present the first global, kinetic simulation of SBS in a high-fluence, hard-sphere, electrostatic ICF plasma. For the first time, we are able to replicate both the fast-electron-beam-driven modes and the slow, spontaneous modes observed in the experiments. Furthermore, the wavevectors and frequencies of the fast modes are in good agreement with full-kinetic simulations of a two-temperature version of the fluid equations, while the slow modes are insensitive to kinetic effects, a result that we attribute to wavevector aliasing due to the discrete electron momentum grid. Inclusion of the full kinetic electron pressure term in the ion equations of motion is also shown to improve the agreement with experiments for fast-electron-driven modes, although the effect on slow modes is less clear. These results suggest that global kinetic simulations will be necessary for future comparison with SBS experiments, and we provide the first comparison of kinetic and fluid simulations for this application.

Group dynamics play an important role in the evolution of social groups, including animal colonies, human collectives and even social networks. Studying group dynamics has often relied on intuition, visualisations and simple measures. Here we introduce a general methodology for quantifying group dynamics. Using a Markov chain Monte Carlo technique, we sample the space of social group evolution trees, and estimate the probability of different group dynamics outcomes. We illustrate the technique using computer simulations of the evolutionary prisoner's dilemma game and the snowdrift game, as well as analysing real data from yeast colonies. We find that while groups typically evolve towards distinct dynamics, some groups frequently undergo repeated change between different dynamics. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of group evolution scenarios, including social network evolution, to quantify the dynamics of group evolution. By coupling Markov chain Monte Carlo methods with techniques from statistical physics and graph theory, we introduce a general methodology for quantifying group dynamics. We illustrate the technique using computer simulations of the evolutionary prisoner's dilemma game and the snowdrift game, as well as analysing real data from yeast colonies. We find that while groups typically evolve towards distinct dynamics, some groups frequently undergo repeated change between different dynamics. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of group evolution scenarios, including social network evolution, to quantify the dynamics of group evolution. In social network analysis, the evolution of social networks has been studied using a generative model of network evolution. Similar approaches have been used to model the dynamics of cooperation in games. Resonantly excited states of neutral iron (Fe) can undergo various autoionization channels. In the case of 13.6 eV resonant excitation, the atomic electron can lose enough energy to form Fe XV, a low-lying, meta-stable K-shell vacancy. The formation and lifetime of this metastable state have been previously studied theoretically [1-3] and via time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) [4]. In this work, the resonant excitation of Fe XV has been observed in the time-dependent spectra of both photoelectrons andAuger electrons, and the lifetimes of the metastable state formed were measured for the first time. Additionally, we have also developed a method to theoretically predict the resonant excitation of metastable states using time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). Our method shows good agreement with the measurements, and additionally allows for the theoretical prediction of resonantly excited states with arbitrary electron configurations. The time-dependent photoelectron spectrum (PES) following resonant 13.6 eV laser excitation of neutral Fe displays a distinct feature at 4.7 eV, well-separated from the ionization continuum at lower binding energies. This feature is characteristic of resonant excitation of Fe XV, meta-stable K-vacancy formation. Subsequent decay of this state through Auger processes is indicated by the evolution of the 4.7 eV feature into a feature at 2.0 eV in the Auger electron PES. Lifetimes of the metastable state were determined for 8-15 eV neutral Fe and were observed to decrease with binding energy, with a measured lifetime of 3.1 ± 0.3 ns for 13.6 eV excitation, in good agreement with the previous TR-XAS measurement of 2.3 ± 0.4 ns. The decay of Fe XV into Fe XIV has been theoretically investigated previously [1-3], using a combination of time-dependent configuration interaction and multiconfiguration perturbation theories (CADX+CI+RPA). These calculations were performed in the soft-core approximation, using a global parametric form of the potentials. Time-dependent DFT can provide an alternative approach to study this decay, since it provides an accurate description of strong-field processes. Using a previous implementation of TDDFT for f-ions [5], we have calculated the resonant excitation and decay of Fe XV, for 13.6 eV excitation. The agreement between theory and measurements is very good for both the excitation and decay processes, with a shift in the peak positions, most likely due to uncertainties in the long-range form of the one-electron nuclear potential. In summary, our measurements and calculations agree that the decay of Fe XV to Fe XIV has a lifetime of 3.1 ± 0.3 ns for resonant excitation at 13.6 eV. The experimental and theoretical methodologies presented can be applied to investigate the decay dynamics of other low-lying vacancies in various heavy elements.

Personal archives hold a unique record of our lives and experiences. Often these collections are a mix of mementos, documents, and computer files that reflect different points in time and generate from different applications or sources. Providing a seamless and secure experience for the user has been a key challenge for archival service providers. In this paper, we propose a service model for personal archives that is complementary to existing cloud and backup offerings. In our model, users retain ownership and control of their data, and service providers offer access to files based on established security criteria. In return, users are paid for the services they use. In this way, service providers can utilize data while allowing users to monetize their assets, benefitting both parties. To demonstrate our approach, we have integrated with a File-hosting service to provide access to a sample of user files. Our preliminary evaluation suggests that users are able to access their data quickly and securely through this interface, with the service generating significant revenue for the host. We also discuss key considerations and challenges for this model, and highlight opportunities to further integrate with security services, enable access via Web browsers, and promote user privacy. This work was sponsored by the Institute for Advanced Technology & Public Policy (IATP) at George Mason University. The digital assets of individuals are growing increasingly large in volume and diverse in source and type, including documents, images, videos, and computational artifacts created by individuals and their interacting with digital systems. Many individuals would like to ensure the availability and accessibility of their digital assets into the future, and would prefer to monetize their use of these assets while they are still accessible. A challenge for service providers is to assist individuals in meeting these goals while maintaining the privacy and security of the data and providing a sustainable business model. We present a model that enables individuals to own and monetize their data while providing a seamless, secure experience for the user. Service providers will be able to access data while meeting security criteria established by the user, and users can generate revenue for the services they use. We present our approach to integrating with a cloud storage service to demonstrate the compatibility and security of this model. We also discuss additional considerations necessary for fully integrating with security services and show preliminary revenue results. We conclude by discussing the potential challenges and opportunities for this model and identify next steps to address these challenges and develop this idea into a sustainable business. Personal archives, like those of Alan Turing or Edward Snowden, provide a unique perspective on current affairs. The long-term accessibility and security of these collections is increasingly a concern. Encryption methods improve annually, but remain cumbersome to use and are vulnerable to motivated or unknowledgeable attackers. In addition, the quantity and variety of digital assets generated by individuals grows increasingly large and complex. Personal archives must adopt a user-centric approach that allows owners to control their data and ensure its accessibility while meeting the unique needs of each archive. Mapping the shapes of stars is a powerful way to learn about the formation and assembly history of galaxies. Methods from integral field spectrographs (IFSs) enable us to measure the stellar kinematics across the surfaces of galaxies, and derive information such as the mass of dark matter halos in which they formed and how rapidly they are rotating. We present a method for extracting spatially-resolved spectra that, for the first time, combines high quality IFS data with the wide wavelength coverage and high signal-to-noise of multi-band photometry, enabling us to robustly extract stellar absorption line strength maps that encode the full spectrum of information about the stellar populations. We combine our maps of stellar populations with high-resolution mapping of the stellar kinematics to study the dynamical structure of the galaxies. We find that our derived maps of stellar population properties are robust and provide an accurate view of the histories of the stellar populations in these systems.

The magnetic groundstate of an experimental $S=1/2$ kagom\'{e} antiferromagnet was studied by means of magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, and NMR experiments. The previously proposed axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange model, which takes into account the latest experimental observations was used to simulate the experimental results. The axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange interaction between the third neighbor ions was found to be extremely important to reproduce the experimental results, achieving a qualitative agreement for the susceptibility and the Curie-Weiss temperature dependence on the temperature, and a quantitative agreement for the nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate and the specific heat with a entropy correction factor of around 0.6. The axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange interaction was also shown to induce a tiny ferromagnetic component in the z direction, which was successfully reproduced by the simulation. Finally, the simulation indicates the existence of a small temperature region below 0.5K in which the system undergoes a magnetic phase transition. The obtained exchange interactions and anisotropies agree with a renormalization-group analysis of the experimental results, providing further support for the axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange interaction model. The results presented herein may shed light on the nature of the more general class of materials described by this model, which includes a significant number of actual materials, and suggest a novel approach to their experimental study. The axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange interaction is currently the only symmetry-allowed second-nearest-neighbor interaction in the kagome lattice, and it is thus a potentially significant energy scale in a wide range of systems. The axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange interaction has recently attracted considerable interest, owing to its potential application in novel quantum information processing and quantum simulation architectures, as well as in the general understanding of frustration in quantum many-body systems. In this work, we present magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, and nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate experiments on an iridate kagome lattice antiferromagnet. We find that the previously proposed axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange model can qualitatively reproduce the susceptibility and Curie-Weiss temperature dependence on the temperature, as well as part of the specific heat data. However, the simulation fails to reproduce the experimental nuclear spin-lattice relaxation rate data, and a correction factor to the specific heat data is also required. The latter can be explained by the existence of a small temperature region below 0.5K in which the system undergoes a magnetic phase transition. We then show that the obtained exchange interactions and anisotropies agree with a renormalization-group analysis of the experimental results, providing further support for the axial next-nearest-neighbor exchange interaction model. Mykyta the Fox is a fox who has lived most of his life in captivity. Despite this, he has learned to speak two languages: human and fox language. This paper presents a model of Mykyta’s language learning. It assumes that Mykyta’s knowledge of human language is based on auditory instructions provided by his trainers. Linguistic knowledge of fox language is represented as a network, where each word is a node and connections between nodes represent semantic relations between these words. The network evolves according to a basic algorithm that takes into account the probability of the word occurrence given the preceding and following words in the sentence. The initial network is random and, through the learning process, acquires structure that resembles that of fox language. The process is extremely slow in the beginning, and human language requires many thousands of hours for the network to acquire the structure comparable to that of fox language. The model suggests that fox language has a grammatical structure and that it differs radically from random networks. The model can be a base for studying aspects of language acquisition and can be extended to other languages.

This paper presents a formulation of the yield stress design in poro- hydraulic systems using approximate pressure field and "calcul'a la rupture en présence d'un "ecoulement". The approximation of the pressure field is based on a solution presented in [1] and it was validated for different examples. The work presents an original method that can be applied to a wide range of problems. As an example, the formulation is applied to the problem of a saturated with water soil subjected to the flow of water. The yield surface is shaped as a penalty function of the absolute value of the differences between the local equivalent saturation and the desired value. The difference between the actual pressure and the imposed pressure, called "enthalpy", is considered. The obtained results are compared to the ones obtained with the classical solution based on "calcul'a la rupture en présence d'un "ecoulement". The proposed method is more realistic from a hydraulic point of view and the number of iterations to achieve the stabilisation is reduced.

The universality of Mixed Action Extrapolation (MEA) formulae, which link free energies of lattice models to the covering radius of the lattice, is demonstrated by explicit calculations of the five- and six-state Potts models in two and three dimensions. For the first time MEA is shown to be exact in the thermodynamic limit, both in the two- and three-dimensional Potts models. This is done using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. The universality of MEA formulae implies that, for any given lattice and lattice models, the free energy difference between two arbitrary boundary conditions separated by a distance R in the thermodynamic limit can be written in the form \[ \Delta F(R) \approx f(R/L) \sim \ln R/L + \cdots \text{, as } R \to \infty, \] where L is the lattice size and R is the covering radius of the lattice. The covering radius is a geometric property of the lattice and has a simple expression in terms of the interaction parameters of the lattice models.

The breakthroughs in String Theory and its proposed compactification on T$^{4}$ and Calabi-Yau threefolds provide a natural framework for cosmology. In this perspective, we review the different cosmological scenarios that can be obtained by simply considering the effect of the moduli fields present in these scenarios on cosmology. Finally, we present two new scenarios based on the existence of stabilizing fluxes, which present different phenomenology than the ones previously proposed. The theory of cosmic inflation provides a compelling solution to the problems of the standard hot Big Bang model. However, explaining the observed flatness and regularity of our Universe still requires additional fine tuning. In the moduli stabilization scenario, the small scale fluctuations in the density of our Universe can be naturally explained without requiring additional tuning. In particular, the warped compactification of Type IIB String Theory on Calabi-Yau threefolds contains a universal light modulus (the volume of the internal manifold) whose long wavelength fluctuations directly generate the observed curvature and regularities of the universe. Alternatively, the situation can be significantly enriched by the inclusion of additional light fields. Two prominent examples of this are the inclusion of flux and anti-flux. Such fluxes can stabilize the curvature of the internal manifold, and lead to an inflationary epoch at a later stage of the universe. We present a complete catalog of models of moduli stabilization consistent with the assumptions of the described flux compactification schemes, and indicate the regions of parameter space that lead to interesting cosmological consequences.

The nuclear symmetry energy is one of the most important inputs for modeling neutron-rich nuclear systems. Highly precise experimental data for the energy difference between finite nuclei and their neutrons drops can provide constraints on the density dependence of nuclear symmetry energy. With the recently developed energy-weighted momentum-dependent effective interaction (EWMDPI), we perform theoretical calculations of the nuclear symmetry energy using Skyrme interactions with and without relativistic corrections in the particle-hole channel. With the available Skyrme parameter sets, we first examine the density dependence of the nuclear symmetry energy at sub-saturation densities by using the experimental data for the energy differences between different binding energies of mid-heavy nuclei. We then use the nearly -$1/3$ power-law behavior of the symmetry energy at sub-saturation densities to determine its density dependence at supra-saturation densities. We find that the symmetry energy at supra-saturation densities is about 30 - 50 MeV higher than that extracted from the neutron-star observation, though it is well constrained by the properties of heavy elements. We also examine the temperature dependence of the nuclear symmetry energy and its slope. The results indicate that the symmetry energy is much more dependent on temperature than previously believed.

The large-scale structure (LSS) of the universe today exhibits a complex spatial distribution of galaxies, seemingly at random, with an amplitude of a few tens of millions of light-years at low redshifts. This "cosmic web" is a powerful cosmological tool, which, combined with other cosmological measurements, is helping to nail down the nature of dark energy. As the largest nonlinear structure in the universe, the LSS strongly depends on the combination of matter density and dark energy density. We perform a complete LSS analyses using the halo model and Liang-Mocular method in the latest cosmological simulations, including the state-of-the-art simulations (e.g.,, Auriga and Illustris) and classic simulations (e.g., Millennium and GHALO). We then use five popular parametrizations of dark energy to modify the evolution of the linear growth factor and the evolution of the rms fluctuation of the matter density field to predict the formation epochs of halos and their impacts on the shape of the galaxy power spectrum. We finally summarize the possible results in terms of projected art maps and make a summary plot. We find that the amplitude of the galaxy power spectrum is able to break the degeneracy of the five dark energy models at the 0.5% accuracy level in the future survey, i.e., the Euclid and WFIRST missions.

The quantum mechanical Dyson indices have been related to various separability properties of the corresponding quantum systems. In this paper, we show that the Hilbert-Schmidt separability probabilities and the related Hilbert-Schmidt separability functions can be expressed in terms of the corresponding Dyson indices. As an application, we show that the probability that a random pure state is unseparable equals 1/2. This generalizes a corresponding result for the Dyson indices. We also derive a recursion relation for the Hilbert-Schmidt separability function. As a simple example, we consider the two-particle Separable Quantum Systems with the one-particle Hamiltonians being either separable or not. We find explicit expressions for the corresponding Dyson indices and for the Hilbert-Schmidt separability probabilities and functions. Searching for photos on Flickr is a popular activity, and the photo search results can be sorted by most liked, latest added, and most viewed. In this work, we use a neural network to predict the click-through-rate (CTR) of each photo, and use the predicted CTRs to re-rank the photo search results. The results show that using predicted CTRs rather than the original photo metadata can boost the query-independent photo search performance. Our model can be easily trained on the publicly available Flickr dataset, and can be readily deployed to other photo search platforms. Overall, this work shows that using deep learning to model the photo search ranking can be a promising approach to improve the photo search experience. Yingzhe Yan, Quanquan Nie, Ping Zhou, Liming Liu Link to the paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.10455.pdf

Distributed network topologies are commonly established by some central authority according to geographic proximity, link availability, or other arbitrary constraints. In this work, we design a decentralized, localized approach to network topology formation, whereby each sensor node randomly and independently forms links to other sensor nodes. We present conditions under which this decentralized approach leads to substantially denser networks compared to existing centralized approaches based on similar assumptions. We also present two versions of the proposed protocol for partially and fully random networks. In partially random networks, some connectivity constraints, such as a minimum number of neighbors, are fulfilled; in fully random networks, all constraints are fulfilled. We evaluate our protocol through extensive simulations and illustrate its applicability to sensor networks in large venues such as a college campus.' We envision a wide range of applications for our approach. For example, it can be used to generate ad hoc networks for emergency services with the goal of expediting the delivery of emergency services communications, or for wireless sensor networks deployed in large venues such as a college campus, where the generated networks have the desired properties of high density and full randomness.

The pulsar PSR J1930+1852 in the Crab-like SNR G54.1+0.3 was observed with the satellite XMM-Newton on 2011 April 7. The observation was made following the precise solar ephemeris generated by the PREM model. A search for a sinusoidal modulation in arrival times of the pulsar signal with period equal to the Earth's sidereal day was performed. No such signal was found, but a strict upper limit on the root mean square of the sinusoidal signal with periods equal to the Earth's sidereal day and the sidereal year was established. This limit, depending on the assumed properties of the signal, translates to a bound on the free parameters of possible physics models that could account for the observed properties of the pulsar J1930+1852 and the Crab Nebula in general. The most straightforward explanation of the signals detected in the pulsar timing data so far is the so called ”Shapiro delay” due to the curvature of space-time around the pulsar. A more exotic explanations, such as coupling of the axion field to the neutron, should also be considered.

Galactic globular clusters (GCs) are among the oldest objects in the universe. Over time, primordial nucleosynthesis processes act to produce a homogeneous mix of light elements (heavier than helium) throughout the cluster. Over the past decade, it has been demonstrated that several GCs show light nuclei (carbon, nitrogen and oxygen) abundances that are significantly higher than the local interstellar medium (ISM) values. This observation presents a challenge to the commonly accepted model of GC formation. Current solutions to this problem invoke an external source of fresh elements, but this has not been able to reproduce the observed abundance patterns. A more elegant solution would be for the GC to itself produce the observed quantities of the freshly synthesized elements. In this manner, the self-enrichment model does not require external enrichment and is, therefore, a more broadly applicable solution to the problem of explaining the light nuclei observations in GCs. Here we present a nucleosynthesis calculation showing that an idealized self-enrichment scenario is capable of producing the observed quantities of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen in globular cluster mass models.

The Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) universe is the most common theoretical description of the universe based on the general theory of relativity. In this article, we examine the possibility that the universe is undergoing a phase of current acceleration. To do this, we will use the fundamental energy conditions, which are necessary conditions for the universe to be described by general relativity. We will show that the strong energy condition is satisfied, and so no anomalous current is required. However, the weak energy condition and the additional condition of local causal structure cannot both be satisfied, and thus a violation of the dominated energy condition is required for current acceleration to occur. We consider the consequences of this on the nature of the current acceleration, and its implications for cosmology. We consider the energy conditions, which are necessary conditions for the consistency of the Einstein field equations. The strong energy condition (SEC) states that stress-energy is always positive,, local causal structure requires that if a sufficiently small region has a positive stress-energy, then the entire region has a positive stress-energy, and the weak energy condition (WEC) requires that if a object has positive energy then all the observers measure a positive energy density. The standard FLRW universe satisfies the necessary conditions for the SEC and WEC, but not the additional requirement of local causal structure. Thus, the universe cannot be undergoing a phase of current acceleration unless this is caused by a violation of the SEC or WEC. We will consider the implications for cosmology of the possibility of such violations. We show that, if the violation of the SEC is caused by a fluid with negative pressure, then this negative pressure fluid must be dominant, and so the current acceleration must be caused by a repulsive gravity effect of this fluid. On the other hand, if the violation of the WEC is caused by an ordinary negative energy matter field, then this causes the acceleration of the universe to be superluminal, which is ruled out by observations.
