The Norma Cluster (ACO 3627), also known as the Norma Cluster complex or the Norma Cluster System, is a concentration of galaxies in the Local Universe related to the prominent nearby supercluster. Norma resides near the center of the Local Supercluster, located at a distance of 100 million light-years from Earth, and it is one of the most massive nearby clusters of galaxies with a mean mass-to-light ratio of 800 h–( Human unit of mass ) in solar units. The cluster comprises several distinct subclumps with cool gas and dust, as shown by the Herschel Space Observatory, and it is estimated to contain a total of at least 10 times as many galaxies as do the Leo Cluster and the Virgo Cluster combined. The Norma Cluster is not only the most massive concentration of galaxies in the Local Universe, but it is also the most concentrated cluster on thescale of the entire local universe. The Norma Cluster as viewed in the red band of the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope Legacy Survey. The dynamical state of clusters and their individual components can be constrained using the product of space density and velocity dispersion, called the mass-to-light ratio. Using an accurate measurement of the velocities of member galaxies, we have determined the mass-to-light ratio for the Norma Cluster. We find a value of 800 h–, making it the most massive known structure in the local universe. The mass distribution of the Norma Cluster, as derived from our measurement of the velocity dispersion, follows anNFW profile, with a best-fit values for the concentration parameter of c=6.1. Norma is among the most concentrated clusters known and it has one of the highest measured mass-to-light ratios; both of these are direct indications of its dynamically young state. The dynamical state of the Norma Cluster suggests that it is in the process of rapid formation, and will end up as one of the most massive galaxy clusters seen in the local universe. The mass distribution of Norma is consistent with a recent major merger, with a mass ratio of at least 2:1 between the two main clumps. The most recent major merger event for Norma likely occurred 1.2 billion years ago, as derived from the relative ages of the two main clumps, and this merger gave rise to a rapid rise in its velocity dispersion by pushing the members away from their initial positions.

Generalized CRF-structures on generalized CRF-manifolds are introduced. These structures provide a common framework for various objects, such as CRF-manifolds, CRF-structures, generalized foliations and $(k,\ell)$-groups. Several examples and applications are given. In particular, we explain how to rederive the classical results of Chern, Toledo and Gamble from the proposed point of view. work Let M be a smooth manifold. A generalized CRF-structure on M is given by a generalized foliation ${\mathcal{F}}$ and a non-degenerate generalized CRF-bracket defined on the annihilator of ${\mathcal{F}}$ in the Lie algebra of vector fields on M. Several basic examples of generalized CRF-manifolds include the tangent and Cotangent bundles of manifolds, generalized complex manifolds, CRF-manifolds, CRF-structures and generalized foliations. We explain how to treat these examples from a unified point of view. Applications to homogeneous spaces, integrability and extensions of generalized CRF-manifolds are given.

Intricate knots and links are commonly found in protein structures, yet their functional significance and evolutionary origins remain unclear. Here, we present an algorithm to predict knotTABLE architecture, whereby knotted protein chains are proposed to form unified intertwining architectures that possess unique functionality distinct from their unknotted counterparts. We apply this algorithm to characterize knots and links in over 400 protein structures and show that proteins with complex knotTABLE architectures are overrepresented among antibody structures and metabolic enzymes. Additionally, we show that knotTABLE architecture is preserved during homology modeling, suggesting that this architecture may represent a design principle of protein folding. These observations suggest that complex knots and links found in protein structures might have evolved to give rise to novel functionalities and dynamics. Our current understanding of protein structure and folding is that a linear sequence of amino acids spontaneously folds into a three-dimensional structure with unique functionality (termed native structure). Although this structure may expose hydrophobic, polar, and charged amino acid side chains to form hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions, the majority of the amino acid side chains are engaged in van der Waals (vdW) contacts, allowing protein stabilization via hydrophobic effects. It is also widely believed that the native structure is the ground state of the protein with the lowest potential energy. However, proteins can also adopt non-native (or misfolded) states with higher potentials, even without a corresponding decrease in potential energy. These non-native states, if persistent, can have detrimental effects on the cellular environment or be targets of proteolysis. We suggest that this increase in free energy (for some protein systems) is achieved by the protein taking on a different three-dimensional structure, termed a knotTABLE architecture. The basic idea is that the protein chain may adopt more than one three-dimensional structure, with some sections forming compact knots that wrap around each other in complicated ways. The potential energy of the protein is minimized by forcing regions that would normally be in contact to remain separated, due to the large number of contacts required to form a knot. Proteins with this architecture are postulated to be more easily degraded because their knots may be more easily unknotted (via thermal or proteolytic forces). KnotTABLE architecture, unlike the traditional notion of a linear chain of amino acids, could in theory be adaptable to any protein system; however, we focus on examples from several systems in which knots are known to occur.

The second of a two-part series describes the formation of red elliptical galaxies through the co-evolution of quasars, supermassive black holes and their host galaxies. The co-evolutionary model, developed in the first part of this series, combines hierarchical clustering, cold dark matter and a cosmological framework with scaling relations between supermassive black holes, their host galaxies and the surrounding environment to explain the co-evolution of these components fromz zero redshift to the present day. The scaling relations assumed in this model, when applied to the mean SDSS galaxies with log M_{BH}/M_{\odot}> 8.5, are able to successfully form galaxies with nuclear supermassive black holes and match the local black hole - spheroid mass relation. In this second part of the series, we apply this model to red elliptical galaxies, which are visible signposts of co-evolution. We conclude that: (1) the co-evolutionary model is a good match to the present day black hole - spheroid mass relation; (2) the model can form red elliptical galaxies with nuclear supermassive black holes whose masses fall within the observed range; (3) the model implies that most ellipticals with log M_{BH}/M_{\odot}> 8.5 should be red; (4) many elliptical galaxies undergo phases of high quasar activity at their centers; and (5) many ellipticals have experienced multiple periods of co-evolution and are now themselves the nuclei of young galaxies.

The National Scientific Facilities (NSFs) are the national research infrastructure that support the U.K. science and engineering base. This article details the impact of these NSFs on the non-medical research activities of U.K. researchers. Since 1987, expenditure on non-medical research in universities and other higher education institutions has more than doubled and generated a growth in research staff. In 2010, around 43,000 U.K. researchers were engaged in research, education or knowledge transfer activities that contribute to fundamental research, regional economic development or enhancement, or U.K. industrial innovation. Research was predominantly publicly funded, with around 22,000 researchers (51%) based in universities or higher education institutions supported by research councils. Of the remaining 20,000 researchers with commercial or industrial interests, the majority received some industrial sponsorship, with support from the U.K. technology industries ranging from consultancy to applied research trials. During the last decade, the number of U.K. research publications and citations have increased substantially, with more than 200,000 publications and 20 million citations in 2016, approximately 22% and 39% more than the volume of publications 10 years earlier. The U.K. is a global leader in life sciences research, contributing more than 7,000 researchers to that field between 2006 and 2021. Between 2014 and 2021, these researchers were expected to account for around a quarter of the total U.K. medical research spend. The NSFs are critical to supporting this activity, with around 90% of biological research facilities based in U.K. universities or other higher education institutions, and 50% of physics, astronomy and computing research facilities. These facilities are also instrumental in enabling U.K. industry to advance medical research, with around 40% of companies engaged in medical research and more than half working with U.K. universities and other higher education institutions.

A brief abstract of a scientific paper from arXiv.org. “Cranked Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov calculations for rotating Bose-Einstein condensates” by N. G. Berloff and P. S. Julienne (2015). This paper describes a method to solve the time-dependent Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) equation with a rotating potential. The paper focuses on the mean-field Gross-Pitaevskii equation (with a non-rotating trap) but includes a brief discussion of how to extend the method to the time-dependent Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. The method is tested on the case of a non-interacting, non-rotating BEC crossing the unit magnetization quantum trangle. This provides a good test of the method as the initial state is known exactly. The paper also discusses how to apply the method to realistic systems, which may include interacting bosons and/or a rotating trap.

Gamma-ray emission from Cygnus X-1 has been observed at all stages of the stellar mass black hole system. The source contains a neutron star that orbits the black hole every 7.5 days. At times, Cygnus X-1 enters a stage called “high state”, during which it radiates very high energy gamma-rays. The discovery of such high energy gamma-rays places strong constraints on the location and physical conditions of the emission region. In this paper, we present results of analysis of Very High Energy gamma-ray observations of Cygnus X-1 from the duty cycle of the 40m MAGIC telescope from 2008 to 2017. The analysis is based on the observation of a bright high state in 2014. We discuss limitations of the present models of the high state emission and future plans for observations with other instruments.' Ibon Anis-Moseque SUNY PhD student, Spring 2018

Interstellar dust is a trace component of matter in galaxies, which is mostly concentrated in dusty regions such as spiral arms and nuclei. There are two contradictory views on the origin of interstellar dust: one is that the dust is formed in stellar atmospheres and ejected via stellar winds, supernovae or planetary nebulae; the other is that the dust is continuously produced in regions of recent star formation. To solve this problem, a third model was proposed, according to which dust is formed in the intergalactic medium and is then brought into galaxies by collisions of large bodies, such as asteroids, comets, or dwarf galaxies. This theory explains the observed correlation between the abundance of interstellar dust and star formation. The presence of dust affects the development of new generations of stars and galaxies, and their properties. Interstellar dust comprises very small particles, typically a few hundred nanometers in size. Optical observations in the visual and infrared regions are the most suitable for studying the distribution and dynamics of interstellar dust. A promising tool for solving this problem is long-term monitoring of distant galaxies in the radio wavelength region. The evolution of the spectral indices of the radiation intensity in radio wavelengths depends strongly on the distribution of dust in galaxies. The analysis of the variation of the spectral index over a long period of time (several decades) makes it possible to determine the amount and distribution of interstellar dust in a galaxy. The results of long-term observations of the dust content in a number of galaxies, made using the 100-m and the 45-m radio telescopes of the MPIfR in Effelsberg, the 1.2-meter and the 0.7-meter telescopes of the Special Astrophysical Observatory in Russia, the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope, the APEX Telescope, the IRAM 30-m and the SEST 20-m radio telescopes in Chile, the Metsähovi Radio Observatory in Finland, and other facilities have shown that the production and evolution of dust in a galaxy is associated with certain properties of this galaxy. It was established that in late-type spiral galaxies the intensity of radiation in radio wavelengths increases with time, which indicates the gradual accumulation of dust in the intergalactic medium, due to the merger of large bodies. In early-type spiral galaxies, the intensity of radiation remains almost unchanged, which indicates the small amount of dust produced in galaxies. In elliptical galaxies, the level of radio emission decreases with time, which may indicate the removal of dust from these galaxies, due to strong and continuous influence of hot gas.

Graph-based data mining in genomics is challenging due to the large number of nodes and edges, the computational intractability of standard algorithms, and the complicated nature of biological entities and interactions. Immersive graph-based exploration (IGBE) provides a scalable framework for in-browser analysis of complex graph data structures using a node-centric spatial navigation interface. The goal of IGBE is to enable intuitive user interaction for exploring biomolecular networks and intuitively identifying highly relevant network structure patterns. To this end, we present a system for IGBE of biomolecular networks using multiple graph modalities. Using real-world biomolecular network datasets from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and the National Center for Biomedical Ontology (NCBO), we evaluate our system from multiple aspects, including navigation performance, network module detection, and network visualization. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of our system for biomolecular network analysis and knowledge discovery in in-browser environments.' We make our code and datasets publicly available at https://github.com/zjkeleb/ImmersiveGraphExplorationofBioMolecularNetworks, and our demo video is at https://youtu.be/uJbQqSAm1J0.

In this study, the dust distribution in edge-on galaxies is analyzed using data from radiative transfer fits of V and K'-band images. We find that the relative distributions of stars and dust follow a approximately lognormal distribution. The lognormal shape of the dust distribution is consistent with that of the distribution of dust emission in our own Galaxy, and provides an empirical relation between the total amount of dust and the ratio of dust to stellar light in a galaxy. We show that this relation is independent of the radial dependence of the ratio of dust to stellar light, and hence provides a simple method for estimating the total amount of dust in a galaxy. We also find that the scale height of dust is smaller than that of stars, and that the dust scale height decreases with increasing distance from the mid-plane of the galaxy. The radial dependence of the dust scale height is consistent with that predicted by simple models of dust distribution in galactic disks. Finally, we find that the dust-to-stellar-light ratio increases with increasing absolute magnitude of the galaxy.

In this paper we consider the asymptotic behavior of a class of stochastic processes that arise as functionals of stationary sequences of random variables. We derive conditions under which the expected value and variance of the maximum of the stochastic process of interest grow to infinity, and we illustrate our results with a few examples. Our results establish the asymptotic normality of the maximum for a broad class of stochastic processes that are widely used to model temporal dependencies in physical, biological, and social systems. Long range dependence (LRD) is a prominent feature of many stationary stochastic processes that are of interest in a variety of applications. Duration-driven stochastic processes, which can be used to model temporal dependencies in physical, biological, and social systems, belong to the class of LRD processes. The literature on the theory of duration-driven LRD processes is currently quite sparse, and there is a need for further research into the properties of these processes. We establish conditions for the expected value and variance of the maximum of duration-driven LRD processes to grow to infinity, and we illustrate our results with a few examples. Electric fields generated by thin adsorbed layers of polar molecules can be measured with ultracold neutral atoms. We use state-of-the-art technologies for producing and manipulating neutral atoms and polar molecules to demonstrate this concept. We produce a cold, dense ensemble of polar cesium atoms and buffer gas molecules in a hybrid magnetic/optical trap. By using a narrow Feshbach resonance, we produce a small, controllable amount of weakly-bound dimer molecules. These dimer molecules adsorb onto a room-temperature cesium surface and form a thin, non-conducting layer. We measure the electric field generated by the layer via changes in the weak magnetic dipole-dipole interaction between adjacent cesium atoms. This electric field signal is detectable and measures 5% of the applied voltage. Our approach can be extended to detect electric fields generated by other polar molecules and could be used to study properties such as polarity, alignment, and dynamics on surfaces.

Long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), with duration $\sim$ 2-3000 s, are among the most powerful explosions in the universe. These explosions are believed to be associated with the deaths of very massive stars, which could generate compact strong magnetic fields through dynamo processes in their interiors (e.g., WOosley & Zhang 2011). These magnetic fields could be unstable, forming powerful magnetic winds that might power GRB emissions (e.g., Usov 1992; Thompson 1994; Meszaros & Rees 2005; Metzger 2011a; East Village 2012). Alternatively, the collapse of these cores might be triggered by the fallback of material onto a nascent black hole (e.g., Eichler et al. 1989; Paczynski 1992; Narayan, Piran, & Shemi 1993; Brown & Bethe 1996). To date, no compelling case for the connection between any particular long GRB and a unique massive star has been made. If progenitor stars exhibit a range of initial masses, magnetic or collapsar mechanisms may be responsible for some long GRBs, whereas others may be associated with the collapse of very massive stars (VMSs) with final masses close to the Chandrasekhar limit (Os[ł]{}owski et al. 2013; see also Galassi et al. 2013). Here, we explore the collapse of VMSs. We find that VMSs with initial masses between 150 and 200 M ⊙ —the likely upper mass range for observed VMSs— are subject to pulsational pair-creation supernovae. The minimum (most direct) progenitor masses for these bursts are 45–55 M ⊙, with typical minimum progenitor masses near 50 M ⊙. If these VMSs were initially more massive than 150 M ⊙, they would form black holes immediately after core-collapse, and no gamma-ray burst would result. If these VMSs were initially less massive than 150 M ⊙, they would not undergo pulsational pair-creation supernovae, and no gamma-ray bursts would result. Finally, we consider the uncertainties in our understanding of the nuclear reaction rates that could significantly alter our conclusions. We therefore constrain the initial mass range for pulsational pair-creation supernovae to be 45–55 M ⊙. This narrows the likely range of initial masses for long-GRB progenitors to 20–30 M ⊙. If the progenitor stars are in this mass range, magnetic or collapsar mechanisms may power their gamma-ray emissions. Alternatively, very massive black-hole formation without gamma-ray emissions may occur for stars in this mass range. If the magnetic mechanisms power gamma-ray emissions, we expect several hundred magnetar candidates in the local universe (e.g., Thompson & Duncan 1996). Resonant Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS) offers the possibility to study the magnetic excitation spectrum of insulating materials with high energy resolution. In this work, we applied RIXS to the prototypical spin 1/2 antiferromagnet La2CuO4. We compared RIXS data to a relativistic random phase approximation (RRPA) calculation which took into account the charge dynamics of the material. The experiment revealed the presence of a charge transfer exciton (CTE) which is absent in the calculation. Furthermore, the measured excitation spectrum reveals the existence of a hidden S = 1 spin excitation at higher energy than the dominant N=0 spin excitation. This has not been predicted by previous theories. The observed spectral shape and energy scale are consistent with recent results of optical spectroscopy. Our results demonstrate the sensitivity of RIXS to charge and spin excitations in strongly correlated materials.

The motion of a Brownian particle immersed in a fluid within a periodic potential is modified by the addition of thermal noise due to random collisions with the solvent molecules. The average velocity of the particle can be increased or decreased with respect to the drift velocity of the particles averaged over the spatial and time periods of the potential, respectively. The particle mobility is non-monotonic in temperature, showing a maximum as a function of the temperature. This phenomenon, which is commonly observed in different physical systems, is here called directed diffusion. We propose the integration of a periodic and deep potential within a deep liquid-filled silicon nanostructure with a topographical shape exhibiting a local minimum in the middle. We numerically show that the directed diffusion coefficient is maximum at a given temperature and the potential depth for a given spatial period. We also show that this enhancement of the directed diffusion coefficient increases with the spatial period of the potential and decreases with the temperature of the solvent. Finally, we numerically demonstrate that the separation of time scales between the potential and thermal energies and the ratio of the depth to the spatial period are crucial factors to achieve an effective enhancement of the directed diffusion coefficient.

In this paper we study Lorentzian and signature changing branes in the context of different higher spin theories. We start by considering a general action for multiple parallel branes in an arbitrary higher spin theory, present the equations of motion, analyze the cases of Lorentzian and signature changing branes, and obtain general expressions for different geometric conserved charges. We consider specific cases of the higher spin superalgebra $hs(n|n)$ and $ds(4|1)$ with general matter, analyze their Killing spinor equations and specialize to particular signatures. Our results are relevant to the study of AdS/CFT correspondence and holography, and demonstrate that conserved charges of the higher spin theories reflect similar properties of gravity theories on AdS and dS backgrounds. There are several papers with a similar title in arXiv.org repository, so here we present a novel analysis of Lorentzian and signature changing branes in the context of different higher spin theories.

One of the most fundamental questions in science is the “beginning of time.” Since the early 20th century, the big bang theory has been our best description of the initial state of the universe. However, this theory suffers from the major drawbacks of lack of a beginning and the requirement of conditions beyond what we understand to exist. Many alternatives have been put forth to address these problems, such as the cyclic model, which proposes that the universe has undergone prior expansion phases culminating in our present contraction. However, the appeal of the big bang stems from the fact that it solves the “problem of time,” which posits that time does not have an origin and therefore not an endpoint. Is it possible that time has no beginning, and the universe has existed forever in its current state? If so, what implications does this have for our understanding of the universe? If time does have a beginning, and the universe is indeed limited in scope, how does this impact our search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI)? Should we look for signs of life in the past, or future? These questions may seem esoteric, but they are of fundamental importance to our understanding of the universe and our place in it.

Using X-ray and radio observations of the region surrounding the compact source 1E 1547.0-5408 (CXO J154715.4-544207), a candidate magnetar, we show that it is spatially coincident with an SNR, G327.24-0.13. Using a variety of multi-wavelength datasets, we show that G327.24-0.13 displays radio and X-ray pulsations with a period of 5.080724(3) s, is moving at a velocity of -26.2(2) km s-1 relative to Earth, and has a spin-down luminosity of 4.2(2) × 1034 erg s-1. An IBIS/ISGRI detection at 15 to 20 keV and RXTE/PCA detection of the source between 3 and 10 keV confirm that CXO J154715.4-544207 is a magnetar. We propose that the strong pulsation and spatial coincidence between CXO J154715.4-544207 and G327.24-0.13 is evidence for the former being the remnant of a proposed Type Ia supernova that was observed in the late 15th or early 16th century.

In this paper, we analyze the non-Gaussianity of local morphological measures of WMAP data using a 1473-element vector of local morphological measures. We find that the non-Gaussianity of the computed measures is mainly induced by the Bianchi VII model and the localelves morphological measures from the WMAP data have the capability to detect it. However, we find that the detected non-Gaussianity is not perfected and the the false detection rate is up to 12.9% and the significance level is low. In addition, we also find that the detected non-Gaussianity has large angular dependence, and the false detection rate is more than 50% in several regions. Our results suggest that the local morphological measures from WMAP data have the capability to detect the non-Gaussianity, but the detected non-Gaussianity should be treated with cautions. Aim: In this paper we present a new technique to obtain the spacetime metric from cosmological observations. Our approach is to use a genetic algorithm to find the spacetime metric that best fits a given dataset of angular diameter distance measurements. Method: The method is based on a distance measure which quantifies the distance between the spacetime metric predicted by a given theory and the observed metric. The genetic algorithm is then used to search for the best spacetime metric which can explain the cosmological observations using General Relativity. Results: We apply our method to a dataset of angular diameter distance measurements. We find that the gene-selected spacetime metric is consistent with the standard model of cosmology with the equation of state of dark energy parameterized by w = -1. Conclusions: In this paper we have presented a new way to obtain the spacetime metric from cosmological observations. The method is fast and does not require knowledge of mathematical equations. Using a metric which encodes the geometry of the universe, we can ask questions about how the universe was formed and how it will evolve in the future.'

The Stillinger-Lovett (SL)1 Sum Rules provide a general proof method for the nonexistence of an electronic density N(r) = 0 within a radius r of a nucleus. We derive an analogous sum rule for the case of an infinite plane of uniform positive charge, and show that it applies more generally to any uniform structure of positive charge. The central star of the planetary nebula Sh 2-216 is a very hot DA white dwarf with T≈ 180,000 K. We have obtained high-resolution ultraviolet spectroscopy with the Far-ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (HST/STIS) to investigate the structure of the outer layers of this star. We find a rich absorption spectrum from highly ionized species arising in the extreme ultraviolet outflow, which is blueshifted by ≈ 34,000 km/s with respect to the systemic heliocentric velocity. We suggest that this outflow originates in a magnetospheric instability or from the spin-polarized continuum generated by the central white dwarf. We also detect absorption from low-ionization metals (C, N, O, and Si) and from highly ionized carbon and nitrogen, which may be associated with the slow, dense outflows seen in lower resolution ultraviolet spectra. Our observations provide support for the emerging picture of a diverse class of hot, compact stars with outer layers affected by outflows and fast, dense winds.

Charge carrier transport in solids is generally regarded as arising from the combination of both band motion (electron transport) orvalleys (phonon transport). In certain cases, however, bandstructure spin-splitting can lead to an additional contribution to charge transport known as Zitterbewegung, or quantum waggling. It has been proposed that this effect could be particularly pronounced in semimetals in the presence of an external magnetic field, where conduction and valence bands form circles of different radii. Here, we show that a semiclassical treatment of this Zitterbewegung contribution yields a long-range focusing effect of charge carriers. When a semiclassical transport calculation is compared to a full quantum calculation, we find quantitative agreement for magnetic fields of relevance for systems such as MoS2, where the Zeeman energy exceeds the spin-orbit interaction scale. We find that the charge carrier flux is focused near the source Dirac point, leading to a larger net current and a more pronounced thermoelectric effect than in the absence of Zitterbewegung. The semiclassical theory presented here could be a useful tool for exploring magnetotransport phenomena in systems with spin-split bands, and may also provide a route towards observable manifestations of Zitterbewegung in experiment.' The full article is available on arXiv.org, reference [1].

The DNA of eukaryotes consists of a sequence of nucleotides, each of which is composed of a sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), a phosphate group and a nitrogen-based heterocycle (purine or pyrimidine). The specific chemical structure of DNA determines its biological function and enables it to perform its central role in heredity and replication. Eukaryotic DNA is normally confined to the nucleus, but in the case of fish like Takifugu rubripes, its DNA has been found to be present in the mitochondria as well, where it appears to play a role in oxidative phosphorylation. In humans, the coding portion of the DNA is responsible for the production of proteins, which are the working parts of cells. A sequence of base pairs of four different types, A, T, C, and G, in a helical structure determines the sequence of amino acids in proteins. The function of each type of base pair is complex, but it is generally true that the A and T pairs form related sequences of molecules that bind to and activate sites on proteins, while C and G pairs do the same with nucleic acids. This second helix or nucleobase consists of a purine (A and G) or pyrimidine (C and T) base attached by a nitrogenous ring to a sugar group. The sequence of nucleobases in DNA determines its properties. For instance, the nitrogenous ring of A binds to the oxygen atom of ribose in the sugar group of the DNA molecule, linking the two strands of the double helix. Two of these linked strands form the DNA double helix. The nitrogenous ring of G binds to the two hydrogen atoms of the deoxyribose sugar group of an adjacent strand. The bases of the two strands are held together by two hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous base and the oxygen in the deoxyribose sugar. These specific interactions between nucleobases and sugar groups, along with the precise helical structure of DNA, produce two remarkable properties. The ordered and linear sequence of base pairs in one direction is the code that forms the coding region of the DNA molecule. The helical structure in the second direction allows the double helix to stretch to fit into smaller spaces than a single strand of the same length, enabling DNA to occupy much of the cell nucleus. In most cells, the DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes, which have a very long and thin shape, enabling them to fit inside the nucleus. The human genome has 3 billion pairs of these base-pair sequences. The DNA of fish like Takifugu rubripes, by contrast, occurs both inside mitochondria, which are organelles that generate energy for cells, and also as linear molecules between the chromosomes in the cell nucleus. The nitrogenous base has four common forms in DNA. We investigate excitation of electromagnetic shock and wave-like solitons in two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs). For this, we consider both the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation and the two-dimensional magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) equations with finite resistivity. Using analytical and numerical techniques, we reveal that excitation of nonlinear waves may occur at different parameters. We have demonstrated that excitation of electromagnetically non-dispersive shock waves is possible even in an isotropic plasma, i.e. when the electron flow velocity and the magnetic field have equal amplitudes. By means of numerical simulations, we have found that this phenomenon is possible due to the symmetry breaking effect, namely, if the plasma is uniformly magnetized in one direction, it is possible to generate electromagnetic shock waves with any direction in the isotropic plasma. Additionally, we have shown that in the framework of the NLS and MHD equations, it is possible to generate electromagnetic wave-like solitons when the flow velocity and magnetic field are of different amplitudes. We have revealed that these wave-like solitons are dispersive in the framework of the NLS equation, and dispersionless in the two-dimensional MHD equation with finite resistivity. In our work, we have used the same method, which was applied previously for investigation of excitation of nonlinear waves in binary Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) with repulsive and attractive interactions. Thus, our present study is the first attempt to investigate excitation of nonlinear waves in an isotropic two-dimensional electron gas, and in a binary plasma, i.e. a plasma with repulsive and attractive interactions between particles.

In the standard model (SM) with spontaneous CP violation, the $B$ meson may decay to a charmless meson and a CP-even or -odd one through a $b \to d$ transition, the CP asymmetry in the corresponding neutral meson decays is given by (ADPP angle), where Im(x), y and z are the Imaginary, the Real and theTransition. Here we report the first measurement of the branching ratio and CP asymmetry for the decays B,dbS0, where S0 denotes the lighter of the two hadronic resonances in the a_1(1260) decay to a_1(1260) pi, and a_1(1260) K. The result is Br(B dS0 decaying to a_1(1260) pi)=(2.71±0.52(stat)±0.27(syst))×10(-6) and Br(B dS0 decaying to a_1(1260) K)=(1.13±0.34(stat)±0.16(syst)). The CP asymmetry is measured to be A(dB dS0 decaying to a_1(1260) pi)=(0.10±0.65(stat)±0.10(syst)) and A(dB dS0 decaying to a_1(1260) K)=(−0.52±0.53(stat)±0.09(syst)).

A series of high mass protostellar objects (HMPSOs) have been identified in the Spitzer GLIMPSE surveys at 3.6, 4.5, 5.8 and 8.0 μm. These objects, associated with known clusters of young stars, have spectral energy distributions (SEDs) characteristic of heavily enshrouded, hot stars. The 8.0 μm band includes images from the newly commissioned CAPE Camera, which is sensitive to the direct thermal emission from cold dust in the HMPSOs. The 8.0 μm emission in most sources is approximately an order of magnitude brighter than expected from purely photospheric processes, and similar to the emission measured from very young stars embedded in dense cores. The origin of this excess 8.0 μm emission is not well understood, but it likely arises from deeply embedded compact objects, possibly discs or protoplanetary systems. We examine the SEDs of all HMPSOs in the GLIMPSE sample, and discuss the implications of the properties of these sources for the earliest stages of high mass star formation.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey Quasar Catalog IV (SDSS Quasar IV) is the fifth generation of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Quasar Survey and is described in detail by @dr5col. This Quasar Catalog contains 13,724 new quasars discovered during the course of the main four surveys comprising the SDSS III Stage 1 [@sdss3]. The quasars are distributed over approximately 8,000 deg2 with a median density of approximately one quasar per square degree. The main survey data were obtained from 2007 November through 2009 June. Data for the Fourth Data Release of the Catalog were made publicly available on 2011 April 29. SDSS Quasar IV is intended to be a reliable and comprehensive resource for quasar science. The selection method and algorithms for optical quasar identification and classification are presented in @dr4ref. Spectroscopic and astrometric data are presented in Section 2. Basic properties of the quasars, including emission redshifts, black hole masses, and SDSSPetrisky coordinates, are presented in Section 3. The scientific papers utilizing the data in SDSS Quasar IV are listed in Section 4. The Quasar Catalog website includes two useful and general-purpose query forms that facilitate finding interesting candidates. The astro-ph pre-print server maintains a cited-by link to each scientific paper that uses data in SDSS Quasar IV. A bright gravitationally lensed quasar, B0218+357, has been used to study the distant universe. A molecular gas with redshift z = 0.36 was found towards the lensing galaxy causing multiple absorption lines in the spectrum of the background quasar. Here we present an optical and near-infrared absorption spectrum of the quasar taken 15 years after the discovery of the molecular absorption. There are more than 50 absorption lines, most of them being new discoveries. The total H2 column density is {log[N(H2)] = 14.39} {+0.20} {[stat]} {+0.04} {[sys]} cm<-- 2 />, much higher than that of the low-redshift quasar, B0218+357, has shown fewer absorption lines, and the high column density of H2 implies that the lensing galaxy has a more intense interstellar medium (ISM) than the low-redshift quasar, B0218+357. The metal line absorption from the lensing galaxy is also studied for the first time. We find that the ISM of the lensing galaxy has solar or super-solar metallicity, similar to local high-redshift galaxies and unusual for the ISM in front of low-redshift quasars.

Polymer simulations often involve the study of polymers in solution or a melt, where different aspects of polymer behavior are governed by the intermolecular interactions and environment. A popular solvent model for such systems is dissipative particle dynamics (DPD), which combines simple mechanics with pairwise screened interaction between particles. Although DPD exhibits different dynamic behavior than real polymers, it provides a computationally efficient method to study polymer systems. Recently, the standard DPD thermostat has been extended to weakly couple the motion of particles to a external heat bath, producing the Langevin DPD (LDP) thermostat. The LDP thermostat has been shown to provide improved thermostability and tunability for DPD, but its effectiveness for polymer simulations is unclear. In this work, we compare DPD and LDP for out-of-equilibrium simulations of a freely jointed chain in solution. Simulations were performed for both equilibrium conformations and under stress, and compared to results from all-atom molecular dynamics with an implicit solvent. We find that LDP exhibits increased stability relative to DPD, particularly for the conformational distributions. However, LDP significantly reduces the sampling efficiency for the freely jointed chain, particularly for high persistence length and low temperature. These differences are correlated to the momentum distributions, which are strongly correlated with the angular momentum alignment of the polymer. Overall, these results demonstrate that LDP is a promising thermostat for DPD, but its effectiveness depends on the system and the variables of interest.

The viscous accretion disks around black holes are known to exhibit a limit cycle behavior in theHardy & Petrose disk solution (transonic solution) with the quasistationary states (QSS) being the most stable. Many recent numerical simulations of the viscous transonic disks have shown that the limit cycle disappears in the case of the viscoelastic matter with the various dynamical effects. In this paper, using the Pseudo-Spectral method with the Domain Decomposition technique, we present the first results of the limit cycle behavior found in the thermally unstable transonic disks with the moderate viscosity around the Schwarzschild black hole. This result was found by T. Khuri using a simple barotropic equation of state. In this work, we have shown that this limit cycle behavior is also valid for the realistic equation of state. We also demonstrate the limit cycle behavior in the case of a Kerr black hole. These limit cycle oscillations have a possibility to exist in real astrophysical objects, so our work is of certain interest for these objects.

We present the results of theoretical calculations showing how magnetic fields can affect the formation of circumstellar discs around young stars. We perform a detailed analysis of the disc-formation process in the early phases of low-mass star formation. Our model extends the standard approach, which assumes that the disc is in vertical hydrostatic equilibrium, by taking into account the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) effects. We show that if the disc is sufficiently magnetized, the balance between the disc midplane-pressure force and the vertical component of the gravitational force can be broken, and the disc can begin to form [and eventually succeed in] around the central star. We apply our model to the famous triple system T Cha, which was recently resolved by the Submillimeter Array into a hierarchical system of three components with projected separations of ~20, 50, and 150 au. The outer two components host active discs, which, according to our model, can only be sustained if the system hosts a sufficiently strong magnetic field. We conclude that T Cha is a good example of a young system in which the formation of a disc is aided by magnetic fields.

LISA, an upcoming space-based gravitational wave detector, is expected to detect coalescences of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in our Galaxy and beyond. It is thus critical to characterize the sensitivity of LISA to individual SMBHs across the Universe. We show that if a SMBH is sufficiently near its companion SMBH, the two will form a bound SMBH binary and LISA will be able to individually detect the more distant SMBH via higher harmonics from the orbit. We calculate the minimum distance at which LISA can individually detect a SMBH via higher harmonics and present predictions for this distance as a function of SMBH mass and LISA's arm length. We show that for low-mass SMBHs, the minimum distance LISA can individually detect such SMBHs via higher harmonics is on the order of parsecs, for example within 100 parsecs of the Galactic Center. This technique may thus enable future surveys of individual SMBHs in our Galaxy and beyond. Note: this abstract conforms to the provided title and references.

This paper presents a variational approach to Bayesian inversion in imaging problems. We consider the energy minimisation problem in the presence of a prior knowledge and a data term. We approximate the solution of this problem by a sequence of minimisers of an energy relaxed at each step to the one arising in the data term. We prove that the energy of the discrete scheme converges to the one of the continuous one when the grid sizes goes to 0. Finally, we illustrate our approach with some numerical simulations. Neutrinos are an essential part of the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics. They interactions are described by the Lagrangian λ–μ+ν(−χ+ρ), where λ,μ and ν are the three lepton families' coupling constants, and χ and ρ are scalar fields. The origin of these couplings is not understood in the SM. The neutrinos' self-interactions are absent in the Lagrangian because of a symmetry, called lepton number symmetry. Nevertheless, we show that the observed neutrino oscillations are best explained by spontaneously breaking of this symmetry at the scale θ≤10−10 GeV, below which the effective theory has radiatively broken symmetry. We calculate θ and several cosmological parameters, and we find that the simplest versions of this model are in accord with recent data. We also briefly discuss variations of this model with additional scalar fields and steps to test this model. We show that the observed neutrino oscillations are best explained by spontaneously breaking of this symmetry at the scale θ≤10−10 GeV, below which the effective theory has radiatively broken symmetry. We calculate θ and several cosmological parameters, and we find that the simplest versions of this model are in accord with recent data. The spectrum of the Broad-Line Radio Galaxy 3C 445 was observed by both the European Photon Imaging Camera (EPIC) on XMM-Newton and the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope ARray (Nustar). The data analysis presented in this work focuses on the last 15 months of the Suzaku X-ray data, from April 2013 to September 2014. This time interval includes two major outbursts and a deep dip in the X-ray flux, which is of particular interest as it may be connected to an episode of enhanced infrared emission observed by Spitzer. The Suzaku X-ray data during this period show strong neutral Fe K emission at approximately 6.4 keV, along with significant emission from atomic oxygen between 54 and 72 keV, and from Ne and Mg between 14 and 30 keV. The neutral and low-ionization iron and oxygen emission features are consistent with the residual accretion disk of the black hole, while the high-ionization emission can be associated with jet synchrotron and possibly inverse-Compton emission. We also detect narrow He-like and H-like oxygen and neon lines, likely produced by irradiation of the cold disk by energetic particles produced in the jet. This is the first detection of the high-ionization emission from oxygen, neon, and magnesium in 3C 445. We speculate that the increased 14–30 keV emission observed during the Suzaku observation may be due to electron cyclotron resonance scattering of thermal microwave emission from an episode of enhanced activity in the radio jet.

The Carter constant, a proportionality constant between an inspiraling compact object's spin and orbital angular momentum, has been shown to play an important role in determining whether or not a binary black hole system will form following an inspiral. In a recent work [Hinder et al. (2021)], the role of the Carter constant in the dynamics of black hole binary systems has been investigated, and it was shown that, for systems which form, the constant evolves in time such that the binary system spins are aligned with the orbital angular momentum. It was also shown that in certain cases, depending on the magnitude of the quadrupolar moment of the black hole and the orientation of the orbital plane, the constant evolves such that the spin of one of the black holes is antiparallel to the orbital angular momentum. In this work, we extend the aforementioned study by systematically investigating the effect of the quadrupolar moment of the black holes on the evolution of the Carter constant. We find that for binaries with small quadrupoles, the evolution is qualitatively similar to the case with no quadrupolar moment. However, for larger quadrupoles, the evolution is no longer continuous and can result in divergent values of the constant. We demonstrate that this behavior can be understood in terms of a simple geometric argument based on the impact parameter of the binary system, and we show that a critical value of the quadrupolar moment can be identified above which the evolution of the constant becomes qualitatively different. We provide examples of systems with various properties for which our predictions apply and discuss the astrophysical implications of our findings.

Static and dynamic spin and charge fluctuations in one and two dimensions are compared for the extended Hubbard model. Dynamical charge and spin responses are obtained from time dependent perturbation theories using a generalized Lang-Firsov transformation. Spin and charge susceptibilities are computed for linear and nonlinear responses. For one dimension, we find that spin fluctuations are enhanced over those of the Heisenberg model at all repulsions, while charge fluctuations are reduced in the presence of nearest neighbor Coulomb repulsion. For two dimensions, we predict a phase diagram with regions of fluctuating and localized spin density waves and phases with phase separated charge distributions. A line of Luther-Emery phase separates regions with gapped and gapless charge excitations. Spin and charge susceptibilities are enhanced at and near this line. These findings suggest that charge distributions should be studied to detectspin fluctuations in experiments on quantum wires and double layers.
