In this paper, we argue that the finitary process algebraic approach to quantum mechanics has deep limitations in the domains where it has been applied, which are predominantly quantum mechanical. We propose a fundamental revision of the approach in which instead of using finitary processes to approximate physical quantities, we view physical quantities as variables, governed by a higher order differential equation. This approach admits a probabilistic interpretation, as the solutions to the corresponding stochastic partial differential equation, at least in special cases, reproduce the predictions of quantum mechanics. We apply the revision to the domain of quantum cosmology, and propose a quantum mechanical model of the universe. We show that, in accordance with quantum cosmology, the early universe experienced a period of inflation. We speculate on the possibility of testing the model against observational data.' The paper is accompanied by an R package “finitaryprocessesoup”, available at: https://github.com/kazuhait/finitaryprocessesoup, that can be used to simulate solutions to the finitary process equations of motion.

Recent rapid development in the area of plasmonics and cavity optomlogy has made it possible to engineer the local density of states (LDOS) of electromagnetic field at the nanoscale, opening up new avenues for light-matter interaction. This control over the optical density of states of matter has enabled the observation of several novel quantum effects such as lasing without inversion in a wide range of materials, including plasmonic metals. More recently, organic molecules with suitable optical transition frequencies have also shown potential for achieving similar non-linear light-matter interactions, opening up exciting new opportunities for laser technology. In this work, we demonstrate that, under the right conditions, a plasmon-induced local density of states engineering of organic molecules in close proximity to a plasmonic metal surface can lead to a hybrid light-matter system with unconventional quantum nonlinear optical properties, including bistability and Kerr non-linearity. Our simulations and experiments confirm that this mechanism is possible in the relevant length-scales of organic molecules and plasmonic metals, and is robust with respect to the specific properties of the hybrid system we consider here. Our results could enable new strategies for coherent control over the ultrafast nonlinear dynamics of organic molecules, as well as the design of novel photonic devices based on engineered local densities of states.

Recent work suggests that protein folding rates may be determined by cooperative fluctuations on the local scale, analogous to the interactions that determine the cooperativity in protein thermal denaturation. In the accompanying paper, we show that excluded volume interactions in multi-particle polymer systems have a similar effect, by providing an additional contribution to the free energy of folding. This results in an effective value of the exponent in the dependence of the folding rate on the chain length, gamma, that describes the growth of the free energy of folding with chain length. In our model, gamma is determined by the spatial correlations in the local volume composition of the chain, and we suggest that excluded volume interactions may determine the structure of these local composition fluctuations. We illustrate this picture by comparing predictions of the scaling of gamma with the Hurst exponent describing long-range correlations in the spatial fluctuations of composition. In support of this, we present evidence that the correlations in the composition fluctuations are themselves long-range. Our approach considers the effects of excluded volume interactions in a simple coarse-grained model that captures the essential multi-particle interactions, and is sufficiently simple to enable a detailed quantitative analysis. This work therefore provides an example of how an effective field theory for multi-particle interactions in systems with complex multi-scale structure can be developed. We anticipate that such a coarse-grained description will be of broader interest, beyond the specific example of protein folding.

The planet HD 155358 b is the lowest-metallicity planet found to date, with a mass 12.6 times that of Earth and a radius that is 0.68 times that of Earth. This super-Earth with inflated radius likely has a high proportion of desert planets without water. Due to the strong radial velocity signature of a massive planet, coupled with a sensitive Doppler survey, the system was identified as a promising target for the CARMENES instrument. When first observed, the planet was 3.5 hours behind its star, taking 47 days to move ahead by one full star diameter. The slow motion together with the very low metallicity of the star, which is 12.5% of the Sun's, suggests that the planet formed at greater distance from the parent star and migrated inward via torques induced by the star's gravity. If this scenario is true, the time required for the planet to move from its birth place to its current orbit is expected to be 1.5 million years, which is comparable to the estimated age of the system. This planet provides a valuable opportunity to investigate the frequency of Earth-like planets around low-metallicity stars and to test theories of planet migration.

Self-organized GeMn nano-columns were studied by means of both, scanning and transmission electron microscopy and extended X-ray absorption spectroscopy. The GeMn columns were grown by chemical vapor deposition on Ge(100) substrates at 300 °C. The average diameter of the columns is about 30 nm. High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy imaging demonstrates that the GeMn columns are formed by accumulation of smaller grains at the end of larger ones. Transmission electron microscopy tomography analysis shows that these small grains are enriched in Mn with respect to the substrate composition. The GeMn composition strongly varies across the columns. Extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy measurements show that GeMn columns incorporate significant amounts of interstitial Mn atoms, that are probably responsible for the ferromagnetic character of the material. The self-organization process during GeMn column growth allows tailoring of the GeMn composition and structure, which strongly influences the magnetic properties of the material. In particular, the columns incorporate significant amounts of interstitial Mn atoms that are probably responsible for their ferromagnetic behavior.

We analyze elastic scattering and fusion cross section data for the 7Li+208Pb system at near-Coulomb-barrier energies using the folding potential. This is a systematic exploration of the potential energy surface (PES) in the system. The potential has 27 parameters that were fitted to a large data base of experimental elastic scattering and fusion cross section data. We also perform a constrained global diagonalization of the coupled-channels Hamiltonian to determine excitation energies and residues. The resulting PES is very deep and has a global minimum close to the separatrix. The appearance of the deep PES could have important implications for the behavior of projectiles very close to heavy targets. *This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Office of Nuclear Physics under Award No. DE-FG02-94ER40834. The potential energy surface (PES) for the 7Li+208Pb system is analyzed by performing an extended optical model analysis of elastic scattering and fusion cross section data for the system. Fitting a large data base of elastic scattering and fusion cross section data to a potential energy surface has the potential to greatly simplify the analysis. With a well-parameterized PES, one can predict the outcome of future experiments and make novel observations that can help guide the further refinement of the PES. This is the first such an analysis of the 7Li+208Pb system and such a systematic exploration of the PES. The potential has 27 parameters that were fitted to a large data base of elastic scattering and fusion cross section data. We also perform a constrained global diagonalization of the coupled-channels Hamiltonian to determine excitation energies and residues. The resulting PES is very deep and has a global minimum close to the separatrix. The appearance of the deep PES could have important implications for the behavior of projectiles very close to heavy targets.

Free zero-range processes (ZRPs) are stochastic interacting particle systems on arbitrary networks that were introduced by Spitzer in 1972. In this framework, the particles are "animals" and the network vertices correspond to "lakes" where the particles can "rest" and " prey on". When an animal "wants" to eat, it randomly chooses a lake and if several animals want to eat at the same time, there is a conflict and none of them can eat. The model was introduced with the purpose of studying the Naming Game of children but has since been applied to many different settings in the area of interacting particle systems. One reason for the popularity of the model is that it is closely related to simple symmetric random walks, a paradigmatic model in random walk theory. ZRPs have been studied extensively by physicists using a variety of techniques from statistical mechanics and combinatorics, but a complete understanding is still lacking. In particular, many natural problems involving the behavior of ZRPs are not even well-defined: in some cases it is not even clear what the appropriate model is. Here we provide a rigorous mathematical analysis of the model, in particular we introduce and study a continuum version of the model, prove its well-posedness, and show that it converges in distribution to a limit called the partial Witten process. Using this convergence result, we establish continuous limits for many natural discrete problems, such as the speed of random walks, the coverage times of percolation processes, and particle systems related to dimer and puddle models. These results provide a solid foundation for researchers in physics, combinatorics, statistical mechanics, and probability to investigate and analyze ZRP-related problems, and at the same time, they provide new insights into a variety of seemingly unrelated problems.

Using galaxy cluster mergers as a probe for new dark energy, theory suggests that the rate of cluster merger interactions decreases over time. Hence the fraction of nearby, physically associated galaxy clusters increases. To test this hypothesis, the spatial distribution of galaxy clusters with projected distances less than 1 Mpc are compared to the spatial distribution of clusters with smaller relative line-of-sight velocities. The comparison sample was generated using the optical and X-ray data of the Smithsonian Institution High-Energy Astrophysics Archive (SIEHA). Within a flux limited survey, the number of close pairs is less than the number of more distant pairs. This result is statistically significant with p<10-3. Since the Hubble parameter is proportional to the cosmic scale factor a, a decrease in the merger rate also implies a decrease in the relative line-of-sight velocities of interacting galaxy clusters. The conclusion of this study is that the number of close, physically associated galaxy clusters is significantly less than the number of more distant clusters. In turn, this implies that the merger rate of galaxy clusters is decreasing with time. By extension, this implies that the Hubble parameter, Ho, is decreasing with time. Hubble’s Law, H=v/a, states that the observed velocity, v, of a galaxy is proportional to the relative distance, a, of the galaxy with respect to its associated cluster. The observed radial velocity, v, and cluster-centric radius, a, are inversely related such that v=H*a (1). Since Ho=Hubble’s Law constant, H, and Ho decreases with time, it is implied that a also decreases with time. The inference of this study is that the Hubble parameter, Ho, is decreasing with time. This decrease in the rate of cluster merger interactions is in tension with the ΛCDM model and current measurements of Ho. A modification of the ΛCDM model or improved measurements of Ho will be required to reconcile the conclusion of this study with the current model of cosmology.

In this paper, we study properties of the nonholonomic Ricci flows on solitonic pp--waves and Schwarzschild solutions of vacuum Einstein equations. Such flows generalize the well-known Einstein flow and they are defined by the expressions, which describe the nonholonomic deformation of a certain Plano-Projective metric in terms of a (non-holonomic) Lagrange derivative. We prove that the nonholonomic Ricci flow, whose "potential" is the squared of the unique M-curvature, is equivalent to the nonholonomic flow envelope (NFE) for the class of vacuum Einstein equations with anholonomic variables. It means that solutions of the considered equations for the M-curvature define the same solutions of the nonholonomic Ricci flow. We prove that the considered vacuum Einstein equations with anholonomic variables define the Riemann geometry, which never Ricci flows, but only nonholonomic Ricci flows. We find the formulas for variation of some geometric objects, defining the induced nonholonomic distribution and nonlinear connection (ND) in the corresponding deformations. Such formulas can be used for redefinition of the solution parameters for generating new families of solutions by such nonholonomic deformations. We show that such formal transformations are not uniquely defined and there are some some solutions, which cannot be transformed into each other by such nonholonomic formal parameter transformations. The Abelian and non-Abelian conservation laws for the nonholonomic Ricci flows are found. Such conservation laws are very useful for integration of nonlinear partial differential equations, corresponding to the considered flow. The solitonic geometry with nonholonomic constraints allows to define some classes of exact solutions of the vacuum Einstein equations with inhomogeneous (such like parametric) deformations, preserving some special symmetries. Such symmetries can be used for constructing exact solutions with some symmetries, using corresponding generating functions. In the Appendix we prove that our nonholonomic deformations of the vacuum Schwarzschild solution define the corresponding parametric families of such solutions, with a Killing symmetry and a parametric deformation parameter being the rescaled parameter from the classical Schwarzschild metric. Such solutions have a big roche type hump on the Lifshitz type hyper-surface and they are compared with corresponding Einstein flows.

Dirichlet sigma models and mean curvature flow are widely studied in geometry and physics, with important applications in surface and interface motion, phase transitions, and material science. In this paper we show how to derive sigma models from the more fundamental theories of quantum gravity. We use the background independent quantization of 2+1 gravity, Vasiliev theory, to derive sigma models for interfaces in (2+1)-dimensional quantum gravity. This provides a geometrical interpretation of the (2+1)-dimensional quantum gravity dynamical variables as an (2+1)-dimensional analogue of the relativistic membrane. We show that the mean curvature flow is the $0$-th order perturbative expansion of the gradient flow for the quantum gravity action, and describe the higher order corrections in the flow. This theory provides a geometrical interpretation of higher order corrections to the mean curvature flow. By analogy with the example of the relativistic membrane, this may give us new insights into the behavior of these flows in general, and the behavior of solutions near singularities in particular. The theory also has implications for the potential experimental tests of this theory: In various regimes of physical interest, the gravitational interaction between probes is weak and may be described by a sigma model with a world-sheet metric independent of the target space geometry. This means that many proposed experiments to test two-dimensional quantum gravity cannot distinguish this theory from sigma models based on otherworldly targets. However, there are regimes where the theory deviates from a sigma model, such as at strong coupling or near a critical point, and in these cases gravity may give a detectable signal. This work was performed within the program of theoretical physics of fundamental interactions of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and was supported in part by the Russian Found for Fundamental Research, Grant No. 16-32-00137. The abstract has been approved by the arXiv.org moderators and may be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.07497

We present the results of our two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of the evolution of Type II supernovae in circumstellar wind bubbles blown by evolved massive stars. We studied three explosion sites with different stellar parameters: a 1000 [...][...] of a 20 M$_{\odot}$ star with a wind parameter of 10; a 120 [...][...] of a 10 M$_{\odot}$ star with a wind parameter of 1; and a 20 [...][...] of a 5 M$_{\odot}$ star with a wind parameter of 0.1. Our reference models include 60- and 90-degree half-angle rotations around the z-axis and mixing of axial and equatorial regions. We characterize the evolution of the density, velocity, radiation fields, and explosion energy of the resulting supernovae. In most cases, the outer shockwave of the explosion runs into the wind and is soon slowed down or overtaken by the faster moving inner bubble wall. The shockwave progressively weakens and becomes radiative, eventually being overtaken by the forward shock. In the extreme case of the 20 [...][...] star with a wind parameter of 0.1, the forward shock never reaches the ejecta and is instead reflected at the interface between the expanding bubble and the inner wind region. Despite this special case, the total amount of nickel produced is comparable in all three models. We discuss the influence of various input parameters on the evolution of the explosion, including the effects of non-spherical explosions and rotation. We compare our results to observations of nearby supernova remnants and examine the possibility of identifying individual SN explosions within them.

The fossil record is one of the most valuable resources for understanding how life on Earth has changed over time. As such, it is frequently examined for evidence of cyclical patterns in biodiversity. Despite over a century of study, the presence of biodiversity cycles has been a highly contentious issue. This is largely due to a lack of replication of previous results and a reliance on weak null models that have since been shown to give false positives. We apply the most robust tests available to the fossil record and identify significant evidence of biodiversity cycles in equatorial stratigraphy, the record of near-shore marine biodiversity over the past 60 million years. These results, and their dependence on temporal aggregation and fossil sampling, are consistent with previous studies and highlight the need for replication and improved data analysis in previous studies of the fossil record. As biodiversity has rarely been characterized by truly static states, our results suggest that the static view of biodiversity observed in many taxa may not be representative of life on Earth as a whole.

The double pulsar system J0737-3039A belongs to a rare population of pulsars that exhibit a stable orbital decay. This phenomena can be described as a result of the loss of energy and angular momentum due to the electromagnetic spin-spin interaction. The precise nature of this interaction, together with the physical characteristics of the two pulsars allows for very accurate determination of the system's age. In this work we present a detailed study of this system and its constrain on the possible companions its components could have. We show that current observations allow for existence of either white dwarf, red dwarf or low-mass giant companion, excluding a neutron star or black hole companion. In addition, we show that the low-mass companion should have a surface gravity lower than that of a white dwarf and be younger than that of a neutron star. We argue that the most probable companion is a low-mass giant, providing a possible explanation for the observed orbital decay.

In quantum mechanics, coherent superpositions of macroscopically distinct states are typically expected to rapidly decohere due to environmental interactions. For example, the interference pattern of a classical solvable model system quickly decays after the initialization. In contrast, it is theoretically proposed and experimentally demonstrated that a large amount of superposition coefficients remain significant after tens of millions of measurements in a Ramsey interferometry with weakly coupled quantum systems andclassical fields. This observation indicates that the system exhibits 'environment-induced superdecoherence'. The system remains highly mixed while still supporting coherent superpositions with significant amplitude. This work provides a foundation for observing and utilizing quantum superpositions in practical systems. Here, we experimentally demonstrate 'environment-induced superdecoherence' with a large amount of superposition coefficients remaining significant after tens of millions of measurements in a Ramsey interferometry with a many-body quantum system and classical fields. The key idea is to decouple the system of interest from the environments using a Hamiltonian evolution, at the cost of increasing the energy of the system. In the present case, this can be achieved by appropriately engineering the classical fields in the Ramsey sequence. We further show that a good measurement scheme can minimize the impact of quantum systems, and the coherence time can be extended to more than tens of millions of measurements. This work provides a foundation for observing and utilizing quantum superpositions in practical systems.

Social annotation, the process of adding descriptive content to digital content by authors who participate in online social communities, is a rapidly expanding paradigm. In the context of computer-assisted resource discovery, social annotations may provide precise geospatial and structural metadata, as well as rich opinions and descriptive fragments. However, the generation and processing of large collections of social annotations for the purpose of resource discovery has thus far received little attention in the literature. In this work, we present CollectiveEye, an end-to-end framework for the automated collection and curation of social annotations for scientific papers. Through a series of benchmarking experiments using our framework, we demonstrate the ability to efficiently and accurately harvest social annotations from Twitter, YouTube, and Wikipedia and use these annotations for the purpose of resource discovery in the scientific paper domain. In particular, we demonstrate the value of social annotations for accurately determining geospatial and structural metadata, including precise publication venue, as well as providing sentiment analysis, opinions on specific figures and other topics, and descriptive fragments. Furthermore, we show that the use of multiple social platforms for annotation improves coverage, and we demonstrate the efficacy of a host of novel data processing and representation techniques for leveraging noise and sparse annotations. Overall, we demonstrate the practicality of social annotation for the purpose of computer-assisted resource discovery in scientific paper domain.

The estimation of the residual life of individual components or machines through the application of artificial intelligence methods continues to be an issue of great relevance to companies in the industrial sector. Neural networks have been applied to this problem with positive results, thanks to their capacity to obtain robust estimates of residual life with few input variables, thus facilitating the decision making process of companies. In this paper, we present a descriptive and empirical study of residual life estimation with artificial intelligence methods, using the example of a cryogenic industrial compressor. mj; Abstr:Residual life estimation with artificial intelligence methods, using the example of a cryogenic industrial compressor. In this paper, we present a descriptive and empirical study of residual life estimation with artificial intelligence methods, using the example of a cryogenic industrial compressor. Neural networks have been applied to this problem with positive results, thanks to their capacity to obtain robust estimates of residual life with few input variables, thus facilitating the decision making process of companies. In this paper, we present a descriptive and empirical study of residual life estimation with artificial intelligence methods, using the example of a cryogenic industrial compressor. We analyse the residual life of a cryogenic industrial compressor based on time series data, using the artificial intelligence method of artificial neural networks. The application of neural networks has given positive results, allowing us to obtain robust estimates of residual life with few input variables, thus facilitating the decision making process of companies.

In this paper we develop a neuronal model with the simplest possible functionality: a neuron that spikes when active, and that connects to other neurons according to a simple Hebbian rule. We show that this model can exhibit a stable dynamics with three distinct regimes, corresponding to quasislow, fast and chaotic spiking, and that displays two types of asynchronous irregular activity. We explore the relationship between these different dynamical regimes and their robustness to changes in model parameters, and discuss how this type of dynamics may be connected to the maturation of the nervous system. We then show that, in the chaotic spiking regime, the connectivity between the neurons can be organised in a stable, self-organising way that resembles a small-world architecture, with a high clustering coefficient and a short average path length. We argue that such self-organisation plays a crucial role in allowing the system to perform novel tasks, and that its disruption might play a role in pathological conditions such as epilepsy.

Quantum dots coupled to electron reservoirs are archetypal devices for studying fundamental aspects of quantum physics. A low-frequency electric potential varying with time, or "pump", can have an effect on the charge distribution in the device. Since electrons in quantum dots interact with a fermionic environment, a charge pump corresponds to a redistribution of electrons between the reservoirs. A celebrated example of a quantum charge pump is the integer quantum Hall effect, where the pump transports one unit of charge every period. Similar quantum pumps have been proposed for quantum dots, but because of strong electron interactions at low temperatures, the actual behaviour can be more complex. Here we show that for a quantum dot in the Kondo regime, subjected to a periodically varying applied voltage, the system exactly reaches a steady state where each reservoir contains a different, time-dependent, population of electrons. The population is transported adiabatically and maintains a memory of the initial time dependence of the voltage. These results have clear parallels with the integer quantum Hall effect and suggest that the steady-state properties of quantum dots coupled to fermionic environments can be more complex than previously appreciated.

ABrand new high energy X-ray transient IGR J11321-5311 was discovered by the INTErnational Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL) on February 11, 2010. Subsequent rapid follow-up observations with other space and ground-based telescopes revealed that IGR J11321-5311 is a highly obscured OB supergiant, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The distance to the source was estimated to be approximately 50 kpc (which is about 20 times closer than the Andromeda galaxy, M31). IGR J11321-5311 is the second example of a supergiant fast X-ray transient (sfxt), an uncommon class of X-ray transients that are accreting binaries hosting a highly obscured massive star. To date, six such systems have been identified. This is the first report of its kind for the LMC. The available data do not allow to firmly establish the nature of the compact object, if a neutron star or a black hole. The large column density and high spin period of the pulsar (inferred via periodicities in the quiescent X-ray flux) point to a neutron star. However, the high inferred mass transfer rate and peculiar properties of the pulsar (such as an unusually slow pulse period and a high absorption column density) could also be explained via the acquisition of material via stellar wind from a highly magnetized companion. Moreover, the source lies in a globular cluster which, given the highly old age of these objects, might also point to a black hole accretor. Finally, based on the large column density and peculiar X-ray variability, a possible explanation for this source could be that IGR J11321-5311 hosts a new subclass of ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs), dubbed “hyper-compact binaries”, with a compact star orbiting a neutron star or a black hole in a very tight orbit (less than a few tens of solar radii) and being significantly more obscured than classical ULXs.' The fast nature of the X-ray transient and the high luminosity (assuming a distance of 50 kpc) make this source a promising candidate to investigate the process of mass transfer from a companion on the highly-accreting regime. Finally, the upcoming sensitive monitoring with the currently operational modules of INTEGRAL (IBIS and JEM-X) as well as with other X-ray instruments (e.g. the proposed LOFT mission) is expected to provide a more detailed characterization of the physical phenomena taking place in this system, and to provide a definitive identification of the compact object.

Superluminous supernovae (SLSNe) are a recently discovered class of supernova (SN) that exhibit significantly brighter luminosities than regular core-collapse SNe. The observed peak absolute magnitudes are up to a few hundredth of that of a normal SN, and the light curves are extremely luminous for several months. Eta Carinae is a famous and popular namesake of the supergiant star at the center of the Carina Nebula. Owing to its proximity and strong radiation field from the ejecta, Eta Carinae was long considered a strong candidate for a SLSN explosion. However, recent studies have revealed that Eta Carinae is not likely a SLSN but rather a normal type IIn SN that was observed in 1890, before evolving to a supergiant star. The unusual observational features of Eta Carinae can be well explained by the interaction between the ejecta and surrounding medium, and the strong radiation field from the central star does not significantly enhance the luminosity of the SN. Thus, Eta Carinae does not represent a hazard for observations of SLSNe at cosmological distances. This work highlights the importance of detailed observations of Eta Carinae, since it can help to clarify the true nature of similar and possibly related transients.

We present spectroscopy of clusters in the merging/interacting galaxy NGC 3256, obtained as part of a survey of star clusters in galaxies undergoing similar dynamical activity. We obtained integrated spectra of 73 clusters with the Gemini South telescope, and measure radial velocities for 65 of these. We compare these velocity measurements with those from the alternate HyperLEDA database, as well as results from our own double-blinded visual classification of the spectra, and find an error rate of ~15%, likely dominated by systematic errors in the redshift measurements from absorption lines in the spectrum of a star cluster. We find a large rotation axisymmetric distribution of cluster velocities, with a mean difference of 107 km/s with respect to a "zero-velocity surface" fit to the spatial distribution, indicative of substantial net rotation for this galaxy. We also compare the integrated colors of the clusters to those expected from population synthesis models, finding evidence of differential extinction. The age-velocity dispersion and color-magnitude diagrams for the clusters also suggest evidence for substantial multiplicity in some clusters. Overall, we find that clusters in this system are in a late stage of development, and likely associated with two colliding spiral arms in NGC 3256.

In this paper we consider light scattering by particles much larger than the wavelength. We develop a discrete dipole approximation (DDA) for this case. The DDA is a simple and accurate method to simulate light scattering. The scattering pattern is obtained as a sum of patterns originated from individual particles. The DDA method is widely used to calculate electromagnetic fields of arbitrary scatterers. However, the applicability of the method is currently limited to particles smaller than the wavelength. We propose a variant of the DDA method that allows to simulate light scattering by particles much larger than the wavelength. The proposed method is based on the lattice sum representation of the electromagnetic Green’s tensor. The discrete dipole approximation (DDA) is used to compute the fields created by particles. The method is illustrated by simulation of light scattering by a composite material with embedded clusters of nanospheres. SPPs on a metal surface separated by a thin layer of a dielectric can exhibit much larger light scattering cross-sections than the corresponding volume scatterers. The large scattering cross-sections make these structures promising candidates for surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) and surface-enhanced infrared absorption (SEIRA) experiments. Due to the simplicity of the fabrication, large electromagnetic fields are achievable with Au-Ag Janus particles, however control of the plasmonic resonance is difficult. The silver core of the Janus particles is difficult to chemically functionalize, and the small gap between the core and the gold shell tends to collapse during the high temperature process of creating the SERS enhancement sites. Here, we propose to use Au@Ag@SiO2 Janus particles with a thin SiO2 shell. The plasmonic resonance of the inner Ag core is visible in the near-IR. The SiO2 shell prevents collapse of the gap during high temperature synthesis and enables chemical passivation of the gold surface. These composite particles have high chemical stability and stable, well-defined plasmonic resonances at visible and near-IR wavelengths, making them good candidates for SERS and SEIRA applications. The extinction cross-section of the proposed composite particles can be two orders of magnitude larger than the volume plasmonic gold-nanoparticle clusters. The proposed composite particles are promising for applications in SERS and SEIRA due to their large scattering cross-sections, chemical stability, and well-defined plasmonic resonance.

A nearly 150 years old law of thermodynamics, the Third Law of thermodynamics, is being empirically verified with increasing precision in nanoscale materials. Here we report nearly six orders of magnitude decrease in the cubic term of the PbS phase specific heat capacity with a 19.9% difference between heavy and light isotopes, in good agreement with the theoretically expected value of 18.5%. This discovery paves the way for new studies of phonon-glasses and supercooled liquids in the deep nanoscale, where traditional techniques of thermometry and quantum fluctuations are absent. Lead sulfide (PbS) is a promising thermometric material for use in nanoscale systems where traditional techniques of thermometry are unavailable due to the scale of the system. At these scales, quantum fluctuations play a significant role in the thermodynamics of the system. This creates the possibility for new studies of phonon-glasses and supercooled liquids in the deep nanoscale. The law of Thermodynamics, third law, states that the heat capacity of a system is positive, negative, or zero, with zero being most probable. The law was initially stated and proved true for larger objects at normal temperatures. The validity of the law has since been verified with increasing precision in nanoscale materials. Recently, nearly six orders of magnitude decrease in the cubic term of the PbS phase specific heat capacity with a 19.9% difference between heavy and light isotopes has been observed. This observation is in good agreement with the theoretically expected value of 18.5%. This study has significant implications in the development of thermometry in nanoscale systems. With a better understanding of thermodynamics at these scales, the effects of quantum fluctuations can be better modeled, leading to a better understanding of phonon-glasses and supercooled liquids. This study was conducted at the University of British Columbia and is published on arXiv.

The 4C 74.26 galaxy at a redshift of 0.045 is amongst the most X-ray luminous active galaxies known. Its isotropic 0.5–200 keV luminosity of 2.2 × 1046 erg/s is nearly one hundred times higher than that of the Milky Way Galaxy, and makes it an ideal candidate to study the accretion of material onto supermassive black holes and their jets. The high-energy emission of 4C 74.26 is usually explained by inverse-Compton scattering of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) photons by the same electron population that produces the relativistic jets. The study of the variability of the optical/UV/X-ray emission can test this model, as it should vary simultaneously with the variability observed in the inverse-Compton emission if the two are produced by the same population of electrons. However, in 2009 the source exhibited an extended and massive radio hotspot with an observed superluminal motion, which could not be reproduced by such a simple model and instead suggested the presence of an additional population of relativistic electrons. Observations of 4C 74.26 between 2009 and 2016 using the Chandra X-ray Observatory yielded no detection of the nucleus or of the hotspot, but did detect a substantial increase in the core X-ray emission as well as a persistent, compact, and variable X-ray emission component coincident with the location of the hotspot. The latter is best explained by synchrotron emission from a population of very high energy electrons, possibly produced by the shockwave of a colliding relativistic jet. If confirmed, this would be the first detection of synchrotron X-rays from a radio hotspot and would have profound implications for both the study of the accretion and jet phenomena in the 4C 74.26 system, as well as for the origin and physics of very high energy particles in extreme particle environments.

The statistics of supersonic isothermal turbulence, a fundamental problem in fluid mechanics, has been a subject of intense research for more than seven decades. In 1936, Wilcox found that the relative velocity of eddies and the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) velocity field appear to be proportional to the sqrt(Re) and Re, respectively, where Re is the Reynolds number. The energy spectrum also exhibits a steeper power law at the viscous range, which was found by Rhines in 1963 and by Braginskii in 1965. Further theoretical and numerical studies have confirmed these findings. More recent experimental and numerical studies have established the existence of a multi-fractal spectrum, in which the smallest-scale energy is not necessarily concentrated in the viscous range. To date, a complete theoretical treatment of this phenomenon has not yet been achieved. This article presents the first detailed experimental study of the statistics of supersonic isothermal turbulence in the viscous range. Numerical simulations corroborate the experimental results. The key new findings are: (1) the existence of a multi-fractal spectrum, in which the smallest-scale energy is not necessarily concentrated in the viscous range; (2) a close agreement between the experimental spectra and the numerical simulations; and (3) a clear discrepancy between the experimental and numerical results for the scaling exponents, which were difficult to measure in the laboratory.

A large number of studies have shown that many properties of real-world networks, such as the Internet, power grids, cell phone networks, and the semantic network of pages on the Web, can be captured by modeling them as networks of networks, in which nodes are networks of nodes and each link represents a strong ties between nodes of distinct networks. Despite this success, relatively less is known about the structure and dynamics of the networks of networks themselves, especially their characteristic size and the importance of network components. Here we shed light on these questions by using a combination of network-level measurements, computational modeling, and theoretical analysis on a large data set of human cognitive networks from multiple experimental studies. We find a robust power-law scaling of many topological properties, such as the number of nodes and links, degree distribution, and clustering coefficient. We also discover a heavy-tailed distribution of component sizes and a small but significant differences in connectivity across components. We develop a theoretical framework that describes the emerging patterns using a simple model of network growth. The results of this model agree very well with the data, suggesting that the growth of cognitive networks follows a power-law with heavy-tailed distribution.

The idea that Newton’s third law of motion does not apply to gravity has many variants. For example, it has been suggested that the fifth force – the force mediated by a scalar field – might give a different interaction law between the particles than the one dictated by Coulomb’s law. To test this scenario, we can consider the behavior of orbiting bodies around the source of the fifth force. In this article, we consider the case in which the fifth force has a spontaneously broken symmetry. The model leads to a force which is long-range, but does not depend on the acceleration of the test bodies. We find that the fifth force does not explain the gravitational anomaly in the orbital motion of bodies around the Sun, provided the range of the fifth force is between 0.2% and 3% of the distance between the Sun and the Earth. This range for the range is allowed by laboratory experiments and cosmological observations. We conclude that, at present, the model with a spontaneously broken dilation symmetry does not give a worse fit to the gravitational physics than the standard general relativity with the cosmological constant.

In this paper, we study quantum dynamics of a one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnetic spin chain with random interaction following a global quench from a disordered initial state to a target quantum critical point. In the framework of quantum adiabatic evolution, we compute the time evolution of the the Loschmidt echo, an indicator of quantum non-equilibrium properties, for different system sizes and show that its long-time behaviour is well captured by an envelope function that decays as a power-law with the system size, $\Lambda^{-\eta}$, where the length scale, $\Lambda$, is either the quantum correlation length or the typical length scale of the system's inhomogeneity and the exponent, $\eta$, is system-dependent. The pre-factor of the power law depends on the system parameters but is independent of system size. These results suggest that a dynamical scaling theory might be applicable to describe the long-time behaviour of the Loschmidt echo. To test this hypothesis, we compute the dynamical scaling exponents and show that they are independent of system size, suggesting that the expected scaling behaviour exists for this particular system and critical point. The presented scaling behaviour could be tested in future quantum simulators based on Rydberg atoms or polar molecules in optical lattices.

We use perturbation theory to classify cosmological singularities, and show that they are generically either locally de Sitter or locally Friedmann-Lemaître (FL), depending on the number and connectivity of their Misner-Sharp fingers. In four space-time dimensions, this results in seven possible topologies of spatial sections, corresponding to a cusp, plain, helix, hyperboloid, cone, and fright ring. We give an example of each type, for both closed and open Friedmann-Lemaître universes. We also show that these generic singularities are unstable to further perturbations, and argue that this implies that we can always find regions in which Einstein’s equation either smoothly converge to a cosmological singularity, or to an asymptotically Friedmann-Lemaître universe. We conclude by discussing the implications of this work for the classification and treatment of cosmological singularities in general relativity and cosmology.

High-redshift quasars are unique probes of the universe, as they are visible when the age of the universe was approximately 0.6-5.4% of its present age. During that time, the universe went from adense fog of dark matter and gas to the current moment of uniform density and temperature. Studying the growth of structure in the young universe can give us insights into how structures form in the universe today. In this paper, we analyze the LMT19 telescope, designed for the long-term observation of distant quasars, in the search for absorption from neutral hydrogen in the high-redshift universe. Using data from 20 epochs between October 2022 and February 2023, we set new upper limits on the absorption cross section at the redshift range 7.5<z<8.1, 5.4<z<6.8, and 8.1<z<8.7 with 5 sigma significance. These measurements correspond to an effective optical depth of 0.07, 0.09, and 0.14 at the respective redshifts. These are the first such limits for these redshifts and will be used by future 21 cm cosmology studies.

In this paper, we present a new solution to the hierarchy problem of particle physics. The solution is based on the existence of large n species of dark matter, each with a particle mass of order 1 GeV. These dark matter particles interact via new forces, with strength parameter λ, which are suppressed by a large compactification volume Ω. As a result, the lightest of the dark matter species, Δ, has a freeze out temperature of order λΩ and a abundance matching current observational bounds. As Δ subsequently annihilates to Standard Model particles, it releases sufficient energy to cancel the vacuum energy density indicated by current observations. The relationship between λ, Ω and the hierarchy problem is explored. It is shown that by having Ω depend exponentially on n, large n species can lead to the correct dark matter relic density without the need for a cancelation at the global level. We conclude by outlining a mechanism for realizing this model with non-abelian dark matter.

The VIMOS VLT Deep Survey (VVDS) is a survey conducted with the VLT Survey Telescope (VST) deepening the census of the stellar mass in galaxies, from the young to the old universe. The total sample includes 980 early type galaxies and 1069 late type galaxies between redshifts 0.2 and 5, drawn from 44 independent fields (VVDS-44) in 32,000 arcmin2 of the sky uniformly distributed over three sky releases (VVDS-007, VVDS-Europe and VVDS-Omega). The VVDS-44 observations have already been presented in the single fields (hereafter SF) papers. These data are used to investigate the assembly history of galaxies by measuring the evolution with time of the scaling relations between the stellar mass, colour and environment, between 0.2<z<2.3. These are compared with local relations and with high-redshift analogues computed from mock galaxy catalogues built from hydrodynamical simulations, to infer the role of merging and of environmental processes in shaping the evolution of galaxies. The VVDS-007, VVDS-Europe and VVDS-Omega surveys cover 32, 24 and 18 % of the sky respectively. The paper describes the survey strategy, the dataset and the measurements made, as well as the analysis methods. The paper concludes with an overview of the main results and of the progress in the early data analysis of the wider VVDS-Infinity survey, which will study the evolution of galaxies as a function of their luminosity and rest-frame colour out to z = 6.

A large area deep field X-ray survey has been performed using the chandra satellite. In this work, we present the number counts from this survey in three bands: full band (0.5-8 keV), soft band (0.5-2 keV) and hard band (2-8 keV). The full band number counts are well fitted by a single power-law with a slope of 1.42 ± 0.02, whereas the soft and hard band counts are well fitted by a double power-law with a break at 2.0 keV. The number of sources per sq. arcmin in various luminosity bins show strong evolution with increasing luminosity. At high luminosities, the number counts follow a Euclidean slope while at low luminosities, the slope is much shallower than Euclidean, which is consistent with the population model predictions. We also study the properties of the X-ray sources. We find 57percent of sources have optical counterparts, most of which are quasars and active galactic nuclei (QSOs). We measure the X-ray spectrum of 77 sources, and find that the spectrum of the X-ray absorbed sources are soft with a photon index < 1.8.

Three Galactic Cepheids were observed with the North American Multi-Conference Array (NAMCYA) using the Optical Fiber Array (OFA) in the near-infrared. Together, the three Cepheids span a period range of 8.2 - 22.2 days, and thusly their individual photospheric radii evolve on different timescales. Two of the Cepheids, Y Oph and AL Peg, show extended NIR emission that is not seen in visible band photospheric models. This emission, which has been observed in optical bands by previous studies, may be caused by a dusty, extended photosphere or a hotter, more extended region. We demonstrate that for Y Oph and AL Peg, a double-component photospheric model is able to simultaneously reproduce the visible and NIR emission. In contrast, for the third Cepheid, Alpha Per, a single-component model is sufficient to describe the NIR emission. We also observed the Cepheids during pulsation using the Center for High Angular Resolution Astronomy (CHARA) Array. We found that the photospheric diameters determined from the FLUOR data are consistent with those determined from the NaStYS data, lending additional support to the results from the OFA data.

In this work, we present Keck spectroscopic and Spitzer photometric observations of the outer disk of the Triangulum Spiral Galaxy M33. The stellar population in this region of the disk exhibits unusual properties, including an elevated stellar velocity dispersion and the presence of an over-density of red giant stars. Using optical integral field spectroscopy, we measure heliocentric radial velocities for 180 stars in this region. After removing likely members of the M33 halo, we measure a significant, ordered stellar rotation of about 30 km s-1 around the major axis. Combined with the apparent thickness of the outer disk, this implies a deprojected stellar rotation amplitude of about 200 km s-1. We compare our observed rotation curve with the expected contributions from a stellar bar and an eight-armed spiral pattern. We argue that the outer disk of M33 most likely formed through an external accretion event, most likely from a small satellite that was already slowly rotating.

Pulse-shape discrimination with the Counting Test Facility (CTF) was presented for the first time at a large electron-positron collider, the LEP Experiments Committee reported. The pulse-shape discriminating variable was the rate of detector signal counts, rather than the energy of clusters of these counts. This was found to be adequate for separating particles according to their electric charge and their strangeness, and for some purposes was even better than using the energy of the clusters. The article reports on the method's development and its application to top and antitop production. The Counting Test Facility, referred to here as CTF, is an acronym for Cluster-tau-detector-for-Pulse-Shape-Discrimination. It is based on counting the number of clusters of detector signals in a fixed time window, and using this information to distinguish between different particle types. The method was first proposed by F. James and R. Meh00; it has been implemented for the first time at the LEP Experiments Committee meeting in 2000, for top and antitop production at centre-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s}=176$ GeV. It was shown that the method works well, in particular for separating particles according to their electric charge and their strangeness, and for some purposes was even better than using the energy of the clusters. The method was also found to be adequate for separating electrons and muons.

Galaxy clusters are among the most massive structures in the universe and essential tools for studying large-scale structure and cosmology. Through measurements of their fundamental properties, clusters can reveal information about the underlying cosmology, particularly the properties of dark energy. X-ray and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) surveys have been used to identify large numbers of galaxy clusters, and the wealth of scaling relations between these quantities have been used to both confirm the validity of these surveys and to simultaneously estimate the properties of clusters. Here we present joint X-ray and SZ scaling relations based on the first results from the Cluster survey (CLAIRE II) and from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT). We find X-ray luminosity–SZ signal amplitude relations of Lx ≈ 7.2 × 1044 × Am (at 10keV) and Lx ≈ 5.1 × 1044 × Am (at 14.5keV), with uncertainties of 20% and 15% respectively. These are the first such scaling relations derived from a combination of X-ray and SZ data, and are important inputs to the next generation of cosmological studies utilizing large cluster samples.

A comprehensive analysis of a neutron star (NS) pulsar wind nebula (PWN) located in the Southern Galactic plane (G328.4+0.2), its compact object (CXO), and the associated supernova (SN) explosion. Using multifrequency observations, we show that the PWN is powered by a young, energetic pulsar that has a slow spindown rate, as indicated by the long periods and large period derivatives. This is possible only if the initial period was above about 20 ms. The X-ray spectrum is very soft, and the extended region is highly polarized. The broadband spectrum is best fit by a broken power law, with a low-energy spectral index of −2.1 and a high-energy spectral index of −0.7. These indices are atypical of young PWNs, which typically have much softer spectra. We propose that the PWN has a jet-like structure with a jet that expands at roughly the speed of light, in agreement with predictions of theoretical models for the dynamical evolution of CC SNRs. The PWN luminosity is only about 5% of the luminosity of its associated CC SNR. This is possibly due to a long interval between the explosion of the progenitor star and the formation of the PWN, combined with an efficient mechanism for extracting spin energy from the pulsar. The pulsar has a very stable light curve, with no detected timing noise or glitches. However, we discovered a gamma-ray signal from the source, and we discuss the implications for the interaction of the pulsar wind with a possible surrounding pulsar magnetosphere nebula.

A Circulating Hydrogen Ultra-High Purification System for the MuCap Experiment at the Canadian Neutron Facility at the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) in Victoria, British Columbia was designed and constructed for the MuCap experiment, which aims to search for theMajorana dark matter interaction. A circulating hydrogen-based mixture of tetrahydrofuran and trifluoromethane is intended to simulate the Muon-dedicated Antarctic Storage Facility (MADAF) material composition, and is projected to reduce the background rate from the decay heat of tritium by more than ten- orders-of-magnitude. The ultra-high purity hydrogen is required to eliminate active and passive mechanical and structural isolations between the cold volumes and the warm instruments. A series of cryogenic systems have been developed and integrated for System integration, testing, and long-term operation are ongoing to deliver a demonstrated minimum detectable rate of 10−47 cm−3s−1/12, which is six orders of magnitude lower than the corresponding background.

Several models have been proposed in the last decades to explain the smallness of the three active neutrino mass-squared differences compared to the grand unification scale, called problem of the floppy masses. One of them is based on the see-saw mechanism which uses particles around the Grand Unification scale (GUT scale) to provide small masses to the standard model (SM) neutrinos. We present an extension of the see-saw mechanism based on the introduction of several additional symmetries. This leads to a realization of the inverse seesaw mechanism. We show that in the framework of this new class of models, contrary to the original see-saw mechanism, one of the heavy Majorana neutrinos can have a very large mass, even above the TeV scale. This implies the existence of a distinguished GeV-TeV collider channel for this neutrino, making this model testable in the near future. We present the realistic realization of this class of models with both normal and inverted neutrino mass hierarchy. The deviation from unitarity of the first column of the PMNS matrix is used to explain the normal hierarchy, while the deviation from zero in the first row of the mixing matrix explains the inverted hierarchy. This model can be tested by the measurement of the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. We present the one-loop contribution of the lightest active neutrino and the heaviest right-handed neutrino to this magnetic moment. We find an upper bound on their masses for a given value of the lightest neutrino mass. This model can be considered as an example of an unbalanced See-Saw mechanism, where the violation of the conservation of one or several of the additional symmetries leads to the presence of massless and/or very massive particles. This model has some other interesting phenomenological implications, in particular the existence of keV sterile neutrinos. We show that this model leads to the observed enhancement of the Higgs decay to a pair of muons, presented at the Moriond EW session as an excess. Massive and massless neutrinos were hypothesized in the 60s in order to explain the solar and atmospheric neutrino oscillations. The experimental confirmation of these oscillations has completely changed the face of particle physics and cosmology. The standard mechanism to explain these oscillations is the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix through theDirac theory of the neutrino, the Glashow-Weinberg-Salam (GWS) theory of the photon and the Fermi theory of the electron. These three particles are now called the Standard Model (SM) neutrinos and they have a zero mass. Oscillation experiments prove that at least two of these neutrinos have a non-zero mass. However, the cosmological observations of the Baryon Asymmetry of the Universe (BAU) indicate that at least two of these neutrinos should be exactly light. Using the multiple-population magnetohydrodynamic modeling, we investigate the effects of the kinetic electron collisions on the low-frequency (ion-cyclotron) beam instabilities within the multi-fluid description. It is shown that the anomalous (cross) current density and the potential drop, which are generated by the beam-heated plasma waves, may affect the mirror and theBenford instabilities. Moreover, the instability thresholds of the both beam-heated modes increase with the decreasing of the temperature anisotropy. The analysis of the linearized non-linearities has been also carried out. The results of the presented study can be used for a more accurate modeling of the low-frequency instabilities within the tokamaks and heliotrons plasmas morphology June 30, 2023 Using the multiple-population magnetohydrodynamic modeling, we investigate the effects of the kinetic electron collisions on the low-frequency (ion-cyclotron) beam instabilities within the multi-fluid description.

We formalize the equivalence between Nash equilibria and subgame perfect equilibria in game theory. This equivalence is strong enough to imply various properties of Nash equilibria, like their existence or uniqueness. Unfortunately, in general these properties are not true for subgame perfect equilibria, and we give explicit examples of games which disprove these properties for subgame perfect equilibria. This disproves a conjecture by H. Brézis that subgame perfect equilibria, and hence also Nash equilibria, must be acyclic. We give a constructive version of the above equivalence, and use it to show that in any game, a subgame perfect equilibrium always contains all the information about the game, in the sense that any path in the subgame perfect equilibrium graph yields a Nash equilibrium. We also give a combinatorial proof that in two-player zero-sum games, any subgame perfect equilibrium is also a Nash equilibrium, thus providing a simpler and more direct proof of this well-known result than previous constructions using fixed point theorems.

The critical Casimir effect (CCE) is an indication of a phase transition in quantum vacuum, associated with a change of an essential parameter of the vacuum. The change of the parameter, for example, temperature or chemical potential, leads to a modification of the vacuum structure and to a dynamical Casimir force acting on some bodies of arbitrary shape and separated by the force. I investigate the CCE in a system consisting of a superfluid film and a sphere in its critical point fluid near a wall. In the case of a rough wall with many peaks and valleys the critical point film demonstrates a new type of long-range ordering, which I call “superwetting”. I show that close to the wall the film order parameter decays as a power law with a distinct critical exponent, which characterizes the new phase. In the case of an ideal flat wall, the film demonstrates short-range order. I calculate the corresponding critical scaling function and show that it remains short-range ordered. However, close to the wall the film is perturbed by the weak lateral confinement. This perturbation leads to the breaking of the translational symmetry in the direction parallel to the wall and, as a consequence, to the decay of the order parameter as a power law with a different exponent. I calculate this new critical exponent and show that it characterizes the long-range order in this case as well. The investigated system provides an example of both critical phenomena (superwetting and critical exponents) and spontaneous symmetry breaking. My findings could be verified in the experiment with critical films and spheres, or at least their theoretical explanation could be useful in the development of the predictive capabilities for the behavior of such systems.

In this paper, we study the pseudospectrum of elliptic quadratic differential operators of second order on a compact manifold. We give sufficient conditions for the pseudospectrum to be empty, a disk, a circle or the whole complex plane. Moreover, we establish a relation between the pseudospectrum and the pole order of the determinant of the laplacian on the bundle of $(0,2)$ tensor fields. In particular, we prove that the pseudospectrum is empty if and only if this bundle is flat, which is a generalization of a result by K. Uhlenbeck for the case of compact manifolds with boundary. The pseudospectrum is an interesting object to study as it gives more information on the essential spectrum of the laplacian than this spectrum itself. It also allows to detect non-smoothness of the laplacian, in this case the existence of non-flat $(0,2)$ tensor fields.

The line intensities of several key molecules have been measured in molecular clouds located in different Galactic environments. These include translatory thermal lines of CO, an excellent tracer of molecular hydrogen, as well as the HCN, CS and CO isotopes' rotational thermal lines. Conversion factors are derived between the line intensities and the properties of the molecular clouds, such as their mass, temperature and density. The derived factors are specific to the different types of galaxies and are given for Sa, Sb, Sc, Sd and Irr galaxies. It is shown that the line intensities of CO, HCN and isotopes can be used as quantitative measures of the masses of molecular clouds. The large-scale structure of the universe is often described in terms of the distributions of galaxies, dark matter, and large-scale gravitational potentials. These surveys have constrained the matter distribution to follow a ruled distribution on large scales, as indicated by the pattern of galaxy clustering. However, this does not describe the distribution of galaxies within these catalogs, which often has lower clustering amplitude and follows a simple Hubble flow pattern. In this work, I present a theory for how these differences arise from the distribution of galaxy orientation relative to the observer. The theory follows the dynamics of individual galaxies, starting with initial conditions set by the Cosmic Microwave Background. Large scale structure grows under gravity and substructure forms in galaxies, which host central black holes that heat and reprocess host galaxy gas and stars. Black holes that form from high redshift stars have satellites from high redshift that form along filamentary structure. As these satellites fall into the center of larger galaxies they have higher probability of falling along the galaxy's weaker axis, such that they form an anisotropic distribution with more galaxies along one axis than another. The theory presented here, based on large-scale structure growth, is able to reproduce observed large-scale patterns of galaxy clustering and radial alignment. I also show that this model can explain the observed near-symmetry of galaxy velocity dispersion with the observed cosmological anisotropy.' --- Large-scale structure in the universe evolves over time. This evolution is driven by the distribution of energy and momentum in the initial conditions, which define the distribution of mass, and subsequently the gravitational potentials, that define the large-scale structure. These large-scale structures later form galaxies, which host central black holes that heat and reprocess host galaxy gas and stars. Black holes affect the structure of their environment by galaxy formation and by their active nucleus, which can feedback energy and momentum into the surrounding medium. This series of interactions forms the physical foundation of the presented theory for how the observed large-scale structure of galaxy clustering and radial alignment arises from the initial conditions of the Cosmic Microwave Background.

An exactly solvable model of statistical mechanics, the chiral Potts model, is generalized to an SU(N) invariant model on a ring. The Hamiltonian and the generator of SU(N) spin rotation are derived by a fusion procedure. The model exhibits an infinite set of conserved charges, which lead to a set of algebra commutants, the latter of which is shown to correspond to an integrable quantum chain with cyclic representations of $U_q(sl_2)$. The model is related to the XXZ quantum chain with twisted boundary conditions in a magnetic field. The chiral Potts model is a generalization of the Ising model which incorporates lattice chirality. The model was introduced in 1988 [1], and since then has attracted considerable attention in the theoretical physics literature. The model has been solved exactly on an arbitrary graph [2,3] as well as on a ring [4]. The latter case generalizes to an SU(N) invariant model, which we will focus on in this letter. The charges in the model are generated by $\{\tau^l\}$, the generators of the Lie algebra su(2), and the conserved charges are bilinear in the charges. We present late-time X-ray observations of the nearby Type Ibc core-collapse supernova 2018crp with the Chandra X-ray Observatory and review its observational and modeling signatures. We measure an X-ray luminosity of (4.6 ± 1.0) × 1033 erg s−1 at a Galactocentric distance of 4.4 ± 0.3 kpc, assuming the distance to the Large Magellanic Cloud is 50 kpc. We compare this luminosity with modeling predictions from three distinct progenitor models for the Type Ibc SN 2018crp: a naked helium star (a Helium star with no external hydrogen or dust layer), a stripped-envelope star (a star with a hydrogen or helium envelope, but not enough to classify it as a blue supergiant), and a compact Wolf-Rayet star. All progenitor models predict X-ray luminosities that are highly inconsistent with the observed value. We determine that the X-ray emission from the forward shock radius must be suppressed via a break in the electron energy distribution; the suppression could be due to either a significantly steeper electron energy distribution (which requires a much faster ejecta expansion velocity or larger explosion energy), or a low-density environment surrounding the shock-suppressed region. We thus present evidence against the compact Wolf-Rayet star progenitor model for Type Ibc SN 2018crp and, in general, favor more extended, lower-velocity explosion models for these transients. Type Ibc supernovae, or hypernovae, are a rare class of explosive stellar events that are generated by core-collapse of massive stars. Their classification is based on their observed spectra, with Type Ibc supernovae showing hydrogen or helium features in their spectrum, but lacking sufficient features of a broad absorption line supernova. The recent discoveries of long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), also known as hypernovae, have opened up new possibilities to probe their origin. Observational constraints on the location of long GRBs suggest they are associated with the deaths of very massive stars, though the details of their progenitors are not fully understood. Two long GRBs ( GRB 170729A and GRB 160821B) were observed in the local group of galaxies, and in one of these (GRB 160821B) late-time X-ray observations were also obtained. Constraints on the progenitor star and explosion geometry can be obtained from the observed properties of these transients. For a few weeks to months following the GRB explosion, the X-ray, ultraviolet, and optical emission are powered by the forward shockwave from the escaping ejecta interacting with the circumstellar medium (CSM). This emission can be used to measure the radial distance of the shockwave from the explosion center as a function of time, the so-called light curve, and to obtain the total energy of the explosion. In this paper, we present a spectral method for solving the Einstein field equations on a fixed background grid. We do so by expressing the system in first-order form and using a pseudospectral method to advance the fields in time. We provide proof of well-posedness for the evolution and present a series of tests to ensure that our numerical methods behave as expected. In particular, we demonstrate second-order convergence in space and time for a variety of smooth solutions of the vacuum Einstein equations, without needing to use a basis with positive spectral radius. To demonstrate the robustness and performance of our code, we present a suite of simulations of binary black holes. Introduction We present a spectral method for solving the Einstein field equations on a fixed background grid. We do so by expressing the system in first-order form and using a pseudospectral method to advance the fields in time. First-order form of the Einstein equations The vacuum Einstein equations can be formulated as a first-order symmetric hyperbolic system of partial differential equations (PDEs). In this form, the equations are highly constrained and allow for an elegant, coordinate-free description of the evolution. In particular, one can prove the existence of solutions to the constraint equations that are smooth everywhere (including at the black holes) under fairly general circumstances (e.g. the absence of hair for charged black holes). This enables us to use a high-resolution numerical grid to accurately resolve the singularities at the black holes. We express the equations in first-order form by introducing a connection 1-form on the space-time, and employing the Weitzenböck connection to express the curvature in terms of the non-dynamical connection 1-form rather than the dynamical (metric) connection. The resulting system then takes the form of a first-order pseudodifferential equation (elliptic in the Lorentzian case). In practice, we discretize the equations on a uniform spatial grid (using either a finite differences or finite element method) and employ a one-sided spectral method to advance the fields in time. Pseudospectral methods for first-order PDEs Since the fields are expressed in terms of spectral functions, we employ pseudospectral methods, which are based on discretizing the equations using trigonometric polynomials. These polynomials are then adapted using spectral techniques to ensure that the discrete approximation satisfies the appropriate boundary conditions (at infinity and on the spatial grid). We provide proof of well-posedness for the evolution and present a series of tests to ensure that our numerical methods behave as expected. In particular, we demonstrate second-order convergence in space and time for a variety of smooth solutions of the vacuum Einstein equations, without needing to use a basis with positive spectral radius. The study of the rho meson within the framework of the K-Matrix theory was performed for the first time in the framework of the Regge theory of fundamental particles. The role of the rho meson is important for a clear interpretation of pion electroproduction experiments at JLab (Mainz, Buhler, CExchange, and A2). In particular, it was shown that the inclusion of the rho meson in the analysis leads to a considerable improvement of the description of these experiments. The work was performed within the Regge theory, which is a fundamental theory of strong interactions. The Regge theory states that the total cross section of hadrons increases with the energy level in an approximate power-law dependence:. The approximation is good for hadrons with large masses, such as the pions. The Regge theory is based on the assumption that the exchanges between particles in the different reactions have a common pattern, which can be described by the exchange of fundamental particles called reggeons. The reggeons correspond to intermediate states in the quantum field theory between two hadrons. The first description of hadron interactions at high energies within the framework of quantum field theory was developed by G.V. Efimov in the framework of the simple Regge theory. A number of later theoretical and experimental studies of the high-energy interaction confirmed the main assumptions of the simple theory, in particular, the universal character of the exchanges of reggeons. Pions appear in the description of interactions at high energies due to the unique possibility of electromagnetic interaction of pseudoparticles. Population III stars were the very first stars to form in the universe. Due to their high inward flux of Lyman-Werner radiation, the H<--->H2 reaction became rapidly inhibited, and subsequent H2 formation was suppressed. As a result, the lack of hydrogen caused these stars to become predominantly core-dominant, leading to the stellar dynamical collapse of the cores of these very first stars. Magnetorotational collapse, as the name suggests, involves a combination of magnetic and rotational forces that aid the gravitational force in collapsing a population III star. This process has never before been observed in such old, very first stars, and its implications for the early life of the universe are discussed. The very first stars to form in the universe, Population III, had no hydrogen due to the H<--->H2 reaction becoming inhibited by the suppression of subsequent H2 formation. These first stars were extremely massive, with typical masses of a few hundred solar masses. Population III stars, like our Sun, were initially dominated by their cores. With further contraction, radialGreg Anglin instability caused the formation of an iron core. This led to a dynamical collapse of the core, which is ultimately triggered when iron nuclei reach absolute zero pressure. At this point, electronuclear reactions supported by neutronization become so rapid that the infall velocity of the rest of the star becomes super-elastic. This results in a blast wave of nuclearfire, which completely encompasses the core. The stellar dynamics of these events have never before been observed in such very first stars, and their implications for the early life of the universe are discussed.
