Grazing-incidence X-ray telescopes (GIXTs) are designed to collect X-ray signals from space that are emitted nearly perpendicularly to the optical aperture, thereby minimizing the optical throughput and avoiding optical distortions. GIXTs are therefore necessarily equipped with grazing-incidence mirrors that are extremely compact to fit within the volume and mass constraints of the satellite. As a consequence, these mirrors are made of thin layers of extremely high-Z materials (usually gold or silver), making them very sensitive to electron contamination, i.e. to the presence of low-energy electrons that might be present in the satellite volume and that might be released by the modules that are attached to the telescope. We present a model to evaluate the electron contamination of the satellite volume based on measurements of the X-ray signal that is collected by the telescope, and we apply this model to evaluate the degradation in the electron contamination induced by the presence of a low-voltage power unit (LVPU) that is attached to the satellite. We show that this degradation can reach several tens of percent and that it is correlated with the intensity of the X-ray signal that is incident on the satellite.

Recently, technological innovation has been spurred by invention leverage resulting from invention clubs or communities of technology holders. This phenomenon has been well studied with regard to trends in single technologies, for example wireless local area networks (WLAN) and Worldwide interoperability for microwave access (WiMAX). A complementary trend to this innovation is invention relocatability or joint applicability, that is, the capability of an invention to be applied to various technologies. We investigate trends in joint applicability by mapping patents to technology classes using a mixture of descriptive and class-based hierarchical Bayesian techniques. We find that joint applicability increased over time with spikes in the late 1990s and early 2000s, possibly reflecting rapid development of the semiconductor industry and the diffusion of mobile communication, respectively. We also find that joint applicability exhibits clear geographical patterns: joint applicability was higher in regions where corresponding technologies are highly developed, including the Kanto district in Japan and California in the United States. These geographical differences may reflect differences in regulations, competition, and consumer preferences.

Pulsars are typically characterized as fast spinning neutron stars with small rotational period ($P=1/f$, s) and large period derivative ($\dot{P}=dP/dt$, s s -1). The rotating neutron stars have an associated neutron star magnetosphere, which is divided into two regions by the light cylinder, the region where the speed of light rotates around the neutron star. The light cylinder radius is denoted as $R_{lc}=P\dot{P}^{-1}$. Pulsars typically generate huge amounts of rotational energy via emission of electromagnetic radiation. The power is extracted via a pair-created-region, the pulsar magnetosphere, which extracts spin-energy and funneling it down to the polar caps. The energy extraction relies on rotational energy being converted to particle energy, which eventually annihilate in a conversion gap above the star surface, giving rise to two highly energetic beams of electrons and positrons which move towards the star's surface with almost the speed of light. The beams of electrons and positrons, which are considered to be a plasma, produce electron-positron pairs through curvature radiation. The model presented in this work describes a pulsar whose energy extraction mechanism relies on an annular gap accelerator, or rotator. This model can explain the observed radio-to-high-energy emission from pulsars, even without the need of any additional processes, such as pair production. It is shown that the required Lorentz factors of the particles to explain the data are naturally achieved in the model. Furthermore, it is shown that the model can reproduce neutron star surface temperatures that are consistent with observations.

The peak of the Black-body spectrum in the gamma-ray burst (GRB) emission, assigned to the thermal Comptonization of scatters in the fireball, is usually fitted with a single-broken-power-law function with two peaks. In this work, we find that the thermal component can be decomposed into two separate black-body functions through a robust non-linear fitting, and the two black-body temperatures (kT) are significantly different with high statistical significance (7.3σ). The goodness of the decomposition is confirmed by the low value of the residual sum of square, the high values of the reduced χ2, and the absence of systematic errors in the residuals. Furthermore, when the kT of the soft thermal component is fixed to the value obtained in our work, the two-piece function still provides a significantly better fit than a single-broken-power-law function to the spectra of more than 60% of the observed bursts. We argue that the two-temperature black-body components are naturally produced by the hotspots of two independent jets with different Lorentz factors.

The integrated spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of star-forming galaxies at intermediate redshifts (z~2) are reconstructed from multi-wavelength Spitzer mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy for the first time with data from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS). Infrared luminosities are dominated by star-formation, rather than an active galactic nucleus (AGN), as revealed by the consistent shapes of the dust-reprocessed energy distribution with the stellar initial-mass function (IMF). The stellar Initial Mass Function (IMF) is flatter than theSalpeter IMF that is typically assumed for local galaxies, but more consistent with that observed for galaxies at higher redshifts. We investigate the origins of this evolution by comparing the inferred IR luminosity density of star-forming galaxies with the predictions of galaxy evolution models. The physical parameters of the models indicate that the evolution in the characteristic scale height of the galaxy potential wells is most closely linked to the decrease in the amplitude of the stellar Initial Mass Function (IMF). An increase in the redshift dependentMadau-Lilly relation amplitude explains the rest of the increase in IR luminosity density, but only if 60% of the total IR luminosity of high-redshift galaxies is from AGN activity. These results emphasize that more than one mode of star formation is responsible for the growth of the stellar mass density of the Universe over the last 9 billion years, and provide new insight into the competing effects that influence the evolution of the characteristic scale height of the galaxy potential wells.

Tidal fields reconstructed from the distribution of dark matter contain a wealth of information about the growth and merger history of galaxies, as well as their current dynamical state. We present strong and weak-lensing mass reconstructions of the Corullo-IATA1638+29 cluster, and show that the two correlated structures comprise a triple merger with the central galaxy’s associated tidal field revealing the orbital plane of the cluster and its projected separation. We additionally show that the orientations of the projected spins of the galaxies cluster around this same plane, and quantify the alignment using two-dimensional Kuiper test significance, testing for spatial correlation with the orientation of the cluster’s tidal field. We additionally test the hypothesis that the galaxies’ spins are uniformly distributed, finding a probability of < 10-4 that the orientation of the spins are random. We conclude that the galaxies in this structure have aligned their spins with the orbital plane of their merger.

The symbiotic star H1-36 was observed across the radio through ultraviolet wavelengths for this study. The spectra are presented as a composite of line and continuum spectra with Hbeta excluded. The spectra were modeled using methods that take into account orbital changes in the absorption lines of the white dwarf and red giant components of the system. The white dwarf is estimated to be 10,000-30,000 K, and the giant is estimated to have a radius of 500-1000 R⊕. This is the first time that the white dwarf effective temperature has been estimated from ultraviolet data. The ultraviolet spectrum is dominated by cyclotron absorption in the white dwarf, which allows the field strength to be constrained. The strength of the field suggests that the white dwarf has a fossil dipole field, as in many cataclysmic variables, but the dipole is significantly tilted with respect to the rotation axis. The strength and orientation of the magnetic field could impact the stability of the accretion flow onto the white dwarf.

IGEC-2 (International Gravitational Event Collaboration 2) is a global network of several major laser interferometric gravitational-wave observatories. During 2005, the IGEC-2 network was continuously operational and the search for gravitational wave bursts was conducted. No gravitational wave signal was detected in association with these events. We present the observational results from the IGEC-2 network and place upper limits on the rate of gravitational wave bursts in 2005. Our most sensitive search covered short (10-30 s) bursts with frequencies in the range 10-1000 Hz, and used 10-second data samples from all threeIGEC-2 observatories. We also present a less sensitive all-sky search covering longer (10-1000 s) bursts and lower frequencies (10-300 Hz). 2017, 13, 2, pp. 28 ersonnel: Arvin B. Hayes, Jose Luis Jaramillo, Joseph D. We give a method to compute the Seiberg-Witten basic invariants for any Ozsvath-Szabo 4-manifold invariant. We use our results to give product formulae for the invariants, that is, formulas relating the Seiberg-Witten invariants of fiber bundles whose fibers are copies of a fixed 4-manifold to the Seiberg-Witten invariants of the base and the fiber union the reversed fiber bundle. As an application, we rederive the formulae of Szabó and Witten for the Seiberg-Witten invariants of K3 and Taured manifolds. We use our results to give product formulae for the invariants, that is, formulas relating the Seiberg-Witten invariants of fiber bundles whose fibers are copies of a fixed 4-manifold to the Seiberg-Witten invariants of the base and the fiber union the reversed fiber bundle. Let M be a closed, oriented 4-manifold withSW homology sphere type, and let (B, p, F) be a fiber bundle with B is a 5-manifold, p is a point in B and F is a closed, oriented 4-manifold, such that the inclusion-induced map of the fundamental groups extends to an embedding of B into a connected sum of multiple copies of S4. We assume further that for each i we have - The SW basic invariant of the pair (M, B\ p) is nonzero. - The SW basic invariant of the pair (M, F) is defined.

In this paper we study the problem of finding rational points on elliptic surfaces. Elliptic surfaces are surfaces of the form y2 = x(x^2 +Ax +B), where A and B are constants, and they can be viewed as minimal models for certain elliptic curves. Finding rational points on elliptic surfaces of this form would give integer solutions to the elliptic curve given by the following Weierstrass equation: y2 = x^3 + Ax2 + B x + C. This curve has been of interest in the study of QEC, and a proof of its integer points was announced in 2013 by H. Davenport, C. Lewis, and Y. Tang, but this result has not appeared in print to date. Modern physics abandons the concepts of absolute, including that of space and time. However, in the field of statistical mechanics, the most important theory of classical physics, it makes sense to define an advanced potential (A-P) to consider only the variations that occur in the system. Therefore, a system with A-P is anomalous. This article presents the most important concepts of statistical mechanics, the definition of A-Ps, applications, and some physical experiments that can be used to verify this theory. ytics Modern physics abandons the concepts of absolute, including that of space and time. The strong chemical bonds in molecules and the high opacity of particules in medium to low temperatures limit the study of Ultracool Dwarfs (UCDs) and Exoplanets. The most massive UCDs have a temperature lower than 20000 K and an effective temperature below 300 K; they are in a gaseous state. The Opacity Project (OP) computes theoretical line and mean opacities for plasmas of different temperatures and compositions, which can be used as input for radiative-transfer simulations and then to fit the observed spectra of these UCDs and Exoplanets. In this work, the authors compute line and mean opacities for plasmas with temperatures lower than 20000 K and effective temperatures lower than 300 K. The inclusion of impurities and traces of metals (like H2O, CO2, NH3, CH4, etc.) extend the computed range of opacities for such kind of plasmas. For example, for plasmas at 10000 K with 90% Hydrogen and 10% Carbon, the authors computed line and mean opacities within 10% of the OP simulation results for pressures between 10-7 and 10-9 torr. Thus, these computed line and mean opacities can be used to simulate the thermal emission and reemission spectra of UCDs and Exoplanets with good accuracy.

In this paper, we compute the linearized graviton propagator in a class of massive gravity theories that arise by a Ghost Free Massive Gravity (GFMG) mechanism. These theories are built from a linear, second-rank tensor metric fluctuation about an AdS background, coupled to a general, derivative-coupling scalar field that acts as the graviton mass. We do this by separating the linearized fluctuations into three distinct fields, which we then decompose into plane-wave modes. The resulting propagator is not positive-definite, but we show that it is well-defined by considering a particular parametrization of the theory's parameter space. Finally, we consider applications of this propagator to gravitational wave astronomy, using upcoming pulsar timing arrays as a foreground monitor, and we argue that the graviton described by our propagator is a viable effective field theory (EFT) for parameter estimation in the proposed framework.

Daemons (or DAMA, forDark Matter Astronomical Mountaineer) were my car's (a Mercedes-Benz 600GD) celestial mechanics measuring engine, with the following salient features: - It worked by counting the number of steps motorized wheels made as it drove around the earth in a circular route. - It was highly accurate, with a mean error of about 1% of a full circle (360 degrees). - It was robust, in that it worked well on all four wheels, and over several decades (until the car was scrapped in 2014). - It was minimally invasive, in that it required no change to the car, the wheel bearings, or the car's suspension, and no physical connection to the car other than the four wheels. - It was compatible with existing electrical systems, using the same engine start circuit as the car's diesel engine. It follows that the car was a low-mass, highly accurate, robust, minimally invasive detector ofdark matter particles, and I was its engineer.

The Bonn Lensing, Optical, and X-ray selected Galaxy Clusters (BLOX) is a sample of massive, X-ray emitting galaxy clusters constructed using data from X-ray, optical, and lensed Einstein ring surveys. BLOX clusters are detected in three steps. First, a HEC cluster finder identified groups and clusters in the Deep XMM-LSS (XMM-Newton Merged Serendipitous Survey) field. Next, a red-sequence cluster finder identified high-redshift galaxy clusters in the HEC clusters' redshift slices. Finally, a strong lensing cluster finder identified the most significant clusters from the red-sequence analysis. The final BLOX cluster catalog consists of 823 clusters, out of which 752 are at z>0.1 and 91 are at z>0.18, covering a sky area of 1.34 steradians and containing 18,314 cluster members. After applying various tests for sample contamination and cluster finding biases, BLOX stands as one of the largest and most reliable cluster samples constructed to date. The BLOX clusters' weak lensing mass and X-ray properties are presented in cosmological lensing papers associated with this release.

Neutron stars (NSs) are highly magnetized, strongly-magnetized compact objects. The interior of a NS is composed of degenerate neutron matter, together with a small amount of leptons and free nucleons, which may be in a neutron gas or nuclear droplet state. The composition of the inner crust of a NS is determined by the equilibrium between the pressure of the neutron-rich material and the strong gravitational pull. The outer core of a NS is composed of electron-rich matter, in which nucleons are largely spaced apart by a sea of electrons. Because of quantum effects, electrons act as both a liquid and a gas, exhibiting Fermi motion and Bose-Einstein statistics, respectively. It is believed that strong magnetic fields exist in the interior and exterior of a NS, and the respective magnetizations are likely to be equal (parallel) in the interior and opposite (antiparallel) in the exterior. In the present work, we report on the behavior of axisymmetric magnetic fields in magnetized neutron-star matter within the framework of quantum magnetohydrodynamics (MHD). We have found the existence of a new type of drift—the Hall drift—which depends on the relative magnitudes of the magnetic field, the matter velocity, and the magnetic field strength. The Hall drift transports poloidal magnetic flux into the regions of stronger magnetic field, with the associated flux conservation providing a mechanism for Ohmic dissipation. Our results suggest that Hall drift could play an important role in the evolution of magnetic fields in both compact-star interiors and relativistic jets emanating from such objects, with implications for low-energy flares, the emission of gravitational waves, particle acceleration, and pulsar timing.

Exoplanets are common around main sequence stars like our Sun. But less than 1% of these planets reside in the surrounding system of their host star, also known as the stellar neighborhood. Such an extreme isolation of planets around main sequence stars is difficult to explain via current planet formation theories. Much more hospitable zone around evolved stars offer a solution. Here we report the detection of 49 planets around 14 evolved stars. Nine of these planet host stars are confirmed to be members of the double-star system. Planets around these systems tend to be more massive, have shorter orbital periods and are more likely to reside in their host stars’ habitable zones than planets around main sequence stars. Our results suggest that planets around evolved stars could have higher potential to support life than those around main sequence stars. The research was presented in a preprint on arXiv.org, which is a repository for scientific papers before they are published in a journal article.

Using a simple model for advection-dominated accretion, we show that the conventional implementation of the $\alpha$ prescription for viscosity may not be causal. We propose a new prescription for viscosity that has the same instability properties as the conventional $\alpha$ prescription, but is causal. We show that for this viscosity prescription, shock waves are stable and accretion is stable. If magnetic fields are not strong enough to prevent diffusive transport of momentum, the standard approach of solving the problem with a conductive or stochastic viscosity may lead to unphysical cooling of matter near the event horizon of a black hole. We note that the recently proposed hyper-viscous method (see Proga et al. 2014), although very effective at preventing unphysical cooling, may have stability issues that have not yet been resolved (see Malagoli et al. 2014). We suggest that the newly proposed causal viscosity may prove to be a suitable replacement for hyper-viscosity. We also provide a simpler test-case calculation to illustrate the effects of the new viscosity prescription.

In this paper, we analyze the real estate market in the Las Vegas Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA). Sales of individual properties account for 92% of all transactions in the area, and we examine this 1-month aggregate using time series methods. We find that the time series of the sales aggregate follows a non-stationary seasonal pattern, which we characterize with a harmonic sum model. We then use this model to make predictions of the CSW indexes, which are published monthly by the Greater Las Vegas Association of Realtors (GLVAR). We compare the actual CSW indexes with the predictions made using the seasonal pattern from the previous month, as well as with seasonal patterns from random data and with random data adjusted to match the seasonal pattern of the actual data. We also examine predictions made using other methods, such as the Holt-Winter method and ARIMA. We find that the CSW indexes can be well predicted using a seasonal pattern from the previous month with no further adjustments.

In this work we present a general study of the energetic and dynamical behavior of a reduced version of the fully non-linear Kolmogorov-Lorenz equations, often referred to as the Lorenz-Kolmogorov equations. These equations, which describe the spatio-temporal evolution of a dynamical variable representing the areal density of particles in a fluid, are used to model a vast spectrum of physical, biological and chemical systems. As in classical Lorenz models, the dynamical variables in the Kolmogorov-Lorenz system consist of three state variables which denote the magnitude of velocity, density and temperature fluctuation, respectively. Contrary to the classical system, however, these state variables are not normalized to a difference of unity, but are related via an energy function which depends on the total energy of the dynamical system. We explore the parameter space of the model and identify regions where the system undergoes transitions between different dynamical states as well as exhibits chaos. We then perform a similar energetic analysis to the one recently proposed by Rudiger et. al. [Rudiger et al., Phys. Rev. Lett., 2015] for the classical Lorenz equations, and show that, despite the apparent difference in the dynamical behaviour of the two systems, the underlying structure of the two analyses is quite similar. We also explore the possibility of using linear and non-linear methods, typically employed in statistical mechanics to predict the long-term dynamics of the system. We show that both methods yield precise predictions in a large fraction of the dynamical regions explored, indicating that these systems may be used to generate long term predictions.

Recently, a lot of research has been devoted to the idea that the standard model (SM) particles might be understood as constituents of higher-dimensional objects, called branes. These higher-dimensional objects appear as zero-modes of chiral fermions on the 4D universe brane. In a supersymmetric version of these models, all Standard Model particles and their interactions can be understood in terms of three special extra spatial dimensions compactified down to a small enough radius that allows gravity to confine below the weak scale without conflicting with present experimental bounds. In this scenario, the weakness of the weak force is explained by the large size of the extra dimensions. The richness of the Higgs sector of the supersymmetric standard model (SSM) can be understood as arising from the multiplicity of contributions from the different branes. The standard model Higgs boson appears as the zero mode of the second spin 1/2 Dirichlet brane, while the first and third spin 1/2 branes give mass to the up and down type quarks. The muon and the electron masses can be generated by the mixing of the first and third spin 1/2 branes with different chiralities. If the radius of the compact dimensions is very large, the SSM Higgs potential can have a global minimum at any value between 0 and 2.43 m_e (the electron mass). This allows for a complete theory of fine-tuning, including both the the cosmological constant and the weak scale parameters.

The magnetic Cataclysmic Variable HS 0922+1333 was observed by the OGLE project in the photometric R band. The obtained data were analyzed. The obtained observations can be best described with the sinusoidal function with the period of 6.965 hours. Such a long period is extremely rare among magnetic Cataclysmic Variables. Possible causes of this phenomenon are discussed. The magnetic Cataclysmic Variable HS 0922+1333 was observed by the OGLE project in the photometric R band. The obtained data were analyzed. The obtained observations can be best described with the sinusoidal function with the period of 6.965 hours. Such a long period is extremely rare among magnetic Cataclysmic Variables. Possible causes of this phenomenon are discussed. The magnetic Cataclysmic Variable HS 0922+1333 is an asynchronous magnetic rotator. Such objects usually have shorter periods of variability. Possible reasons of the long orbital period in HS 0922+1333 are discussed. It is suggested that apsidal rhythmical motion due to the presence of a distant companion may be the most probable explanation. The orbital period of HS 0922+1333 was not observed before and was not expected from the theories. The obtained result significantly expands the knowledge about this unusual Cataclysmic Variable.

Pi-pulses, with a frequency of approximately 3 GHz, are commonly used in solid state quantum information processing to coherently manipulate the spin of single electrons. In practice, the application of such pulses is often accompanied by an undesired, strongly inhomogeneous local magnetic field, which causes undesirable admixtures of multiple spin states. Here we show that such spin echoes can be induced by directly manipulating the nuclear spin configuration, and that these echo signals can be spectrally and spatially resolved using dynamical decoupling techniques. We present analytical and numerical calculations of the heteronuclear decoupling sequences needed to suppress the local magnetic field and observe the generation of long-lived spin echoes in both Ramsey and spin-echo experiments. Our results show that spin echoes are not only a limiting factor in creating robust quantum registers, but are also a manifestation of the strong exchange interaction between the electron and nuclear spins. The authors are Christof Weis, Michael Kowalewski, Andreas Friederich, Michael Chung, Martin Mühlberger, Markus Brink, and Tilman Pfau. "The Intrinsic Origin of Spin Echoes in Dipolar Solids Generated by Strong Pi Pulses." arXiv:1908.04812v1 [QE, PP, Optics]. Published August 5, 2019.

Asteroseismology has proven to be a powerful tool for determining the properties of stars. The observed frequency spectrum of a star is a characteristic of its interior: the stellar mass, the arrangement and composition of its interior pieces, and the possible presence of rotation. The rotational splitting of starcoseismic modes can be used to detect the presence of surface rotation and thus map the differential rotation of the star. Here, we report seismology of the roAp star alpha Centauri A using observations spanning 4.5 years. We detect two triplet starcoseismic modes. From this we are able to measure the differential rotation of alpha Cen A and conclude that it has a complex structure, with a pole-to-equator gradient in the equator-on component of differential rotation of nearly 3%. This is the first detection of differential rotation in a binary system and demonstrates that stars are not zombies following rigid, global rotation.

Debris disks are remnants of protoplanetary disks, which are the precursors of planets. Many debris disks exhibit surprising uniformity in dust properties and luminosities, suggesting that planet formation may occur rapidly, over a span of <1000 years. Nonetheless, there is compelling evidence for the ongoing generation of planetesimals in many debris disks, including dynamical evidence for embedded planet-mass bodies, and collisional evidence for rapidly produced large planetesimals. The collisional evolution of planetesimals is responsible for the accretion of debris disks, which can cause observable features such as infrared excesses and gaps. The onset of this collisional evolution is delayed by the generation of embryo bodies. I summarize observational constraints on embedded planet-mass bodies in multiple debris disk systems, present new dynamical limits on their existence, and suggest that the dynamical evidence for planet-mass bodies is compelling. I also summarize constraints on the collisional evolution of planetesimals via large body collisions, presenting constraints on the time-span of planetesimal growth, and discuss the implications of these constraints for the generation of short-lived planets. I conclude that the concurrent generation of planetesimals and embryos in debris disks is a robust conclusion, and that an explanation for their concurrent existence is likely required.

We propose to distinguish a gravastar from a black hole by observing the event horizon of the former but not the latter. Unlike a black hole, a gravastar has an additional surface, called the coat hanger hole, through which matter can fall but out of which it cannot escape. Thus, a test particle in a gravitational field of a gravastar will accumulate ergs trying to climb up the coat hanger hole, but will fall behind the event horizon. In contrast, a test particle in a gravitational field of a black hole will not experience such accumulative erg energy transfer, but will be pulled into the event horizon. The proposed distinguishing observational signatures may help to address the current debate on the nature of dark matter. In contrast, a test particle in a gravitational field of a black hole will not experience such accumulative erg energy transfer, but will be pulled into the event horizon. The proposed distinguishing observational signatures may help to address the current debate on the nature of dark matter.

Heavy quarkonia, e.g. J/ψ, etc. due to the suppression of the strong interaction between heavy quarks, are suitable platforms for the detailed investigations of the properties of nucleons and the non-perturbative nature of the strong interaction. With the newly developed approach based on the QCD multipole expansion, in which the interactions between heavy quarks and between heavy quarks and gluons are considered via multipole expansions, the ratios of various heavy quarkonia decays can be calculated in terms of the well-known quarkonium heavy quarkonium coupling constants and the spectra of hybrids. With the calculation of the spectroscopy of hybrids, the magnetic moments and polarizabilities of hybrids can also be obtained. It is found that the calculated spectra of hybrids are in good agreement with the lattice results. Finally, by taking into account the heavy quarkonium--hybrid interactions, the decay widths of various heavy quarkonia transitions are also calculated, and the ratios agree with the experimental data well. Therefore, both the spectroscopy and strong interactions of hybrids are well determined by the new approach.

This paper presents results of the 2PN approximation of the relaxed Einstein equations, which yield post-Newtonian (PN) metrics and equations of motion for a test particle in a Schwarzschild spacetime. The full system of equations includes both the Euler and Lagrangian perturbations, and is solved for the first time to second post-Newtonian (2PN) order in an appropriate (gauge-invariant) phase space. The 2PN solutions are then used to derive a new version of the Pound-Rebka experiment, in which the detector is treated as a scalar, vectors, and tensors of post-Newtonian order. The force acting on the detector is shown to equal the rate of change of the metric of post-Newtonian order, in agreement with the strong equivalence principle to 2PN order. In addition, the precession of the polarization plane of an electromagnetic wave is computed to 1.5PN order, and it is shown that the equations of motion are compatible with the theorem derived by Will on the retro-propagation of gravity waves. This paper is an update and extension of the original version published in 2014 [20], with two new results: (i) the computation of the energy shift of the Pound-Rebka experiment to 2PN order (previously done to 1.5PN order in [20]), and (ii) the derivation of the equations of motion to 2PN order (previously done to 1PN order). Both of these latter results are in agreement with the strong equivalence principle to 2PN order. In addition, several typos and other small mistakes have been corrected.

Noise is one of the most common phenomena in real world systems. It is always present, in forms like thermal noise, or shot noise. In control system perspective, measurement noise is another type of noise, which is arising from imprecision in measurements. This type of noise is also common. This research, focuses on the effect of measurement noise, on the stability of discrete time Markov processes. Particularly, it is shown that if measurement noise is strong enough, then even if the underlying Markov process is stable, its stability is compromised. Another interesting finding is that the effect of measurement noise diminishes with the increase of order of the system. Markov Processes are widely used to model uncertainty in dynamic systems. One of the assumptions in this modeling is that the underlying system is deterministic, and that a stochastic element is only due to uncertainty in the model itself. However, there are many examples in the real world where this modeling assumption does not hold. An example of this are physical systems with uncertainty due to measurement error. In this research, a discrete time Markov process is modeled as: dX(t)=f(X(t),t)dt+g(X(t),t)dW(t),X(0)=x, where X(t) is the state of the system, W(t) is a Wiener process, which models Brownian motion, and f and g are functions. By using the weak formulation of this equation, and applying the Ito isometry, this can be written as: dX(t)=f(X(t),t)dt+g(X(t),t)dW(t)+hg(X(t),t)dt, where h is a positive constant. In the special case that h=1/2, this reduces to the standard form of the Markov process. In this model, it is assumed that f and g are known functions of the state X(t), the time t, and some parameters, which are not part of the state. However, in real world applications, it is almost always the case that X(t), t and the parameters are only known up to some uncertainty. For example, in system identification, the functions f and g might represent the model, and the parameter are the unknown states. In these cases, it is not possible to observe f and g with arbitrary precision. The uncertainty in the model due to this imprecision is reflected in the system identification literature as Uncertainty set, which is a hyper-ellipsoid in the parameters space. In this case, the true value of the parameter is contained in the interior of the uncertainty set, and the true value is surrounded by a boundary that is an approximation to the inherent imprecision in the observation of f and g. The non-Gaussian characteristics of the cosmic density field induce scale-dependent effects that can be measured through the gravitational lensing of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). These effects imprint themselves in the two-point statistics of the temperature and polarization maps. We quantify how the detectability of these effects is impacted by the intrinsic levels of non-Gaussianity measured by Planck in the Synchronous scenario as well as by the presence of additional cosmological parameters, in particular the presence of early dark energy. We find that, for a wide range of observable scales, the detection of these effects would improve the sensitivity to the amplitude of the amplitude of the primordial non-Gaussianity of a factor 2 for a detection significance of 4σ. Additionally, we find that the effects of non-Gaussianity are best seen on relatively large angular scales, namely those probed by S-Z data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), and that those data are particularly well suited to constrain the presence of early dark energy.

Internal state evolution during mechanical loading of model isotropic granular packings is analyzed. In a companion paper (1) we described the development of local stresses and contact forces in a granular packing under quasistatic, smooth, linear, and progressive loading protocols. In the current paper we analyze the changes in internal structure and packing connectivity that accompany the development of the macroscopic stress state. We quantify the formation and growth of microcracks that appear in regions of tensile stress and discuss the manner in which these microcracks coalesce to produce macroscopicFailure. The observed responses of the packing are compared to those predicted by a model for the evolution of local states of mechanical stress and damage within granular media. 1. R. Pan, N. Wang, Internal states of model isotropic granular packings. I. Development of local stresses, contact forces and granular pressure, J. Rheol. 58, 1135-1170 (2014).

The photoproduction of the ground state of the charmonium J/ψ in hadron collisions has been observed for the first time by the BRAHMS, PHENIX and STAR collaborations at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). In this paper we report the first measurement of the exclusive J/ψ photoproduction in proton-proton and proton-antiproton scattering at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The J/ψ photoproduction was identified through the detection of its dimuon decay mode in the zero degree dimuon trigger region. The monitored multiplicity and the luminosity-weighted cross section as a function of the J/ψ transverse momentum are presented. The nuclear modifications of the J/ψ photoproduction cross section are presented as a function of the J/ψ transverse momentum, the rapidity, the transverse momentum imbalance and the photon-proton center of mass energy. The results are compared to models.

A recent proposal for a physical implementation of the quantum NOT gate [1] has the potential to enable scalable quantum computing using superconducting qubits, opening the door to the construction of a large-scale quantum computer. Here, we show that the reliability of this physical realization of the quantum NOT gate is ultimately limited by dissipation arising from the preservation of the von Neumann entropy of the quantum system during its dynamics. In particular, we find that the infidelity of the quantum NOT gate in this realization, due to entropy accumulation, is constrained to be less than 0.067 over timescales required for quantum computation, significantly outperforming other proposed physical approaches to quantum computing. This analysis sets a new bar for quantum computing precision that can be exceeded only by approaches based on error suppression by active control. [1] M. S. Allman, et al., Implementing the Quantum NOT Gate with superconductive Qubits, arXiv:1809.07413 (2018). *ACTIVE CONTROL* is used to suppress the accumulation of entropy in our physical realization of the quantum NOT gate, allowing for an error rate less than 0.067 over timescales required for quantum computation.

We report the discovery of extreme asymmetry in the debris disk surrounding the star HD 15115. The rotation vector of the outer belt is oriented at a PA of 167° compared to 180° for the inner belt. The axis of the extreme asymmetry is tilted with respect to the axis of the planet orbit such that the midplane of the disk is aligned with the planet orbit at a PA of 25°, or 90° - 167° = 83°. This is the first detection of planet-induced warping of a debris disk and the first detection of planet-induced tilting of a circumbinary disk. The observed tilt of the midplane of the disk is 1.7°. We discuss a few plausible scenarios to explain the observations including Kozai migration of a small body toward the star, enhanced eccentric instability of large particles in the outer belt, and satellite sculpting. The paper is titled "Discovery of planet-induced warping and tilting of a debris disk" and is authored by B. C. Kelley, J. B. Reylé, C. D. Russell, S. Casassus, and J. Schneider. It was published in ApJ 870, L14 on December 4, 871, and can be accessed on arXiv.org with this DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aaf803

The Richard Thompson groups, first discovered independently by A. W. W. Rouse and H. Zeller, are a family of discrete groups acting on simplicial trees. In 1982, J. H. Brown, C. K. growing and J. W. Gross III discovered that these groups satisfy the special case of a generalized word problem, making them a counter example to the Quick conjecture. In 2010, M. Brin found that these groups act on squares of complexes, making them an example of a quasiconvex subgroup of the mapping class group. In this paper, we observe that monoid generalizations of the Richard Thompson groups act on labeled mobiles, generalizing Brin's result. We also show that these groups satisfy a generalization of the generalized word problem which implies they are quasiconvex. In particular, we show that the mapping class group of a finite graph of finite presentation acts on a labeled mobile where the labeling is given by a Thurston realization.

Solar heavy element abundance: Constraints from frequency separation ratios of low-degree p modes. Solar heavy element abundance is one of the longstanding questions in solar physics. Thanks to the high precision of helioseismology, it is now possible to put strong constraints on the heavy element abundance in the solar core. In this work, by using recent White Dwarf sound speed profile with detailed chemical composition, we show that the heavy element abundance should be less than 0.08 Solar abundances, at 3-$\sigma$ confidence level. Heavy element abundance less than 0.08 Solar abundances at 3-$\sigma$ confidence level Researchers have long suspected that the heavy element abundance in the solar core is much higher than the current measurement. Many proposed solutions invoked extreme physical processes, such as magnetic activity enhanced atomic diffusion, deep internal meridional circulation, or helium settling. Recent works indicated that these proposed solutions might not be necessary. Using the helioseismic diagnosis on the solar sound speed, which is the first direct measurement of the solar composition, we can tightly limit the heavy element abundance. The current measurement of the heavy element abundance in the core is about 0.08 Solar, at 3-$\sigma$ confidence level.
