SBF is a photoionization code that calculates the propagation of stellar photons in multi-wavelength data and models, and produces spectra and images. It can generate synthetic spectra and images from observations of either the stellar or quasar continuum or any specified features. It has been used to model H II regions and stars. It can also calculate the ionizing properties of populations and stellar clusters. SBF can generate spectra and images at any desired resolution. It can also output images at a series of specific wavelengths, ranging from common ultraviolet and optical wavelengths to the longest wavelengths emitted by the gas and the most energetic ionizing photons. SBF also includes modules to simulate the emission from gaseous nebulae and hot plasma. It uses a flexible computational method that can be adapted to any kind of problem. SBF was written to be easily extensible so that it can be used to analyze a wide range of astrophysical problems. SBF can use data from a variety of telescopes and telescopes/instruments combinations. It can process optical and infrared observations from telescopes on Earth, in space, and on other planets. It can also use ultraviolet and X-ray observations from telescopes on Earth and in space. It can use any desired observations and their corresponding models. SBF has been successfully used to study hot plasmas and gaseous nebulae, star clusters, and the integrated light of galaxies. SBF has been used to study a planetary atmosphere, with complete consistency between the calculated and observational spectra. SBF has also been used to analyze one solar spectrum and to calculate the corresponding radiation force and resulting velocity distribution of the solar wind. The ionizing properties of single stellar populations and the star formation histories of galaxies have also been studied with SBF.

In this paper we prove the hyperbolic rank rigidity for a large family of flows on surfaces, thus showing that an initially arbitrary 2-frame flow is fully determined by its first two time-integrated flow patterns. To achieve this, we provide a detailed analysis of the dynamical behavior of the hyperbolicity detection maps, proving several key rigidity properties for this dynamical system. As a corollary, we show that the hyperbolic rank rigidity also holds for (partially) uniform 2-frame flows. As another important application, we provide the first periodic solution in this family to a long-standing open problem, which was proposed in 1982 by Plante. The results in this paper greatly extend our previous work on the 2-frame flow on surfaces, where we focused only on the case where curvature is nonpositive. By taking the initial 2-frame as a canonicalarsh--the closed positive 2-form associated with any other orthonormal frame--, this paper also greatly strengthens the implication "frame flow on surfaces determines initial frame flow up to scale" to the case of nonpositive curvature.

Recent simulations of galaxies have included nearly all particles in their representation of the dark matter and stars. Such simulations afford significant advantages over previous methods in allowing systematic exploration of the impact of modeling subgrid physics on the evolution of galaxies, particularly at low-redshift. Here we explore the impact of particle number on a subset of simulations included in a previous paper (Dolag et al. 2009). To do so, we rerun all simulations with at least 4x as many dark matter particles, with a minimum of 8 times as many stellar particles. For each rerun we report relevant numerical and physical parameters. We find that energy loss due to artificial viscosity in the inter-particle contact algorithm (IMvAT) causes a systematic drift in many of the relevant properties. Including this drift in a comparison with data would lead to an underestimate of the level of required accuracy for simulations. The impact of IMvAT is larger for more elliptical galaxies, which tend to have stronger concentration parameters and thus more rapid energy losses. Including an effective viscosity algorithm similar to the one of Agarwal et al. (2013) limits the drift to less than 20% in most properties. We also find that, independent of drift, the statistical accuracy of measurement for each property decreases with decreasing particle number. This decrease in accuracy is stronger for higher-concentration galaxies, and is likely the dominant source of uncertainty for most applications. These limitations suggest that galaxy simulations that are touted as providing “precision physics” (e.g., Duffy et al. 2008) require at least 16 times as many particles to achieve the same precision for a given property as otherwise implied by the 20% drift. In addition, some properties may not be measured at all with simulations of this resolution due to limited statistical accuracy. Our results have implications for a broad range of numerical and physical effects. Simulators of galaxy collisions must either resolve much smaller impact parameters, or use a much more efficient scheme for simulating such events (e.g., Barnes & Hut 1992). Stochastic effects in the physics of satellite galaxies may no longer be treated using simple techniques (e.g., Gnedin et al. 2007), and must be modeled using stochastic simulations. Similarly, properties such as the formation of central black holes (e.g., Di Matteo et al. 2007) may no longer be treated as if they followed an individual merger tree, as this would require essentially subgrid modeling at the limited resolution of current simulations. Our results demonstrate the value of additional numerical resolution beyond the minimal requirements to simulate galaxy subgrid physics. However, as our results suggest, current simulations fall short of providing the precision of physical insight that has driven the field’s recent interest in subgrid modeling.

Massive galaxies at 2<z<2.5 are observed to have distinct MZR with elevated stellar mass and bulge mass surface densities (Sérsic index n > 4.5). We present the results of a uniform multiwavelength analysis of 14 such galaxies and find that this elevated mass structure is accompanied by elevated star formation rates (SFR>100M⊙yr-1), low concentrations (Congo et al. 2013), and high sSFR (Gargiulo et al. 2015). With high significance, elevated dynamical mass estimates and lensing signals imply massive black holes (MBH) in excess of 10^{9} M⊙, with the majority (11/14) having MBH ~10^{8.7}-10^{9.3} M⊙. Five of these massive galaxies have Spitzer/SWIRE MIPS 24μm detections, all are detected in the hard X-ray band with (0.5-2)keV luminosities ~10^{43}-10^{44} erg s−1, and eleven are Compton-thick in the hard X-ray. These observations strongly imply that the majority of these massive, rapidly growing galaxies have central massive black holes with masses at or above the regime of "monster" black holes. We combine our dynamical estimates with archival VLT and ALMA data to study the cold gas and far-infrared fine structure line energetics. Most (9/11) of these systems have signifcantly elevated CO SLEDs and high estimated He 2-10 radiated powers, with estimated starburst masses MSB ~10^{10.6}-10^{11.2} M⊙. There are three broad approaches to growing such massive bulges and central black holes in the peak epoch of star formation. In the "top-down" or mergersill scenario, the majority of these massive galaxies are the product of mergers over several hundred million years. The second is "in-place" or "normal" growth whereby these systems are growing through concurrent, normal, secular processes like gas accretion and star formation. The third is that these galaxies are growing entirely through gas accretion. Using rough constraints on the cold gas fueling rate and Eddington limit at the heart of the "maintenance mode" accretion growth, we show that these monster growth events likely require significant growth fueled by gas accretion. We combine this with Bayesian growth tracks for matching black hole and bulge masses, and find that over half (7/14) of these galaxies have double-mass milestones at z~2.3-2.6, concurrent with both the epoch of peak star formation and 24μm Spitzer/SWIRE detection. By z=0, 9/14 have stellar masses ~M∗>10^{12.6}M⊙, bulge masses Mbulge>10^{11.2}M⊙,

In this paper we combine ideas from parametric approximation, Monte Carlo methods and optimism to develop an algorithm that efficiently finds high-quality solutions to combinatorial optimization problems. We present an algorithm that starts with any algorithm for solving a problem and provides a flexible way to customize the solution by tuning a few parameters. The algorithm generates many trials by running the base algorithm for a number of parameter values and picks the best ones. The approach is illustrated on a numerical optimization problem. We also develop a theory for analyzing the performance of this algorithm and proving its convergence. We demonstrate that the algorithm consistently finds high-quality solutions to a wide range of combinatorial problems. Learning and optimization have several key components. We need to have a good model of the problem and an efficient method to search over the model parameters. This allows us to find high-quality solutions to a problem. These components have been separately studied in different communities for different types of problems. We present an algorithm that can effectively combine these components to find high-quality solutions to a broader range of problems. The algorithm can start with any algorithm and provide a way to custom design the algorithm. We use this framework to develop a theory for analyzing the performance of this algorithm. We demonstrate that the algorithm consistently finds high-quality solutions for a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems. There are multiple ways to design algorithms for learning and optimization. Our framework focuses on combining model-based and black-box optimization techniques. We use the first technique to find good initial points for the second technique. We present a theory for analyzing this algorithm and provide performance guarantees. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a number of experiments. We develop the algorithm and the theory for solving a discrete problem. The approach can be adapted to work on problems defined on continuous spaces. The algorithms in this framework can be used for many machine learning problems. This includes the following areas: - Supervised learning - Unsupervised learning -reinforcement learning -dimensionality reduction -colaborative filtering -semi-supervised learning -reinforcement learning -perturbation-based method The approach can also be used for many different optimization problems. This includes the following areas: - combinatorial optimization - continuous optimization - semidefinite optimization - quantum optimization - operations research The algorithm has three key steps. We first develop methods to efficiently search over the parameter values. We then present a framework that uses a model to find high-quality solutions. We then combine the two components to find high-quality solutions. This approach can be applied to a broad range of problems. However, the approach will not work well if the base algorithm is not efficient or if the parameter space is not well structured. The algorithm will also not work well if the objective function is not well behaved or if the answer has to be close to a solution with high probability. We demonstrate the approach for a

The Young-Fibonacci insertion algorithm is an insertion algorithm that can be used to sort in linear time a sequence of n elements so that the i-th element is inserted after the (i-1)th and (i-2)th element. The Young-Fibonacci insertion algorithm is named after its discoverers Richard P. Young and Marc D.het Veld. The algorithm was described for the first time in 2001 and its time complexity was calculated in 2004. A detailed proof of its time complexity and a short discussion of its space complexity were published in 2006. The Young-Fibonacci insertion algorithm belongs to the class of level-index insertion algorithms. The time and space complexity of level-index insertion algorithms depends on the maximum number of levels in the insertion tree. It is therefore straightforward to simulate the Young-Fibonacci insertion algorithm on a parallel computer with multiple processing units so that the total runtime is reduced.

We present deep optical integral field unit (IFU) and multi-wavelength observations of the Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) in the cool core cluster 2A0335+096. The BCG, the brightest cluster galaxy in the 1H 0323+022 HRI cluster, was observed with Gemini-N/GMOS in IFU mode. We detect dust in the central 1.5 kpc of the BCG. The equivalent width of the aromatic feature indicates an old stellar population with less than 5% of the light arising from recent star formation. Integral field spectroscopy and grism data show that there is a large reservoir of warm molecular gas with large scale shocks distributed between 1 and 4 kpc from the nucleus. The derived molecular gas mass is 2.2 × 10 8 M ⊙, about 35% of the expected molecular gas mass from the X-ray cooling rate. The total energy of the molecular gas must be approximately 5% of the total energy of the galaxy based on its impact on the dynamics. We also detect an unusually large sample of low mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) in the core of 2A0335+096. We measure the LMXB population and find a total of 4.2 × 10 40 ionizing radiating LMXBs, 1.5 × 10 39 strong-ZLMXBs, and 2.2 × 10 38 weak-ZLMXBs. This results in a LMXB brightness within 2 kpc of 4.2 × 10 39 erg s -1, and is several times higher than other systems of similar mass. The higher than average LMXB population may indicate a higher than average encounter rate in the group environment, or a higher fraction of strong magnetic field sources in this group. We also detect a large radio halo, which may indicate an ongoing merger between the cluster and a diffuse radio source to the south.

Using data from the fourth data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-DR4), we study the X-ray properties of a complete sample of the most-luminous quasars at ~z>4, drawn from the luminous quasar (LQ) catalog ofWarner et al. (2006). Compared to the local luminous quasars, these highest-redshift objects have extremely high space density, and therefore are excellent tools with which to investigate the growth of supermassive black holes and their host bulges and galaxies. We find that the highest-redshift quasars have similar X-ray properties to those at low redshift, but with broad EWs and X-ray luminosities that are a factor of ~10 higher. This emission is most plausibly interpreted as thermal coronal gas in the host galaxies with broad emission lines. When compared to a radio-loud control sample matched in X-ray luminosity, the quasars have significantly enhanced radio emission, although not as much as predicted by models in which the powerful radiation emitted by the quasar promotes gas into a hot, kpc-scale torus. The small difference in radio emission may indicate that, at high redshift, quasars have less obscured nuclei than locally. We suggest that this may be due to the brighter cosmic background at high redshift, which can penetrate more easily through a putative torus. In addition to its intrinsic interest, this paper offers a cautionary example of how the analysis of a single flux-limited sample can lead to erroneous conclusions when applied to high-redshift populations.

In this paper, we show that superconducting correlations can be induced in a ferromagnetic layer of a superconductor-ferromagnet (S/F) structure due to the proximity effect. When a magnetic field is applied to such a S/F structure, nonhomogeneous magnetization occurs inside the ferromagnetic layer. This gives rise to a Doppler shift of the ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) signal and a superconducting current in the superconductor. We find that the triplet component of the induced superconducting correlations exhibits a local maximum near the FMR resonance frequency and the magnetic field at which the nonhomogeneous magnetization occurs. These results indicate that it should be possible to detect FMR in S/F structures by using the techniques of superconducting spintronics. The full paper "Nonhomogeneous magnetization and superconductivity in superconductor-ferromagnet structures" can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.07446

A thermal instability leading to the formation of an oscillatory secular mode is described in the context of stellar pulsations. This instability is demonstrated in the presence of a temperature gradient, with the cold side of the interface unstable. The resulting oscillation is analogous to the well-known Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, but with a cyclic rather than monotonic dependence on the wave number. Using modern opacity computations, the possible loci of the instability are explored and the condition for its appearance is determined. Results of numerical calculations confirm the validity of the proposed theory and demonstrate the appearance of oscillatory secular modes. The authors suggest that oscillatory secular modes, similar to the ones described herein, may also appear in other astrophysical systems (e.g. in accretion disks, gaseous halos of galaxies, etc.) and therefore could be ubiquitous. The oscillatory secular mode is of particular interest since it can explain certain features of old and warm stars, such as their ellipsoidal shape and the existence of equatorial features (e.g. bright spots, bright rings).

In this work, we present the first comprehensive study of a compact object merger simulated with both a full numerical relativity (NR) evolution and an approximate treatment using calibrated analytic methods. We analyze an equal-mass, nonspinning binary of black holes (BHs), examining two different NR treatments of the spacetime evolution and two different Cauchy treatments of the binary dynamics. The two NR treatments are one that employs high-accuracy waveforms for the spacetime dynamics (Hann) and one that employs an analytic kludge to approximate the dynamics ( kludge). We find that the NR simulations result in more angular momentum and higher total radiated energy than the kludge simulation. We additionally analyze two different ways of approximating the NR dynamics with an analytic evolution, comparing two different amplitudes of NR waveforms in the corresponding analytic fits (NRWA and NRWT). The two analytic fits produce very similar results and are in significantly better agreement with NR than the kludge approximation. We conclude that data-analysis methods for modeling the spacetime dynamics of coalescing binaries can produce results that are substantially more accurate than current kludge approximations, provided that data suitable for modeling the full spacetime dynamics is available.

One widely used assumption in demography and evolutionary biology is that populations are discrete, that is, they are composed of a large number of small, non-interacting groups called demes. In this framework, the joint probability distribution of the ages of individuals is typically assumed to be known (e.g. the Gompertz law for mortality or the logistic law for fertility) and to reflect the Only Fit (OF) principle, according to which only the fittest (that is, individuals with the largest predicted reproductive value) are able to reproduce. While this approach has provided many important insights, it has been recently argued that demographic stochasticity—the variability in reproductive value arising from, for example, variability in ability to find a mate or resistance to infection—may lead to underestimation of demographic parameters such as survival and fertility and bias in parameter estimation. To date, this has largely been explored using linear approaches, but we here demonstrate that demographic stochasticity can also lead to nonlinear selection. We provide numerical evidence and a simple analytical approximation to show that the evolutionary stable age of a population will be close to the Gompertz law only if demographic stochasticity is weak and populations are large or if variation in reproductive value is small. We also demonstrate that demographic stochasticity can lead to apparent Fisherian runaway evolution, in which selection for early age at maturity leads to decreased longevity and increased rates of juvenile mortality. These results demonstrate that demographic stochasticity can, in principle, lead to selection against demographic stochasticity.

This paper presents a novel method for investigating the collisional evolution of spatially extended debris discs. The method is based on the comparison of the observed size distributions of the planetesimals with the simulated size distributions resulting from various sets of parameters which specify the strength and frequency of the perturbing interactions. The method is illustrated with the example of the debris disc around 48 Herculis. The preliminary results of the application of the method to spatially extended debris discs show that, contrary to the common belief, the evolution of these discs is likely dominated by collisional grinding rather than by fragmentation of larger planetesimals. The method is based on the comparison of the observed size distributions of the planetesimals with the simulated size distributions resulting from various sets of parameters which specify the strength and frequency of the perturbing interactions. The method is illustrated with the example of the debris disc around 48 Herculis. The preliminary results of the application of the method to spatially extended debris discs show that, contrary to the common belief, the evolution of these discs is likely dominated by collisional grinding rather than by fragmentation of larger planetesimals. The observed size distributions of the planetesimals in spatially extended debris discs are usually approximated well by a log-normal distribution. The average of the log-normal function corresponds to the logarithmic mean radius of the disc. The comparison of the observed and simulated size distributions allows one to determine the best-fitting value of this logarithmic mean radius, which can be interpreted as the average spatial density of the disc. The disc average spatial density constrains the product of the maximum planetesimal size and the strength of the planetesimal interaction kernel, which is the product of the maximum planetesimal radius and the strength of the planetesimal interaction kernel. The preliminary results of the method application to spatially extended debris discs show that the spatially extended discs with average spatial densities between 10(-5) and 10(-4) kg/m 3 are best reproduced by models in which the maximum planetesimal size is between 10 and 100 m, and the strength of the planetesimal interaction kernel is moderate (less than or equal to 1). Higher average spatial densities are usually reproduced by discs in which the maximum planetesimal size is larger, which means that the strength of the planetesimal interaction kernel is higher, or by discs with more complex composition, i.e. with the presence of large planetesimals that interact very frequently with the smaller ones.

A new 60-cm radio survey telescope with the sideband-separating SIS receiver for the 200 GHz band is described. The sideband-separating SIS (SS-SIS) receiver can simultaneously observe the total power and the sideband separated by a double-sideband modulation scheme. The SS-SIS receiver has been developed for the SIMBENEDA 60-cm radio telescope. The instrument has been tested at the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan and the 200 GHz band has been opened for the astronomical community. The angular resolution is about 3.5 arcmin at 200 GHz, which is sufficient to observe the Galactic radio sources. The sideband-separating SIS receiver is an efficient instrument for the SIMBENEDA 60-cm radio telescope in the 200 GHz band. Seven decades have passed since Einstein's gravitational field equation was introduced. From this seminal work, general relativity (GR) has been shown to be a very elegant and successful theory of gravity, accounting for a wide range of observations and successfully describing the universe on large scales. Despite its enormous success, however, several significant challenges remain. In particular, we still do not know what caused the accelerated expansion of the universe, which marks the end of the 'era of curvature', and we do not understand what are the dark matter and dark energy, which constitute nearly 95% of the matter and energy in the universe and thus nearly 98% of the total energy in the universe. In this talk, I will present several recent gravitational wave (GW) measurements from LIGO and Virgo, and highlight how these results have already begun to test general relativity in new and exciting ways. I will then describe the Laser Interferometer Space antenna (LISA), a mission concept to test general relativity using gravitational waves in space, and provide an update on the on-going design study. Finally, I will describe how major technological breakthroughs in the fields of gravitational wave astrophysics and aeronomy could enable breakthroughs in our understanding of the origins of the universe and the role of gravity in the evolution of the cosmos.

In this paper we consider induced subgraphs of the random graph with edge probability $\lambda$, where the expected number of edges between any pair of vertices is $\mu$, and $\mu \ll \lambda$. We call such graphs locally sparse. We show that the independence transversals of some simple graphs constitute wide sets with positive density in such graphs with $\mu = \omega(\log n / \log \log n)$, where $n$ is the number of vertices. That is, we prove that they are still significantly denser than expected in such graphs. This implies that the local edge distribution is essentially irrelevant for the transversal density. We also show that in the random graph with $\mu = n^{-1/2 + \varepsilon}$ for some fixed $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\lambda = \lambda(n) = n^{-1 + o(1)}$ the independence transversals are still wide with positive density. We thus confirm a suspicion of Holmgren that this behaviour is generic.

Wireless communication systems employing multicarrier signals, such as orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) and multi-carrier modulation (MC) techniques, have been widely used in current wireless networks because of their efficient bandwidth utilization and ease of implementation. The widely separated antennas used in these systems, however, tend to render the channel as sparse multipath, i.e., the channel is flat in the frequency domain but has impulses at specific delay points in the time domain. This work investigates the capacity and reliability of such a sparse multipath channel in the wideband regime. The capacity is shown to be logarithmically dependent on the coherence time of the channel whereas the reliability is shown to be exponentially decreasing with respect to the coherence time. The capacity-reliability tradeoff is then studied in terms of the exponent of the logarithm of coherence time. Numerical results verify the accuracy of the derived capacity and reliability expressions and demonstrate that the latter consistently overwhelms the former, in all cases. This work is valuable for evaluating the potential performance gain of multi-antenna deployment in current and next-generation wireless networks operating in the wideband regime.

One-range addition theorems for Coulomb interaction potential and its derivatives were reviewed by Guseinov (Chem. Phys., Vol. 309 (2005), pp. 209-213). In this Comment, we briefly respond to some of the points raised in the extended rejoinder by Guseinov. In the first place, Guseinov raised a concern about the completeness of the addition theorems. In fact, these theorems are complete with respect to definition of the special functions entering these theorems, including the Struve function, the Tricomi function, the Bessel functions and their derivatives (in particular, the Hankel functions), and the Lommel function. Next, Guseinov claims that the theorems given by us are valid only for highly symmetric situations. In fact, these theorems are valid for arbitrary interaction potentials if they satisfy the conditions (i) the interaction potential depends only on the distance between the particles and (ii) the range of this interaction potential is much less than the mean interparticle spacing. Guseinov’s last comment is that our reply “…contradicts to well-established rules of quantum mechanics” does not make any sense since we have only clarified some inconsistencies in Guseinov’s calculations and not introduced new inconsistencies. As an example, let us consider the response to the third comment. The theorem is valid only for highly symmetric situations, that is, when the nuclei have spherical symmetry. This is reflected by the integral in Eq. (7) through the function $F(kr)$ which is rapidly decreasing as $r$ tends to zero (this is possible only if $l = 0$ and the potential is spherical). If there are linear term(s) in the expansion of the potential in a vicinity of the nuclei, then the theorem is not valid anymore. The theorem can be applied only to the potential which decreases as $1/r$ at large distances.

The Carina Nebula, one of the most massive and most evolved regions in the Milky Way, contains dozens of historical supernova remnants, most of which are interacting with molecular clouds. Thus, the Carina Nebula is an ideal region to study the feedback process between stars and the interstellar medium. In particular, the origin of diffuse X-ray emission from this region has been a long-standing mystery. Using data from the Suzaku observatory, we have found clear detection of this diffuse X-ray emission. The spectrum can be modeled with a thermal plasma model with a temperature of 0.7 keV and a 0.5-2.0 keV surface brightness of 5.2x10^-6 W m-2, which corresponds to about 6.7% of the observed X-ray emission from the region. The X-ray properties and the distribution of the diffuse X-ray emission are both consistent with predictions from fast shocks caused by the winds and explosions of massive stars. We therefore suggest that the observed diffuse X-ray emission is created by wind-driven shocks interacting with the surrounding molecular clouds.

We derive entropy inequalities for the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) for the perfect gas. The lattice Boltzmann equation is a popular discretization of the continuum Boltzmann equation for rarefied gases, and provides a simple algorithm for computing Navier-Stokes-like moments. However, the Chapman-Enskog analysis of the LBM demonstrates that it provides no cooling, an entropy mistake first identified by Zhou et al. [J. Stat. Phys. 165, 1 (2016)]. Our first result is an upper bound on the heat flux in LBM conserved moments. We then prove a discrete entropy inequality using entropy Corrigan relationships and monotonicity properties of the discrete chain velocity. We show that this discrete entropy inequality is satisfied by LBM conserved moments provided that the solution has at least second order accuracy in space and time. We present LBM discretizations that satisfy the discrete entropy inequality with first and second order accuracy in space and time. Numerical evidence demonstrates the practicality of our entropy corrector LBM schemes, in that they yield statistically accurate solutions to the fluctuating viscous compressible Navier-Stokes equations in two and three spatial dimensions.

Phylogenetic mixtures represent phylogenetic patterns found in nature, in which multiple species (or populations, or biogeographical regions) group together, but not necessarily in the usual, well-supported monophyletic clusters. Such groups are not considered here as evolutionary anomalies, but rather as expected outcomes of evolution, and thus they are called ‘phylogenetic neighborhoods’; they are predicted by many current evolutionary theories, and have been observed across a broad range of organismal groups. A common example is the clustering of several genotypes of the same species (e.g., hosts of the same pathogen) together in space or time. Another example is the coexistence in the same region of sister species with different fossil records (‘mosaic evolution’). Yet another one is the grouping together of species with similar functional or life-style characteristics, even though they may have very different evolutionary origins (as in the previously mentioned case ofhosts of the same pathogen) Despite their prevalence, phylogenetic neighborhood relationships are often hard to discern in traditional, bifurcating phylogenies because they do not conform to classical notions of monophyly. Here, I introduce a statistical framework to detect and quantify phylogenetic neighborhoods in any bifurcating phylogenetic tree, regardless of their nature or branch length (quantitative or qualitative, instantaneous or ultrafast, harmonic or anagenetic). It is based on an inference of the frequencies of random bifurcations under a simple, explicit model of tree evolution, and on an estimation of the maximum-likelihood (ML) tree under a mixture of prior topologies. The resulting ‘mixed-up trees’ expose patterns of evolutionary mixture, and can be explored using popular phylogenetic software. I illustrate the method by applying it to two large-scale empirical datasets of DNA sequence, and show that neighborhood relationships are more pervasive than expected under a null model of random trees. Mixed-up trees will hopefully become a standard method for detecting and quantifying evolutionary mixtures in both the molecular and organismal biodiversity communities.”

Effects of electron-electron interaction on the phonon-mediated spin relaxation in quantum dots have been studied. Spin relaxation time T1 and T2 coefficients are proportional to 1/N3, N being the total electron number. This result is robust with respect to variations in the strength of the electron-phonon coupling and the electron density. However, T1 and T2 become infinite at the Coulomb repulsion value U=2E( dot energy level ) where E(dot energy level) is the energy level quantization in the dot. This is because for U>2E(dot energy level), formation of singlet and triplet configurations of electrons with different spins becomes forbidden and the lowest spin states of the system are effectively spinless. Thus, the system becomes nonmagnetic and the spin-flip processes vanish. Since singlet and triplet configurations are connected by spin-exchange processes, spin-relaxation also becomes forbidden in this case. The results are illustrated by studying the symmetric and asymmetric quantum dots.

Modern nanotechnology enables precise fabrication of various kinds of nanometer-scale structures, which have been employed to investigate the interactions of electromagnetic waves with subwavelength structures. In this paper, we investigate the interactions of electromagnetic waves with metallic and semiconducting nanospheres. By employing both exact and semiclassical descriptions, we demonstrate that both metallic and semiconducting spheres can support both Surface Plasmon Polariton (SPP) and Surface Phonon Polariton (SPhP) resonances, which are separate phenomena. SPP resonances require both bulk and surface modifications and are less sensitive to the geometrical size and shape of the particles, while SPhP resonances require only bulk modifications and are more sensitive to those variations. We further demonstrate that the SPhP resonances in semiconducting spheres can have much larger q (wave vector) values than the light in air and therefore have much longer radiative lifetimes.

The discovery of the Higgs boson with a mass of 126 GeV at the LHC experiments has a strong implications on the electroweak symmetry breaking. In particular it has been shown that the Standard Model (SM) Higgs boson must have a significant Yukawa-type coupling to the top quark. This raises the question of the nature of the Higgs sector inComposite Higgs Models, which provide a simple realization of the idea of Electroweak Symmetry Breaking (EWSB) through the formation of a strongly coupled phase of gauge theories. One such model, the Minimal Composite Higgs Model, has a strongly coupled sector which is $SO(5)/SO(4)$ gauge theory with 48 spin-1 resonances, known as light scalars, which are minimally coupled to the fermions. This minimal model, however, has some drawbacks, the first and most important one being the lack of a true dynamical breaking of the electroweak symmetry, as it is based on a hidden sector which remains strong at all scales. One possibility to solve this problem is to allow for a additional strong sector, leading to a larger strongly coupled sector, for example $SO(N)/SO(N-1)$ with N spin-1 resonances. Such a theory, known as Generalized Minimal Composite Higgs Model, was introduced in[1]. The resulting theory has a weakly coupled sector at low energies which is described by an $SO(N+4)/SO(N+3)$ gauge theory, with $N$ light spin-1 resonances. In this framework, it is possible to generate the Higgs doublet from the extra four dynamical directions of the gauge theory, leading to a composite Higgs model with a partially dynamical EW symmetry breaking. The new strong dynamics, although still conformal, allows for electroweak precision tests consistent with the recent observations, and leads to a larger effective potential which allows for a dynamical electroweak symmetry breaking with a weak-strong coupling hierachy. Finally, this theory naturally leads to top-quarks with a Yukawa coupling close to one, as the Higgsing of the strong sector produces a large top quark condensate.

Aim: In this work we model the high-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (HFQPOs), also known as mHz QPOs, observed from some black hole X-ray binaries. We focus on a particular example, the European Photon Imaging Camera (EPIC) instrument on the European Space Agency's (ESA's) XMM-Newton space telescope, which has detected several HFQPOs between 30 and 300 Hz, during the first months of 2015 in the X-ray emission from the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary Serxajs A. The energy dependence of these HFQPOs cannot be well-described by current accretion disc models, where the observed frequencies are determined by the Keplerian orbital frequency of material in an accretion disc around a compact object. We, therefore, introduce a new model for the HFQPOs, in which the QPOs are produced by resonantly driven warps in the inner parts of the accretion flow, near the black hole or neutron star. The warps are driven by global instabilities in the accretion flow, in particular the magneto-rotational instability. The model is able to successfully describe the energy-dependent behaviour of the HFQPOs. Additionally, we show that this model can also simultaneously explain other observed spectral behaviours of Serxajs A, such as the variability in the iron Kα fluorescence line, as well as observed X-ray spectral hysteresis.

Neutrino absorption instability is among the most promising mechanisms to transform the bulk kinetic energy of a gamma-ray burst (GRB) outflow into flares and/or scintillation light in their wake. The instability occurs when the drift rate of the heavier, inhibiting-density neutrinos is faster than the local sound speed. This is possible in part because the electrons and the inhibiting-density neutrinos can drift apart due to the thermal difference. Such an instability in the time-dependent neutrino disc of a GRB outflow has been suggested to produce rich variability in high-energy neutrino and light curves of gamma-rays, potentially resolvable with future large neutrino telescopes. However, this idea has never been investigated in full 3D or cosmological context. We perform 2.5D simulations in full 3D, self-consistently resolving the thermal, viscous, and neutrino transport. We find that even a sub-Eddington, solar-wind-like outflow is subject to the instability. The instability grows on dynamical time-scales and produces moderate fluctuations in both the light curves and the total neutrino luminosity. The fluctuations show rapid growth at early times and slower saturation at later times, with saturated fluctuations of up to 50%. The neutrino lightcurve and spectrum also become increasingly multi-modal and skewed, with softer neutrinos depleted. Overall, the results suggest that the instability may limit the detectability of high-energy neutrino and lightcurves from recent and even nearby gamma-ray bursts.

The hierarchical multithreaded (HMT) architecture has been proposed as a future-proof computing paradigm, which combines the best of both multithreading and multiprocessing. It allows the current coarse-grained multi-core processors to efficiently carry out today’s computation-intensive workloads without extensive redesign. However, it suffers from several impediments, including limited portability and ease of programmability. In this work, we introduce BubbleSched, an HMT runtime system, to provide portability and ease of programmability. In BubbleSched, there is a small number of high-level scheduling primitives to express fine-grained thread scheduling. Benchmark results show that BubbleSched provides a wide range of parallel performance with a high efficiency for both matrix multiplication and blockchain workloads. BubbleSched is an easy-to-use runtime system for hierarchical multithreaded (HMT) processors that provides portability and ease of programmability. It reduces the communication and manages resources efficiently to achieve good parallel performance for both matrix multiplication and blockchain workloads. BubbleSched schedules threads using a small number of high-level scheduling primitives. The high-level primitives are: (1) parallelization and replication, which distributes the workload across the available threads and processes; (2) synchronization, which avoids data races and improves the performance by using locking when needed; and (3) affinity and scheduling, which groups threads according to the similarity of the work and distributes the groups to different processes. Benchmark results show that BubbleSched provides a wide range of parallel performance with a high efficiency for both matrix multiplication and blockchain workloads. BubbleSched is easy to use: it provides three coarse-grained scheduling primitives, which are lightweight and easy to program, and automatically handles all the fine-grained optimizations for good performance. Benchmark results show that BubbleSched achieves good parallel performance for both matrix multiplication and blockchain workloads.

In recent years, a number of highly accurate distances to Cepheid variable stars have been published. These distances are based on novel geometric techniques that compare the size of Cepheid variable stars to other nearby stars. Using multiple techniques, distances that are statistically independent have been obtained for a sample of Cepheids in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) and the Distance modulus to the LMC has been determined. These distance measurements allow a new determination of the Hubble constant. The new value of the Hubble constant is statistically identical to the values obtained from type Ia supernovae and baryon acoustic oscillations, and is consistent with prior estimates based on the cosmic microwave background. The new Hubble constant is 13.71 ± 0.27 (stat) ± 0.32 (syst) km s-1 Mpc-1. This is the first direct determination of the Hubble constant independent of the assumed distance to the Virgo cluster.

We present the first complete simulations of the collisional evolution of Kuiper Belt (KB) objects (KBOs). We calculate the dynamical evolution of test particles placed in heliocentric orbit typical of those of the KB objects Eris, Sedna, and Orcus. From these simulations, we calculate the physical evolution of these objects' surfaces, collisional lifetimes, geology, lithologies, compositions, and dynamical membership in the Parenago segregation category. All of the relevant processes studied herein have observational signatures in the emitted light that we also model. We also calculate how the spectra of these objects would change if they had differentiated. The majority of the observed colors, reflectance spectra, and visible-light spectra of the KB objects we studied are the result of static clouds of regolith superimposed on underlying differentiated surfaces. We suggest that visible-light spectroscopic observations of such objects might allow discrimination between these models, if, for example, albedo or feature spacing data were available. Additionally, a global color observation may be possible if the object's spectrum was measured at multiple phases. We provide appropriate recommendations for future observational searches for surface differentiation and present an observing strategy to maximize the probability of observing this phenomenon.

The $\eta$ meson has been identified for the first time in the nuclear reaction $p d \to p d \eta$. The proposed missing links diagram is responsible for the formation of this meson. An analysis of the corresponding missing mass spectrum is performed and its behaviour is well reproduced by the proposed diagram. The decay properties of the $\eta$ meson have also been studied, finding a fair agreement with previous results. -- The $\eta$ meson has been an interesting subject of study since its first observation in 1925. It was initially believed to be a light spin-1 anti-tagging odd particle of the s-wave scattering between known nucleons, though later theoretical speculations suggested it to be a Goldstone boson resulting from the spontaneous breaking of a $U(1)$ global symmetry in a dual version of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). In spite of its theoretical significance, the $\eta$ meson was missing in the corresponding spectrum up until recently, when it was observed in the $p d \to p d \eta$ nuclear reaction for the first time by the joint Japan and Russia spectrometer HADES (from German word for survey) at the electron-proton collider ELSA. -- The proposed missing links diagram is responsible for the formation of this meson. The corresponding invariant mass spectrum is well reproduced by the proposed diagram. The decay properties of the $\eta$ meson have also been studied, finding a fair agreement with previous results.

Using the long baseline interferometry operating in the optical domain could lead to an improvement of the detection limits of measurements of fundamental stellar parameters (such as diameters and masses). These parameters are closely linked to the nature and evolution of the stars. Therefore, investigations of stars in different stages of their lives (such as formation, evolution, and pulsation) could be significantly accelerated through the use of long baseline interferometry in the optical domain. These capabilities will be particularly significant for massive stars that evolve quickly and have dimensions much larger than the wavelengths involved in their optical spectra. The study presented in this paper deals with two such massive stars, HD 37366 and HD 54662. We have obtained spectra and carried out an astrometric analysis of these stars that showed that HD 37366 is a double star, while HD 54662 is a binary with an orbital period of approximately 21 years and a total mass of approximately 22.5 solar masses. The study of these objects’ orbital motion has shown that theHD 37366 system is a stable hierarchical quadruple system with an inner pair of stars, HD 37366 AB, that are eclipsing with a period of 3.6 days. The masses of the components of this system were estimated from the light curve solution to be M A = 1.13 solar masses and M B = 0.89 solar masses. The estimation of these masses provided a validation of the results of the astrometric study. For theHD 54662 system, only the component HD 54662 C was detected in the spectrum; the mass of this component was estimated to be M C = 2.14 solar masses. Additional observations are needed to study the properties of the companion of HD 54662, if it is also a star, and to detect the orbit of the AB pair of HD 37366. The discovery of these two systems suggests that the study of their orbital motion could yield new results about the evolution of star clusters, the structure of stellar interiors, and the stability of hierarchical multiple systems.

In this paper we study the asymptotic behavior of the solution to a typed branching diffusion, describing the growth of a colony of individual agents that reproduce and die. The limiting growth rate is characterized in terms of the branching ratio and the allelic type, which govern the rate at which individual agents reproduce and die. We show that when the allelic type is 0 or 1, the solution converges exponentially to an equilibrium density. When the allelic type is between 2 and 4, the solution converges at a linear rate to a time-shifted version of the equilibrium density. When the allelic type is larger than 4, the solution converges at an exponential rate to 0. The result is consistent with a phase transition at the allelic type of 2, where the rate of exponential growth changes from 0 to non-zero. The asymptotic results are complemented by a method of moments calculation which matches the solution to the model with direct simulation. The paper provides foundational work for a general theory of typed branching diffusions. The result applies more broadly to differential equations of the form: $\frac{\partial f(t, x)}{\partial t} = \mathcal{L}[f(t, x)],$ where $\mathcal{L}$ is a linear partial differential operator and $f(t, x) > 0$ is the density function of $X(t)$, the number of individuals of type $x$ at time $t$. The theory of typed branching diffusions will have numerous applications, for example in epidemiology, where it can be used to model the spread of an infection through a population, and in population genetics, where it can model the evolution of allele frequencies over time.

Exoplanets are found across the spectrum of size, temperature, and formation. While their locations can tell us about the makeup of their host stars, the diversity in planet types allows us to study the diversity in planet formation. XO-2b is a transiting hot Jupiter with a mass of 1.33 MJup orbiting a F6V star at a distance of 0.0735 AU. This planet is notable for being found in a metal-rich circumstellar disk, yet its mass and radius are similar to those of other hot Jupiters. In addition to being a useful comparison object, XO-2b's metal-rich nature allows for a probe of weathering. The planet's radius is not significantly different than what is expected for a planet of its mass, implying that XO-2b has a compact layer of scorching rock around its core. With a mass roughly 75% that of Jupiter and radius similar to that of Jupiter, XO-2b is likely surrounded by a dense layer of hydrogen gas. If this planet has a moon, its tenuous atmosphere may be detectable via secondary transits.

This paper is an exposition of two mathematical techniques that can be used to find elements of an infinite dimensional Hilbert space. The first technique is the Rayleigh-Ritz method, which uses the operator analytic definition of the sine of the angle between two Hilbert space subspaces to find the angle between them. The second technique is the Alternating Projector Method, which in a more general setting uses the analytic definition of the cosine of the angle between two projectors to find the angle between them. The exposition is illustrated with several examples, including the calculation of the angle between the Riesz projections associated with the Laplacian on Euclidean domains, the Hodge Laplacian on Euclidean domains, and the integer and fractional laplacians on smooth domains. The techniques demonstrated here also allow the calculation of the angle between the Riesz projectors associated with the Laplace operator on arbitrary domains in Euclidean space. However, the analytic definition of the cosine of the angle between the projectors requires the introduction of a kernel, and as such this exposition is restricted to the case of domains that are relatively compact with respect to the entire Euclidean space. Additionally, while the techniques demonstrated here apply to finding angles between subspaces of arbitrary Hilbert space, the exposition is initially restricted to the case of subspaces that are finite dimensional. An example is provided of the calculation of the angle between two subspaces of an infinite dimensional Hilbert space that are each spanned by a sequence of basis elements. Finally, the techniques demonstrated here are illustrated with a discussion of the connection between the angles between subspaces and the Rayleigh-Ritz and Alternating Projector methods of finding eigenvalues. Rayleigh-Ritz and Alternating Projector methods are two techniques that can be used to find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of linear, self-adjoint operators. The Rayleigh-Ritz method evaluates the Rayleigh quotient and searches for the value of the parameter for which this quotient is stationary, i.e., for which the norm of the gradient of this quotient is zero. The Alternate Projector method evaluates the projector of the operator onto the kernel of the adjoint of this operator onto the range of this operator.

The Coma cluster (z=0.023) is one of the most massive and X-ray luminous clusters in the local universe, and is a key cosmological landmark. Although the central galaxy in Coma, NGC4839, is luminous and massive, it is substantially obscured by dust and its star formation rate is likely strongly depressed relative to other cluster members. Previous studies of the Coma cluster have generally been limited to bluer wavelengths, thus precluding the study of the obscured star formation in the central galaxy and other cluster members. Using data from the Spitzer Infrared Array Camera, we perform a study of the cluster's near-infrared (NIR) luminosity function, which is sensitive to obscured star formation. In particular, we detect 1622 galaxies down to a star formation rate of 0.2M$_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$, about 35 times more galaxies than detected in the optical. The majority of this NIR population appears to be associated with the Coma cluster, based on available redshift data. Using simulations, we demonstrate that this extremely high detection fraction is unusual, and likely indicates the presence of a significant population of extremely dusty, Compton-thick galaxies associated with the cluster. The contribution of this population to the overall Star Formation Rate density of the Coma cluster is discussed.

This is a very brief abstract of a highly technical paper from the arXiv.org archive. The full version can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06755. The main result of the paper is a generalization of the Riemann zeta function to the setting of arithmetic manifolds. The Zeta-Function is defined using the von Neumann term for the trace of the Laplacian. This can be extended to manifolds with a p-adic metric, which leads to a p-adic analogue of thezeta function. The main theorem of the paper is the computation of this p-adic zeta function for hyperbolic manifolds. This is used to prove a theorem about rational points on such manifolds, which in turn is used to prove a number of equivalent formulations of the Riemann Hypothesis. This work was inspired by the analog result for real manifolds, due to Dwork, and the associated Dwork Theory for physicists. My hope is that this p-adic version will be of interest to physicists in the same way that Dwork Theory is. In particular, this work uses the methods of non-Archimedean geometry and arithmetic geometry, so may be of interest to non-specialists who are interested in this area.

This paper lays the foundations of thermodynamics, building upon previous work by @Planck, @Planck2 and @Gujrati. This is important as many foundational concepts in thermodynamics are counterintuitive and cannot be easily derived from basic statements about energy conservation. This is because those statements do not distinguish between different forms of energy and therefore cannot reveal the fundamental distinction between heat and work. We do this by developing a general theory of Clausius inequalitites, which provide a basis for defining what heat and work are. We then apply this framework to microscopic systems, obtaining a general form for the second law of thermodynamics. Finally, we apply this to the irreversible processes observed in macroscopic systems, deriving the well known forms of the first and second laws. In summary, this paper lays the foundations of thermodynamics, building upon the work of Planck, Planck 2 and Gujratit and presents a general framework which can be applied to microscopic as well as macroscopic systems to derive well know forms of the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

Recent developments in harmonic analysis provide new computational tools for imaging. These tools, termed needlet methods, are flexible representations of multifrequency information and provide a unified approach to a wide variety of imaging techniques. In this work, we introduce two such methods for variational image reconstruction. The first, termed hybrid needlet frame Implementation, combines the two most popular needlet methods, the variational multitaper needlet and the variational wavelet needlet, into a single algorithm. The second method, termed hybrid needlet renormalization, allows the hybrid needlet method to be applied to an almost arbitrary needlet frame. We present numerical results to demonstrate the efficacy of these methods, and suggest potential extensions to volumetric imaging and other inverse problems.' Studies of the chemical and dynamical properties of the stellar halo have been performed in two separate, but complementary, directions. Observationally, candidate members of the stellar halo have been identified by their unusual kinematic characteristics in the Milky Way's observed gravitational field, leading to the characterization of several stellar streams. For some of these, high-resolution spectroscopy has confirmed them to be old, sparsely populated systems with Galactically isotropy spatial distributions and large apocentric distances. While the radial velocity components of some of these systems may be interpreted as resulting from recent accretions, other system-proper motions are wholly consistent with those of the classical satellites of the Milky Way. More direct clues to the nature of the stellar halo come from surveys of the outer Galaxy. Searches for variable stars and RR Lyrae variables have identified the stellar halo as a metal-poor population. Stellar neighbors of several candidate halo stars are being scrutinized for chemical peculiarities through medium-resolution spectroscopy. A clear gap in the metallicity distribution of nearby stars is observed for several stars with strongly retrograde Galactic velocities. Recent evidence from studies of the chemical and dynamical properties of the stellar halo has confirmed the long suspected nature of its metal-poor nature and provided further hints of its accretion origin. While its stellar number density is in remarkable agreement with expectations based on simple dynamical models of the Milky Way's outer components, the available evidence is less compelling for its accretional origin. At present, there is still room for more direct clues to the nature of the stellar halo through searches for chemical peculiarities.

Object classification is a key step in difference imaging, the study of galaxies when they were younger than they are now. Historically, this has been a laborious process that has limited the kinds of galaxies that have been studied. We introduce a technique for object classification that both increases the efficiency with which we can study galaxies and improves the reliability of our results. The technique uses a convolutional neural network trained on high-quality images of galaxies to classify low-quality difference imaging images of the same galaxies. This allows us to identify candidate galaxies and to reject images of stars that otherwise might have been incorrectly labeled as galaxies. Our method improves the reliability of our results and significantly increases the number of galaxies that we can study. As a test, we apply our method to the difference imaging survey of a field in the southern sky, K2, identifying 80% as galaxies instead of the approximately 50% that are identified by eyeball inspection. The resulting catalog will be useful for studying the evolution of the population of galaxies as a function of redshift and will aid in our understanding of galaxy morphology and population statistics. The technique described here is not limited to difference imaging. Similar methods can be applied to other contexts in which object classification is a necessary preliminary step.

Late Long-Term Potentiation (L-LTP), also known as Long-Term Memory, depends on the presynaptic activation of group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs), and postsynaptic protein synthesis. Maintenance requires NMDA receptor activity and new protein synthesis. In this work, we present a model of late L-LTP that incorporates these three basic components. The model can produce long-term depression (L-LTD) and long-term memory, which are also observed in late L-LTP. Thus, the model may be a useful tool in elucidating late L-LTP’s basic mechanisms. Late Long-Term Potentiation (L-LTP), also known as Long-Term Memory, depends on the presynaptic activation of group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluRs), and postsynaptic protein synthesis. Maintenance requires NMDA receptor activity and new protein synthesis. We present a model of late L-LTP that incorporates these three basic components. The model can produce long-term depression (L-LTD) and long-term memory, which are also observed in late L-LTP. Thus, the model may be a useful tool in elucidating late L-LTP’s basic mechanisms. The model includes three parts: presynaptic, postsynaptic, and the interaction between the two. The presynaptic component includes an mGluR that is activated by an increase in the concentration of a presynaptic neurotransmitter. This leads to the mobilization of calcium via a diacylglycerol/protein kinase C cascade. This calcium influx results in the synthesis of critical proteins involved in L-LTP maintenance. The postsynaptic part includes the synthesis of glutamate receptors that have a half-life of several hours. Finally, the interaction between the two parts includes the production of long-term depression (L-LTD) when the combined postsynaptic glutamate and presynaptic neurotransmitter concentrations decrease. Our results show that this model can produce long-term depression, as well as long-term potentiation, that is similar to late L-LTP. We conclude that this model may be a useful tool in elucidating late L-LTP’s basic mechanisms. Acknowledgments This work was supported by NSF grants 1719653, 1719564, 1820822, 1834991, and 1900094. Omega Cen is 4.2 million years old with a current mass of approximately 4.6 million M☉[1]. Its name is derived from its radius of approximately 16,500 light-years and its proximity to the Galactic Center. Omega Centauri is one of the brightest globular clusters in the sky, second only to the core of the Milky Way in terms of visual brightness. It is a powerful testbed for astrophysics as well, since it contains the Omega Cen stellar boson, a large, concentrated group of relatively very old, very low mass stars (at most half a solar mass), that behaves, from a dynamical point of view, as a single unit, from a stellar population standpoint. The space around Omega Centauri is also filled with numerous other stellar systems. At the cluster's core lies the supermassive black hole, 4.2 million times more massive than our Sun, which is surrounded by a cluster of at least 20,000 stars. This cluster, called the Quintuplet, is too distant to be observed individually, but the combined light of its members outshines the black hole. The Quintuplet is home to at least 12 blue stragglers, meaning it hosts the most massive, brightest stars in the cluster. In addition to these compact objects, Omega Centauri has long been known to contain dozens of hypervelocity stars - stars that were pulled from the cluster through the galaxy's mighty gravitational field. Finally, Omega Centauri is the site of the oldest and most recent supernova in our local universe.
