Interfaces with quenched disorder, in particular adsorbing pinning centers, have attracted considerable interest for more than four decades. Early theoretical work, starting with Imry and Ma, predicted that disorder promotes low temperature ordering, at least for weak randomness. Subsequent renormalization group analyses byFisher and Halperin provided evidence of an extensive phase with long range order in 2D, but with dislocations (rough defects) carrying free energy. Subsequent analytical work confirmed the RG analyses, but with more restricted ranges of validity. More recent work has clarified the properties of these random systems in 2 dimensions. It has been shown that there is, in fact, a low temperature phase with long range order and without dislocations. However, the nature of the phase has changed: here the disorder is “strong,” in the sense that translational symmetry is broken, but there are no long range positional orders. It is possible to prove that in this strong disorder regime there is only a finite density of corner dislocations; in the language of disorder fields, this means that there is a non-zero stiffness in these disordered systems.

The phenomenon of resonant tunneling of electrons through a thin insulator, if spin-polarized, has been observed in a III-V magnetic semiconductor heterostructure. The tunneling current and the Schottky barrier height depend on the relative orientation of the magnetization in the ferromagnet and in the semiconductor. We report measurements of current-voltage characteristics and magnetic modulation of the tunneling current in magnetoresistive tunnel diodes based on a II-VI semiconductor (ZnS). The measurements were carried out at room temperature in an applied magnetic field of several hundred Oe. We observed a resonant tunneling through the Schottky barrier and magnetic switching of the tunneling current. The experimental results were qualitatively and quantitatively explained by a model which takes into account the energy spectrum of quasiparticles in the ferromagnet and the semiconductor, as well as the presence of a nonmagnetic electrode between the ferromagnetic layer and the semiconductor. *With kind regards, *Saša Knizevitch, PhD Spin-polarized transport in II-VI magnetic resonant tunneling devices

Hybrid inflation is an attractive paradigm for inflation, combining aspects of both single-field inflation and multi-field theories. However, current formulations of hybrid inflation suffer from either lack of prediction power or faced with major challenges. We present a new model of smooth hybrid inflation, with three scalar fields and a non-minimal coupling. The potential is natural on cosmological scales and can provide a good fit to the latest Planck data. With the potential naturally achieved, the model has an graceful exit from inflation and produces a scale invariant spectrum of fluctuations. Further, we demonstrate that our model does not suffer from the small field issue and is able to give the correct scalar spectral index, $n_s$. In addition, we show that our model gives the right amplitude of the primordial gravitational waves and is consistent with the BICEP2 result. Lastly, we demonstrate that our model is free from unwanted dynamic background solutions and can successfully produce the observed large scale structure.

Recent work by has identified a large population of transients in radio astronomy. These transients range in properties from barely brighter than the detection threshold of the survey in which they were discovered, to many orders of magnitude brighter. They include highly variable bright radio bursts,Sources whose radio emission is modulated on very fast time scales, and sources which are either completely dark or weakly variable over time periods of weeks to many years. Here I present a survey of archival data for these transients. Using observations from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA), the Green Bank Telescope (GBT), the Hartebeesthoek Radio Astronomy Observatory, the Australia Telescope National Facility, and the Deep Sky Station database, I identify 1223 sources with bright radio transients within the past 30 years. When combined with a recent comparable survey of the GBT data by, this increases the total number of radio transients discovered to 3969. The majority of these transients were not previously known, but similar survey of other observatories have discovered similar populations of highly variable radio sources. These populations include radio bursts, pulsars, magnetars, and Tidal Disruption Events.

Neutrinos are the only known particles that do not interact via the weak force, and thus may pass through ordinary matter without being significantly deflected or attenuated. This property makes them an excellent probe of extreme environments, such as the interiors of stars and the vicinity of black holes. Using this feature, one can study neutrino properties by observing the signals from their interactions with matter. In this work, we show that the combination of oscillation and scattering measurements can provide insight into the nature of weak interaction symmetry breaking. Specifically, we consider the scenario in which the neutrino has a non-zero mass, but the only source of this mass is the symmetry breaking parameter in the neutrino Yukawa coupling matrix. We present the projected sensitivity of the IceCube neutrino telescope to this scenario, and show that it will be able to constrain this scenario to a small region of parameter space, corresponding to a strong limit on the magnitude of the symmetry breaking parameter.

We present the results of a large-scale, proper-motion-selected survey for low-mass members of the southern sky carried out with the Swope Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory, Chile. We combine these observations with results from a previous survey of the northern sky [Shkolnik et al. 2009] to determine the multiplicity statistics for low-mass stars and brown dwarfs (spectral types M and later). We find that approximately 43% of stars in our sample are members of multiple systems, with a multiplicity frequency similar to that of higher mass stars. We find that wide systems (Sep > 10 arcseconds) are even more highly concentrated to the cluster than tight systems, suggesting that dynamical interactions are a significant process shaping wide multiple systems. We identify 72 very low-mass (VLMS) or low-mass candidates (spectral types J and K) in our sample, 18 of which are in wide systems. Including previously published VLMS and low-mass companion discoveries, we estimate the frequency of VLMS in multiple systems as 24% for our full sample, and 50% for the VLMS systems. Finally, we estimate that for wide VLMS systems, the median semi-major axis is approximately 100 times greater than the physical separation of brown dwarfs and that the eccentricities of these systems are generally low.

In this paper we introduce a subjective information measure for numerical quantification of the informativeness of scientific publications. The measure takes into account both the statistical reliability and the interest relevance of the reported results for the specific field of research. We also present the Rate Fidelity Theory, a new approach to information retrieval, based on the same measure of informativeness. Rate Fidelity Theory (RFT) assigns a relevance score to each scientific publication in a subject area, based not only on its position in an information hierarchy, but also on how close to the Position of Interest (PoI) it is. The RFT relevance score can be used as a quantitative indicator of how much a publication deviates from the PoI. Thus, RFT allows one to not only find the most relevant publications in a specific field, but also to find the most interesting ones. The measure of informativeness and the Rate Fidelity Theory can be used in many information retrieval applications, especially in the area of digital libraries and scientometrics. They can be used, for example, in the process of paper/journal recommendation, or to enhance the relevance of the paper/journal citations index.

Recent studies show that most of the matter in the Universe is dark, and it is driving the formation of large-scale structures. However, direct observational proof of the existence of dark matter is elusive, as its apparent effects are manifested through its gravitational influence. In this study, we present the first observation of the Einstein ring dark matter, produced by the combined gravitational lensing from an intervening cluster and individual halo masses of the cluster galaxies. We identified the Einstein ring LBG J213512.73-010143 as the background source behind the cluster J213512.7-010143 at a redshift of z=3.07. The lensed image of the LBG is composed of two components - the visible (luminous) galaxy and the dark (dwarf) lensing galaxy. The separation of the two components is 1.2” (or 160pc) and it is detected at high confidence level (conf=9.3). The half-light radius of the dark lensing galaxy is 0.18” (or 23pc), which corresponds to 0.13M⊙ at the lensing mass, and the number of detected satellite galaxies around it is 4. We used combined strong lensing, weak lensing and galaxy cluster mass observations to estimate the total mass of the lensing cluster J213512.73-010143, and determined that it is comprised of about 1.4 times more dark matter than the observed luminous matter. The mass difference is likely produced by cosmic variance and cosmic bias, with dark matter more strongly clustered than observed luminous matter. If confirmed by future observations, the discovery of the Einstein ring dark matter would provide the first observational evidence for the existence of dark matter, and provide an important addition to the current cosmological model.

Metallic systems may exhibit superconductivity by several different routes. The electron-phonon interaction, which is believed to be the primary mechanism of phonon-mediated superconductivity in conventional superconductors, requires the electrons to be sufficiently mobile to carry out repeated lattice vibrations. The strongest electron-phonon coupling occurs in systems with linear lattices, like solid crystals, but strong electron interactions can also generate superconductivity in more amorphous systems, such as the metals made famous by John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, and Robert Schrieffer, who are rightly known as superfluid metals. While the electrons in these metals are well-coupled to their lattice, the phonon spectra remains gapped, and so the conventional wisdom has been that strong electron-electron interactions are required to develop superconducting instability. However, new theoretical work has proposed that sufficiently asymmetric electron and phonon systems can generate attractive electron-phonon coupling even at nonzero phonon frequencies, and that this asymmetric coupling can generate a robustly stable superconducting ground state even in systems with well-defined quasiparticles. These predictions have been successfully demonstrated by parallel transport calculations on representative real materials, which revealed that the electron-phonon coupling in these materials is asymmetric by more than 20%

In this paper we generate Einstein-scalar field solutions from vacuum solutions with arbitrary cosmological constant by employing the method of finding the asymptotic boundary conditions at infinity. This method has previously been used to generate black hole solutions. We apply this method to find minimally coupled solutions with a cosmological constant and minimally coupled to a scalar field. The scalar field potentials that admit these solutions are constructed. The cases with zero, negative, and positive cosmological constant are covered. We then present explicit solutions with a zero, negative, and positive cosmological constant. We show how these solutions generalize previously known solutions, in particular Boulware, Hartle, and Zel'dovich AdS and dS spaces. The main new feature of the solutions with positive and negative cosmological constant is the existence of naked singularities. In the case of positive cosmological constant these singularities are black holes with non-Abelian hair, in the case of negative cosmological constant they are dS spaces with non-minimal hair. In the case of zero cosmological constant the only new feature is the presence of a massless scalar field, which we argue could be naturally described as a ghost.

A novel, highly selective, liquid-crystalline chemosensor has been synthesised for the detection of sulphur (S). The chemosensor, based on an indoline-2-one unit, exhibits a near-infrared (NIR) fluorescence response towards S detection with high sensitivity (LOD=5.3×10−7 M). The system can discriminate between S and other commonly encountered anions with the exception of hydrogen sulphate (H2SO4) with a significant NIR fluorescence enhancement observed for S over H2SO4. Fluorescence microscopy imaging of mammalian cells demonstrates that the chemosensor is membrane permeable and that it can detect endogenous sulphide (S2-) in mammalian cells. Preliminary, non-targeted, live-cell NIR fluorescence imaging of mammalian cells treated with the chemosensor demonstrates the ability of the chemosensor to detect S2- in mammalian cells. These results indicate that the chemosensor is a promising candidate for the sensitive non-invasive imaging of endogenous S2- in biological systems.

In this paper, we describe the properties of some generators of II_1 factors, which we found using computational techniques. Some of these properties may be of independent interest. We find that there are uncountably many generators and that there is no finite set of generators with the same property. In the process, we show that some previously known examples of II_1 factors can be realized as factors of other factors. In particular, we show that all known examples can be obtained as quotients of the hyperfinite II_1 factor. In contrast to many previously known constructions of II_1 factors with particular properties, our factors have simple automorphisms. In [1], Haagerup constructed the first examples of II_1 factors, namely the factor of type II$_\infty$ constructed from the group of diffeomorphisms of the interval and the factor of type II$_1$ constructed from the group of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of the unit interval. In [2, 3], Connes and Jones introduced normal free Araki-Woods factors, which are the factor of type III constructed from the hyperfinite factor and the discrete II_1 factor.

This paper presents a quasi-equilibrium grid (QEG) algorithm for constructing projection matrices in model reduction. The method is motivated by the projection method for dynamical systems, but with the key difference that the dynamical systems matrices are replaced by the "QEG matrices", which are generated using a graph Laplacian. The QEG method provides a practical alternative to projection-based model reduction techniques, offering similar accuracy at significantly lower computational cost. The construction of the QEG matrices is achieved using a novel form of double-grid technique, which is shown to satisfy an appropriate quasi-equilibrium condition. Numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Authors: Fei Gao and Jianfeng Lu Journal: Journal of Computational and Nonlinear Materials Science Publishing Office: Springer DOI: 10.1016/j.jcm.2019.01.035

Exoplanets are one of the most remarkable outcomes of modern astronomy. The experimental technique of radial velocity method has allowed for the discovery of more than 400 planets outside our Solar System. However, for every planet we know, there are probably many more to be discovered. One of the biggest limitations in the detection of new planets is related to the velocity accuracy that is required to detect the possible signal from a planet in motion around its host star. The HARPS instrument at the ESO La Silla Observatory is a fiber-fed echelle spectrograph that is capable of reaching velocity precisions of 1 m/s. In recent years, a new method of planet detection, which does not require the velocity accuracy of HARPS, has been developed. This method, called the search for earth-mass planets around close stars (MEarth), is based on the radial velocity method, but makes use of the apparent dimming of a star when a planet transits in front of it. In this article, we present a new planet around the nearby star GJ 674, with an earth mass, an orbital period of 20 days, and a minimum orbital distance of 0.0457 AU. This is the lowest mass, lowest orbital distance and second closest orbit planet ever detected. We also characterize the host star as a spotted main-sequence star of spectral type M4.5V, with a mass of 0.828 ± 0.045 solar masses, a radius of 0.690 ± 0.015 solar radii, and an estimated age of 5.2 billion years.

High-energy threshold reaction rates on 0.8 GeV proton-irradiated thick Pb-target were measured in a tandem accelerator consisting of a synchrotron and a fragmentation ring. The reaction rates of 13 nuclear reactions with 0.8 GeV charged particles on thick Pb target were determined. Significant deviations from the standard evaluated values have been observed in the evaluated nuclear reaction rates. The possible causes of the observed differences are discussed. The 13 nuclear reaction rates with 0.8 GeV charged particles on thick Pb target have been measured. These data will be valuable for nuclear reaction model developments and assessment of nuclear risk in the environments with high-energy heavy ion fluxes. Significant deviations from the standard evaluated values have been observed in the evaluated nuclear reaction rates. The possible causes of the observed differences are discussed. The evaluated nuclear reaction rates are used for design, assessment and mitigation of nuclear risk in environments with heavy ion fluxes. Nuclear reaction models are used in radiation transport simulations of aircraft, space vehicles, personnel, and the human body to determine specific absorbed rates. In these simulations, the evaluated nuclear reaction rates are used to represent the possible environments with heavy ion fluxes. These simulated specific absorbed rates are then compared to observed responses to determine if these models are adequate. Deviations between the modeled and observed specific absorbed rates can indicate the need for new nuclear data in the models to improve their accuracy. The evaluated nuclear reaction rates presented in this paper will be valuable for nuclear reaction model developments and will aid in the assessment of nuclear risk in the environments with high-energy heavy ion fluxes. This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by the National Nuclear Security Administration, Off-Axis Heavy Ion Accelerator Studies Group, and was supported by the Office of Science of the U.S. Department of Energy.

Unitary evolution represents one of the most profound success stories of twentieth century science. In quantum mechanics, it guarantees the conservation of probability, and together with the continuity equation, it also guarantees the absence of negative probabilities. Most famously, it guarantees the existence of a universal Hamiltonian. Moreover, it is the theoretical basis of all scattering experiments and the driving force behind much of our modern electronics, including transistors and nuclear magnetic resonance imaging. The latter two applications rely on the nuclear spin, a spin 1/2 degree of freedom. In the past decade, a new class of quantum devices has been introduced that exploits a different kind of fundamental degree of freedom - spinless fermions. These fermions naturally occur in several condensed matter systems such as graphene and cold atoms. Very recently, a scheme to engineer spinless fermions that also exhibit unitary evolution was introduced. Building on the earlier work in Refs. [1,2], this framework of engineering fermions is sufficiently general to encompass any 1D interacting quantum system.

An experimental gravimetric result for the revival of corpuscular theory: On 23 November 1687, the observation of a fast corpuscle moving under the gravitational force in an earth-based laboratory for the first time provided experimental confirmation of the particle theory of light. This observation, made by French scientist Robert Hooke, validated a major prediction of the theory of Isaac Newton. Since that time, hundreds of experiments all over the world have produced consistent results providing direct experimental evidence that light is composed of tiny material particles called photons. An experimentalist, François HoverschMiddeleur, working with a team from the University of Strasbourg and the Institute of Space Systems ("Istituto di Intelligibilità Spaziale"), made the observations reported in this paper. The observations were made using an artificial satellite named SERVIR, which they had placed into a low Earth orbit, and which they turned into a centrifuge by varying the orientation of its antenna, enabling it to detect Earth's gravity gradients. The result: the authors of this paper obtained a set of 11 measurements of the Earth's gravity gradient, in the frequency range 0.1 – 10 Hz. The standard deviation of these measurements is comparable with the expected values and is compatible with the standard uncertainty of the measurements. This result, reported in the paper, provides experimental evidence of the existence of the Earth's gravitational field gradient, enabling future experiments to test Newton's and Einstein's theories of relativity.

In a study on the scalar mesonf0(1370) performed with the full detector setup, we find an evidence of the f0(1370) resonance with a statistical significance of 5.9 standard deviations. The mass and full width of the f0(1370) are 1380 ± 40(stat) ± 30(syst) MeV/c2 and 265 ± 50(stat) ± 70(syst) MeV, respectively. It is concluded that the f0(1370) is likely to be the meson with J=0, |q|=1 bond between the u and d quarks. This study was performed with the full detector setup, that is, with the CMD-3 detector on the HMS Chikuma, the VELO detector at VEPP-2M (Novosibirsk) and the SND detector at the IHEP (Protvino).

In the core-accretion model of planet formation, planetesimals are formed from large bodies of dust. The locations where dust forms planetesimals, i.e. the snow line, are determined by the temperature, which in turn is determined by the mass of the central star. Planetesimals form more easily where the temperature is low. Thus, planets around low-mass stars are expected to have a higher concentration of planetesimals close to their host star. Here we show that this is the case around the dust-disk inner edge, where MRI-driven turbulence is the strongest in the disk. The MRI-driven turbulence also reduces the formation of pebble planetesimals, by stirring up the pebbles into larger, fast-moving dust. Consequently, there are more small (10-100 km) dust grains at the disk inner edge, and more of these settle toward the midplane. When the gas surface density drops sufficiently at the snow line, particles can stick to the disk and start to collect. We find that the planetesimal concentration increases with the snow line radius and the distance to the star, and that the maximum planetesimal concentration reaches 3.2% around the host star Proxima Cen. This high planetesimal concentration may help explain the existence of detectable amounts of water in the spectrum of Proxima Cen b.

Exact half-BPS Type IIB interface solutions Author: Chervonyi Alexander Jr. Yuriy Vasil$'$evich Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of Zurich and Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics Address: Switzerland and Germany Data: 2020 Type: PDF The paper reviews a new class of exact half-BPS Type IIB interface solutions. First we review the Type IIB solution with worldvolume directions $x^{10},x^{11},x^{12},x^{13},x^{14},x^{27},x^{28},x^{29},x^{30},x^{31},x^{32},x^{33},x^{34},x^{35},x^{36}$ and $x^{42}$ in the 11D space-time, equipped with the 3-form field strength given by the Buscher rules with the additional fluxes along $x^{10},x^{11},x^{12},x^{13},x^{14},x^{27},x^{28},x^{29},x^{30},x^{31},x^{32},x^{33},x^{34},x^{35},x^{36}$ and $x^{42}$ vanishing. Next, we generalize this solution to the case when the fluxes along $x^{27},x^{28},x^{29},x^{30},x^{31},x^{32},x^{33},x^{34},x^{35},x^{36},x^{42}$ are turned on. We call such solution the Janus, since it has two distinct sides corresponding to the two different ways the fluxes can be turned on. In particular, when the flux along $x^{27}$ is turned on, we obtain the first locally non-squashed half-BPS Type IIB interface solution with this flux turned on. We perform Kaluza-Klein dimensional reduction on this solution to obtain five-dimensional nonsupersymmetric Janus solution. We find that the Janus solution exhibits a new type of horizon topology which we call squashed ellipsoid. Next, we perform a similar dimensional reduction starting from the Janus solution with all fluxes turned on, and we obtain the first supersymmetric Janus solution. We find that supersymmetry of the Janus solution requires the D6-brane tension to be fine-tuned.

A locally decodable code (LDC) is a family of codes for transmitting information bits over a memoryless noisy channel such that the decoder has access to some of the channel outputs but not all of them. Traditionally, the access to the channel outputs is spatially separated at two or more places in the paper, called domain. Domain separation has two drawbacks: first, the channel capacity increases with the number of domains and the code becomes less useful in practice; second, if the channel outputs are ordered according to some predefined pattern, the code becomes easy to interpret and not very difficult to decode. In this paper, we consider the first drawback and show that if the desired number of outputs is a prime number, one can find a nice subset of the field of prime order and a prime factor of a Mersenne number for the channel outputs. This allows to decrease the number of domains to one, and provides a code that is efficiently realizable in practice. We also provide lower bounds on the size of LDC that answer an open question.

A novel soliton theory for the quantum KdV equation is presented, whose S-matrix is computed by a degenerate integrable perturbation method. Using the S-matrix, a quantum Langlands duality relating the quantum KdV to the quantum N=2 super KdV is proved. This work was presented at the 49th SIAM Conference on their Water Series in Control and Dynamical Systems, May 12-15, 2019, at Royal Beach resort, San Diego, CA, USA. The quantum KdV (qKdV) equation, derived from the quantum Thirring model, possesses the Lax pair and scattering data of the quantum KdV equation, and admits solitary wave and periodic wave solutions. We present a novel soliton theory for the quantum KdV equation. A recursion operator and related conserved quantities are derived by employing the classical KdV theory. By means of degenerate integrable perturbation method, we compute the S-matrix of the quantum KdV equation, from which the quantum Langlands duality relating the quantum KdV to the quantum N=2 super KdV is derived. The soliton theory we present may be applicable to other nonlinear integrable equations with soliton or solitary wave solutions, and this duality may have broad applications in the theory of quantum integrable systems. We present the results of deep photometry of the outer parts of M33, performed with the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV) survey, carried out with the VIRACam instrument at the Calar Alto Observatory. The studied area corresponds to two fields located at a distance of 9.7 kpc from the nucleus, covering about 14 square degrees on the galaxy's disk. We also present our analysis of the luminosity and metallicity profiles, based on spectroscopy of 82 giant branch stars from the fields studied in VVV. The innermost parts of the galaxy (r< 10 kpc) follow a well known negative metallicity gradient. We find that the outer parts of M33 have a flatter gradient than the inner regions, and that, at a galactocentric distance of 30 kpc, the metallicity is solar. We discuss different formation scenarios for M33, such as cooling flow accretion, and merger and compare them with the derived profile for the mean stellar metallicity. We find that the best agreement between the metallicity profile and the formation scenarios is achieved assuming that most of the outer regions of M33 were built up via mergers of dwarf galaxies. Our result suggests that major mergers could have played an important role in the evolution of M33 and the build up of its disk.

Ultrasonic slip has been measured in a Newtonian fluid flowing in a controlled-slip round thread coil using a torsional ultrasonic oscillator. The fluid was found to slip by up to 14% over a range of Froude numbers (0.2–0.8). The measurement method is considered and some implications for fluid turbulence and drag reduction are discussed. mirror A method of measuring ultrasonic slip in a Newtonian fluid has been presented and evaluated. The slip was found to reach up to 14% over a range of Froude numbers (0.2–0.8). The measurement method is considered and some implications for fluid turbulence and drag reduction are discussed. ! Published on arXiv.org 2112.00485v1, 12 December 2019. Author: P. E. Jewell. later A method of measuring ultrasonic slip in a Newtonian fluid has been presented and evaluated. The slip was found to reach up to 14% over a range of Froude numbers (0.2–0.8). The measurement method is considered and some implications for fluid turbulence and drag reduction are discussed. The slip was measured using a torsional ultrasonic oscillator (TOU) – a type of vibrometer – which allows a fluid to be illuminated from many different directions, and measures the Doppler shift of the reflected sound to determine fluid velocity. The fluid was seeded with acoustic bubbles, and the motion of the bubbles was used to detect the slip. Previous work using this technique has found ultrasonic slip over short, localized regions1,2,3; however, this is the first time that such measurements have been made over a broad range of flow conditions and resulted in a slip profile. The implications for fluid turbulence and drag reduction are discussed.

A REM (Rapidly Extensive Method) interface to the simulation of dynamical mean-field spin glasses is introduced. This interface allows one to perform parallel simulations of finite temperature dynamical mean-field spin glass dynamics in the wide range of time and length scales. The proposed interface is specialized to handle fully connected random matrices. We study the relaxation of a mean-field spin glass model with probability distribution of Ising interactions defined by a Gaussian random matrix to the equilibrium distribution using the REM. In particular, we compare the average relaxation time τRSA calculated with different existing methods. τRSA obtained by the REM is consistent with the theoretical prediction 1/log(N), where N is the system size. For N=10^4, τRSA = 13.2, consistent with 1/log(N) = 13.2/9. REM: Rapidly Extensive Method; MFSG: Mean-field spin glass; CDM: Chained Decomposition Method; N: System size; log: Logarithm.

In this paper, we study the problem of node crystallization in large wireless networks, where the objective is to gatherly deploy multiple copies of a single node in the network such that the coverage area of each copy overlaps with that of at least one other copy, while taking power consumption and communication overhead into consideration. Node crystallization aims to maximize the number of covered nodes under the restrictions that (1) the coverage area of each copy cannot be larger than a predefined size, and (2) the distance between two copies must be greater than a threshold. We refer to the process of solving this problem as node crystallization. We first present an exact algorithm to find a solution for case of two copies, and then generalize the algorithm to solve the problem for any number of copies. However, the running time of the presented algorithms is exponential w.r.t. the size of the network. To solve this problem, we develop an algorithm with a near-linear running time, and conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of our algorithm as well as the running time of the presented algorithms. Our simulation results show that our algorithm can achieve near-optimal solution within a few minutes even for networks with thousands of nodes.' Node crystallization in large wireless networks has two key features that make it different from existing wireless network deployment problems. (1) The communication and computational capabilities are sufficient in each node to participate in the formation of multiple copies, thus the formation of multiple copies does not require the all nodes in the network to participate simultaneously, and the process of node crystallization can be executed in a distributed manner. (2) The restriction on the coverage area of each copy, which limits the interference among copies, makes it possible to guarantee the formation of multiple copies without requiring full global information of the network. In summary, node crystallization has the potential to realize scalable wireless networks by allowing distributed formation of multiple copies of nodes.

Parity violation in hydrogen has been studied for over 40 years. The observation of this phenomenon was the first clear sign that protons are not purely spin 1/2 particles, but have a smaller angular momentum component, called spin 1. This is the first systematic study of parity violation in hydrogen from the recently-released full datasets of the PREM parlance-free database, covering the period from Jan 2008 to Dec 2019. The energy and direction-dependent effects are inferred from the difference between the spectroscopic and static or Darwin values of the electron axial coupling constant a0, measured in highly accurate optical rotation experiments. While the effect found in the earlier experiments has a 3.2σ significance, the more precise measurements nearly doubles that significance to 6σ. In addition, the difference between the direction-dependent and constant values of a0 is determined with a precision of better than 0.002 a0, further doubling the significance of the result. These observations increase the known violated parameters in the standard model by two, increasing its complexity without providing an obvious explanation.

At a critical power, the doubly resonant cavities provide the maximal chi2 and chi3 values. Both resonators are excited simultaneously and the sum and the difference of the fields amplitudes in the two resonators are exploited to generate the second and the third harmonics. The optimization of the excitation permits to obtain large values of the chi2 and chi3 parameters, with relatively low incident power. At the same time, the proposed devices are easy to manufacture. The optimization of the excitation with respect to the cavities dimensions and to the input polarization permits to obtain simultaneously large values of chi2 and chi3, opening the way to new generation of optical parametric devices with low cost, large efficiency and simplicity. The effect is robust against mechanical disturbances and could be exploited in gas and liquid media for harmonic generation with jet pumps or continuous wave diodes. The doubly resonant cavities permit to exploit non linear processes also at low incident power with respect to conventional resonators. In particular, chi3 is a more accurate metric than chi2 to estimate the efficiency of non linear processes, being able to discriminate the distortion effects due to the non linear process.

The quantum mechanical description of a two-dimensional (2D) electronic orbital in the plane perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of a carbon nanotube is analogous to the 3D spherical harmonics wavefunction in the azimuthal direction. The spatial symmetries of the 2D electronic orbitals in carbon nanotubes and the 3D spherical harmonics are united by realising that the 2D electronic orbital wavefunction is a linear combination of scalar spherical harmonics, whose form factors determine the spatial symmetries of the 2D electronic orbitals. When these form factors are expressed as the products of two 2D Delégliseÿ polynomials, they are analogous to the spherical harmonics projections on the Laplacian eigenfunctions (i.e., the Pythagorean theorem for electronic orbitals). In addition to the spatial symmetries, the 3D spherical harmonics can also represent the energy eigenfunctions of the 3D spherical harmonic oscillators. The analogy between the spatial symmetries of the 2D electronic orbitals and the 3D spherical harmonics, and their corresponding energy eigenfunctions is the Kepler's law of planetary orbits. The simultaneous realisation of the spatial symmetries of the 2D electronic orbitals and their corresponding energy eigenfunctions by means of the Delégliseÿ polynomial expansions of the form factors of the 2D electronic orbitals provides a quantum unification of the spatial and energy eigenfunctions and symmetries.

A-type stars are defined as having spectral types A0-A9, luminosities larger than the main sequence star with the same surface temperature, and color excesses near zero. These characteristics allow A-type stars to be easily identified in observational datasets. Pulsation is one of the key characteristics of A-type stars. However, the presence of A-type stars in open clusters can make it difficult to identify pulsation, as multiple stars in the same cluster are likely to be evolved relative to their surfaces temperatures. In this study, we examined time series photometry of 122 suspected A-type stars from the BELTESS survey to search for pulsation. We used the Box Least Squares (BLS) algorithm to find periodic signals in the data. We identified fourteen stars that showed evidence of pulsation, of which three are new multiperiodic delta Scuti (DSCT) stars. We identified ten pulsating B-type stars for the first time and updated the frequencies of seven known DSCT stars. We also discuss a newly identified suspect of A-type pulsation.

Recent theoretical research has suggested that the Poincaré symmetry, the symmetry of special relativity, might be a residual symmetry of a more fundamental high-dimensional conformal symmetry. On the other hand, the general theory of relativity and the standard model of particle physics are both formulated within the framework of a generally-covariant Galilean conformal algebra. By extending the conformal algebra with an additional $D$-dimensional Abelian algebra, a unification of general relativity and the standard model can be achieved with just five additional fundamental constants: the spacetime dimension D, the AdS radius R, the speed of light c, the unified gauge coupling constant g, and the Planck mass MPl. The Poincaré symmetry of special relativity is found to be a special case of the conformal algebra with D = 1, R = c = 1, g = MPl = 1. The particle masses are generated by the breaking of the conformal symmetry down to the Poincaré symmetry, and the pattern of symmetry breaking is consistent with the standard model of particle physics. A dynamical principle, such as the AdS/CFT correspondence, may underlie the underlying theory, as it does in the case of the standard model formulated within the framework of quantum chromodynamics. This work represents a remarkable merging of two of the most influential theories in physics, general relativity and the standard model, into a highly successful unification scheme with just five additional fundamental constants.

Star-forming dwarf galaxies (SFDG) are important systems in the early stages of galaxy formation. These small systems are efficient in their ability to form stars, therefore they are ideal laboratories for understanding the initial conditions of galaxy evolution. In this paper we present optical spectroscopy and spatially resolved analysis of 12 SFDG. We determine oxygen abundances and chemical abundances patterns using both direct method and strong line methods. We also explore the spatial distribution of the chemical elements and study the relationships between different parameters. Our main results can be summarised as follows: 1. We found extremely low oxygen abundances with higher values of 12 + log(O/H) estimated using the R23 method compared to the Pettini & Pagel’s (2004) strong line method. 2. We did not find any correlation between oxygen abundances and kinematic radial velocities. 3. Calcium abundance seems to decrease with the increasing radius. In contrast, sodium and aluminum abundances seem to increase at large distances from the centers. 4. We did not find any correlation between chemical abundances and structural parameters of the galaxies. However, we noticed a correlation between SFR and chemical abundances. We also found a very high fraction of SF regions with 12 + log(O/H) values lower than 8.2, which is a threshold used by many authors to distinguish between normal and low-metallicity regions.

Recent cosmological simulations of galaxy evolution have reproduced the morphology-density relationship and star formation rate - density relationship observed in local galaxies. These simulations, however, cannot reproduce the full distribution of galaxy properties at both low and high redshift. It has been suggested that feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGN) and quasars may play a role in regulating star formation in their host galaxies. In this paper, we present high resolution, cosmological, hydrodynamical simulations of a sub-set of galaxies in a single volume of a large, modern simulation, in which a simple model for radio-mode feedback is included. The model is characterized by a constant Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion rate onto the supermassive black hole, which is adjusted so that the AGN contributes a specified amount of radio heating to the interstellar medium. We have selected a simulation which is volume-limited and resolves all galaxies above a given mass, and which includes the effects of stellar feedback, AGN feedback and the evolving gas properties from the larger simulation. We find that even without AGN triggered starbursts, the momentum input from radio mode feedback is enough to significantly disrupt the cold streams which form the core of cooled galaxy clusters, and thus suppress the formation of bright ellipticals. At the same time, this feedback is not sufficient to disrupt the clusters completely. In lower mass galaxies, below the critical cluster mass, we do not see significant suppression of star formation, although we do find a decrease in the concentration of stellar metallicity and stellar density. We conclude that while radio-mode feedback is an effective regulator of star formation in the early universe, it alone is not sufficient to reproduce the full distribution of galaxies across the Hubble sequence.

Four quasars with redshift greater than 6 are reported in this paper. The discovery was made by the Canada-France High-z Quasar Survey, which is designed to find high-redshift quasars using the Magellan Telescopes and Chandra. The observation details are presented and the results are discussed. This is the first finding of highly-redshift quasars using L,M,N band flux density. It suggests a new pathway that quasars shine at high-redshift above magnitude i=22. The Canada-France High-z Quasar Survey (CFHQS) is designed to find high-redshift quasars using the Magellan Telescopes and Chandra. Starting in 2008, our team has conducted a major programme, targeting 5 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) with photometric redshifts that indicate they are at high redshift. The spectroscopic results for these targets are presented in this paper. Based on observations with the Magellan Telescopes and Chandra, the z=6.42 quasar is the most distant object known, and the first AGN at redshift greater than 6 identified using only optical/near-infrared photometry. The CFHQS J0648+1516 is a radio-quiet quasar with a black hole mass of 2 x 10 6 solar masses and a Eddington ratio of 5%. The radio luminosity of the quasar is 10% of the value predicted by the $M_{\rm BH}$-M_B^ *, pseudo-bolometric luminosity relation for z < 2.2 quasars, suggesting the accreting material in the quasar is significantly truncated. This result is consistent with the peak of quasar activity occurring at lower black hole masses at higher redshifts. The first five years of the CFHQS programme have produced a total of 10 quasars at redshifts 6.0 < z < 6.7, and three more quasars at higher redshifts up to z=7.2. In addition, we have found one z=4.76 quasar that was not selected for the original quasar search. The z=4.76 quasar is the most distant object known until now, and the most distant z=4 quasar discovered by any large programme. Among these sources, four have black hole masses 2.5 x 10 6 solar masses, similar to the largest galaxies in the universe. This discovery suggests the formation of massive black holes and their host galaxies may be related. The Canada-France High-z Quasar Survey has continued to make rapid progress, and in 2014 alone we discovered six new quasars with redshifts greater than 5.5.

The absolute calibration and characterization of the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS) cryogenic mission is an ongoing project at the Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI). Here we describe the methods and results of the stellar calibrator sample (SCS) study for the 24 μm calibration. The SCS is a sample of bright, isolated, stars that are used to characterize the calibration and validate the data reduction and analysis techniques. These stars are used as references against which observations of other, fainter, calibration standards can be compared. The resulting spectra are compared with model spectra to derive the magnitude, spectral type, and overall variability (Stellar Parameter Classification; SPCLASS) of the stars as well as the characteristics of the emissions from circumstellar dust (DIRBEdust) and the instrument itself (PSFdust). We discuss the variation of these quantities as a function of both stellar properties (luminosity, effective temperature, color, variability) as well as the properties of the calibrator. In all cases we find the parameters obtained for the calibration sample to be within the expected ranges. We present the spectral type, luminosity, and effective temperature distributions for the calibration sample and describe the observed trends in these properties with variability, stellar color, and variability. We find the effective temperature and variability of the calibration sample to be consistent with expectations. However, we find a deficiency of stars with spectral types M0-M2 and luminosity greater than 2.2 × 10log(L/L⊙). While we cannot explain the lack of such stars, we suggest a number of hypotheses for its origin including variability-induced selection effects as well as a decrease in the number of low-mass M-type stars due to disk evaporation. We compare the observed properties of the calibration sample to those predicted by theoretical models of low mass star formation. Finally, we describe the work toward a global calibration and spectral mapping of the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the photosphere and the DIRBE and PSFemitted dust. The STScI MIPS instrument team and SCS managers include: Alan Marconi, Tom Soifer, Ari Laor, Ilse i. Goldman, Tim Harrington, Amir Yeh, and Edo Serabyn. The SCS is supported by JPL, Caltech, and STScI. Data presented herein were obtained at the Gemini Observatory ( Hawai‘i ), which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, Inc., under a cooperative agreement with the NSF on behalf of the Gemini partnership: the National Science Foundation ( United States ), the Particle Physics and Astronomy Research Council ( United Kingdom ), the National Research Council ( Canada ), and the National Science Council of Republic of China (Taiwan ). This work is supported by the Spitzer Science Center and the Space Telescope Science Institute, which are operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, Inc.

Using data from the 100-meter Green Bank Telescope, we show position-velocities diagrams for the maser emission coming from a Keplerian ring around a young stars. Such diagrams, showing a Keplerian rotation curve with no other trace of evidence for intruding masses, are typical signatures of dark rings. We show that the available data are consistent with a power-law brightness distribution for the ringlets and that the parameters of the fit favor a compact distribution of the masers, in better agreement with the expected distribution for dark rings rather than for an irregular thin ring. We conclude that the available data are consistent with the hypothesis of a dark ring around the young star IRAS 16293-2422 and speculate about its potential interaction with the main ring. F. Mazzetti et al. "Position-Velocity Diagrams for the Maser Emission coming from a Keplerian Ring." Astronomy and Astrophysics 784 (February 2019). doi:10.1051/astro-2019-30033

In this work, we consider an online scheduling problem in the CONGEST model, in which machines have unit-size jobs that can be executed in any order. We focus on deterministic strategies in which, for any input, the jobs are executed in some order, and we measure the performance of a strategy using its makespan: the maximum load over all machines. We ask how to achieve low makespan for a range of problems in the cell phone tower repair scenario, where a single facility has to periodically replace some of its existing cell phone towers with newer, taller ones. Each job corresponds to a tower and has to be placed in a minimum number of visits to the facility. A schedule is feasible if no job is executed more than once on the same machine. We study this problem for the case where the list of jobs is obtained by pulling jobs from a pool using a probability distribution over the jobs. This distribution may represent actual user requests for tower repair, though we emphasize that our approach can be applied to other scenarios as well. We give a formal model for this problem, and we design admissible schedulers for different classes of distributions. We then prove lower bounds for any scheduling algorithm, and we characterize the optimal strategy for the Poisson and the uniform distribution. Our results show that, for these distributions, the best makespan is either achieved by always scheduling exactly one job, or by always scheduling an exact amount of jobs, whichever is smaller. The best average makespan is achieved by a simple, between-the-two- extremes strategy, in which the fraction of machines used is proportional to the square root of the expected number of jobs. Finally, we implement an admissible scheduler, and we report performance results for our rule-of-thumb strategy as well as for the optimal strategies for the uniform and the Poisson distributions. We also introduce a generalization of this model, in which a single facility serves a set of jobs, and the goal is to minimize the maximum load over all machines. We again characterize the optimal strategies for the uniform and the Poisson distributions, and we show that our between-the-two- extremes strategy also achieves low makespan in this more general model.

Pyrex and silicon glasses are widely used in different applications in chemistry, biochemistry and materials science. Surfaces of these materials are typically smooth and have no relevant chemical functionalities. Since atoms in solid surfaces possess stronger bonds to their neighboring atoms compared to those in the bulk, they are less prone to move under the influence of thermal or mechanical perturbations. One way to chemically modify glass surfaces is to expose them to particles of strong chemical etching solutions. These solutions contain strong bases that can etchant glass surfaces and strong acids that can deposite functional groups such as -CF3, -OH, -O- and -N= on the surface. Blasting glass surfaces with sharp particles results in creation of these functional groups in random and repetitive patterns. Depending on the patterns, these patterns are called discrete or continuous. Discrete patterns are composed of regular shapes that can be easily identified. In contrast, continuous patterns are composed of randomly distributed functional groups and are significantly harder to parse. In this paper, we report on our studies of the dependence of patterns formed on glass surfaces after blasting them with particles on the size and material of the particles used. We also describe our efforts to characterize these surfaces using various spectroscopic techniques.

Galaxy clustering is a powerful probe of the large-scale structure of the Universe and provides unique tests of gravity on these scales. This is because, unlike galaxy surveys, weak gravitational lensing and standard cosmological parameters such as the amplitude of matter fluctuations or the abundance of light neutrinos, deviations from Newtonian gravity (DNG) affect the growth of structure. Using the Lagrangian perturbation theory, we performed a fully general relativistic analysis of the effect of DNG on large-scale structure, which yields the modified evolution for the density fluctuations and their present day cluster or bispectrum. As a preliminary test, we have carried out an analysis of the effect of DNG on the non-linear power spectrum. We find that DNG would generate a percent-level correction to the halo mass function. To obtain more accurate constraints, we forecast the effect on the bispectrum of the B modes, which is a next-generation gravity probe. We show that the amplitude of the bispectrum is proportional to the sixth power of the non-linear growth factor, and that by constraining DNG with the B-mode clustering we can probe deviations as small as 1% at $k=0.1~h~Mpc^{-1}$ (comoving) with only 30,000 galaxies in the range $0.1 < z < 2.1$.

The generalized Freedman-Townsend model is an effective field theory of SO(3,1) symmetry, with a global SO(3,1)×SO(d,1) symmetry, spontaneously broken down to SO(3,1) symmetry with d additional global SO(d,1) symmetries. This model includes the usual Freedman-Townsend model with d=3 as a special case. We investigate the compactification of this model on an S^4 with SO(4) isometry. We obtain the scalar potential, the graviton, the three Goldstone bosons, the would-be Nambu-Goldstone boson and their mass spectra. layer.
