Einstein's general theory of relativity is a powerful theory that has withstood all experimental tests thus far. However, recently released hypothesis suggest that the theory might not be complete and that it might leave open the possibility of rogue solutions, so-called wormholes. Wormholes are tunnels that could connect two distant regions of space and time. The existence of wormholes would mean that information could be transported from one distant region to another faster than the speed of light, thus violating the tensor constraint of the theory. Here I propose that Gödel's incompleteness theorem might prevent general relativity from being fully self-consistent and that this would imply the possibility of wormholes. If correct, this would resolve the black hole information paradox and significantly modify our understanding of gravity. G\"odel's incompleteness theorem states that any finitely axiomatizable partial theory in a formal language that contains the basic arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency. This suggests that general relativity, which contains the basic arithmetic, might not be self-consistent. In particular, if general relativity withstood all experimental tests thus far due to the absence of rogue solutions, then this implies that the theory might not contain all the assumptions necessary to prove its own consistency. If this is the case, then there exists the possibility of wormholes, which would allow information to be transferred between distant regions of space in a faster than light manner, violating the tensor constraint of the theory. If correct, this would resolve the black hole information paradox and significantly modify our understanding of gravity. In particular, this would imply that general relativity might not be fully predictive and that new physical phenomena might arise from rare situations within the framework of the theory. This hypothesis remains to be proven, but it is a logical possibility that general relativity might not be fully self-consistent and that this would imply the existence of wormholes. If correct, this would significantly change our understanding of gravity and resolve the black hole information paradox.

In this work, we study the covering number of the exponential of a matrix and the behavior of its approximation by the cut-off matrix. This matrix can also be seen as a limit of a sequence of positive definite matrices. Under various assumptions on the sequence we show that the covering number of the cut-off covering spectrum is equal to 1, therefore the cut-off matrix can be approximated by the exponential of the matrix in the cut-off covering spectrum. We apply this result to stochastic matrices, band matrices and positive definite matrices. We also study the connections between the cut-off covering spectrum and the peripheral spectrum, the algebraic and topological sepctra. The cut-off covering spectrum was introduced in a recent work [1] where it was used to approximate matrix functions with bounded variation. In this work, we build on this approach to study various properties of the cut-off covering spectrum. [1] B. Barman, M. Tikhomirov, B. Zhu, Covering numerical range with exponential of a matrix, (2018). https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.00754

Neutron, deuteron, and Mercury EDMs are constrained by experiments, and recently the existed constraints on the neutron and Mercury EDMs were largely superseded by new measurements. In the framework of minimal supersymmetry without R parity (MSSS), we calculate the quark loop contributions to neutron and Mercury EDMs, and find that the contributions can account for the new data and are much more naturally large than previous expectations. For example, for the MSSS scenario with heavy gluino and light sbottom, the calculated neutron EDM can reach $|d_n|\sim 10^{-26} e$ cm, which is close to the experimental upper limit and far beyond the previous best values. Therefore, the MSSS scenario is strongly constrained and could be tested in the ongoing or upcoming experiments. This article discusses the neutron and Mercury EDMs in the framework of minimal supersymmetry without R parity (MSSS). We calculate the quark loop contributions to neutron and Mercury EDMs, and find that the contributions can account for the new data and are much more naturally large than previous expectations. For example, for the MSSS scenario with heavy gluino and light sbottom, the calculated neutron EDM can reach $|d_n|\sim 10^{-26} e$ cm, which is close to the experimental upper limit and far beyond the previous best values. Therefore, the MSSS scenario is strongly constrained and could be tested in the ongoing or upcoming experiments.

We present a general framework for generating approximate nearly horizon-skimming orbits in Kerr spacetime, and apply it to derive families of circular and non-circular orbits that have near-zero Carter constant. The Carter constant measures the slope of the effective potential and hence the stability of the orbit. Our solutions cover a broad parameter range, including nearly circular orbits with arbitrarily small radii, as well as eccentric non-circular orbits with high Lyapunov exponents and tilted angles of attack. In a suitable limit, all these orbits approach the critical value of the dimensionless angular momentum at which both the circular and the non-circular orbits in circular restricted three-body problems are circular. Additionally, we describe a family of non-circular orbits with the maximum possible value of the tilt of the orbital planes, including the novel circular orbit with two revolutions per period. All these orbits are essentially stable over one orbital period, as their instability radii are several orders of magnitude larger than the orbit radius. Our results may find potential applications in the study of gas accretion onto supermassive black holes and the high-energy emission from their accretion disks, especially in connection with relativistic jets.

Simulations have been performed to study the structure of the boundary layer between a white dwarf and its accretion disk. We solve the Euler equations of hydrodynamics, including self-gravity of the gas and nuclear energy production term in the energy equation. The equations have been solved in a Cartesian grid domain with dimensions of 1000 x 1000 x 300 Schwarzchild radii of the white dwarf. The models presented have explored the effects of varying the strength of the nuclear energy production term and the mass flux through the inner boundary. It is found that in all models a sufficiently strong nuclear energy production term leads to the formation of a shock transitioning across the inner radial boundary. In addition, it is found that a modest mass flux through the inner boundary results in the formation of a persistent boundary layer structure. In particular, we find that the presence of a boundary layer greatly alters the emission spectrum of the system. It is expected to result in double-peaked emission lines, such as the C III emissions lines detected in the cataclysmic variable AE Aquarii. We also find that there is significant supersonic motion in the boundary layer, likely accounting for the persistent broad emission line components observed in some systems. The simulations presented in this work were performed with AMRAII, a three-dimensional, three-dimensional, resistive, hydrodynamical simulation code developed at the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics in Garching, Germany.

Recent measurements of the hadronic parameter $\alpha$ by a large B physics community has lead to a flurry of research on the implications of these measurements. Reparametrization Invariance, an under studied property of the $\chi$Expand[α] model independent analysis technique used to extract α, implies that α is not a physical parameter. However, α has the useful property that α = 0 is an boundary of the allowed parameter space for theckmfit. Consequently, α is often interpreted as the minimal value of an angle. With that in mind, we apply reparametrization invariance to the strict no New Physics (SNP) case, where α = 0, and to the general 1% SNP case. We find that α can only have a posterior probability greater than 99.9% that it is non-zero if there is no SNP, and a 95% probability that α is non-zero if there is only a 1% probability of SNP. Thus, the current data does not disfavor α being zero. However, α must be studied further in the SNP case as a way to quantify SNP.

In this paper, I investigate the dynamical stability of polytropes, which are bodies formed by rotating uniformly an entropy stable solution of the Spherem equation. Polytropes are generalizations of the ideal gas law, and are typically represented by the function : p = K ⁢ ( 1 + θ - 1 ) 1 + θ ⁢ ⁢ ⁢ where ⁢ ⁢ θ ≥ 1 , and K is a constant. I find that polytropes are generically dynamically unstable, with three different instabilities. The first, called the radial runaway, occurs when the velocity of sound waves in the polytrope, computed with a linearized Lagrangian, is real and has the same sign as the derivative of the potential energy with respect to density. When this occurs, density fluctuations grow and the sound waves carry negative energy away from the region of stability. The second instability, called the angular runaway, occurs when a sound wave with positive energy traveling along the rotation axis changes sign in the rotating frame. This occurs when the sound wave velocity in the meridian plane, computed with a linearized Lagrangian, is real. Lastly, the polytrope becomes unstable to modes that simultaneously compress and distort the polytrope, a type of hydrodynamic instability not present in an isothermal gas. For each of these instabilities, I find a threshold amplitude at which the instability occurs. I then show that polytropes with zero radial velocity of sound are dynamically stable, as are polytropes with constant radial velocity of sound. The constant radial velocity of sound polytropes have been proposed as models for dark matterhalos.

In this paper, we study a two-component symmetric exclusion process (ASEP) on a one-dimensional lattice with open boundaries. The boundary sites are injected and extracted with species-dependent rates. This system can be realized as a lattice gas model with one type of particles (ASEPs) that hop to the right and an other type of particles (holes) that hop to the left. In the ASEP without extraction, the system exhibits phase separation: ASEP particles form domains surrounded by a gas of holes. When the extraction rate exceeds a critical value, the system undergoes a phase transition to an active state: Active sites become depleted and holes rush to the boundaries and accumulate at the extraction sites. A pair of density and flux gap are identified at the transition point. The model with two components generalizes the ASEP to asymmetric exclusion processes (ASEP(2)) in which both ASEPs and holes hop to the right and left with different rates. The behavior in the open boundaries with two species of particles is much richer than the previously studied cases with one species. For example, the two-ASEP(2) system shows three phases: gas, coexisting liquid, and active liquid. The density and flux gaps exist only in the liquid phases. We identify the order of the phase transitions using spatially resolved kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in a new axiomatic approach to physics, called the deformation principle. This framework allows one to rigorously formulate physical theories without referring to particular solutions or parametrization. Instead, one works with a locally-defined action, which, for specific applications, may be chosen to approximate the systems of interest. Invariant properties of the action are used to define the corresponding models. In particular, dynamics are represented by a formal path integral. A model is called physical if the action is stationary with respect to all possible deformations of the model within a given equivalence class. The resulting theory is then fully consistent and independent of the choice of the action. An explicit example of a gravitational model following from this approach is given. The main idea of the deformation approach to physics is that all physical theories may be treated as special cases of a larger, generic scheme, and it is the deformation principle which provides the unifying mathematical framework. This approach can be applied not only to classical, but also to quantum theories, in particular, to quantum gravity.

Primate brains are among the most complex among mammals, and show a high level of variability across species. While there is extensive evidence for structural and functional connectivity between regions of cortex in non-human primates, much less is known about the connectivity patterns within single regions or between regions of different functional networks. In this work, we used graph analysis to predict features of cortical connectivity from anatomical and functional properties of individual brain regions. We first created weighted, signed, and correlated structural networks using MRI data and a new measure of cortical surface distance. We then predicted network connections between brain regions by training a machine learning model using brain region-specific values of topological and spatial node properties. The model was able to predict positive and negative weights for networks with correlated structural and functional connection data, predicting stronger positive weights between regions with similar topological and spatial node property values, and weaker positive or negative weights between regions with different values. When trained on a subset of data and tested on held-out data, the model could also predict connective networks that were significantly similar to observed structural and functional networks. These results demonstrate that features of node-specific topological and spatial properties can predict features of their connectivity, suggesting that these properties may play a causal role in determining the observed connectivity patterns.

In string theory, Wilson loops provide a powerful tool to analyze the classical string configurations. For more general gauge theories, in particular for quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at large nucleon momentum transfers, the color confinement is better described by quark-antiquark bound states, or mesons, rather than freely moving colored fermions. In particular, a fundamental quantity in the QCD calculation of the hadronic spectrum is the Wilson loop, which, in the light-front formalism, is defined as the path-ordered exponential of the gluon field along a closed loop $C$ in space-time. The fundamental representation of the gauge group is usually chosen. The dependence of the Wilson loop on the loop dynamics is more complicated. In particular, the area law for large loops is no longer true. For small loops, the area law is modified to be proportional to the perimeter of the loop $C$. This phenomenon is called perimeter law. The relation between the area and perimeter laws has been observed for more than 40 years. Recently, by using the supergravity in eleven dimensions, a string theory realization of a long Wilson loop in the fundamental representation of the $SU(N_c)$ group is proposed. The corresponding string configuration is the graviton with one temporal and one spatial infinite size. This allows a detailed comparison between the field theory and gravity results. For finite-size loops, new Quantum Mechanics-like phenomena may arise. For example, it may admit discrete energy levels with a spectrum linearly proportional to the area of the loop. In this article, we present a more general class of string configurations, which are the finite-size gravitons corresponding to loops with arbitrary shapes. We use the second fundamental representation of the $SU(N_c)$ to represent the loops. The corresponding gravity background is a truncation of type IIB supergravity on S^5 x T^{11}. The quantum mechanics-like spectrum on such backgrounds has been studied before. In particular, the different classical shapes of the loop have different behaviors for the quantum mechanics-like states. We also propose a string interpretation for the observed spectra. Finally, we briefly discuss the implications of our results to QCD and discuss possible future work.

In this paper, we explore a cosmological scenario where the observed accelerated expansion of the universe is driven by the curvature instead of a dark energy fluid. The background spacetime is described by a solution to the Einstein field equations with a non-positive constant curvature. The acceleration of the universe occurs because the spatial sections of the universe have an effective negative curvature that causes the volume of the universe to grow more rapidly than the surface area. The transition from a decelerating to an accelerating phase of the universe occurs because as the curvature inspired dark energy density increases the effective equation of state of the universe crosses the -1 barrier. We discuss how the model can accommodate recent observational data and generate a successful inflationary era leading to the current period of accelerated expansion. The background spacetime is described by the $$ ds^2 = -dt^2 + a^2(t)d\vec{x} \cdot d\vec{x} $$ where the scale factor satisfies the following equation $$ \ddot{a} + \frac{\dot{a}}{a}\left(3H + \frac{1}{\Lambda}\right) + \frac{\Lambda}{3}a = 0 $$ This can be derived by writing the metric in the form $$ g_{\mu \nu} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & a^2(t) \end{pmatrix} $$ and splitting the Einstein tensor in terms of the spatial divergence and the trace. The constant $\Lambda$ sets the magnitude of the effective negative spatial curvature. We set the scale of this curvature to be $a^{-2}$ and choose the numerical value of $\Lambda$ so that the present day expansion of the universe is standard luminosity distance based upon the Hubble parameter $H_0 = 100 h \ \mathrm{km} \ \mathrm{s}^{-1} \ \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ given an assumed value of the Hubble constant $h$. Then, $\Lambda \approx -0.82 h^{-2}$ is a suitable value. The solution is expressed in terms of the conformal time $\eta$ where the scale factor is given by $$ a(\eta) = \begin{cases} \cosh(\sqrt{|\Lambda|/3}\eta) & \Lambda < 0 \\ \eta & \Lambda = 0 \\ \sinh(\sqrt{|\Lambda|/3}\eta) & \Lambda > 0 \end{cases} $$ This describes a universe that initially has a positive effective spatial curvature that becomes increasingly negative and eventually mimics a positive cosmological constant in the far past and the far future. The transition from the decelerating phase to the accelerated phase of the universe occurs at $$ \eta_T = \sqrt{|\Lambda|/3} \ln \left( \frac{3}{2|\Lambda|} \right) $$ This

The W3 giant molecular cloud (GMC) is a prominent region in the constellation Aquila. Located some 20 kpc away, W3 is one of the nearest grand design spiral galaxies and hosts an extreme cluster of massive young stars. Historically, W3 has been used as a prototypical GMCs with significant ongoing star formation. In this study, we present far-infrared and submillimeter data from the Herschel Space Observatory, as well as molecular line and radio continuum data from the data archives, to characterize the star-forming content of W3. Far-infrared and submillimeter data are an ideal probe of thermal dust emission, which is well-correlated with young stellar populations. We find that W3 has a bolometric luminosity of 9.5 x 10^9 L⊙ and a total mass of 1.2 x 10^10 M⊙. At a column density of 1.87 x 1021 cm-2, its mass surface density is 221 M⊙ pc-2. We estimate that W3 has a mass of 250 x 10^3 M⊙ within its estimated star-formation density threshold of 2.2 x 10^4 M⊙ pc-2. This suggests that star formation is ongoing within W3 but is not significantly active. In this context, W3 likely does not qualify as a typical GMC with significant ongoing star formation, but rather is a very massive, very old (5-10 Myr), quiescent, and extremely dense star-forming region.

Simulating non-small cell lung cancer with a multiscale agent-based model could provide insights into therapy efficacy and optimization. Existing NCI MaM models are limited in their scope, simulation time, and heterogeneity resolution, and their clinical translation has been limited. We developed MADMaM, a multiscale agent-based model of the lung, that addresses these shortcomings. We developed MADMaM to perform thousands of individual simulations in clinically plausible time frames for therapy evaluation. MADMaM includes representations of non-small cell lung cancer cell phenotypes, stroma, immune system, and vascular and lymph systems. We calibrated MADMaM by comparing simulations with empirical clinical data from patients with extensive stage non-small cell lung cancer treated with radiation combined with targeted therapy. MADMaM exhibits clinically relevant heterogeneity in cell phenotype, stromal abundance, immune cell infiltration, and vascular density and connectivity. Simulated therapies exhibited expected effects on tumor growth and response. Simulated immune-cell infiltration agreed with independent observations. MADMaM may be used for large-scale therapy evaluation and optimization, facilitating the development of precision therapies for non-small cell lung cancer.

Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are fast-spinning, strongly magnetized neutron stars. Binary MSPs are routinely detected in close orbits about their companion stars, and some of these systems become radio loud due to interaction between the pulsar and its companion star in a process known as accretion disk ablation. The very similar solitary MSPs are much less frequently detected, and have thus far been found in about half of transient gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). These systems, lacking companion stars, are expected to be radio quiet. Here we report the detection of PSR J1453+1902, a solitary MSP previously known only at 1400 MHz, for which we obtain a 1.4 GHz pulsed radio upper limit that is more than an order of magnitude deeper than the average of other solitary MSPs. We use the Large Sky Area Multi-band Transit Satellite (LSAM). We compare the upper limit on the radio luminosity of PSR J1453+1902 with the distribution of radio luminosities for the much more commonly observed binary MSPs and find it to be a very high-luminosity outlier. We therefore suggest that PSR J1453+1902 is the first solitary MSP found in a transient GRB.

Astrophysical accretion, resulting from the collapse of large scale structures or galaxy mergers, is a widespread phenomenon which shapes the evolution of galaxies and the structure of the Universe. Despite of the fact that a significant amount of energy is released due to gravitational potential, most of the energy is trapped on relatively large scale of a few Kpc. Here we propose a mechanism to tap a significant amount of energy, that is radiated away due to gravitational potential, through the thermonuclear instability of gas on sub-kpc scale. We find that when the gas temperature exceeds the ignition temperature, $T_{ign} \sim 10^{10}$ K, nuclear reactions start and the accretion disk becomes thermally unstable. As the instability proceeds, the disk expands, radiate more energy, and further increases its temperature, leading to a positive feedback cycle. The energy released from the nuclear reactions, called Novel Nuclear Instability, NNI, is estimated to be $\sim 10^{50} - 10^{52}$ erg, which is much larger than typical gravitational binding energy of the disk, $\sim 10^{49}$ erg. This indicates that NNI is a more efficient energy reservoir than gravitational potential and can power quasar activity for a long time, ∼1010 yr. The feasibility of this scenario is tested with three dimensional radiation hydrodynamics simulations. The nuclear reaction effectively increases the disk temperature, leading to the positive feedback cycle. The NNI is also found to lead to the ejection of high velocity shells, which could explain multi-wavelength broad emission lines and high velocity offsets in some quasars. Our findings suggest a new paradigm for supermassive black hole growth: rapid growth via merging of sub-kpc scale nuclear disks, rather than through cold gas clouds.

Moons around other worlds are called exomoons. To date, fewer than ten exomoons have been identified via direct detection, most of which are satellites around Mars-sized planets. This is in part due to the small size and low surface gravity of exoplanets compared to terrestrial planets in our own solar system. "Super-Earths" and "mini-Neptunes" have sizes similar to many Earth-mass exoplanets but possess densities like small celestial bodies such as satellites or comets. This makes it difficult for current telescopes to resolve these worlds, as the low surface gravity and size make them appear roughly the same angular size as the planet they orbit. One method to detect exomoons is via the transit method. Planets gravitationally interact with their satellites, causing them to move around the parent star in a deterministic fashion. Transiting exomoons will appear to "perturb" the timing of transits of the parent star, causing variations in the star's illumination pattern. Timing these variations with high precision can in principle determine the mass, radius, and density of the satellite. We used observations from the K2 mission to identify an exoplanet with a large, likely partially transiting exomoon, and used time-variability analysis to determine the satellite's mass, radius, and density. The exomoon exhibits substantial deviations from a pure atmospheric density model, and we speculate on possible origins for this novel structure.

Graph codes are a powerful family of error-correcting codes that find many applications in storage, transmission, and computation. For high performance, usually high rate codes are desired. But for high rate codes, maximum a-posteriori (MAP) decoding (optimized for maximum likelihood (ML) decoding) often requires large graph sketches that cannot be stored or transmitted efficiently. In this work we consider codes optimized for source/channel coding and binning. We introduce the concept of graph codes that are optimal for source/channel coding and binning (called cCBC-optimized graph codes). We then describe a simple algorithm to construct graph codes that are cCBC-optimized. We apply these codes to the compression problem and show that they allow to reduce the bandwidth of sum product decoding by a factor of 2, at the cost of only a small increase in storage. We also apply these codes to the problem of shaping and show that they allow to reduce the buffer size of list joint source channel coding by a factor of 2, at the cost of only a small increase in computation.

Using observations from the Fermi Gamma Ray Space Telescope, we have detected gamma-rays from 37 supernova remnants (SNRs). The gamma-rays are dominated by hadrons, with a smaller component from bremsstrahlung. The observed gamma-ray spectra are well fitted by a single power-law in kinetic energy, with indices between 2.0 and 2.7. The gamma-ray efficiency, the fraction of supernova explosion energy deposited in the form of gamma-rays, is about 1% for young SNRs and increases with age as the amount of shocked gas increases. Hadronic gamma-ray production rates are a few percent of the historical yields, suggesting that cosmic-ray particles propagate through a dense medium with relatively mild interactions. We conclude that the observed gamma-rays are consistent with production in nuclei interactions with background protons, although uncertainties in the local cosmic-ray density and composition are large enough to allow significant contributions from electrons and Dark Matter particles. The detection of gamma-rays from young and middle-aged SNRs without corresponding radio synchrotron emission challenges existing models of gamma-ray production in SNRs.

Topological cluster classification, which organizes clusters according to the topology they possess, has proved to be very useful for understanding phase diagrams and for capturing phase coexistence. In this paper, we present a topological classification of clusters in condensed phases, where the global symmetries of the system are taken into account. We illustrate our method by applying it to several important types of clusters, such as islands, stripes, and bubbles. Furthermore, we show that our classification has direct physical interpretations, connecting the different classes to different phases, including solid, smectic, nematic, and cluster phases. As an example, we apply our classification to the rich phase diagram of the easy-plane anisotropic Heisenberg model, where our analysis explains recent numerical work on the nature of cluster phases. Overall, our classification provides a natural way to organize clusters in condensed phases according to the phase in which they occur. This will be of great utility for understanding phase diagrams and for capturing phase coexistence.

In this Letter, we report experimental and theoretical results on the oscillatory behavior of the magnetization in a free layer in the proximity of a magnetic layer with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. This system constitutes a building block for spintronic memory devices in the form of racetrack memories. By using point-contact samples with a conductive atomic force microscope, we are able to drive magnetization oscillations with a spin-polarized current at room temperature. We characterize the resulting damped harmonic motion by measuring the Nyquist plot of the magnetization, from which we retrieve the Gilbert damping parameter and the amplitude of the magnetic forces exerted by the reference layer on the free layer. We demonstrate that the amplitude of these oscillations are strongly dependent on the value of the damping parameter, which is known to be a material property. In addition, we observe a spin-torque induced frequency shift of the mechanical oscillator, which depends on the frequency of the driving current. These two observations illustrate the strong influence of damping and frequency on the dynamics of the magnetization. Based on micromagnetic simulations, we show that both effects can be attributed to spin-polarized current-driven domain wall motions in the reference layer.

The present paper is concerned with geometry of parallelizable manifolds in the context of generalized Lagrange spaces. We introduce the concept of (generalized) Lagrange structure and establish the corresponding characterization theorem, which extends the classic result by Sir J.L. Synge to the broader framework of generalized Lagrange spaces. Furthermore, we present the notion of (generalized) Lagrange vector bundle and establish an expression for the curvature of such a bundle, which generalizes the celebrated expression for the curvature of a Yang-Mills vector bundle. As a first application, we establish a Hamilton–Jacobi–Maupertuis principle in the context of generalized Lagrange spaces. As a second application, we discuss the corresponding constrained Hamiltonian dynamics and establish the corresponding phase-space characterization theorem. In particular, we establish a version of the transport equation for any projectable vector field on a generalized Lagrange space, which generalizes the celebrated transport equation for projectable vector fields on Riemann manifolds. As a third application, we discuss the geodesics of Lagrange-Rund geodetic structures on a generalized Lagrange space and establish the corresponding integral curves. As a fourth application, we discuss the moment maps of Hamiltonian group actions on generalized Lagrange spaces.

In this study, we present new spectra of the transitions between the ground states, D1 line at 50892.334 Å and the D2 line at 58946.523 Å, which are strongly sensitive to the magnetic field. We observed variations of the integrated intensity and polarization parameters of the D1 line and of the ratio between the intensities of the D1 and D2 lines, which we observed in the vicinity of MDI surface field data, acquired with the Deep Space Climate Observatory (DSCO). The correlation between the intensity variations of the D1 line and of the DSCO data was r = 0.85. We also observed a decrease in the ratio between the integrated intensities of the D1 and D2 lines, which correlated with a decrease in the field strength, according to the MDI data. This decrease is probably related to the emergence of the new magnetic region on the Sun's surface. We obtained the average vector of the MDI field for the time period between February 2001 and January 2003. In this time interval, a weak region emerged near the center of the MDI field, with a magnetic field of 50 G. The new region has a total area of about 10,000 km2, which is approximately one-tenth of the solar surface. The field strength in the emerged region has decreased to about 45 G. The correlation between the variations in the D1 line intensity and those in the MDI data indicates that the new region may have played a role in the observed variations in the intensity of the D1 line.

Tori are circular ring domains in the complex plain. The complex affine linear transformations of the complex plain that preserve the torus structure form the Lie algebra of the modular group. This Lie algebra is semisimple and has an irreducible representation of highest dimension. This yields the highest dimension of a torus that can be extended to a projective linear group. A higher-dimensional torus can be extended if and only if the corresponding Lie group can be equipped with a projective linear structure. This happens if and only if the dimension of the torus is a prime number that is either 2 or 3 or a multiple of 4. A modular group torus is 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, or 48-dimensional. The 48-dimensional torus has the simplest properties. It can be extended to a projective linear group that preserves a quadratic form. This quadratic form defines the projective projective linear group. A normal subgroup of the modular group with a similar action on the torus is the full modular group or a subgroup of it generated by a 2-element rotation and a 6-element translation. This yields the projective projective linear groups: projective rotations, projective special orthogonal groups, projective special linear groups, projective symplectic groups, projective orthogonal groups, projective unitary groups, and the exceptional symplectic group. Each torus preserving subgroup of the modular group is isomorphic to one of these groups. The projective linear groups act on the 48-dimensional torus transitively and their orbits cover the 48-dimensional projective projective linear group. The corresponding Lie algebras are isomorphic to one of the following: the algebra of pseudo-orthogonal transformations, the algebra of special linear transformations, the algebra of symplectic transformations, the algebra of orthogonal transformations, the algebra of unitary transformations, or the exceptional Lie algebra. The exceptional Lie algebra is the unique algebra of dimension 27 admitting an irreducible representation of highest dimension. All other Lie algebras admit extensions that preserve the quadratic form that defines the corresponding projective projective linear group. This yields one projective projective linear group per algebra of special transformations and one projective projective linear group per special orthogonal, symplectic, orthogonal, unitary, or exceptional group. This article analyses these extensions in the case of the algebra of pseudo-orthogonal transformations and the algebra of exceptional transformations.

Astronomers using the Submillimeter Array (SMA) have made the first clear detection of the Infrared Extinction Law (IEL) at extreme depths in a dark cloud core. Previous studies suggested the IEL could be violated at extreme depths in dark cloud cores, potentially due to the effects of dust opacity. We observed clear evidence for the IEL at far-infrared and submillimeter wavelengths toward the center of the starless core L1544 with a dust opacity of ~2.2 cm-2 g-1 at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. This is the first clear detection of the IEL in a dark cloud core and the first direct evidence of the existence of interstellar dust at depths of more than 20 Marcellin masses (about 17 MMSN). We present high-resolution 1.3 mm observations of the core L1544 made with the SMA. We have imaged the dust and gas contents of the core, finding clear evidence of the Infrared Extinction Law at a wavelength of 1.3 mm, the first clear detection of the IEL in a dark cloud core and the first direct evidence of the existence of interstellar dust at depths of more than 20 Marcellin masses (about 17 MMSN).

A geometric invariant theory (GIT) approach to the moduli spaces of stable rank 6 bundles over smooth projective algebraic curves is presented. A remarkable family of vector bundles over the curve C0(x,y,z)y3+x3z+x2z2+xz3+z3, with Hilbert polynomial 3×(n+1)(n+2), is constructed. It is shown that the corresponding [stable] variety of vector bundles is isomorphic to the F4-curve. A concrete realization of the F4-curve as the moduli space of smooth cubic surfaces in P3 is given. This invariant theory approach allows us to construct a moduli space of stable vector bundles over the above curve. This moduli space has the property that it is isomorphic to the F4-curve. It is shown that the F4-curve can be realized as the moduli space of cubic surfaces in P3. This curve has an interesting geometry and carries a remarkable family of vector bundles.

We present the first precision measurement of strange form factors in the nucleon, $K^+\Lambda_c$ and $\bar K^0 \Sigma^+$, using recoil polarisation asymmetries in deep inelastic e + p and neutrino + p scattering. We compare our results to a global parameter-free analysis of nucleon strange form factors using data from a wide range of processes and observables. Our results show good agreement with global analyses of existing data, however, we find significant discrepancies at the 2.5 σ level for the strange magnetic and strange electric form factors, when comparing to our data. We identify the sources of these discrepancies and consider alternative hypotheses to explain our results. If these discrepancies are confirmed, it will have significant implications for our understanding of the flavour structure of the nucleon and will likely necessitate the introduction of new degrees of freedom to the standard model description of low-energy particle physics.

Resolving the spectra of individual galaxies is one of the most promising methods to measure their physical properties, as it would allow to separate starlight from active galactic nuclei (AGN) and potentially to map the spatial distribution of different types of galaxies. While recent large surveys like the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS; @SDSS) have provided large samples of spectra of galaxies, their analysis still requires significant effort. Modeling individual galaxies, on the other hand, is time-consuming, as it requires the knowledge of numerous parameters that describe a galaxy. A combination of the two approaches — a library of synthetic galaxy spectra, which would parametrize the basic properties of galaxies and allow to fit the spectra of individual galaxies, could significantly simplify the process of galaxy spectrum analysis and could be a key to unlock the full potential of current and future spectroscopic surveys, like the Gaia mission. To this end, we have started building a library of synthetic galaxy spectra, based on state-of-the-art physically-based models of galaxies, which we are making publicly available to the community. Here, we present the first results of the galaxy sample classification based on a Random Forest algorithm, trained on a sample of 3 million galaxy spectra, which we made available together with the library. We show that it is possible to separate the library galaxies according to four basic properties: starlight fraction, AGN fraction, the spatial distribution of the starlight and the physical size of the galaxies. We also present preliminary results of the preliminary parametrization of unresolved galaxies in the Gaiaspectro library by means of Random Forest regression.

We develop a polymer quantum mechanics (PQM) where the fundamental variables are continuous twists on a non-compact group, whose Lie algebra is an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. The Hilbert space of the quantum polymer is the space of sections of a vector bundle over the group with the standard fiber at the unit element, whose Lie algebra is identified with the abovementioned one. The coordinate algebra of the polymer is completed with respect to a natural invariant trace. This allows us to construct an invariant Schrödinger equation on the entire space of continuous twists. The quantum polymer is also shown to be continuously deformable to the standard (commutative) quantum mechanics, where the polymer-like features appear as a self-similar fine structure in the spectra of some exactly solvable models. We also show that the polymer quantum mechanics can be approximated by a corresponding sequence of ordinary quantum mechanics for increasingly large degrees of polymerization, with errors vanishing in the limit. The limit transition can be performed in two steps. In the first step, the continuous twists are replaced by a projective limit of finite-dimensional matrix groups with the normal subgroup that keeps only the diagonal elements and the corresponding subalgebras. In the second step, these matrix groups are replaced by their projective limits, which are the compact Lie groups. Finally, we show that the strong operator limit of the corresponding sequence of ordinary quantum mechanics corresponds to the commutative limit of the polymer quantum mechanics.

A set of differential equations for modeling transient enhanced diffusion in shallow ion-implanted layers is presented. The proposed model combines kinetics of the surface layer transport with diffusion equation in the entire depth of the implant. It accounts for three physical processes in the diffusing atoms transport: spatial non-stationarity of the process rate, temporary trapping and subsequent release from the surface defects states, and diffusion in the defect-related channels. The equations are solved numerically for a number of examples and the obtained results are compared to the outcomes of the Monte-Carlo simulations. The proposed model provides an adequate description of the diffusion transport in the wide range of the physical and geometrical parameters of the process and has the ability to reproduce the directional dependence of the atomic flux density. The online version of the paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.02546 The author is ELI ALHADI,corresponding author: elhadi@elma.media.mit.edu Paper title: Set of equations for transient enhanced diffusion in shallow ion-implanted layers. Added: Feb 20, 2020. Developed and tested on the examples of hydrogen and helium ion implantation in silicon. Citation: Alhadi ELI, Eliassafi S, Eisenkraemer E, Roy KV (2020). "Set of equations for transient enhanced diffusion in shallow ion-implanted layers". Communications in Computer and Information Science, 425: 445-453. DOI: 10.1016/j.cins.2019.11.024.

V1186 Scorpii (Nova Scorpii 2004 #1) was observed by P.A. van der Werden on 2004 October 22.5 (UT dates are used throughout this document) using the telescope at CTIO, Chile. This was approximately 10 days before its typical optical peak at γ = -15.2 magnitude. The early spectral evolution can be divided into 3 distinct phases. During phase I the emission is characterized by a steeply rising blue continuum and strong emission lines of HeII, CIV, and NV. No broad band emission is present. The Balmer continuum subsequently grows in intensity as phase II commences. In this phase II, the helium emission weakens while stronger emission lines of NIV, SiIV, and CIV appear. At this stage, the Balmer continuum has increased in intensity and is able to produce broad emission components, corresponding to an observational characteristic of Nova spectra. The spectrum eventually moves into phase III with a distinct decline in the emission line intensities. At this stage, the spectrum resembles that of a Wolf-Rayet star. The classification of this star is likely a intermediate type Nova and is remarkable for the early appearance of the characteristic Wolf-Rayet spectrum.

Small balls in high dimensions have been studied extensively in recent years. In particular, a central question in this field is whether or not a small ball in high dimensions remains the Euclidean unit ball with appropriate dimension-dependent radius. Inequalities for such dimension-dependent radii have been established for both even and odd dimensions but their sharpness has been widely open. In this short note, we show that a sharp dimension-dependent radius inequality for odd dimensions fails to be sharp for even dimensions. More precisely, for n ≥ 3, we construct odd dimensions n + 1 and even dimensions n such that the n + 1 small balls of dimension n + 1 around the origin form a Clifford's Multivector. By comparison, n small balls of dimension n around the origin do not even form a vector space. We also discuss some of our immediate applications of these findings to general quantization theory. We also discuss some of our immediate applications of these findings to general quantization theory. The main theorem and its corollary below address this issue. More precisely, for n ≥ 3, we construct odd dimensions n + 1 and even dimensions n such that the n + 1 small balls of dimension n + 1 around the origin form a Clifford's Multivector. By comparison, n small balls of dimension n around the origin do not even form a vector space. We also discuss some of our immediate applications of these findings to general quantization theory. The main theorem is the following: Let n be a positive odd integer. For each x ∈ Rn+1 with |x| < (4/3)n, there exists a rotation θ around the origin such that θ * x = 0 and thus |θ * x| = |x| < (4/3)n. This theorem tells us that the boundary of the unit n + 1 dimensional ball around the origin in Rn+1 does not intersect the interior of the unit n dimensional ball around the origin in Rn. To see this, note that if x/|x| = (x 1, x 2,..., x n + 1)/x 1 could be written as (4/3)n for some θ around the origin, then θ * x/|x| = 0, which is a contraction. As a corollary, we have the following: Let k and n be integers such that k ≤ n and n is odd. Then n − k is even. The article argues that a negative Poisson ratio in a metallic glass is a signature of a liquid-like behavior rather than a solid-like one. Such a behavior is commonly expected for a system in a vibratory excitation at a GHz frequency. However, to reach such a conclusion the authors statistically analysed the already published data from much lower frequency vibrations and came to the conclusion that the data does not support a solid-like behavior. I reanalysed the same data and I conclude that the analyzed data does in fact support a solid-like behavior, and even a liquid-like one for the specific composition of the sample. found that the analyzed data does in fact support a solid-like behavior, and even a liquid-like one for the specific composition of the sample. * The authors conclude that the observed frequency dependence of the Poisson ratio is more consistent with a liquid-like behavior than a solid-like one. The data indeed seems to be more consistent with a liquid-like behavior rather than a solid-like one. However, it is unclear whether the actual observed frequency dependence is indeed more consistent with a liquid-like behavior. In the authors’ own Figure 3, the Poisson ratio does not seem to approach -1 at low frequencies (the predicted value for a liquid). In addition, the authors did not test the prediction of liquid theory that the Poisson ratio is independent of frequency (if the sample is indeed a liquid). More data at different frequencies is needed to draw a more quantitative conclusion. The article can be improved by adding more analysis of the existing data to reach a more quantitative conclusion.

Noise in the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE) is an important aspect that can often be overlooked in the study of this novel state of quantum matter. Both emission and absorption noise have been theoretically predicted to occur in the FQHE. While emission noise can affect transport measurements through the sample, absorption noise cannot and can be observed via noise spectroscopy. We present two distinct experimental realizations of this noise spectroscopy, one utilizing microwave radiation and another optical Raman scattering, both of which are in good quantitative agreement with theoretical calculations of emission and absorption noise in the FQHE. This noise spectroscopy is an essential tool to study transport in the FQHE and will enable future studies of many-body dynamics in this quantum many-body system. This study of noise in the fractional quantum hall effect (FQHE) is an important one as often a study of this novel quantum state involves overlookinh the noise aspects of the FQHE. Emission noise can affect transport measurements through the sample but absorption noise cannot and can be observed via noise spectroscopy. We present two distinct experimental realizations of this noise spectroscopy one using microwave radiation and another optical Raman scattering, both of which are in good quantitative agreement with theoretical calculations of emission and absorption noise in the FQHE.

We analyze the motion of a local volume of approximately 1.2 billion galaxies, located roughly 10 billion light-years distant in the Shapley Supercluster, away from the Local Void. Our data indicate that roughly 5% of the galaxies in this volume have recently entered the Local Void from behind the Shapley Concentration, with a significant portion of these galaxies being accreted in the last 7 billion years. The galaxies in our volume that have recently exited the Void have average velocities relative to the Local Group of 1,660 ± 460 km/s, some 20% of the LG's recession velocity at the present day, implying these galaxies have been propelled away from the Void at 39,000 ± 11,000 km/s. We compare our results to cosmological simulations, finding good agreement given that these simulations under-represent the effects of background structures on galaxy motion. These measurements have important implications for our understanding of the Shapley Concentration, the role of the Local Void in the broader context of the observed cosmology, and the efficacy of simulation methodologies.

Deep inelastic neutron scattering (DINS) was used to study the low energy in-plane transport properties of single crystalline YBa_2Cu_3O_6+x (x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5). Surprisingly, for all compositions studied, a well defined magnetic dispersion curve was observed in the low energy regime. This dispersion curve crosses the low energy transverse acoustic phonon branch at // q = 2 q_D, yielding a strong magnetic resonance peak. The presence of this resonance in the excitation spectrum of the antiferromagnetism leads to a peak in the in-plane thermal transport at a wavevector of // q = 2 q_D. This // q = 2 q_D peak has not been observed in previous studies of the in-plane thermal transport in YBa_2Cu_3O_6+x using Raman spectroscopy or in-plane thermal imaging. The // q = 2 q_D peak grows in size and intensity with decreasing temperature until it reaches a maximum intensity at T = 60 K. This // q = 2 q_D intensity maximum coincides with the half-height temperature of the low temperature in-plane magnetic susceptibility, as determined by both DC susceptibility and Mössbauer spectroscopy. We suggest that this // q = 2 q_D peak is directly linked to the presence of static antiferromagnetic order in YBa_2Cu_3O_6+x, as it only appears above T = 60 K in materials that exhibit long range antiferromagnetic order.

A team of scientists from South Korea, Germany, and the United States has succeeded in loading nearly $10^{7}$ single $^{1}$S$_{0}$ calcium atoms into an optical dipole trap (ODT). The team was able to load $^{1}$S$_{0}$ calcium atoms in a continuous manner by using a magnetic micro-fluidic trap and an optical dipole trap, instead of a conventional two-step procedure which requires stopping the atomic flow to load the atoms into a magnetic trap. The high atom number in the ODT allows for efficiently loading not only multi-optical traps (MOTs) but also single-optical tweezers (SOITs). The longterm ability to load a large number of atoms into an optical dipole trap opens up new possibilities for studying many-body physics with degenerate quantum gases. The loading of $^{1}$S$_{0}$ calcium atoms into an optical dipole trap (ODT) has been demonstrated by several research groups. In this work, a nearly pure atomic sample with nearly $10^{7}$ atoms is loaded in a continuous manner by using a magnetic microfluidic trap and an optical dipole trap. The continuous loading scheme not only provides the opportunity to load many-optical traps (MOTs) but also single-optical tweezers (SOITs). The high number of atoms in the ODT not only makes it possible to study many-body physics with degenerate quantum gases but also holds the promise of a wide range of applications in quantum information science and precision measurements.

The node deleting is an important strategy in the network structure perspective. It can imitate the attack on the nodes in the network and reflect the relationship between the nodes. It can also reflect the performance of the network from different angles. The 1%–40% node deleting has a very important influence on the scale of the network. It can achieve the network topology change and also has an important influence on the characteristic parameter of the network, such as the node degree distribution. This paper analyses the influence of different deleting strategies on the characteristic parameters of the network, including the node degree distribution, average shortest path, clustering coefficient, and so on. At the same time, we give the algorithm to achieve these deleting strategies. The experiment results show that 1%–40% node deleting has a very important influence on the network structure. When the deleting strategies change from 1% to 40%, the performance of the network is from the robustness perspective gradually damaged. The network characteristic parameters are affected significantly.

Anomaly mediated supersymmetry breaking (AMSB) is a promising paradigm for explaining the weak scale without the need for a Grand Unified Theory (GUT) at the expense of introducing additional parameters. We propose that, in addition to the AMSB contribution to the gaugino masses, there is a F-term contribution to the scalar masses which depends on the anomalous dimensions of the relevant fields. We show that in a wide range of plausible models this generates the right order of sfermion masses and avoids tree-level flavor violations. Furthermore, we present one explicit model realizing this paradigm. Phenomenologically this model has the distinctive feature of generating a Higgsino-like LSP with a mass in the several hundred GeV range. --- Signatures {#signatures.unnumbered} ========== The LHC has already set strong constraints on many SUSY parameter spaces. The main challenge of the AMSB paradigm is explaining the weak scale without the need for a GUT. The most relevant parameter space for AMSB are m0, the initial scale of SUSY breaking, and tanbeta, the ratio of the two Higgs v's. Generically m0 is expected to be of order 10-100 TeV. In such high scales we expect the MSSM to be broken. However, in order to avoid anomalies, a GUT is generally required to give masses to the Higgses and to certain scalar partners. Typically this requires a E$_6$ or SO(10) GUT. These additional GUT models normally introduce a large number of extra parameters. Anomaly mediated SUSY breaking (AMSB) is a viable realization of the weak scale without the need for a GUT. In AMSB SUSY breaking is mediated by the trace of the gauge boson kinetic energy, as opposed to gravity mediation which is mediated by a graviton. Thus the SUSY breaking scale is closely connected to the strength of the gauge groups, and not directly related to the GUT scale. Anomaly mediated SUSY breaking has three distinct features. First, the first two generation scalar masses are zero at the unification scale, and are generated by one loop. This avoids the need for a complicated doublet-triplet splitting mechanism. Second, there is a large mass gap between scalars and fermions. This avoids flavor violation. Third, the sleptons and squarks are often the lightest sparticles, therefore requiring R parity. We propose a new paradigm of GUT-less AMSB. In this paradigm the gauginos and third generation scalars receive a one loop AMSB contribution to their masses, mamsb, while the scalars and first two generations, as well as the Higgs, receive a F-term contribution to their masses, MsF. The sfermions of the first two generations receive a direct tree-level mass from the spurion associated with the breaking of EWSB. The F-

On 2014 December 24, a massive outburst was detected from the eclipsing slim hydrogen-burning star EX Hydrae. It has been observed in highcadence mode, which enabled us to precisely follow the outburst evolution. The initial outburst showed an exponential decay with a characteristic timescale of 12hr, but later on it showed a rebrightening after exponential decay with a characteristic timescale of 3.5hr. Additionally, a dwarf-nova-type rebrightening was observed after the second exponential decay. Using multi-wavelength data, we constructed the outburst profile in several energy bands and found that the energy generation mechanisms were changing during the outburst evolution. During the initial exponential decay, the outburst energy was dominated by the residual nuclear energy generated by the gradually cooling accreted material. During the later stages, it was likely powered by the release of gravitational energy as the accreted material further cooled and settled into a steady state.

Hot Molecular Cores (HMCs), traced by powerful and synchronous maser emissions, are an important signpost for the investigation of high-mass star formation. In this article, we present simultaneous multi-wavelength observations of a sample of HMCs (G33.82+0.10, G34.26+0.15, and G35.80-1.75) with the Very Large Array (VLA), the Methanol Multi-Beam (MMB) survey, and the NRAO 12-meter Telescope. We find that all three HMCs show bright ammonia (23 ${\rm km~s^{-1}}$) emission and 24 GHz continuum emission with a detection rate of 100%. We calculate the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the ammonia and 24 GHz continuum emissions, which indicates that all three HMCs possess thermal-infrared components. In addition, we find that there are steep spectra at both ammonia and 24 GHz continuum wavelengths, suggesting the presence of cores with bright thermal emission. We also compare our results with existing single-dish observations of methanol masers, ammonia, and 24 GHz continuum emissions and conclude that the three HMCs contain multiple high-mass clumps. Finally, we discuss some implications of our results for the early evolution of high-mass stars and high-mass cluster formation.

In this note, we construct IIB supergravity backgrounds with five-form flux, and show that they solve the equations of motion of the theory with zero entropy. We focus on the warped product structure and consider an Ansatz with two internal three-tori and one external geometry. We present explicit solutions on each of the internal spaces and show that they are compatible with the equations of motion. The resulting solution is smooth, and has an AdS3 factor in global coordinates, and a warped AdS4 geometry. We then show that the total solution has zero entropy. To do so, we consider an alternative conformally flat metric, and show that it has zero Killing entropy. We conclude by discussing some further directions for this note, such as developing the solutions we find as M-theory backgrounds, and computing their dyonic spectra. This work was performed at the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, under the auspices of the Planck Sciences Community and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada. This note is based on a talk given by one of the authors (James implements) at the Black Holes and Gravity Program at the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics in Santa Barbara, California, on February 7-9, 2018.

Reconnection is an important process that shapes the energy release in many magnetised systems, such as the solar atmosphere, the laboratory magnetosphere and in Earth’s magnetotail. In these systems, large-scale structures reconnecting and evolving on time-scales of tens of seconds to tens of minutes – micro-scales. In this Letter, we show that a kinetic approach to reconnection – the electromagnetic tearing mode – resolves a number of micro-scales. The process is inherently global, connecting across scales, and produces steady-state solutions in agreement with recent simulation. Moreover, in the limit of strong guide fields, the model is reduced to a wave equation and solutions are easily constructed in appropriate physical variables. We conclude that the tearing mode is an important micro-scale process that resolves the slower-evolution reconnection dynamics, and predict that plasmas with high energy e.g. in the solar atmosphere, will manifest a steady tearing-mode reconnection regime.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used to image living subjects and provides a non-invasive method for diagnosis and monitoring. However, images are distorted by artifacts due to turbulent Transport of dissolved gasses within the subject's body. Here, we present a theoretical framework to study the efficiency of MRI-induced turbulent transport. We perform a global parameter survey to identify the most impactful dimensionless numbers for imaging. We find that the importance of these numbers depends on the region of interest (ROI). In the case of the abdomen, the rate of molecular diffusion is the most impactful number, while the effectiveness of the MRI signal in the ROI depends most strongly on the Larmor frequency and the ratio of magnetic susceptibility and the volume-averaged field strength. In the brain, the volume-averaged field strength is the most impactful number. The efficiency of MRI-induced turbulent transport depends on these numbers in complicated ways. The optimal MRI protocol may depend on the ROI, requiring synthesis of local images based on global parameters. Our results provide a foundation for developing new strategies for optimizing MRI protocols.

New close binary systems were found in the data release five (DR5) of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. These systems comprise a white dwarf and a companion that is a possible low-mass black hole, a pre-white dwarf, a red giant, a neutron star or a main-sequence star. In addition, the search for magnetic white dwarfs in these close binary systems is presented. This paper focuses on the new close binary systems discovered in the DR5, but we also present the results of the search for magnetic white dwarfs in these systems. A description of the new binary systems is presented, and information about the optical variability of the systems is provided. We find 14 new close binary systems with a possible low-mass black hole, 2 new pre-white dwarf systems, 5 new red giant star systems, 2 new neutron star star systems and 2 main-sequence star systems. We find that SDSS J012952.08+141444.7 is a double-lined spectroscopic binary system, while SDSS J075005.88+321644.9, SDSS J080754.76+202304.2, SDSS J082803.53+272832.4, SDSS J084942.94+093831.8 and SDSS J091339.96+224909.3 are trinary systems. The low-mass black hole has a mass range of 7.5-15 M Sun and the companion star has a mass between 0.8 and 5 M Sun. The companions are most likely red giant or neutron star stars. Some of these new close binary systems have the potential to evolve into cataclysmic variable systems. SDSS J091339.96+224909.3 is a good example of this, since this system has the characteristics of a symbiotic system, since the low-mass black hole is orbiting around the red giant star and the system has strong emission lines. We present the results of the search for magnetic white dwarfs in these close binary systems. We find no new magnetic white dwarfs. SDSS J142914.74+111559.6 and SDSS J082803.53+272832.4 have already been identified as magnetic white dwarfs. In summary, we present 14 new close binary systems with a possible low-mass black hole, 2 new pre-white dwarf systems, 5 new red giant star systems, 2 new neutron star star systems and 2 main-sequence star systems.

High redshift galaxies are known to exhibit strong neutral and ion outflows (e.g. Schenker et al. 2013;Trainor et al. 2015).The presence of strong winds at high redshifts poses a challenge for successful reionization, as Lyman limit systems (LLS) produced by these winds potentially suppress transmission of ionizing radiation from the first galaxies.We present the results of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations which demonstrate that the strong winds observed in some of these galaxies are broadly consistent with observations of the $\ Hogan\alpha$ absorption feature, suggesting that the associated LLS may not have fully suppressed the ionizing background. Although the exact frequency and distribution of such systems as well as their spatial structure are sensitive to various assumptions made in the modeling of high-redshift gas, these winds could have significantly contributed to the total ionized volume fraction at $z>6$ without requiring over-production of LLS by the simulations. Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations were used to investigate neutral and ion outflows from galaxies at high redshift ($z\sim6$). Simulated galactic winds are broadly consistent with observations of the Hogan alpha feature, suggesting that the associated Lyman limit systems may not have fully suppressed the ionizing background. Although the exact frequency and distribution of such systems as well as their spatial structure are sensitive to various assumptions made in the modeling of high-redshift gas, these winds could have significantly contributed to the total ionized volume fraction at z>6 without requiring over-production of LLS by the simulations.

On 2013 August 15, the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.) Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) detected an excess of gamma-rays from the region of the Galactic plane close to the position of the star ESO 243-23. The emission is spatially and temporally consistent with that expected from the interaction of a energetic particle beam with interstellar matter. The most likely origin for this beam is the putative pulsar B0127+11, the most plausible of at least seven identified in the vicinity of ESO 243-23. The observation of gamma-rays in the spectrum of the putative pulsar suggests that it may be powered by a radio pulsar wind, as is the case for the famous Crab pulsar. Assuming this is the case, the energy release by ESO 243-23 in the form of gamma-rays has implications for the energy loss of the putative pulsar compared to expectations, and so the possibility of the system being a pulsar wind nebula (PWN) is considered. The paper examines the theoretical relationship between the properties of PWN and those of their pulsars, as well as whether the properties of ESO 243-23 can be reconciled with those of a PWN. It concludes that the evidence is not yet conclusive as to whether ESO 243-23 is a PWN, but that such an identification would be striking and suggest a possible link between the source of the energetic particle beam and the wind of the associated pulsar.

Relativistic jets are key to the observed phenomenology of active galaxies. Such jets carry away the angular momentum of the central black hole and collimated region, and therefore must transport energy and mass efficiently to offset their loss through jets. In contrast to non-relativistic winds, relativistic jets can stabilize through entrainment of external gas; however, there are also numerous examples of collimated outflows that are unstable to global modes. This Letter presents the first-principles theory of such instabilities in the relativistic hydrodynamic and magnetohydrodynamic regimes, and describes how the growth rates and saturated amplitudes of global modes depend on the background accretion and jet parameters. In particular, we find that the most unstable modes are local perpendicular modes and non-axisymmetric torsional ones, with the former growing faster and likely driving rapid variability. This Letter provides the theoretical foundations for interpreting the rich phenomenology of relativistic jets, and motivates intensive scrutiny of systems with the potential to destabilize via these processes.

Uncompensated charge doping or excessive charge localizations in conductive \theta-(ET)2X conductors can lead to Coulombic interactions and, consequently, phase separation or long-range order. The \theta transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDC) are particularly susceptible to excessive electron-lattice coupling, as evidenced by the observation of commensurate charge order at 1/2 the average electron density of the system. Despite this finding, the impact of electron-lattice interactions on charge order in \theta-(ET)2X remains poorly understood. Here we report theoretical evidence that lattice instabilities in \theta-(ET)2X can drive charge order through rapid decay of quantum spin liquid (QSL) states, even in the absence of spontaneously broken symmetries. We predict that charge order in \theta-(ET)2X should exist at quarter-filled, 1/4 electron per unit cell, which is a density previously observed to coexist with a proximate spin-liquid state. In this case, a proper description of the coexistence region should account for mutual biasing of competing orders by strong, frustrated coulomb interactions. As an illustrative example, we propose that charge and spin order in \theta-(ET)2X may be stabilized via explicit coupling to an emergent Higgs mode of the spin liquid. Finally, we propose that QSL states can be tuned into critical phases with emergent fluctuating charge order, through subtle symmetry breaking arising from a temperature dependent lattice distortion. Our work establishes a proximate relationship between the electron-lattice interaction and the nature of charge order in \theta-(ET)2X, and highlights the potential for exotic orders to emerge near QCPs with strong frustration.

In this work, we develop a novel approach to study the contact process (CP), a stochastic process that reflects the evolution of the concentration of infected individuals in a population where individuals either have or do not have the CP. In the case of a homogeneous and neutral environment, the CP belongs to the directed percolation (DP) universality class. In the presence of quenched disorder, the system exhibits two distinct phases. For high infection rates, the system is in the absorbing disordered phase, where each realization of the disorder has one or more active absorbing states. For sufficiently low infection rates, the active phase extends over the entire infinite volume limit and the system is in the inactive disordered phase. Here, the average number of infected sites, <I>, decreases with system size but remains non-zero. We study the CP in the active phase where we can assume the existence of a small deviation from average values, known as a supercritical series expansion. This approach is exact in the limits of high and low infection rates and provides a quantitative description of the critical behavior at the phase transition between the active and inactive phases. We evaluate the $\beta$- and $\gamma$-functions that characterize the critical behavior, allowing us to determine the locus of the critical points in the parameter space of the model and to establish the universality of the phase transition. The non-trivial critical points are in excellent agreement with numerical simulations of the CP in one, two, and three dimensions on lattices of arbitrary size. Our results can be used to make predictions and simulate the critical behavior of various processes that can be represented as a CP with different values of the model parameters. The known universality of phase transitions and the presence of quenched disorder make CP interesting for applications in a variety of areas, such as catalysis, epidemic spreading, and interface dynamics.

NGC 5033 is a Sy 1.5 galaxy, located in the Fornax Cluster at a distance of 22.4 Mpc. It has a massive active galactic nucleus (AGN), which is also the power source of the observed broad optical and ultraviolet lines and strong X-ray emission. Continuum emission at centimeter wavelengths from this source has been little studied. We have carried out new cm-wavelength continuum observations with the Very Long Baseline Array that reveal a core-jet structure for the first time. The spectrum, which is fairly flat from 80 to 6 cm, is consistent with optically thin free-free emission from a thermal electron population with a temperature of approximately 0.2 keV. The derived cm-wavelength flux density is approximately 110 mJy, which corresponds to a luminosity of L ∝ 1.2 × 10 31 W. This is slightly higher than the values estimated from lower-frequency measurements, but it is within the errors of those estimates. We speculate on the possibility that the cm-wavelength spectrum is affected by free-free absorption.

A wide-field imaging survey identified 500 Cepheid variables in the galaxy NGC 4838. The HSOY global Survey mapped these Cepheids over a 3.2 sq. degree region of the galaxy in the g, r, i, and z bands. Combined with existing optical data, this yielded a sample of distant Cepheids with WLM, the local group galaxy located just below the ordinary galaxies in the Local Group. This allows the distance to the galaxy to be determined without the assumptions inherent in local galaxy distances, such as the Hubble flow. This technique can be applied to more galaxies in the local volume and will allow for a greater understanding of the impact of local galaxy density on local group formation. Neutrinos streaming out of a supernova enter the earth and may interact with the constituents of the earth. These interactions can reveal signatures about the nature of neutrinos. In particular, recent studies have suggested the possibility of non-standard interactions (NSI) of neutrinos withStandard Model (SM) particles. These interactions, if present in nature, could reconcile various experimental findings, such as theexistence of dark matter, the mass differences among the neutrino species, and the reactor anomaly. We study the sensitivity of forthcoming supernova neutrino experiments to NSI parameters. We show that several existing experiments already place significant bounds on these parameters, and that upcoming experiments will be able to probe a sizable region of the NSI parameter space. In particular, we show that the DUNE experiment will be able to probe NSI parameters up to tenths of an power of GeV. This opens up the exciting possibility of probing new physics with supernova neutrinos, which could revolutionize our understanding of the universe.

We study the nature of the continuous phase transition in the three-dimensional random field Ising model by using extensive numerical simulations. We find that the distribution of the magnetization exhibits a second order phase transition at the critical temperature, with a non-zero magnetized fraction in the ordered phase. Our analysis using the spherical approximation for the critical components shows that the order parameter distribution belongs to the same universality class as the three-dimensional Blume-Capel model. In addition, we observe hysteretic behavior in the magnetization that changes sign between the paramagnetic and magnetized phases, suggesting that the zero temperature phase transition is of first order. We carry out our simulations on a three-dimensional hypercubic lattice with Gaussian random magnetic fields with zero mean and power-law form dependence on the distance between the sites. The critical exponents obtained from the critical scaling of the Binder cumulant and the leading irrelevant variable correction to the magnetized volume fraction at the phase transition agree with the mean field results and the values predicted by the spherical approximation for the leading irrelevant variable.

In this work we consider a model for the early universe with a dynamical scalar field and a Chaplygin gas. The Chaplygin gas belongs to a family of models with a real scalar field with an effective negative pressure depending only on the density of the fluid. We assume that the radiation and the Chaplygin gas are two interacting fluids. We study the evolution of the corresponding scale factors and of the physical quantities describing the fluids. We show that this system of equations allows for a non-singular inflationary solution. Moreover, we compute the perturbations generated by this dynamics and we study their scale dependence. We show that the scalar spectrum of density perturbations is scale invariant for super-Hubble modes, in agreement with observations. Modeling the early universe as a dynamical system allows us to understand its evolution as the result of the interactions between its different components. This allows us to find non-singular inflationary solutions and to compute the scalar perturbations that they generate. Our results suggest that a model with a Chaplygin gas and radiation leads to a scale invariant spectrum of density perturbations, in agreement with observations.
