In recent years, the measurement of vibration-induced conductivity fluctuations has been suggested as an effective method for soil analysis. Conductivity fluctuation signals are readily obtained by instrumenting an area with many pairs of electrodes and measuring the electrical potential fluctuations between the electrodes caused by excitation with a broad-bandwidth noise source. Vibration-induced conductivity fluctuations are particularly attractive because they do not require a external excitation source and are inherently broad band. Thus, the effect of soil compositional and structure information can be decoupled from that of soil water content and temperature. In this study, we demonstrate that vibration-induced conductivity fluctuation signals can be used to characterize soil bulk density. Soil bulk density is related to soil particle size and is an important factor influencing soil settlement in active construction sites. The measured soil bulk density is validated with soil samples with known bulk densities collected from the same construction site. The validation demonstrates that the measured soil bulk density is proportional to the true bulk density with a correlation coefficient of 0.97. The relative measurement error is 4.3%. This study indicates that the measurement of vibration-induced conductivity fluctuations may have the potential to be used for in-situ soil bulk density analysis.

The rapid neutron capture process, known as the r-process, is responsible for most of the heavy elements in the universe. The fundamental properties of this process, including the reaction network, kinetics and site of the r-processing, are not well understood. This has led to a proliferation of models, each designed to reproduce specific aspects of r-processing, and a corresponding absence of consensus. While considerable success has been achieved in modeling key features of r-processing, including the solar system r-process andMESSie abundance, many r-process elements are over- or underproduced relative to the solar abundance and there is no consensus on the astrophysical site of r-processing. Moreover, the most rapid neutron capture process, known as the "ist875-a" process, continues to elude robust theoretical explanation. I will review the current state of understanding of the r-process and its associated astrophysical and nuclear physics open problems, and discuss potential solutions and avenues for progress.

Magnetar starquakes can emit high-energy photons via a process called central engineDisk instability, launched dipole radiation, or winds from a rapidly-rotating magnetar, can produce collimated outflows in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Historically, it was thought that these outflows were powered solely by energy lost by stretching of the GRB jet, which launches at nearly the speed of light. However, we demonstrate that collimated outflows can also be powered by baryon-loaded winds from a magnetar, and that the majority of observed GRB central engines are spinning down rapidly via this mechanism. If enough energy is coupled to the winds, then the outflow is mildly relativistic (Gamma > 2). The combination of baryon-loaded magnetar winds and ultra-relativistic jets remains a viable model for the observed diversity of long-duration GRBs. A rapidly-rotating neutron star (NS) known as a magnetar is a popular model for the central engine of long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). During a GRB, the surface of the magnetar may emit gravitational-wave (GW) radiation, which could power a cosmological population of highly-relativistic jets, in addition to baryonic winds. While some baryonic-wind models produce mildly-relativistic jets that could account for some of the diversity of long-duration GRBs, these models tend to over-predict the amount of energy that can be extracted from the central NS. We demonstrate that a better coupling of magnetar energy to baryonic outflows via neutrino annihilation or Poynting flux can solve this problem. In particular, we consider a combination of a baryonic wind from a magnetar with a mildly-relativistic jet, and find that the total energy coupled to the winds can account for the majority of long GRBs. We conclude that a model with a baryonic-wind component and a jet remains a viable model for the long-duration GRB phenomenon. A rapidly-rotating NS, such as a magnetar, is a popular model for the central engine of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). During a GRB, the NS surface may emit gravitational waves (GW), which could power a cosmological population of highly relativistic jets. While some baryonic wind models have been able to account for the diversity of long-duration GRBs, they tend to over-predict the amount of energy extracted from the NS. We demonstrate that coupling of NS energy to baryonic outflows via neutrino annihilation or Poynting flux can solve this problem. In particular, we consider a combination of a baryonic wind from a magnetar with a mildly-relativistic jet, and find that the total energy coupled to the winds can account for the majority of long GRBs.

Massive galaxies at high redshift (z ~ 2) are thought to build up the massive galaxies observed in the local universe1, 2. In this study, we exploit the unique capabilities of the combined GOODS and CANDELS multiwavelength dataset to study the physical processes active in the most massive galaxies at these early epochs. We find that the dominant mode of star formation at these redshifts is quiescent, dry merging, in contrast to popular expectation based on studies of local galaxies3. More quantitatively, we find a continuous increase in the specific star formation rate of massive galaxies from z = 2 to the present day, with corresponding decreases in the ratio of recent to past-average star formation rate and galaxy size. We show that these trends cannot be easily reconciled with a model in which star formation in these galaxies is uniformly delayed until the present day, without otherwise changing their evolution. We conclude that the dominant process setting the star formation rate in the most massive galaxies at these high redshifts is distinct from that in present-day galaxies. We show that while this mode of star formation is inefficient, it drives the growth of the massive galaxies we observe in the local universe. We show that this growth is also non-uniform, with massive galaxies growing by accretion of both companions and smooth ("dry") mergers with similar fractional contributions from each. This growth through dry merging is sufficient to explain the observed size evolution of massive galaxies. This picture also naturally explains the observed correlation between galaxy structure and star formation: as galaxies continue to grow by dry merging, the growth of the brightest central regions is quicker than that of the outskirts. These results may help to explain several long-standing puzzles about the early growth of massive galaxies. In particular, they suggest that present-day elliptical galaxies grew largely by dry merging throughout much of their lifetimes, a conclusion which may help explain the observed correlation between galaxy structure and star formation. They further imply that massive galaxies at high redshift were not predominantly "downsizing"3-5 in their star formation, as would be implied by the extended periods of intense star formation observed in some high-redshift galaxies6-8. Instead, we suggest that observed differences in the physical processes and rates of star formation in present-day massive galaxies and those in the most massive galaxies at these high redshifts may instead be driven by the much longer timescales since the peak of most recent dry merging. While the details of these differences are still subject to considerable debate, our results point to the importance of the early growth of massive galaxies via dry merging, perhaps even preceding the "monumental" merger class, in explaining the present-day galaxy populations we observe.

In the early X-ray afterglow of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), a decrease in flux density is usually observed, known as the "dips". The dip behavior in the X-ray afterglow of the Circinus X-1 (Cir X-1) was studied by a broad band (0.3-70 keV)Rossi X-ray timing explorer (RXTE) observation taken in 2007. We find that the dips are more obvious at lower energies, with the 2.5-5 keV and 5-10 keV dips having a detectable amplitude of 70% and 90% respectively. The dips become shallower and broader with increasing energy. No detectable dip is observed above 10 keV, suggesting that the deeper dips may be associated with the compact object gravitational radius passage, while the broader dips may be related to the accretion disk falling toward the compact object.' The deeper dips may be associated with the compact object gravitational radius passage. The broader dips may be related to the accretion disk falling toward the compact object.

Local interactions with not-completely-positive maps can generate entanglement increase. By local we mean the action of the map is restricted to act on a part of a multipart system. We show that this leads to a notion of distillable entanglement, for which we give an analytical expression for the general case. We then show that if the action of the map can spread to the whole system, then we can generate entanglement increase even from a classical source. For quantum and classical periodic dynamics, we give explicit constructions of maps that achieve this. aisy. Entanglement increase from local interactions with not-completely-positive maps. Distillable entanglement of a state $\rho_{AB}$ is the max over all ensembles $e_n$ of $\rho_{AB}^{\Gpd}$ with maximal concurrence over all possible decompositions $A_n B_n$, $\rho_{AB}=\sum_n p_n \rho_{A_n B_n}^{G_n}$, where $G_n=\tr_{A_n B_n} \rho_{AB}^{\Gpd}$. For a completely positive map $\Phi$, we denote the concurrence of $\Phi(\rho_{AB})$ obtained from a classical source by $C_{\text{cl}}$. For local maps $\map L_{\text{ncp}}$, we show that $\text{distillable entanglement}(\map L_{\text{ncp}}(\rho_{AB})) \geq C_{\text{cl}}$. We give an analytical expression for the general case. For quantum and classical periodic dynamics, we give explicit constructions of maps that achieve this.

Borromean halo nuclei, also known as hierarchical haloes, are spatially localized regions with unusual atomic and molecular spectra. The spectra are characterized by an absence of absorption or emission lines, but rather a near-continuum of small, sparse absorption lines. Recently, the phenomenon of Borromean halos has been observed in mass-25 Cs molecules, opening up the exciting prospect of studying three-body recombination collisions in an unexplored mass domain. The phenomenon is attributed to quantum interference effects in three-body collisions which produce a suppression of electric dipole interatomic transitions. We present an analysis of the geometrical structure of Borromean halo nuclei based on the Fano-Machi Hamiltonian. We find that the halos can be understood as a coherent mixture of three limiting configurations with resonant-tunneling couplings between them. The molecular binding is shown to arise from a resonant-tunneling coupling between a deeply-virtual state in the interaction region and a halo state in the molecular core. The geometrical structure of the halo is then a resonant-tunneling waveguide formed by the direct coupling of a deeply-virtual state in the interaction region and the molecular core.

The HI distribution in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) has been extensively studied. It has been proposed that the LMC is a possible satellite of the Milky Way and its motion relative to the Milky Way suggests that the LMC has had a significant impact on the morphology of the HI layer around the Milky Way. A detailed comparison of the HI distribution between the LMC and its likely progenitors, the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and the Milky Way is crucial in understanding the evolution of the LMC and the interaction between the LMC and its environment. The LMC interacts with its environment through gravitational forces. The gravitational potential of the LMC, the Milky Way and the SMC cannot be modeled accurately using analytical methods and requires the calculation of the integrals of motion using numerical methods. The location and morphology of the HI layer is determined by the strength of the self-gravity of the LMC and the SMC and the gravitational forces exerted by the Milky Way. In this paper, we present the results of an observational study of the HI distribution in the LMC. The LMC is an ideal target for this study as it is close enough to observe with modern day telescopes and has a significantly lower mass than the Milky Way. We compare the observed HI morphology of the LMC to that of the SMC and the Milky Way as derived from numerical simulations. Our study reveals that the observed HI distribution in the LMC is largely influenced by the Milky Way's gravitational forces.

The standard model with neutrino mixing extends the standard model with three lepton families, Higgs bosons and weak interaction bosons, to include neutrino mixing. This mixing, however, requires an extension to the standard model gauge group, typically the addition of a new heavy gauge boson and scalar that communicate the additional symmetry breaking. One possibility is that this extra symmetry is broken by Higgs fields localized to a four dimensional defect, warped AdS, or Little Randall-Sundrum. In this paper we consider the standard model with neutrino mixing in the context of noncommutative geometry. The noncommutative geometry in this model is realized as a curved phone book Deformed Poincaré symmetry (DPS). We provide finite temperature corrections to the standard model with neutrino mixing on a phone book DPS warped deformed conifold. In particular, we demonstrate that embedded strings arising from background DPS gravity are a resolution mechanism for singularities in the deformed conifold. This warped deformed conifold is an example of a soft breaking of the warped/compositeification/decompactification limit of the five dimensional anti-de Sitter space, Little Randall-Sundrum, proposed as a solution to the hierarchy problem.

Luminous Compact Galaxies (LCGs) are among the most luminous objects in the universe and haveMorphologies which may be largely determined by the environment in which they reside. Using the HST/ACS GOODS survey, we investigate the morphologies of LCGs in the redshift range 0.4 < z < 1.2, and split our sample according to their local environment. We find that cluster LCGs are more likely to have disturbed morphologies than their field counterparts, even at fixed stellar mass, showing significant signs of harassment and/or mergers. Additionally, we detect significant amounts of clustering of spheroidal morphology at fixed mass, with approximately 40% of spheroids being found in multiple structures. We do not find any environmental trends in the disky LCG population, however the surface brightness of these galaxies is found to be significantly higher on average than those with spheroidal morphologies. We discuss the possible origins of these differences, which may be due to variations in formation time, mass, or viewing angle.

We present a dynamical computation of the electroweak chiral Lagrangian parameters, namely the weak angle and top-quark mass, in two models with dynamical electroweak symmetry breaking, namely one-doublet and topcolor-assisted technicolor. The starting point of our analysis is a global, spontaneous symmetry breaking of the approximate global electroweak and color symmetries of the standard model into the standard model global symmetry, with the EW symmetry breaking induced radiatively through the Coleman-Weinberg mechanism. We compute the resulting Goldstone boson interactions with the standard model fermions, and show that these parameters can be expressed in terms of dynamical quantities of the underlying models. Our results for the one-doublet model are consistent with current measurements of the weak angle and top-quark mass. In the topcolor-assisted technicolor model, we find that the top-quark mass is dominated by the topcolor anomaly and is in the range of 175-200 GeV, while the weak angle, due to current measurements, is in the range of 0.22-0.28. We further discuss how the inclusion of additional vectorlike fermions may allow for a more precise prediction of the electroweak chiral Lagrangian parameters, namely the weak angle and top-quark mass. We also discuss the strong CP problem in these two models, and show that the vacuum structure can be chosen to naturally avoid the strong CP problem.

We present a method for determining the equation of state (EOS) of nuclear matter, which is based on the path-integral formalism and extends the well-knownSkyrme force in a consistent and thermodynamically self-consistent way. For the first time, we present results for the sound velocity, the spinodal, the Landau potential, the curvature, the speed of sound, and the incompressibility in the full density range. We compare our new EOS to other many-body methods and global parameterizations. We also determine the effective nucleon mass in the EOS and show that it decreases with increasing density, which is in contradiction to most parameterizations. The method is completely general and can be applied to any Lagrangian that has a well-defined path integral. As an example, we apply it to derive the EOS of solar interior from first principles. The calculated structural quantities are in good agreement with seismic and observational data.

The Kohn-Sham (KS) scheme is one of the most important and widely used methods in theoretical chemistry and quantum physics to solve the Schrödinger equation for the system with Coulomb potential. The efficiency of KS scheme relies on the choice of the approximate electron-electron interaction. For strong interaction, one has to use more elaborate KS-potential, which is numerically expensive. One of the efficient and low-cost approximations for the KS potential is the so-called exact exchange (EX) potential. This potential is constructed as a functional derivative of the exact exchange energy with respect to the electron density. The density obtained from the KS equations with the EX potential as a part of the exchange-correlation (XC) potential is very close to the actual one. However, the KS equation with the EX potential as the KS-potential yields a very large gap in the excitation spectrum, which does not correspond to the experimentally observed excitability of the systems. This discrepancy is referred to as the paradox of the correlated electrons. It was shown by Vydrov and Scuseria in 2008 that the gap in the excitation spectrum of the KS system with the EX potential can be made closer to the experimental one by introducing an artificial dependence of the potential on density, which they called the non-local dependence (NLD). In this work we show that the existence of NLD in KS potential is a consequence of the fact that it is obtained as a solution of the KS equations with the XC potential containing a non-local term. The non-local term appears due to the dependence of the Fock operator on the electron density. We derive the formula for the NLD term that takes this into account. We present the KS equations with the new XC potential and prove that the solutions of the equations coincide with those with the potentials used before and with the KS equation with the EX potential as the KS potential. This solution eliminates the gap in the excitation spectrum and reconciles the correlated electron systems described by the KS scheme with the Exact exchange potential and the Fock operator with the reasonable density dependence of the Coulomb potential.

Unitary random matrix ensembles exhibit a fascinating critical behavior at their spectral edge. The scaling limits of the corresponding spectra, known as edge scaling variables, involve correlations between nearest and next nearest neighbors in the spectra. These variables are known to be expressed in terms of solutions of the thirty fourth Painleve transcendnt. In this work we show that the spectra of unitary random matrices, averaged over the real Ginibre ensemble, also exhibit a distinct critical behavior at their spectral edge. This behavior can again be expressed in terms of solutions of the thirty fourth Painleve transcendent. We also show that edge scaling variables for real Ginibre spectra satisfy the same recursion relations as those satisfied by the spectral edge variables of unitary random matrix spectra, and thus that the two families of variables are identical upon conjugation by a redefinition of the scaling parameter. This work was prepared for publication by participants of the Caltech workshop: “Random Matrices: Theory and Applications”, January 29-31, 2015.

In recent years, the notion of emergent spacetime has been introduced to try to unify gravity with other physical forces, most notably quantum mechanics. These emergent spacetimes have been shown to arise in a bottom-up fashion from consistent theories in a higher dimensional spacetime, general relativity in d dimensions plus a scalar field. In this paper, we show that for a particular choice of coupling between the scalar and gravitational fields, this higher dimensional spacetime admits a higher symmetry, and the theory appears in one higher dimension as a dual gravitational theory with a doubled number of spacetime dimensions. Specifically, we consider the theory of a scalar field with a non-linear self-interaction on d+1 dimensional Minkowski space. The corresponding equations of motion have a critical point corresponding to empty spacetime. We show that by introducing a new scalar field conformally coupled to the first one, the system admits a higher symmetry, and reduces to a theory in d dimensions with an emergent ((d-1)+1) dimensional Minkowski spacetime. This theory allows for non-trivial solutions describing black holes with multiple horizons and with a length scale set by the charge of the black holes. In addition, in the classical solution, there is a smooth lower dimensional region behind the black hole horizon, in which the original (d+1) dimensional spacetime is smoothly extended, with the extension encoded in the structure of a solitonic string connecting the black hole horizon with the smooth region. We analyze the solutions with a single black hole and a cosmological horizon, finding that for large enough charge the black hole and cosmological horizons coincide, giving rise to a tri-horizon solution. We compute the entropy of the black holes in the dual gravitational theory, and find that it matches the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the black holes in the tri-horizon solution. Finally, we argue that the general solution of the theory includes the Reissner-Nordström black holes in higher dimensions, for which the gravitational theory reduces to five dimensions. We end with a discussion of the results and possible extensions. Wide binaries are pairs of main-sequence stars that are separated from each other by more than their orbital radius. They are excellent laboratories to study the properties of both components as they can be separated spatially. The semi-major axis of their orbit can be approximated by half of the binary separation. The mass of each component must be greater than 5% of the total mass of the system in order for the orbit to be consider wide. The dynamics of wide binary systems are governed by the conservation of energy. The variations of the semi-major axis are related to the variations of the orbital energy through the following equation: Here, n is the mean motion, G is the gravitational constant, M is the total mass, and is the average radius of each component. This equation implies that the distribution of the semi-major axis is directly related to the constitution of the system. The orbital evolution can be divided into two stages. During the first stage, the two components are essentially in isolation and evolve independently according to their initial properties. This is commonly known as ‘Case A’ evolution. During this phase, the average radius of each component increases as they evolve away from the main-sequence. As a result, the semi-major axis increases. In the second stage, the two components interact through their mutual gravitational field. During this phase, they co-evolve according to the requirements of ‘Case B’ evolution. The outcome of this co-evolution is ‘soft’ binaries with small semi-major axes and ‘hard’ binaries with large semi-major axes. It is important to note that the outcome of the second stage depends on the properties of the system when the first stage ends, which is related to the constitution of the binary system. ‘Soft’ binaries are systems with a large average radius for the primary component and/or a large mass ratio. ‘Hard’ binaries are described as those with a small average radius for the primary component or a small mass ratio. Currently, binary population synthesis models aim to reproduce the observed distribution of wide binaries in the Galaxy. These models consider only ‘soft’ binaries. The predicted distribution does not reproduce the number of hard wide binaries that is observed in the Galaxy. Thus, there is a clear discrepancy between observations and theory.

Web data has evolved with the growth of Web and the introduction of new concepts such as social networks and mobile applications. The volume of this data increases day-by-day and new research in the field of data management is needed for effective data analytics on this data. In this paper, a distributed data model for Web data integration in data warehouses is proposed. The main advantage of this model is that all the data associated with a website is represented as a single row in the target relational database, which makes it easy to perform joins between this table and other tables. This model uses case-change style rules to add new columns to the base table to represent the new concepts and these rules can be extended easily to add new concepts. The proposed model has been implemented in MySQL database and the performance of this model has been evaluated using real-life data and it is shown that this model can handle large volumes of Web data compared to other models.

The Magellanic system is an interacting pair of satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. Among other features, the Magellanic system includes a nearly collisionless gaseous component, the Magellanic Clouds, and a ~300 kpc long leading arm, called the Magellanic Stream. The origin of the Magellanic Stream and its leading arm is a longstanding mystery. Several competing explanations have been proposed, including ram pressure stripped gas from the SMC, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, tidal interactions between the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way, and extragalactic positrons. In this paper, we present simulations of the Magellanic System that simultaneously explain the origin of the Magellanic Stream and its leading arm, the Magellanic Bridge. The simulations, performed using the Versatile Advection Code (VAC), include a Milky Way potential, a MWPotential9+ dark matter potential, and a simple SMC ISM model. VAC solves the Euler and diffusion equations with multiple time steps and adaptive spatial resolution, capturing the dynamics of gas, stars, and dark matter simultaneously. The model successfully reproduces the main structures in the Magellanic System, including the Magellanic Bridge, Magellanic Stream, and Magellanic Counter-Bridge. The origin of the Magellanic Stream is caused by ram pressure stripping of the SMC gas, which is pushed toward the Milky Way, leading to an extended gaseous feature that connects the Magellanic Clouds. The simulated Magellanic Stream is metal-rich, in agreement with spectroscopic observations of the Stream's leading edge, and is coincident in space and velocity with the Magellanic Stream. The simulated Magellanic Bridge and Magellanic Counter-Bridge are tidal structures that form as the Magellanic Clouds are perturbed by the Milky Way potential. The Magellanic Stream and Bridge are the two most significant structures in the Magellanic System, and the simulated Magellanic System successfully captures the observed relationship between the two.

The basic idea of this approach is to introduce a new chromosome encoding for a set of corresponding mappings, called meshes, between the given test functions and their corresponding lower levels in the topology. The EAs are applied to find meshes corresponding to low level set covers. Preliminary experimental results are presented to show the feasibility of the approach and its potential. Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) have been successfully applied to many difficult search problems. However, most existing EAs are designed for continuous search spaces. When the search space is discrete (as in the present case), they do not perform well. Evolutionary Mesh Numbering (EMN) is the first discrete EAs for solving discrete optimization problems. The basic idea of EMN is to encode the mapping between the test functions and their corresponding lower levels in the topology. The encoding is called mesh numbering and is inspired by graph theoretical concepts. The search process is also designed to be related to the mesh numbering. The search process is designed related to the mesh numbering. Preliminary experimental results are presented to show the feasibility of the approach and its potential. CFIRB stands for Cosmic Far-Infrared Background and it is believed to be radiated by galaxies in the early stages of the Universe. So far, the detection of this background is extremely challenging because it is fainter and cooler than the thermal emission from interstellar dust in our own galaxy. A satellite mission, called AKARI, observing the far-infrared and submillimeter wavelengths, is the first mission with the sufficient sensitivity and resolution to detect this faint radiation. Using data from the Diffuse Infrared Background Experiment (DIRBE) and the Faint Infrared Surveyor (FIS), AKARI observed a 4.5° x 4.5° region of the sky 5 times from 2006 to 2010. It detected emission above the expected brightness of the cold dust in our galaxy and this is likely the CFIRB. This is an initial detection and further observations are required to confirm this result.

The dynamical evolution of binary neutron stars depends crucially on the extent to which their components couple hydrodynamically and become tidally entrained as they inspirate and coalesce. We find that, for equal-mass, irrotational neutron stars described by a Skyrme model at zero temperature, as the stellar inspiral proceeds, the tides generate a dynamical non-axisymmetric instability that grows and deforms the stars’ shape, changing the torques and rate of energy and angular momentum loss. We carry out an axisymmetric stability analysis in the slowly-rotating, weak-tidal limit and confirm the growth of a bar-mode deformation, whose saturated amplitude increases proportional to the compactness of the neutron stars. We then numerically integrated the coupled time-dependent Euler and Poisson equations in axisymmetry and confirmed the linear growth of the bar mode and the saturation of the deformation, over the full range of initial amplitudes explored. Finally, we use the ZEUS-MP hydrocode to carry out 2.5D numerical evolutions of tidally-distorted, equal-mass, irrotational neutron stars with a range of initial bar-mode amplitudes, and confirm the growth and nonlinear saturation of the bar mode and the deformation mode, over a broad range of initial distortions. Thus, we identify the dynamical bar-mode instability as a potential new source of dissipation in inspiraling neutron-star binaries. The amplitude of the induced tidal dissipation correlates strongly with the initial amplitude of the bar deformation, and the energy and angular momentum loss may be sufficient to stall the inspiral and lead to a rapid instability to spontaneous fission.

In the curvaton scenario, the fluctuation of the scalar field determining the number density of dark matter contributes to the gravitational waves at the level of the parameter Omega_GW, which is related to the speed of the gravity during the period of inflation. However, if the potential of the scalar field has a lower bound, the contribution of the fluctuations of this field to the gravitational waves is not effective. In this work, we study the maximal amount of gravitational waves generated in the curvaton scenario, taking into account the effects of the effective speed of gravity during inflation. We find that the maximal amount of gravitational waves in the curvaton scenario is equal to the general relativity value, Omega_GW=1. We show that this result does not change even if the potential of the scalar field has an upper bound. In this work, we consider the case of two scalar fields: the real inflaton field and the complex curvaton field. The complex curvaton field determines the fluctuation of the number density of dark matter, while the real inflaton field determines the variation of the expansion rate of the universe. During the inflaton oscillation, the speed of gravity is nearly equal to the light speed, while it is slower than the light speed during the period of the complex inflaton field evolution. Thus, the fluctuation of the scalar field determining the number density of dark matter contributes to the gravitational waves with the parameter Omega_GW, which is related to the speed of the gravity. We find that the maximal amount of gravitational waves is equal to the general relativity value, Omega_GW=1. In addition, we study the perturbation of the gravitational wave during the sub-Hubble scales. We find that the perturbation of the gravitational wave is dependent on the effective speed of gravity during inflation. If the effective speed of gravity is equal to the light speed, then the amplitude of the perturbation of the gravitational wave is inversely proportional to the square of the effective speed of gravity. This result has an upper limit, which is 1/3 for the case of two-field models and 1/7 for the case of multi-field models. Finally, we discuss the gravitational wave background from the inflationary universe. If the effective speed of gravity is larger than the light speed, there are many modes with the scale of the Hubble radius at the time of inflation, which lead to a large gravitational wave background. In this case, it is difficult to explain the recent gravitational wave experiments such as B-mode experiment and LIGO/Virgo. However, if the effective speed of gravity is equal to the light speed, then we obtain the consistent gravitational wave background with the current value. We can realize a model with the maximal amount of gravitational waves by adopting the potential of the scalar field with a lower bound, which determines the maximal effective speed of gravity during inflation. Advanced LIGO performed a series of preparatory zeroing passages coincident with target instrumental configuration changes in late 2019. TheseZeroing Passages were analyzed for noise transient signatures. This analysis led to the development of physicalinstrumental vetoes for coincident Advanced LIGO and Virgo trigger buffers during early 2020.Physical instrumental vetoes were deployed during the first months of Advanced LIGO’s fourth observing run andcontinue to be developed and applied. Virgo was also observed during this period. The effects onAdvanced LIGO sensitivity of physical instrumental vetoes applied in this way are demonstrated. so, As the Advanced LIGO and Virgo detectors reached theirdesign sensitivities in the early 2020s, preparatory zeroing passages coincident with target instrumental configuration changes drew largenumbers of transient noise signatures. These were removed using physical instrumental vetoes. The effects ofphysical instrumental vetoes on Advanced LIGO sensitivity are demonstrated.

LIGO has made remarkable discoveries about gravitational waves since the detector's first observation in 2014. The first direct detection of a compact binary coalescence (CBC) heralded the beginning of the multi-decade era of gravitational-wave astronomy, and opened the unprecedented opportunity to study the universe via astronomy's most energetic emission. Yet, all of LIGO's discoveries to date have come from observing the coalescence of black hole binaries, whose host galaxies are extremely hard to study observationally. Fortunately, most black hole binary coalescence events occur much farther away than the stellar distances of their host galaxies, permitting LIGO to ignore the latter in their search for CBCs. However, searching for CBCs in the crowded fields of host galaxies required large observation volumes and exquisite alignment control. In a recent development, the LIGO-Virgo Observatories have introduced a new observing strategy: identifying host galaxies ofCBC candidates from larger electromagnetic datasets (e.g., from X-ray, gamma-ray, or optical observatories), and then using near-infrared spectroscopic methods to identify galaxies within the LIGO localization regions that are likely to be the actual host galaxies. This “Galaxy Catalog” approach allows the LIGO observations to target theseCBCs in smaller, more densely sampled regions, achieving greater sensitivity by optimizing the localization of the CBC and enabling multimessenger astronomy. In this work, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by presenting the results from the first such search, O1. We identify two new CBC candidates that are consistent with being in galaxy clusters, and show that the localization of one of these events was improved by a factor of two after including galaxy catalog information. We present these results as an example of the potential of combining gravitational-wave and electromagnetic astronomy in parallel, and we discuss prospects for future CBC searches that make use of galaxy catalog information.

Five new planets were discovered around nearby stars using the N2K Consortium's near-infrared K2-3Ne standard mask photometric survey. Host stars of these planets have masses from 0.7 to 1.4 solar masses, and distances from about 19 to 60 parsecs. The relative semi-major axes of these planets span from 0.025 to 0.15, and they have equilibrium temperatures between 34 and 59 K. Assuming these planets have typical Uranus and Neptune masses and radii, they have equilibrium temperatures between 34 and 59 kelvin. The lowest mass host star with a planet found by this survey is 0.7 solar masses, and the most distant planet with an equilibrium temperature above 59 kelvin is 55 AU from its star. The rate of detection of these planets as a function of their estimated equilibrium temperatures is higher than what is expected for hot Jupiters, with a probability of 48% for predicted temperatures between 58 and 63 kelvin, corresponding to Neptune and Uranus-like objects. If these planets have followed similar formation pathways to our own Solar System, their initial locations should be located outside of their star's snow line, with the most likely scenario being that the planets formed farther out and then migrated in. Therefore, the results of this survey provide strong evidence for an outer region of the system being stable against mass loss, in which case the substellar objects could be either super-earths or truly Neptune-sized planets.

Harmonic Oscillator Nuclear Matrix Elements Arising in Semileptonic Electroweak Interactions ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A Mathematica script to compute nuclear matrix elements arising in semileptonic electroweak interactions is introduced. The amplitude of the process can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric functions, and the expression is simplified using series and special function identities. The matrix elements can be further simplified using the Heisenberg equations of motion. The resulting expression can be evaluated efficiently using built-in functions in Mathematica. History The nuclear matrix elements (NMEs) are fundamental parameters in the theories of nuclear reaction. In nuclear reaction network simulations, the NMEs determine the rate of changes of reaction cross sections with energy. Additionally, NMEs appear in the calculation of detectability of neutrinoless double beta decay, a hypothetical process that would reveal the Majorana nature of neutrinos. Therefore, precise calculation of NMEs is crucial for understanding fundamental particle physics and for the interpretation of future nuclear reaction network simulations and neutrinoless double beta decay experiments. Semileptonic electroweak interactions provide a rich source of NMEs, which have been studied experimentally for many years. The most accurate NMEs are from the study of muon capture on hydrogen, M(mu) - H, in hydrogen barrels of heavy water D 2 O which are located at Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNG S) in Italy. Experimentally M(mu) - H NMEs are calculated as the capture rate in 12.5 cm heavy water barrels relative to the capture rate in 10 cm light water barrels; that is, M(mu) - H = [rate(captured particles in 12.5 cm barrels)/(rate(uncaptured particles in 12.5 cm barrels))]/[rate(captured particles in 10 cm barrels)/(rate(uncaptured particles in 10 cm barrels))]. The theoretical calculation of M(mu) - H NMEs involves computing the overlap of the nuclear wave functions of the participating particles with the spatial wave functions of the bound states of the corresponding charged weak current operators. Calculating NMEs for a given process requires the computation of these overlap integrals. In the last decade, thanks to the development of effective methods and computer power, NMEs have been computed for many semileptonic electroweak interactions. A consensus on the most accurate NMEs has not been reached, however. In this work, we provide a Mathematica script which computes NMEs for semileptonic electroweak interactions arising in muon capture on hydrogen and other nuclei, as well as some NMEs from charged current reactions on free nucleons.

Mass and temperature of the TWA 7 debris disk were measured using Herschel and Spitzer observations. This disk is unusual in that it exhibits at least four clear breaks in its spectral energy distribution (SED), which are suggestive of four spatial regions with distinct temperatures. The inner two breaks at radii of 19 and 47 AU can be explained by an irradiation dominated belt and a transitional Kuiper belt, while the outer two breaks at radii of 180 and 500 AU are likely due to the depletion of solids beyond the frostline location at 100-150 AU. The temperature in the middle break region is best explained by a compositional gradient in the residual dust grain population, with a temperature of 50 K at 47 AU increasing to 200 K at 180 AU. This indicates the presence of a relatively warm region at intermediate disk radii. The detection of these distinct regions with different temperatures is only possible with Herschel and Spitzer observations, as previous far-IR observations with the Infrared Astronomical Satellite had compromised the ability to discern the multi-temperature nature of the disk.

Researchers study the composition and evolution of dust in the early stages of galaxy evolution using Primordial Supernova Remnants (P31 in the image below, also known as Cas A) as aRosetta Stone to help interpret the observed abundances and physical conditions in young supernova remnants (SNRs) throughout the universe. By performing state-of-the-art dust formation and evolution simulations, we find that silicate dust grains formed in the P31 ejecta can survive for a Hubble time and be injected into the surrounding early Interstellar Medium (ISM). These dust grains can then grow via accretion of metals from the presolar ISM to form nanometer-sized particles. We also find that titanium and vanadium are the most abundant elements at the grain surface and that the overall stoichiometry is roughly Ti-26V-4Si, with a high sulfur to oxygen atomic ratio of 0.5-1.5%. These sulfur-rich compositions are distinctive from those of chondritic meteorites and are most consistent with carbon-rich pebble materials, such as enstatite andagnetite, as injected dust precursors. We conclude that the P31 supernova remnant, as observed and modeled here, provides a rich platform to test theoretical predictions of dust formation and subsequent evolution. The bulk compositions of silicate dust grains injected into the early ISM can serve as fingerprints to help identify these unique grains among the Galactic and extragalactic background population. The silicon, titanium, and vanadium abundances can be used to confirm the formation of silicates, oxides, and carbides, respectively, as expected for core-collapse supernova ejecta interacting with the surrounding ISM. Furthermore, the sulfur-to-oxygen ratio can be leveraged as a clock to date the injection event to within roughly 30-330 million years, depending on the assumed density and composition of presolar ambient gas. The recent detection of an unusually large sulfur mass fraction in the wake of SN1987A supports an age estimate of ~30 million years, given that most of the injected sulfur would have likely been consumed in the formation of new dust grains. Ultimately, dust identified in young SNRs will provide a unique window into the nucleosynthesis and chemical enrichment history of the very first stars and galaxies in the early Universe. This is a descendent post of this entry in the Darwin Award Contest.

We have performed a detailed analysis of the HI structure in a sample of 45 galaxies with no identified optical counterpart at other wavelengths. We have found that a significant fraction of isolated galaxies have large HI disks with maximum scale lengths of 13 kpc and velocities widths of 250-450 km/s. We interpret these large HI disks as remnants of previous major mergers. We do not find any correlation between the presence of a large HI disk and the properties of the underlying stellar disk. The HI fractions and velocity widths of the galaxies are consistent with those of normal late type galaxies, indicating that these galaxies have undergone periods of gas accretion rather than having a pervasive HI halo. This implies that the incidence of dark matter halos in local isolated galaxies is much lower than the dark matter content inferred from the velocity dispersion of their visible components. The total atomic hydrogen masses of the isolated galaxies are consistent with those of normal galaxies of the same optical luminosity, and they show a correlation with the stellar mass of the host, similar to that observed in clusters. This supports the hierarchical model of structure formation in which galaxies grow through the merger of smaller entities. We conclude that most isolated galaxies have undergone periods of gas accretion and of stellar mass growth but not all through major mergers. The efficiency of forming large gas disks through minor mergers seems to be very high.

In this paper we introduce a quasi-exactly solvable (QES) spin chain which contains nearest-neighbors interactions. The Hamiltonian of the chain can be factorized into a sum of two-site terms which commute with one another. We show that the spectrum of the chain consists of a set of doubly-degenerate eigenvalue bands and a set of non-degenerated eigenvalue bands. Moreover, we derive the total number of the energy bands and the corresponding wave functions. Finally, we apply the Yang-Baxter equation to analyze the spectrum of the whole spin chain. Our chain could be realized in experiment with ultracold atoms in an optical lattice, with bosonic or fermionic atoms, or with photons. It would be interesting to study the properties of the chain and the method proposed in this paper by numerical methods and study the relations with models studied in literature. A compelling aspect of theories with gravity is their ability to give a complete description of the universe, from the largest-scales to the smallest. String Theory, for example, or M-Theory, are compelling frameworks for such a description, unifying all the interactions of particle physics into a single, complete, elegant theory. One such aspect, not yet fully realized, is the unification of the fundamental forces: the Strong and Weak nuclear forces, and the electromagnetic force. Supersymmetry, realized a quarter century prior to the unification of these forces, predicts that for every symmetry that preserves one force, there is another force, requiring a symmetry-conjugate, but slightly different, force. The manifestation of this in the real world is the hierarchical structure of the force-couplings: the Strong and Weak nuclear forces are tied together, and the Electromagnetic force is tied to the Weak force via the photon, which is itself an interaction of the electromagnetic force. The realization of unifying the three forces is a primary aspiration of high-energy physics, one that has yet to be realized. The challenge of realizing this, however, is one of engineering, for no current theory realizes this unification. While String Theory - which at its core is a quantum-mechanical theory of extended objects in a 10-dimensional manifold - offers a framework in which to realize this unification, it is a highly abstract framework, with no realization in terms of local quantum field theories. While the challenges of realizing this dream of physics have driven theoretical endeavour for nearly 70 years, a realization in terms of a local quantum field theory is yet to come. The latest, and most promising, framework for realizing this dream is that of M-Theory, unifying all of the physical interactions via the existence of 11-dimensional membranes. Unfortunately, these membranes, while realizing the dream of unification, also run into the same roadblock - no realization of M-Theory in terms of local quantum field theories. While this is a challenge that many believeString Theory to be, it is one that M-Theory does not address, leaving a major gap in the unification of the three known forces. One possible solution to this unification challenge is that of the graviton, the quantum of the gravitational interaction. If realized, this unification of the forces would be a profound achievement, and could open up the discovery of a new universe of phenomena and insights, offering a new way for theorists to understand our world. We report on the observation of an odd-frequency pairing component in the conductance of hybrid normal-superconducting structures. The pairs have nonzero spin projection along the direction of the applied magnetic field and zero total momentum. We observe this effect in structures with highly transparent interfaces in the limit of an incoming electron spin paired with a reflected hole with spin parallel to the interface. The observation of this spin-triplet pairing is supported by a quantitative fit of the data, and we discuss the relation of this effect to other odd-frequency pairings observed in superconductors or superfluids. model and results The unexpectedly large conductivity of superconducting hybrid structures with highly transparent interfaces (e.g. ~70% of the quantum of conductance 2e2/h) has been the subject of many studies, both experimental and theoretical1,2. It is commonly accepted that the excess conductivity is due to coherent singlet pairing of electrons and holes with opposite spins. However, recently a triplet component has been proposed3,4 as an alternative explanation of the data. This theory is based on the assumption that the triplet component of the pair wave function has a pronounced spatial structure (distant from the interface) and has opposite sign on the different sides of the interface. This sign difference produces a finite triplet proximity effect. As the conductance is a sum of singlet and triplet contributions, the presence of a nonzero triplet contribution would explain the unexpectedly high proximity effect observed in experiments. In this letter we report results of studies of a possible triplet component in the conductance of hybrid structures. The triplet component would have zero total momentum and nonzero spin projection along the direction of a static in-plane magnetic field. In order to study the odd-frequency pairing we used a spin-resolved Andreev interferometer with a normal metal "mirror" placed on the opposite side of the superconductor. We observed the conductance for spin-triplet pairing with relative phase differences of 0 and $\pi$ between the incident and reflected waves. We were not able to observe a dependence of the result on the angle between the magnetic field and the direction of propagation of the incident electrons.

The conformations of single polyelectrolytes play an important role in determining their functionality in biological systems as well as their responses in various chemical and physical stimuli. To gain an insight into the influence of various factors governing the conformations of single polyelectrolytes, we have performed all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of a flexible polyelectrolyte (poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate)) and a rigid polyelectrolyte (poly(ethylene oxide)). We have systematically changed the chain stiffness of the flexible polyelectrolyte, while keeping the length and the monomer charge of the chains fixed. The conformational statistics have been analyzed using the radius of gyration and the end-to-end distance. We have observed that the flexible polyelectrolyte is significantly more coil than the rigid polyelectrolyte in all the regimes of the stiffness. The conformational differences between the flexible and rigid polyelectrolytes increase with the increase in stiffness. Further, we have analyzed the conformations in the solvent-excluded volume. We have also observed that the conformations of the flexible polyelectrolyte in the solvent-excluded volume differ significantly from those in the bulk, while the conformations of the rigid polyelectrolyte are similar in both the regimes. The flexibility of the chain fundamentally alters the conformation of the polyelectrolyte in the solvent-excluded volume. We have also computed the excluded-volume interactions between the chains using the center of mass separation and the end-to-end distance. We have found that the excluded-volume interactions are not sensitive to the chain stiffness, except at short center of mass separations. The differences in the conformation and the excluded-volume interactions lead to differences in the pair interactions between the polyelectrolytes in different regimes. *This work was performed under the DST Inspire Programme, and DST has not been involved in the study in any way. Exoplanets are of great interest to astronomy because they can provide information about the prevalence of planets around other stars. Planets that are both large enough to be readily detected and have orbits that are not unstable over long time periods are termed "giant planets". Giant planets are relatively rare, comprising only about 0.8% of the total number of planet types that could potentially exist around other stars. I present a model for giant planet formation that includes pebble accretion, gravitational instability, and migration. The model is calibrated to yield a giant planet population that agrees with the observed population of giant planets. My model shows that around 15% of systems with solid material between the inner edge of the planetesimal annulus and the outer edge of the giant planet's orbit will form a giant planet. Systems with multiple giant planets are also favored by this model, with approximately 1/3 of multiple giant planet systems having three or more planets. The most common final configuration is a single giant planet with a large adjacent planetesimal disk.

A steep drop in the infrared spectral energy distribution (SED) of T Tauri stars is commonly explained by settling of small grains in a dust disk inner region1,2. This observational signature, however, has not yet been unequivocally detected for any star, and instead alternative scenarios invoking grain growth3,4 or flat disk geometries5 have been proposed. IRS 48 is a T Tauri star in the Taurus-Auriga molecular cloud complex with a nearly face-on debris disk that shows a steep drop in the infrared SED at roughly 40 μm, but the origin of this emission remains unclear. We combine ALMA 890-930 μm imaging with PACS 70 and 160 μm imaging from the Herschel Space Observatory to detect the disk at shorter wavelengths. We find that the IRS 48 system contains three debris disk components: a large grain belt in the outer disk that could be analogous to the Kuiper Belt in our solar system; a broad gap in the middle of the disk where temperatures are low and small grains likely reside; and an inner disk detected at wavelengths as long as 890 μm that exhibits a steep drop in fluxes at shorter wavelengths due to small grain settling. The inner and middle disk components are mutually exclusive and cannot coexist in a single system, suggesting that processes intrinsic to the disk (e.g., gravitational interactions) sculpt the evolution of the disk surface density.

The dwarf irregular galaxy ESO 364-G 029 was observed in the BVI bands and with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) in the F775W and F555W bands, respectively. The data were used to produce colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) as a function of radius. These revealed the presence of multiple star formation episodes over the last Gyr. Radial surface brightness profiles were constructed for the galaxy and showed that it is consistent with having a low surface brightness system. The overall morphology was also determined from the images, and this revealed that ESO 364-G 029 has an exponential profile with an effective radius of 5.4 kpc. The global HI velocity width is 235 km s−1, which corresponds to a dynamical mass of Mdyn = (6.5 ± 0.5) × 1011 M⊙, where the error corresponds to 1σ. The HI rotation curve is consistent with an exponential profile with an effective radius of 5.4 kpc. The HI surface density profile was also determined and this suggests that the dark matter content of the galaxy is significant.

Modern approaches to quantitative structure-activity/property-relationships (QSAR/QSPR) seek to link chemical structure to a range of biological and physico-chemical properties. This has lead to highly predictive models, which in turn have fed back into chemical design. For example, we can use chemical structure to guide search strategies for drug candidates with optimal properties. However, such ‘design’ processes rely on the initial QSAR/QSPR models being sufficiently accurate. This requires better definition of what it is that we wish to model. Many biological and chemical processes are complex, and depend on a range of inter-related properties. The challenge therefore is to develop chemical descriptors that reflect the full complexity of molecular structure and account for inter-relationships between properties. We describe a robust methodology for such ‘multiphilic’ descriptor development. We illustrate the approach by developing a multiphilic descriptor for chemical reactivity and selectivity. The approach is readily extensible to other properties, and other descriptor types.

A rotating stratified flow, such as a planetary boundary layer, contains combined vortical and wave modes. We perform a numerical simulation of an statistically uniform rotating stratified flow, with strong stochastic rotation, temperature and density variations, and double periodic boundary conditions in the horizontal directions. The flow becomes turbulent after a time transition related to the initial conditions. We compute time-averaged flow statistics, energy spectra, and kinetic and potential enstrophies. While potential enstrophy is concentrated at large scale and seems to decay with an infrared loglaw, kinetic enstrophy is concentrated at small scales and seems to be cascaded. The initial large-scale forcing is mostly into vortical modes, with a broadband energy distribution in the flow. However, after some time, a more local energy distribution, with a large share of energy at small scales, develops and evolves according to the cascaded spectral model. This dynamical range is too large to be fully captured with a direct numerical simulation with a small grid spacing. This is the first direct numerical simulation of a statistically uniform rotating stratified flow that reveals both vortical and wave modes. It also reveals the dynamical range and cascade range spatial and temporal scales, and suggests directions for further research.

Thin magnetic flux ropes are fundamental to the activity of solar active regions. This activity includes flares, eruptions, and coronal loops. In this paper, we show that thin flux ropes are the organizing principle of dynamos and anti-dynamos. Dynamos are regions of rotational convection in which large-scale magnetic fields are generated. Anti-dynamos are regions in which rotational convection leads to the destruction of large-scale magnetic fields. Thin flux ropes, and the principles that govern their equilibrium and dynamics, provide an organizing framework for the complex behavior of dynamos and anti-dynamos. The thin flux ropes can generate their own flux, minimizing energy costs, while the thin magnetic walls of the flux ropes limit the effects of the free energy released by the convective motion. We illustrate these principles with a detailed case study of a dynamo simulation performed in a spherical shell, using a novel Riemannian geometry that enables the dynamics of thin flux ropes to be described. In this dynamo, the free energy generated by convection is rapidly and efficiently converted into large-scale fields. The thin flux ropes themselves evolve into tall, stable anti-dynamos that promote magnetic field annihilation.

In this letter, we consider the problem of distributed sensing over networks, where a network of nodes can collaboratively monitor an environmental process, but the nodes are only able to communicate a noisy version of the process vector. This scenario arises in numerous applications, such as collaborative monitoring of environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity, gas levels, pollution levels), surveillance video monitoring, and detection networks. The problem of distributed sensing is to use the network topology and local observations to design networks that can collaboratively detect the presence or estimate the value of the process, while incurring a limited total communication and computational cost. We study the case where the environmental process is linear and can be represented by a matrix, and the goal is to design linear network observations that result in efficient distributed matrix sensing. Our framework allows the communication and computational costs to be modeled via a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which captures the effects of noise and communication rate on sensing performance. We study the optimal distributed matrix sensing problem for a range of network scenarios. First, we consider the case when the network topology is random and show that this problem can be exactly recast as a linear programming problem. We show that for any network with a sufficiently high level of regularity, no better than linear performance in network parameters is possible. Next, we study a more challenging scenario where the network topology is fixed, but flexible computation at the nodes allows the network to be decentralized. We develop a general algorithm that enables each node to locally compute an optimal linear observation based on locally observed processes, while achieving an average network error that is near optimal. Furthermore, we show that a simple greedy algorithm that independently selects nodes to communicate with at each time step, with uniform randomness in the selection, yields a high-probability (1-1/e) nearly-optimal distributed solution. Finally, we perform a performance analysis that characterizes the performance of the greedy algorithm. We illustrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm via simulation results for various network topologies and illustrate that the proposed algorithm can achieve near optimal performance.' Note: this is an abstract of the full text paper here.

In a previous work [1] it was shown that in the quasilinear regime the halo response to a perturber can be modeled as the superposition of transient growth and linear responses. In this work, we generalize this result to Lagrangian perturbation theory (PT), which allows us to compute halo responses to arbitrary initial conditions. This allows us to construct a simple and accurate modeling of halo responses to intermediate length and time scales, without requiring prohibitively expensive simulations. To illustrate our results, we apply this framework to simulations of the L5/L6 Lagrangian pair, which are characterized by a relatively weak response on large scales. By construction, Lagrangian PT simulations reproduce the mean relative separation and velocity dispersion of L5/L6 at high accuracy. Applying the model presented in [1] to these simulations yields reasonable agreements for both the transient growth and the subsequent linear response, at the price of using a single parameter to fit the simulations. We show that this parameter, which measures the strength of fluctuations in the large-scale density field, can be estimated directly from L5/L6 simulation data. Using this parameter, our Lagrangian PT model yields accurate predictions for the mean response of L5/L6 at various time and length scales, without requiring additional expensive simulations. This is in contrast to other models, such as the haloFit model, which requires calibration on large scales, and may lead to significant errors on shorter time and length scales. Our model is thus very flexible, and can be applied to arbitrary density field fluctuations. We apply it to L5/L6 and L6/L5 halo pairs separately, which allow us to characterize the response of individual halos to density field variations on a range of scales. Furthermore, we show that our model can be applied to halo pairs that exhibit strong responses on short scales. We conclude that Lagrangian PT is a promising approach to study the statistics of halo response to density field fluctuations, and apply this approach to a set of 48 halo pairs, with different initial separations and time separations. We find that pairs with initial close separation tend to have large, positive response on large scales, whereas pairs with initial intermediate separation tend to have strong but short-lived response. Moreover, the response of a halo pair on a given scale increases with increasing length and time separations of the pair. These findings are consistent with previous studies based on more direct approaches. We illustrate our results with several examples, and find that pairs that show strong response on small scales may exhibit almost no response on larger scales. We discuss the physical mechanisms responsible for these observed trends, and emphasize that while Lagrangian PT is promising, more work is required to apply it to individual halos and make contact with observations. This work revisits the ideal fluid dynamics on Lie groups from a control perspective. It is well-known that such theories can be obtained from the Lagrangian formulation of the celebrated Euler equation on the diffeomorphism group of a three dimensional Riemannian manifold. An equivalent Hamiltonian description using the theory of Lie groupoids and Lagrangian mechanics on Lie groupoids is proposed, and explicit constructions are given for some important special cases including fluid dynamics on Lie groups, Newtonian gravity on the special orthogonal group and the general linear group, and the classical ECSK theory of non-relativistic gravity. In the Hamiltonian description, the fluid dynamics on Lie groups and ideal hydrodynamics are described by a Lie groupoid, with the fluid dynamics being a particular case in which the source of the gauge groupoid morphism is the diffeomorphism group of the fluid domain. In particular, in the particle description, the fluid dynamics on Lie groups and ideal hydrodynamics can be seen as resulting from a deformation quantization of the source groupoid. It is shown that the Schrödinger equation, which describes the evolution of quantum mechanics, arises as the geodesic equation for the magnetic connection of the deformation quantization. This permits the construction of a mechanical system which realizes ideal hydrodynamics in the large, namely which exhibits the geodesic flow of a specific left-invariant metric on the solution groupoid. The resulting system is presented in explicit form for the example of ideal fluid dynamics on the special orthogonal group. It is also shown that the system so constructed is Hamiltonian with respect to a modified symplectic structure, corresponding to that of Dubois-Viallet on the Lie group corresponding to the special orthogonal group. Some exact solutions are also presented.

We present the observations of the dust and gas contents of a complete flux-limited sub-sample of luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs; log(L[8-1000keV]_\odot) = 11.0–12.0L[8-1000keV] = 10.1–46.7) selected from the all-sky 2 Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS). The sub-sample was further divided into ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs; log(L[8-1000keV]_\odot) = 11.0–12.0L[8-1000keV] = 46.7–47.5) and hyperluminous infrared galaxies (HyLIRGs; log(L[8-1000keV]_\odot) = 12.0L[8-1000keV] = 47.5). We detect atomic hydrogen in 11 out of 12 LIRGs, and 9 out of 11 ULIRGs. Four ULIRGs are undetected in HI, whereas two LIRGs have upper limits that are inconsistent with the detection in these sources. We detect polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission features at 3.3, 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, and 11.3 micron in all but two LIRGs. The LIRG dust masses are a median of 2.1 x 10^8M_\odot (2200M_\odot), with a spread of 1.2–4.9 x 10^8M_\odot. The ULIRG dust masses are a median of 1.0 x 10^9M_\odot (1100M_\odot), with a spread of 8.0–4.5 x 10^8M_\odot. The HyLIRG dust masses are a median of 1.2 x 10^9M_\odot (1300M_\odot), with a spread of 8.0–8.7 x 10^8M_\odot. The average LIRG, ULIRG, and HyLIRG gas-to-dust mass ratios, assuming a canonical gas-to-dust ratio of 160:1, are 685, 280, and 320, respectively. If we scale the gas-to-dust ratio to that found in the Milky Way of 150:1, the gas-to-dust ratios are 880, 300, and 370. These results suggest that the HyLIRGs have higher dust masses than LIRGs and ULIRGs, as measured by a factor of 3.3 on average, with a 1σ dispersion of 0.7. However, we estimate that the LIRGs and ULIRGs have similar gas masses, with a 1σ dispersion of 0.5.
