Coherence is a property that ensures that past events don't conflict with future expectations. For databases, it ensures that update operations can be performed atomically. This guarantees that updates either happen completely or not at all. The same idea can be applied to other distributed data types such as hypergraphs or DAGs. Unlike previous models which assumed unique normal forms, coherence does not require this assumption. This makes it applicable to a broader range of scenarios. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that my implementation of coherence is faster and more scalable than existing systems. The database community has focused on three properties that ensure database consistency: 1.transaction consistency (a sequence of updates either happens completely or not at all), 2. schema consistency (the structure of the database satisfies the business requirements), and 3. data consistency (the updates are valid according to the underlying data model). These three properties have been unified into a single property: coherence. A distributed data type has coherence if any finite sequence of updates happens completely. Coherence does not require the underlying data model to satisfy any unique normal form property. This makes it more scalable. My implementation of coherence is faster and more scalable than state-of-the-art distributed data type coherence systems.

The Falicov-Kimball model (FKM) is an important model in the study of Mott transition and thus superconductivity. The model consists of electrons and spin-less fermions called slave bosons that interact through an onsite repulsion. In this work, we construct a slave boson theory of the extended FKM, which includes additional hopping and onsite repulsion terms. The theory is shown to be a well-defined effective low energy theory of the half-filled repulsive Hubbard model on a triangular lattice. We apply the slave boson theory to study the model away from half filling as well as at half filling. In the half filled case, we find two phases: an insulating phase with charge density wave order at small parameters, and a trivial superconductor phase at large interactions. At finite but small dopings, we observe a Beresinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition and a crossover between the insulating and superconductor phases. At large dopings, we find a first order Mott transition separating the uniform metal and a density wave state. We conclude that slave boson theory provides a consistent low energy description of the extended FKM for all values of the parameters.

The stability of shock waves in a transonic gas flow is studied. The inviscid and isentropic case is solved and a transcritical shock wave is found to be most unstable. The result is confirmed by a stability analysis for viscous shock waves, which are shown to be stable for all possible wave numbers. The stabilizing effect of viscosity is discussed. The equations of isentropic gas dynamics in one spatial dimension reduce to a nonlinear wave equation for the pressure in case of inviscid flow and to a semi-linear degenerate hyperbolic equation in the viscous case. A shock wave is thus stable to viscosity for the inviscid case and stable for all wavenumbers for the viscous case. The results are of interest in several areas of astrophysics and gasdynamics, where shock waves appear as a result of e.g. nucleosynthesis or star formation, and viscosity may be an important effect.

Z(N) spin systems in d = 4 continuous dimensions with self-dual (N=0) scaling behavior at their quantum critical point exhibit the conformal field theory description of the renormalization group (RG) invariant scaling theory of a self-dual N=0 SLE(8/3, 2/3) process. The SLE(8/3, 2/3) process is critical at its Gaussian free field scaling dimension and SLE curve parameter, and describes the scaling limit of real-space interfaces in self-dual N=0 critical quantum spin systems in d = 4. The paper derives this SLE description, and tests it by exact prediction of the scaling dimensions and operator products of a Z(N) spin chain with N>or=4. This SLE description provides a proof of the quantum Riemann mapping property of the self-dual N=0 Z(N) spin chain, and predictions for scaling dimensions and operator product coefficients are verifiable by DMRG computation of the spin chain critical point spectrum.

Hybrid networks have been widely used in recent communication systems owing to their benefits of increased network capacity and enhanced network support. However, existing localized support for injection point election (LSE) mechanisms for hybrid networks cannot guarantee the election of a same injection point (IP) among all the networks, which restricts their applicability in hybrid networks. In this paper, we propose a localized supported injection point election (LSIPE) mechanism, which ensures that all the networks will elect to the same injection point. Moreover, we prove that LSIPE is close to optimal with respect to the objective of maximizing the minimum network utility while guaranteeing that the same injection point is elected among all the networks. Extensive simulations validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed LSIPE mechanism.' LSIPE mechanism is a novel localized support for injection point election (LSE) mechanism for hybrid networks. In hybrid networks, some physical networks and virtual networks coexist, and each physical network or virtual network can connect to multiple other physical networks or virtual networks. Thus, the network injection management in hybrid networks becomes a multipoint-to-multipoint problem, which is much more complex than the point-to-point problem in single networks. Existing LSE mechanisms for single networks cannot guarantee the election of a same injection point (IP) among all the networks. Therefore, we propose a LSIPE mechanism, which can achieve the goal that all the networks will elect to the same injection point. Furthermore, we prove that LSIPE is close to optimal with respect to the objective of maximizing the minimum network utility while guaranteeing that the same injection point is elected among all the networks. Extensive simulations validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed LSIPE mechanism. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Related works are described in Section II. The system model is introduced in Section III. The proposed LSIPE mechanism is presented in Section IV. Performance evaluation and analysis are presented in Section V. Section VI concludes this paper.

A fundamental measure functional for the fluid of aligned hard hexagons is presented. This functional is based on a close approximate of the hard hexagon particle shape that allows for an analytical treatment and the resulting expression is a functional of the weighted density, a functional which has not been considered before in theories of the hard hexagon fluid. A systematic gradient expansion of the free energy leads to a direct correlation function and a simple Padé approximant for the functional. The resulting fluid exhibits square order at high densities, as found in computer simulations and as observed experimentally for real hard hexagons. At low densities, however, we predict a phase transition to a hexatic phase. Further, we predict a reentrant nematic phase which has not been observed in computer simulations. Our functional forms a solid angle subtended by neighboring particles as a critical independent variable for the first order phase transitions. We discuss the connection of our findings to recent computer simulations of the hard hexagon fluid and propose that some computer simulations have found an incorrect transition to the solid phase.

The spectrum of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) is typically assumed to follow a power-law, dN/dE = K E-α, where α is the spectral index and K is a normalization constant. One popular mechanism for accelerating cosmic rays to such high energies is the shock acceleration process, where particles scatter back and forth between longitudinal waves until they cross a relativistic shock at which point they attain a non-zero energy corresponding to the jump in the relativistic downstream speed across the shock. Consequently, a popular method for constraining the cosmic-ray power spectrum is by observing the flux ratio of UHECRs above and below the Greizen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin (GZK) cutoff. However, such a cutoff is not observed in the flux of UHECRs and its absence has led to the development of possible solutions involving new beyond-Standard-Model physics, such as neutron decaying to electron-antineutrinos. One such beyond-Standard-Model scenario is that cosmic rays are produced via the decay of dark matter particles, which can be motivated by the recent hints for dark matter provided by numerous cosmological, astrophysical and laboratory observations. In this paper we consider the recently proposed model that the dark matter particles are bosons with zero spin, and thus are maximally correlated, and that the decay channel is to standard model particles via a mediation channel involving a real scalar field. We show that under these assumptions the energy in cosmic rays produced via this decay channel cannot explain the observed fluxes above the GZK cutoff. Furthermore, this scenario is excluded by recent observational results from the Pierre Auger Observatory and Telescope Array, which are able to detect a flux of UHECRs at Earth with an overall spectral index of 4.6 and a cutoff at around 56 Ee+19 eV. We therefore conclude that this scenario is disfavoured by existing observations.

The OGLE (Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment) microlensing project has discovered numerous planets around the Milky Way stars. To date, the mass and eccentricity of these planets are poorly constrained because of the required annual monitoring from the ground. Furthermore, the typical Galactic planet detection rate is low due to overwhelming contaminations from field stars. Both of these difficulties can be overcome by a space-based microlensing survey, but the costs are extremely high. We describe a survey using Exoplanet Satellite (EXPLO), which is a cheaper alternative that can achieve the same sensitivity with proper observations from the ground. By performing gravitational microlensing parallax observations from the ground and space, we can measure the mass and orbital parameters of extrasolar planets with uncertainties of 20% in mass and 50% in orbital elements for 70% of the detectable planets. When applied to the known planets discovered by OGLE, EXPLO will discover nearly all with the proper monitoring strategy. In addition, EXPLO will discover several planets with pericenter distances less than 2.2 AU around bright host stars, which are presumably difficult to be discovered by current surveys due to stellar crowding. Furthermore, EXPLO can measure the atmospheric conditions of these planets and identify potentially habitable ones.

Liesegang patterns are generated by self-assembly of nanoscale building blocks into periodic structures. In the Liesegang model, these patterns form in a single selective chemical reaction occurring in a narrow spatial region over several days. We demonstrate that Liesegang patterns may also be generated by self-assembly of phase-separating mixtures into spatially periodic patterns. When quenched from equilibrium, such mixtures separate into two phases of different composition. In this case, Liesegang patterns emerge due to spontaneous breaking of inversion symmetry, which stabilizes the pattern of chemical phases. We show that the frequency and symmetry of the Liesegang patterns may be tuned by adjusting the composition and temperature of the quench, allowing the patterns to be used as a "controlling template" for self-assembly. Here we introduce a framework to predict the formation of Liesegang patterns by mixtures separating into two phases. This approach may be used to optimize Liesegang patterns for a wide range of applications, from constructing micron-sized machines to synthesizing materials with highly desired physical or chemical properties.

Bok globules are small, dark clouds without bright centers, and they represent an early phase of star formation. It has been suggested that the high concentrations of molecules such as H2CO and CS observed in Bok globules are formed in the cold interior of newly formed low-mass stars, and that the dark globules will eventually become solar systems with associated planets. This study examines the distribution of young stellar objects (YSOs) within the Bok globule CB54. CB54 was selected because it is nearby (approximately 11.4 light years) and contains an unusually high number of YSOs; there are 54 YSOs projected within a 260 parsecs (approx. 825 light years) region around the globule. The young stars are indicated by infrared emission, radio free-free emission, or visual extinction. The high number of young stars projected near the globule CB54 suggest that the formation of planets may be more likely in this region of the universe than in others.

supernova explosion signals may encode a wide range of information about the nature of the explosion and its environment. In this paper, we investigate one such encoded signal: the temporal evolution of the neutrino signal. We find that the overall signal follows a simple hierarchy: at early times, there is a brief, rapidly oscillating burst of neutrinos corresponding to electron-capture on free nucleons; at intermediate times, there is a decaying burst of neutrinos corresponding to the beta spectra of various nuclear processes; and at late times, the signal has a component in addition to this broad, slowly-varying signal: an oscillatory burst of neutrinos corresponding to the evolution of the three neutrino mass eigenstates. We determine that the mass-splitting between the first two eigenstates is 7.5 x 10 -5 eV 2, which corresponds to a timescale of 14.7 seconds. This is substantially longer than previously expected, but may be important for upcoming supernova neutrino observations.

Turbulent transport is an important process in space and astrophysics, but the plasma physics of low-collisionality regimes remains poorly understood. Gyrokinetic theory, originally developed for the Solar Proper Motion System, provides a powerful framework for studying turbulent transport in weakly collisional plasmas. The theory has been recently extended to include finite Larmor radius effects and correspondingly enhanced turbulent cascade rates. In this Letter, we present the first implementation of gyrokinetic theory for turbulent transport in collisionless plasmas, termed Astrophysical Gyrokinetics, which is capable of simultaneously describing kinetic and fluid turbulent cascade processes in magnetized weakly collisional plasmas. This Letter focuses on the development of turbulence via the Orszag-Tangetsu theory, which accurately describes the relative displacement between neighboring magnetic surfaces due to isotropic fluctuations at high wavenumbers. The corresponding nonlinear equations are solved using a hybrid finite difference-spectral method. First- and second-order statistics of the turbulent structures in the electron temperature and magnetic field variances, as well as the energy transfer rates across the kinetic and fluid cascade bands, are presented and discussed. The results demonstrate the simultaneous existence of kinetic and fluid turbulent cascade processes. Furthermore, the fluid cascade rates are found to be significantly enhanced by the finite Larmor radius effects, which is beneficial for the transfer of energy to smaller scales and better modeling of turbulent transport in the solar atmosphere.

Grains of ice behave much like particles and will flow when introduced to a fluid with sufficient kinetic energy. The distribution of ice grains in the lab is typically close to a log-normal, and so ice grain agglomerates will naturally form. We performed collisions between agglomerates of same size, and found that they stick after a short period of time, which we attribute to friction between the agglomerates. We also performed collisions between agglomerates of different sizes, and find that the smaller agglomerate moves around the larger one, with some sticking and breaking. We speculate that the sticking observed in the collisions between agglomerates of same size is due to the buildup of static charge on the surfaces of the agglomerates. We have submitted this paper to [arXiv.org]. It is available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.12147

Transcritical bifurcations are a novel type of criticality in dynamical systems first observed in maps. Here we demonstrate that they arise naturally in Hamiltonians as a universal feature of phase transitions. We numerically compute the critical indices for the transcritical bifurcation in the classical N-body problem, finding excellent agreement with the theoretical value for the 3D Hamiltonian Mean Field (HMF) model. We also establish the presence of this bifurcation in the low-energy classical dynamics of the Symplectic Map Version of the Particle Physics Hamiltonian, arising naturally as the system is tuned across a phase transition in this case as well. These results suggest that transcritical bifurcations may be a generic feature of phase transitions in non-integrable Hamiltonian systems, and could provide a simple paradigm for studying the critical dynamics of long-standing problems in physics and astronomy.' --- arXiv.org version: https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00872

The complex multiconfigurational charge distribution in the 4f shells of lanthanides often gives rise to a complicated energy level structure that leads to numerous phenomena, such as multiple phases of the same material, different behaviour of isostructural compounds, and variable interactions with external perturbations. PrOs_4Sb_{12} is a rare-earth stibnite exhibiting two successive superconducting transitions at 0.3 and 0.75 K. The upper transition is commonly referred to as the first-order transition, while the nature of the lower transition is still controversial. Theoretically, both second-order and first-order phase transitions have been predicted for the lower transition, while the nature of the first-order transition is still under debate. We present a comparative study of the low-temperature specific heat of several single-crystalline samples of PrOs_4Sb_{12}, with and without prior mechanical grinding. The results of this study suggest that the two transitions are of similar magnitude and of first-order nature. In addition, our data reveal the coexistence of a Schottky anomaly at the first-order transition and a double Schottky effect at low temperatures, suggesting that at least two order parameters coexist.

Quark-gluon plasma (QGP) formed in heavy ion collisions exhibits many properties similar to nuclear matter at high density and temperature. As a consequence, properties of QCD at high densities may significantly affect description of particle production in heavy ion collisions at beam energies per nucleon-nucleon collision up to 200 GeV. In this article, the authors present the dependence of jet transport parameter, $\hat{q}$, on parton saturation momentum, $Q_s$, in QGP. The $\hat{q}$ is derived from theGy-Kolmogorov-Sonine (GKS) spectrum by applying a hadronization and finite detection volume correction. The results for 0-20% most central Au+Au and pp at 200 GeV are compared to previous studies at lower beam energies. The increase in $\hat{q}$ with center of mass energy is consistent with expectations based on the Glauber model of nucleus-nucleus collision which assumes local equilibration between constituents. However, a detailed energy dependence of $\hat{q}$ does not match the data well. The results are compared to a pQCD motivated parameterization of parton saturation momentum dependence of $\hat{q}$ and a conclusion is drawn that QGP formed at top RHIC energy does not manifest parton saturation physics via modification of $\hat{q}$ at this time.

Template based image registration is an important problem in medical image analysis and computer vision, with applications in structure segmentation, quantification and tracking. In this paper we present an evolutionary algorithm based optimisation approach for solving this problem. The optimisation framework is formulated as an evolutionary algorithms can naturally solve, and is additionally adapted to the specific form of the problem, by using a sum of difference terms and an exponential transformation to approximate the technically challenging rigid transform energy function. Using simulation examples we demonstrate that the proposed approach is capable of providing high quality solutions for a variety of challenging registration problems, including difficult examples with large deformation and significant noise corruption. The effectiveness of the approach is further illustrated through its application to the real-word problem of cardiac Motion Tagging. The proposed approach presents a practical and effective solution to image registration problems and we expect it to have wide applicability in clinical imaging, medical diagnosis and rehabilitation.

The MINOS Experiment at the University of Minnesota uses a broad beam of protons from the northwestern shuttle tank of the Fermilab booster ring to measure the atmospheric muon charge ratio at very high energies. This is the first direct measurement of the atmospheric neutrino flux at these energies and provides the highest precision inclusive charged-muon flux to date. The systematic uncertainty on the measurement is 7.5% (5.1%) in theMC generated40-GeV (450-GeV) range. The ratio of the predicted charged-muon flux to the flux calculated using Bartolomeo and Baroletto as the primary flux agrees to within 4.4 (5.7)% in the 40-GeV (450-GeV) range. The MINOS experiment observes atmospheric neutrinos by measuring the energy and direction of upward-moving muons produced by neutrinos interacting in the ice surrounding the detector. Using data from 2007 through 2018, MINOS measures the flux of atmospheric neutrinos over three energy regions: 40-GeV muons, which are most likely produced by tau neutrinos; 450-GeV muons, which are likely produced by all neutrino flavors; and 800-GeV muons, which are produced by chargino and neutralino decays in supersymmetric models. The most precise flux measurement is for the total charged-muon flux, which consists of contributions from all flavors of neutrinos and antineutrinos. This is the first observation of the tau neutrino contribution to the total charged-muon flux. The observed tau neutrino flux is consistent with the expected flux within the standard model total flux uncertainties of 19.5% at 40 GeV and 10.3% at 450 GeV. MINOS also observes the charged-muon flux in the very high-energy region, or VHE, which includes events with an energy greater than 0.5 TeV. The observed charge ratio of contained events to through-going events is consistent with the standard model expectation of 5.4% in the 1.2-TeV to 3.3-TeV range. However, the standard model prediction of the ratio of the charged-muon flux to the flux calculated using Bartolomeo and Baroletto as the primary flux agrees to within 4.4% in the 40-GeV range, and this ratio is used to predict the contained- muon flux in the 1.2-TeV to 3.3-TeV range. The MINOS measurements of the contained-muon flux are 2.0% (2.3%) above (below) the standard model prediction in this range. MINOS also measures the atmospheric muon charge ratio using data from 1997 to 2005. The results are consistent with those from the 2007-2018 analysis. The total uncertainty in the average atmospheric muon charge ratio is reduced to 7.5%. One of the biggest open problems in particle physics and cosmology is the understanding of the Electroweak Scale (EWS) and the origin of mass. String theory, one of the leading candidates for a Theory of Everything (ToE), has thus far been unable to explain the electroweak scale. This is because in the past forty years or so, we have progressively increased the precision of our experiments, and for string theory to make sense, all these experiments would need to be much better explained by something more basic, namely some new strongly coupled regime of string theory. While this is plausible, and there is recent growing evidence that this may be the case, it is a huge and wide open question. On the other hand, since the last few years, a great deal of progress has been made in formulating string theory in backgrounds with warps, namely in the context of warped and orientifold compactifications. These geometries naturally lead to very different metrics from the usual ones in string theory, with non-factorisable metrics and moduli spaces. Most importantly for us, they allow for a natural uplift to ten dimensions where 6 of these dimensions are small and Minkowskian, and 4 are large and roughly analogous to the dimensions of space-time in 4D general relativity. In this way, one can naturally explain the huge gap between the weak and gravitational scales of around 30 orders of magnitude. Moreover, one can also explain the fractional electric charge of the electron by localising the sixth internal dimension on a cycle, and coupling the standard model particles to the zero mode of the cycle. The same explanation can also be used to generate fermion mass terms, which are naturally of the right order of magnitude. This all fits very naturally with the observed pattern of quark and lepton masses and mixing angles. In this talk, I will review this development, showing how it provides a natural solution to the electroweak hierarchy problem, as well as how it explains the patterns of fermion masses and mixing angles. Moreover, I will describe some of the recent developments that have made it even more concrete, with particular emphasis on how the localisation of the 6D gravity mode on a cycle can be made robustly calculable and transmogrify it into a mechanism for gauging the standard model Yang-Mills gauge symmetry and couplings. I will end by outlining some of the crucial remaining questions in the subject, and point to some directions for further research that may help answer these questions in the near future. November 2018 Title: Connecting String/M Theory to the Electroweak Scale and to LHC Data. Authors: Tom Drummond Rehman Murid Prateek Jain Krishnendu Mandal Abhijit Majumdar Link to paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.11766 November 2018 Abstract: One of the biggest open problems in particle physics

Surface gap solitons (SGSs) are localized pulses solutions to nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation with saturable nonlinearity. Saturable nonlinearity, often encountered in real physical systems, gives rise to the nonlinear loss, rendering the NLS equation valid only for propagation distances shorter than the nonlinear loss length. Saturable nonlinearity interface is formed at the meeting point of two different nonlinear media, with linear gain in one and nonlinear loss in another. SGSs can be fully stable at such an interface, even in the absence of Kerr self-focusing and saturable absorption. We find that the SGS profile oscillates in the transverse direction, and the oscillation period is inversely proportional to the propagation constant of the SGS, which can be larger than the linear loss length. Such large-period, non-Kerr-stable SGSs could be potentially useful for all-optical information processing.

Using data collected by the H1 and ZEUS collaborations at DESY HERA, we study the production of multiple jets in the current -rapidity region of the Breit frame in deep inelastic scattering at low values of the product of the proton beam energy and Bjorken scaling variable, xBj. A calculation within quantum chromodynamics (QCD), based on the factorisation of the hard-scattering and the soft-scattering cross sections, describes the data well in a region with a minimum transverse momentum between the jets of 5–30 GeV. Events with three or more jets are observed with rates of approximately 10–20%, depending on the cuts applied. A significantly higher rate is observed for events with at least one jet with a large transverse momentum with respect to the others. These events may be considered as containing a hard scattering contribution from a parton with a high longitudinal momentum transfer, indicating that they may be caused by the exchange of objects with high invariant masses.

In this work, we study the so-called tensionless limit of strings in the light-cone gauge. In this limit, the fluctuations of the string disappear, and the remaining theory is a sigma model. We show that this sigma model can be obtained from the dimensional reduction of type IIA supergravity in the limit in which the string tension becomes zero. This allows us to find the sigma model exactly and provide its global symmetries. We also show that the sigma model is invariant under the AdS group. This research has been partially supported by the Czech Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports (MŮLYSH finances – Exceptional Minnesota University, CASE project No..). We would like to thank Sergio Cecotti, Olaf Lechtenfeld, Fernando Quevedo and especially Jan Moller for their comments on a first version of this paper.

In modern cosmology, the dominating content in the universe is 27% energy density of dark energy, while the classic model believes the ordinary matter accounts for 23% and the dark matter accounts for 46% (including 5% light nuclei), and the rest is energy density of empty space. This defined the "matter dominated" universe, which was successfully realized in the early universe before cosmic inflation, when the energy density of the vacuum state was much larger than the energy density of matter. In this paper, we first review two exotic models: Negative Matter and Phantom, which aim to recover the 23% ordinary matter in the universe. We show that these two models can be realized in a consistent way, by considering a new kind of interaction in the framework of general relativity, named as repulsion force. We name this new interaction as dark matter, and show that it can account for 46% of the matter content in the universe. Then we discuss the theoretical relation between inflation and the new force, which provides a possible mechanism for inflating the universe. Finally, we discuss the relation between the negative matter and the Phantom model, which shows that they are different manifestations of the same underlying theory.

The article considers the imprint of the distortions in the Oort Cloud on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies. The approach is based on the idea that the Sun is located close to the boundary of the Oort cloud, where the galactic gravitational force starts to dominate. The article presents the analytic estimations of the temperature variations within the Planck units caused by the gravitational perturbations of the perturbers located in the Oort Cloud. The calculations were carried out for several models of the Oort Cloud structure derived in the recent years. The calculations show that the perturbers in the Oort Cloud could produce the anisotropies of the CMB temperature of the degree that are observed in the CMB radiation. The article shows that the method of detecting the signals from the Oort Cloud proposed in the article could be used to test the models of the Oort Cloud structure and to estimate some parameters of the galactic potential.

The main motivation of this paper is the search of a pure spinor superfield formalism for 10D and 11D supergravities. The motivation is based on the observation that 10D and 11D supergravities only have two (utility) gauge invariances. One is the pure spinor gauge invariance, which plays an important role in the uncompactified M-theory and type IIA superstring theories. The other is a local supersymmetry (SUSY) gauge invariance. Using only local SUSY gauge invariances leads to the so called ‘ massive supergravity’ formulations. However, this is not so useful in the M-theory and type IIA superstring theories since the Higgs mechanism in those theories break local SUSY. A pure spinor gauge invariance cannot be obtained from local SUSY transformations. The pure spinor gauge invariance can be reformulated in a superspace formalism. It was known that the pure spinor superspace was the unique superspace to formulate the 10D and 11D supergravities (with local SUSY). However, the pure spinor superspace is not convenient for some purposes. It is technically complicated. In addition, the number of fermionic coordinates is the same as the number of bosonic coordinates, which is in contrast with the requirements of supersymmetry. We propose the pure spinor superfield formalism to overcome these drawbacks. The pure spinor superfield has the same number of fermionic and bosonic variables, which is the minimal requirement for supersymmetry. But the pure spinor superfield formalism is simpler than the pure spinor superspace formalism. We present the 10D and 11D pure spinor superfield formulations. The pure spinor superfield for 10D supergravity was proposed in 2014. The pure spinor superfield for 11D supergravity was proposed in 2015. The new proposals of pure spinor superfield for 10D and 11D supergravities are obtained by generalizing the ideas and techniques of previous works on 10D and 11D supergravities. The pure spinor superfields have similar properties as the usual spacetime fields. The pure spinor constraints are first class constraints of the super-$p$-branes. They generate local SUSY (and gauge symmetries) in the fermionic directions. They generate the double space generalizations of the various supersymmetric transformations in the bosonic directions. In addition, the pure spinor constraints are used in the Lagrangian formulation of the super-$p$-branes.

Resistivity and magnetoresistance of polycrystalline samples of Ce1-xLaxOs4Sb12 (0<or=x<or=0.15) were studied. CeOs4Sb12 is a 4f$^1$ electron system with a superconducting transition temperature Tc of 2.75 K. Upon substituting 4dLa orbitals with additional electron density, Tc is suppressed with a superconducting dome centered at x=0.10. Unlike other 4f-based superconductors, where lattice expansion by Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) coherent pairs causes superconductivity to be quickly suppressed by random foreign impurities, x=0.10 Ce1-xLaxOs4Sb12 appears to have a high degree of purity. However, a second phase transition is observed below T* approximately 30 K. For 0.10<or=x<or=0.15, the in-plane resistivity decreases with decreasing temperature below T*, most likely due to an increased carrier density. The low-field magnetoresistance reaches a maximum of 1480% at 1.8 K for H//c, and the Kohler’s rule is clearly violated. Both the residual resistivity and the magnitude of magnetoresistance decrease with increasing x, which is consistent with the higher La-content alloy phase having a smaller carrier density. This study shows that high purity 4dLa alloying is an effective way to suppress the superconducting transition temperature of CeOs4Sb12 without significantly altering its lattice parameter. As an effective way to tune the carrier density of Ce1-xLaxOs4Sb12 without introducing further disorder, this material system appears to be ideal for studying the interplay between superconductivity, magnetism and topology.

A wide range of masses, from 3 to 18M_odot, has been found for Single stars. This range includes 4 to 18M_odot for White dwarfs. The maximum masses of neutron stars have been found to be 2.2-2.5M_odot, but there is a large uncertainty in this number. For binary systems, it is much harder to form such massive compact objects, because a larger amount of matter must be compressed for a longer time. The origin of these very massive objects is not clear. It has been proposed that these very massive objects might be the remnants of very massive Population III stars. These very massive Population III stars might have formed in metal free regions of the early universe due to the bottom up creation mechanism for these very massive objects. Very massive Population III stars might have formed with approximately 40-200M_odot. When these very massive Population III stars eventually exhaust their nuclear fuel, they could end their life as very massive compact objects. Currently, there are very limited models for these very massive compact objects, and this hampers our understanding of their evolution. Current very massive compact object models assume the compact objects have a constant mass equal to the initial mass of the progenitor. However, a more realistic model for the compact object masses should take into account the possible loss of mass during the formation process.

18um-selected galaxies in the AKARI/IRC Monitor field towards the North Ecliptic Pole (NEEP) are studied in the wavelength range from 3.2 to 230 μm, with the HSC, GALEX, UKIDSS and WISE data used as references. Galaxies in the AKARI/NEEP field have lower SFR, lower fraction of galaxies with 24um detected galaxies and higher fraction of 70um-detected galaxies than those in the AKARI All-sky survey (AAS). NEEP 18um galaxies have slightly lower SFR than AAS 18um galaxies on average, but still have considerable star formation. NEEP 18um-detected galaxies have lower average SFR and higher fraction of 24um-detected galaxies than AKARI All-sky 18um-detected galaxies. WISE 3.4um - WISE 22um luminosity ratios of NEEP 18um-detected galaxies are significantly larger than those of AKARI All-sky 18um-detected galaxies. These results indicate that AKARI/NEEP 18um-selected galaxies are likely to be very young with high dust content.

Recently scaling laws have been shown to be very good at predicting the scaling relations of various cluster observables including X-ray luminosity and temperature. These include the simple model where scaling relations are formed via selection effects arising from flux-limited X-ray surveys and variations of the mean relations with scale (cosmology). In this paper, we study the scaling relations of galaxy clusters from the REFLEX and South pacific Chandra Cluster Samples (SPCCS). The new relations presented here do not require any a priori knowledge of the scaling relations or the cosmology and are very well described by a model in which scaling relations are formed via both selection effects and intrinsic scatter arising from a log-normal distribution of cluster masses. We also explore the relationship between the shape of the scaling relations and the scaling relations themselves. We find that the average temperature–Y scaling relation (kT-Y) has the smallest intrinsic scatter and that the luminosity–Y scaling relation (L-Y) has the largest intrinsic scatter. We also find that in an analysis of the kT-Y and L-Y scaling relations separately, the intrinsic scatter of the L-Y scaling relation is entirely due to scatter in the mass-observable scaling relation. The selection terms in the scaling relations have simple forms which allow us to de-couple the selection and intrinsic scatter terms in the scaling relations and find that the flux-limited selection effect causes a decrease in both the measured temperature and luminosity, whereas the intrinsic scatter is unchanged by the flux limit. We also find evidence for a mild evolution in the scaling relations. The evolution parameter appears in the L-Y scaling relation but not the other relations and we discuss various possible reasons for this. Background: Scaling laws have been shown to be good at predicting the scaling relations of various cluster observables such as X-ray luminosity and temperature. These scaling laws require neither a prior knowledge of the cosmology nor any a priori knowledge of the scaling relations themselves. Rather, the scaling laws are constructed by plotting observable(s) versus cluster mass or some other easily observed parameter and then finding the best fit line or fit to the data. These scaling laws have been shown to arise from both selection effects arising from flux-limited X-ray surveys and from variations of the mean relations with cosmology. In this work, we study the scaling relations of galaxy clusters from the REFLEX and South pacific Chandra Cluster Samples (SPCCS) and explore the relationship between the shape of the scaling relations and the scaling relations themselves. We also find that in an analysis of the kT-Y and L-Y scaling relations separately, the intrinsic scatter of the L-Y scaling relation is entirely due to scatter in the mass-observable scaling relation. A Secure Broadcast scheme is proposed for efficiently transmitting the same secret material to multiple receiving nodes over a wireless network. The broadcast is protected from eavesdropping, tampering, and masquerading. The transmitting node first secret material generate a random sequence of secret key and encrypts the random sequence using the Encrypt-Then-Encrypt (ETE) approach. The ciphertext is then shuffled and split into multiple parts and transmitted to the multiple receiving nodes using zero-profit random access protocols. Finally, the receiving nodes jointly decrypt the ciphertext and recover the original secret material. The broadcast secrecy is achieved by exploiting the difficulty of recovering the secret key from the received signal despite the low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). We analyze the performance of the proposed scheme under the wire-tapping model and the Moore heterogenous network model. The simulation results show that the proposed scheme is efficient in terms of the number of transmissions, the encryption and secrecy performance.

Animal behavior is frequently modulated by changes in the perceived safety of the surroundings. An organism's response to danger can have profound consequences for its fitness. Animals often adjust their behavior in response to aversive stimuli such as intense heat or severe injury. Here, we present a neurodynamical model that captures the learning and decision-making processes that underlie such behavioral plasticity. Our framework assigns a value to each behavioral response based on a probabilistic mapping to outcomes, represented as a multivariate normal distribution. These values are updated by means of a variant of contrastive estimation that enables the model to account for both positive and negative reinforcement. The model can be applied to a broad class of behavioral optimization problems, and we illustrate its application by applying it to scenarios that pose conflicting demands on a creature's behavior. The model predicts that rats exposed to a danger stimulus will exhibit an initial rapid behavioral response but will ultimately optimize their behavior, as measured by time-averaged heat loss, over a gradually shifting optimum. Furthermore, we show that the model can account for heat-induced analgesia, one of the most striking examples of behavioral plasticity, by computing a probability distribution over expected pain intensities. Thus, our model can generate accurate predictions about how organisms respond to danger, providing a foundation for understanding how behavioral flexibility emerges from a Bayesian optimization framework in which outcomes are predicted using neural networks. Symbolic models have been widely used for the analysis and design of nonlinear control systems. For systems with a known model structure, it is possible to construct an approximately bisimilar symbolic model using an SMT solver. However, the procedure for model construction is challenging since the state space model is first constructed and then refined by symbolic permutations. In this paper, we present a framework that combines the symbolic model construction and refinement steps in a unified framework. The key idea of the framework is to combine several techniques, including encoding symbolic constraints into an SMT formulation, converting SMT solving for model construction and refinement into sequence of optimization problems, and using fast linear algebra techniques to efficiently solve the resulting large-scale problems. We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method through the examples from both theory and practice. This work was partially supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) grants CCF-1704825, CCF-1815855, and CNS-1926804.

Aim: To model the clumping-induced polarimetric variability of hot star winds. Observations: Spectropolarimetric monitoring of O-star wind clumps has revealed highly variable circular polarisation signals that vary on short time-scales. These findings cannot be fully explained by current polarisation theories. Potential problems: These variations could be attributed to magnetic field variability on small spatial and short temporal scales, if the relevant polarimetric signals are formed in small-scale clumps located in the wind. Model: Here, we develop a three-component, structured-wind model to simulate spectropolarimetric light curves and circularly polarised signatures for comparison with observations. We find that the model can successfully reproduce the short-timescale variability seen in the observations. Significance: These observations provide the first glimpse of how the dynamics of clumps in hot star winds may affect their magnetospheres. The model presented here can be readily applied to other stars with known wind clumping properties, to help further elucidate the structure of these critical regions.

In decision-making processes, a player may be attracted to outcomes with a high payoff despite the risk of a lower expected payoff. This phenomenon, called the "illusion of control," is well known in Parrondo's games, in which a player chooses either a high-yielding but neutral game or a losing game and enjoys a surprise winning streak because of the addition of the winning game to the losing game. This effect, however, does not always occur, as demonstrated by the minority game, in which a player chooses either to repeat a sequence of spins of a wheel with twice as many black as white spindles or to repeat a sequence of spins of a wheel with twice as many white as black spindles. Despite the opposite odds, this game does not exhibit a winning streak, but instead causes the player to lose more frequently than if they had chosen to repeat the neutral game. These contrasting effects arise from the order in which the games are played: the order in which the games are played affects the likelihood of the illusion of control.

On December 12, 2015, a Be/X-ray binary system named 1E0102.2-7219 was observed by the Suzaku satellite. 1E0102.2-7219 is an eclipsing X-ray binary system, in which a neutron star primary star is permanently accreting matter from a low-mass companion star in a close orbit. The system enters an eclipse every 3.8 hours, during which no X-rays are emitted. 1E0102.2-7219 showed two bright episodes of X-ray emission, with peak 0.2-10 keV luminosities of 1.2 x 10 35 and 4.8 x 10 35 erg s−1, respectively. The higher-luminosity episode was observed to end less than 30 minutes after the start of the observation, a completely unprecedented delay for a source in this class, which cannot have an obscuring cloud of material obstructing the line of sight to the neutron star. This outburst, which we dub the supersoft outburst, is the only one of its kind detected during a 170 ks Suzaku observation. The supersoft outburst shows similarities to novae, however the inferred low mass donor star and short delay between start of the outburst and detection indicate that the accreted material did not accumulate in a disk. Instead, we suggest that the material was directly released from the compact object into a accretion disk around it. In either case, the supersoft outburst marks a dramatic increase in the rate of mass transfer from the companion star to the compact object.

Large-scale simulations of structure formation in the concordance cosmological model suggest that dark matter (DM) halos naturally organize themselves into two distinct phases, a dense central core and a more diffuse outskirts. The DM density profile in the central regions can be well fit by an inwardly-decreasing, power-law (Γ-profile), while the outskirts are better fit by an exponential-law. We investigate the time evolution of the phase-space density in DM halos from high-resolution dissipationless N-body simulations, and show that it follows a similar profile, where the phase-space density at a given radius is defined as the number of DM particles in a space volume at that radius, divided by the volume of the space itself. Using the definition of phase-space density in terms of the density and velocity divergence of the DM particles, we show that it can be computed directly from the simulation data without the need for binning. We find that the time evolution of the phase-space density is well fit by a triple-power law that depends on both radius and time. At a given radius, the time-evolution at high-redshift is well fit by an exponential with a scale radius of a few hundred pc, while at low-redshift, it is well fit by a power-law with an exponent of -0.23. The exponents at different redshifts are consistent with the self-similar solution for halo formation. These trends can be understood in terms of the differential growth of halos and their material components, with the density and velocity divergence of the halo components scaling with the scale radius of the halo.

We live in a universe that is growing ever more complex. Galaxies join clusters together to form larger structures. These structures eventually come together to form superclusters. Astronomers have recognized this trend of structure growth for decades, giving us a picture of our universe as a network of structures. However, a new study has found that this structure formation may be even darker than we thought. By analyzing the galaxy positions from large galaxy surveys, the researchers found that even regions where no galaxy observation is taken exhibit structure. These regions are known as the "cosmic microwave background," and they provide important information on the early history of the universe. This implies our standard model of structure formation is too simplistic, and we should perhaps search for a more complex equation of state to describe the universe's dynamics. This paper studies the galaxy spatial distribution in different environment bins at various scales, and highlights the dynamical range enabled by the large-scale structure dataset from SDSS-DR7. The galaxy distributions in high density regions, such as clusters and superclusters, are strongly correlated with their apparent shapes and tend to reside in stable orbits around the corresponding cosmic structures. However, the galaxy distributions in low density regions are far more complex and contain signals beyond gravitational instability. These signals are present on separations of tens to hundreds of megaparsecs, corresponding to the correlation lengths of 0.5-1.5 billion years. The signals from voids are persistent, spanning at least six billion years. Since these correlations are incompatible with gravitational instability, the authors conclude that the standard theory of structure formation, which is based on gravity, is incomplete and hypothesize a new equation of state that ties the dynamical range of large-scale structures to the early universe. The techniques in this paper could be applied to a broader range of data to explore similar signals from other cosmologically important processes, such as weak lensing and galaxy bias. Furthermore, by identifying these signals, we may be able to develop a better theory of structure formation that can more accurately describe our universe. --- SDSS-DR7 is a spectroscopic galaxy survey which has been used to study the large-scale structure of the universe. The large-scale structure of the universe grows over time through a process of gravitational instability. Galaxies move toward overdense regions, where the density of galaxies is higher than the average density of the universe. Once a region becomes dense enough, the galaxies will collapse into galaxy clusters. Some galaxies may also be pulled into superclusters. These processes can be studied by comparing the spatial distribution of galaxies in different environment bins (e.g., clusters vs. superclusters) and at different scales (e.g., megaparsecs vs. billion years). Using this dataset, the authors compare the spatial distributions of galaxies in different environment bins (density environments) and at different scales (luminosity-limited samples). The year 2020 has been characterized by several events that profoundly changed our world. It began with the first reports about a newly discovered virus, causing an outbreak that soon led to a pandemic. In parallel, the year has seen the rise of chaotic and apocalyptic cults, usually referred to as “cults”, among which the “Bio-Agent 7” and “Children of God” cases. Simultaneously, other events took place in the scientific community, such as the reemergence of smallpox for the first time in over 20 years. Finally, the beginning of the year saw the unexpected death of the most famous scientist of all times, Albert Einstein, a true icon of humanity. The Einstein’s life can be seen as a unique meeting point of the sciences, arts and humanities. The son of a celebrated scientist, he studied physics at Zurich, where he gained notoriety with his special relativity paper. After his early experiments in the field, his findings did not meet with widespread acclaim, and he was even accused of commercialism. He was then more or less forced to give up his research on quantum electrodynamics, considered the most promising path in his field. In 1925, Einstein was offered the presidency of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics, but he turned it down, preferring to remain an active researcher. Einstein’s later years were devoted to playing a leading role in the German Resistance, with all the ensuing risk for his family. During the final years of the war, the Nazis tried to deport him to Russia, but the American military authorities rescued him and brought him to the USA. The vindication of his genius, however, was not to come easily: not only did he have to struggle with serious health issues, but also the most ordinary tasks had become virtually impossible for him, given his deafness. Despite the apparently dark events of his life, Einstein remained a humanitarian, and saw the usefulness of science even in the darkest times. Throughout his life, he maintained a philosophical outlook on the world, trying to approach it with reason and logic, without fanaticism and cultishness. In the end, Einstein passed through the most difficult times with resilience and calm, accepting his destiny and remaining an example of humanity.

Imaging synaptic transmission by fluorescence microscopy is challenging because of the small opening of the synaptic cleft between two neurons. This implies that molecular scale details of the trafficking of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate are concealed. The vallinamain hypothesis states that an increasing calcium concentration in the presynaptic terminal will promote the fusion of secretory vesicles containing glutamate with the neuronal membrane, ultimately leading to the release of glutamate into the synaptic cleft. Despite its conceptual simplicity, the underlying molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Using real-time imaging of synapses expressing fluorescence labelled glutamate receptors, we were able to record the trafficking of individual glutamate receptors at nanometre resolution. We show that the vallinamain hypothesis does not account for the full complexity of these events, and we propose a set of detailed molecular processes underlying the trafficking and exocytosis of glutamate receptors. These findings not only advance our understanding of synaptic transmission, but also present a framework for understanding other membrane trafficking events.

Early-type galaxies are key galaxy populations in the structure formation paradigm. The strong correlation between their properties, such as mass and luminosity, indicate that early-type galaxies assembled most of their mass at high redshifts. However, the physical processes driving their assembly are still not well understood. In this work, we study the structure of early-type galaxies in the galaxy population of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), focusing on their photometric morphology and isophotal shapes. We find that, independent of galaxy properties such as stellar mass, concentration, and dynamical and star formation activity, early-type galaxies show different structural properties along the their isophotal shape. In particular, we find that early-type galaxies split in two distinct families when separating the sample into quiescent and active galaxies. The two families are well separated in terms of their central dominance, which is a proxy of their total mass, their sizes, and their distribution of axis ratios. The active galaxies show lower central dominance and higher degree of prolateness. Furthermore, we show that the environmental density is a key factor in determining the physical properties of the galaxies, including their morphology and central dominance, and we propose a model to explain these dependencies based on the effects of environment on galaxy properties. This work suggests that the structure of early-type galaxies is a complex phenomenon influenced by several physical processes acting in different ways in different environments.

We present the first Swift X-ray Telescope (XRT) observations of 35 gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). These observations span a wide range in time and luminosity, with 12 high-fluence, high-luminosity flares. We perform a detailed spectral analysis of each flare, finding that the spectra are best fit by an absorbed power law with photon index ˜1.8 in the 10-1000 keV band, and include flux estimates in the 0.3-10 keV band. The inferred total energy release in these flares is 9%–93% of the gamma-ray burst energy release. We also compare the flare luminosities to the afterglows of these bursts, and find no evidence of anti-correlation. We briefly discuss implications for emission mechanisms. We describe the results of the first survey of X-ray flares from gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) observed by the Swift telescope. The sample contains 35 GRBs with a total of 48 X-ray flares. We detected X-ray flares from 12 bursts out of the total sample. The temporal and spectral properties of the observed X-ray flares were examined. We found that the spectra are best fit by an absorbed power law with photon index ˜1.8 in the 10-1000 keV band and 0.3-10 keV band, and included flux estimates in the 0.3-10 keV band. The inferred total energy release in these flares is 9%–93% of the gamma-ray burst energy release. We discuss the implications of these results for emission mechanisms. We find no anti-correlation between the X-ray flare intensity and the intensity of the afterglows. This study was made possible by the Swift satellite, which was financed by NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA).

Local probing of electromechanical responses in cellular and biomolecular systems in aqueous environments is a crucial step towards understanding of their functions and mechanisms. Despite recent technological progress in the field of Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEMs), in situ probing of mechanical responses of cellular systems (such as live cells) within an aqueous environment remains an experimental challenge. Here, we present a method combining Micro Electro Mechanical System (MEMS) technology and an aqueous environment to develop a new family of probes suitable for such in situ probing. We apply this technology to develop the first MEMS cantilevers in the 1-10 μm length scale (1 μm being the diameter of a human red blood cell) with integrated functional channels for precise perfusion of cellular systems with aqueous environments, and electrolytes in this case, in real-time. In this work, we demonstrate the capabilities of this technology by monitoring the local mechanical responses of a live cell cultured on the surface of the probe. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of this technology to the investigation of the local mechanics of cellular systems in aqueous environments and biomolecular interactions in real-time.

Minkowski's question mark function (?(x)) is a multi-valued function that gives the frequency of the prime numbers up to a number x. It is known that the derivative of?(x) is not defined at some points, which are called quasi-prime numbers. In this work, we apply a fractal approach to study the pointwise behavior of the non-differentiability of?(x). We prove that there exists a universal constant C such that for almost all quasi-prime numbers q, we have |?(q+1) -?(q+2)/2| > Cq^{-(1+2)/4}. This improves the best known exponent of q^-1/2 obtained by Laurent. Our proof combines classic methods from analytic number theory and large sieve for the Cartwright Littlewood method. This work was completed during my PhD studies at EPFL, in the lab of Pierre-Henri Laurent. I would like to thank him for his help and support.

Recent advances in computer technology and algorithm development allow molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of strongly coupled dynamical systems over extended periods of time. In order to monitor the energy and momentum conservation over such long time periods, switchings of various force fields become necessary. In this work we present a general algorithm for the energy and momentum conservation in MD simulations using force fields with switching potentials. The general case is considered. The switching potentials are obtained from analytical solutions of the corresponding equations of motion. The general solution contains only parameters which have to be fixed by the initial conditions. Therefore, the proposed method is easy to apply and inexpensive in computational terms. We illustrate the efficiency of the approach on the example of the Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential. Applying the proposed algorithm, we obtain the results of the energy and momentum conservation over 600000 time steps of the LJ system with a relatively low cost, which is ~27% of the cost for the same time step with the conventional algorithm.

A new comprehensive set of elemental abundances in damped Lyman alpha absorbers (DLAs) is presented. The dataset is based on high-resolution spectroscopy of 19 quasars, aimed at the Zn and Y lines, which together provide 18$<$Z/H$<$27 and 26$<$Y/H$<$0.5 and cover almost 4 orders of magnitude in DLA [N$_2$H$^+$](+)[H$_2$]{}abundance. In addition to these Zn and Y lines, we also analyze other Zn and Y abundances from the previously published data of B13 and HS15. The paper includes re-analyses of the data from B13 and HS15, as well as new results for the previously analyzed elements O, Si, Ti, V, Cr, Co, and Ni. It also includes the first results for Al, Cu, and Mn. The full dataset allows, for the first time, detailed studies of the star formation histories (SFHs) in DLA galaxies. The new Y/Zn atomic ratios as a function of metallicity allow us to exclude models with a constant SFH with time (including exponentially declining ones). This significantly increases the number of SFHs that can be allowed by the data. We find that a two-burst model with a 5 Gyr-old secondary burst is the best model for the majority of the galaxies, with an additional very small fraction of galaxies best described by a constant SFH. The new dataset will be valuable for studies of the early evolution of galaxies, understanding of the chemical evolution of galaxies, and the testing of models of the formation and evolution of galaxies.

Non-backtracking random walks have been shown to be efficient algorithms for sampling from large networks with difficult weight distributions. The standard algorithm is inefficient for networks with community structure, for example, social networks with groups of friends. We analyze a novel algorithm for sampling from networks with community structure that is both more efficient and theoretically justifiable. We show that the eigenvalues of the transition matrix of the non-backtracking walk satisfy the Poisson distribution, just like in the case of a uniform random walk. This allows us to develop a novel algorithm, based on the Dinkelbach method, which improves the sampling efficiency of the non-backtracking walk. We apply this method to the problem of sampling communities in social networks, showing dramatic improvement over the standard method. The non-backtracking walk has applications to other sampling problems in networks. Tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs) are identified as structures in tidal debris fields. They may form in response to high-speed collisions between dwarf galaxies, and as such, are excellent probes of hierarchical structure formation. Their properties can be predicted by a simple empirical law, and they are used as tools to study the processes of galaxy formation and evolution. In this work, we compile a database of TDGs from the literature, with a total of 77 TDGs in 21 Hickson Compact Groups (HCGs). We present detailed models of the photometric evolution of these systems, and compare the predictions of these models to available data for 53 systems. We find that (1) the most massive TDGs in HCGs must have acquired more than 90% of their current mass by less than 8.5 Gyr, with most acquiring more than 50% of their current mass by less than 6 Gyr; (2) low surface brightness TDGs are predicted to have masses of 0.1-1.0%, with a median of 0.3% of the total group mass; (3) the characteristic mass scale for TDGs scales with the total mass of the HCG; and (4) there is no strong correlation between the age of a TDG and its mass, color, or environment. This suggests that tidal stripping and merging have been important processes in shaping the TDG population in HCGs. We conclude by discussing the implications of these results for hierarchical structure formation and the evolution of low surface brightness galaxies.

A scientific paper titled "Near-Infrared and X-ray Observations of the Enigmatic G70.7+1.2" by D.J. Kennea, L.V. Tchekhovskoy, R.F. Elsner, S.D. Nadiga, N.A. Webb, R.C. Hickox, K.T. Schachter, S.S. Dimopoulos, R.G. Kron, M.H. Soffitta, A. Pimayer, J.D. Tran, S.T. Brandt, R. Matsuoka, Y.U. Lee, M.Nagai, Y. Kato, M. Tsujimoto, M. Oizumi, M. Iwai, Y. Mizuma, T. Yoshikawa, M. Miyoshi, M. Tashiro, T.M.izuno, A. Elyiv, O. Reimer, T. Cunninghan, R.F. Mailly, and A.J. Wagner, published on arXiv.org on 2018 Aug 30, described new observations of the mysterious source G70.7+1.2, discovered with FERMI in the second half of 2012. The source was initially detected in gamma-rays and later in X-rays and radio, but its nature remained a mystery. Thanks to new observations with the both the infrared VLT and Chandra X-ray Observatory, the authors were able to better understand the nature of this intriguing object. G70.7+1.2 is likely a young, low-mass black hole X-ray binary in the intermediate stage of formation, where the optical counterpart is either swamped by the intense emission of the black hole or strongly absorbed. The authors argue that the unusually hard X-ray spectrum is most likely produced by synchrotron self-Compton mechanism.

Networks are found in almost all aspects of our lives, ranging from infrastructure such as power grids and transportation networks to interpersonal interaction such as friendships and social media followerships. One way of studying networks is to represent them as graphs, in which the nodes represent individual entities and the edges represent their relationships. Studying the structure of these networks can provide useful insights into their function. For example, the small-world phenomenon, where nodes are clustered into modules, has been observed in many real-world networks. One method of analyzing network structure is to look for patterns in their nodes and edges. These patterns may represent functional groups of nodes and edges, or they may simply be a byproduct of the network having some underlying structure. For example, the wheel andBridge patterns have been shown to significantly enhance the complexity of real-world transportation and social networks, respectively. In this work, I consider chain motifs, patterns in which a core node is connected to adjacent nodes that themselves form a pattern. Examples include a diamond pattern in which four nodes form a chain and an inverted diamond pattern in which a node forms a chain in reversed orientation. I show that many real-world networks contain one or more chain motifs. These patterns can enhance the functionality of a network, and their absence in random networks suggests that chain motifs are, on average, over-represented in real-world networks. I also study the structural effects of chain motif disruption, showing that removing a core node from a diamond motif harms its stability, while removing a core node from an inverted diamond motif helps its stability.

Two-photon ionization of hydrogen-like ions is studied via a fully relativistic description based on the Riccati-Hankel method. The angular distribution of the emitted electrons is calculated for a number of fixed values of the principal quantum number N and the angular momentum quantum number J, including N = 2 and J = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. It is shown that the relativistic corrections generally smooth the behaviour of the non-relativistic patterns and shift them to lower values of the electron's emission angle. In particular, relativistic effects considerably modify the values of the peak of the emission distribution for some values of the quantum numbers N and J. The obtained results can be used to determine the influence of relativistic effects on the energy levels and electronic transition probabilities in hydrogen-like ions, as well as the possibility of testing the relativity through the study of these effects on the emission patterns of the ionized electrons.

In this article, we study J-class operators, a class of operators introduced by Arveson. We first show that an operator on a Hilbert space is in the J-class if and only if it is hypercyclic. We then study some sufficient conditions for a single J-class operator to be hypercyclic. Among other things, we find that if the operator has a non-dense range and its essential spectrum is not identically equal to the whole complex plane, then the single operator is hypercyclic. We also give examples showing that all these conditions are necessary. USE CASES: This article is mainly interested in studying hypercyclic properties of a particular class of operators known as J-class operators. These operators were introduced by Arveson in 1969 and form the set of all those operators that are mixing, positive and hypercyclic. They also have some other interesting properties like a) The J-class operators are closed under taking adjoints. b) An operator in the J-class is densely defined if and only if its adjoint is also in the J-class. c) An operator is in the J-class if and only if its minimal normal extension is in the J-class. d) If f is a J-class operator on a Hilbert space H, then so is $\lambda f$ for every complex number with modulus one. e) If f is a J-class operator and z is a non-zero vector in the Hilbert space H, then so is $z f$. f) If f is a J-class operator and $A$ is a subalgebra of the $C^*$-algebra generated by f, then either f is a scalar multiple of the identity or $A$ is commutative.

Cosmic rays are high energy particles that permeate the entire universe. Their high energy density pose a challenge to the standard model of cosmology, suggesting the possibility of new physics. One consequence of new physics could be the local attenuation of cosmic rays due to the interaction with a dense medium. This attenuation could potentially be observed via an increase in the gamma background radiation emitted from the dark matter halo of our solar system. We test this possibility by analyzing the gamma background radiation recorded by the Advanced Thin Ionization Technique (ATI). We do not observe an increase in the gamma background radiation from the direction of the nearby remnants, implying a cosmic ray flux at least 1,000 times higher than observed. We argue that this discrepancy can be resolved if a nearby supernova occurs every 50-200 Myr, corresponding to a distance of 7-30 kpc away from the sun. In this scenario, the supernova remnants have positivenergy effects by accelerating cosmic rays to ultrahigh energies, but the local cosmic ray flux is still sufficiently low to explain the lack of a gamma signal.

A hot and young pre-cataclysmic variable (P CVn) star has been discovered in the constellation of Vulpecula. The star has a white dwarf companion, and is estimated to be 14% of the present age of the universe and has a surface temperature of 14,000 K. Its companion is radiating 1000 watts at its surface. The most likely scenario for the formation of such an object is the merger of two white dwarfs. This object exhibits several of the defining characteristics of a pre-cataclysmic variable star, including a very low eccentricity for its inner Lagrangian point, and a substantial spin-orbit axis misalignment. This is surprising for such a young system, and implies that evolution has acted very rapidly to realign the inner binary.' This system may have interesting dynamical implications for the evolution of these systems and could provide a strong constraint on theories of dynamical evolution of binaries. Further high cadence monitoring of this system will be required to further refine its characteristics and confirm its suspected young age.'

Dynamic screening in a two-species asymmetric exclusion process has been studied by using an external species of noninteracting fermions. We find that the correlation between the particles changes the effective diffusion constant of the system dramatically. The dependence of the diffusion constant on the concentration of the external particles exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with a maximum at a particular concentration. The maximum of the diffusion constant occurs because the dynamic screening effect enhances the transport of particles with low hopping probability. This maximum is sensitive to the external particles’ parity and is absent for the lower symmetry case with a larger diffusion constant. We demonstrate that the dynamic screening effect can be viewed as a distinct phase of the system. This work was published in Physical Review E 92, 042123 (2015). Researchers have shown that dynamic screening, i.e., the interaction between different species of particles, can dramatically change the transport behavior of particles. This has been observed in both experiments and simulations for one-dimensional models. However, less is known for two-dimensional systems. In this work, we study dynamic screening in a two-species asymmetric exclusion process using an external species of noninteracting fermions. The external particles are restricted to move in one direction and cannot change the species or the number of particles of the system particles. We find that the dependence of the diffusion constant of the system on the concentration of the external particles exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with a maximum at a particular concentration. The maximum of the diffusion constant occurs because the dynamic screening effect enhances the transport of particles with low hopping probability. This maximum is sensitive to the external particles’ parity and is absent for the lower symmetry case with a larger diffusion constant.
