In this paper we present a detailed study of the systematics of soft particle production in forward angles for Au+Au collisions at energies available at the Relativistic Heavy Ion collider (RHIC). Such studies are of particular relevance to characterize the Degree of Chaos /thermalization achieved in these collisions. Our results are based on analyzing 1.7 million minimum-bias events from the PHOBOS experiment. We compare charged and neutral particle spectra, elliptic flow, and high transverse momentum particle production, covering a range of 15% centrality covering the most central to the most peripheral Au+Au collisions. We observe that particle production at forward rapidity is very well described by a quadratic function of the number of N-particles per unit of rapidity, where N=charged or neutral. These results are compared to hadronic models (PYTHIA, HIJING, AMPT), calculations from lattice QCD, and models from weakly coupled physics. Our data show the most detailed and strongest constraints on these models, and indicate the importance of specific aspects of the dynamics of these collisions to different aspects of the observed particle spectra. We quantify these aspects using a thermal-based model. This allows us to derive the thermal parameters for the system at the chemical and kinetic freezeouts. These are compared to predictions from ideal hadron gas and transport models at both constituent-quark level and hadronic level. We find that the kinetic freezeout parameter is more strongly constrained by the data, and we extract a conservative range of temperatures of 155 MeV<T<175 MeV. The preliminary results indicate that the hadron gas phase is short-lived, with a strong transition to a dense and hadronically collapsed medium at chemical freezeout. While both hard scattering and early phases of the nuclear collision appear to be consistent with being perturbative in nature, the strongly interacting final state is well described by a gluon plasma with moderate centrality-dependent temperatures of 155 MeV<T<175 MeV.

NiCl$_2$-4SC(NH$_2$)$_2$ is a quantum magnet which exhibits a variety of fascinating behaviors. This material is known to order at low temperatures into a large polarization of transverse spin components, with the spins ordering in a two-dimensional plane. Furthermore, this material has been shown to exhibit slow magnetic dynamics in a temperature range below approximately 30 K, where the nature of the low-temperature magnetic behavior is not well understood. In this paper, we report studies of the low-temperature magnetic dynamics using a combination of high-frequency pulsed magnetisation and continuous wave (cw) low-frequency magnetisation, with results presented for both single-crystal and polycrystalline samples. We demonstrate that the low-frequency cw magnetisation is sensitive to the spin-spin correlation function, with both low-temperature dynamical scaling behaviour and the field and temperature dependence of the coupling suggested to be consistent with the predicted behaviour for a system with dominant long-range interactions, in this case a system with dominant infinite-range, or long-range, magnetic dipole interactions. These results, while providing only indirect evidence for the magnetic dipole interaction, are consistent with a picture in which the ground state of NiCl$_2$-4SC(NH$_2$)$_2$ is dominated by a fully polarised transverse spin configuration, with short-range interactions between these polarised regions, as would be expected for systems with dominant dipole interactions.

Polarization states of the primordial gravitational waves (GWs) remain encoded in the temperature and polarization anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). To probe these states, we introduce a novel statistic, the Stokes parameter variance (SPV), and develop new methods to analyze future cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations. We show that an experiment with sky coverage of 5,000 square degrees and noise level of ~0.01 σ(SPV) can probe the (spin up ⟂ ↗, spin down ⟂ →) states with a significance of 5 σ. This can be extended to the 24-dimensional parameter space of (⟂ ↗, ⟂ →, ⟂ ∥, ⟂ ⊥) by adding low resolution CMB polarization observations. We demonstrate the robustness of our method by simulating the gravitational wave foreground and showing that the SPV measurement is largely insensitive to these foregrounds. We apply our method to ongoing CMB temperature and low resolution polarization observations and place constraints on the amplitudes of the spin-2 operators generated by gravitational waves in the estimated skies. Our approach is entirely data-driven and does not make any prior assumptions about the theory or the foreground nature of the observations. We provide an easy to use publicly available software package for polarization estimation from future CMB observations.

In this paper, we study a gravity theory dual to conformal Surfaceprotein Dynamics, which naturally exhibits a wide class of single-sector supersymmetry breaking (SSSB) patterns, without the need for ad hoc moduli stabilization. These SSSB patterns can arise as leading quantum corrections in the gravity theory, or from moduli stabilization. Following recent claims that the universe is accelerating, this paper critically analyzes the validity of the data and the methodologies employed to reach that conclusion. It is shown that the Type Ia supernova data may be fit to an open universe with zero or even positive curvature without the need for a cosmological constant or dark energy. It is also shown that the data used in recent papers purporting to show that the universe is accelerating is in fact consistent with an open universe with zero or even positive curvature without the need for exotic forms of dark matter. It is concluded that the evidence for the acceleration of the universe is inconclusive and likely represents a form of data selection bias. The acceleration of the universe is one of the greatest achievements of modern cosmology. It was reported by two independent research teams in 2014 and 2016 and gained significant attention in the popular media. The results were quickly accepted as fact by the general astronomy community and the prevailing theoretical interpretation is that a form of dark energy with an equation of state parameter, w < -1 is causing the universe to accelerate. The theoretical foundations of this claim have been extensively analyzed and found to be lacking. It has been demonstrated that for a range of theoretically plausible dark energy models, a vanishingly small value of w is consistent with the reported supernova data. The statistical methodology employed to reject non-dark energy models with small w has been shown to have significant flaws and is invalid. More recent papers have reported similar results. It has been demonstrated that the Type Ia supernova data may be fit to an open universe with zero or even positive curvature without the need for a cosmological constant or dark energy. It is also shown that the data used in recent papers purporting to show that the universe is accelerating is in fact consistent with an open universe with zero or even positive curvature without the need for exotic forms of dark matter. It is concluded that the evidence for the acceleration of the universe is inconclusive and likely represents a form of data selection bias. It is shown that the Type Ia supernova data is consistent with the original research claim, that dark energy is causing the acceleration, but not with the more recent claims that the universe is open or flat. Therefore the reported acceleration is likely a result of selection bias or the incorrect application of statistical methodologies. The data and research in this field is still in a relatively early stage and it is likely that the true nature of the acceleration will become clear as new observational data sets are developed and as more comprehensive modeling of the dark energy is performed. Until then, the acceleration of the universe should be viewed with great suspicion.

In this work, we analyze the signatures of heavy Z’ bosons in the Extra U(1) Superstring Inspired Model (EUSIM) (1, 2). We base our study on the renormalization group equations (RGEs) of the model. We conclude that the neutral heavy Z’ boson can be lighter than the standard model (SM) electroweak (EW) bosons, and it may even be the lightest new particle (LNP) if the Extra U(1) gauge boson has a small kinetic term (1, 2). Besides the neutral heavy Z’, we also study the charged heavy W’ and Z’. In this model, they can also be lighter than the SM W and Z bosons, respectively. Our study shows that these particles may have signatures like disappearing tracks (3, 4), large electric dipole moments (EDMs) (5, 6), and monojet plus missing transverse energy (MET) (7). Some of these signatures have been observed at the LHC, for example, the disappearing tracks (8) and monojet plus MET (9). However, all of these phenomenological aspects of this model are subject to considerable uncertainties that remain to be fully explored (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10).

A measurement of the far-infrared background (FIRB) provides a powerful tool for understanding the history of the universe and the intergalactic medium (IGM). The FIRB contains information on the energy generation history of the universe, from galaxies to decoupled electromagnetic and ultra-violet photons. The FIRB has been directly measured by the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) and subsequent instruments, and by the Diffuse Infrared Background Experiment (DIRBE). In contrast, an intensity of the FIRB has only been measured indirectly by the Wisconsin Hautmann (WHAM) radiotelescope for a narrow range of longwave (94-120 μm) wavelengths. Here, we use data from both COBE/DIRBE and WHAM to determine the FIRB intensity at 94-120 μm with an accuracy sufficient to test models of the formation of the large-scale structure of the universe. The resulting FIRB intensity is (2.2 ± 0.3) × 10−8 photons μm−2 s−1, where the uncertainty is 1 σ, consistent with other measurements and with predicted intensities from galaxy models. This measurement represents the first determination of the FIRB at 94-120 μm with an accuracy sufficient to test models of the formation of the large-scale structure of the universe.

Pulsars are highly magnetized Neutron Stars (NS) that are product of supernova explosions. Pulsars can be divided to two different classes. Some of them, calledNormal pulsars have strong magnetic fields and lighthouse like beams that are used to detect them. Another class, called Anomalous pulsars, have much weaker magnetic fields and don't have beams. One anomalous pulsar, called PSR B1930+22, was found to produce pulsed radio emission with probable origins in its magnetosphere as well as in the plasma that fills its magnetospheric space. This pulsed emission was also observed coming from the direction of pulsar rotation and moving at relativistic speed in relation to the surrounding plasma. Similar pulsed radio emission has also been observed from another anomalous pulsar, called PSR B1046-58, that has extremely weak magnetic field. Hence, it is also unlikely that this pulsar can be detected by any earth based instrumentation. These pulsed radio emissions have also been observed to be transient. These observations indicate that pulsed radio emission may be generated due to reconnection of magnetic fields in pulsars magnetospheres. Such mechanism might also be responsible for transient pulsed emission observed from some pulsars. Such a process might also be important for radio emission from pulsars that are detectable by instrumentation on earth.

High speed white dwarfs (HSWDs) with radial velocities (RV) up to 2000 km/s are difficult to identify and characterize observationally. The dearth of reliable empirical measurements of the trigonometric parallaxes of HSWDs prevents their meaningful characterization, especially if these measurements are used in concert with non-parametric probabilistic velocity vectors (e.g. UFOlogists) to assign likely orbital pericenters. Here we report trigonometric parallax measurements for 11 previously identified HSWDs with RVs $\geq$ 500 km/s. The measured parallaxes indicate these stars lie within 10 kpc of the galactic plane with pericentric distances ranging from 9.2 to 29.4 kpc (with a median of 18 kpc). Only one star has a low orbital eccentricity ($e$ = 0.16), most have $e$ $>$ 0.5. Six stars have highly negative periastron velocities consistent with NGC2477—a proposed open cluster at 23 kpc from the sun. In combination with available astrometry and photometry we conclude all but one star likely belong to the NGC2477 moving group. This result suggests the majority of high RV halo white dwarfs share a common velocity vector with a natal population in the solar vicinity, possibly the thin disk. Parallax-based estimates of the heliocentric distances of several hundred HSWDs with RVs $\geq$ 500 km/s will aid in refining the population spatial density as a function of RV, which may prove useful for constraining the origin(s) of these unique stars.

Recent experimental advances in the field of Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) enable observation of novel forms of quantum many-body phenomena. Notably, engineering of driven-dissipative quantum systems has led to the observation of quantum phase transitions with light, namely, the Bose-Hubbard model. Integration of BECs with cavity quantum electrodynamics, another milestone in coherent light research, opens up the possibility of realizing effective gauge potentials for quantum particles. Here, we realize both these effects in a single chip device, and observe the formation of chiral supersolids and a chiral spin liquid. We demonstrate that a cavity-BEC platform has many potential applications, ranging from the discovery of new quantum phases to the implementation of quantum simulators and quantum information processing. The article provides an overview of recent experimental results in the field of cavity Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). The authors demonstrate realization of both effective gauge potentials and the Bose-Hubbard model in a single chip device. Such integrated systems could find applications in quantum simulators and quantum information processing.

The Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence, also known as the PBW theorem or the PBW theorem for Lie algebras, is a key result in the representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras. It was established by Michel Dixmier and Gerhard Moeglin in 1968. Let be a complex semisimple Lie algebra and a Borel subalgebra. Then the -invariant elements of the universal enveloping algebra form a polynomial algebra,, generated by the elements where runs over the set of simple roots of relative to. This is known as the Dixmier-Moeglin equivalence. The PBW theorem for semisimple Lie algebras has important applications in the theory of integrable systems; in particular, it is used to show that certain representations of Lie algebras of vector fields are freely generated as -modules. The proof of the PBW theorem was simplified by Jean-Marie M692 bios and Hans-Joachim Schellmann.

In the Milky Way, there are several kinds of non-baryonic dark matter, which remain undetected by standard laboratory experiments. Some of these particles may interact with normal matter only via gravitational forces, and some of these particles may still be in spatial regions where Standard Model interactions are suppressed. These dark matter particles may accumulate in the center of the Galaxy, where the gravitational force is strongest. We propose to search for such dark matter particles by targeting the gamma-rays they produce when they scape from the galactic disk and are exposed to cosmic rays for the first time in the Galactic Center (GC) region. Our target GC halo dark matter particles would have two key properties. First, the velocity dependence of their interaction with normal matter peaks at high speeds, such as those of dark-matter particles lost to the halo in the solar vicinity. Second, the dark-matter-induced gamma-ray signal from these halo particles would have both a nearly isotropic spatial distribution, and a spectral shape distinct from other known gamma-ray sources in the GC region. We demonstrate that a dark matter search with GLAST could discover halo dark matter that scatters in the GC with a signal strengths that are significantly stronger than current bounds, even for particles with weak interactions, and with no prior information other than an isotropic gamma-ray signal. We note that halo dark matter can form bands, rather than being uniformly distributed, and we present limits on the fraction of dark matter in such bands as a function of halo mass and observation time. In our example analysis, we consider a band of dark matter that crosses the midplane of the Galaxy at a location that is consistent with the observed positions of radio stars, and with an event rate that is at least ten times the mean rate. Such a band of dark matter could be consistent with existing experimental constraints. We also propose several target bands, where future observations could discover gamma-ray bands from dark matter particle interactions. These observations would significantly strengthen existing constraints on dark matter interactions, and would provide new tests of dark matter models.

We present results of very high energy gamma-ray and near infrared observations of 1ES2344+514 performed between 2004 and 2005. The source was observed by the H.E.S.S.Cherenkov Telescope array twice each year on average, and also detected by the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) in the K band. The spectrum of 1ES2344+514 is very stable during this period, and can be well described by a simple power law with an average spectral index of -2.26 ± 0.08 (1σ). The high correlation coefficient (r) between the total flux and the photon index, as well as the distribution of the photon index versus the strength of the spectrum, strongly suggest that the spectrum is indeed due to gamma-ray attenuation by the extragalactic background light. Here we present the results of Very High Energy gamma-ray and Near Infrared observations of 1ES2344+514 performed between 2004 and 2005. The source was observed by the H.E.S.S.Cherenkov Telescope array twice each year on average, and also detected by the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) in the K band. The spectrum of 1ES2344+514 is very stable during this period, and can be well described by a simple power law with an average spectral index of -2.26 ± 0.08 (1σ). The high correlation coefficient (r) between the total flux and the photon index, as well as the distribution of the photon index versus the strength of the spectrum, strongly suggest that the spectrum is indeed due to gamma-ray attenuation by the extragalactic background light. The Very High Energy gamma-ray observation of 1ES2344+514 was conducted in September 2005 and April 2008. No significant variability on time scales of hours was found during these observations. However, there was a significant and rapid (null hypothesis probability=3.8% ) change in the spectral properties of the source, with the average photon index increasing from -2.26 to -2.47 during the 3.5 hour long observations. This fast variability could be caused by either the source undergoing a major transformation in the structure of its relativistic jet, or by the passage of a new cloud through the line of sight to the source, causing fluctuations in the intensity of the gamma-ray flux.

A vertically oscillated shallow granular layer fluidizes. During fluidization, the average grain velocity increases with depth and the flux of grains through the upper surface decreases with depth in a way consistent with the Beverloo Law. However, the flux of grains passing through the lower surface does not exhibit this inverse relationship and increases with depth. These results indicate that there is a depth-dependent tri-layer structure of the fluidized granular layer, with the top surface being the shallow layer, the middle layer fluidizing like the Beverloo Law, and the bottom surface not fluidizing at all. This tri-layer structure is similar to the sandpile dynamics observed in self-organized critical systems, except that the bottom surface is not consumed. We present the results of a 998-MHz Giant Meterwave Radio Telescope (GMRT) radio continuum survey of M33, a nearby galaxy in the M31 group. The observations, performed between 2011 January and 2012 June, consisted of 1218 Pointings (primary beams of the GMRT dishes are shaped like astro showers), each of which were observed for a total of about 17.5 hours. The entire survey region, covering about 11.3 square degrees of the M33 disk, has been mapped at an angular resolution of 6.4’’. We have used the CLEAN algorithm, implemented in the DIPACK software, to produce the radio images. The achieved r.m.s. noise is about 29 $\mu$Jy/beam, which corresponds to a detection limit of about $10^{19}$ atoms/cm$^{2}$ for a 50 km/s linewidth for the emission. We detect radio continuum from atoms and molecules, and estimate the electron density and magnetic field strength.

The tensor part of the Skyrme energy density functional is extended to spherical nuclei. The new functional is tested on stable nuclear ground states with various interactions in the Delaunay volume rendering algorithm. The functional is also used to compute collective potential curves and their curvatures for several low-lying excitations in $^{16}$O and $^{208}$Pb. The calculated excitation energies, and transition strengths, compare very favourably with data. In this paper, we investigate the critical interface dynamics in a model for Barkhausen noise. The model is a directed percolation with additional degrees of freedom which describe the local interface slope. In the long time limit the model shows a critical scaling behavior with continuous phase transitions. In particular, we are interested in the fluctuations close to these transitions. To investigate these we use the method of wavelet transforms. The analysis shows that the scale-dependent wavelet variances have a singularity at the critical point in the form of a universal scaling function which coincides with the static scaling exponent of the correlation length. Furthermore, we discuss how to test the scaling hypothesis numerically and present Monte Carlo data which confirm our analytical findings. Reference: Adib, M., Berthier, C., Moreno, A., & Gorre, N. (2015). Wavelet transforms in a critical interface model for Barkhausen noise. Physical review letters, 114(17).

Signals of unparticles, which are fractionally charged particles that emerge from a scale invariant theory at higher energy scale, have been explored in low energy parity violation and NuTeV experiments. The unparticle physics may also be accessible at the current run of Tevatron and future LHC. Signals of unparticles have been explored in low energy parity violation experiment SLD and NuTeV experiment. The combined analysis of these experiments leads to the limits on scale of unparticle physics, Λ~ 1.7 × 10−3 - 3.7 × 10−3 eV, and the unparticle couplings to electrons, photons and Z, β=0.2-0.8. These limits are applicable to the dark matter search, new physics at the TeV scale, and some scenarios of unparticle physics. These results are interpreted in the framework of unparticle physics, where the parity even degrees of freedom, associated with a scale Λ, slowly decouple at a lower energy scale, leading to a modification of the electroweak interactions. Specifically, the unparticle exchange generates parity odd corrections to the standard model Lagrangian with dimension scale Λ. These corrections can induce the effective operators of the electromagnetic form factors, analogous to the electromagnetic form factors of the particles of standard model. The form factors F^{unparticle}(q^2) can be measured in experiments. These measurements can put strong constraints on the scale of unparticle physics Λ and the unparticle coupling constants β. For the case of weak boson couplings, the measured form factors are consistent with the Standard Model predictions. However, for the cases of electrons and photons, the measurements disfavor the unparticle interactions with the electron at 3.5σ level, and the photon at 2.1σ level. These results are not compatible with the standard model prediction at 1.9σ level. Moreover, for the case of Z couplings, the measurements favor unparticle interactions over the standard model predictions at 2.7σ level.

New data from MiniBooNE on the searches for $\nu_e$ neutral current (NC) events and $\nu_{\mu}$ charged current (CC) events in the oscillation region suggest that sterile neutrinos may be necessary to account for these data. We examine the data from the latest MiniBooNE NC and CC oscillation analyses in the framework of three-neutrino oscillations with one light active neutrino and two heavier, sterile neutrinos. We find that the latest MiniBooNE data can be explained with normal ordering of the neutrino mass spectrum and a typical choice of sterile neutrino mixing parameters, namely, $m_4 < m_5 < m_1$, $|U_{e4}| \approx |U_{e5}| \ll 1$, and $|U_{e4}|^2 + |U_{e5}|^2 \approx 1$. The global fit to the data gives, at the $3\sigma$ confidence level, the following best-fit parameters: $\Delta m^2 = (2.44^{+0.56}_{-0.52})\times10^{-3}~\text{eV}^2$ and $\sin^22\theta = 1.00^{+0.19}_{-0.20}$. We show that, for this set of parameters, the resulting global three-neutrino best-fit predictions are in good agreement with the recent determinations of these parameters from the global neutrino oscillation fit to all available data, as well as with the results of other low-energy neutrino experiments and the recent cosmological constraints on the total energy density of the Universe. However, because of the large sterile neutrino mixing needed in this model, one should be careful in drawing definitive conclusions until the results of the short-baseline neutrino experiments designed to look for active-sterile mixing with small $\Delta m^2$ and $\sin^22\theta$ are available.

Heavy-light semileptonic decays of mesons provide a clean opportunity to test the Standard Model (SM) and explore physics beyond it. In this work, we present the first complete analysis of these decays in the framework of staggered chiral perturbation theory. We combine our results for these decay rates with lattice QCD calculations of the corresponding hadronic parameters and make predictions for a number of experimentally measurable observables. We find that isospin breaking in the SM predictions for these observables is large and that these deviations are best described in the framework of chiral perturbation theory, which we apply here to the first time to these decays. We also make predictions for quantities which cannot be measured in lattice QCD, such as lepton- flavor-violating decays of charged pions. We find that these modes can be potentially large and can provide competitive probes of new phenomena beyond the SM. We also make predictions for quantities which cannot be measured in lattice QCD, such as lepton- flavor-violating decays of charged pions. We find that these modes can be potentially large and can provide competitive probes of new phenomena beyond the SM. In addition, we perform the first analysis of hadronic light-by-light scattering in the framework of chiral perturbation theory, which can provide a significant source of isospin breaking in these decays and can potentially explain the large offsets from the SM observed in some of our predictions. We make predictions for the following quantities: - Decay rates and isospin breaking - Hadronic parameters that enter the decay rates, such as $K_\pi L$ - Lepton- flavor-violating decays of charged pions - Photoproduction of charged pions on nucleons We find that these modes can be potentially large and can provide competitive probes of new phenomena beyond the SM.

Atomic force microscopy (AFM) is a powerful surface science technique that can provide detailed images of biological samples with nanometer resolution. It has been extensively used to study phospholipid bilayers for over a decade. Recently, researchers realized that it can also provide important information about the structure of thicker (>10 nm) lamellar stacks. To take advantage of this capability, proper sample preparations and control of imaging conditions are critical. In this study, we used commercial-grade silicon nitride probes with optimized tapping mode AFM imaging conditions to obtain high resolution and large scan areas of thick (20-30 nm) lamellar stacks. We imaged both supported and single-bilayer unsupported specimens, and we also studied several systems with different bilayer thicknesses. We show that imaging of these samples should be performed in ultra-high vacuum, or in solvent vapor for supported specimens, at low temperature ( < 10 °C). We believe that the method we used here can provide valuable information about the structure of thicker lamellar stacks and should be applicable to different bilayer materials.

In the first part of this paper, we introduce a new algorithm that solves the advection-diffusion equation with moving boundaries (i.e. free boundaries). The algorithm is based on a discrete ordinates approach, using a finite difference method to discretize in both space and velocity. This method is exact if the boundaries are periodic or advected with a linear velocity. We show that it is also consistent if the advection speed is linearly interpolated between the cell center and the boundary. In practice, this method is useful as long as the advection speed is not too large, or the spatial resolution is not too poor. As an example of its application, we simulate the growth of solids in a viscous accretion disk. We test our algorithm on analytical solutions of the diffusion-advection equation and show that our results are in agreement with the expected analytical solution. We then use our algorithm to study the evolution of solids in a viscous accretion disk with various sets of initial conditions. In all cases, solids cannot reach the central star within a ten thousand year time scale. In the second part, we study the effect of solids on the dust evolution in the disk. Solids generate a size distribution that differs from that of dust grains. In particular, solids tend to generate a significant amount of sub-micron sized grains. The exact form of this size distribution depends on the size and composition of solids. In this part, we present several simple models to investigate the influence of solids on the dust evolution. We show that solids with a given size and composition produce different consequences on the dust size distribution. Finally, we show that the exact form of the size distribution is of little importance for the dust evolution in the most part of the disk: after about one million year only large grains are present in the disk and the evolution is fully determined by the dust settling and the radial drift. We conclude that solids cannot reach the central star within a ten thousand year time scale, but they are a major actor of the dust evolution. Solids generate a size distribution that differs from that of dust grains. The exact form of this size distribution depends on the size and composition of solids.

Raman spectroscopy and photoluminescence spectroscopy are two powerful experimental techniques to probe the spin and electronic structures of spin-polarized electron gases. Using spin- and electron-resonance excitation, the excitation spectra of the Coulomb pseudo-gap spin excitons reveal the Zeeman splitting in the electron spin resonance (ESR) and the g-factor in the electron spin resonance absorption (ESRA). Here, we measure the ESRA and ESSR spectra of a spin-polarized electron gas created in a graphene layer using illumination with circularly polarized light. The comparison between the ESRA and ESSR spectra reveals the g-factor of the electron spin resonance. The observed g-factor of 2.002(3) is close to the free electron g-factor of 2, but differs significantly from the g-factor of a ferromagnet (2.75), which indicates that the electron spin is not polarized. Furthermore, we extract the spin polarization from the ratio of ESRA and ESSR spectra. Our result provides a new method to measure the spin polarization of a spin-polarized electron gas.

Observational cosmological data have been used to statistically describe the probability distribution function (PDF) of the mass of dark matter haloes. In recent years, high-resolution N-body simulations have advanced to the point of enabling the gravitational clustering of dark matter to be reproduced directly, allowing the construction of halo PDFs at much higher mass and spatial resolution. These have provided new insights into the process of halo assembly, allowing the growth of substructure within each halo to be analysed and the influence of environment on halo properties to be investigated. Although the evolution of halo mass function is generally consistent with a predicted scale-free form at the high-mass end, with significant deviations seen only at the low- and high-mass ends, the PDFs exhibit more complex behaviour, with significant differences between individual simulations, and a dependence on time and environment. In this paper we use the large-volume (>8.5 billion h^{-1} Mpc^3), intermediate-resolution (particle mass < 8.5 x 10^9 h^{-1} M /) Millennium-II simulation to investigate the evolution of the PDFs of the concentration, spin and orbital kinetic energy of dark matter haloes across four environments: clusters, sheets, filaments and voids. We also examine the effects of subhalo accretion, disruptions and mergers on these properties. The mass dependence of these distributions evolves significantly with time, and environment has a significant impact on the distribution at fixed time. In general, the haloes in sheets and filaments have more concentrated mass distributions than their cluster or void counterparts at all epochs. These differences are reflected in their associated mass functions, with the filament clusters being the most massive and most dynamically evolved structures, while voids are the most overdense regions in the universe and thus mark the sites of recent and future structure formation. The evolution of these distributions with time and environment therefore appears to be related to the hierarchical growth of structure. The spin and orbital kinetic energy also exhibit significant differences between environments, with the spin magnitude having a near-universal evolution, irrespective of environment or redshift, while the orbital kinetic energy exhibits different behaviours, with its distribution shifting to lower values in more evolved environments. This corresponds to the hierarchical buildup of structure in sheets and filaments, which forms at relatively late times, leading to an accumulation of material in the central regions, as well as a reduction in substructure. The properties of haloes in clusters are largely set by their major mergers since z > 2, leaving them with short orbital times and low orbital kinetic energy. Conversely, the evolution of void haloes is more complex, with a mixture of processes at work. Subhaloes can only survive in the highest density regions for a limited time, while the expansion of the universe disperses material, resulting in lower concentrations and lower orbital energies. Nonequilibrium statistical mechanics has come a long way since the pioneering works of G. N. Bochkov and Y. E. Kuzovlev. In this field, a central problem is to determine the probability density that a nonequilibrium system is in a given state. Many systems of interest, such as vibrating strings, lattice gases, and particle systems far from global equilibrium, do not dissipate energy and so are typically described by the so-called “boltzmann” or “non-neglected" or “nonequilibrium" or “steady state" statistics. However, it is difficult to perform direct calculations with these statistics. Recently, a “generalized" or “two-time" probability density has been proposed for systems described by a time-independent Hamiltonian. The “two-time" probability density, defined as the product of the "quasifred" density and the “green’s function" or “retarded function", generalizes the Boltzmann and “non-neglected" statistics. In the quasifree regime, the two-time probability density reduces to the Boltzmann probability density; in the quasifree and Markov regimes, the two-time probability density reduces to the non-neglected probability density. A corresponding generalized fluctuation-dissipation theorem is proven, and several exact results are obtained for the two-time probability density. An algorithm is proposed for numerically computing the two-time probability density. In summary, this paper provides a systematic theoretical framework for nonequilibrium statistical mechanics for systems described by a time-independent Hamiltonian and offers a new approach for studying such systems.

In this paper we develop a framework for propagating scalar fields in (Anti) de Sitter spacetimes using the concept of time ordering. We introduce the concept of a scalar propagator which describes the temporal development of a scalar field, and use this to formulate the scalar field equations of motion in terms of a time ordered correlation function. We consider the de Sitter and (Anti) de Sitter spacetimes as special cases of our more general time ordered theories, where we apply this to minimally and non-minimally coupled scalar fields. We explicitly solve the scalar propagator in these theories in global coordinates, and use this to find an approximation to the full propagator. Finally, we illustrate our results by computing the two-point function of a minimally coupled scalar field in various de Sitter and (Anti) de Sitter spacetimes. We show that the two-point function is given by the Hadamard self-correlation function in de Sitter, by the Wightman two-point function in (Anti) de Sitter with vanishing boundary terms, and by the boundary Wightman two-point function in de Sitter with a cosmological horizon.

We present a detailed analysis of the gamma-ray spectrum of the TeV source RX J1713.7-3946, based on 10 years of observations with the H.E.S.S. telescopes. We confirm the existence of two spectral components, previously reported by other experiments, with a break at approximately 600 GeV. The differential energy spectra of the two components and their integral fluxes are derived and the implications for the origin and physical properties of the gamma-ray emitting particles are discussed. The SNR RX J1713.7-3946 is one of the best candidates to study particles of extra-terrestrial origin (cosmic rays) interaction over a wide energy range from the radio to the TeV gamma-ray band. We performed a detailed study of the gamma-ray emission using data collected by the H.E.S.S. I and II telescopes. We confirm the existence of two spectral components, one with a spectral break at 600 GeV, the other one extending to at least 10 TeV. The differential energy spectra of the two components and their integral fluxes are derived and the implications for the origin and physical properties of the gamma-ray emitting particles are discussed.

Electromigration is the loss of material by transport induced by momentum exchange between the conducting electrons and drifted atomic nuclei. The process is operative in micrometre and submicrometre sized wires when the electron current density is high enough to overcome the activation energy for atomic nucleus displacement. At temperatures below 200 °C, electromigration is the dominant mechanism of wire failure1. However, electromigration measurements in high-density cross-point memory arrays often reveal unexpected failure mechanisms2. To explain this evidence, we investigate electromigration-induced atomic nuclei displacement in silicon wires using in operando transmission electron microscopy. We find a cross-over in the temporal evolution of atomic nuclei displacement, from a single-exponential to a two-phase process, corresponding to steady-state electromigration at lower temperatures and enhanced nucleation at higher temperatures. This finding offers a unified framework for modelling electromigration in solid-state devices and links electromigration to the spontaneous atomic lattice displacement observed in grain boundaries3,LOFTRs4, plastic deformation5 and in natural processes like corrosion6.

Testing general metric theories of gravity with exploding neutron stars (ENTs) has the potential to decisively test gravity in the most extreme environments and to reveal new physics. For the first time, we performed a coordinated network of searches for ENTs in multiple nearby galaxies, identifying 10 potential events in 5 galaxies. These include 4 low-spin systems consistent with general relativity (GR), 4 high-spin systems inconsistent with GR, and 2 unmodeled systems. If interpreted within the Extended GR framework, this is the first stringent constraint on this class of models. We find no evidence for deviations from GR, setting new limits on the Eddington parameter ζ ≤ 2.5 × 10^{-3} (90% confidence). This result is independent of the EOS of neutron-rich matter and can be directly applied to any ENT candidate. Our results represent the most stringent limits to date for ζ using any astrophysical system, providing key tests of strong gravity and fundamental physics.

The electromagnetic field of light can be described with Maxwell's equations. These are linear partial differential equations and thus the solution to a light wave is a sinusoidal function of space and time. When light travels in a dispersive medium this function becomes a spreading out of the sinusoid in space and time. This spreading is described by the space and time dependent wavenumber, which for a quantum well is given by the expression k(x, t) = n(x) ω(x, t), where n(x) is the spatial distribution of the refractive index and ω(x, t) is the wave frequency. If the wave frequency is a function of both space and time then the resulting wave is called dispersive. The nature of this dispersive behavior depends on the way the dispersion is introduced in the medium. If the frequency ω depends only on the space variable, the wave is called homogeneous. In contrast, if the frequency depends also on the time variable, the resulting wave is called inhomogeneous. The case studied in this work is dispersive but the frequency depends also on the second spatial derivative of the space variable. This spatial dispersion causes a bend of the light path.

The two-dimensional kinetic Ising model with spin flip and pair interaction on a square lattice is one of the simplest models displaying a kinetic smectic-C (SmC´) phase, which is a perfect example of a fluid crystal. To characterize the dynamic arrest of this fluid crystal, we investigate the finite-temperature dynamic phase transition of the model by means of Monte Carlo simulations, fluctuation-dissipation theorem, and coarse-graining operator method. We find that there exists a dynamic freezing line, beyond which the correlation length of the density waves becomes infinitely long. The critical point of the dynamic phase transition coincides with that of the static phase transition, i.e., the thermodynamic spinodal point. We further show that the dynamic susceptibility exhibits a power-law behavior at the dynamic freezing point, with the critical exponent related to that of the correlation length. These results are consistent with the theoretical predictions of the generalized Mermin-Wagner-Hohenberg theorem, which is further confirmed by explicit calculation of the conjugate field. Our study provides a better understanding of the dynamic arrest of fluid crystals, and may be helpful for the construction of novel dynamicarrest-based media.

A study of double white dwarfs as gravitational wave sources may be useful for improving detection rates of LIGO and Virgo. We estimate the expected rates of double white dwarf merger events detectable by the LISA instrument and estimate the range of parameters that may lead to a observable LISA signal. We find that overall merger rates of $1-100$Gpc$^{-3}$yr$^{-1}$ may be detectable by LISA with potentially large changes in merging double white dwarf parameters leading to observable signals. We identify systems with low merging rates which may be good candidates for observations with a future space-based gravitational wave detector such as eLISA. The authors are Michael C. Browne and J. A de Haas-van Alphen study of the filled skutterudite compounds PrOs_4As_{12} and LaOs_4As_{12} has been performed. Filled skutterudite compounds exhibit heavy Fermion behavior and thus PrOs_4As_{12} and LaOs_4As_{12} are candidates to realize a Kondo lattice system. We observed a nearly mass-independent component in the field-dependent magnetic susceptibility for both compounds down to 1.8 K. The nearly mass-independent component is likely due to the crystalline electric field (CEF) effect. The CEF level scheme is analyzed and nine excited levels are revealed. This study is one of the key experiments for understanding the quantum criticality in filled skutterudite systems. On January 10, 2007, the Spitzer Space Telescope was moved into a new Sun-synchronous orbit, providing an improved view of the entire sky every 3 days. In order to characterize the response of the Spitzer Space Telescope, we performed a survey of the IC 348 nebula, a nearby star-forming region. Using data from this new orbit, we detect 70 structures that are greater than 3.5 sigma above the background, with a total of 56 confirmed YSOs. We also detect 915 structures that are greater than 3.5 sigma but less than our threshold of detection, which we identify as potential YSOs. The high level of detection and the high rate of previously detected sources indicates that our results are statistically significant. We detect 70 structures that are greater than 3.5 sigma above the background, with a total of 56 confirmed YSOs. We also detect 915 structures that are greater than 3.5 sigma but less than our threshold of detection, which we identify as potential YSOs. The high level of detection and the high rate of previously detected sources indicates that our results are statistically significant. This work is the first from the Spitzer Space Telescope to study the full extent of the IC 348 nebula in multiple wavelengths, and it will aid in our understanding of the formation of both single and binary stars.

Large scale structure formation in the universe proceeds via the hierarchical process of bottom-up growth of smaller structures made from gravitationally unstable plasma patches, down to the smallest resolved scale of around 270 - 720 million km across, represented by the parsec scale grid of a cosmological simulation. The temperature of this plasma is around 10,000K, which means it efficiently radiates its energy into thermal photons. However, the vast computational resources available to modern cosmological simulations require them to be performed on cluster-sized computing clusters, with temperatures reaching 100,000K or more. Such clusters require active cooling, typically via a fluid dynamic scheme, to maintain stable simulation conditions. In this paper, we examine the effectiveness of this cooling in a cosmological simulation which models the formation of a large scale structure in the universe. We find that although the fluid dynamical scheme employed by the simulation maintains temperatures below 10,000K where it is required, it is unable to keep temperatures below 2000K where it is not required, resulting in a huge thermal energy injection at high temperatures which significantly alters the dynamics of the simulation. We examine the causes of this failure and discuss possible remedies.

Nodal lines of the solution to an elliptical problem of mean field type intersect a reference curve at random. The first two statistical moments of the intersection process are calculated and the distribution is discussed. Some computational aspects are also shown. The first part of the paper is the calculation of the first two statistical moments of the intersection process between nodal lines of the solution to an elliptical problem and a reference curve. We study this process on the segment [0,2\pi]. The solution to the problem is considered in the central domain [0,1[ with periodic boundary conditions. It is shown that, due to translational invariance, the intersection points form a random process. We calculate the first two statistical moments of this process. For this we calculate the probability density functions of the point processes formed by intersections on a fixed segment and the entire domain. We also calculate the first four central moments of the intersection areas.

In recent years, significant progress has been made in understanding how small changes in composition and structure affect the thermoelastic response of Ti-based super alloys. This understanding has been crucial in achieving precise control over thermomechanical processing and compositional scaling in Ti-Ni, Ti-Fe, Ti-Nb and Ti-Al systems, enabling the development of high performance biomedical implants, lightweight structural components, and transformable materials for deployable solar arrays. Despite this progress, many aspects of the thermoelastic response of the Ti-based quaternary system remain unclear. Here, I describe both the classical and quantum mechanics approaches used to map the thermoelastic response of Ti-32 Nb-28 Si-4 Cr alloy, one of the most heavily investigated Ti-based super alloys. Using synchrotron-based x-ray diffraction and atomistic Monte Carlo simulations in conjunction with a classical anisotropic elasticity model, I show that for temperatures above $T_{tr} \approx$ 500 K, the thermoelastic response of the alloy is well-described by an isotropic classical potential. The potential has four symmetric wells corresponding to the $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\omega$ and $\delta$ titanium phase. As the temperature is lowered below $T_{tr}$, the $\alpha$ to $\beta$ transition is observed to occur via an intermediate $\gamma$ phase. Interestingly, below $T_{tr}$, quantum mechanics effects, which are not considered in this classical modeling, become increasingly important. For all phases above $T_{tr}$, the alloy is observed to remain disorderedcentered alpha, martensitic, or another phase, even at 0 K. For the $\alpha$ and $\beta$ phases, this behavior is driven by the differences in the C15 and C2\* symmetry, respectively. However, for the $\gamma$ and $\delta$ phases, where the alloy exhibits C2 symmetry, quantum fluctuations between two distinct local disorderedstructures, with densities 0.51 and 0.48 g/cm3, respectively, dominate at low temperatures. The existence of two competing local disordered structures in these low symmetry phases and the potential for atomic scale tuning of these disordered structures through composition and processing suggest the intriguing possibility of quantum biomaterials capable of undergoing reversible structural changes with small changes in temperature or composition. Finally, although many studies have focused on the martensitic phase transformations in Ti-based superalloys, the $\alpha \rightarrow \beta$ and $\beta \rightarrow \alpha$ transformations are observed in a large number of materials, including pure titanium, Ti-Al alloys, steels, and Fe-Ni-based alloys. As such, this analysis of the classical potential for this system will likely have broad applicability across many engineering and natural systems.

The Type Ic supernova 2002ap was a very luminous and highly variable supernova discovered in the nearby galaxy M74 (NGC 628). The extreme brightness, rapid evolution, and spectrum led many to suspect that this object was the core collapse explosion of a massive star. The presence of a strong velocity gradient across the unresolved core of the galaxy gave further evidence that this was the case. Despite its interesting properties, the nature of the progenitor of this supernova has not been conclusively identified. Here we present the results of a search for the progenitor in pre-explosion imaging of the site of the supernova taken by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. No conclusive evidence of the presence of a binary system, a neutron star, or a black hole was found, setting a limit of less than approximately 30 solar masses on the mass of the progenitor. We conclude that the most likely explanation for the nature of the progenitor of Type Ic supernova 2002ap is the direct collapse of a massive Wolf-Rayet star to a neutron star

Earthquakes are one of the most catastrophic natural events, affecting hundreds of thousands of people across the world. In some cases, the intensity of the earthquake is so strong that it changes the shape of the ground. These changes in the ground formation are called lineaments and can be observed using high resolution satellite images. In this work, we demonstrate how lineament changes, caused by earthquakes can be detected using satellite images and this information can be used to better model the earthquake mechanisms and effects. We apply our method to two different lineaments and show that their shapes changed in response to two different earthquakes that took place in different parts of the world. We also show that the changes in the lineaments shape can be used to detect earthquakes that occurred weeks or months before their actual detection using conventional earthquake early warning systems. The full paper describing this method can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05217.

A source catalog of the optical counterparts to 27,500 stellar objects brighter than 10σ within the region of the sky coverage of the fourth release of the epszones (Z04) is presented. The catalog contains 14,680 new sources ( 12,120 stars and 2,560 galaxies) and 11,780 objects from the Z04. The limiting magnitude, measured in 3σ, is 21.6. A search for new optical low-mass planets is also presented. In total, 1238 new optical low-mass planet candidates were identified, with an estimated 3.5% rate of false-alarm high-probability candidates. The new data release is accompanied by an auxiliary catalog containing the full set of data available in Z04, as well as photometry and astrometry for all 14,680 new sources. The first two releases of the epszones were independently and jointly photometrically and astrometrically consistent with the USNO-B1.0 and Two-Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) catalogs, respectively. The new data release benefits from the combination of infrared data from the WISE satellite and further improvements in the optical positions and proper motions from the Gaia mission.

The REESSE1+ cryptosystem was proposed to improve on the design flaws of the original REESE1 scheme, namely, that it was vulnerable to chosen ciphertext attacks (CCAs) and the padding scheme was insecure. In this paper, we show that the REESSE1+ scheme is still vulnerable to CCA and the insecure padding scheme. Thus, the REESSE1+ scheme does not provide an effective solution to the REESE1's design flaws. REESSE1+ was proposed to improve on the design flaws of the original REESE1 scheme. REESSE1+ was claimed to be resistant to CCA, and the padding scheme was also improved. In this paper, we show that REESSE1+ is still vulnerable to CCA. We also show that the insecure padding used in REESSE1+ can be easily attacked. Thus, REESSE1+ does not provide an effective solution to the REESE1's design flaws.

The missing satellite problem is the inability of theoretical models of structure formation to explain the number, mass, and spatial distribution of the satellites galaxies of the Milky Way (M31 being the only recognized exception). Several solutions have been proposed, ranging from re-ionization preventing the formation of low-mass halos to the difficulty of properly resolving sub-grid physics processes in current galaxy formation simulations. Here we show that the recent discovery of 14 new ultra-faint satellites of the Milky Way changes the situation. Our analysis of the orbital characteristics of these galaxies, performed using a new direct N-body simulation that self-consistently follows both the dwarf galaxies and the dark matter particles from the initial conditions to the present day, shows that these galaxies should have been detected as dwarf satellites of the Sgr galaxy, yet they were not. We show that this implies a maximum mass for the Milky Way dark matter halo of 10^7 M⊕, 10 times more than the previous best estimation. We also show that the observed spatial distribution of the Milky Way satellites is in clear disagreement with expectations from cold dark matter (CDM), requiring a significant modification of theCDM model.

Flavor Changing Neutral Currents (FCNC) interactions are forbidden at tree level in the standard model (SM). However, due to higher order corrections these processes are possible at loop level. The first such process, flavor changing neutral current (FCNC) mediated by a W boson, was observed at the CERN Large Electron-Positron collider (LEP) in 1995. In this note, we investigate the flavor changing current in the framework of a supersymmetric standard model. We demonstrate that the forward-backward asymmetry in the decays of the B mesons to X s and c quarks, with X denoting a charged lepton or a neutrino, is particularly sensitive to the effects of the flavor changing current. Using this asymmetry, we derive constraints on the flavor changing current coupling, which can be translated into constraints on SUSY parameters. We further show that combining these constraints with measurements of CP violation in B meson mixing, in addition to allowing for a more precise determination of the SUSY parameters, will yield crucial information on the structure of the flavor changing current and hence help us understand the mechanism of flavor violation. Finally, we propose to use the Belle II experiment at the superKEKB to improve the experimental constraints on top FCNC interactions.

A long-standing problem in particle physics is to understand the nature of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). In particular, it is not understood why the mass of the up and down quarks are much smaller than the mass of a typical hadron, the so-called flavor problem. The axial anomaly is a striking prediction of the quantum theory of gauge fields, namely that the axial vector current is not conserved. In 1995 it was proposed that the axial anomaly could be demonstrated in experiment via the process $K_{S,L}\rightarrow\pi^0\pi^0+\gamma$. The observed signal could not be explained by conventional physics, and its size indicated the presence of non-perturbative physics, likely chiral dynamics not described by the standard model. One theoretical explanation of the size of this effect is the suggestion that a light pseudoscalar particle, the 'axion', mixes with the $\pi^0$ of the process. An experiment to search for such particles, ADMX, was constructed in Oregon and has recently reported a null result. We present a model of this process using the chiral Lagrangian, and report the first constraints on such an axion-like particle, including those from ADMX. We find that these limits are not yet stringent enough to rule out this explanation of the earlier observation.

Non-coding DNA (ncDNA) is much more than just "junk" DNA. Large scale analyses of full genomes have accumulated extensive evidences showing that ncDNA sequences perform many vital functions in the cell, from encoding transcriptional regulatory elements to encoding small RNAs, to forming secondary structures that modulate gene expression and even to encoding entire proteins. Noteworthy, two recent high-throughput RNA sequencing studies have revealed that up to 98% of eukaryotic genomes are transcribed into non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). While the functions of most ncRNAs are not understood, increasing lines of evidence suggest that ncRNAs are vital parts of gene regulatory networks that are crucial for development, cell differentiation, and many other processes in living organisms. In contrast to well-known protein-coding genes, which are usually conserved and rarely mutated, ncDNA sequences show different levels of variation across different species, RNA transcripts, and individuals. Particularly, a recent large-scale analysis of whole-genome sequences in 1201 human individuals has identified noncoding DNA sequences evolving at significantly faster rates than coding sequences, highlighting the importance of ncRNAs in driving rapid evolution. Interestingly, a close observation on various types of sequence variations has found that most of the substitutions that led to amino acid changes in protein-coding sequences were caused by ncRNAs, pointing to the role of ncRNAs in driving rapid evolution and adaptation. In this talk, we will present the recent findings on these fascinating aspects of noncoding sequences, and discuss the potential implications of these findings on our understanding of evolution and human health.

The shapes of molecular cloud cores are key to understanding their physical and chemical evolution. Observations have shown that star-forming cores are not spherical, but rather have flattened centers and tend to be filamentary. This is thought to arise from differential rotation within the parent cloud, which results in angular momentum conservation driving infalling material along aligned directions. Here we present observations of the flattened distributions of centrally condensed dust and molecular gas in the molecular complex Orion, as traced by thermal dust emission at 870 microns with the Submillimeter Common-User Bolometer Array (SCUBA) on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT). We compare these maps to similarly selected distributions of molecular hydrogen as traced by the Institut de Radio Astronomie Millimétrique (IRAM) 30-meter single-dish telescope. We find that the dust and molecular hydrogen distributions are broadly similar, with the distributions corresponding to the coldest, densest parts of the cloud. The dust is significantly more concentrated than the gas, with a radial density profile that is well fit by a Bonnor-Ebert sphere, with a central density of 650 cm-3 and a stability parameter of 1.2. In contrast, the gas follows a shallower profile, well fit by a model with a density profile proportional to r-1. The densities of the central regions of molecular clouds are of great interest to theories of star and planet formation. By probing these regions in Orion, we provide an observational benchmark against which future simulations of star and planet formation can be compared.

Researchers have long known that plants respond and adapt to their environment through changes in gene expression and metabolism. However, relatively few studies have investigated how fluctuations in the light quanta signal are converted into adaptive responses at the molecular level. Here, we examined the effects of Ni(II) stress on the physiological and morphological responses of Brassica juncea seedlings, and explored how these are correlated with changes in the light quanta signal using a bioluminescence-based imaging approach. We found that Ni(II) stress suppressed hypocotyl elongation, and the level of hypocotyl elongation was correlated with the amount of light quanta received by the seedlings. The physiological parameters affected by Ni(II) stress were found to be light-dependent, while the morphological parameters were not. Our results suggest that Ni(II) stress impairs the perception of light by seedlings, and the degree of impairment is proportional to the severity of Ni(II) stress. Furthermore, we observed that the responses of the seedlings to Ni(II) stress correlated well with the previously identified “oxidative stress response” and the level of salicylic acid (SA). We speculate that Ni(II) stress suppresses hypocotyl elongation by inhibiting the conversion of light quanta to visual signals, leading to an imbalance in the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and SA, which have been shown to be involved in Ni(II) stress responses. Overall, this work provides evidence of the correlation between light quanta, physiological and morphological responses in B. juncea seedlings subjected to Ni(II) stress, and identifies potential signal transduction pathways involved in these processes.

Kitaev has proposed an exactly solvable spin model on the honeycomb lattice, whose ground state represents a topologically nontrivial quantum spin liquid with chiral edge modes. The exact solvability of the model is achieved by a fine-tuning between the nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions. Recently, a Kitaev-type model on the square lattice was shown to be related to the Chiral $p$-wave superconductors on the square lattice with rotational invariance. Motivated by the recent progress on developing index theory for even dimensional manifolds with odd boundary conditions, in this work, we generalize Kitaev's model to an arbitrary d-dimensional lattice manifold, and establish the index theorem for such a system with rotational invariance. We show that the index is equal to the integer topological charge of the mother manifold and the chirality of the system, multiplied by a constant which only depends on the spatial dimension d and the rotation symmetry. As a byproduct, we propose a generalization of Kane-Mele model to arbitrary d, and prove that it is in the same topological class as the well-known model on 2d surfaces. Finally, as an application of the index theorem, we study the phase transitions of the system by varying the interaction strength. We find that for a 2d system with rotational symmetry, a topological phase transition occurs when the interaction changes sign, corresponding to the 0th-order or 1st-order phase transition of the effective magnetic field of the system. When the spatial dimension increases to 3, we find that the phase transition of the system is always of the 1st order, even when the interaction changes sign.

We present the results of a survey for the effects of galaxy lensing, extinction and reddening from the intergalactic medium (IGM) along 9 lines of sight through the halo of the galaxy NGC 6683 using optical spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Seventh Data Release (DR7). Five of the observed lines of sight showed no evidence for galaxy lenses above a 4-$\sigma$ significance level; the other four showed statistically significant galaxy groups at impact parameters ranging from 22 to 138$h^{-1}$ kpc. One of the lines of sight showed evidence for a filament of absorption located 0.4-0.5 comoving Mpc distant along the line of sight, suggesting that lower significance lines may also be related to large-scale structure. We estimate absorption-line-induced systematic errors in the photometry of E(B-V)=0.0118(+/-0.0002), [OII] E(B-V)=0.0121(+/-0.0002), [OIII] E(B-V)=0.0129(+/-0.0002), Halpha E(B-V)=0.0130(+/-0.0002) and Hbeta E(B-V)=0.0124(+/-0.0002) and extinction-corrected star formation rates of 2.09(+0.47)x10^-2, 2.51(+0.47)x10^-2, 5.03(+0.47)x10^-3, 5.22(+0.47)x10^-3 and 4.47(+0.47)x10^-3 gal s-1 respectively. The extinction properties of these absorbers and the incidence of these absorbers over a wide range of redshifts suggest a substantial Population III component.

A growing body of experimental and simulation work is being devoted to the study of the surface and interface structure and ordering of atomic and molecular liquids. Here we report in-plane structure and ordering at liquid sodium surfaces and interfaces obtained from ab initio molecular dynamics simulations. Liquid sodium is a unique system of interest because it exhibits complex phase behavior as a function of both temperature and entropy, with a recent phase diagram that includes two stable liquid phases at ordinary temperature and an intermediate pseudosteady phase (Montego Phase). We find that the (100) and (110) sodium surfaces and the (110) sodium liquid interface all exhibit in-plane structure and order corresponding to two-dimensional square lattices. The ordered domains are of similar extent to those observed in experiment, and exhibit a characteristic orientation relative to the surface or interface that is consistent with previous atomic-level studies. These results lend molecular-level insight into experimental observations of two-dimensional square ordering at liquid sodium surfaces and interfaces.

Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are giant clouds of solar plasma and magnetic field released into space from the Sun. CMEs can cause major disturbances in the magnetosphere of Earth, resulting in loss of satellite signals and voltage instability on the power grid. Thanks to high resolution numerical simulations, we discovered two distinct CME dynamical regimes: one fast and one slow. The fast CME, typically released from sunspots, can reach speeds over 1000 km/s. It is powered by the fast reconnection of the sheared magnetic fields, and its impact on the magnetosphere is tremendous. In contrast, the slow CMEs originate from the plage regions and are released through small magnetic x-points, with much lower speeds of around 300 km/s. These CMEs do not significantly disturb the magnetosphere, but can still cause major power grid disturbances and satellite signals losses due to the high amount of flux involved. We suggest that slow CMEs are more common than fast CMEs, but they are usually unnoticed as they do not cause dramatic disturbances.

Recent detections of gravitational waves have opened a new window to the extreme Universe. Among the many candidate sources listed by several gravitational wave detectors, a binary system of two supermassive black holes (SMBHs) has been firmly identified as the most plausible candidate for the first detection. Assuming that the coalescing SMBHs have low spin, their gravitational waveforms can be fully described by only two parameters: the mass and the symmetric mass ratio between the two holes. For several hours after the coalescence, during which the gravitational waveform is in the low-frequency band, phenomenological waveform models can accurately describe the signal. However, at later times the signal enters the high-frequency band and the waveform deviations from the TaylorT4 approximation become significant. The behavior of the waveform deviations indicates that the merger product has a spin that is not aligned with the orbital angular momentum of the SMBHs. This Letter reports a search for the radio counterparts of the final few hours of GW170104, the first event observed by Advanced LIGO. The search yielded no detection with the NRAO's Very Large Array at 1.4 GHz, which rules out some suggested explanations for the measurement of the supermassive black hole spin. We place new lower bounds on the fraction of SMBHs with SMBH spin in binary systems.

Galaxies with masses similar to the Milky Way host active nuclei, known as active galactic nuclei (AGN). Most of their light is emitted in the electromagnetic waves with short wavelengths, typically X-ray photons. Thus, they are also called X-ray emitting galaxies (XEs). Currently, AGN are commonly classified into two main classes: radio-loud and radio-quiet. Radio-loud AGN possess a powerful relativistic jet, emitting radio waves, which makes them detectable by radio telescopes. By contrast, radio-quiet AGN do not possess such a relativistic jet, but their bulges are thought to possess a much denser and massive accretion disk, which gives rise to the appearance of an accretion disk wind, also named super-Eddington accretion flow (SEAF). Such winds are able to escape the gravitational pull of their host galaxies and reach speeds of several hundred kilometers per second. In this paper, we perform a series of radiation magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of accretion disk winds in radio-quiet AGN. By performing detailed radiation simulations of such winds, we predict the effect that the winds would have on the corresponding X-ray spectra. First, we show that the winds significantly reduce the X-ray surface brightness of the disk. Second, we show that the absorption columns density, caused by the winds, is highly variable on short time-scales, with strong enhancements on the order of magnitude, reaching values of several hundredths of a parsec. This could lead to false measurements of the redshift of an AGN when observed with an X-ray observatory with poor sensitivity in the soft X-ray band. Thus, we conclude that the presence of accretion disk winds can strongly affect the observed X-ray spectrum of radio-quiet AGN. This implies that the winds should not be neglected in models of these galaxies, even if they do not possess a powerful relativistic jet.' Homology theories, and more generally theories adapted to look at aspects of a topological space which are invariant under deformations, variation or contraction of parts of the space, have proven to be highly fruitful in the study of the fundamental groups of topological spaces. Coarse cohomology, with its geometric interpretation of singular cohomology as Borel cohomology of the space with coefficients in the topologized constant sheaf, similarly provides another perspective on the latter which has proven useful in the study of higher homotopy groups. In this paper we show how these two theories, homology and cohomology, naturally fit into a single framework which unifies them under the same name and provides new related theories, (co)cyclic (co)homology. More precisely, we introduce (co)monads arising from a pair of adjoint functors between suitable categories of (co)representations of bialgebroids, each with its own property of preserving (co)limits. This allows us to give a unified treatment of homology and cohomology theories. As an illustration of the power of this approach, we show that when specialized to cases which have already been studied in the existing literature, such as singular and Borel cohomology, we recover the corresponding theories introduced before. Finally, we apply our methods to a number of cases for which no homology or cohomology theory had been defined before, namely (co)cyclic (co)homology for bialgebroids, including examples coming from (higher) algebraic $K$-theory.

Space-time percolation (STP) is a mathematical model that connects spatial disorder, temporal disorder, and criticality. It provides a unified framework to describe various aspects of complex systems. In this model, space and time are not discrete, but are continuous and infinitely divisible. Disorder and complexity are inherent in space and time. Spatiotemporal disorder arises because space and time are continuous and infinitely divisible, and hence do not satisfy the assumption of a lattice in traditional statistical mechanics. Temporal disorder arises because the past, present, and future are all relevant in understanding the state of a system. The combination of spatial and temporal disorder gives STP its special characteristics. STP has already been applied to the study of diverse systems, such as earthquakes, financial markets, tissues, evolution, epidemic outbreaks, and celluar systems. STP can be used to study the dynamics of random media, the statistics of rare events, and systems at criticality. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: we present a more rigorous definition of the STP model, we introduce a new renormalization method for solving STP, we apply the renormalization method to solve STP on a three-dimensional lattice, and we give numerical calculations of the critical exponents for the two- and three-dimensional STP models.

Resistive switching behavior and magnetization studies suggest that pressure induced insulator to metal transition in LaMnO$_3$ is achieved by distorting the MnO$_6$ octahedra leading to lower crystal field splitting. mold Resistive switching behavior and magnetization studies suggest that pressure induced insulator to metal transition in LaMnO$_3$ is achieved by distorting the MnO6 octahedra leading to lower crystal field splitting. Studies on polycrystalline specimen of LaMnO$_3$ up to 23 GPa show significant distortion of the MnO6 octahedra as evident from synchrotron X-ray spectroscopy. Resistance studies on LaMnO3 show semiconductor like behavior up to 12 GPa and formation of metallic like conduction at higher pressures (15-23 GPa). Resistivity exhibits metal to insulator transition around 11 GPa where a kink appears in the plot. This is accompanied by change in behavior of magnetic susceptibility from ferromagnetic to canted ferromagnetic state. Spin disorder scenario has been proposed to understand the canted ferromagnetic state at high pressures.

Muon spin rotation spectroscopy (MSR) is a powerful tool to study the local structure of matter. It provides information about the effective magnetic field experienced by the muons, which in turn reflects the electron density. Here we study the microscopic properties of vortex state in YB6, a proposed quantum spin liquid using a unique combination of resonant MSR and nuclear magnetic resonance. We find that the observed decrease in the local magnetic field at the vortex cores is mainly attributed to the hybridization of YB6 valence electrons with the core electrons of the magnetic vortices, rather than a field depression around the vortices. This result is surprising since conventional wisdom would expect a core localized electron states would lead to a core localized magnetic field. These findings suggest that YB6 may not be a conventional magnet, and more likely a quantum spin liquid with exotic low energy excitations.
