The commonly accepted theory to explain the chemical peculiarities of the R stars suggests that they are descendants from former late-type (mainly G and K) giants, which lost their external hydrogen envelopes due to either stellar evolution or close encounters with planets. This scenario, however, has a serious difficulty explaining the small number of observed R stars, since even a small fraction of giants losing their envelopes due to stellar evolution would imply a sizable population of R stars that is not observed. In this paper, we present an alternative scenario to explain the origin of the early-type R stars, which involves the merger of two red giants. This unusual evolution sequence, although extremely rare, is consistent with the number of early-type R stars observed today and does not have the same difficulties associated with the standard scenario. We find that the observed chemical peculiarities of the early-type R stars can be reproduced by the merger of two red giants with a small degree of rotational distortion, and a main-sequence companion in a close binary. This binary system is the end result of a previous much more extensive merger between a red giant and a compact object. The merger occurred within a dense stellar cluster, which provided the necessary conditions for the binary system to be formed. We present a series of detailed binary-evolution calculations that demonstrate that the system would survive for a long time as a close hierarchical triple, with the inner binary consisting of the merged stars and the tertiary component being the initially more massive compact object. The inner binary is driven towards Roche lobe overflow by the decreasing radius of the less massive component, and finally undergoes a merger due to dynamically unstable mass transfer. We demonstrate that for the observed range of physical parameters of the merger products, the merger of two red giants is expected to lead to the formation of a slowly rotating star with a convective envelope, similar to the observed early-type R stars. We therefore propose that the early-type R stars represent a new channel for the formation of chemically peculiar stars in the Universe. The proposed formation scenario for the early-type R stars can also provide a natural explanation for the origin of the binary companions that are observed in close orbits around several of these stars, since in our scenario these will be the result of previous mergers between two red giants. Finally, we discuss the possibility of this formation scenario being responsible for the large number of chemically peculiar white dwarfs that have been discovered in recent years, since both merger products of two red giants and the compact remnants of such mergers may end their lives as white dwarfs. Our preliminary investigation indicates that for a typical range of parameters, the remnant white dwarf will be rapidly spinning and possess a thin hydrogen layer, possibly explaining the large observed numbers of observed chemically peculiar DQ and DC white dwarfs. We also predict that a significant fraction of these stars will be expected to be rapidly rotating, strongly gravity-affected polars, which would be detectable via their aperiodic and highly variable optical/UV emission.

Networks self-organize to efficiently perform the functions that they are assigned. They may form clusters to improve communication efficiency, grids to improve computation efficiency, or a combination of the two. The process by which networks self-organize is relatively unexplored. We propose a multi-agent based approach that allows networks to self-organize without the need for pre-defined organizing objectives or assumptions about network topologies or rules. Our approach is modular and applicable to a wide range of network architectures. We demonstrate its ability to self-organize networks to efficiently perform multiple communication and computation tasks. We model a network of agents as a system of coupled ordinary differential equations. The agents can communicate with each other, but cannot directly interact with physical nodes in the network. We propose an approach to adjust the weight of links in the network based on the differences in the communication and computation efficiencies of connected nodes. Using this approach, the network can self-organize in an efficient manner, without the need for pre-defined organizing objectives or assumptions about network topologies or rules. We present results on both synthetic and real-world networks. In the case of real-world networks, we show how our approach can be used to self-organize communication and computation clusters in data centers. We also show that the approach is scalable to larger networks and synthetic architectures. The source code, videos, and data used in our experiments are available at https://github.com/avivah/selforganization.

In this work, we study the statistical properties of fluctuations of shot noise power in quantum dots in the limit of strong quantum fluctuations. Using the Keldysh Green's function technique and a diagrammatic technique for averaging, we derive an effective action for the leading-order statistical moments of these fluctuations. We find that for weak interaction the dephasing time does not saturate, and for strong interaction the saturation value is proportional to the interaction energy. The result for strong interaction is in contrast with the phenomenological predictions of generalized Thouless and Pekar models, and is supported by recent experiments. The effect we study in this work was observed recently in many experiments. An example of such an experiment is provided in Fig. 1. A sketch of the measurement setup is also shown. A conducting channel, connected to electron sources and sinks, is embedded into a quantum dot (depicted by the box). The box is formed in a quantum point contact (QPC), the quantum channel, by applying suitable voltages to the substrate. Electrons are fed into the channel at the source contact, and the current is measured at the drain contact. We study the fluctuations of the shot noise power, $S_I$, in the channel, $\delta S_I=\delta I^2/2$, carried by the electrons, $\delta I$, arriving in bunches of duration $\delta t$. The measurement is performed at a particular fixed frequency, $\omega$, which lies in the interval, $\omega_c<\omega<\omega_s$, between the cut-off frequency, $\omega_c$, imposed by the response time of the equipment, and the frequency, $\omega_s$, imposed by the inverse duration of electron bunches. The value of $\delta S_I$ is measured in the frequency domain, by the photo-multiplier connected to the drain contact. The relative strength of quantum fluctuations in the channel is characterized by the dimensionless parameter, $\lambda\sim Q/\sqrt{L}W$, where $L$ is the channel length, $W$ is the channel width, and $Q$ is the von Klitzing constant of the channel. We assume that $\lambda\gg1$. The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect is a potentially powerful cosmological tool, as it can be used to detect clusters of galaxies and measure the degree to which their inner regions have been thermalized by Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) or other cold structures. The thermalization of the ICM gas, due to its mergers, plays an important rôle in the SZ detectability of clusters and the accuracy of their WIMP mass limits. We carry out the study of the merging process of galaxy clusters using the SZ effect and show that it is crucial to properly model the SZ signal coming from these systems in order to accurately study their merger state. We provide a new and complete description of the SZ signal, allowing us to accurately characterize clusters that are likely to be undergoing a merger. We also investigate the effect of applying a naive de-mergerization method on the SZ signal, which will introduce a strong bias in the measurement of the projected mass of merging clusters and the distribution of the redshift space distortion parameter, ultimately affecting the cluster dynamical state reconstruction.

Cobalt doped ZnO nanoparticles show a sharp metal-insulator transition at 250 K. The ferromagnetic nature of the cobalt doped ZnO nanoparticles has been confirmed from the measurement of magnetization. The ferromagnetic nature is found to be inhibited at low temperatures. The electrical resistivity decreases with increasing temperature and shows an anomaly at 250 K, suggesting presence of Metal-Insulator transition (MIT). The optical studies further corroborate the occurrence of MIT. The band gap decreases with increase in cobalt concentration and exhibits a sudden jump at the transition temperature. The observed features are mainly attributed to the Metal-Insulator transition(MIT) driven by electronic modification due to Cobalt doping. The work provides an easy way of engineering the electrical and optical properties of ZnO by doping with Cobalt. The research was published in Nature Communications The team included Sankalp Thoudam, Ramesh C. Rai, S. Ramadhan, N. Islam, A.K. Pal, A. Kumar, S. Seffai, J.S. Ahopella and V. Prakash.

Three-dimensional equations for a system of three equal mass particles interacting via a pairwise Yakubovsky potential and subject to a three-body force (3BF) are presented. The three-body force is taken to be a monopole form with a complex scaling parameter γ which determines the strength of the force. Bound state solutions of the two-body reduced Schroedinger equation (SchildM Applicability) are found via a Variational Method combined with a Multi-Configuration Gaussian Expansion. The two-body interaction is represented in separable form and the three-body force is incorporated non-perturbatively. The resulting system of three-dimensional coupled non-linear equations are solved in Cartesian coordinates, and bound state solutions of the full Hamiltonian, representing Efimov trimers, are presented for various values of the scaling parameter γ. The binding energy of the obtained bound states is found to scale like ε ~ γr2, where r is the range of the interaction. For the particular value γ = i, the obtained scaling is consistent with that of a three-body scale invariant system. In addition to the binding energy, the differential cross-section is also calculated and found to be in agreement with available experimental data for the particular value γ = i. The structure of the paper is as follows. The three-body problem with a three-body force is introduced in. The three-dimensional reduced Schrodinger equation for the two-body subsystem in the presence of a three-body force is presented in. The Variational Method and Multi-Configuration Gaussian Expansion are discussed in. Numerical results are presented in, and a short conclusion is provided in.

The resonant state in quantum mechanics plays an important role in the scattering theory. For Schrödinger equations with potential satisfying certain conditions, the resonant state exists and is purely imaginary. When the energy of the incident particle is equal to the resonant energy, the resonant state causes the most strong scattering. The computation of the resonant state is based on the Fourier transform and iteration algorithm. The convergence of the algorithm relies on the magnitude of the imaginary part of the resonant state. This paper will introduce some properties of the resonant state and its computation algorithm. In quantum mechanics, the scattering process is one of the most important research topics. The total potential of a particle is the sum of the incident potential and the potential of all the particles in the surrounding environment. For a specific energy, the particle with that energy will meet the potential and cause some scattering. The most important thing in the scattering process is the resonant state. The scattering is strong when the energy of the incident particle is equal to the resonant state. This paper will introduce some properties of the resonant state and its computation algorithm. In quantum mechanics, the Hamiltonian operator can be represented by $$ H = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu} \nabla^2 + V(x) $$ where $\mu$ is the reduced mass of the two particles and $V(x)$ is the interaction potential between the two particles. The Schrödinger equation is $$ H \psi = E \psi $$ If $V(x)$ is a local potential, the solution of Schrödinger equation can be expressed as a linear combination of the incident wave $\psi_0(r)$ and the scattered waves $\psi_k(r)$: $$ \psi(r) = \psi_0(r) + \sum_k f_k(E) \psi_k(r) $$ where $f_k(E)$ is the scattering coefficient and $\psi_k(r)$ can be expressed as a linear combination of the spherical waves. When $k=\ell+1$ is a positive integer, the function $\psi_\ell(r)$ is called resonant state because it satisfies $$ \Delta \psi_\ell(r) + k^2 \psi_\ell(r) = 0 $$ and $$ \lim_{r \to \infty} r^{k+1} \psi_\ell(r) \to 0 $$ The resonant state is purely imaginary and is in some sense the most "dramatic" wave in the scattering process. If $V(x)$ is a smooth potential, $V(x)$ satisfies the so called "asymptotic nondegeneracy" condition if there is at least one $\ell+1$ resonant state with a nonzero amplitude. A population of Lyman alpha emitters (LAEs) at redshift ~ 4.5 was found to form over-densities by narrow-band Lyman alpha imaging, a sign of ongoing galaxy formation at early times. Subsequent spectroscopy of these over-densities revealed lower redshifts (~ 4.5), though, for the most part, the LAEs were observed to remain at z ~ 4.5. This apparent clustering was confirmed with numerical simulations and interpreted as evidence for the existence of substantial neutral hydrogen reserves in these early systems. Itai M. R惠and Andrea G。Crocce led a team that used imaging with the UltraVio survey to find this clustering and confirmed it with subsequent spectroscopic observations. The study is published in the journal Science. UltraVio (University of Vienna Observatory), an imaging survey using the robotic 2.2m telescope of the University of Vienna, is described at http://www.ifs.org.ua/usno/auto/auto.htm. The survey imaged eight square degrees of the sky in five passbands between 4000 and 9000 Å. The observations, from 2011 to 2016, were made with a wide-field camera designed by the University of Vienna and equipped with a InSb detector with a pixel size of 18 μm, covering a field of view of 1.76° × 1.76°. The survey is 95% complete to DM = 24.7. The data are available from the University of Vienna Science Archive (URL: http://tagc.ifac.tuwien.ac.at/ultravio/).

The large scale structure (LSS) of galaxies contains powerful information on cosmological models and our understanding of galaxy formation. The Luminous Red Galaxy (LRG) sample of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has 27,000 galaxies with median redshift 0.38 and photo-z errors of 0.03 out to a redshift of 0.7, making it the largest contiguous high-redshift LSS sample to date. We use this sample to measure the halo occupation distribution in a comprehensive suite of Monte Carlo simulations of six popular galaxy formation models. The measured correlation functions are compared to the measured two-point correlation functions of the LRG sample. The six model comparisons allow us to limit the sum of the virial temperatures of the dark matter halos hosting LRGs to be greater than or equal to 4.5 keV, and the sum of the stellar feedback heating rates to be less than or equal to 12.7 keV. These limits correspond to typical WIMPs masses less than approximately 15 GeV for a standard thermal WIMPs model.

The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will be an orbiting telescope designed to detect weak gravitational waves. Space-borne gravitational wave detectors are most effective at detecting the most strongly bound systems: supermassive black hole (SMBH) binaries. Accretion-driven phase relations in such systems can be predicted using mass and angular momentum accretion rates, and when the SMBH mass is measured by other means, such as stellar velocity dispersion or gas dynamics, the most precise tests of general relativity come from LISA's sensitivity to measurement errors of these parameters at the milli-arcsecond level. Here we report the result of a three-stage search for SMBHB candidates in LISA data. The first stage was a matched filter search using error models; the second was a genetic algorithm search for coherent sinusoidal signals in the LISA data; and the third was a hierarchical Bayesian analysis using population synthesis models for SMBHB populations to quantify the sensitivity of the first two stages to SMBHB signals. No significant candidates were found in the three stages of the search, and this resulted in a false alarm rate of less than 1 per billion years. These results place significant bounds on the space density of SMBHBs and constrain scenarios for their evolution.

A rotating photoevaporating disk has been discovered in the Cepheus A HW2 star cluster. The disk, which is 100,000 degrees Celsius, was detected via spectral analysis of light from the cluster. It has a mass of at least 1 million times the Sun and an outer radius of more than 5000 times the distance between the Sun and Mars. These observations suggest that the disk wasphotoevaporating, rather than being ejected from the system. The disk may have been caused by the strong ultraviolet radiation emitted by the Young Stellar Object (YSO) Irditable. I describe how I used high-dispersion spectroscopy to identify the disk. I also analyze the dynamics of the disk and the YSO, and I discuss the implications of this discovery for our understanding of the YSO's environment and early star and cluster evolution. I obtained this result with the help of the FLAIR instrument on the Subaru Telescope, which is operated by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan. This research was funded by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology of Japan, grant 15K05019. This research makes use of data obtained from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the SpeX Prism Spectral Libraries (http://www.browndwarfs.org/spexprism).

The VLT-FLAMES survey of massive stars (VMSS) is aimed at studying the evolution of hot massive stars in the Local Group galaxy the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Wind properties and evolution of hot massive stars are key to understand feedback from massive stars in their environment, from the morphological structure of the interstellar medium to the chemical evolution of their host galaxy. Combined high-resolution spectroscopy from VLT-FLAMES allows to determine mass-loss rates from H emission, temperature of the bi-conical winds and thus analyze the evolutionary status of these stars. From the mass-loss rates, Ionic masses can be derived and eventually be used to investigate other properties of the winds, such as ionization degrees and acceleration regions with potential effects on simulations of the feedback into the environment. In this contribution we present the first results on the evolution of hot massive stars in the LMC and the impact of this evolution on the galactic feedback. We confirm previous studies which concluded that the initial mass function (IMF) is top-heavy in the LMC, with respect to the Milky Way. The most massive stars show stronger IMF divergence from the initial mass function (IMF) with increasing age, suggesting that these stars were affected by significant mass-loss episodes. We found more extreme cases of stars with abnormally high nitrogen to carbon (N/C) and nitrogen to oxygen (N/O) abundance ratios, which might be the consequence of a thermohaline mixing process occurring in their winds, an hydrodynamic process taking place in the strong winds of massive stars.

Massive black holes in the centers of galaxies are relatively rare, with only about one million solar masses observed in the centers of galaxies throughout the universe1. Yet, many galaxies have black hole masses many orders of magnitude larger2. One proposed solution to this “black hole mass problem”3 is the hierarchical galaxy assembly model, in which small black holes were created in the centers of collapsed Population III stars, and subsequently grew by accreting gas and merging with other black holes4. However, while gas accretion is expected to increase black hole masses rapidly, growth by merging is limited by the non-existence of intermediate-mass black holes (between stellar-mass and supermassive black holes)5,6, which would otherwise act as merger seeds. Theoretically, intermediate-mass black holes with masses ≳ 108 solar masses are unstable against spherical infall7, and would have already depleted the population by emitting gravitational waves8. However, it was recently proposed9 that massive black holes could exist in a new form of compact stellar system known as a globular cluster, which is stabilized by the large distance between stars in the cluster. If these black holes were ejected from their host galaxy, they would receive a large recoil velocity due to the mutual gravitational interactions between the black holes. In this Letter, we present the first calculation of the recoil velocity of a massive black hole ejected from a globular cluster. We find that, for typical globular cluster masses and velocities, black holes with masses ≳ 105 to 107 solar masses have recoil speeds of ≳ 0.3 to 0.6% of the speed of light, which may be sufficient to allow clusters to retain intermediate-mass black holes in their cores. We present the results of an observation of the elliptical galaxies NGC 2992 and NGC 3081 performed with the HEAO-1 mission. We find a well-defined peak in the energy distribution of both galaxies between 1 and 200 keV. The energy distribution can be well fitted with a single temperature bremsstrahlung model with a low temperature of 0.25 keV and 0.58 keV for NGC 2992 and NGC 3081, respectively. The 1-200 keV luminosity of NGC 2992 is 7.54 x 1037 erg/s while that of NGC 3081 is 1.89 x 1037 erg/s. gainers abstract: The 1 keV to 200 keV X-ray spectrum of NGC 2992 and NGC 3081 is presented. The spectra can be well fitted with a single temperature bremsstrahlung model with a low temperature of 0.25 keV and 0.58 keV for NGC 2992 and NGC 3081, respectively. The 1-200 keV luminosity of NGC 2992 is 7.54 x 1037 erg/s while that of NGC 3081 is 1.89 x 1037 erg/s.

eternal inflation, de Sitter entropy In physics, entropy is a measure of the disorder of a system. At early times in the history of the universe, the spacetime on sufficiently large scales was conjectured to obey de Sitter geometry, and the entropy was associated with the dimension of the corresponding de Sitter space. However, this conjecture was found to be incorrect on quantum gravity grounds. In particular, it was later shown that quantum corrections to the entropy of de Sitter space actually converge to a finite value. This was taken as a convincing example of the failure of the de Sitter entropy conjecture. In this paper, we will introduce a measure of de Sitter entropy which correctly accounts for quantum gravity corrections. We will then argue that this entropy is exactly equal to the Hubble rate during eternal inflation. We will also show that this entropy matches the Bekenstein–Hawking entropy of de Sitter space, leading us to propose that the latter is an exact quantum gravitational scale. This connection between the entropy of de Sitter space and the rate of expansion of the universe during inflation solves the paradoxes of de Sitter entropy and provides further evidence for the validity of the holographic principle in gravity. The proposed measure of de Sitter entropy, while not being a new fundamental constant of nature, does seem rather surprisingly analogous to the Hubble rate. We speculate on the possible implications of this analogy for the cosmic landscape, the multiverse, and string theory. Thesis: Entropy and the Geometry of Spacetime The entropy of a system is a measure of its disorder. Informally, it is the number of possible states that the system can be in minus one. This intuitively makes sense for systems consisting of many particles, where the number of ways the particles can be arranged is a measure of the system's entropy. In physics, the most common entropy measures are the Gibbs entropy (also known as the Boltzmann entropy) and the von Neumann entropy. They are both defined in terms of the partition function of the system. In general relativity, one defines the entropy of a spatial region to be the surface area of the region's unit normal sphere in a given vacuum geometry, as measured by an observer with appropriate idealizing physical assumptions. There are a number of reasons why this prescription for calculating the entropy is natural. First of all, the normal sphere is a natural generalization of the notion of a point to higher dimensional spacetimes. It is a minimal surface, and minimal surfaces are well-known to be sensitive to topology. In particular, the normal sphere is compact without being topologically a sphere, and this is why the entropy is a diffeomorphism-invariant. Moreover, it is reasonable to require the entropy to be calculated from an ideal observer without feeling too guilty about implicitly making assumptions about the mass and size of the region. The normal sphere also correctly accounts for Hawking radiation, as an observer in a slightly higher dimensional boundary layer would perceive

The Charge Injection Capability (CIC) of the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) on board the Suzaku satellite was measured by exposing the devices to a narrow spectrum of charge-injection neutrons with energies of 25-100 keV. The measured CIC (7.5 $\times$ 10$^{12}$-5.1 $\times$ 10$^{13}$ nsec/cm2) is a factor of 2.3 - 9.2 larger than that predicted by the weak binding model based on the measurements of high-energy charged particles. Thus, the measured CIC represents the limit of the weak binding model for charge-injection neutrons. The Suzaku XIS detectors successfully detected these low-energy charge-injection neutrons for the first time, and these results significantly improved the understanding of high-energy neutron spectra and the CIC in the space environment.

Power control has been studied extensively in conventional cellular networks. However, energy consumption has become an increasingly important issue in new types of cellular networks, such as wireless sensor networks and smartphones, where a large number of wireless devices are equipped with processing capabilities and battery lifestyles are crucial. Moreover, increasing demand for machine-type communications (MTC) poses additional challenges to the existing power control schemes. In this paper, we propose a unified approach that can seamlessly apply to both conventional cellular networks and new types of cellular networks. The proposed approach jointly optimizes both power control and bandwidth allocation to maximize the lifetime of wireless devices while ensuring a minimum quality of service (QoS) for delay-sensitive traffic and guaranteeing energy efficiency. The proposed algorithm is validated through extensive simulations, which demonstrate that the proposed approach can achieve significant energy savings and QoS improvement compared with conventional power control approaches for both conventional cellular networks and new types of cellular networks.

The central limit theorem (CLT) is a fundamental result in probability theory stating that the sum of a large number of independent and identically distributed random variables (r.v.s) approaches a normal distribution. Turbulent flows are known to deviate from the predictions of the CLT. For decades, such deviations have been attributed to multiplicative disorder in the statistics of vorticity increments, a measure of turbulent dissipation. Here we prove that this multiplicative nature is not required. We introduce the relative transfer entropy, a quantification of correlation transfer along arbitrary trajectories in dynamical systems, and show that it satisfies a weak form of the data processing inequality, a fundamental result in information theory. We provide explicit dynamical and statistical conditions for the relative transfer entropy to be positive, and show that it is positive in a statistical simulation of an isotropic, homogeneous, and statistically steady turbulent flow. We conclude that the strong form of the CLT—i.e., the entropy convergence version—is a sufficient condition for the Gaussian departure from the observed statistics of turbulent flows. This result casts doubt on the current paradigm that assumes the observed statistical behaviour of turbulent flows to be the result of multiplicative disorder in the statistics of vorticity increments, and has far-reaching consequences for data analysis in turbulent flows. In particular, it provides a theoretical foundation for the recently proposed anomaly cancellation mechanism, in which exact compensation of positive and negative anomalies is enforced, thus possibly offering a route towards accurate numerical prediction of the statistics of turbulent flows from first principles.

Astronomy is a powerful tool for determining fundamental parameters of stars, and in particular their temperatures, masses and ages. In recent years, considerable advances have been made in the spectral domain, with the implementation of new theory and the development of efficient data analysis techniques. I describe a method to derive these parameters from high-resolution optical spectra, using current evolutionary tracks and the strengths of certain atomic and molecular lines. To demonstrate its effectiveness, I present an application to the open cluster IC 4651 and field stars of similar spectral type. The required observational data are provided, including high-resolution optical spectra and relevant atmospheric parameters, from the literature and my own observations at the Haute-Provence Observatory. The main limitation of this approach is the requirement of high-resolution optical spectra, which are not always available for large samples of stars. Nevertheless, this methodology can be applied to a wide range of applications, and I present a first application to open clusters and field stars, which can help us understand the properties of these populations. In particular, these results demonstrate that intermediate-resolution spectrographs on large telescopes (such as MuSiC; Probeca) provide high data return and low cost, making them good candidates for surveys of large samples of stars.

Boolean networks have been used to study the dynamics of genetic and logical networks. Such networks can be used to model the qualitative behavior of systems. Average sensitivity (ASS) is a metric which has been used to analyze the stability of Boolean networks. In this paper, we present a novel approach to compute ASS by approximating the solutions of the average K-th order sensitivity equations using an iterative procedure. The solution of the average K-th order sensitivity equations is approximated by first order systems which are solved using a novel iterative method. The iterative procedure is initialised using the solutions obtained using the approximate linear system solver built into BoolNet. We demonstrate the efficacy of the approach on two models and show that the solutions computed using the iterative approach closely approximate the solutions of the average K-th order sensitivity equations. In this paper, we study spherically symmetric spacetimes in f(R) gravity theories. We show that these spacetimes are generally geodesically complete and Nariai solution is the only static, spherical symmetric solution. The Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black holes exist only in limited ranges of the metric parameters. We also show that these black holes can be completely described by the three parameters: the mass, the electrostatic potential and the charge. We conclude that the metric function of these black holes is entirely determined by these three parameters. The results show that the black holes in these spacetimes are more general than those in general relativity. In particular, the possibility of separating the gravitational field into a product of an arbitrary function of the geometry and a Riemannian space allows the modelling of more complex structures such as multishell black holes or even collapsars, the latter being models for hypernovae and gamma-ray bursts. The paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we present the theory and equations. In section 3, we discuss the case of a point mass. In section 4, we study the general case of a spherically symmetric distribution of matter. We study the existence and properties of the solutions. We also show that the metric can be written in a separated form. In section 5, we present our conclusions and outlook.

In this paper we present results from an investigation of the structure and properties of dark matter (DM) halos in the largest Lambda Cold DM model (LCDM) simulation to date, a hydrodynamical resimulation of 4 billion particles representing a (570 Mpc/h)3 region of the universe. We identify DM halos in this large volume simulation using a technique combining friends-of-friends (FOF) with a high-order multivariate filter and characterize their inner structure using the radial distribution of their DM and substructure (stellar and gaseous) components. We find that at all masses, DM halos can be cleanly separated into two primary structural components: a relatively smoothly distributed "central" region and a more clumpy "substructure" component which comprises a distinct secondary distribution having an asymptotic power-law slope of -3. The fraction of substructure within a halo, and the power-law slope of its structural distribution, are both significantly correlated with the halo's maximum identified gravitational attraction: the more substructure a halo has, the stronger its central gravitational pull. We refer to these two distinct structural components as the "core" and "fossil" distributions, respectively, and suggest that fossil groups, comprising a halo with a significant fraction of central substructure, may be identified by an algorithm combining the FOF halo-finder with the inverse of this power-law slope. We apply our algorithm to a selection of clusters and groups from the Bolshoi simulation, finding that, while the scheme correctly classifies most clusters as fossil or non-fossil groups, it fails to identify some fossil groups with diffuse stellar components and halos having shallower central cusp slopes. Finally, we propose that the fractional abundance and clustering properties of fossil groups may provide a useful probe of the normalization of the galaxy cluster mass function and the dark matter power spectrum at high masses.

A binary model for the UV-upturn of elliptical galaxies is presented. It consists of a static, non-rotating stellar component, resembling a 5 Gyr old single stellar population, which forms the host galaxy, and a compact object (black hole or neutron star) that accretes matter from the companion and produces a UV excess by emission from the accretion disk. Different model parameters can reproduce the UV color, the near-IR brightness, the UV spectral slope and the UV emission line strength of elliptical galaxies. The presented model, that combines simple assumptions and physically motivated parameters, can be a useful tool to interpret the UV-upturn of elliptical galaxies. Researchers often wish to keep their research secret until they have obtained formal consent to share this information with the general public or until they have developed a proprietary product. While formal ethical committees evaluate the merits of proposed research, it is often not possible to obtain consent to research until a future date. In many cases, it is not feasible to develop a proprietary product without sharing initial research findings. It would be advantageous if a single measure could be used to weigh the merits of research in these two distinct contexts. A common definition of "merit" would allow for objective comparisons between research projects. In this paper, we describe a mathematical framework for comparing research projects based on defining a research program as a search in a solution space for the best solution. Our framework assigns a score that balances two competing concerns: the need to share information early on, so that failures can be corrected before distributing costly resources, and the need to obtain consent to distribute information in a more widespread manner. We demonstrate the feasibility of this framework with a number of examples.

Recently, the existence of localized waves in binary solids with equal concentrations of the two components, called binary Laves phases, has been established. These waves, called gyration waves, were observed experimentally for the first time in a eutectic alloy by Xia et al. [1]. They are characterized by a compact support in the transverse direction and a (non-trivial) crystal structure in the longitudinal direction. The existence of these waves was theoretically predicted by Nesterenko [2] and later confirmed by various authors using different modeling approaches [3-7]. This Letter presents an analysis of gyration waves in the framework of the Landau-Lifshitz equation for nonlinear dispersive waves. The existence of two branches of wave dispersion is established: a heavy branch corresponding to the density wave and a light branch corresponding to the spin wave. Moreover, the linearization spectrum includes two eigenvalues corresponding to the in-phase and out-of-phase oscillations of the heavy and light wave branches. The spin wave has a finite amplitude at the threshold of instability. Thus, gyration waves can be regarded as localized modes consisting of the superposition of a heavy and a light waves with the corresponding wavelengths (Goldstone modes). This picture is confirmed by the numerical solution of the full Landau-Lifshitz equation.

We present dielectric spectroscopy studies of a 0.65[Pb(Ni_1/3Nb_2/3)O_3]-0.35PbTiO_3 (PNN) relaxor-based ceramics across the so-called supercooled liquid and smectic-C* (Sm-C*) transitions. We demonstrate that the temperature dependence of the dynamical susceptibility, χ″(T), and dielectric loss factor, ε″(T), strongly differs in the two states. We argue that the presence of two relaxations corresponding to two energy scales in the supercooled liquid state is a precursor phenomenon of the phase transition to the Sm-C* state. We compare our results with the most recent theoretical models for relaxors and discuss the implications of our results for the physics of the phase transition in relaxor systems. In this paper, we introduce and apply a new model to describe physical properties of disordered materials. The model is a generalization of the well-known two-dimensional (2D) Ising model, including an extra term describing competing interactions. The model is studied via Monte Carlo (MC) simulations and real-space renormalization group (RSRG) methods, and it is found that it exhibits a continuous, second-order phase transition for a range of values of the model parameters. Furthermore, the model can be used to describe magnetic properties of disordered materials consisting of arrays of $\pi$-rings and lattices of alkane molecules. Finally, we show how the model can be simulated in adiabatic quantum computing by utilizing a dressed spin basis that eliminates the need to reverse Hamiltonian parameters at various critical points during the simulation. A newly discovered satellite of the Milky Way is announced. It is around 10 thousand light-years in diameter, and it is named "Bootes". It was found during the Galactic microlensing survey. The first detection of the satellite was announced in 2018, and it was confirmed with full 6-dimensional phase-space information in 2019. It has a very eccentric orbit around the Milky Way and it moves far from the center of the galaxy. It might have been captured by the Milky Way's dark matter halo and it might be a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy in the future. The discovery was made by a team of astronomers from several countries, led by Dr. Yossi Bekerman from Weizmann Institute of Science. The discovery was published in The Astronomical Journal on February 21, 2023. The authors are Yossi Bekerman, Jonathan Brink, Noa Noffset, Yuval Aron, Lia Filippenko, Ehud Nakar, James Bullock, and John Grunsfeld.

Mixtures of rectangular particles at high composition develop distinctive long-range order, consisting of layers of rectangular particles parallel to the mixture's composition vector,separated by symmetric interstitial regions. The long-range order develops because rectangular particles of different composition tend to separate spatially. Rectangular particles of different composition have different orientational order; at high composition, they develop a tendency to align along the layer or layer-like regions in which they lie, with the composition gradient. The tendency to align exhibits wave-like behavior,with wavevector that lies in the compositional plane and points from higher- to lower-composition regions. The wavevector governs the character of the long-range order: particles that align along the wavevector are in close contact within layers but extend past each other between layers. These features are revealed by numerical simulation and real-space renormal group calculations. In a previous study of the extragalactic x-ray background, AGN and X-ray binaries were suggested as possible sources of the unresolved cosmic x-ray background (UcxRB). These populations were unable to completely explain the excess in the Chandra data and further studies were required. In this study we test for the contribution of 24 micron Spitzer sources to the UcxRB by modelling their distribution and characteristics and then performing a stacking analysis on archival Chandra data. The model is able to describe the characteristics of the sources and produces a stacked spectrum which is in agreement with a Compton y-distribution, with a best-fit temperature of 1.4 keV and normalisation of (5.3 ± 2.3) × 10−4 cm−2 s−1 keV−1 at 30% confidence. These results suggest that 24 micron Spitzer sources may contribute up to 20-30% of the UcxRB and may be able to explain some of the excess population observed by Chandra.

Neutrino oscillations are established facts with well-known parameters. In contrast, the nature of the three remaining neutrinos, the corresponding mass eigenstates, is still a mystery. A possible mechanism to generate neutrino masses is the so-called See-Saw mechanism. In this context, heavy singlet fermions are introduced, which could appear at the TeV scale. The latter could be explored at the LHC. In this note, we present the first study of the sensitivity of the LHC to this framework. The considered channel is the direct production of the heavy neutrinos, with subsequent decay into a lepton and a photon. A dedicated simulation, based on [GEANT4]{}, taking into account the main characteristics of the LHC detectors, is presented. We show that the LHC, with 14 TeV centre-of-mass energy and 30 ab$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, is capable to give rise to quite some sensitivity to this new scenario, should it be indeed accounting for the nature of the neutrino mass eigenstates.

13CO observations of candidate massive YSOs are presented from the RMS Survey, a Large Program with the IRAM 30m Telescope designed to map the chemically-rich inner regions of low-mass star-forming regions in the Southern Hemisphere. In this paper we present 13CO observations of 17 candidates, 10 of which were previously identified in the Mid-Infrared Survey of Pointed surveys (MIPS). All observations are reported as ϵ(13CO), the line width defined as FWHM at/width 2.35 M_{\sun}/cm^2/ K km/s. Spectra are examined for the presence of infalling, Keplerian disks, and if disks are present, determine the mass of young planets by modeling the spatially-resolved 13CO spectra. Two of our sample demonstrate clear evidence of Keplerian disks, while the remaining candidates do not show any signs of flattened structures. We combine our observations with published results from other surveys to discuss the various evolutionary states and gas accretion properties of our sample. Infall is common throughout the sample, and in many cases, multiple patterns of gas infall are present. High accretion rates are rare, although high accretion rates do exist in our sample. We compare our results to those from other studies and discuss potential explanations for differences in the evolution of sources across different samples. We also compare the properties of our sample to those of previously-identified young stellar clusters in the region, and discuss implications for high-mass star formation in Southern Hemisphere.

In eighties, Hitchin introduced a twistor space for every signature (4p, 0, s), generalizing the usual cases p = 0, +4 and s = 0, -4. In this paper we study the family of double solid twistor spaces, corresponding to the signature (4, 0, 0). We provide a new simple description in terms of finite flat groupoids, which has the advantage to work for arbitrary genus. This article is a transcription of a paper submitted to the arXiv on May 10, 2020. It remains available there for 15 days and then, by acceptance, it will become available in the www archive of the author's institution. Introduction. The Hitchin's double solid twistor space is the twistor space over the signature (4, 0, 0). It was introduced in the eighties by Hitchin [1], generalizing the usual cases p = 0, +4 and s = 0, -4. Let Ω be the vector bundle of the octonions, with the quadratic form defined by the intersection with the imaginary four-sphere. Ω is a positive line bundle over 8-dim quadric surface Q. The twistor space is defined by the orthogonal split of the twistor space Χ(Q) over Q, whose fiber is the Stiefel manifold of Ω-spinors. Such an orthogonal splitting allows to identify the total space of Ω with the projectivized spin bundle of Q, where the projectivized spinor bundle is defined as the quotient of the bundle of two-forms by the complexification of the orthogonal of Ω. We provide a new simple description in terms of finite flat groupoids. This description has the advantage to work for arbitrary genus. Finite flat groupoids were introduced by Kobayashi andNomizu [7]. Finally, we discuss the conformal and projective structures on a double solid. * Groupoids. Finite flat groupoids were introduced by Kobayashi and Nomizu [7]. Let G be a Lie groupoid over M, where M is a smooth manifold. Such a structure is given by the following data: 1) an orthogonal structure on the tangent bundle TM of G; 2) an action of G on its unit space Υ(G) such that the differential restricts to an action on the soul Υ(M) of G; 3) an injective morphism of groupoids from G to the projectivized frame bundle of the orthogonal structure on TM; the structure of groupoid on G induces an injective morphism from G to the projectivized spin bundle of Υ(G). An example of finite flat groupoid is the structure of Lie groupoid on the orthogonal frame bundle of a Riemannian manifold. Another example is the automorphism groupoid of a Lie group, considered as a groupoid structure on the left cosets of the group.

The largest structures in the Universe are called superclusters. We identify 58 superclusters in the nearby Universe up to a distance of 4 Mpc using the algorithm by Voronoi tessellation and the clustering algorithm DBSCAN. The superclusters are divided into two main groups by the mean height of their members - low-height superclusters with a height of less than one tenth of the dimension of the supercluster, and high-height superclusters with a height of more than one tenth of the dimension of the supercluster. The high-height superclusters are divided into two subgroups - superclusters with main axes aligned with the supercluster axis and superclusters with different orientations. The first subgroup consists of superclusters with right-left orientation, which are more abundant than the superclusters with other orientations. The second subgroup is divided into superclusters with north-south orientation and superclusters with east-west orientation. The distributions of supercluster parameters between the subgroups have different signs, which indicates that they had different primordial origins.

Extreme mass ratio binaries (EMRBs), comprising a very massive black hole (VMBH) and a companion object, such as a star or planet, are sources of gravitational waves (GWs). Such systems are of great interest to gravitational wave astronomers, as they may generate detectable signals throughout the universe, and they may present promising sources for Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO). However, when a EMRB emits a detectable gravitational wave, its companion will be perturbed, and the system may become unstable. During this instability, the VMBH may be dramatically displaced from the system's center of mass, as the two objects are essentially tidally disrupted apart from their very high relative velocities. Here we demonstrate that the motion of the VMBH in this regime is affected by relativity, and that this effect can be significant, even for displacements as small as 1% of the Schwarzschild radius of the VMBH. We characterize this relativistic effect, derive a corresponding criterion for EMRB tidal disruption, and demonstrate the accuracy of our approximation by computing EMRB tidal disruption Events in the LIGO S6 data and applying our relativistic criterion to these events.

Interacting fermions on a lattice, described by the Hubbard model, can develop a long-range order when the on-site interaction is larger than the kinetic energy. At low temperature and near half-filling, the ground state is antiferromagnetic (or sometimes referred to as Néel order). However, away from half-filling the nature of the ground state is more complex. At small Hubbard interactions, at low but non-zero temperatures, fermions develop a Fermi surface and a jump in the specific heat evidences the phase transition into a Fermi liquid state. In between the critical Hubbard interaction and the critical temperature, for a wide range of fillings, fermions develop an anomalous Fermi liquid (AFL) state, which is a quantum critical phase. The nature of the quantum phase transition between the Néel and the AFL phases is still under debate. The stability of the AFL state has been established both by perturbative approaches and by non-perturbative variational methods. In this work we study the stability of the AFL state in the non-perturbative infinite dimensional limit of the Hubbard model. Using a variational wavefunction based on matrix product states, we determine the stability region of the AFL phase in the space of parameters. Our results suggest that the AFL phase is stable in a finite region of the phase diagram, thus providing additional evidence in favour of its existence.

In Europe, FP5 has been an important initiative for open research and the participation of industry in scientific research. FP5 was ended in 2015 and it was replaced by Horizon 2020. This study analyses the impact of FP5 on the interplay of universities and industry. It is based on a critical review of the publicly available reports of the participating projects. These reports were analysed with respect to pre-defined categories, looking at the novelty of the proposed research, the efficiency of the project management and the potential applications of the resulting technologies. It is concluded that FP5 had a positive impact on European science and industry, by attracting a high number of participants and supporting cross-border, interdisciplinary research. The social impact, economic benefit and the internationalisation potential of FP5 can be considered quite positive as well. The main shortcomings were the poor follow-up of most projects, and the lack of industry involvement in some critical stages of the research process. The analysis also shows that FP5 was successful in implementing changes to the research process to encourage industry engagement, but did not manage to implement adequate measures to prevent conflicts of interest.

The paper is an update of the model of nonleptonic two-body B-decays including axial-vector mesons in the final state, published in Phys. Rev. D76, 014017 (2007) (1). The updated model contains the following new elements: the light quarks flavors have been split in its Goldstone-like and Gell-Mann-Okubo-like components, the effective chiral and axial U(3) symmetries have been incorporated to reduce the number of free parameters; three different descriptions of the axial-vector mesons are considered, since the existing descriptions are conflicting. The updated results fit the experimental data better than the previous ones, with 18 free parameters vs. 32 previously. The two-body nonleptonic B decays represent one of the main tools for the studies of the CKM matrix and of the flavor structure of the strong interactions. Thanks to the recent and future experimental activities on B-factories and hadron colliders, more precise measurements will be available in the near future, which will allow to study these aspects of the Standard Model with greater accuracy. Besides this standard model (SM) aspect, this kind of studies can give information on the CP-violation mechanisms and on the properties of exotic particles. Therefore the experimental study of nonleptonic B-decays remains an active field of research. For the two-body nonleptonic decays of B-mesons into two light mesons, the factorization approximation is applied. Electron dephasing in a AuPd alloy has been studied using angular resolved photoelectron spectroscopy in a wide temperature range from 5 K to 300 K. At temperatures above 20 K the electron dephasing is well described by the weak localization theory. At lower temperatures an additional dephasing component appears, increasing faster than linearly at low temperatures. We suggest that the dephasing is caused by electron-electron interactions and can be described by the mechanism of weak localization in a 1D liquid of fermions. The resulting temperature dependence of the dephasing time corresponds to a 1D Fermi gas with effective mass depending on temperature: t* = const * mexT/h, where me is the effective mass of electrons, x = 1.3 and me = 0.19 m0 in AuPd alloy. Much of the material formed in the early stages of planet formation is thought to be contained in the mm-cm sized grain population of protoplanetary disks, which cannot be directly observed. We present the first detection of this population in the material orbiting a young low-mass star. Augereau et al. (2014) searched for signs of gas and dust in the G 196-3 system, but were unable to detect any material around the host star, except for one Neodymium isotope (97% atomically pure) which may have been accreted during the AGB phase. This isotopic signature places an upper limit on the amount of mm-cm size dust in the system. We used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to search for continuum emission from Augereau’s limit and found a robust detection of the mm-cm size dust component in the disk around G 196-3B, with a flux density of 12.6 ± 0.7 mJy at a frequency of $\sim$ 796 GHz (or a total mass of 4.5 ± 0.3 × 10^{-3} M_{\earth}$). We also detect emission at the 2.22 mm and 2.70 mm bands, but not at longer wavelengths where the emission is typically associated with larger, more micron-sized dust. The total mass in mm-cm size grains in the disk is estimated to be 1.1 ± 0.2 × 10^{–2} M$_{\earth}$. The particle size distribution has a shape similar to that of the planetesimal disk of the solar system, with a steep decrease in number density at radii greater than 1 mm. The unusual properties of the mm-cm size dust population are discussed in the context of models of dust evolution in protoplanetary disks.

Recent experimental results on the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and the proton spin structure function indicate the importance of quark orbital angular momentum (OAM). In particular, an analysis of the latter shows the presence of an approximately chiral symmetric component. It has been suggested that this component arises from chiral pion- and rho-exchange interactions, which lead to chiral mechanisms for the generation of quark orbital angular momentum. We provide a general parameterization of these mechanisms, which exhibit chiral scale invariance and allow for a separation of spin and orbital contributions. We also discuss various sources of model uncertainty, and suggest strategies for their reduction. This intriguing conclusion can be drawn from recent experimental results on the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and the proton spin structure function. These results, together with the intrinsic quantum fluctuations of the nucleon’s partons (quarks and gluons), provide direct access to its quark orbital angular momentum (OAM), and its quark spin structure. The chiral symmetry of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), which is an essential property of the strong interaction, implies the conservation of quark spin and the generation of quark orbital angular momentum through spontaneous spin-orbit interactions. In particular, in the limit of massless quarks, the quantum number corresponding to the chiral (or axial) symmetry, namely, chirality, should be locally distributed in such a way that the total chirality is conserved. The spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry in the QCD Lagrangian gives rise to quark masses, which generate spin-orbit interactions between the quarks through the so-called center of mass (CM) motion. The resulting chiral symmetry breaking, associated with the dynamical generation of quark OAM, provides an explanation for the magnitude of the observed orbital momentum component. On the other hand, although chiral symmetry does not directly apply to the strong interaction between the quarks and the gluons, certain mechanisms can induce chiral symmetric spin-orbit interactions in which chirality emerges from the intrinsic quantum fluctuations of the partons, namely, the quarks and gluons. Such mechanisms have been suggested to generate a chiral symmetric contribution to the quark OAM, which could explain the observed experimental trends. The chiral symmetric component of the quark OAM is expected to scale in the large nucleon spin limit, as dictated by the Wandzura-Wilczek relation. The precise measurement of the orbital contribution to the spin structure function, in combination with the corresponding theoretical understanding, may help in distinguishing between these chiral mechanisms. Several proposed mechanisms for the dynamical generation of quark OAM can be classified according to the origin of their chirality. These include explicit chiral symmetry breaking generated by current quark masses and spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in the QCD Lagrangian, the latter being the basis of the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model and low energy effective field theories based on it. In this work, we will focus on the dynamical generation of quark OAM through spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in the QCD Lagrangian. Recent theoretical developments suggest the presence of

A differentially rotating force-free magnetosphere of an aligned rotator is studied. We derive an analytical solution in split-monopole approximation, which can be used for construction idealized models of the magnetosphere. The solution depends on two parameters, which can be chosen to approximate the geometry of the magnetosphere and the flux functions in the polar regions. We demonstrate how the solution can be used for construction models of the magnetosphere with different properties. In particular, the surface magnetic field is chosen so that the solutions can produce magnetars and gamma-ray burst jets. Magnetic fields and plasma in magnetospheres of rotating neutron stars are usually considered to be force-free. However, force-free magnetospheres were found only in special cases, for example when the neutron star has a very strong magnetic field or when the star is not rotating. In contrast, general rotating magnetospheres are described by the induction equation, which allows for electric currents and moving charges. The force-free and induction magnetic field models describe the same magnetic fields in different regimes and can be connected by their perturbative departures. We study analytically a general differentially rotating force-free magnetosphere with general equations of state and current distribution. We solve these general equations in the split-monopole approximation. This solution can be used for construction idealized models of the magnetosphere. The solution depends on two parameters, which can be chosen to approximate the geometry of the magnetosphere and the flux functions in the polar regions. We demonstrate how the solution can be used for construction models of the magnetosphere with different properties. In particular, the surface magnetic field can have different geometries (poloidal and toroidal) and can be time dependent. Such magnetospheres can produce magnetars with huge magnetic fields (about 10^14-10^15 G) and gamma-ray burst jets with observed fast rotating electrons.

Understanding the origin of ferromagnetism is one of the key issues in materials science. In this paper, we report an unexpected ferromagnetic (FM) behavior in a non-magnetic material, TiO2. When Ti atoms are removed from the TiO2 crystal lattice (specifically the Ti4+ sites), the crystal structure evolves to anatase type and acquires a net magnetic moment, which is found to be persistent above room temperature. This Ti4+ disorder induced magnetism (TDIM) has been observed in a number of materials such as TiO2 nanoparticles, TiO2 thin films and nanotubes. We hope that our work will stimulate more research activities in this field and motivate further experimental and theoretical investigations on this interesting problem. In the supplementary material, authors have provided more experimental data and also some hints for the theoretical explanation of TDIM. First-principles calculations show that Ti4+ disorder, on substitution of O2- anions for TiO2- anatase, leads to a net ferromagnetic moment. In addition, our experimental studies indicate the persistence of this moment up to at least 300 K. These observations are in contrast to previous reports of anatase type TiO2 being nonmagnetic. Various mechanisms for the persistence of this net moment are explored. While substantial ionic coupling in Ti4+ sites is necessary to explain the observed moment, substantial spin-orbit coupling is required to explain the observed moment value. The theoretically predicted ordering temperature of this moment is consistent with experimental results. Our work demonstrates that Ti4+ disorder is an overlooked mechanism to induce ferromagnetism in nonmagnetic materials. We have provided possible evidences to support the hypothesis that Ti4+ disorder accounts for the persistent ferromagnetism observed in a number of materials. Since Ti4+ disorder has been observed in a number of anatase type TiO2 samples, our work raises the possibility of persistent ferromagnetism in TiO2 based materials and related systems. This study was motivated by the recent report of persistent ferromagnetism in Ti4+-disordered TiO2.[1] While much research has been devoted to understand the origin of ferromagnetism in metals, understanding ferromagnetism in nonmagnetic materials is still an active area of research. TiO2, which is used as a semiconductor in many devices, is nonmagnetic. However, recent work has demonstrated that certain forms of TiO2 can be ferromagnetic.[2,3] Since ferromagnetism has been observed in a number of Ti4+-disordered materials, understanding the origin of ferromagnetism in TiO2 is of both fundamental and applied interest. This work explores the Ti4+-disorder induced ferromagnetism (TDIM) mechanism in TiO2 anatase. To explore the TDIM mechanism in TiO2, we synthesized TiO2 nanoparticles with a wide size distribution using a sol gel technique. We explored three distinct synthesis methods to control the amount of Ti4+ disorder

In this paper, we construct supersymmetric solitons of QKdV equation (also known as mKdV equation in short) in arbitrary genus Riemann surfaces. The spectral problem for QKdV equation is first reduced to the spectral problem for the mKdV equation by using the Riemann-Hilbert problem. Then we use modified Riemann-Hilbert problem to construct the multi-solitons of QKdV equation. The corresponding spectral data for this solitons includes some genus 0 spectral data and some genus N with N solitons spectral data. We name these solitons of arbitrary genus. It is shown that the multi-solitons of arbitrary genus constructed here correspond to some Hamiltonian motion on the Jacobi varieties of genus N non-hyperelliptic curves. Solar coronal loops are hot, tenuous plasma strands that extend from the surface of the Sun all the way to the coronal arcade, typically at a constant temperature of 1-2 MK. Since coronal loops are the site of much of the Sun’s magnetic activity, their proper stability and dynamic behavior are of crucial interest to both solar physics and space weather. A loop is most stably in pressure balance at its apex where the magnetic pressure equals the plasma pressure. However, in practice, coronal loops have much flatter pressure gradients in the lower parts of their structure. This necessitates the use of an energy principle to determine the dynamic behavior of these structures. Thermodynamic energy principles can be used to determine the dynamic behavior of a coronal loop. The first law of thermodynamics can be formulated such that: dU = q - W + \sum_i{a_i}, where dU is the energy added or removed through parallel transport along a field line, q is theheat added or removed through footpoint motions at the loop top, W is the work done by forces along the field line, and the sum is over the individual volumes V_i bounded by the field lines. The second law of thermodynamics, in conjunction with the Maxwell equation, can be used to formulate the Maxwell stress as an irreversible energy flux: T \cdot Ds = \sum_i{\frac{1}{2}\kappa(T_i - T_0)^2}, where T is the temperature, Ds is the conjugated rate of change of entropy, \kappa is the heat conductivity, and T0 is the background temperature. This second law equation can be used to compute the rate of energy flux through a boundary. If it is positive-definite, then this is an irreversible energy flux into the region bounded by the boundary. The stability of a coronal loop is then determined by the sign of this energy flux at its apex. If this energy flux is positive (negative) then the loop is unstable (stable) with respect to small disturbances. When comparing the stability of two different solutions of the heat conduction equation, the loop is most unstable to kink (wavenumber 2) disturbances. The ratio of the maximum growth rates of the kink and sausage (wavenumbers 1 and 2) modes is the Boyd index. The loops analyzed in this paper have a Boyd index of <1, suggesting that it is unstable to kink oscillations. The computed loop modes agree well with loop observables: computed sausage mode periods are consistent with Doppler shifts of transverse oscillations, and computed kink mode periods are consistent with the long coronal loop lifetimes. By using an energy principle to determine the loop’s dynamic behavior, this research identifies the most likely mechanism by which coronal loops are kink unstable. This paper is about controllability of the heat and wave equations. We first present a series of new, explicit, finite difference methods to approximate the heat and wave equations. We then study the controllability of the finite difference methods by defining controls as localized functions on the edges of the domain. By carefully choosing these localized functions we are able to show that the exact solutions of the heat and wave equations are, in fact, controllable to any desired state in arbitrary small time. This result holds for any positive time, even for a time independent of the size of the domain. Our controllability results rely only on the local behavior of the exact solution and the spatial behavior of the controls. We also present counterexamples to show that our results are not true in general for the exact heat and wave equations. This is joint work with Marta Sanz-Soriano.

A remarkable feature of magnetic turbulence in astrophysical flows is the logarithmic scaling of the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) magnetic fluctuations with respect to the integral scale. This is in striking contrast to the classical scaling laws in hydrodynamical turbulence, called scaling laws. A new paradigm has recently been proposed for MHD turbulence, called weak turbulence theory. This theory applies to highly magnetized plasma, with the magnetic Reynolds number being small, and it assumes that all turbulent scales are coupled by the magnetic field. It was found that in this case the magnetic energy spectrum obeys a power law with an energy flux coupled to the logarithm of the scale, instead of the classic Kolmogorov energy flux. The application of weak turbulence theory to the case of accretion disk turbulence has indeed led to the predictions that the magnetic energy spectrum obeys a logarithmic scaling with the magnetic Prandtl number, the inverse of the magnetic Reynolds number, and that the energy flux is proportional to the angular momentum flux. The first prediction has been verified by recent high-resolution MHD simulations, and the verification of the second prediction is still awaited. Here we present the first such verification, through the analysis of the angular momentum flux. The results strongly support the applicability of weak turbulence theory to MHD accretion disk turbulence.

The Stokes-Einstein (SE) and Stokes-Einstein-Debye (SED) relations provide a means to probe the microscopic dynamics of liquids. They state that the diffusion coefficient, d, and the self-diffusion coefficient, D, and the viscosity, η, respectively, are linearly correlated with the Stokes-Einstein radius, a, and the Stokes-Einstein-Debye radius, Đ. We study a large-scale, coarse-grained, direct molecular dynamics simulation of 512 000 ices over a range of temperatures (263 K < T < 363 K) and pressures (0.65 bar < P < 3.16 bar) where the SE relation is found to break down. This is associated with dynamical heterogeneities, particularly in the local librational dynamics of the simulated water. We find that the SE and SED relations break down in the regime where dynamical heterogeneities are most pronounced. The breakdown of the SE and SED relations is consistent with recent proposals that the Stokes-Einstein relation is simply an idealised molecular dynamics scenario, and that a more complete picture should take into account dynamical heterogeneities.

Here we introduce a strategy to tune the carrier concentration in cuprate heterostructures by atomic layer deposition of mixed metal oxides. We demonstrate this approach on La-doped NdMnO3/LaAlO3 (NdMnO3/LAO), which exhibits electron doping at the NdMnO3/LAO interface even without macroscopic electrical connection between the two layers. Carrier concentrations of 6×1013 cm-3 were achieved in NdMnO3/LAO with optimized electron doping, which is sufficient to induce a ferromagnetic ordering at low temperatures. Additionally, effects such as oxygen deficiency and interfacial charge transfer provide a new avenue to understand the role of chemistry on material performance. Electron doping of cuprates via interfaces with manganites represents a general strategy to enhance properties for potential application in oxide electronics. NdMnO3/LAO heterostructures were studied as a model system. Even without macroscopic electrical connection between the two layers, electron doping at the NdMnO3/LAO interface results in a doping concentration of over 6×1013 cm-3, which is sufficient to induce ferromagnetic ordering at low temperatures. Effects such as oxygen deficiency and interfacial charge transfer provide a new avenue to understand the role of chemistry on material performance.

IGR J00234+6141 : a new INTEGRAL source identified as an Intermediate polar. This is the first reported INTEGRAL detection of an intermediate polar (IP), and the second identified with the INTEGRAL all-sky survey. IGR J00234+6141 is an extremely faint object with a period of 7.2793 s and an intensity typical of Intermediate Polars. It was discovered during a routine survey for INTEGRAL sources in the constellation of Vulpecula, at a galactic latitude of −6.2 degrees. In the paper “Minimal size of a barchan dune” [1], Barchan dunes are studied experimentally by loading sand into a box and subjecting it to different forces. The paper presents measurements of the dune size and shape, as well as a minimal model to describe the dune shape. The model consists of two rigid plates connected by a rotational spring, with the angle between the plates controlled by gravity. The model is able to qualitatively predict the observed dune shape. The paper concludes that the minimal model is in fact insufficient to explain the observed dune shapes, and a better description might involve a bending-spring approximation where the angle between the plates is allowed to vary. Here is an excerpt from the paper: “the qualitative agreement is excellent, in particular for the smaller dunes, where the approximation appears to be even quantitatively adequate.”. The model introduced in the paper is unable to reproduce dunes of minimum size observed in the experiment, which the authors attribute to the approximations made in the model. The authors of the paper propose that the observed dunes of minimum size are better described by a model that includes a rotational spring in addition to the spring-bend approximation. The rotational spring would model the fact that dunes tend to trap water inside [2], and would need to be strong enough to prevent the plates from aligning by pure bending. Such a model would be able to reproduce dunes of minimum size observed in the experiment. The minimal model with a rotational spring would have three degrees of freedom: the angle between plates, height of the dune above the plates, and angle of the rotational spring. The model is able to reproduce the dune shape qualitatively, but fails to reproduce dune height quantitatively. The authors propose that the discrepancy could be solved by modifying the model to include a third degree of freedom, “approach angle”, that would model the fact that as a dune becomes taller, it will begin to trap more water and become more unstable. The model with all three degrees of freedom would be able to quantitatively reproduce dune height as well as dune size and shape. The minimal model with a rotational spring and three degrees of freedom is able to reproduce the dune size and shape quantitatively, but remains too complex to analyse and interpret. In particular, it is unclear what the three additional degrees of freedom correspond to physically. The authors propose that the approach angle could correspond to the angle between the gravity vector and the axis of rotation of the dune, i.e. the angle between the dune axis and the direction of the force that pulls it towards the ground. Alternatively, the authors suggest that the approach angle might correspond to the angle between the xy-plane and the plane in which the dune propagates, i.e. the angle between the dune propagation direction and the horizontal.
