Recent advances in nanoscale magnetic functionality have led to a burgeoning interest in utilizing these structures for magnetic imaging and magneto-optical signals detection. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) are uniquely attractive for these applications due to their tunable, localized surface magnetic moments. Here we present the atomic scale magnetic characterization of uniformly 15 nm Fe Nanodots. We employ aberration-corrected, high resolution transmission electron microscopy (AC-HR-TEM) to probe the local magnetic properties of these particles. Our measurements reveal distinct magnetic fingerprint patterns of individual Nanodots. These patterns correspond to the engineered multi-domain states of the Nanodots, which we image with nanometer-scale spatial resolution. Finally, we exploit the spatial dependence of the magnetic fingerprints to rapidly image small volumes (~2 × 2 × 2 nm3). Our experiments provide a detailed, nanoscale magnetic characterization of sub-100 nm single-domain particles and represent an important step toward the development of MNP-based devices for high resolution magnetic imaging.

The Santa Fe Light Cone Simulation Project: I. Confusion and the WHIM in Upcoming Sunyaev-Zel'dovich Effect Surveys Recent observational results from the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH) and the Satellite Axis Viewer (SAV) of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey show evidence of systematic uncertainties in the measurement of cluster masses. While these uncertainties are likely caused by the intrinsic non-Gaussianity of the density distributions of the clusters, they may also arise from poorly understood sources such as thermal noise, calibration errors, and contamination from discrete sources such as galaxies and galaxy clusters. Here we report the results of a large cosmological simulation that resolves both the cosmic web and the galaxies that populate it. The simulation incorporates a novel treatment of thermal conduction and radiative cooling that enhances the efficiency of cluster formation. This enables the mass function of galaxy clusters to be robustly determined over a dynamic range of five orders of magnitude in mass. We apply a series of selection effects to the resulting population of galaxy clusters that approximate the conditions of current and future Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect surveys. Inclusion of discrete sources of thermal emission is found to have a significant effect on the measured masses of galaxy clusters. The combination of these two effects causes significant uncertainties in the inferred cosmology. We investigate both the dependence of the bias on the cosmological parameters and observational selection effects, and demonstrate that an uncertain cluster mass function can mimic a cosmic web topology characterized by a spatial variation in the local density parameter.

In the study of condensed matter, defects are often observed at the interface between different phases. The nature of these defects is conceptually easiest to understand in the case of continuous phase transitions, where the different phases are ordered. For example, near the ferroelectric to paraelectric phase transition in potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KDP), the different phases - the ferroelectricc, low-temperature anti-ferroelectric and paraelectric - can be distinguished by the symmetry of the electric polarisation they exhibit. Defects are best characterised in terms of the continuous distortions that they break the symmetries of the ordered phases. Such distortions are called dislocations and are analogous to the Burgers vector in the case of lattice distortions. In this short paper we discuss the nature of defects in the anti-ferroelctric phase of KDP. We focus on a particular class of defects, continuous defects, which continuously distort the anti-ferroelectric lattice but preserve the periodicity of the local polarisation direction. Such continuous defects break the polarisation rotation symmetry, but preserve the in-phase and out-of-phase symmetries, and therefore are different to the dislocations that were discussed in the previous paragraph. We describe the nature of these continuous defects and present the results of atomistic simulations of their formation. In the ferroelectric phase of KDP, atoms are displaced by approximately 25% from their positions in the idealised rhombohedral structure. The polarisation direction that these displacements form is only approximately regular, and the local polarisation directions change by approximately 10° between neighbouring ions. In the anti-ferroelectric phase, the structure of KDP is fully tetragonal, and polarisation is entirely rotationally invariant. As described in the preceding paragraph, continuous defects in the anti-ferroelectric phase are characterised by the polarisation direction changing by approximately 10° between neighbouring ions, but these defects form a fully rotational distortions of the polarisation direction. We present the results of calculations that show that the distortion energy of anti-ferroelectric crystals with continuous defects is lower than that of crystals without defects. We conclude that defects in the anti-ferroelectric phase of KDP are likely to be dislocations, that is, discontinuous defects, rather than continuous defects. In the case of KDP, this conclusion was aided by the discovery of a second anti-ferroelectric phase at high temperature, in which the structure and polarisation direction are identical to those in the tetragonal structure of the low-temperature anti-ferroelectric phase, but in which the continuous defects predicted by our calculations were observed. In the literature, continuous defects and dislocations have sometimes been confused, and this has sometimes led to unfortunate confusion in the study of defects. We believe that our results contribute to a more clear definition of the nature of defects in crystals, and we hope that the discussion presented here will encourage more careful definitions of continuous and discontinuous defects in the future.

In this paper, we propose a physically motivated approach to generating entangled graph states with spin chains that undergo Gaussian noise and decay. The noise and decay allow us to engineer various strengths of interactions, topologies of the underlying graphs, and fidelity of our desired target states. We show how to efficiently simulate the spin chain using a classical Ising model and develop an analog Hamiltonian engine to generate target states with high fidelity. We numerically optimize our strategy and show that by harnessing dissipation, thermal noise, and imperfect gates, we can produce highly entangled graph states in a probabilistic manner with fidelities above 0.97. These results provide a path to generating high-fidelity graph states with dissipative spin-chain engineering, a technology that is readily implementable with current experimental capabilities. Resistivity of an obliquely deposited atom chip is measured using scanning magnetoresistance microscopy. The atom chip was produced by laser-induced oxidation of a silver wire. Atomic resolution is demonstrated down to 20 μΩcm. Resistivity is uniform across the chip and drops to zero at the centre. From the former, the zero-point energy of the chip is estimated to be 246 nK, which corresponds to 41 atoms per cubic millimetre at 1 atm. From the latter, the distance between the atomic wires is estimated to be 16(4) nm. The centre of the atom chip, which is likely to be free of defects and contaminations, would be useful as a smooth potential surface for atomic interferometry and inertial sensors. -- Han Miao, Jingchang C. Shock waves moving through interstellar and intergalactic media heat and compress the gas, triggering the formation of new gas structures with very different physical characteristics from those in the ambient medium. We report new observations of such a structure in the vicinity of a young supernova, PTF11dsf (SN 2011ih), using archival data from the Chandra and Subaru telescopes. The newly-formed cloud, which moves at ~14,000 km/s with respect to its environment, is characterized by extremely high temperature (over 10^8 K), very low gas density (10-100 atomscm−3), and strong magnetization (B ~ 10μG, μG = microgauss). These physical characteristics are all very different from those of the colder, higher-density ambient medium and provide new insight into the interaction between SN remnants and the interstellar medium. We report new observations of such a structure in the vicinity of a young supernova, PTF11dsf (SN 2011ih), using archival data from the Chandra and Subaru telescopes. The newly-formed cloud, which moves at ~14,000 km/s with respect to its environment, is characterized by extremely high temperature (over 10^8 K), very low gas density (10-100 atomscm−3), and strong magnetization (B ~ 10μG, μG = microgauss). These physical characteristics are all very different from those of the colder, higher-density ambient medium and provide new insight into the interaction between SN remnants and the interstellar medium. In particular, we show that the newly-formed cloud is strongly magnetized and approximately isothermal. This implies that the compression and heating of the gas were so great that the gas achieved a stable, hot, condensed phase, perhaps after reaching some threshold of magnetization due to previous shocks with the ambient medium. The observed cloud thus represents a novel phase of the ISM, which we term “shock-triggered formation of magnetically-dominated clouds” (SMMDCs). This is the first clear detection of a condensed phase of interstellar gas with magnetic fields amplified by orders of magnitude relative to the surrounding medium. These clouds may represent an important stage in the evolution of gas in the ISM, from the warm, diffused phase, to the cold, dense phase that eventually forms stars. We also present analysis of a similar cloud located behind the Tornado Loop supernova remnant, suggesting a possible evolutionary sequence for such objects. Finally, the dense, magnetized gas observed around SN 2011ih may explain the high-energy emission recently detected from the SN remnant, which could be synchrotron radiation from relativistic particles confined in the magnetic fields of the SMMDCs. Short duration gamma-ray bursts (SGRBs) are among the most powerful explosions in the universe. Their progenitors have not been identified, but some hypothesis, such as neutron star-black hole coalescence or magnetar giant flares, predict the production of high-energy neutrinos and cosmic rays in addition to gamma rays. Assuming the gamma rays arise from the Thomson regime, their flux should produce a corresponding excess in the very-high-energy (VHE, 100 GeV - 100 TeV) electromagnetic spectrum, observable by ground-based gamma-ray observatories. Using data from the Milagro gamma-ray observatory, we search for such an excess and find a 5.99σ detection of VHE radiation from a small region of the southern sky during the hours following the 2008 triggers of short duration gamma-ray bursts. We derive limits on the total fluence and duration of any VHE emission from these bursts, as well as on the maximum isotropic-equivalent gamma-ray energy. These limits disfavor models that predict a spatially uniform emission from SGRBs and span a parameter space where alternative explanations of the gamma-ray signals are still possible.

In particular, we will show that the geometry of time, which is the time interval between two consecutive events is related to the axiom of choice and this axiom of choice is related to the well-known quantum zeno effect. More precisely, we will show that the more the geometry of time is curved the more the axiom of choice becomes necessary to connect the events. Conversely, we will show that the more the geometry of time is flat the weaker the axiom of choice becomes and this may explain why we do not observe quantum behavior of the neuro-biological systems. Finally, we will show that a zeno effect may also occur at the quantum level and this may have dramatic consequences on the neuro-biological quantum universe. The axiom of choice states that for a given collection of choices, there exists at least one choice. The issue with this axiom is that when we try to apply it in the real world, we face some difficulties, for example, when I ask you to select one element from a set of choices, such as selecting a color or a dressed, you may seem to have a lot of elements to choose from but when I select one, you suddenly have none. To explain this, we may think that the set of choices is too large, which is impossible because we can always create an equivalent set with a smaller number of choices by, for example, separating those choices that may be ill defined (such as red hair) from the rest. GRB 060614 was one of the most observed gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Early after the initial detection of the prompt emission, a multi-wavelength afterglow was observed for the first time. The initial afterglow was typical of many long-duration bursts: a shallow decay followed by a period of rapid decline, eventually making a normal behaviour comeback as the afterglow entered the X-ray and radio windows. Such a comeback had never been observed before for a long burst and was quite unusual. These results, and the properties of the prompt emission, were very surprising and have since then been associated with this event being a so-called 'anomalous burst'. This article summarises the main results of the prompt and afterglow analyses of this burst, highlights the most surprising findings and discusses the implications of this event. stem On 6 June 2014, the [*Fermi*]{} satellite detected a gamma-ray burst, GRB 060614. This short and intense gamma-ray burst was localized with an accuracy of a few square degrees and the X-ray, optical and radio afterglows were promptly discovered. The early afterglow behaviour was typical for most GRBs, but the normal comeback in the afterglow flux had never been observed before for a long-duration burst and was quite unusual. These intriguing results have since been associated with this event being an 'anomalous burst'. In this article, we summarize the prompt and afterglow analyses of this burst, highlight the most surprising findings and discuss the implications of this event.

The inner jet of radio galaxy NGC 315 (NGC 315) is examined using data from the NASA Chandra X-ray Observatory and the National Radio Astronomy Observatory's VLA. The jet is found to contain a continuous flow of particles. As the jet moves along its axis, its spectrum becomes gradually dominated by the presence of a population of very high-energy particles, with no evidence of a cutoff in the energetic emission as suggested by previous observations. The magnetic field strength in the jet is found to be within the range 0.3-0.9 microGauss, which is typical of jets in radio galaxies. The precise nature of the progenitor of the jet is not clear. The lack of strong shocks and the detection of a large population of very high energy particles in the jet both argue against a direct link with the AGN that appears at the nucleus of NGC 315. The most likely hypothesis is that the jet is powered by a normal active galaxy in the course of formation, through a process known as merger-induced gas accretion. A large-scale radio source is commonly associated with mergers of galaxies, and may be fueled by the gas being driven into the central black hole.

The inner magnetosphere plasma pressure distribution around the planet was obtained using satellite measurements from Geosynchronous satellite (GSO) and polar satellites during the March 1-8, 1982 geomagnetic storm. The radial distribution shows that pressure was depleted from approximately 8 R_E (earth radii) to 4 R_E during the storm. There was no radial pressure enhancement noted during the storm. The depletion of pressure began at around 6 R_E and extended to 3 R_E during the night of March 2nd. This pressure depletion coincided with a period of intense negative Bz in the midlatitude regions, and can be explained by adiabatic expansion of plasma in magnetic fields. However, the pressure depletion during the storm was more extensive than that predicted by the adiabatic expansion model. Additional depletion may have been caused by interaction of the storm plasma with the ring current. Recent advances in the AdS/CFT correspondence have lead to the development of a stringy realization of this correspondence, where a classical string in AdS space is dual to a quantum string theory in a corresponding superconformal field theory. The classical strings in question are Type II superstrings in ten-dimensional Minkowski space, performing an orientifold projection to obtain a Type I superstring in ten-dimensional AdS space. Using the AdS/CFT correspondence, the spectrum and symmetries of this string theory have been determined. Two-loop world-sheet corrections have been shown to correspond to the entanglement entropy of the CFT. This Letter provides the first two-loop world-sheet corrections to the Type I superstring in AdS space. It is determined that the world-sheet corrections correspond to the entanglement entropy of the CFT. The Type I superstring consists of a both a bosonic string as well as a ten-dimensional Type II superstring. Two-loop world-sheet corrections have been known in the latter case for many years, while for the bosonic string the first two-loop world-sheet correction has just been obtained in this Letter. The result is expressed in terms of a simple integral representation, with UV and IR fixed points. It is also shown that for appropriate linearized perturbations of the fixed points, the world-sheet corrections are captured by the scaling dimensions of the operators in the CFT. This result provides new information about the AdS superstring and the AdS super-CFT correspondence. Finally, a few applications of the entanglement entropy representation of the world-sheet correction are discussed. The first is to determine corrections to the semi-classical graviton and dilaton scaling dimensions. The second is to evaluate the world-sheet correction to the energy of the giant graviton configuration. Finally, it is shown how to determine the anomalous contribution to the world-sheet stress tensor. A tomographic analysis of the Lyman-alpha absorber associated with PKS1302-102 is presented. Using observations from the Cosmic Variance Survey (CVN) and the Spectroscopic Survey for Impostor NuSTARS (SSINS), the neutral hydrogen distribution in this system is characterized over a velocity interval of -1000 km/s to +500 km/s with respect to the quasar rest frame. The absorbing column density is high, N(HI) ~10^{20.5}-10^{21.5} cm^-2, indicating that this is a stable structure within the evolving Universe. Analysis of the differential ionization parameter Q(H) shows the absorber is largely ionized at all impact parameters. A simple photoionization model with a uniform radiation field from the quasar is found to be sufficient to simultaneously reproduce the measured column densities and differential ionization parameter across the line of sight. We rule out scenarios involving a pre-ionized absorber or gas within the strong cool/warm phase of the cosmic web at z=0.54. This is the most comprehensive study of the intergalactic medium towards PKS1302-102 to date and provides a reference for future observations of this system.

The CO J=6-5, 4-3 transitions are critical for testing models of the starburst/AGN interface, given their low critical density and high excitation temperatures. As such, the first such transitions in a typical ULIRG, Mrk231, were sought with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA). The spectroscopic images are naturally curious: the symmetric distribution of dense gas around the active nucleus, in combination with the asymmetric distribution of star-forming molecular gas, suggest that the starburst and the putative black hole accretion are not co-spatial. Mrk231 is thus a clear demonstration of the powerfulness of ALMA, and the importance of studying the cool Universe with it. By ignoring the potential influence of the AGN on the nearby molecular gas, a method for estimating its mass reservoir is laid out. Further measurements in other molecular lines are recommended to fully assess this method, as well as the ability of this method to properly characterize high-redshift quasars with potentially disrupted cool gas reservoirs. Mrk231 is a prototypical low-redshift (z = 0.0483) ultraluminous infrared galaxy (ULIRG), of which the CO J=6-5 line has recently been detected with ALMA. The detection presented here, at an inferred luminosity of L'_{CO(6-5)} = 1.2×10^9 L_{\odot} kpc^{-2}, is the first such detection in any ULIRG. With the superior resolution of the ALMA data, the distribution of molecular gas around the active nucleus is clearly seen to be asymmetric. The star-forming molecular gas is distributed around the nucleus in a ring approximately 200 pc in radius, whereas the dense gas (as traced by NH3) extends out to at least 600 pc in radius. The latter is likely consistent with the gravitational influence of the active nucleus, which would thus be located between the inner starburst ring and the more extended, dense molecular gas. Using a simple radiative-transfer calculation, the total molecular gas reservoir in Mrk231 is estimated to be between 1.1×10^10 and 6.2×10^10 M_{\odot} based on this observed distribution, corresponding to 450-25000 L'_{CO(6-5)} (K km/s Mpc2). Thus, even in the extreme environment of a ULIRG, where a large fraction of the molecular gas may be in the form of dense gas as opposed to star-forming gas, the reservoir of molecular gas is substantial. The radiative-transfer calculation, however, raises a caveat: it assumes that the gas is in thermal equilibrium with the radiation field, whereas typical dense molecular gas has temperatures of 50 K or less. Assuming LTE will overestimate the column density by a factor of 2-3. Underscoring the importance of modeling the cool gas in local ULIRGs

Animals were randomly divided into different groups and were subjected to different experimental conditions as following: 1- No treatment: control group 2- Exposure to physical stress: stress group 3- Social stress: social stress group In the chronic social stress protocol, mice were exposed to several hours of social defeat every day for 21 days. On the 22nd day, all mice were subjected to a home cage without any threat. Two days after the last stress exposure, open field, elevated plus maze, novelty suppressed feeding, open field-repeated exposed to the chamber for three consecutive days, fasting blood glucose test, fasting insulin test and measurement of plasma corticosterone levels were conducted. The results of this study showed that mice exposed to physical stress only developed an anhedonic-like behavior (increased immobile time in the forced swimming and novelty suppressed feeding tests) and displayed altered corticosterone and insulin levels (marker of HPA axis activity). However, mice exposed to chronic social stress not only developed an anhedonic-like behavior but also became hypersensitive to novelty and exhibited altered glucose levels (insulin resistance). In conclusion, the present study suggests that physical stress per se is not sufficient to induce affective disorders like anhedonia but requires an additional psychological component, which is likely stress related. This study was performed using C57BL/6J male mice. The influence of experimental context on the behavioral, endocrine and metabolic effects of stress were analyzed.

In this paper we study the dynamics of the heavy quark-antiquark $qqq$ wave function in the high momentum limit of QCD at the light front. This limit has the advantage of simplifying the momentum dependence of the wave function and thus facilitate a numerical study. We use a combination of relativistic effective field theory and QCD sum rules to compute the heavy quark-antiquark light-front wave function at two different levels of sophistication. We use the wave function to compute the resulting spin dynamics for a proton with three heavy quarks. The model is then used to make a number of qualitative predictions for observables that can be experimentally tested. Heavy quark-antiquark systems provide a unique window into the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). A powerful method to study such systems is the heavy quark effective theory (HQET) (1), which separates long distance dynamics, which are described by heavy quark symmetry (often called heavy quark scaling), from the short distance details of the QCD interaction. The heavy quark symmetry has been shown to be a powerful tool for calculations in the heavy quark limit, in which the heavy quark mass is assumed to be infinitely large compared with the QCD scale. In this limit, the effective theory, HQET, simplifies to a non-relativistic theory, whose Hamiltonian corresponds to a kinetic energy term and a potential term which couples the heavy quark velocity to its angular momentum (called the “ chromomagnetic” Hamiltonian). The potential in the chromomagnetic Hamiltonian is a fundamental parameter of the heavy quarkonium system. The strong coupling constant can be estimated by comparing the spectrum of heavy quarkonium with the corresponding spectrum of heavy hadrons with the same heavy quark content. The value of the potential at the origin, V(0), can be determined from leptonic decays of heavy mesons, and a range of values of V(0) has been determined by studying decays of both mesons and baryons (2). The strength of the potential can also be determined from high-precision measurements of the electronic energy levels in heavy ions (3). These studies have resulted in a consensus on a “standard model” value for V(0) of about 0.94 GeV, with a very small error (about 10%). One approach to determine the potential is via QCD sum rules (4, 5). QCD sum rules are based on the short distance (two-point) operator product expansion, in which the time-ordered product of two local operators is expressed as a series of positive powers of the short distance scale, the momentum transfer. The Wilson loop, which is a path ordered exponential of the gauge field, plays an essential role in the application of the operator product expansion to the heavy quarkonium systems. At leading order in the heavy quark expansion, the long distance (four-point) correlation function is completely determined by the heavy quarkonium wave function, which is basically the light front wave function (LF

GPCRs, also called G-protein coupled receptors, are membrane proteins which transfer a signal across the cell membrane by means of a guanine nucleotide binding protein, G-protein. Based on their structure and sequence similarity, GPCRs are divided into seven families (7-TM receptors, adenosine receptors, chemokine receptors, dopamine receptors, opsin receptors, secretin receptors, and latrophilin receptors). Functioning as a gateway to the cell, GPCRs play a vital role in signal transduction, metabolic regulation, and cell-cell communication, and are thus of significant interest to pharmaceutical researchers. Because of the important role GPCRs play in the onset and development of various diseases, their classification is of high relevance. Traditional methods for GPCR classification make use of multiple feature descriptors which are extracted from GPCR three-dimensional structures. However, these methods typically rely on a non-adaptive algorithm, making them inefficient and insensitive to changes in input data. In this work, a method for GPCR structural classification is proposed which makes use of a feature descriptor and an adaptive algorithm. The feature descriptor is based on gravitational bag of words (GBOW), a type of distributed word representation which assigns a vector to every token in a given text. These vectors are learnt using word2vec, a commonly used tool for training word2vec models. The GPCR sequences are converted to corresponding four-letter DNA words using single letter correspondences, and then converted to GBOW vectors using word2vec. The model is trained on the Edinburgh GPCR dataset using three different learning rates. Using a 5-fold cross validation scheme, the lowest mean average error (MAE) is achieved with a learning rate of 0.0001. The GBOW vectors of all the sequences in the Edinburgh GPCR dataset are subsequently used as features to train an Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) algorithm. The AdaBoost model is tested on the Matthew and Anderson (2017) GPCR dataset, achieving a 3-way MAE of 0.36. Compared to previous work, the proposed Adaptive Boosting algorithm significantly outperforms both non-adaptive algorithms and other existing methods for GPCR classification.

Galaxy collisions can produce powerful radio sources, gamma-rays and gravitational waves. In this paper, we calculate the gravitational wave signature of close encounters between galaxies, using a three-body approximation to model the system. We perform the calculation for a range of parameters, and find that for typical galaxy properties the expected gravitational wave strain is extremely low, but may be detectable by future space-based gravitational wave observatories, such as eLISA. In most cases, however, the frequency of gravitational waves is too high to be detectable by eLISA. We also investigate the parameter space which could lead to a merger, and find that for close encounters with sufficiently high energy the merger time may be shorter than the current age of the universe, suggesting that galaxy collisions might be a mechanism for gas accretion and subsequent star formation in extreme systems. This work was supported in part by STFC.

IGR J11215-5952, briefly IGR J11215, was first detected by INTEGRAL on 2011 August 15 (error circle 5 sq. deg.) during an outburst that lasted about 21 days. The source subsequently made at least four further detections with INTEGRAL and Swift/XRT between 2012 February and 2013 January. IGR J11215 is a highly variable X-ray source, with a periodicity that has been observed between 20 and 30 days with different instruments. The source has a likely Galactic association but the distance and nature remain uncertain. IGR J11215 was first observed by Swift/XRT on 2012 February 9 (obs. ID 0003414001) during its fourteenth outburst. Here we present an analysis of all 14 Swift/XRT observations of this source performed between 2011 August and 2013 January. The data were analysed using standard procedures, with the results being plotted using Pyrolithic Graphical User Interface (PyroPLUS) and FTOOLS. The X-ray light curve shows that the source intensity varied by a factor of about 30 between the lowest and highest observed fluxes. The source remained within $15''$ of the centre of the field of view throughout each observation, with a peak count rate of about 7000 c s$^{-1}$. The highest luminosity observed was $2 \times 10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, occurring during the brightest outburst in 2012 December. Spectral analysis shows that the spectrum was well fitted by a simple power law throughout each observation, with no significant deviations apparent between the observations. The average hydrogen column density was found to be about $3 \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$, which is relatively stable over time. IGR J11215 underwent its fifth outburst between 2011 August and 2012 February. The light curve shows that the intensity varied by a factor of about 30, with a maximum luminosity of $2 \times 10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$. During the brightest outburst in 2012 December, the source reached a maximum luminosity of $4 \times 10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$. Spectral analysis showed that the source exhibited a simple power law spectrum, with no significant deviation between the observations. The average hydrogen column density was relatively stable at $3 \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$.

Quarkonium-based QCD tests extend into low quarkonium masses, providing sensitivity to the strong coupling constant evaluated over several orders of magnitude in momentum, from 1 GeV scale in quarkonium masses to 1/1000th of an MeV scale at which the strong coupling runs. We report results from running and latest theoretical calculations of the quarkonium spectrum. Including relativistic and quantum chromodynamics radiative corrections, we calculate spin-dependent quarkonium ground state masses for the six quarkonia, and use them to determine QCD coupling. QCD coupling evaluated in the 1 GeV region is much smaller than that evaluated at much higher scales, providing evidence for the improvedrunning of the strong coupling constant down to 1 GeV. Running and latest theoretical calculations of the quarkonium spectrum are included. QCD coupling evaluated in the 1 GeV region is much smaller than that evaluated at much higher scales, providing evidence for the improved running of the strong coupling constant down to 1 GeV. Spin-dependent quarkonium ground state masses for the six quarkonia are reported. These masses include relativistic and quantum chromodynamics radiative corrections. QCD coupling evaluated in the 1 GeV region is reported along with that evaluated at much higher scales. The smaller coupling evaluated at 1 GeV demonstrates the improved running of the strong coupling constant down to 1 GeV.

The High Energy Astronomy Observatory (HEAO) 1 was launched by NASA in June 1967. It was the first satellite designed to study high-energy gamma-rays and had a large detector plane with sodium iodide (NaI) crystals that was sensitive to energies in the range of 10 keV to 300 GeV. HEAO 1 collected data until 1980. In particular, it performed an experiment to search for gamma-rays from the universe in the GeV band. This experiment was called the GeV-rays experiment. Results of the GeV-rays experiment were surprising. For the first time, a galaxy was observed to make gamma-rays in this band. The source of these gamma-rays was not known at the time. In subsequent observations, the GeV-rays telescope confirmed the source was relatively steady and strong. Furthermore, its spectrum was compatible with very high energy (VHE, GeV energies) photons originating from electrons accelerated to such energies in electromagnetic waves in the gamma-ray range emitted by the galaxy. This phenomenon was later called the primary electron-positron pair production. Several models were proposed to explain this observation but none of them matched all observations. The most likely explanation for the origins of these gamma-rays is that they were produced by Primary Cosmic Gamma-Rays (or PCG). Pairs of high energy gamma-rays emitted by distant active galaxies would interact with the photons of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) producing electron-positron pairs in the so-called Bose-Einstein condensate. After a series of interactions and losses, the electrons and positrons would acquire relatively low energies and could emit gamma-rays in the GeV band. The proposed distance at which this interaction occurs depends on the energy of the gamma-rays but it is generally in the range of tens to hundreds of megaparsecs. According to recent data from the MAGIC telescope, a very strong candidate for the production of PCG has been identified: 1ES 1959+650. In this work, we will analyze this source through different models and its implications for the Poynting-Robertson effect, the spin-rotation coupling and galactic center gamma-rays anomalies.

Ultra-low-field MRI (ULF-MRI) has recently emerged as a promising candidate for in-situ medical diagnosis as it allows for non-invasive visualization of microstructural and molecular features within early stage disease development and treatments. This new MRI modality, although presenting great potential, is severely limited by the low SNR associated with sensitive detectors used in most systems. To address this challenge, we have developed a SQUID-based ULFMRI system, which combines the low-noise performance of SQUIDs with the multiplexing capability of RF coils, to achieve ultra-low-field MRI detection. A voxel size of 0.1 mm3 and a noise level below 3 aT/√Hz have been demonstrated, which are the smallest volume and the lowest noise level for an MRI scanner operating at the magnetic noise level of 360 aT/√Hz. Preliminary animal and human studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the ULF-MRI technique. Our work establishes a SQUID-based ULF-MRI system and demonstrates its capability for in-situ medical diagnosis. This ULF-MRI system has the potential to accelerate the clinical translation of ultra-low-field MRI.

The self consistent treatment of quantum field theories provide a unique approach to the inter-relation between hadronic physics and QCD. The aim of the present article is to review some selected aspects of such an approach in quantum chromodynamics (QCD). The basic idea is to perform a simultaneous expansion of the theory around a number of well-defined mean fields. Such an approach, which we call self-consistent approach, has proved to be extremely useful in accounting for the main features of hadrons, even though much remains to be done to fully exploit its potential. The review is organized as follows. We start by discussing the phenomenon of spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking and the associated occurrence of light pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone (pNGB) mesons in the spectrum. Next we present a description of the light meson octet in terms of the effective Lagrangian (massless quarks). Subsequently, we move on to discuss the phase structure of QCD and in particular the phenomenon of deconfinement. Finally, we present a discussion of possible scenarios of color superconductivity and of the novel color-flavor locked phase.

We develop a general framework for discrete thermodynamic modeling and analysis of dynamical systems, with an emphasis on laser-based devices. We start with an arbitrary dynamical system, describe its state space using a countable state space model, and define the corresponding state vector and the relevant probability distributions on this vector. Next, we define the dynamical flows on the state space induced by the system, the action function describing the change of the state space average induced by a single system transition, and the Jacobian matrix describing the linearization of the dynamical flows around the invariant measures. We discuss important special cases and examples of such modeling and thermodynamic analysis, and apply our approach to study the internal energy consumption in a generic optical laser. We have developed a general discrete thermodynamic framework for dynamical systems with an emphasis on laser-based devices. We start with a generic dynamical system and define its state space using a countable state space model. Next, we define the dynamical flows on the state space induced by the system, the action function describing the change of the state space average induced by a single system transition, and the Jacobian matrix describing the linearization of the dynamical flows around the invariant measures. We study important special cases and examples of such modeling and thermodynamic analysis. As an example, we apply our approach to study the internal energy consumption in a generic optical laser. This research will help us to fully understand the thermodynamic processes in laser-based devices and may help in developing more efficient devices with respect to energy consumption.

An optical lattice is a periodic standing wave of light with wavelengths corresponding to the spacing between the barriers in a laser optical lattice. By using a Bose-Einstein condensate as a quantum wave reservoir, it is possible to control the effective strength of the optical lattice. Here, we report an experimental measurement of the speed of sound of an optical lattice, revealing a good agreement with the theoretical prediction. The obtained result can be used for monitoring and controlling the dynamics of the condensate in the optical lattice. Authors: D. Skryabin and A. In recent years, several analyses using high-energy gamma-ray and neutrino telescopes have been performed to search for cosmic ray accelerators, which are candidates of sources of high-energy cosmic rays. None of these analyses has found significant evidence of these accelerators, and thus an unambiguous discovery of these objects remains elusive. However, uncertainties in the cosmic ray propagation models lead to the possibility that some of these gamma-ray and neutrino signals could be produced by hadrons accelerated in a hypothetical cosmic ray proton accelerators (pevatrons), but not detectable with current instruments due to their large distance from Earth. In this work, we present a search for these pevatrons using several analyses of high-energy gamma-ray and neutrino data. No significant excess was found and thus we put upper limits on the flux of these pevatrons. *Reference: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.11439

Fossil groups are large clusters of galaxies captured by the gravity of a larger central halo. The galaxies in the groups are early-type, similar to the way in which the central galaxy is described as cuspy. We examine the dynamics of galaxy groups and compare to a subset of the Millennium Simulation. While the average groups masses in the simulation agree with observational values, the fraction of groups with multiple luminous members is less than that in observed groups. We investigate the causes and conclude that the low multi-occupancy of the groups in the Millennium Simulation can be reproduced by standard treatments of galaxy-galaxy interactions and mergers, without the need for modification to the mass or dynamics of the groups. The Millennium Simulation is a $N$-body simulation of our universe, run by the Virgo Consortium and funded by the American Astronomical Society. The resolution of the simulation is approximately 108 times better than that of the Las Campanas survey. I compare the dynamics of galaxy groups in the Millennium Simulation to that in the Las Campanas survey. The fraction of groups with multiple luminous members in the simulation is less than that in the survey. I investigate the causes and conclude that the low multi-occupancy of the groups in the simulation can be reproduced by standard treatments of galaxy-galaxy interactions and mergers, without the need for modification to the mass or dynamics of the groups. I confirm this by comparing the dynamics of groups in the Millennium Simulation to that in the Las Campanas survey. In the simulation, the average groups masses agree with observational values. However, the fraction of groups with multiple luminous members is less than that in the survey. I investigate the causes and conclude that the low multi-occupancy of the groups in the simulation can be reproduced by standard treatments of galaxy-galaxy interactions and mergers, without the need for modification to the mass or dynamics of the groups.

Bacterial populations are often modeled using partial differential equations, whereby the density of individual bacteria is represented by a spatial variable and time is propagated implicitly (hereafter, “modeled bacteria”). Such models have proven effective at describing the qualitative behavior of bacterial populations, but tend to exclude bacterial interactions which occur on length scales comparable to the average bacterial separation. To account for this, a field of individual bacteria has been modeled using a set of integrodifference equations, whereby bacterial interactions are explicitly modeled. In this article, we study a generalized version of such a model which includes a control volume-type term representing chemotaxis, the ability of bacteria to detect and respond to chemical cues in their environment. In certain parameter regimes, we show that solutions of the model approach a critical mass in the limit of an infinite-sized control volume; namely, a finite population density at which point spontaneous pattern formation occurs due to self-enhancement. We present a phase plane analysis of the model and investigate the linearization about a flat solution, which we use to obtain an analogy with the Chandrasekhar limiting mass of a white dwarf star.

Entanglement is one of the most remarkable features of quantum mechanics, and is at the heart of several key principles, such as the No-Cloning Theorem and the uncertainty principle. The entanglement present in a quantum state of a composite system, say $\rho_{A_1...A_N}$, is typically quantified by means of the entropy of entanglement, which is the entanglement entropy of the state when one of the parties is replaced by a reference system, namely the environment. Such entropy of entanglement has been shown to be a proper entanglement measure only for product states. In this paper we consider a natural generalization of the entanglement entropy to multipartite quantum states, the so-called squashed entanglement. We establish bounds for the squashed entanglement of a general state of multipartite systems, and we introduce an entanglement monotone based on the so-called mixed convex roof. The latter generalizes the well-known convex roof construction to the case of composed quantum states. We apply our results to separability and negative partial transpose (NPT) detection, showing that our entanglement monotone is higher than negativity in detecting bound entangled states. Moreover, we prove that the corresponding optimization problem is equal to the optimal cost of a semidefinite program, thus providing a convex roof dual for the mixed density matrix, from which several interesting addenda can be derived, including an entanglement measure based on the convex hull of the partial traces.

In the standard fireball model of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the afterglow emission is thought to be mainly powered by the transferred shock wave ploughing through the circumburst medium (CM). In this paper, we point out that the circumstellar wind (CSW) from the GRB progenitor can also form a wind-shaped CM. The inner part of the CSW has a velocity of a few hundred km s-1, which is much higher than that of the photonuclearCompton scattering shell. As a result, the wind would sweep up the shell and form a density structure like a cocoon, while the swept-up material would cool the shock front and produce an observable X-ray afterglow. We show that this mechanism can potentially explain the extended X-ray emission observed in some afterglows. For some specific parameters of the CSW and GRB, this model can also account for the optical/IR afterglows in some GRBs, and can naturally produce the shallow decay phase in some X-ray afterglows. We conclude that the X-ray and optical/IR afterglows of some GRBs may involve a wind-shaped CM.

A function is holomorphic if its complex derivative is zero. We introduce the concept of norm and numerical peak holomorphic functions. A function is norm-peak if in addition to being holomorphic, it satisfies an additional inequality. We present several examples of norm-peak functions, and prove some existence theorems for norm-peak functions. We conclude with a discussion of our results and open problems. We introduce the concept of norm and numerical peak holomorphic functions. A function is norm-peak if in addition to being holomorphic, it satisfies an additional inequality. We present several examples of norm-peak functions, and prove some existence theorems for norm-peak functions. We conclude with a discussion of our results and open problems. Motivation and background The notion of holomorphy has played a prominent role in complex analysis for more than a century. Holomorphic functions have many nice properties that make them very useful in analysis. For example, all of their derivative functions are also holomorphic, and they satisfy a number of other fundamental properties. A function is holomorphic if its complex derivative is zero. In this sense, holomorphic functions represent the "functions that are constant along complex derivatives". The holomorphic functions form a sub-ring in the ring of all functions. We introduce the concept of norm and numerical peak holomorphic functions. A function is norm-peak if in addition to being holomorphic, it satisfies an additional inequality. We present several examples of norm-peak functions, and prove some existence theorems for norm-peak functions. What is norm-peakness? The term "norm-peak" was coined by the present author in an article published in Complex Variables and Geometric Analysis in 2011. Norm-peak functions generalize holomorphic functions in a number of ways. First, we allow the functions to have more than one complex derivative. In this sense, norm-peak functions have more than one constant along "complex derivatives". A function is norm-peak if in addition to being holomorphic, it satisfies an additional inequality. In the case that a function is holomorphic, its derivative is zero. In this case, the derivative function satisfies an equality. We require that our norm-peak functions satisfy an inequality in addition to being holomorphic. A function is numerically peak if in addition to satisfying an inequality, the inequality is a equality. If a function satisfies an equality, then it is constant along every complex derivative. Thus, numerically peak functions are constant along all of their complex derivatives. Examples of norm-peak functions include the normal functions and log-normal functions. Both of these functions were introduced in the present article as examples of norm-peak functions. The normal function and log-normal function are norm-peak. The normal function is also the unique solution of a certain partial differential equation. It satisfies a fundamental existence theorem. In general, there can be more than one numerically peak function for a given function.

Exclusive charmless B decays into two-body hadronic final states containing a $D$ or $D_s$ meson, provide a rich source of information on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix elements, as well as on the dynamics of the underlying weak interaction. Over the last decade, an impressive amount of data has been obtained from B-factories and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), and next-generation experiments at super-b-factories and the LHC upgrade are expected to collect samples in the range of 100 billion events. Over the years, several high-performance theoretical calculations for these decay rates have been performed, using a variety of approaches. Of particular interest are QCD radiative corrections, which are known to modify the decay rates by approximately 20%–25% [1–3]. The current state of the art calculation is based on the conformal expansion of the QCD amplitude [4], combined with several modern techniques for the numerical evaluation of Feynman diagrams. In this paper we present a new theoretical calculation of the QCD corrections to the aforementioned decay rates, using the semi-analytic approach of brilliant unitarity [5], based on a model for the strong interaction amplitude with a limited number of adjustable parameters. In our implementation, the model enters as an Ansatz for the decay amplitude as a function of the mass scale μ, and parameter-free strong interaction unitary constraints at high energy scales are used to determine the model parameters. We apply this approach to the calculation of the exclusive charmless B decay amplitudes into two-body hadronic final states, with a $D$ or $D_s$ meson, at next-to-next-to-leading order in the strong interaction coupling constant α_s, and to all orders in the heavy quark expansion. We perform a matched calculation of the hard scattering functions, as well as of the corresponding soft functions, i.e., the propagator and vertex corrections. The remaining infrared singularities are isolated in the renormalization scale and are absorbed in the parameters of the model. The strong interaction kernel is obtained from the dispersive representation of the two-particle intermediate states, and the light degrees of freedom are integrated out in the spirit of hard scattering and heavy quark effective theory.

In this paper, we study the transition matrices between the 24 bases for a Leonard pair. It is shown that each Leonard pair has a 3-term recurrence relation whose coefficients depend only on the ranks of the pair. This allows us to completely describe the transition maps between the 24 bases, as well as their inverses. Leonard pairs were introduced by Leonard in 1965 [1]. Later work by Herschberger and Stitzel [2] classified all Leonard pairs up to order six. Leonard pairs are a generalisation of both symmetric and orthogonal matrices and they have numerous applications in various areas of mathematics and physics [3]. We use the framework of Lie theory to show that each Leonard pair has a 3-term recurrence relation whose coefficients depend only on the ranks of the pair. Recent advances in thin film fabrication technologies have led to a renewed interest in the study of magnetic thin films. This is due to the coexistence of ferromagnetic and strongly Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yoshida (RKKY) interacting layers in sub-micron scaled thin films, leading to novel magnetic ground states and complex phase diagrams. In this study, we present a magnetic characterization of Co/Pt multilayer thin films, synthesized using selective area epitaxy. Our x-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements on the remanent state show that a nanometer-sized uncompensated magnetic region persists at low temperatures. Our results are discussed in light of existing theoretical descriptions of thin film magnetic phase diagrams. hrs. The early-time light curves of supernovae (SNe) are important in determining their fundamental parameters and their host-galaxy environmental properties. The homogeneity of the light-curve shape of SNe Ia suggests that they result from the thermonuclear disruption of a carbon-oxygen (CO) white dwarf (WD) in most cases, although alternative scenarios, including the merger of two WDs, have been proposed. A newly discovered class of normal SNe Ia, named 2005hj, exhibits light-curve diversity that cannot be reconciled with a standard CO-WD scenario. Here we report a well-observed normal SN Ia, 2005hj, that has a relatively fast rise and decline in its optical light curve and a normal-looking light curve at later phases. The SN Ia is relatively more distant than the majority of normal SNe Ia and has a low $^{56}$Ni mass. We suggest that this may be evidence for a distinct class of normal SNe Ia, which can be explained by the merger of two WDs. This provides strong evidence that at least two distinct classes of SNe Ia exist, with distinct origins and cosmological applications.

A well-known problem in solar physics is the lack of a unifying model to explain the existence of prominences in the Sun's coronae. Observations indicate that prominences are formed by cool and dense plasma suspended in hot, tenuous solar coronal plasma. Moreover, these filaments are confined to within narrow magnetic field structures that often exhibit complex, non-potential magnetic configurations. Here we present magnetohydrostatic equilibrium models that naturally produce magnetic fields consistent with those observed around quiescent filaments, with the added bonus of supporting both cool, dense plasma and the hot coronal plasma in approximate magnetic equilibrium. Furthermore, the cool, dense plasma, supported by the magnetic field, experiences only very weak gravitational forces. Therefore, these structures may be able to survive atmospheric drag and can accumulate into long-lived features that could explain the existence of quiescent filaments, which have lifetimes that range from several days to many years. These structures are also naturally confined to within narrow, stable magnetic field structures.

Prompt emission of high energy photons has been suggested as a signature of multi-TeV particles in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). However, uncertainty remains about the efficiency and expected energy spectrum, due to limited understanding of the physical processes involved. We report observations of prompt emission high energy photons from two long-duration GRBs observed by the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. These observations constrain emission models and provide the first direct evidence for multi-TeV particles in these astrophysical jets. We report the observations of prompt emission high energy photons from two long-duration gamma-ray bursts, GRB 141028A and GRB 160821A, which were detected by the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. These observations provide important new constraints on emission models and directly prove the existence of multi-TeV particles in gamma-ray bursts for the first time. According to the standard picture of gamma-ray bursts, high-energy photons are produced by particles accelerated in a relativistic shock wave that forms at the surface of the expanding fireball as it sweeps up colder material from the surrounding space. The production of such high-energy photons via the synchrotron radiation process requires that electrons be accelerated to very high energies, and that the accelerated electrons radiate significantly before being subject toenergy losses. This process has been invoked to explain the observed high-energy spectral shape and the very high-energy emission detected in some cases by experiments such as ATHENA and ACTs, but particle acceleration in gamma-ray bursts has not been conclusively proven. The observations reported here provide the first direct evidence for the existence of multi-TeV particles in gamma-ray bursts, and allow us to tightly constrain emission models. We discuss a model in which electrons are first accelerated to TeV energies in internal shocks, and then up-scatter CMB photons to high energies via the inverse-Compton (IC) process. This model is constrained by the observations of the spectral shape, as well as by the fluence and energy spectrum of the observed high-energy photons. Our observations provide the first direct evidence for the existence of multi-TeV particles in gamma-ray bursts, and allow us to tightly constrain emission models. We discuss a model in which electrons are first accelerated to TeV energies in internal shocks, and then up-scatter CMB photons to high energies via the inverse-Compton (IC) process. This model is constrained by the observations of the spectral shape, as well as by the fluence and energy spectrum of the observed high-energy photons.

Resonant interaction of carrier spins in semiconductor quantum dots represents a powerful tool for implementing quantum information processing and quantum computing1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Indeed, robust long-lived carrier spin correlations and entanglement have been demonstrated in coupled quantum dot devices5,6,7,8,9. Entanglement is a critical requirement for solid state quantum computing10. Long-lived entanglement also provides a mechanism for performing quantum state read out with high efficiency11,12,13. Here, we implement and characterize two spin entanglement in a semiconductor quantum dot coupled to separate contacts. Spin-entanglement in this architecture arises from the resonant interaction between carrier spins in spatially separated quantum dots. Carrier spins in the two quantum dots interact through an inter-dot exchange interaction, leading to resonant ferromagnetic Heisenberg coupling. This coupling occurs even in the absence of long-range magnetic interactions such as super-exchange, as is the case for carriers in semiconductor quantum dots. Spin-resonance is observed in the regime of strong resonant coupling as a splitting of the single-dot spin resonance into two distinct energy states. The coherence time of the coupled quantum dot spin resonance is estimated to be > 1 ms, corresponding to a distance over which the spins can be spatially separated by > 200 nm, limited only by device dimensions14. We characterize the spin resonance with three non-collinear ferromagnetic quantum dots configured into a Hanbury Brown and Twiss geometry15. Measurement of the correlations between the emitted photons demonstrates the long-lived nature of the spin-entanglement. Entanglement is confirmed by a violation of an upper bound on the linear entropy, with observed values of linear entropy approaching 6.9 percent, corresponding to near-maximal entanglement16. These results demonstrate the robustness of the long-lived spin-entanglement arising from carrier-carrier exchange interactions in semiconductor quantum dots. The ability to generate and characterize entanglement between carriers in spatially separated quantum dots may be used to realize quantum communication and quantum computing protocols17,18,19,20,21,22.

Open clusters are groups of stars that form together from a single cloud of gas and dust. Over time, most open clusters dissolve due to gravitational interactions with the surrounding interstellar medium. However, some open clusters survive as remnant clusters after escaping from the surrounding parental cloud. Using data from the Gaia mission, we characterized the positions, radial velocities, and proper motions of 22,958 open cluster candidates. We then used a likelihood-based method to estimate the likelihood of a cluster's survival, and identified 2976 remnant clusters. We found that these remnant clusters have ages ranging from 0.01 to 13.26 Ga, and that they are distributed across most of the disk of the Milky Way. These remnant clusters provide a useful archive of star formation within the Milky Way, and can be used to study the formation and evolution of the Galaxy. This work was performed under the auspices of the observing program GNCS, funded by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

Stochastic processes are often described by their time evolution equations. In continuous time random walk (CTRW) approach the description is based on the assumption that the waiting times between consecutive jumps are characterized by an arbitrary probability density function (pdf) and the jumps themselves are independent and have a known probability distribution. The former property is referred to as non-Markovian and the latter as Markovian. The non-Markovian property of a process allows to describe the waiting time distribution alon g with the knowledge of a single parameter - the tail of the distribution. This is impossible in the Markovian case. As an example non-Markovianity can be observed in the memory effects typical for many systems with feedback or delayed interactions. In this contribution we propose a generalization of the CTRW approach to the case of non-Markovian stochastic process with arbitrary distributions of waiting times and jumps. An equation for the joint distribution of waiting times and a jump is derived. The obtained equation is the non-Markovian variant of the celebrated stochastic Liouville equation. The Markovian version of the obtained equation is also presented. This version generalizes the previously used continuous time random walk approach. The obtained equations are applied to the particular case of waiting time distribution with power-law decay and Fréchet distribution of jumps. The results are verified by simulation of the corresponding Markovian equations.

Cyclopentane and cyclohexane are widely used in laboratory testing and actual explosions as they have low vapor pressures and auto-ignite at relatively low pressures. In this study, we investigate the auto-ignition pressures of these two compounds in a shock tube. The results show that the autoignition pressures for these compounds are 25.3 kPa and 22.2 kPa for cyclohexane and cyclopentane, respectively. These results are compared with a recent global chemistry model (GCM) evaluated ignition pressures and demonstrate good agreement between the experimental autoignition pressures and the GCM model. The auto-ignition of cyclopentane and cyclohexane in a shock tube. Lambda and Lambda-bar hyperons were produced in quasireal photoproduction in the process \Ne+->n Lambda. The lambda polarization was measured for the first time. It was found to be substantially transverse: sin 2- theta = -0.47+/-0.26(stat)+/-0.13(syst), where theta is the angle between the lambda polarization direction and the incident photon direction in the cm frame. This measurement implies that the photon can be described by a mixture of vector and scalar couplings to the nucleon, in disagreement with helicity conservation. Further theoretical work is needed to fully understand this observation. Submitted to arXiv.org on May 10, 2020. Published on August 22, 2020. Revised on December 18, 2020. In this work, we revisit the expansion history of the universe using model independent methods, with the goal of testing whether the redshift-distance relation can be extended to higher redshifts. A general relation between the redshift and the distance for the recession of an object is given by, $$1+z = 1/a_r + 1/d_L,$$ where $a_r$ is the scale factor of the recession velocity and $d_L$ is the luminosity distance. The luminosity distance can be expressed in terms of the scale factor and the expansion history, $a(t)$, as, $$d_L(z) = (1+z) \int_0^z \frac{d z'}{H(z')}$$ where $H(z)$ is the Hubble parameter and $H(z=0)=H_{0}=100h$ km s-1 Mpc-1 is the current value of the Hubble parameter with h being its present day value. To test the validity of the relation at higher redshifts, we use the redshift data from quasars with z=2.3, 3 and 4 and the luminosity distance can be estimated from the angular divergence of the quasar light due to the transverse Doppler redshift. We calculate the transverse Doppler redshift as, $$1+z_T = \left(1+z_s\right) \left[\frac{\int_0^{z_s} \frac{d z'}{H(z')}}{\int_0^{z'} \frac{d z'}{H(z') }}\right],$$ where $z_s$ is the screen redshift at which the light emitted from the quasar is screen redshifted. Using the latest observational data for the angular divergence of the quasar light from the Planck 2017 results, we find that the transverse Doppler redshift at z=4.15 which is in excellent agreement with the quasar redshift of z=4.15. We also estimate the luminosity distance for z=4.15 and find, $d_L = 1044$ Mpc, which is in excellent agreement with the estimated luminosity distance of z=4.15 from the angular divergence of the quasar light i.e., $d_L = 1044$ Mpc. Thus we show that the redshift-distance relation can be extended to higher redshifts and the angular divergence of the quasar light can be a promising technique to measure the luminosity distance at higher redshifts.

This paper uses a multilevel statistical analysis to examine the role of behavioural and demographic factors in determining the size of firms. We find that differences in firm sizes among agents are significantly related to the behaviour, i.e. strategies, that these agents use in their interactions, but not to demographics factors such as gender, age or position. We also find that the same behavioural factors are significantly related to the size of groups of agents, but only to a smaller degree. These findings have significant implications for the understanding of why firms differ in size and provide a new perspective on the discussion of strategy and organizational behaviour. We study the Firm Size Effect (FSE), which is the observation that large firms tend to be larger than small ones of equal measures in an economic system. This size variation, commonly observed in the data, has provoked decades of debate about the causes. We analyse large data from Poland and show that the FSE is mostly explained by variation in behaviour. We partition the sample in groups of agents using hierarchical clustering based on similarity in their strategies. The analysis reveals that groups of similar agents with similar strategies account for most of the FSE. Within each strategy group, however, the FSE disappears. These findings have significant implications for the understanding of the FSE and provide a new perspective on the discussion of strategy and organizational behaviour.

Using data from the ELAIS N1 field observed with the Westerbork radio telescope, we have performed a search for compact polarized radio sources. The Stokes Q and U images at 6cm have been convolved with different beams (Gaussian and top-hat) and signal-to-noise (S/N) thresholds (5, 3 and 1). We have detected a total of 58 sources at 6cm with polarized intensity greater than 5.5μK. The number of sources detected as a function of beam and S/N is reported. Monte-Carlo simulations have been used to compute the significance of the detections. The entire ELAIS N1 field has been imaged in total intensity at 20cm and detection of the same sources at 20cm has been performed. We have cross-matched our 6cm sources with those detected at 20cm and computed the radio spectral index. Compact sources show a median spectral index of 0.8 and our observations are not sensitive to sources with a spectral index less than this value. We show that the sensitivity of our observations in the total intensity is sufficient to detect these steep spectrum sources, if they are smaller than about 4.5 kpc. Based on this, we present a new estimate of the total population of radio sources. This value is a factor of 2 smaller than that computed by 1.5 million sources in the ELAIS N1 field were detected at 20cm. We attribute this discrepancy to compact, steep spectrum sources being missed in our 6cm observations.

Radio astronomers, working in collaboration with the planetary scientists, have developed innovative new techniques to detect and characterize exoplanets. These techniques, which use very long baseline interferometry and radio astrometry, have the advantage of being extremely sensitive (can detect the tiny wobble of a small Earth-mass planet in a neighboring system), have high spatial resolution (can determine an orbiting body's distance from its host star to an accuracy of a few percent), and have very few systematics (are not subject to the same interpretive challenges as other techniques, such as radial velocity). In this paper, we describe these techniques and demonstrate their scientific promise by presenting an example of their recent success: the discovery of a planet with a 3-day period orbiting the star Gliese 864 in the so-called "habitable zone" of its star. We also describe the next steps in the development of these techniques: the realization of international networks of very long baseline interferometers, such as the EHT, and next-generation large radio telescopes, such as theaperture array. These developments will allow us to characterize the atmospheric composition and oceanography of potentially "Earth-like" planets around other stars, providing vital information on their potential to support life.

Smectic phases of hard rod--hard sphere mixtures are known to undergo a series of structural phase transitions as the composition of the mixture is varied. The sequence of these phase transitions has been mapped out for a wide range of mixture compositions using X-ray scattering and computer simulations. Here we present an analysis of the structure of the smectic-C* phase using small-angle neutron scattering. We find that in the limit of high dilution, the inter-rod separation in this phase exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on concentration, which we rationalize by considering the changes in effective pair interactions between neighboring rods induced by the presence of non-interacting solvent particles. We also examine a related phenomenon, “depletion attraction”, which occurs in semidilute concentrations due to enhanced attractive correlations between the central rod and the solvent particles. We show that this depletion interaction can be approximately modeled by considering a solvophobic hard core attractive interaction between the central rod and the solvent particles. Our results should provide useful insight into the structure of complex fluids composed of elongated particles and can be tested in liquid-state NMR spectroscopy of fluids with variable particle size.

The Serpens Molecular Cloud complex is located within the view of both the Spitzer Space Telescope and the Infrared Space Observatory (ISO). These two datasets allow us to trace the history of star formation in this cloud complex over a wide range of wavelengths. First, the infrared spectral energy distribution (SED) of each YSO candidate was fit with an outer hullien-layer dusty disk plus a nearly dust-free stellar photosphere. These fits are compared to simultaneously observed broadband magnitudes in order to identify likely young stellar objects (YSOs). The resulting Serpens YSO candidate list was then used as the input for a series of Monte Carlo simulations which generate a complete distribution of spectral types for Serpens YSOs. These simulations suggest that Serpens contains about 1,500 YSOs with visible disks, spread across at least six distinct age clusters. The global properties of these Serpens YSOs appear consistent with the previously characterized relation between disk frequency and age in which the Serpens stars exhibit the highest disk frequency of all known star-forming regions. In addition, the Serpens YSOs exhibit the full range of SED classifications, including those with little or no near-infrared excess (Class III objects), consistent with the picture that Serpens contains not only fully accrete objects, but also those in which significant circumstellar material has been removed by, for example, winds from the central stars.

Graphene, a one-atom-thick planar sheet of carbon, is a unique two-dimensional (2D) material with remarkable properties. One of its most interesting properties is its linear dispersion in the vicinity of the so-called Dirac points, which give rise to several exotic phenomena, such as unusual quantum Hall effects and high-speed transport. In this work, we develop a general elastic scattering theory for charge carriers in graphene, based on the corresponding Dirac equation. We consider both the intralayer and the interlayer cases. In particular, we derive formulas for scattering cross sections for arbitrary directions of incidence and for any value of the Fermi energy. Moreover, we discuss how to obtain the elastic scattering matrix from an arbitrary potential. In our treatment, we assume that the Fermi energy is not too large, so that the Born approximation is valid. With this formalism at hand, we explore the possibility of tailoring the transport properties of graphene through elastic scattering. Specifically, we explore the modifications that occur to the transmission probability when particular potentials are present, and we provide guidelines for the implementation of controllable scattering. As a result, we identify the regions of the wavevector-space plane where the transmission is almost unity or almost zero. We apply our general theory to study tunneling and localization phenomena. In this regard, we derive approximate analytical expressions for the localization length in the vicinity of the conduction and valence bands' Dirac points. With the help of our theory, it should now be possible to tailor the transmission properties of graphene through elastic scattering. Such tailoring may find applications in the fields of nanophotonics, sensor technology, and nanoelectronics.
