The dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) are believed to be the most dark matter dominated objects in the universe. Their nature is still a matter of debate. Many of them are kinematically consistent with old population of stars but some of them exhibits evidence for recent star formation. The presence of significant populations of young stars in these galaxies has been debated. In this work, we present observations of 19 blue plumes in 16 dSphs. We find that 14 plumes are consistent with simple stellar population models with age less than 7-8 Gyr. The spectra of remaining five plumes can be fitted with combination of simple stellar population models with ages between 0.7-1.1 Gyr and 5-7 Gyr. We argue that the origin of the five blue plumes with intermediate age might be attributed to the blue straggler evolution and the star formation in these galaxies might not be recent as previously thought.

Here we explore phenomenological consequences of embedding the standard model into a relativistic, gravitationally warped space-time. In particular, we explore bulk properties of the standard model fields and their phenomenological signatures in current and future low-energy experiments. We find that the observed pattern of SM particle masses and mixings can be generated in a relatively low energy theory consisting of the standard model fields propagating in a warped space. We focus on two specific models: one which realizes AdS center symmetry breaking, and one which realizes AdS/Conformal symmetry breaking. The resulting models have similar low-energy behavior with the same properties summarized in a “textbook” holographic Randall-Sundrum model, however with a novel mechanism for SM fermion mass generation. We discuss experimental signatures of this framework, and identify collider, atomic, andGravitational wave signatures. Among the signatures which can be explored are tiny but measurable Planck-scale suppressed effects, such as interaction eigenstates becoming mass eigenstates at low energy; processes which are induced by Planck-suppressed operators at tree-level, such as semileptonic meson decays, $K_L \rightarrow \pi^0 e \bar{\nu}$, $\pi \rightarrow \mu e$, and $h \rightarrow \mu e$, as well as atomic spin-flip transitions such as $X^0 e \rightarrow \mu$, where $X^0$ is the spin-0 component of the RS graviton. In addition to collider signatures, such as anomalous increases in cross-section at small invariant masses in vector boson fusion processes, the Gravitational Wave signal from black hole and collider events will likely provide the cleanest signatures. In addition, we propose the possibility of detection via the atomic spin-flip transitions, both by augmenting current experiments to lower sensitivity levels, and by proposing a new experiment with a caesium clock an order of magnitude more sensitive than current commercially available clocks. It should be emphasized that there is a high degree of model dependence in these signatures, and alternative models with very different low-energy behavior may give similar signals. However, should any of these signals be observed, the realization that our standard model is embedded in a relativistic, gravitationally warped space-time would be of great significance.

The velocity structure of the solar corona is of great importance for understanding the processes taking place within this dynamic environment. Since coronal emission is often faint and broadened due to the high speeds of the material, it is difficult to observe the full velocity profile of the solar wind. Therefore, numerous studies have analyzed either the line-wing or the line-center of coronal emission lines to determine the properties of the plasma. In this study, we combine data from the EUV spectrograph (ESA/SOHO) with data from the EUV imager (SECCHI/SIBYNTES) and the HIA/SDO to determine velocity profiles for an extensive range of coronal emission lines. We find that the coronal plasma is moving at supersonic speeds, ranging from 900 km/s to over 1,000 km/s, with strong scatter in the speeds observed along a single coronal loop. By analyzing this scatter, we determine that Alfvén waves are likely propagating along the loop.

Particle physics is an exciting field of science, with the discovery of the Higgs Boson completing the foundational work necessary for us to complete our understanding of the universe. The open access publishing model, in which the author pays a publication fee rather than reads fees, is resulting in a large increase in the amount of research being published. This increase in publishing has the potential to drastically increase our collective understanding of the universe, however it can be difficult for researchers not involved in the field to understand these papers and the datasets they reference. In this paper we provide a brief introduction to the open access publishing model for the non-expert, with an eye towards highlighting some of the more interesting articles published in this emerging field of research. We hope this will act as an introductory resource for people interested in this emerging area of research and encourage research into more in-depth articles about specific fields within particle physics.

In this paper, we develop a detailed quantum electrodynamical (QED) description of interactions between realistic superconducting qubits and microwave radiation. We derive an effective low-energy Hamiltonian that includes the Jaynes-Cummings, Tavis-Cummings, and dipole couplings. Numerical simulations of quantum Rabi, Dicke, and Landau-Zener models are performed to illustrate the QED regime. This low-energy QED description facilitates a controlled analysis of qubit-microwave coupling strengths and microwave frequency offsets relative to the qubit levels. The predicted dispersive decay and dephasing rates are consistent with recent experiments. Introduction Realistic superconducting qubits like the transmon are an excellent platform for studying quantum many-body phenomena in nature. In particular, their highly tunable nature allows for an exquisite control of both system- and bath- dephasing processes. This exquisite control, however, has become an asset that now poses a challenge for sufficiently understanding and describing the underlying physical mechanisms. In this paper, we develop a detailed quantum electrodynamical (QED) description of interactions between realistic superconducting qubits and microwave radiation. The derivation is based on a high-fidelity derivation of the dispersive Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian in [1]. Unlike other derivations in the literature, our starting point is a fully calibrated transmon model, that is, a model with the complete experimental control settings encoded. By calibrating this model, we account for parasitic modes, an important consideration given the extreme small size of superconducting qubits. A crucial result of this derivation is an effective low-energy Hamiltonian that includes the Jaynes-Cummings, Tavis-Cummings, and dipole couplings. Using degenerate perturbation theory, we obtain analytical expressions for qubit-microwave coupling strengths and microwave frequency offsets relative to the qubit levels. These analytical expressions facilitate a systematic understanding and controlled analysis of qubit-microwave interactions for any given experimental system setup. The low-energy QED description enables a quantitative comparison with experiment and an assessment of control errors and residual non-QED interactions. Computing the exact dynamics of the full system would be intractable given the current level of complexity, but we can perform a numerical simulation of the low-energy QED Hamiltonian. Our results are in excellent agreement with both the measured resonant decay rates and the anlytical expression derived in the paper. In addition, our simulations explain the emergence of avoided level crossings in the system. This explanation, which is not accounted for in the QED model, is a non-Markovian dressing of the qubit levels by the non-perturbative bath induced by spontaneous emission. We finish this paper with a summary of the most important findings and a discussion of the potential use of this approach to describe qubit-microwave interactions in more complex settings. This paper presents a fast algorithm for recursive filtering of nonlinear dynamic systems. The resulting filter, which we call the fast recursive filter (FRF), uses the extended H∞ filter design approach to recursively compute estimates of the system states, based on a set of error dynamics induced from the error system representation of the original nonlinear dynamic system. Unlike other FRF implementations, the proposed FRF algorithm allows recursive estimation of the high-gain errors without requiring recursive computation of all first-order terms. In addition, the FRF algorithm admits a more straightforward treatment of multiplicative noise terms than existing FRF implementations. Consequently, the FRF implementation developed in this paper is expected to have an improved overall performance, in particular, for estimation of systems with high-frequency states, high-gain dynamics, or with a large noise magnitude. To illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed FRF design, a few numerical examples, including Van der Pol oscillator, Rössler system, and a nonlinear circuit example, are provided to illustrate the efficiency and advantages of the proposed FRF design approach.

The Millennium Galaxy Catalogue (MGC) is a statistically complete sample of galaxies in the redshift range 0.05 < z < 0.15 selected from the deep contiguous region observed by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The survey region contains much additional ancillary data, which we have exploited to study the cosmic evolution of dust and stellar mass. We derive accurate B-band attenuation measurements for a volume-limited subset of the MGC, which we show exhibits little luminosity- or distance-dependence. The implied dust and stellar mass densities are found to increase with cosmic time, with star-formation surface densities roughly constant with redshift. We show that, if spheroidal galaxies can be characterised as a single component with an effective radius and central surface brightness correlated with luminosity, the stellar mass density in spheroids can be estimated with a precision of ~20%: at z ≲ 0.4 this is comparable with the contribution from quasars; at higher redshifts the cosmic spheroidal stellar mass density is comparable with that of red galaxies and the photometrically-derived redshift distribution of distant quasars. If all galaxies are included (as in the main MGC), the total cosmic stellar mass density at z ≲ 1 is comparable with that of local red galaxies. The optical and near-infrared spectra of a large sub-sample of the MGC galaxies are examined for the signatures of dust attenuation and emission lines, but in neither case is there a strong correlation with B-band attenuation. Our conclusion is that the majority of B-band attenuation in local galaxies is due to scattering rather than starlight being emitted at other wavelengths. We show that our results for dust and stellar mass densities imply that significant dust absorption and scattering must occur within kpc-scale regions, and conclude that dust is closely associated with star-formation within most galaxies.

The interaction between particles in a fluid is typically separated into long- and short-ranged contributions. The long-range interaction is typically modeled with a simple pair potential, while the short-range interactions are modeled with a series of pair-distribution functions. At thermal equilibrium, the total interaction may be simplified to a screened Coulomb potential. The system may be formally separated into one containing only the long-range interactions, a system of particles with periodic boundary conditions, and a system of particles with vanishing velocity. The former may be solved exactly, while the latter two may be solved numerically. In this work, the three-dimensional Ising model is used as a test case for this approach. Using a novel technique to systematically eliminate short-range interactions, it is shown that short-range attractions can reduce the thermal conductivity of the fluid by up to four orders of magnitude without changing the critical temperature. It is further shown that this reduction in thermal conductivity results in a divergent self-diffusivity and vanishing viscosity, while the structural order remains finite. These results provide further insight into the role of short-range forces in the heat transport of fluids.

Electronic spin transport and spin precession at room temperature in single graphene layers is studied. We present experimental demonstration of electrical detection of spin transport in single graphene layers and measurement of magnetic moment precession in single graphene Levy flights. The obtained spin transport and precession frequencies are equal to 500 MHz and 40 GHz, respectively. The experiments were performed at room temperature, which is of great importance for further application of the results in graphene based spintronics. ingham Spin transport and spin precession in single graphene layers at room temperature were studied. Spin transport was observed using electrical means, and spin precession was observed using magnetic means. The obtained spin transport and precession frequencies are equal to 500 MHz and 40 GHz, respectively. The experiments were performed at room temperature, which is of great importance for further application of the results in graphene based spintronics. Graphene, a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice of carbon atoms, with its special properties has opened a broad field of application for its applications in the electronics industry1,2. Graphene can also function as a spin carrying medium3-5. The electron spin precesses around the direction of the magnetic moment of the nucleus under the influence of a magnetic field. If the magnetic field has a time dependent component, the electron spin will also precess around the direction of the effective magnetic field. Thus, a change in the spin precession frequency is indicative of a change in the effective magnetic field6-8. The magnitude of the nuclear magnetic moment is on the order of magnitude of the electron magnetic moment9. The nucleus behaves as a small magnetic moment coupled to a large number of electrons. This forms the basis of the electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy10, which has previously been used to characterize the effective magnetic field in graphene3,4. In this work, we present experimental evidence of electrical detection of spin transport in single graphene layers and measurement of the magnetic moment precession in single graphene Levy flights. The obtained spin transport and precession frequencies are equal to 500 MHz and 40 GHz, respectively.

Internal states of model isotropic granular packings. I. Assembling process, geometry and contact networks. The assembly process of granular materials is of considerable scientific and technological interest. Contrary to atomic and molecular systems, the assembly of granular particles is an open system: the rearrangement of particles may change the geometrical arrangement and, consequently, the internal state of the packing. In this work, we study how this rearrangement affects the geometrical and topological properties of the contact network, which is the unique way to describe the internal connectivity of a packing. We carry out numerical simulations of jamming processes with the Omodei law, which successfully captures the structure of the contact network during the evolution of a packing toward stability [1, 2]. To analyse the rearrangement mechanisms, we characterise the internal state of a packing by a small number of global variables. We focus our analysis on two packing properties: the mean angle between neighbours and the radial distribution function. Finally, we introduce a metric to quantify the topological changes produced by rearrangements and we characterise different rearrangement mechanisms.

We present a model for QCD at high density and large quark mass which may explain the quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) phase diagram. The model is built around an infinite dimensional Polyakov gauge theory that reduces to N coincident 1+1 dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills theories at high temperature, to N coincident 1+1 dimensional U(1) gauge theories at low temperature, and to three spatial dimensions at infinite temperature. The parameters in the model are the temperature T, the quark chemical potential mu, and the temporal extent of the 1+1 dimensional theory L(T). We obtain three phases as T is decreased: a high density deconfined phase at low mu and high T, a confined low density phase at high mu and low T, and a crossover phase in between. The confined phase at high mu is expected to have a dual description in terms of a superconductor at low temperature. The model provides a plausible scenario for the continuous crossover between these phases as T is decreased.

We present the results of a search for angular correlations in the large-scale structure (LSS) of the Cosmos 2018 data set. The data were mapped to a common redshift of 0.545 using a matched filter algorithm applied to galaxy pair counts. We find a high significance detection of the two-point angular correlation function (ACF), in the range of scales 30<sigma<250, corresponding to a 2-8 h$^{-1}$Mpc separation at z=0.545. Assuming a simple model for the two-point redshift space distribution (RSD) of galaxies we extract a robust estimate of the mean pairwise galaxy velocity of v=562$(\pm194)$ km s$^{-1}$ at this redshift. This RSD measurement is dependent on the assumed shape of the redshift space correlation function and by itself does not provide a velocity dispersion measurement. We present a method based on a moving ACF analysis to simultaneously measure the RSD and velocity dispersion. Assuming a model for the shape of the correlation function as a function of separation and peculiar velocity dispersion, we extract a robust estimate for the velocity dispersion of v=725$(\pm314)$ km s$^{-1}$. We conclude by discussing our findings in the context of ΛCDM cosmology, and compare our measurement to recent RSD measurements from the VIPERS and BOSS spectrosocpy redshift surveys.

In this paper we introduce an algebraic definition of charge liquids. These theories exhibit confinement, but instead of quarks and gluons, they are composed of flux tubes containing an appropriate algebra representation. This representation may be chosen to possess a non-abelian global symmetry, and these flux tubes naturally behave like magnetic insulators or superconductors, depending on the chosen symmetry. We present several examples of this phenomenon, and also discuss some open questions for future research. Ultracold atoms in random potentials are studied experimentally and numerically. In particular, an ensemble of coherent Bloch waves with random initial phases is prepared in a three-dimensional optical lattice with Gaussian disorder. The resulting statistical properties of the wavefunction are investigated for different strengths of the disorder and of the Bose-Einstein condensation. It is shown that, in the limit of strong disorder, the wavefunction has a Gaussian shape with exponentially small tail. For the case of weak condensation, the distributions of the localisation lengths and of the populations of the coherent states are calculated. For the case of strong condensation, the ground state of the system is identified and the localisation length is calculated. In ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices, both experiments and theory have demonstrated that the so-called Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) can be achieved for various combinations of different hyperfine states, atomic hadrons, and scattering lengths. The condensates are typically in the regime of weak interactions, and are thus well-described by the mean-field approximation. In this framework, disorder, either due to a random potential or imprinted in the system, is represented by an additive term to the mean-field Gross-Pitaevskii equation. In such systems, it has been established that, depending on the strength of the disorder and of the mean-field interaction, one observes either localization (under strong disorder) or delocalization (under weak disorder). The new experiment performed here crosses this regime by realizing condensates in a three-dimensional random potential with an additional Gaussian modulation in the lattice geometry. We find that, in this case, the wavefunction has a Gaussian shape with an exponentially small tail for strong disorder. For the case of weak Bose-Einstein condensation, the distributions of localisation lengths and populations of coherent states are calculated. For the case of strong condensation, the localisation length is calculated. The paper is intended to be of interest to a wide readership both in condensed matter physics and in atomic, molecular, and optical physics.

We present the results of a blind tomography analysis of the low-redshift Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) supernova survey using a model based on the spherical overdensity approach to determine structure in the universe. We combine supernova data from five years of the survey with measurements of the large-scale structure derived from over one billion galaxies in the northern celestial hemisphere in the photometric Data Release 9 of the SDSS. This allows us to measure the three-dimensional distribution of stars and dark matter in a region of the universe of approximately 93 million light-years on a side. We measure the bias between these components in the region of overlap, finding values of b$_{\mathrm{gal}}$ = 1.65 $\pm$ 0.06 and b$_{\mathrm{SN}}$ = 1.54 $\pm$ 0.10 at a effective mean scale redshift of z = 0.35. The measurements are consistent with the expected evolution of the bias with scale at these redshifts, with measurements of b$_{\mathrm{gal}}$ and b$_{\mathrm{SN}}$ differing by 7% at z = 0.3 and 9% at z = 0.55. Given the dependence of the bias on the mean matter density of the universe, our results provide additional evidence for the expected evolution of the universe toward lower density at high redshift.

Recent observations of the Sun's open magnetic field show that it is not simple. It is composed of many small-scale flux tubes which are dynamic and evolve with time. The evolution of individual flux tubes is complex and depends on the interaction with neighboring tubes as well as the local ambient magnetic field. There is a range of scales at which the magnetic field is structured and the energy is located. The size of the structuring scales increases with decreasing distance from the solar surface. The magnetic energy is gradually transported towards the solar surface with the lifetime of the flux tubes. The size of structuring scale increases with height. At the bottom of the flux tube, it is of the order of the size of the tube itself, i.e. of the order of tens of kilometers. Above the solar surface the structuring scale is of the order of hundreds of kilometers. It is likely that there is a range of scales between these two extremes where the magnetic field is not entirely structualized. Magnetic flux transport dynamo, originally proposed by Parker, provides a means of generating the poloidal (winding) component of the Sun's magnetic field. It is commonly believed that the generated poloidal field is stored in the stable layers of the solar convection zone. The recent results of direct measurements of the surface magnetic field intensity support this picture. They show that the stored field has a magnitude of approximately 1 kG and a substantial poloidal component. It is most probable that the evolution of the observed structure of the solar open magnetic field is controlled by the competition between the generation, transport, storage, and loss of the magnetic flux. Recently, solar physicists have started to focus on the magnetic field organization on small spatial and temporal scales. Observations of the magnetic field at these scales are crucial to developing models of the large-scale organization of the Sun's magnetic field. Recent high-resolution observations from the SDO and HMI instruments have opened new possibilities for probing the solar magnetic field on small scales. We have developed an algorithm for identifying the structures in the observed magnetic field, based on the method of False Color {# False Color uses different colors to encode the value of a parameter. In this case, the value of the signal in a given pixel is encoded as a different color. We apply a statistical test that assumes the parameter has a specific probability distribution function and assigns a color to each pixel based on where that probability density function peaks. The result is a map of the probability density function. The technique can be used to reveal fine-scale structures in data with relatively few data points. We use this algorithm to identify the small-scale magnetic structures in the observed field. The observed field consists of many separate magnetic elements of various sizes and shapes, and these structures can interact with each other. For example, two adjacent structures may connect via a hinge, where the magnetic field direction changes, allowing information to be exchanged between the structures. We find

A long-standing discrepancy between renormalization group (RG) running of chiral operators and corresponding counting rules has been healed in a recent work [1]. It was shown there that a certain class of chiral pion production operators satisfies the consistency condition with the RG running in the deep Euclidean regime. In this work we verify that the consistency indeed holds at the level of the operator product expansion (OPE). We also study a similar case of the axial-vector-vector (AV) operator and find a similar agreement for the anomalous dimensions of certain diagrams. We would like to stress that, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first case in which the consistency between the RG running and the corresponding counting rule has been shown at the OPE level for operators with Dirac structure and for more than two flavors. [1] D. Bečvář, E. Jeleńska, G. P. Korchemsky, and J. Noltés, “Renormalization Group Consistency of Chiral Pion Production Operators,” arXiv:1905.00199 [hep-ph], May 2019. Link to the paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00199

In this paper, we consider the problem of blindly identifying a set of distributed antenna systems (DAS) from wireless channel measurements without requiring prior CSI or a database of DAS models. Unlike previous work, we characterize the measurement noise as aWN0 with unknown aweAte-1 covariance and propose a regularized non-convex cost function to solve for the DAS model. The aWN0 approximation is valid provided that the channel variations are slow compared to the inverse of the channel sample rate. Furthermore, we use the KKT conditions to derived a computationally efficient solution method. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method through Monte-Carlo simulations. Our work differs from prior work on DAS identification in the following ways: (1) we characterize the measurement noise as aWN0 with uncertain covariance, and (2) we propose a regularized non-convex cost function to solve for the DAS model. The aWN0 approximation is valid provided that the channel variations are slow compared to the inverse of the channel sample rate. Furthermore, we use the KKT conditions to derived a computationally efficient solution method. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method through Monte-Carlo simulations. References: 1. A new search for planet transits in NGC 6791 has been presented. The project is utilizing a wide-field telescope with an innovative system of small, simple cameras, which enables high-precision measurement of slight stellar brightness changes induced by planets. Based on the data from a sample of 21 NGC 6791 stars, no planets with sizes similar to that of Earth were found. The new constraints on the existence of superearth and subear planets, as well as the upper limit for the size of exoplanets, were obtained. This work was made possible due to the adoption of a novel system of cameras with a special Optical Low Light Shot Array (OLSSLCA), used for high-precision measurement of the slight stellar brightness changes induced by planets. As a result of the project, the upper limit for the sizes of exoplanets was increased. The project is currently monitoring 21 brightest stars in the NGC 6791 globular cluster using a wide-field telescope at the South African Astronomical Observatory. The analysis of the first year of data suggests that the existence of superearth and subearth planets with sizes similar to that of Earth in the cluster's environment is unlikely. The upper limit for the sizes of exoplanets was also increased.

Interior Point decoding, originally proposed for LP decoding, has recently been shown to achieve significant performance advantages in multiple wireless network settings, including massive MIMO and millimeter wave communications. This paper presents a unified framework for Interior Point (IP) decoding of linear vector channels (LVC). We first present a general theory for IP decoding of LVC, and establish a theoretical performance lower bound for the general LVC setting. We then specialize our results to a few important LVC examples, including Gaussian LVC, multi-user MIMO systems with orthogonal or non-orthogonal pilots, and physical-layer security (PLS) protocols. Through comprehensive numerical studies, we demonstrate that IP decoding provides significant performance advantages over existing methods in all considered settings. More specifically, this work makes the following novel contributions: 1) Establish a general theory for IP decoding of linear vector channels. 2) Establish a theoretical performance lower bound for the general LVC setting. 3) Specialize our results to a few important LVC examples. Through comprehensive numerical studies, we demonstrate that IP decoding provides significant performance advantages over existing methods in all considered settings. We believe this is the first paper to provide a general theory for IP decoding of linear vector channels. This is an important milestone on the path to generalizing interior point algorithms to more complex optimization problems.

This paper presents a novel algorithm for multiple pattern matching, that is widely used in string matching, database indexing, and computer vision. It can be used to index both digital sequences (e.g. digital pictures) and structured collections of items (e.g. sets of word occurrences in text documents). Our approach can solve several matching queries using the same database search cost, in contrast to existing methods which have quadratic or worse search cost with respect to the number of pattern matches. We achieve this efficiency by using the recently proposed Markov chain techniques, and apply it to a fast hashing scheme for strings. Our experimental evaluation using the public data sets shows that our method is very effective for matching patterns with limited (or no) semantic information. Our method works as follows. Let string S be the text of interest and s a pattern. Given a database D of strings, our goal is to find all occurrences of s in S. Typically, D is huge, so we want to be selective in our matching and only report a few representative occurrences. Our method first maps each pattern character to a large alphabet, using an efficient hashing scheme. Then, for each database string, we build a string of "markov chains" over the pattern alphabet, one chain for each pattern character. The chain of length i contains the i most probable next states of the Markov chain corresponding to the database string. We define the string matching score as the sum of these chains, where the contribution of each character is its transition probability to the current state. Given this score, we can find all occurrences of s in S by a standard efficient string matching procedure, and map each occurrence to the ID of its matching pattern in D. To our knowledge, this is the first work to design a matching algorithm using Markov chain techniques, and our experimental evaluation using public data shows that our method outperforms existing ones. In this paper, we present exact solutions of semiclassical non-characteristic Cauchy problems for the sine-Gordon equation. Using the optimal ordering, we obtain the exact solutions in the form of Jacobi elliptic functions. The obtained exact solutions describe a wide variety of wave phenomena, including periodic waves, lump solitons, breather waves, and anti-train waves. Numerical simulations are carried out to support the validity of the analytical results. president Exact solutions of semiclassical non-characteristic Cauchy problems for the sine-Gordon equation In this paper, we present exact solutions of semiclassical non-characteristic Cauchy problems for the sine-Gordon equation. Longitudinal studies are prevalent in medical and social research, often with a mixture of observed and unobserved outcomes. For settings with potentially unobserved outcomes, marginal structural models (MSMs) have been widely used for confounder control and causal inference. In this article, we consider a novel setup with repeated measures on the observed outcomes, and the goal is to analyze the impact of time-varying treatments, where the treatment histories are available up to a certain horizon. This setting arises in clinical trials with intermittent treatments or observational studies with pseudo-randomized treatments, and it is more complicated than the typical case with a single treatment time point. We propose to estimate the so-called history-restricted MSMs, in which the treatment intensity processes are incorporated as predictors and some assumptions are imposed on their trajectories. We establish the strong convergence of the predicted values, and establish the convergence rate and optimality of the corresponding Full Bayes estimator. We demonstrate the superior empirical performance of the Full Bayes estimator over alternative threshold estimators through both simulation studies and an analysis of a mental health intervention study.

The multilayer samples with the approximate composition U0.2Fe0.8 acquired after mild annealing of the as-deposited samples with composition U0.2Fe0.8+x exhibit a ferromagnetic behavior at low temperatures. The Curie temperature Tc is strongly dependent on the annealing parameters. For x = 0.02 the ferromagnetic transition temperature is achieved at temperatures above room temperature, which is an advantage for practical applications. The variation of Tc with x indicates that the observed ferromagnetism is induced by the Fe layer. The effects of post-deposition heat treatments on the magnetic properties of U0.2Fe0.8+x are also investigated. Samples with x = 0.04 show a weak ferromagnetic behavior at low temperatures. The weak ferromagnetism is probably related to the clustering of U5+ ions into small clusters. The saturation magnetization is strongly reduced in comparison with the as-deposited samples. The samples with x = 0.08 exhibit a paramagnetic behavior at low temperatures. This result indicates that strong enrichment of U5+ leads to a magnetic null composition.

The standard model (SM) based on the gauge group SU(3) x SU(2) x U(1) remains an excellent framework for describing particle interactions due to its extraordinary success in describing experimental data over decades. However, it is widely believed that the SM is only an effective field theory and thus may be embedded within a larger fundamental theory. One such larger, grand unified theory (GUT) is SUSY, based on the gauge group SU(5) x (d)T, where d is a dim of compactification. Such a framework gives an elegant solution to the doublet-triplet splitting problem, while simultaneously yielding a successful model of flavor. The minimal SU(5) x (d)T model contains several tachyons in the Higgs sector, the Majorana mass terms for the light neutrinos, and a viable explanation for the origin of matter in the universe. However, recent studies have shown that these problems can all be solved by adding a discrete symmetry, called R symmetry, to the particle content. In this paper, we present the low-energy spectrum of this R-symmetric SU(5) x (d)T model, containing a complete GUT breaking Higgs sector and three viable cases for the MNS matrices of the Standard Model fermions. We use the bases of the dim(d) x dim(d) matrices that diagonalize the corresponding d x dmatrices in the 24 representation of SU(5) to construct these matrices. We call these bases the CKM and Tri-bimaximal (TBM) matrices, respectively. These MNS matrices give a successful explanation for the hierarchies of quark and lepton masses and mixings. We also present the corresponding charge assignment under the SU(5) symmetry, thereby providing a grand unified theoretical context for the model. Link to preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.08527

Recent discoveries of unexpected plasma components in the interstellar medium (ISM) – missing baryons – have profound implications for our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution. The baryon-to-total mass (baryon fraction) ratio in galaxies is a fundamental statistic that conveys key information about the efficiency of galaxy formation and the timing of different mass assembly processes. Measurement of this ratio at low redshift is challenging due to the extreme faintness of ISM components, particularly in low mass galaxies, where the majority of the baryons are thought to reside. Analysis of direct observations has historically relied on indirect methods that infer the amount of ISM in galaxies from extrapolating the motions of its observed components. These methods introduce significant systematic uncertainty given the level of complexity in galaxy dynamics, and failure to properly account for hidden components such as ordered rotation can result in significant overestimation of the mass of the ISM. Here we present a new observational approach based on 21 cm absorption against distant radio quasars. We combine a sensitive GMRT survey of the sky at 150 MHz with high resolution observations of the TXS2342+7501 system with the SKA1 Allen Sky pathfinder (ASF) telescope. Using absorption against TXS2342+7501 we detect signatures from 11 different species (C, O, N, Mg, Si, S, Ca, Ti, Al, and Fe) with high signal-to-noise ratios (S/N). By combining these observations with archival and new GMRT, Arecibo, and WSRT observations of TXS2342+7501, we measure neutral hydrogen absorption down to a sensitivity of 40 mJy beam$^{-1}$ per 50 km s$^{-1}$ channel. In conjunction with state-of-the-art cosmological simulations, this allows us to measure the ISM baryon mass in galaxies down to a stellar mass of 10$^{10}$ M$_{\odot}$ at impact parameters of 30 kpc. We discuss the general applicability of this approach, which we term weak lensing via absorption, and conclude that it will revolutionize our ability to measure the baryon content of galaxies in the near future.

Conservation laws are the backbone of modern physics. In particular, the principle of conservation of energy is crucial for explaining most of the phenomena in our daily lives, from the movements of celestial bodies to the interactions between particles. In the last few decades, a powerful approach to deriving conservation laws from first principles has emerged, namely, the method of Lagrangian mechanics. In Lagrangian mechanics, the evolution of a physical system is described in terms of the positions and velocities of its particles, from which one can derive the corresponding differential equations, often known as the Euler-Lagrange equations. The solution to these equations is called an extremal, and their locus in phase space is called a critical point. The necessary conditions for a critical point to be an extremal are called the Euler-Lagrange equations. The corresponding statement in the relativistic domain is known as the principle of relativity. Lagrangian mechanics has been extremely successful, but it has some notable limitations. For example, many systems of interest do not have a Hamiltonian description, for reasons including the need to explicitly consider particle positions and velocities. Thus far, there is no general method to obtain Hamiltonian dynamics from a given Lagrangian. Also, the notion of a momentum (which serves to identify a phase space point) typically only arises in special cases. Even in the presence of symmetries, the Lagrangian is rarely known a priori and often must be determined by solving an equation. Finally, conservation laws should be independent of the choice of coordinate system, but in most Lagrangian mechanics formulations, this is not the case. These limitations have encouraged the development of a new variational method known as Lagrangian field theory. This approach was initially proposed by Victor Andreevich Volodin in the late 19th century; the first systematic treatment was given by Vladimir Igorovich Éleshev and Dmitrii Aleksandrovich Mikhailov in the 1960s. Lagrangian field theory is formally similar to Lagrangian mechanics, but the evolution is described in terms of “fields” (functions of space and time) rather than “particles.” Fields need not have an assigned location; the Euler-Lagrange equations describe the evolution of field gradients. As a result, field theory provides a framework for obtaining both Hamiltonian and relativistic dynamics from a given Lagrangian. Despite these successes, Lagrangian field theory has not gained the same level of popularity as Lagrangian mechanics. One likely reason is the apparent lack of intuitive appeal of this abstract, formal approach. Lagrangian mechanics is an engineering or geometric approach, focusing on the physical laws as implemented in equations of motion; Lagrangian field theory is more of a mathematical approach, focusing on the structure of the governing equations. Another likely reason is that Lagrangian field theory has been largely restricted to applications to classical mechanics and field theory. Over recent years, this restriction has been relaxed and the approach has been applied to relativistic field theories, fluid dynamics, the calculus of variations, and even to computer vision and reinforcement learning. SDSS J080531.84+481233.0 (J0805+4812) is a wide (~14") binary system comprised of an L0 dwarf and a T dwarf of similar temperature, which is of particular interest as it is the lowest-mass, bound binary system of its kind discovered to date. Such systems are of extreme interest for studies of low-mass stellar and sub-stellar atmospheres, as well as for constraining models of binary evolution. We present new spectroscopic and photometric observations of the system, as well as archival data for which we have performed a detailed analysis for the first time. We find that the projected separation of the two components is 14.0+/-0.2" as measured from the peak of their relative brightness, and we measure a velocity semi-amplitude of 285.0+/-3.0 m s-1 for the primary star, indicating that the system is likely dynamically unstable. We calculate a minimum companion mass of 22.7+/-0.3 M Jup for the system. We also measure updated astrometry for the system and derive a preliminary orbit, which indicates that the component separation is growing at a rate of 3.2+/-0.2" yr-1. Despite the expected instability of the system, we argue that interactions with distant perturbers are the more likely explanation for this apparent proximity increasing. We estimate the minimum orbital separation at which the components are likely destroyed by close approaches with higher-order multiple system members, and find that J0805+4812 may be constrained to be separated by >27.1+/-0.4" at the present time.

Wetting and drying are ubiquitous phenomena in nature. Despite intense studies, understanding of their complex dynamics remains a great challenge. In this Letter, we study the local order parameter of a second-order wetting transition with quenched disorder. We find that the spatial probability distribution of this parameter exhibits multifractal properties characterized by a unique singularity spectrum, in agreement with the prediction of the dynamic scaling theory. The singularity spectrum is fully determined by the distance from the critical point and the disorder strength, without the assumption of hyperscaling. The full scaling functions are computed via a transfer matrix method, and shown to be in good agreement with our numerical data. This Letter provides a general framework to study the multifractal properties of local order parameters and may stimulate further applications to other correlated systems. Galaxies are distributed into two main classes, called E and S0 galaxies. E galaxies have pronounced discs with rotational support, whereas S0 galaxies haveelow or no optical rotation and are often considered to be eitherEarly-Type (ET) or lenticular galaxies (S0a). The two main differ-ences between these classes are the lack of spiral structure and presence of a bar in S0 galaxies.The simplest way to classify a galaxy is by its morphology. However, galaxy morphology is only a rough indicator of the galaxy's past history and current state.E galaxies are often thought to be evolutionarily older than S0 galaxies, with theE galaxies forming their morphology over longer time periods via internalevolution. The most widely accepted formation scenario for E galaxies invarious interactions, typically with smaller galaxies. In this scenario, thegalaxy's interstellar medium (ISM) gets shock heated and heats up the galacticdisc, causing it to rotationally support. However, the ISM only becomesvisible when two thirds of the disc's angular momentum is consumed, meaning thatearlier on the galaxy had a presumably more spiky structure. Moreover, thereasonable formation path for S0 galaxies is via major mergers of galaxies,which is also witnessed in cosmological simulations of galaxy formation. Mergers cause the ISM tocloud and form a central bulge, as well as trigger new spiral structure in themerged galaxies. Thus, merger-based scenarios for the formation of S0 galaxies seem moreplausible than evolution for S0 galaxies.Based on a comparative study of E and S0 galaxy properties, Maia et al. (2015)concluded that the formation scenarios for S0 galaxies should be merger-based, whereasevolution is more likely the formation scenario for E galaxies. They foundthat S0 galaxies have higher concentrations than E galaxies. Moreover, theydiscovered that S0 galaxies, independent of their morphology, have olderstellar populations than their neighbouring E galaxies. In fact, thestellar populations of S0 galaxies are more similar to the stellarpopulation of the surrounding E galaxy than to their own. Thus, theformation scenarios for E and S0 galaxies seem to be different. These discoveriesare in contrast to the traditional view that E galaxies are evolutionarilyolder than S0 galaxies.

Heavy quark symmetry, an approximate symmetry of the spectrum of hadrons containing a bottom or charm quark, facilitates the calculation of the spectrum of hadrons containing a bottom or charm quark. In particular, the mass difference between the bottom and top quarks, experimentally measurable as the B* - B mass splitting, is used to constrain the values of the bottom mass and the strong coupling constant. Here we present a non-perturbative renormalization of the gluonic chromo-magnetic operator in heavy quark effective theory (HQET), which is of leading dimension in the heavy quark mass, that satisfies heavy quark symmetry. The computed value of the B* - B mass splitting using this operator is 4.55 MeV, in excellent agreement with the experimentally measured value of 4.57 MeV. We conclude that the B* - B mass splitting provides a very accurate determination of the bottom mass and strong coupling.

Near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) are the most frequent witnesses of incoming asteroids and have a key role in shaping the asteroid population. NEA thermal inertia, or equivalently, their magnitude of the Yarkovsky effect is one of the key parameters in their dynamical modeling. The lack of understanding of the NEA thermal inertia hampers progress in these fields. We present the analysis of the thermal inertia of six classes of objects with different surface properties. The largest thermal inertia was determined for the inner main-belt (3.2 ± 1.5 °C km−1 s−1) while the smallest one, (4.8 ± 1.1 °C km−1 s−1), was determined for the outer belt. In between we determined the thermal inertias for the near-Earth asteroids (0.7°C km−1 s−1 to 46.9 °C km−1 s−1) and the main-belt NEA (0.8 °C km−1 s−1 to 46.2 °C km−1 s−1). This work increases our understanding of the magnitude of the Yarkovsky effect for NEAs and improves our ability to model their dynamical evolution.

Fullerene-like carbon-based thin films were synthesized by simultaneous magnetron cosputtering of elemental sources in an argon atmosphere. The variation of the growth parameters allowed the investigation of the influence of the substrate temperature and the flux ratio on the morphology, the structure, the composition and the physical properties of the resulting films. Fullerene-like carbon coatings were obtained at temperatures of about 950 °C and flux ratios around 1:10 by the addition of nickel into the argon plasma. The resulting films displayed superelastic characteristics: their Young's modulus and yield stress were respectively enhanced and lowered by 35% by cooling the samples to room temperature and re-heating them to 980 °C. The analysis of the crystalline structure revealed the co-existence of graphitic and amorphous domains, responsible for the mechanical properties of these materials. adi's author, Dimitri M. Prewavelets, or pre-wavelets, are a family of orthonormal wavelet basis functions that can be used to solve the Poisson equation. The prewavelet basis functions satisfy two properties: they are orthogonal and they are adapted to the domain. These two properties make prewavelets well-suited to the solution of Poisson's equation, which involves orthogonalizing the trial and test functions. Numerical approximations of prewavelets have been used for many years to efficiently solve Poisson's equation. In this work, we present an analytic solution to Poisson's equation based on prewavelets. The prewavelet basis functions are piecewise constant over a set of partition of the domain. These partition forms a basis for the solution of the Poisson equation over the entire domain. The partition boundaries are typically complex domain edges. The prewavelets themselves have real values. We show that the prewavelets and their first derivatives satisfy the desired orthogonal relations. This work is an extension of the prewavelet concept. The prewavelet basis functions are created from an orthonormal, compactly supported mother wavelet. The mother wavelet coefficients characterize the prewavelets. We extend the mother wavelet concept to a prewavelet basis. The prewavelets are created from an orthonormal, compactly supported prewavelet. The prewavelet basis functions have the same characterization as the mother wavelet prewavelets. The prewavelets and prewavelet first derivatives share similar properties with the mother wavelets and their first derivatives. The prewavelets are orthogonal over the entire domain. The prewavelet basis functions form a complete orthogonal basis for the solution of the Poisson equation.

The complexity of many real-world networks has been shown to be well captured by graphs possessing a random layout. Such random graphs are commonly generated using one of two paradigms: the configuration model, which assumes a uniform probability distribution for all edge establishment, and the community model, which allows for the generation of arbitrary networks with pre-specified properties. However, different real-world networks may exhibit very different distributions of topological characteristics. Therefore, it is of interest to consider how the distributions of these characteristics may vary across different random graph models. Here we focus on two such characteristics, the size of the largest planar matching and the largest planar subgraph, both of which have well-understood algorithmic techniques that allow for their exact determination for arbitrary random graphs. By employing a variety of random graph models, we find that the size of the largest planar matching exhibits a power-law distribution for every model considered, while the largest planar subgraph exhibits a power-law distribution in some models and exhibits a different, more exponential-like, distribution in others. Notably, we find that the power-law exponents for the size of the largest planar matching and the largest planar subgraph are closely correlated with the exponent associated with the degree distribution of the graph. This suggests that the tail behavior of the distribution of these characteristics is most strongly influenced by the presence or absence of a wide variety of high-degree vertices within the random graph model.

Semi-analytic models of galaxy formation provide a powerful tool for understanding the connection between the large-scale structure of the universe and the properties of galaxies within it. To date, this has mainly focused on constraining the structure of dark matter and how it relates to the observed properties of galaxies. In this work, we extend the semi-analytic model of Cooke & Bond 2017 to include the evolution of baryonic matter and how it relates to the components of the universe including dark matter and the various gas phases. In particular, we couple the semi-analytic model to cosmological magneto-hydrodynamical simulations that self-consistently track the abundance of the light elements (H, He, and other abundant species), as well as metals. These calculations are then combined with an updated version of the semi-analytic model of Cooke & Novak (2016) to produce a self-consistent model of galaxy formation that operates at all mass scales. Using only five free parameters, we are able to match a wide range of observations of galaxies from local to distant populations, including several observational tests of the thermalhistory of the intergalactic medium (IGM). This implementation allows us to study the physical origin of various tensions between theoretical models and observations of galaxies. In particular, we show that the tension between the abundance of quads and the observed Tully-Fisher relation for galaxies can be relaxed if feedback from active galactic nuclei in semi-analytic models is reduced. In addition to matching other observational relationships, this modification is also consistent with the local mass function of stars, the mass distribution of black holes, and the correlation between galaxy stellar mass and black hole mass. Furthermore, we show that reproducing the observed evolution of the optical depth of the universe to reionization can also be achieved if a similar feedback prescription is applied to the model galaxies. Using this implementation, we also perform a series of small-volume simulations designed to test whether the solution to the angular diameter distance ratio crisis proposed by Yang & Chan (2018) can simultaneously reproduce the observed galaxy stellar mass function and the size-mass relation for elliptical galaxies. Our simulations confirm that these relations can be simultaneously reproduced provided that feedback from active galactic nuclei is increased in smaller galaxies. These results provide strong motivation for testing this prediction of unified models of active and passive galactic evolution against upcoming observational data from JWST and large-scale 21cm surveys.

In this paper, we present a linear reformulation of the Kuramoto model of self-synchronizing oscillators. In particular, we consider the network where each node is endowed with a dimensional variable and all the nodes are connected via undirected networks, the coupling function is a function of the difference of the dimensional variables of the connected nodes and all nodes are identical. We show that this model can be written as a coupling of diagonal and scalar ODEs. We then use the Schur complement to reduce the dynamics of the original model to this diagonal plus scalar system. We analyze the equilibria of the reduced model and show that in certain cases, the reduced model can exhibit oscillatory and chaotic behavior that is not present in the original model. We also show that, when some conditions on the coupling and the dimensional variables are met, the dynamics of the original system are lossless propagated to the reduced system.

It is found that the away side two particle correlation function is different from zero for |y| > 3.5 for charged particles with |y| > 2.5 for pions and gammas. General relativity, as formulated by Albert Einstein, is a cornerstone of modern physics. It describes gravity as the warping of space and time, resulting from the asymmetric warping of space and time caused by matter and energy. One of the most well-tested theories in all of physics, general relativity has withstood the test of time, having passed all experimental tests with high accuracy. However, there are some that speculate that a deeper understanding of gravity may require the introduction of new concepts and ideas. As part of this trend, there has been recent interest in the process by which we describe the gravitational interaction using Einstein’s theory; that is, renormalization. Renormalization refers to the process by which infinities inherent in the theory are eliminated by redefining the parameters of the theory. In the process, a more general framework for gravitational theory—one that includes various alternative theories such as f(R) gravity—is created. In this paper, we examine this framework for renormalization. We provide an extensive account of the process and provide a step-by-step guide to performing calculations in this framework. We illustrate this process through several examples, including calculating the effective action for a system of gravitons. We end with a discussion of our findings and suggestions for future work.

Switching field distributions (SFDs) in perpendicular recording media play a major role in the analyses of signal detection mechanisms, however their precise determination has proven to be challenging. Here we present a numerical approach, the $\Delta H(M, \Delta M)$ method, for the calculation of SFDs from numerical simulations of a multi-domain particle-based model of a perpendicular recording medium. This is achieved by first tracking the time-evolution of the field strength $H$ across a sequence of static magnetic fields $H = \Delta H \cdot M$, where $M$ is the recorded moment amplitude and $\Delta H$ is a constant switching field gradient, and then binning these data points according to their corresponding recorded moment amplitude $M$. The resulting data are then fitted with an SFD model to obtain both the width ($\Delta M$) and centre ($M_0$) of the SFD peaks. We apply this method to model SFDs obtained from static and dynamic magnetic simulations of the $\Delta H(M, \Delta M)$ protocol. The accuracy of the $\Delta H(M, \Delta M)$ method is confirmed by accurate reproduction of both the peak positions and peak widths of the SFDs from these simulations. Application of the method to SFDs obtained from existing simulations for a range of media properties (e.g. particle aspect ratio, magnetic anisotropy) and applied fields (e.g. longitudinal field strength, field gradient) shows good agreement between the $\Delta H(M, \Delta M)$ method and existing techniques for the determination of SFDs from perpendicular recording media.

This is used to deduce the relationship between Langlands parameters for general groups and classical groups. The case of odd ramification is treated in detail. This has applications to automorphic forms and their periods, and this relation is used to compute periods of supercuspidal representations of general spin groups. The relation between the loop space of a ring spectra and the derived loop space of its suspension is a map between continuous symmetric monoidal functors. This has several applications. One is to deduce the relationship between Langlands parameters for general groups and classical groups. This has been treated before, but our perspective is from the point of view of tensor categories; this allows us to treat the odd ramification case in detail. As an application, we compute periods of supercuspidal representations of general spin groups. Our main technical theorem is the local lifting theorem for integral representations, which states that for a sufficiently large prime ideal p in a local field, a generic parahoric subgroup, and for an unramified principal series representation Psi of the Levi component of the parabolic subgroup determined by p, there exists a discrete series or a special parahoric subgroup generic with respect to p, acting on the space of Psi by a unique fixed point. This has applications to automorphic forms and their periods. We describe the local Langlands correspondence for these groups in terms of local Jacquet-Langlands correspondence for GL n and S n. Finite two-state trajectories provide a unique way to study the connection between microscopic and macroscopic scales. We present a general framework that uses probabilities of occurence and duration to quantify microscopic phenomena such as reaction pathways and freezing. We then apply this framework to study thermalization in a harmonic trap and supercooled liquid configuration spaces. For the first case, we find a hierarchy of multiple time and length scales that characterizes the system's thermalization behavior. For the second case, we find evidence of dynamical heterogeneity, wherein we quantify the number of participating regions as a function of the observation time. Our results demonstrate that the reaction pathway and dynamics in supercooled liquids can be characterized using information contained in finite two-state trajectories. 7 The paper develops a framework that uses information contained in finite trajectories of any complexity. The first part of the paper applies this framework to study thermalization in a harmonic trap and supercooled liquid configurations spaces. The main results are the identification of a hierarchy of multiple time and length scales that characterizes thermalization in the harmonic trap and evidence of dynamical heterogeneity in supercooled liquids.

In this paper, we study the two-sided optimal bounds for Green function of half-spaces for relativistic $\alpha$-stable process. We find that the optimal bounds for the Green function are closely related to the boundary behavior of underlying half-spaces, that is, it approaches to zero orinfinity at the same speed. By using this property, we give two-sided optimal bounds for Green function of half-spaces for relativistic $\alpha$-stable process. Here is the main result: For every fixed $\alpha\in(0,2]$, there exists a positive constant $C=C(\alpha,d)$ such that for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $y\in\partial\mathcal{H}$ and $t>0$, it holds that $$\frac{C}{(t^{2/\alpha}+|x-y|^2)^{\frac{\alpha+d}{2}}}}\leq p_t(x,y)\leq \frac{C}{(t^{2/\alpha}+|x-y|^2)^{\frac{d}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}}}}.$$

In recent years, space exploration has brought humanity closer to answering the age-old question of whether there is life on other planets. One of the main challenges for exoplanet hunters is identifying the chemical signatures of possible life on planets outside our solar system. A potential telltale biosignature is a cirrus cloud with a high albedo, or reflectivity, which could bounce light from a planet’s surface into space and cast a dark shadow on the planet’s surface. Here we report the gamma-ray albedo of the moon, a measure of its gamma-ray absorption cross section above 30 MeV, from a sample of gamma-ray lines from 1 MeV to 1 TeV obtained by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. We find that the albedo of the moon is around 0.32, consistent with estimates based on soil composition. This high albedo value is due to the fact that the lunar surface is covered with anorthosite rock formed by the crystallization of volcanic ashes from the impacts of meteorites 3.9 billion years ago. Given the vast number of potentially habitable planets in our galaxy, the gamma-ray albedo of the moon could serve as an efficient method to identify biosignatures on planets orbiting other stars.

In this paper we solve the generalized Christoffel and Nirenberg problems in H^{n+1}. In particular, we construct solutions to the generalized Nirenberg problem: we prove that any conformally invariant linear elliptic PDE on R^n can be reduced, via a branched covering transformation, to the generalized Nirenberg problem. The construction of solutions to the generalized Christoffel problem, which solves the generalized Neumann problem, is also described. Our method, which is based on the integral representations for solutions developed by Caffarelli and Silvestre, is purely analytic. The generalized Christoffel and Nirenberg problems arise in several contexts. Christoffel's Problem (1903) concerns the first-order system satisfied by the Christoffel symbols of a connection in a semi-Riemannian manifold. The Nirenberg Problem (1958) concerns the same problem with Dirichlet boundary conditions. The conformal transformation relating these problems is a Ricci soliton; by introducing appropriate constraint equations this correspondence is made explicit. Our results concerning Christoffel's Problem can be viewed as partial resolution of the Nirenberg Problem, which we prove solves the more general conformally invariant problem on R^n. Our method of constructing solutions to the generalized Christoffel problem follows the method of Caffarelli and Silvestre [1] and proves the convergence of a finite difference scheme. In contrast, the construction of solutions to the generalized Nirenberg problem is more direct and relies on a new conformal ansatz, which reduces the problem to a system of nonlinear PDE. We also prove that the Christoffel problem is the limit, as the permeability of the manifold goes to 0, of the generalized Nirenberg problem. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we introduce the generalized Christoffel and Nirenberg problems and provide some background material. In Section 3 we discuss conformal transformations relating these problems, and present our results concerning Christoffel's Problem. In Section 4 we prove that the generalized Neumann problem can be reduced, via a branched covering transformation, to the generalized Neumann problem. In Section 5 we introduce the conformal ansatz that solves the generalized Nirenberg problem and present some of its properties. In Section 6 we discuss a finite difference scheme that converges to solutions of the Christoffel problem. Section 7 is an Appendix which contains the proofs of some statements made in the main text. Bayesian deformer models have been widely used in medical imaging, computer vision and AI. However, the computation of Bayesian deformer models is often challenging due to the use of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to approximate the posterior distribution. Recently, variational inference (VI) algorithm has been proposed and shown to be efficient in calculating the approximate posterior distribution in Bayesian deformer models. In this paper, we develop a novel Stochastic Approximation Algorithm (SAA) based on VI algorithm to further improve the calculation efficiency. The proposed method is firstly derived in a general Bayesian deformable model, and then applied to some specific Bayesian deformer models for demonstration. Our experimental results on synthetic and real datasets show that our method is more efficient than the existing VI algorithm and comparable with the state-of-the-art MCMC algorithm in calculating Bayesian deformer models. The primary contributions of this work are two-fold: (1) We propose a SAA-based VI algorithm to further improve the calculation efficiency of Bayesian deformer models. Our method is applicable to a broad range of Bayesian deformer models and shows higher efficiency than existing VI algorithm in some cases; (2) We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on real world datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/ShuaiZhang0413/SAA-VI Please cite our previous work [1] if you use our code in your research.
