In this work we present the results of a study into modeling epidemic spread in synthetic populations – Virtual Plagues. In particular, we focus on modeling the spread of diseases in computer-generated, synthetic populations. The Virtual Plague research has three main components: 1. Modeling the physical world and including its dynamics in the virtual world; 2. Developing synthetic biological entities that resemble real life biological entities, but also allow for expansion of the population to support high player counts and runtime speed; and 3. Implementing a global simulator that can model the interaction between entities and predict outcomes in the physical world. In this work, we present the first results of the Virtual Plagues project, applying these techniques to the spread of epidemics. We create a virtual world in which the player population lives in cities that are themselves dynamic entities that can be built, destroyed and migrated to in response to different factors, such as disease prevalence and player actions. The cities are populated with synthetic biological entities that behave as both individuals and members of a collective, interacting with each other and with player characters. Together, these form a closed system, in which epidemics spread from one biological entity to another based on proximity and contact-based infection, and behaviors such as social distancing and wearing face masks affect the likelihood of an entity becoming infected. Our results show that using this approach we are able to achieve realistic spread of epidemics in the virtual world and generate patterns of behavior – both individual and collective – that are consistent with real-world data. In particular, we find that when individual behavior is calculated based on the expected behavior of the majority, rather than an abstract system-wide average, then the patterns of collective behavior are also realistic. Overall, our Virtual Plague approach to modeling physical world dynamics in virtual worlds, allowing for high player counts, has proven to be effective and robust, and can be applied to many simulation domains. We present a first step toward modeling epidemics in this way and hope that our research into this area will help lay the foundations for future studies in the area, as well as a potential area of commercial application."

Phonons are the collective motion of the ions in a crystal, and they can travel through solids by various scatterings. While the dynamics of electrons are affected by the crystalline structure, that of phonons is determined by the interaction between atoms. This implies that phonon transmission across different crystalline structures may show unique features. Here we report measurements of the longitudinal and transverse sound transmission through epitaxial interfaces. By varying the orientation of the two crystals, we are able to isolate the interface vibration from the bulk modes. We identify three resonant interface modes and their phonon counterparts in the transmission spectra. The first resonant mode is the lateral surface mode, also known as Rayleigh wave. The interaction between the surface and the longitudinal and transverse waves show quite different behaviours, which is attributed to the change of the polarization of the propagating waves. The second mode is a bending vibration of the reconstructed interface, which is allowed due to the symmetry of the coupled crystals. The third mode is a two-dimensional interface mode. It has zero transmission for longitudinal sound and only transmits transverse sound. These resonant features are further analysed in terms of the atomic displacement patterns.

We construct the explicit twisted $N=2$ superstring theory that consists of the 2D black hole background and the Neveu–Schwarz sector with the reversed worldsheet spin. The R-R sector of the theory contains the space-time bosons and fermions as well as the corresponding solitonic states. This model can be obtained from the usual FZZ T-duality transformation applied to the reversed NS-NS sector of the Type IIA superstring theory with O8-planes, with the O8-planes representing the twisted R-R sector. As an application, we study this theory in the low-energy limit and demonstrate that it is a consistent truncation of the four-dimensional $N=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory coupled to matter hypermultiplets in the quiver gauge group, with the R-R bosons corresponding to the vector superfield of the low-energy effective theory. We also demonstrate that the low-energy limit of this superstring theory possesses the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)$ global symmetry, which is the same as the global symmetry of the four-dimensional effective super Yang-Mills theory with respect to the $N=2$ supersymmetry.

The $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson, first discovered by the BaBar and BESIII experiments, is an s-wave resonance with mixed charm and strangeness. Its discovery reported by the LHCb and other experiments has opened a new field of opportunities to study the properties of exotic hadrons. The first measurement of $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson production at midrapidity in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV was carried out by the CMS experiment at the LHC. This article reports on the measured $D_{sJ}$(2317) meson production cross section at forward rapidity and in the low mass region in p+p collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV, based on the integrated luminosity of 1.15 $\text{fb}^{-1}$. 875 fb^{-1}$ of data were recorded with the CMS detector, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1.15 fb$^{-1}$. The nuclear modification factor is found to be consistent with 1, independent of the $D_{sJ}$ mass, and the cross section is compatible with no modification.

Lithium Iodine Oxide (LiIO3) is a promising material for solar thermal to near-infrared (NIR) spectra due to its wide bandgap (5.6 eV) and high absorption coefficient. Bandstructure and optical properties of $\alpha-LiIO_{3}$ crystal are investigated by using the density functional theory (DFT) with GGA+U method, and the quasi-harmonic approach is used to calculate the harmonic spectra. The calculated results show that $\Gamma_{7c}$ conduction band minimum (CBM) and $\Gamma_{6v}$ valence band maximum (VBM) are both at $\Gamma$ point, which means $\alpha-LiIO_{3}$ is an indirect-bandgap semiconductor. The energy bandgap of $\alpha-LiIO_{3}$ is determined by the highest optical indirect bandgap $E_{opt}’=2.2$ eV. The strong $\Gamma_{7c}$ CBM and weak $\Gamma_{6v}$ VBM lead to a large Brillouin zone center indirect bandgap of $E_{BZ}(CBM-VBM)=2.2$ eV. The polarizations of all optical transitions are along c-axis, which is consistent with its inter-layer weak van der Waals force. The average energy gap, lattice parameters and dielectric constants are provided for designing ultraviolet optical devices and THz optics devices. Finally, a promising candidate for solar thermal to near-infrared (NIR) spectra is introduced and demonstrated by theoretical calculation and experimental verification.

A new type of thermodynamic cycle has been proposed, which violates the First Law of Thermodynamics but satisfies the Second Law. The new cycle is comprised of two isenthalpic processes, where the total volume entropy increases, and it connects two states with different temperatures but equal volume. The first process is isothermal compression with external heating; the second process is isothermal expansion with external cooling. Based on the generalized Clausius–Duhem inequality, we prove that the total volume entropy increases in both processes. Thus, this cycle may generate work. In addition, we demonstrate that this cycle is equivalent to the Carnot cycle with a demon. Thus, the total volume entropy increase implies the violation of the First Law. At the same time, the Second Law is satisfied because the total entropy increases in both processes. Hence, this cycle might have some potentials in industrial applications. This is an original paper and was published on 12 January 2023 with the URL https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.11651.pdf. Since the late 18th century, the First Law of Thermodynamics has been well established, stating that the entropy of isolated systems cannot decrease over time. However, there are still some aspects that need to be further explored. The aim of this paper is to propose a new thermodynamic cycle that violates the First Law, but satisfies the Second Law. The new cycle is comprised of two isenthalpic processes, where the total volume entropy increases, and it connects two states with different temperatures but equal volume. The first process is isothermal compression with external heating; the second process is isothermal expansion with external cooling. Based on the generalized Clausius–Duhem inequality, we prove that the total volume entropy increases in both processes. Thus, this cycle may generate work. In addition, we demonstrate that this cycle is equivalent to the Carnot cycle with a demon. Thus, the total volume entropy increase implies the violation of the First Law. At the same time, the Second Law is satisfied because the total entropy increases in both processes. Hence, this cycle might have some potentials in industrial applications. Keywords: Thermodynamics, Entropy, Second Law of Thermodynamics, Violation of the First Law, Proposed Cycle 1. A near-infrared polarimetric study of the bipolar nebula IRAS 19312+1950 was conducted using the UKIRT telescope. Linear and circular polarisation was detected for the first time from this object. The polarisation angle is aligned with the direction of motion of the lobes and not perpendicular to the symmetry axis of the source, suggesting that magnetic fields play a role in the evolutionary process of this object. The physical parameters of the bipolar nebula determined from the NIR data are: - Distance: 2.5 ± 0.5 kpc - Lobe size: 0.25 ± 0.03 kpc - Outflow velocity: 310 ± 40 km s-1 - Mass: 3.0 × 10−4 M⊙ - Momentum: 6.3 × 10−7 ~ 4.9 × 10−7 g cm² s-1 This research was conducted as part of the UKIRT Infrared Deep Sky Project.

Central type groups and cohomology classes Let G be a Lie group and g its element. We say that g has central type if the Killing form of the Lie algebra of G vanishes at the origin, i.e. vanishes on the Lie algebra of G. In this case, the mapping g−1 : g−1 (g)↦g is an automorphism of G called the Zassenhaus automorphism. We say that a cohomology class in Hn(G,M;R) has central type if its projection to Hn(g−1(g),g−1;R) does. We give two criterions to know when a cohomology class with central type is non-degenerate: it is non-degenerate if and only if its inverse is non-degenerate and we give an explicit cup-product. We also explain how to compute cup-product between two cohomology classes with central type in terms of pairing between the corresponding Lie algebras' cohomology classes. We finally show that any cohomology classes with central type is bijective if and only if it is non-degenerate and then exhibit an explicit formula for its inverse.

In quantum mechanics, a density operator is a projection valued, Hermitian operator that represents the state of a quantum system with uncertainity. The density operator is a fundamental and important mathematical object in quantum mechanics, which encapsulates the statistical information of the quantum system. In this paper, we study the geometry of the set of all density operators on a complex Hilbert space, i.e., the quantum state space. First, we present a generalized von Neumann entropy and characterize the entropy landscape of the set of all quantum states. We then study the extreme points, the convolution structure, and provide alternative characterizations of the set of physically allowed quantum states. Next, we show that a quantum state is a density state if and only if it can be expressed as a tomographic probability distribution. As an application of these results, we derive a unified geometric framework for the construction of positive maps and use it to completely classify super-operator positive maps on trace-class operators. As an example, we provide an explicit formula for the operator Jordan map, which can be considered as a quantum analog of the complex equator of the Riemann sphere.

Recently, cognitive radio has been paid much attention due to its capability to automatically find available unused spectrum for new utilizing, which is particularly useful in the scenario of spectrum shortage. In order to avoid interfering with the primary spectrum user, the secondary cognitive radio transmitter has to adopt the rate adaptation to control its transmitting rate based on the interference received by the primary user, which is, however, unknown and difficult to observe. To this end, this paper proposes a non-Bayesian rate adaptation with two design approaches: one is the restless multi-armed bandit based approach for finding the unavailable spectrum in an automated and adaptive manner; the other is the Lyapunov optimization based approach for finding the operating point that achieves the worst average interference to the primary user. Specifically, the former adopts a large number of discrete channel states to approximate the dynamic and continuous interference levels, while the latter adapts the transmitting rate from a static to a dynamic mode according to the observation of the interference, and gradually converges to the operating point that achieves the worst average interference. Simulation results show that the proposed approaches achieve near-optimal performance, in terms of both effective spectrum utilization and average interference to the primary user.

In this paper, we introduce a new flow model named width flow. This model is able to flow a surface towards a circle with a fixed radius. We prove that this flow will exist for all time and will smoothly converge to a round point. In addition, we can compute the evolved surface at each time by simply inverting this flow model. We also apply this model to solve mean curvature flow, which is to flow a surface toward its mean curvature, and we will get the same nice results. These two flows have similar usages in brain modeling. We can start with a thin initial surface, and flow it towards the curvature of a brain sphere. Then we can get a thick surface which can approximate a cortex. Width flow: Let M be a compact surface without boundary in an n-dimensional Euclidean space. For each x0 in M, we define a vector tangent to M at x0, denoted byux0. Let d2x0 represent the area element of M at x0. The width of M at x0 is defined as the area of the parallelogram spanned byux0 and ux0. In other words, the width of M at x0 is the function w: M×R→R, w(x) = |ux0 − ux0|, where |•| is the euclidean norm. At each x0, we define a vector normal to M at x0, denoted bynu0. Fermionic quantum criticality is a long-standing and much debated topic in many-body physics. Mott’s archetypal Fermi-liquid-based explanation of the metallic state in heavy fermions, i.e., based on Landau-Fermi-Golden-Rule electron scattering, has remained a classic example of effective theories based on a microscopic many-body framework going beyond traditional phenomenological approaches. Over the years, however, criticism of Mott’s theory has increased both in the quantum and statistical mechanical communities, in particular, concerning the neglect of quantum zero-point motion and spin-orbit coupling. This article presents a modern generalization of Mott’s Fermi-liquid theory of heavy fermions, which is capable of explaining these and other low-dimensional fermionic strongly correlated systems (e.g., thin film superconductors). We establish the existence of a unique finite-temperature quantum critical point where standard Landau-Fermi-Golden-Rule perturbation theory becomes invalid and non-Fermi-liquid anomalous transport emerges, yet the system remains a Fermi liquid. In particular, Fermi liquid quasi-particle weight vanishes at the QCP and the non-Fermi-liquid scale is set by the energy/temperature scales (e.g., Kondo scale or spin-orbit energy) and interaction-induced coherence factors, rather than by the size of the quantum critical fluctuation. We argue that similar exotic non-Fermi-liquid behavior might universally emerge in low-dimensional strongly correlated fermionic systems with spin, orbital, and/or other degrees of freedom (e.g., systems with particle-hole or fermion–boson mixed symmetry). This article reviews a comprehensive description of quantum criticality in low-dimensional fermionic systems with or without symmetry, including spin, orbital, and other degrees of freedom. Within the framework of “proximity” to a low-dimensional system, we discuss the applicability of the conventional Fermi-liquid theory, in particular, those strongly violated by the existence of zero-point motion and spin-orbit coupling. We establish the existence of a novel quantum critical point which controls non-Fermi-liquid behavior despite being a Fermi liquid. In particular, Fermi-liquid quasiparticle weight vanishes at the critical point and non-Fermi-liquid behavior is set by a non-Fermi-liquid scale that is independent of the control parameter as well as the size of the quantum critical fluctuations. We also discuss potential physical realizations of such a Fermi-Liquid to non-Fermi-Liquid quantum phase transition, which are manifested by non-Fermi-Liquid transport behavior but which can still be well described by Landau Fermi liquid theory. We argue that such an exotic quantum critical phenomenon might universally emerge in strongly correlated low-dimensional fermionic systems with or without spin, orbital, or other degrees of freedom.

We present a theoretical study of high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos from semi-relativistic hypernovae. During the explosion of a very massive star (at least 30 times more massive than the sun), the inward force of gravity overcomes the pressure exerted by electrons and neutrinos on its surroundings, forming a shockwave that propagates outward through the star. We show that in some circumstances, a significant amount of energy is transferred from the shockwave to high-energy particles as it sweeps up, with 99% of the energy going to electrons and positrons and 1% going to neutrinos. These energetic particles emit a spectrum of high-energy neutrinos and gamma rays that could potentially be detected by future experiments. We demonstrate that models of hypernovae naturally produce neutrino and gamma-ray spectra that could potentially explain the spectra observed by IceCube. We also show that models that produce gamma-rays in the observed energy range could also potentially explain the measurements by Fermi-LAT. In our models, the dominant source of high-energy gamma-rays is the decay of mesons produced in interactions between neutrinos and target nuclei. The mesons produce decay products that gamma-rays through photopion production, similar to models of blazars. Neutrinos could contribute to the observed gamma-ray and neutrino spectra either through synchrotron radiation from secondary electrons and positrons, or through more exotic processes such as neutron decay. In order for these models to be potentially detectable, we must account for the fact that very massive stars are rare. We show that gamma-rays can be suppressed in the case that hypernovae arise from magnetorotationally driven core-collapse of low-mass stars. We also show that the measured flux of high-energy cosmic rays could potentially be explained by the decays of long-lived TeV scale particles if these particles are created in the process of generating the black hole in the neutron-rich collapsar model of hypernovae. In order to test these models, we must identify observational signatures that could potentially distinguish between models of hypernovae and other hypothesized sources of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays. We argue that the evidence from IceCube and Fermi-LAT can be explained by models of hypernovae if high-energy neutrinos are observed over multiple years with a typical flux of 1 neutrino per 4 GeV of observed energy, and if gamma-rays are observed in the 100 GeV to 10 TeV range with a typical flux of 1 gamma per 2 GeV. Our theoretical framework for hypernovae provides an explanation for the observed flux of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays, as well as a potential explanation for the observed flux of high-energy cosmic rays. In particular, it explains the potential distinction between models of hypernovae and other hypothesized sources of high-energy neutrinos and gamma-rays. This suggests that we must observe neutrinos for multiple years with a typical flux of 1 neutrino per 4 GeV

A quasar outflow, perhaps powered by a radio galaxy analogue, is identified in the narrow-line region of z = 0.1723 quasar SDSS J154141.33+155426.6. The outflow has a kinematic width of at least 1000 km s-1, a dynamical mass of at least 1042 M⊙, and is moving at high velocity (v = -0.999995 c, relative to the quasar frame). The width, dynamical mass, and velocity are all similar to, but slightly lower than, those of broad absorption line outflows. The narrow-line region gas is asymmetrically distributed around the quasar, with one side closer to the quasar than the other. The closer side is coincident with the radio galaxy analogue, suggesting that the quasar wind has been partially turned around by the AGN radiation pressure, and is interacting with the radio galaxy host. The density of the outflowing gas, calculated from the X-ray absorption, is high enough ( approximately 1011 cm-3) to affect the spectrum of the quasar, providing a natural explanation for the unusually blue UV/optical/near-infrared colours of the quasar, as well as the detection of the MgII absorber in previous radio galaxy observations.

A resonating valence bond (RVB) state, which is a variational wavefunction for the quantum Heisenberg antiferromagnet, is proposed for the first time for the quantum disk, a plausible precursor of the familiar quantum Hall state at filling factor 1. The flux quantum in the quantum disk is treated as a perturbing parameter, and low-lying spin singlet excitations are identified. The triplet excitation spectrum is also calculated and found to be highly unstable against strong spin correlations. The ground state energy is computed in the sector with no triplet excitations, and it is shown to be lower than that of the conventional Néel state by a resonating valence bond solid (RVB) energy, α²q² - (α-q²)q, with α = 0.32 and q = 0.75. Furthermore, the susceptibility of this state to various perturbations is also computed and is shown to be very robust. The proposed resonating valence bond quantum disk is observed to have the correct low-energy behavior for all calculable quantities. The emergence of the resonating valence bond state from the conventional Néel state is analogous to the onset of superconductivity from a Fermi liquid, and there are some tantalizing similarities between these two transitions. Furthermore, there is now strong evidence that high-temperature superconductivity emerges from a near-Fermi-liquid state, and a spin-gap insulator with superconducting fluctuations may well describe the Mott insulator cuprate superconductors. In a similar manner, it may be that the quantum Hall state at ν=1 arises from a near-Fermi-liquid quantum disk and an associated resonating valence bond quantum disk is a natural subsequent phase. The intriguing idea of resonating valence bonds between Quantum Hall edges is already a fact, with Jain’s heterogenous electron gas as the most famous example. We predict a heterogenous valence bond solid of Quantum Hall edges, where half of the electrons remain unscreened.

In a recent paper, we have presented the first explicit half-BPS flux solution in Type IIB supergravity that depends on all ten original spacetime coordinates and it generalizes the well-known five-dimensional octic extremum with two centers to IIB. Here we extend this result by showing the existence of multi-Janus solutions, which are generalizations of multi-domain walls to the flux compactifications. The general existence proof relies on a refinement of the phase transition method and it involves a system of differential equations with many arbitrary functions of seven variables. We present a particular solution that interpolates three different domain-wall solutions in seven planar transverse space dimensions. This solution generalizes the well-known McGuire multi-kink to the flux compactifications with localized sources and admits a consistent truncation to an 11-dimensional solution, where it represents a warped horizon of a smooth AdS$_{4+7}\times$S$^{7}$ solution with all periodic directions compact. The flux solution in question preserves four supercharges and has a massless three-form field in the internal seven-dimensional space. It has an interpretation as a stack of M2-branes on top of two five-branes and the competition between the forces from the worldvolume fluxes and the M2-branes produces an interesting warped supersymmetric solution with AdS factor in 11-dimensions.

By taking a continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo method, Gaussian-Basis Monte Carlo method, as an example, this paper presents an application of it to strong correlation physics. Using continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo method to simulate an interacting electron system needs a complex number computing, which is not only time consuming, but also inefficient. To solve this issue, we develop a novel approach: employing a discrete number-theoretic computing and using a Gaussian wave function as a basis function, namely Gaussian-Basis Monte Carlo method. This approach not only reduces the complexity from the computation perspective, but also has a good performance in balance between efficiency and accuracy. With the continuous-time quantum Monte Carlo method as a benchmark, we apply Gaussian-Basis Monte Carlo method to study some typical strongly correlated electron systems, such as the Hubbard model, the iterant model, and the periodic Anderson model, and observe the evolution of ground state as the correlation strength changes. This approach can provide a new perspective for solving strongly correlated physics problems.

Here we present a very deep, rest-frame 0.3-10 keV survey of X-ray spectra of broad-line AGN (18,900 individual observations from 70 journal papers between 2008 and 2018), which we combine with analysis of all available contemporaneous X-ray and optical data for the same sources (197,165 spectra from 130 journal papers between 1974 and 2018). We introduce a new diagnostic to classify the X-ray spectral shape: the fractional variability amplitude, Amp, computed from the standard error of the difference between each spectrum and the median spectrum. Amp ≥ 5% defines the broad-line (BLR) region, Amp < 5% defines the narrow-line region (NLR), and an intermediate value is a mixture (BLR + NLR). Although originally defined for photon counting data, Amp is easily computed from simple count rates and well separates the three regions, with no misclassifications in 145,805/18,900 = 80% of the AGN, and 76/197,165 = 0.004% with BLR + NLR. For BL Lacs, Amp < 5% in 122,630/122,630 = 99.99% of sources, and 80/197,165 = 0.004% have BLR + NLR. For radio-loud quasars, the corresponding numbers are 112,620/123,095 = 92.4% Amp < 5%, and 1,490/197,165 = 0.8% have BLR + NLR. The remaining 0.6-1.0% of radio-loud quasars have intermediate Amp, and likely have very complex and variable obscuration. If obscuration is constant, but the X-ray flux varies, Amp serves as a very sensitive detector of such flux variation, and for Seyfert 1 galaxies and quasars, Amp is approximately proportional to flux, with a best fit powerlaw index of 0.53-0.56. For BL Lacs the corresponding powerlaw indices are 0.5-0.58 for flux increasing and 0.59-0.82 for flux decreasing, suggesting a greater contribution of the BLR variability, perhaps by larger scale height (or faster response) variations in the BLR clouds. The fractional rms variability amplitude correlates well with other classification schemes, and supports an interpretation of Amp as approximately proportional to flux for most sources, with a small contribution from BLR variability for BL Lacs and quasars. For 44,165 observations of 20 sources from 10 papers with multiple observations, Amp shows the expected variability between successive observations. For 32,330 observations of 12 sources from 10 papers with a single observation per source, Amp is constant to within the estimated measurement uncertainties, except in one case with three observations of 3C 273, for which an argument is made that the spectrum is not constant between the third and fourth observations. A meta-nematic (MNT) phase occurs in a layer structure where the molecules in one layer order, but the coupling with the molecules in the other layer lacks such symmetry. The MNT phase is characterized by a non-zero complex twist vector density, which can be measured by its Carol TERMA code, C-Term. In this work, we report the discovery of two distinct MNT phases in a bilayer ruthenate Ca_{2}RuO_{4}} using resonant x-ray diffraction. While one C-term signal indicates an in-plane c-axis rotation between the layers, the other signal implies a staggered c-axis rotation, which we interpret as a half-integer octupolar MNT phase. Using first-principles electronic structure calculations, we show that the coupling between the layers in Ca_{2}RuO_{4}} originates from antiferromagnetic superexchange between the adjacent Ru layers. With the introduction of a small next-nearest neighbor Heisenberg interaction, the proposed magnetic model is found to be consistent with the C-term signals. Our work establishes Ca_{2}RuO_{4}} as the first known example of a MNT phase in the bilayer lattice, and offers a potential playground for studying intriguing physical phenomena arising from mixed symmetries between inter- and intralayer couplings.

Representations of tame quivers and their finite-dimensional modules are in one-to-one correspondence with continuous integral representations of affine Weyl groups. A classification of irreducible modules over various types of finite-dimensional algebras was achieved by cellularity of corresponding represen-tations of tame quivers. A realization of this classification in terms of canonical bases of quantum affine spaces gives a geometric interpretation of canonical bases. An introduction to the classical canonical bases (CB) of quantum groups was given by Lusztig in 1990. These bases are in one-to-one correspondence with irreducible representations of finite-dimensional quantum groups and their characters. It was conjectured by Soibelman and Deodhar that this correspondence can be interpreted in terms of canonical bases of quantum affin spaces, and it was realized in type A by Mitzima. Soibelman and Kodera gave a proof of this conjecture for type GLn, while Demazure gave a proof for type Lie. This correspondence can be generalized to the case of quantum affin groups and canonical bases of quantum affin spaces, see recent papers of Stroppel and Ginzburg for GLn, and Ginzburg for Lie. These bases are in one-to-one correspondence with irreducible representations of quantum affin groups and their specializations at points of the exceptional nilpotent orbit. This correspondence can be interpreted in terms of canonical bases of quantum affin spaces. It is known that canonical bases in a quantum affin space can be realized in terms of Fock space constructed over certain representations of a Borel subalgebra, which in type A coincide with the fundamental representations. These representations are in one-to-one correspondence with semilattices in $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. Moreover, each semilattice defines a canonical basis in the corresponding quantum affin space. The main result of the present paper is a construction of canonical bases in quantum affin spaces of any symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebra and any of its types, in terms of representations of the corresponding Borel subalgebra. This gives a proof of the Soibelman-Deodhar and Stroppel-Ginzburg-Ginzburg conjectures for all symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebras. More precisely, we prove the existence of a special order on the indexing set for a family of canonical bases. The corresponding semilattices are partially ordered. The main result is a construction of a family of bar complexes, whose subcomplexes are dual to the canonical bases. This gives a spectral sequence with nonzero terms in dimensions grading and restriction to a sublattice, and consequently the duality between these bases.

In this paper we present a global approach to the theory of special Finsler manifolds. A special Finsler manifold is one that satisfies an homogeneity condition of a particular form. The global approach is based on the study of Cartan geometries defined over the non-void space of parameters that characterise the manifold. We develop an abstract framework for Cartan geometries, showing that many well-known geometric structures fit into this framework. We then apply this general theory to the study of special Finsler manifolds, and deduce several unique features of these manifolds that had gone unnoticed in the local approach based on the study of metrics. Our framework allows us to describe in a uniform way general relativity and other theories with Lorentz-violating interactions as special Finsler geometries. Finally, we briefly discuss the prospects of applying the results of this paper to general relativity with a non-zero cosmological constant.

This paper shows the existence of a pure inductive limit state for the pair of measures consisting of Lebesgue measure on the interval and the Dirac delta mass at the endpoint, in contrast to the trivial and well-known example of the pair of measures consisting of the counting and Lebesgue measures on the Integer, which has pure state but not inductive limit state. The proof makes use of unique path decomposition for generalized functions. It is shown that the unique path decomposition for the regularization of the Dirac delta mass is weakly isomorphic to the double sequential limit of the unique path decompositions for regularized distributions that appear as simple components in the generalized decomposition. It is further shown that this double sequential limit coincides with the desired pure inductive limit state. The Kolmogorov's property for this pure inductive limit state is then shown to follow from its uniqueness and general properties of inductive limit states. It is further argued that the existence of this pure state but not inductive limit state for the pair of measures described above has several potential applications in mathematics and theoretical physics. The paper presents the results of joint work with E. Posta and I. Damián M. Medina.

UScoJ1609-2156 is a low-mass (M_ultimatum=0.69 ± 0.04M⊕), close (d=5.52 ± 0.21 pc) transiting planetary system. UScoJ1609-2156 was first identified by Dieterich et al. (2020) as part of a large transit survey using data from the Dark Energy Camera, and its discovery was announced at the arXiv pre-prints website. Although originally classified as a single-lined spectroscopic binary (which is usually taken to indicate a planetary system), UScoJ1609-2156 actually consists of at least three components, two of which are currently visible with the naked eye. Both USco1609A and B are M-dwarf components in a close hierarchical orbit, with periods of ~1 day and an apsidal alignment such that their combined transit duration is ~6 hours. UScoJ1609-2156C is a wide companion at a projected separation of ~14.7" (~400 AU), and is the most distant component amenable to atmospheric characterization with current facilities. My initial characterization of UScoJ1609-2156 involved a joint session with the American Astronomical Society (AAS) and American Institute of Physics (AIP) in Seattle, Washington, on April 9-11, 2020. I will present an overview of the discovery and analysis of UScoJ1609-2156, along with an overview of current methods of describing, parametrizing, and detecting multi-planet systems. Finally, I will conclude by discussing future opportunities for atmospheric characterization of UScoJ1609-2156C and the overall prospects for characterization of low-mass companions to solar-type stars.

Researchers have long sought to determine the factors controlling the location, amount, and timing of snowfall, since falling snow effectively radiates heat from the Earth's surface and plays a critical role in the development and maintenance of atmospheric circulation. The variability of midlatitude snowstorms has profound implications for regional and local hydroclimates, ecological habitats, and aviation routes. In this study, we use satellite-derived cirrus cloud data, collected between 2002 and 2006 by theSnowengulf instrument on the NASA TIMED satellite, to investigate the variability and determine the drivers of midlatitude cirrus clouds and their relation to regional and global tropopauses. We find that, during wintertime, midlatitude cirrus clouds form and are primarily influenced by the unequal heating of the tropics and the upper and lower altitudes. The tropical heating anomaly (THA), which is a measure of the temperature difference between the equatorial region and the region midway between the Equator and the Poles, promotes the growth and persistence of midlatitude cirrus clouds. The zonal index, which is a measure of the temperature difference between the Southern and Northern hemispheres, inhibits cirrus cloud growth and convection and, therefore, their ability to develop into thunderstorms. The THA and zonal index vary in phase with the Arctic and Antarctic Temperature Anomalies, which, in turn, drive the Niño-3.4 and South Atlantic Anomaly indexes, which are the primary indicators of tropopauses. Thus, we demonstrate a clear connection between the variability of midlatitude cirrus clouds and regional and global tropopauses.

An optically-trapped lightbeam can be formed by a gravity-like potential created by light itself in a photonic crystal fiber (PCF). The light beam could be either a stable lump or a ringing wave packet that oscillates in time. The packet is induced by a femtosecond pulse supercontinuum in the PCF and it can carry a large amount of energy over a long distance. The research is interesting from both fundamental and applied viewpoints. The paper [1] reports on the experimental observation of gravity-like optical potential and supercontinuum-induced light packet. The potential is optically simulated by the supercontinuum, which is a femtosecond pulse train, in a photonic crystal fiber. The light pulse train is shaped in the time domain to create a gravity-like optical potential. The light propagating in the PCF forms a pulse train itself, which interacts with the supercontinuum and forms a light packet. The packet can carry a large amount of energy over a long distance. The light-induced potential has different features from other optically-trapped light, such as a lump or a ringing wave packet. The packet has a stable shape that depends on the fiber parameters and it could be used as a light source. The potential could be used in all-optical switching and energy transport.

Reverberatory activity is found in many neuronal networks during states of high network activity, and has been associated with various brain states and behavior. In this paper, we study a minimal model of a neuronal network in which reverberatory activity is observed as a multiple spiking state. Through a reduction of the model to a mean field theory, we find that reverberatory activity is present due to a strong mean field interaction term that arises from the dynamical interaction of calcium and potassium channels. We validate our theory using large scale computer simulations of the full model, and we present a functional role for reverberatory activity in the brain by discussing its possible associations with the dynamical state of the brain. Model the brain as a network of spiking neurons. The dynamical state of the brain can be approximated as a state of high network activity, during which all network components are in nonlinear dynamic regimes. The two most common nonlinear dynamic regimes observed in networks of spiking neurons are continuous wave bursting and reverberatory activity. Continuous wave bursting is characterized by the spontaneous emergence of self-sustaining, fast spike frequency oscillations in the form of "bursts". Reverberatory activity is instead characterized by the presence of spontaneous slow oscillations, and can be thought of as a dynamical state of "hyperconnectivity" in which many feedback loops exist within the network. Both bursting and reverberatory activity have been observed in experimental studies of the dynamical state of the brain. We hypothesize that reverberatory activity may have a functional role in the brain, acting as a dynamical state of high neural activity that may assist the brain in transitioning between different states.

Insect locomotor activity cycle is a key element in ecophysiology and could be recorded by a variety of methods. Recently, progress has been made in developing spectral sensors to detect movements. In this study, we developed a procedure for automatic detection of locomotor activity from insects captured by infrared phototransformers (PT). This procedure has been applied to a sylph-like Psocoptera, Eupelmus orientalis Boheman and a leaf insect, Eupelmus vuilleti Rondani. Both species were recorded in the wild and in laboratory conditions. The procedure consists in detection of different body movements by a single algorithm trained on several exemplars. The algorithm was applied to a new example by adapting it to its specific body characteristics. The feasibility of this approach was validated on several exemplars. The algorithm reached an accuracy of 95.6% for E. orientalis and of 98.1% for E. vuilleti, evaluated on a set of 20 exemplars. The number of detected activities was similar for the two species, but their temporal organization was species-specific. Moreover, when recordings were performed on the same individuals in the laboratory, the temporal organization was similar but the number of detected activities was slightly lower, indicating a possible habituation. Thus, the method is a promising tool to investigate the temporal organization of locomotor activity for different species. Moreover, these results provide a methodological basis for a multitaxic analysis of locomotor activity, evaluating the number of activities, their characteristics and temporal organization.

Recent discoveries of exoplanets have opened a new chapter in the field of astronomy. With the upcoming transit missions such as TESS and PLATO, the number of known planets is expected to increase by several folds in the coming decade. Most of the known exoplanets are smaller and more dense than our Earth. When we look at the data from Kepler, it appeared that the surface of most planets are covered with water. However, when we observe the same planets with more accuracy, we find that the existence of oceans on those planets is uncertain. As the technology to detect those planets improves, the tendency of astronomers is to characterize the planet in terms of its atmosphere, not its surface. This implies that in the future, we might only identify the existence of life, not the existence of surface water. In other words, we could be oblivious to the existence of most planets. Dynamical research is a key enabler in the detection and characterization of exoplanets, and this field will significantly benefit from state-of-the-art technologies in computing, data analysis, and system identification.

Representations of general linear groups over discrete valuation rings (DVRs) were extensively studied. Over a decade ago, Schneider and Teitelbaum constructed such representations via adèlic locally analytic vectors. Since then, many new constructions have been given using narrow frames, local orbits, and seminorms on representations. Each of these new constructions provided additional insight into the problem of constructing irreducible cuspidal representations. In this paper, we give a unifying construction, which applies to any DVR with perfect residue field and fraction field of characteristic zero, and yields irreducible cuspidal representations. Our construction is direct, and provides many additional examples of irreducible cuspidal representations that were not previously known. Finally, we show that our construction interpolates between the existing constructions. This work was performed while the author was in residence at the American Institute of Mathematics in Palo Alto, CA, during the spring 2017 semester.

The semi-classical description of black hole evaporation has been an extremely successful framework to understand the final states of quantum gravity theories. Such an approach assumes that the black hole quantum gravity dynamics can be effectively described by a 2+1 dimensional gauge theory living on the black hole horizon called holographic CFT. The entropy of the black hole is then identified with the CFT maximal symmetry breaking pattern. This framework has been very successful at reproducing black hole properties for a broad class of quantum gravity theories including string theory. This success suggests that the gravity description provides the right degrees of freedom to account for the statistical mechanics of black holes. I discuss recent results that put this framework on a more rigorous basis by taking into account higher quantum gravity corrections. The higher order corrections become significant at late times near the black hole singularity and provide the black hole with a natural equilibrium description as a semi-classical state with a thermal density matrix. I present the corresponding description of the black hole entropy and dynamics as that of a closed system in equilibrium at a temperature determined by the higher order gravitational couplings. I discuss several phenomenological consequences of this new description including new predictions for black hole production at the LHC.

We prove that for any connected surface with nonempty boundary and any $\Sigma_g \in$ Map$(\Sigma_{g,1})$ (the mapping class group of the genus $g$ surface with one boundary component), the orbit of the Teichmüller geodesic determined by any non-arithmetic foliation on $\Sigma_g$ under the mapping class group action is locally rigid. Roughly speaking, a foliation is arithmetic if it has a transverse measure (i.e. a measure which is singular with respect to the transverse measures on the leaves). Our result not only resolves conjectures of Penner, Harer, and Sagelberger but also generalizes a result of Kapovich, Leeb and Porti on surface groups. We also remark that when $g=0$, our result recovers the classical rigidity theorem of Prym, which states that the orbit of the Prym foliation under the mapping class group is locally rigid. Our result is a combination of several techniques in geometric group theory, dynamical system, deformation theory and transversely affine geometry, and relies crucially on the work of Hahn and Strubel on the local rigidity of the mapping class group action on the moduli space of abelian differentials with prescribed conical singularities. Our results also has implications to the study of entropy for measured foliations and the Thurston metric on the Teichmüller space, and to the growth of Bers embeddings of Teichmüller space into projective space. We also provide an alternative, more concise proof of a special case of our result when the Riemann surface is a once-punctured torus. This work is in collaboration with Kang-Kuen Huang, Mladen Bestvina, and Richard Wentworth.

Planets are an important part of any planetary system, and giant planets are of particular interest because of their potential to host life. Although planet detection is typically the first step in determining if a planet lives in the "habitable zone," where temperatures are suitable for water to be liquid on a planet surface, there are few observations of this critical zone for planets around young stars. This work presents the first direct detection of infrared radiation from the region around giant planets in the habitable zones of nearby stars. This is done using L-band (3.78-3.84 μm) spectroscopy, which has not been widely used for planet detection because it is more difficult to observe from space than other bands, and does not provide the same level of detail as shorter wavelengths. Using the Infrared Telescope on board the Spitzer Space Observatory, we obtained high-quality spectroscopy of two nearby stars, named Tucana and Beta Pictoris, that are members of the moving groups corresponding to their age. We observed each star in the L' (3.74-3.81 μm) and L" (3.84-3.94 μm) water vapor filters, which are extremely sensitive to reflected infrared radiation from planets in the habitable zone of these stars. No planets were detected in these observations, placing upper limits on the planetary water abundance of 1.2×10−5 and 1.3×10−5 for the Tucana and Beta Pictoris systems, respectively. These results are consistent with theoretical predictions for the typical water abundance on a planet in the habitable zone of these stars.

On September 14th, 2015, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO), part of the worldwide Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory network, detected gravitational waves for the first time. The waves, generated during the collision of two black holes some 1+ million light-years from Earth, marked the beginning of observational astronomy with sub-atomic sized particles. This Letter describes the first search for short, intense gravitational-wave bursts, or sequences. Bursts of this type may occur naturally during the core collapse of massive stars, thermonuclear explosions, collisions of double black holes, and certain cosmological events. The search is based on data from the fourth science run of LIGO and covers a time period of 90 days between September 14, 2015 and April 15, 2016. We search for signals in the data with very short time durations, 20 milliseconds, and high signal-to-noise ratios, greater than 30. We find no plausible bursts within the data. Informed by this result, we set upper limits on the rate of short, intense bursts at the levels of a few hundred per year for 20 millisecond bursts with signal-to-noise ratios of 30 or greater, and at the level of a few per year for bursts of duration 1 second with signal-to-noise ratio of 30 or greater.

In this paper we introduce two novel and easy to implement algorithms to assess wine risk based on neural networks. The first is a hybrid algorithm that uses both transfer learning and recursive neural networks for wine assessment, and the second is an algorithm that uses only recursive neural networks, which is more simple but sometimes less accurate. The proposed hybrid algorithm was tested on a database of 3278 wines belonging to 18 countries, achieving a correlation of 0.81 with a professional assessor. Compared with the other algorithms tested, it was the one that obtained the best results. In particular, it was the only algorithm to assess 100% of the test samples as average risk, very close to the group of low risk wines, and the only one to correctly assess 24% of very high risk wines. Neural networks have shown to be a very good option for the wine assessment problem due to their ability to learn complex non-linear patterns from big datasets. However, despite the progress made with these models, their implementation is usually complex, and sometimes the models show errors by over-fitting the training set. To overcome these problems, we introduce two new algorithms that can be easily implemented. The first is a hybrid algorithm that uses transfer learning to quickly adapt a pre-trained model to the wine assessment problem, and also incorporates other techniques to improve the generalization of the model. The second algorithm is the simplest, but sometimes less accurate, because it only uses recursive neural networks, which are more simple than deep learning models but sometimes perform better. Both algorithms have been tested on a large wine dataset and have obtained very good results. The datasets and implementation details are available at https://github.com/aburgosvelez/wine-risk-assessment.

Nonlinear on-line learning has recently been proposed to tackle the problem of ensemble diversity, where a weighted combination of a set of shallow independent models are trained to improve the overall performance. Although encouraging results have been achieved with the simple convex combination, the search for better ensemble designs remains an active area of research. In this paper, we present a statistical mechanics point of view on nonlinear on-line learning and develop a framework that identifies the design space of effective ensemble strategies. Our analysis suggests that a hierarchical Bayesian model with separate Dirichlet processes for the weights of individual teachers and the shared prior over parameters can capture the intrinsic diversity of individual teachers and their commonality while effectively sharing information between them. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on several machine learning tasks, including image classification and semantic segmentation, where we construct a teacher ensemble for image segmentation using different network backbone, head, and training data. Our method substantially outperforms the state-of-the-art approach based on simple convex combination without using additional labeled data. The Orion Nebula is one of the most famous regions in the sky, and a jumping off point for many observing runs with both amateur and professional telescopes. Originally thought to be an example of a low-mass star forming region, it was later found to actually be a compact stellar cluster with an apparent emission temperature of over 10,000 K. The primary luminosity of the region comes from two massive stars within the inner region, also known as the Trapezium, but it is this nearby that has lead to significant analysis of the region's dynamics, surrounding gas, and galactic background. The region has also been used as a testbed for many different astronomical techniques. The first infrared imaging study of the region was published in 1955 and in 1956, Russell H. Bowey described the region as "a tiny globular star cluster" with a density between 1022 and 1023 m−3. In 1962, van den Bergh was the first to suggest that the cluster was in fact in an early stage of gravitational collapse. In 1964, Daniel Kerr described the region as "a concentration of some 50,000 stars... forming a beautiful, expanding cluster of nebulosity... almost certainly once a part of Orion's Nebula." In 1968, David Whitmore detected an infrared counter-part to the Trapezium stars and in 1970, Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky independently suggested that the Orion Nebula was in fact a star cluster. In 1973, Whitmore published the first deep survey of the region in visible light, detecting of an additional 60 stars, and in 1974, the first infrared survey of the region was published, reaching a limit of 15 Myr and approximately 2000 stars. In 1977, Alfred Landoldt and W. J. Moons independently calculated the age of the cluster to be between 2.1 and 2.5 million years, in close agreement with the most recent calculations. The Orion Nebula is now regarded as an example of a very young, massive star forming region and this has significant implications for its subsequent interaction with the interstellar medium. The region is within 1,200 light years of Earth and the Orion Molecular Cloud Complex, the nearest large molecular cloud, is approximately 1,000 light years across. This close interaction has profound implications for the radiation and winds from the Trapezium stars, the feedback this has on the region's interstellar environment, and the potential for disruption of the entire region.

Privacy is an issue in eLearning for people who seek privacy and/or security. However, privacy is not often a top priority for people who only consider eLearning if it is useful. What if privacy was an issue that users were truly concerned about, and eLearning solutions helped protect privacy? This paper investigates eLearning users’ attitudes towards privacy and presents a trend analysis reflecting the attitudes over time. The results show that privacy was not an issue for most users up to 2017; however, it is an increasingly important issue that users really care about. This trend is encouraging for companies that aim to provide privacy-preserving eLearning solutions. The results also show that a small number of eLearning users are expressing their concern about privacy. Thus, a handful of privacy-preserving eLearning solutions may be able to gain wide user acceptance. The results of this study can be used to help companies provide privacy-preserving eLearning solutions and improve their solutions to satisfy users’ needs. A multi-transition molecular line study of candidate massive young stellar objects associated with methanol masers was conducted using recently commissioned millimetre-wave observations with the Australia Telescope Compact Array. Eight sources were observed, of which five sources had clear detection of multiple transitions of methanol, water and carbon monoxide, indicating these sources host both high-mass Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) and an associated early phase of high-mass star formation. The results provide constraints on the physical and chemical conditions in these YSOs, and suggest that several may be good candidate high-mass YSOs. The methanol (3$_{\rm { 1,3}}-$2$_{\rm { 0,2}}$), water (2$_{ 0,2}-$1$_{ 0,1}$A$^{+}$ ), and carbon monoxide (J =$\rightarrow$ K = 1–0) lines were observed with high spectral resolutions (0.26, 0.16, and 0.26 km s$^{-1}$, respectively). Methanol and water trace similar gas components, and both show clear evidence of active motion and strong infall in all sources. Three sources also show evidence of strong outflow, which is most likely driven by the earlier high-mass star formation. The CO line width is broader than the other two lines in many sources, which may be attributed to a combination of large-scale outflow and infall. The various lines probe different environments, and thus can be used to trace different gas components in the same region. The three transitions of methanol, water, and carbon monoxide simultaneously observed provide critical diagnostic information on the gas properties, which can be used to trace physical and chemical conditions in the YSOs.

In this paper, we study the evolutionary dynamics of a system that can be modeled by a Markov chain with a finite state space. The state of the system represents the population composition, and the transition probability depends on the fitness difference between the current and the next population. We calculate the fixation probability, the mean convergence time, and the longest common subsequence count for this system. We show that for some parameter values the mean convergence time is exponential in the system size, while for other values it is super-exponential. In some cases, we can obtain an exact expression for the mean convergence time. We also calculate the spectral radius of the so-called Jacobi matrix, associated with the chain, and show that it characterizes the exponential growth rate of the mean convergence time. We obtain our results by using methods from the theory of Markov chains and extremal flows on graphs. We also study the case when the fitness function is two-tiered. We use random initial conditions to show that the probability of the system reaching the region with higher fitness is higher for two-tiered fitness functions than for one-tiered fitness functions, which means that two-tiered fitness functions produce a more robust result than one-tiered fitness functions.

The structure of the A=14 mirror nuclei with mass number 12+12 has been studied for the first time in a wide range of masses covering the continuum between the ground state and the alpha particle using the combination of the rapidity method and the Gaussian expansion method. A large variance of the isospin asymmetry for the excited states with the same quantum numbers as the corresponding ground states was observed. It was shown that the $D_{33}(1520)$ nucleon resonance appears as the first excited state with the isospin T=1 in the considered mass region. The appearance of the excited states with the isospin T=0 in the same mass region is most probably caused by the fact that the $S_{11}(1535)$ and $D_{13}(1520)$ resonances can decay directly into the isospin T=0 channel, nucleon-nucleonchannel. The calculated excitation energies of these resonances are in good agreement with the available experimental data.

In the large-scale structure of the universe, virialized objects, such as galaxies and clusters of galaxies, are surrounded by enormous amounts of hot gas, which remain largely undetected. This is because the virial temperature of a galaxy is about 4 keV, which is too low for this hot gas to be easily detectable in X-rays. However, in recent years, there has been a growing interest in the detection of diffuse hot gas in galaxy groups and clusters, using both X-ray and radio observations. Moreover, there is now a general consensus that this hot gas is very important for various aspects of galaxy evolution. In this paper, we present an extension to previous work (see, e.g., Ma 2008, 2008) on the relativistic dynamics of a multi-component fluid in the Newtonian regime. We consider a configuration involving a flat Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker universe containing a pressureless fluid and a non-relativistic ideal fluid, as well as a stiff fluid and a viscous fluid. We derive the full set of linearized perturbations for each fluid about an FLRW universe. This leads to a closed system of four partial differential equations, describing the two modes of the pressureless fluid and the two modes of the stiff fluid in the perturbed FLRW universe. The perturbations of the viscous fluid can be derived from a conservation equation. We discuss the main relativistic contributions due to pressure, curvature and rotation. In order to test the viability of this model, we compare the theoretical predictions to numerical results from an N-body simulation, which we perform for a $\Lambda$CDM model. We conclude by discussing some possible observational effects of the main relativistic contributions due to rotation, pressure and curvature.

Geophysics and cosmology have a lot in common in their objectives to understand the structure of the universe. The former aims to reconstruct the subsurface structure of the earth, while the latter tries to understand the origin and evolution of the universe. The data that are employed to achieve these goals are measurements of the earth's reflected wavefield and of the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation, respectively called earth-reflection and satellite-microwaves. Both reflection and microwaves are a result of photons travelling from an isotropic distribution in the universe to an anisotropic one due to gravity, passing through the earth and reaching the observer. The physics of this scenario are described by the Telegrapher's equations. Solving these equations is the goal of spectral estimation on a sphere (SOS). In this short abstract, we provide the necessary background information and describe recent advances in this field. Background Earth-reflection and satellite-microwaves are caused by photons, which are waves of electromagnetic radiation. These waves can travel in several ways. While traveling along a straight line with constant velocity, they consume energy and corresponding frequency, called linear propagation. Alternatively, they can be polarized, where the waves' crests and troughs swap places, emerging with altered frequency and direction, called nonlinear propagation. Finally, they can change frequency and direction while wrapping around a non-trivial topology, also called Fermi-Szilard-Dirac picture switching, where they encode Topological Entropy. Telegrapher's equations describe the linear propagation of a wave on a continuous 1D manifold. If we represent the manifold as the one-dimensional line, the equations describe the wave as propagating with a constant velocity. The corresponding observable, the earth-reflection, exhibits a frequency modulation caused by the photons' nonlinear propagation. On the other hand, the Cosmic Microwave Background radiation, called satellite-microwaves, is a measurement of the electromagnetic waves' linear propagation. The corresponding observable exhibits a frequency shift caused by the photons' energy consumption during nonlinear propagation. Solving the Telegrapher's equations for the line, Earth, provides two solutions. The trivial one, called reflection, is the case where the wave is completely reflected. This corresponds to no frequency shift and thus to no signal in the earth-reflection. The non-trivial solution, called diffusion, describes a wave that, once reflected, partially diffuses forward and backward. This corresponds to a signal with frequency shift in the earth-reflection. For decades, geophysicists have employed the reflection coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the earth-reflection over the linear propagation, to infer the Earth's subsurface structure. Recently, the Diffusion Probe Geodynamics discipline employed the Diffusion Scatterer Spectroscopic model, which is an eigen-decomposition of the diffusion equation. This model is based on the diffusion approximation of the earth-reflection

Resummation effects in the search for the standard model (SM) Higgs boson at hadron colliders have been examined. We have computed the normalized p-value distribution for the leading-order (LO), next-to-leading order (NLO), and next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) calculations using the Fully Unintegrated onto PDF (FUNPDF) formalism with a (NN)LO~QCD+NLO+NLLA+HERA2 effects summation. A distinct pattern of higher normalized p-value at the invariant mass of the Higgs boson has been observed at the (N)NLO and (N)N(N)LO orders. The level of the observed pattern and the size of the increase in the p-value depends on the renormalization/factorization scales and the choice of scale for the fixed-order perturbation theory calculations. We have also demonstrated that a distinct enhancement in the normalized p-value can be achieved at (N)NLO and (N)N(N)LO orders with the computed summation effects up to NLLA and HERA2 accuracy.

Recent research has discovered a larger family of Type D solutions of 10 or 11 dimensional supergravity, whose low dimensional analogs are the Eguchi-Hanson and Taub-NUT manifolds. The general solution with NUT and/orbolt singularities is cohomogeneity one and only unique in (10+2n) dimensional supergravity. Unlike their lower dimensional counterparts, all of these solutions have Kaluza-Klein Reduction to (9+2n) dimensional supergravities with matter, leading to AdS geodesics and various dual field theories with higher spin symmetries. These solutions provide strong evidence that 11 dimensional supergravity should be viewed as a non-linear realisation of (10+2n) dimensional supergravity, with the number of tensor multiplets equal to the number of vector multiplets. The most general solution with no-flux dstributional constraints, hatted gauge invariances and 3 special holonomies is an affine version of the Schwarzschild-Taub-NUT-bolt solution. It admits a Killing spinor with all of the same asymptotic symmetries of the AdS boundary, which in turn implies that it is dual to a 1/4 BPS state in a particular large N limit of a particular dual field theory with three free scalar fields. Interestingly, this solution admits 5 different Carter-Penrose diagrams, each corresponding to a different null geodesic singularity, and therefore different quantum gravity realisations. The two types of singularities corresponding to infinite local symmetries have already been encountered in solutions with fewer Killing spinors. The second case, admitting an additional 1/2 BPS state, was discovered only recently in the context of AdS holography. It would be interesting to understand whether it can also be interpreted as local symmetries of quantum gravity. These results demonstrate that the holographic dictionary cannot always be applied to local quantum field theories, and that the simple higher spin symmetries of gravity need not match the higher spin symmetries of the dual field theory. This work was supported in part by the ERC advanced grant 2304alloig 76viol, the FNR French national grant 20450203, the Max Planck Foundation, and the China Scholarship Council.

The spectrum of a magnetic cataclysmic variable contains a number of discrete lines, such as the cyclotron line and the LL...LL transition. We have examined several magnetic cataclysmic variables using both moderate resolution detectors on BeppoSAX and High-Energy X-ray Timing Experiment (HEXTE) on Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer, and have found a strong, narrow line near 70 Å. We show that this line is the Fe Kα triplet, and is therefore a strong signature of cool, covered, shock-heated plasma. We show that the characteristics of the triplet line are best explained by Thomson scattering, rather than fluorescence. Additionally, we find the line is highly variable, sometimes disappearing entirely. This variability is likely caused by changes in the physical conditions in the heated plasma, such as changes in covering factor or Thomson depth. We propose that this line is the first direct detection of a magnetic CV in the high-energy X-ray range. Observations of magnetic CVs in the high-energy X-ray range could help us understand accretion in these systems, as well as the relationship between these systems and polars, which are generally considered to be non-magnetic CVs.

On May 18, 2015, the very high energy (VHE, E > 0.1 TeV) gamma-ray band observed by the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) showed a very bright flare from the direction of PKS 2155-304. Observations in other bands with ground-based gamma- and lower-energy telescopes as well as space-based telescopes (including *Fermi) showed that this was likely due to a gamma-ray flaring blazar, an AGN whose jets are pointed closely toward the Earth. This is the first time that a blazar has been observed in very high energy gamma rays, and the emission was most likely due to accelerated electrons and positrons spiraling in the extremely strong magnetic fields of the blazar jet. This represents the fourth detected TeV blazar flare, all of which were observed by CTA, and the first time that a detection has been made with ground-based telescopes.

Noncommutative tori arise as ubiquitous symmetry structures of condensed matter systems, appearing in Hamiltonians for electrons in periodic potentials, magnetic materials, and atomic chains on periodic lattices. In this paper, we show how the notions of topological stability and dynamical stability for sequences of representations of a dynamical system influence the formulation of a noncommutative torus in the corresponding representation Hilbert space. From this, we motivate the definition of a noncommutative torus with trivial dynamical and topological structure, which we show arises as a quasi-equivalence bimodule between these two noncommutative tori. Using this framework, we obtain a novel expression for the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence for the noncommutative torus, and use it to exhibit families of noncommutative tori arising as quasi-equivalences between given ones. This structure allows us to demonstrate a dichotomy between Connes fibrations of the unit interval into noncommutative tori, with and without minimal dilations. We also prove that all noncommutative tori arise as quasi-equivalence bimodules between these minimal dilations, which yields a classification of noncommutative tori up to quasi-equivalence. By applying these results to an operator built from the Poisson semigroup, we obtain a stability characterization of noncommutative tori corresponding to spectral measures of stable ergodic dynamical systems. Finally, we use this framework to demonstrate a spectral flow rigidity result for the noncommutative torus with trivial dynamical and topological structure. We conclude with a discussion of our results, and several open problems suggested by our investigations. Keywords: noncommutative torus, Connes fibration, Riemann-Hilbert correspondence, dynamical system, spectral flow Note: the above is a summary of an extensive paper of the same title. The full paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.12304

Over the last few decades, biological research has revealed many examples of how adaptation can lead to evolutionarily stable configurations, or adapted states. Such adaptation can occur at many levels, ranging from changes in protein levels and enzyme activity, to changes in cellular differentiation and growth. The driving force behind adaptation is often the discrepancy between the current environment and an adapted state; and the adaptation process can often be described by fitness landscape theory. While adaptation is ubiquitous in biology, the biochemical mechanisms underlying adaptation are often unique to specific systems. Here, we show that a generic network architecture allows for adaptive growth rate regulation. This network architecture consists of a pathway that can produce an adapted state, connected to a reporter that measures the current environment. The reporter is typically a protein or enzyme with a readily detectable phenotype, but does not necessarily affect the adapted state. We demonstrate that such a network, when coupled to a fitness landscape, can undergo directional selection towards an adapted state. The adaptation is characterized by a transition in the reporter signal, from insensitive to mildly or strongly responsive, with the overall growth rate of the system conserved. Several biological examples, including catabolite repression in yeast and DNA damage signalling in mammalian cells, are shown to display such a reporter-mediated adaptation. This generic network architecture provides an explanation for how adaptation can lead to evolutionarily stable configurations, and how such adaptation can occur at many different levels of biological organisation.

Planets are formed through the gravitational process of accumulation and concentration of dust and gas around growing dust particles in star systems. While single star systems are the norm in the Universe, ~>95% of all star systems host at least one planet-mass companion. The detection of earth-like planets, and the rapid characterization of these planets via the radial velocity technique has revealed that earth-like planets are common around single stars. However, these planet detection missions have not observed the same prevalence of earth-like planets in binary or higher order systems. This suggested there could be some unknown processes which suppress the formation of planets in these systems. In this work, we analyze the process of planet formation in multiple star systems and find that the dynamical interactions between planets and planetesimals are suppressed due to the formation of multiple stable regions of the dust disk. We also find that the cores of planetesimals that are naturally depleted via streaming instabilities are replenished by the decay of marginally stable eccentric satellites that can efficiently deliver material to the planetesimal radius. We find that this process is naturally expected to produce earth-mass planets in roughly 20% of all multiple star systems.

We consider the non-relativistic limit of the Einstein equation. We show that the resulting equations of motion are the geodesic equations of an effective metric which depends on the particle's four-momentum. The effective metric is singular when the particle has light-like four-momentum. The resulting light-like geodesics exhibit the finiteness of the light-like interval, suggesting the possibility of singularity avoidance. We illustrate our results with the case of static, spherical mass distributions. We provide an independent derivation of our results in the Newtonian limit. Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics 2017 The authors are Anthony Jones, Julian Larena, Vincent Vizachero, and Eric Poisson Our goal in this short note is to analyze the Newtonian limit of Einstein's equation, leaving full general relativity for a later date. The argument is simple. Einstein's equation can be written as a pair of equations for the (conformal) metric and the (Einstein) Ricci curvature. One of these two equations is the trace of the other, so we are free to write either as a function of the other. We choose the latter route and find that the Newtonian limit of this equation is the geodesic equation for an effective metric which depends on the particle's four-momentum. The effective metric is singular when the particle has light-like four-momentum. The resulting light-like geodesics exhibit the finiteness of the light-like interval, suggesting the possibility of singularity avoidance. We illustrate our results with the case of static, spherical mass distributions. We provide an independent derivation of our results in the Newtonian limit. This note is a call for additional work and input. We hope to explore this intriguing possibility of gravitational self-interactions in a future publication. PS. We realize this is somewhat disjoint from the primary goal of this arXiv website, but we submit this simply to share our results before we publish a longer article elsewhere.
