Algorithmic reduction is a fundamental and challenging problem. By now, two distinct but related logics of algorithmic reduction have been developed and explored. One focuses on computational complexity, and is based on relativization. The other focuses on language shift, and is based on Rewrite Rule Semantics (RRS). This work unifies these two logics by introducing a novel intermediate level called behavioral equivalence, and develops a framework to capture both computational and language shift aspects of algorithmic reduction in a unified way. As a by-product, this framework greatly simplifies and systematizes the previous work on both relativization and RRS. We illustrate the usefulness of our framework by applying it to a series of long-standing open problems, including Champarna’s open problem on the limits of nonuniform samplings, and finally settling it for any $n$, any samplings allowed. Moreover, we propose parameterized solutions to two-sidedif and three-sided pathfinders, and show their equivalence to a well-known open problem on related classes of pushdown systems. We also show that a seemingly different problem called testing emptiness of L systems, which has been a major open problem for more than three decades, is captured by our framework as well.

In this work, the main characteristics of the imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescope system at the Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma (CODATA Position: 17.908,-63.716) are presented. The CATS (CTA Core Arrays for the Telescope System) collaboration was created with the purpose of developing the technological requirements, studying the technical challenges, and performing the feasibility study for the future next-generation Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). Currently, the CATS collaboration includes 13 institutions from seven countries. The collaboration has created an own detector model that simulates CTA-like configurations with different systems and choices of novel technology. The results show that the expected sensitivity for the detection of very high energy gamma-rays is within the level of current observatories, like HAWC or the future CTA in some regions of interest. However, significant improvements on the sensitivity and angular resolution for photon energies below 1 TeV can be obtained with the Cherenkov Telescope Array, particularly in the case of the CODATA position.

Galaxies across a wide range of cosmic time and environments can be roughly segregated into two distinct populations based on their color: Blue cloud galaxies predominantly span the range −16.7 < $g - r$ < 5.6, with significant number density at $g - r$ < −20.5 and $g - r$ > 5.6; red sequence galaxies, predominantly spanning −0.3 < $g - r$ < 1.3, have significant number density at $g - r$ > −0.3. These two populations are commonly thought to be the product of major and rapid wet merger events, respectively, or the gradual transformation of early-type galaxies via their central black holes radiatively heating their interstellar media (– –). We present an analysis of the normalized color magnitude distribution of field galaxies to z~3. These data show that, while the color distribution of blue cloud galaxies is consistent with a passive evolution of a Gaussian star formation history, the high-redshift population is best modeled by a passively evolving, non-Gaussian-distributed galaxy number density evolution (AND/GPB models), whereAND refers to the faint-end Gaussian rise, and GPB refers to a bright-end power-law fall. The amount of star formation at high-redshift must have been extraordinarily rapid, such that galaxies at the bright end of the distribution are evolving passively today. We propose a physical model for this evolution involving a system of Pop III stars photo-dissociating H2 in the early Universe, which allow galaxies to rapidly transition from a blue to red population. In addition to affecting the blue cloud, this process likely contributed to the red sequence at high-redshift, explaining the steep faint-end slope of the red sequence evolution and the steep bright-end rise of the blue cloud distribution. This is the first direct evidence for Pop III star formation at redshifts > 6, and highlights their vital role in galaxy evolution.

Using density-functional theory in the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) and including a mean-field Hubbard-U correction for the iron atom, we simulate the porphinoids, the conjugated rings of heme that bind oxygen-rich blood. This first-principles approach gives the electronic structure, density, spin density, and magnetic properties of the oxygen-bound water and carbonmonoxy complexes, and of carbonmonoxy as a function of pressure. The calculation explains the anomalous behavior of C-O bond length and spin state compared to experiment, and it promises improvements in calculated heats of formation and spin state energetics. The approach paves the way for spin-state energetics and molecular properties in other bioinorganic systems that are challenging to simulate with standard DFT. Iron atoms in porphinoid models bind oxygen-rich blood with colors ranging from red to orange depending on the number of oxygen atoms. The stability of these complexes under physiological conditions is crucial for biological function. For example, myoglobin, the oxygen carrier in muscle, changes color from red to purple upon oxidation to oxymyoglobin. Although heme is an essential cofactor in several enzymes, such as cytochromes, catalases, and peroxidases, its energetic stability is challenged by the thermodynamics of the spin state and the covalent geometry of its C-O bond. High-spin iron has a four-electron fee forO bond, whereas low-spin iron has an imperfectly saturated porphin ring, with a formal iron(IV) center. Although the identities of the true spin state of heme and myoglobin remain debated, spin state energetics is a central topic in bioinorganic chemistry and molecular biology. It influences, for example, the g-values of electron-spin resonance spectra and the thermodynamics of oxygen binding and the electron transfer reactions catalyzed by heme enzymes. Furthermore, stable hemes require precise control of spin state in applications such as oxygen sensing, biolabels, and biomimetic catalysts. Current methods for calculating spin state energetics from first principles are unable to explain the anomalous bond lengths and spin state of heme and myoglobin. We present the first-principles calculation of porphinoids (the conjugated rings of heme), including the water- and carbonmonoxy complexes. This approach recovers the correct bond length and spin state, explaining why heme and myoglobin have the spin states they do. With this achievement, DFT+U opens the possibility of predicting the energetic stability of other bioinorganic complexes. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are powered by accreting massive black holes in their centers. Over millions of years, gas in galaxies gets funneled toward the center of the galaxy, where it is compressed and heated by the black hole, and finally falls toward the black hole itself. In the process of falling, the gas collapses onto the black hole and forms an accretion disc. While the accretion process is very active, surrounding gas can be disturbed, and as a result star formation can be triggered. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as AGN feedback. To test this scenario, we obtained adaptive optics assisted spectra of the region around the Seyfert 1 galaxy NGC 1068, which is one of the closest AGN. We found several hundred solar masses of young stars in the region only 15 pc away from the center of the AGN. At the same time, there is no sign of current star formation in this region. This implies that the star formation was caused by the previous activity of the AGN, and was most likely triggered by AGN outflows. We also performed radiative transfer modeling of the gas, and tested if such high star formation rates are possible. We find that the high star formation surface density is consistent with being directly related to the amount of AGN outflowing material, suggesting a strong connection between the two processes.

The anionic graft copolymers of methacryloyloxyethylphosphorylcholine and vinylpyrrolidone (PlyMPC) and stearyl methacrylate serve as stabilizing building blocks for the self-assembly into nanoparticles under formation of non-covalent interactions at low pH. The characterization of the resulting soluble nanoparticles includes determination of average diameter, analysis of size distribution, analysis of the presence of aggregates using light scattering, and determination of the zeta potential. It was determined that the diameter of the resulting nanoparticles ranges from approximately 130 to 270 nm, the size distribution is rather narrow with a width of approximately 40-80%, and no signs of aggregates were present. The zeta potential is highly negative with a value of approximately -40 mV. The presence of the stabilizing building blocks PlyMPC, stearyl methacrylate, and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), acting as a size and charge stabilizer, is further confirmed by 1H NMR spectroscopy. The results indicate that the assembly of these building blocks into nanoparticles is possible at low pH.

The discovery of quasars with small masses (mbh < 10^6$) and low-mass black holes in the local universe (z < 0.3) has led to the development of scaling relationships between the mass of supermassive black holes (Mbh) and other properties of their hosts, such as the velocity dispersion of the host bulge (sigma) or the luminosity of the galaxy (L). These scaling relationships are typically interpreted as indications of co-evolution between the growth of supermassive black holes and the host galaxy, with the former affecting the latter, either directly or indirectly. The discovery of a tight correlation between Mbh and host galaxy velocity dispersion at low black hole masses has been used to argue for a top-down mechanism, in which seeds of black holes formed during the early growth of galaxies, and then grew by gas-accretion after the host became a distinct galaxy. Such low-mass black holes would be difficult to grow by accretion in the hot halo of the larger black hole, and so may require a substantially longer time for co-evolution to operate. We test this hypothesis by using the Sloan Digital Sky Survey selection function to generate mock datasets with the observed black hole-host scaling relationships, and analyzing these in the same way as previous observational studies. We find that the datasets with the observed scaling relationships produce a stronger correlation between Mbh and sigma than the datasets without the scaling relationships, even when using conservative statistical methods for detecting correlations. However, our results depend on the (relatively arbitrary) choice of parameters for generating the mock datasets, and we are unable to rule out alternate scenarios in which the scaling relationships are generated by correlated noise. Further observations with improved control of systematics, especially at low black hole masses, would be valuable for fully testing the significance of the scaling relationships.

Weak lensing surveys allow us to study structures on large scales, making them powerful tools to test cosmological models and search for subtle signatures of gravity. To extract the largest possible information from these surveys, it is desirable to break the degeneracy between the lensing potential and the cosmological parameters, which introduces cross-correlation between different redshift bins. Although ground-based telescopes provide the required precision for these cross-correlations, space is much more advantageous due to the high accessible volume and the reduced cloud coverage. Here, we present the first results of a lensing tomographic analysis with weak lensing reconstructions in 8 redshift bins from space with Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) onboard the Hubble Space Telescope (HST). We combine this with accurate, simultaneous optical and near-infrared photometry from the VisibleISS. We find very good agreement with current ground-based results with similar quality datasets, with errors of ~0.35 on the galaxy bias parameter and ~0.1 on the mass ratio spectrum. This technique has the potential to achieve 0.1% uncertainty on cosmological parameters from cosmic shear with WFC3 and the VisibleISS, as well as break parameter degeneracies with other imaging surveys with similar telescopes.

Recent observations have demonstrated that Barnard 68 is likely no longer bound to the Sun, but instead resides in a distant Centaur orbit with a semi-major axis of approximately 34au and an eccentricity of 0.19. The calculation of core-envelope structures suggests that 68 cannot have retained its icy envelope after its host system formed. Instead, we suggest that 68—like many other distant Centaurs—formed beyond the Classical Solar System and was subsequently implanted into the current location of Barnard 68 by a recently disintegrated comet or asteroid. The previous existence of an icy envelope would imply that 68 formed beyond the proposed water snow line at 20au, and thus provides further evidence for an outward migration of planet formation. We calculate the ionization of Barnard 68’s atmosphere and compare it with that of several other Centaurs and Kuiper Belt Objects. The strong dissociation of 68’s atmosphere indicates that Barnard 68 is likely the most primordial Centaur currently known.

The formation of massive stars is closely linked to the formation of globular clusters, as the most massive stars evolve into compact remnants—black holes and neutron stars—that are required to unbind globular clusters through their energetic core-collapse supernova explosions. Thus, the formation of massive stars is intimately tied to the process of globular cluster formation. In this regard, massive stars can be used to probe the density of the surrounding matter, which can in turn be used to characterize the formation environment of globular clusters. Early work found that the masses of young massive stars were distributed around the center of their host molecular clouds with low probabilities that could not be explained by Poisson noise. This observed offset, which is commonly known as the “massive star dispersals,” was first interpreted as evidence for expulsion of the clouds from massive star clusters via three-body interactions involving the massive stars themselves, as has been shown to be possible via high-precision collisional calculations. However, more recent work has cast doubt on the likelihood of three-body interactions disrupting the parent molecular clouds, and it has been suggested that rapidly-moving clouds may not be able to withstand the tides generated by massive stars during their explosive burning phases. New calculations have shown that the observed offset distributions are consistent with purely statistical fluctuations arising from a small number of massive stars, and that there is no evidence for massive stars disrupting their parent clouds. Thus, the formation of massive stars is still poorly understood, and further studies aimed at measuring the local densities of their parent molecular clouds may be required to better characterize the environment in which globular cluster formation takes place.

Star formation is an important process in the evolution of galaxies, as it provides new members to the subsequent stellar population and injects energy and momentum into the interstellar medium (ISM). In this work, we use the FIRE-1 cosmological simulation, which follows the dynamical evolution of baryon only, from high redshift, $z\approx16$, to the present day, $z=0$, to explore star formation in galaxies of different masses. We calculate the molecular, atomic and dusty star formation rates (SFRs) for each galaxy and find that the bimodality in galaxy property space is driven primarily by the relative distribution of these SFRs. The high-mass galaxies, which dominate at high redshift, have high atomic and molecular SFRs but have suppressed dust-enshrouded SFR due to the limited available cold gas. In contrast, lower-mass galaxies have relatively less cold gas but have elevated amounts of dust-obscured star formation. We construct histories for the stellar and halo masses of individual galaxies and find that the two trends are linked. Galaxies that are more gas-rich have both larger stellar and halo masses and higher rates of growth. Conversely, galaxies with larger stellar or halo masses are more efficient at funneling gas to the central regions where star formation can proceed. In addition, we find that star formation rate density (SFRD) peaks at $z\approx2-3$ for all galaxies and that the relative contributions from the different modes of star formation change with time.

A longsword into the bizarre: NGC6908 is a barred spiral galaxy located in the Ursa Major constellation. Discovered by Barnard in 1916, it was later observed by van den Bergh in 1967 to have an unusual feature: a small secondary bar inside the main one. As more observational data became available, the second bar seemed to get bigger and bigger, until it finally decoupled from the main one. This is probably the most bizarre galaxy ever observed. NGC6908 is located at a distance of approximately 85 megaparsecs, or 290 million light years. It has a diameter of about 80,000 light-years and a mass of about 6.9 billion times that of the Sun. It is visible with the naked eye and has been studied extensively. It was assigned the designation 7436-02 in the 'Late Printed Blue Catalog' of Mark Watkins. The galaxy exhibits a main bar and a smaller secondary bar. The latter got so big that it finally decoupled from the main one and formed a new larger bar. Photographic evidence of the secondary bar goes back to 1967, and there are even studies dating back to 1901 which mention it. Why is this such a big deal? Well, so far no evidence of a spiral galaxy having multiple bars has ever been found. Multiple bars are quite common in spiral galaxies with several different classifications being used to distinguish between different types of multiple bars. NGC6908, however, seems to be an anomoly. Observations show that the secondary bar slowly grew over time as gas from its circumnuclear region was funnelled to the main bar. As the two bars became more and more different, their relative strengths started to differ as well. When the secondary bar finally decoupled, its stars were set on a collision course with those of the main bar. This likely explains the large stellar bar in the centre of NGC6908 as well as the offset distribution of its 2nd and 4th brightest nuclear ring structures from the principal bar. All in all, this galaxy is an oddity in several ways: not only does it have two bars, it also seems to have grown more and more separate from the point of view of its general appearance and behaviour over time. As this phenomenon has never been observed before, we can only speculate about what causes it and what its long-term effects will be. The small separation between the two bars, for example, could mean that they interact or even merge in the future. We will have to wait and see. In this paper, we construct a general $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{EM}$ sigma model with external sources, dynamical breaking and spontaneous vacuum symmetry breaking. The model has a global $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{EM}$ symmetry and contains gauge fields, a three-index antisymmetric tensor field, a dilaton field, and three complex scalar fields in the representation $\mathcal{R}=(\mathbf{2},\mathbf{2},0)$. The bosonic Lagrangian is constructed by using the method of covariant differentiation. We show that the model has a global $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{EM}$ symmetry and dynamical breaking of the symmetry to the subgroup $U(1)_{EM}$. At the same time, the model has a vacuum where the symmetry is spontaneously broken to $U(1)_{EM}$. In this vacuum, the Faddeev-Popov ghost terms and the gauge-fixing terms become invariant under the global symmetry. The global symmetry and the gauge symmetry are both broken by the vacuum and the gauge boson masses are generated. This theory may provide a consistent description of the low-energy world, including the standard model (SM) particle spectrum and weak and strong interactions, as well as a new particle spectrum including spin-0 and -2 particles. Our model is motivated by the recent discovery of the Higgs particle with a mass of about 125 GeV. In our model, the scalar fields $\sigma_i$ ($i=1,2,3$) have vacuum expectation values (VEVs) and give mass to the gauge bosons, while the three gauge-neutral fields $\chi_i$ have masses of the order of the scale of dynamical symmetry breaking (DSSB) $f$. This scale can be naturally as large as the Planck scale, if we take the coupling constants of the model to be of the order of one. The three gauge-neutral fields $\chi_i$ form a complex Higgs field which is a reasonable substitute for the SM Higgs field. The gauge-invariant composite field $\Sigma=\sigma_1+i\sigma_2$ also has a VEV, which causes the spontaneous breaking of the vacuum symmetry. The vacuum expectation value of the composite field $\Sigma$ generates a Majorana mass for the neutrinos, which is of the right order of magnitude to explain the neutrino mass. Besides the SM fermions and the Higgs field, we also predict new spin-0 and -2 particles, which can be tested in future experiments. As a consequence of the spontaneous vacuum symmetry breaking, the model also has a U(1) symmetry, under which the three Goldstone bosons $a_i$ become the longitudinal components of the gauge fields $W_i^{\pm}$ and $Z^0$. Intervening metal systems in the line of sight to Gamma-Ray Bursts and Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) offer the opportunity to measure the distribution of heavy elements in the early universe. Using observations from the Keck I telescope and Hubble Space Telescope, I examine the Carbon, Oxygen, and Magnesium distributions in the Universe back to z > 6.5. While Carbon and Oxygen remain relatively uniformly distributed, Magnesium is depleted at a 4.2σ significance level in the highest redshift QSO host, at z = 6.5. If the abundance pattern of the Milky Way (MW) interstellar medium (ISM) can be applied to these distant galaxies, the implied redshift of formation for the majority of this Mg depletion is z = 9.1 ± 2.3. If instead we apply the abundance pattern of the local group gas, the implied formation redshift is z = 6.5 ± 0.7. In the Gamma-Ray Burst host, a possible local group interloper at z = 0.48 is depleted at the 2.6σ level at z = 6.5, consistent with the formation at z = 9.1 ± 2.3. No depletion is observed in the highest redshift QSO and Gamma-Ray Burst sight-lines, at z = 6.5 ± 0.7 and 9.1 ± 2.3, respectively, suggesting that the first galaxies may not have undergone the same processes of chemical enrichment as local group gas. This study represents the first measurement of the chemical evolution of the early universe beyond the range of the EUCLID satellite, and will likely remain the most precise measurement until galaxies can be observed to significantly higher redshifts using the James Webb Space Telescope or other future telescopes.

Recent studies have shown that the iron Kα spectral line is emitted from regions close to the supermassive black hole (SMBH) in active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Timing studies of this emission could, in principle, yield information on the geometry and velocity field in the immediate vicinity of the black hole. By combining X-ray timing and continuum timing observations of the Seyfert galaxy NGC 3783, we demonstrate the existence of a correlation between the X-ray flux and the high-frequency (milliseconds) X-ray variability time delays. This correlation is consistent with reflection-based models for the X-ray emission, in which the X-rays incident on the accretion disk are scattered into our line of sight by cold electrons in a corona that surrounds the disk. We further demonstrate that the iron Kα emission is consistent with being emitted within a few gravitational radii of the black hole, lending support to the hypothesis that the X-ray flux is modulated at the black hole's fast-spinning rates. Our results demonstrate that X-ray timing observations can, in some cases, provide unique insight into the physical processes occurring close to supermassive black holes.

In numerical analysis, integration is the process of finding the numerical solution of a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) by a computer. Numerical integration of a system of ODEs starts with an initial condition, and generates a corresponding numerical solution. The numerical solution at a given timestep is called an integration step, and the total number of steps needed to reach a specified final time T is called the total simulation time. The numerical solution is an approximation of the exact solution of the ODEs, and has an associated numerical error. The objective in integrating a system of ODEs is to calculate the numerical solution with as low a numerical error as possible. The method of integration refers to the algorithm used to calculate the numerical solution. It is usually specified in the article associated with a simulation result, along with the step size and other simulation parameters. When the simulation result is expressed as a time series of numerical solutions, the method of integration is also referred to as a solver. Lie group methods are a class of techniques that allow the calculation of the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) by a computer. The equations are first transformed into an initial value problem (IVP), where the solution at a given timestep depends on the values assumed by the dependent variable at both the beginning and the end of the timestep. An important class of Lie group methods are Lie group integrators, which are derived from a infinitesimal approximation of the flow of the ODEs. These integrators are composed of a sequence of groups, each representing the flow of the ODEs over a small time interval. For a system of ODEs, the overall numerical solution is the composition of the groups. The numerical error of an integration step is controlled by the error in each group. The performance of Lie group methods depends on the structure of the differential equation, as the Lie group structure means that the flow of the ODEs can be broken down into a sequence of simpler flows. The computational cost is therefore generally proportional to the number of steps required to calculate the solution, rather than the number of ODEs. The method requires that the differential equation be divergence free, or exact, which is generally not true of the systems of ODEs that arise in applications. The divergence free constraint can be imposed a posteriori by subtracting a steady state solution. This can result in numerical oscillations if the steady state is unstable. To remove the steady state, the initial value problem can be completed (added a sink term) or an a priori knowledge of the long term behaviour of the solution can be used to prevent the numerical oscillations. Alternatively, weak Lie group methods may be used, which approximate the steady state and the long term behaviour, but do not enforce the divergence free constraint exactly. Lie group methods have found application in the analysis of differential equations. In particular, their application to Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) is founded

The plasma torus around Io, the smallest of the four Galilean satellites of Jupiter, has been the subject of numerous observations over the past several decades. Voyager, Galileo, and Cassini each made observations of the plasma torus, but only Cassini had the capability of making ultraviolet (UV) measurements of the torus. We present an analysis of the temporal and azimuthal variability of the torus using Cassini Ultraviolet Imaging Spectrometer (UVIS) observations from December 2000 to May 2006. Models of the plasma torus emission should account for thermal effects, non-LTE ionization and excitation, free electrons, and electron impact excitation and ionization. We compare two models, a two-fluid model, which has been successful at modeling the global atmosphere of Io, and a hydrodynamic model. While the two-fluid model has generally been adequate for modeling Io’s thermosphere and exosphere, it cannot model Io’s plasma torus. The hydrodynamic model has been successful at modeling the plasma torus, however it cannot explain the variations in emission observed by Cassini. This suggests that the variability of the plasma torus is caused by changes in the mass flux entering the torus.

Recent theoretical and experimental activities in ultracold gases have lead to a realization of isolated quantum systems with tunable interactions and unprecedented control. These systems, originally proposed for the experimental realization of correlated quantum phases and quantum dynamics optimization, now give access to a broad class of strongly correlated quantum systems whose complexity defies a na�ve description. Among those, one-dimensional Bose gases allow for the study of strongly correlated phases such as Mott insulators, solitonic excitations and superfluidity. Here we report on the experimental study of the dynamical properties of one-dimensional Bose gases via Bragg spectroscopy. By modulating the coupling between the gas and light waves, we engineer non-equilibrium quantum dynamics and access the intermediate-time dynamics where correlations play a role. We identify and characterize dynamical phase transitions between various regimes. In particular, we provide conclusive evidence for the dynamical Mott phase transition in the vicinity of the solitonic solution. This work paves the way for the experimental exploration of strongly correlated quantum dynamics in one-dimensional Bose gases and opens avenues for the study of the intricate connections between quantum and classical dynamics.

Quantum mechanics allows for the same physical system to be in different states, with each state corresponding to a different probability distribution. This concept of quantum indistinguishability, first proposed by Lev Landau, suggests that the act of observation in quantum mechanics changes the state of the system. In this paper, we propose that, in addition to changing the state of the system, observing a system also changes the effective number of particles associated with the system. We illustrate our argument with the example of a double-slit interference pattern, and show that the pattern observed may not reflect the actual interference pattern of the particles. However, we also show that the observed interference pattern may be reproduced by integrating the wave function over a region smaller than the slit width, which we argue is equivalent to observing only a portion of the system. We illustrate our argument with a simulation of single-photon interference using a quantum emulator, and show that our hypothesis holds true for this system. Our results suggest a novel form of uncertainty principle in quantum mechanics, where the act of observation not only prevents the exact determination of certain variables but also contributes to a new kind of uncertainty.

In this paper we consider the problem of variable selection in the linear regression model. We compare several algorithms for this problem, starting from a forward stagewise approach, which is known to be consistent, and ending with the recent nonconvex approach of cyclic and global minimization of the regularized loss with the $\ell_1$ norm. For the forward stagewise approach, we consider two versions: the standard version, which is also known to be consistent, but is known to select many false variables, and the modified forward stagewise algorithm, which has the advantage of not selecting many false variables, but might be inconsistent. For the nonconvex approaches, we use the penalty of Kurdyka and Mitrushak (2001) with the special case of totally monotone convolution kernel, which we call the monotone lasso. We show that this method is consistent and has an oracle property with the true model being a local minimizer of the penalized loss. We also show that this method is order-optimal for the convex case and prove its non-convex convergence.

In this short note we relate three notions that can be used to describe singularities of plane curves: ordinary singularities, quasi ordinary singularities and the support of the albanese dual curve of the curve. We show that, in the case of an ordinary singularity, the first and second notion are the same and coincide with the support of the albanese dual, i.e. the singularity is of type Q_8. In the case of a quasi ordinary singularity the notions differ but we give sufficient conditions to distinguish between these two types. Finally, we exhibit an example of a curve with a quasi ordinary singularity that is not ordinary and another one with an ordinary singularity that is not quasi ordinary. We deduce from these relations some consequences on the the existence of albanese maps of these singularities and on the structure of the arithmetical equivalence of plane curves. We assume the reader is familiar with the basic notions of scheme theory. If $f \in K[x,y]$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ we denote by $V(f)$ the projective curve defined by $f$ in $\mathbb{P}^{2}_K$, by $C$ the projective curve in $\mathbb{P}^{2}_K$ defined by $F$ and by $R$ its coordinate ring. We denote by $\overline{K(P)}$ an algebraic closure of the function field of a curve. If $P$ is a closed point of $\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\overline{K(P)}}$ then we denote by $\mathrm{ord}_P$ and $\mathrm{quord}_P$ the normalized value and the quasi normalized value of the formal affine equation of $\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\overline{K(P)}}$ at $P$ (see e.g. [\[\]]{} for the definition of normalized value). If $P \in \mathbb{P}^{2}_K$ is a closed point we denote by $\mathrm{Res}_{K(P)/K}$ the residue class field of $P$ and by $e(P)= \mathrm{ord}_P \mathrm{Res}_{K(P)/K}$ the absolute ramification index of $P$. If $f \in R$ is a nonzero polynomial we denote by $\mathrm{supp} (f)$ the support of $f$. We say that $P \in \mathbb{P}^{2}_K$ is an ordinary singularity of $C$ if the local ring of $\mathbb{P}^{2}_K$ at $P$ is a discrete valuation ring and the residue class field $\mathrm{Res}_{K(P)/K}$ is equal to $\overline{K(P)}^m$ for some $m \geq 0$. The weighted complexity and the determinant functions of graphs are defined. These two new graph invariants generalizes several existing graph invariants such as vertexcover, edgecover, matching, determinant, branching number, independence number and total graph domination number. Weights are assigned to the vertices according to their importance in the sense that vertices with higher weights are preferred. We show that the weighted complexity of a graph is equal to the matching complexity of the line graph of the graph, and the determinant of a graph is equal to the branch-width of the line graph of the graph. We give several relationships between these invariants. In particular, we show that the weighted complexity and the determinant are both lower bounds for the matching complexity, branching number and independence number. On the other hand, we give two graphs with different weights for which the weighted complexity and the determinant are the same but their matching complexity and branch-width are different. We conclude by observing that the problem of computing the weighted complexity and the determinant is -complete even when the weights are all one.

In this study, we present a method to analyze structural properties on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) that can be applied on multiple domains, for example, speech, text, or images. As a first step, the given HMM is converted to a profile HMM. Profile HMMs capture the interdependence between observation and state emission probabilities, which enables us to derive a set of structural equations that can be used to calculate the probability of any given sequence of observations given the HMM. We apply our method to four popular HMM architectures for text: the HMM, the Baum-Welch HMM, the left-to-right HMM, and the bilateral HMM. We show that our method correctly recovers the HMM structure for the given examples, while showing that the Baum-Welch and left-to-right HMMs do not accurately model the given data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to images and shows that the HMM is an appropriate model for raw pixel data.

A Type Ib supernova (SN Ib) is generally believed to be the explosion of a star that lacks hydrogen and/or helium in its outer layers. Such a star is known as a Wolf-Rayet (WR) star. The most commonly accepted theory to explain the disappearance of the hydrogen layer is a two-step process in which the stellar envelope is stripped by the pulsational mass loss of a non-H superbubble. To explain the observations, hydrogen-free (helium-free) SN Ib models must possess several unique characteristics. First, hydrogen-free but helium-rich ejecta must dominate the early-time spectrum, with helium becoming more slowly-scattered than hydrogen at $\sim$30 days after the explosion. Second, the photosphere must be located in helium-rich regions at later times. Third, the photospheric velocities and kinetic energy of the ejecta must be low. The latter two characteristics arise from the high compactness of the helium core. Using the comprehensive non-LTE radiative-transfer code [tardis]{}, we have calculated several detailed spectra for a large set of hydrogen-free, but helium-rich, SN Ib models. Our approach differs significantly from previous works in that we have considered the full spectral energy distribution from radio to X-rays; we account for line blocking and scattering; and we have included an extensive treatment of Doppler shifts from the asphericities in the ejecta. We also investigate the influence of heavy-element condensation on the opacities. We discuss the key discriminating features between our models and current observational constraints. The most distinguishing features between our models and current observations are (1) the photospheric location (i.e., helium-rich vs. hydrogen-rich), and (2) the photospheric velocities (i.e., low vs. high). These properties can be attributed to the compactness of the helium core. The compactness parameter is related to the mass, radius, and central density of the helium core, and is approximately equal to the ratio of the mantle mass to the core mass. The compactness parameter, η, controls the essential opacities and thus has a strong influence on the time evolution of the photospheric radius and velocity. In our models, the helium core mass ranges from 0.6 to 1.2 M⊙, the mantle mass is similar to or slightly less than the core mass, and the corresponding η ranges from 0.2 to 0.5. For the less compact models, η < 0.3, the photospheric velocity is relatively high (∼12,000 km s−1), and the photosphere is positioned in a hydrogen-rich region (near 60 days after the explosion). For the more compact models, η ≥ 0.4, the photospheric velocity is lower (∼9,000 km s−1) and the photosphere is positioned in a helium-rich region (near 100 days after the explosion

With rapid increase of human population and development of industry, water shortage is becoming a critical issue for human beings. It is estimated that by 2025, about 58.5 million people will be affected by water stress. In addition, most of the world’s population relies heavily on fossil fuels to meet their energy needs. This trend of energy consumption will significantly increase greenhouse emissions and global climate change. These factors raise the question of how to use water and energy from the air, which is the most abundant substance in the universe. Water vapor is the most abundant solute in the atmosphere, and can be captured with existing technologies. The captured water vapor can be used for numerous beneficial applications, such as: production of fresh water, production of hydrogen fuel, and etc. This process can be implemented at a large scale and is economically feasible. Meanwhile, the captured energy can be used to vaporize the water and generate green electricity. Thus, the dual use of water and energy from the air can significantly alleviate water shortage and decrease carbon emission simultaneously.

Neutral genetic drift, a form of genetic polymorphism occurring due to random genetic mutations, can aid protein sequence evolution. Such a scenario may occur frequently during early protein evolution, when long protein sequences are less likely to contain strongly deleterious mutations. Under this model, although most new mutations are deleterious, some are weakly beneficial or even neutral. These weakly beneficial mutations fix by chance in a population, because their slightly increased frequencies are due to genetic drift. Due to their small effect, these weakly beneficial mutations do not contribute to an organism's Darwinian fitness. However, they contribute to protein sequence evolution, by helping compensate for the negative effect of strongly deleterious mutations. This "fine-tuning" through neutral drift can increase the organism's protein functionality and Darwinian fitness, even though its average fitness is still close to zero. In contrast to previously proposed protein adaptation scenarios, this model explains how protein functionality can be maintained over long periods of time in the absence of positive Darwinian selection.

DNA hashing (or DNA hash, dna hash) is an advanced hashing technique to generate short, fixed-length hash values from long, variable-length sequences of nucleotide bases. It was first proposed by Chew et al. [1], and was shown to be highly resistant to hash collision attacks [2, 3]. In 2014, DNA hashing was adopted by the EU FP7 ProjectDNA Consortium for building EU digital DNA sequences [4]. In late 2017, DNA hashing was adopted by Google for generating short nucleotide sequences, called Thumbprints, for authentication and identification purposes [5]. In 2018, DNA hashing was proposed for protecting digital signatures [6]. In 2019, DNA hashing was adopted by Apple for generating secure key files for TouchID [7] and for encrypting user photos on the Apple Photos service [8]. In 2020, DNA hashing was proposed for generating secure and unique biometric identifiers [9] and for addressing the jitter issue of fingerprint sensors [10]. DNA hashing is also adopted by Google for digital identifier protection [11]. It was shown that DNA hashing can protect the privacy and security of digital identifier users [12]. As a digital identifier is often correlated with sensitive information (such as fingerprint information, facial recognition information, and biometric identification information), DNA hashing can protect the privacy and security of the identifier owner. DNA hashing shares the same basic principles as cryptography-based one-time password (OTP) schemes. Like cryptography-based OTP schemes, DNA hashing protects against offline password recovery attacks by incorporating a unique salt into the hash function. Like cryptography-based OTP schemes, DNA hashing enables password change without exposing old passwords, because old password hashes cannot be reused to calculate new hash values. Unlike cryptography-based OTP schemes, DNA hashing can generate and memorize short, fixed-length hash values from long, variable-length sequences of nucleotide bases, thereby significantly reducing the storage and computation costs. DNA hashing was also designed to satisfy other design requirements. For example, it should satisfy the hardware constraints of the embedded system, as it can be implemented in low-cost, small-footprint circuits. It should be compatible with existing Watson and MegHash hardware architectures. It should be extendible to multiple algorithmic choices. It should be easily expandable to different signature schemes. We believe that DNA hashing is a novel, promising digital identifier technology, with important security, privacy, and usability advantages over existing technologies. -- First Author: Kun Qian Xiamen University, China Last Modified: 26 March 2023 -- Kun Qian is the first author of this paper. The paper was last modified in March 2023. This is a long abstract, but it gives a good overview of the field of DNA hashing, an application of the technique,

The electronic properties of dry DNA have attracted considerable interest in the recent years due to the potential applications in electronic technologies. The electronic properties of dry DNA are significantly different from those of its hydrated counterpart. For example, dry DNA has much higher conductivity and becomes semiconducting at room temperature. Understanding the electronic properties of dry DNA is important for its potential applications in electronic technologies and DNA-based sensors. Despite the great technological importance, the electronic structure and mechanism of dry DNA has not been fully understood. In this work, we developed a multiscale model for dry DNA which can capture its electronic transport behaviors from the atomic scale to the macroscopic scale. The local structure of a stretch of dry DNA is modeled using the energy functional theory. A transport model is developed using the tight-binding method to describe the electronic transport behavior of the full stretch of dry DNA. The developed model can capture the electronic transport behaviors from the atomic scale to the macroscopic scale and represents a major step forward for understanding the electronic structure and mechanism of dry DNA.

Two-band superconductors, also known as multi-band superconductors, occur in nature in some heavy fermion systems, and in particular in multi-band correlated superconductors such as (oxy)aniline, (oxy)nitrosulfatemediated by copper and sulfur (eg. sulfur passivated regions in oxyacetylene or sulfur doped iron pnictides). The oxyacetylene-based oxy nitrates (e.g. La(OCH(CH3)2)0.9Ce0.1NO3) have two strongly overlapping bands near the Fermi level originating from the oxygen p and σ* orbitals. Here we report resonant inelastic x-ray scattering experiments on a sulfur doped sample revealing the coupling between the two bands at low energy. The results are compared with recent specific heat and muon spin relaxation measurements performed on a similar sulfur doped compound which reveal evidence of fluctuating full gap and nodal states, respectively, at low temperatures. These results suggest that the full superconducting gap may be closed and reopened by small additional internal or external perturbations, making these systems good candidates for further studies of exotic superconductivity such as topological superconductivity or phase separation.

The neutron rich oxygen isotopes have been studied using the shell model quantum Monte Carlo (SMQMC) method. It was found that both theintrinsic, i.e. the two neutron hole coupled to the two proton vacancy, and the two neutron particle-hole coupling configurations play a significant role in the behaviour of these nuclei. It was observed that both the size and the nature of the deformed single particle energies are crucial for the detailed behaviour of these nuclei. In particular, the ground state is favored for ^{24}O, presumably because of the closed spherical shell, whereas for the neighboring nuclei, the high lying 2$^{+}$ state is mostly favored. The results presented in this work will be helpful in planning further studies of these nuclei with more complex interactions. The paper [1] was authored by Alia Mugford, Eric Navbras, Anthony G. Martin and Tomasz Malawski and submitted to arXiv.org on 22nd December 2022. It has been validated and is currently being processed for publication.

A long-standing problem in cosmology is to explain the observed isotropy of the sky. One of the main arguments against an early period of anisotropy is the relatively low degree of isotropy on scales of the order of the size of the Earth's orbit about the sun (i.e., approximately 30 degrees). In recent years, several groups have claimed to observe higher degrees of anisotropy on smaller scales. These include, for example, regions of the sky devoid of galaxies and quasars, high-density regions within large-scale voids, and the entire gravitational wave horizon. In this work, we perform a direct, all-sky comparison of the Hubble diagrams of the northern and southern hemispheres. We compute the ratio of the distances to galaxies (i.e., the Hubble parameter) separately for each hemisphere and find no significant evidence for anisotropy. The best-fit amplitude of anisotropy, as determined from our analysis, is |2%|, which is consistent with the currently observed sensitivities of measurements of anisotropy on large angular scales.

In this paper, we consider the energy-efficient resource allocation in wireless networks with both bandwidth and quality-of-service (QoS) constraints. We consider the most energy-consuming communication event in wireless networks, i.e., channel access, as the performance metric and provide an algorithm to minimize this metric subject to different constraints, including the bandwidth and QoS constraints. Due to the coupled structure among these constraints, the traditional optimization techniques cannot be directly applied. We first decouple the constraints and then propose an iterative optimization algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. In a recent comment, "Essence of intrinsic tunnelling: Distinguishing intrinsic features from artefacts", Abhishek Kasliwal and Yogesh Jaiswal (arXiv:2004.12376 [quant-ph], APPNL-PRL) make several objections to an earlier paper, "Intrinsic features of quantum tunneling", Yi-Xin Liu, Hai-Yao Ma, Xiao-Dong Song, and Weiping Zhang (arXiv:1903.10262 [quant-ph], arXiv:2004.12376 [quant-ph] submitted to PRL). We address these objections point by point in this reply. In addition, we show that the results of the recent comment contradict an earlier one of the same authors. The essence of intrinsic tunnelling: Distinguishing intrinsic features from artefacts https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12376 Abhishek Kasliwal, Yogesh Jaiswal Abstract: Intrinsic tunnelling has recently been shown to occur in systems without regard to explicit consideration of intrinsic dynamics. However, a recent comment claims that intrinsic tunnelling is an artefact of considering a system without an explicit intrinsic dynamics. Here, we show that such a claim is incorrect by responding to the points made in the comment.

In this work, we explore how observations of the Dark Ages, the Epoch of Reionization, and the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) can be used to determine the energy density of dark energy (the 68% confidence regions shown). We use measurements of the optical depth to reionization (Planck) and the gamma-ray opacity (eROSITA, the Extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope array) to place conservative upper limits on the contribution of dark energy. In the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, these combined bounds rule out 26% of models with a spatially-flat dynamical dark energy, and 56% of non-flat models. This can be improved by combining with large-scale structure information, though not all models that are consistent with other data are also consistent with these low-redshift probes of dark energy. We explore the impact of relaxing assumptions about the astrophysical priors, finding that under reasonable assumptions these data alone still significantly restrict the parameter space of many popular dark energy models.

The standard model (SM) is the most successful theory in describing elementary particles. However, several theoretical problems suggest the need for a more comprehensive framework. Two notable examples are the hierarchy problem and the unnaturaliveness of the coupling constants. Furthermore, theories with higher spatial dimensions and theories with supersymmetry (SUSY) have been shown to be highly consistent with the SM predictions. In this work, we consider theories with an additional spatial dimension compactified on a wall, and show that this minimal modification to the SM leads to a consistent theory with surprisingly few free parameters. We then study the localization of various SM fields to zero and two dimensions, and demonstrate the unique properties of the electroweak interactions on the wall. In particular, we show that the weak scale wall radion and Higgs may provide a solution to the hierarchy problem and that the observed weak mixing angle may be explained by the higher-dimensional nature of the Higgs field. Furthermore, the radion develops a mass of the order of TeV through a Stückelberg mechanism, and can provide an explanation for the Fermileran collider resonances.

A widely accepted and broadly used method to clean a dirty floor is a gravity method. It starts with piling up the dirty stuff in the middle of the floor and letting it flow to the edges. The obvious problem here is that this may not completely clean the floor and as more and more dirty stuff accumulates in the middle, the floor may become dirtier. This article develops an alternative method which is to start with spraying some cleaner around the floor and let it spread around by gravitational force. The article then develops a probabilistic framework to analyze this method. First, it derives a probabilistic model for the amount of dirty stuff on the floor and uses it to calculate the probability that this method completely cleans the floor. Then it uses this result to answer the more important question of how much dirty stuff the method can clean up. This analysis reveals that for a moderately dirty floor, this method will completely clean the floor with a high probability, but the amount of dirty stuff it can clean up is only about 50% of the actual amount. The article then uses this result to propose a more efficient method which starts with twice as much cleaner and instead of spreading it around the floor, directs it to the areas with higher dirt density. This method can completely clean the floor and also clean up almost all the dirty stuff.

Radio emitting active galactic nuclei (AGN) are abundant at low and high redshift. The latter are known to host supermassive black holes (SMBH) with masses as high as 10^9-10^10 Msol, and it has been suggested that these SMBH could form seeds for supermassive black holes in the nuclei of galaxies at high redshift [1]. While their relevance in the early growth of supermassive black holes is well established, their role in the formation of galaxies has been more uncertain. The large growth time scales compared to the typical lifetimes of galaxies, as well as the negative impact of radio jets in galaxy clusters have led to the consensus that AGN feedback must be ineffective in this context [2-4]. I present cosmological simulations which suggest that radio feedback from SMBH can in fact have a profound influence on the growth of galaxies. AGN feedback operates via radio feedback, and here I focus on the feedback mechanism in cosmological context for the first time. The simulations presented in this work were performed with the state-of-the-art cosmological code Gizmo, which combines high resolution adaptive mesh refinement in the relevant region, with dark matter, radiative, and hydrodynamical physics. The inclusion of radio-mode AGN feedback, which couples the growth of SMBH to the host dark matter halo potential well, dramatically affects the population of central galaxies in the universe. These systems now show regular disks that are stable against catastrophic disk instabilities, as well as the frequent occurrence of bulges. Fully half of central galaxies in the simulation now have prominent bulges. In comparison to the similar runs without radio feedback, the difference is striking. This surprising result is in contrast to most theoretical studies, which tend to assume that radio feedback is either ineffective, or drives galactic winds that prevent the formation of cool, dense gas disks. The inclusion of radio feedback in these simulations is necessary to explain the observed correlations between the masses of central black holes and their host galaxies, in particular the "knee" of the distribution at 10^9 Msol. The direct connection between the two enables the SMBH to set the growth rate of the host galaxy, and thus regulate cold-gas accretion and star formation. Finally, we show that the inclusion of radiative feedback (cosmic rays) has the potential to substantially increase the impact of AGN feedback in galaxy formation, as it may inhibit the radio mode in low-accretion systems. These results suggest that radio feedback may have had a crucial role in the evolution of central galaxies in the universe, as well as in setting the observed population of galactic disks and bulges.

CP violation, a vital phenomenon in the era of the early universe, has also been observed in many aspects of modern particle physics. One of its important manifestations is the difference in the conjugate properties of the particles, such as the branching fractions of $B$ mesons that each of their parents is a different CP eigenstate. Here, we report a large, CP-violating, direct signal of $\bar{B}^0$ meson decays to $\rho^0(\omega)\rho^0(\omega)$, with $\omega \to \pi^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-$, where $\rho^0(\omega) \to \pi^+\pi^-$. The measured branching fraction is ${\cal B}(\bar{B}^0 \to \rho^0(\omega)\rho^0(\omega)) = (2.76 \pm 0.72({\rm stat}) \pm 0.32({\rm sys}))\times 10^{-6}$, which is two orders of magnitude larger than the previous best measurement and more than 7 standard deviations from the CP-conjugate channel $\bar{B}^0 \to \rho^0(\omega)\rho^0(0) \to \pi^+\pi^-\pi^+\pi^-$. The experimental study of CP violation is usually performed in the framework of the standard model (SM), and so far, no significant evidence of new physics has been found. Therefore, the observation of large direct CP violation in $\bar{B}^0$ meson decays would be a sign of new physics. The associated New Physics models with such possibility include supersymmetry, two Higgs doublet models, and left-right models. The present result is based on a data sample containing an integrated luminosity of 3.65 fb$^{-1}$ of $\bar{B}^0$ meson decays collected with the Belle detector at the KEKB collider. The main sources of systematic uncertainties in this measurement are the signal efficiency and the background shape.

Icosahedral model quasicrystals are very rare examples of natural quasicrystals with a long-range order. First discovered in 1993, their icosahedral symmetry has never been matched in human-made crystals. They have many remarkable mechanical properties (e.g. 5-fold quasicrystalline symmetry enhances their resistance against cleaving) and provide a nice laboratory for studying a myriad of interesting scientific problems. While quasicrystals have been intensively studied theoretically and numerically, their dynamic fracture properties are relatively unknown. In this work, we perform molecular dynamics simulations of quasicrystal cleavage. To model quasicrystal cleavage we performed molecular dynamics simulations of a system consisting of a 500 atoms piece of the quasicrystal face-centered cubic structure subjected to a moving blade mimicking brittle fracture. We observe a catastrophic failure of quasicrystals similar to previous observations in other systems with quasiperiodic order. However, as opposed to previous studies, we observe an extremely interesting micro-failure pattern. The failure is not homogenous and occurs at specific'motifs' that consist of five 'ice' particles arranged in a cubic lattice. In this way, quasicrystal fracture shares many similarities to crack pattern in disordered systems. We also find that quasicrystal cleavage is very sensitive to changes in temperature or simulation parameters (especially to the initial atomic configuration).

Testing the Accuracy of Synthetic Stellar Libraries by Charles W. Rodi Published on July 31, 2023 Stellar is a framework for distributing financial instruments through a computational substrate. Stellarspring is a sample dataset composed of actual trades from the dark pool XIV. Stellarport contains trades from two independent dark pools. Each port represents a single trade between two entities, who agree on a price and quantity but do not publish them. The accuracy of Stellarport as a stellar library has not been previously tested. I compare the prices and quantities of the Stellarport trades with the actual trades from the Stellarspring dataset. The average percent difference in price is -2.4%, with a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 5.3%.[1] The average percent difference in quantity is 8.7%, with an RMSE of 21.9%. By design, dark pool prices are not revealed to the market. Trade concentrations deviate from 50% match-up in both the actual and synthetic datasets. The actual dataset has a higher proportion of large discrepancies, with over 20% of the differences exceeding 30%. The synthetic dataset exhibits more moderate errors, with only 13.2% of the differences exceeding 30%. Stellarspring contains trades where both parties’ APIs failed, but neither party will disclose the reason for the failure. It is possible that some of these failures were due to mistakes made by Stellarport, and the results presented here underestimate the library’s effectiveness. However, it is more likely that some of the failures were deliberate attempts by traders to circumvent market rules, and the library’s effectiveness reflects the limits of its design.

V471 Tau is an eclipsing (white dwarf + red dwarf) binary system. I present the most up-to-date measurements of its photometric and spectroscopic properties, obtained using the Johnson-Cousins MOST satellite and the 6m telescope of the SAO RAS in Bulgaria. We derive the system parameters: the white dwarf's mass 0.87 ± 0.02M⊙, radius 0.0121 ± 0.00022 R⊙, the red dwarf's mass 0.4725 ± 0.0075 M⊙, radius 0.2632 ± 0.0064 R⊙, the orbital inclination i = 79.91 ± 0.05° and the linear size of the semiaxis a = 0.4032 ± 0.0044 pc. We also re-determine the atmospheric parameters of the red dwarf: T = 3540 ± 90 K and log g = 5.55 ± 0.02.

The variability in cataclysmic variable stars (CVs) is produced in an accretion disk around a white dwarf (WD) when material from a low mass companion (M {sub 2}> M{sub star}), transfers from a Mercury-like to a Brown Dwarf-like orbit. The disk, launched from the inside of the Roche limit, is puffed up by the pressure of gas, but a singularity still exists at the inner edge where the hydrostatic force from the pressure is balanced by the force from the Keplerian velocity. I calculate the equilibrium surface structure of such an accretion disk, and show that the ratio of radiation to gas pressure at the surface, can exceed the mid-plane pressure by a large factor. Hence, this surface is also radiatively inefficient and the transition to a hard state is prevented. Thus this mechanism for sporadic bursty variability is not only applicable to CVs, but may also explain the periodic outbursts observed in certain dwarf novae and soft x-ray transients.

Modern information technology is based largely on electrical and electronic devices. The continued miniaturization of these devices and their component parts, along with the introduction of new capabilities through novel materials and fabrication methods, is propelling the development of even more compact information processing systems. Significant progress in this direction has been made using micromechanical resonators that convert thermal energy into acoustic waves, thus avoiding the need for direct electrical or electronic interfacing. However, this method is limited to applications where the thermal energy is available and the spatial structure of the computing elements is irrelevant. An alternative approach that can synthesize both microwave and millimeter wave radiation and allow for true three-dimensional information processing is based on the magnetic properties of spin waves. These low-power, small-form-factor devices could revolutionize computing by providing compact, efficient units capable of converting information into microwaves or millimeter waves for transmission over distances, while minimizing energy consumption for on-chip or nearby communication.

In this paper we present a deep infrared search for companions to 67 members of the Pleiades cluster. We combine data from the UK Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS) with data from the WISE satellite and other literature to search for evidence of stellar, brown dwarf and planetary companions. We find no companions at distances of less than 5 arcseconds, and set 3-$\sigma$ upper limits on the occurrence of brown dwarf companions in the same separation and separation ranges of 12-240 M_{Jup}$ at 20% and 1%, respectively. Using these results, along with an empirical estimate of the binary frequency in the Pleiades, we place new constraints on the substellar binary fraction and the form of the low mass IMF in the range 0.1-2.5 M_{Jup}$. We find no companions at distances of less than 5 arcseconds, and set 3-sigma upper limits on the occurrence of brown dwarf companions in the same separation and separation ranges of 12-240 MJup at 20% and 1%, respectively. Using these results, along with an empirical estimate of the binary frequency in the Pleiades, we place new constraints on the substellar binary fraction and the form of the low mass IMF in the range 0.1-2.5 Mjup. The occurrence of substellar companions as a function of mass and separation is a powerful discriminant between different proposed forms for the low mass IMF. The occurrence of free-floating planets is a particularly powerful discriminator because planets above a certain mass are expected to have formed and survived their parent protoplanetary discs. The derived substellar companion frequency therefore provides a fundamental constraint on the form of the proposed initial mass function (IMF) between the stellar and substellar regimes. In particular, if most stars and brown dwarfs form in the same fashion, the inferred IMF is characterized by a distinct flattening at low masses. Conversely, if the IMF varies significantly with mass, the substellar companion frequency will correspondingly depart from that predicted for an approximately flat mass spectrum. We adopt a frequency of 33% for the binary fraction of the Pleiades, which was measured using data from the NASA Wide Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) satellite and other literature and is in good agreement with previous surveys. We then compare this with predictions from two candidate star and brown dwarf formation models. The core accretion model of core growth and planetesimal growth, which produces a flat mass spectrum, is disfavoured based on the lack of Jovian-mass free-floating planets in our Solar System. The competitive accretion model, which produces a more top-heavy mass spectrum, better agrees with the observed low-mass companion frequency.

Observed spectra of black hole may consist of multiple components, one of which is the thermal component. We show that a string theory dual of this system is a gas of strings and particles, termed fuzzballs. This implies that the evaporation of black holes produces not simply a black hole with a certain temperature but a fuzzy black hole consisting of many non-commutative pieces. In particular, we argue that a precise definition of the Barbero-Immirzi parameter for fuzzballs is the string statistical parameter, /b/ = 2pi/3. We provide strong circumstantial evidence for our claim by reproducing the semiclassical limit of the degeneracy of states (Bekenstein-Hawking entropy) and the spectrum of low-lying states (greybody factors) from first principles in string theory. We find that the spectrum and symmetries of the low-lying states are in good agreement with those of a scalar field in the Hartle-Hawking state, which is related to the thermal state by a Penrose process. We also show that the entropy of small black holes can be reproduced by counting the entropy of fuzzballs, which implies that the decay of a small black hole consists of fissioning of a large fuzzball. Our results establish fuzzballs as the proper objects within string theory that reproduce the standard description of black holes. Because the fuzzball partition function is likely to have an asymptotic expansion in powers of 1/b, where b is the Barbero-Immirzi parameter, we also establish /b/ as a physical observable of string theory.

A new mechanism for producing s-process elements in the massive stars (M > 8M⊙) is presented. The newly suggested Super-AGB channel is the so-called super-sNACC process. In this process, a carbon- and neon-rich layer forms on the surface of an AGB star through the s-process nucleosynthesis in the fp-shell. The produced s-process elements are dredged-up to the surface due to the thermal pulses and accumulated in the carbon-rich layer. The newly suggested Super-AGB star, with an initial mass of 1.5M⊙, has a sufficient mass to produce s-process elements throughout its lifetime. The duration of this process is longer than that of the usual AGB scenario (approx. 500 thousand years). Therefore, the suggested Super-AGB channel has a major influence on the chemical evolution of galaxies.

The idea that the universe was created out of nothing has profoundly deep philosophical and theological implications. Theories of creation generally fall into two main categories. The first considers the universe to be a physical object that already had a beginning in time and requires an explanation for its current existence. The second posits that the universe was created out of nothing for no apparent reason. This second idea has far-reaching consequences, because it implies the existence of an unsearchable infinity of worlds, each with its own physical attributes and living creatures. The universe may have begun from nothing, but it is still an unsolved problem why this happened. The birth of the universe from nothingness or a “big nothing” is the best way to explain the existence of the universe. However, this term seems counterintuitive, because the idea of nothing is inherently ambiguous. According to the Hindus, the universe was originated from a huge and infinite nothingness known as Mahalakshmi. In contrast, nothingness is often considered to be an absence of form or content, so the creation of the universe from nothing would mean creating form out of formlessness. Scientists are still debating the question of why there is something instead of nothing. New theories and research on the origins of the universe are being continuously published, but the answer to this question remains elusive.

The standard model of cosmology assumes that only 4% of the universe’s energy budget is composed of ordinary matter – the “baryonic” matter comprising stars, planets and other objects we can see. The remaining 96% is composed of a mysterious substance known as dark matter, which can only be observed through its gravitational effects. As dark matter particles themselves participate in the usual matter-based interactions, they have a finite chance of leaving behind traces in a particle detector. Such signatures – while extremely weak – would confirm the existence of dark matter and shed light on its particle properties. Many experiments have been searching for such signs of dark matter, with no success. This has lead many to question whether dark matter particles actually exist. However, a growing body of evidence from both astronomical and terrestrial experiments suggests that the standard model of cosmology may need revision. We now have compelling observational evidence that a substantial component of dark matter consists of very faint dwarf galaxies, rather than a sparse population of massive particles. These objects would be undetectable without their dark-matter content, which would have collapsed into even smaller objects long ago. On the other hand, small dark-matter particles would be insufficient to reproduce the observed dynamics of these dwarf galaxies, even if all of their dark matter were 100 times more energetic than the electron. This apparent contradiction has led many to hypothesize that the dark matter may consist of much lighter particles than previously thought, or else of entirely new types of particles. These alternative hypotheses still leave many observational signatures which could be tested by future experiments. We thus conclude that, while the current evidence for dark matter is compelling, it is not definitive. Continuing to search for dark matter will be important for understanding our universe’s composition and dynamics, and for testing the many theories that have been proposed to explain it. Despite extensive searches, no dark-matter particles have been observed. This suggests that either dark matter has spin 0 or 2, or it consists of entirely new particles, with no prior theoretical motivation. Alternatives to the standard dark matter hypothesis include warm dark matter, self-interacting dark matter and light dark matter. These differ from standard dark matter in spin, interaction strength or mass, and could produce different observational signatures. There is considerable agreement that further searches for dark matter are warranted. Some of these searches are already making important progress; others are under way or proposed. If further experiments fail to find evidence of dark matter, or if subsequent observations reveal inconsistencies with the current model of dark-matter structure, the standard model of cosmology will need to be revised. Although observational evidence for dark matter is compelling, it is not definitive. Continuing to search for dark matter will be important for understanding our universe’s composition and dynamics, and for testing the many theories that have been proposed to explain it. A neutral hydrogen (H I) absorption spectrum of the radio-emitting magnetar XTE J1810-197 is reported. This is the first such observation of a magnetar and probes the gas surrounding this ultralight neutron star. The observed properties of this absorber are consistent with it arising in the outer atmosphere of the magnetar, and imply a distance of 13.2-14.5 kpc (90% confidence). The results are consistent with a magnetar birth scenario in a binary system that subsequently managed to remove most of the mass in the system via the influence of some external agent (likely a supernova explosion). The large distance derived from these observations of the magnetar’s environment has important implications for the physics of magnetars, and for the nature of the explosion that made this neutron star. Neutral hydrogen absorption spectroscopy of magnetars provides information about the environment near these neutron stars. Such observations of XTE J1810-197 have been obtained toward both the radio-emitting magnetar and the persistent X-ray source (which likely traces the collapsed outer core of the star). These results are consistent with the magnetar environment being the outer atmosphere of the neutron star, with a distance of 13.2-14.5 kpc. The results are also consistent with magnetars being born in binary systems, and subsequently gaining much of the material in the system via the action of some external agent (likely a supernova explosion). This provides a mechanism for removing the vast majority of the original material from the equation, potentially solving the mystery of the very faintness of typical magnetars. In particular, the detection of neutral hydrogen near magnetars such as XTE J1810-197 is remarkable, as it had not been observed toward any other magnetar. This work was performed using the radio astronomy facilities of the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory, the University of Toronto, and the National Astronomical Observatories of China. This work was performed within the framework of the National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2017YFA0403503) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC, No. 11773014, 11533002, and 11851300).

Vortex in axion condensate as a dark matter halo Axion is a plausible explanation of dark matter (DM), and it can naturally generate vortices. I show that a vortex in DM density can form in the intergalactic medium (IGM) in the early universe and survive to the present time. The dynamics of formation is constrained by the cosmological gravitational effects. The core size of the vortex is of order of comoving Mpc and the mass is from the order of a hundred million solar mass to the order of a billion solar mass. The core size and the mass are consistent with the observed size of dwarf galaxies and the missing satellite problem, respectively. The stability of the vortex is also discussed. I consider two-component dark matter model, where the Axion and WIMP DM interact via gravity. The axion field has a global modulus and two real part, and it can generate a topological vortex during the evolution of the universe. The dark matter consists of the WIMP and the axion condensate, and the vortex in the axion condensate can be a dark matter halo. Then, the vortex can form the intergalactic medium (IGM) and survive to the present time. The core size of the vortex can be of order of Mpc scale and the vortex mass is in the order of a hundred million to a billion solar mass. The vortex size and mass are consistent with the observed size of dwarf galaxies and the missing satellite problem, respectively. The vortex is also stable against gravitational collapse. The vortex like structure in the axion condensate can be a dark matter halo and can survive from the early universe to the present time. It provides a new interpretation of the dark matter phenomena and suggests new phenomenology for the axion.
