RX J1713.7-3946 is a rare shell-type PSR (RX J1713.7-3946) which is located in the Small Magellanic Cloud. This object emits a young and energetic light, gamma-rays, produced in interactions between high energy cosmic-rays and the ambient gas. The emission has been recently detected by the H.E.S.S. and Fermi Large Area Telescope, but its TeV-band spectrum has not yet been measured. In this work, a diffusion model is used to calculate the gamma-rays emission and the spectrum is estimated in the energy range of 0.3-10 TeV. The result is compared with the observations and it is concluded that the diffusion model is capable to describe the emission and the spectrum of the TeV radiation from RX J1713.7-3946. Authors: Sergio Catalano and Nicola Mavromatakis Journal: arXiv preprint arXiv:1902.10546 Year: 2019

We present a detailed chemical and dynamical analysis of five protostellar clusters in intermediate-mass star forming regions, around the sources I18198, I22134, I22134A, I22135, and I22134B. Through the combination of CH3OH and deuterated organic molecules (dcoms) data with dynamics from carbon monoxide (CO) observations we are able to determine the luminosities, gas masses, disk masses and binding energies of the protostars and their associated class 0/I outflows. We find that the protostellar disk mass distributions are similar to those seen in low-mass systems, with a median value of 0.015 M⊙. The four younger sources (I18198, I22134, I22134A, and I22135) are still embedded in protoclusters and present binding energies that are an order of magnitude greater than those measured for more evolved IM protostars (such as IRAS 16293-2422). In contrast, the older source I22134B is dissociated from its protocluster and its binding energy is consistent with that measured for more evolved systems. We suggest that the evolution of protostellar binding energies is not driven by the energetic effects of outflows, as has been previously proposed, but is instead intimately linked with the evolution of their natal protocluster.

A double main sequence turn-off is observed in the rich star cluster NGC 1846 in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The two main sequences have a different temperature, which is consistent with the hypothesis of two populations of stars in this cluster. The fraction of more massive stars is higher in the brighter main sequence, suggesting that the most massive stars are forming first in this cluster. The observed characteristics of this double main sequence turn-off point towards a dynamical origin for this population division, for example from two distinct epochs of cluster collapse or from a recent merger with a tidal tail. Ben Skari and Olivier Ivanov acknowledge the support from the ERC Grantham Centre. The authors thank the operators of the Canadian Astronomical Data Centre and the SDS director Tim Brown for their help with downloading the ESO data and images used in this paper. The authors used the data obtained with the X-Shooter Spectrograph at the VLT, programme ID 094.D-0914. The X-Shooter data were processed using the ESO X-Shooter Data Reduction pipeline (version 2.2.0) and followed the standard reduction procedures as described in @Godart2019. The photometry was done with DAP 2.0.0, which is a modified version of DAP 2.5.1. The standard EROSpec on-source calibration procedure was used, including calibration of the nightsights and an estimation of the background. The FLAMES observation logs and the positions and basic parameters for the observed targets are listed in Table 1. The observed sample includes 5947 stars in the region of the cluster center. The observed color-magnitude diagram (CMD) is shown in the left panel of Fig. 1. The right panel of the figure shows thecmd after the fine adjustments of the distance modulus and the reddening, using a two-parameter fit. The best fit gives = 21.34 ± 0.09 mag and E(B-V) = 0.55 ± 0.02 mag, with a reduced $\chi^{2}$ of 1.51 for 6 degrees of freedom. We adopt the latter value in this paper. The cluster is rather compact, with a core radius of about 12". The sharpness of the red main-sequence turn-off is a sign of a low age. In particular, it implies that the more massive stars have reached the end of their life cycle. On the other hand, the much lower sharpness of the brighter, bluer main-sequence indicates that the lower-mass stars have much shorter lifetimes.

Increasing network vulnerability to cascading failures represents a dynamic effect, which occurs when the existing failure scenarios are improved upon through evolutionary optimization. Here we consider a scalable network model that exhibits a second-order phase transition to become more vulnerable to random failures as network size increases. We further demonstrate that this dynamic effect can be greatly magnified by optimizing the existing failure scenarios in a non-intuitive way: specifically, we show that increasing network vulnerability to targeted attacks can lead to greater dynamic effects of enhancing vulnerability to random failures, as long as the attacks further accelerate the vulnerability-booster strategy that increases network vulnerability to random failures. These results provide insights into the vulnerability of real-world networks to random and targeted attacks. By combining targeted attacks and improvements to the existing failure scenarios, networks can become more vulnerable to random failures, a finding with wide-ranging implications for resilience in real-world systems.

Transitive powers of Young-Jucys-Murphy elements are central elements in the unitary group representation. We give a proof that these elements are a norm in the C*-algebra of the unitary group and we compute their spectrum. In particular, we show that for odd N these elements are a root of unity, and for even N they are a primitive root of unity. These results were conjectured by A. Connes and D. Shklyarov, and partially proven by R. Longo and M. Weiner. Our proof is different and based on the character theory. The main ingredients of the proof are the Good deformation functor and character theory for infinite dimensional representations of classical Lie groups and their subgroups. This paper is a part of my PhD thesis under supervision of R. Longo. Young-Jucys-Murphy elements were introduced by V. K. Dzyadko, A. Mironov and A. Alexandrov in 2012. Since then these elements have been studied by several authors and applied to various problems in theoretical and mathematical physics. Journal version of this paper is available at arXiv:1607.00667 [math.QA]. It was also presented at QMath14 conference in Stockholm. Isovector density dependence, Lane potential and symmetry energy have been suggested as an effective mean to approximately describe the isospin dependent interactions in heavy ion reactions. In this work, the influence of isovector density dependence, symmetry energy and Lane potential on the isobaric analog transition (IAT) was studied in a folding model based on the isospin dependent quantum molecular dynamics (IQMD) approach. It was shown that the stiff symmetry energy and Lane potential favor the IAT while the soft symmetry energy and weak Lane potential tend to suppress it. The competition between the stiff symmetry energy and strong Lane potential enhances the IAT probability. Besides, the isovector density dependence was also found to have an important effect on the IAT, i.e., a good density dependence facilitates the IAT. It is expected that the suggested effective mean would provide a deeper understanding of the IAT and further stimulate the research on the IAT induced reactions. The article is uploaded on arXiv.org with the identifier of arXiv.org:1906.04568.

HH212-mm is a nearby low-mass multiple system in the Aquila Rift, whose ejection axis makes an angle of ~30° with the local dust filaments. It drives a prominent microjet in the 1.3 mm continuum, and exhibits a rich molecular line emission. The latter has been shown to trace the dynamics of the underlying jet/wind. We report new, very high spatial resolution (0.3“), observations of the 1.3 mm continuum, and fine structure line emission of SiO using ALMA. The continuum source is spatially unresolved, consistent with previous observations, but the detected jet has a total width of only 0.15" (35au), which is much narrower than in previously observed similar jets. The kinematic shift between the blueshifted and redshifted jet is also very small (less than 5km/s), indicating that the jet is well-collimated and likely driven magnetocentrifugally. These observations imply that the jet has been collimated and accelerated within the past 200-400yrs, and its initial width must have been significantly larger than that of the current day, implying that the jet/wind is being continuously refilled from the envelope. This is the first spatially resolved study of the microjet dynamics in this source, showing that it is an excellent target to study the launching and collimation of low-mass Class 0 jets in fine detail.

A quantum system that obeys the laws of quantum mechanics is said to be Markovian if the future depends only on the present, but not on the past. Although widely used in modeling open quantum systems, the canonical definition of a Markovian quantum system, dating back to the 1970s, is based on a weak notion of dependence. We introduce a stronger notion of quantum Markovianity, based on the idea that a system's dynamical maps should leave the system's quantum statistical properties invariant. By invoking the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, we provide a simple definition of this stronger notion of quantum Markovianity in terms of the interaction of a system with its environments. We demonstrate how to diagnose quantum Markovianity via a set of efficiently checkable conditions. Finally, we establish the existence of efficient means of controlling and steering quantum Markovian systems. Our results provide an analysis of the entire spectrum of Markovianity, from totally uncontrollable non-Markovian processes to fully controllable Markovian ones, via a unified framework that accommodates a broad scope of quantum systems and open dynamics.

A simulation of ASTROD I test mass charging due to solar energetic particles has been carried out with the Marenostrum Space Supercomputer. The energy deposition by the particles is modeled by means of a Gudermannian function with time-dependent amplitude and smoothing length. The resulting temperature increase in the test mass as a function of time shows a sudden increase due to the initial conditions used in the simulation. The temperature peak and the time necessary to achieve it depend on the primary energy and arrival direction of the particles. The response of ASTROD I can be used to determine the characteristics of solar energetic particles. The simulation of a charged particle bombardment of a mechanical structure subjected to temperature variations can be modeled by the following equation, adapted from [1] $$\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}= \frac{a}{2} + bT^2 - \frac{6\sigma S(t)}{\rho C_p}$$ where a is a coefficient related to the properties of the mechanical structure, b is the temperature coefficient, T is the temperature variation, σ is the Stephan-Boltzmann constant, S is the radiating surface, C p is the specific heat at constant pressure, ρ is the density of the mechanical structure and t is time. The model can be simplified assuming that all terms but the first are constants (t-independent), leading to the equation $$\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = a + bT^2$$ which has an analytical solution given by $$T(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2a}{b}}\ \mathrm{cosh}\left(\sqrt{b/2a}t\right)$$ The temperature variation in time is shown in the Figure 1 for different initial conditions. It can be seen that the temperature has a sudden increase, which amplitude depends on the primary energy of the particles and the arrival direction. The simulation was performed for 10 MeV protons and 5 MeV alpha particles with energy values similar to those observed by interplanetary spacecraft. The sudden temperature increase in the test mass causes thermomechanical excitations which, depending on the mechanical structure, can cause damage or produce acoustic emissions which can be detected by ASTROD I sensors. The analysis of the simulations shows that it is possible to determine the characteristics of the particles using only the temperature response of the structure.

Recent observations revealed extended thermal emission and highly variable non-thermal emission from the inner 30- 200 pc of the Galactic centre (GC). Here, I examine the physical processes which may be responsible for the observed emission. I argue that the variability in the observed luminosity is most likely driven by the accretion of material onto compact objects in the GC. Such objects have recently been detected via pulsations, and I demonstrate that their illumination may account for the observed emission in the 3-30 keV band. Furthermore, I argue that the winds of normal stars in the GC may also power the relativistic jets recently observed in the region. The variability in the strength of these jets may be explained by variations in the density of the GC stellar winds, and such winds may provide the momentum flux required to drive the observed gas along rotation curves seen in all bands. I conclude by presenting a model for the variability observed in the light curves of Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) and the radio source Sgr A*. I find that the winds of less than 10% of the massive stars in the GC are required to power the observed emission.' Based on work by Paolo Pauletta and MengWang.

In this work, we analyze the spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems. Spectrum pooling systems allow harnessing the spectrum resources across multiple bands and carriers, e.g.,mmWave and LTE, to improve spectrum utilization. The primary benefit of spectrum pooling is the flexibility to assign non-orthogonal spectrum bands and carriers to different uses, e.g., future mmWave services can be co-located with LTE services in the same band. However, the spectrum diversity may lead to inter-band interference, which could be mitigated by spectrum sharing policies that assign equivalent spectrum bands to the same use in different bands. In this paper, we investigate the potential rate region and spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems with spectrum sharing policies. We derive the spectral efficiency upper bounds with fractional spectrum sharing, which show that spectrum pooling can significantly increase the spectral efficiency compared to non-pooling counterparts. For the case of integral spectrum sharing, we show that under the proportional-share spectrum sharing policy, the spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems is limited by the minimum rate requirement, and spectrum pooling and non-pooling systems have the same spectral efficiency. Our results provide insights into the performance of spectrum pooling systems from the perspective of spectrum sharing, and can be used for system design, e.g., multi-user MIMO techniques can be used for improving the spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems with fractional sharing.

We examine the effects of nonlinear interactions between fluctuations and mean flows in two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence on the effective drift velocity of mean magnetic fields. The equations for turbulent fluctuations are reduced to a matrix form using the correlation approximation, and then a perturbation method is used to calculate the effective drift velocity. The most important finding of the present work is that the nonlinear interaction between fluctuations and mean flows in two-dimensional MHD turbulence makes the effective drift velocity considerably large even in the case of zero average magnetic flux and/or zero correlation time of the large-scale magnetic field. We estimate the effective drift velocity of large-scale magnetic field in the two-dimensional MHD turbulence with zero correlation time and obtain the scale dependence of the effective drift velocity. The obtained effective drift velocity is as large as the rms fluctuation. Therefore, our results imply that a mean magnetic field which was created by some small-scale dynamo by itself can be transported by the large-scale dynamo owing to the large effective drift velocity of mean magnetic fields in two-dimensional MHD turbulence.

In this paper we show that the presence of a fundamental string in AdS3 requires the string to have an infinite energy. The proof is based on an observation that fundamental strings in AdS3 arise as solutions to the classical equations of motion of the corresponding superstring compactified on a circle of small radius. We argue that the spectrum of string states that are trivial under this compactification must be bounded from below in order to maintain finiteness of the string energy. We derive an inequality that string states must satisfy in AdS3, which we call the Hagedorn condition. We show that the Hagedorn condition is equivalent to the requirement that the string energy be infinite, and we provide evidence that this condition is also necessary. Our results imply that fundamental strings in AdS3 are therefore ghostlike. We also discuss an application of our results to the correspondence principle in AdS3, and we conclude by summarizing some of the key ideas in our paper.

In this paper we study a 4D Z_2-symmetric thick brane solution in an AdS spacetime. We compute the Wightman function and vacuum densities corresponding to this solution. We show that these densities are nontrivial and depend on the spacetime and the fifth dimension. mselves, we consider the 5D Einstein-Maxwell action with the 5D Minkowski space-time metric and with the potential that generates a Z_2-symmetric thick brane solution with the corresponding 5D Riemann and 4D induced metrics on the brane, and with the appropriate jump in the 5th dimension component of the 5D vector potential across the brane. Solving the 5D equations of motion with this brane configuration, we compute the Wightman function and vacuum densities for this system. We show that these densities are nontrivial and depend on the spacetime and the fifth dimension. Welfare, in this paper we show that the nontriviality of the vacuum densities has an interesting physical implication. It leads to the breakdown of the additivity of the energy in 4D effective theory, for the system of the brane and the bulk fields.

A periodic modulation of radio emission with a period of 1.29 seconds was observed from the ultracool dwarf 2MASS J1119-3141. This is the first observed radio signal from an ultracool dwarf and the first observed periodicity in a dwarf star other than our own Sun. The observed periodic signal is likely the rotation of the ultracool dwarf itself, possibly due to formation of coherent surface magnetospheric emission. The observed signal represents the first confirmed rotation period of an ultracool dwarf and the first measured periodicity in a dwarf star other than our own Sun. This rotation period is longer than predicted by theoretical models, indicating that the ultracool dwarf may possess a subsurface hydrogen layer. If confirmed, this result would suggest that ultracool dwarfs can undergo additional gravitational settling over timescales of millions of years. This article includes a synopsis of previously unpublished results obtained with the pulse-stretch ephemeris rotation method. It also presents new evidence for the rotation of the ultracool dwarf 2MASS J1119-3141 using radio pulses from the slowly precessing radio magnetar PSR J1119-6127. The observations span over six years and indicate that the ultracool dwarf is not stationary, but is instead rotating at a rate of approximately 1.29 seconds, longer than any rotation rate predicted by theoretical models. Further observations at different radio frequencies and of different polarisation characteristics may help determine the exact nature of the signal and the processes determining the rotation period of this ultracool dwarf. The rotation of ultracool dwarfs may be of interest to studies of low-mass star formation, since some studies have suggested that slow rotation and weak magnetic fields may facilitate the gravitational collapse of gas clouds to form such objects. The observed rotation periods of ultracool dwarfs are similar to or longer than the rotation periods of Jupiter and Saturn. In contrast to these gas giants, ultracool dwarfs are sub-stellar objects with thin subsurface hydrogen layers. This may result in faster differential rotation than would be expected for similarly aged objects with similar mass and radius. This work was presented at the 2014 meeting of the International Society for Plasma Physics.'

NGC 3377 (Leo Minor) is an early-type galaxy, located approximately 55 million light-years from Earth in the Leo Group, a sparse collection of galactic clusters that stretch across the observable universe. Studied in detail using the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), the galaxy's thin disc of old, bright stars is accompanied by a halo of fainter, younger stars. The halo was shaped by merging events with other galaxies throughout its life, and provides a unique glimpse into the galaxy's accretion history. In this study, I combine HST/WFC3 ultraviolet and visible imaging with previous HST/ACS observations in the optical wavelength range to precisely measure the starlight density in NGC 3377's halo. I construct projected density profiles and fit stellar population synthesis models to the resulting photometry to determine the galaxy's halo starlight composition. Results show that the majority of stars in the halo are metal-poor and old (78 per cent are 12+ billion years old), with only 22 per cent of the population being more metal-rich and younger (8-12 billion years old). This result is consistent with what is expected given the frequency with which early-type galaxies are found to host halo populations, and highlights the utility of HST photometry for studies of galaxy evolution.

Manganites R_{1-x}A_{x}MnO_{3} (R is a rare-earth and A is a alkaline-earth element) are widely studied due to their interesting physical properties such as colossal magnetoresistance. There are two coupling mechanisms which are believed to be responsible for the colossal magnetoresistance effect in these materials: the double-exchange (DE) mechanism and the Jahn-Teller (JT) mechanism. The former assumes that the spins of the Mn ions are coupled through the double exchange and depends only on the spatial structure of the material, while the latter assumes that the JT effect (e.g. the local distortion of the MnO6 octahedra) is related to the electron-phonon (el-ph) interaction and depends also on the atomic structure (i.e. the unit cell). In this letter, we show that the el-ph coupling in manganites is very weak, similar to other transition metal oxides. In contrast, the el-el (i.e. the lattice) coupling in manganites is very strong and increases with volume. As a result, the strain coupling is a much more important effect than the el-ph coupling in manganites. Therefore, the double-exchange plus JT effect cannot be the sole origin of colossal magnetoresistance in these materials.

Temporal event sequencing is an important capability for intelligent agents, such as autonomous vehicles, and is essential to reasoning over complex dynamic scenes. Current state of the art approaches to sequence prediction are reliant on long short term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks, which are parameterized by their sequence length and are therefore not scalable to long or variable length sequences. In contrast, in this work, we demonstrate that a mixture of RNN experts with adaptive variance (Movel) is a simpler and more scalable alternative to LSTM for sequence prediction, and we apply it to a task of dynamic scene parsing. We train a single model to simultaneously perform sequence prediction and sequence segmentation, wherein each sequence segmentation is represented by a small number of Movel components. We compare to the state of the art on the publicly available CamVid dataset and show that our approach outperforms existing approaches, even without finetuning on this dataset. Furthermore, we show that our approach is easier to train than LSTMs with similar performance on this task, making it more suitable for applications with limited resource training budgets, such as self-driving cars.

Ergodic Model for the Expansion of Spherical Nanoplasmas As nanotechnology improves, there is great interest in understanding the electrical and mechanical properties of nanoparticles. One of the main problems in these studies is that it is very difficult to simulate the behaviour of a nanoparticle in a realistic material using a continuum model due to the enormous differences in scale. In this article, we develop a discrete dynamical model for the collision and evolution of finitely many nanoparticles, inspired by recent continuum theories for composite materials. The model is derived as an approximation of a continuous model for a finite number of particles, and consists of coupled nonlinear delay equations for the time-dependent positions and shape of the particles. We apply this model to study the scaling of a nanoplasma, and find that for certain parameter regimes the particle dynamics are ergodic, in which case mean values can be estimated by time-averaging the positions and shapes of the particles. We show that in the ergodic regime the size and shape of the nanoplasmas are well approximated by the radius and inverse convex hull of the particles' equilibrium positions, respectively.

We study various aspects of the AdS/CFT correspondence relating a class of four dimensional, N=4 supersymmetric sigma-models with (super)-symmetry groups U(1) × SO(4,n) to superstrings on AdS_4 × X_6, where X_6 is a 7-dimensional manifold of special holonomy. In particular, we discuss the fermionic part of the sigma-model, the role of fermions in the AdS/CFT correspondence and their description in terms of the superconformal algebra, and the construction of local observables in the field theory. We also suggest a formula for the fermionic partition function which can be used in the holographic approach to fermionic quantities in superstring theory. The Sr I 4607 \AA line (Z = 40) is mostly used for Doppler spectroscopy of exoplanets and is usually found in the spectral range of Earth-Like planets. The line is very sensitive to atmospheric conditions and can be used to study the mechanism of the water formation. In this work, the authors present the first model-independent analysis of the scattering polarization of the Sr I 4607 \AA line at the diffraction limit resolution of a 1-m telescope. The model-independent approach allowed the authors to detect the presence of the atmospheric sodium and water vapor, and to study the thermal structure of the dayside atmosphere of a transiting hot Jupiter. The sodium can be present only above the clouds whereas the water vapor is usually formed above the hot thermosphere and detected only when the planet is in phase 2 of the water vapour radio cycle. The Sr I 4607 \AA line has very complex behavior and can be used for a much more detailed studies of the atmospheric conditions than using the conventional Doppler spectroscopy.

Sim PlanetQuest, a flagship science mission of the Scientific Highlight Series of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, was designed to find and characterize gas giant planets around a sample of bright nearby stars. These characterized planets are vital for understanding how the universe developed over time, and are also prime targets for follow-up with other observatories (such as the Coronograph Chlorine model mission). The initial target list was generated from studies of young stars that are significant members of nearby star clusters, and these studies concluded that ~30% of such stars have gas giant companions within 0.5 AU. Follow-up observations are therefore recommended to characterize the properties of these planets and their host stars. The observations recommended by the study are ones that will provide constraints on the mass, radius, atmospheric composition, and eccentricity of the planets. A major challenge of such observations is their timing. The characterization of a planet's atmosphere via transmission spectroscopy requires the planet to pass through the star's projected 'zone of avoidance' at inferior conjunction. The amount of time for which this happens can vary by several hours each time the planet orbits its star. Successful characterization of the atmospheric properties therefore requires frequent and precise monitoring over short durations. The observations recommended by the study should enable detection of the typical radius of a planet in the habitable zone of its parent star, and place an approximate upper bound on the atmospheric scaleheight. The recommended observing cadence and duration is one evening of continuous coverage over two weeks. JWST might be able to provide precise characterization of the atmosphere of such a planet (or the equivalent for a sufficiently nearby Earth-analog planet).

Leaf venation is a beautiful example of highly branched, complex hierarchical vascular networks that protect plants from drought, high light intensity, and insect attacks. Despite its aesthetic and functional importance, the morphogenesis of leaf venation is a challenging problem because it involves multiple length and time scales. While it was initially hypothesized that secondary cells are only patterned after they are morphologically distinct from primary cells, it is now clear that secondary cells pattern prior to their morphological distinctness from primary cells. The signaling pathway responsible for this patterning was recently identified as a novel form of intercellular heterogeneity: elastic stresses. This elastic stress signaling theory of venation morphogenesis may be general and apply to other branched hierarchical vascular networks. profile Elastic stresses signaling is a recently proposed mechanism for leaf venation morphogenesis. In this note we study the number of topological types occurring in a parametrized family of arrangements. Let $\mathcal{A}_n(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ be the family of all real hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with normal vectors $a_1,\dots,a_n$, and where all $a_i$ are distinct. For generic choice of parameters, the number of topological types of this parametrized family is computed. We show that the number of topological types depends only on the combinatorial type of the $a_i$, and not on the particular choice of parameters. We also study the situation where some of the hyperplanes become equal. In this case, the question of the number of topological types is not even well-defined. We present a case where the topological types do depend on the parameters, and where a formula is given for the number of topological types.

A superbimonte discovered in 1703 by a Swedish amateur astronomer, Georgius Barwick, is known today as the Nobeyama molecular cloud. The molecular cloud is located in the southern celestial hemisphere around 5.5 kiloyears away, which makes it the most remote object for which a spatial mapping of thedistribution of molecular gas has been performed so far. Using the Nobeyama radio observatory, we have mapped the carbon monoxidedistribution in a sample of 25 nearby spiral galaxies and found that barred spiral galaxies have a larger quantityof molecular gas than non-barred spiral galaxies at the same optical luminosity. We propose that the strongerbars, which are associated with bigger bulges, stabilize the potential, and this in turn promotes theformation of more molecular gas. It is now well known that barred spirals are more abundant in the universe than non-barred spirals, which indicates that bars are important mechanisms in the evolution of galaxies. Our finding supports the view that bars promote the evolution of the host galaxies, probably by promoting the transfer of gas to the central region1,2. Non-resonant and resonant x-ray scattering have been used to study magnetoelectric TbMn2O5. Resonant scattering results evidence short range magnetic interactions between adjacent rare earth ions in the ab-planes, while non-resonant scattering reveals a narrow spin continuum centered at ≈35 meV. Resonant magnetic excitation spectrum displays two sharp spin waves modes, with the high energy mode at ≈29 meV. Magnetic structure determinations from both methods show commensurate helical order at low temperatures. The observed spin excitation spectra are very similar to other Tb based multiferroics, and the helical order with multi-q waves is likely a key factor in TbMn2O5's multifunctionalities. The scientific paper "Resonant and Non-resonant X-ray Scattering Studies on Multiferroic TbMn2O5" was published on arXiv.org on March 28, 2019. The full text of the paper is available from the author's website.

On the early stages of supernova explosion, the shock wave propagates through the pre-existing stellar material, breaking and heating the molecules. Microwave radiation with frequency range of 10-1000 GHz is produced due to superradiance, a phenomena when waves emitted by a rotating sub-system speed up to the speed of light along the axis of rotation. This microwave radiation may be detectable by CHIME andfuture high-frequency telescopes. I calculate the frequency of the peak superradiance emission and show that it is in the detectable frequency range. In addition, I show that the high pressure of the shockwave created by the supernova explosion can also stimulate coherent scattering of light, which may also produce detectable emission. I propose that the recent detections of radio waves from SN 1987A was due to superradiance and stimulated scattering This work was done while the author was at McGill University.

In this paper we examine the time evolution of Gaussian entangled states of the electromagnetic field inside an optical cavity. We demonstrate that for a given average photon number the temporal shape of the entangled state and its diffraction pattern is strongly correlated. We also show that for sufficiently low mean photon number the entanglement temporal profile exhibits lobeshaped sections that evolve in a periodically repeated pattern. We explain this phenomenon by observing that the time-dependent optical Kerr non-linearity leads to a phase-dependent frequency shift of the field that can be interpreted as a periodic effective cavity length modulation. The resulting wavepacket dynamics is thus Bloch-like and the structure of the temporal entanglement profile is directly linked to the underlying wavepacket dynamics. These results are of importance for quantum optical communication and signal processing applications where the temporal structure of the field is exploited. In particular, they suggest that for the efficient creation of Gaussian entanglement one should adjust the shape of the created state to the period of the underlying wavepacket dynamics. The statistics of core lifetimes describe the decay time or stability of a process. They are of central importance in the theory of dynamical systems, specifically the theory of Markov chains, and in many fields of applied probability. Applications include areas such as reliability, electronics, telecommunications, economics, and finance. Here we report statistics of the core lifetimes in numerical simulations of turbulent, magnetically supercritical molecular clouds, a problem of current interest in astrophysics. The statistics are computed in the frame of reference of a local (starless) region of the simulation, and for comparison also in the rest frame of the average flow of the region. We find that the distributions are nearly, but not exactly, exponential, and that the decay times depend upon the choice of reference frame. The implications of these results for the core evolution in the simulation, and for the applicability of kinetic theory and dynamical systems theory to the problem, are discussed.

Self-assembly has been widely used to produce large-scale interconnect networks on the microscale for the classical electronic circuit. The scaling limits of this technique, however, have largely restricted its applications on the nanoscale. In this work, we employ bottom-up nanofabrication techniques to develop an assembly approach inspired by biological self-assembly to achieve wafer-scale integration on the nanoscale. Specifically, the approach leverages the polar and surface energy interactions between low-stretch dielectric nanowires and polyethylene oxide self-assembled monolayers (PESLs) on standard silicon substrates to assemble electronic circuits from wafer scale up to millimeter-scale dimensions. The integration densities achieved exceed those produced by existing top-down approaches by several orders of magnitude. We demonstrate the successful integration of circuit building blocks including antennas, inductors, and resistors as well as a single-layer routing architecture, which are key components for reconfigurable networking, on a 100 mm × 100 mm chip. Furthermore, by developing open source software tools, our work enables practical designers to leverage this approach to rapidly develop system-level network-on-chip (SoC) designs using a high-level design approach to build custom applications in a modular fashion. We also present three case studies that show how these networks can be leveraged to build fully functional SoCs, including a case study where a networked FPGA fabric solves the Traveling Salesperson Problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that such a large-scale nanoscale interconnect network has been demonstrated on a wafer-scale substrate.

3C 382 is a well-known radio galaxy with a highly Compton-thick active nucleus. The obscuring column density is estimated to be a few times 1025 cm−2. Observations of this object have traditionally been difficult, and very few spectra of its nuclear emission were known. We report on the results of recent X-ray observations of this object with both the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer and the Chandra High Energy Transmissions Gratting Facility. We fit the data with a model that consists of a Compton-thick thermal accretion disk corona component and a complex reflection spectrum. We find that the coronal temperature is surprisingly low at kT ≈ 0.65 keV, and the coronal ionization parameter is large at 0.7 erg cm s −1. The size of the coronal region is extremely large, extending out to a radius of 14 parsecs (or 40 kiloparsecs), as indicated by the large value of the light-crossing time for the corona, τ cross = 57 light- days. These results challenge models in which the primary emission is blackbody radiation from a cool, thin accretion disk. Instead, we suggest that the primary emission is produced by a hot, thick accretion disk that is optically thick not only to direct emission, but also to Compton scattering. If the primary emission extends down to the last stable orbit, as appears to be the case in this source, then we must be viewing the inner regions of the accretion flow almost exactly edge-on. We discuss alternative geometries that may explain the large-scale coronal emission without requiring such an extreme viewing angle.

Spherically and axially symmetric solutions of the Einstein equations contain Killing vector fields, which define a family of conserved quantities. Using a regularization of the black-hole area, computed by the Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) null code, as a penalization term in an evolution code, leads to the resolution of critical boundaries in the evolution and thus to the improvement of the stability of the numerical solutions. The improvement is similar to the constraint-damping procedure in parabolic problems, but in the present context it occurs on a characteristic domain. The regularization is applicable to equations in any spatial dimension and in any formulation of the numerical problem. The method is applied to various spherical and axial solutions in vacuum general relativity, including the late-time approach to the Klemm-Wilzcek solution. In order to illustrate the generality of the method, an example is presented in which a spacetime containing a black hole and a neutron star is evolved from a Cauchy surface far from the neutron star. The gravitational radiation generated by the Cauchy evolution is reflected by the neutron star and observed by an observer at the Cauchy surface far from the star.

Landau levels (LLs) of Dirac fermions were observed in a van der Waals heterostructure consisting of highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) as the bottom layer and bismuthene as the top layer. The HOPG/bismuthene heterostructure was grown by chemical vapor deposition on a NiAl(110) buffer layer and subsequently transferred onto a SiO2/Si substrate. Scanning tunneling spectroscopy reveals characteristic resonance peaks in form of multiple nearly equidistant horizontal lines, which are interpreted as LLs of spin-up and spin-down Dirac fermions with an LL spacing of 2.6 meV. This is the first observation of LLs in a hexagonal lattice system other than graphene. The successful growth of a top-layer bismuth coating on graphite promises application potential of van der Waals heterostructures in future molecular electronics devices.

Heavy quark jets are an interesting probe of the dynamics of hadron colliders, since their masses provide a natural scale in the strong force coupling constant, quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Using data from p–Pb collisions at the LHC and from Tevatron experiments, we present the first precise theoretical predictions for the production of heavy quark jets, or heavy-flavour jets, at hadron colliders. We describe these predictions using the modern parton distribution function set nnPDF, which includes information on parton distributions from data up to a large value of x, or momentum, the scales of the process, and the finite mass of the bottom and charm quarks. We also present predictions for the production of other heavy flavours, including bottom and charm, for comparison. We compare the theory predictions with recent LHC data and with CDF and D0 measurements of differential heavy-flavour jet production in p–Pb collisions at the LHC. Finally, we make our code nnPDFnn/nlo/heavy-quark available to the community for use in simulations and analyses of heavy-quark jets at hadronic colliders.

Recently, measurements of the branching fractions and polarizations of $B$-mesons decaying to $\phi K^*$ final states by the LHCb and the CKMfitter groups have led to unexpected results for the averaged polarization fractions: $$\bar{F}_L=\frac{N_L}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=0,u,c,t} N_i} = 0.51 \pm 0.17 \text{ and } \bar{F}_H=\frac{N_H}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=0,u,c,t} N_i} = 0.49 \pm 0.17$$ where $N_L$ and $N_H$ are the numbers of longitudinal and transversely-polarized $\phi$ mesons in the sample, respectively. The dominant Standard Model (SM) sources of $B\to\phi K^*$ decays are $b\to s \bar{\phi} K^*$ and $b\to d \phi K^*$ amplitudes, which lead to longitudinal and transverse $\phi$ polarizations of $F_L=\bar{F}_L$ and $F_H=\bar{F}_H$, respectively.

Complexity Science has established methods for nurturing breakthroughs. Despite the recognized importance of complexity science in the innovation economy, the processes and practices through which its discoveries emerge are not well understood. In this article, I provide examples from a complexity science framework for discovering breakthroughs. These examples illustrate how a diversity of stakeholders can stimulate new ideas and how experiments can rigorously test hypotheses. Complexity Science’s rigor about assessing its hypotheses and its investment in supporting diverse trial and error offer promising pathways forward for other research traditions. The increasing pace of technological innovation in the information economy creates great incentives to study its dynamics. While it is well understood that failure is an essential component of progress, the mechanisms through which breakthroughs are achieved are not well understood. As Nobel Laureate Eric Maskin notes, “Our understanding of innovation is still very poor and we need more research on the ways to increase it.” In this article, I draw from Complexity Science, a framework for studying breakthroughs, to illustrate how other research traditions might increase their own understanding of innovation. Complexity Science identifies breakthroughs by considering the properties of complex systems. Complexity Science has established methods for identifying emergent behavior and resolves debates about the nature of complexity by using computational simulations that isolate variables. These simulations provide generalizable knowledge through rigorous experimentation and monitoring. Despite its importance in the innovation economy, the emergence of complex systems knowledge through rigorous experimentation is not well understood in other research traditions. Based on these observations, this article illustrates how to increase the emergence of rigorous knowledge through diverse trials and errors supported by a diversity of stakeholders. First, it describes the features of successful stakeholders who stimulate breakthrough ideas. These stakeholders include experts, early-stage investors, academic researchers, and open-source developers. These examples provide evidence that the collective intelligence of a diversity of stakeholders stimulates breakthrough ideas. Second, the article illustrates how rigorous experimentation can guide diverse trials and errors. These experiments, called “het programs,” rigorously test hypothesis by randomly partitioning stakeholders into groups to isolate variables. Het programs provide evidence on a trial-by-trial basis. Third, the article shows how to expand the domain ofrigorous experimentation from a single innovation effort to the continuous invention of several innovations. These innovations include the number of trialations, the number of stakeholders who participate in each trial, and the forms that stakeholders contribute. The articlesupports these recommendations by providing several case studies from Complexity Science that illustrate how to increase the diversity of trials and the range of rigorous experimentation. Finally, the article provides recommendations for supporting Het Program efforts to increase the emergence of rigorous breakthrough knowledge.

This paper presents an analysis of the near-infrared (NIR) background, extracted from the deepest observations of the HETDEX pilot survey and the Data Release 8 of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-DR8). This is the first time that such a dataset has been used to study the NIR background, and we present new evidence for a very faint NIR background that is spectrally identical to the hot intra-halo medium (IHL) expected from high-redshift star formation. We also show that, although at a much lower intensity, the NIR background likely contains contributions from low-redshift sources that were previously undetected. Using physical arguments and a hierarchical model for structure formation, we demonstrate that the hot IHL and low-redshift contaminants can jointly explain the existing constraints on the NIR background amplitude. We show that the strong clustering of the high-redshift galaxies needed to produce the observed hot IHL is consistent with current constraints from the optical and UV background. If this scenario is correct, the near-infrared spectra of high-redshift galaxies should show the absorption features expected from metals in the IHL, and upcoming infrared spectrographs on ground-based telescopes and the James Webb Space Telescope will be able to test this hypothesis. Finally, we show that the combined amplitude for the NIR background and the existing bounds on the abundance of high-redshift galaxies can be used to predict the amplitude for the “extra-galactic stars” UV background, and we present new upper limits on this background from the spectra of galaxies in SDSS. Taken together, these results strongly imply that the vast majority of stellar mass in the present-day universe was formed at $z \lesssim 8$, in galaxies much less massive than those observed at high redshift. Planetary nebulae (PNe) are the stellar result of a dying star's outer layers being swept up into a round and beautiful shell via a fast moving wind. Abundances in PNe can reveal information about their natal star's environment and evolution. Abundances of neutron-capture elements can provide insights into a star's origin and evolutionary history. However, the nature of PNe and the lifetimes of the various neutron-capture processes means that their elemental abundances do not necessarily reflect the history of the interstellar medium from which the star originated. Abundances of neutron-capture elements can also be impacted by internal processes occurring within the star. The s process involves slow neutron capture and is thought to occur in the He-intershell in massive, evolved, low-metallicity AGB stars. The lower mass stars above the limit for AGB processing, with lower initial metallicities, are predicted to undergo the same process but additionally experience fast neutron capture, called the r process. This results in a spread in neutron-capture element abundances, with the amount of s process (slow) and r process (fast) varying with each star. The upper left quadrant of this abundance plot, with low s and high r process abundance ratios, contains predicted stars with only thermally pulsing AGB progenitors. The other quadrants contain stars of multiple origins. This presentation will discuss the observed elemental abundance patterns in the sample of 22 PNe and present the expected elemental abundance patterns based on evolutionary theory. The abundances are presented as the logarithmic abundance of an element with respect to that of iron, [X/Fe]. The analysis was performed by the team of C. Fröhlich (IITK) using theMagellan Telescopes and the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo. Most PNe show enrichment consistent with slow s process nucleosynthesis. Only two PNe show enrichment consistent with only fast r process nucleosynthesis. Abundances in the remaining PNe are consistent with stars of multiple origins. The elements with the highest s process enrichments, beyond the observed scatter, are Pd, Ag, and Au. These three elements are expected to have similar s process patterns. The observed s process pattern for these three elements is consistent with He-intershell s process and is not consistent with the pure s process occurring in AGB stars. The observed abundance pattern for one PNe shows clear evidence of a partially processed origin, with [Na/Fe] consistent with that of the r process, but the elements [Mg, Si, Ca, and Ti] with significantly higher s process enrichments than expected. The observed abundance pattern is consistent with a slow He-intershell s process origin and a fast AGB s process origin. This result indicates the importance of using multiple elements when interpreting the s process pattern in PNe. Three distinct classes of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are distinguished in a statistical analysis of a large data set, using two components of the GRB prompt emission as classification parameters. The sample includes long, normal, and short bursts, and the divisions are correlated with the burst peak flux and duration. These results are interpreted as evidence for separate classes of progenitors, with two of the three classes originating from compact binary mergers. The division into three classes is more evident when data are classified according to peak flux rather than fluence (total emission duration-normalized). This might imply that the duration of the prompt emission is affected by the envelope of the burst central engine rather than the mass-energy actually emitted. * Long bursts are attributed to the merging of two compact objects, such as two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole. * Normal bursts are considered to be of Galactic origin, possibly arising from binary systems that include a neutron star or a black hole. * Short bursts are attributed to merger of three compact objects (two neutron stars and a neutron star-black hole). These results are in contrast to the traditional classification of GRBs as either long or short, based on the duration of the burst. The data set was collected by the *Fermi*/LAT, a $\gamma$-ray satellite, from 2008 August to 2016 November. The sample includes 93 long (T90$>$ 2s), 150 normal (2s $<$ T90 $\leq$ 10s), and 132 short (T90 $<$ 2s) bursts. The number of bursts in each class is representative of the size of the sample.

Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) are highly star-forming galaxies at high redshifts. They can be identified through their Lyman-break dropout signature in the spectrum and are observed to exist up to z ~ 6.7. We have obtained spectra of three Lyman break galaxies at z = 5.7–5.9 using the LRIS instrument on the Keck telescope. These data are used to measure rest-frame UV spectroscopy through visible wavelengths for these galaxies, complementing recent studies in the near-infrared (NIR). These observations have considerable implications for galaxy formation and reionization, as the Lyman continuum radiation from massive young stars is responsible for driving the return of UV radiation with redshift. These observations indicate that the epoch of galaxy formation was considerably delayed with respect to the NIR spectroscopy, perhaps to as late as z ~ 5.7–5.9, corresponding to a period of only 250–500 Myr after the Big Bang. It is also likely that the escape of ionizing radiation was limited by the harder ionizing radiation from young stars at these early times. The observed absorption lines in the UV spectra of these galaxies provide important clues to the physical conditions in these young galaxies, and comparison with high-redshift galaxies with later-generation telescopes such as HST and Spitzer will allow us to study how the escape of ionizing radiation was altered as these sources passed through the period of reionization.

Blood consists of various cells, such as red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells, and platelets, and these cells maintain its normal structure and functions by absorption and elimination of oxygen and carbon dioxide. In this study, we examined the light scattering properties of individual RBCs by use of scanning flow cytometry and discrete dipole approximation (DDA). We compared the experimental results with the calculated light scattering results, and the calculated scattering direction of the RBCs was similar to that of the experimental data. The absorption and scattering properties of individual RBCs were examined at the single-cell level. The observed light scattering distribution and the spectral analysis of the RBCs showed that the characteristic peaks of RBCs were obtained in the forward scattering direction at a scattering angle of 90°, and a well-defined dipolar-like light scattering pattern was observed at scattering angles of 120° and 240°. The results suggested that the RBCs exhibited dipole-like light scattering properties. The RBCs exhibited dual absorption and scattering properties; however, the absorption cross section was dominant in the scattering direction. Our research provides new experimental data on RBC optical parameters that will facilitate the design of diagnostic optical measurements and optical devices for medical applications, such as biodiagnostics and blood component separation.

The paper studies massive gravity in the TeV scale, following a previous attempt by Feng and Huang who used a hyperbolic background instead of a compact one. In the context of the Horava-Witten theory, the authors obtain the following solution for the metric: $g_{ab} = e^{-2\Phi(x)} \bar{g}_{ab} + \tilde{h}_{ab}$, where $\bar{g}_{ab}$ is the metric of a hyperbolic three-space of constant negative curvature, and $\tilde{h}_{ab}$ describes the quantum fluctuations around this classical metric. By comparing the results with the previous work, they conclude that the quantum correction becomes more significant for massive gravity in a hyperbolic background instead of a compact one, which provides a framework for testing this theory in the future. This work is performed in the framework of the Horava-Witten theory, which provides the lowest-order perturbative theory for gravity in the TeV scale. The model obtained yields the following solution for the metric: $g_{ab} = e^{-2\Phi(x)} \bar{g}_{ab} + \tilde{h}_{ab}$, where $\bar{g}_{ab}$ is the metric of a hyperbolic three-space of constant negative curvature, and $\tilde{h}_{ab}$ describes the quantum fluctuations around this classical metric. By comparing the results with the previous work, they conclude that the quantum correction becomes more significant for massive gravity in a hyperbolic background instead of a compact one, which provides a framework for testing this theory in the future. The authors also study the issue of vacuum instability. They adopt the method of semi-classical analysis by calculating the first-order perturbation of the graviton field, and demonstrate that there is a negative energy region in the bulk. Assuming that the boundary of this region corresponds to the spatial infinity, it means that the usual Minkowski vacuum is not stable. The authors propose a new solution for the stable vacuum, which has already been adopted in other models such as bigravity and Hořava gravity. The high energy emission of GRO J1655-40 as revealed with INTEGRAL spectroscopy of the 2005 outburst is described. This well-known black hole X-ray binary is a system composed of a Neutron Star primary orbiting a black hole of 18 Meters in close orbit (13-31 R_s) every 2.87 hours. It is suspected that disk accretion onto the neutron star occurs in this system, as evidenced by its spectral class of Z-source, which is characterized by having strong, sometimes regular, neutron star high-speed winds. These winds are likely due to the transfer of energy from the accretion disk onto the neutron star. The 2005 outburst of GRO J1655-40 was detected with the INTEGRAL observatory on Jan. 28, 2005, and reached a maximum on Feb. 24. The work presented here focuses on the high energy spectrum of GRO J1655-40 over this time period. The major result of this work is the discovery of acutoff powerlaw component in the high energy spectrum of GRO J1655-40, with a flux contribution of approximately 50% over nearly 3 decades in energy. This component is not commonly observed in X-ray binaries, and therefore its discovery with INTEGRAL represents a new paradigm for high energy production in these systems. The cutoff powerlaw component is believed to be an extension of the accretion disk blackbody component which is often seen in black hole X-ray binaries, and is generally thought to be the signature ofNETWORK GAMMA RAYS radiated by the inner part of an accretion disk around a black hole. The discovery of a cutoff powerlaw in this system, with a neutron star at its core, represents a new paradigm for high energy production in black hole X-ray binaries, and may indicate that disk accretion is not the only form of high energy production in these binaries. It is possible that this component is the result of a new form of high energy production unique to this system, which may be a result of the strong neutron star winds. This may be a promising area for exploration with further, more detailed analysis of these data.

In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the vev of the Higgs doublet, which triggers the electroweak symmetry breaking, generates a potential for the neutral Higgs bosons which has a minimum at zero at tree-level. This minimum causes a naturalness problem, because the quadratically divergent corrections to the neutral Higgs mass-square parameters from the SM particles are unacceptably large. The solution to this problem requires a supersymmetry (SUSY) spectrum with superpartner particles at accessible energies. A minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model (MSSM) contains two additional Higgs bosons, namely, the higgsinos and the heavy scalars, which appear in supersymmetry-breaking mass matrices. These are the supersymmetric partners of the goldstino, the photino and the zino. By proper alignment of the parameters in the SUSY-breaking mass matrices, these heavy scalars can be made relatively light, of order of the SUSY-breaking scale, while preserving the electroweak symmetry breaking. We perform a phenomenological study of the potential corrections to this alignment, and demonstrate that this reduces the mass of these scalars below 1 TeV, in a portion of the MSSM parameter space, and can be as low as 400 GeV for some parameter space points. The lightest of these new particles is a good dark matter candidate. We also study the collider phenomenology of the model, and demonstrate that this light Higgs sector can be tested at the upcoming hadron colliders, namely the CERN LHC and the Future Circular Collider, as well as the Folding@home Distributed Processing Cluster. We study the phenomenology of a minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model with heavy scalars (MSSM-HS) sparticles, at the tree-level. These new particles appear in the supersymmetry-breaking mass matrices for the supersymmetric partners of the goldstino, the photino and the zino. We perform a phenomenological study of the potential corrections to the alignment, which allows us to reduce the masses of these particles below 1 TeV, in a portion of the MSSM parameter space. We also study the collider phenomenology of the model, and demonstrate that this light Higgs sector can be tested at the upcoming hadron colliders. Here we study the following points: 1. We briefly introduce the MSSM-HS model and discuss the symmetry principles which the superpartners should satisfy. 2. We describe the spectrum of the model. The fundamental objective of wireless communication is to deliver the message from the sender to the receiver in the most efficient way possible. One way to improve efficiency is to exploit the extra knowledge about the communication channel that the sender has, and encode the message according to this knowledge. This approach is known as physical layer network coding (PLNC). We investigate the case when the physical layer transmission is confined to a single channel use. In this case, we characterize the capacity achieving probability of message transmission, and we show that it is possible to achieve this probability strictly larger than unity by judiciously choosing the message to be transmitted. We consider the general discrete memoryless channel with channel input, channel output and channel transition probabilities denoted by ${\bf x}$, ${\bf y}$ and $p({\bf y}|{\bf x})$, respectively. The physical layer transmission takes one use of the channel, and is denoted by $x^n$, where $n$ is the length of the channel use. The objective is to communicate a message $m$, where the central objective is to achieve high probability of message transmission. We consider the binary alphabet and exponential input distribution, and focus on the general discrete memoryless channel with i.i.d. channel inputs. Our goal is to characterize the message rate $R_m$ and the probability of message transmission $P_m$ that achieve the capacity of this channel. It will be seen that the achieved message rate is a function of the codebook used to convey the message, and the probability of message transmission depends on the channel input $x^n$. In order to characterize this dependence, we define the entropy of the channel input as a measure of channel uncertainty. We then characterize the tradeoff between the message rate and the probability of message transmission. We then exploit the idea of multi-resolution coding, and split the message into several layers, and use a high rate short layer to convey coarse information about the message, and a low rate long layer that conveys detailed information about the message. We use the channel input to modulate the long layer, and use the short layer to help convey the detailed information about the message. We show that by judiciously choosing the codebook for the short layer and the detailed layer, it is possible to achieve a high probability of message transmission strictly larger than unity. It is further shown that the message rate achieving probability of message transmission is a monotonically increasing function of the codebook used for the short layer. As a result, it is possible to achieve the capacity achieving message rate and message transmission probability if and only if the codebook used for the short layer achieves capacity. This characterization has a clear stochastic dominance interpretation. If the codebook used for the short layer is selected according to the distribution $p_1(x)$ and the codebook used for the detailed layer is selected according to the distribution $p_2(x)$, then the codebook for the short layer dominates the code

The abundance and size distributions of globular clusters (GCs) are key diagnostics of the formation processes of galaxies. GCs are primarily old, self-gravitating systems of stars, thus providing a fossil record of the star formation events that gave rise to their constituent members. As such, the GC systems (CGCS) of galaxies offer a valuable tool with which to study the formation and evolution of galaxies. We study the CGCSs of 13 massive, X-ray selected, optically dull galaxies (SDGs) with masses 1.3 - 4.5 x 10 11 M⊙, redshifts z = 0.02 - 0.33, and 13 - 105 Gyr of age using Hubble Space Telescope (HST) WFC3/G band images. We find that 7 of these SDGs exhibit bimodal or multimodal GC systems. We compare our observational results with predictions of the classical early-major merger scenario, the delayed-merger scenario, and a novel merger-binary-spiral-component scenario. We argue that the SDGs likely formed through a variety of pathways. At low redshift, these pathways included major mergers of comparable-sized galaxies, as well as more minor mergers and accretions. At high redshift, SDGs likely experienced more minor and major mergers, as well as purely dry minor mergers. However, we suggest that the late-stage mergers of gas-rich spiral galaxies formed the dense central GC systems of the SDGs. The lack of strong rotational support in the nuclei of these galaxies likely reflects the gas-richness of these mergers. In this scenario, we expect to find kinematic signatures of recent or ongoing major dry mergers in galaxies with predominantly diffuse GC systems, and we identify 3 such galaxies. Using our spatially resolved color data, we show that both the SDGs and their constituent GCs have intermediate-age to old stellar populations, with the fraction of young stars increasing with distance from the center of the galaxy. We find that the spatial distribution of the GCs is more extended than that of the old stars and that the GC systems exhibit truncation radii (average projected distances within which half of the GC system’s GCs are found) and power-law slopes consistent with the predictions of recent major merger and purely dry minor merger scenarios, respectively. We argue that this suggests that either a major merger or a purely dry minor merger has already occurred within the truncation radii of at least 5 galaxies.

This paper presents surface brightness profiles for a sample of 27 globular clusters located in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and Fornax galaxy. Globular clusters are gravitationally bound collections of millions of stars. Because they are so compact, the light from the individual stars in a globular cluster can substantially pollute its surface brightness profile. Therefore, accurate measurement of surface brightness profiles for globular clusters is critical for studying their structural parameters, especially their half-mass radii, which can be used to place constraints on the halflight radii of their host galaxies. In this study, we obtained $VI$ images of the globular clusters using the photometric system of the CTIO 0.9-m telescope. A PSF-fitting program was used to measure the surface brightnesses of the clusters, and the resulting profiles are presented here. The profiles are presented for two intervals in radius, one centered on the half-mass radius and one centered on the half-light radius, and have been fitted with the models of the truncated isothermal sphere, the logarithmic sphere, and the generalized-Sersic model. For Fornax globular clusters, the generalized-Sersic profile provided the best fit to the data. In general, the globular cluster surface brightness profiles follow the same general trends in all three galaxies, i.e., the Fornax globular clusters have the steepest profiles, the LMC globular clusters have profiles between the Fornax and the SMC profiles, and the SMC globular clusters have the shallowest profiles. The surface brightnesses at a given radius for the globular clusters in a given galaxy tend to increase with the total luminosity of the galaxy.

Non-Gaussian distributions of financial returns are one of the distinctive features of financial markets. These distributions are commonly described by the third and fourth order statistical moments, namely, mean, variance and skewness, or more comprehensive measures such as the kurtosis. In the past decades, it has been shown that financial returns are weakly non-Gaussian, with the probability density functions (PDFs) of price increments conforming to the Gaussian distribution with high precision. By contrast, more recent studies have found deviations from the Gaussianity in the returns’ non-linearity, cyclicity, and multifractality. To uncover the microscopic origins of these non-Gaussianities, we develop a novel approach based on multifractal random walks (MWRW). We construct a stochastic process with the stationary, strongly multifractal, and non-Gaussian PDFs of increments. Applying this process to measure the price movements of a wide range of assets, we demonstrate that financial returns are statistically non-Gaussian. The statistical non-Gaussianity of returns is positively correlated with their liquidity, reflecting the fact that high-volatility assets with frequent price changes tend to have non-Gaussian returns. Moreover, we find that the distributions of the logarithmic returns have universal form, which is different from the non-Gaussian distributions of price increments. This finding indicates that the statistical properties of financial returns are more related to their absolute values than to their changes. We further uncover the multifractal nature of financial time series and their interrelations with non-Gaussian returns. The multifractal nature of returns implies their non-stationarity, which is consistent with previous findings based on other methods. Our work provides new insights into the statistical mechanics of financial returns and has important implications for risk management and quantitative finance.

We present the first large, homogeneously selected sample of supermassive black hole (BH) pairs in paired galaxies. We combine our sample with recent analyses of bulge properties for individual galaxies to explore how host galaxy properties relate to BH pairs. We find that galaxies with higher bulge masses tend to have greater BH masses. Higher bulge mass is also correlated with higher Sersic index, which measures the shape of a profile, and with younger stellar populations. Higher Sersic index is associated with more disky isophotes, which can be linked to faster rotation in galaxies. We combine these results with models of galaxy evolution and BH growth to propose a scenario in which more massive bulge stars form in more rapidly rotating galaxies, which are more likely to host active black holes. BH pairs that form in such galaxies are then likely to have higher mass ratios, consistent with observations. Our results provide new constraints for simulations of BH growth and galaxy evolution, and suggest a connection between high-mass BH pairs and galaxy evolution processes, such as major mergers.

In this paper, we present a random access broadcast (RABC) protocol that allows a large number of nodes to exchange information in a small amount of time, without the need for central coordinating nodes or clock synchronization. Nodes that want to transmit a message construct a packet by choosing random access signatures (RAS) from a large space of signatures. The RAS act as a node ID and enable a node to state its full power and capabilities. The recipient of the broadcast can verify the sender's capabilities and accept or reject the broadcast based on the type of application and QoS requirements. We provide stability and throughput analysis of the RABC protocol. We also discuss how our RABC protocol can be modified to support more complex broadcast types such as multicast and zeroconf. We have implemented a random access broadcast (RABC) layer on top of UDP. Using the ns3 simulator, we demonstrate the efficacy of RABC by comparing it against other random access protocols in terms of throughput, delay and stability. We show that RABC is efficient in terms of both latency and message payload. Compared to the Z-bus, an existing random access broadcast protocol, RABC shows better performance in terms of throughput, delay and stability. We also show that RABC provides multicast and zeroconf support through simple extensions to the protocol.

This paper aims to analyze the internal structure of the Indian financial market using high-frequency data. Specifically, the stock prices of the National Stock Exchange (NSE) are analyzed for evidence of positive or negative co-movements. The analysis is based on two tests that are adapted from the field of finance, the vector error correction model (VECM) and the Granger causality test. The NSE dataset from January 2009 to June 2017 was analyzed and results indicate that there exists significant correlation across different markets across different time lags, where the strongest lags are 2 hours and 4 hours. These results help provide a deeper understanding of the internal structure of the Indian financial market. The Indian financial market is an important market that contributes significantly to the GDP of the country. It is an open economy and a hub for foreign exchange transactions. It has a high liquidity and shares global financial information due to its presence on the global stage. In addition to this, India is one of the fastest growing major economies. The stock markets in India have shown considerable growth in the past decade, increasing from ~USD 400 billion to ~USD 2.5 trillion in the period 2009-2017. Despite its importance, the Indian financial market is also one of the least understood. Unlike the U.S. or western markets, the Indian market has a highly centralized structure where a few major stock exchanges play a significant role. These major stock exchanges are BSE (Formerly Bombay Stock Exchange), National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the S&P Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index. There are a few smaller stock exchanges, which include the National Stock Exchange of India, Indian Stock Exchange and Reliance Industries Share Value System. The Indian financial market has also been criticized for having delayed reporting mechanisms and surveillance due to which, most transactions do not get reported and hence the available information is minimal.

A highly significant gamma-ray burst (GRB) was detected from the site of a lensing-corrected $z=5.47$ galaxy. The inferred isotropic equivalent gamma-ray energy of this burst is $E_{\gamma,iso} = (2.9 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{54}$ erg, one of the largest of any observed gamma-ray burst (GRB). The inferred radiated energy is nearly two orders of magnitude larger than the expected energy from tidal disruption events (TDEs), placing significant constraints on the rate of both events at high redshift. Using the detection of this burst in conjunction with an upper limit on the dimming of subsequent GRB afterglows places interesting constraints on the reionization history of the intergalactic medium (IGM), namely that reionization must be occurring at $z \geq 6.5$ if the IGM were fully reionized by $z = 5.5$ and the factor of $500$ decrease in luminosity from the end of the dark ages to $z = 5.47$ was due only to passive evolution of the galaxy.

Stochastic Loewner Evolution (SLE) is a one-parameter family of random processes in a plane. It was introduced to describe the growth curves of clusters of mobile particles, but it has found many other applications. We consider two stochastic differential equations (SDEs), one corresponding to the chordal version and the other to the radial version of SLE. We give Feller-type conditions ensuring that the solutions to these SDEs exist and are unique in probability. We also show that the solution to the radial SDE converges in distribution to the solution to the chordal SDE. Finally, we use martingale methods to establish the convergence in distribution of the half-plane percolation generated by random curves of the SLE variants.
