A relativistic effective field theory (REFT) for nuclear many-body systems has been developed. The effective Lagrangian for describing nucleons and medium-modified nucleons together with their mutual interactions is based on the instantaneous single- and two-pion exchange with nucleons and several irreducible two-nucleon contact terms (two-pion exchange plus contact terms), consistent with the proper symmetries of nuclear dynamics and causality. The leading parameters in the effective Lagrangian are the binding energy and the scalar and vector self-energies of infinite nuclear matter. By employing the standard techniques of perturbative quantum field theory, we have calculated the two-loop corrections to these quantities in a genericREFT. The results indicate that the cutoff dependence of the two-loop corrections is significantly reduced as compared to the one-loop results. The calculated properties of nuclear matter at both normal and high densities are in good agreement with those from both effective field theories and many-body theories, including self-consistent meson-exchange models, non-relativistic and relativistic Hartree-Fock models, Brueckner-Hartree-Fock models, and QCD sum rules. Thus the calculated results from this work provide a very good description of both the nuclear forces and the nuclear many-body systems.

Lithium-like ions have been widely used as tests of quantum electrodynamics (QED) calculations due to their simple structure. In this work QED calculations of the 2p1/2-2s and 2p3/2-2s transition energies and the ground-state hyperfine splitting in lithium-like scandium are presented. Theory and experiment agree to within 4.2% and 5.2% for the two transition energies and the ground-state hyperfine splitting, respectively. The 2s2 2p(1/2)2p(3/2) and 2s2 2p(3/2)3s bound-states energies of lithium-like scandium were calculated using the multiconfiguration Dirac-Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) theory including all single and double electron relativistic, quantum electrodynamic (QED) and electron correlation corrections. The 2p1/2-2s and 2p3/2-2s transition energies and the ground-state hyperfine splitting were estimated by combining the MCDHF energies with the relativistic many-body perturbation theory and all order charge delocalization correction methods. The results were compared to the available experimental data and good agreement was obtained.

A neutral Higgs boson may decay into a lighter Higgs boson and a b quark pair, with a branching ratio as large as 40% in the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM). Depending on the mass difference between the two Higgs bosons, this decay may occur through either an intermediate chargino or a sneutrino. In this paper we present an effective Lagrangian for the $\chi^{+}_j \chi^{-}_kH^{0}_l$ interaction that parameterizes the chargino and sneutrino contributions to this decay, and show how this Lagrangian can be used to model the neutral Higgs decays in the MSSM. The effective Lagrangian is constructed in the super-CKM basis, where the neutral Higgs mixing matrices and the chargino and sneutrino states are all expressed in terms of super-CKM rotation angles and phases. Numerical results are presented for this effective Lagrangian in the context of the first and second benchmark scenarios proposed by the LHC Higgs cross section working group, corresponding to a light SM-like Higgs boson with a mass of 125 GeV, and a heavier Higgs boson with a mass of about 600 GeV, respectively. Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) have been used as "standard candles" to study the expansion history of the Universe. The current leading survey to discover thousands of SNe Ia is the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope Supernova Search (SNLS), which is targeting 7.5 deg2 area in distant Universe [1]. With the discovery of SNe Ia at such high redshifts, it will be possible to measure the dark energy properties with unprecedented precision. The LSST, which is projected to discover tens of thousands of SNe Ia in 10 square degrees by 2021, is expected to dramatically improve the measurement of the dark energy parameters [2, 3]. To achieve the optimal science return from these future surveys, it is essential to measure the structure growth rate from redshift 7.5 to 10 accurately. This requires much larger galaxy surveys in the near-infrared (NIR), and breaking the *visibility period gap with NIR galaxy surveys has become a high priority for SN cosmology research. In this work, we measure the galaxy clustering rate using BOSS DR12 galaxy samples in three non-overlapping regions of the LSST visible footprint, and demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed NIR galaxy clustering measurement from BOSS DR12 by testing the impact of systematics from the light-to-number count relation. We find that the uncertainty from this relation is smaller than 0.5% in wavenumber space, and the bispectrum information beyond the nonlinear scale can be exploited to further reduce the uncertainty to 0.1%. We forecast the uncertainty from using BOSS DR12 in the LSST full footprint by combining three regions with these NIR constraints, and find that the galaxy clustering measurements will achieve 1% precision at nonlinear scales (0.2% at one eighth of the nonlinear scale) in the dark energy analysis with only 25% more galaxies than the BOSS DR12 clustering measurement alone. We also show that combining the BOSS DR12 clustering measurements with the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurement from the planned SPHERIC power spectrum measurement can significantly tighten the dark energy constraints, and the parameter errors can be decreased by a factor of two compared to using the BOSS DR12 clustering measurement alone. The measurement from BOSS DR12 can be completed by 2021, and the full LSST NIR clustering measurement will be achieved in 2023. The NIR galaxy clustering measurement from BOSS DR12 will provide strong synergy to the optical SN Ia measurement from the LSST, and significantly improve the dark energy measurement with the next generation cosmological surveys.' Hot molecular cores (HMCs) are strongly obscured regions located in the centers of protoplanetary disks. They are believed to be the early stages of planets. Recently, complex N- and O-bearing molecules such as HCNO, HCON, NH3, and OH have been detected in HMCs and interpreted as potential molecular precursors to prebiotic compounds. In this work, we present the results of a search for these molecules in 10 HMCs from our IRAM 30m survey of C-type stars using both ASA and boldy re-extract the spectra. We also present the results of new observations of 6 HMCs with the IRAM 30m, ASA, and Divertor aborratory and show that HCNO, HCON, NH3, and OH are not ubiquitous in HMCs. We estimate the column densities of these molecules in HMCs and find that HCNO, HCON, and NH3 exhibit high abundances relative to each other while OH is always below the detectable limit. HCNO is a good prebiotic precursor. HCON and NH3 may also be important prebiotic precursors. OH may not be a precursor given the low inferred column density.

A deep optical imaging and H I absorption study of the high Galactic latitude interstellar neutral hydrogen structure revealed two distinct high column density structures along a high galactic latitude sight line, G281.65+1.32. The more compact structure (0.47 kpc comoving) appears to be aligned with the large scale galaxy structure over 3 Mpc. We suggest that the galaxy filament to which this structure is aligned and its clumps are the sites of active star formation, which have produced enough Lyman continuum radiation to ionize and characterize the observed compact H I structure. The second H I structure (1.3 kpc comoving) is more filamentary and extends perpendicular to the galaxy structure. The G+0.47 galaxy group lies at the intersection of this structure and the sight line. We suggest that this filamentary structure may represent a nascent galactic halo, which has not formed stable clouds, or else has not ejected enough H I through galactic super-winds to be observed as a small scale high column density structure. We explore the implications for high frequency (~23.6 - 100 cm-2) continuum emission from this region expected from the Free-Free and Thomson scattering of H I radiation. We predict significant absorption of such emission at frequencies from ~43 to 44 cm-2 and suggest this as a means of probing the distribution of neutral gas in our local galactic neighborhood.

Deep near-infrared spectrograph on board the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) will allow probing the interior of stars, and determine surface properties, such as masses, radii, and ages with high precision. With this in mind, we simulate the observations of an F-type star with a 3-5% abundance of metals, which has a fully convective outer envelope, with a JWST-like spectral resolution and sensitivity in a 1.65 μm region of the stellar spectrum. The star exhibits a broad absorption feature near ē = 5.9 μm, which is expected to be caused by rotational splitting of the - [FeH] fundamental band, due to the star's rapid rotation (P < 1 day). The depth, shape, and position of the ē = 5.9 μm feature can be explained by simulating the heating and evaporation of upper convective layers, which are then carried to the surface by rapid rotation-induced gravitationaldarkening. These features could be readily detected by JWST, and could potentially serve as a validation of models of rapidly rotating, low-mass stars.

A key resource in quantum information processing and communication is entanglement, which underpins many of the remarkable applications of quantum mechanics. In particular, it enables powerful quantum information processing tasks such as quantum key distribution and quantum computing. The ability to generate and manipulate entanglement represents an important challenge in the field, and there is ongoing research into the mechanisms by which entanglement can be generated and transformed. We present a novel method for manipulating entanglement which makes use of separable operations and allows for the controlled generation of any desired form of entanglement. This technique can transform one form of entanglement to another, and furthermore can also be used to generate an entangled state from an initially separable state. Using our method we are able to transform pairwise entangled quantum states to a mixture of separable states and maximally entangled states. Furthermore, we demonstrate the generation of entanglement from an initially separable state. We present a general framework for the optimal control of entanglement, and illustrate the applicability of our technique through a range of example scenarios. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of quantum information processing systems and represents an important step towards the full exploitation of entanglement in quantum technologies.

A recent proposal for counting BPS black holes in AdS solutions of eleven and ten dimensions is that they are in one-to-one correspondence with supersymmetric solutions of ten dimensional non-linear sigma models, whose target spaces are half-flat geometries. These half-flat geometries are embedded into maximally supersymmetric solutions of type IIB supergravity, which in general may also have non-trivial NSNS flux. In this paper, we examine classes of such geometries with various Killing vector fields. For such geometries, we find that if the half-flat factor is realized as a saddle point of the Yang-Mills theory then the string theory dual corresponds to a bubbling AdS solution. On the other hand, if the half-flat factor is realized as a fully-supersymmetric AdS vacuum then the string theory dual is a droplet solution. We present several examples of such AdS solutions.

Transit timing variations (TTVs) have been used to detect planets around other stars, but many TTV detection techniques cannot distinguish between TTV caused by star-planet interactions and TTV caused by other astrophysical processes. Using TTV amplitudes to distinguish between these signals is difficult because the amplitudes depend on both the sensitivity of TTV detection and the mass, spin, and obliquity of the host star. We present the first detections of the TTVs caused by interactions between a star and two planet systems. The TTVs were caused by a relativistic shift in the Keplerian semimajor axis of each planet's orbit. The observed TTV amplitudes depend on the masses, spins, and obliquities of the host star, the planets, and their orbits, and are inconsistent with models of TTV caused by other astrophysical processes. Our observations provide the most precise measurements of the masses and spins of the host star and its planets, as well as upper limits on the obliquities of the planets' spin axes and their orbits. Future analyses of the TTVs caused by star-planet interactions may allow these parameters to be determined for planets around other stars.

We prove a meromorphic extension of the Tame exponential relative to a projective hypersurface, generalizing previous results for the special case of a hyperplane section. We then use this to compute the Euler characteristic of a hypersurface, and to give another proof of a known theorem of Kouchnirenko. As an application we calculate a multiple Milnor number of a Brieskorn singularity, thus extending a theorem of Danilov to this case. use We prove a meromorphic extension of the Tame exponential relative to a projective hypersurface, generalizing previous results for the special case of a hyperplane section. author(s) Yuri G. The most interesting is a calculation of a multiple Milnor number of a Brieskorn singularity, which extends a theorem of Danilov to this case.

The article concerns the probability distribution of economic profits. It traces the profit distribution back to the value distribution of the involved factors of production and postulates a log-normal distribution for the profit with two log-normalrandom variables: the factor-specific log factor-turnover and the specific log surplus production. The model parameters are estimated by matching the distribution of profits in U.S. economic data for the year 2005. The empirical investigation shows that the model fits the data well and explains the profit distribution in the middle scale region better than the widely applied Gibrat's law. Triplet nucleon-nucleon scattering is important to many areas of nuclear physics. For example, the scattering describes how free nucleons interact via the strong force and is directly involved in the binding of atomic nuclei. In addition, it is the fundamental process by which some ion induced nuclear reactions occur. Recently, a dedicated partial-wave analysis (PWA) of this process has been undertaken. Historically, these PWAs have been performed independently of each other, although a global PWA is an appealing concept that can increase the insight of separate analyses. In this work, a global PWA is performed that explicitly accounts for the systematic uncertainty of each separate analysis. As a result, new insights into the systematic uncertainties of past analyses and the correlation between them are revealed. In addition, previously overlooked constraints from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) are found. These new constraints will help guide further experimental and theoretical work toward a fuller understanding of this fundamental process.

Galactic globular clusters are generally identified from their high galactic latitude, low optical surface brightness, and redness in the color-magnitude diagram. However, a handful of globular clusters can also be found near the center of the Milky Way, within its historic luminous profile. These “central” clusters are particularly interesting due to their past association with galactic nuclei and their present potential to be tagged as loci of ongoing nucleosynthesis. Here we report on a study of the central cluster NGC 2419. We have obtained spectra for over a hundred red giants, from which we have measured chemical compositions and mapped the cluster metallicity and spatial distribution. We have uncovered a previously-unrecognized spatial structure in the distribution of calcium abundances that is correlated with that of the iron-peak elements. These compositional structures are suggestive of multiple epochs of star formation in NGC 2419, with the iron-peak showing evidence of chemical enrichment from the most recent (and presumably, central) generation of stars. NGC 2419 is thus the most promising galactic nucleus-related cluster currently known.

Nova explosions are powered by the rapid conversion of hydrogen to helium via the pp chain. The reaction rates in simulations are set by fitting to experimental data from the sun, but how well do these rates represent nova explosions, which can occur in a vastly different environment? I find that changes in these rates can alter the amount of explosive hydrogen produced, the amount of fallback, and the amount of radioactive nickel synthesized. In some cases, the nova fails to explode at all. The rates may need to be adjusted to better represent nova explosions, and I propose a simple method to do so. I also analyze how the explosion dynamics are affected by the chosen reaction rates. Increasing the hydrogen reaction rate too much increases the amount of explosive hydrogen produced and thus the strength of the explosion. In contrast, decreasing the hydrogen reaction rate too much decreases the amount of explosive hydrogen produced. Decreasing the hydrogen reaction rate too much leads to weak explosions that do not achieve nuclear statistical equilibrium. Examining these rates reveals that there is an optimal hydrogen reaction rate that results in a good explosion with the correct amount of explosive hydrogen, amount of fallback, and amount of radioactive nickel.

A small number of particles have been proposed to interpret the anomalous results obtained in the PVLAS experiment. These include, among others, hypothetical massive bosons, quantum liquid crystals, non-Abelian massless higher spin fields, axion-like particles, ythios, nanoscaled condensed matter, muons promoted to Dirac particles, nondiffusing spin-0 particles, and photons with integer spin. These interpretations assume that the PVLAS data are due to photons and do not explain the apparent violations of Lorentz invariance and other experimental results. None of these explanations are conclusive; further experimental tests are needed to identify the nature of the observed effects. It is remarkable that several of these particles have already been or soon will be tested against PVLAS data. The theoretical bases of these interpretations are described, and the experimental tests needed to determine the true nature of the effects are proposed. It is concluded that the simplest explanation of the results obtained in PVLAS so far is the photon hypothesis, although more complex interpretations cannot be ruled out. New, more conclusive tests are needed to distinguish between these hypotheses and determine the true nature of the effects observed so far in PVLAS. New, more conclusive tests are needed to distinguish between these hypotheses and determine the true nature of the effects observed so far in PVLAS. Photon hypothesis The PVLAS experiment initially reported anomalous results and, after a major upgrade, confirmed a larger number of initially observed effects. These include: - Parametric light amplification in a Vacuum Magnetic Field (PVMF): the experimental data show a peak in light emission at precise frequencies, corresponding to the effective magnetic fields at which the PVLAS cavity was resonant. - Intense slow light pulses: the PVLAS data also showed an intense slow light pulse, or ")", at a particular intensity value. These anomalous results could not be explained by the usual model of electromagnetic vacuum interactions and were thus the focus of a large number of theoretical papers proposing different particle explanations. These include, among others, hypothetical massive bosons, quantum liquid crystals, non-Abelian massless higher spin fields, axion-like particles, ythios, nanoscaled condensed matter, muons promoted to Dirac particles, nondiffusing spin-0 particles, and photons with integer spin.

Two-dimensional N=(2,2) super Yang-Mills theory is conjectured to be a compactification of ten-dimensional Type IIA superstring theory on a CY three-fold. In the weak coupling limit, the theory has been shown to flow to a non-trivial superconformal fixed point with 8 supercharges. Until now, this theory could only be analyzed on a single space-time dimension by performing perturbative computations in the weak coupling constant or by using AdS/CFT correspondence. Here we report a fully non-perturbative test of the superconformal theory for N=(2,2) super Yang-Mills theory on a computer. We use a domain wall formulation to simulate the theory on a two-dimensional spatial lattice, with both left- and right-movers. This work is an important step towards the full nonlinear understanding of the superconformal theory and the elucidation of its potentially important elliptic genera.

Ferromagnetism in doped graphene remains an important open issue despite extensive research in recent years. There is strong evidence for Stoner ferromagnetic instability in the electron-doped case, while for the hole-doped system a large body of evidence supports a nonmagnetic ground state. Here we show that the magnetic properties of hole-doped graphene can be understood in terms of a SU(4) C1S0-symmetric bosonized theory. Our approach starts from a generalized Hubbard model with full SU(4) symmetry. Using a combination of non-perturbative methods, namely the Functional Renormalization Group and the Cluster Perturbation Theory, we find that this model yields ferromagnetism at low energies. This leads us to propose that C1S0 symmetry might be generally relevant to ferromagnetic ground states in hole-doped graphene, and possibly in other systems with strong electronic correlations such as high-temperature superconductors.

Combining weak lensing tomography and halo clustering is a powerful tool to probe the cosmological parameters and trace the dark energy evolution. We apply this method to our cosmological N-body simulation and show that the joint data of tomographic flexion and two-point correlation function can break the parameter degeneracy in the $\Lambda$CDM model and can tightly constrain the parameters, such as the equation of state of dark energy (w) and the spatial curvature (k). Moreover, we find that the tomographic shear-shear correlation function has similar constraining power as the two-point correlation function. We expect that combining tomographic shear and galaxy cluster number counts can also tightly constrain cosmological parameters. We also show that a combination of tomographic flexion and galaxy number counts can further break the degeneracy between the normalisation of matter power spectrum and the growth rate of structure. The combination of these five methods can achieve the dark energy study in the era of precision cosmology.

Interstellar dust grains are normally observed and studied in the infrared, where their thermal emission helps trace the distribution of dust in our galaxy and in other galaxies. However, a robust measurement of the mass of molecular clouds requires observations at shorter wavelengths, where the emission is not dominated by the thermal dust emission but rather by the much more subtle Rayleigh-Jeans thermal dust emission. Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we have performed such observations of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). We detect multiple peaks in the thermal dust continuum emission from six regions known to host giant molecular clouds. The derived masses of these molecular clouds are between 430 and 1580 million solar masses, with a total mass of the SMC molecular clouds between 840 and 2380 million solar masses, making up between 25 and 63 per cent of the entire mass of the SMC. These numbers are significantly higher than previous mass estimates that did not account for the clumpiness of the SMC dust emission.

The central kiloparsec of galaxies is a region of intense star-formation and nuclear activity. It is also of great interest to galaxy evolution studies as the region within which two-thirds of the mass of a galaxy will usually form within $\sim 1$Gyr of its accretion onto a cluster (Fall 1973). It is now well established that the central kiloparsec of most galaxies contains a compact nuclear star cluster (NSC) (e.g.@2002AJ....123..855T; @2006ApJ...643..212H) as well as a central supermassive black hole (SMBH), in the form of either a Seyfert or an inactive black hole (respectively), whose gravitational influence will be evident in the kinematics of the nuclear stellar and gaseous components. The high densities and intense SF of the nuclear regions in most galaxies imply that the dynamical influence of the SMBH on the surrounding stellar and gaseous components will be substantial, and can usually be detected. Previous studies have shown that the nuclear dynamics of nearby galaxies is well described by a two-component model comprising a Newtonian point-mass (the SMBH) and a cusp (possibly describing the influence of a SMBH on stellar dynamics in the vicinity of the black hole). In this work we study the nuclear dynamics in a sample of 22 nearby galaxies, selected to comprise both active and inactive galaxies, using new IFU data from the KMOS multipurpose science sensor and published long-slit data. By applying high-resolution dynamical models to the resulting three-dimensional kinematic maps, we are able to measure the enclosed mass (and therefore the presence and dynamics of a SMBH), and the influence of the SMBH on the surrounding stellar and gaseous components. We find that while in general the dynamical influence of the SMBH is significant, we are unable to distinguish between different descriptions of the enclosed mass distribution in most cases. The mass discrepancy in these galaxies (where $\mbh/\langle\mstar\rangle\gtrsim0.4$) may indicate the presence of other non-baryonic mass components, such as a dark matter halo. This result runs contrary to the expectation that a two-component model should be sufficient to describe the nuclear dynamics of galaxies, and so may imply that either the simple Newtonian description of the SMBH is not adequate, or that the influence of the SMBH on the surrounding stellar and gaseous components is not purely Newtonian in nature. We present a simple phenomenological model to describe the contribution of the SMBH, which does not assume a particular description of the mass distribution, but does require three parameters: the mass of the SMBH ($M_{\rm bh}$), the fraction of dynamical mass contributed by the SMBH ($f_{\rm bh}$), and the radius within which the influence of the SMBH begins to dominate the dynamics of the system ($r_{\rm crit}$). A new large sample of radio-loud AGN, selected at different frequency ranges, is presented. The sample consists of 1724 quasars and blue broad-line AGN (46% of the entire SDSS DR7 Quasar sample) with observed frame wavelengths 280 nm < \lambda_{obs} < 600 nm detected by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) in the magnitude range 19.5 < r < 20.8. About 60% of the sample has observed frame wavelengths longer than 350 nm. The simultaneous optical/near-infrared spectrophotometric observations with the 2.3m Otto Struve Telescope at McDonald Observatory, Texas, USA and the WHT, Gemini, Subaru, UKS, VLT, and Gemini South telescopes provide, for the first time, measurements of rest-frame ultraviolet-to-optical spectral energy distributions for more than half of the sample (1419 objects). The redshift range of the sample is 0.04 < z < 5.44 with the median value of 0.39. Approximately 19% of the entire sample has z < 0.2. The multi-frequency selection enables investigation of the optical spectral energy distributions in a wider range of AGN physical parameters than is possible with smaller and less well-representative individual samples.

A tensegrity structure is a framework of bars and struts which forms a stable structure when all the bars and struts have equal stiffness. The structure is able to maintain its cubic form by minimizing its potential energy. Continuously tensegrity structures have been developed by Archigram in the 1960s and by DHK in the 1970s. This paper revisits continuously tensegrity structures by introducing a dynamic nonlinear unit that can be controlled through various activation signals. Each unit is a nonlinear tensegrity which models material, structural and dynamical behaviors. The framework is able to form various polyhedral structures and shows multiple stable states. The potential energy of the system can be reduced by changing the shape of the system. This paper presents a method of generating activation signals based on golden ratio and demonstrates multiple stable states of the generated tensegrities. The method can be applied to various types of tensegrity structures.

Optimizing future imaging survey of galaxies (TFIS) is proposed to confront models of dark energy and modified gravity. The survey will cover 1500 square degrees to obtain high-redshift enough galaxy samples to probe cosmology with redshift $2 < z < 3.5$ and supernova coverage to $z > 1.5$, and will employ a novel patch-based imaging strategy to enable efficient targeting of luminous galaxy clusters, the most efficient cosmological discriminants known. We demonstrate that this strategy will deliver cosmological constraints competitive with current optical andnear-infrared surveys, with the advantage of targeting far more efficient cosmological probes. We optimize the survey design with simulated annealing to achieve 2% precision in the dark energy figure of merit z 2 p(z=2|fzo) and 2.5σ deviations in the distance-redshift relation at fixed other parameters for f(R) and DGP models, respectively. We also show that the survey would detect evidence of modified gravity at the 3σ level if it exists at the level suggested by models, without assuming a prior on the background expansion history. We present the first design for this large and critical survey, and demonstrate that it is realizable with current technology. A long-standing controversy in X-ray astronomy is whether high energy (HE; 100-300 keV) X-rays are generated by the magnetic threads that connect the neutron stars (NSs) in neutron star binaries or by an accretion disk around a black hole (BH). Recently, absorption-like features at ~60-300 keV in a few magnetar candidates, including Mkr 841, were reported and attributed to either a cut-off power-law (CPL) or cyclotron resonance scattering feature (CRSFs), depending on the spectral analysis method used. The feature at 100-300 keV in Mkr 841 can be modeled equally well by a CPL or a CRSF. However, both the CPL and CRSF models are acceptable with large reduced χ2 values, 1.8 and 3.2 for the CPL and CRSF models, respectively. To better understand the spectral complexity of Mkr 841, we reanalyze the publicly available NuSTAR and *-Newton data using different methods. We confirm the CPL model with an exponential cut-off at ~120-180 keV, but not the CRSF model, in Mkr 841. The sharp cut-off at ~120-180 keV is well represented by a pure absorption model. Furthermore, we detect a broad band X-ray continuum extending to at least 50 keV. The phenomenological model consisting of an attenuated CPL and an absorption model successfully accounts for the broad band X-ray continuum, which likely originates from electron scattering in the magnetosphere or in the vicinity of the NS. The broad band X-ray spectrum can also be interpreted as a NS wind. These findings indicate that the magnetar scenario is a more reasonable interpretation for Mkr 841 than a black hole scenario. Mkr 841 is known as a highly magnetized neutron star with the surface magnetic field of approximately 4.8∼8.3 × 10^{13} G, the highest magnetar surface magnetic field known. It has a spin period of 2.0378 s and a fast-down jump of the period between 2010 and 2016, which is among the fastest observed in magnetars. Several absorption-like features have been reported in Mkr 841 at ~60-300 keV, including a absorption line at ~93.3 keV reported by INTEGRAL in 2004, an absorption edge at ~130 keV reported by Swift in 2010, and an absorption feature at ~60-300 keV reported by NuSTAR and *-Newton. However, the spectral complexity of Mkr 841 has not been fully understood until now. To study the NS matter environment of Mkr 841, we analyzed the publicly available NuSTAR and *-Newton data. We found that the phenomenological model consisting of an attenuated CPL and an absorption model can fit the broad band X-ray spectrum of Mkr 841 equally well, which likely originates from electron scattering in the magnetosphere or in the vicinity of the NS. In this work we solve the equation for the high energy evolution of parton distribution functions (PDFs) including the first running coupling corrections. To this end, we use the principle of maximum conformality (PMC) introduced byliusly, which provides a novel solution to the renormalization group equation (RGE) for the PDFs in the perturbative regime. In this approach the solution is achieved by adding a particular RGE solution for the QCD beta function into the PMC one, which introduces a new parameter. We demonstrate that the PMC solution fulfills all requirements of the formal perturbative expansion in QCD. Running coupling corrections are included via the PMC parameter, which is fixed by the corresponding momentum sum rule for the corresponding coupling. To validate the approach, we consider the total and polarized distributions of the neutron for a given target mass number A. For the first time, our result for the neutron structure function F2(x, Q2 = 2.2 GeV2) presents a complete leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) nuclear corrections calculation. We predict that the gluon distribution function in the neutron is significantly smaller than that in the proton at large x values, which can be tested by future experiments.

MgB2, a new superconductor with critical temperature higher than 30K, has recently received a great deal of attention due to its remarkably high transition temperature. The reasons for such a high transition temperature are not completely clear so far. The main reason is the special structure of the boron layers where two boron layers are separated by a strategic misalignment of the magnesium and aluminum layers. Substituting some magnesium atoms with lithium atoms allows the critical temperature of the resulting compound to be increased up to 37K. In the case when some of the magnesium atoms are substituted with lithium together with a small addition of carbon into the crystal structure, the critical temperature can be increased up to 41K. The introduction of lithium and/or carbon may have different effects on the superconducting properties of MgB2. The exact reason for the superconductivity increasing effect of lithium is not clear so far. Researchers from the Center for Studies of Hetero-structures at the National Technical University of Ukraine, Kiev, have carried out a comprehensive study of the effect of lithium and carbon additions into the structure of magnesium diboride on its structural and superconducting properties. For this, single crystals of magnesium diboride with different compositions were grown by the spontaneous negative crystallization method. The phase composition of the obtained crystals was determined by X-ray diffraction method. The authors of the article used the following empirical rule to characterize the relations between the structure and superconducting properties of the investigated materials. MgB2 – stable phase in the structure of magnesium diboride,possesses high transition temperature (Tc = 39K); the presence of carbon in the composition increases electron density in the conductive band, increasing the superconducting transition temperature; the addition of lithium into the structure of magnesium diboride increases the distance between the magnesium layers, increasing the Tc to 37K; the addition of lithium and carbon at the same time increases the superconducting transition temperature to 41K. The addition of lithium changes the chemical composition and structure of the obtained crystals in a way that increases the distance between the magnesium layers. As a result, a three-dimensional superconductor with a record high transition temperature of 37K was obtained. The addition of carbon causes an increase in the electron density in the conductive band and in turn increases Tc to 37K. The addition of lithium and carbon results in an increase in the distance between the magnesium layers to a value that is larger than that in the case of a three-dimensional superconductor with a record high transition temperature of 37K. As a result, a three-dimensional superconductor with a record high transition temperature of 41K was obtained.

Half-metallic materials are promising candidates for spintronic devices owing to the 100% spin polarization of the conduction band. However, most of the known half-metals are ferromagnets with slow spin-polarized electron propagation, which limits their device applications. Here we report the synthesis of edge-oxidized zigzag graphene nanoribbons (ZGNRs), in which a polarized half-metal state is retained despite the addition of oxygen edges, a commonly observed reconstruction in experiments. The emergence of the half-metal state is elucidated by ab initio calculations, which indicate that the half-metal state is stable due to the enhancement of the [Formula: see text] carbon-skeleton orbitals in the edges of ZGNRs. As a result, the spin relaxation rate is strongly reduced and the calculated spin polarization of the conduction band is about 92%, making the ZGNRs potential candidates for high-speed, low-power spintronic devices.

Silicon based minerals are widely distributed in the solar system, especially in asteroids and meteorites. They are the most abundant minerals in the solar system and comprise over half of the chondrite class of meteorites. Silicates are thought to be key materials for prebiotic chemistry on early Earth. However, to understand the delivery and processing of these materials in protoplanetary disks, we analyzed crystalline silicates and dust in the Taurus molecular cloud complex with the spectral infrared identify and structural spectrophotometer (SEDAR) on the Hubble Space Telescope. We find the following abundances for three Taurus star systems: 12 Tau, 14 Tau, and 37 degrees 31' west: 21, 22, and 50% for for crystalline foramina; 5, 12, and 20% for crystalline forsterite; and 17, 42, and 49% for crystalline enstatite. Abundances in the disk are correlated with the concentration of crystalline silicates in the natal gas complex. Thus, crystalline silicates are an excellent tracer of recent and ongoing planet formation. In addition, we find many sight lines with at least one structure that has a thin layer of crystalline dust along the line of sight. The dust layer is ~10% the thickness of the photosphere for the Taurus stars. We suggest the dust is left over from the formation of planetesimals, when runaway accretion resulted in the formation of rocky cores larger than one meter in radius. The cores created small cm-sized fragments, leftover from their formation, which were then bombarded by projectiles in the surrounding region. These fragments produced a thin layer of crystalline dust along the orbit of the planetesimals, left behind when the planetesimals cleared out the region of material formed by condensation.

Recently, a mysterious parallel sorting algorithm known as dualheap selection has been discovered and demonstrated to be faster than Quicksort on both real and simulated computer systems. Dualheap selection works by swapping selected items into a well-balanced dualheaps, which apparently facilitates the sort. Dualheaps are internally heap structures in which the least-recently-swapped element is at the top. The mechanics of the sort are rather deep and mysterious, and the parallelism seems to arise from the interaction between dualheaps and cachelines. The algorithm seems to work well on modern multicore architectures, but it is not obvious how it should be adapted to work on shared-memory systems such as GPUs. Interestingly, dualheap selection is related to a stack-based sorting algorithm known as quick stack. The two algorithms share a number of similarities in their implementation and motivation. In fact, dualheap selection is faster than quick sort on some random distributions, suggesting that the unusual algorithm is more than just a trick. Dualheap selection and the quick stack were discovered independently around 2008 by separate computer scientists pursuing apparently unrelated research interests. There has been some speculation that dualheap selection may be a complex building block in some kind of a data structures continuum, similar to heaps, tries and chmaps. Dualheap selection has so far resisted all attempts at rigorous analysis, although it appears to have useful approximation properties and can be made stable with some tuning. No serious algorithm has been devised yet based on dualheap selection, although certain theoretical improvements and empirical successes have been demonstrated. Despite its success on real computer systems, dualheap selection has not been proven to be correct. In particular, it is not known whether the theory has all the right properties or whether there are exotic inputs that lead to incorrect behaviour. This article provides an overview of dualheap selection, with an eye toward explaining how and why it works. We also discuss some recent developments in understanding the algorithm and ways in which it might be adapted to work on different computer systems.

RBS 315 is a radio-loud quasar at a high-redshift of z = 2.653. It was observed by both Suzaku and previous XMM-Newton observations in 2005 and 2012, with a gap of 6 years in-between. During this time the sources spectrum could have significantly changed. New data shows that the source also displayed cut-offs in its spectrum at approximately 100-150keV in 2005, which were not previously observed. The cut-off softens to 20-50keV in the later observation in 2012, and can no longer be detected by Suzaku. The difference between the two observations is probably related to a change in the strength of the primaryContinuum source, with a possible association to a change in the black hole's mass. In both observations, the source also displayed a very hard power-law component with a photon index of 1.9-2.0, which seems to be intrinsic to the object and not likely due to Compton reflection from a neutral medium.

A newly discovered X-ray transient XMMU J174716.1-281048 has been observed by multiple X-ray observatories over a period of a few days in the beginning of February 2017. This new transient is located in a close binary system with a neutron star. From the analysis of the publicly available data we determined the source characteristics and studied the X-ray behavior of the source. We found that the source was bright (count rate about 0.02 counts/sec in the 0.3-10 keV band) at the beginning, but faded at a slow rate (about 1 count/sec in 3 days). This is very unusual for X-ray transients with a neutron star accretor. We did not detect the source at the end of the monitoring period (3 days later). The possible nature of this object is discussed. The source was discovered by multiple X-ray observatories on 2017-02-07 at coordinates R.A. = 17h47m16.1s and Dec = -28d10m48s (J2000). Preliminary analysis of the data obtained from the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory (INTEGRAL; 1 day integration) and the European Photon Imaging Camera (EPIC) on XMM-Newton did not reveal its presence. However, the object was later observed by the X-ray telescopes Chandra (0.3-10 keV band, 3ks observation) and XMM-Newton (0.3-10 keV band, 3 days of observations). The spectral characteristics of the source, the lightcurve and the distribution on the sky make this source very unusual, and call for further detailed study. We determined the source's basic parameters using the X-ray spectral characteristics: the spectrum can be well fitted with a simple absorbed power-law model with a hydrogen column density of N_H = 1.1x10 21 cm -2 and a photon index of 1.8. The 0.3-10 keV luminosity of the source at the beginning was about 3x10 33 erg/s. The source reached a peak count rate of about 0.02 counts/sec, and then faded at a slower rate of about 1 count/sec over 3 days. No additional observations of the source were conducted after the 3 days of initial observations. A more detailed study of this source is planned. In particular, follow-up optical and radio observations are required to determine the nature of the object. It is very unlikely that the source is a normal star, since the luminosity and fading rate do not correspond to the behavior of a normal X-ray binary system with a neutron star accretor. Using an ultracold atomic cesium Feshbach resonance, we prepare molecules in the collision channel of ground state KRb molecules. By varying the magnetic field, we induce coupling between different molecular spin configurations, which we use to carry out spectroscopic studies of the KRb potential energy surface. We measure avoided crossings between vibrational ground state quantum states and first excited state quantum states, showing evidence of a repulsive core in the potential. Furthermore, we measure coupling between the ground state spin-orbit doublet and first excited state, which we use to study inelastic decay into a weakly bound excited state. We measure spin-orbit coupling and widths for the lowest lying avoided crossings. Finally, we show that variation of the Feshbach resonance position with magnetic field can be used to control the KRb molecular scattering length. These studies of ultracold molecules coupled by Feshbach resonances open up new possibilities for molecular quantum simulation and quantum engineering.

A growing network is a general network model in which nodes can be in one of several states (such as "alive" or "dead") and can activate (or "arrive") and become nodes of the network according to a scheduling rule. In this model, nodes are allowed to have an arbitrary out-degree which may change over time. In this model, we study the maximum in-degree that can be supported for a network whose out-degree is one and nodes arrive according to a Poisson process. It is proven that the maximum in-degree is one if and only if the out-degree is two, and it is two if and only if the out-degree is one and the in-degree distribution is constrained to be delta_0. In other words, the maximum in-degree is limited by the arrival process and by the out-degree of the network. In this paper, we assume that nodes arrive according to a Poisson process and the out-degree of the network is one. We study the maximum in-degree that can be supported if the in-degree is limited by the out-degree of the network and by the arrival process. It is shown that this maximum in-degree is one if and only if the out-degree is two, and it is two if and only if the out-degree is one and the in-degree distribution is delta_0. It is an open problem to determine the maximum in-degree for other out-degree distributions and other arrival processes.

The Carina Nebula, a large region of stellar formation in the southern sky, has long been of interest to astronomers for its beauty and intriguing complexity. In recent years, new instruments operating in the near-infrared have opened up new avenues of study, allowing investigation of gas and dust structures obscured by dust in optical wavelengths. Using data from the Subaru Telescope’s near-infrared instrument (SCam), we have mapped out the distribution of warm hydrogen gas in this cloud complex. The resulting picture of the cloud structure, while still containing some complicated features, shows a clearer division into distinct filaments and regions of active star formation. These results illustrate the value of new near-infrared instruments for studies of our Galaxy’s vast, complex interstellar medium. On December 30, 2006, the Swift satellite detected a gamma-ray burst (trigger number 0003265). It was one of the longest observed gamma-ray bursts with more than 10000 seconds of persistent emission. X-ray afterglow of this gamma-ray burst was observed by XMM-Newton and Swift. The XMM-Newton observation was performed 4.3 hours after the trigger and the Swift observation was performed 39.8 hours after the trigger. During the first 26.5 hours of the Swift observation the source was fading steadily, with a factor of 2.2 decrease in the soft (0.2-2 keV) X-ray flux. The decay was however exceptional, with an increase by a factor of 5.2 between the 24th and the 40th hours of the observation. The soft X-ray spectrum during the first 6 hours is well fitted with a single power-law with an energy index of −0.9 with a reduced chi-square of 0.74 for 6 d.o.f. After the rapid increase the decay is well fitted with a power-law with an energy index of −0.76. The unusual behavior of the flare, together with the soft spectrum observed during the first 6 hours make this a good example of chromaticjet break, in which the low energy part of the observed spectrum changes. The Swift satellite has also observed other gamma-ray bursts, but this flare in the X-ray afterglow of GRB 050730 was observed only with XMM-Newton and Swift. Journal article: Munoz-Darias, T., Froning, A. S., Bracker, S. W., & Strom, T. G. 2012,, 765, 73

ANALYSIS OF SINGLE SPECTRA IN THE QUIET SUN SPECTRA FROM HMI AND MDI A single spectrum from the magnetic diagnostics on board SOHO and NASA's Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SUN / HDต Backasch et al. (1995): Two photospheric lines with opposite magnetic polarity are clearly visible in the intensity profiles. A possible explanation is the Zeeman effect. The result is in disagreement with the notion that the quiet Sun has no magnetic field. The signal to noise ratio in the quiet Sun, obtained with current technologies, is not sufficient to detect the weak fields of a few Gauss. The weakest fields in the solar atmosphere are observed in the photospheric layers, where the gas pressure and temperature are high. In particular, two photospheric lines with opposite magnetic polarity are clearly visible in the intensity profiles. A possible explanation is the Zeeman effect. The result is in disagreement with the notion that the quiet Sun has no magnetic field. The quiet Sun has a magnetic field of several hundred Gauss, although it is much weaker than the fields of active regions.

Theory predicts that stars more massive than about two solar masses will develop degenerate cores, and will consequently become magnetic stars known as Ap stars. Observational evidence for such a link, if it exists, could provide strong constraints on stellar evolution models. Here we report spectropolarimetric observations of 150 candidate Ap stars belonging to open clusters and associations. We measured longitudinal magnetic fields and from this, assuming the relation between magnetic field strength and rotational spin down rate, obtained estimates of the stellar rotation rates. We find a significant anticorrelation between the stellar age and the strength of the measured magnetic fields, such that the most slowly rotating stars have the strongest magnetic fields. This is consistent with the existence of a spin-down magnetic field strength evolution timescale of order 10^6 years, much longer than the estimated lifetimes of stars with convective cores. This is the first observationally-based evidence for the link between magnetic fields and stellar evolution.

The physics of the early universe is well understood, at least up to a point near the moment of decoupling. Forced period of late time acceleration, if it exists, is expected to be driven by a dark energy component with an equation of state parameter near -1. As the temperature of the universe fell below the electron mass threshold, electrons and protons recombined into hydrogen and helium, and photons decoupled from the rest of the universe. Electromagnetic radiation remained accessible to the laboratory until nearly a minute after decoupling, at which point all remaining photons were a billion times more energetic than visible light. This photon bath, created during the famous Recombination Epoch, is crucial to the formation of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and the subsequent history of the universe. However, despite its importance, the bath remains largely unstudied. In this work, I compute the subsequent radiation authored by charged particles as they "unplugged" from the bath of background radiation. This radiation, which comprises a stochastic background of electromagnetic waves, has potentially observable signatures in radio astronomy, very high energy gamma ray astronomy, and cosmology. It is a unique probe of structure in the early universe and a new source of anisotropy with a distinct spectrum and distinctive evolution with time.

Jupiter and Saturn are the two largest planets in the solar system. They both formed in the gaseous proto-planetary disk, from which the solar system planets were formed. Planets are supposed to form in a circumstellar disk of gas and dust, surrounding a newborn star. Interactions between the forming planets and the disk can have a significant influence on the dynamics of the planets and the formation of the Solar System as a whole. Jupiter and Saturn orbited the Sun in the early phases of the Solar System's formation, but as the planets' orbits shifted, they ran into planetesimals and pebbles in the disk. In the early 2000s, scientists started to detect the signatures of these bodies through observation of dust in the disk. In this paper, we investigate the orbital dynamics of Jupiter and Saturn in the context of a gaseous proto-planetary disk. We use symplectic maps, a modern technique from dynamical systems that solves the particle equation of motion on a discrete mesh in phase space. We find that, in our model of the Solar System, which includes the disk, Jupiter and Saturn migrate inward until the the ice line is reached. After that, the Solar System stabilizes with the two giants forming a 1:2 mean-motion resonance. We also see a 7:8 outer resonance between the orbits of the two planets and a 1000:2000 mean-motion resonance with a planetesimal. This last resonance creates an additional damping in the eccentricities of the giants. Our results suggest that the Solar System formed through a process of convergent migration, in which Jupiter and Saturn migrated towards the Sun while the disk protected them from distant planetesimals. This mechanism could not have worked if Jupiter and Saturn did not start close to the Sun. The formation conditions for the Solar System may therefore be looked for in the vicinity of the Sun.

The current standard model of cosmology, $\Lambda$CDM, suffers from several tensions, including the lack of a compelling explanation for the observed accelerating expansion of the universe. Many solutions have been proposed to explain this behavior, the two most popular of which are the cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, and dark energy, represented by the density parameter, $\Omega_\Lambda = \Lambda / (3 H_0^2)$. The cosmological constant was introduced to explain an early period of cosmic acceleration in $\Lambda$CDM, and after ruling out potential contributing factors, such as modified gravity, remains the simplest explanation. However, the $\Lambda$CDM model, with its constant $\Omega_\Lambda$ fails to explain the present day accelerated expansion. Dark energy, as evidenced by the density parameter, is a dynamically evolving component of the universe, and thus it does not reside in an equilibrium state. Furthermore, $\Lambda$ is an ill-defined term - it is often assumed to represent a constant, but this is a logical fallacy. While assuming a time-independent $\Lambda$ is a simplification, it does not reflect how one would actually measure a constant. More fundamentally, there is no compelling theoretical reason to assume $\Lambda$ should be a constant, or even a dynamical parameter. Since the introduction of the cosmological constant, there have been several measures to determine whether its dynamical nature has been established, and each of these measures has concluded that $\Lambda$ is a constant. While the theoretical arguments against treating $\Lambda$ as a dynamical parameter are often summarized, the mathematical proofs of the theoretical arguments are typically not presented. Instead, this paper aims to present the theoretical arguments against treating the cosmological constant as a dynamical parameter.

The paper is mainly concerned with a mesoscopic version of a diffusive Josephson junction with arbitrary transparency of the interlayer connection and arbitrary magnetic field in the “barrier”-layer. Within the quasiclassical Usadel theory the supercurrent through this junction is determined by the Green’s function which satisfies the appropriate boundary condition at the barrier. The problem of finding the supercurrent reduces to the problem of solving a system of nonlinear algebraic equations involving the Usadel equations and the normalization condition. The method of ”uniformization of eigenvalues” is used to explicitly find the supercurrent for arbitrary barrier transparency, at zero and finite temperatures. It is shown that supercurrent has a finite maximum at intermediate temperatures and abruptly decays to zero at zero temperature. The paper is noteworthy for novel exact results for the supercurrent through a mesoscopic diffusive Josephson junction. This problem is of practical interest, for example, for studying low-temperature characteristics of hybrid SQUID prepared by assembling several Josephson junctions in a single superconducting loop.

Unconventional superconductors have been discovered in several families of materials with various crystal structures in the last decade. One such superconductor is Moiré superconductor which is made of two misoriented sheets of hexagonal boron nitride. Moiré superconductivity is sensitive to strain and emerges only in carefully engineered heterostructures. It was suggested that the superconductivity is mediated by phonons, however the pairing symmetry was not known. We use a unbiased functional renormalization group approach combined with unbiased weak-coupling limit checks to demonstrate that the Moiré phonons mediate conventional s-wave superconductivity. This elucidates the nature of superconductivity in Moiré superconductor and paves the way for design of generic phonon-mediated superconductors. This research was published in Nature Physics (DOI: 10.1038/s41563-020-0651-z) Dr. Jian-Xin Cai (Assistant Professor, University of Michigan) The conventional phonon mediated superconductivity in Moiré superconductor The recent discovery of superconductivity in the van der Waals heterostructure formed by two sheets of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) with different orientations (1,2). The critical temperature (T~c~) of the Moiré superconductivity in these heterostructure is very high, up to hundreds of kelvin. Although the crystal structure of the Moiré superconductor is very distinct from those of conventional superconductors, the superconducting pairing mechanism is very similar to that of high-Tc cuprate superconductors. However, there are some key differences. For example, (1) The charge-carrier bandwidth in Moiré superconductor is a few tens of meV, much smaller than that in cuprates (around 100-200 meV). (2) The Moiré superconductor is highly asymmetric, while the conduction band in cuprates is almost symmetric. (3) The Moiré superconductor is naturally very thin with a very small Hillman parameter (0.5). (4) The Moiré superconductors are ferro-magnetic with spin-rotation symmetry. Functional renormalization group approach To understand the physical nature of the Moiré superconductor, it is helpful to first discard the effect of some unphysical high-energy structures through a method like DFT. After removing the high-energy structures, we then use a functional renormalization group (FRG) approach to study the dynamic fluctuations of the effective interactions. In this approach, we write the quantum fluctuations of the many-body system in terms of the interaction function, using the Wilson method. The functional renormalization group is used to calculate the effective interaction function with a certain cutoff. Compared with the direct computation of the many-body problem, this method only considers the long-distance interactions, and is therefore effective and accurate. In this paper, we describe a novel approach to exact numerical computation of Casimir energies and forces. Our approach is based on the observation that both the Casimir energy and the full electromagnetic field dynamics can be cast as eigenvalue problems for the same Laplacian operator. We then show how this operator can be numerically approximated inexpensively on arbitrary 3D meshes. Using this approach, we demonstrate stable and accurate computation of the Casimir energy and forces for a wide range of problems, including configuration with nontrivial boundary conditions. We conclude by applying our method to the case of two metallic plates in vacuum, for which we obtain results in excellent agreement with those obtained via traditional, perturbative methods. This work was done at Harvard University. Authors are Yi Liu and Robert M. Millner. IGR J16194-2810 is a new symbiotic X-ray binary (SXRB) detected with INTEGRAL. The compact object is probably a neutron star, accreting from the donor star, which is most likely a white dwarf. The optical counterpart of IGR J16194-2810 was first identified by HETE-II observations and classified as a Be/X-ray binary. IGR J16194-2810 was also detected with Swift and Chandra. IGR J16194-2810 was observed to be undergoing flares similar to Gamma-Ray Bursts. The orbit of the compact object around the center of mass of the system is most likely elliptical with a long period. There is an ongoing outburst, and the emission of the source was detected with a 2-20 keV flux of ~ 10^{-9} erg cm{-2} s{-1}. This source was previously catalogued as HD 154417B, an O8.5 III-IV((f)) star located at a distance of 19.7 kpc from the Sun. The nature of IGR J16194-2810 as a member of the class of X-ray binaries is further strengthened by the discovery of periodic radio flares, and the presence of a strong optical/X-ray correlation. The extreme ultraviolet spectrum of IGR J16194-2810 measured with HST/COS is rich in emission lines and features. The spectrum resembles that of a system in outburst more closely than that of a steady system. Strong variability, and the possible identification of a cyclotron absorption feature suggest that IGR J16194-2810 contains a magnetic neutron star with a spin period of 9.4hours. The possible link between this source and other members of the symbiotic X-ray binary family is further strengthened by the discovery of a possible extended supersolar metallicity plasma around the compact object, which is typical of those observed in symbiotic binaries. This rich multiwavelength behavior make IGR J16194-2810 a very interesting system to understand the late stages of binary star evolution. The source is located in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) which allows to study this system in great detail. This will allow to trace the mass loss of the O8.5 III-IV((f)) star progenitor of the compact object, study the effects of tidal friction on the orbit, and examine the impact of the close proximity of the compact object to the stellar surface on the acceleration of particles around the magnetic neutron star. In this paper, we study simple shear flows in inelastic Maxwell models, where the material particles have pairwise linear forces. In particular, we consider the constant-shear-stress case. Through Chapman-Enskog analysis, we obtain a set of nonlinear differential equations for the model-specific distribution functions. For a one-dimensional model, we observe dynamic instability in the form of periodic density waves and calculate the growth rate. For a two-dimensional model, we show that the Navier-Stokes equation is restored in the large-time and large-length-scale limits. change-verification This paper studies simple shear flows in inelastic Maxwell models, where the material particles have pairwise linear forces. The Gemini Deep Planet Survey (GDPS) was a Large Strategic Program conducted by the Gemini Observatory, which was dedicated solely to the discovery of transiting planets around faint stars (i.e., GDPS is a Transit Survey). The survey utilized both Gemini North and South telescopes from 2010–2013, and produced the largest sample of transiting planet candidates with precise photometry to date. The initial survey yielded 312 planet candidates, and many of these candidates remain candidates today. The detection efficiency, physical characteristics, and the diverse systems of the GDPS planets make this survey highly complementary to the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), which began observing in 2017. The long period nature of some GDPS planets suggests a higher frequency of large planets in this sample, and the parameter space of the smallest planets can be explored with the MEarth Project, which has been monitoring these systems since 2012. GDPS planets also have median orbital distances that are significantly more distant from their host stars than the orbits of planets around the same apparent brightness found by the [*Kepler*]{} mission, and as a result, GDPS has the potential to detect an excess of small planets compared to the Solar System. The precise ephemeris information from the *TESS* mission can be used with GDPS follow-up observations to search for planets around nearby stars, facilitating the discovery of Earth-analogs.

Networks have been studied in various fields of science. From the physical point of view, the underlying mechanism and structure of a network can reveal a lot about the system. On the other hand, much of the modern science is built on the hypothesis that the behavior of large systems can be explained in terms of the behavior of their constituent parts. Complex networks offer a perspective on systems that are composed of many parts and exhibit behavior that cannot be explained by the behavior of their individual parts. In a complex network, a system of many different elements are linked and interact with one another in a non-trivial way. A striking feature of such networks is the prevalence of highly clustered structure. In particular, the degree of clustering in a complex network, k- clustering, is robustly determined by a single parameter, the clustering coefficient, which in turn is strongly correlated with the characteristic path length of the network. In this work we show that this robust correlation is disrupted at a critical value of the clustering coefficient. We analyze the percolation properties of networks with different values of the clustering coefficient and show that the clustering has a strong effect on the survival probability of nodes in the network after the removal of a fixed number of nodes. For clustering coefficients above the critical value, the removal of a small fraction of nodes decreases the robustness of the network by disconnecting large portions of the network. In contrast, for clustering coefficients below the critical value, the removal of a small fraction of nodes has little effect on the robustness of the network. We test our analysis on several real-world complex networks and show that several of these networks have clustering coefficients above the critical value, indicating that these networks are particularly susceptible to targeted attacks.

In this paper, we discuss (non) gauge invariance of Wilsonian effective actions in supersymmetric theories. For this purpose, we first recall the definition and key features of the gauge invariant effective action, the effective potential, and the effective average action. Next, we demonstrate that the corresponding gauge invariant Wilsonian actions are not invariant under ordinary diffeomorphisms. In other words, their operator count and field content are not (manifestly) invariant under these transformations. As a counterexample, we consider the Abelian Higgs model in the Wilsonian picture. Finally, we argue that this lack of gauge invariance severely hampers the derivation of gauge invariant quantum theories from classical ones, i.e. the renormalizability proof. In particular, it prohibits the application of the standard methods of quantum effective field theory to these theories. For these reasons, we advocate the systematic use of the gauge invariant effective actions, effective potentials, and effective average actions in theoretical physics.

On April 6th, 2005, the gamma-ray burst (GRB)050906 was detected by both the Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) on board the Swift satellite and the REM telescope in Maui. This burst was very short, with a duration of only 0.06 s. The X-ray, optical, and radio afterglows were very weak, with decay indices of -1.2, -1.6, and -2.2, respectively. Several authors suggested that this short duration might be related to a compact object merger event. Here, we report the detection of a double-humped feature in the lightcurve, with the peak-to-peak amplitude of 6% and an intra-peak separation of 3.5%. If interpreted in terms of opacity from Thomson scattering, this feature indicates a cloud with an electron density of at least 2.5 × 10^{17} cm^{-3} and a radius of about 0.4 μm. Such a cloud could be created as a result of a stellar collapse event or a compact object merger. If this feature is interpreted in terms of a photospheric emission component, the temperature of the photosphere is about 3.8 × 10^5 Kelvin. This very hot photosphere, with an emission measure of 2.8 × 10^{58} cm^{-3} and radius of about 3.2 km, is more consistent with a compact object merger event than a core-collapse event. Thus, we suggest that the short duration of the GRB050906 event was caused by the tidal disruption of a compact object by the supermassive black hole at the center of its host galaxy.

A two-dimensional analytical framework is presented to study the capacity of sparse multipath channels in the ultra-wideband regime. The underlying physical model considers a multipath channel as a superposition of a large number of weakly coupled paths. Each path is characterized by a unique delay, complex gain, and amplitude, which enables the modeling of the multipath channel as a sparse vector of complex Gaussian variables. Via statistical mechanics techniques, the average capacity of the sparse multipath channel is obtained by averaging over the random channel parameters. The proposed analysis provides accurate and insightful characterization of the capacity in the multi-gigahertz frequency regime, where the conventional wisdom of using tight complex Gaussian input signals is no longer valid. Numerical results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and demonstrate that the maximum capacity is achieved when the ratio of the propagation delay to the signal wavelength is equal to an integer divided by half the ratio of the signal frequency to the bandwidth of the channel, which provides useful insight into the optimal waveform design for millimeter wave communications.

Theoretical physicists have recently proposed a new paradigm, called the Slingshot mechanism, to explain the success of the inflationary paradigm. In this model, our universe popped into existence near a boundary of another, larger universe. This boundary has a highly curved geometry, which could lead to fluctuation of the metric across the boundary. These metric fluctuations can act as a stochastic gravitational wave background (SWB), which seeds the formation of structures in the universe. We calculate the power spectrum of SWB generated in the Slingshot model, and compare it with the power spectrum of Primordial scalar spectrum (PS) calculated by the WMAP team. We show that, for some parameter choices, the SWB and PS are nearly identical. We conclude that a concrete realization of the Slingshot model could account for the success of inflation without the need for fine-tuning. The full paper is available here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.11164.pdf

The dust temperatures of the prestellar cores in the Rho Oph main cloud and in other star forming regions have been measured with the Mopra telescope at 12mm wavelength using the technique of spectral line thermal broadening. These dust temperatures are related to the physical parameters of the cores and thus to their masses and provide a means of testing current theoretical models of the initial conditions of star formation and their evolution. The results show that the dust temperature in the cores in the Rho Oph main cloud is higher than in other clouds. The reason is the action of external stellar radiation pressure in the dense cores, which raises the dust temperature beyond the value predicted by the theoretical models unless some other mechanism, such as YSO heating, is acting to remove the excess energy. The data are consistent with there being a near-linear correlation between core mass and temperature over about four orders of magnitude in core mass. In addition, there is clear evidence that the dust temperature in the cores rises steeply with core mass toward the high mass end of the function. If this is an accurate picture of the evolution of the core mass function then it has profound implications for theories of the collapse of the density fluctuations responsible for producing stars.

Pulsars are amazing rotating neutron stars that emit beams of radiation that can be observed over enormous distances. They are natural laboratories for relativistic gravity and have been important tests of Einstein's general relativity. The double pulsar system J0737-3037 contains two pulsars, A and B, in a relativistic Keplerian binary with a 5.76 day period. We report the detection of a characteristic radio frequency chirp from the system and show that it is consistent with the general relativity prediction of the Shapiro delay due to the gravitational field of the companion pulsar, B. Our observation of this Shapiro delay from such a compact system provides the most direct evidence to-date for the preferred frame effect predicted by alternative theories of gravity.
