Networks have been a powerful tool to analyze relationships between entities, and uncovering structures behind networks have led to remarkable advances in many disciplines, including physics, biology, social sciences, and computer sciences. The most common types of networks areUndirected networks where the connections between any two nodes does not depend on whether other nodes are connected to the first two nodes. Most social and economic networks are undirected, and the vast majority of theoretical network studies have been based on undirected networks. Weighted networks and directed networks where the direction of connections is used to encode directional information are also popular, and have provided significant new insights.In this paper, I introduce a novel network construction technique based on a class of nonlinear models with long-range interactions. A network structure is encoded into the model by considering a generic function of pairwise distances between nodes, and the model is fitted to data via maximum likelihood. Unlike existing network models that often involve intractable integrals or computationally prohibitive Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, my method is based on fast Fourier transform that allows for likelihood computations in polynomial time in the number of nodes. The approach is validated on a number of synthetic and real networks, and shown to provide significantly better fits than existing techniques.

Here we present a study of the star cluster system in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), using the Dragonfly Cluster Survey. We measure the ages of 215 clusters in the sample, and compare them to stellar population models. In contrast to earlier studies, we find that the mass distribution of SMC clusters is best fit by models in which most clusters form with a broad range of initial conditions, and no single set of parameters (e.g. star formation rate, initial mass function) can fully explain the entire sample. As such, the SMC cluster system provides a useful testbed for models of cluster formation. This supports the picture in which many clusters form with a broad range of initial conditions, rather than the classical view that most clusters have a unique star formation history and were born with similar parameters. A full understanding of this difference will likely require the study of larger samples of clusters in other galaxies, which will be possible with wide-field multi-object spectroscopy on next-generation telescopes.

A photometric study of stellar structures throughout the disk of the barred galaxy NGC 3367 is presented. This is a nearby (distance of 23.9 ± 0.7 megaparsecs, or approximately 62 million light-years), interacting (T = 5.1 ± 0.3), face-on spiral (inclination of 13°) which exhibits some of the most extensive and low-level star formation of any known spiral. I obtain UBVRI photometry of 54 areas across the disk of NGC 3367, including spiral arms, inter-arm regions, and nuclei. The data are used to study the star formation history of the galaxy and the changes in the stellar populations across the disk. Stellar population studies are complicated by several factors. First, different parts of the disk may have different reddenings, so colors can provide only partial information. Second, even within a given structure, there is likely some random sampling variance: the oldest stars are the most widely distributed, so sampling a given region more densely will cause younger populations to be over-represented relative to the global average. Third, dust attenuation can reduce the flux of young stars; this effect is wavelength dependent, so broad bandpasses such as those of the BVR filters I employ here are not suited to accurately tracing recent star formation. Finally, because the light of individual stars is so much fainter than that of galaxies, even a low level of background contamination can significantly skew measured colors and star formation rates. These concerns are illustrated by Figure 1, which compares synthetic colors to the data. The synthetic model galaxy is composed of three simple stellar populations (SSP) with ages of 0.1, 0.5, and 5.0 Gyr, respectively, and a fourth with a constant star formation rate (SFR). The distribution of stars in NGC 3367 is compared to a model with solar metallicity, and a two burst SFH, one 0.1 Gyr ago and the other 0.5 Gyr ago. The fits are not ideal; given the simplicity of the models, the SFH appears to have varied dramatically in the last 0.5 Gyr, and, while a constant SFR seems an adequate fit to the bulk of the disk, the central regions are very poorly fit at all epochs. The great width of the arms and clear change in the relative numbers of blue and red stars between the arms and inter-arm regions suggest that a two burst SFH provides a much better description of the evolution of NGC 3367's disk than a constant SFR. Ultraviolet to blue light is dominated by very short lived, massive stars which are present only in the most active parts of a galaxy's star formation. In contrast, the visible and near infrared are dominated by less short-lived, less massive stars, whose creation is strongly suppressed in low activity regions such as arms. A popular supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking scenario is the constrained minimal supersymmetric standard model (CMSSM), in which the minimal supergravity (mSUGRA) assumption is made about the initial conditions of the soft supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking parameters. In this scenario, the parameters of the CMSSM are fully determined by just four input parameters: the universal scalar mass parameter, m0, the universal trilinear scalar coupling parameter, a0, the ratio of the vacuum expectation values of the two Higgs doublets, tan beta, and the sign of the Higgs mixing parameter, sign(mu). Current experimental data, in particular the measured values of the physical masses of the quarks and leptons, can be used to determine preferred values for these CMSSM parameters. However, in this paper we show that in addition to the parameters m0, a0, tan beta, and sign(mu), another SUSY breaking parameter, the gluino mass, MLsp, also takes on a preferred value when these experimental constraints are imposed. We call this new and significantly more general CMSMS scenario the constrained minimal supersymmetric standard model (CMSSM). We perform a global fits to the CMSSM and CMSMS parameters m0, a0, tan beta, sign(mu), and MLsp to the measured masses of the sparticles and the HPS1 parameters, alpha(GUT), m0(3), and A0, determining the best-fit points and 1 sigma errors for these parameters. The global best-fit point for the CMSSM is found for m0 = 150.7 GeV, a0 = -3.14 TeV, tan beta = 5.9, sign(mu) = 1, and MLsp = 985 GeV. For the CMSMS, the best-fit point is m0 = 131.6 GeV, a0 = -3.2 TeV, tan beta = 8.4, sign(mu) = -1, and MLsp = 983 GeV. Thus, we observe that, within the context of the CMSMS, the gluino mass can be significantly lower than in the CMSSM. This is very significant, as lower values of MLsp greatly expand the LHC LHC phenomenological realm, with larger values of MLsp yielding a more constrained LHC phenomenology. We find, however, that the best-fit points for both the CMSSM and the CMSMS are quite close and are consistent with one another, indicating that the difference between these two scenarios is not statistically significant. The values of the universal scalar mass parameter, m0, the universal trilinear scalar coupling parameter, a0, the ratio of the vacuum expectation values of the two Higgs doublets, tan beta, and the sign of the Higgs mixing parameter, sign(mu), that are preferred by current experimental data within the context of the CMSSM are also consistent with those favored by current data in the CMSMS. A strongly lensed Lyman break galaxy at z = 7.085 behind the cluster Abell 1689 is presented. Using the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH), we show that the arc configuration is likely produced by the cluster halo with a high concentration parameter of c = 12.2. The smooth deconvolved light profile of the arc suggests an elliptical galaxy, and the spectroscopic redshift supports the presence of ionized gas and young stars. The combined strong lensing and spectrum data indicate that this galaxy has a total stellar mass of (2.3 +/- 0.3) x 10 11. In the near-infrared spectral energy distribution, the galaxy falls in the green pea stage between normal spiral galaxies and green peas, and is likely forming stars at a high rate. The arc is the most distant confirmed strongly lensed galaxy with both spectroscopy and image reconstruction. This galaxy gives a rare glimpse of galaxies during the epoch of reionization, one week after the big bang.

The Stueckelberg extension of the Standard Model (SM) is a simple and minimal extension that admits dark matter (DM). In particular, it is charged under a new global U(1) symmetry, with the lightest particle, a Majorana fermion, forming a stable DM candidate. In this model, the global U(1) symmetry is radiatively broken by the vacuum expectation value (vev) of an SM-singlet complex scalar field. The model predicts the existence of two new particles: the Stückelberg particle, which is a ghost-like particle that helps us understand the underlying symmetry of the model, and the radion, which is the Goldstone boson associated with the spontaneous breaking of the vev of the SM-singlet complex scalar field. The radion plays an important role in explaining the tiny Planck scale as compared to the weak scale, and can explain the Cosmological Constant problem. We show that, in contrast to the radion, the Stückelberg particle has a definite mass, and can interact with the known particles via the weak, strong, and gravitational interactions. Therefore, it is a promising DM candidate. We show that, under the correct DM density, this model can simultaneously account for the observed Universe’s expansion, its rotation, and the gravitational interaction between galaxies. In particular, we show that under such circumstances, galaxy clusters can form naturally, without the need for some form of dark energy. Furthermore, we discuss the phenomenology of this model, and show that this model can be tested at current and near-future experiments.

The evolution of solitary waves and undular bores in shallow-water flows over a gradual slope with bottom friction is studied. The behavior of these waves is strongly affected by the nature of the bottom, and in particular, by the strength of the bottom friction. In the absence of bottom friction, these waves always propagate rightward and break down into undular bores after some time. When bottom friction is taken into account, solitary waves can still propagate rightward, but they may also leftward, form spirals or even turn into undular bores. The behavior is explored via numerical and asymptotic methods, and good agreement between the two is found. It is also shown that the dispersion relation for undular bores can be obtained as an expansion around the KdV regime, and a truncation of this expansion is provided. The truncation is shown to be valid if the undular bore travels significantly faster than the mean speed of the underlying wave packet.

Finite-size effects in roughness distribution scaling are discussed for interfaces in statistical physics, social science, and Earth science. The finite-size effects are important when the length scale of interest is comparable or smaller than the system size. This is typically the case for real-world roughness data, where the length scales of interest are typically within one order of magnitude smaller than the system sizes. For such data, the statistical properties may deviate significantly from the corresponding theoretical predictions based on infinitely large systems. In particular, two-point correlations in roughness are shown to be directly proportional to the surface area-to-volume ratio of the system. Examples of applications include but are not limited to evolution of power-law correlations in random growth models, and fitting of power-law roughness scaling to real-world data. Here we consider two well-known examples of the latter application: evolution of roughness correlations in random growth models and fitting of power-law roughness scaling to real-world data. For both applications, the surface area-to-volume ratio plays an important role. First, it determines how far two-point correlation functions can sense the length scale of interest. Second, it modifies scaling exponents that are determined from the slope of correlations at large length scales. These two factors are shown to conspire to yield the finite-size effects on the scaling of the surface area-to-volume ratio with length scale. Two scaling relations for two-point correlations are derived for system sizes from one to infinity. They are shown to be asymptotic to the theoretical predictions for large system sizes. Fitting of power-law scaling to real-world data is found to be particularly susceptible to the finite-size effects. This is because the range of correlation length scales of the data is very narrow, leading to large relative surface area-to-volume ratios. In contrast, theoretical predictions for infinitely large systems break down for the data. This article provides an overview of finite-size effects in scaling relations for real-world data, and points to some common pitfalls that should be avoided.

The CDF experiment at the Fermilab Tevatron proton-antiproton collider has searched for the production of single-top quarks in p \bar{p} collisions, with both W boson and top quark decays to a bottom quark and a muon or electron, resulting in a signature with an energetic isolated muon or electron, large transverse momentum imbalance due to the momentum of the underlying W boson, and a b-quark jet resulting from the top quark decay. Observation of this signature would indicate that single-top quarks, a predicted but rare class of particles, were produced in p \bar{p} collisions. No evidence for single-top quark production was found in the data, and therefore 95% confidence level upper limits on the production cross section are set as a function of the assumed cross section. Among various theoretical predictions for the single-top production cross section, the x \bar{x} production via the weak interaction is most promising for the discovery with the Tevatron, due to its high cross section and clean signature. The CDF results are consistent with the expectation from the standard model (SM) prediction for the production of single-top quarks via the x \bar{x} interaction. However, various beyond the SM theories can also enhance the production of single-top quarks and produce signatures with different characteristics from those of the SM single-top quark production. A direct search for single-top quarks in the CDF data provides a powerful tool to test the SM and to probe new physics.

Galaxy clusters are powerful cosmological telescopes that can be used to study structures and composition of the Universe on large scales. Here we present a census of galaxies, cold hydrogen (Hi) and hot X-ray-emitting plasma in 65 galaxy clusters and groups observed with the [*Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE)*]{}. We determine the masses of dark-matterhalos hosting these systems, calculate the masses of their central galaxies, and study the evolution of the relations between these mass scaling relations with lookback time. We find that while most of the clusters have central galaxies that are massive and are consistent with the observed mass–scaling relations for groups and clusters at similar redshifts, a significant fraction of clusters appear to have had recent or even ongoing major galaxy overdensities, with observed central galaxy masses that are significantly higher than those expected from their host dark-matterhalos, implying the likely disruption of substructure within their dark-matterhalos, a process that would be enhanced by preheating of the cluster environment by early generation of galaxies. We conclude by discussing the likely origins of this excess baryonic mass and its implications for the mass–scaling relations of clusters and groups over cosmic time.

Five-quarks bound states, also called molecular states, have long been predicted to exist in quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Until recently, their existence was not verified experimentally. Now, the exotic $X(5568)$ meson, with its unusual properties, has been unambiguously confirmed by the Belle and LHCb experiments to be a weakly bound hadronic molecule of the $D^0$ and $\bar{D}^{*0}$ mesons. In this work, we report lattice QCD studies of this bound state using both the quenched approximation and two dynamical flavors of twisted mass fermions. We find that the binding energy is much smaller than previously estimated, bringing into question the existence of this state and suggesting that the $X(5568)$ is best interpreted as a quirk of the current lattice action. The $X(5568)$ was first discovered by the Belle collaboration in the $B^+\rightarrow K^+ X(5568)$ decays, with a measured mass of $M=5568\pm 3\mathrm{ (stat)}\pm 8\mathrm{ (sys)}$ MeV, and an absolute decay width of $\Gamma=205\pm 21\mathrm{ (stat)}\pm 35\mathrm{ (sys)}$ MeV. This particle was subsequently confirmed by the LHCb collaboration, with a measured mass of $M=558\mathrm{ (stat)}\pm 2\mathrm{ (sys)}$ MeV.

In high energy physics, the photoproduction of pion, i.e. the collision of the laser or high energy photons with the high energy protons, plays an important role due to its sensitivity to the content and characteristics of the proton. The theoretical framework to describe this process is the generalized parton distribution function, that allows to access the distribution of quarks and gluons among the protons, at the distance scale comparable to the size of the protons themselves. Among these, the axial density, that is the probability of finding a quark with a certain flavor and spin aligned, has been measured only recently by the CLAS collaboration at JLAB, using the exclusive $\gamma^* \pi^0 \to \gamma \pi^0$ reaction. In this article, we present a next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) resummation for this distribution, at the first time this is done for a hadronic process. The resummation is performed using the effective field theory method, to all orders in the coupling constant between the electro-weak and strong interactions. As a by-product of the resummation, we also calculate the large logarithmic contributions beyond NLL, using the method of expansion in $\alpha_s$ around the heavy quark effective theory, which is valid at very low momentum scale. We compare the resummation and the perturbation theory results, and estimate the theoretical uncertainties in the results. We also present a prediction for the next CLAS12 experiments.

In 4D Riemannian geometry, the geometric product of two vectors is zero. In 5D Kaluza-Klein theory, this product is non-zero, and defines an extra dimension with geometric properties reminiscent of the role of speed of light c in Special Relativity. We show that the zero-field limit of a Higgs model in 5D yields an enlarged 4D spacetime with metric described by a Kaluza-Klein tetrad. The tetrad fields are identified with the inverse of the metric and its first and second derivatives, in agreement with general relativity. The fifth force appears as a torsion of the Kaluza-Klein spacetime, due to the geometric product of the v5 vector with itself. In the vicinity of particles, the fifth force exhibits the Yukawa potential form. We compute the leading term in this potential, and compare it with the current limits on the fifth force. The theory presented in this paper has not yet been experimentally verified. However, the mathematical concepts used to formulate the theory, such as the product of vectors, the tetrad formalism, and the zero-field limit of a Higgs model, are all commonly used in gravitational and electroweak theories. As such, an experimental test of this theory would simultaneously test gravity, the zero-field limit of the Higgs model, and the mathematical formalism of tetrads.

Trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) are a heterogeneous population of objects, most of which are likely scattered disc objects (SDOs) that formed within the trans-Neptunian region of the Solar System. Their existence was predicted in 1664 by Johann-Heinrich Schroter, and the first such object was identified in 1801. TNOs are considered a key testbed for theories of planet formation, as their current orbit distribution provides evidence of the processes by which the Solar System evolved over time. Recent high-resolution images from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) have revealed that a significant fraction of TNOs are in fact in compact multiple systems. This fraction is particularly high for larger TNOs, with about 15% of 2499+ objects with diameter >50 km being in multiple systems, and as many as one third of trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) with a diameter of 100 km or more being part of multiple systems. Although many of these observed companions are likely remnants of shattered embryonic asteroids, several systems with centaurs, comets, and classical Kuiper belt objects are also clearly identified. Chaos-assisted capture (CAC) has been proposed as a mechanism to form these companions through resonant interactions with the giant planets, but recent theoretical work suggests that resonant capture may not be sufficient to explain the existence of so many multi-chained systems. In this paper, we propose another mechanism by which TNOs in the trans-Neptunian region could have been members of multiple systems: fission. We show that the sudden merger of two SDOs in a near-contact configuration can lead to the formation of a third SDO thanks to an instability that creates an additional gravitational torque. This mechanism, which we dub chaos-assisted fission, has the advantage of explaining the high observed fraction of binary TNOs without the need for planets to be responsible for their origin. We show that this dynamical process is likely to occur frequently in the trans-Neptunian region, especially during close encounters. By conducting a series of N-body simulations, we show that the instability that creates a new companion tends to occur for SDOs with a diameter of 100-150 km that are dynamically caught in an inward migration region between 35 and 40 au. For the conditions typically found in the trans-Neptunian region, the instability occurs more frequently for SDOs with an initial orbital radius of 30 au than for those with an initial orbital radius of 50 au. Finally, we show that two SDOs with initial semi-major axes of 300 au and 1.5 au could have been members of a binary system through this process.

We present the results of a systematic study of the diffuse optical light in a sample of galaxy clusters observed with the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT). The cluster sample was selected from the Data Release 4 of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The optical light is extracted from the flux measured in a circular region centered on the X-ray emission peak and with a variable radius, depending on the cluster richness. The intracluster light (ICL) fraction in optical bands is strongly correlated with the cluster X-ray temperature, showing a higher ICL fraction in hotter clusters. The stellar mass of the cluster galaxies is also a factor that correlates with the ICL fraction, showing that more massive galaxies have formed more extended tidal tails and envelopes that contribute to the ICL light. Finally, we find that the optical light is more centrally concentrated than the X-ray emission. This effect becomes more marked toward the cluster center, and we suggest that it may be explained by the dissipation of the stripped galaxies' dark matter halos within the cluster potential.

IEEE 802.11e has been widely accepted as the primary standard for WNM (Wi-Fi network management). However, its reliance on leasing asymmetric-bandwidth bandwidth for announcement and confirmation purpose, might be unfair to low-traffic stations (LTSs). In this paper, we present the design of an efficient, layer-2 bandwidth sharing mechanism for IEEE 802.11e, to reduce LTSs’ implicit bandwidth leasing. The mechanisms are implemented and evaluated in an emulated 802.11e IBSS. The results show that our mechanisms can reduce the L5-L14 latency of the emulated IBSS by ~13.5% on a saturated channel, compared with the state-of-the-art unloader. Besides, our mechanisms do not degrade the Wi-Fi QoS of the non-LTS clients, and maintain a high fairness and a low leasing cost on LTSs.

In quantum mechanics, the angular momentum (AM) and linear momentum (PM) operators have a spectrum of eigenvalues that is far more extensive than that allowed by classical Physics. For example, the eigenvalues of the square of the total AM operator in a given quantum mechanical state are proportional to the total nuclear spin, a property with theoretically unlimited resolution. In addition, the eigenvalues of the square of the total linear momentum operator in a given quantum mechanical state are equal to the square of the reciprocal of the reduced Planck's constant, a physically observable property with theoretically unlimited precision. Since these quantities are numerically equal to, respectively, the total AM and total PM of the quantum state, this work concludes that quantum mechanics does in fact adhere to the AM and PM properties expected from classical Physics. These extraordinary results are the consequence of rigorous mathematical theorems from the field of Quantum Mechanics, which state that the eigenvalues of these operators are theoretically unbounded. Classical Physics would suggest that the values of these operators be limited by the product of the reduced Planck's constant and the corresponding spatial dimension of the system. The eigenvalues of the square of the total AM operator in a given quantum mechanical state are equal to the square of the reciprocal of the reduced Planck's constant, a physically observable property with theoretically unlimited precision. Since these quantities are numerically equal to, respectively, the total AM and total PM of the quantum state, this work concludes that quantum mechanics does in fact adhere to the AM and PM properties expected from classical Physics. Similarly, the expectation value of the square of the total angular momentum operator in a given quantum mechanical state is equal to the reduced nuclear spin of the quantum state, a property that theoretically has no upper limit. Furthermore, the expectation value of the square of the total linear momentum operator in a given quantum mechanical state is equal to the reduced Planck's constant, a physically observable property with theoretically unlimited precision. Since these quantities are numerically equal to, respectively, the reduced nuclear spin and the reduced Planck's constant, this work concludes that quantum mechanics adheres to the AM and PM properties expected from classical Physics.

We report the discovery of a population of AGNs composed of galaxies with double peaked optical emission lines, along with a smaller population of galaxies with single-peaked lines. The AGNs with double-peaked lines are predominantly low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINERs), while the Seyfert 2 galaxies contain both low-ionization (Baldwin, Phillips & Terlevich 1981; Veilleux & Osterbrock 1987) and high-ionization (FWHM$\ge$1000 km s$^{-1}$) lines. This coexistence suggests that the low-ionization and high-ionization lines are emitted from two different gas-rich nuclei, where the low-ionization lines are from an accretion disk around a SMBH and the high-ionization lines are from a merger-driven nuclear starburst. Our data suggest that nuclear mergers are more frequent in late-type galaxies with double-peaked lines, and support a scenario where double-peaked lines are produced by the incidence of gas-rich mergers in intermediate mass galaxies. This work was performed on the Nebula telescope, which is supported by the University of California Instatewiderocket science program.

Researchers in theoretical high-energy physics have been developing a powerful method called supersymmetry or SUSY for nearly thirty years. In particular, SUSY has proved very useful for solving problems in quantum field theory that are too difficult to handle with more standard techniques. One well-known example is the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry in the standard model of particle physics, which describes the properties of particles like the proton and electron. In this work, we show how to apply SUSY techniques to a system with an important application in condensed matter physics, namely antiferromagnets with doped dopants. These materials have proven useful for quantum information processing as well as exhibiting a number of fascinating phases as a function of doping. We show that doped antiferromagnets are adequately described by a massive version of the standard model quantum field theory known as CP$^1$ theory. CP$^1$ is a special example of a two-dimensional field theory, a topic of active research with tantalizing connections to string theory. We present results for a single hole in an antiferromagnet, though our technique will also work for any spin. This paper demonstrates the utility of SUSY techniques for studying quantum many-body systems, and provides a pedagogical example that can be reproduced by nonexperts.

In this paper we apply the tools of information geometry to study the geometry of the space of holonomic probabilities on the letter space of an iterated function system (IFS), and in particular to study the variational problem of maximizing the entropy under constraints imposed by a holonomic probability. We establish several results which illustrate that the maximization of entropy subject to holonomic constraints is not a linear program and describe its geometry. In particular, we describe a stratification of the space of holonomic probabilities by Kolmogorov complexity. We also provide an explicit formula for the gradient of the entropy functional in our setting. We then study the geometry of the level sets of the entropy and show that they are geodesics with respect to the spatial distance defined on our space of holonomic probabilities. This result allows us to show that the entropy is strictly concave on the interior of the simplex of holonomic probabilities. We show that the space of holonomic probabilities with maximal entropy is smooth, and is the exponential proportional to a Gaussian. We also show that the volume of the maximal entropy simplex is finite and show that it is equal to the unique real number whose logarithm is proportional to the Kolmogorov complexity of the maximal entropy probability distribution.

Power-law distributions have been observed in a variety of empirical datasets, arising in a variety of contexts, such as the sizes of human settlements1, the masses of objects2, the income of individuals3, the stride lengths of individuals4, the cell diameters of plants5 or the bark widths of trees6. The broad applicability of power-law distributions has led to the suggestion that such distributions may arise naturally as the outcome of a number of simple generative processes, such as the product of independent random numbers7, the catastrophic failure of a single component in a random failure system8 or phase transitions in discrete models9. However, it has also been suggested that power-law distributions may result from the superposition of a large number of more common distributions10, the simple permuation of a single common distribution11 or a logarithmic distribution12. Indeed, there are a variety of processes capable of generating such distributions. For example, the superposition of a large number of common distributions may generate a distribution with a power-law tail13. In addition, heavy-tailed distributions with similar mathematical forms to power laws have been observed in a variety of contexts, arising from different generative processes. For example, the late stages of a logarithmic distribution may be similar in appearance to a power law14, and it has been suggested that the size distribution of computer files may be consistent with a power law, even though this is often attributed to finite size effects15. Similarly, one may speculate that certain types of networks may exhibit a power-law degree distribution, though this has not been demonstrated rigorously. In addition, there are processes which generate power-law distributions which are not generative processes. For example, the removal of nodes from a network with a power-law degree distribution may result in the removal of nodes with degree distributions similar to a power law16. It has also been suggested that heavy-tailed distributions may arise as a result of the sum of a small number of more common distributions17. For example, a truncated power law may arise as the result of a superposition of common distributions18. In this case, it is interesting to note that there are many examples of power-law distributions which arise as a result of a small number of generative processes. For example, the distribution of human settlement sizes appears to arise as the result of two generative processes - the growth of human populations through the coalescence of settlements and the natural variation in the size of settlements as dictated by geographical and environmental constraints19.

The classical magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) theory, proposed independently by @Alfvén and @Goldreich, explains that plasma waves are the elementary particles that underlie various types of electromagnetic radiation. In this framework, @Sturrock originally proposed that an electron plasma wave is responsible for causing kHz-frequency fluctuations in the emission from pulsars. This hypothesis, known as the @Sturrock dispersion relation, has been confirmed by subsequent MHD simulations [e.g., @Heikkila]. It is remarkable that there is an excellent agreement between the observed and predicted phase velocities of the waves, as the product of the electron density and magnetic field strength in a pulsar plasma is known a priori. However, there are several studies that question the validity of the @Sturrock dispersion relation. First, @Kelley re-examined it based on previous work by @Krause. They claimed that the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability may give rise to a frequency-dependent correction to the phase velocity. In addition, a three-wave interaction process, between an electron plasma wave, a ion plasma wave and a proton sound wave, was proposed by @Schmidt. They argued that the second and third waves combined to form an infinite set of coupled oscillations, in contrast to a linear analysis that predicted a single dispersion relation. Some other research teams supported these arguments by performing different kinds of analysis [e.g., @Chen; @Chandran]. Therefore, the validity of the @Sturrock dispersion relation remains controversial.

The capillary-induced interactions between two cylindrical rods in an aqueous solution are investigated beyond the superposition approximation. The excess free energy of the system is expressed by two equivalent formulas, one in terms of the direct interactions between the rods and the other in terms of the Fourier transform of the microscopic density profile. The direct interactions are evaluated by the finite-size-scaled numerical solution of the interaction energy between two spheres. By considering an external cylinder of one orientation adjacent to an external cylinder of another orientation, an intuitive procedure to extract the rod-rod interaction is developed. The validity of the approximate treatments and the applicability of the method are examined by comparing the theoretical predictions with the available simulation and experimental data. It is shown that the present theory can qualitatively describe the impact of finite sizes, orientations, and concentration on the pair interactions between the rods. Author: Wang Yue, Hu Yin, and Ren Xu Journal: Physical Review E 93, 043306 (2016) DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.93.043306 URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.1897 Click here to visit the article on arXiv.org.

In this paper we present the first evidence of the transverse proximity effect in spectral hardness towards HE 2347-4342. Hard x-ray observations of this quasar, performed with the Chandra satellite, revealed a proximity effect typical of a forest of absorption systems along the line of sight. However, new optical observations carried out with the William Herschel Telescope (WHT) revealed a proximity zone with a filamentary structure and a transverse size of 30-40 kpc in radius, showing that the forest of systems is transverse the line of sight. We discuss the evidence for the transverse proximity effect and its implications in terms of the transverse distance between the forest of systems and the central quasar.' Sikora, published on 17th September 2023 on the arXiv pre-print server [ https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.09983 ] The transverse proximity effect in spectral hardness on the line of sight towards HE 2347-4342 In this paper we present the first evidence of the transverse proximity effect in spectral hardness towards HE 2347-4342. Hard x-ray observations of this quasar, performed with the Chandra satellite, revealed a proximity effect typical of a forest of absorption systems along the line of sight. However, new optical observations carried out with the William Herschel Telescope (WHT) revealed a proximity zone with a filamentary structure and a transverse size of 30-40 kpc in radius, showing that the forest of systems is transverse the line of sight. We discuss the evidence for the transverse proximity effect and its implications in terms of the transverse distance between the forest of systems and the central quasar.

In this paper we introduce a method for constructing Einstein manifolds of any desired signature (2m+1,1), admitting a space of twistor lines of any prescribed flag type. These twistor spaces are constructed as moduli spaces of holomorphic curves with given asymptotics, in some simply-connected Riemann surface with complex structure deformed by a holomorphic differential. This deformation complexifies the structure group of the tangent bundle, reducing it from the special orthogonal group SO(2m+1,1) to the isometry group of the corresponding Einstein metric. The moduli spaces of holomorphic curves considered here are related to the generalized Krichever construction of Einstein metrics. We classify all the obtained Einstein structures when the Riemann surface is the complex plane or the sphere. As an application, we present explicit Einstein metrics on some of the orbifolds of the standard sphere S^{2m+1}/Ω, where Ω is a fixed point free symmetry of the underlying Fefferman-Graham ansatz for the anti-de Sitter metric.

A possible evolutionary scenario for the S Ori star is presented. S Ori is a Mira variable with a thick circumstellar dust shell, a bipolar molecular outflow, and a SiO maser shell. The star has a photosphere and a neutron star companion. S Ori was observed in 2002, 2004, 2007, and 2010 with the Spitzer Space Telescope, the Submillimeter Array, the Infrared Telescope on Mount Mauna Kea, and the Very Large Telescope, respectively. The IR emission from the dust shell was declining at a rate of 2.2 ± 0.2 MJ kg-1 yr-1, while the SiO maser shell was expanding at a rate of 10.0 ± 0.7 km s-1. From 2002 to 2010, the photospheric radius expanded at a rate of 19.2 ± 1.3 km s-1, while the radius of the molecular layer remained approximately constant at 7.2 ± 0.3 km. There is a large discrepancy between the observed expansion rates of the photosphere and those of the molecular layer and SiO maser shell. The photosphere and SiO maser shell are thought to be moving at relative velocities of +11.5 km s-1 and +34.7 km s-1, respectively. It is proposed that S Ori has a binary companion with a more rapidly moving photosphere and SiO maser source. Such a companion is likely to be a neutron star formed through a collision between a white dwarf and a red giant. The energy source for this companion is the radioactively decaying neutron star.

A search for radiative decays of the Upsilon(1S) meson into eta and eta' has been performed with the full dataset of the L3+00 experiment at the LEP collider. No evidence for these decays has been found, and upper limits at the 90% confidence level of Br(Upsilon(1S)-->eta) < 5.0x10(-8) and Br(Upsilon(1S)-->eta') < 2.5x10(-8) are obtained. These results improve previous ones from the L3 and OPAL experiments. The L3+00 experiment, which was performed at the LEP collider, is described. The data sample consists of 202 x 10(exp - 7) positive mesons, collected from 1996 to 2000, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 208 pb(s). The results of a search for the radiative decays of the Upsilon(1S) meson are presented. No evidence for these decays has been found, and upper limits at the 90% confidence level of Br(Upsilon(1S)-->eta) < 5.0x10(-8) and Br(Upsilon(1S)-->eta') < 2.5x10(-8) are obtained.

Turbulent flows are complicated, chaotic systems that can not be well approximated by finite-dimensional models. The evaluation of the complete Reynolds-Averaged-Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations—typically involving a solution procedure with a computational cost proportional to the eighth power of the Reynolds number—is therefore often avoided and an alternative approach is followed, based on a closure to model the unresolved scales. One possible approach consists in introducing some modeled correlation between the fluctuations of the Reynolds-Averaged-Variable (RAV) and the instantaneous Reynolds stress. Among all the possible correlation tensors, the one ensuring the maximum Reynolds-Averaged-Navier-Stokes (RANS)equation-consistent (RA Conserving) is often chosen, see e.g. [1] for a review. This closure, however, does not take into account the fact that the fluctuations of the Reynolds stress are not fully known, and therefore the Reynolds-Averaged-Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations are not closed. In this work, we propose to model the fluctuations of the Reynolds-Averaged-Variable (RAV) via an Exponential-based solution of the Reynolds-Averaged-Variable equations, where the exponential is computed using the (analytical) matrix exponential of the (unclosed) Reynolds-Averaged-Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations. This new closure, that we call Matrix Exponential-Based Closure for the Turbulent Subgrid-Scale Stress (MEC-TS), ensures the RA Conserving property and greatly reduces the cost of the evaluation of the Reynolds-Averaged-Navier-Stokes equations at each time step, at the same time accounting for the unresolved contributions in the Turbulent Subgrid-Scale (TSGS) model.

Dynamical 3-space, also known as Ernie Newton's stage, is a four-dimensional theory in which spacetime is considered to be a dynamic entity that can interact with and be affected by events occurring in three-dimensional space. Unlike four-dimensional theories of gravity that assume the conservation of energy–momentum, Dynamical 3-space assigns a privileged status to the three spatial dimensions of space. The theory assumes that space and time are interchangeable, and that the observed spatiotemporal curvature of our universe is the result of motions occurring in three-dimensional space. In this review, the fundamentals of Dynamical 3-space are outlined, as well as several applications and experimental tests of the theory. The main aim of Dynamical 3-space theory is to provide a deeper insight into the working of the universe, and specifically gravity. Since the beginning of the 20th century, we have been living in a three-dimensional world. We experience the world in terms of height, width and length. It was Ernie Newton, in the 1920s, who first considered the possibility that space could also have a fourth dimension, depth. In Dynamical 3-space, time is not considered separate from space. Space and time are considered to be different aspects of the same entity, and the universe we experience in our daily lives is just a projection of how three dimensions of space have been projected onto a two-dimensional surface. We shall outline in this review how Dynamical 3-space could explain gravitational interaction as a four-dimensional phenomenon. In this way, it could explain the imbalance between the four fundamental forces of nature: the three forces occurring in our everyday life (electromagnetic, strong and weak nuclear forces) and the Gravity force, whose imbalance is responsible for the development of galaxies and solar systems. We shall start by providing the main tenets of Dynamical 3-space. This will be followed by a summary of the experimental tests of Dynamical 3-space carried out up to now, including the latest tests using the gravitational anomaly, GAP-7, which took place in June 2022. We shall then discuss the main applications and predictions of Dynamical 3-space theory. Finally, we shall outline the main objections and shortcomings of the theory and discuss possible solutions to these problems. Theory of Dynamical 3-space was developed by Ernie Newton in the 1920's. The fundamental assumption of Dynamical 3-space is that space and time are interchangeable. The theory was originally developed as a means of reconciling Albert Einstein's theories of relativity and the Newtonian universe, but it also explains how the universe we experience on Earth, with its three spatial dimensions, came to be. A new analysis of the physical and spectral characteristics of the T8 and later-type dwarfs is presented here. We assemble multi-wavelength photometry and spectra for a sample of 240 T8 to T10.5 dwarfs. Photometric parallaxes are calculated and compared to values from previous studies. We use these photometric parallaxes to estimate absolute magnitudes, and separate the sample into bins of luminosity and color. We find the distribution of spectral types in each bin, and use these to calculate spectral types as a function of luminosity and color. We also analyze the full sample of T dwarfs observed by previous studies and calculate the same distributions. We find that the relationships between spectral type, luminosity, and color are the same for all samples, with the distribution of objects following a clear trend of decreasing radius with later spectral type. We also find a correlation between effective temperature and spectral type that can be well-approximated by a black body relation. We use this to estimate the effective temperatures of the new samples, and confirm that the trends in temperature with spectral type and luminosity are the same for the new samples as in the full sample of previously-studied T dwarfs. The physical relationship between spectral type, luminosity, color, and effective temperature has important implications for the nature of these objects, and the origins of their atmospheres. The observed trend of decreasing radius with later spectral type can not be reconciled with theories of T dwarf evolution if these objects are primarily planetary in nature. Instead, it is likely that the observed trend corresponds to a lack of fully-convective objects at later spectral types. This interpretation is also supported by the observed correlation between spectral type and effective temperature, which implies that later-type T dwarfs must be cooling off rapidly to have the same temperatures as previously-studied T8 and T9 dwarfs. It is possible that the distribution of temperatures for these later-type objects is altered by evaporation of subsolar layers, though this requires a more complex evaporation model than is currently available.

The predictability of solar activity has been a subject of interest to solar physicists and solar activity forecasting for purposes such as space weather. Historically, the Sun's global activity, or solar cycle, has been observed to occur in periods of approximately 11 years followed by a period of approximately 5 years during which the activity levels are reduced or "minimum" activity. Using data from the Helios satellite, Richardson et al. (2011) found that they could accurately predict the length of the solar cycle 7 based on the mean strength of the maximum of the field strength of solar Magnetic Flux Ropes (MFR) at the solar cycle start, or minimum. The model was further refined by Richardson et al. (2013), who found that the length of the solar cycle could be accurately forecast given the total magnetic flux in the MFR, as well as the magnetic flux in individual flux ropes. Using data from Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO), Schou et al. (2015) further developed the model, showing that the model could also accurately predict the strength and length of the next two solar cycles, but not the following two cycles, when the parameters were again based on the MFR strength at the start of the current cycle. Using now Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO)/Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) data, Hudson et al. (2017) found that the MFR strength at the start of the current cycle did not, in fact, predict the length of the current cycle, but instead, the amplitude of the magnetic field of the active region at the start of the cycle, as well as the length of the current cycle, could be accurately predicted. Using a neural network model based on these parameters and a data set that extended back to the 1850s, Hudson et al. (2018) found that the model was capable of predicting the solar cycle accurately up to three years in advance. The model was also tested on data from Solar and Heliospheric Observations (SOHO), where it was shown to have an overall skill score of approximately 70% at predicting the cycle minimum level. In this work we present results from using a mean-field model to predict the solar cycle from its start. Mean-field models have previously been used to successfully predict solar phenomena such as filament eruptions, flares, and CMEs from the photospheric level, to coronal phenomena such as solar transients, and eventually, to predict solar cycle strength. Richardson et al. (2011) found that the maximum MFR strength at the start of a solar cycle could be used to predict the length of the solar cycle with an accuracy of approximately 77%. In this work, we show that the mean-field model can also be used to predict the solar cycle start, given information about the current cycle. In quantum field theories (QFTs), the local symmetry according to which particles have definite values of certain conserved quantum numbers, known as isotopic or conserved charge symmetries, restricts the form of local interactions. In particular, isotopic spin, isotopic isospin and hypercharge symmetries each require different types of interactions between particles with different symmetries, and consequently QFTs with these symmetries are constrained to have different particle content. In particular, the low energy effective field theories (EFTs) of quantum gravity, denoted General Covariance (GC), are expected to be described by the general covariance (diffeomorphism) EFT (diffeomorphism EFT), in which all particles are coupled to the metric and gravity. However, there are several known scenarios in which isotopic or other charge symmetries are spontaneously broken, resulting in a dimensional reduction (DR) whereby local symmetry implies a lower symmetry, resulting in a less constrained local interactions. Several classes of such scenarios are based on extended gravity, including Kaluza-Klein reduction (KKR), as well as minimal de Sitter and Projective Special relativity (dS/PSR) scenarios. These all share a common feature that there exists a background field, namely a gauge field (a connection), whose field strength is nonzero and consequently a local symmetry is explicitly broken to a global one. However, the effects of the symmetry breaking are independent of the local symmetry transformation parameters, and so in particular the symmetry transformation parameter becomes a Goldstone boson. This can be used to deduce universal features of DR schemes, independent of the explicit details of the symmetry breaking mechanism. For example, it is expected that all spontaneously broken isotopic or other charge symmetries will result in a reduced local symmetry, with the local symmetry transformation parameter corresponding to a Goldstone boson. In particular, for the minimal de Sitter and Projective Special relativity scenarios, there is an exact symmetry between the local de Sitter (dS) and global Poincaré symmetries, resulting in an exact Goldstone boson equivalence. Furthermore, under certain conditions, it is expected that the spontaneous breaking of isotopic or other charge symmetries results in the universality class of the Conformal, CPT and extended Conformal symmetries. These results imply universal features of DR schemes, independent of the explicit details of the symmetry breaking mechanism.

One of the current challenges in string theory is to construct realistic models that account for the macroscopic features of the world we perceive around us. While it is in principle possible to construct models with the required properties based solely on the ten space-time dimensions of the heterotic string or the eleven dimensions of type II string theory, such scenarios typically require the stabilization of other charged moduli fields, which in general conflict with experimental constraints. An appealing solution to this problem is the possibility of intersecting branes, i.e. three dimensional objects arising as higher dimensional supersymmetric loci in the context of string theory. Intersecting brane models contain a large number of light particles, as they arise from the low energy limit of string theories with many symmetric fluxes. Furthermore, these particles often carry charges under currents, leading to the general expectation that they should be present in abundance in our universe. In this work, we study the phenomenological viability of intersecting brane models in light of recently obtained experimental constraints on the electric dipole moments of neutron and electron. We conclude that the vast majority of these models are in conflict with these constraints, and that therefore generic intersecting brane models require some extra ingredient to be considered phenomenological viable. We propose that the presence of a small number of sectors that do not violate the above bound might allow for a consistent phenomenological picture, and construct a simple example of such a scenario.

In this paper we analyze the properties of Zero-Lag Long-Range Synchronization (ZL-LS) via Dynamical Relaying. ZL-LS is a recently discovered phenomenon in dynamical systems, in which two chaotic systems can synchronize their dynamics not only when the former systems interact with each other but also when a sensor System merely observes the latter system’s states. In the original setting of ZL-LS, two chaotic systems interact with each other. In this work, we study the case in which a “dynamical relay” observes one chaotic system and passively conveys its state to the other chaotic system. In this manner, the two chaotic systems do not need to interact with each other. We derive sufficient conditions for the passive observation to enable Zero-Lag Long-Range Synchronization. In addition, we propose three numerical examples to illustrate the effectiveness of the derived conditions. Finally, we discuss the relations between our work and two existing synchronization scenarios, i.e., Asynchronous and Zero-Delay Long-Range Synchronization.

I present radial density profiles of strongly-lensed galaxies from the BELLS GALLERY (BGC) survey. BGC is a strongly lensing survey for galaxies behind the North American Galaxy Cluster Sample (NAGCS). The BEST method was used to identify 14 galaxy-strong lens systems from a total of 32 possible systems, for an efficiency of 0.44. Photometric redshifts and grayscale imaging in theVisible with Hubble Space Telescope (${I_{VST}}$) guided the selection of target galaxies to ensure strong lensing and appear in the resulting mass models. Multiple images of the same galaxies appear in many regions of the strong lensing field, enabling spatially-resolved spectra of lensed galaxies for dynamical studies of the background source galaxies. Radial density profiles of the background galaxies are described using the following functions: r^2 (squared radius), I(r) (radial brightness profile), n(r) (radial number profile) and ln(r) (radial luminosity profile). The BEST method yields correct galaxy redshifts in all cases, enabling robust density profile calculations for 11 of the 14 systems. Analysis of the remaining 3 systems (BGC 05-clean, BGC 08-clean and BGC 09-clean) is restricted to approximate profiles based on the galaxy brightness and position relative to the critical line. The 3 approximated profiles have 2 hump shapes, although with low significance. The BEST method identifies counter-images that are spatially separated from the lensed images. These 2 images are known as "discrete images" and are valuable for investigating the mass distributions associated with the galaxy halo. I find that the radial density profiles of the lensing galaxies are consistent with r^2, I(r) and n(r), although with significant scatter. Lens galaxies have galaxy density distributions that range from singular to cusp-like, and are typically not similar to the luminosity profile of the galaxies. This implies that galaxy clusters may not fully trace the matter distribution on small (sub-cluster) scales.

SNR G18.8+0.3 (G32.4+0.1) is a member of a small class of Galactic SNRs interacting with molecular clouds. In this letter, we report on new VLA 20 cm, ATCA 1.1 and 8.6 GHz, and EVN 5 and 8.4 GHz observations of G18.8+0.3. We also include X-ray data from a Chandra ACIS observation. In our new radio images, we find a compact structure, as previously seen at 8.6 GHz, but with a more complex and unusual morphology at 20 cm and at 1.1 GHz. In addition to a shell-like structure, we find a prominent central peak, a secondary peak to the south, and a filamentary structure to the southwest, most likely indicating shocked clouds or compressed magnetic fields. The secondary peak is visible only at 1.1 GHz, but not at 8.6 GHz or in the 8.4 GHz image. Comparing the radio and X-ray emission, we detect X-ray emission coincident with the peak of the secondary and filamentary radio peaks and to the southwest of the shell. We also see X-rays from hotter gas along the southeastern and southwestern edges of the shell. In addition, we see X-ray emission from the radio SNR itself. We discuss the implications of our results for the mechanisms responsible for the radio emission from G18.8+0.3, the evolution of the interaction between SNRs and molecular clouds, and the potential formation of population of mini-pcgs.' The Lorentz transformations form a group that shows how the laws of physics change when things move at constant speed. A group is a set of transformations, with an identity, that can be composed with one another. In this sense, the Lorentz transformations express how things change with velocity. In particular, if one knows the velocity of an object, one can use the Lorentz transformations to find how it changes with time. In turn, this allows one to find the spatial transformation. This article shows that, although the Lorentz transformations were introduced a very long time ago, they can still provide useful lessons for how to approach mathematics and physics. In particular, it discusses the finding that it is useful to distinguish between first and second order equations in physics. The article then explores the origins of the Lorentz transformations and shows that they can be derived from more general transformations, which in turn can be derived from the requirement that certain laws of physics should not change over time. From this more general perspective, the Lorentz transformations can be considered a specific case, whose use can lead to confusion. The article then considers an example from special relativity of a person measuring the speed of light in two different inertial frames of reference. It is shown that this requires one to consider both the spatial and the temporal component of the Lorentz transformations, as the speed of light is a function of both. In this example, the temporal component of the Lorentz transformations can be interpreted as a change of reference frame, which alters the rate at which clocks in the different reference frames move with respect to each other. From this, the authors find that if one specifies the spatial transformation between the two reference frames, one can in turn find the temporal transformation. In the second part of the article, the example is generalised to two inertial reference frames that move with respect to one another, leading to a situation called the Relativistic Doppler effect. This again requires the consideration of both the spatial and temporal components of the Lorentz transformations. The article then considers the situation in which the observers in the two reference frames agree that light should travel with a fixed speed, and that this should remain true regardless of their motion with respect to one another. In this case, the temporal component of the Lorentz transformations reduces to a simpler transformation rule for the light’s frequency, which can then be interpreted as a standard way to compare the observers’ own reference frames when they move with respect to one another.

Detecting gravitational radiation from binary black holes is one of the most promising ways to observationally confirm their existence. Previous efforts to detect such radiation have focused on detections from sufficiently nearby binary black holes with sufficiently large observable spin parameters, but such binary black holes are unlikely to form via normal astrophysical processes. Some researchers have proposed that black hole-massive star binaries could represent the significant production channel for binary black holes, and that such systems may thus be detectable via observation of their emitted gravitational radiation. The authors conduct a search for binary black holes in the galactic halo and put limits on the population of binary black hole MACHOs. This Letter reports the most sensitive search for binary black holes in the galactic halo to date. We analyze archival data from the Microvariablility Interferometer (MIDI) on the European Extremely Large Telescope (E-ELT) using theiryringe instrument. The data span a time period from November 2011 to October 2017 and consist of multiple wavelength configurations, all of which consist of simultaneous visible (VIS) and near-infrared (NIR) observations. We search for signals from binary black holes with various component masses and with a wide range of orbital separations. Our most significant detection, with a signal-to-noise ratio of 4.3, corresponds to a black hole with a mass of 70 Msolar and an orbital separation of 2.8 Astronomical Units (AU). We place upper limits on the number of compact binary black holes in the galactic halo with component masses between 1 and 100 Msolar and with orbital separations between 1 and 1000 AU. We derive 90% confidence level upper limits of 6.2% and 0.18% of the expected abundance of black holes with component masses between 1 and 10 Msolar, assuming uniform distribution in orbital separation and galactic evolution models, respectively. We also place constraints on the parameter space of models for the production of binary black holes in the galactic halo. For models that produce binary black holes with component masses between 1 and 10 Msolar, we exclude 43-90% of the region for binary black hole semimajor axes between 1 and 1000 AU and binary black hole mass ratios between 0.1 and 10. Organic conductors are unique systems for studying criticality and quantum phase transitions due to the unusual nature of the charge, spin, and orbital degrees of freedom that are involved. Here we report observations of critical scattering and scaling behavior in quasi one-dimensional conductors based on the Bechgaard and Fabre salts. We find that the charge degrees of freedom are critical over the full range of temperatures, with dynamical critical exponent z=2. We present evidence for logarithmic corrections to scaling, and estimate the central charge c=1. The spin and orbital degrees of freedom are found to be either Heisenberg or Kugel-Khomskii models, with spin-orbital separation clearly evident in the single crystal samples. Although there is some evidence for quantum critical points in the system, our data are consistent with the spin and orbital degrees of freedom being separate chains coupled by a uniform Heisenberg coupling with an effective lower critical interaction strength. This material can be viewed as a testing ground for interesting theoretical questions related to quantum many-body effects and the limits of criticality.

Planets are commonly discovered around other stars. The finding increases with the number of stars that are searched for planets, and today almost 70% of all discovered exoplanets are found around another star. These planetary systems are frequently observed to have orbital properties between those of a compact system with several super-Earth planets and those of a period desert, that is a dearth of planets with periods smaller than 10 days or larger than 100 days. Here, we report the discovery of a system with a single Neptune-sized planet in a compact orbital configuration around a high-mass host star. The planet, named HAT-P-32b, has a mass of 1.88 M⊕, an orbital radius of 0.0457 AU, and an orbital eccentricity of 0.26. Its long orbital period of 5.2 days is only second to the recently announced HAT-P-23b among the highest known period planets. Despite this compact arrangement, its mass is only 18% of that of the Saturn-mass planet Jupiter, which places it in the category of low-density planets. Assuming an irradiated thermal evolution, we estimate the minimum planetary mass such that HAT-P-32b could have retained an atmosphere when its interior was heated sufficiently to outgas the atmospheric gases. We find that the core mass of HAT-P-32b must be more than 25 M⊕, and less than 32 M⊕ at 95% confidence, to have retained an atmosphere with an observable escape rate. Thus, while atmospheric loss appears to be complete, HAT-P-32b may still retain an atmosphere like the most likely member of its system, HAT-P-23b. We also rule out the presence of a second planet more massive than 4 M⊕, and with an orbit wider than 0.039 AU, within a disk passedULAR examination at the 99.73% confidence level. This work was made possible by the HATNet Project, a collaboration between the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, the Harvard College Observatory, and the Las Cumbres Observatory.

High-energy gamma rays (>30 GeV) are of particular interest because of their unprecedented ability to penetrate the Earth's atmosphere and backgrounds beyond our atmosphere. Many of these gamma rays are caused by the attenuation of gamma-rays from distant astrophysical sources by the Photoproduction of pions in the atmosphere. However, such gamma-rays cannot penetrate the Earth's magnetic field lines, leading to a small probability for air showers initiated by such gamma-rays to occur in an extensive air shower array. An analysis of 3720 h of atmospheric neutrino data taken by the atmospheric neutrinos experiments at the KGF (Karlsruhe Gamma-ray Factory) suggest that such gamma-rays do, in fact, lead to extensive air showers in substantial numbers, producing electron- and muon-type Cherenkov light with energy equivalent to several hundred GeV. This result, if confirmed by further extensive air shower measurements, may provide the first evidence for High-Energy Gamma Rays from Outside the Solar System.

In the paradigm of evidential reasoning, a conclusion is warranted by a given amount of evidence, if that evidence fully justifies that conclusion. Traditional notions of full justification are subject to a demanding quadruplecontext condition, which rules out warranted conclusions from sufficiently weak evidence. We consider an intermediate notion of minimal justified conclusions, which is sufficient for some applications but weaker than full justification. We describe a formal framework for reasoning about such conclusions on the basis of finite evidence, and provide a general method for computing minimal justified conclusions for arbitrary formulas. As a sample application, we consider the problem of covering a finite domain with balls of a given radius, and provide algorithms for computing minimal justified subdomains and covering problems in these domains. Finally, we describe how the proposed approach can be used for solving a fundamental problem of automated plannning: the construction of construction sequences with bounded tolerance and guaranteed length. We describe a formal framework for reasoning about conclusions on the basis of finite evidence, which is intermediate between full justification and the justified reachable from the available evidence. This is sufficient for some applications but weaker than full justification. Minimally justified conclusions enable planning in the face of limited information and incomplete knowledge. We illustrate the approach through two examples: (i) the covering problem in the considered domains, and (ii) the problem of construction sequences with bounded tolerance and guaranteed length. Our framework is general and can be used for solving other problems in automated planning. This is a joint work with Marek Chrobak and Tom['a]{}[š]{} Bil[' y]{}.

Fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe) cell cycle is sequentially triggered by repeated assembly and dissolution of mitotic spindle pole bodies (SPBs). The SPB assembly initiates at the site of previous SPB separation and is maintained by the Cdc2 kinase. SPB separation is the hallmark of the Start transition. Subsequent SPB separation triggers Start-dependent gene transcription and mitotic entry. In this work, we developed a Boolean network model of the fission yeast cell cycle and found that it accurately predicts the sequence of Start, SPB separation, and mitotic entry.
