The evolution of the chemical composition of a population of stars—their "aspect" or "chemical signature"—can reveal information about their past evolutionary path and their present-day locations. One such aspect is the abundance of isotopes of elements such as carbon and nitrogen. These nuclei experience nuclear reactions at different rates, and the rates of the most common reactions together determine which isotopes will be produced or "created" in significant amounts. The abundances of these isotopes in the population as a whole then reflect the history of the last major nuclear reaction to occur in the light-curve-averaged composition of the Universe at the time each population of stars formed. The abundances of carbon and nitrogen isotopes that are created in the interiors of stars are known to depend strongly on the temperature and density at the base of the surface convection zone. Because the convection zones of low- and intermediate-mass stars undergo very large and abrupt changes during the main sequence, and because the time required for the processes governing these nuclear reactions to operate is shorter than the main-sequence lifetime of these stars, the interior abundances of carbon and nitrogen are also strongly dependent on the chemical composition of the surrounding medium when the main-sequence lifetime of the star is brief compared to the nuclear reaction rates. This includes the chemical composition of the gas out of which the star formed, which in turn reflects the composition of the evolving sun, which itself is a function of the abundances of key nuclear reaction products in the planet-forming regions of the sun's solar system as observed by remote sensing. These dependencies can render the observed abundances of carbon and nitrogen isotopes a very strong constraint on the chemical composition of the sun at the time of the main-sequence lifetime of a given population of stars, given that the observed abundances can be compared to computed rates of change for the main-sequence lifetimes of the stars. For this reason, measurements of the abundances of key carbon and nitrogen isotopes in very old stars can be used to inform us about the early history of the sun, and specifically about the abundances of key nuclear reaction products in the planet-forming regions of the sun's solar system as observed by remote sensing. In this paper, we compare results of simulations of the evolution of the chemical composition of populations of stars under the assumption that the abundances of the products of key nuclear reactions in the planet-forming regions of the sun's solar system are within the uncertainty ranges of current estimates to the analogous results when those abundance ranges are set equal to the observed ranges for values of the main-sequence lifetime that are consistent with the computed rates of change for those abundances. Specifically, we find that even if the uncertainty ranges for the abundances of products of key nuclear reactions in the planet-forming regions of the sun's solar system are at the lowest levels observed to date (1.5% for carbon and 7.2% for nitrogen), then if the main-sequence lifetime of the star is greater than about 10 million

IGR J17254-3257, an X-ray burster, was discovered in an all-sky monitor performed with INTEGRAL, an international gamma-ray astronomy mission. It exhibited recurrent bursting, with one burst showing two peaks. Follow-up observations with the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) revealed a modulation at the pulse period of the source, and classified the burst as a Type I burst. Subsequent observations with the Prognoz-5 and -6 satellites discovered periodic pulsations with the period of 6.7 seconds, rendering IGR J17254-3257 a new bursting neutron star, for which the naming symbolizes J17254–3257. The source was also detected with the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The source showed two different states during the observations, with the harder state occurring more frequently. During the hard state, the spectrum can be well-fitted with a Kerr black hole cross section. When the source changed to the softer state, the color-color diagram and the time-averaged spectrum became similar to those of low-mass X-ray binaries, indicating an accretion disk surrounding a compact object. Based on the spectrum, the distance to the source was estimated to be approximately 11.2–12.5 kpc.

Recently, there has been a lot of interest in the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZE), which is the Compton scattering of background radiation off of hot gas in clusters of galaxies or dark matter filaments. In this paper, we show that there is an additional contribution to the SZE from the free electrons in our galaxy. We calculate the spectrum of this so-called kinetic SZE for two different cases: one in which the scattering electrons are in a maximal motion and another in which they are in thermal motion. We find that this new SZE can be observed by the future Heat Sunyaev-Zel'dovich Effect (HSE) experiment and expect to detect it in our galaxy out to distances of a few hundred megaparsecs. Our galaxy consists of two distinct phases of matter: hot diffuse gas, which is predominantly ionised hydrogen and helium, and a population of cold electrons, which is primarily due to synchrotron radiation from a population of radio emitting electrons. The electrons from both of these populations will scatter the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation as the galaxy rotates, causing a spectral distortion of the CMB. We show that the kinetic SZE has a very distinct signature from the thermal SZE, and therefore can be distinguished using future experiments. This research was carried out at the University of Leicester'sAstrophysics Group and Department of Physics and Astronomy and the Science and Technology Facilities Council's (STFC) Kellnersley Orchestra Centre.

Geometrical engineering is a powerful tool to probe the deep relationships between symmetries, energy scales and manifolds. In this work, we propose to engineer the standard model (SM) on the local supergravity (SUGRA) breaking geometry in the Minimal E(8) Symmetric universe. We consider the Pati-Salam (PS) symmetry as local E(8) and break the symmetry down to local SU(4) x SU(2) x U(1) at the heart of the SM. The resulting Higgs field and mass hierarchy naturally solve the fine-tuning problem of the SM. Moreover, we show that the gauged B-L symmetry in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) is the subgroup of the global E(8). By making E(8) global symmetry local, we demonstrate that the compactification of the 10-d superstring theories on the local E(8) symmetric manifold produces the gauge mediated supersymmetry breaking and the splitting of the triplets and doublets of Higgs fields. Finally, we propose the current LHC search for the colored particles can be reinterpreted as the LHC search for the white particles in the long-standing problem of the missingenergy in the collider experiments.

Evolutionary Neural Gas (ENG) is a model of a self organizing network (SON) that helps machines understand how to categorize input data. It is an extension to the well known NeuroEvolution of Genes (NEO) algorithm. ENG uses a generative neural network based on the extended generative stochastic network (GENSNET) model to categorize the training data. The activation of eachHidden Layer Neuron in the Generative Neural Network (GNG) is represented as a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). Each GMM represents one category in the training data. The mean of each GMM is used as a vector to a Vector Quantizer (VQ) which determines the codebook size. Each codebook is a set of prototypes, where each prototype is a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). One GMM from the codebook represents one category in the codebook. The codebook size is equal to the number of categories in the training data. The codewords of each input data sample are the indices of the codebook that the GMM in the GENSNET is fit to.The Neuroevolutionary Algorithm (optimizes the GENSNET parameters so that the activation of theHidden Layer Neurons in the GENSNET best match the codewords of the training samples. This leads to a more effective codebook that better represents the categories in the training data. The final result is a SON that can be trained to do input categorization.

Modern electronics are largely based on silicon devices, which have enabled extensive automation and remarkable progress in quality of life. However, silicon is a fragile, indirect band gap material, which makes it difficult to integrate into high-power, high-temperature, and high-frequency circuits. Graphene, a two-dimensional hexagonal lattice of carbon, provides an ideal contender for the future electronics. The large carrier mobility of graphene, the ability to modulate its band structure via stretching or bonding, and excellent compatibility with current lithographic techniques make it a promising material for next-generation electronic devices. One potential application for graphene is in transistors, which are the basic devices of integrated circuits and represent the most challenging obstacles to graphene’s real-world implementation. One approach for graphene transistors is based on ballistic transport through one-dimensional nanoribbons, called ballistic graphene nanoribbons. This approach has potential advantages compared to existing two-dimensional devices, but fully exploring this potential will require a fundamental understanding of device characteristics on the nanoscale. Here, we present a full quantum real-space study of ballistic graphene nanoribbon metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors. From atomistic simulations of electron transport, we observe room-temperature device characteristics and characterize the influence of various device parameters. We show that ballistic graphene nanoribbon devices can compete with existing silicon devices, while offering significant benefits, such as a higher on/off current ratio and significantly reduced parasitic capacitance. Our work is significant because it bridges the gap between the nanoscale understanding of device performance and the microscale semiconductor device physics necessary to make practical devices. The principles developed in this work should be readily extendable to other one-dimensional materials and have implications for the design and understanding of other one-dimensional nanoelectronic devices. Our work is significant because it bridges the gap between the nanoscale understanding of device performance and the microscale semiconductor device physics necessary to make practical devices. The principles developed in this work should be readily extendable to other one-dimensional materials and have implications for the design and understanding of other one-dimensional nanoelectronic devices.

The c2d Legacy Project mapped the emission from gas and ice particles frozen onto the surfaces of dust grains in 14 molecular clouds. This, combined with complementary millimeter and submillimeter continuum data, provided estimates of the dust temperature, column density, and mass for these clouds. In this paper, we compare the spatial distributions of recent star formation in these clouds as revealed by Bolocam 1.1 mm dust continuum observations. In general, the star formation appears to be more extended in Perseus and Ophiuchus than in Serpens, though the signal-to-noise ratio of the data for the former are relatively low. The Perseus and Ophiuchus clouds also exhibit distinctive centrally-condensed structures that do not appear in the Serpens data. In particular, the Perseus and Ophiuchus clouds exhibit clear two-dimensional features that are not present in the Serpens data. The Perseus cloud also appears to be undergoing global collapse on large scales, indicated by the central concentration of filamentary structure and depletion of dust mass toward the centers of some of the brighter 1.1 mm condensations. If real, this implies that the star formation in Perseus has recently been even more spatially concentrated than suggested by the Bolocam data. Although the spatial scales sampled by the Bolocam observations are large (0.1-2 pc), the mass of material involved in recent star formation in Perseus is comparable to or greater than the typical mass of gas and dust in these clouds. Given this, the comparison between the spatial distributions of recent star formation in Perseus and Serpens may not be particularly meaningful. Finally, the Perseus and Ophiuchus clouds exhibit comparable levels of recent star formation, given the amounts of cold gas and dust observed in these regions.

In this essay, I describe my research into stellar evolution over the last sixty years. I discuss how my initial training in theoretical physics helped me to develop an observational approach to this research, and how this in turn helped me to develop our understanding of mass loss on the main sequence and throughout red giant and asymptotic giant branch phases. I also describe how this in turn helped to confirm the basic assumptions of stellar evolution theory, and the limitations of this approach. I describe how this approach also led me to study mass loss in other stars such as Wolf-Rayet and blue supergiant phases. I describe how the detailed chemical enrichment history of globular clusters can be used to study the intermediate-age population of the Galactic disk, and how this has led me to study the formation history of the thick disk component of the Milky Way. I finish by outlining some of the current challenges for this research area, and the issues I am currently working on addressing.

The baryonic antidecuplet was observed by the DSPNEP report in 2016. The antidecuplet is the next-to-lowest-mass hybrid multiplet consisting of 10 particles, consisting of 7 scalar states, 1 pseudoscalar state, and 2 positive-parity spin 1/2 states. The antidecuplet's spin-3/2 members will interact with photons via spin-1/2 sea quarks. Therefore, these spin-3/2 members will typically be excited states with relatively low masses. The antidecuplet couples preferentially to SU(3) octet vectors and SU(3) singlet axial vectors. In this work, the mass and electromagnetic transitions of the first three members of the antidecuplet are calculated. The spin-1/2 members are calculated using the chiral quark-soliton model (CQSM). The spin-3/2 members are calculated using the diquark-cluster model (DCM). The interaction Lagrangian is described. Feynman rules for these models are presented. Results for the scalar members of the antidecuplet are presented in the first three sections. Results for the spin-3/2 member of the antidecuplet, $\Theta^{+}$, are presented in the final section. The masses and electromagnetic transitions of the first three scalar members of the antidecuplet are calculated in the CQSM. For the $\phi$, $\chi$, and $\psi$ members, the predictions are within 10 MeV of the empirical values. The $\rho$ member has a larger disagreement. The discrepancy may be due to the $\rho$ meson not being an ideal mixing of the ideal octet and singlet members, or due to the CQSM not including all possible interactions. For the $\phi$, $\chi$, and $\psi$ members, the electric dipole transitions are an order of magnitude or more above the competing magnetic dipole transitions. The $\rho$ member has an extremely small electric dipole transition compared to the competing magnetic dipole transitions. The diquark cluster model (DCM) is used to calculate the mass and electromagnetic transitions of the spin-3/2 member of the antidecuplet, $\Theta^{+}$. The $\Theta^{+}$ is identified as the $\delta^{++}$ baryon. In DCM, the $\Theta^{+}$ is a diquark-diquark molecular state. The $\Theta^{+}$'s strong interaction may be understood as a mixture of $SU(3)$ singlet axial-vector and octet vector diquark pairs, each with their own coupling strengths. The $\Theta^{+}$'s electromagnetic transition is purely electric. The $\Theta^{+}$'s electric dipole transition is approximately 1.0 MeV. The $\Theta^{+}$ has a very small electric dipole transition compared to the other spin-3/2 members of the antidecuplet. The first three members of the antidecuplet

Using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we examine the connection between the sSFR (specific star-formation rate), stellar mass, dark-matter halo mass and the color and presence of a hard-spectrum nucleus in early-type galaxies (ETGs). We find that the sSFR and stellar mass of the central host galaxies are tightly correlated, with high sSFR galaxies being more massive. By splitting our sample into red and blue subsamples using the Dα* diagram, we see a clear link between the presence of a nucleus and the sSFR of the host galaxy. Significantly more red ETGs have a hard-spectrum nucleus compared to blue ETGs at a high confidence level. We also find that the fraction of ETGs with a hard-spectrum nucleus is dependent on the stellar mass of the host galaxy, with low-mass hosts having a significantly lower probability of hosting a nucleus. These results imply that central black-hole growth and star-formation are either causally linked or co-regulated. By plotting the average fraction of each population in each bin of the Dα* diagram, we show that the transition between blue and red galaxies occurs at a higher specific star-formation rate in more massive dark-matter halos. Using semi-analytic models, we explore two co-evolutionary models in which the central black hole and host galaxies are either completely decoupled or co-evolve following the growth of the host galaxy. We find that the latter model provides a better fit to our observations.

Radiochemical solar neutrino experiments are based on the capture of electron anti-neutrinos on protons, which results in the production of low energy beta particles. These electrons undergo a radiation belt consisting of a sequence of filters and detectors that determine their ultimate landing location. The dominant reaction $^{71}Ga$($^2H$, $\anti\nu_e$)$^{71}Ge$ was used for all experiments except one (DANSS) between 2001 and 2015. We perform a combined analysis of the gallium and copper-formed indium experiments Daya Bay, Reno, Borexino, and click here for the DANSS data. The new analysis includes the individual detector response functions as well as their absolute cross-sections. We show the evidence for sterile neutrinos, performing a hypothesis test via Bayes’ theorem. We introduce a new, nearly Feldman-Cousins like procedure for combining neutrino oscillation and neutrino decay results. We also point out the problems of using beta-beams to build large scale neutrino factories.

The nature of the plasma in the vicinity of black holes is a central question in high energy astrophysics. The intense gravitational and magnetic fields near black holes cause plasma to deviate from its collisional equilibrium state. These so-called collisionless plasmas are believed to harbor energetic particles and non-thermal processes. Since accreting black holes in different classes of celestial objects, such as active galactic nuclei and X-ray binaries, are often observed in different observational states, the plasma properties near these black holes may vary accordingly. Until now, however, there is no reliable means to study the plasma near black holes, as the extreme brightness of the source can obscure its reflection signature. Recently, there has been a strong observational hint that relativistic distortions might be present in the iron Kα lines from the vicinity of some supermassive black holes, and this has fuelled considerable theoretical interest in the predictions of relativistic reflection spectra from close to rotating black holes. The signal is yet to be positively detected from any source, but if confirmed, such a detection would prove intense matter around black holes can non-thermally process energy, and hence challenge our understanding of the behavior of black holes and their environment.

The Lagrangian density of sixth-order gravity is non-linear in the Riemann curvature, and the theory may not be unitary. Irreducible forms for the metric variations of the action terms of sixth-order gravity and approximated stress-energy tensor are derived. The irreducible forms are expressed in terms of the Ricci tensor, the Riemann curvature and their covariant derivatives up to the fourth order. The actions and stress-energy tensor corresponding to the second and third order variation yields the correct field equations. The correct Einstein equation may be achieved by adding a perfect fluid term with negative effective pressure. The fluid and gravity combination terms give the same equations of state as for a pure fluid, however the model admits vanishing effective pressure and density at finite energy density. The gravitational waves and the matter perturbations propagate at the speed of light in the absence of a dissipative mechanism. The second and third order variations give rise to a consistent theory with a unitary description. The Lagrangian density of sixth-order gravity depends on the Riemann curvature tensor, and the theory may not be unitary. Irreducible forms for the metric variations of the action terms of sixth-order gravity are derived. The resulting actions and stress-energy tensor are equivalent to the second and third order variations of the Lagrangian density of sixth-order gravity.

The supergravity (SUGRA) models, in which the soft supersymmetry (SUSY) breaking parameters are expressed as functions of only a few universal parameters, have been very popular since the early days of supersymmetry (SUSY). These models predict a specific correlation between some of the SUSY parameters, namely the masses of the Higgs bosons and superpartners, which could be tested at the Tevatron and the LHC. We point out that the current data on the masses of the superpartners, namely the lightest neutralino and the gravitino, can be accommodated in the minimal supergravity model (mSUGRA) with non-zero trilinear SUSY breaking couplings (A terms). Depending on the value of the A terms, LHC may or may not see signals associated with these interactions. In the region where LHC sees signals, the signatures are very similar to the signals expected at the Tevatron, which has currently the best sensitivity for these signals. We emphasize that this correlation is a consequence of the SUSY models and would not hold in the standard model (SM) with arbitrary SUSY breaking terms.

A paper investigates the possibility of a universality in nature on the basis of the nonlinearities suggested by the post-Newtonian (PN) approximation of general relativity. It is shown that general properties of gravity, such as the emission of gravitational waves by compact objects in close orbits, the instability of circular orbits, and the deflection of light, can be expressed by a surprisingly small number of parameters. The corresponding parameter values can be related to the post-Newtonian parameters, which have been known for decades but until now could not be connected to each other. By means of a new method based on an effective field theory of gravity, the conformal transformations of the metric are mapped to a potential, which can be associated with a universality. It is demonstrated that in the limit of a high velocity of light, the Riemann-flat gauge is obtained, which is frequently used in the investigation of gravitational wave signals. The analogy to superconductivity is also demonstrated.

Five-loop maximal super Yang-Mills amplitudes are presented, computed via on-shell unitarity methods. The corresponding series of open superstring theories are subsequently identified, and the corresponding series of partial amplitudes are deduced. The four-loop planar MHV amplitudes are found to match previously conjectured numerators, and five-loop amplitudes are found to match conjectured numerators for NMHV and non-MHV theories. A recursion for the series of five-loop amplitudes is conjectured, involving analogous four-loop integrals. Several lower point results are also deduced, some of which are new. --- Maximally supersymmetric amplitudes at five loops in planar $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills have been presented. These amplitudes contain all two-loop MHV and NMHV components, as well as all three-loop MHV and NMHV components, and some four- and five-loop MHV components. Using the explicit form of the integrals present, several new recursion relations are conjectured for these amplitudes, as well as lower point results that are partially known.

The host galaxy of GRB 980425, a high-redshift supernova, was observed in the CO(J=3-2) line with the Atacama Submillimeter Telescope Experiment (ASTE) in April 2004. The 1.3 mm continuum emission is also observed with APEX at lower angular resolution and with the 12 m telescope of the Arizona Radio Observatory (ARO) at higher resolution. The ASTE CO(J=3-2) image reveals a compact structure of $\sim$ 120 pc in size with two peaks (separated by $\sim$ 210 pc) and an overall extent of $\sim$ 200 pc. The 1.3 mm continuum emission is also resolved, with a deconvolved size of $\sim$ 160 pc. The relative strength of the 1.3 mm continuum and the CO(J=3-2) emission suggests that the molecular gas has an amount comparable to that of the dust, and is highly concentrated toward the two peaks of the CO(J=3-2) emission. The peak line and continuum emission are offset by $\sim$ 50 pc from the geometrical center of the 1.3 mm continuum emission. Assuming that the molecular gas and the dust are closely coupled, this spatial offset is likely caused by the existence of two nuclei within the past $\sim$ 1000 years, as inferred from the supernova lightcurve. This is the first direct evidence for the presence of a rapidly rotating disk of molecular gas in the host galaxy of GRB 980425.

Information-theoretic proofs of entropy power and complementary entropies inequalities for discrete random vectors are presented. In particular, inequalities for the joint entropy of dependent random variables are obtained. The novel inequalities are employed to derive vector formulations of well known entropy power and complementary entropy relations in information theory. The new results provide a theoretical framework for estimation-theoretic characterizations of entropy power, entropy rate, and conditional entropy, and related quantities. The inequalities are relevant to theories of multivariate dependence and have potential applications in mathematics, information theory, and statistics. Here is an excerpt from the paper: A remarkable property of entropy is its monotonicity under statistical mechanisms. For example, if two random vectors are statistically independent, then their entropies add. More generally, if statistical mechanisms transform into , their entropies increase. The entropy power inequality (EPI) and the entropy rate (ER) entropy power inequality are fundamental and well known results in information theory. The former states that the entropy of a random vector cannot be greater than the sum of the entropies of its components, while the latter states that the entropy of a random vector cannot be greater than the entropy of its mean. Both these inequalities hold for any random vectors. Here we present information-theoretic proofs of the entropy power and entropy rate entropy power inequalities. Our starting point is the information inequality (FI), which gives a lower bound on the mutual information. Under suitable conditions, we obtain a new family of information inequalities, which imply the entropy power and entropy rate entropy power inequalities. We demonstrate the use of these general inequalities through vector forms of fundamental entropy power and entropy rate relations. The inequalities presented here complement existing approaches to proving the entropy power and entropy rate entropy power inequalities. These include information-theoretic proofs based on Young’s inequality, probability distributions and sufficiency. In this paper we also present information-theoretic proofs of some related entropy inequalities, including relations for the conditional entropy and the joint entropy of dependent random variables. We observe that the proofs are unchanged if joint distributions are replaced with distribution functions. The new results presented here have several important applications, including to theories of multivariate dependence, mathematics, information theory and statistics. For example, the new results are used to obtain a vector entropy power inequality for statistically dependent random variables, an application that has received considerable attention in the information theory literature but which has not previously been available via an information-theoretic approach. Another application of our results is to obtain a vector entropy rate inequality for time series. We also prove a vector joint entropy power inequality. We argue that the new vector forms of fundamental relations may be of independent interest. We present

Entanglement is a fundamental non-classical feature of physical systems. Such systems which possess entanglement could have applications in areas such as quantum information processing and quantum computing. As a physical system evolves, its entanglement can change in nature. We investigate the time evolution of entanglement in the Jaynes-Cummings model which describes the interaction between a two level system and a single mode of the electromagnetic field. The model includes the coupling of the system and field via rotating wave and the Born-Markov approximations. For initial states comprising the two level system and electromagnetic field in an equal superposition, we examine the entanglement generated between the two particles as well as between the particles and the field. We find that the system, field, and entanglement exhibit periodic behaviour. We characterize these behaviours and present waveform diagrams for the different regions of behaviour. We also examine the effect of changing various parameters of the model on the dynamics of entanglement. We find that the initial amount of entanglement present in the system and field has a significant influence on the amount of entanglement generated throughout the evolution. Specifically, we find that the entanglement exhibits sudden death and sudden birth. We also determine that the frequency of the oscillations exhibits maxima at particular values of the coupling constant and initial photon number.

In this paper, we investigate a scenario of brane inflation within the context of string-theory. We study a very simple realization of brane inflation in which the inflaton is the distance between two stacks of branes. For distances greater than the so-called threshold value, the effective theory is that of a $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ gauge theory with three colors and three flavors. In this theory, the relaxion is an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ gauge field, and it can drive slow-roll over a wide range of parameters. We compute the energy spectrum of the relaxion and show that it depends strongly on the initial conditions. The energy spectrum is red at large wavenumbers, in accordance with observations. Furthermore, we find that the energy spectrum is rather insensitive to the initial conditions in the range $0.3\lesssim \alpha \lesssim 1$, where $\alpha$ is a parameter that controls the Vachaspati-Vilenkin potential. Thus, the relaxion scenario with moduli stabilization via Stückelberg massive gravity is consistent with current observations.

The IC1396N proto-cluster is a nearby ($d\sim260$ pc), spectacularly dusty star forming region. It contains hundreds of stars in the process of formation, including several recently formed brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars. The region is surrounded by a gigantic, cross-shaped cloud of gas and dust extending for at least 12000 au in perpendicular dimensions. The dynamics and 3-D geometry of the cloud suggest that it has only recently come together, perhaps by coalescence from smaller subunits. The region has a high space motion and is likely to remain distinct from the local cloud population for at least the next 100,000 years. The members of the IC1396N proto-cluster have distinct ages, as determined from signatures of protoplanetary discs, accretion, and the presence of associated extrasolar planets. The oldest members have fractional disk masses similar to those of field objects of the same age, but the masses of younger members are consistent with the reservoir of material required to form additional planets in the same region. The difference between the masses of young and old objects indicates that most of the material in the region has been consumed in the formation of the youngest members. The presence of material that is at least 5 million years old suggests that the cluster may have started with a very large core, perhaps as large as 30,000 au in radius, which then consolidated into a more conventional size of 10000-25000 au within 5 million years. The high fractional disk masses of the very youngest members suggest that further inward migration, usually ascribed to higher-mass planets, might also have occurred. IC1396N provides an unusually direct and quantitative window into the early stages of star and planet formation. It demonstrates that, in many ways, the process appears similar to that in the field, but on larger scales and over a shorter time period.

Twenty three globular clusters (GCs) in the inner region of the Milky Way are called the bulge globular clusters. These clusters are very old and have low metallicities. Consequently they have red horizontal branches (RHBs). Terzan 5, Liller 1, UKS 1 and Terzan 4 are very luminous and massive, and are known to have extended cores. HST observations in the F110W and F160W bands were used to obtain their relative proper motions and consequently their 3D space positions. These four clusters are on average 31.2 kpc from the Galactic center. Terzan 5 is at a distance of 25.3 kpc from the Galactic center, which is closer than the Galactic center. This cluster is the closest to the center of the Milky Way among the known globular clusters. The other clusters are at distances of 32.4 kpc (Liller 1), 33.7 kpc (UKS 1) and 38.1 kpc (Terzan 4). The spatial distribution of the bulge globular clusters has important consequences for the formation and evolution of the Galaxy. Terzan 5 is a possible globular cluster progenitor that may have been disrupted by the central supermassive black hole. The other clusters are likely to have formed during the early stages of the Galaxy's formation.

An accretion disk can be regarded as a thermodynamical system. The gas pressure and radiative cooling are two important non-static variables in the system. This Letter focuses on the dynamical aspects of the disk by considering the radial dependence of these two variables. It is found that the inner disk is dominated by gas pressure, while the radiation pressure dominates the outer part. The transition radius is around 3-4 times the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. The temperature is 100-1000 K at the pressure-dominated region and 10^9-10^{10} K at the radiation-dominated region. The adiabatic index is between 2 and 7, which is comparable with the computed adiabatic indices of some other systems in astrophysics. The inner part of the disk is dynamically important for the following two reasons. First, it is the site of powerful radiation-dominated accretion. It has been suggested that the jets and outflows in some high-mass binary systems and active galactic nuclei are probably related to the activities in the inner disk. A high adiabatic index may be required by the presence of radiation at such a high temperature. Second, it may be a trigger to supply fresh gas to the outer part of the disk, where the gas pressure is dynamic irrelevant. A "gas pump" has been proposed to explain the high radiative efficiency of active galactic nuclei. It was speculated that a cool dense disk around a Kerr black hole may be an ideal gas pump. A low-temperature and high-density "accretion funnel" has been observed around supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies. If the inner disk is indeed a low-temperature gas pump, the gas supply at large radii may be related to the mass of the black hole, rather than the mass of the surrounding bulge. This Letter reports an example of a numerical simulation to a self-consistent system, which may be helpful to understand the interaction between the inner part and the outer part of an accretion disk.

We report on the first results from the 2500-2750 MHz band of the Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope (GBT) Large 2010A deployable feed array, used for a sensitive search for neutral hydrogen absorption toward BRI 1335-0417 at $z = 4.4$ (OM 1365+1549). We use the 1000-hour data set from November 2010 to March 2011 to place an upper limit on the neutral hydrogen fraction of $f < 0.26$ at $4.4 < z < 5.2$ in a region of 21 Å (with 2σ conf. level). If the absorbing region covers the background QSO, as proposed in some scenarios for the nature of dark matter, this limit provides the most stringent constraint on the neutral fraction at high redshift to date. If the neutral hydrogen is distributed in small clouds distributed smoothly around the QSO, this limit corresponds to an upper limit on the velocity-integrated optical depth of Υ<0.027, or a lower limit on the fraction of neutral hydrogen of f≥0.95. This limit is an order of magnitude more sensitive than the previously best measurement at this redshift, and will reduce the region of uncertainty by a factor of 2, offering the most precise test to date of the nature of dark matter.

The Local Group (LG) dwarf irregular galaxy IC 1613 is an ideal galaxy for studying the effect of environment on star formation. Being at a distance of 3.9 Mpc (1 Mpc == 1 million light-years), it is the closest LG member without a prominent halo. In addition, it is the third brightest LG galaxy after the Andromeda galaxy (M31) and the Milky Way (MW). Due to proximity and richness of observational data, it has been the subject of many studies on resolved stars. Here, I present the results of resolved star photometry and spectroscopy from HST WFPC2 imaging of the red giant branch (RGB), along with ground-based spectroscopy of aasurys of horizontal branch (HB) and main sequence (MS) stars. The colour-magnitude diagrams (CMD) reach deep enough to probe the oldest generations of stars in the galaxy. As expected, there is little to no star formation in the galaxy's central regions, while the outer regions have recent (1-2 Gyr) star formation. This pattern is similar to that seen in other LG dwarf irregulars. I compare the age, metallicity and spatial distribution of different stellar populations. I also investigate the dynamics of the galaxy, using a large sample of radial velocities for various stellar populations. While the stellar populations appear distinct in some respects, there are significant overlaps in others, making it difficult to distinguish between a simple monolithic collapse and a series of mergers.

A low-complexity STBC from a new class of Clifford algebras, which admit a simple representation, is proposed. The proposed scheme is based on the mapping between a complex STBC and itsQLF, which are constructed using a finite field, onto a real Clifford algebra, which belongs to a special type called proper even Clifford algebra. This mapping allows to exploit the properties of the real Clifford algebra, for example, the existence of a simple representation, to design a low-complexity and near-optimum STBC. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the performance of the proposed scheme. The proposed scheme allows to exploit the properties of the real Clifford algebra to design a STBC with low-complexity and near-optimum performance. The mapping between a complex STBC and itsQLF and a real Clifford algebra allows a low-complexity and near-optimum design. This can be useful to provide a low-cost solution for next generation OFDMA cellular systems, where the flexibility in the transmitter and the cost of the network equipment are important design goals.

Wireless networks often involve multiple cooperating nodes in which some nodes forward their received signals for other nodes to decode. This cooperation increases the decoded signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and improves the overall decoding reliability. However, cooperation increases inter-node communication and hence worsens the overall energy consumption of the network. In this paper, we study the problem of efficiently controlling the cooperating nodes such that the total energy consumption of the network is minimized while reliably delivering the message to the destination. We consider two different scenarios. In the first scenario, the source node knows the cooperative topology and can communicate with all the nodes. The focus of this scenario is to minimize the total energy consumption of the network by choosing the best subset of nodes to cooperate with. In the second scenario, we consider a more general network model where the source node does not have global knowledge of the network topology but can communicate with a fixed receiver. In this scenario, we first establish the connection between the node cooperation and the partial message delivery and then study the problem of minimizing the total energy consumption of the network while ensuring the reliability of message delivery. We develop distributed algorithms to solve the problem in both scenarios. Extensive simulations confirm the efficacy of our algorithms.

The process of reionization ended the darkness of the universe and is a powerful tool for studying its physics and astronomy. 21-cm emission and absorption traces the neutral fraction of the intergalactic medium (IGM) and is influenced by the structure of the underlying density field and the dynamics of galaxies. Early stages of cosmic reionization are challenging to observation as these are localized features in the large-scale 21-cm signal. Correlated random walks (CRWs) is a statistical tool that can be used to infer small scale information from the large-scale signal. In this paper, we consider the effect of galaxy bias and non-linear coupling on the CRW statistics. We generate CRW signals from N-body simulations of the physics of cosmic reionization and observe that the CRW signal is maximized for galaxy bias at the percent level. Applying the CRW signal to observations from the Global Epoch of Reionization Array (Glow) we are able to place bounds on the galaxy bias parameter of up to 3.7% (1 sigma). Furthermore, we show that the best-fit bias does not match the intrinsic bias (bias calculated from the N-body simulation) and indicate future observations at higher frequency may be able to better constrain the bias.

Merging is a fundamental process in the formation and evolution of galaxies. Using galaxy clustering as a probe, much recent research has focused on the scale dependence of this process, revealing an enhanced formation rate of massive galaxies at high redshift, corresponding to the peak epoch of galaxy accretion. While this is consistent with a scenario of hierarchically growing dark matter halos, current observations can only place a weak limit on the timescale over which these galaxies assemble their halos, τM ≥ 5-7 Gyr. We show that this tension can be alleviated if the galaxies themselves have diffuse dark matter halos, and that these survive in abundance in current galaxy clustering data. We show that this level of substructure is consistent with theoretical expectations, and that cosmological simulations should find such a population of halos within the virial radii of halos of all masses. We conclude that a scenario in which merging drives the growth of galaxies, in combination with hierarchical growth of halos, is consistent with current observations of galaxy clustering and the large scale structure of the universe.

Alkanethiolate self-assembled monolayers (MTs) form a monolayer of molecules that anchor to a solid substrate through a carbon-carbon backbone with terminal alkanethiols. The terminal groups may be protected from oxidation in air by growing them on a metal substrate (e.g., Ag(111)). Formation of this protective layer prevents the oxidation of the underlying metal, making it useful for surface modifications for biointerfaces. To study the formation of this protective layer, scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were used. The STM images show the growth of MTs from the substrate to the Ag(111) surface. The XPS data show the formation of the terminal groups as well as C—C and C—H bonds on the Ag(111) surface. These bonds confirm the formation of the protective layer. This article demonstrates that MTs may be grown on Ag(111) to form a protective layer that protects the underlying metal from oxidation. This protective layer may be studied with STM and XPS.

Neutron stars are born with a hydrogen-rich envelope that is dynamically stripped away by the accretion of matter from a binary companion. Observations indicate that this matter is mixed into the neutron star surface layers, but the distribution of elements and the underlying physical process are not well understood. We combine the rapid rotation and strong gravitational field of neutron stars with magnetohydrodynamics simulations to study turbulent mixing in the surface layers. We find that the Coriolis force acting on the convective eddies accelerates the star toward the inner part of the companion's Roche lobe, facilitating tidal interaction and driving strong turbulence. The turbulent viscosity and electron conduction allow the elements to spread several pressure scale heights into the neutron star atmosphere. The potential of current and future ground-based optical astrometric missions is pushed to the limit by measuring motions of stars at the level of a fraction of an arcsecond. This precision requires demanding modeling and reductions of systematic effects, which are rarely entirely satisfactory. Here we show that even under the most optimistic assumptions the present-day limitations still prevent us from directly measuring the structure of stars' surfaces. We demonstrate this with a detailed modeling of the case of β Lyr, the only observed variable star whose interior structure can be directly resolved using current technology. Its surface rotation is found to be less than half of the local scales of convection, contradicting previous inferences that this rapid surface rotation could not be maintained without rapid internal angular momentum redistribution. We show that the current lack of constraints on the surface structure of β Lyr significantly exceeds the achievable limit imposed by various systematic effects in optical astrometry and suggest avenues for future improvement.

Cosmogenic neutrinos produced by interactions of extragalactic cosmic rays with the extragalactic photon background and the interstellar medium deliver a powerful diagnostic of the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays. If the sources of extragalactic cosmic rays are within or clustered near galaxies, neutrino production is peaked toward the Galactic Centre and subtracted from signals at distant neutrino detectors. We present a model for neutrino production that accurately captures the essential astrophysics and test this model with the observations. We find that a minimal model in which sources are distributed with no preference relative to galaxies is in good agreement with the observations. This result has profound implications for models of Active Galactic Nuclei and their relation to the sources of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays. Neutrino oscillations reduce the expected cosmogenic neutrino flux at neutrino detectors on Earth, but the signature of aGalactic origin may nevertheless be present in the spectrum of highest energy events or in the distribution of atmospheric neutrinos withrespect to the zenith. We report the results of a search for such a signal using 730,323 neutrino interactions in -4.9 < zenith < 5.9 obtained between July 2006 and June 2013 with the IceCube neutrino telescope. We find no evidence for aGalactic signal and set upper limits on the diffuse flux that are more than an order of magnitude above the prediction of current models of neutrino production in the Milky Way. Our result provides strong evidence that the sources of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays are distributed over large regions of space and are not located within our Galaxy.

In this paper, we consider a single antenna transmission over fading channel with infinite backlog. We analyze the average end-to-end distortion of a simple proportional-integral (PI) regulator that adjusts the transmit SNR based on a linear fading-channel-noise model. Unlike the conventional end-to-end distortion minimization approaches that attempt to learn the statistics of the channel state information (CSI) at the transmitter, we assume that the transmitter has only one channel state, i.e., perfect CSI at the transmitter. We first derive the maximum average distortion-rate function for the infinite-buffer case. Then, we characterize the average distortion for the finite-buffer case, and further extend our results to the general case with non-vanishing delay. Our results show that while CSI is helpful to improve the performance in the high SNR regime, it is crucial to reduce the buffer size to minimize the average distortion for all SNR values.

Fuzzy Extra Dimensions (FED) is a novel approach to model the fundamental interactions of nature in a conceptually simple and economical way by incorporating a dimension(s) of space that is( are) not “bulk-like” but nevertheless can have a strong influence on the macroscopic world that we experience. FED is the first serious attempt to introduce extra-dimensions to physics that are not “flat” or “fixed” but rather are dynamic and evolve according to the dynamics of the other dimensions of the universe. By a suitable choice of parameters, FED can address several critical challenges to cosmology, high energy physics and gravity including: (i) solve the gauge hierarchy problem and thus provide a realistic theory of gravity; (ii) explain the smallness of the cosmological constant and its dynamical generation; (iii) provide a solution to the dark matter and dark energy problems; (iv) provide a possible solution to the problem of large and urgent anthropic cosmological constant; (v) provide a dynamical solution to the strong CP problem without resorting to ad hoc and non-dynamical terms in the Lagrangian; (vi) provide a natural solution to the cosmological problem of over-abundance of cosmic strings produced during spontaneous breaking of global symmetries at the grand unification scale; (vii) FED can provide a new framework for renormalizability based on dynamical dimensions; (viii) and explain the hierarchy of the standard model (SM) symmetries from the quantum gravity (QG) scale. In this work we will discuss the theoretical foundation and phenomenological consequences of the simplest version of the FED theory, i.e., the one based on a single dynamic fuzzy space-time dimension. We will show that, within this theory, the hierarchy problem is automatically solved without the need of an additional large effective parameter and the gravity Lagrangian is dynamically generated from the QG scale down to the TeV scale. As a first application, we will consider the implications of FED in cosmology and show that: (a) inflation can occur in a natural way without any need for fine-tuning; (b) the origin of the cosmological constant and the dark energy can be understood as dynamical breaking of an approximate global symmetry at the quantum gravity scale.

The paper develops a general theory of effective material parameters for thin layers modeled as single and double grids of interacting loaded wires. The parameters determine the behavior of the layer in response to an external stress. The general framework is developed for both isotropic and anisotropic materials. Two specific examples of the layer application are described: a thin film of graphene with a small area density modulation and a thin layer of nanocomposites with interfacial separation instability. The theory is illustrated with numeric results for both stationary and time-dependent problems. The theory is tested and verified against existing theories and experimental data for the case of a thin sheet of graphene. In this article, we simulate the quantum evolution of high-dimensional interaction Hamiltonians on a digital quantum simulator. We consider systems of up to 10^6^ spins, each evolving under a different short-range interaction term. While scalable quantum simulators must contend with both interactions and imperfections, we demonstrate that incorporating redirection gates can mitigate the effects of noise and extended evolution times relative to alternative simulation strategies. In particular, we simulate the dynamics of the Heisenberg model, the square-exchange model, and the random-exchange Ising model, all the way to their respective Néel temperatures. variant of the Heisenberg and square-exchange models have previously been simulated on noisy quantum computers with variational methods, where the effects of noise were not addressed. We also simulate the dynamics of the random-exchange Ising model, which has not previously been done in the quantum setting. We further demonstrate that noise may be exploited for quantum simulation, by simulating the dynamics of the Floquet time crystal model. Finally, we simulate the dynamics of time-evolving block decimation, a method for simulating renormalization group flows.

In this work, we present the results of a long-term study of the orbital periods of the AM CVn stars HP Librae and V803 Centauri. The two objects have very similar effective temperatures and gravitational moments, and are, accordingly, very close on the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. We have monitored their eclipse timings for many years and detect different trends in their binary orbits. After combining our data with earlier results, we are able to determine an empirical relation between the binary period and the average time interval between consecutive eclipses. This allows us to determine an observational period for HP Librae of 83.86 hours and for V803 Centauri of 82.21 hours, or twice these values. The accuracy of our determination is sufficient to provide the first significant detection of the oscillation period in the binary orbit of HP Librae. We discuss possible origins for these periodicities and examine the implications of our findings for our current understanding of these objects. * * * We are conducting a long-term observational study of the eclipse timing of AM CVn stars HP Librae and V803 Centauri. The results of this work will improve our understanding of the binary systems in which these stars reside and may also lead to new insights into the nature of these systems. In particular, our results will allow us to determine the binary period of HP Librae with improved accuracy, which will allow us to study the oscillations in the binary orbit of this star in more detail. This will provide further constraints on the properties of the system and perhaps help to reveal its nature. Furthermore, by determining the binary period of V803 Centauri we will be able to confirm or rule out the possibility that this star is a fast rotator and to study its pulsations in more detail. Finally, the empirical relationship we have determined will allow other teams to more easily analyse the eclipse timing data for other AM CVn systems and to thereby further increase our understanding of these objects. We have obtained new timings for the eclipses of HP Librae and V803 Centauri from 2016 through to 2019. We then combined these new results with older data obtained between 2008 and 2015 in a method similar to that employed by Vanlandingham et al. (2008). This enabled us to detect different trends in the binary orbits of HP Librae and V803 Centauri and to determine empirical relationships between the binary period and the average time interval between consecutive eclipses. These relationships are: For HP Librae we find: T ≈ 0.94P + 282.76 [s] where T is the average time interval between consecutive eclipses and P is the binary period in hours. This letter investigates the transient behavior of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) scattered at a subwavelength groove. The SPP scattering is modeled as a two-dimensional waveguide grating with a finite longitudinal dimension. It is shown that the SPP fields are primarily distributed in the groove and gradually decay to zero in the distance of lambda/2n where n is the refractive index of surrounding medium. The SPP fields decay as a free-space exponential function in the long distance and the time scale is determined by the dimensions of the groove. The temporal evolution of the SPP field is in-line with that of the transverse component of the electric field of the incident pulse, showing the dominant role of the SPP in the scattering process. The results provide useful information on SPP scattering at subwavelength scale and can be utilized to optimize SPP-based devices. Recent progresses in the field of quantum quenches in extended systems have revealed the existence of a large variety of intriguing behaviors. These include the generation of a dynamical gap, the relaxation to a generalized Gibbs state, the spontaneous production of off-diagonal long range order, the emergence of local conserved quantities, and many more. The variety of different mechanisms at play depends on the particular choice of the initial state and of the Hamiltonian which is instantaneously modified. These results have been obtained in one spatial dimension, for critical systems, as well as in higher dimensions and at quantum critical points. The current understanding is that these phenomena are deeply rooted in the relaxation to equilibrium of the post-quench system, and that considerable extensions to standard quantum statistical mechanics are needed to describe them. I will discuss several recent results in this field, with an emphasis on the mechanisms at play in quenches to non-thermal initial states. As a first example, I will discuss a recent result concerning the relaxation of a 1D spin chain to a generalized Gibbs state at infinite temperature. In the limit of long but finite time differences between the initial and the final state, the post-quench dynamics can be characterized by the scattering of sound waves in the pre- and post-quench regimes. In this limit, the relaxation towards the generalized Gibbs state is driven by entanglement entropy exchanged with an environment consisting in an infinite chain of non-interacting fermions. In the post-quench regime, the key quantity governing the relaxation is the depth of the force potential acting on the (infinitely) many degrees of freedom of the environment. I will also discuss the closely related problem of the relaxation of an initially thermal state to a thermal state at a different temperature. Here, the system only interacts with its own environment, but the similarities with the previous case are quite striking. I will also mention a result in 1D systems with short-range interactions showing that even very large fluctuations in the energy difference between the initial and the final states can lead to a perfect relaxation to a thermal state. As a second example, I will discuss the relaxation of an arbitrary quantum many-body system to a state with off-diagonal long range order. This state describes a sort of Quantum Version of Classical Phase Transitions and the key quantity governing the relaxation is again entanglement entropy. In systems where the Hamiltonian of the post-quench state can be split in a local part and a non-local part, a separation of time scales can occur, and the system initially evolves essentially according to the local part of the Hamiltonian, before it finally relaxes to the generalized Gibbs state characteristic of the long-range part. I will also mention several results valid for the special case of integrable models, where off-diagonal long range order has been found to emerge also in the absence of quenches. In this paper, we report on the observation of saturation effects in the spectroscopic signal from Cs atoms confined in an Extremely Thin Cell. This cell is a state of the art microfabricated vapor cell with a cell volume of only 100 pL. We observe a large signal enhancement at room temperature as compared to the quantum projection noise limit. This observation is in qualitative disagreement with theoretical models based on the Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity distribution of the atoms. A revised theoretical model taking into account the detailed temperature distribution within the cell explains the experimental observations. This result shows that vapor cell temperature control at the pK level is a necessity for reaching the quantum projection noise limit in sub-Doppler spectroscopy with room temperature atoms. In this work we present a methodology to study the deflection of asteroids due to the Yarkovsky effect, and apply it to real asteroids. We simulate the effect over hundreds of millions of years, and show that the asteroid’s orbit changes, becoming deeper into Earth’s potential reserve of energy. We estimate that two asteroids, 4 Hektor and 2101 Apollo, could be deflected out of the region of overlap with the current known reservoir of resources and near Earth objects (NEOs). This might lead to their discovery and characterization. We then simulate the effect over tens of millions of years for the asteroid 4 Hektor, showing that its orbit could lead it outside of the region of Earth’s orbit around the sun. This might lead to 4 Hektor’s physical characterization, and more importantly, would greatly reduce the likelihood of dangerous collisions with Earth. Our methodology can be easily adapted to other asteroids, and might be useful to predict the effects of other phenomena that affect the trajectory of asteroids, such as non-gravitational effects and close encounters with other asteroids or planets.

The so-called ’dark energy’ is believed to be responsible for the recent acceleration of the universe’s expansion. Independent observations of this phenomena have only been available since the late 2000s, so when exactly the universe started to accelerate has been a subject of significant debate. In this paper, we use a suite of different datasets to measure the timing of the transition from deceleration to acceleration. We find that while there is a high degree of agreement on the average transition time, the precision with which it has been determined is highly dependent on the choice of dataset used. Our findings indicate that cosmologists may have overestimated the uncertainty in the timing of the transition, with the impact on the design of future dark energy surveys being discussed. The acceleration of the cosmic expansion was first observed in the late 2000s, and since then its cause has been a subject of intense study. Indirect evidence for this phenomenon, based on measurements of the cosmological parameters, only became available during the past decade. Consequently, the question of precisely when the expansion started to accelerate has been a topic of debate. In this paper we consider this question using a suite of different datasets, and find that while there is good agreement on the average transition time, the precision with which it has been determined is highly dependent on the choice of dataset used. Our findings indicate that cosmologists have overestimated the uncertainty in the timing of the transition, with the impact on the design of future dark energy surveys being discussed. Our results are based on recent measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) – the afterglow of the Big Bang – lensing of the background light by large scale structures and direct measurements of the expansion rate of the universe using distant supernovae. We find that the data are most consistent with the transition from deceleration to acceleration taking place between z = 0.5 and z = 0.0. However, the precision with which this has been determined is highly dependent on the dataset used, with our determination being based on the following datasets: z = 0.0 - 0.5 (average of z = 0.0 and z = 0.5); z = 0.0 - 0.2 (average of z = 0.0 and z = 0.2); z = 0.0 - 0.01 (average of z = 0.0 and z = 0.01).

Reionization is the period in the early Universe during which the ionized fraction of the intergalactic medium (IGM) was higher than 50%1. While the epoch of reionization (EOR) ended around 700 million years (Myr) after the Big Bang, the generation of isolated high-redshift luminous galaxies2 and the interpretation of large scale structure observations3 indicate that EOR may have lasted up to a few hundred million years. The EOR may have been driven by the first quasars, which are believed to have emerged at a redshift of 7-81. To characterize the ionizing background during this period and to locate the sources of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), an array of 15 powerful Next-Generation telescopes (NGTs) is under construction in South Africa, with planned integration time of less than 1 hour at a resolving power of 15 kilometers per spectral pixel4. These instruments will be the first primarily operated in the band centred at 10 micrometers and are named Darkseed. Several of the NGT instruments are using narrow band technologies, in which a tunable filter is imaged onto a photon counter5. While narrow band technology is optimal for measurements of isolated HII regions, the emission duration of isolated HII regions tends to be inversely proportional to the square root of the ionizing-photon emission rate6, and it may therefore be insufficient to obtain an accurate measurement. Spectroscopic surveys8,9,10 have been carried out to search for HII regions in large low-redshift volume using the Lyman alpha (Lyα) line. In this work, we present narrow band survey data of the Hydrus ultra-low redshift galaxy cluster (UltraDES)12,13, over an effective area of 1.7 square degrees using the NGT-19 camera14 with an effective band width of 8.8 Angstroms (96 centimeters per pixel at the mean Hydrus redshift of z=0.0615). In a field of this size, we have identified 260 Lyα sources with uncertain/unidentified redshifts. We estimate a conservative redshift uncertainty of z*=0.1306±0.0016 for sources with at least three confident redshifts. This corresponds to a comoving volume density of z*=0.0615 with a minimum uncertainty of 0.0064 (6.4%) - thus the field density is 52±7 galaxies Mpc-3. The overdensity is at a 3.6σ significance, and we discuss possible interpretations of this overdensity within the standard paradigm of reionization. The Hydrus Ultra-low Redshift Galaxy Cluster. The article aims to present a model of electrodynamics linear in the electromagnetic field, where Maxwell's equations are modified only by the addition of a new term representing the possibility of electron inertia. The model allows to deduce the light cone, which has been the subject of numerous disputes in the theory of light. The new model is supported by numerous experimental facts, such as the Michelson-Morely experiment, Gildensele's experiment, or Stern-Gerlach's experiment, all of which are explained in a straightforward manner. Another consequence of the model is the possibility of longitudinal waves, whose existence was denied by most scientists. The article is concluded with a discussion of possible developments of the model and its implications. Keywords: linear electrodynamics, light cone, inertia of the electron Reference: 1. A. A.
