Galactic discs are warped due to the non-sphericity of the gravitational potentials in which they are embedded. I calculate the warps that are due to the attraction of large scale dark matter distributions, including cosmological haloes, that are found around late-forming massive galaxies. In addition to these “internal” warps, which are typically small and focus close to the galaxy’s centre, I also calculate the large-scale “external” warps that are generated by the infall of material from large-scale cosmological flows onto the galaxy’s disc. I show that these “external” warps are most significant at large radii from the galaxy, with amplitude and pattern speed depending on the rate of accretion and the depth of the potential well of the host dark matter halo. The external warps are typically significantly larger than the internal warps, and the warp pattern speed is directly related to the pattern speed of the infalling material. Thus the presence of large-scale warps in galactic discs provide a potentially powerful method of identifying when infalling material has affected a galaxy. Because the warp pattern speed is strongly dependent on the pattern speed of infalling material, the change in warp pattern speed over time provides a method of constraining the rate of infall. I show that the amplitude of the warp increases with time as matter accumulates, following a track like that of the warp amplitude due to a single major infall event. The rate of increase is also dependent on the rate of infall, with more rapid increase for higher infall rates. The amplitude and pattern speed of galactic warps provide a novel means of estimating the mass and rate of accretion of large-scale flows in the universe. Because the warp amplitude is a strong function of the pattern speed of the infalling material, which in turn depends on the rate of accretion, the amplitude of galactic warps can be used to estimate both the mass and rate of accretion of large-scale flows in the universe.

In this work we generalise the construction of gauge invariant factorisations of linearised topologically massive gravity in four dimensions [1] to arbitrary dimensions, and apply it to the construction of a canonical quantum field theory (CQT) defined on any background. In particular we find that the four dimensional theory can be canonically quantised on a general background, producing a unique Hilbert space and a unique Hamiltonian, satisfying a self-adjointness condition which is equivalent to the existence of a conservation law. We also generalise this to arbitrary dimensions and find that the unique Hamiltonian takes the same form, with the additional requirement of general covariance. We show that in any dimension a unique solution to the constraint equation exists, which for any choice of group manifold parameterisation defines a CQT. We provide the complete component form of the general covariant constraint equation and demonstrate that it is first class, independent of the choice of parameterisation and generates a symmetry of the theory. We also construct the induced representations of the symmetry algebra and provide the explicit form of the induced Hamiltonian.' This work continues the programme initiated in [1], for which we provide a detailed review, and which provided the starting point for our approach. We show that by including the local degrees of freedom of the additional, more general, backgrounds we are considering the gauge symmetry is enlarged to general covariance. We also include some additional motivation and technical detail which might be of interest to the reader, and present the main results in a form suitable for reference and future work.' --- On 26 September 2016, we submitted [1] to arXiv as a preliminary version. Since then we have made major revisions to the manuscript, incorporating many suggestions made by referees, and have incorporated further aspects suggested in discussions with Zackaria Brown. In this version we also correct an error in our discussion of the induced representation of the symmetry algebra. These changes have resulted in a substantial improvement to the readability and flow of the text, and we hope that this will be the final version.

Ulman estimates the time-dependent density corresponding to a given potential by minimizing the expectation value of the potential under the time-dependent von Neumann equation. We prove that the solution to this minimization problem is unique and given by the Feynman-Kac formula. We also examine the possibility of mapping the potential onto the density rather than the reverse, and we show that for the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator potential this is possible only at positive times. The mapping of a time-dependent potential onto its corresponding time-dependent density has applications in imaging, kinetic theory, and quantum mechanics. In quantum mechanics this mapping is useful in determining candidate ground states for numerical solutions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. This article examines the nature of this mapping and its limitations for the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator potential. Time-Dependent Density Operators and the von Neumann Equation The expectation value of an operator $\hat{A}(t)$ in the state $\hat{\rho}(t_0)$, $$\begin{aligned} \langle \hat{A}(t) \rangle = \text{Tr}\left( \hat{\rho}(t_0) \hat{A}(t) \right),\end{aligned}$$ can be expressed in terms of the time-evolution of $\hat{\rho}(t)$, the von Neumann equation: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \hat{\rho}(t) = \frac{i}{\hbar} \left[ \hat{H}, \hat{\rho}(t) \right] + \hat{D} \left( \hat{\rho}(t) \right), \quad \hat{\rho}(t_0) = \hat{\rho}\end{aligned}$$ where $\hat{D}(\hat{\rho})$ is the dissipator. For a time-independent Hamiltonian, $\hat{\rho}(t_0) = \hat{\rho} = \exp[-\beta(\hat{H}-\mu\hat{N})]\rangle$, where $\beta = (k_B T)^{-1}$ is the thermal wavelength, $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant, $T$ is the temperature, and $\mu$ and $\hat{N}$ are the chemical potential and particle number operators. The density operator may be expressed in terms of its eigenstates $\vert n \rangle \langle n \vert$, $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\rho} = \sum_n p_n \vert n \rangle \langle n \vert \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \hat{\rho}(t) = \sum_n p_n \vert n \rangle \langle n \vert e^{-i E_n(t - t_0)}.\end{aligned}$$ The eigenvalues are given by the Boltzmann distribution $p_n = e^{-E_n(t - t_0)}/

In a wireless broadcast channel with multiple antennas at the transmitter and one antenna at the receiver, it is possible and beneficial to allow some of the transmitter antennas to be turned off, as long as the signal energy is spread across the antennas. This article studies the system design question of how many transmitters should be turned on, and how much transmission power should be used, to maximize the number of receivers who can recover the transmitted information at an arbitrarily low cost. We consider the case where the transmitter has perfect knowledge of the channel state information (CSI), and the case where the transmitter only has statistical CSI. In the case where perfect CSI is available at the transmitter, we determine the optimal number of active transmitters and corresponding transmission power that maximize the number of receivers who can recover the information at an arbitrarily low cost. We then characterize the scaling of the number of active transmitters and corresponding transmission power with the blocklength of the channel code, up to logarithmic factors, for the symmetric case where the channel is invariant under permutation of the antennas. When only statistical CSI is available at the transmitter, we provide sufficient conditions for low-complexity effective coding and interference management to achieve nearly-optimal performance, and we describe a specific coding and interference management scheme that achieves within a factor of 2/3rd the maximum possible number of receivers.

Large electric polarization and magnetic order coexist at room temperature in BiFeO3, a material with Curie temperature above 1000 K. The large spontaneous electric polarization (8.2 μC/cm2) and anomalous Hall effect indicate the coexistence of ferroelectricity and improper magnetism. Such exotic multiferroic behavior is unexpected in simple perovskite structure materials and highlights the unusual properties of BiFeO3. section Large electric polarization and magnetic order coexist at room temperature in BiFeO3, a material with Curie temperature above 1000 K. The large spontaneous electric polarization (8.2 μC/cm2) and anomalous Hall effect indicate the coexistence of ferroelectricity and improper magnetism. Such exotic multiferroic behavior is unexpected in simple perovskite structure materials and highlights the unusual properties of BiFeO3. technical details BiFeO3 single crystals exhibit both large spontaneous electric polarization and spontaneous magnetic moment with rare long-range order. Electric polarization is aligned along the a axis and the magnetic moments are organized along the b axis, i.e. both are improper. Large coupling strength between polarization and magnetic order is responsible for the coexistence. Such exotic multiferroic behavior is unexpected in simple perovskite structure materials and highlights the unusual properties of BiFeO3.

Magnetic fields exist in a wide range of physical systems ranging from massive stars to the largest domains of the interplanetary plasma. The very small-scale fields, ubiquitous in biology and technology, are challenging to simulate. The traditional brute-force finite difference or 3D Maxwell solvers are simply not scalable to this challenging problem space. Recent years have seen the development of scalable simulation techniques based on the Finite-Difference-Collocation (FDC) method. In this review, we provide an overview of these recent progresses, as well as point to outstanding challenges and applications. For more information, please visit: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.08422 *Towards the scalability for small-scale magnetic field simulation* Simulating the very small-scale magnetic fields in biology, technology, and the interplanetary plasma requires both huge dynamic ranges and a scalable algorithmic solution. While the former requires a fine grid resolution and a large dynamic range simulation, the latter requires solvers that are able to handle very large systems with strong P{DIV}=0 and C{DIV}=0 constraints. Finite-Difference-Collocation (FDC) algorithms provide such a solution, and have recently made rapid progress in computing the small-scale magnetic field, especially in the biophysical case of the magnetotail and in the technological case of the photonic bandgap. In this review, we provide an overview of these recent progresses, as well as point out some of the outstanding challenges.

Young early-type galaxies are particularly interesting because they are believed to be the most straightforward manifestation of "mainstream" galaxy evolution: the fading of "blue" star-forming galaxies and the emergence of more evolved “red and dead” systems. In this sense, the study of young early-type galaxies could give us an idea of how typical the whole process of galaxy evolution is. We present results of a search for "young" early-type galaxies (ETGs) in the GOODS-South field using high-quality HST imaging from the CANDELS survey. We identify 134 potential "blue-coupon" candidates (i.e., galaxies that exhibit substantial evidence of on-going star formation) with robust spectroscopic redshift measurements and measure their structural parameters. In an effort to remove low-mass post-starburst galaxies from our sample we also use a photometric redshift analysis to identify a further 987 "candidate" blue-coupon galaxies. We find a total of 1124 massive ($M_{*}>10^{10.5}M_{\odot }$) galaxies with $z<1$ and structural properties consistent with those of local early-type galaxies. This represents a dynamical merger fraction of 13-19% for the present-day massive galaxy population at $z<1$ and is in good agreement with the predictions of semi-analytic models of galaxy formation. We conclude that, at least up to $z\sim 1$, the majority of the most massive galaxies have already formed a compact nucleus and shut off their star formation through a combination of dry mergers and AGN feedback.

A decaying wave packet on an atom in vacuum is retarded by a surface due to the mismatch of the dispersions. The resulting difference in propagation speeds leads to a non-zero probability of the system to enter into an excited state of the potential. We call this phenomenon super-Speedup. The probability of super-Speedup is numerically shown to increase with the strength of the surface potential and decrease with the wave packet momentum. Super-Speedup may offer a novel pathway for protecting quantum information from decoherence. An atom in vacuum decays to vacuum, however if the atom is subjected to a surface this can lead to an enhanced probability of the atom to transition to an excited state. We demonstrate this phenomenon, termed super-Speedup, and show that it is due to the difference in propagation speeds of the decaying wave packet and the induced surface potential. We compute the probability of super-Speedup and find that it increases with the strength of the surface potential and decreases with the momentum of the wave packet. Super-Speedup may offer a novel pathway for protecting quantum information from decoherence.

This paper shows that, in addition to the usual Heisenberg algebra, the canonical commutation relations between the coordinates and the momenta in quantum mechanics can be derived from a Lie algebra, which is isomorphic to the so-called quantum group of isometries. The isomorphism between the two Lie algebras is given explicitly, in the form of a nonlinear Fourier transformation. The obtained commutation relations resemble a deformed Poincaré algebra, which includes a $\kappa$-deformation and a quadratic, Carrollian boost. As an application of these results, quantumroup of isometries are used to quantize a free particle on the Poincaré patch of the Schwarzschild metric, obtaining a deformation of the standard Kepler-Coulomb law. Dissipative processes in superfluid neutron stars are investigated within the framework of three dimensional, isotropic, and local momentum conservation equations. We adopt the microscopic theories for superfluid nuclear interactions and calculate the couplings between the superfluid components and the normal matter. In particular, we include the processes associated with the exchange of pions and their anapole counter parts. Within the approximations made, we found the criteria for the existence of pure superfluid neutron star solutions. Further, we identified various possible mixed phase configurations and computed the ranges of the various parameters over which each of the three phases is stable. The numerical computations of dynamical evolution show the occurrence of three different types of unstable modes in the mixed phase stars namely, fundamental Kelvin-Helmholtz, Rossby and Chandrasekhar (convective) modes. The global Rossby and Chandrasekhar modes could result in fusion of normal and superfluid regions leading to the formation of a single core plus mantle star. The collapsing cores of massive pulsars are usually expected to be more than 90% superfluid. The realization of this instability could lead to an interesting scenario for the formation of massive black holes

Longitudinally inhomogeneous coronal loops are known to undergo torsional oscillations when the longitudinal twist exceeds a critical value. This Letter shows that the twist evolves as a function of time and forms longitudinal inhomogeneous kinks that are then twisted. This process can explain many features of torsional oscillations that have been observed. This model can be used to understand the dynamics of twisted coronal loops in the solar atmosphere. Longitudinal inhomogeneity is essential to the formation of kinks. An analytical kink solution is found and numerical results are provided for both the kink evolution and the oscillation of twist. A twisted kink loop is simulated and shown to reproduce many features of observed torsional oscillation loops. The oscillation period is sensitive to the half-length, thickness and twist of the loop. These results may have applications in solar magnetohydrodynamics and in the interpretation of solar UV bursts. Longitudinally inhomogeneous coronal loops undergo torsional oscillations when the longitudinal twist exceeds a critical value. This critical twist increases with the longitudinal loop inhomogeneity. A twisted kink loop is a fundamental solution of the equilibrium twist evolution. By developing, we mean twisting more than is necessary to satisfy the twist evolution equation. The twist evolves as a function of time and forms longitudinal inhomogeneous kinks that are then twisted. This process can explain many features of torsional oscillations that have been observed.

In this paper, we propose a fully differentiable convolutional neural network (CNN) model that can approximate arbitrary two dimensional (2D) path curves. The model, referred to as 1-layer Excitable CNN (ECC), only consists of a single layer of 1D CNN, with the convolution filters shaped in a particular fashion so as to excitable. Unlike existing 2D path curve approximation methods that typically require multiple layers of convolutions and nonlinearities, ECC only requires a single 1D CNN layer. We show that the 1D filters in the 1st layer of ECC are actually hyperbolic tangent functions (HTF) and that by proper initializations, the 1D representations of different 2D path curves generated from ECC all collapsed into a single 1D band after a few singular value decompositions (SVDs). Through carefully studying the SVD factors, we are able to identify the number of factors to equal the number of path points in a path, and thus ECC can be viewed as a dynamic lower dimensional Hankel matrix completion method. We further propose a path evolution strategy to use this implicit representation to generate 2D path curves, achieving smooth path evolution and thus path curvature. We demonstrate that 1-layer ECC is capable of approximating complex path curves with high fidelity, even those with very thin or sharp turns. We show that ECC, with its single layer representation, is much more efficient and has much less parameters than existing 2D path curve approximation methods. We also conduct thorough experiments to analyze the influences of various factors on the path curve approximation performance of ECC. With the 1-layer ECC model and the path evolution strategy, we build an automatic path approximation pipeline which is easy to train and robust to various path types. We show that our pipeline is effective on multiple public benchmark path datasets and that it can even generate better results than existing methods on some difficult path datasets. We would like to take this opportunity to express our sincere gratitude to the authors of [1] for their inspiring work on designing 1D CNN filters that can excitable, to the authors of [2] for introducing the SVD technique into neural networks and providing a rigorous and comprehensive SVD analysis of ECC, and to the authors of [3] for their seminal work on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) and the development of the Lyre tool that is indispensable to our path curve evolution and alignment algorithm research.

Recent years have seen remarkable progress in sequencing the DNA of a large number of diverse organisms, yielding a significant increase in the number of protein-coding genes described and many genome-scale biochemical networks fully annotated. Despite these rapid changes, little is known about the evolutionary mechanisms that shaped these networks, leaving a major gap in our understanding of the origins and design of biological networks. Here, we conduct a large-scale, genome-wide analysis of protein interaction and transcriptional regulatory networks in 20 diverse bacterial species. We find that these networks share a striking core with median node degree that varies only two- to fourfold across species. Strikingly, we find that the correlation in degree across species – while low within each network – is significantly higher across all three networks examined: protein interactions, transcription factor binding site networks, and operon structures. We show that these high correlations are not due to species-specific network ‘parasites’ (i.e., network modules with high node degree across species but uncorrelated with the rest of the network), and cannot be recapitulated by a model in which network structures simply ‘copy and paste’ from one species to another. We conclude that although local network connections, or ‘modularity,’ are independently preserved between species, these networks also have a highly conserved global ‘topology’ – the correlation in the level of connectivity across nodes. We propose that this topology, and specifically the correlations observed in protein interaction, transcription factor binding site, and operon networks, are necessary consequences of genome evolution. This article is free to read on arXiv.org

Vibrations strongly influence the electronic structure of atoms and molecules. They determine, for example, fundamental properties such as melting and vibration frequencies, and are at the same time sensitive indicators of the molecular structure. The coupling between electrons and vibrations is known as electron-vibration interaction. The coupling leads to a broadening and modification of the spectral distribution of electronic excitations. The electron-vibration interaction is treated in many-body perturbation theory as a weak interaction. In this approach, properties of the system are analyzed with reference to an effective Hamiltonian that describes the electronic excitation spectrum. In the framework of many-body perturbation theory within the functional integral formalism (dynamical mean field theory), the electron-vibration interaction is described with the help of a systematic expansion in the electron-vibration coupling constant. In this expansion, the first non-vanishing term is called the electron-vibration coupling constant. Up to now, this coupling constant was obtained in second-order many-body perturbation theory. Here, we present the first calculation of the electron-vibration coupling constant in covariant density functional theory (CDFT). We show that the commonly used frequency-independent random-phase approximation, which is based on Fermi's golden rule, gives only the first non-vanishing term of this expansion. The result of the calculation in CDFT agrees well with that of theGW method. In addition, we demonstrate that for strongly anharmonic molecules the dominant contribution to the electron-vibration coupling constant stems not from diagonal matrix elements of the electron-vibration interaction, but from nondiagonal off-diagonal matrix elements. These off-diagonal matrix elements are induced by the anharmonicity of the potential energy surface. The corresponding non-diagonal Wick contractions are frequency-dependent. Our result indicates that anharmonic effects must be included in a fully consistent calculation of the electron-vibration coupling constant.

Open clusters play an important role in studies of stellar evolution, because the stars in the same cluster share the same initial conditions of formation and evolutionary stages. One of the best studied open clusters is the DAwarf-main sequence stars of the magnitude 7.5 star cluster M67, commonly referred to as NGC2682. It is an ideal place to study the effects of stellar evolution, as it is comprised of mostly main-sequence stars that have left the main sequence band in the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and are on the route to their future white dwarf configurations. To study the stellar population of NGC2682, Strömgren uvbyHβ photometry was obtained. The observed color–magnitude diagram (CMD) was used to evaluate the effects of photometric contamination and incompleteness, along with the membership selection method designed for the Hyades cluster. The CMD revealed a population of probable blue stragglers, which was also confirmed by the variability analysis. A simulation was performed to analyze the effects of the uncertainties in the input parameters on the output results. The results of this work can be summarized as follows: (1) the contamination level in the CMD of NGC2682 is estimated to be about 6.7% among the analyzed stars, (2) blue stragglers comprise at least 0.26% of the total cluster members, and (3) the simulated uncertainty of the output parameters does not exceed 14%.

This paper presents a family of numerical methods for solving the hyperbolic equations that comprise the outer boundary of a computational domain in simulations of gravitational collapse. The methods are based on a high-resolution shock capturing (HRSC) scheme and an approximate Riemann solver, and make use of the characteristic structure of the equations and of characteristic initial data to increase the order of accuracy of the solution at the outer boundary relative to other methods. We test the methods by performing several calculations of the nonlinear collapse of a spherical cloud of gas, with and without a rotation law that introduces a degree of differential rotation, and find that the methods are able to capture the formation and propagation of a shock front through the solution. To demonstrate the methods’ robustness, we also perform calculations in which the initial conditions, either the velocity or the density, are varied either smoothly or abruptly, and recover accurate solutions throughout. We conclude by discussing the outlook for future development of these methods.

This paper investigates interval conjectures for Hilbert functions of graded artinian modules over a graded polynomial ring. The Hilbert function of a graded artinian module $M=\oplus_IM_i$ is the vector of its graded parts $H(M):=(h_i(M))_i$ where $h_i(M):=\dim_K(M_i)$. The $r$th graded section of $M$ is the vector $h_M(r):=(h_i(r))_i$ where $h_i(r):=$ the $r$th graded part of $M_i$. The Hilbert function is said to be level if all its graded sections are level. The $m$th initial central degree of $M$ is the vector of degrees $\mathrm{in}_C(M):=(d_i)_{i=m}^{m+h-1}$ where $d_i=\deg(M_{i+1}\cdots M_{i+h-1})$ and $M$ has a minimal graded free resolution $0\longrightarrow \oplus_{i=1}^RA_i\longrightarrow \oplus_{i=1}^RB_i\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow 0$. The graded Betti table of $M$ is the $h_M\times h_M$ matrix $B(M)$ with $(i,j)$ graded Betti number $B_{i,j}(M)$ equal to the number of elements of $ \mathrm{in}_C(M)$ which are equal to $i$ and difference $j$ from $i$ modulo $h_M$. The paper first studies level Hilbert functions with constant graded Betti numbers $b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_h$ and establishes upper and lower bounds on the number of such functions with fixed height and constant difference between $b_h$ and its immediate neighbours $b_{h-1}$ and $b_h$. The bounds are then applied to a special class of level Hilbert functions which are shown to be realisable as Hilbert functions of graded artinian modules over a polynomial ring. An example is given of a level Hilbert function which is not realisable as Hilbert function of a module.

Galaxy colours in the AKARI Deep SEP Survey are presented. The DEEP SPITRS (Drop-Out High Redshift Emission Prop");- rerly SDSS) survey is the first large survey utilising the newly launched ASTRO-F/SPITZER satellite. In this survey approximately 3,000 h of observations were obtained at X-ray/near-IR wavelengths, providing deep and extensive coverage to large area (1.8 deg2) surveys. The galaxy population at high redshift is of great interest due to the pro- perties of the early universe, and the evolution of galaxies from high-redshift to the present day. Using simple models of galaxy spectral energy distributions, we investigate the rest-frame UV through near-infrared colours of galaxies in the DEEP SPITZER Large Area Survey (DSL) data release 7, which provides the deepest X-ray to near-infrared colours to date. These colour-colour diagrams are compared to the predictions of models including star-forming galaxies, passive elliptical galaxies, and active galactic nuclei at various redshifts. The resulting redshift distribution, coupled with the colour information, allows for the unique identification of separate populations of galaxies. We find that the galaxy populations at various redshifts can be robustly distinguished with the aid of these multi-wavelength data. Specifically, our results show that: (i) the majority of the galaxies in the high-redshift sample are massive passively evolving galaxies; (ii) the rest-frame UV - NIR colours of the galaxies at z>1.5 show little dependency on their stellar mass; and (iii) a significant fraction of high-redshift galaxies are likely highly dust-extincted, with a high average dust attenuation of A(H) = 2.2 ± 0.2 mag, and a high average specific star formation rate of (0.92 ± 0.12) -1, both of which are higher than those of local galaxies of the same mass.

Recent improvements in the integration of quantum dots (QDs) into optical nanophotonic structures have resulted in the availability of coherent spin oscillations from individual QDs. However, the physical principles that enable the control and read-out of spin states from these nanoscale structures are only beginning to be understood. Here we demonstrate coherent spin dynamics in individual self-assembled InGaAs QDs through photoluminescence intensity time-correlation and emission frequency correlation spectroscopy. Spin lifetimes of up to 20 ns are observed, corresponding to a coherence time of 120 ps. The exchange interaction between the confined electron and nuclear spin systems is identified as the dominant source of decoherence, allowing for spin lifetimes of several ns in high-quality quantum dots. The demonstration of coherent spin dynamics in QDs extends the range of system dimensions for which spin-based quantum information processing can be achieved and provides a useful platform for investigations of QD nanophotonics in the context of quantum information science.

The AKARI infrared astronomy satellite was launched in February 2006, and has provided a unique opportunity to perform infrared observations across the mid-infrared wavelength range of 3.5 – 26 μm. The Astronomical Multi-BEam Instrument (AMBI) was successfully implemented onboard AKARI as the first light instrument. AMBI is equipped with three cameras covering two bands simultaneously with wide fields of view and fast readout modes. The Infra-Red Camera (IRC) covers two 4.2° × 4.2° sub-fields of view with dual-channel staring MCT (Meridianized Combiner Module) arrays and fast readout modes. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-orbit focal adjustment (IAF) for AKARI using IRC images obtained during the same night and perform precise astrometry for the detected sources by comparing with UKIRT Infra-Red Deep Survey (UKIDSS) and GALEX ultraviolet imaging data. Our best-fit rms distortion values for the IRC images are 11.1 μas for x-direction and 8.0 μas for y-direction, corresponding to linear rms wavefront errors of 5.7 nm and 4.1 nm for x- and y-directions, respectively, at the near-infrared wavelengths. Finally, we present proper motion measurements for the detected sources in the IRC images and find that the weighted mean value of the motion vectors is -0.1146 ± 0.0063 pixels/frame (or 0.12 ± 0.006 arcsec/frame) in the x-direction and -0.1055 ± 0.0176 pixels/frame in the y-direction (or 0.11 ± 0.019 arcsec/frame).

A network tomography based on 1-D projections is proposed. This approach reconstructs the inter-vertex connection weight matrix from nodal metrics, known as 1-D projections. Nodal metrics include, for example, degree, clustering coefficient, betweenness centrality, and eigenvector centrality. The connections in the weight matrix correspond to the connections in a adjacent graph where the weight of a connection is proportional to the absolute value of the corresponding element in the weight matrix. The adjacent graph captures the relationship between vertices according to the corresponding 1-D projections. Thus, the original network can be recovered through matrix multiplication. Network tomography based on 1-D projections is simple, requiring only 1-D projections and no 3-D measurements. In contrast to existing tomography methods based on 3-D measurements, this method does not require expensive instrumentation or complex measurements. Moreover, it can be used to reconstruct networks with arbitrary structures and does not require a small, regular, or complete graph. This method has been applied to synthetic networks and real-world networks. Results show that the method can reconstruct the underlying connections with high accuracy.

A new I-band Tully-Fisher catalog is presented based on the SFI++ II imaging data. Based on a revised tilted-ring model, thecatalog contains 584 TF galaxies in the A3625 field. Using global colors and a novel iterative decomposition technique, we obtain a first-order approximation for the disk effective radius ($r_e$) and surface brightness ($\mu_e$) and construct a three-dimensional photometric model for each galaxy. The final Catalog includes a table of rotation curves, distance measurements and observational data. We also present the Peculiar Velocity dataset derived from the new catalog. The dataset includes z values calculated from the new TF data and optical photometry data, as well as z distances derived from a new peculiar velocity model. The Catalog and Peculiar Velocity dataset provide new and important information for studying the large-scale structure in the local universe.

Nanometer-scale tribology has recently been identified as a particularly interesting area of scientific inquiry due to the possibility of discovering novel frictional mechanisms and functionalities. In recent work, synergistic effects between methylodinitrosoacetoacetate (MoDTA) and zodi-Trojan intermolecular disulfide (ZDTP) were found to produce uniquely low friction tribo-performance. This paper describes a quantitative study of the mechanism of this behavior. A new molecular mechanism for the observed friction reduction is proposed based on a population of transiently formed interface monolayer crystals, which we term tribofilms. The tribofilms, possessing amphiphilic character and orientation stability reminiscent of surface films, are proposed to greatly enhance the mobility of molecular components between asperities, providing a lubrication mechanism distinct from other conventional mechanisms such as boundary layer shear or solid-solid contact area modification. A quantitative model for tribofilm formation is developed and applied to explain the low friction and wear data. The results indicate that tribofilm formation is the critical contributor to the synergistic reduction of friction and wear. The reported study provides new insight into the interfacial mechanism of nanometer-scale friction reduction, and could serve as a foundation for the development of future antifriction materials, lubricants, and coatings.

Media is a double-edged sword: while it can amplify messages and stimulate individual and societal discussion, it can just as easily amplify whims and prejudices, promoting particular thoughts and opinions, and suppressing opposing viewpoints. It is not immediately clear whether feedback effects arising from these informational asymmetries are constructive or destructive. Using an agent-based computational model of cultural dynamics, I explore a range of simulation scenarios in which media can amplify or suppress different aspects of cultural diversity, and discuss the possible implications for social stability and innovation. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. IIS-1715946. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation. Media has become an indispensable part of human communication and entertainment. From classical books to modern technology, people rely on it for information and cultural background. Thanks to the advanced communication technology, the distribution speed of media content is extremely fast. As a result, the effect of information feedback becomes more and more evident. With the help of computational model, I study the impact of media in the society from two aspects: the amplification of different aspects of cultural diversity and the promotion of social stability or innovation. In the scenario where only negative feedback is considered, I find that the diversity of opinions is suppressed. A small group of individuals can dominate the whole society. Although this outcome is not that surprising, the simulation result is quite depressing. In the scenario where both positive and negative feedbacks are considered, I find that diversity of opinions is promoted. Small groups with diverse opinions can coexist peacefully. I further examine the underlying mechanism. In the long-term simulation, with the help of social labels, each individual can easily recognize different opinions. Since different opinions correspond to different social labels, they can be separated naturally. With the aid of the reinforcement learning, the individuals with similar opinions are likely to gather and form clusters. With the increase of time, clusters with similar opinions become bigger and bigger, while the small clusters with diverse opinions are broken. As a result, the whole society becomes more and more homogenous. Nevertheless, as long as all opinions can survive, the stability of the whole society can still be promoted. This research indicates that although media can help amplify different viewpoints, it can also promote social stability by amplifying the survival of different opinions. Optimizing scrip systems have been the focus of both praise and criticism in the cryptocurrency community for several years. Scrip systems are plugins for cryptocurrency wallets that allow users to make incremental payments to pay people, services, and machines. Many view scrip systems as a fundamental missing piece to cryptocurrency, enabling practical applications which are difficult or impossible without them. Scrip systems can automate the task of paying people for things they produce, like content, labor, or data. They can also make it easier to manage large payments or payments to multiple recipients, which can be a challenge with cryptocurrency. Critics, however, have warned that scrip systems can be vulnerable to crashes, can cause erroneous payments, and can create opportunities for abusive or unethical behavior by virtue of their design. In this work, I compare three commonly used scrip systems: Bitwage, Libera, and Wagepoint, and describe several ways in which they could be improved. First, I describe design decisions behind each scrip system that I believe could be reconsidered. Second, I discuss research into alternative designs for scrip systems that I believe could improve security and reliability. Third, I describe ways in which scrip systems could be designed to reduce the opportunity for abusive or abusive behavior. I conclude by describing some ways cryptocurrency projects could adopt and fund this work, through development partnerships or sponsorships.

In this paper, we explore the phenomenology of neutralinos that are nearly massless and thereby are excellent dark matter candidates. These supersymmetry (SUSY) scenarios are characterized by the parameter MSUGRA, the common mass of the supersymmetric partners of theStandard Model(SM) fermions. We focus on the co-annihilation region of this scenario where nearly mass- degenerate superpartners can have similar masses and therefore contribute significantly to the dark matter density of the universe. We consider the implications of current XENON1T observations of dark matter density and further put strong constraints on the SUSY parameter space. We identify the regions of the parameter space that are compatible with the observed dark matter density and Xenon1T constraints, and also satisfy other constraints such as Higgs mass and B-physics constraints. In the regions of this parameter space, the nearly massless neutralinos are within the reach of future colliders like the International Linear Collider.

In this paper, we present an algorithm to find the optimal order-one algorithm for computing the spectral norm of a matrix. The spectral norm of a matrix measures the largest eigenvalue of the matrix; it is of central importance in analysis and algorithm design for linear algebraic problems. Traditionally, the optimal order of the computational complexity for computing the spectral norm is known. In this paper, we present an algorithm to solve the eigenproblem for a polynomial equation, and the resulting rational function satisfies the same degree bounds as the optimal order. We show that the corresponding order-one algorithm for computing the spectral norm finds the optimal order of precision when applied to the matrix representation of the rational function. The spectral norm has wide-ranging applications, ranging from PAC learning theory and robust optimization to semidefinite programming and sum of squares programming. The first sub-cubic algorithm for the spectral norm was given by Lee, Meka, Recht and Huang (FOCS 2011). Since then, the best known algorithms for the spectral norm have had running times that were super-cubic in the best-known lower bounds on the precision. Until recently, even improving the asymptotic complexity of computing the spectral norm to better than super-cubic was out of reach. Chang, Huang, and Wang (STOC 2020) gave the first sub-quartic algorithm, and Chan and Scholkopf (FOCS 2020) gave an algorithm with order-one reduction that computes the spectral norm to within precision of 0.25. Since the lower bounds on the precision of the best known algorithms were super-quadratic, this implies that sub-quartic algorithms for the spectral norm are possible. We present a novel approach to order-one algorithms for the spectral norm. We solve eigenproblems for rational functions, which is to say, we solve a linear equation in the form y = P(x)/Q(x) for a given matrix P and a polynomial division Q, with the goal of computing the spectral norm of the matrix representation of the rational function. We give two algorithms for solving such eigenproblems. The first algorithm is a straightforward generalization of the algorithm of Chang et al. (STOC 2020) for solving eigenproblems for linear functions, and it is inspired by their proof. The second algorithm is inspired by the work of Chan and Scholkopf (FOCS 2020) for constructing an order-one algorithm for semidefinite programming by solving a hierarchy of eigenproblems. Both of our algorithms run in time that is at most quartic in the precision, for which we give an explanation based on the Dantzig selector. We show that the rational function computed by our first algorithm gives an order-one reduction for the spectral norm, and that the rational function computed by our second algorithm has precision at most 0.25. This implies that our first algorithm gives an optimal order-one algorithm for computing the spectral norm

In the early phase of star formation, the angular momentum is a critical factor in the formation process. To avoid the collapse to a point singularity, the central core first form an accretion disk, through the fragmentation of the parental gas cloud. The presence of an accretion disk can effectively inhibit the further collapse, and form a rotation supported core. Such rotationally supported core, named as pre-stellar core, will eventually collapse to form a protostar. In such a process, some of the material with high angular momentum is expelled from the vicinity of the forming star along with the infall motion, forming a jet-like structure. With the help of numerical simulations, we reveal the dynamic process that the formation of jets and outflows in star formation. This article is a must read for anyone interested in star formation and related topics. This article presents the dynamic process that the formation of jets and outflows in star formation. With the help of numerical simulations, we reveal the dynamic process that the formation of jets and outflows in star formation. We perform several three-dimensional global simulations of collapsing pre-stellar cores. The included physics is simplified but adequate to follow the early dynamics of star formation, and enable us to capture the key processes such as gravitational instability, dynamical interaction among cores, rotation, magnetic field, convection and fragmentation. In particular, magnetic field is included in the resistive MHD system. We find that, along with the contraction of the whole pre-stellar core, the fragments will get more concentrated near the center due to the angular momentum, and a rotationally supported core is gradually formed. When the rotationally supported core reaches ~0.1 pc, it starts to launch a jet-like outflow along the rotation axis. As the outflow propagates outwards, some of the materials around the jet launching region will be swept into a narrow shell, and further launch a spherical symmetric outflow. The launched outflows carry large amount of energy and momentum, and play an important role in the star formation process. To understand the launching mechanism of the jet and outflows, we further decompose the energy equation and magnetic flux equation in the dynamical calculation domain. Through the analysis of different physical processes, we find that the magnetic flux is extremely tightly related to the launching process of the outflows. For example, the rotational energy of the central compact core is mainly converted into the magnetic flux through magnetic flux transport and winding, and the launching process of the jet is just a natural process resulted from the conversion from magnetic to kinetic energy. In addition, the magnetic flux also tightly regulates the formation and evolution of the jet launching regions, and forms multiple-peaked helical magnetic fields in the jet launching regions. We summarize our main findings as follows: 1. The formation and evolution of pre-stellar cores is regulated by both gravity and thermal/non-thermal pressure of the gas. 2. A0620-00, an X-ray binary in the center of the globular cluster NGC 6Most likely consists of a black hole accreting from a Be star companion (Menou, et. al. 2001). The system is nearby (4.3 kpc; Reipurth, et. al. 2001), and the black hole has a low mass (6.6 M⊙; McConnachie, et. al. 2009) which makes it visible in the near-infrared. We have obtained near-infrared (NIR) spectra of the system with the NIRSPEC spectrometer on the W. M. Keck II Telescope. The NIRSPEC spectra have a spectral resolution R ≈ 22,500 and cover the 1.0-2.4 μm wavelength range. We use these data to determine the absorption and emission spectrum of the donor star. The donor is an A-type star, and the absorption spectrum displays Balmer and P-Cygni lines consistent with expectations from a spectral classification of A0 Ve. We also detect CO bandhead absorption in the donor spectrum, and measure an equivalent width of W(CO) ≈ 1.0 ± 0.2 Å. This detection of CO bandhead absorption in the spectrum of an X-ray binary donor is surprising and raises new questions about the composition and evolutionary state of the companion star. We compare the NIRSPEC spectra with spectra from the VLT/ISAAC NIR spectrophotometer and find that the NIRSPEC data are consistent with a constant temperature photosphere, as expected for an A-type star. However, we detect strong emission in the Br γ line at 2.16 μm, as well as weak He I 2.06 μm and Ca II triplet emission. This emission is not present in the VLT/ISAAC spectra. We model the NIRSPEC data as a simple shell of gas and dust surrounding the star, and we show that this model is capable of producing the observed Br γ emission and excess near-infrared flux. We discuss the origins and implications of the gas and dust in the environment of the donor star.

The Standard Model (SM) works very well in describing the interactions of fundamental particles, except for three notable shortcomings: i) the lack of a dynamical mechanism to explain the smallness of the electroweak symmetry-breaking scale, ii) the initial flavor symmetry structure of the theory - introducing three generations of fermions - is not explained, and iii) the lepton and quark sectors seem different, with neutrinos having a mass while the three charged leptons are massless. Quark-Lepton Complementarity (QLC) postulates that there exists an additional high-energy symmetry that manifests differently for quarks versus charged leptons and neutrinos, with a direct correlation between their observed values and the types of fermions with which they are associated. For three generations of non-degenerate coupled fermions - considered here - this manifests as having one large angle, comprising the Cabibbo angle, and two small angles, one defining the up-down quark block and the other the down-strange quark block. Using this QLC-based ansatz, a simple, novel, and predictive model of spontaneous symmetry breaking is presented. The model accommodates the origin of the electroweak scale and the quark and lepton sectors' respective differences while simultaneously preserving the underlying similarities between them.

The problem of counting colourings of the vertices of a graph, or equivalently, the problem of computing a count of the number of ways that a multinomial coefficient can be partitioned, has long been a problem of interest to combinatorists and probabilists. A significant advance was the introduction of the dimer / coloring / bijection / Rosetta Stone (as first described by Kasteleyn and McCoy, 1966) by statistical physicists Ken Ono, Chetan Nachbagauer and Chris Janjic, which allowed for the development of a bijective framework for more general partitioning problems (Araujo, 1980, 1981; Temperley, 1971). However, even this framework was unable to count certain multinomial coefficient partitions (e.g. partitions into squares) without extensive case-by-case analysis. In recent years, significant advances in computer algorithms have allowed for the study of these hard partitions via the Counting Principle (Dousse, Di Matteo, Rafieier and Cerf, 2013) and these algorithms have resulted in the enumeration of some hard partitions (e.g. all 2-partitions of a partition into squares) without case-by-case analysis. In this paper, we carry out a systematic enumeration of 2-colourings of all facets of the cubic lattice (a total of 3779 facets). We find 20 distinct2-colourings, each arising via a different bijective framework.

This paper investigates the performance of a downlink MIMO system with multiple co-channel and cross- channel transmit antennas. We consider a case where the base station (BS) has perfect channel state information (CSI) but the user equipment (UE) only has statistical CSI. We propose to use a combining technique at the UE, based on antenna switching, to exploit the benefit of using multiple antennas at the BS. We establish a simpleclosed-form expression for the achievable rate, and obtain the optimal BS beamformer that maximizes the achievable rate for a given UE combining vector. Numerical results show significant performance gains using our proposed techniques in comparison to using only UE CSI or only BS CSI. Authors: Liugong Cai, H. Two perfect fluids are considered to interact within a cylindrical domain of circular cross section and length L. The total amount of energy in the system is fixed. The equations of motion are solved analytically for a range of interaction parameters, permitting the character of the collapse and the nature of the interaction sustained by the fluids to be described. When the fluids are non-interacting, the collapse proceeds in a hierarchical fashion, with shock waves appearing first at the center, then shocks reflecting from the domain boundaries, and finally, following reflection at the domain boundaries, a quasiequilibrium configuration is formed in which a cavity of depressed amplitude gradually expands. When the fluids are interacting, the character of the collapse is more varied, including quasiequilibrium and blow-up modes. In all cases the domain wall(s) separating competing quasiequilibrium configurations is/are capable of sustaining shock waves. The paper is inspired by the problem of colliding water waves, in which two shallow wave tanks are set up side by side and a solitary wave launched in one tank interacts with the wave train in the other.

Free core nutation, also known as temporal nutation, is a relatively fast component of Earth's rotation. It is directly proportional to the axial wobble, which in turn is driven by the planet's mass and moment of inertia. Temporal nutation is measured by satellites with very high precision, which has enabled detection of Free Core Nutation Frequency (FCNF). FCNF is caused by modulation of Earth's axis of rotation in the Free Core Nutation Mode. The amplitude of FCNF may vary with time and gives information about dynamics of Earth's core. In this study we analyze an existing database of FCNF observations from space. We apply two methods to extract theFCNF signal from the noise. The first one is based on statistical hypothesis testing and calculates the significance of FCNF signal. The second one is based on empirical mode decomposition and identifies components of FCNF signal. The results of both methods are consistent and show that the amplitude of FCNF varies with time. This indicates that dynamics of Earth's core may be of interest for scientists.

A collective state of the odd-mass nuclei is described in the framework of the Interacting Vector Boson Model (IVBM). In the frame work of this model the nucleus is viewed as a condensate of interacting vector bosons. The boson fields are associated with their individual quasi-particle states. Interactions between quasi-particles are described by means of the Brueckner reaction matrix. The model accounts for the ground state band structure and first excitation bands in many even-even as well as in odd-mass nuclei with high accuracy. The interaction between the vector bosons gives rise to the monopole and dipole phonon modes. These phonon modes generate the systematic patterns in the even-even and odd-mass nuclei spectra. In particular, the high-K electric transition operator excites the vibrational (phonon) states in the even-even nuclei and the wobbling vibration (phonon) states in the odd-mass nuclei. The wobbling mode in the odd-mass nuclei has been recently observed and discussed in several experimental papers. The theoretical description of the wobbling mode within the IVBM remains an open problem. In this work we report the theoretical analysis of the wobbling mode based on the IVBM approach and predict the excitation energy and the transition probability for the first excited state of several odd-mass nuclei in the vicinity of the closed shell N=Z nuclei. The calculated excitation energies are compared with the corresponding experimental data. The article contains also a short discussion of the monopole and dipole phonon modes.

Non-cooperative multiparty programming, also known as parallel scheduling, consists in deciding the start time of multiple agents so as to maximize a common global objective. Although various approximation algorithms and highly restricted models have been studied, non-cooperative multiparty programming under a generic model with general time windows and hard deadlines remains open. In this work, we consider the schedulability testing problem for this general model. Specifically, we consider the case in which there are m parties and n tasks, and each party can only participate in one task. We present a polynomial-time algorithm that can decide the feasibility of a task deadline violation subset of size 2 in this general model, thereby generalizing the corresponding results in prior work. We further propose a simple $(1 - 1/e - \epsilon)$approximate algorithm and show that it cannot achieve better than $(1 - 1/e)(1 - 1/e - \epsilon)$ approximation for any positive constant $\epsilon$. We also present a lower bound of $m$ on the number of agents required to guarantee feasibility of any task deadline violation subset of size 2.

The Reionization Epoch of the universe was characterized by the gradual dispersal of the intergalactic medium (IGM) gas into discrete pockets of clustered gas known as cosmic structures. The period of Cosmic Reionization was signaled by the full occupation of neutral hydrogen (HI) states, resulting in the complete suppression of 21-cm neutral hydrogen signals. Measuring this signal is one of the most powerful ways of understanding the process of Reionization, yet observational limitations have historically made this task difficult. Most prior efforts to measure the 21-cm signal have been hampered by bright foreground sources and the untargeted nature of radio surveys, limiting the volume and fidelity of the signal that could be studied. Using data from the COsmic IDentification over aeles radio (COrE) survey, we develop a novel probe of the Epoch of Reionization, the differential brightness temperature, that is directly constructed from the spatial distribution of the 21-cm signal. By stacking the data in Fourier space onto large grids we are able to sample the 21-cm power spectrum at scales beyond what has been feasible in the past, and directly measure the amplitude and shape of the 21-cm power spectrum at various stages of the Epoch of Reionization. Our data reduction process additionally corrects for a number of systematic effects, including those from foreground sources and sample variance. We find that the amplitude of the power spectrum decreases rapidly as the IGM begins to be reionized, and is consistent with zero by z = 7, providing strong evidence for the conclusion of Reionization at that time. These results are consistent with recent observational constraints from the Epoch of Reionionization Explorer (Sharp et al. 2016) as well as from modeling, and we demonstrate the constraining power of our technique through comparison to large astrophysical simulations.

The LBNE Collaboration has studied the potential of the long-baseline neutrino experiment to determine whether or not short-baseline muon neutrino disappearance is caused by neutrino oscillations. We find that such an observation would be highly statistically significant and have a good chance of making a discovery. We determine projected sensitivities to total mixing, inverted mass hierarchy, and CP violation in the MNS matrix. We also discuss potential spinoff experiments, which could confirm or exclude the null result with higher statistics, and address experimental challenges. Finally, we compare the LBNE proposal to other long-baseline neutrino experiments and to proposed neutrino sources. We find that the LBNE proposal has excellent potential to make a discovery and set strong constraints on neutrino parameters. The Long-Baseline Neutrino Experiment (LBNE) is a proposed neutrino physics program at the Sanford Underground Facility (SONGS) in South Dakota, USA, and the Soudan Mine in Minnesota, USA. The LBNE has the scientific goal of establishing whether or not short-baseline (~15 km) muon neutrino disappearance is caused by neutrino oscillations, and if so, to determine the nature of the disappearance; that is, whether it is due to normal or inverted mass hierarchy, and whether it involves maximal or minimal neutrino CP violation. If confirmed, these phenomena would indicate the presence of new particle species, leading to possible discoveries in particle physics. LBNE could also shed light on a possible conceptual conflict between the short and long distance scales implied by neutrino oscillations. The LBNE has a two-detector configuration using massive 200 kt-Trititanium (TT) detectors with a baseline of 1210 to 1610 km. It has been shown that this configuration would be sensitive to total neutrino mixing < 13% C.L. at the 3x10-3 baseline resolution, and to neutrino mass-ordering and CP violation at the 5x10-2 to 5x10-3 C.L. levels. We describe the determination of projected sensitivities to neutrino parameters using a Feldman-Cousins method that includes systematic uncertainties. This study is preliminary and does not include a cost-benefit or risk assessment. We conclude with a discussion of proposed spinoff experiments that would confirm or rule out the null result with higher statistics and discuss experimental challenges.

Exoplanet populations are dominated by the population of super earths and mini Neptunes. While many of these worlds may be amenable to characterization and discovery by the transit method, a robust classification scheme for exoplanets has not been developed. In this work, a statistical approach to exoplanet population characterization is presented. A new taxonomic scheme based on a new metric, Caplan, is introduced and demonstrated on a set of observed exoplanet systems. Using a bootstrap resampling procedure, uncertainties on Caplan values are derived. These values have obvious utility in evaluating potential dynamical interactions between planets in multi planet systems. In addition, the statistical approach introduced here may be applicable to additional characterization metrics for exoplanets, such as potential habitability or identification of biomarkers. * Kazutomo Arimura, Joseph Cassan, Gábor Apai, Naoki Katza, Robert S. Matharu, Eugene A. Wallace, and David Ciardi * arXiv preprint arXiv:1903.01125 [astro-ph.EP] submitted to MNRAS (February 19, 2019) * Planets are classified by the statistical approach introduced here into one of four categories: super earths, mini Neptunes, earthlike planets, and gas giants. The metric introduced here, Caplan, is related to the area of the planet divided by the area of the host star. The metric has a value of zero for earthlike planets and one for gas giants. Super earths and mini Neptunes are intermediate in the spectrum, with typical values between 0.5 and 1.0. As Caplan is heavily influenced by observational uncertainty, bootstrapping is performed to characterize the associated uncertainties. On average, Caplan values for observed exoplanets fall within the ranges of super earths (0.7 $\pm$ 0.3), mini Neptunes (0.8 $\pm$ 0.2), and earthlike planets (0.6 $\pm$ 0.2). Earthlike planets tend to have the lowest value of Caplan due to high observational uncertainty on their radius. The statistical approach introduced here is demonstrated on a set of observed exoplanet systems and has obvious utility in evaluating potential dynamical interactions between planets in multi planet systems.

Dust plays an important role in the evolution of massive stars. For example, it may significantly affect the distribution of metal-rich materials in the vicinity of the supernova explosion, which in turn may affect the dynamics of the resulting remnant and the distribution of materials exploded in second generation nucleosynthesis. Dust may also have significant observational consequences in the form of extinction and thermal emission. The interaction of newly formed dust with the violent environments of supernova ejecta has not been extensively studied, however. We performed two-dimensional hydrodynamic calculations of dust coagulation in Type II and Type Ibc supernova ejecta, accounting for the full range of dust size and composition. We obtained good fits to the observed size distribution of interstellar dust and to extinction measurements of a sample of Type IIb supernovae. Our results indicate that dust in supernova ejecta forms and survives under conditions generally thought to be hostile to dust growth; our calculations do not require modifications to standard dust growth parameters. We discuss the potential implications of our results for the nucleosynthesis of elements beyond iron, the heating and extinction efficiencies of dust in supernova remnants, and the development of precise observational techniques for the detection of supernova remnants.

Researchers have long pondered whether time travel is possible, and if so, whether paradoxes such as the grandfather paradox are logically disproofed. In a recent article, Albin, et al. proposed a test to search for "time-travel paradoxes", using neutral $K$ and $B$ mesons that coherently transform from an incoherent to a coherent quantum state. Such a transformation entails removing the meson from its current incoherent state and placing it in a coherent superposition of all possible momentum states. CP symmetry, which is a fundamental property of the universe, ensures that the transformation is reversible, and a CP-violating disturbance is invoked if the time-travel paradox is logical disproofed. The team at the Jefferson Lab achieved the transformation, and performed a search for CP violation, with null results. A null result rules out the possibility of logically disproving the time-travel paradox, and further illustrates that the universe possesses a logical consistency.

A theoretical study of dense granular fluids is presented. By employing a self-consistent density functional approach, we are able to construct a unified theory for both the equilibrium fluid and inelastic non-ideal dynamics (including heating/compression) of inhomogeneous granular fluids down to the mean-field level. Exact evolution equations for both the total and granular density are derived, along with consistent equations of motion for the fluid-density and granular-density correlation functions. These equations of motion are numerically solved and shown to reproduce the crossover from crystalline to diffusive dynamics with increasing amplitude of the inelasticity parameter. More importantly, we are able to analyze the influence of thermal fluctuations on the inelastic dynamics. It is shown that the cooling and heating rates of the granular temperatures display a crossover from exponential to linear dependence on the amplitude of the inelasticity parameter at intermediate inelasticity. This is in sharp contrast to the corresponding temperature (or granular heat) fluctuations of elastic granular fluids, which are predicted to be widely independent of inelasticity. In addition, we have shown that the dissipation functional for the inelastic dynamics can be expressed in a simple and transparent form in terms of the granular temperature and density-density correlation functions. These exact results obtained here should be of interest to both the granular physics and statistical mechanics communities.

In this work, we consider the phenomenological implications of the Dvali-Gabadadze-Poratti (DGP) braneworld model. The model is designed to provide a self-consistent solution to the dark energy problem by introducing a modification to the gravity on small scales. While the theory possesses two gravitational couplings, (one for large and one for small distances), in order to be self-consistent the strength of the small distance coupling has to be fine-tuned to a tiny value of 0.01%. We propose a modification to the DGP model, which allows for a stronger small distance coupling that does not suffer from such a fine-tuning problem. However, we show that this modified model also gives rise to new problems. In particular, we find a new resonance in the system that can render the theory unstable. While the existence of the new resonance is generic, we find that the strength of the resonance is highly dependent on the choice of parameters. We explore the parameter space of the model, and identify regions where the new resonance is strong enough to render the theory unstable. We show that this instability corresponds to the loss of ghost-like behavior in the system, and that the theory becomes unitary. We discuss the implications of these results for parameter space and for the self-consistency of the model.

7 Aql and 8 Aql are two Delta Scuti stars that have been under the STEPHI (Search for Variable Star in the Eyes of Hipparcos) observing campaign for many years. In 2003 we obtained multi-site observations of these stars in order to study their lightcurve variations in a more extensive way. New times of minimum and variabilities were found. This new analysis suggests that 7 Aql is a new Delta Scuti variable and that its amplitude of lightcurve variations is lower than that of 7 Aql. The observational data used in this analysis were obtained at different sites around the world using different telescopes and photometers, such as the 1.2m RCC Telescope at the Llano del Hato Observatory (Almería, Spain), the 0.6m TRASCA telescope at the Teide Observatory (Tenerife, Spain), the 1.5m STELLA robotic telescope at the European Southern Observatory (Chile), the 0.76m Plata 60m telescope at the Complejo Astronómico El Leoncito (Argentina), the 0.6m Fin humanitarian young scientist program (FHS) telescope at Haleakala (Hawaii, USA) and the 1.22m Mark VI telescope at Anderson Mesa Station (Arizona, USA). The analysis of the times of minimum and the amplitudes of lightcurve variations shows that the observed lightcurves of both stars present a large fraction of variations with low amplitudes. This kind of variations can be produced by cool starspots, which can be related to the recent passage of these stars through the solar tachocline.

Stretching Homopolymers. One of the central problems in the statistical mechanics of polymeric systems is the response of a polymer to an external force. Consider a semi-flexible homopolymer of $N$ repeat units of length $a$. The statistical mechanics of this polymer in a three dimensional space of volume V is described by the famous “Flory-Huggins” potential $$ U = -k_{\text{B}}T \left( \ln \left( 1 - \frac{\Lambda^3}{N a^3} \right) + \frac{\Lambda^3}{N a^3} \right)$$ where $\Lambda$ is the thermal de Broglie wavelength. At high temperatures this depends only on the volume and not on the conformation of the polymer. At low temperatures however, fluctuations about the extended chain configuration become important and can be accounted for using the “ Poland-Sheraga” free energy. In this case, the energy is expressed as a function of the end-to-end vector $R$ and of the angle $\phi$ between the vectors linking successive monomers along the chain. Minimisation of the energy with respect to these variables yields the following force-extension relation for the polymer: $$\frac{F}{k_{\text{B}} T N a} = \frac{1}{2 \sin^2 \phi} \left( \frac{F_{\text{lam}}}{N a} - \frac{\kappa \cos \phi}{a} \right)$$ where $F_{\text{lam}} = \Lambda^3/(N a^2)$ is the force required to stretch the chain from a straight to a canonical conformations and $\kappa$ is the (fluctuation) Hessian. For small extensions $F/k_{\text{B}} T N a \sim F_{\text{lam}}/(N a)$. However, if $F/k_{\text{B}} T N a \gg 1$, then $\kappa \cos \phi/(a) \gg 1$ and one has the interesting result $F/k_{\text{B}} T N a \sim 1/(2 \sin^2 \phi)$. This indicates that the polymer strongly attracts itself towards a straight configuration. In fact, the two limits correspond to an “ideal” polymer (imagine a nylon fishing line) and an infinitely flexible one (a very stiff spring). In between these two extremes lies the polymer coil.

Here we examine the morphologies, gas fractions, and star formation rates (SFRs) of a sample of low-mass, largely blue compact dwarfs (BCDs). Our sample is representative of the lowest-mass galaxies with ongoing star formation, and consists of 24 BCDs from the SWINGES survey (SINGS With HST EVOLUTION Study) and SINGG (Spitzer INfrared Nearby Galaxy survey with Hubble). We use SINGS data to measure integrated properties of the galaxies, while SINGG provides near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy and, in some cases, optical imaging for a subset of our galaxies. We use new observations of a sub-sample of our sample to measure their properties. We find that most of our galaxies have disturbed morphologies, though many also have regular disks. We find that the morphologies are often linked to those of the stellar components, and that disks are commonly found in galaxies with irregular orMagellanic-like morphologies. We compare these observations to numerical simulations of low-mass galaxies, finding that current simulations cannot reproduce the disturbed morphologies of most of our galaxies. We also find that even the most extreme feedback efficiencies investigated can only reproduce the morphologies and gas fractions of the least disturbed galaxies in our sample. Finally, we compare our observed trends of morphology with global properties such as stellar mass, mass, SFR, and sSFR to those seen in larger galaxies, and find that the small galaxies in our sample follow the same general trends. However, we also find a number of low-mass galaxies with unusual properties: some have very low content and high SFRs, while others have highly regular morphologies despite having high sSFRs. We discuss these results in the context of current theories of galaxy evolution.

Recent surveys such as ZENI, POINT-MAD and MOA have been extremely useful in detecting planets around other stars, particularly super earths and Neptune mass planets. A very interesting aspect of these surveys has been the use of the gravitational microlensing effect to search for planets around other stars. Microlensing occurs when a star passes in front of an object such as a star or a star system and the light of the background star is affected by the passage of the foreground object. If a planet is passing in front of the background star, the planet will exert a small but significant gravitational force on the light of the background star and this will cause a deviation from the straight line trajectory of the light path. The angular separation of the background and foreground objects as well as the time scale of the event are determine by the size of the planet and the distance of the planet from the star. These surveys have used the observations of lensing events to search for planets with a wide range of masses and distances from the host star. These surveys have also been successful in detecting planets that are at the same distance from their star as the Earth is from the Sun, i.e. between 0.01 and 1 AU. This in turn has lead to the development of new strategies for the direct imaging of planets. The results of these surveys have led to the detection of planets around a wide range of host stars including red dwarf stars which are common in the galaxy but have very low masses and small radii. Planets play an important role in the evolution of systems including our own Solar System. The detection of planets outside of our Solar System and in other solar systems allows us to determine the distribution of planets as a function of distance from their star and also the characteristics of the planet. In this paper we review the results of these surveys and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the microlensing method for detecting planets.

In this paper we compare numerical relativity (NR) and post-Newtonian (PN) waveforms for neutron-star binaries with mass ratios up to 6:1. We build on recent publications that established effective methods to match the two waveform families at a specified post-merger frequency (known as the hereditary or spectrally truncated approximation). We show that accurate waveforms for physical properties, such as the radiated energy, can be obtained by matching the numerical and analytic waveforms at the effective center of mass (CCM) frame frequency. For nearly equal-mass systems, we find an excellent match with a maximum discrepancy of 3.3% in the total radiated energy, 1.3% in the phase, and 2.7% in the amplitude at twice the CCM frame frequency. For higher mass ratios, we find that total radiated energy estimates are accurate to 1.7%, and phase and amplitude corrections are accurate to 2.4%. We discuss optimizations to the matching procedure and present additional corrections to improve the waveform accuracy for a wider range of binary parameters. Finally, we provide the reader with a software tool that computes gravitational waveforms for neutron-star binaries using both the spectral truncation method and a novel hybrid approach that combines the strengths of both methods. The tool, named PyEFT, is publicly available and written in Python for general-purpose use.

Swift/X-Ray Telescope (XRT) has observed gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) since December 2005. The GRB catalog maintained by the Swift Science Data Center (SSDC) includes 648 Swift GRBs as of April 2023. For each burst, the SSDC provides basic metadata, such as the time and zenith angle of the observation, and the detailed light curves in various energy bands. The XRT light curve repository presented in this work is built upon the Swift Database application service, and provides a user interface for browsing and searching the XRT light curves. It also provides an API for programmatic access to the light curve data. We describe the motivations for building this repository and the architecture of the system. We also present several examples of using this data for research purposes and possible applications in the widerSwift community. LightCurves.org is a website that hosts machine-readable light curve files and provides a simple web interface for browsing the data. The SwiftGamma-Ray Burst Analyser (SGRAA) is a joint effort between multiple research groups to automate the process of extracting and analyzing gamma-ray bursts using Swift/XRT data. SGRAA provides a user interface for SQL queries of the database of light curves maintained by the Swift Science Data Center (SSDC). To complement these applications, we developed the SwiftXRTLightCurvesRepo, a Swift application providing an easy interface to query and download the database of light curves maintained by the Swift Science Data Center.
