In particle physics, the hierarchy problem is the difficulty of explaining the smallness of the electromagnetic force compared to the stronger nuclear forces. This has led to the suggestion that there is a vast overdensity of vacua in string theory, so the hierarchy problem is analogous to the way that there are many more galaxies than expected within each observable universe. It has been proposed that this supersymmetry (SUSY) may stabilize the weak scale. However, this assumes that all regions of the string landscape are highly connected, which is a natural consequence of current wisdom but has never been proven. I will present two new mechanisms by which this connection can be lost, creating forbidden territories in the string landscape. The first is uplifting a discrete symmetry, which can create a new domain wall at the string scale. This will generically divide the landscape into multiple domains, each with a different pattern of Kähler moduli stabilization and different fractions of the supersymmetry breaking hidden sector gauge group. The second is creating a new light species by deforming the worldsheet theory. This will create domains in the string landscape separated by forbidden zones where closed strings are not able to propagate, leaving the standard model fields localize on a domain wall. I will argue that both of these effects can naturally arise in a class of string theory models with dilaton stabilization, leading to a landscape with a large number of domains, with different patterns of SUSY breaking and moduli stabilization within each domain.

DeconSTRUcting FUNCTIONS on Quadratic SURFACES into Multipoles PDF Version S. G. Randle, P. J. Treadway, and R. P. Behringer arXiv:1908.04856 [sc29] September 24, 2019 (From the Abstract) We present experimental evidence for the surprising discovery that discrete functional forms can be constructed on quadratic surfaces into multipoles. These multipolar forms were discovered and fit to experimental data obtained from particle-jammed granular surfaces, whose quasistatic contact properties are governed by the equations of motion of the square and multipole solid harmonics. We anticipate that these multipolar constructions may find utility in a variety of contexts, such as the rational design of particle-based systems. Experiments on jamming granular surfaces generate data that is well-described by the square and spherical solid harmonics. Building on this observation, we posit that these two harmonics are sufficient to construct discrete functional forms on quadratic surfaces into multipoles. This is in direct contrast to most conventionally assumed functional forms (e.g., polynomials), which must possess continuous differentiable curvature to accommodate local function maxima and minima. This work is built on the foundation of discrete models, which are of growing interest in systems and computational science, particularly in addressing the "curse of dimensionality" that plagues the use of traditional modeling approaches in high-dimensional spaces. We investigate empirically the construction of multipolar forms using polynomials and basis sets with $p\leq 4$. We fit our multipolar models to experimentally obtained quadratic surface geometries and observe statistically significant improvements in the fit $R^2$ values using higher order multipolar models. We additionally show that these multipolar forms can also be used to classify data according to the polynomial order $p$. Our results provide experimental evidence that multipolar constructions can be applied to discrete geometries generated from particle-based systems. Furthermore, we make our quadratic multipolar construction code and associated data available online. We anticipate that this work will find utility in discrete system modeling, discrete model enumeration, and the rational design of discrete systems. # Computational Science, Discrete Models, Experimental Robotics DeconSTRUcting FUNCTIONS on Quadratic SURFACES into Multipoles S. Third-order cosmological perturbations of zero-pressure multi-component fluids are studied in the framework of general relativity. The fluid has a general equation of state and can be non-barotropic. As an example, the case of an adiabatic fluid with zero heat flux is considered in full detail. It is shown that, in the case of zero cosmological constant, the propagation of third-order cosmological perturbations in an ultra-stiff fluid differs from that in a fluid with a conventional equation of state only by the value of the effective gravitational constant. The problem of obtaining this constant in the case of a non-zero cosmological constant is considered, and it is shown that the propagation of cosmological perturbations in an ultra-stiff fluid with a non-zero cosmological constant differs from that in a fluid with a conventional equation of state only by the value of the effective gravitational constant in the case of zero heat flux and by the value of the effective gravitational constant and the speed of sound in the case of non-zero heat flux. In all the cases considered, there is no general instability of density perturbations. The stability of gravitational collapse of a spherical distribution of a zero-pressure multi-component fluid with an ultra-stiff equation of state is studied. It is shown that for such an equation of state there are no critical conditions on the entropy of the initial data under which the dynamics of gravitational collapse will inevitably lead to the formation of a shock wave. The case of a fluid with a polytropic equation of state and with a heat flux is also considered. In this case, it is shown that, in addition to the propagating acoustic mode, there is another mode with zero speed (the mode with a moving sonic point). It is shown that this mode may be stable or unstable, depending on the value of the adiabatic index. The characteristic features of the dynamics of gravitational collapse in each case are analysed in detail. The case of an ultra-stiff fluid with a non-zero cosmological constant is also considered. It is shown that in this case there is no general instability of cosmological perturbations. The stability of gravitational collapse of a spherical distribution of a fluid with an ultra-stiff equation of state is studied. It is found that in this case the critical values of the adiabatic index and the speed of sound for which the dynamics of gravitational collapse leads to the formation of a shock wave depend on the value of the cosmological constant. It is shown that there is a critical speed of sound for which the dynamics of gravitational collapse inevitably leads to the formation of a shock wave if the speed of sound exceeds the critical speed of sound, but does not lead to the formation of a shock wave if the speed of sound is less than the critical speed of sound.

In this paper, we consider the analytical properties of finite Euler products, which arise in various contexts in number theory. We show that such products often possess analytic continuation, and under suitable hypotheses, we can prove the meromorphic continuation and unique, simple pole at $s=1$ of such products. As an application, we prove the Riemann Hypothesis for many zeta and L-functions. We also discuss generalizations of these results to a certain class of periodic functions. We denote the product over all natural numbers $n \geq 1$ by $$\zeta(s) := \prod_{p} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p^s}\right)^{-1},$$ where the product is taken over all prime numbers $p$, and where $s \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\mathrm{Re}(s) > 0$. The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) is the statement that $\mathrm{Re}(s)=1/2$ is a zero of $\zeta(s)$. We consider similar finite Euler products which arise in the study of L-functions. Given a primitive Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $q$, we define the $L$-function associated to $\chi$ by $$L(s,\chi) := \prod_{p} \left(1 - \frac{\chi(p)}{p^s}\right)^{-1},$$ where the product is taken over all prime numbers $p$. Assuming certain standard conjectures, we prove the meromorphic continuation and unique pole at $s=1$ of such products. As an application, we prove the RH for many $L$-functions associated to characters modulo $q$ when $q$ is a product of distinct Fermat primes. We also discuss the generalization of these results to periodic functions. For $r \geq 2$, we define the Dirichlet $L$-function $$L(s,\chi_r) := \prod_{n=1}^r \left(1 - \frac{\chi_r(n)}{n^s}\right)^{-1},$$ where the product is taken over the first $r$ prime numbers, and where $\chi_r$ is the (unnormalized) principal character modulo $r$. Assuming the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), we prove the meromorphic continuation and unique pole at $s=1$ of such products. As a consequence, we obtain the RH for many $L$-functions associated to the principal character modulo $r$ when the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet $L$-functions is assumed. We make use of well-known properties of the Riemann zeta function in our proofs, as well as some simple identities for Dirichlet $L$-functions. Cool stars play an important role in the dynamics of galaxies by delivering energy and material away from the core. However, their influence extends far beyond their host galaxy, as they can also affect the structure of the interstellar medium (ISM) and even the galactic halo via feedback effects. Here we present new optical and ALMA observations of a peculiar cool star, named HK loops, in the metal-rich circumnuclear disk of the spiral galaxy M83. This star is located near the galactic center, only few kiloparsecs from the supermassive black hole, and is possibly growing by accretion. We report a probable ejection event of gas and the resulting broad molecular and atomic hydrogen lines, the first such detection for a cool star other than the Sun. We also detect a flow of dusty plasma from this star, which is further evidence of the complex interaction between this star and its environment. We discuss the potential implications of this discovery for our understanding of cool star feedback in extreme environments, and its connection to galaxy evolution.

Peer-to-Peer IPTV (Internet Protocol TV) provides quality video streaming over the Internet. This white paper presents the results of an ongoing research project, examining the protocol and traffic characteristics of an IPTV service, iPlayer by BBC, when delivered to users via the P2P protocol. Using passive monitoring, we characterize the protocol and traffic characteristics of the iPlayer IPTV service. iPlayer is one of the most popular IPTV services, providing high-quality streams of TV shows and sporting events. The P2P IPTV service is built upon the popular eDonkey/Bear P2P protocol, which has been in use since the early 2000s. We present the results of an ongoing research project examining the scaling properties of P2P IPTV services, by monitoring eDonkey servers running the P2P IPTV service iPlayer. The iPlayer service is one of the most popular Internet Protocol TV (IPTV) services, providing high-quality streams of TV shows and sporting events. We examine the scaling properties of the eDonkey IPTV server by monitoring a set of eDonkey P2P servers hosting the iPlayer IPTV service.

In this work we report direct measurement of the interfacial tensions between coexisting phases of a canonical, simple, model liquid-liquid system. This is possible due to the recent development of a scheme for the determination of interfacial quantities from computer simulation of only the solute particle system. This approach is based on constructing interfaces in the simulation box that match a geometrical definition of interfacial surface, and monitoring various interfacial properties, such as average position and orientation of solute particles as a function of simulation configuration. In this way we are able to measure the interfacial tensions between two coexisting phases of tangent hard sphere chains (THC), a model system used extensively to test methods for computational interfacial studies. We find that the interfacial tensions between coexisting liquid and vapor phases and between liquid and solid phases are all positive and of similar magnitude (ca. 27 mN/m), in contrast to the typical situation in liquid-vapor and oil-water systems (ca. 40 mN/m), and hence more representative of real liquids. This is the first time that such direct measurement of interfacial tensions has been reported. A simple fundamental measure theory (FMT) approximation is shown to provide an excellent description of the interfacial tensions, and hence the FMT interface potential can be evaluated quite accurately. Such accurate evaluation of the interface potential is not possible from analysis of the interfacial configurations or from standard Surface Evolver calculations, which typically need to make uncontrolled assumptions about the form of the potential, or perform a tedious parameter search.

The von Karman flow with mass loading is a standard benchmark for studying turbulence. It consists of an ensemble of non-interacting vortices, with energy concentrated in enstrophy and well-defined packets of each vortex sign. The vortices are self-similar and exhibit scale-invariance in the high-Cascade regime. In this paper, we develop a simplified 2D dynamical model that captures the essential features of the high-Cascade state. The evolution of the vorticity, Omega, is modeled by a diffusion equation with no-flux boundary conditions. Dissipation of enstrophy arises primarily through two distinct processes: direct viscosity, which leads to local smoothing of the vorticity field, and cross-helicity flux, which transfers enstrophy from near-core vortical zones to outer regions. We demonstrate that these two processes lead to a scaling solution with time-independent enstrophy and energy dissipation, in agreement with the dynamical model. We then show that the evolution of large-scale kinetic energy is controlled by the rate at which enstrophy is transferred to the outer regions. We derive an evolution equation for the scale-dependent enstrophy flux and perform a linear analysis to compute the scaling of the flux. This analysis, which neglects quadratic enstrophy-flux terms, gives excellent agreement with the full dynamical model in the high-Cascade regime. This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy under award number DE-SC0019468.

Fourier analysis on homogeneous spaces has a long tradition in analysis. Convolution on locally compact groups is one of the most important and widely studied operation. In contrast, Fourier analysis on semisimple Lie groups and their homogeneous spaces has been less developed, although they appear naturally in the representation theory of Lie groups. In this paper, we establish convolution results on these groups, by imitating the locally compact case. In particular, we show that if G is a semisimple Lie group and K a compact subgroup, then the natural analogue of the convolution map on the unitary dual of G, is also a associative algebra product on the algebra of functions on the coset space G/K. We also discuss some related results and examples. This work is part of a series, in which we explore the structure and representation theory of semisimple Lie groups, and their homogeneous spaces. This work was completed during the summer of 2022 as part of the MIUR summer program SFAE at Northeastern University.

M31 is the Andromeda galaxy. It is a large spiral galaxy located at a distance of 786 kpc from the Sun (McConnachie et al. 2009). This galaxy has a halo with more than 1000 globular clusters (GCs), the largest such population of any individual galaxy (Forbes et al. 2005). Many of these GCs are part of large, extended clusters (Zaritsky, Harris, & Thompson 1997). GCs in M31 are well suited for studying the formation and evolution of galaxies, owing to their ability to act as probes of their host galaxy's potential and environment (e.g., Goerdt et al. 2006; Lan, Brodie, & Huchra 2008). These GCs are valuable for addressing many open questions in the field of GC research, such as (1) the processes involved in the formation of GCs, (2) the environments in which GCs form and evolve, (3) the origin of multiple GC populations in galaxies, and (4) the orbits and origins of the extragalactic GCs in M31. In this paper, we present a new, updated catalog of GCs in M31 based on very deep, wide-field images taken with the 4m Mayall Telescope at the Kitt Peak National Observatory. This catalog includes 85 new globular clusters discovered in 12 new CCD fields covering a region 4 magnitudes fainter than that covered by our former survey (Mackey & Gilmore 2003). The total number of GCs in M31 now stands at more than 1000. We describe the data and our new methods of analysis in §2. Our new catalog is presented and discussed in §3. A discussion of our results and the conclusions we draw follow in §4.

In the standard model (SM) extensions with additional gauge symmetries, the dark sector may interact with the ordinary matter via mediation of the bosons in the dark force carrying-interactions, e.g. W' and Z'. If the dark force is strong, it could affect Electroweak precision measurements. The former limits from the direct searches and the latter from the precise measurements of the electroweak observables put strong constraints on the parameters of these models. If the dark force is mediated by the gauge boson interacting with the ordinary matter only through the weak force, it leads to the violation of the standard model (SM) relations between various electroweak observables. Recently it was shown that a very simple extension of the SM with additional global $U(1)_{DF}$ symmetry can explain these two phenomena simultaneously. In this model, the dark photons can interact with the standard model particles, both, weakly via photon and via the new strong force carrying bosons - X'. There are two free parameters in the model - the scale of the new physics, $f$, and the dark photon mixing angle, $\chi$. If $\chi \approx 10^{-8}$, as suggested by the model predictions to the $K_L-K_S$ mass difference and the atomic parity violation, the experimental limits from the direct search for the dark photons, put strong constraints on the model parameter space. Unfortunately, until now the most precise test of the SM relations between various electroweak observables is the $e^+ e^-\to \mu^+\mu^- \pi^+\pi^-$ cross section measurement with initial-state radiation. In this paper, using this test, we put a new limit on the parameter space of the model with $f\gtrsim 1$ TeV.

A probabilistic cellular automaton (CA) simulating the evolution of a preys population coupled to a predator population is introduced and studied. The system is composed of coupled maps, where the density of preys evolves according to a discrete stochastic iteration and the density of predators is governed by a continuous deterministic approximation. Each prey can randomly become predator at each time step with a given probability. The population goes through two phases: a disordered one where the populations evolve toward a uniform distribution, and an ordered one where the system converges to a non-trivial spatio-temporal pattern. In the ordered phase, a travelling wave seems to appear propagating at a constant velocity. Its shape and the velocity of the wave can be accurately predicted by a self-consistent equation arising from a mean-field approximation of the probabilistic CA. The self-consistent equation displays two branches of solution: a stable one corresponding to the travelling wave, and an unstable one leading to an uniform distribution of the populations. These results highlight the ability of the proposed CA to capture both local and non-local interactions, and to reveal the impact of randomness on the pattern formation. This work is a contribution to the Theory of Everything initiative. References: Bányai, E., & Thome, V. (2020). Stable oscillations of a predator-prey probabilistic cellular automaton: a mean-field approach. Physical Review E, 101(2), 022909.

In experiments with ultracold atoms, quantum mechanics allows for effects that would be reversible in classical physics, such as quantum backaction or measurement backaction. We observe quantum-measurement backaction with an ultracold atomic gas. Using state-selection spin echos, we detect atoms that experienced a unitary transform associated with the measurement of an operator that has no mean value in the system’s initial state. We perform a quantum process tomography of this unitary transform and show that our measurements reproduce the dynamics predicted by quantum mechanics. Our results establish measurement backaction in an essentially pure system and withdB/dt ≥ |h|/τ, where dB is the change in operator expectation values and τ is the characteristic evolution time. These results could enable new approaches to quantum control and precision measurement, with potential applications to quantum information and ultra-low light-noise measurements. We observe quantum-measurement backaction with an ultracold atomic gas. In experiments with ultracold atoms, quantum mechanics allows for effects that would be reversible in classical physics, such as quantum backaction or measurement backaction. We perform a quantum process tomography of this unitary transform and show that our measurements reproduce the dynamics predicted by quantum mechanics. In general, quantum backaction occurs when a quantum system responds to a measurement. Quantum measurement theory describes the statistical relationships between quantum systems and measurements, and the act of measuring an observable affects the state of the system. Measurement backaction occurs when the measured observable has no mean value in the system’s initial state, and it is defined as the rate of change of the expected value of that observable. It can have a variety of forms. For example, if an operator is the observable of a quantum system, the measured system can become entangled with a meter system in a process called quantum entanglement, and backaction corresponds to how the measured system and meter system evolve together in time. Alternatively, if the operator is a parameter of a unitary transform, backaction could enable control and measurement of the parameters of unitary transforms, for example in quantum process tomography. Thus far, measurement backaction has only been observed in the presence of quantum entanglement or incoherent forces (e.g., gravity or the spin-force associated with magnetic fields). We demonstrate measurement backaction without entanglement or additional incoherent forces. Instead, we observe measurement backaction in an essentially pure system, without loss due to interactions with a large environment. The dynamics are reversible because our experiment operates near the quantum limit of few-atom systems. Our results establish measurement backaction in an essentially pure system and with dB/dt ≥ |h|/τ, where dB is the change in operator expectation values and τ is the characteristic evolution time. These results could enable new approaches to quantum control and precision measurement, with potential applications to quantum information and ultra-low light-noise measurements.

The cell nucleus is arguably the most sophisticated level of control in a biological system. It has long been established that the cell nucleus has the ability to compartmentalise various biochemical species within the nucleoplasm and chromatin domains. It has also been established that this compartmentalisation has an important role in regulating key cell signalling pathways. More recently, it has been shown that, in addition to these chemically based compartmentalisations, the cell nucleus also has a diffusional compartmentalisation. Diffusional compartmentalisation is such that water molecules, which are normally highly mobile within the nucleoplasm, display anomalous mobility within the chromatin domain. The anomalous mobility is such that it may be exploited for imaging and therapeutic purposes. Here we present a biophysical model of diffusional transport in the interphase cell nucleus. We first develop a coarse-grained chromatin bead-spring model and use this to identify two length scales governing water mobility in the chromatin domain. We then exploit this insight to develop a continuum model of diffusional transport within the chromatin domain, using a modified Fick's law approach in which the flux of water molecules across inter-chromatin space is determined by the anomalous mobility exhibited by water within the chromatin domain. Using the anomalous mobility parameters from our coarse-grained chromatin model, we are able to accurately predict, both qualitatively and quantitatively, the spatial and temporal behaviour of nuclear water transport in response to applied thermal and osmotic stresses. We believe this to be the first biophysical model of diffusional transport in the interphase cell nucleus.

CAST (CERN Axion Solar Telescope), an international experimental programme for searching for the DM axion, reported the first result with solar photons collecting in the CAST scheme. These data show an excess of solar photons compared to the background, opening the way to potential discovery scenarios for the axion. Change log (from CAST website): Results on axion physics from the CAST Experiment at CERN CAST (CERN Axion Solar Telescope), an international experimental programme for searching for the DM axion, reported the first result with solar photons collecting in the CAST scheme. These data show an excess of solar photons compared to the background, opening the way to potential discovery scenarios for the axion. CAST experimental collaboration consists of the Institute of Physics of the Academy of Sciences of Czech Republic, the University of Vienna, the University of California Berkeley, the University of Chicago, Harvard University, the Laboratory for Ultrafast Physics (LNE-SYSCParis), the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics (MPG), and the European Southern Observatory (ESO). A global fit to the data (with light-sigma terms and subject to certain constraints) yielded a best-fit particles parameter of ; these particles, dubbed "saxions", couple to photon particles in an anisotropic manner, with a best-fit coupling of. The data are consistent with a single component, but a two-component fit has slight, although not statistically significant, advantages. Discovery potential for the axion-photon coupling in the CAST experimental configuration was estimated as, assuming a two-year exposure with a 1-GHz CAST assembly with 10% system uncertainty and an additional 2% background uncertainty. These results, if confirmed, would be of great significance for the LHC searches, because they are the first experimental results on the new light, boson-like particles - axions, beyond the scope of the Standard Model of particle physics. For references, see [1].

Lambda, the cosmological constant, is anathema to cosmology because it leads to a vacuum energy dominated universe in violation of the observed cosmological principle. Despite this, Lambda is very useful as an observable cosmological parameter, allowing for tests of the Copernican principle, tests of the inflationary paradigm, constraints on dark energy, and probe of the ultimate fate of the universe. The cosmological constant is determined by thecci parameters and its value must be very close to zero in order to satisfy the aforementioned tests. While this may suggest that the value of the cosmological constant is fine-tuned, this could also be explained by the anthropic principle, which states that parameters of the universe must be favourable for the development of intelligent life. In this paper we test this latter hypothesis by using the Maximal Miniature Cosmos (MMC) device to simulate the development of intelligent life in a universe with a non-zero cosmological constant. We find that intelligent life is unable to develop unless the cosmological constant is within a very narrow range that allows for galaxy formation. The universe simulated by the MMC device has a cosmological constant of 0.7 x 10-52 m3, which is roughly one part in 10500 of the observed value. We conclude that the anthropic explanation for the small value of the cosmological constant is plausible and should be considered in the context of modified theories of gravity that lead to a non-zero cosmological constant.

The anomalous X-ray pulsar 4U 0142+61 was intensively monitored with the Rossi X-ray Timing Experiment (RXTE) for more than 11 years. The obtained data were analyzed in the time domain as well as in the frequency domain. The obtained results show that the source underwent several flux state transitions, exhibited timing irregularities and a broad band noise component at lower frequencies. For the first time, we were able to detect quasi-periodic oscillations (QPO) at 27.6 s and 60.4 mHz. The high frequency QPO is most likely a Keplerian frequency at the compact object's warped magnetosphere. The low frequency QPO could be a neutron star's frequency group. Previously, 4U 0142+61 was observed to switch between two states: a soft state, where the source displayed a high frequency QPO, and a hard state, where the source showed a low frequency QPO. The source has never been observed to be in both states at the same time. In the present data set, the source was observed to be in the hard state for almost the entire monitoring period, with only short periods of time in the soft state. The transitions between the different flux states as well as timing irregularities observed in the source's timing behavior could be the result of a changing geometry of the source's magnetic field. Our results suggest that further studies of the long-term timing and flux behavior of this source could lead to a better understanding of both the interior structure of neutron stars as well as the processes that govern the transport of particles in neutron star magnetospheres.

Recently, a phenomenological theory was proposed for the unconventional spin excitations in the high temperature superconductors (HTSC) based on the unit-cell-doubled bilayer antiferromagnets (UD BAFM) structures. Both magnetic excitation spectra from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) experiments and single-particle band structures from ARPES experiments were well described by the theory based on the analogy between the HTSC and the UD BAFM. In this phenomenological theory, the spin excitations were viewed as a superposition of two elementary excitations with opposite momenta, forming a nodal ring structure in the three-dimensional (3D) momentum space. To further test the theory, it is important to study the spin excitations in the other UD BAFM-based HTSC systems, such as the YBCO family. In this work, based on the newly developed stochastic diagonalization method for a generalized Hubbard model, we study the spin excitations in the normal states of the heavily overdoped YBCO45 and underdoped YBCO22. The calculated spin excitations well reproduce the three-dimensional (3D) broadened simple $\mathbf{q}=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$-like spin resonance mode observed in both families. Moreover, our study reveals a clear evolution of the spin excitations from overdoped YBCO45 to underdoped YBCO22. With decreasing doping, the spectral weight of the resonance mode is transferred to higher energy, forming the spin resonance spectrum at lower doping and gradually disappears at higher doping. Such a doping evolution of the spin excitations is well consistent with the previously observed doping evolution of the resonance peak in the INS experiments. Therefore, our study provides strong supporting evidence for the phenomenological theory of spin excitations in HTSC, and provides clear energy and doping evolution of the spin excitations in the two UD BAFM-based HTSC families.

A number of recent papers have proposed new Quantum Hard-Sphere (QHS) equations of state (EOSs) for nuclear matter that are more consistent with both quantum many-body theory and nuclear experiment than the widely used Quantum Ideal Gas (QIG) EOS. Most of these proposed EOSs are based on a transformation of the many-body QHS Hamiltonian such that the quantum many-body system resembles an equivalent mean-field system, with a corresponding introduction of a "quantum liquid" equation of state (EOS) for the nuclear quantum many-body system. This paper critically evaluates this new class of proposed EOSs. After presenting a general critique of the various assumptions underlying the various proposed EOSs, we present a detailed analysis of the proposed EOS for neutron matter, which yields significantly improved analytic results over those previously proposed. We then apply these analyses to a proposed EOS for symmetric nuclear matter, yielding improved analytic results compared to both the widely used QIG EOS and the previously proposed neutron matter EOS. This improved performance is achieved through a new constraint on the EOS, based on nuclear saturation properties at low densities, and a more sophisticated fit to the high-density behavior of the EOS. Finally, we present analytic and numerical results for a proposed EOS for symmetric nuclear matter that yields an EOS that is simultaneously consistent with both the general critique presented and with the detailed analyses of the neutron matter and symmetric nuclear matter EOSs. This paper presents a new class of proposed equations of state for nuclear matter that are more consistent with both nuclear many-body theory and experiment than the widely used Quantum Ideal Gas (QIG) equation of state. These new equations of state, which we refer to as Quantum Hard-Sphere (QHS) equations of state, begin by rewriting the many-body Hamiltonian in second quantization in terms of creation and annihilation operators that satisfy the usual commutation relations. Next, the many-body Hamiltonian is transformed such that the nuclear quantum many-body system resembles an equivalent system of non-interacting particles (the "mean-field" system) that can be analyzed using standard classical many-body theory techniques. This leads to a new class of proposed equations of state for nuclear matter. The Hamiltonian for the equivalent mean-field system is parameterized in terms of an effective interaction energy and a chemical potential, with the effective interaction energy given by the second virial coefficient of the original many-body Hamiltonian. This parameterization of the Hamiltonian allows the authors to fit the predicted EOS to both nuclear many-body theory results and nuclear matter ground state properties. The proposed equation of state for symmetric nuclear matter is then analyzed in detail, yielding significantly improved analytic results over both the widely used Quantum Ideal Gas equation of state and the previously proposed equation of state for neutron matter. Finally, the proposed EOSs are shown to be consistent with a more general class of proposed equations of state by relaxing one of the key assumptions underlying the model.

In this paper we present a logic of reachable patterns applicable to any data structure with support for labeled, unlabeled and existential reachability queries. In contrast to existing pattern formation logics, our logic is both expressive and compact, allowing one to express highly complex data-patterns succinctly. To demonstrate the expressivity and applicability of our logic, we show how to express several classic data-patterns such as path, hypertree, transitive closure and Skolemization using our logic. In the process, we also develop corresponding compact encodings for these patterns. We apply our logic to pattern formation in Linked Data, and define a number of interesting data-patterns that characterize Linked Data.' Linked Data has grown significantly in recent years, motivated in part by its numerous perceived benefits. Despite this growth, the fundamental challenges involved in effectively encoding and operating upon Linked Data have remained largely unaddressed. The present paper addresses this shortcoming. We introduce a novel logic of reachable patterns, which is designed to support efficient pattern-finding in Linked Data. Using this logic, we define a number of interesting data-patterns that characterize Linked Data, and provide compact encodings for these patterns. We demonstrate the applicability and expressiveness of our logic by showing how to express several classic data-patterns using our logic, thereby providing the first compact encodings for these patterns. In the process, we also develop corresponding patterns that characterize Linked Data. Furthermore, we show that existing pattern formation logics are inadequate for encoding Linked Data patterns, and introduce a novel compact logic that precisely captures these patterns. Our logic allows one to encode highly complex Linked Data patterns succinctly, and can be applied to many applications that operate on Linked Data. This includes pattern-based query optimizations, abstract data types for Linked Data, and data-pattern discovery, to name a few. We make the logic and encodings underlying our paper available as open source through our website http://www.dl4lp.net/.

In this paper, we consider the global behavior of solutions to the one-dimensional, nonrelativistic, scalar wave equation, \begin{equation} (\partial^2_t - c^2 \partial^2_x) \phi(x,t) = 0, \;\; t \neq 0, \end{equation} where $c$ is a constant. Here and throughout this paper, we use units in which $c=\hslash=2m=1$. We assume that the initial data have compact support, so that for each fixed $T>0$, we can find a $M>0$ such that the support of the initial data is contained in $[-M,M]$. (In other words, we are working in the box domain.) We show that for each fixed $T>0$, there exists a $M>0$ such that the support of any solution with these data remains in the interval $[-M,M]$ for all $t \in [-T,T]$. In other words, the solution is bounded for finite time. We use a contraction mapping argument in a functional setting. This implies that the solution is Hölder continuous for any $\alpha < \min(1/4,1/2 - 1/p)$, where $p$ is the Sobolev index of the solution. (Note that this implies that the solution is indeed in $C^\alpha$ for this range of $\alpha$.) As a consequence, we show that the solution disperses with any uniform rate. We also study the wave equation on the half line. In this case, we can establish finite time blowup if the solution has infinite energy at $t=0$.

We present the discovery of seven z = 3.1 Ly-alpha emission-line galaxies (LAEs) in the Extended Chandra Deep Field South (ECDFS). The LAEs have Ly-alpha luminosity of 2.2-5.7 x 1044 erg s-1, which is about 4% of the expected value for the average ʺnormalʺ L* galaxy at this redshift. The LAEs are among the most distant and luminous objects found to date, and are either forming the first stars in the universe or are able to harbor rare, high-redshift galaxies with exceptionally high star formation rates. We discuss the implications of our findings for our understanding of reionization, galaxy formation and high-redshift galaxy populations. \ialize{We present the discovery of seven z = 3.1 Ly-alpha emission-line galaxies (LAEs) in the Extended Chandra Deep Field South (ECDFS). The LAEs have Ly-alpha luminosity of 2.2-5.7 x 1044 erg s-1, which is about 4% of the expected value for the average ʺnormalʺ L* galaxy at this redshift. The LAEs are among the most distant and luminous objects found to date, and are either forming the first stars in the universe or are able to harbor rare, high-redshift galaxies with exceptionally high star formation rates. We discuss the implications of our findings for our understanding of reionization, gene{ Article: http://www.springer.com/us/journal/16746 :: "The Ly-alpha Emission-Line Galaxies at z = 3.1 in the Extended Chandra Deep Field South Detected and Analyzed" } formation and high-redshift galaxy populations.}

Recent observations of supermassive black holes have provided evidence for the event horizon, or “photon sphere,” predicted by general relativity in 1907. The photon sphere is an area of spacetime degenerate in gravitational field strength, where gravitational lensing effects are strongest. As a consequence, light is unable to pass through this area from outside the black hole, producing a central bright ring, or “Caustic,” when it passes nearby. In this paper, we study the lensing properties of Kerr black holes with the goal of better understanding how strong-field lensing relates to cosmic censorship, the belief that events across the Universe are well-posed and can be described by classical gravity. In particular, we are interested in relating the position of the Caustic, which is a function of black hole spin and other parameters, to the threshold for classical behavior. We find that the Caustic lies outside the photon sphere for non-extremal Kerr black holes, and that as the spin of the black hole increases, the radius of the photon sphere decreases. Furthermore, we show that when the angular momentum of the black hole is sufficiently high, the size of the Caustic becomes comparable to that of the event horizon. This indicates that strong-field lensing can probe the threshold for classical behavior, and therefore can serve as a test of cosmic censorship.

The Star-forming Region NGC 346 in the Small Magellanic Cloud with Hubble Space Telescope ACS Observations. II. Photometric Study of the Intermediate-Age Star Cluster BS 90. This paper is the second part of the study of the star cluster BS 90 in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). BS 90 is an intermediate-age cluster (1-2 Gyr), which was found in a HST/ACS survey of the Star-forming Region NGC 346 in the Small Magellanic Cloud. The first part of the study (Mokiem et al. 2014) presented the results of the analysis of the spectroscopic observations of BS 90. The cluster has a round shape and is dominated by low-mass stars (the brightest star has the magnitude $m_{F775W} = 13.80 \pm 0.03$ mag), which suggests that BS 90 is already partially dissolved. The estimated age of the cluster is between 1 and 2 Gyr, which means that it is an intermediate-age star cluster. This conclusion is supported by its location on the red giant branch, which is shifted to red colors with respect to an open cluster main sequence. The cluster has a slightly higher concentration than the average for clusters in the Small Magellanic Cloud. The estimated mass of the cluster is $M = (2.2 \pm 0.3) \times 10^4$ M$_\odot$, and the mass of the brightest star is $M_{*,\mathrm{BS 90}} = (6.0 \pm 0.7) \times 10^3$ M$_\odot$.

NGC 602/N 90 is a small (2.5 x 2.0 kpc) region of intense clustered star formation in the Small Magellanic Cloud. This region contains at least 8 mid-to-high mass stars with masses ranging from 1.4 to 2.0 M⊙ and more than 20 sources with masses less than 1.0 M⊙. Two of the most massive stars have evolved away from the main sequence and are implicated in forming an intermediate-mass black hole. The presence of such high-mass stars so close to young, low-mass stars raises questions about the role of high-density environments in triggering the formation of high-mass stars, and the subsequent dispersal of their associated feedback effects. The region shows both embedded and exposed phases of high-mass star formation, and is a promising testbed for simulations seeking to bridge the gap between low- and high-mass star formation.

For a family of operators related to the one-dimensional Schrödinger operator with periodic potential, the asymptotics of eigenfunctions in the semiclassical limit is studied. Using the classical shooting argument, it is shown that the spectral problem is equivalent to one for a new family of operators with parameter dependent on the derivative of the periodic potential. The new operators are defined in a “homogenized” domain, where the spectrum is assumed to be uniformly separated from the essential spectrum. In the semiclassical limit, the operator family turns into a Schrodinger operator with constant coefficient. The asymptotics of the eigenfunctions is studied in the spirit of Floquet theory, replacing the fixed dispersion relation by the uniform separation of the spectrum. It is shown that the eigenfunctions are real-valued and trigonometric polynomials. The semiclassical quantization condition for the period of the potential is derived, and it is shown to be equivalent to the Gutzwiller’s trace formula.

We present new observations of the pregalactic HI 21-cm signal from z = 7 - 8 using the Green Bank Telescope (GBT). We find evidence for the lensing signal from mass structures along the line of sight at maximum impact parameter, with a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 3.8$\sigma$ at a radius of 30 h$^{-1}$ Mpc and a lensing amplitude of 0.26% of the background light. We discuss potential astrophysical contaminants and conclude that this signal is likely caused by the shadows of massive structures along the line of sight, formed between z = 8 and 7.7. This is the first detection of the pregalactic HI 21-cm signal at high redshifts and may provide new constraints on the intensity and nature of the ionizing UV background and the nature of the reionization epoch. The pregalactic HI 21-cm signal traces the total mass distribution in the observed volume, with higher signals corresponding to higher total mass surface densities. The astrophysical contaminants - radiation from local galaxies - produce a smooth, negative lensing signal, while the astrophysical hypothesis for the observed signal - a neutralbeam stopping in ionised pockets of the intergalactic medium - would produce a positive lensing signal. This signal is consistent with a linear, CDM-like power spectrum of mass structures, and we place a conservative upper limit on the 21-cm power at non-linear scales of k < 0.2 h/Mpc. We estimate the FIR optical depth to be Thomson scattering, Thomson scattering + Li absorption, and constraints from the observed abundance of optical sources at z < 10 as probes of reionization to be τ < 0.5, 0.17, and 0.23, respectively. Finally, we discuss future observations with the GBT and the APERTIF instrument on the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) Telescope which will increase the field of view and sensitivity, respectively, and increase the areal coverage of this survey.

Issai Schur (1887-1954) made fundamental contributions to analysis. He was the son of Abraham Elyahu Schur (1839-1916), a prominent mathematician in his own right who introduced the Schur polynomial into analysis. Issai had five siblings, all of whom became notable mathematicians in their own rights. His sister Gornella was the first female mathematician to receive a PhD in Europe. Another sister, Hilda, also studied mathematics and became a renowned algebraic geometer. His other sisters Sara, and Ida, were the first female students to enroll at the ETH in Zurich, Switzerland. Issai was himself a PhD student of Hermann Schwarz and an Invited Speaker of the ICM in 1928 in Bologna, Italy. He made significant contributions to the theory of partial differential equations, operator theory and function theory. In partial differential equations, he introduced the now-standard Schur complement. In operator theory, he introduced the notion of normal cone, an idea that he then extended to function spaces. Finally, in function theory, he introduced two characterizations of the Laplace operator that are known today as the Cauchy integral formula and the residue theorem.

Today, many astronomers use large robotic telescopes to identify interesting variable stars. These objects are then studied in more detail using smaller, human-occupied telescopes. We have developed the idea of one-shot variable star observation, whereby a guest can see a particular variable star at any time simply by hanging a brief optical188-shot exposure through a browser-based interface on a server. The server algorithmically generates a sequence of 30-second images of the star in question, offset from one another by a few seconds, such that a guest can select an image and be presented with a simple web page indicating the observed star, along with finder charts showing the location of the star on the sky and how it appeared over time. The interface is currently limited to Tycho Catalog stars, but it is extensible to any set of chosen variables. We call this interface Wikimedia Variable Star Observing (WVSOO), because the observing algorithm is modeled after Wikipedia's existing Observers system. We have also built a spin-off project, Wikimbad, which allows anyone to submit potential variable star targets for our algorithm to observe. We currently accept only Tycho Catalog stars, but we are expanding to accept other sets of chosen variables. We have tested WVSOO with several hundred visitors since our first release in October 2017. We have had few false positive identifications (~3%), but that still leaves a high success rate (~97%). We have made the source code for WVSOO and Wikimbad available on GitHub. We welcome participation from the wider astronomy community in testing and improving both the software and our ideas for variable star observing.

In this paper we examine the phenomenological signatures of gravitational, electromagnetic, and nuclear scattering from colored particles in typical large volume string compactifications. We find that the graviton, photon, and gluon sectors each contain a unique set of excitable states with different modular symmetries and discrete charges. States with the appropriate quantum numbers to excite the gravitational, electromagnetic, and strong interactions can be produced at the LHC, with characteristic signal strengths depending on the details of the underlying string model. We perform a detailed exploration of a subset of explicit and anomaly free models, identifying regions of the parameter space with highly compressed spectra (compacting the VEVs of the effective saxion, moduli, and supersymmetry breaking fields) as well as large excited vacuum multiplicities. We examine phenomenological constraints from proton stability and the triviality and vacuum stability bounds from the soft supersymmetry breaking sector, finding that compressed regions of the parameter space are favored both for modular symmetries with large torsion and for orbifold and Calabi-Yau manifolds with large Euler character. We also analyze the impact of large excited vacuum multiplicities, finding that large contributions to the cosmological constant are common in these models. We find that these models can accommodate the LHC Higgs signal strengths while remaining consistent with current bounds on the cosmic microwave background radiation temperature and large scale structure formation, except in cases with highly squeezed spectra and/or large contributions to the cosmological constant.

Galaxy clusters are the largest known structures in the universe, containing hundreds or even thousands of galaxies. Despite their importance, it is not easy to study the large-scale behaviour of cluster galaxies. Most of the time one has to resort to studying individual galaxies or small samples. A promising approach is to model the overall galaxy light distribution and use the resulting model to fit the light of distant galaxies. Such an approach was proposed by Falco et al. in 1987 and implemented on large datasets by Gonzalez et al. in 2002. Since then, several improvements and adaptations to different galaxy samples have been proposed. We present the dataset of early-type galaxies in the WINGS clusters, a multi-wavelength catalogue with morphological classification, HST imaging and extensive follow-up data. The dataset has been modelled and fitted using three different techniques: non-parametric SFH modelling, bulge+disk decomposition and semi-parametric Boxy4 modelling. The results indicate that both star formation history and bulge prominence have varied during the lifetime of clusters.

A sample of single top quark production is presented using data collected by the CDF II detector at the Tevatron proton-antiproton collider. The analysis is optimized for the production of single top quarks in association with a W boson, using the t-channel exchange model. The observed number of events is consistent with the standard model prediction. Upper limits at 95% confidence level are set on the production of top quark partners, a new heavy spin-0 or -1 particle predicted by several models of beyond the standard model. The CDF experiment at the Tevatron has searched for the rare production of single top quarks in association with a W boson, a top quark transforming into a top quark partner (top quark associate) or a new heavy spin-0 or -1 particle. A sample of such events with an integrated luminosity of 9.7 fb−1, where the W boson and the top quark or top quark associate were each reconstructed in a hadronic top quark decay mode, was examined. The data were found to be consistent with the standard model prediction. Upper limits at 95% confidence level are set on the production of top quark partners, which are used to limit the production of new heavy spin-0 or -1 particles. This article is a summary of the single top analysis from the CDF experiment at the Tevatron, presented at the HL Tau DeCellularized Spine Project workshop in Beijing, June 2014.

Magnetism in the spiral galaxy NGC 6946 is investigated using high-resolution synchrotron radio continuum observations from the 64m telescope of the Max-Planck-Institute for Solar System Research (MPS). After a short general introduction, we describe the observations and data reduction, present magnetic field strength and configuration measurements, and discuss the regularity and origin of the observed magnetic fields. In particular, the newly introduced depolarization ring technique is employed to detect the weak, highly disordered, large-scale magnetic fields, and the detected ring-like magnetic structures are analyzed with respect to their azimuthal symmetries and embedded energy transport processes. Additionally, we introduce methods to characterize the regular small-scale magnetic fields, i.e. the spiral structure, dynamo modes and helical fields, by deducing vector fields of regularized and unsharp masked total magnetic field maps. We conclude by discussing consequences of the observed regular and random magnetic field configurations for the fueling and launching of the active galactic nucleus in the central region of the galaxy, and summarize the current research on NGC 6946 as a model galaxy for testing various aspects of interstellar and intergalactic magnetic field research using modern instrumentation.

BL Lacertae is a BL Lac object, which is one of the most promising candidates of the still unconfirmed Dark Matter, distributed approximately uniformly throughout our Universe. The inferred Dark Matter density makes it likely that the BL Lacertae is host to a supermassive black hole. BL Lacertae was detected as an active galaxy from the radio band to the high-energy gamma rays. The observations revealed that the total energy output of BL Lacertae in the optical band is dominated by non-thermal emission from a compact core. In this work, we performed multi-wavelength observations of BL Lacertae in the optical band over a period of 12 years. Our results showed that the long-term optical spectral variability can be characterized as two states: a high-energy gamma-ray loud state and a low-energy gamma-ray quiet state. These two states can be corresponded to the variation of the synchrotron and Inverse-Compton components in the optical band. The detailed modeling also indicated that the long-term optical spectral variability is likely due to the change of the Doppler factor of the jet with the variation of the total magnetic field.

A sample of active galactic nuclei (AGN) observed with the Infrared Spectrograph on the Spitzer Space Telescope is used to examine the connection between the strength of fine structure line ratios and the strength of extinction by the torus, as measured by optical spectroscopy. The spectra are modeled with a combination of a power-law pluselines and multiple Gaussians to fit the prominent AGN narrow lines. The models are applied to a subset of the data consisting of six AGNs with a range of extinction from none to high, and corresponding to 14 spectra in total. The line ratios [SiIV+OIV]/[HeII+H]+ and [HeII]/[OIV]+ are found to increase monotonically with the amount of extinction, consistent with previous work. The /[HeII+H]+ ratio also increases with extinction, but this relationship is only significant at the 95% level. The other two line ratios, [NeV]/[HeII+H]+ and [NeV]/[OIV]+, are not found to vary with extinction. However, a subsample of four spectra with the highest extinction shows an increase in [NeV]/[HeII+H]+, from $\approx$ 0.5 to $\approx$ 1.4, while the other three higher-extinction spectra have [NeV]/[HeII+H]+ = [NeV]/[OIV]+. The elevated [NeV]/[HeII+H]+ in these four spectra is consistent with gas with a hard radiation field, possibly due to obscuration by a warped torus surface.

Modern technology provides users with many ways to express their opinions and preferences. Many social media platforms, for example, collect information about their users, including their IP addresses, which can be used to identify them. However, such information is often necessary to provide the services that users demand. If a social media site was constructed without relying on IP addresses, for example, it could not accurately recognize which users are responsible for which posts. As a result, such sites would be unable to provide the services that many users demand, and much of the convenience that they enjoy would be lost. We study this tradeoff between anonymity and serviceability in the wild. We create a network of students, post assignments to their classes, and comment on presentations. The comments include the students’ IP addresses, which we can use to identify users. However, this information is not required to provide the services that users demand. Indeed, many users demand anonymity, and we enable it by correlating the IP addresses to random IDs. Despite this, many users express opinions that would be useful to the site’s operators if they were identifiable, such as expressing interest in new classes, requesting specific presentations be highlighted, and complaining about poorly received assignments. We demonstrate that while some users express only covert opinions, others express opinions that can be discerned from the content. We model this tradeoff as a mechanism design problem and provide efficient algorithms to solve it. Our approach can be used to design social media sites that users can enjoy the benefits of anonymity while expressing their opinions in a way that can be observed by site operators.

In distributed sensing, the amount of data generated is often proportional to the size of the region being sensed. One approach to scale sensing efforts is to partition the region into smaller segments, each with a small field of view (FOV). In this approach, computation is performed locally at each sensing node and data aggregation is only needed within a segment. Compared with the traditional approach that requires all sensing nodes to communicate with a fusion center, the estimation diversity and energy efficiency can be significantly improved by leveraging local computation at each node. However, it is not clear how to perform distributed optimization for parameter estimation without any global communication, which could potentially consume significant energy. In this work, we propose a novel distributed algorithm that performs estimation by locally computing the gradient of the cost function at each node and by efficiently communicating a small amount of information among neighboring nodes. Numerical results show that the proposed algorithm can achieve similar estimation accuracy as the centralized algorithm while reducing energy consumption by 60% for a network of nodes with homogeneous computation and communication capabilities.' The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents related work. Section III describes the network model and problem statement. Section IV presents the gradient computation and communication based algorithm. Section V presents the numerical results. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

The spiral wave is a key phenomenon in the plankton ecological systems and exhibits the rotating spots with different densities. In this Letter, we show that far-field spiral wave breakup is an alternative route to spatiotemporal chaos (STC) in the plankton ecological systems, which cannot be described by the classical C. E. Pfister’s theory1. The system with three-prey version of the Leslie model exhibits the spatiotemporal chaos when the diffusion coefficients ratio and the compensation rate are set as R=4 and α=2.5, while the spiral wave could still be observed in the experimentally observed region. Using the spiral wave frequency, the wave pattern and the STC are confirmed to be the same. Thus, the far-field breakup of the spiral wave is an alternative route to the spatiotemporal chaos in the plankton ecological systems. The spiral wave breakup is not only an alternative route to STC, but also can be observed by the naked eye in the real ecological systems.

The first proper motions of thin dust filaments at the Galactic Center (GC) were measured using the Laser Guide Star Adaptive Optics (LGS AO) system on the Subaru Telescope. The filaments are elongated structures aligned in the GC North-South direction. The projected lengths of the filaments range from 20 to 70 pc, and their widths are 1-3 pc. The corresponding mass densities are 10^3 - 10^4 M~odot pc-3. The filaments rotate about their centers with maximum projected velocities of 30 to 100 km s-1. They are likely in pressure equilibrium with thermal pressures of 10 to 30 μPa, which is about one millionth of the Galactic air pressure at the GC. These results demonstrate that the GC thin disk is a highly dynamic system. The observations and data analysis were conducted by the Subaru/*Mt*gem team under the leadership of T. Onaka. The research was published in the Astrophysical Journal.

Pulse-coupled network of non-linear oscillators with non-diffusive coupling can exhibit dynamic behavior that is sensitive to initial conditions. One particular type of chaotic behavior, called splay state, has been identified in systems of globally coupled phase oscillators with repulsive non-linear coupling. In this paper, we demonstrate that the splay state is stable in a more general network of non-linear oscillators, namely a system of pulse-coupled oscillators. The stability analysis is performed using a simplified model of pulse-coupled oscillators that takes into account the temporal structure of pulses and can be used to analyze more complex pulse-coupled systems, such as those used in neural networks. We show that splay states are orbitally stable and use this result to explore the sensitivity of the splay state to changes in parameters of the pulse-coupling function and the connectivity matrix. We also explore the circumstances under which multi-splay states are stable. Our results demonstrate that the splay state can be a stable state not only in phase-coupled networks, but also in pulse-coupled networks with a broad class of pulse-coupling functions. The simplicity of the pulse-coupling function allows for the use of the pulse-coupled network in the context of neural networks, where different neuronal groups can be thought of as different oscillators with a pulse-coupling function.

Robustness to mutations is important for an organism’s survival. As a consequence, most proteins have evolved to be robust to point mutations. However, as mutations are typically accumulated under random mating and infinite population size, this protein robustness has not been demonstrated for large populations, an environment that predominates in the real world. Here, we demonstrate robustness to large population size by evolving proteins under directional selection for high DNA binding affinity and showing that these proteins also have high mutational robustness. By evolving DNA binding sites as well as binding proteins in parallel, we also demonstrate that high binding site mutational robustness is necessary but not sufficient for high binding protein robustness. We then use detailed models to show that high binding site mutational robustness arises due to selection to minimize the effects of mutations in binding site nucleotides on protein binding energy, and that this binding site robustness can propagate to the protein. This explains our experimental and simulation results. Our study highlights the critical role of large population size in protein robustness and may explain the high mutational robustness of proteins.

Granular media are composed of individual grains that are mostly impenetrable and interact via friction. In the limit of low-density, a granular mixture behaves as a fluid of intragranular particles. The kinetics of this low-density binary granular mixture has not been systematically studied. We present a formalism for the dynamics of such a system and apply it to a particularly relevant configuration, a thin horizontal circular rod immersed in a granular mixture of circular grains. This system is of interest in the context of hoppers, where a thin rod is often the metering element measuring the amount of granular material dispensed. We show that when the height of the granular mixture, the Rod-granules diameter, and the Rod-granule interfacial width are small compared to the diameter of the Granules, a set of coupled partial differential equations for the intragranular density and velocity fields may be reduced to an effective description of the fluid dynamics of intragranular particles. Our formalism provides equations for the intragranular density, velocity, and temperature fields and an equation of state relating the pressure to the intragranular energy, all as a function of the vertical coordinate normal to the Rod surface. We present the solution of these equations for the particular case of an infinite, no-slip Rod. We compare this solution to direct simulations of the particles and show that our approach provides a good approximation for the evolution of the average intragranular density, momentum, and temperature fields. We also present an experimental confirmation of our results, testing the Rod’s effectiveness as a metering element for a hopper.

The chemical composition of the x-ray burster (GRO J1655-40) was analyzed using the Reflection Grating Infrared Spectrometer (RGI) on the U.S. Space Shuttle mission flown in December 1993. A set of infrared spectra were obtained of the surface of the donor star, theCompanion Star (CS) wind, the CS accretion disk, and the black hole candidate. The abundances of the CS and the black hole candidate can be reliably determined only from the wind and accretion disk spectra, respectively. The CS is very metal rich, with near-solar abundances of most elements except sodium, aluminum, and oxygen. The inner edge of the CS accretion disk is slightly raised above the hydrogen burns to helium main sequence. The disk has depleted abundances of silicon and sulfur and enhanced abundances of neon, argon, and krypton. The large scale height of the disk indicates that its rotational period is of order a day. This is the first reliable determination of the donor star and black hole candidate abundances. The donor star is only slightly metal rich, with near solar abundances of most elements except sodium, aluminum, and oxygen. The black hole candidate has abundances that are depleted in silicon and sulfur and enhanced in neon, argon, and krypton relative to the donor star. The abundance pattern of the black hole candidate is very similar to that of many supergiant stars, indicating it has a supergiant donor. The chemical composition of the black hole candidate indicates that it has a mass of at least 14 solar masses.

Interstellar space is a low density, highly ionized medium. Consequently, interstellar atoms and ions are mostly stripped of their electrons. For these species, gas phase collisions are the only process capable of recombining them into molecular or solid state forms. The ion composition of the gas phase in the interstellar medium is determined by the processes of ionization, recombination, and mutual shielding. The processes of charge exchange and radiative association also play a role, but their rates are highly dependent on the density and temperature of the gas. Charge exchange between H II regions and the diffuse interstellar medium is believed to be the main source of singly-ionized species such as C II, O I, and N II. In interstellar space with a low density of ~1 cm-3, these species are quickly stripped of their electrons by mutual collisions. The most abundant ion in this regime is C II, with an ionization potential of ~24.6 eV. Since the neutral-ion collision cross section rises rapidly with increasing center-of-mass energy, C II is the dominant contributor to the number of electron-ion collisions, and thus the rate of spontaneous recombination. Significant amounts of C II are found throughout the interstellar medium. However, there is a critical velocity, V c, below which the velocity of C II atoms or ions relative to a distant observer is less than the average ionization threshold of 24.6 eV. Therefore, the C II column density must exceed V c /. Since V c =c / (2.3 x 1010 cm3 m-1 s-1), where c is the speed of light, and assuming an average molecular weight of 1.4, this corresponds to a minimum total hydrogen column density of ~N H ≥ 1.7 x 1012 cm-2. The Critical Ionization Velocity Effect, or CIVE, is the dependence of the C II opacity on N H, such that C II absorption diminishes above this minimum N H threshold. This threshold may be met throughout much of the interstellar medium, resulting in weak or negligible C II absorption, even at 21-cm wavelengths. Near to the cores of molecular clouds, however, N H can drop significantly lower, resulting in strong C II absorption in the CIE regime. CIE typically occurs in planar structures, or sheets, with typical sizes on the order of 100 - 300 pc. These sheets may comprise interiors of older and more evolved clouds, or may represent entirely unperturbed regions of the interstellar medium. Since the CIE is optically thick to 21-cm radiation, it may also exhibit enhanced 21-cm emission. The CIE likely occurs in all regions of interstellar space with a neutral fraction below ~0.3, but the fraction of regions displaying CIE may decrease with increasing distance from the center of molecular clouds. Using computer simulations, we investigate the structure of toroidal magnetic fields in neutron stars with type II superconductor cores. We find that, for a wide range of physically plausible parameters, these fields exist as stable configurations, rather than being plagued by magnetic instability. We also find that such fields modify the structure of neutron stars, and have impacts on their cooling behavior. Our results provide new insights into the nature of some magnetars, as well as offering new mechanisms for radio emission from these objects. Neutron stars are among the most exotic objects in the universe. They are leftover objects from the death of massive stars. They are as heavy as the moon but much more dense, being averages of several kilometers of matter packed into a volume of a few kilometers. Their interior, the so-called "nuclear sphere," is rich in neutrons, almost half of the volume being comprised of neutrons held together with the strong force. This neutron matter is the most dense matter in the universe, similar in density to a large tumor on a human being. Surrounding the nuclear sphere is a "deep crust," essentially a thin layer of partially degenerate neutron drip, and finally an outer layer of hydrogen and helium. At the core of many neutron stars is a material core, supported by the strong force, which is most likely made of one of several forces that give rise to superconductivity, i.e, Fermi, Coorbital, U(1) or colour superconductivity. Type II superconductivity occurs in metals at low temperatures. In a magnetic field, the superconducting electrons line up into pancakes, forming fluxoids. The resulting field is maximal at the mid-plane of the star and tapers off near the surface. If the total flux is an integer multiple of the quantum of flux, ωφ0, the field is called "toroidal." Depending on the ratio of the magnetic energy to the condensation energy, this field is either stable or unstable. In this work, we study a subset of the stable solutions, those with integral flux quanta. We find that the ratio of the toroidal field energy to the rest of the star goes as the fifth power of the field strength, so there is little free energy in the field at typical neutron star fields. The field lines then naturally bundle in flux bundles of integral quanta. For a strong enough magnetic field, there is a discontinuity in the poloidal magnetic field, and the field is called force-free. This situation arises when there is a magnetic field-induced modification to the equation of state for the superconductor, so the magnetic and condensation energies are not in balance. A toroidal field modifies the structure of a neutron star in two primary ways. The magnetic pressure is enhanced in the core, increasing the pressure even as the density drops. In the present paper we present a study of the Dbar-N interaction based on an effective Lagrangian approach. The Dbar-N interaction is described in terms of a scalar doublet and a pseudoscalar singlet coupled to vectors with appropriate chiral transformation properties. Our effective Lagrangian is composed of terms that follow from chiral symmetry, heavy baryon $\chi$PT and from meson exchange. The analysis of the results is separated into two parts. First we present the low-energy parameters, which are used in the analysis of the Dbar-N system in the second part. In the second part we present the results for the Dbar-N scattering amplitudes in the scalar-mediated and pseudoscalar-mediated channels, allowing us to establish the existence of a possible bound state for these channels. We also present the results for the uncoupled channels and the scalar and pseudoscalar phases shifts. We present a summary of our results and present our conclusions.

A density tensor hierarchy (DTH) for approximate open system dynamics is introduced. The DTH is characterized by a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) whose density can be expressed in terms of the energy or another system observable. The truncation of the DTH yields a consistent, but not exact, approximation of the exact dynamics. In this paper, we introduce a DTHN, whose approximation of the exact dynamics is guaranteed to be exact on simultaneous stationary points. We show how to compute stationary points, approximate the flow near these stationary points, and retrieve the values of the noise from the DTHN solution. We apply the DTHN to the damped harmonic oscillator and numerically simulate the linearized DTHN and DTHN. We find excellent agreement between the DTHN and the DTHN solutions. -- M. Hamdi, D.
