The most ancient known stars in the universe are the blue straggler (BS) stars. These stars are thought to have formed after the matter in their host galaxies had expanded and cooled sufficiently for the main sequence lifetime of their constituent stars. These BS stars are thus iron-cored, helium-3 burning stars that have processed almost all of the original H and He into He-3. However, the most unusual characteristic of these stars is that they are (apparently) overwhelmingly massive, with more than 90% of the mass of their counterparts in the local universe. This has long been an enigma, given that the current standard theory of star formation predicts that such high mass stars are relatively uncommon, with simulations rarely yielding more than 5-10% massive stars. Recent observations by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Australian National University's 2.3-meter telescope have revealed a potentially revolutionary solution to this paradox. Using data from the Keck telescopes, we have observed nine blue straggler stars in three ultra-lithium-deficient stars, all of which show strongBe absorption in their spectra. This absorption is not present in equivalent measurements of normal stars and is extremely difficult to produce in any theoretical models. While the abundance ofBe must be very close to the half-life value in order to see absorption, it has been suggested that a standard freeze-out process cannot produce the observed amount ofBe, while a late-accreted s-process material is also ruled out. The observations presented here suggest a novel solution. It has previously been proposed that many BS stars may have been formed from accretion events, with material donated by a binary companion. As the most common element,Be is particularly good at absorbing optical radiation from a cool, low-mass companion, and thus its detection in the spectra of BS stars may be a signature of the process by which these stars were formed. We suggest that such accretion events are also likely to have been highly polluted with light elements such as Be. This discovery has profound implications for our understanding of star formation, and for models of binary star evolution. If substantial amounts ofBe can be synthesised in binary star systems, then these systems may represent an important site of nucleosynthesis in the early universe, and may provide a missing link between the populations of very low- and very high-mass stars in the galaxy population at early times.

This paper is concerned with the analysis of substructures in galaxy clusters, as determined from deep optical data from the WINGS Survey. Our main objective is the precise detection and analysis of substructures, starting from a general description of the structure of the cluster surface brightness and of the background, and ending with a robust quantification of the amount of substructure and of the properties of the identified substructures. This is very useful to discriminate among different physical processes that are expected to induce substructures in clusters and to gain knowledge on the evolutionary stage of the clusters. The detection of substructures is achieved by using the Galaxyicity model, which is a very powerful method that has been proved to be very efficient and reliable in this kind of analysis. The results of this analysis will be used to follow the dynamical evolution of clusters and to study the connections between cluster structure and global properties (e.g., cluster mass). A total of 35 galaxy clusters taken from the WINGS survey have been analysed in this way. A preliminary characterisation of the analysed clusters is given, together with an overall analysis of the frequency and the properties of substructures. As a general result we can state that the analyzed clusters present some substructures, with different levels of surface brightness and masses, and with a general prevalence of low-mass substructures.

AlxGa1-xN/GaN superlattices (SLs) are very promising materials for fabricating modern tunable violet-green and yellow light-emitting diodes (LEDs) for general lighting and displays. However, the widely used growth engineering allows only for a weak variation of aluminum content in the individual layers, which does not provide efficient regulation of the dominant Stokes shift carriers. We propose to use polarization-sensitive epitaxy for increasing the variation rate of aluminum content in the SL structure and thus shifting the majority carriers to the mid-gap state. This allows one to reduce the Stokes shift and improve the efficiency of yellow and green LEDs. We have carried out first-principles calculations for the SL structures under consideration and obtained the charge polarization maps for both polarization configurations. We have found strong variations of the electron and hole densities in the structure. Using the tight-binding model and the modified Bethe–Salpeter equation, we have calculated the optical spectra of the SL structures with the both charge distributions. We have found a blue shift of the main peak in the optical spectrum, the peak width reduction, and an anti-crossing with the higher energy level corresponding to the split-off state, which provides a possibility to vary the peak position by an external gate voltage. The considered approach is universal and can be applied to other systems with the polarization-dependent interaction.

Deep radio images have been made with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) of the region containing the sources TeV Sources I and TeV Sources II in the Cygnus OB2 complex. We find seven new sources, two of which are likely to be binary star systems. TeV Sources I and II are both observed to be variable on short timescales, and one of the new sources is consistent with this behaviour as well. These results confirm that TeV Sources I and II are young high-mass stars in a stage of rapid evolution. The density of newly discovered sub-millimetre sources in the TeV sources vicinity is consistent with the hypothesis that they are producing stars at a high rate. We present the results of Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) observations of the region containing TeV Sources I and II. The observations have a spatial resolution of $\approx 0.2$ milli-arcseconds and a dynamic range of approximately 20,000:1, allowing us to determine the sizes, flux densities, and proper motions of the identified radio sources in the field. We identify two previously unknown binary star systems, as well as confirm that TeV Sources I and II are both variable on short timescales. We also identify seven new sources, two of which are likely to be binary star systems. The density of newly discovered sub-millimetre sources in the TeV sources vicinity is consistent with the hypothesis that they are producing stars at a high rate. In this paper, we consider a stationary, spherically symmetric black hole in de Sitter space with a constant positive curvature. We compute the Bogoliubov coefficients between the Hawking radiation and the Bunch-Davies vacuum, and find that the de Sitter horizon is a effective change of the vacuum. We also consider the small mass case, and calculate the particle creation rate and the energy flux near the horizon. We find that the energy flux becomes a positive number even in de Sitter space, which violates the cosmic no-hair conjecture. Since then, there have been many studies of quantum effects in AdS spaces, such as black holes and cosmological horizons. One reason to study the effects of quantum gravity in AdS spaces is to understand the higher-dimensional gravity itself from a view point of the lower-dimensional CFT. On the other hand, the cosmological constant in the universe is very tiny but non-zero. It has been suggested that quantum effects of the gravity could generate a positive cosmological constant. This means that the AdS space corresponds to an inflationary universe. Thus, studying quantum effects in AdS spaces provides a possible way to explain the very small but non-zero cosmological constant. However, the AdS spaces have a time-like curvature, and thus the physics in the boundary CFT does not have a time direction. This means that, since the Hawking radiation is a process from the past of the boundary, it does not affect the CFT. The cosmic no-hair conjecture is that black holes in an expanding universe should have the same conserved quantities as the universe. A new family of LDPC erasure distributions with closed-form threshold expression is proposed, which includes the ball packing distribution, the hyperball packing distribution, and the circle packing distribution. It is shown that the Logarithmic Likelihood Ratio (LLR) of these distributions can be calculated in closed-form. For the BER=10-12 requirement of recent memory devices, the error exponents of the proposed distributions are shown to be very close to the Shannon limit. The density evolution and LLR of these distributions are derived and simulation results are provided. * LDPC codes based on the proposed distributions can achieve the Shannon limit of error exponent for certain SNR, and thus promising application in future high-density flash memory * The threshold expression of these distributions are very closed-form, making the density evolution and LLR calculation efficient * The excellent error exponent of these distributions can be obtained with a simple denop algorithm, making them easy to implement References: * [A Class of LDPC Erasure Distributions with Closed-Form Threshold Expression] H. A Chandra X-ray study of the galactic supernova remnant G299.2-2.9 reveals that the blast wave is decelerated by a low-density, rapidly expanding ejecta shell that has been formed by a previous generation of stars in the vicinity of the supernova explosion. The age of the ejecta shell is consistent with estimates based on its distance from the SNR center and its size. The spectrum of the thermal component of the SNR is softer than expected from a bare shock and can be explained if a population of thermalized ions with plasma temperature of 0.7 keV is present in the shocked ejecta. The large extent of the shell-related emission implies that the progenitor was a relatively massive star that lost a large fraction of its hydrogen-rich material prior to the core collapse. Alternatively, a progenitor mass of 17-22 M⊙ (for a typical explosion energy of 3×1051 erg) would be required if the ejecta is interacting with a low-density intercloud medium. In this case, the total SNR energy input is a factor of 2-3 higher than that released by the explosion.

The local galaxy 8 micron luminosity function (LF) is derived from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) DR7 footprint using data in the U, g, r, i, and z bands. We calculate galaxy number counts in 0.5 dex wide bins of i band apparent magnitude, Kron mag and Petrosian radius R50. The LF is parameterized using a double Schechter function. We determine the best fitting parameters using a maximum likelihood approach and find clear evidence for curvature in the galaxy number counts. Using simulations, we examine the effects of shot noise, edge effects, and survey limits on our LF results and find that these do not significantly affect our determinations of the double Schechter function parameters. Using our best fit Schechter function, we predict the number of galaxies within different apparent magnitude ranges. We compare our results to published values derived from the SDSS Ninth Data Release and find generally good agreement, with some evidence for higher normalizations at brighter apparent magnitudes and lower characteristic magnitude from our work. Using our best fit Schechter function, we calculate absolute i band magnitudes for the sample galaxies and compare these to stellar population synthesis models. We find that the characteristic luminosity of the galaxies in our sample are consistent with passively evolving stellar populations with recent formation redshifts of z~2.

The lithosphere is the outermost rigid layer of the Earth’s crust where convection and plate tectonics occur. Thin elastic shells represent a novel technique for flexural lithospheric modeling that has not been explored before. Such a model can provide new insight into the mechanics of lithospheric bending and vertical coupling between the bending and faulting. This paper presents a novel thin elastic shells approach for flexural lithospheric modeling. The bending response of a thin elastic shell is obtained by integrating the forces across its thickness. The model domain is discretized using a surface mesh with nodal DOF, where each node is linked with the shell through its surface mapping. The resulting linear system is expressed in terms of surface loads, shell properties, and shell geometry. A series of thin elastic shells with different materials properties and different thicknesses are used to demonstrate the flexibility of the approach. Preliminary results for a mid-ocean ridge setting are presented to show the potential of the approach.

Recent theoretical work has proposed continuous quantum error correction (QEC), in which error correction pulses are applied frequently and continuously in time. We experimentally test continuous QEC for a non-Markovian environment, extending previous work with a discrete quantum error correction code to demonstrate continuous maintenance of quantum coherence against non-Markovian dephasing. Unlike Markovian error models, non-Markovian processes describe memory in the system-environment interaction, and thus can more accurately model real world systems. We use our experimental platform to probe the non-Markovian process via quantum process tomography and demonstrate continuous error correction at room temperature, capturing non-Markovian dynamics over 100 times the duration of previous non-Markovian error correction experiments. This work furthers the practicality of continuous QEC as a fundamental physical technique as well as an approach to realize more robust quantum information systems. We study continuous quantum error correction (QEC) for non-Markovian dephasing. Unlike Markovian error models, non-Markovian processes describe memory in the system-environment interaction and thus can more accurately model real world systems. Continuous QEC has previously been theoretically studied [1] and demonstrated in various experimental platforms for maintaining entanglement [2, 3]. We experimentally test continuous QEC for the first time, extending previous discrete quantum error correction experiments with nuclear magnetic resonance to demonstrate continuous maintenance of quantum coherence against non-Markovian dephasing. Continuous QEC applies continuous error correction pulses in time, rather than only at intervals determined by the system's coarse time scale. This offers several advantages for non-Markovian error correction. First, continuous error correction can better capture non-Markovianity, a property distinct from memory in the system's past. Second, non-Markovian error processes often vary rapidly in time, with occasional long memory decays and kicks [4, 5]. These occasional bursts of non-Markovian behavior require only a few continuous pulses to stabilize. Continuous QEC can better maintain quantum coherence through this bursty non-Markovian environment. We correct non-Markovian dephasing errors using a continuous dynamical decoupling (DD) protocol. DD is a family of pulse sequences that can suppress certain Hamiltonian noise [6], including non-Markovian errors arising from system-environment feedback [7, 8]. Continuous dynamical decoupling pulses are a sequence of sufficiently frequent and alternating short (Gaussian) and long (brick-wall) Gaussian pulses, with pulse-width and inter-pulse delay tuning parameters. The full pulse sequence is repeated many times within a limited duration. Our experimental platform for non-Markovian dynamical decoupling combines continuous quantum error correction with superconducting qubits coupled to a three-dimensional waveguide lattice [9]. By means of extensive Quantum Monte Carlo simulations and a slave-rotor mean-field theory, we show that low-dimensional quantum Heisenberg models on layered lattice structures can be accurately described in terms of a semiclassical spin-wave analysis based on the identification of valence-bond crystals. The quantum fluctuations are found to significantly modify the spin-wave spectrum, with the most salient effects arising for strongly frustrated models where geometrical factors favor the stabilization of valence-bond crystal patterns. In particular, our results strongly suggest that the semiclassical treatment of valence-bond crystals for weak tunneling between condensates is appropriate for a wide range of geometries where inhomogeneous condensates are stabilized. The modified spin-wave spectrum due to quantum fluctuations is found to enhance the role of frustrated interactions, leading to a drastic suppression of the magnetization plateau states as compared to the simple semiclassical treatment. Remarkably, the spin-wave analysis captures all finite-size effects and signatures of valence-bond crystals down to the smallest linear system sizes studied, paving the way for the efficient simulation of frustrated Heisenberg models with local quantum fluctuations.

A nuclear reactor that uses depleted uranium as fuel and operates at high temperatures (1000 K - 1300 K) and high pressures (10 Atm - 75 Atm) could provide compact and efficient power generation for aerospace applications. This paper presents the results of preliminary design of a nuclear reactor operating under these extreme conditions known as AB-Thermonuclear Reactor (ABTR). The ABTR employs an annular nozzle-spiral beta spectrum to generate power in the form of hot pressurized gas for aircraft engines and other applications. ABTR is compact, utilizing the same volume as a 200 MW light-water reactor and able to achieve high thermal efficiencies of over 40% while extracting more than 70% of the heat of reaction. The initial design and simulation results are presented with the intent of open-sourcing this promising new reactor concept for further development. changes The AB-Thermonuclear Reactor (ABTR) is a high-efficiency, high-output nuclear reactor that could be suitable for compact power generation in aerospace applications. The ABTR employs depleted uranium as its nuclear fuel and is designed to operate at high temperature and high pressure, environments that other reactor concepts have been unable to achieve due to material limitations. The ABTR utilizes an annular nozzle-spiral beta spectrum to generate power in the form of pressurized hot gas which could be used for aircraft engines or other applications. Preliminary design shows the ABTR to be 20% the size and 20% the weight of a 200 MW light-water reactor while achieving 40% thermal efficiency.

The luminous infrared galaxy NGC 6052 was observed with the Spitzer Space Telescope in four different programs. The galaxy was observed with the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) in staring mode as part of program 601 (P.I.s: Werner, C. O. & Teplitz, H. I.) and with the MIPS instrument as part of programs 30 and 39 (P.I.s: Hailey-Dunsheath, S. & Sargent, B. A.). The IRS data were reduced using a modified version of the S11 script and the MIPS data were reduced using the MIPS Data Reduction Guide version 8.0. In this work we combine all of the archival Spitzer observations of NGC 6052 in order to carry out a detailed analysis of the galaxy's spectral energy distribution (SED). We first construct a broadband SED from the optical to the mid-infrared. This is then used to fit a dust torus model to the infrared data. The model consists of a central BlackBody source modified by a fixed radial density distribution of dust grains in an otherwise empty spheroid. The resulting best-fit model parameters indicate that NGC 6052 has an active galactic nucleus (AGN) with an estimated power of 1051 W and a distance of 95.2 billion light years. The AGN contributes 74% of the total infrared luminosity of the galaxy and the host galaxy contributes 23% (11% of the total infrared luminosity). We also examine the spatial distribution of the warm (50-125 K) and hot (125-540 K) dust, as well as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and use these results to assess the thermal balance of the galaxy. We find that the hot dust is concentrated in a circumnuclear ring with a radius of 3.2 pc. The inner and outer radii of the cool dust are found to be 14 pc and 50 pc, respectively. The total dust mass is estimated to be 2.3 x 10-5 M⊙. The PAH luminosity is 5.5 x 10-8 L⊙ and the star-formation rate is 1.2 M⊙/year. The relative strengths of the PAH bands indicate that the predominant energy source heating the dust is star-formation, rather than the AGN. We also examine the ionized gas component of the galaxy, finding that it contributes 1% of the total infrared luminosity. We estimate that the star-formation rate in the ring is 235 M⊙/year. We perform a analysis of the spectral line energy distribution to determine the distribution of dense gas in the ring. We estimate the gas mass to be 1.1 x 10-4 M⊙. We find that the measured CO-to-H2 mass conversion factor of 4.3 x 10-4 cm3/kg is consistent with that expected in the molecular-rich ring but is a factor of

Two laser pulses, separated by a meter, are used to demonstrate frequency upshifting by a relativistic flying mirror through two colliding laser pulses. The key element in the demonstration is a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) holding a quantum mechanical number of 87 sodium atoms. The BEC is cigar-shaped and is flying at a speed of 7 × 108 m/s through the space between the two laser pulses. The two laser pulses have wavevectors forming an angle of 23.5 degrees, leading to a well-defined Bragg interaction between the BEC and the photons. The frequency of the BEC is observed to upshift by 7.6 MHz, which corresponds to a phase shift of 11 radians. The BEC is found to remain intact with almost all atoms in the initial ground state. The experimental demonstration of frequency upshifting by a relativistic flying mirror is an important step towards achieving faster-than-light communication and transportation by exploiting quantum nonlinear dynamics.

Dust emissions at long wavelengths (far-infrared, or FIR) are a powerful diagnostic tool for tracing the distribution of mass in galaxies and are of critical importance for studies of galaxy evolution. We present new statistical analyses of the far-infrared emission from the Revised Guide to Galaxies’ and Mean redshifts 0.2 and 0.4. The M51- Nearby Galaxy Sample (M51-NGS) consists of 126 normal galaxies at low and high redshifts with Spitzer Infrared Nearby Galaxies Survey (SINGS) and Hershel Heritage Area Survey (HHAS) data, observed with similar far-infrared wavelength coverage and resolution. Using a Bayesian maximum a posteriori method, we characterize the spatial distribution of the total far-infrared luminosity, L{FIR}, the surface density of star formation (which we term {Sigma}sf) and the power-law index of the stellar initial mass function ( IMF) in each galaxy. We also examine correlations between {Sigma}sf, L{FIR}, and the galaxy stellar mass, M*, and find that L{FIR}, {Sigma}sf and the power-law index of the IMF are all independent of redshift within the errors, while {Sigma}sf and L{FIR} both increase with stellar mass for both the local and high-redshift samples. Our results provide a comprehensive view of the physical processes that regulate star formation in normal galaxies and also provide a basis for understanding the role of star formation in galaxy evolution.

In this paper, we present a quantum gauge theory in Euclidean space-time, defined by a path integral over connection configurations A μ = − i β ̂γ μ A β ̂ + ω μ, where γ μ are vierbein 4 × 4 matrices, A μ are gauge field configurations, β are Lagrange multiplier matrices, and ωμ are a divergence-free vector gauge field. In the Hamiltonian formulation, the resulting effective action has a local term, proportional to | det ( β ) |2, a standard Yang-Mills term, and a non-local Pontryagin-like term. For flat space, the non-local term gives rise to an effective, 4D gravitational action, with Newton's constant | det ( β ) |2 and a renormalizable, non-local Planck mass proportional to the scalar curvature of β. We discuss renormalization and cosmological constant problems in this theory, as well as possible higher curvature corrections to the effective action.

ANNNI model is an archetypal paradigm for studying phase transitions in physical systems. This paper reports the discovery of a floating phase, wherein the interface between two different phases remains bound to the system boundary. This was discovered during the course of studying the model on a square lattice using Monte Carlo simulation. The discovery was validated using renormalization group analysis for the defect-free version of the model and finite size scaling for the case with defects. The implications of this discovery for understanding phase transitions in physical systems with boundary constraints is discussed. The ANNNI model [1] is a paradigm for studying structural phase transitions in physical systems. The model has three competing interactions, two of which are nearest neighbor and one is next-nearest neighbor. The model has two phases: ferromagnet (FM) and antiferromagnet (AFM). The transition between these phases is second order and characterized by the rise in temperature or some other control parameter. The model has been used to understand phenomena as diverse as the glassy nature of spin systems, competition between biological species and influence of social pressure on human behavior. The discovery of a floating phase, wherein the interface between two phases remains bound to the system boundary is reported in this paper. This was discovered during the course of studying the model on a square lattice using Monte Carlo simulation. The discovery was validated using renormalization group analysis for the defect-free version of the model and finite size scaling for the case with defects. The implications of this discovery for understanding phase transitions in physical systems with boundary constraints is discussed.

In this paper, we report the vortex formation by merging and interference of multiple trapped Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). We have prepared a double BEC consisting of two different hyperfine states of 7 atomic bosons and successfully observed the merger and interference of two independent vortices. The merger process of the two vortices was clearly observed as a dark-bright pair, which was finally reduced to a single vortex with a clear phase singularity. We also observed the phase singularity of the single vortex behavior under a rotational oscillation and observed that the decay of this phase singularity was affected by the interaction between the two vortices. Our results demonstrate that by merging and interference of multiple independently prepared vortices, one can potentially generate highly non-trivial and novel quantum many-body states. This research was published in Nature Physics on June 6, 2019 and was led by Dr. Dmitry Petrov (Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology).

We present the results of a CCD $B$ and $V$ photoelectric survey of a 5$\times$ 5 area in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). The complete sample consists of 575 stars in the magnitude range $17.5 < B < 18.5$. The analysis of the turnoff region is used to determine the distance to the Cloud. The color of the turnoff region, which is due to the Spread in Magang Allen parameter, is used to derive an upper limit on the age of the system. Furthermore we find evidence that the star formation in the SMC was more extended in the recent past than at present. The observed width of the Turnoff region is in reasonable agreement with model predictions for an instantaneous burst of star formation 10-12 million years ago and an age of the system of between 11 and 13 million years. The turnoff region in the SMC is affected by the presence of old stars which contaminate the sample. The distribution of these stars is analyzed and used to evaluate the completeness of the sample. The analysis was performed on three fields, each with a different spatial coverage, and revealed that the completeness is $\approx$ 95% for stars brighter than the turnoff region and $m_B \leq 16.5$.

Graphene is a flat monolayer of carbon atoms tightly packed into a two dimensional honeycomb lattice. It has been studied for decades due to its unusual physical properties. Depending on its interaction with light, graphene exhibits either conductive or reflective behaviour. Graphene is perhaps best known for its perfect reflectivity in the visible spectrum. While this remarkable property has been widely exploited in scientific research, optical studies of graphene have mostly relied on its reflection using traditional light microscopy. This experimental method provides only surface measurements and does not allow access to the underlying microstructure. Scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) can probe the nanoscale structure of surfaces, but its application to graphene has been limited by its inherent interaction with light. Here we demonstrate high resolution, optical transmission microscopy of graphene with atomic resolution. We employ sparsely roughened graphene samples to avoid interference from surface scattering. This enables us to detect contrast variations arising from atomic displacements in the substrate, which we attribute to graphene’s atomic structure. The analysis of atomic periodicity reveals threefold symmetry characteristic of the hexagonal structure of graphene. This is the first observation of ripples in graphene by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The measurements were performed at 120keV electron energy on large area graphene samples. Our approach can be applied to study other two-dimensional crystals, such as molybdenum disulphide, a promising material for next generation electronics.

Wreath products are generalizations of semidirect products, in which one factor is embedded in the other in a way that preserves the group structure of each. Examples of wreath products include the diasoup product, in which a finite group acts on itself by conjugation, and the normalizer, in which a subgroup is embedded as a normal subgroup. We introduce a new family of examples generalizing both of these, the entrelacement, in which the vector representation of a Lie algebra is embedded as a subrepresentation. We study its representation theory and interpret certain symmetric and exterior powers as symplectic reductions. We also determine all examples for type A and B, and compute the example for type C in two special cases. This paper studies a family of examples of wreath products generalizing both diasoup products and normalizer products. In the normalizer product, one group is embedded as a normal subgroup of another, and the subgroup acts on the first by conjugation. Diasoup products are a special case of normalizer products in which one group is embedded as a normal subgroup. We introduce the entrelacement product, in which a Lie algebra is embedded as a subalgebra. We study its representation theory and interpret certain symmetric and exterior powers as symplectic reductions. We also determine all examples for Lie algebras of type A and B, and compute the example for type C in two special cases. Entrelacement occurs in several areas of mathematics, including symplectic geometry, quantum mechanics, dynamical systems, and algebraic combinatorics. The cohomology of homogeneous spaces for these groups has a rich representation theory, and in particular, symmetric and exterior powers often appear as representations. In these cases, we can study the action of the embedding Lie algebra on these subrepresentations, which leads to our definition of the entrelacement product. In particular, we apply this to study the symplectic reduction of the vector representation of a Lie algebra by an associated Lie subgroup. We study examples from several areas, including classical mechanics, semisimple Lie groups and Poisson Lie groups, algebraic combinatorics, orthogonal and symplectic groups, and quantum groups. We find, as special cases, well-known examples such as symplectic reduction, diasoup product, and normalizer product. We compute all examples for Lie algebras of type A and B, and in two special cases for Lie algebras of type C. An important application of our construction is in understanding the cohomology of symplectic reductions. For example, for an adjoint group G, a subgroup H, and a linear representation V of G, the subspace of invariants forms a representation of the central extension of the normalizer N(H), and restricting to H induces a symplectic reduction of V modulo H, whose symplectic structure may be retrieved from the Poisson structure on N(H). We compute the same symplectic reduction for many examples arising from entrelacement. This allows us to determine the cohomology of symplectic reductions and in particular, we compute the cohomology ring of symplectic

Quadratic forms in computer arithmetic are commonly evaluated using multiplication, which is efficient only for relatively large values. We present a fast algorithm for evaluating quadratic forms based on reducing the number of digits using p-adic arithmetic. This algorithm, which we call the p-adic quasi-quadratic point (PQPA), avoids computational complex exponentials and powers, making it faster for small values. We prove that our method is effective for PQPA and apply the algorithm to explicit points on curves. The PQPA algorithm uses the three operations in computer arithmetic: addition, subtraction, and multiplication. These operations can be evaluated more quickly by keeping the number of digits small, avoiding computational complex exponential and powers. We will evaluate a quadratic form as a sum of terms of the form x*x, where each x is a digit in some base. The algorithm recursively reduces the number of digits of each x, as long as this does not change the quadratic form. It reduces the problem to evaluating a sum of terms x0*x0*x1*x1, where x0 and x1 are the leading digits of the x's. We call this sum PQ1(x0,x1). This sum is either 0 (if all of the x0's and x1's are 1) or can be evaluated using PQ1(divide each x0 by some prime p, multiply each result by some prime q, and add the results). The algorithm terminates when the sum is 0, because this means all the x's are 1, or when the sum cannot be so evaluated for some reason, which we call PQ0. PQ0 implies that the quadratic form is zero, but not the other way around. We prove that the algorithm is correct, and thus find all the PQ0's, by showing that PQ0 and PQ1 satisfy the same recurrence and that the same initial values lead to the same sum. We evaluate each quadratic form using PQ1 when possible and switch to multiplications when this is not possible. We test our algorithm on random quadratic forms and on the evaluation of points on elliptic curves. For random forms, we find that quadratic forms in small integers are typically nonzero, with probability 0.5, and that all nonzero forms have at least one nonzero term. For the evaluation of points on elliptic curves, we find that our algorithm typically terminates in a few minutes using a single-threaded implementation on a laptop computer, even for very small explicit points. We present this algorithm in order to introducep-adic arithmetic and the PQ1 recurrence. We highlight two applications: fast evaluation of quadratic forms and finding all quadratic forms that evaluate to 0, which are often related to zero-dimensional systems in number theory.

In standard cosmological models, structures form from the gravitational instability of Gaussian random initial density perturbations. As a result, the phase-space distribution of gravitationally bound structures is typically closely approximated by a multi-variate Gaussian in position and velocity. Observations of the motions of stars and gas in galaxies and clusters can be used to determine the mass distribution of these systems. In contrast, measurements of the distribution of dark matter suggest the presence of significant small-scale power, even at very large cosmological scales: the dark matter possesses an (approximately) infinite set of spherical shells of preferred radius. If dark matter is colloidal particles with similar properties to dust, formed from an ordinary matter ‘sweepup’ in the early structure of the universe, then it is a logical expectation that the local environment of a dark matter halo will differ from the global average, due to fluctuations in the gravitational potential associated with the large-scale structure.

We present optical imaging spectroscopy of six galaxy clusters identified in the redshift range 0.2≤z≤0.6 from the Dark Energy Survey year 1 data. The clusters were observed as part of the KiDS (Kilo-Degree Survey) cluster survey, and the data have been reduced with the dielectron pipeline. We measure the red sequence luminosity function (RSLF) and colour distribution for each cluster, and estimate the total cluster light by scaling the individual RSLF galaxy contributions using the observed red sequence width. We fit a Schechter function to the RSLF and measure the bright end slope, α. We measure a median value of α=-1.22±0.03, with a distribution that peaks at α=-1.28. These values are consistent with previous studies in this redshift range, and suggest that luminous red galaxies dominate the cluster member population out to z=0.6.

We present cosmological parameter constraints from a joint analysis of thewiggle tomography and cosmic shear power spectra, with focus on the impact of intrinsic alignments (IA). Our tomographicwiggle power spectra include the intrinsic alignment shear contribution defined in @Hirata:Kodama:Padmanabhan:2012, and we present the first cosmological parameter constraints from this analysis. We forecast the constraining power of future surveys by calculating the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for varying level of IA parameter, $\alpha_{\mathrm{IA}}$. We show that for a Ly$\alpha$ survey like the Mitchell Spectrograph, with $\sigma_P(l_{\mathrm{max}})=0.023$ ($95\%$ confidence level), $\alpha_{\mathrm{IA}}=0.35$ (which corresponds to a bias of the IA model of $b_{\mathrm{IA}}=1.1$), and a photometric redshift error of $\sigma_z/(1+z)=0.05$, one can obtain a maximum of SNR=2 for the neutrino mass of $\Sigma m_\nu<0.22$ eV (95% confidence level). For a tomographic survey like SPT-3G with $\sigma_P(l_{\mathrm{max}})=0.016$ ($95\%$ confidence level), one can constrain the sum of neutrino masses to $\Sigma m_\nu<0.12$ eV at maximum SNR. The neutrino mass is most affected by IA for SPT-3G and Ly$\alpha$ surveys, while the neutrino mass constraint for PLANCK is dominated by the uncertainty in the CMB measurement. The inclusion of IA weakens the constraint on the sum of neutrino masses by $\sim 50\%$ for Ly$\alpha$ and SPT-3G surveys, while it has a negligible impact on the PLANCK measurement. The inclusion of IA yields approximately 10% error on the Hubble parameter $H_0$, and the impact on the other cosmological parameters are of the order of a few percent.

We present a new mechanism for the emergence of a shallow decay phase in the X-ray afterglows of some gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The canonical late time decay index of a typical afterglow is -1.2, but we show that a shallower decay index of -0.8 is possible if the initial fireball is relatively loaded with circumburst matter. The shallow decay phase emerges due to late time absorption by circumburst material of X-ray radiation from a relativistic wind that is driven by the activity of the central engine. The conditions for this to occur are that the wind is relatively slow, with a Lorentz factor of γ_w < (0.3-0.5)γ_b, where γ_b is the bulk Lorentz factor of the initial fireball. The wind interacts with the initially narrow shocked blastwave, producing a forward and reverse shock configuration. The forward shock driving the initial blastwave stalls, and the resulting circumburst density profile is consistent with that of a constant density atmosphere with scaleheight z_c= 500-1000 m. The shallower late time decay phase can account for the relatively bright X-ray afterglows of several GRBs, including the unusual short GRB 150903A. We suggest that a significant fraction of short GRBs may have a circumburst medium with significant scaleheight.

The variation of sunspot number is one of the important indicators of solar activity. However, the accuracy of sunspot number data obtained by observation stations is affected by random error and short-time effect. Therefore, to predict the future solar cycles, it is necessary to take both these factors into consideration. Here we propose a data-driven method to predict future solar cycle by using all available cycles since 1750 and employing artificial neural network. The prediction result shows that there will be 15 solar cycles between 2016 and 2116, and the maximum sunspot number of next cycle will be about 220. The prediction result is consistent with the past two cycles, and the accuracy is higher than most of the existing method.' The key to successfully predict the future solar cycle is to eliminate the impact of short-time effect and random error. This is achieved by using the Neural network with sufficient neurons and sufficient training cycles. The strong self-adaptive capacity and nonlinear mapping ability of Neural network are very suitable for this problem, which can not only eliminate the impact of short-time effect, but also reflect the periodic regularity of solar activity. The prediction result shows that the maximum deviation of sunspot number between prediction and observation is less than 10%, and the average deviation is about 7%.

A significant number of galaxies have been detected in the deep field surveys with luminosities far in excess of their estimated star formation rates. These Hyper-Luminous Infrared Galaxies (HyLIRG) are of particular interest as possible probes of galaxy evolution in extreme environment. In this paper, we study six HyLIRGs with available X-ray data from the XMM-Newton observatory. These include four E+A (post-starburst) galaxies, IRAS F09230– Mo1, IRAS F00183–7 Jam1, IRAS F00397–7537 and ClG J2218.1+0052, and two late-type HyLIRGs, IRAS F00183–7 Jam2 and ClG J2218.1-0053. All except IRAS F09230– Mo1 have starburst-driven winds which are well detected in X-rays, but none have elevated absorption, suggesting that the HyLIRG phenomenon may be caused by extreme gas-rich mergers.

In this paper, we develop a mathematical model for tuberculosis (TB) infection considering three different states: susceptible (S), latent (E) and active (I) TB. The model incorporates TB infection process, as well as the transfer between the three TB states. The model is analyzed using dynamical systems theory, and we find that the system has both stable and unstable manifolds. Then, we use the pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) data from Hunan Province, China from 2012 to 2016 as reported by The National Health and Family Planning Commission of the People's Republic of China to simulate the model, and the results show that the model can correctly represent the PTB dynamics. We also apply the model to forecast the possible future of PTB in China until 2022. Finally, possible extensions of the model are discussed. Keywords: tuberculosis, pulmonary tuberculosis, nonlinear dynamics, transfer. Impedance of electroceramic functional oxide thermistors was measured over a frequency range of 10 mHz to 10 kHz and temperatures between -55 °C and 150 °C. The measurements were performed using a network analyzer in the reflection mode. The electroceramic functional oxide thermistor is a solid solution of barium and strontium lanthanum zirconate (Ba,Sr)(La,Zr)2(Sn,Ti)3O12. The impedance decreases with temperature between -55 °C and 100 °C and levels off above 100 °C. The imaginary part of the impedance decreases with frequency between 10 mHz and 0.1 kHz and increases above 0.1 kHz. The real part of impedance increases with frequency between 10 mHz and 0.1 kHz and levels off above 0.1 kHz. The material properties and the temperature and frequency dependence of the impedance can be modified by varying the composition and the doping of the electroceramic functional oxide. These modifications suggest that the impedance is dependent on the domain size of oxygen vacancies.

This work presents the sensitivity analysis of MICS Asia Phase II Daily Gridded Data products to the Aerosol Module for both Drought and Non-drought seasons. The analysis indicates that the MICS Asia Phase II Aerosol product are generally robust to the choice of Aerosol optical depth for both seasons. However, there are a few channels which were found to be significantly impacted by choice of AOD inputs. These are the channels corresponding to AOD measured by IASI over Southern India, and the AOD measured by MISR over the Eastern Pacific Ocean. The analysis also indicates that MICS Asia Phase II AOD product are more sensitive to AOD computed using the correlated thinNRG and DRF models for the drought season. This can be due to the contribution of AOD over the Indian region in the drought season which is not well captured by the correlated models. In terms of AOD sources, the analysis suggests that ignoring the AOD contribution fromBoundary layer and molecular species may significantly impact the MICS Asia Phase II AOD product in the drought season. This paper is a product from the MICS Asia Phase II Technical Internal Review.

Infrared data from 11 μm is crucial for studying cooler objects in our Solar System, such as small bodies and comets, and for tracing materials in the interstellar medium. AKARI is a cryogenic infrared telescope with three channels centered at 3, 4, and 11 μm. The AKARI North Ecliptic Pole Deep survey observed a large area of the northern hemisphere in the extended mission phase. 11 μm data provide more complete picture of the source properties and its variation than other channels. Fluxes of point sources at 11 μm are presented as a function of various parameters including heliocentric distance, plane-of-sky position, and the wavelengths. The 11 μm sources are categorized as follows: 1) Crystalline silicates such as enstatite and forsterite; 2) Amorphous silicates such as forsterite and olivine; 3) Carbonaceous dust; 4) Other sources such as comets and YSOs. The 11 μm fluxes from these sources show similar heliocentric distance dependence. Comparison with optical data suggests that the 11 μm fluxes from some YSO candidates are overpredicted. We discuss the implications for planet formation around observed small bodies and the interstellar medium.

Aim: We present the results of a multi-year Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) survey of 27 RL AGNs selected from the Red-sequence Cluster Surveys (RGB) with H band data from the ground-based Relativistic Jet Monitoring program (RJMF). Seven of our targets have not been previously reported to undergo strong parsec-scale relativistic de-magnification. From our data we detect radio structure on milliarcsecond (mas) scales for 18 out of the 27 sources, some of which show dramatic variability across our 4 year observing window. This variability strongly suggests that the SMBHs in these targets are undergoing episodes of relativistic de-magnification, an event which has previously only been observed in the jet of M87. Here we discuss several key implications of our findings, including the frequency of occurrence of parsec-scale de-magnification, the connection between parsec-scale structure and broader-band variability, and the extent to which parsec-scale structure in RGs may reflect lower-energy versions of the more extreme features seen in quasars. We discuss future work that can be done using the RGB program and the VLBA, as well as potential physical implications of our findings.

In this article, we study the distribution of the strongest of a subset of fixed size of peak points of a probability measure. This is motivated by statistical problems arising in processing High-Definition Television (HDTV) material. The analysis of the distribution of the strong peak points has three purposes: 1/ signal enhancement in Television signals, 2/ image processing (e.g. for noise reduction or detail enhancement), 3/ denoising (removing unwanted noise from an image). We show that the distribution of the strongest of a subset of fixed size of peak points of a probability measure exhibits two well-distinguished regimes. In the first one, the density of the strong peak points is lower than the density of all peak points (the so-called sparse regime). In the second one, the density of the strong peak points is higher than the density of all peak points (the dense regime). The article is organized as follows: The second section presents some preliminary notions on the notion of strong peaks and the properties of the strong peak functions. The third section is devoted to the proof of the lower bound of the strong peak densities. The fourth section is devoted to the proof of the upper bound of the strong peak densities. The last section is devoted to some practical applications of these new densities. Our article is an updated and expanded version of the work published on arXiv.org on June 1, 2015 (doi: 10.1016/j.jcvs.2015.05.004).

An ansatz for the asymptotics of hypergeometric multisums is given. It involves applying Laplace's method to integral representations for hypergeometric multisums. Assuming a certain non-vanishing condition on the parameters, it is shown that the Laplace transform of the multisum tends to a positive or negative constant, depending on whether the sum comprises even or odd values only. Explicit error bounds are derived in terms of elementary functions, and numerical examples are presented for some small values of the involved parameters. The ansatz is illustrated by the analysis of two specific multisums. It is first shown that, for any positive integer $n$, one has $$\label{1} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(a+k)^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}x^2}\bigg\vert_{x=0}F(a+k,a+n;a+n;1-t)=\frac{n}{a}F(a,a+1;a+n+1;1)+\mathcal{O}\big(n^{3/2}\big)$$ as $n\to +\infty$, where $F(a_1,\dots,a_r;b_1,\dots,b_r;1-t)$ is the Watson series defined by the iterated integral $$\begin{aligned} F(a_1,\dots,a_r;b_1,\dots,b_r;1-t)&=\prod_{i=1}^r\frac{\Gamma(1-b_i)}{\Gamma(a_i+1-b_i)}\cdot\frac{\Gamma(t)}{\Gamma(t+1-a_1-\dots-a_r)}\\ &\quad\times\int_0^{1/(1-t)}\dots\int_0^{1/(1-t)} \prod_{i=1}^r\frac{dt_i}{t_i^{a_i+1-b_i}\Gamma(t_i)}\prod_{1\le i<j\le r}(t_j-t_i)^{-1}.\end{aligned}$$ The right-hand side of the above equation is interpreted as $0$ when any one of the $a_i+1$s is a non-positive integer. Secondly, it is shown that, for any odd integer $n$, one has $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^{(n-1)/2}\frac{\cosh(\pi(a+k)/2)}{(a+k)^2}\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}x^2}\bigg\vert_{x=0}F(a+k,a+n;a+n;1-t)&=\frac{1}{2

A paper introducing viability, limitations and potential sources of error of using gyrochronology to determine stellar ages. The viability of the method is demonstrated using a sample of 48 stars for which rotational period, T_{c}, and surface age are known from other means. The limitation of the method, expected from the theory behind it, is also demonstrated using the sample. The limitations of the method arise from the dependence of T_{c} on composition, which results in a degeneracy between age and metallicity. The potential sources of error are also discussed. The sample is from the IAC-80 visual binary star catalogue (IAC-80), consisting of 48 G-type stars for which rotation period (T_{c}), effective temperature, surface age and metallicity are known. The projected equatorial rotation rates (VΩ/sin(i)) were obtained from T_{c}, which were calculated using the rotational period and temperature from the Infrared Flux Method. Using the Babel code, an estimate of the gyrochronological age was made. The surface age was compared with the true age to determine if the gyrochronology is viable for determining ages of G-type stars. The reliability of the method is demonstrated using a two-sample t-test, the proportion of constant stars, the Scholz radius test and the gyrochronology - chromchronology plot. Gyrochronology is shown to be viable for determining the ages of G-type stars, with a mean error of -2.2% indicating that for most stars the gyrochronological age is within 10% of the true age. The limitations of the method arise from the dependence of T_{c} on composition, which results in a degeneracy between age and metallicity. The gyrochronology - chromchronology plot demonstrates the limitations of the method by showing T_{c} versus surface age with metallicity over-plotted as a separate series.

The observed changes in the length of the sidereal day allow one to determine the motion of the Earth around the sun in the galactic reference frame with an accuracy of 10 km/s. For the first time direct measurements of the rotation curve of the dark matter halo of the Milky Way are performed. The resulting value of the rotation velocity at the distance of the Sun from the Galactic Center V0 is equal to 254.23 ± 0.55 km/s. remnance of a long paper... The observation of the sidereal day change (SODC) opens new possibilities for the investigation of the motion of the Earth around the sun (planets' orbit) and more generally of the motion of the Solar System in the galaxy (Galilean satellites). The most precise SODC measurements are obtained for the outer planets of the solar system (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune). The accuracy of the distance determination from the SODC depends on the quality of the satellite laser ranges (SLR) used and on the knowledge of the satellites' parameters, their positions, velocities and representations in the Earth's reference frame (equations of state). The knowledge of the positions and velocities of the planets requires the use of observational data, for which various ephemerides are developed, based on either observations or theories. A frequency analysis of the SODC allows one to determine the solar system's motion with an accuracy of 10 km/s. It also allows a new determination of the rotation curve of the Milky Way's dark matter halo. The resulting value of the rotation velocity at the distance of the Sun from the Galactic Center V0 is equal to 254.23 ± 0.55 km/s. The SODC of the sidereal day (sidereal year = 365.25 days) is the variation in the length of the day as observed from a given location in the sky due to the motion of the Earth around the sun. The SODC is proportional to the mass of the planets and to their mean motion around the sun. The latter can be expressed in terms of the eccentricity e, the inclination i and the longitude of the ascending node $\Omega$. The frequency of the SODC is the mean motion of the planet divided by the sidereal day, i.e., 2π/Ne, where Ne is the mean motion. The SODC was observed for the first time in 1639 by Christiaan Huygens, using the satellite body of the deities of the Seven Churches of the Apocalypse which he had placed under his personal protection. For many years, this was the only possible way to measure the Earth's motion. The SODC is currently measured for the outer planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune). From the SODC, the variation in the sidereal day (sidereal year) is determined by measuring the arrival time of a laser

Recent observations have revealed that a large fraction of main sequence stars have companions. Planets around these stars, known as planet circumbinary, are expected to have different formation histories from planets around single stars. Planet circumbinaryimals can form in situ in the circumbinary disk via planetesimal growth; however, core accretion typically takes longer than the disk lifetime and lacks the necessary leftover material to grow gas giants. In situ formation also requires planet compositions to be mostly icy, which conflicts with the the detection of hot Jupiter systems which have mostly rocky compositions. Here, we suggest that the cores of circumbinary planets can be formed outside the binary system and migrate in. The cores can then grow further via pebble accretion within the inner stable orbit of a much wider circumbinary disk. This avoids the need for icy compositions and fast migration times. We confirm that our model can form super-Earths within the habitable zone of current observations, while still permitting stable systems of gas giants similar to our single star systems.

The kappa1 Ceti system, located about 39.3 light years from the Earth, is an excellent candidate for the detection of extrasolar planets. The most recent data from the MOST satellite, which provide the best measurements of the system's rotation period to date, reveal that kappa1 Ceti is impacted by an unseen companion that causes a Differential Rotation effect. The kappa1 Ceti system was the first system to be proposed for detection of extrasolar planets by the Line-Of-Sight Satellite (MOST) satellite. MOST observed kappa1 Ceti over multiple nights in 2007, 2009, 2011, and 2013 and were able to significantly detect the wobble of kappa1 Ceti due to the effect of an unseen companion on the host star. Observations over multiple years confirm the change in the direction of the Companion's motion relative to the star, providing evidence for a massive companion orbiting the star in a nearly circular orbit. The Companion's minimum mass was estimated at 3.16 times the mass of Jupiter, and its expected orbital period was determined to be approximately 5.2 years. The differential rotation effect, which causes a slower-than-average surface rotation on stars that are orbited by massive companions, was first detected in the kappa1 Ceti system. It has since been observed in at least 21 additional systems, most of which are also suitable candidates for detection of extrasolar planets. In addition to the companion, kappa1 Ceti appears to host a stellar activity cycle of approximately 30.4 days. Although the cause of this cycle is not well understood, it may be related to the existence of a planet-migration mechanism, in which giant planets interact with their host stars and disturb orbital resonances that cause periodic changes in the host star's activity. Overall, the kappa1 Ceti system provides an excellent observational laboratory for studying star-planet interactions and planet migration, as well as a potential target for the detection of exoplanets. Inter comparison of the magneto transport of La2/3Ca1/3MnO3: Ag/In polycrystalline composites was performed at different temperatures. La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 is a robust layered perovskite-like structured material which offers an attractive option for high temperature solid oxide fuel cell applications due to its high working temperature (around 700 °C). The magneto transport properties were studied by measuring the magnetic susceptibility, electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility simultaneously with varying temperature and magnetic field. La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 showed a mixed- valence electron ferromagnetism with S = 1/2 at low temperature. At intermediate temperatures (around 200 °C), a slight deviation from the Curie-Weiss law was noticed which may be related to spin fluctuation. Finally, at high temperature (around 700 °C), La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 revealed a Pauli paramagnetic behaviour with a drastic decrease in the electrical resistivity. The variation of magneto transport properties with temperature were well correlated and this correlation may be useful in order to evaluate the suitability of La2/3Ca1/3MnO3 for various high temperature applications.

In three-dimensional topology, the Thurston norm is a natural generalisation of the Euler characteristic. Although its definition makes sense for any 3-manifold, it has been characterised only for representations of its fundamental group in the special linear group, over the field of complex numbers. We show that the Thurston norm may be computed by considering any such representation in the standard 3-space, over the field of real numbers. As a consequence, we provide a new proof that certain normal surfaces in knot complements are taut: every smoothly embedded disk in these surfaces has odd multiplicity at each of its points. The proof is based on work of Agol,boileau and C.T.CTseng, and of Rosenthal and of Sivek, on the prime decomposition of the normal surface, and of Gay, on the field of complex numbers--real number version of the classical theorem of Grauert-Remmert. We also provide a new proof that the fibre surface of a normal surface in a knot complement is strongly norm SP surfaces.

The stability of compressible viscous shock profiles has been a subject of intense research for many decades. Existing results are primarily limited to low Mach number shocks, for which disturbances grow at most exponentially with distance behind the shock. In this paper we consider the stability of high-Mach number isentropic viscous shock profiles, or more specifically their expansion at large Rayleigh number. We prove that disturbances with small wavelength in phase space—in a sense defined precisely below—satisfy a linearized version of the extended Prandtl equation, from which one can conclude linear growth of the disturbances at least in a bounded spatial domain. To show nonlinear stability, we exploit a heuristic analogy to the inviscid Burgers equation and show self-similar growth at the maximum possible rate. Our analysis does not cover disturbances with large wavelengths—prohibiting a proof of nonlinear stability by energy methods—but nonetheless suggests that such waves are not present. We provide some numerical evidence for this in the form of direct simulations, and also compute the relevant growth rates for certain wavelengths, confirming the linear analysis.

A real-time renormalization group (RT-RG) is applied to a quantum dot system in the Coulomb blockade regime. The conductance through the dot is computed as a function of the system’s parameters, namely the gate and bias voltages, as well as the plunger (i.e., orbital) number of the dot. A separation between low- and high-energy scales is established by a smallness parameter which is assumed to be the bias voltage scaled by a large energy, e.g., the plunger energy. Exact solution is obtained by truncating the hierarchy of integro-differential equations at the second member. In this approximation the conductance is parameterized by the solution of a closed set of differential equations. Our solution method allows us to study a wide range of the system’s parameters. In particular, we compute a crossover from tunneling to charge-transfer regimes as the system is tuned from an initial almost empty dot to a filled dot. Furthermore, we compute a cutoff energy and a cutoff scale that separate slow (i.e., flowing with the system’s parameters) from fast (i.e., independent) scales in the system. The former dependence is captured by the effective theory, whereas the latter is absorbed into therunning (i.e., evolving) cutoff scale. This provides a powerful method to explore a nonequilibrium quantum dot problem as one varies the plunger (orbital) number and gate voltage. In particular, this allows one to locate a parameter regime where a given nonequilibrium steady state was not reached during the system’s evolution from some initial conditions. For example, we find that if the initial state of the quantum dot is almost empty (filled), then the conductance through the dot is minimal (maximinal) at the Coulomb blockade peak of the dot’s conductance.

Recently, the B0 -> D*- l+ nu_l decay was observed by the LHCb Collaboration. The analysis of the corresponding semileptonic decay B0 -> D* l nu_l was performed, using a data sample of 658x10^6 B0 decays, recorded by the LHCb experiment in 2012 and 2013, and containing 37.9x10^6 semileptonic B0 decays. The form factors for this decay were obtained from a combined isospin and heavy quark expansion, with the parameters obtained from a combined light-meson and heavy-quark effective theory analysis of the B0 -> D* l nu_l decay. The obtained form factors were used to calculate the branching fraction, which was found to be (1.20 \pm 0.06)x10^-4. The resulting value of the ratio |V_{cb}| of the CKM matrix elements between the D* l and D l semileptonic decays was calculated using the heavy-quark symmetry. The result, |V_{cb}|=(40.6 \pm 1.5 \pm 2.8)x10^-3, is the most precise measurement to date, and it is consistent with the result of the global fit of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix.

This paper develops a continuum theory of thin fluid-like sheets with in-plane axial stretch and bending. The resulting nonlinear theory encompasses many models in mechanics of materials and condensed matter physics and describes a wide range of physical phenomena ranging from mechanics of biological structures and polymer electrolytes to a quantum Hall effect on the surface of a three-dimensional topological insulator. The generic model introduced here can be realized in engineered systems of electrons or vacancies embedded in graphene, topological insulators, phosphorene, or other similar two-dimensional materials. The rest of the paper is focused on application of the theory to electromechanical systems, in particular, to nanostructures like two-dimensional crystals, polymer films, and opal films. Special attention is payed to the transverse electric (transverse magnetic) phonons in a two-dimensional crystal (film) as well as to optical modes in a thin photonic crystal. The analysis is illustrated with a number of examples of the application of the theory to concrete nanomechanical and photonic systems.

The relationship between Albert Einstein and the avant-garde art movements in the early part of the 20th century was tenuous at best. For instance, Einstein was an outspoken critic of Marcel Duchamp’s Readymades, and even refused to call his prize winning theory on the photoelectric effect ‘his’ theory. Yet, while most art historians have long since rejected the idea that Einstein was an admirer of the radical new movements that swept the European continent in the early part of the last century, Einstein’s opinions on these movements are still a matter of debate. In this article, I will examine the relationship between Einstein and three of the key figures of early 20th century avant-garde art: Francis Picabia, Marcel Duchamp, and Kurt Schwitters. I will argue that while the two were clearly in opposition to one another, there are several points of contact between their respective artistic practices. For example, both Duchamp and Einstein made use of appropriation as a part of their respective artistic expression, they were both interested in disrupting the realistic expectations of their audience, and they were both interested in pushing the boundaries of what it meant to be a ‘artist’. I will also discuss how each artist’s relationship to Einstein may have been colored by their respective locations in Europe at the time. In particular, I will argue that while Duchamp was based in France, and thus may have been more exposed to Einstein’s criticism than the other two artists, who were based in German-occupied Europe, and thus may have been more sympathetic to Einstein’s attitudes. I will close by discussing the implications of these points of contact for how we should think about the relationship between art and science.

A microscopic theory of macroscopic quantum tunneling (MQT) in high-T_c c-axis Josephson junctions is developed. Based on a two-well tunnel Hamiltonian and an instanton method, the theory can well explain a series of recent experiments, including the MQT peak structures in I-V curves, the temperature dependence of the MQT currents, and the parametric resonance driving MQT without invoking any (spontaneous) symmetry breaking. The theory unifies the descriptions of both reversible and irreversible MQT processes. Moreover, a small bias current may induce a large resonant MQT current, in sharp contrast to the almost negligible resonant tunneling current in previous theories. It is also found that the theory can well predict some new interesting experiments, such as the opposite temperature dependence of the MQT currents in two parallel junctions. The theory is also applied to explain the recently reported enhanced MQT in asymmetric junctions. Furthermore, since the theory can well describe both MQT and conventional (non-MQT) DC Josephson effects, it can explain a large portion of the highly non-linear I-V curves observed in some recent experiments.

Soft repulsive-spheres (RSS), when mixed in varying composition, generally segregate into distinct global phases, with the midrange RSS partial mixing quantity, Q2, being small. Here we report the identification of a wide Q2 range of strong attractive depletion interactions in RSS binary mixtures, even for high RSS packing fractions. Strong depletion interactions emerge as a competition between two distinct interparticle forces, namely, hard sphere steric repulsion and RSS attraction. Using three independent techniques, we find that these depletion forces dominate over other pairwise forces, such as RSS particle wetting, RSS electrostatic interactions and short-range chemical bonding, for a Q2 range spanning three decades. The attractive depletion interactions lead to enhanced RSS demixing at high RSS packing fractions, and formation of unexpectedly rich phase diagrams with two and even three coexisting global phases. The identified strong attractive depletion interactions could find potential uses in tailor-made RSS mixtures with programmable phase diagrams, and for controlling RSS self-assembly in bottom-up nanotechnology and soft robotics.

In this paper, we study the following two stage hybrid and modular inflation: 1. Early hybrid inflation driven by a gauge field coupled to a fundamental scalar and its superpartner. 2. Modular inflation driven by a charged scalar field coupled to gravity. We find that generically these two stages can occur sequentially with the decay of the false vacuum of the first stage producing the curvature perturbations needed for the second stage. This allows the flexibility to choose the parameters of each model without compromising the feasibility of the subsequent stage. The spectrum of the density perturbations is flat in this model. This work is related to the previous paper arXiv:1908.05761 [hep-th] in that we consider a slightly different scenario where the decay of the false vacuum of the first stage does not produce the curvature perturbation but rather enhances it. This work is also related to arXiv:1907.11961 [hep-th] in that we consider a model with multiple stages of inflation and find conditions on the parameters of each stage such that they can follow each other.

Boolean networks have been extensively used to model and study biological systems. Since the models are discrete in nature, they often generate synchronous dynamics, which is hard to validate in real biological systems. Recently, external regulation, a generalization of inhibitions, has been proposed to relax the synchronous assumption and allow for more biologically relevant behavior. In this work, we study the dynamics of random Boolean networks with external regulations. We show that under some conditions on the in-degree of the nodes and the probability of regulations, the network exhibits asynchronous dynamics with a non-trivial phase. We characterize the phase diagram in terms of the threshold parameters, and illustrate its dependence on the parameters via simulations. We also investigate the cluster size distribution and find that it can be either exponential or power law in nature. Finally, we present a mean-field theory that is capable of predicting the overall cluster size for arbitrary system size. @article {osti{128672567{/V uint78} }@files wnio5879 [PDF version of this story] Abstract writes: Asynchronous dynamics has been recently proposed as a generalization of inhibitions in Boolean network models of biological systems. In this work, we study the propagation of external regulations in random Boolean networks. We show that with proper parameters, the network exhibits asynchronous dynamics with a non-trivial phase. The phase diagram is characterized in terms of the threshold parameters, and we illustrate it's dependence on the parameters via numerical simulations. We also investigate the cluster size distribution, and find that it can be either exponential or power law in nature. Finally, we present a mean-field theory that is capable of predicting the overall cluster size for arbitrary system size.

Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have been widely used for monitoring various environments because of their easy deployment and low cost. However, the single-hop structure of WSNs inevitably suffers from serious energy depletion and data transmission bottleneck. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a collaborative beamforming and cooperative transmission scheme to extend network lifetime and improve network connectivity. In the proposed scheme, each sensor node can cooperatively transmit data to the sink with the help of beamforming technique, and these cooperative transmissions can offload the data transmission over the common wireless channels. In addition, a joint relay and beamforming design is proposed to maximize the number of cooperative transmissions and further prolong the network lifetime. Both theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate the significant lifetime improvement of the proposed network model over the conventional schemes. + Bernstein, Eytan; Chi, Ming-Chiang; Golovinski, Ido; Sendonaris, Erkmen; Taylor, John E. The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is an effective theory valid up to the Planck scale, which, despite its remarkable empirical success, remains a profound mystery. Although the SM exhibits an exact electroweak symmetry, this symmetry is actually broken at low energies due to the lack of a true bare symmetry. The SM Lagrangian is chiral, and the presence of this global symmetry (hereafter called chiral symmetry) can be thought of as arising from certain quantization conditions on the underlying manifold on which the theory is defined. To uncover the origins of this symmetry, it is natural to consider unifying the electroweak and strong interactions into a single force mediated by a hypothetical Higgs boson. Such a unification would naturally suggest a larger symmetry group than that of the SM, such as SO(10) or E(6). However, the most common family of such grand unified theories (GUTs) predicts a seemingly small residual symmetry known as the horizontal symmetry, which treats different families differently (for instance, assigning different scalar assignments to up-type and down-type fermions). One can argue that such a horizontal symmetry is an accidental one, arising from the specific scalar representations of the GUT. However, an important loophole in this argument is the lack of a compelling rationale for the observed chiral structure of the SM Lagrangian. If we assume the latter holds at high energies but fails at some low energy scale, this horizontal symmetry would be spontaneously broken, predicting the existence of massless Goldstone bosons. Such bosons, also known as flavors, correspond to the low-energy degrees of freedom from which the electroweak and strong interactions arise. It has been shown that the electroweak and strong interactions can each be described by an affine symmetry, which contains a global symmetry corresponding to the chiral symmetry of the SM. In this letter, we argue that lattice chiral symmetry, rather than horizontal symmetry, may be the correct theory to describe the low-energy behavior of the SM. By carefully studying the phase diagram of a massless two-flavor lattice Dirac fermion at general cubic and quartic couplings, we find that only two phases are consistent with the known empirical facts of the SM. The first, which we refer to as the phase of approximate lattice chirality, exhibits a spontaneously broken reflection symmetry, corresponding to an exact axial symmetry (in the infinite lattice spacing or regularization limit). The second, which we call the phase of exact lattice chirality, exhibits a remnant global symmetry, which is sufficient to decouple the electroweak interactions. In particular, the SM particles are interpreted as the low-energy Nambu-Goldstone bosons of the former phase. As an interesting aside, it is shown that in this phase, the lightest quark carries electric charge. The implications of this result on the landscape of string theory are also discussed.
