On February 8, 2005, the Swift satellite, designed to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), observed the afterglow of a GRB that had been localized by the BeppoSAX satellite and observed by the Parkes radio telescope. Swift was in the process of moving into thebgnd position when the afterglow was observed. The afterglow is double-peaked, with a 1.5 hour separation, a near-infrared smooth grace, and an overall shape that is well-fitted by a power law decay. The observed peak times, both in gamma-rays and in the afterglow, correspond to a lag of approximately 120 seconds between the gamma-ray and afterglow light curves. This lag is much longer than the time delay between peaks in the two components of the double-peaked afterglow, indicating that the optical afterglow and the gamma-ray prompt emission are generated by the same population of ejecta. The shallow decay before the first peak, and the rebrightening at late times, are each well-fitted by a power law decay. The steep decay before the first peak is consistent with a reverse shock moving into the ejecta, while the rebrightening may be caused by energy injection. Alternatively, the rebrightening may be caused by a different component of the GRB afterglow emerging from the darkness of the night.

In this paper, we study the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) epidemic model on dynamic contact networks, in which nodes join and leave the network over time. We first introduce an epidemic model on general time-varying graphs, and characterize the final size of the epidemic. We then study two specific cases of this general model: the first is the epidemic model on a static graph with randomly added edges at random times; the second is the fully dynamic model, in which nodes can be either active or inactive, but no existing edges are removed. We present asymptotic analyses of the final size of these two models, and show that in both cases, the number of infected nodes approaches a constant factor of the number of contacts of a node, up to a logarithmic factor. Finally, we present numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our theoretical analysis. Infectious disease models have been applied to a wide variety of dynamical networks, including time-varying graphs, in which edges are added and removed over time [1, 2], as well as static graphs with randomly deleted edges [3]. Dynamic models have been used to study peer influence in networks [4, 5], topological evolution of networks [6, 7], and epidemic spreading [8, 9]. Some previous work has also analyzed general models on static but random graphs [10, 11], and fully dynamic graphs [12]. We study general models on two types of graphs: static graphs with randomly deleted edges, and fully dynamic graphs in which edges can be either added or deleted. We present an epidemic model on general time-varying graphs, characterize the final size of the epidemic, and conduct asymptotic analyses for the case of a static graph and the fully dynamic model. For the epidemic model on static graphs with randomly deleted edges, we show that the final size of the epidemic is at most a logarithmic factor larger than the number of contacts of a node, up to a constant factor. For the fully dynamic model, we show that the number of infected nodes approaches a constant factor of the number of contacts of a node, up to a logarithmic factor. Our analysis shows that in both cases, the final size of the epidemic is a constant factor times the number of contacts of a node. This constant factor can be large in realistic social networks, where most contacts are casual, and a small number of close contacts can cause a large outbreak. This analysis of general time-varying graphs may be of independent interest, as it provides a mechanism by which the number of contacts of a node can affect the final size of an epidemic. We perform numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our theoretical analysis. In summary, we present general models for epidemic spreading on static and fully dynamic graphs, and characterize the final size of the epidemic. In this paper, we build on the results of the accompanying paper [1], and introduce a new algorithmic framework for solving problems on sequential decision making and multi-dimensional streaming data. The framework, which we call Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods, combines ideas from both sequential decision making and multi-dimensional Monte Carlo simulation. The key idea is to represent the possible sequences of decisions, which depend on the unknown, multi-dimensional filtering distribution, as samples from a suitable probability distribution. We call this distribution the Sequential Monte Carlo distribution, and the corresponding sampling scheme the Sequential Monte Carlo method. The framework of Sequential Monte Carlo methods allows for a very general class of sampling schemes. In the accompanying paper [1], we considered a particular sampling scheme, called Population Monte Carlo, which can be shown to correspond to sequential importance sampling (SIS). In the present paper, we extend the Sequential Monte Carlo framework to Sequential decision making by developing Sequential Thompson Sampling (STS). We show that, under mild conditions, the resulting algorithm, called STS with Thompson Sampling (STS-TS), yields asymptotically optimal sequential decision making, in an information theoretic sense. The proof uses variational characterization of the information optimal sequential decision rule, along with a suitable relaxation of the Sequential Monte Carlo method. The extension of Sequential Monte Carlo methods to Sequential decision making also allows us to consider scenarios in which the decision maker is forced to make a sequence of decisions sequentially, even if the quality of information available improves significantly between successive decisions. In the noisy case, where the available information is random samples, we provide analysis for the simple but effective case of deterministic sequence generation. The extension to the noisy case, where the available information is random samples with noise, is also discussed. Simulation results are presented for both the simple and noisy cases." Reference: [1] K. Saber, “Scanning and sequential decision making for multi-dimensional data - part I: the exact case," arXiv:1908.10395 (2019).

Magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) based on the magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) configuration consisting of a MgO barrier layer sandwiched between two ferromagnetic layers ( tunneling layer and reference layer ) provide the means for recording high density magnetic memories and magnetic logic. In conventional (CPP) ferromagnetic tunnel junctions, the spin-polarized current flowing across the interface between the ferromagnet and the tunnel junction leads to a spin-transfer torque (STT) that can rotate the magnetic direction of the free ferromagnetic layer. For magnetic tunnel junctions, this effect can be used to write information by manipulating the magnetic orientation of the reference layer. Here, we report a novel technique to characterize STT-based magnetic memories by measuring the spin transfer torque vector rather than the STT vector itself. This technique employs a modified Hanle effect to measure the projection of the STT vector onto the direction of an applied magnetic field. We apply this technique to a MTJ and measure the projection of the STT vector onto the x-axis, which is parallel to the easy axis of the free ferromagnetic layer. The sign of this projection, which we denote as sxt, indicates whether the effective field was applied from the positive or negative side of the easy axis. We observe a relatively large sxt for positive applied fields, corresponding to an “in-plane” configuration, and a small sxt for negative applied fields, corresponding to an “out-of-plane” configuration. This technique enables measurement of the projection of the STT vector onto a fixed direction, rather than the measurement of the STT vector itself, which has been the standard for decades. The advantage of this approach is that it is applicable to any STT-based devices, including STT MRAMs, STT spin valves, and STT thin film transistors. Thus, it can be used to characterize device performance and map the device write fields and switching currents. This work was performed in collaboration with the IBM Almaden Research Center and was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, Materials Sciences and Engineering Division.

A debris disc around a white dwarf is a natural outcome of gravitational perturbation of orbiting debris by the central star. Such a disc offers an excellent chance to study dynamics of planetesimals and their evolution under the forces of gravity. Recently, two such discs have been discovered around white dwarfs, but the planetary nature of the systems could not be confirmed. Here we present a model-independent confirmation of the planetary nature of SDSSJ104341.53+085558.2 via an analysis of its light curve. The model fitting shows that the system consists of a white dwarf with a 12.5 per cent above the mean density, and a 0.062+0.018/-0.014 Mjup planet on a 2.72+-0.21/-0.18 day orbit. The planet likely has a M DNO 1.2 earth-like composition and is the first exoplanet discovered around a white dwarf. Such a planet could have formed beyond the snowline of its parent star, suggesting that giant planets are not uncommon around white dwarfs.' Author: Dimitri Veras, Vasily Belov, Sergey Nasergieva, Oleksandr Shchekinov

Silicon surfaces present many intriguing phenomena owing to the large difference in electronegativity between silicon and oxygen. The regular stepping pattern on the (100) surface is one of the most notable examples, which has been observed for more than seven decades. The (110) surface, on the other hand, presents a similar structure but with a two-fold symmetry, which was first described in 1952 and termed the “densité échelonnée” (“stepped array of chains”). Due to its highly faceted shape, the (110) surface has been the subject of many recent studies. Here, we report high-resolution low-energy electron microscopy experiments that reveal a detailed reconstruction model for vicinal (100) and (110) surfaces. In addition to the well-known surface step density-wave pattern, we observe facet-induced bending of the steps and chains at the triple points between steps, leading to the formation of “V”-shaped steps. Using a simple model, we are able to explain the main features of this unusual reconstruction. The information we provide here should facilitate future experiments and simulations on these interesting surfaces.

A simple phenomenological model is presented to interpret the cosmic-ray electrons (CRe) electron spectrum in the galaxy cluster Sersic 159-03 discovered by the the Fermi-LAT. It is shown that both the gamma-ray flux and the radio upper limit can be well accounted for if the spectral break of the CRe spectrum is below the energy threshold of the radio telescope used (1.5 PeV). Compared to hadronic models which suffer from the extreme high density discrepancy problem, this model can naturally explain the relatively low gamma-ray luminosity for the observed hard X-ray tail while keeping most of the CRe population in the halo of Sersic 159-03. The model is also shown to be compatible with the tentative detection of the lepton asymmetry between the north and the south of the cluster. Finally, we briefly discuss the detectability of such a model with the current and future IACTs and CTA.

Researchers around the world are making large, ever more complex simulations of the universe. These simulations, called “models,” are used to make predictions about the universe, and they can be tested against observations of the universe. One such model, which has been very successful at explaining a lot of data about the early universe, is the “Lambda Cold Dark Matter” model, or ΛCDM for short. It assumes that the universe is composed of about 72% dark energy, 23% dark matter, and just 5% ordinary matter, including light particles such as photons, electrons and neutrinos. The neutrinos are particularly important as they are extremely difficult to directly observe, but their presence is essential to keeping the universe flat and stopping it from collapse back onto itself. The model neutrinos are called “neutrino masses,” and the phenomenon of neutrino mass is one of the most mysterious in all of science. In the early 2000s, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) detected a significant decrease in the speed of neutrinos moving through space-time, which suggested that neutrinos might have a tiny but non-zero mass. Many observations since then, however, have failed to find this decrease in speed, which would be expected if the neutrino mass was a tiny 0.1eV. On the other hand, various extensions of the standard model of particle physics suggest that neutrinos might have a non-zero mass. These include the see-saw mechanism, which postulates the existence of right-handed neutrinos. By adding a symmetry which forces right-handed neutrinos to have a non-zero, but tiny, mass, the standard model of particle physics can be extended to the see-saw model. Additional experimental evidence in favor of neutrino mass includes the observation of neutrino oscillations, which show that at least two of the neutrinos have non-zero, but differing, masses. Additionally, cosmology shows that if neutrinos have non-zero masses, then they must have a “normal” mass of approximately 0.05eV or less. If neutrino masses are confirmed, then they will be the first elementary particles shown to have this property. While their interactions are so far unsolved mysteries, neutrinos are the only known particles that can interact via the weak force, which interacts in this way over such large distances. The observation of neutrino masses would be a major breakthrough in our understanding of the universe.

Excitation spectrum gaps and spin-wave stiffness of quantum Heisenberg chains are obtained via global renormalization-group (RG) calculations. For an XXZ spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain with uniaxial anisotropy, anisotropy and magnetic fields in the direction of the easy axis, we obtain an excitation spectrum gap of 0.408(5) for the spin-fluid phase and 0.532(5) for the Néel phase, and the spin-wave stiffness of 0.932(5) for the spin-fluid phase and 1.050(5) for the Néel phase. For the isotropic case, exact results are compared with the numerical estimates for the excitation spectrum gaps and spin-wave stiffnesses, and good agreement is found. The excitation spectrum of the quantum XY model is also examined, and the spin-wave stiffness is computed for the isotropic case. The excitation spectrum gaps and spin-wave stiffnesses of quantum Heisenberg chains obtained by the present RG calculations show good agreement with the known exact results and numerical estimates.

A Type II-P supernova was discovered in the galaxy UGC 4461 approximately 3 years after it had exploded as a short-hard gamma-ray burst (SBOGRB). Despite this extraordinary delay, the SN was observed to have transitioned into the thermonuclear explosion phase 1.5 years after theburst and was visible to optical telescopes. The light curve of the supernova can be fit with a cooling function that is characterized by an exponential rise time of 17 days and a peak magnitude of -17.4. In this paper, we analyze time-resolved X-ray and ultraviolet photometry of SN 2006bp and demonstrate that the lightcurve evolution is consistent with radiative transport in a spherically symmetric, homologuous, massless gas. We compare our results to previous studies of Type II-P lightcurve shapes and find that SN 2006bp is brighter but otherwise matches other SNe 2006bt, 1999ac, 1998bw, and 1993J. In particular, the similarities between SN 2006bp and SBOGRB060218 point to a unifying origin for these diverse transients. We suggest that the immediate progenitor of SN 2006bp was a very massive star (M>30 M⊙), possibly a binary system, with a compact merger yielding a rapidly rotating, strongly magnetic neutron star. In this picture, the SBOGRB and the lightcurve of the supernova are produced by the interaction between the magnetar magnetic field and the circumstellar medium.

Magnetic materials that do not exhibit long-range magnetic order at low temperatures are of great scientific interest. In some of these cases, “geometrical frustration” has been shown to lead to novel behavior. Sr3NiRhO6 and Sr3NiPtO6 are isostructural frustrated, antiferromagnetically interacting magnetic systems that do not exhibit long-range magnetic order down to 20 mK. To characterize this, we have utilized magnetic neutrons scattering, which reveals a number of interesting features, including spinon Fermi surface fragmentation. We discuss the implications of our results on the nature of quantum spin liquids, as well as possible relationship to recent proposals for room-temperature superconductivity in this system. An X-ray spectral analysis of the central regions of NGC 4593 was performed with data obtained from the Chandra X-ray telescope. The spectrum could be well fitted with a simple phenomenological model comprising a narrow emission line component, generated by reflection from cold matter, and a continuum component. The continuum is well represented by a single-temperature blackbody with temperature kT = 0.65 keV. The equivalent width of the emission line is $510^{+230}_{-200}$ eV. The observed line energy is consistent with an emission feature from highly ionised Iron, but more data are needed to confirm this. The gravitating mass, electron density and gas cooling rate in the central regions of NGC 4593 were estimated by modelling the reflection spectrum. It was found that the gravitating mass is 1.3 x 10^9 M_{\odot}$, the electron density is 1.3 x 10^8 cm^-3 and the gas cooling rate is 8.8 x 10^{39} erg s^-1.

Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) are limited in terms of scalability and connectivity by their own medium (i.e., broadcasts) and the bandwidth of the underlying wireless channel. To overcome these limitations, in this work, we propose a collaborative beamforming (CF) protocol and a cooperative transmission (CoT) protocol to allow multiple nodes to cooperatively transmit their data to the sink node. These protocols jointly optimize the transmission beamforming vectors and the cooperative transmission times at each node such that the throughput of the network is maximized. Simulation results show that the proposed protocols significantly outperform a baseline transmission protocol in which each node randomly selects other nodes to cooperate with, both in terms of the average throughput and the typical-user throughput. The proposed protocols significantly outperform a baseline transmission protocol in which each node randomly selects other nodes to cooperate with, both in terms of the average throughput and the typical-user throughput. Mobile wireless networks are facing ever-increasing data traffic and rising consumer demand for mobile broadband services. In this context, cooperative communications have recently been considered as one of the promising techniques to achieve better spectral efficiency and energy efficiency at the cost of additional computational requirements at each node. However, most of the existing cooperative communications techniques for mobile networks were designed for broadcast channels, and thus, were not suitable for the more restricted wireless channels in WSNs. In this work, we propose cooperative beamforming and cooperative transmission techniques to allow multiple nodes to transmit their data to the receiver via cooperative beamforming, thus improving both the spectral and energy efficiencies. In the proposed cooperative beamforming technique, the transmit beamforming vectors are jointly optimized by each node to maximize the achievable rate. In the proposed cooperative transmission technique, the data packets are first divided into cooperative groups such that the interference between the nodes can be cooperatively mitigated at the receiver. Then, each node in the cooperative group sends its data packet with a joint transmit beamforming vector chosen by the group, and the received signals at the receiver are cooperatively processed to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and thus the reception performance. We also investigate the impact of the imperfect channel state information on the performance of the proposed cooperative transmission technique and develop low-complexity design algorithms. The performance of the proposed cooperative transmission techniques are assessed through both numerical simulations and theoretical analyses. Our simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed cooperative transmission techniques in terms of the spectral and energy efficiencies.

In the standard LCDM model of galaxy formation, spheroidal galaxies grow gradually via a combination of a continual merger of existing galaxies, as well as the accretion of smaller galaxies. These processes, as well as that of bar instability, are expected to generate random motions that significantly influence the internal dynamics and perhaps even the structure of the galaxies over time. In this work, we study a sample of spheroidal galaxies from the local universe and examine their assembly histories. We find that approximately two-thirds of the sample formed through the growth of single galaxies by gradually modifying their structures via processes that can generate significant random motions. The rest appear to have grown through the major mergers of two or more smaller galaxies. While this result is consistent with the findings of other studies of large samples of local galaxies, it implies that the processes that lead to the growth of spheroidal galaxies are significantly more frequent than those that lead to their growth via the merging of similarly-sized galaxies. This has important implications for galaxy formation models.

L'Univers en expansion est une expérience menée par Lawrence Krauss qui consistait à faire fondre un métal à température constante à une température croissante pour observer les effets d'entropie générés. L'expérience a été menée dans trois lieux différents suivant la température auquel le métal a été chauffé. La première étape correspond à une température de 330°C, entre 330°C et 310°C la chaleur produite était suffisante pour alimenter un château de jeu, mais les résultats étaient contradictoires. Après avoir fondu à la température de 310°C, le métal a été tempéré au noyau d'un certain nombre de heures, la raison principale pour laquelle le noyau a durci est que les atomes étaient partis en expansion dans le vide à la vue de puissants jets de rayons X. De nombreuses expériences ont montré qu'il s'agissait d'une expérience réussie, mais d'autres scientifiques ont soutenu que les résultats obtenus n'étaient pas valides en raison de l'absence de chaleur de ce noyau allumé. La chaleur produite a été insuffisante pour faire fondre les blocs de métal et pour générer l'entropie nécessaire pour les preuves avancées. L'expérience a également comporté un problème en termes d'énergie, car le métal doit être chauffé à très haute température alors qu'il est composé principalement de piles au cours du métal ces dernières utilisent de l'énergie considérablement plus efficacement. L'Univers en expansion est un rapport par Lawrence Krauss, où il présente les conclusions d'une expérience menée dans le but d'étudier les effets d'entropie générées, à la lumière de récents développements, Krauss soumet l'expérience qu'il a menée pour révision. La critique se concentre principalement sur l'absence de chaleur produite par le noyau, qui aurait pu générer les effets d'entropie postulés. Quantile and probability curves without crossing is a challenging problem in statistics. The curves have to be able to intersect, but they should never cross. The challenge is that many traditional methods to solve this problem, such as monotone lsm, only ensure one curve intersects the others at most at one point. To the best of our knowledge, all current methods can neither ensure that all the curves intersect nor guarantee that they do not cross. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, sequential monotone lsm, which can ensure all the curves intersect and avoid crossing. The advantages of our method over other related methods are also discussed. Our algorithm, implemented in an open-source R package, is also demonstrated to be effective on several synthetic and real data sets.' Landau, S.; Morozov, V.N. (1983). Optimization of functions with different types of constraints. Bulletin of the USSR Academy of Sciences, Physics Engineering, Volume 19, pp. 325–357.

Symbiotic stars are unique astrophysical systems which consist of a white dwarf accreting material from a nearby companion star via a strong outflow. The latter is often associated with a compact jet-like structure. The nature of the companion star is not well understood, but most likely it is a red giant. Symbiotic stars are usually found in theLocal Volume of the Milky Way, and several hundreds of them have been discovered in recent years owing to the the modern astronomical surveys. Symbiotic stars provide important clues to better understand the mass-transfer process in such systems. We obtained near-infrared spectra of HD330036, a symbiotic star candidate identified from the optical surveys, using the HERMES spectrograph mounted on the 30-cm Mercator telescope. We derived radial velocity curve of the secondary star, which is in agreement with the Roche lobe geometry. We also found that the spectra show prominent features of CH, CO, and??? typical for symbiotic stars and also signs of rich interstellar medium environment. The observed gas and dust emission spectra can be reproduced using the photoionization and gas-and-dust geometry models, respectively. The elemental abundances obtained from the gas emission spectrum are supersolar, in agreement with those found in the optical spectra of symbiotic stars. The circumbinary disk with Hubble flow-like velocity distribution and the partial covering of the hot component in X-rays are also confirmed. We assume that the hot component in theHD330036system is a white dwarf with the surface temperature of approximately 10 million Kelvins.

The core of the starless region FeSt 1-457 was mapped in C$^{18}$O ($J = 1 \rightarrow 0$) and DCO$^{+}$ ($J = 2 \rightarrow 1$) at the angular resolution of $23.88''$ ($\sim 0.07$ pc). The region is centrally condensed with a diameter of $\sim 20$ AU and about 10 times more concentrated than the median core from @mc_krish_1983. We identify one centrally condensed core source and seven quiescent protocluster candidates based on their C$^{18}$O velocity dispersion. The condensed source has two peaks with a full-width-half-maximum (FWHM) linewidth of $0.35 \pm 0.05$ km s$^{-1}$ (thermal), corresponding to a typical size of $\sim 20$ AU at 3.2 kpc. Both peaks are coincident with SMA 7.7-mm continuum emission. A precise astrometric fit positions the peak motions at the core centre with an annual uncertainty of $0.16''$ (0.04 AU), which is consistent with the source radius. These results strongly suggest the two peaks represent a rapidly orbiting disk around a central object with a mass of $\sim 0.5$ M$_{\odot}$. We rule out the presence of a binary companion down to a separation of $\sim 10$ AU, the likely deuterium burning limit for such a low-mass system. The dynamical state of FeSt 1-457 is surprisingly evolved for its mass of $< 0.5$ M$_{\odot}$. Based on these observational results, we discuss the evolutionary states of the core and the likely origins of the central source.'

The late-M multiple system LHS 1070 is a benchmark for studies of stellar magnetism due to its strong and unique magnetic field. We report the results of our discovery spectroscopy of this system with the WIYN 3.5-m telescope and subsequent Doppler imaging analysis of the components' stable and unusual abundance of elements other than hydrogen and helium. We find that its moderately fast rotator, LHS 1070 B, has a strong, stable magnetic field that dominates its atmosphere and slows its rotation at a rate consistent with rigid body rotation. In contrast, the even faster rotating components, LHS 1070 C and D, have much weaker magnetic fields and faster rotation rates than expected for their respective spectral types, consistent with previously reported magnetic braking acting on their surfaces. The rapidly spinning LHS 1070 C has a field that is only slightly stronger than that of a typical late-K star, while the nearly non-rotating LHS 1070 D has no detectable magnetic field. We conclude that LHS 1070 C and D may be the first example of a close binary where the more rapidly spinning component has strong enough magnetic braking to significantly slow its spin rate below that of rigid body rotation. We further speculate that the strong magnetic field of LHS 1070 B may be a clue to its unusual chemical composition, which is rich in elements other than hydrogen and helium.

Buffer gas evaporation is an effective technique to reduce the background pressure in an ion trap and thus increase the duty cycle of ion experiments. We demonstrate buffer gas evaporation out of a multipole rf ion trap, achieving a buffer gas inventory of 20% without reducing the number of detectable ions. The buffer gas is thermalized with the ions and thus cools the ion ensemble. As an example application, we study sympathetic cooling of Yb^{+} ions to the zero- kinetic-energy state using Sr^{+} ions. Sympathetic cooling is a method to reduce the temperature of a ion ensemble by magnetically coupling the ion populations via dipole-dipole interactions. We observe a sixfold reduction in Yb^{+} temperature, corresponding to a sympathetic cooling rate of 2.2(2)×10^{-19} K/s, or 1.4(1) Hz, at 295(5) mK. Our sympathetic cooling scheme does not require any unique quantum characteristics for the Sr^{+} ion, and should thus be generally applicable to many ion species.

Astrophysical jets are very powerful, collimated outflows driven from compact objects, such as active galactic nuclei (AGN) and X-ray binaries. They are key to how galaxies and clusters obtain most of their energy and momentum. The formation of astrophysical jets is still a mystery, but various theoretical models have been proposed. In particular, it has been proposed that magnetic fields are important in generating, collimating, and sustaining astrophysical jets. In this paper we study the resonant coupling between the fast Kelvin-Helmholtz wave and the magnetosonic wave in a sheared, relativistic plasma, with special emphasis on the astrophysical systems in which this process may take place. Our analysis is carried out in the framework of general relativity. We find that in these systems the resonant mechanism can efficiently channel energy from the shear into the fast Kelvin-Helmholtz wave. For simplicity we consider a system consisting of a sheared plasma, moving with a Lorentz factor γ in a quasi-neutral plasma with an external magnetic field B0 along the y-direction. We study the modes that are possible when the linear propagation speed of the magnetosonic wave is equal to the phase speed of the Kelvin-Helmholtz wave. The most unstable mode has a short wavelength in the y-direction and a non-zero phase speed in the x- and z-directions. The growth rate of the most unstable mode is proportional to the square of the fluid vorticity in the y-direction, which means the instability is most efficient for differentially rotating systems. However, the most unstable mode also depends on the ratio of the shear to the sound speed, γShc, and increases with γShc, meaning that the stronger the shear, the more efficient the mode. We also study the stability of this most unstable mode against non-linear effects. When the amplitude of the magnetosonic wave becomes comparable to the amplitude of the Kelvin-Helmholtz wave, the two waves interact non-linearly and the most unstable mode evolves into a stable shock wave with smooth contact surfaces. We conclude that the resonant coupling between Kelvin-Helmholtz and magnetosonic waves may have an important impact on astrophysical jets, which makes it an important area for future study. The resonant coupling discussed here could also be important in microquasars, the envirnment of black hole systems like SS 433, where a pair of stars orbiting each other eject high-energy jets. The stars are in nearly circular orbits, but the jets are highly relativistic and tend to ejection in a direction perpendicular to the orbital plane. This parallelism between the orbital plane and the jets strongly suggests the extraction of energy and momentum from the orbital motion. Noise can induce phase transitions in dynamical systems. It has been shown recently that a proper noise might only cause a qualitative change in the dynamics of the system, but a grossly wrong noise can lead to a discontinuous phase transition. In this work, we study how the noise’s spectrum and statistics affect the noise-induced phase transitions. We consider a noisy time-discrete map and compute the phase diagram as a function of noise’s amplitude and spectrum. We find that the noise-induced phase transitions are the more complex the more different the noise’s spectrum is from the system’s deterministic spectrum. The noise-induced phase transitions are also affected by the noise’s statistics. We find that the noise-induced discontinuous phase transition is more likely to happen when the noise is Gaussian and the noise’s amplitude is low. We use a recurrence plot and dimension reduction techniques to characterize the different dynamical behaviors in the phase diagram and find that they are associated with distinct correlation patterns in the recurrence plot. These findings deepen our understanding of noise-induced dynamics and provide guidelines for control design of coupled systems. It is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.08892

The experimental search for a small mismatch between the neutrino and the anti-neutrino masses has recently exceeded the world-leading sensitivity. The new result from the muon (g-2) experiment at Brookhaven National Laboratory brings the total computed discrepancy between the observed and the predicted values to over 2.6 standard deviations, lending strong support to the existence of a small, underlying sterile neutrino mass. The new result is in perfect agreement with the standard model prediction, providing further evidence in support of the so-called "normal" neutrino mass ordering. Should the central value of the upcoming new result be lower than the current best fit, it would be an unambiguous sign of new physics and would call for an update of the current model building. However, given the current statistical and systematic uncertainties, even an order of magnitude improvement on the sensitivity would not significantly change the current best-fit three-neutrino model.

In this work, we develop a discrete computer network model with expanding dimensions. This model can capture the structural organization of computer networks and simulate the dynamics of node addition and removal. We start with a regular lattice and let a network expand by duplicating the nodes and bonds of the original structure. The structure grows larger, but retains the initial properties of the starting network. We then duplicate the nodes and bonds of the expanded structure, generating a network that grows both in physical size and dimension. We show that this process can capture the structural organization of computer networks and simulate the dynamics of node addition and removal. We demonstrate our method on real-world networks, beginning with a local network in Silicon Valley and moving to internet-scale graphs from Berkeley’scentral routing table and PlanetLab. Our model has several key advantages over existing approaches to network analysis. Most models of networks focus on nodes and their connections, but ignore properties such as node “volume” and dimensionality. These models are typically continuous, making it difficult to model systems with discrete nodes and numerical attributes. Our model is discrete and uses “node volume” and dimensionality to describe networks. In particular, our model can capture the structural organization of computer networks and simulate the dynamics of node addition and removal. Many real-world networks exhibit an exponential or power-law degree distribution, where a few nodes have a large number of connections, while most nodes have a small number of connections. In this work, we show that our model has self-organized critical properties. We find that, after a slow start, the average degree of a network grows exponentially with the size of the network. The average degree provides a simple measure of how “scale free” a network is. We also find that the distribution of node degrees follows a power law. The self-organized criticality in our model may help us understand the structural organization of real-world networks and the ubiquity of power laws in their degree distributions.

Comprehensive calculations are performed on the OZI-forbidden nonleptonic decays of orthoquarkonia $J/\psi(\Upsilon)\to \pi\pi,\rho\pi$, where the orthoquarks (strongly interacting quarks) are assumed to be exchanged in the t- and u-channels. We find that the strong phases of most of these decay modes are large and the typical values of the strong phases from the color-singlet current are much larger than those from the color-octet current, except for the decay $J/\psi\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0$, which may have a large color-octet contribution. The differential branching ratios of some decay modes with low masses of the two final mesons are relatively large. These features may be useful in searching for the scalar or vector tetraquarks, and should be tested by the LHCb and forthcoming BESIII and BelleII experiments.

Noether’s theorem is one of the fundamental principles of physics, stating that in any symmetry of the laws of physics, there is a conserved quantity. In this Letter, we show that it is possible to obtain conservation laws in modified gravity theories by invoking a hidden symmetries. We demonstrate this for the class of f(R) theories of gravity and show that the standard Einstein-Hilbert term of General Relativity gives way to a modification that has no conventional Newtonian description. Despite the non-linearity of the field equations, the curvature scalar is not an appropriate variable to describe the dynamics of our universe, and a reduced description based on the development of a new scalar degree of freedom is needed. We explore this theory quantitatively through the analysis of solutions to the field equations and show that this leads to modifications to the Poisson equation and the form of the matter density in the universe, which can lead to new physical effects in the large scale structure of the universe. We present a simple and general procedure for finding exact solutions to the field equations of these theories, and demonstrate its use with some specific examples. We show that these solutions give way to inhomogeneous stellar distributions of stars with compact cores, which have not been identified in previous solutions to the field equations of modified gravity theories.

A review of biological molecular computers is presented with a focus on the bacterial cell and how it could be programmed to carry out various tasks. Various aspects of biological molecular machines are discussed along with an outline of how such a biological computer could be realized by engineering proteins on a surface. The possibility of the living cell itself being used as a molecular computer is explored with a discussion on how molecular signals can be processed by the cell itself using transport and enzymatic reactions. A survey of a number of molecular tasks that the cell could carry out is presented along with several experiments that could be performed to validate the cell as a biological molecular computer. Several key issues that must be overcome to build a biological molecular computer are also discussed. The possibility of programming the bacterial cell to carry out various tasks is explored. Various aspects of biological molecular machines are discussed. The living cell itself could be used as a molecular computer. Molecular signals can be processed by the cell itself using transport and enzymatic reactions. A survey of a number of molecular tasks the cell could carry out is presented. Several key issues that must be overcome to build a biological molecular computer are also discussed. BioBrick assembly, logic gates, sensors, computers, robots and networks could all be built from bacterial cells. An essential part of this technology is the use of reliable methods of intracellular synthesis and assembly. A prime requirement in this respect is that the DNA templates employed in the construction of these molecular systems be obtained intracellularly. Current methods based on in vitro transcription or PCR amplification of DNA templates for direct biosynthesis are generally unreliable. We believe that the cell itself, by providing an environment with suitable pH, temperature and salt concentrations, and protected from direct physical injury, could serve as an ideal host for the biosynthesis of DNA. Theory suggests that significant barriers to intracellular DNA synthesis include the thermal stability of DNA in bacterial cells (which favors nascent DNA strands in their natural double-stranded form), cell membrane instability (which prevents larger DNA pieces from escaping the cell once transcription begins), and nuclease attack (which degrades DNA strands). In order to solve these problems, we have designed synthetic DNA structures with optimized thermal and membrane properties. In addition, we have identified potent nuclease-resistant DNA structures that have yet to be utilized in bio-nano fabrication. All of these DNA properties should facilitate the production and assembly of complex nanoscale structures from within bacterial cells. The versatile genetic information encoding capacity of DNA allows the digitalization of any signal for processing by the cell. An analogy may be made to the molecular computer that performs calculations by processing digital signals in a sequence of logic operations. These logic operations may be encoded in the form of DNA. As a result, any biochemical signal could be converted into a digital form suitable for processing by the cell. We are proposing the concept of digital biochemistry, where all biochemical signals are converted into digital form and processed by the cell.

Localization in the Anderson Transition is understood in terms of a deformation of the Fermi surface into closed loops. In the supercritical regime, a fluctuation theory is developed in [1] based on the Kotliar-Ruckenstein representation [2] of the Anderson Transition. The resulting Coulomb gas (CG) is studied on the Keldysh contour, and a one-loop calculation is performed, which leads to a boson representation of the (nonequilibrium) Anderson-Yuval-Hamann (AYH) transition. The CG parametrization is generalized to include anti-ferromagnetic next-nearest neighbor interactions, as is known to be important in certain strong localization regimes. The resulting CG action is evaluated exactly on the Keldysh contour, and yields an asymptotically exact resummed Fermi surface deformation, fermion pairing, and a dynamical slaving of the localization field to the pairing field. Most theories of the Anderson Transition focus on the average behavior of the system. The result presented here is a fluctuation theory based on the Kotliar-Ruckenstein representation of the Anderson Transition. A one-loop calculation is performed, and leads to a boson representation of the Nonequilibrium Anderson-Yuval-Hamann (AYH) transition. This CG representation also yields an asymptotically exact resummed Fermi surface deformation, fermion pairing, and dynamical slaving of the localization field to the pairing field.

The very existence of luminous quasars (QSOs) at high redshift is difficult to explain within the paradigm of pure cold dark matter cosmology. As the most massive dark matter halos at high redshift, QSOs are good laboratories to test evolutionary models of the universe, as well as the supermassive black hole - host galaxy co-evolution. Using a sample of 12 luminous high-redshift QSOs with X-shave archived, we investigate the host galaxy dust covering factor (defined as the ratio of solid angle covered by dust to the total solid angle), and the silicate strength and colour of the mid-infrared emission, which are potential probes of the star formation rate (SFR). We find that compared to local luminous and ultra-luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs and ULIRGs), high-redshift luminous QSOs have a significantly higher covering factor of dust, lower silicate strength, and redder infrared colour. The high covering factors suggest that these QSOs have significant on-going or recent star formation. The trends are consistent with that expected from an evolving dust-to-stars ratio, with a dust covering factor of 0.4-0.6 at z = 2.2-3.4 (where z is the cosmological redshift). There is no strong evidence for a higher proportion of IR-luminous, or active galaxies in the QSOs than typical for the bright sub-population at these redshifts, in agreement with previous studies. The observed dust and silicate properties are, however, more similar to those of local sub-millimetre galaxies (SMGs) than normal ULIRGs, suggesting the QSOs may evolve into SMGs at lower redshift. We discuss several scenarios to explain our results, including QSO-driven winds clearing out interstellar medium (ISM) and/or molecular clouds. However, we note that without measurement of the velocities and densities of the obscuring material, and the strength and shape of the quasar continuum, it is difficult to distinguish between these scenarios and to test the influence of the QSO on the host galaxies evolution.

The recently discovered SDSS J233325.92+152222.1 provides us with the opportunity to study an object which straddles the boundary between the class of AM CVn systems (which comprise both interacting magnetic CVs and semi-detached polars) and the class of polars. SDSS J233325.92+152222.1 has a projected orbital period of 7.8 hr and its spectrum is characteristic of a magnetic white dwarf. However, it shows far stronger Balmer lines and far weaker HeII 4686 than is typically seen in polars. We show that SDSS J233325.92+152222.1 fits the (very loosely defined) intermediate polar classification and that it is potentially one of the most rapidly rotating polars discovered to date. We also show that the combination of the intermediate polar nature of SDSS J233325.92+152222.1 and its rapid rotation implies that the accretor must be nearly spherical. This is in contrast to the well-known class of tidally-locked polars, for which the accretor is often significantly oblate due to tidal distortion. We discuss the implications of this discovery for our understanding of the evolution of AM CVn systems and polars.

A new development in the field of Quantum Optics is the control and understanding of interactions among elementary quantum entities1, namely photons and excitons. Typically, the approach is to use a method of quantum mechanics known as the Heisenberg equation, where the time evolution of a system is described in terms of the operators for the corresponding quantum mechanical entities. In typical optical experiments, it is the light field which is modulated (e.g. by reflection or transmission through a controlled optical element) that is of interest. The problem with describing interactions between photons and excitons is that photons and excitons have different properties - in particular, photons have a wave-like behavior and excitons have particle-like behavior. Therefore, a method of describing these interactions which has been developed is to use the coupling of Heisenberg equations for the corresponding quantum entities. This paper considers an example of application of the method of coupling of Heisenberg equations to quantum optical theory - specifically, coupling of the Heisenberg equations for photons and excitons to describe the interaction between these entities, including applications to photonic crystal slabs with embedded quantum wells. We present a method of solution of the coupled equations which is easily generalizable to more complex geometries and interactions. Our results are in good agreement with experimental data in the literature for two very different types of sample - semiconductor quantum wells and molecular crystals, suggesting that the method used here is generally applicable to more complex systems.

Simulations of the preheating scenario for the formation of galaxy clusters have been performed using a modified version of the GADGET-2 code. The simulations were initialized at z=49 with Gaussian fluctuations with a wave number corresponding to a scale of 8.4 kpc/h at z=0, consistent with the WMAP7 results for the amplitude of mass fluctuations on these scales. Cluster-sized objects formed at z=0 in the regions with the highest peaks of the initial density field. To reproduce the observed X-ray luminosity function of galaxy clusters, the thermal energy of the gas in these high-density peaks had to be transferred to it by means of non-linear interactions between sub-relativistic particles of the plasma, known as preheating. Such interactions became possible after the energetic particles from the decay of the particlehardtype curvatons had settled down into the potential wells of different over-densities. The results of the simulations demonstrate that the non-linear interactions between the produced particles of the plasma become very efficient in raising the temperature of the gas after passing the period of reheating, called the warm phase. The mean gas temperature in the clusters reaches a level of 10 keV at z=0, in good agreement with the observed X-ray luminosity of the clusters. The temperature difference with respect to the universal mean value at different redshifts is used to estimate the strength of the preheating interaction rate. The simulations also describe the development of inhomogeneities in the distribution of the dark matter after preheating. Comparison of the distribution of the density peaks in the dark matter field with the distribution of galaxy clusters in the nearby universe allows us to estimate the rms mass density fluctuations in the epoch of galaxy cluster formation. These simulations predict the amplitude of the dark matter fluctuations to be ~40% higher than that inferred from observations of the galaxy distribution, although it is consistent with the results of earlier simulations. The presented results demonstrate that the preheating scenario for the formation of galaxy clusters is consistent with a wide range of observations, ranging from the X-ray luminosity function of clusters to their spatial distribution and the mass fluctuations in the dark matter field, as well as with the temperature and the clustering of the intergalactic medium inferred from the observations of the cosmic microwave background.

We present global, three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamical simulations of turbulent disks in cylindrical co-ordinates. The basic state is in pressure equilibrium with a flat rotating equilibrium, which is embedded in a static, purely vertical, solenoidal magnetic field. Small-scale stochastic forcing is applied to the velocity and imposed on large scales to simulate the effect of gravitational instability. The linear growth of the waves and the decay of the imposed flux have been confirmed for a range of parameters. We present the first results for a turbulent model with self-consistent gas and dust transport, and discuss the important effect of Ohmic resistivity. We find an effective diffusivity consistent with the effective viscosity inferred from global disk properties. The effective magnetic Prandtl number is between 0.01 and 0.1, showing that resistive MHD effects are essential for accurately modelling these disks. We also find that radial transport of solids occurs via a streaming instability with the particles on elliptical orbits.

Existing studies of extragalactic background light (EBL) used measurements in the optical and far-infrared wavelength regions. These measurements are subject to various systematic uncertainties, and the EBL in the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray wavelength regions remains largely unconstrained. In this paper, we use gamma-ray data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope to place a constraint on EBL in the EUV wavelength region down to a few eV, i.e., the effective photon energy of 10-511 keV electromagnetic radiation. We employ a numerical model of galaxy formation to predict the optical depth to gamma-ray pair production. We find the total EBL in the EUV wavelength region is (3.0 ± 0.9) × 10-13 h erg -2, or equivalently, the star formation rate is (1.2 ± 0.4) × 10 -12 h 1.6 -1.2 × 10-13 h cm -2 s, where h is the reduced Hubble constant in units of 100 km s -1 Mpc -1. If we adopt a universal Simon-Glover-Glotch (SGG) disk mass scaling relation, the resulting EUV luminosity density is (2.2 ± 0.7) × 10 -23 h erg -1 s -1, consistent with previous estimates derived from direct UV measurements. Given the significant uncertainties in the modeling of star formation and the gamma-ray opacity, the constraints on EBL presented in this Letter should be interpreted as a range of possible star formation rates and total EUV luminosity densities. However, the measurement of the EUV luminosity density is an important step in understanding the energetics of galaxy formation over cosmic time.

PKS0537-441 is a blazar at a redshift of 0.859. It is one of the most variable AGN and has been detected by the Swift satellite as well as the REM telescopes. In 2005 simultaneous monitoring with both satellites as well as the REM telescopes detected changes in the high energy behavior of the source during the appearance of a new supermassive black hole in the center of a nearby galaxy. Swift observed a flare in X-rays before the REM observation of a corresponding absorption decrease in the optical bands. This and other similarities between the short-term variability of different bands for the first time demonstrated the link between these wavelength regions, which was previously suspected. 2012 Astolfo et al. reported the discovery of a supermassive black hole in the centre of a nearby (14.4 billion light years) galaxy. In 2005, simultaneous monitoring with both Swift and REM telescopes detected changes in the high energy behavior of the source during the appearance of a new supermassive black hole. A single letter from the input bit stream can imply multiple output symbols, achieving maximum diversity in a collection of outputs. For any monotonic, right-continuous input distribution, the associated optimal output distribution has a combinatorially simple form. This universal source coder can be implemented efficiently, with computation and feedback per letter logarithmic in the length of the codeword. The corresponding maximum likelihood decoder is fast and approximately maximum a posteriori, for all realizable input distributions. We present evidence of the effectiveness of this coding strategy through empirical evaluation on synthetic and real datasets. This letter studies the problem of coding for an abstract alphabet, maximizing the entropy of an output sequence subject to an average cost per bit. We show that for any right-continuous, monotonic input distribution, there exists an output distribution achieving these costs, whose support can be described by a small, regular graph. We present efficient algorithms to generate codes for such distributions, with computation and feedback both logarithmic in the length of the codeword. We evaluate our scheme empirically on synthetic and real datasets, and demonstrate that our codes achieve low cost per bit while incurring little redundancy.

Recent observations of gravitational waves and electromagnetic signals have revealed the mergers of black holes (BHs) of millions of solar masses, opening a new window to the study of galaxy evolution and the early Universe. The detected events were deep in merger, with separations of tens of Schwarzschild radii. However, the observed electromagnetic signals were emitted on a dynamical timescale of the black holes, longer than the light crossing time of the orbit. This raises the question of how these massive black holes (MBHs) were brought to their close separation, at such high velocities. The answer may lie in a dense cluster of smaller mass black holes, that acted as a massive perturber and changed the dynamical evolution of the system. I here present a suite of three dimensional, fully hydrodynamical simulations that probe this scenario, focusing on the extreme mass ratio scenario with the secondary MBH a thousandth the mass of the primary. The simulations start from generic parabolic encounters with different impact parameters and show that the configuration with the closest approach of the centres is approximately 5% of the initial separation. The high velocity dispersions of a few hundred kilometers per second are achieved after just 0.2% of the initial orbit, corresponding to 20 dynamical times, in the case of closest approach.

The Examples against The Generalized Jacobian Conjecture (Examples for GJC) by Brent Everly is an interesting paper showing that the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture (GJC) is not generally true. The GJC, proposed in 2001 by Luis Barreira, was a bold claim suggesting that generic topological chaos, a key feature of irregular dynamical systems, occurs in a large class of dynamical systems. The Examples against The Generalized Jacobian Conjecture demonstrates that a specific dynamical system, known to be in this large class of dynamical systems with no generic chaotic behaviour, does not satisfy the GJC. The Examples against The Generalized Jacobian Conjecture shows that the GJC is false in a generic sense, but leaves open the possibility that the GJC may be true for a smaller class of dynamical systems, for example those systems with some additional generic properties. The implications of this result are far-reaching and many resonances with diverse areas of science. For example, the Examples against The Generalized Jacobian Conjecture has applications to classical mechanics, the foundations of statistical mechanics, certain dimensions in coding theory, the statistical properties of weather and water clouds, and the combinatorics of words. The paper is well-written and very clear. The Examples against The Generalized Jacobian Conjecture has broad interest to a diverse audience of dynamical systems scientists and mathematicians.

A robust detection of an age-metallicity relation in planet-hosting solar analogues has important implications for our understanding of planet formation. The mechanism that establishes the age-metallicity relation is likely related to the timescales for gas accretion, disk lifetimes, and planet migration; all of which are strongly dependent on the stellar host's properties such as mass, temperature, and metallicity. Here we search for an age-metallicity relation in the disk age–metallicity relation and find an offset of 150 Myr, indicating that stars similar to the Sun formed with approximately the same metallicity 150 Myr ago. With a spectroscopic sample of 59 stars within 2.2 kpc, we find this offset robust: we obtain an offset of 170 Myr by considering only stars within 200 pc and an offset of 150 Myr with the entire sample. This is the first detection of an age-metallicity relation in disk-hosting solar analogues and suggests that the onset of planet formation was coeval throughout the inner regions of the Solar Neighbourhood. We further identify the the sample as incomplete for stars with ages $<300$ Myr, with approximately 25% of stars less than 50 Myr old lacking measured kinematics; these young stars are likely associated with the birthcloud. The transition from inside-out to outside-in disk formation, which is marked by the metallicity dependence of the disk age-metallicity relation, provides a direct probe of the time taken for planet migration.

Here, we present floating-gate transistors based on a high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) with a floating, inverted silicon dioxide tunnel gate. The HEMT was defined in a vertical-stacked silicon-on-insulator (VSOS) device, allowing us to make transistors with very thin active regions. The floating gate is completely separate from the control gate, avoiding charge loss and interfacial traps. We investigate the effects of plasma exposure on the device, and find that the work function of the floating gate changes by over 1.5 eV after 200 seconds of exposure to plasma, corresponding to a loss of trapping charge of 35%, much faster than charging the gate in an electron microscope. This enables optically erasable floating-gate transistors using a similar technique to electrically erasable floating-gate transistors, with potential uses in digital operations for logic, memory, and imaging.

In this paper we introduce dynamical objects for cohomologically expanding maps. We first recall the definition of topological entropy and the definition of measure of maximal entropy. Then we introduce the $\alpha$-limit set and the $\omega$-limit set for a cohomologically expanding map. We give several examples and applications of the introduced dynamical objects. First we show that for any countable system the $\omega$-limit set always exists. Then we apply this result to extend the definition of topological entropy for countably infinite systems. We show that the $\alpha$-limit set and the $\omega$-limit set could be strictly contained in the phase space. Finally we apply this result to give an example of cohomologically expanding map such that the topological entropy is not equal to the measure of maximal entropy. In the end we give an explicit example of two dimensional cohomologically expanding map such that the topological entropy is not equal to the measure of maximal entropy.

Network communities, or clusters of nodes with a higher density of connections between nodes in the same community than between nodes in different communities, are important structure in networks. Most current algorithms only detect large groups, or clusters, ignoring the detailed structure of communities. Here we introduce a resolution limit for network clustering, and develop a hierarchical method that detects both large and small communities in networks. The proposed method works by first identifying super-communities at many resolutions, and then clustering each super-community at the given resolution. We validate our method on random and real-world networks, and show that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art community detection algorithms. The full paper, along with technical details and data, is available here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.09755 Ian O. Tolstoy, Han Wang, Paul J. Mucha, and Mihaela Van con, “Network Communities with a High Resolution,” arXiv:1711.09755 (December 13, 2017). There has been a recent resurgence of interest in network clustering, sparked by the development of a wide variety of network data, as well as the ubiquity of network datasets in other fields, such as social media and biology. The study of network communities has traditionally focused on detecting large groups or clusters of nodes with high density within the network, or networks. Community detection algorithms have been shown to be sensitive to a resolution parameter, which determines the granularity of clusters to be detected. Higher resolution generally leads to higher quality clusters, although the tradeoff is that more computationally expensive algorithms are needed to detect lower resolution communities. In this paper, we introduce a hierarchical method for community detection that identifies both large and small communities at many resolution levels. The method identifies super-communities, or large groups of nodes that are highly dense and well connected within but low density with respect to other super-communities. The method then clusters the identified super-communities, refining the cluster structure at each resolution. This hierarchical approach allows us to detect both large and small communities at many resolutions. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both synthetic and real-world networks, showing that our method is highly accurate in detecting clusters and outperforms state-of-the-art community detection algorithms.
