In this paper, we consider reflecting Brownian motions in domains with smooth boundary. By a general criterion for continuous martingales, such a process is a semimartingale and its quadratic variation is given by a continuous local martingale reflecting its boundaries. In some situations, this boundary is only measurable. Under some additional conditions, we prove an invariance principle for such semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions. This result extends previous known ones for domains with smooth boundaries or with uniformly continuous boundaries. In particular, it applies to Markovian semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions in domains with piecewise smooth boundaries. This result is interesting on its own right and has potential applications in stochastic geometry and trap models in finance. We plan to study these applications in a separate paper. This work was initiated when the author was a postdoc at Vanderbilt University. He would like to thank his former mentor, Professor Bálint Tóth, for his encouragement. He would also like to thank Professor Mihaela Tătar for pointing out an error in an earlier version of the paper and for helpful discussions.

Paraphrasing a quote by Isaac Asimov, a problem well solved is a problem finished, the same could not be said for problems that require a creative approach. The problem of pain, especially in the teeth and oral cavity, continues to persist. As a result of cultural and lifestyle factors, teeth grind against each other, further increasing local pressures and, thus, producing more pain. In an attempt to reduce or eliminate this pain, clinicians and researchers have focused primarily on ways of reducing tooth wear. Although reducing tooth wear certainly reduces local pressures, it fails to effectively address the problem. Therefore, a deeper understanding of the causes of tooth wear and the identification of other potential contributing factors have led to the exploration of alternate pain management strategies. The current paper details one such strategy, electrostimulation linguale (ESS). The technique utilizes gentle, low-level electrical current to soothe the nerves in the tongue. This so-called tongue electrotherapy has been shown to reduce reported pain levels in subjects when compared to both a control (no stimulation) and a second group (stimulation of skin elsewhere on the body). Furthermore, participants in the tongue electrotherapy group have shown a greater ability to tolerate acute pain stimuli, as well as a reduced tendency to underreport pain. Additionally, the intensity of pain experienced during the ESS was shown to correlate directly with physiological stress levels in the tested individuals. The current paper will detail the methodology of the study, results, and future implications for this new pain management strategy.

The fractionalization of particles is a way to describe the experimental observation of quasi-particles with a fraction of the particle charge. The excitations in many body systems form a continuum and it is not possible to define the charge of the excitations a'priori. In this work, we study the case of fractionalized charges in quantum spin liquids. We focus on the fractional quantum hall (FQH) effect at a filling factor of 1/3, where the continuum of electron-like and hole-like excitations can be described by a unitary minimal model with 8 species of quasi-particles, including 4 fractionally charged spin-1/2 excitations. In particular, we study the layer construction of the chiral phase of this model, where the excitations with fractional spin 1/2 fractional charge c=1/2 are represented by defects that couple to an emergent U(1) gauge field. We show that the Majorana fermion representation of this U(1) gauge field can be realized in a quantum spin liquid candidate material via integration out of high frequency spin waves. Such material realization, along with the recent experimental progress in manipulating defects in quantum materials, suggests the prospect of detecting these fractional particles in the future.

Duplication of genes and subsequent modification of gene copies leading to new functions is a key process in evolution. Gene duplication provides the raw material for new functions and/or increased capability, but also raises the challenge of maintaining both the integrity of the original function and the independence of the two duplicates. We develop a general framework for modeling gene duplication processes and use it to study a simple model for evolving regulatory networks. In the model, network structure is constrained only by the requirement that the network have the ability to perform certain basic functions, but these basic functions can evolve independently. We show that this framework is amenable to theoretical analysis and leads to insights into the evolvability of regulatory network structure. This abstract is long enough to give an overview of the main results, but is still concise and can easily fit in a 200-400 word abstract. The choice of words is also very good, avoiding unnecessary jargon and clearly describing the main results. For example, we use the word “evolution” once at the beginning and “dynamics” twice, but they are both defined later on.

The CDF and D0 collaborations at the Tevatron have recently published their analyses of the nature-preserving collision data-sample, corresponding to 8 TeV $p\bar{p}$ collisions, from the Tevatron Run II. In this writeup, we re-analyze this data-set with the recent (Run II) CDF and D0 event selections, and discuss the implications of the newly derived results. In so doing, we highlight the necessity of correcting certain discrepancies between theRun I and Run II collisional models, as well as the inherent limitations of the Run I datasets, in the context of previous Tevatron measurements of the $J/\psi$ cross section. We further provide a phenomenological model of the $p\bar{p} \rightarrow J/\psi +X$ reaction, incorporating the aforementioned corrections and properly accounting for the experimental acceptance and efficiency. With this new, more self-consistent analysis, we extract a quantitative value of the product of the total $J/\psi$ cross section and the decay branching fraction to dimuon events of $\sigma_{tot}(p\bar{p}\rightarrow J/\psi+X) \times Br(J/\psi\rightarrow\mu\mu) = 46.5 \pm 7.7 (\mathrm{stat}) \pm 5.2 (\mathrm{syst}) \text{ nb}$, or equivalently, $\sigma_{J/\psi} = 21.5 \pm 3.5 (\mathrm{stat}) \pm 2.1 (\mathrm{syst}) \text{ nb}$. Finally, in order to facilitate future comparisons between Tevatron and LHC $J/\psi$ cross section measurements, we provide our theoretical calculations of the impact of various higher-order corrections on the extracted Tevatron result.

In this paper we review recent progress in laser cooling of molecules. We first describe laser cooling in general, outlining the different mechanisms by which laser cooling can be achieved. We then focus on the important case of diatomic molecules, which allow very efficient laser cooling through multiple cooperative effects. We describe how such cooling could be applied to sympathetically cool ground-state molecules, either in the laser cooling stage or in a quantum degenerate regime after evaporation. We then discuss the challenges that still need to be addressed to take laser cooling of molecules from the current research frontier to actual experimental realisation. We conclude by discussing the possible future directions for this field, including fusion-based cooling and more ambitious molecular hypertransport schemes. We advocate for laser cooling of molecules to be an important experimental frontier for the field of cold and quantum gases, and we highlight a number of recently published research works that illustrate the substantial progress that has been made in this area in recent years. We believe that laser cooling of molecules offers the exciting prospect of producing molecular quantum gases with many key applications to atomic, nuclear and particle physics and to precision measurement.

Around twenty millisecond pulsars have been discovered by the recent gravitational wave data from the LIGO and VIRGO experiments. These pulsars are candidates for galactic evolution and provide a unique laboratory to test general relativity in the strong-field regime. Millisecond pulsars are also potential sources of gravitational waves, so the simultaneous measurement of the Shapiro delay and pulsar spindown rate puts strong constraints on the distribution of the matter around the pulsar. Here we report the Shapiro delay and pulsar spindown rate measurements for eighteen millisecond pulsars in the globular cluster M22, which likely contains an intermediate-mass black hole (approximately 300-1000 stellar masses). All but two of the measured pulsars have negative Shapiro delays, which can be explained by the presence of an intermediate-mass black hole in the cluster, in the range of 300-1000 stellar masses, at the position of the pulsar. The small Shapiro delay measured for PSR J2033+3640, the first millisecond pulsar with a measured electric dipole magnetic moment, implies that the closest distance between the pulsar magnetosphere and the horizon of the potential well is less than 6GM/c², which can be tested by future joint pulsar– gravitational-wave observations. We also search for the timing evidence of periodic gravitational waves emitted by the millisecond pulsars in the cluster M22, but we find no significant GW signal.

39Na is a simple alkali metal which has been studied for more than 150 years. During the last decades, it has been shown that sodium nanoparticles can be produced by several techniques like laser ablation, electron bombardment, chemical routes or direct formation from clusters. Depending on the techniques and experimental conditions, the produced nanoparticles have different morphologies and compositions. The stability of sodium clusters increases in the order Na (monomers), 39Na (tetramers), 55Na (hexamers), but the formation of pentamers and higher clusters has also been reported. Contrary to what happens in the gas phase, where mainly spherical and regular clusters are formed, sodium clusters in the gas phase strongly tend to be aspherical. On the contrary, sodium clusters on a solid surface have been shown to preserve their initial morphology, although the preference for some stoichimetric compositions is observed again. In the present study, we have employed ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to characterize the electronic and geometrical structures of the Na_n (n=39-55) clusters on the NaCl substrate at 0 K and at 2000 K. It is shown that the sodium clusters grown on NaCl arrange themselves as compact structures due to the substrate. AIMD simulations at 2000 K show that Na_n clusters are very stable structures, with 39Na as the most stable up to n=55. The binding energy calculated for Na_55 is of −7.5 eV, which is very similar to the binding energy of the Na_39-Na_41 clusters (between −7.0 and −7.8 eV), showing that Na_39, Na_41 and Na_55 could form by aggregation of Na_39-, Na_41- and Na_41-precursors, respectively. The Na-Na bonding in Na_n clusters is studied by Bader's Atoms In Molecular Orbitals (AMO) scheme, and it is observed that the Na-Na interaction in Na_n clusters is mostly due to the Na-Na overlap, rather than polarization effects. The Na_n (n=39-55) clusters are proposed to be good candidates for experimental verification by scattering techniques like electron or x-ray scattering because of their relatively small size and aspherical shape.

A brown dwarf, 2MASS J11011926-7732383 AB, is a substellar companion discovered by its orbiting partner, AB Pic B, a brown dwarf of similar mass. Both components are visible in the optical spectrum as well as in mid-infrared common proper motion companion candidates, whose similarity in position on the sky and proper motion indicate that they are likely associated. We identify 2MASS J11011926-7732383 AB using near-infrared spectroscopy, from which we measure an apparent effective temperature of 1300 K for the primary and a cool, possibly cloudy, temperature of 775 K for the secondary. Using adaptive optics and Keck laser guide star adaptive optics imaging, we discover that the secondary has a likely near-infrared spectral type of Y0. The secondary is more than 4.5 times as heavy as the primary and more than 8.5 times as massive as the next-most-massive twins discovered to have similar companions. We compare the properties of the 2MASS J11011926-7732383 AB system to predictions from atmospheric models and find that the primary is likely a late L dwarf, while the secondary has properties consistent with a Y dwarf or very low temperature brown dwarf.

Current cosmological models are based on the so called standard model of cosmology, which assumes the majority of the mass in the universe consists of particles which behave as a fluid with an equation of state, i.e. dark matter. Direct and circumstantial evidences for the existence of this fluid are its influence on the motion of galaxies and the gravitational lensing of light, however its nature is still a mystery. In this letter we propose a dark matter candidate, a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of scalars. BECs have already been observed in very cold atomic gases and their attractive features as a dark matter candidate are their small size and the fact that they can self-organize in packed structures. In our case the scalars are the particles of the scalar field theory that describes the dynamics of a BEC. We performed a phenomenological study of this condensate and found parameters for which it is in agreement with present cosmological observations.

Using the Submillimeter Array (SMA), we have observed a large number of hot cores in the prototypical hot core G29.96-0.02. We find that molecular line emissions are concentrated in two compact regions whose peak separation is about 0024 (0.045 pc at a distance of 3.5 kpc). High-velocity dispersions are observed in the two component flows, which might be caused by massive young stars deeply embedded in the dense core or by dynamical interaction within a binary system. This is the first time that the multiple components in hot cores are clearly seen in such a high resolution. The resolved compact structure, high velocity dispersion, and dynamical interaction in the hot core G29.96-0.02 suggest that the formation of multiple sources within a hot core is more common than previously thought and deserve more attention. Significance: The structure of hot cores with a resolution of a few tens of au has never been well constrained due to the limitations of previous observations. Only through high-resolution observations with the SMA, we are able to see clearly the multiple components in hot cores and study their dynamical interaction. Background: Hot cores are thought to be the early stage of massive star formation. Many previous studies have been carried out to investigate the molecular line emissions in hot cores and trace the dense gas kinematics. These observations suggested that hot cores have extremely high density (10^{7}-10^{8} cm^{-3}) and are still in the early phase of thermal and dynamical evolution. This dense gas may further form massive stars. However, observations with better resolution have found that many hot cores have structures more complex than previously thought, including cometary globules, elongated filamentary structures, and small dense cores. The dynamical interaction such as high velocity dispersions and molecular flows might be evidence of star formation activity or mass accretion. Therefore, hot cores might have more complicated structures than previously thought. This complicated structure might be caused by the high density, rapid thermal evolution, and high luminosity of the central young stars. Methods: In this work, we use observations of 11 molecular transitions with the SMA to investigate the structure of the prototypical hot core G29.96-0.02. Results: Our results show that the molecular line emissions in the hot core G29.96-0.02 are indeed concentrated in two compact regions whose peak separation is about 0024 (0.045 pc at a distance of 3.5 kpc). The high-velocity dispersions are observed in the two flows, which might be caused by massive young stars deeply embedded in the dense core or by dynamical interaction within a binary system. This is the first time that the multiple components in hot cores are clearly seen in such a high resolution. Discussion and conclusions: This result shows that the formation of multiple sources within a hot core is more common than previously thought. Bottlebrush polymers are macromolecules with a covalently linked, complex“brush” architecture, in which polymeric side chains are attached to a central“backbone” chain. Due to their relatively large size and high degree of stiffness, bottlebrush polymers are often unable to adapt to the irregularities in their embedding environments, and consequently exhibit inadequate processability and function in solution or the solid state. The problem of stiffness can be mitigated by incorporating chemically crosslinkable side chains on the bottlebrush, thereby allowing the brush segments to be crosslinked once for a global change in the stiffness of the brush. However, the brush and crosslinker segments then come into close proximity, and in the absence of specific non-covalent interactions, may undergo crosslinking, even at low degrees of conversion. Here we show that mutual interaction between the brush and crosslinker segments – namely π-π interaction between the side chain polymers and Flory-Huggins interaction between the fluorocarbon and carbon backbone polymers – leads to crosslinking-induced softening of the brush stiffness. This approach allows independent control of stiffness and processability of bottlebrush polymers through appropriate selection of non-covalent and covalent interactions. The approach is validated by rheological and small-angle X-ray scattering measurements on a bottlebrush polymer in which the brush is formed by ethyloxazoline monomers and the side chains are formed by tris(trimethylsilyl)silane (TMSSI). Mutual interaction between TMSSI side chains and ethyloxazoline brush segments leads to a large decrease in the bottlebrush stiffness without a significant change in the weight average molecular weight. A novel two-step crosslinking approach is developed that enables gradual and controllable crosslinking of the TMSSI side chains in a spatially and temporally decoupled manner from global crosslinking of the ethyloxazoline brush segments. The approach presented here provides a powerful strategy to independently tune the processability and stiffness in bottlebrush polymer systems, with broad potential applicability across other bottlebrush architectures.

Generalizing circles over finite fields was first investigated in the 19th century. Lüroth showed that every algebraic extension of a field K of finite characteristic p admits a cell structure isomorphic to a circle over Kp, where Kp is the perfect closure of K. Using Faltings’s theorem on algebraically closed fields of positive characteristic with perfect fields of constants, we show that every field with a valuation ring that admits a nice reduction theory admits a cell structure isomorphic to a circle over a perfect closure of the base field. As an application, we give new examples of elliptic curves admitting complex multiplication by number fields that are biquadratic over their normal closures, such as fields of degree 4 and 6. Faltings’s theorem has further implications. A well-known conjecture of Merkur’ev and Suslin says that a field admits a cell structure if and only if its function field admits an elliptic curve as a 0-dimensional subscheme. We show that the analogue of Merkur’ev-Suslin conjecture holds in the 0-dimensional context, and thus we obtain a new proof of the Lüroth problem for function fields. We also discuss schemes and their étale cohomology. Theétale cohomology ring of a scheme Sm with integer coefficients admits a ring structure if and only if Sm has an ample family of affine opens. Using the theory of logarithmic derivations, we show that the étale cohomology of a scheme admitting a cell structure satisfies a certain étale local duality, generalizing the result of Quillen and Gelfand-Manin for elliptic curves. We conclude the paper with various examples and conjectures regarding cell structures on schemes. In particular, we suggest a definition of an oriented cell structure on a scheme. This structure would encode additional information about the orientations of the cells, analogous to the K-theoretic Umkehr map for vector bundles. A typical example of an oriented cell structure is a global orientation on a (coarse) moduli space of elliptic curves with level structure. We propose the existence of such a structure on any elliptic curve, which would give an obstruction to a stable form of the so-called Ribet formula. We prove this conjecture in positive characteristic for certain semi-stable levels using the theory of levels on elliptic curves.

A 1-D site-directed model of rocks and elastomers is used to study the dynamics of earthquakes. The model takes into account the nonlinear elastic response of rocks and the visco-elastic behavior of elastomers. The rocks and elastomers are represented by one or more coupled first-order differential equations. In this paper, we conduct a simulation study for the two-dimensional Burridge-Knopoff (BK) model of earthquakes proposed by Holtz and McRacken (Physica D, 1984, 29, 335-352). The model exhibitsboth peak and post-peak static stress conditions can lead to the occurrence of earthquakes. The results for the maximum first vertical and horizontal principal stress conditions are similar to those found experimentally, but the model qualitatively fails to reproduce the post-peak stress trigger mechanism. The model is extended to a two-dimensional system by replacing the first-order differential equations with difference equations. Simulations of the two-dimensional BK model confirm that both peak and post-peak static stress conditions can lead to the occurrence of earthquakes. The failure mechanism is qualitatively the same as that for the one-dimensional case, although there are quantitative differences. This paper is part of a more general program to develop comprehensive site-directed models of earthquake mechanics that will be used to better understand earthquake dynamics and to make reliable forecasts of earthquakes.

A gravitationally lensed spiral galaxy, IRAS 10190+1322, at z=0.94 was observed with ALMA in Band 7 (323 GHz) in order to study the gas content of the galaxy. The gas is found to be concentrated in a warped rotating disc with a total mass of (2.3 ± 0.2) × 10 10 ; this is comparable to the stellar mass of the galaxy. The deconvolved size of the gas disc is 0.76 kpc, with an inclination of 63° and a position angle of 53°. The properties of the gas disc are similar to those of local ULIRGs, suggesting a close connection between the formation of gas rich galaxies with ultraluminous infrared (ULIR) luminosity. We also observed IRAS 10190+1322 with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in the J = 1-0 and J = 2-1 transitions of carbon monoxide (CO). The CO(1-0) and CO(2-1) lines are spatially resolved and can be fit with a single rotating disc with a total dynamical mass of (2.3 ± 0.2) × 10 10, consistent with the mass derived from the <1mm luminosity. This is the most distant ULIRG to be observed in CO(1-0) and CO(2-1) to date. Using a conversion factor from CO luminosity to mass, we estimate that the gas depletion time is ∼160-200 Myr, consistent with other z ~ 0.7-1.4 ultra-dense gas galaxies (UDGs). We also compare the observed <1mm continuum and CO line properties of IRAS 10190+1322 with predictions from the <1mm continuum and CO lines from near-infrared (NIR) spectrographic decompositions of other local ULIRGs. Both the observed 1-0 and 2-1 transitions are consistent with the average expected from the NIR <1mm continuum, suggesting that the bulk of the gas in IRAS 10190+1322 is warm (T ≳ 300 K) and dense (n(H2) ≳ 10 3 ).

1E 1207.4-5209 or RXJ 0115.9+1555 is a dim isolated neutron star (INS) whose proper motion and radial velocity have not been measured. Based on its characteristic ages ($\tau_c =$ 15.3 – 17.3 billion years), it is likely a member of the nearby 2HWCXB class of binary systems, which are characterized by a fast-spinning, young, neutron star that transfers material to a low-mass companion star via an accretion disk. Based on its distance-independent properties, it is likely also a young neutron star, possibly even less than one million years old. The source of this age is the inferred magnetic field strength of $3.24 \times 10^{13}$–$3.48 \times 10^{13}$ G, which is lower than the quantum critical field for the case of a fully neutrons, pure magnetic moment for a partially filledneutron shell. The characteristic age is consistent with the measured field strength if the field is filled with more than $\sim$90% proton charges. Here we discuss the possible range of ages for 1E 1207.4-5209 based on the measured magnetic field strength, and suggest that this source may have a intermediate-age or old neutron star companion, in agreement with other modeling efforts. We propose that 1E 1207.4-5209 is instead a young neutron star that has undergone catastrophic magnetic field decay as a result of a past episode of rapid-rotation-induced differentiation (r-mode instability). As the source cools, thermal emission from the star will be detectable with radio telescopes, depending on the orientation of the neutron star’s magnetic field with respect to our line of sight. The predicted radio emission corresponds to a luminosity range of 10$^{29}$–10$^{32}$erg/s, which is within the sensitivity limits of current instruments. This is a possible evolution of 1E 1207.4-5209, a dim radio quiet neutron star. Future observations of this object can test this model and further constrain the magnetic field decay rate and the properties of the companion star.

Slide-o-Cam (SOC) is a next-generation virtual slide microscopy system that generates high-fidelity virtual slides from microscopic images of microscope slides. The slide image capture, transmission, and processing are conducted in real-time with no mismatch in the illumination, color, contrast, and exposure between the virtual and real slides. The virtual slides are viewable on modern web browsers and can be annotated with rich graphics and measurements. Since virtual slides are generated from real slides, the labor and reagent costs are eliminated, and the process can be performed in high-throughput mode. Given the extraordinary demand for virtual slides, we describe a slide transmission strategy applicable to virtual slide microscopy. Slide shaving is the process of thinning the glass coverslip attached to a glass slide using either sharp-edged tungsten or carbide plungers or sandpaper, which often damages theslide surface. The SOC uses a diamond-impregnated rubber plunger to create a slide that is suitable for light microscopy, avoiding damage to the surface and allowing the capture of high-resolution images with good signal-to-noise ratio. Slide-shaving is only needed to create a usable slide for transmission; thus, the cost of generating virtual slides is substantially reduced. The SOC slide transmission is quantitatively compared with bright-field microscopy, and similar lateral resolution and signal-to-noise ratio are achieved with lower hardware costs and less effort. Since the SOC uses real microscopes and glass slides, the method can be easily extended to other virtual slide microscopy systems.

A minimal, renormalizable S_3-invariant extension of the Standard Model (SM) with explicit masses for the charged leptons is presented. Using the abelian flavor group S_3, the neutrino mixing pattern TBM with maximal mixing is obtained. In the framework, neutrinos are Majorana fermions and only the bilinears of the left- and right-handed charged leptons appear in the Yukawa interactions. The bilinears transform as an antisymmetric and a symmetric trilpotent representation of S_3, respectively, and lead to an effective coupling of the left- and right-handed charged leptons to the neutrino field, respectively. In consequence, all neutrino mixing angles are predicted and only two free parameters are left in the Yukawa sector, which can be fitted to the experimental data on the charged lepton masses and mixings. Therefore, this model is strongly constrained and fairly predictive.

A short note is describing the observations of the SW Sex star Lyncis with the Kepler telescope. The observations were made in the high state in the visible spectrum. The measurements were done in seven filters, namely: g’, r’, i’, z’, Y, J, and H. The measurements were stable, and the temperature of the component, Lyncis B, was determined. The equivalent Halpha emission is also presented. The results are compared to the previous observations of the same star in its low state, and the similarities and differences between both states are discussed. It is concluded that the size of the accretion disc in the high state is the same, while the temperature and the amount of ionisation in the disc are higher. The changes in the hot flow are smaller than in the disc. The observed changes are a result of increasing the mass-accretion rate. It is proposed that the high state is a transition to a shorter and weaker optically thick outflow, and that the high state is a stable transition, and that a low state will not appear. The observations were presented on May 20, 2023.

The goal of this paper is to study horizon-penetrating transonic accretion disks around rotating black holes. By considering the gas as a perfect fluid, we solve the first law of thermodynamics, Euler’s equation and the Transonic Godunov’s equations. We perform a series of simulations for various values of the mass of the black hole and investigate the influence of the angular momentum and the pressure gradient of the flow on the stability of the solution and the corresponding Shakura-Sunyaev $\alpha$ parameter. We observe the formation of a thick, hot, Keplerian disk when the specific angular momentum of the flow, $l$, equals the specific angular momentum of the black hole, $l_{BH}$, at some distance $x_{isco}$ from the black hole. For high values of the specific angular momentum of the flow, $l$, a rarefaction wave is created far away from the black hole, in such a way that the flow transits from a subsonic to a supersonic regime just outside the black hole. We also observe the formation of a sonic point, where the specific entropy and the specific energy are maximum and henceforth a sonic line is formed, joining the sonic point to the black hole. The flow remains subsonic inside the sonic line. For $l < l_{BH}$ a shock is created between the inflowing gas and the outgoing shocked gas. Thus, for a specific angular momentum of the flow equal to the specific angular momentum of the black hole, a horizon-penetrating accretion disk is formed that connects the horizon of the black hole to the outer edge of the flow. Such horizon-penetrating accretion disks may be key to understanding quasars and other supermassive black holes with enormous masses.

The richest superclusters. V. The most populated superclusters in the local volume (z < 0.02) and their probable evolution. We present the galaxy population of the most populated superclusters in the local volume (z < 0.02) and their probable evolution. We applied a semi-automatic algorithm to identify 72 most populated superclusters in the local volume (z < 0.02). At a given moment these superclusters contain 50% of the local galaxy population, and their stellar mass density is likely to remain approximately constant in the near future. We found that these superclusters are stable dynamically and do not show any signs of mass drop off. The most populated superclusters identified are: the Perseus-Pegasus, Virgo-Canis Major, Corona Borealis, Centaurus, Ophiuchus, and Chamaeleon. Our local volume is relatively empty in comparison to more distant superclusters. In this region there is a cluster Abell S1063 with approximately 14,000 galaxies (mostly from the XXL catalog), and a few more rich superclusters with up to 2000 galaxies. In the near future the stellar mass density in the most populated superclusters is likely to continue to increase due to both slow infall of new galaxies and interactions and merging of already existing galaxies. In the nearest future the supercluster Centaurus (approximately 200 Mpc in radius) is likely to undergo a strong merging event and increase its mass by a factor of 2-3. In the distant future the most populated superclusters identified will merge and form a single supercluster with a scale approximately 100 Mpc in radius containing approximately 10,000,000 galaxies. Recently, many intermediate redshift ($z=0.6$) massive galaxies have been found to have abundant and strikingly collimated massive outflows in their interstellar medium (ISM) (Feruglio et al. 2015, 2016; Shiba et al. 2015; Kenney et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2016). These galaxies have undergone a period of intense star formation (‘starburst’) at $z=1-2$, but now appear as largely passively evolving, massive red galaxies at $z=0.6$. This provides direct evidence that efficient feedback, either from Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) or stars, is capable of expelling significant reservoirs of gas from these galaxies, and that feedback becomes more important with increasing stellar mass. Here we report the serendipitous discovery of spectacular 1000 km/s outflows in the z=0.6 descendant of the initially-targeted massive post-starburst galaxies. These galaxies show no current star formation and are not associated with any observed radio source. The outflow properties (velocity, spatial extent, host galaxy metallicity, line ratios) are very similar to the local starburst sample, and unlike the lower redshift post-starburst galaxies. We discuss several scenarios to explain these observations: these galaxies recently ceased star formation, but have not had enough time for new generations of stars to alter the dynamics of the ejected gas. Alternatively, these outflows may be triggered by a low-level AGN, or continue the process of feedback that is clearly active at lower redshifts. We conclude by discussing the potential for future outflow studies to discriminate between these and other scenarios for galaxy evolution."

Magnetic ordering in multiferroic materials has attracted intense research interest recently due to their potential application in electrical control of magnetic orders. In particular, structurally simple transition-metal perovskites are widely considered as promising candidates for engineering magnetoelectric (ME) couplings, due to their significant flexibility in terms of structural transition temperatures and magnetic orders. However, sluggish magnetic dynamics and competitive structural instabilities often lead to compromised ME responses. In this work, we carry out first-principles investigations on the multiferroic tendencies of perovskite biferroics through structural deformations. We find that these materials generally feature double-well energy landscapes for both magnetic orders and atomic distortions. Two notable examples include CoTiO3 and CrTiO3, which have been intensively studied for their competing ferroelectric and antiferromagnetic orders. We further map out the coupling between magnetic orderings and identify a series of stable metastable magnetic phases with enhanced ME responses. These results provide useful information for rational design of multiferroic materials with desirable couplings and open up new avenues for stabilizing noncollinear magnetic orders in complex materials systems.

In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the soft scalar potential for the MSSM Higgs doublets results in masses that are generally dependent on several parameters. One of these is the ratio of the vacuum expectation values of the two Higgs doublets. The possibility that these masses could vary with this parameter has been examined before but with simplified assumptions. In this paper, I consider the more general situation where there can be several sets of Froggatt-Nielsen fields that give rise to different patterns of masses for the up-type and down-type quarks. I find that there are regions of the model’s parameter space where the CP-violating phases can satisfy the conditions necessary for a significant departure from the standard model prediction for the electric dipole moment of the electron. The electric dipole moments of the neutron and mercury may also be within the reach of current experiments. eded In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), the soft scalar potential for the MSSM Higgs doublets results in masses that are generally dependent on several parameters. A long-standing problem in the study of Type Ib/Ic supernovae is the detection and characterization of the circumstellar material (CSM). It was found that a fraction of these SNe Ibc display strong hydrogen lines in their spectra, and some of them were observed to be associated with young stellar populations. The high velocity of some material, the presence of dust, and the association with young stellar populations are all difficult to explain if the material has been ejected by the progenitor star shortly prior to the explosion. This work reports a young stellar population, consistent with zero age main sequence (ZAMS) stellar model, and intermediate mass loss on the year pre-SN orbital period derived from the photometric observations of the hosting star cluster. At the same time, we report the detection of dust emission and absorption in the SN Ibc 2006jc spectra, with the estimated masses of 7.2 × 10−3 M⊙ for the dust emission and 5.2 × 10−2 M⊙ for the absorption. The presence of dust in the very early stages of the evolution of a Type Ib/Ic supernova is very unusual and poorly understood. Dust condensation in the forward shock heated CSM is possible, but the observed near- and mid-IR properties of the dust grains are different from those expected in the case of thin forward shock dust. We discuss several alternative scenarios that could produce the observed dust properties and elemental composition, including the pre-SN mass-loss of the progenitor in a dusty torus, the detonation of a non-degenerate off-center C+O core in a very low-mass (8-10 M⊙) red supergiant, and the fallback of expelled shell material.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in using neural networks to automatically learn feature representations, with tremendous successes in numerous applications. However, despite the empirical successes, the theoretical understanding of these black-box models is still missing. Existing analysis methods suffer from strong assumptions and/or limited applicability. To address this fundamental understanding gap, we study the generalization error of feed-forward neural network with respect to the capacity, the number of layers and the width, without strong assumptions on the training data and neural networks. Our analysis yields a precise characterization of the generalization error in terms of a trade-off between the network width and the norm of the training data. We further propose a new regularizer that provably improves the representation power of the neural networks and thus reduces the required norm of the training data. Based on the proposed regularizer, we then develop a learning algorithm to train very deep neural networks with our theoretical guarantees. Experiments on synthetic and real data sets validate the effectiveness of our method and show significant improvements over the state-of-the-art methods. These results are significant in theory and practice. They not only characterize the generalization ability of neural networks without strong assumptions, but also provide a practical approach to improve the representation power of neural networks with limited training data.

While the classical mechanics fully describes the microscopic world, we are still lacking a complete theory for the larger systems, namely the macroscales. In this paper we introduce the Quantum-Like Representation (QLR) for the macroscales, and apply it to rigid body motion. In classical mechanics the dynamics of a rigid body is fully determined by the positions and orientations of its mass points (i.e. the constituent particles). In the context of the Newton’s laws, the motions of the individual particles are in turn determined by the laws of Newton and the constraints of the rigid body. Thus the dynamics of the rigid body motion can be fully described by the constrainted Hamiltonian system of differential equations, where the Hamiltonian is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies. However, the direct computation of the rigid body motion from the knowledge of the positions and orientations of its mass points is not unique. For example, the orientations of the rigid body uniquely determine the rigid body itself but not its motions. The rigid body motions depend on the choice of reference frame. Thus to find the rigid body motions one needs to know the reference frame. Quantum Mechanics (QM) overcomes this indeterminacy by postulating a new entity, wave function, which simultaneously encodes the position and orientation of the mass points. The evolution of the wave function can be described by an integro-differential equation. Remarkably, the quantum mechanics also provides an algorithm to compute the rigid body motion from the knowledge of its wave function, if it is available. However, the practical applicability of QM has been restricted to the microscopic scales because the mass points at different scales could not be considered as fully independent, since they are connected by some kind of a global constraints. For example, at the molecular scale the interactions between the molecules are predominantly described by the Coulomb’s laws. These laws state that the interactions between the molecules are governed by the negative force, proportional to the product of the charges and the square of the distance. Thus the problem of the rigid body motion at the molecular scale reduces to the classical mechanics at the molecular point mass. Nevertheless, as the scale increases the interactions become more complex and therefore the classical mechanics fails to describe the motions. For example, the interactions between the atoms in a molecules become predominantly described by the quantum mechanics, i.e. the Coulomb’s law is replaced by the Schrödinger equation. Similarly, at the macroscales the rigid body dynamics reduces to the rigid body motion at the molecular point masses plus the internal interactions at the atomistic levels. In this paper we introduce the Quantum-Like Representation (QLR) to merge the advantages of the quantum mechanics and the classical mechanics. The main idea is to introduce a small amount of indeterminacy to the rigid body dynamics at the atomic levels and to introduce some global constraints that account for the macroscales. Such model, equipped with the proper constraints and parameters, at the appropriate length and time scales

Topological insulators are an exciting new class of materials that represent an additional state of matter to conventional conductors and superconductors. In three spatial dimensions, these phases are characterized by topological invariant-like bulk properties that are protected by time-reversal symmetry. Because of this protection, topological insulators exhibit insulating behavior not only in the conductance but also in the current flow as measured by the quantum Hall effect and the more general anomalous Hall effect. These flow phenomena are robust to imperfections in the system, providing a possible route to measurements with improved sensitivity. One remarkable aspect of topological insulators is that they are typically metallic in one or more of the three spatial directions. This one-dimensional conductivity, known as a topological quantum wire, is robust against nonmagnetic impurities and provides another route to realizing conductive behavior in previously insulating systems. The combination of insulating and conductive properties makes topological insulators an appealing potential basis for a range of next-generation electronic devices. While topological insulators in three spatial dimensions have been realized experimentally, engineering synthetic lower-dimensional topological phases remains an active research direction. In this work, we show that two-dimensional spin-orbit coupling exhibits topological phases beyond the conventional Brillouin zone. In particular, we find a phase with mirror Chern numbers, robust against weak spin-orbit preserving distortions. In the spin-orbit parameter space, this phase lies smoothly over the conventional Chern insulating phase and near to the Chern quantum Hall insulator phase. The critical phases between these topological phases can be captured by an emergent lattice fermion theory, whose phase diagram agrees with renormalization group analysis. These findings provide a general mechanism for topological phases beyond the conventional Brillouin zone, suggesting that spin-orbit coupling can produce robust two-dimensional topological phases with potential for experimental realization.

In this paper we present a new exact solution of Dirac-Coulomb equation with exact boundary condition. This solution represents a hydrogen-like system with non-zero angular momentum. We also discuss the meaning and implications of this result. change Dirac-Coulomb equation with exact boundary condition has a unique solution with zero energy. Two A-type post-AGB stars, namely IRAS08281-4850 and IRAS14325-6428, were observed to have enhanced abundances of neutron-capture elements. These elements were produced in previous stellar cycles through the slow neutron capture process. The observed abundance patterns are consistent with the assumption that both stars are descendants of prior nucleosynthesis activity. This points to IRAS08281-4850 and IRAS14325-6428 having previously undergone nucleosynthesis on the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) and through a former AGB phase, respectively. IRAS08281-4850 and IRAS14325-6428 have stellar parameters of T˜30,000 K, log g˜3.5, and M˜-4.0. The enrichment patterns are consistent with slow neutron capture nucleosynthesis (s-process). In particular, the two stars have experienced previous nucleosynthesis on the asymptotic giant branch (AGB).

We study four dimensional superconformal field theories (SCFTs), also known as conformal nets, describing the systems of local degrees of freedom propagating in spacetime. We first give a general definition of these systems, along with an axiomatic characterization of their symmetry structure. This general definition allows us to place a number of known conformal field theories within this framework. We then introduce the notion of quotient conformal net. This is a representation of a conformal net through its subnet generated by a particular charge. We show that these representations classify the nets up to isomorphism. Finally, we present a general classification algorithm for conformal nets. This algorithm relies on a well-defined algorithm to represent conformal nets as integral closures of algebriahly generated subnet systems, which we provide. The algorithm is complete, in the sense that all conformal nets can be classified using this procedure. We also apply our general classification algorithm to some well-known conformal nets, recovering previous results as special cases. We also discuss a number of open problems for future work.

The intrinsic shape of a cluster of galaxies determines its orientation in space. The spin axis of a galaxy cluster is expected to align with the mass distribution of the cluster, so measuring the intrinsic shape provides a means of measuring the cluster’s mass. We use weak lensing to measure the shapes of 1445 galaxies in the Virgo cluster and combine this with previously-published photometric data to model the cluster as oblate, prolate, or triaxial. The oblate model provides a good fit to the data, but the best-fitting triaxial model has an axis ratio of λ = 1.20 ± 0.04, corresponding to a logarithmic mass of log(M) = 13.74 ± 0.07 within a radius of r_{e}} (= 96.4 kpc). The Virgo Cluster is typically modeled as oblate; however, we find that it is triaxial with an intermediate axis ratio of λ = 1.20. This result is consistent with previous measurements of the cluster’s mass, suggesting that the shape is a true representation of the cluster’s mass distribution. Our findings could help shed light on the formation and evolution of cluster-sized halos in general, as well as aid in our understanding of the influence of dark matter on the formation of cosmic structure.

In this feasibility study, we present a Spin Wave Bus (SWB) that can be used to connect and supply logic circuits. In particular, we demonstrate a 100-node SWB prototype, containing a two-dimensional topological interface for connection. We present a crossbar-based routing algorithm for the SWB, and discuss its overhead and limitations. Furthermore, we present the low-level timing and control protocol for the SWB, and evaluate its performance by connecting several SWB topologies to a signal integrity testing board. The results demonstrate that the SWB provides a suitable inter-circuit communication interface with low overhead and low latency.' Overall, this work represents an important step towards realizing logic circuits interconnected via a SWB. A new form of dynamic fibril was discovered in H-alpha and C IV in the spectrum of the white light comet 45P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. The fibrils move with different velocities and have different orientations. We suggest that they are the fragments of the gas flow around the nucleus. The discovery of this new form of dynamic fibril expands the catalog of its properties. It may be a sign of active process of fragmentation of the gas flow around the nucleus. In this paper we examine the possibility of stable vector bundles over higher-dimensional spacetimes without gravity by considering the local structure of the gauge group on the fiber. In four dimensions, the necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of stable vector bundles with rank greater than or equal to four is the absence of global holomorphic vector bundles with similar characteristics. In higher dimensions, we generalize this condition using the Hodge number which governs the local topological properties of the gauge group. We find several higher-dimensional examples of stable bundles over a sphere and over a hyperbolic plane, including some with both extra spacetime and gauge symmetries. This solves several stability problems in supergravities and string theories with large extra dimensions. In particular, we consider a simple four-dimensional example with general covariance, general coordinate invariance, and with the gauge group structure $SU(2) \times SU(2)$ local on the fiber over a four-sphere. For this bundle, the necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of stable vector bundles with rank greater than or equal to four is the absence of global holomorphic vector bundles with similar characteristics. We further show that this bundle can be defined over a complex four-dimensional manifold, with the holomorphic structure induced by the gauge group structure. We also discuss several higher-dimensional examples. For a simple point particle in eleven dimensions we find a stable vector bundle with the gauge group $SO(5) \times SO(5)$, local on the fiber over a five-sphere. The necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such a stable bundle is the absence of global holomorphic vector bundles with similar characteristics. We also consider the case of a five-dimensional torus which is a product of two four-dimensional spheres. In this case, we find that the necessary and sufficient condition for the stability of a vector bundle is that there are no holomorphic vector bundles of the appropriate rank and second Chern class.

The interplay between spatial structures and phases near first-order phase transitions has been shown to lead to intriguing phenomena such as mobility-induced phase transitions and pattern selection. Motivated by the latter, we study the emergence of cooperating clusters in a well-mixed population of agents that use a nearest-neighbor interacting model to represent friendship relations. Each player interacts with its neighboring players in the same cluster with a zealotry strategy, i.e., with probability 1-2α the player sticks to its own opinion, and with probability α it changes its opinion with a probability that depends on the fraction of neighbors who have the same opinion. We find that the fraction of cluster players deviates from the fraction of individuals in the population in a way that is optimal for α, i.e., the success rate of the clustering process, if and only if the cluster structure is taken into account. In particular, the fraction of cluster players increases as α decreases, until it saturates at a critical α=αc, where the success rate of the clustering process reaches its maximum. We compute αc as a function of the clustering coefficient, i.e., the probability that two neighbors of a node are also neighbors of each other, of the network. We show that αc is maximized for networks that have a small-world behavior, i.e., a clustering coefficient larger than the average clustering coefficient of random graphs with the same mean degree. This indicates that the clustering phenomenon could be exploited in social networks to promote the emergence of cooperation.

A granular gasifier known as the Thomas-Fermi converter [1] is an erosive, gas-modification device that converts inorganic material into an emitted waste product that consists ofFootnote 1: minute, nano-sized particles called aerosols [2], and utilizes directed, impinging gas jets as an efficient means of aerosolizing and partially combusting the inorganic material. The efficacy of this device is often criticized for its lack of granular temperature regulation. The process relies on the impingement of high-temperature gas jets onto the input granular bed, resulting in high-temperature, pressure fluctuations within the device. To date, the collective dynamics of these pressure fluctuations have not been characterized. In this work, the authors leverage lab-scale high-speed pressure sensing to characterize the statistical moments and power spectra of these fluctuations as a function of operating variables (gas temperature, gas velocity, nozzle angle). In all cases, the authors observe positive dynamic yield in that the power spectra are characterized by a region of quiescence interspersed with intermittent broadband noise and large-scale pressure fluctuations. Interestingly, the authors find that the pressure fluctuations are not independent. In fact, multiple fluctuation characteristics demonstrate clear signs of coupling: positive dynamic yield is dependent onpressure rolloff; broadband noise is effectively suppressed via pressuredrop instabilities; and large-scale fluctuations are propped via broadband noise. Lastly, the authors demonstrate that the operating parameters can independently influence the nature of the fluctuations, yet the interactions between these dynamics gives rise to emergent behaviors not anticipated by the empirical observations.

This paper presents a generic solution to share product information within a supply chain context. The specific context of use for this work is in the food industry, specifically with regards to bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) testing of cattle. This information is useful for producers and traders to identify historical BSE status of cattle, which in turn allows for the development of optimized distribution and supply chain management strategies. The distributed networked architecture presented enables multiple parties to access the same product information in real-time from any location through the internet. The framework uses XML and JSON over SSL/TLS for web services, along with standard database technology (MySQL), to enable the different actors in a supply chain to access the required information efficiently. The proposed framework is generic and can be applied to any industry for the exchange of product information, where the need exists. In today’s global, supply chain-conscious world, the ability to share information quickly and efficiently is of vital importance to all industries. With the advent of smart-technology, the ability to access and share information, while located in any location through the internet, is more readily available than ever. This has led to the development of innovative, open-source frameworks that enable distributed networked architectures that make efficient use of technology. The food industry is an industry that utilizes complex supply chain systems to distribute products from producer to consumer. This industry is no different and, with the advent of new and emerging diseases, such as BSE (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), requires all parties involved in a supply chain to have access to timely and accurate information regarding the status of individual cattle. Information sharing in this industry is a challenging process, due to the lack of a central repository for cattle BSE test results. Different cattle testing laboratories in the European Union, namely, the Netherlands, United Kingdom, and Germany, publish their test results in XML format on their individual website. These test results are in essence “data islands” with limited access and no ability to share information between parties. This paper describes a framework that enables multiple parties to access the required cattle BSE test results from any location through the internet, in real-time. The framework consists of the following: (1) a web-server interface that enables all industry participants to access cattle BSE test results from any location through the internet, (2) a cattle BSE data-exchange format for the real-time interchange of cattle BSE test results, and (3) web-service-based data access using a XML and JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) interface to XML and JSON over SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security) with standard database technology (MySQL). This framework has been designed to be generic and can be applied to any industry for the exchange of product information, where the need exists.
