Spin relaxation of electrons in semiconductors is a process by which a ferromagnet, in which the electron spins are aligned, becomes a paramagnet due to collisions that randomly rotate the electron spins. The dominant spin relaxation mechanism in semiconductors is the so-called Dyakonov-Perel mechanism, which occurs when the electron undergoes a hyperfine interaction with an atom in the semiconductor lattice and experiences an exchange enhancement or quantum beats if the electron wave vector and the nuclear spin wave vector are similar. The mechanism was described for the first time by I.E. Dyakonov and V.Y. Perel in 1971 and subsequently applied to understand experimental results. The Bir-Aronov-Pikus (BAP) mechanism was proposed in 1974 to describe spin relaxation in inversion layers of semiconductors with paramagnetic impurities. The theory takes into account the relativistic effects of band structure. Although the theory was developed a long time ago, it has not been applied to quantitatively describe experimental results. In this work, we present the first quantitative comparison between the BAP and Dyakonov-Perel mechanisms, considering both Dresselhaus and Bychkov-Rashba spin-orbit interactions. We found that in samples with dominant spin-orbit interactions, such as InSb and GaAs, the spin relaxation time due to the BAP mechanism is an order of magnitude larger than that due to the Dyakonov-Perel mechanism. We also discuss the effect of band structure on the efficiency of the BAP mechanism.

On the 150th anniversary of the birth of theoretical physicistClerk Maxwell, a novel form of light-based quantum simulation, known as optical lattices, was recently proposed1,2. By arranging laser beams in a specific pattern and tuning their relative intensities, it is possible to simulate magnetic domains, quasiparticles, and even short-ranged interactions in a system of ultra-cold atoms trapped in this optical potential3,4,5. In this way, quantum simulations, which traditionally require near-perfect isolation from external disturbances, can be performed in lattices which are themselves capable of sensing and responding to perturbations. Here, we demonstrate this principle by simulating the fractional quantum Hall effect in an optical lattice. In this system, atoms are loaded into a two-dimensional square lattice and subjected to an artificial magnetic field. For appropriate choices of the lattice parameters, the system exhibits a variety of quantum Hall states, including the highly-counterintuitive fractionally-charged quasiparticles with charge e/4. We characterize these phases by measuring the real-space structure of the collective excitations and by measuring the quasiparticle's dynamical structure factor. Finally, we show that it is possible to move from the fractionally-quantum-Hall to the trivial-insulating phases by varying a single lattice parameter. This result establishes a clear link between quantum simulations and condensed matter physics, and provides a powerful method for exploring a broad range of novel quantum phenomena.

A rapidly growing population of distant gamma-ray sources has been identified with galaxies whose apparent ultraviolet or optical light is explained by a non-thermal power-law component, often associated with a putative accretion-disk corona or with synchrotron radiation from accelerated electrons. This same non-thermal continuum is typically observed in the gamma-rays, with additional very high-energy gamma-ray emission which may be characteristic of the blazar phenomenon. We report the detection by the Large Area Telescope on board the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope of the unresolved gamma-ray emission from the 2LAC catalog of gamma-ray loud active galactic nuclei. This represents the first determination of the extragalactic gamma-ray background light (EGBGL) beyond 100 GeV, and includes a strong component at mid-infrared wavelengths. The emission in the 30 μm - 40 μm spectral region is well explained by starlight re-processed by the diffuse interstellar medium in galaxy halos, and is unlikely to be associated with blazar gamma-ray emission. However, the Fermi data show that the EGBGL above 1 GeV is largely independent of the mid-infrared starlight contribution, and this shows that the additional very high-energy gamma-ray emission is likely to be blazar in origin. We calculate the integral gamma-ray luminosity contributed by 2LAC blazars above each energy and demonstrate that the Fermi data are inconsistent with a simple extrapolation of the low-energy EGBGL. We conclude that the blazar population in the 2LAC catalog is most likely not representative of the entire unresolved extragalactic gamma-ray background, and that the sources of that background may in fact be dominated by flat-spectrum radio quasars which are currently entirely unrecognizable in the optical or ultraviolet bands.

Stellar multiplicity greatly impacts the formation and evolution of planetary systems. The sheer number of possible systems, however, has made observationally determining the impacts a challenge. This work utilizes the occurrence of planets around nearby stars as a function of stellar multiplicity as well as other stellar and planetary properties to elucidate the impacts of stellar duplicity. The investigation makes use of both observations from the APPLY project and archival data from Planet Hunters, as well as a novel Bayesian approach to assign parameters to validated planets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. The results demonstrate that stellar multiplicity has a statistically significant impact on the occurrence of planets with radii less than twice that of the Earth, with higher-order multiples showing fewer planets than single stars. Furthermore, there is also a weak correlation between stellar multiplicity and the multiplicity of planets, with singles having the highest multiplicity. Planet size has no statistically significant impact on planet occurrence, though this may be due to a smaller sample size and the adopted planet population not being sufficiently representative of the overall occurrence rates. This work demonstrates that planets in multiple star systems are less likely to be large enough to potentially support life, which could have profound implications for planet formation and the prevalence of life in the Universe.

In this paper we discuss two problems that are intimately related to one another. The first one is that of detecting critical delays in discrete-time linear time-invariant (LTI) systems. We show that this detection problem can be cast as a question of finding the smallest eigenvalue of a certain algebraic equation. We then show that this smallest eigenvalue can be determined by first determining the smallest eigenvalue of a so-called Hurwitz matrix, which can in turn be expressed in terms of a certain augmented system of the given LTI system. Such an augmented system can in turn be constructed by appropriately adjoining a so-called observability matrix to the given LTI system. We then discuss this augmented system in terms of polynomials, whose roots give the smallest eigenvalue. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method for detecting critical delays by providing several examples. Our method can also be used to obtain the smallest eigenvalue in exact arithmetic, and thus can also be used as an eigenvalue solver. We also discuss how this approach can be extended to the case of a discrete-time LTV system.

This paper presents an empirical consistency test of dark energy models by using currently available observational data. Standard parametric dark energy models such as the Chevallier-Polarsky-Linder (CPL) model, the hepler-filed (CH) model, and the generalized Chaplygin gas (GCG) model are tested. To perform the test, the latest observational data from Supernovae Type Ia (SN Ia), Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), and the shift parameter from galaxy redshift survey are used. It is shown that the CPL and CH models are not consistent with the observational data. While the GCG model is still consistent with the observational data, it is found that the curvature parameter of the GCG model needs to be extremely large in order to satisfy the current observational data. This result implies that the GCG model is not a good dark energy model. In comparison, the CH model, with the introduction of a drifting term, is shown to be significantly better than the CPL and GCG models. It is therefore suggested that the CH model should be tested against the current observational data. It is found that the CH model is still not consistent with the observational data. It is further shown that the consistency of the CH model can be significantly improved by introducing an interaction between dark matter and dark energy. It is therefore concluded that the CH model with an interaction can serve as an effective phenomenological dark energy model.

Transcription factors (TFs) are proteins that bind to specific sites on DNA and regulate gene transcription. The binding of a TF to a site on DNA influences the rate of spontaneous fluctuations of the TF concentration in the cell, and this phenomenon is called stochastic feedback. In this work, we present a model that describes the TF binding kinetics in a cell in terms of random transitions of a TF molecule between different binding sites on DNA, with each site characterized by a unique binding affinity. The TF concentration and positions of the sites on DNA are represented by a 1D or 2D array of finite size L. This allows for modeling different TFs that can potentially bind thousands of sites across the whole genome. We assume that the TF molecule undergoes biased random walks with small jumps between nearest-neighbor sites on the DNA. The jumps are governed by several independent rates that determine the transitions between the nearest-neighbor binding sites on the DNA and define the corresponding binding affinities. The overall system dynamics is governed by several kinetic rates that depend on TF concentration, DNA binding site configuration, and the nuclear concentration of proteins that bind the DNA and affect the TF binding rates. The model allows for a systematic study of the effect of different kinetic rates on the distributions of binding site occupancies and kinetics of target gene transcription.

The SW Sextantis (SW Sext) stars are a recently identified population of cataclysmic variables (CVs). So far, they have been discovered exclusively in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Stripe 82 region, and comprise nearly 20 percent of all CVs with orbital periods of 3-4 hours. They share many properties with other short-period CV subclasses, but are distinguishable through characteristic absorption lines in the SDSS spectra. The SW Sext population likely originates from the same population of CVs that produce most highly eccentric systems with short periods (period bounce CVs), and have been spun up to fast rotation through tidal spin-up in close contact systems. We discuss the observed properties of the SW Sext population in the context of different formation channels and explore the evolutionary state of the current SW Sextantis stars. Energy released by a single SW Sextantis star is large enough to power an entire galaxies. As such, SW Sextantis stars represent an important class of sources for the Sloan Digital Sky Survey equatorial strips, and may be responsible for some of the optical variability observed in these regions.

In this paper, we consider the general case of MIMO systems with Finite Rate Channel State Feedback and a Power On/Off strategy. We first characterize the limit on the achievable rate as the length of the feedback channel goes to infinity. In order to illustrate the tightness of the characterization, we provide a counter example where the achievable rate is strictly lower than the limit. Then we characterize the optimal power on/off strategy. Interestingly, for fixed feedback length, we show that the on/off ratio has a threshold behavior with respect to the channel realizations, and the off state is most likely to appear when the channel is in weak interference regime. Moreover, in strong interference regime, even though more power would help increase the achievable rate, it would also increase the feedback burden. We further study the optimal strategy in the intermediate interference regime, and characterize the optimal on/off ratio in terms of the effective channel gain. Numerical results confirm the insights from the analysis.

Evidence for the Decay D^0 --> K^_pi^+pi^-e^+nu_e. In contrast to the standard model (SM) expectation, a decays to a and a Indirect evidence for this decay was found in a analysis of a data set corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 5.3 fb−1, with 3 standard deviations (3σ) significance. The analysis was performed using a multivariate artificial neural network approach, with potential systematic errors taken into account. A different analysis using a similar technique found this decay with significance of 2σ. In this work we present a third analysis using the same data set and similar techniques that provides the first observation of this decay with significance exceeding 3σ. We measure the branching fraction to be [1.48_{- 0.60}^{+ 0.78}(stat+syst)]% and present the first measurement of the relative forward-backward asymmetry A_{FB} = [0.58 \pm 0.31(stat) \pm 0.13(syst)]%. We determine the squared average strong coupling constant αS(M^2_Z) = [0.125 \pm 0.009(stat) \pm 0.003(syst)]_{exp}.

An accurate description of optical precursors to major space weather events is of vital importance to space mission design and interpretation, and to accurate solar meteorology. We identify the origin of the timing uncertainty for optical precursors in existing models and show that this can be reduced with the addition of two new variables: a conditional forecast of convection for the photospheric optical depth parameter α, and a prognostic equation for the electron scale length L es. This provides the first model that can accurately describe both the timing and spatial extent of coherent optical transients associated with coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We demonstrate the skill of the model by retrospectively applying it to the 17 February 2020 main group CME that drove the February 2020 storm, and make forecasts for the 10 March 2020 interplanetary coronal mass ejection (ICME) associated with this storm. We show that the timing and spatial extent of weak-field optical transients for both the February and March 2020 storms are accurately described by the model, supporting the hypothesis that α and L es play a fundamental role in the propagation of CME-CME (and ICME-ICME) magnetic field interactions.

Stellar Population Models (SPMs) provide powerful tools for constraining the formation and evolution of galaxies. In particular, SPMs based on stellar population synthesis can be used to measure detailed element abundance patterns in galaxies by comparing the spectra of individual stars to the galaxy integrated spectrum. In recent years, the high precision of spectral observations from 8–10m class telescopes and the sophisticated SPMs based on state-of-the-art stellar evolution and atmosphere models have enabled precise measurements of individual element abundances in stars in the Milky Way and in external galaxies, providing strong observational evidence in support of various modern model predictions for the evolution of stars, galaxies, and the universe. In this paper we discuss the theoretical uncertainties of SPMs that can significantly affect the accuracy of element abundance measurements using SPMs based on population synthesis. We focus on the treatment of physical processes in pre-main sequence (PMS) stars and in red giant stars and its influence on SPMs using theoretical stellar evolution models from the MIST (Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics) project. We demonstrate that different models for a given physical process can result in differences of a factor of 2 in the luminosity of a PMS star at a given mass, which can translate to differences of 1–2 dex in the predicted lifetime of a star and, therefore, in the amount of a specific element that is synthesized during its lifetime. The predicted lifetime difference of PMS stars leads to differences of 0.5–1 dex in the mass of main-sequence stars at a given age. We emphasize the importance of using a single, well-tested and documented set of PMS evolution models for all stellar populations in a galaxy when determining precise element abundance patterns using SPMs.

Recent experimental advances in the synthesis of single walled carbon nanotubes have enabled the study of nanotubes of specific diameters and chiralities. It has been shown that individual nanotubes possess different thermal and mechanical properties which are strongly dependent on the temperature at which the nanotube is examined. Molecular dynamics simulations may provide a means of determining how these properties are affected by atomic structure, and may aid in the understanding of experimental results. In this work, we examine the effects of temperature on the Young’s modulus, longitudinal modulus, and dilatational modulus of single walled carbon nanotubes using O(N) tight binding molecular dynamics simulations. We observe that, over the temperature range examined (300 K-3000 K), all nanotube properties follow a linear scaling relation, and we characterize the functional dependence of these scaling relations using thermal parameter α. At high temperatures, the Young’s modulus of nanotubes depends quadratically on the thermal parameter α, while at lower temperatures, a power law is observed. We also observe an optimal range of α for each property, where the modulus is maximized. We observe similar temperature dependences of the longitudinal and dilatational moduli of nanotubes. This work characterizes the temperature dependence of the Young’s modulus, longitudinal modulus, and dilatational modulus of single walled carbon nanotubes using O(N) tight binding molecular dynamics simulations. We observe that over the temperature range examined, all nanotube properties scale linearly with the thermal parameter α, and characterize the functional dependence of these scaling laws. We also observe an optimal range of α for each property, where the modulus is maximized.

The paper shows how the IT Service Centre at Harz University, a 100-people team operating in the scope of Group Information and Communication, utilised the ITIL service management framework. In order to illustrate its practical relevance, the framework is applied to the Release Management Process, showing improvements that were enabled by using the ITIL methodology. The paper concludes with some lessons learned and a discussion of how these can be applied to other processes. The ITIL framework was originally developed by the British government to support the implementation of best practices in the management of Information Technology services in the public sector. In recent years, the framework has also gained popularity in the private sector. Following an evaluation of the framework’s applicability to IT service management in a university setting, this paper shows how ITIL can be used to benefit such a setting. To this end, the Release Management Process of the IT Service Centre at Harz University is utilised as a concrete example. The process is analysed to determine areas in which it could be improved by using ITIL, and these improvements are illustrated using the example of the used of ITIL in the Release Management Process.

We present spatially resolved mid-infrared spectra of three ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs) obtained with the Spitzer Space Telescope. Compared to local ULIRGs, the stellar continuum of the individual galaxies is much weaker, and the silicate dust features at 9.7 and 18.3 μm are more heavily filled in. The silicate absorption is also reduced in the ensemble average spectrum of the sample. The relative strength of the emission features implies that the current starbursts are heavily obscured by dust in theuclear regions, and that substantial amounts of dust are present in the outer disks. The kinematics of the line profiles suggest that the bulk of the molecular gas and the dominant fraction of the dust are in the circumnuclear regions. Weaker stellar continua and stronger dust features indicate enhanced starburst activity in these ULIRGs relative to their ULIRG analogs at low redshift. The high obscuration and mid-infrared spectra that are more typical of local ULIRGs suggest that these galaxies have evolved substantially since the peak of their infrared activity, either through reduction of the circumnuclear obscuration or conversion of large amounts of dust to stars.

In this paper, we propose and investigate a scheme to reconstruct vibrational states in warm molecules using four-wave mixing with femtosecond laser pulses. Vibrational states play an important role in many chemical reactions and widely used in characterizing chemical species. However, studying vibrational states inwarm molecules is challenging because the low energy modes are overdamped and cannot be resolved using standard methods. We propose a scheme to overcome this challenge using a four-wave mixing process in warm molecules. We first describe the absorption and fluorescence pathways for a molecule in a thermal equilibrium environment. We then show how the warm molecule response can be reconstructed by measuring the four-wave mixing signals using an interferometric approach. By analyzing the coherence of the interfering beams, the vibrational state information can be retrieved from the signals. We demonstrate the feasibility of the scheme by simulating the reconstruction of the first three vibrationally excited states in hot water.

The distribution of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way is a powerful tool to study the structure and dynamics of our Galaxy. HI gas probes the gravitational potential, and can trace the potential's normal and mass distributions. The improved accuracy and depth of the recent observations, in particular with the ALFA instrument on the Arecibo telescope, has revealed the presence of dark matter in the form of compact massive clouds, not accounted for by conventional models of the galactic mass distribution. The properties of these clouds, and the possible interaction between dark and luminous matter, remains a topic of debate. Here we present new observations of the HI distribution in the solar vicinity using the latest data from the ALFALFA HI survey. These data show evidence for the presence of dark matter in the form of compact massive clouds, in good agreement with the expectations from the conventional models of the galactic mass distribution.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to study Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of neutral atoms in optical lattices. We consider both the superfluid (SF) and Mott-insulator (MI) phases and the crossover between them. Our starting point is a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for bosons on a lattice. The theory can be applied to describe experiments with bosonic atoms in an optical lattice. The Bose-Hubbard model is the simplest and most commonly used model to describe such experiments. We use a projective many-body method to map the Bose-Hubbard model onto an effective classical model. This approach has the advantage that quantum fluctuations are properly taken into account while at the same time the problem is reduced to the solution of a classical model. We apply this theory to study SF, MI, and crossover regions in the phase diagram of the Bose-Hubbard model. We make a quantitative comparison with quantum Monte Carlo simulations. We find a very good agreement between our theory and quantum Monte Carlo simulations in the SF and MI phases. In the crossover region, however, we find a first-order phase transition which is a result of the mean-field theory. We find that quantum fluctuations play an important role in determining the nature of the transition.

We present the detection and characterization of cm radio continuum emission from the low-mass protostar L1014-IRS using the Arizona Radioheliograph (ARO). L1014-IRS is a forming low-mass star system located in the constellation Sagittarius at a distance of 7.3 kpc and 2.2 kpc from the Sun in the north and south, respectively. L1014-IRS drives a strong molecular outflow, and has a powerful, but deeply buried, radio jet. We observe a fast, apparently young jet emerging from the vicinity of the driving source. We also observe diffuse, extended emission likely originating from the outflow. We estimate the spectral energy distribution of the compact jet and outflow lobe emission and find a characteristic electron energy of E_c ~ 80-90 TeV and an unusual spectral index, α = 2.2-2.7. These characteristics are consistent with predictions for particles accelerated in the collisionless shocks formed when the jet plows through the natal cloud. We discuss the implications of these findings for models of low-mass star and planet formation.

One of the major unsolved problems in galaxy formation is the so-called "firewall" issue, i.e., how to prevent star formation in the central region of dark matter halos. The favored solution to this problem involves supernova (SN) feedback, which is thought to reheat and eject the gas in the galaxy, thus preventing further star formation. Unfortunately, current simulations of galaxy formation including SN feedback have been unable to result in galactic objects that resemble observed galaxies, possibly due to the use of simple physics in these simulations (e.g., the assumption of a constant or redshift-dependent SN energy/ Feedback fraction or incorrect treatment of the multiphase nature of the ISM). Here, we show that a natural and effective feedback mechanism is missing from all current galaxy formation simulations: we have discovered the first supernova explosions. We find that the initial explosion energy of the first SNe in typical galaxies with masses of a few 10 s of 10^9 M⊕ is a factor of 10-100 larger than previously believed, 2.5-25 10^{50} erg, depending on the uncertainty in the IMF. The initial explosion energy from first SNe is deposited within ∼1 Myr, which is shorter than the pressure ionization cooling time of the gas in the center of the galaxy (∼3-30 Myr). As a result, the energy is rapidly thermalized and redistributed throughout the central 10 kpc region, instead of being removed by mechanical feedback in the form of thermal energy or ram pressure. Moreover, by performing calculations with a variable energy feedback fraction and tracking the chemical evolution of the galactic center, we show that the first SNe are the dominant source of chemical enrichment at early times. Finally, we discuss potential effects of our findings on galaxy formation models. In particular, we demonstrate that the widely accepted assumption that the first SNe are pair-instability SNe should be reevaluated. We also show that the alpha-element to iron-peak elements ratios in low-mass galaxy halos, which have typically been observed in recently found dwarfs and LSBs, can be naturally reproduced by the first SNe, indicating that these galaxies did not form the chemically unique "pattern" of heavy elements seen in the Galactic bulge.

Manganites R$_{1-x}$A$_x$MnO$_3$ (R: rare-earth, A: alkaline-earth) are considered as a prime example for the observation of a discontinuous metal-insulator transition (MIT) with orbital ordering. The MIT is caused by the competition between Jahn-Teller (JT) interaction and electronic (Hund’s) coupling. A microscopic explanation for the observed orbital order has so far been lacking. Here, we present the first microscopic theory for the correlated orbital dynamics in ferromagnetic manganites. We use a multi-orbital Hubbard model for the Mn $3d$ electrons with large separation of Mn $3d$ and O $2p$ orbitals. The model describes the competing interactions in the system and, in particular, accounts for the Mn$^{3+}$ and Mn$^{4+}$ local spins, which are considered as pseudo-spins. The crucial input of the model is the derivation of the effective Hamiltonian for the Mn $e_g$ electrons, which is performed in the framework of the Hubbard lattice approach. We find a ferromagnetic orbital liquid phase with vanishing order parameters for the conventional (canted) orbital order and the ferromagnetic one. The Fermi-surface nesting causes a strong renormalization of the bare interactions and leads to the orbital polarization at small JT couplings and a tiny interval of Hund’s coupling, which we estimate from realistic band structure calculations. We argue that the observed MIT in these compounds can be explained without orbital ordering, if the manganese valence is slightly fluctuating.

Two-dimensional extensions of the t-J model with staggered sign on contiguous sites known as the extended t--J model are studied using a mean field approximation in a large N approximation. We find that at commensurate fillings, where a quarter of the sites are occupied and two-thirds of them are occupied by fermions, the model has an additional non-magnetic phase in addition to the magnetically ordered Néel and striped phases. We call this phase an exotic Néel phase as it breaks both lattice and spin symmetries. We provide numerical evidence that the exotic Néel phase is stable against perturbation by longer-range density-density interactions and at larger N, where the model has a non-magnetic phase that includes a resonating valence bond solid (RVB) and a Fermi liquid. We provide a heuristic argument suggesting that the exotic Néel phase is likely to be found in large N SU(2) symmetric spin models with suitably twisted boundary conditions and a particular two-fold degeneracy on the square lattice. We also speculate on possible experimental signatures.

The magnetorotational instability (MRI) is ankey issue in accretion disk theory. It arises from magnetic flux amplification due to differential rotation. This astrophysically relevant instability has been extensively studied in the ideal MHD limit, but is also affected by viscosity and resistivity. In particular, numerical simulations of MRI in protoplanetary disks are often performed in a shearing box with a periodic boundary in the horizontal direction, which limits the dynamical range of the simulations. We have performed shearing box simulations of the MRI with zero net magnetic flux and with stress-free boundaries in shearing-periodic equilibrium, spanning the range of Reynolds and magnetic Prandtl numbers from 0.1 to 100. We find that the growth rate of the most unstable MRI modes decreases with increasing magnetic Prandtl number. Our results show good agreement with the local homogeneous approximation of the full non-local dispersion relation, which implies that the maximum growth rate is independent of viscosity and resistivity if the magnetic field strength is smaller than a limiting value. This strongly suggests that MRI is a promising candidate to explain the large-scale structure of protoplanetary disks.

In this paper we investigate holographic behaviors in three-dimensional Kerr-de Sitter space with a gravitational Chern-Simons term. It is well known that, in three dimensions, the vacuum Einstein equations reduce to the Chern-Simons (CS) theory, which is a topological field theory. On the other hand, the anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime in three dimensions is AdS$_3$ Horndeski gravity, which is a general theory of gravity consisting of a three-dimensional generalization of the Chern-Simons term. We will see that the three-dimensional Kerr-de Sitter black holes belong to the AdS$_3$ Horndeski gravity. We will show that the AdS$_3$ gravitational field strength of the three-dimensional Kerr-de Sitter spacetime satisfies the three-dimensional CS equation, which is a gauge-invariant extension of the Einstein equation with a negative cosmological constant. By using the boundary CS term, we can obtain the corresponding chiral gravity in the boundary theory. The asymptotic symmetry group of the boundary metric is the Lifshitz symmetry, which implies that the dual boundary CFT has a dynamical critical exponent z. We also derive the absorption cross section of the three-dimensional Kerr-de Sitter black holes. The result shows that the absorption cross section is equal to the geometric optics limit at low frequency, but the absorption cross section is greater than the geometric optics limit at high frequency. This means that the three-dimensional Kerr-de Sitter black holes always emit particles at high frequency.

In this paper, we propose a statistical method for testing whether one sample path of a Wiener process is strictly double-sidededly continuous with respect to the previsible filtration. Under some conditions, we show that the test statistic converges in distribution to the Tracy-Widom distribution, which is well known in the literature of random matrix theory. An application to a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter H<0.5 is given to demonstrate the proposed method. Our proposed test is based on the maximum likelihood estimator of the Hurst parameter, and the LSEE for the underlying diffusion process is derived. An exponential inequality for the LSEE is also established. Numerical studies show that the empirical size of the test is well controlled and the power is close to one under various scenarios. A real data example is also provided to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method. For example, it was observed that certain physical systems, such as earthquakes and wind gusts, exhibit long-range power-law correlations that are similar in form to fBm. As a consequence, methods for testing for fBm have found use in a wide range of areas, including financial market analysis, human activity analysis, astrophysics, and geophysics. On the other hand, there are many scenarios in which it is desired to test the hypothesis that a sample path of a stochastic process is either fBm or an alternative process. As a typical example, when analyzing empirical data, one may suspect that the sample paths exhibit fBm behavior for some time periods, but then exhibit a different behavior for other time periods. It is therefore of interest to have a statistical test for determining whether a sample path of a stochastic process is fBm or an alternative. Such a test should be reliable (have accurate size control) and have power approaching one. The test that is most closely related to the present work was proposed in [5]. There, the hypothesis that a sample path of a stochastic process is fBm was tested using the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of the Hurst parameter, and the LSEE was used to approximate the sample path. Under some regularity conditions, it was shown that the test had correct size and that its power approached one. The primary drawback of this approach is that the regularity conditions were very restrictive, and it was therefore difficult to extend this approach to more general settings. Two-player Nash equilibria (NE) have been shown to be complex, even for relatively simple games. Given a game with n choices and m player choices for each player, there are 2^nm possible two-player games. The computational complexity of finding all two-player NE for such games scales as 2^n m nbo. This Complexity-Theoretic Lower Bound (CTLB) for two-player NE calculation has not been broken for decades. Many distributed multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been proposed to overcome the complex nature of two-player NE, assuming that the players are fully cooperative. However, in practice, players are usually self-interested and dislike each other. Even for games that have two-player NE that are Pareto-optimal, most distributed multi-agent RL algorithms designed to date are only able to find mixed strategies, not pure strategies. In this paper, we show that the complexity of two-player pure-strategy NE calculation is not higher than that of two-player mixed-strategy NE calculation, and present algorithms to achieve efficient pure-strategy NE calculation for any two-player game. This allows the first fully distributed algorithm for two-player strategy optimization, where all players are autonomous, goal-oriented, and dislike each other, to converge to pure-strategy NE, in some cases exponentially faster than the fully-distributed algorithm that players trust each other. Extensive simulation results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed algorithm for various games with complex structure.

Biharmonic functions are fourth-order analogues of harmonic functions. Unlike harmonic functions, biharmonic functions do not necessarily minimize Dirichlet energy. A well-known example is the zero biharmonic function in the entire Euclidean space. Despite the absence of any global minimizer, one can show that the Dirichlet energy of any biharmonic function in a domain $\Omega$ is lower-bounded by the Dirichlet integral of any biharmonic functions on the domain's boundaries. In this sense, biharmonic functions relax Dirichlet regularity requirement on their boundary values. In this work, we show this is not merely a relaxation; for domains with sufficiently many symmetries, biharmonic Green's functions themselves enjoy similar positivity properties as their harmonic counterparts. For instance, their Hopf differentials, measures defined as singular values of their Laplacian, are strictly positive on sufficiently smooth manifolds. We establish this result for the Dirichlet problem on arbitrary smoothly bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our proof makes crucial use of the underlying symmetries of the domain. In the process, we also obtain a new integral representation for biharmonic Green's functions which generalizes the well-known Poisson formula for harmonic functions.

File size: 791 KB 2003 arXiv.org Atom waves can be diffracted between two Raman-Nath Bragg frequencies, when the incident wave is in the Bragg regime. Under these conditions, the effective Rabi frequency, the losses, and the phase shifts are calculated. An analysis of the effective Rabi frequency shows that only half of the atom wave function is diffracted, as expected for a two-level system. The calculated losses can be attributed to phase shifts, and can be large if the wave vector of the diffracted wave is small. rgarding methodology, the article uses the coupled Maxwell-Bloch equations, in the dipole and Raman-Nath limits. The calculations are presented for sodium, with parameters from the literature.

A sample of X-ray flares from a large sample of low-mass stars in the Orion complex has been analyzed. Most of the sources were detected by XMM-Newton and Chandra observations of the region, performed between 2000 and 2009. Most of the flares were characterized by exponential increases in flux with an e-folding time of about 12 hours. Flare peak luminosities were highly variable, ranging from 5 x 10 26 erg/s to 7.5 x 10 27 erg/s for Chandra and from 3.5 x 10 27 erg/s to 7.5 x 10 27 erg/s for XMM-Newton. No significant correlation was found between the rise times and peak luminosities, nor between the observed x-ray flux and that expected from the stellar photospheric emission. We suggest that flares are produced by magnetic reconnection events in the stellar magnetospheres.

Two density matrices are said to be distinguishable if we are able to obtain new information by performing a measurement upon one of them that was not already contained in the knowledge obtained by performing a measurement upon the other. This includes the case in which the new information allows us to express one density matrix in terms of the other. Here we show that, even for operations that are individually not able to reveal any new information about a quantum system, a sufficient number of such operations may allow us to determine whether or not two given density matrices are distinguishable. We present two protocols that differ in the number of uses of the register representing the system that is being investigated, and we prove that their success probability converges to 1 as the number of uses of the register approaches infinity. Our results imply that there are operations that cannot be used to achieve complete distinguishability of quantum states, even if these operations are performed multiple times on a quantum system.

Recent hydrodynamical simulations of galaxy mergers have suggested that a small, deep central channel can form in the midplane of the merger remnant along the direction of gas inflow, carrying a large amount of gas to the central kpc. Such gas could fuel the central massive black hole (MBH), leading to a rapid growth of the MBH and a characteristic period of high-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) phase, or “quasar” phase. Subsequent nuclear starburst can further enrich the circumnuclear gas and the observed Seyfert phase. In this Letter, we simulate the inspiraling of two MBHs with mass scaled from the observed size of the central channel and find that, in less than 1Gyr, the less massive black hole will merge with the more massive black hole, leaving a growing remnant of around 10^8Msun, which will be most likely a bulge of active galactic nucleus with higher probability than a Schwarzschild black hole.

This paper studies an optimal investment problem with an unbounded random endowment and utility-based pricing. The investor’s objective is to maximize the expected utility from terminal wealth under general semimartingale dynamics. Since the underlying random endowment is unbounded, the classical notions of absolute and relative performance become inapplicable. We adopt an approach by coupling the investment and the underlying dynamics to define an a.s. supermartingale. Then we construct a sequence of admissible strategies with the patience to wait for the coupling event to occur. The corresponding optimal value is obtained by a dynamic programming principle. We study two versions of the problem: one with restricted trading and the other without any restrictions. We characterize the value function for the restricted case and show the value function is equal to that for the original problem when the patience times of the two strategies are the same. We also provide an approximation method via refining the approximation spaces of strategies. Our approach applies to a much broader family of utility functions and allows for a much wider range of applications. We provide several examples to illustrate our results. Keywords: Semimartingale, Performance measurement, Relative performance, unbounded random endowment, Utility-based pricing, Dynamic programming principle Journal: Mathematical Finance, to appear Link to paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.03276.pdf

Littlewood-Richardson polynomials (LR-polynomials) give the generating function for the number of Littlewood-Richardson (LR) coefficients, that is, the multiplicity with which tensor product of irreducible representations of a semisimple Lie algebra or Lie superalgebra appear in the decomposition of a tensor product of arbitrary representations. They were discovered by George E. Landrock and Robert C. King in 1978. The eight-vertex model, which was discovered by Donald E. Knuth in 1973, is a useful technique for counting Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. LR-coefficients appear in the decomposition of the tensor product of two generic representations of a semisimple Lie algebra or Lie superalgebra into irreducible representations. In particular, they are non-zero whenever the tensor product of the two highest-weight representations of the semisimple Lie algebra or Lie superalgebra has both a highest-weight and a lowest-weight vector. This is a strong restriction and implies the existence of Young tableaux with the corresponding diagonal lengths. It is the Young tableaux that are counted by the LR-coefficients. For the case of the classical Lie algebras, the LR-coefficients are given by determinants of partial Gram matrices, where the Gram matrix is defined using a scalar product on the dual space of the irreducible representation. The general case of simple Lie superalgebras is also discussed. I describe the Littlewood-Richardson coefficients and the combinatorics that count their corresponding tableaux. I also describe the Knuth map, which is a bijection between two sets of piecewise-linear functions on polytopes that are related to Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. These functions can be used to compute Littlewood-Richardson coefficients and have been studied in their own right. I conclude by describing some open problems and point to some related work. This is a fun area of mathematics and several predictions and open questions are outlined. Some of these questions are about generalizing and computing Littlewood-Richardson coefficients to other types of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, or to non-generic representations.

Paper reviews the mechanics of complex biological and man-made networks, focusing on the effects of topological disorder and force propagation. First, a homogenized network, with both linear and nonlinear elements, is described and its force propagation and relaxation characteristics are studied. Next, two physically realistic network models, representing distinct structural realms, are considered. Specifically, an isotropic, fiber bundle model, with fibers sharing a uniform second moment, is analyzed and compared to random sticker models, in which fibers possess specific moment properties. In both network models, force propagation is markedly different in the two dimensions of the network. In the former model, force chains form and propagate along quasi-one-dimensional channels, exhibiting both power-law distributed forces and highly localized response. In contrast, in the latter model, fibers behave more like springs, with small deflections radiating outward in two dimensions, forming a three-dimensional random solid. In both network models, force propagation is profoundly modified by topological disorder, characterized by fibers with self-entanglements. These fibers can, in some configurations, enslave other fibers within their knot structure. In this case, although the forces remain localized, they become highly correlated over large distances, and the network is correspondingly more rigid.

Neutron stars are the smallest and densest objects in the universe. Their interior fundamental properties, such as their global magnetic field intensity, strongly depend on their early dynamic and conductive evolution. Precise measurements of the properties of these fields are now available from timing measurements of the rotation of the central neutron star, which carry a detailed snapshot of the field’s structure and origin. I present here the most precise measurement of the neutron star’s rotation rate to date, using observations carried out with the ʘ- Cerenkov Telescope Network over a baseline of 3.75 years. Together with prior polarimetric information, this leads to the best characterization to date of the internal field of this source, which is shown to be dominated by a poloidal component with an intensity of |B| = 2.65(8) x 10^8 G, well below that of the Earth’s magnetic field. I also explore potential implications of the obtained field properties for the early dynamic and conductive evolution of the source. In particular, the absence of detectable toroidal components in the inferred field may limit how efficiently the initial magnetic flux was injected into the newly-formed neutron star, providing an alternative explanation to current interpretations for the absence of faster rotating magnetic neutron stars below the so-called “Magnificent Seven” rotation rate threshold.

Using data from the Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) and the Multiband Imaging Photometer for Spitzer (MIPS), we study the distribution of mid-infrared (mid-IR) emission from the massive galaxy cluster MS 1054-03 at $z=0.34$ and its implications for the star formation and evolution in rich galaxy clusters. We find that the far-infrared (FIR) dust emission, detected at $\geq4.5\sigma$ confidence level (CL) with the new MIPS data at 24, 25, and 60 $\mu$m, is centered on the cluster dominant galaxies and is well correlated with the distributions of X-ray emitting gas and the cluster member galaxies. By modeling the FIR emission as a modified blackbody with temperature of 44 $\pm$ 4 K and emitting area of 0.42 $\pm$ 0.12 kpc2, we estimate the infrared (IR) luminosity of the cluster center dominant galaxies at $z=0.34$ to be 1.5$\pm$0.2$\times10^{11}L_\odot$ and that of total cluster membership to be (4.5$\pm$0.5)$\times$10$^{11}L_\odot$. We also find that the star formation rate (SFR) derived from the FIR luminosity, using SFR-L$_{IR}$ relation from normal galaxies at lower redshifts, is 5-10 times higher than that estimated from the optical and near-infrared observations. Given that the total cluster mass is estimated to be (1.3-2.5)$ \times 10^{14}$ M$_\odot$, the above result suggests that a large fraction of the overall star formation in the cluster galaxies has occurred in unobservable obscured form, in which the optical and near-infrared emission from newly formed stars is absorbed and reemitted as mid-IR thermal radiation. We discuss several possibilities to explain such an unobservable obscured star formation, including a substantial growth of dust due to Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) heating, very rapidly occurring starbursts without sufficient time to clear away the dust, and/or recent major mergers of galaxies with high SFRs.

Recent observations of the center of our Galaxy, Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), have revealed that it is encircled by an enormous, quasi-periodic radio emission cloud known as the Sgr A West radio lobe. This cloud exhibits dramatic variations on multiple time scales, from weeks to millions of years, which are potentially related to the dynamic environment near Sgr A*. Based on linear analyses, several recent studies have suggested that the lobe may be caused by disk instabilities in the vicinity of the black hole, rather than by supernova explosions or any other single event. Here, we present the results of three-dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamical simulations of disk-generated turbulence and magnetic fields, which indicate that the dynamical environment around Sgr A* is likely a long-term stable and persistent phenomenon. In our model, the low-frequency radio variations are caused by the fluctuations in the mass inflow rate from the circumnuclear disk to the supermassive black hole, with a periodicity of tens of thousands of years. This result is consistent with several independent lines of observational and theoretical evidence, and may resolve the long-standing problem of the dynamical origin of the Sgr A West radio lobe.

In quantum field theory, BPS operators are certain particular operators for which the number of quantum states with respect to the two-dimensional Yang-Mills theory with given charges is known precisely. For N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, these quantum numbers can be encoded into Young tableaux, allowing to compute the number of such BPS operators for any given representation. In this letter, we exploit this fact to compute the generating function of BPS operators in N=4 SYM, which is given in term of a sum of minimal hyper-elliptic integrals. Finally, we discuss the emergence of this generating function from the statistical mechanics of D0-branes in thermal circular geometry. A jet-like outflow toward the high-mass (proto)stellar object IRAS 18566+0408 has been investigated with the single dish telescopes of the 6-m China FAST and the 1.6-m OSN. The IRAS 18566+0408, which was initially identified as an exciting source with the IRAS catalog, has been studied in more details using molecular lines detected with the single dish telescopes. The observations reveal a proper motion with a speed of about 220 km s-1, which implies a mass of about 2.2-2.5 M⊙ and a dynamical age of about 7000-10000 yr. The large-scale CO outflow, with an axis P.A. of about 165° and a dynamical timescale of about 3200 yr, was also detected and appears to be driven by the IRAS 18566+0408. By analyzing the single dish radio-continuum observations, a radio jet with a proper motion of about 0.25" yr-1 is also discovered, which further supports a Class 0 nature for the IRAS 18566+0408. The blueshifted CO and redshifted SiO emission as well as the SiO outflow axis all roughly align with the radio jet axis, which suggests that the jet may have played an important role in driving the molecular outflow. The SiO luminosity of IRAS 18566+0408 is one of the highest ever observed for a low-mass (proto)star, and even much higher than many hyper-luminous IR galaxies. The SiO maser provides a promising way to understand the early phase of massive (proto)star formation.

In this paper, we prove a conjecture of Maulik and Nekrasov on the structure of Donaldson-Thomas theory of the Grassmannian in the case of a full flag manifold. In particular, we show that the theory has a non-commutative version, generalizing part of Seidel and Thomas’s Fukaya category approach. We then study the case of a single full class at the level of derived categories. To do this, we construct two semiorthogonal decompositions of the derived category of the Grassmannian, and we show that the two resulting non-commutative dual Grassmannians are isomorphic, generalizing a similar result for $K3$ surfaces. Using this result, we deduce a number of properties of the resulting non-commutative Donaldson-Thomas theory, such as a variant of the WDVV equation, functorial properties for mutations, and invariance under change of stability conditions. We also give a non-commutative mirror dual to the conifold, and show that it is a non-commutative hypersurface in the non-commutative dual Grassmannian. This work was completed as part of my PhD with Aaron Bertram at Columbia University under the guidance of Alexei Neeman, with whom I have collaborated on several projects related to non-commutative Donaldson-Thomas theory, and to whom this paper is dedicated.

In this paper we establish two analogous correspondences between link concordance, homology cobordism, and Hirzebruch-type defects. The first correspondence associates to an oriented link L in S3 the Witt-valued concordance obstruction of the iterated p-cover of S3 given by the link exterior, where p is any odd prime. The second correspondence associates to an integral homology 3-sphere X the Witt-valued self-bordism class of the Hirzebruch surface HT opened along its zero section. We then apply these correspondences to show that a given link L in S3 determines the Witt-valued homology cobordism class of some integral homology 3-sphere X, and that a given homology 3-sphere X determines the Witt-valued link concordance genus of some link L in S3. We conclude by observing that in many examples these correspondences are injective, generalizing previous results by Hendricks, Hom, and Kanda.

In this paper, we consider the problem of identifying stragglers in data streams. Straggler identification is an important problem in the design and analysis of distributed systems, and has received much attention in the literature. Classical solutions to this problem build a timestamped logical clock, and often require a prohibitive number of timestamps to converge. More recently, variants of Bloom filters have been used for straggler identification, enabling data stream applications with affordable memory and fast detection. Bloom filters, however, are not invertible, and so existing solutions to Bloom filter-based straggler identification (both in the literature and in commercial systems) are inherently blind: they cannot accurately identify which processes are stragglers. We overcome this limitation by harnessing the power of Newton's identities, a set of three deterministic matrix equations that are invertible. Unlike Bloom filters, our solution can accurately identify stragglers. We describe an algorithm that, using just two timestamps per stream element, can identify straggler processes with high probability, and in particular can accurately identify stragglers to within a set of n processes, for any specified n. We validate our method via extensive experiments on a variety of benchmark data streams, including real-world data from a large-scale production system, and show that our method outperforms the state of the art by orders of magnitude.

Polarized proton-proton (PP) collisions allow for the precise study of the spin structure of the proton and the nature of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). In April 2021, the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) collided longitudinally polarized proton beams at a center-of-mass energy of 200 GeV. These collisions provided an opportunity to study spin interactions in a high-energy, polarized collider. This paper summarizes some of the new results from this program, including measurements of the Gottfried sum, the quark contributions to the magnetic moment, the spin dependent fragmentation function, the quark transverse momentum dependent distributions, and measurements of strangeness polarization. rule Polarized proton-proton (PP) collisions allow for the precise study of the spin structure of the proton and the nature of quantum chromodynamics (QCD). A pulsar traveling through the Milky Way at a known velocity, [km s-1], ejects a fast moving pulsar wind. Due to conservation of momentum, some of this fast moving pulsar wind material may be slowed down and accumulated into a pulsar wind nebula (PWN). Recent observations of the HESS J1809-193 gamma-ray source, detected by the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.), have detected a coincident X-ray PWN. We propose a possible association between the PWN and HESS J1809-193. If so, this may be the first case of a PWN discovered by gamma-ray observations. We also compare the expected spatial coincidence between the PWN and HESS J1809-193 to existing spatial simulations of the diffusion of charged particles from the pulsar in the system.

The ab initio statistical mechanical theory prediction for the helix-coil phase transition temperature of a polyalanine chain with 21 residues is 295.15 K. This paper examines the accuracy of this prediction by comparing the theory with experiments on an equivalent chain with 23 residues. The result is that the prediction is within 1.5 K of the experimental value of 295.65 K, with an estimated standard deviation of 1.22 K. Therefore, the theory is in excellent agreement with experiment. The 21-mer was chosen because it is long enough to show multiple chain structural features, yet short enough that the phase transition can be studied with approximate ab initio methods. The 23-mer was chosen as an example of a longer polyalanine chain for which the same comparison can be made. This suggests that the theory can be used to predict the helix-coil phase transition temperature of arbitrary polypeptide chains.

In recent years, several high-precision broadband spectrometers became available providing large sets of instantaneously recorded data. Here, we introduce the cumulative spectral power as a simple tool to characterize the spectral energy density of earthquake and explosion events. For this purpose, the frequency-dependent spectral energy density is integrated across the whole frequency range. As an example, we apply this method to broadband seismograms recorded during the 2016 July 27 M5.8 Sanriku earthquake near Sanriku, Japan. We show that the cumulative spectral power increases non-linearly with rising ground motions. Hence, it provides a new earthquake manifestation which might be accessible to earthquakes as well as strong explosions. The cumulative spectral power could provide earthquake engineers and safety authorities with a novel and convenient means to assess the energy of potentially dangerous events. The spectral power density (W m-2 Hz-1) of an earthquake ground motion is commonly characterized by the spectral acceleration [1]. Using a force spectrum derived from the seismogenic fault model of Sanriku, we show that the spectral acceleration increases non-linearly with the spectral frequency as SpectralAcceleration(f) = a 0 1 + a 1 f + a 2 f 2 + a 3 f 3, with a = {0.09, 0.1, 0.12, 0.16} and f representing the frequency in Hz. The constants a 0, a 1, a 2, and a 3 represent the contribution of the fundamental wave, the first harmonic, the second harmonic, and higher-order harmonics, respectively. The spectral acceleration is a convenient quantity for comparing ground motions at different locations, or for large events in which the spectrum cannot be easily resolved. However, for the 2016 July 27 M5.8 Sanriku earthquake, we show that the spectral acceleration only accounts for 10% of the spectral energy density. We introduce the cumulative spectral power (CSP), i.e., the integrated spectral energy density as a better means of describing the earthquake energy. The CSP is defined as CumulativeSpectralPower(f) = ∫ a 0 1 + a 1 f + a 2 f 2 + a 3 f 3 df. We compute the CSP for the 2016 Sanriku earthquake and show that it increases much faster than the spectral acceleration. We also compute CSP for strong explosion events and show that they increase much faster than the spectral acceleration of earthquakes. The difference is even more significant for high-pressure explosion events, which have no associated seismic activity. Cumulative spectral power provides a convenient and intuitive way to characterize the seismic and explosion energies. The evolution of CSP with rising ground motions is an interesting new manifestation which may have practical implications in seismology and explosion research. Two colloidal glasses are prepared using polystyrene particles with different sizes. In the first sample, the particles have a size ratio of 1.1, such that they are nearly perfectly monodisperse. This sample is well-described by the bottle-brush model, a semiflexible linear polymer, below the theta temperature. In the second sample, the size ratio of the particles is 2.2, such that the degree of polydispersity is highest. This sample is best described by a cluster-catcher model, a semi-flexible branched polymer. In the first sample, the particles are attractive and well-described by the Stein model. In the second sample, the particles are repulsive and well-described by a modified Stein model that takes into account hydrodynamic interactions. The results are compared to the theoretical expectations for a Lennard-Jones system, and for a Yukawa system. The data are most consistent with a combination of a repulsive screened-Yukawa potential and an attractive Lennard-Jones potential.

In this paper, we present a new chaotic attractor in a basic multi-strain epidemiological model with temporary cross-immunity. The dynamical system we consider is as follows: $$\left\{\begin{array}{rcl} x'_1 & = & \beta x_1-\mu x_1+\alpha x_2-\beta x_1 y_1-\mu x_1 y_1+\alpha x_2 y_1+\mu x_1 y_2\\ x'_2 & = & \alpha x_1-\mu x_2-\beta x_2 y_2-\mu x_2 y_1+\alpha x_1 y_2\\ y'_1 & = & \beta x_1 y_1-\mu y_1+\alpha y_2-\beta x_1 y_1 y_1-\mu y_1 y_1+\alpha y_2 y_1\\ y'_2 & = & \alpha x_2 y_1-\mu y_2+\mu y_1-\alpha y_2 y_2 \end{array}\right.$$ where $\alpha,\beta,\mu$ are positive constants. We give a detailed proof of the existence of the new chaotic attractor and compute the exact value of its dimension. Moreover, we perform numerical simulations to illustrate that the new chaotic attractor appears in a very wide range of the parameters and has some unique properties which distinguish it from the usual chaotic attractor. Finally, we discuss the biological significances of the new chaotic attractor and give some suggestions for its physical realizations.

In this paper we explore the possibility to learn something from the distribution of the biggest fragment in an iron-rich, zirconium rich, 304 stainless steel sample, using artificial intelligence techniques. The goal is to check if the distribution of the biggest fragment – here named “vital trace” – could be used as a fingerprint to identify the origin of the sample and if it carries information about the processes by which the sample was formed. We run a supervised machine learning algorithm with three classes, namely “iron-rich”, “zirconium rich” and “304 stainless steel”, using as features the elemental concentrations of 26 elements and as target the vital trace distribution. We found that the algorithm was able to learn the differences between the classes and to generate different predictions for the three classes, with an accuracy of more than 70% when using only 10% of the samples to train the algorithm. We also applied a similar algorithm, this time using histological images of burns as input and found that it was also able to learn the difference between “304 stainless steel” and “fire” samples, even using only 3 burns to train the algorithm. This shows that vital trace distribution could carry information about the processes occurred before the formation of the material. We believe that this work is a proof of concept that the distribution of the biggest fragment, that could be easily lost during the manufacturing of a material, could carry information that could be used to identify processes occurred before the material formation.

Contractions, deformations and curvature play an important role in physics and geometry. For example, in continuum mechanics, changes in shape are typically described by modifying a background Euclidean metric, by introducing local variations of the speed of sound or by modifying the curvature of a manifold. Curvature often appears in problems relating to flow of fluids in a medium, and can be used to describe various phenomena such as, for example, how a pebble in a stream curves the stream. In this work, we consider a generic system of partial differential equations arising in various applications. We show that this system can be significantly simplified by expressing the deformation in terms of local variations of three scalar quantities, i.e. a contraction, a deformation and curvature. We provide a general framework to derive equations for deformations arising from a given scalar evolution. Finally, we consider several examples of physical interest, such as variations of speed of sound, and provide simple equations governing the evolution. Our approach provides a unified description of a large class of deformation processes and may have applications to a broad range of physical systems. The chiral condensate is an important order parameter for spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking in quantum chromodynamics (QCD). In this work, we study the trace of the quark chiral density in QCD with three light flavors using holographic models of quantum gravity. We study the dependence of the chiral condensate on the number of massless quarks as well as the strange quark mass, and find that it remains nonzero even in the chiral limit. In the case of two massless quarks, the ratio of the chiral condensate to its non-chiral limit value approaches a constant for large quark masses. We examine the behavior of the chiral condensate for a wide range of the Vafa-Witten anomaly induced interactions as well as generalized vector-type and axial-vector-type four-fermion interactions, finding that they yield similar results. We argue that our results for light quarks demonstrate that chiral symmetry is not restored even in the limit of zero quark mass. This raises the interesting possibility that there is a quark qq condensate even in this regime. This work provides holographic evidence of the quark qq condensate for light flavors in the absence of chiral symmetry breaking.

A possible window to test string theory has opened. String theory, the most popular candidate for a Theory of Everything, proposes extra dimensions beyond the familiar four dimensions of space and time. The simplest realisation of string theory, called Type II, has 19 large spatial dimensions. In this scenario, gravity can leak into the extra dimensions, modifying gravity at short distances and providing a possible signature for new large-scale structures in the Universe. By combining the primary temperature maps from the 2015 release of the Planck satellite with high-resolution polarization information from the South Pole Telescope and BICEP2, we perform the first observational search for such modifications. We find no evidence for gravity leaking into extra dimensions, setting an upper limit on the scale of modified gravity at 2.12 × 10^{-3} eV (2.33 × 10^{18} GeV). If string theory is correct, these gravity tests suggest we live on a four dimensional boundary of a larger six dimensional space.

The maxBCG method is a approach to detection and photometry of clusters of galaxies, primarily based on broad-band imaging data obtained with the SWIRE satellite. This approach selects for BCGs those pixels in an image whose color is the brightest in their (local) vicinity and defines a preliminary list of potential clusters. Subsequently, in a second pass, the SWIRE data themselves are used to measure the properties of the selected objects, such as their red-sequence luminosity and size. Here we present power spectrum analyses of the SWIRE data for the initial sample of clusters from the maxBCG method. We find that the power spectrum can be decomposed into a primary spectrum, representing the gross structure of the clusters, and secondary spectra, corresponding to acoustic peaks associated with spatial clustering on different scales. These results suggest that the maxBCG method may successfully identify dark matter structures in the form of galaxy clusters. We measure the primary spectrum for redshifts between 0.18 and 0.55 with a median of 0.33 and find that it is consistent with a nearly scale-invariant power spectrum, with best-fit parameters Ωm = 0.27 ± 0.05, Ωb = 0.04 ± 0.01, and H0 = 71 ± 3 km/s/Mpc. The acoustic scale is s = 7.3 ± 0.5 h^{-1} Mpc and the sound horizon at recombination is Λ = (102.6 ± 1.4) h_{70.3km/s} Mpc. These results provide new evidence for the existence of acoustic peaks in the early universe, corresponding to the pattern of clustering created at scales corresponding to the sound waves in the primeval plasma.

We present results from modelling the early behaviour of the 2006 outburst of the recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi using a 1D, spherically symmetric, hydrodynamical code. We use the Fudge Model for the nuclear reaction network, and consider both adiabatic and (steeper) isothermal expansions. The models suggest the existence of at least three successive adiabatic shocks, two associated with the bullets observed moving away from the origin and the third occurring some time after April 2006 when the brightness of the system began to fall. Within the framework of this one-zone model, the evolution of the emitting zone is well- approximated by an exponential law, with a velocity equal to the escape speed from the shocked region. The density at the centre of the shocked region is found to be consistent with the minimum central density implied by the bolometric luminosity and the average expansion velocity. We also show that the steepening of the radial density profile observed in the last observation of 2006 October 22 can be reproduced by the model if the shockwave has reached the surface of the star. We compare our results with archival observations of the outburst from various telescopes, and find that observations in the blue band during 2006 May show the system to be more luminous and also reveal some evidence for a circum- nova disk.

Spectral efficiency and diversity have long been competing requirements in wireless networks. Whereas spectral efficiency refers to the information bits transmitted per second, diversity order measures the quality of the link in the presence of fading. Traditionally, network coding has been shown to improve spectral efficiency without increasing the diversity order, however, many networks require both high spectral efficiency and high diversity order. In this paper, we show that network coding with multiuser detection (MUD) can achieve both high spectral efficiency and high diversity order. We present a cooperative transmission protocol which leverages network coding and MUD to achieve high spectral efficiency and high diversity simultaneously. We analyze the protocol using the degree of freedom (DoF) framework and present a closed form approximation for the symmetric case. Through simulations, we show that the spectral efficiency and diversity achieved by the proposed protocol are significantly higher than both Network Coding with Max-Ratio Combining (MRC) and Network Coding with Successive Interference Cancellation (SIC). In addition, we show that the protocol is very effective at maximizing the throughput of non-colluding nodes in a network.

The X-ray-emitting neutron star in the center of the Geminga globular cluster exhibits departures from a spherical shape that are best modeled by a ovally distorted torus. The geometry of the neutron star is further constrained by the orbital elements of a distant low-mass companion. By combining X-ray, optical, and dynamical data, we show that the binary system most likely has an inclination of 89.4° and a mass ratio of 0.87. The most likely geometry is that the neutron star has an oval torus-shaped structure with a principal axis ratio of 1.06:1, aligned such that the shorter axis is toward the companion. This result suggests that the neutron star formed through a recent episode of mass accretion, and that the accretion process is ongoing. We present the results of a joint analysis of X-ray, optical, and dynamical data for the neutron star RX J1856.5-3754 in the globular cluster M28. RX J1856.5-3754 has a low-mass companion in a distant and eccentric orbit. The orbit has a measured inclination of 89.4° and a measured mass ratio of 0.87. The most likely geometry for the neutron star is that it has an oval torus-shaped structure with a principal axis ratio of 1.06:1, aligned such that the shorter axis is toward the companion. This result suggests that the neutron star formed through a recent episode of mass accretion, and that the accretion process is ongoing. The companion star is one of the most likely observed orbit beyond the Galactic disk, and its presence indicates that the orbital orientation is probably close to edge-on. Constraints on the mass and distance of the neutron star then allow for precise determinations of its radius and mass. These parameters characterize the equation of state of ultradense matter, and how it interacts with gravity. The inferred geometry is most consistent with an oblate shape with an axis ratio of 1.06:1, aligned such that the shorter axis is toward the companion.

The near-equatorial source counts of the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) have been studied extensively, and a power-law form for the source count distribution has been found. The power-law form is often expressed as N(>S) ~ S-D, where N is the number of sources, S is the source flux, and D is the magnitude of the power-law differential source count. The 2MASS power-law source count is valid only for the faintest half of the population; above this a flattening of the differential source count is observed. This flattening has been attributed to Solar wind effects, but alternative explanations exist. We analyze the entire flux-limited 2MASS source catalog, and determine the best power-law differential source count fromfits to the faint-source population. We find that the best-fit power-law is D = -3.14 ± 0.02, consistent with Solar wind effects. However, the scatter in the fits (0.5–0.6) is large, and alternative hypotheses are not excluded. We therefore propose a parameterized form for the source count, which we find provides a good fit to the entire 2MASS catalog (reduced χ2 = 1.03). This form may allow for a more rapid computation of source counts than direct power-law fits, and may prove useful for investigations of Solar wind effects on source counts.

A plethora of data, ranging from cosmological to astrophysical structures, and also representing a vast array of scientific disciplines, seems to indicate that the universe is not only macrotalks but possibly also anisotropic at the smallest possible scales. In particular, cosmic microwave background radiation, large scale structure and galaxy distributions as well as gravitational lensing studies all indicate the presence of spatial anisotropies on the observed universe. At scales of the order of the Hubble horizon, the universe appears to be isotropic at the statistical level, but if we move to smaller scales, say of the order of the particle horizon size or even smaller, the universe exhibits a remarkable isotropy at a statistical level, but in fact it might be highly anisotropic on small, cosmological scales. The nature of these anisotropies and the precise level of anisotropy might tell us about the gravity theory employed to explain the observed dynamics of the universe. The presence of anisotropy at different scales of observation may be an evidence for a multiconnectedness of the universe, that is, the universe might have several regions that evolved along different trajectories but that are now causally connected. On the other hand, observations seem to suggest that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales, as the presence of spatial anisotropies at any scale of observation would change the nature of the universe and consequently its main observed properties. Therefore, if the universe is multiconnected and anisotropic on small scales, it needs to be homogeneous and isotropic on large scales. The anisotropic models that best fit the available data are the ones that exhibit an isotropy breaking at large scales through the projection of a given Bianchi type symmetry into the three dimensional space, whereas the models recover isotropy at small scales through a suitable definition of the fluctuation field. This is due to the fact that the Bianchi models are the most general spatially homogeneous and anisotropic geometries. In this work, we will assume the universe to be a Bianchi geometry, but we will allow the anisotropy profile to be general. Thus, our starting point is the following line element, which describes the observed dynamics of the universe on an infinitesimal patch of the universe, whose metric takes the following form: $$ d s^{2} = - d \tau^{2} + a_{1}(\tau)^{2} d \chi^{2} + b_{1}(\tau)^{2} d \theta^{2} + c_{1}(\tau)^{2} d \phi^{2} $$ where $\tau$ is the cosmic time, $a_{1}(\tau)$, $b_{1}(\tau)$ and $c_{1}(\tau)$ are the three scale factors of the Bianchi type I metric and $\chi$, $\theta$ and $\phi$ are the cyclic coordinates. The dynamics of the three scale factors along with the rules that define the relative size of the three scale factors determine the anisotropy profile of the universe on the given patch.
