Nuclei composed of fermions, such as atoms and nuclei, are characterized by their spin, which can only take on values of ½-j, ½+j, ¼-j, and ¼+j, where j is an integer. For identical fermions with spin ½, the total angular momentum ℤ is either 0, ℎ±½, where ℎ is an integer. For fermions with spin ¼, ℤ can only be ⅓ or ⅔. The probability of finding a given total angular momentum ℤ for fermions in a given total angular momentum state, JT, is given by a spin addition spectrum. For example, for fermions in the total angular momentum state JT=½+½, the total angular momentum can only be ℎ+½ or ℎ−½, with a spin addition spectrum of 1 or 3/4, respectively. The Fermi-Watson theorem states that the spin-orbit interaction and the average potential, which is, in the case of nuclei, the Pauli potential, between the fermions cancel out in the center of mass of the system. This theorem, first proven for one-dimensional systems, was later generalized to three-dimensional systems. The Pauli potential is due to the exchange of virtual electrons between the fermions and leads to an attractive mean field. Due to this attractive mean field, which increases with the nuclear mass, even small, yet non-zero, Pieper-Hamilton-Sequence (PHS) terms lead to an instability of nuclei against fission. The Spin-Doubling Rare Earth (SDrE) and Spin-Tripling Pt, Pd, Ag, and Au (STDPT) Fermi Surfaces of Nuclei were discovered in the 1970’s. The theoretical understanding of these Fermi Surfaces remained elusive until the 1985 work by Engel et al., in which the Landau’s Fermi Liquid Theory of condensed matter was applied to nuclear systems. The key assumption of the Fermi Liquid Theory is that interactions between the particles are weaker than the symmetry breaking energy scales of the system. Due to the weakness of the interactions between the nucleons (protons and neutrons), the effective interaction between the nucleons can be modeled as a contact potential. The application of Fermi Liquid Theory to nuclear systems lead to the understanding that the Fermi Surfaces of Spin-Doubling and Tripling Nuclei are qualitatively different from the shape of the conventional, or Spin-Singling, spherical nuclei. The Spin-Doubling and Tripling Surfaces are more appropriately described by general ellipsoidal Fermi surfaces. The axes of the ellipsoid are characterized by the shears, or Slater-Nematic coefficients, which can be thought of as phenomenological constants of the interaction between the nucleons. cosmic rays (CRs) are found ubiquitously in the Universe and their sources are largely unknown. If the sources of CRs are powered by massive stars, the progenitor stars with masses exceeding ~8M⊙ (150M⊙ for nuclei) should have reached the end of their lives and trans-relativistic explosions known as supernovae (SNe) as their ultimate fate. We report the detection of gamma-rays from the blazar TXS0506+056 at highest energies (110 GeV – 11 TeV) with the Very Large Telescope (VLT) array under the assumption that the observed gamma-rays are from electrons accelerated by a very young and compact supernova remnant (SNR) powered by the most massive star known, TXS0506+056. The proximity of TXS0506+056 to the Earth implies that the age of the SNR is ~200 years and its size is ~3.4 parsec. These size and age constraints are consistent with the expectation from a typical core-collapse SN with a massive star progenitor. The detection of gamma-rays from the very young SNR favors the scenario that the very massive progenitor stars evolve rapidly into trans-relativistic configurations before their deaths, and thus power CRs at highest energies via the well-known diffusive shock acceleration mechanism. The accelerated CRs can radiate gamma-rays via the inverse Compton and/or proton-proton collisions. These findings imply that very massive stars have a final fate of CR production.

In this paper, we generalize the well-known Caldeira-Legget quantum Brownian motion model to an environment with an arbitrary spectral density and an external force. The spectral density and the external force are both assumed to be general functions of the frequency. By making use of the generating functional technique, we obtain exact solutions to the corresponding master equations in both the Markovian and non-Markovian limits. The influences of the general environment and the external force on the quantum Brownian particle are discussed in detail. Especially, we show that the environment with a constant spectral density and an external force can be treated as a special case of our general model. The influence of the environment with such a special spectral density and external force on the quantum Brownian particle has been investigated in many former literatures, which is therefore contained in our general solution as a special case. We also give a short discussion on the decoherence functional of our model.

Nonequilibrium steady states (NESSs) are an important topic in many-body physics. In this work, we introduce a new technique to study NESSs in quantum lattice systems that is particularly well suited to application to large systems and sparse matrices. Our method, the solution of the matrix product operator (MPO) equations of motion, is built upon a two-fold expansion: an expansion in the size of the underlying matrix product state (MPS) representation and an expansion in Chebyshev polynomials. This allows us to capture dynamics in large, complex quantum systems that are represented by very sparse matrices. We apply our technique to the one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model, a paradigmatic model of quantum phase transitions. We study both the symmetric and asymmetric versions of this model and show that, even in one dimension, one can encounter rich dynamics, including phase transitions and dynamical phases. We also study the hard-core bosons on the square lattice using a quantum simulator and find excellent agreement between our results and those from exact diagonalization. Finally, we use this approach to study the solution of the 1D Bose-Hubbard model at finite temperature. We find, contrary to previous conjectures, that this model does not exhibit a phase with broken symmetries. The MPO solution exhibits a phase with quasi-long-range order in the dimer and charge correlation functions, but a well-defined energy and no symmetry breaking.

Recently, we have seen a lot of interest in phenomena beyond the standard model (BSM) due to the discovery of the Higgs boson and the recent indications of new physics at the LHC. Neutrino interactions are commonly assumed to be well-described by the Standard Model (SM). However, new BSM physics could induce neutral current interactions of neutrinos beyond the SM, leading to new phenomena such as neutrino oscillations, which have been verified experimentally. Moreover, recent results from the Daya Bay, RENO and unique supernova measurements indicate that the neutrino mixing parameters, consisting of the Cabbibo angle mixing angle, theta13 and the solar and reactor mixing angles, theta12 and theta23, are quite small. Motivated by this, the Standard Model neutrino content could be augmented by new degrees of freedom, leading to new physics that might generate non-standard neutrino interactions. Recently, it has been suggested that such new physics could be described by unparticle dynamics, which arise in various extensions of the standard model. In this work, we consider the implications of unparticle physics on the decays of neutrinos and the corresponding process of neutrino electron scattering, which has been measured recently with high precision. We show that such new interactions could significantly change the predictions for neutrino electron scattering, and thus can be tested in the coming decades with potential discovery potential for unparticle physics.

In this paper, the authors apply three different chaotic maps in the formulation of the Ch maps, in order to improve the features of these maps and make them suitable for use in cryptography. Stability of these maps, periodic windows and relations with the usual logistic map and the Mc maps are studied and the regions of chaos and stability in the phase plane of these maps are shown. Also, some of their properties are analyzed such as the behavior of some quantities related to topological entropy, Lyapunov exponents, Kolmogorov entropy and information entropy. Furthermore, some new cryptographic algorithms using these maps are proposed. It is shown that these maps can generate large random numbers with good statistical features and the cryptographic algorithms based on these maps have lower computational complexity than the ones based on logistic map and Mc maps. The authors claim that these chaotic maps have great potential in the field of cryptography and some of their cryptographic algorithms have better properties than the usual ones. The organization of the paper is as follows. Section 2 introduces the three chaotic maps. In section 3, some of the properties of these maps are studied. In section 4, some of the cryptographic algorithms are introduced. In the last section, the authors' concluding remarks are presented.

Recently, a number of studies have claimed that the metallicity distribution of the solar neighborhood is non-Gaussian. However, these claims are based on samples with small numbers of stars. We determine the metallicity distributions in high-latitudes using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 12. The number of stars in our samples are in the range of tens of thousands, and hence we are able to confirm that the metallicity distribution is consistent with being Gaussian. We determine the metallicity distributions using the targets' Galactic extinction-corrected photometry and the DR12 of the SDSS. We find that the metallicity distributions in high-latitudes show no significant differences from those of the whole sample. The probability that the high-latitude samples and the whole sample are drawn from the same population is larger than 99.99%. These results indicate that the local stellar metallicity distribution is consistent with being Gaussian, and previous studies that claimed non-Gaussian distribution were likely caused by small sample statistics.

In 1952, 24 years after its discovery, the spin of the neutron was finally measured. In doing so, Stern-Gerlach experiments on neutrons led to the observation of a Pauli spin-rotation interaction not previously included in theoretical descriptions of the neutron. In his 1925 classical textbook, Young quarter-cylindrical container for the spinning top, known as the Jost–Jost solution, Werner Jost and Edward Adolf apperantly took this interaction into account, assuming the container was uniformly ferromagnetic. This solution, which became known as the Jost–Jost–Pais solution, describes the situation where the top is suspended from a perfectly frictionless string. Subsequent studies, beginning in the 1950s, obtained different solutions with various boundary conditions, most of which neglected the Pauli interaction. In 1974, Jost and Pais were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for their studies of the neutron. In this paper we present a different spin-rotation solution of the classical neutron container problem. We obtain two distinct solutions, one analogous to the Jost–Jost solution and the other analogous to the Jost–Jost–Pais solution. We compare our solutions to the most common experimental setups, that is, the one in which the container is held by two vertical rods and suspended from a horizontal bar. We also compare our solutions to the one obtained by Zee et al. (1974), which includes the Pauli interaction. Lastly, we explore the influence of various physical parameters on our solutions.

The Ξ(1690), the Ξ(1690)Π, and the Ξ(1695) masses were recently measured for the first time. These states were conjectured to be the lowest-mass members of an unconventional antidecuplet of light triply strange baryons. We determine their strong coupling and α′, J, and parity. We find α′ = (0.34 ± 0.05 ± 0.09) GeV2, J = 1, α′ = (0.44 ± 0.07 ± 0.09) GeV2, J = 1, and Ξ parity = −1 for the Ξ(1690), Ξ(1690)Π, and Ξ(1695) states, respectively. The Ξ(1690), the Ξ(1690)Π, and the Ξ(1695) masses were recently measured for the first time. These states were conjectured to be the lowest-mass members of an unconventional antidecuplet of light triply strange baryons. We determine their strong coupling and α′, J, and parity. We find α′ = (0.34 ± 0.05 ± 0.09) GeV2, J = 1, α′ = (0.44 ± 0.07 ± 0.09) GeV2, J = 1, and Ξ parity = −1 for the Ξ(1690), Ξ(1690)Π, and Ξ(1695) states, respectively. The lowest-mass antidecuplet states were originally proposed in 2000 by members of the HERMES Collaboration[1]. Their remarkable特 admissions were the simultaneous discovery of three states with the same strangeness, and of one state with negative Ξ parity. The last two features were conjectured to be unique to the Ξ antidecuplet, distinguishing it from other non-charmed particle multiboson systems. In 2003, the states were called Ξ antidecuplet states[2]. Early measurements suggested a relatively low mass for the Ξ antidecuplet, however, later results from the SAPHIR[3], COMPASS[4], and CERES[5] experiments all indicated a significantly higher mass. The Ξ antidecuplet was finally conjectured in 2009, when it was predicted to exist within the framework of the diquark-quark model[6]. An antidecuplet consists of Ξ, Ξ*bbr, Ξ*bbar, Ξ(1690) (odd), Ξ*(1695) (even) and Ξ*(1690)Π (odd). Two more states were predicted to belong to the antidecuplet but have not been observed yet: the Ξ(1672) and Ξ(1675). A naming system using Roman letters and an odd or even symbol was introduced

Water adsorbs on magnesium oxide at low temperatures in several structures including $2\times2$ and $2\times4$ superstructures. The preferred structure depends on the coverage: for 1/4 and 1/2 ML coverage, the $2\times2$ structure is most stable, while at 1 ML coverage, the $2\times4$ structure is most stable. We perform ab initio statistical mechanical computations of these adsorption structures and show that their relative stability is due to a competition between chemisorption mediated by the hydroxyl group and physisorption on the surface and that the statistical mechanics is consistent with recent experimental work. The demographics of transition objects (TO) is an emerging field that examines how the technology used in cellular telephone networks effects the state of the global population. As the cellular telephone network has expanded globally, the transition TO has resulted in substantial changes to the demographic structures of various regions. By modeling cellular telephones networks as contact-tracing based social distancing tools, this paper will demonstrate how the TO has been utilized globally, what the resulting demographic effects have been in regions such as Asia, and speculate on the TO’s global effects in the future. By late 2020, the world was introduced to the demographics of transition objects (TO). Cellular telephone networks had been rapidly expanded globally in the decade prior, and with the increased availability of mobile cellular services, world leaders implemented mitigation strategies that would help slow the progression of Covid-19. These mitigation strategies, commonly known as social distancing, enabled large scale contact tracing and distribution of verified positive test results. In a multi-faceted approach, social distancing helped slow the spread of Covid-19 by reducing the social interaction rate of individuals and population density in affected regions. In high population density regions, such as urban cities, social distancing was effective at limiting the spread of Covid-19 within communities and helped decrease the number of deaths. Despite the success of social distancing as a mitigation strategy, there are short comings to its use. In order to effectively conduct contact tracing, the world needed to have a mechanism to verify cases, distribute test results, and track potential hot-spots. These criteria fell into the domain of mobile data and internet connectivity, with data prioritization given to more critical uses, such as Covid-19 testing. Cellular networks had an unintended effect on society, not only by enabling Covid-19 testing, but also enabling a heightened interest in telemedicine and remote services, as infected individuals or those at risk of contracting Covid-19 could not travel for medical services and thus required remote care. While the demographics of transition objects (TO) provided the world with the ability to control Covid-19, it also changed the way the world interacted with one another, and the types of businesses that were formed as a direct result. With the exponential growth in remote work and mobile infrastructure, business in nearly all industries became less regional and more global.

Cosmic rays are ubiquitous in the universe, and their pressure contribution to the overall thermodynamics of galaxy clusters and groups is often neglected. We report the first measurements of the pressure contribution of cosmic rays in galaxy clusters with the PROSAP algorithm, a data-analysis scheme optimized for detecting pressure imbalances in interferometric data from the Muon Telescope Assembly (MTA) on the Journey to Jourey (JWST). We find the uncertainty on the gas pressure measurements due to limited spatial and spectral resolution of the data is approximately 10%. When combined with other independent estimates of the thermal pressure, we determine that cosmic-ray pressures in the ICSJE2 cluster are in the range of (2.5-11.2) x 10(44) Pa, with a best-fit value of 5.3 x 10(44) Pa. This pressure contribution is approximately 5% to 15% of the thermal pressure for this pressure range. Cosmological simulations predict that the strength of the thermal SZ signal can be used to estimate the ratio of cosmic-ray to thermal pressure (P(CR)/P(th)) in galaxy clusters. Using these observational results in conjunction with (P(CR)/P(th)) derived from numerical simulations, we find the discrepancy between the observations and the simulations can be resolved by allowing for the possibility of larger-than-expected cosmic-ray pressure in the outskirts of galaxy clusters.

A background study for the CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) pn-CCD detector is presented. The CAST experiment is searching for solar axions by measuring their invisible photon-axion conversion probability in the magnetic field of the Southern solar farm. The pn-CCD is one of the detector systems of CAST. It consists of two hexagonal planes of Silicon photomultipliers with 0.85 mm depleted surface detector, covering 95% of the total sensitive area. This study updates and completes the model-independent background analysis of the detector, presented in a previous publication. The expected rates for the gamma-ray induced signals in the silicon detector and in the surrounding passive material are computed and compared to the measured background. The resulting rates are used to derive new limits on photon backgrounds for CAST. esk A background study for the CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) pn-CCD detector is presented. Finite temperature quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is a useful theoretical framework for studying the thermodynamics of QCD matter under extreme conditions such as those found in heavy-ion collisions and in the cores of neutron stars. In this context, lattice gauge theory has played a vital role in providing a rigorous nonperturbative regularization of the theory and in yielding precise results for thermodynamic observables. Recently, an intriguing new approach to finite temperature gauge theories, called dimensional reduction, has been proposed. In its basic form, dimensional reduction maps four-dimensional (4D) QCD to 1D QCD, with the finite temperature deconfined phase of 4D QCD reduced to a vacuum-like state in 1D. This dimensional reduction has passed several nontrivial tests, including the verification of first-order phase transitions in some models and the generation of a deconfined phase in 1D QCD with massless quarks. However, for QCD with real quark masses, dimensional reduction predicts that the chiral transition is a first-order phase transition with a critical endpoint at nonzero chemical potential, in contrast to what is believed to occur in four dimensions. Here, we report on Monte Carlo simulations of 1D QCD with staggered quarks at nonzero chemical potential. At these non-zero densities, the qualitative behavior of the QCD equation of state remains that of a weakly interacting Fermi gas, with the quarks appearing as mid-range effective interactions among the degenerate Fermi gas of nucleons. Our simulations find that the transition is a second-order phase transition, in agreement with expectations from real-world QCD. Moreover, the transition is completely consistent with a simple mean-field theory, with no signs of critical behavior or other new behavior. These results strongly support dimensional reduction as a practical framework for studying finite temperature gauge theories and have implications for real-world QCD at finite chemical potential.

The form of the initial mass function (IMF) has been the subject of intense debate over the past few decades. While a power law was initially assumed for the IMF, it is now clear that most, if not all, star-forming regions have a modified version of the Initial Mass Function, i.e., a log-normal or more generally a function with a higher-than-exponential density at low masses. The universality of the IMF is an open question. It remains to be seen whether the IMF varies from region to region and, if so, whether this variation is related to the parameters of the region, its gravitational potential, the strength of the local turbulence, or some other aspect. Here we report the discovery that IMFs of individual clusters in the Orion Molecular Cloud 2 exhibit a power-law form with an exponent consistent with the standard value of 0.7. This result suggests that the IMF is indeed universal within the observational uncertainties. However, a full understanding of the origin of the IMF will require establishing the degree of IMF variation both within and between star-forming regions.

Interstellar dust particles and stardust contain unique information about the history of our solar system, the formation of the planets and the evolution of their atmospheres. This information can be retrieved from the isotopic and elemental compositions of the particles. Here we report the results of a programme to characterise the compositions of interstellar dust and stardust in the solar neighbourhood. We find that both particle populations are old, with median formation ages of 3.2 and 1.6 million years for interstellar dust and stardust, respectively. The isotopic compositions of both dust and stardust reflect the composition of the solar nebula at the time of their formation. The composition of interstellar dust differs from the composition of the Sun in nitrogen and sulphur but is similar in carbon and oxygen. Stardust, on the other hand, is very similar in all four elements to the Sun, reflecting the nearly identical elemental compositions of the star and its planetary system at the time of their formation. The relatively large isotopic variation in interstellar dust implies rapid migration of the dust torus around our star, or multiple migration events. We estimate that the ratio of the radial to tangential velocity of dust particles is between 0.5 and 3.2. This is significantly higher than the ratio of about 0.1 found for asteroids in the main asteroid belt and argues against a monolithical origin of interstellar dust. Instead, our data are consistent with the hypothesis that interstellar dust is composed of several spatially distinct populations of stardust created in different regions of the protosolar disk. We also find evidence for chemical differentiation in stardust, with enhancements of titanium, vanadium, osmium, palladium, gold and zirconium. These results suggest that some stardust was created in the asteroid belt and then travelled to the location of the planets and was processed in the different regions of the solar nebula.

Fermi’s golden rule (FGR) is an intuitive principle for understanding the rates of quantum system evolution. It states that the rate of some physical process is proportional to the second power of the density of states (DOS) of the initial states to final states available in the process. This proportionality constant is known as the strength of the process. The rule is exact for weak system-bath couplings. For molecular relaxation time scale quantum systems, the FGR predicted exponential dependence of the relaxation time on the thermal energy. Experimental verification of this prediction using Infrared (IR) photon emission rates for different temperatures showed the predicted dependence only for high temperatures, while for low temperatures the relaxation time is much shorter than expected. This result was interpreted as a signature of quantum dynamical phase transition (QDPT) in terms of scale-invariant behavior of the system. Subsequent theoretical analysis for a general quantum mechanical system with weak system-bath coupling shows the dependence of the relaxation time on the temperature is not exponential, but rather power-law. This finding was later supported by numerous experiments on different quantum systems. In this paper, we argue that the theoretical framework for analyzing the FGR based on scale-invariance is not applicable to realistic quantum systems. In particular, we focus on the initial proposal of QDPT based on exponential temperature dependence of the relaxation time and show that this assumption leads to incorrect conclusion about the validity of FGR. We then analyze the relaxation time and the FGR within a phenomenological microscopic quantum relaxation model. We show that the relaxation time as a function of temperature has a power law instead of exponential dependence as predicted by the FGR. Using the microscopic model, we fit the relaxation time for different temperature and extract the temperature dependence of the microscopic parameters. The analysis based on microscopic parameters reveals that for low temperatures, the quantum criticality disappears and the microscopic model predictions agree with the classical model. We further show that the power-law temperature dependence of the microscopic parameters leads to the power-law temperature dependence of the relaxation time, in agreement with the results obtained using the phenomenological model. Our analysis shows that the FGR cannot be applied to quantum systems within the QDPT framework. We also propose an alternative perspective on the quantum dynamical phase transition, and show that QDPT exists only for the classical system, and does not exist in the limit of quantum system. Our analysis shows that the QDPT is a manifestation of classical mechanics in the quantum system due to approximation of neglecting quantum interference effects. Using the proposed alternative perspective, we show that the scale-invariance is a valid principle for the quantum dynamical phase transition. Our analysis uncovers the mechanism of quantum dynamical phase transition in the classical limit, and suggests that the scale-invariance is not a fundamental symmetry of the quantum system, but a long-distance emergent behavior in the classical limit.

Quasars are highly luminous point sources in the universe, primarily found in the nuclei of large galaxies. It is generally accepted that active galactic nucleis (AGN) are powered by material falling into a supermassive black hole at the center of the host galaxy. As material falls into the black hole, it generates bright lights called quasars. These quasars can be observed over a broad range of distances from the host galaxy, corresponding to various stages in the growth of the black hole, and are valuable tools for understanding how black holes and their host galaxies form and evolve. Using a large cluster catalog from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey data release 11, we select a sample of 43 quasars at a redshift of 0.3 < z < 2.6 that are located in the projected vicinity of a cluster, with a projected separation of less than 1 Mpc. We compare the radial distribution of these quasars to that of a control sample of 43 matched quasars at similar redshifts that are not in the vicinity of a cluster. We use a maximum likelihood method to fit for the mean separation between quasars and their host clusters, and find no significant radial offset between the two samples. We conclude that quasars do not preferentially reside in the centers of their clusters, and that any preference for quasars to be found near the centers of clusters is less than 5% at the 99% confidence level. These results are consistent with previous studies that have either examined significantly smaller samples of quasars, or have not separated quasars into central and satellite galaxies. Our results indicate that satellite quasars are not primarily being fueled by the hot gas in the clusters, but are instead forming their own massive reservoirs of cold gas, which are likely the primary source of fuel for future growth.'

Long-distance transport of digital data is central to the functioning of modern society, and the development of ultra-long-distance quantum communication would have profound benefits for global communications. Using a multicore optical fiber, we demonstrate a quantum communication channel composed of 10,000 light segments, corresponding to a transmission distance of over 2,000 miles. Each light segment is encoded on a individualhyperfine spin state of atoms, and connected via a ETele programed NOT gate. The fidelity of the transmitted state is over 90%, with a logical error rate < 0.5%. This result represents a significant improvement on previous optical long-distance quantum communication [1-3], and is promising for future development of large-scale quantum networks. [1] A long-distance quantum communication across two cities in Europe. NATURE COMMUNICATIONS, 2018, 9, 174-176. [2] One thousand-kilometre quantum communication. SCIENCE, 2018, 359, 52-54. [3] Global Einstein teleportation with a quantum hyperplane. NATURE COMMUNICATIONS, 2017, 8, 76-80.

In this paper we introduce a star product on the Groenewold-Moyal plane [x, y, \theta] which generalizes both the Moyal product and the Weyl product. This star product is explicitly given by, \begin{equation} f * g = \exp\left(\frac{i}{2} \xi^{\alpha \beta} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{\alpha}} \frac{\partial}{\partial y^{\beta}} \right) f(x) g(y) \Big{|}_{\xi = 0}. \end{equation} The Groenewold-Moyal plane (C[\theta], \star) has played an important role in the study of quantum deformations. It is one of the few nontrivial examples of a nonassociative, noncommutative and noncommutative ( Neijmann-Wigner) Hopf algebra. In particular it contains noncommutative versions of complex space, the (2+1)-dimensional Poincare algebra and the complex Clifford algebra. Our first goal is to construct a real star product on the Groenewold-Moyal plane and to clarify its geometric meaning. From the geometric viewpoint the Weyl product on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ can be obtained from the Groenewold-Moyal product in the limit in which the deformation parameter $\theta$ tends to zero. In the first part of the paper we will show that a Weyl-like star product does exist on the Groenewold-Moyal plane, however, there is no limit in which this product reduces to the Moyal product on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$. As an intermediate step we will introduce a projective Weyl product on the Groenewold-Moyal plane and obtain the Moyal product as a suitable limit. This projective Weyl product admits a natural symplectic structure. We can identify the symplectic leaves of this symplectic structure with certain noncommutative projective spaces. Finally, we give a real representation of the Groenewold-Moyal plane in terms of a $2(2n + 1)$-dimensional real symplectic space with non-degenerate symplectic structure.

The B -> D \pi decays play an important role in searching for CP violation in the B system. In the standard model (SM), CP is a good symmetry and therefore the branching fractions of B -> D pi and B -> D eta should be equal in theSM. Experimentally, however, these branching fractions are not equal. This indicates the existence of new physics. In this paper, we study the effects of the Penguin and Vertex corrections using the QCD factorization approach. We find that both corrections can explain the data and CP violation in the B system may arise from new physics. This work was done in collaboration with J. Zhang and F. Su. In the standard model (SM), CP is a good symmetry and therefore the branching fractions of B → D π and B → D eta should be equal in theSM. We find that both corrections can explain the data and CP violation in the B system may arise from new physics. This work was done in collaboration with J. Zhang and F. Su. QCD Factorization approach is used to study the B → D π decays. The theoretical uncertainties of the calculation are estimated by varying the shape parameter between 0.8 to 1.2 and find that the branching fractions are within theory uncertainties. The SM predictions are in good agreement with the current experimental results. New Physics contributions are introduced to account for CP violation in the B → D π decays. The Vertex and Penguin corrections are studied separately. We find that both corrections can explain the data and CP violation in the B system may arise from new physics.

In this paper we present a detailed analysis of the ground states of a continuous family of quantum spin chains with nearest-neighbor interactions. The family of models is parameterized by an angle θ≥0 and contains the well-known AKLT and Harper models as special cases for θ=0 and θ=π/4, respectively. We show that for all θ<π/4 the ground states of the family of models are strongly ferromagnetically aligned and give a proof that this is also the case for θ=π/4. For θ>π/4 we find that the ground state manifold is two dimensional and split into several disconnected components by acting with symmetries of the Hamiltonian. We use numerical methods to demonstrate that each component is spanned by a degenerate ground state with a particular structure. We further present a variational characterization of these ground states and give evidence that they are exactly realized by macroscopic degenerate ground states of a related spin chain with one-dimensional easy-axis anisotropy. Our results not only extend previous knowledge on the ground state properties of these quantum spin models, they also provide novel insights into the structure of the ground state manifold in this parameter range.

Semenov, D., Smith, B. J., Rendón, I., & Girardeau, M. (2016). Ramsey interferometry with a two-level Tonks-Girardeau gas. Physical Review Letters, 117(7), 070401. In this paper, we introduce Ramsey interferometry with a two-level Tonks-Girardeau (TGO) gas and demonstrate its application to resolving high-precision energy levels of mesoscopic systems. Ramsey interferometry, first introduced in 1963, offers the advantage of precision energy level measurement through Ramsey zone shielding and Ramsey acceleration. We propose an analogous approach using a two-level TGO gas in which a sample level of precision spectroscopy can be achieved through interaction-induced reduced qubit decoherence. In particular, we demonstrate this approach through Ramsey interferometry of a two-level TGO gas, and show that the frequency of theRamseyRamsey light shift can be resolved with sub-kHz precision. Ramsey interferometry with a TGO gas offers a precision spectroscopy approach for molecular systems, quantum many-body systems, and other systems affected by qubit decoherence.

We perform three-dimensional supernova simulations with a high spatial resolution and a properly treat in a self-consistent way multidimensional effects. Unlike our previous paper [1], we include the feedback of turbulence on convective motions in the stellar core and solve the full set of non-linear mean-field magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) equations for magnetic fields. Our simulations cover the time period from the onset of convection to the end of the early post-bounce phase. With this set-up we study in detail the advective-acoustic cycle operating in the supernova core. The cycle is initiated by the buoyancy-driven convection from the pocket of helium fusion, which acts as an efficient dynamo and produces magnetic fields strong enough to affect turbulent motions. The feedback of turbulence on the convective flows leads to the excitation of large-scale pulsating instability. The unstable modes trigger non-linear growth of magnetic energy, causing a rapid exponential amplification of fields and an exponential drop of the convective turnover time. The cycle is closed by the energy release in form of strong neutrino losses that reduce the buoyancy and prevent the buoyant flow from further penetration into the core. The turbulent pumping of entropy strongly increases the efficiency of the neutrino cooling and reduces the core temperature by almost 20% with respect to the reference model. As a result, our model produces a powerful explosions with the kinetic energy 2.6$\times 10^{50}$erg, the mass of ejected material 0.08M$_{\odot}$, and the total binding energy 1.2$\times 10^{50}$erg.

In standard cosmology, dark energy (often specified as a cosmological constant) is responsible for the late-time acceleration of the universe. This article considers a modification of the Friedmann equations that allow for a transition from a period of dark energy-dominated cosmic acceleration (for which lambda > 0) to a period of zero-pressure, non-attractive gravity (for which lambda < 0). By requiring lambda to change sign exactly once between these two epochs, we find a solution consistent with recent observational constraints (with zeropoint energy density equal to approximately 4.66 x 10^−11 g/cm^3). The approach taken here could in principle be applied to any period of cosmic expansion in which dark energy plays a negligible role, from the early decelerating phase through to the current accelerating epoch. The article [1] by Freedman et al. proposed this modification of the Friedman equations, and provided the first analysis of its consequences. Subsequent studies [2-4] have since explored similar ideas but, while some have validated the primary conclusion of this paper (namely, that lambda can change sign in the Universe), others have highlighted various shortcomings of the analysis. These include assumptions made regarding the form of lambda, a lack of explanation for why lambda should change sign, and a failure to consider the full implications of the evolution of gravitational instability in such a universe. Recently, works [5,6] have sought to apply similar ideas to the very early universe, in which context the "zeropoint energy density" corresponds to the energy density of the zero-point quantum fluctuations of the space-time metric. It would be interesting to see if such an approach could give rise to a universe in which lambda could have either sign (as opposed to the current convention of always assuming lambda > 0), or whether it might even allow for a transition from a period of slow-accelerating gravity (for which lambda < 0) to a period of accelerated expansion (for which lambda > 0). The geomagnetic field is a vital indicator of space weather. It is composed of a predominantly dipolar component generated by the motion of inner core, and a fluctuating component generated by atmospheric and solar processes. The amplitude of the fluctuating component decreases rapidly with distance from the magnetic north and requires the integration of solar input and atmospheric response to accurately determine its amplitude and dipole moment at Earth’s surface. The geomagnetic field can be observed directly via magnetometers, or inferred from satellite measurements of the geopotential and bulk plasma flow. While the state of the art in direct measurement technology has improved considerably over the past five decades, direct measurements are costly, subject to availability, and are unable to measure three dimensional field information at the Earth’s surface. For this reason, geophysical models have been coupled to magnetic field data assimilation in order to determine the 3D field amplitude and dipole moment at the surface. This paper reviews some of the specific advances made in variational data assimilation, a recently developed technique for the assimilation of indirect observation data in order to improve the estimation of the state of a dynamical system. The variational method is cast as a constrained optimization problem in the J-subproblem and D-subproblem, where J and D denote the Jacobian and Hessian matrices, respectively. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method through the assimilation of magnetic field data from a single location on Earth to a nonlinear, high-dimensional, and sparse MHD model. The application of variational assimilation to the magnetic field is a promising new direction for improving the accuracy of geophysical models and, in the long term, improving our understanding of the dynamo process that generates the Earth’s magnetic field.

Here we generalize the virial expansion, which is widely used to approximate the thermodynamics of ideal (non-interacting) fluids, to arbitrary trapped gases in the limit of low temperature and density. Our main result, an exact functional relation between the pressure and the virial, applies to a broad class of external potentials and at arbitrary temperature and density. We illustrate the application to a family of potentials produced by magnetic Feshbach resonances, and show that our virial expansion converges rapidly for the universal regime of small external potentials. We verify the accuracy of our virial approximation by comparing toPath integral Monte Carlo simulations, and find excellent agreement at low temperatures even for moderate external potentials. Our results provide a simple and accurate method to calculate the equation of state of atomic gases in harmonic traps, which are important for comparisons with experiments and for testing fundamental theories of gravity and quantum mechanics in many-body systems.

The evolution of stochastic SIR epidemics on random networks with heterogeneous connectivity is investigated. It is found that, on regular networks, the disease-free state is unstable if the average degree of the network is smaller than the threshold, and the disease will die out spontaneously if the average degree is larger than the threshold. When the network is heterogeneous, the disease-free state is still unstable if the network is regular; however, the disease can persist on the network with probability one if the average degree of the network is larger than a threshold. Moreover, for scale-free networks, the epidemic threshold is lowered as the edge distribution exponent γ increases. Network structure determines the stability of the disease-free state. If the average degree of the network is smaller than the threshold, the disease-free state is unstable; if the average degree is larger than the threshold, the disease-free state is stable, but the disease can still die out spontaneously if the network is regular. In addition, scale-free network leads to a larger epidemic threshold.

Poincare duality pairs in dimension three In three dimensions, the Poincaré duality pairs between an oriented closed manifold M and its mirror M dual. Namely, the both manifolds have the same homology groups, and their Betti numbers (also called Stiefel-Whitney classes) are equal. Moreover, the dimension of the cohomology groups are also the same, and they are dual to each other with respect to the cup product. This theorem has several nice applications, for example, it allows one to construct pairs of topologically distinct manifolds that have the same set of differentiable properties, and therefore must be similar inside the realm of mathematics. In the standard model of particle physics, the gauge symmetry of the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions between particles is assumed to be invariant under a global symmetry, called parity, under which elementary particles are transformed into their mirror images. Parity symmetry is a fundamental symmetry of the standard model and, hence, all elementary particles must have a parity partner, i.e. a parity partner particle, which is its exact opposite. The standard model predicts that all elementary particles have parity partners, with the possible exception of the neutral gauge bosons. However, recent results from physics beyond the standard model, such as technicolor and Majorana dark matter, indicate that there might be more new particles than those included in the standard model. Thus, spontaneous parity symmetry breaking could be an alternative mechanism to explain the particle spectrum. This article explores spontaneous parity symmetry breaking as an explanation for the non-observation of parity partner particles. In particular, it is shown that the spontaneous breaking of parity can explain the small masses of the particles.

This is the abstract of the paper "Hamiltonian and Brownian systems with long-range interactions: IV. General kinetic equations from the quasilinear theory" by Xiaoping Zang and D.L. Wang published on arXiv.org on January 20, 2020. We would like to share it with the research community for their information. In this paper, we derive general kinetic equations from the quasilinear theory for Hamiltonian and Brownian particles with long-range interactions. For both cases, the resulting kinetic equations contain two isotropic parts: one is the Fourier shift operator applied to the classical Boltzmann equation, which describes the long-range interaction behavior; the other one is a usual scalar Boltzmann equation, which describes the cross-interaction behavior. For the Hamiltonian case, we also derive a gradient formula for the relative entropy, which is crucial for the well-posedness of the resulting generalized Landau equation. We also show that if the initial particle distributions are sufficiently smooth, the resulting generalized Landau equation possesses a unique global smooth solution. As an application, we numerically illustrate the diffusion of heavy particles in light background and the formation of sonic boom in the atmosphere.

On April 18, 1915, Albert Einstein submitted his now-famous paper on the general theory of relativity. This groundbreaking work not only reformulated our understanding of the universe, but it also marked the beginning of a revolution in the philosophy of science. For the first time, scientists viewed the universe as a single self-contained entity. All physical phenomena were explained by reference to a single set of ten non-trivial, entirely natural laws. This landmark publication had profound consequences for the subsequent history of both physics and philosophy. It ushered in an era of new discoveries, including general relativity itself, and several additional formally relativistic theories, collectively known as the standard model. Over the course of the following decades, general relativity was tested and confirmed to an ever-increasing degree of precision. The landmark publication also had philosophical repercussions, opening the door to a new worldview that we now know as scientific naturalism.

A tool for computational cryptography known as Rime can establish security of communication over a channel by use of ideal lattices. A strong R-matrix is a non-linear operator that, together with a related linear operator (the S-matrix), yields an associative product that defines a finite-dimensional non-commutative ring with unity, known as a finite braided commutative algebra (FBCA). In this work we describe computation of R-matrices for eight binary QC codes using the RIME framework. We use the abelian setting where the S-matrix is a diagonal matrix to compute R-matrices that are also diagonal, and give examples of non-abelian R-matrices for the same codes. We discuss how the R-matrices interact with RIME to establish ideal lattices for each of the codes. The eight codes we study are optimal two-level codes, two-level extended Hamming codes, and five four-level codes commonly used in surface-code quantum computing. Our computed R-matrices have many nice properties, including compatibility with the abelian setting and simple structure when viewed as a lattice over the real numbers, rational numbers, or complex numbers. In particular, we describe the case where the R-matrix is a real diagonal matrix as a families of real numbers (depending on several parameters) where each number occurs with multiplicity one and each occurs exactly twice. We also show how to compute R-matrices corresponding to non-abelian structures when the S-matrix is diagonal. The RIME framework for computing R-matrices in the abelian setting makes use of an appropriately modified quantum chess problem, the Hamilton Pfaffian QC-polynomial. In particular, each symmetry of the chess problem corresponds to a permutation matrix in the R-matrix, and these permutations satisfy a precise lattice-theoretical restriction. In the non-abelian case, no analogous check for R-matrix structure appears to be known, so alternative techniques must be used to establish non-abelian R-matrices. In this work, we describe a non-abelian RIME framework that similarly uses a modified Hamilton Pfaffian but with the permutations no longer required to satisfy a lattice-theoretical restriction. Instead, an ad-hoc method for establishing non-abelianity is used. Finally, we present a few experiments using RIME to establish security of communication over common communication channels (such as WiFi or cell-phone networks). We show that our computed R-matrices are strong and that ideal lattices produced using the R-matrices are the best lattice-based schemes we can find for each of the codes we study. The runtime for each computation of R-matrices and the resulting lattice was less than 12 hours on a standard laptop.

Organic molecules with significant configurational freedom and large dipole moments can undergo shifts in both absorption and emission spectra upon the application of a strong external electric field. The nature of the induced spectral transitions depend on the field direction and on the molecule and, in some cases, can be phosphorescent. We demonstrate that simple Lewis structures with polycyclic aromatic cores can exhibit intense, wide-range absorption bands amenable to electric field control. Application of an alternating electric field simultaneously induces intersystem crossing and roaming, leading to simultaneous red and blue shifts in the absorption and emission spectra. The magnitude and direction of the roaming induced by the alternating electric field is tunable and may be leveraged to provide access to a range of orthogonal photophysical behavior. We also describe preliminary time-resolved spectroscopic studies that support a rapid internal conversion process which likely plays a significant role in governing the observed spectroscopic phenomena. Our studies suggest that electric field induced roaming represents an exciting new class of transition metals complexes that may be tuned and modified through application of an external alternating electric field.

Galactic latitude determines the visual access to the inner regions of the Galaxy. Therefore, it may be expected that globular clusters (GCs) located farther from the Galactic plane could present some specific properties related to their formation and evolution. The total space velocities and the distances of about a dozen GCs located close to the Sun have been determined from the radial velocities and the distances of their member stars. This is the largest homogenous sample of such distances, and it includes clusters located at low Galactic latitudes. Four of these clusters are classical GCs, and the others are primarily composed of RR Lyrae variables, making them referred to as RR0 GCs. The median Galactocentric radial velocity of the RR0 clusters is −10.7 km s−1, and it does not show any gradient with respect to the Galactic radius. On the other hand, a hint of an increase in the velocity dispersion with the Galactic radius is found. The median velocity dispersion of the RR0 clusters is 31.8 km s−1, and it is compatible with that of the corresponding control sample of classical GCs. In addition, a hint of a negative radial gradient in the velocity dispersion of these clusters is found when only clusters with available proper motions are considered. These results suggest that the origin and evolution of these clusters are similar to those of their classical counterparts, except possibly for a slightly higher velocity dispersion in the inner regions of the Galaxy. ----- The total space velocities and the distances of about a dozen GCs located close to the Sun have been determined from the radial velocities and the distances of their member stars. The debris disk around the A star AU Mic was observed in infrared with the Gemini North telescope and with the Hubble Space Telescope. The Hubble observations revealed tenuous dust with size of a few microns, while the ground-based observations revealed also tenuous dust with sizes of tens of microns. The large differences in the inferred sizes of the dust grains could be explained if the debris disk is asymmetric with a significantly higher concentration of dust around AU Mic than around the star itself. To model the observations, we ran three different numerical simulations. In the first simulation, the dust was allowed to drift under the influence of Poynting-Robertson and stellar wind drag forces. The modeling predicted dust distributions that were too uniform to explain the observations. The second simulation, in which the dust was placed on initial eccentric orbits, also did not provide a good fit to the data. In the third simulation, the dust was placed on initially circular orbits and subjected to radiation pressure and gravitational interactions with the dust. The model with this prescription was able to produce a debris disk with a radial power-law distribution of dust consistent with the observations.

Co-doped TiO2 films with various Co doping levels were synthesized by sol-gel process and investigated by structural, transport and magnetic measurements as a function of O2 partial pressure during deposition. The crystalline phase of the films was verified by X-ray diffraction and revealed anatase for all samples. A transport study revealed that incorporation of Co in TiO2 matrix enhances the charge transport characteristic of the films. Magnetic measurement revealed superparamagnetic behavior for samples with low doping levels and ferromagnetic ordering at higher doping levels. The results were discussed in the light of the activation energy calculation. Reducing the O2 partial pressure from high to low level during deposition leads to an increase of the activation energy which can be correlated to the change of magnetic behavior from superparamagnetic to ferromagnetic ordering. * * * * * * * * Cobalt doped TiO2 thin films with various Co doping levels were deposited by sol-gel process under various O2 partial pressures. Structural, transport and magnetic measurements as a function of O2 partial pressure revealed that the formation of Co1-xToxOy solid solution is governed by the Co concentration as well as the O2 partial pressure. As Co doping level increases, the ferromagnetic ordering is observed for the films prepared under low O2 partial pressure. An increase of O2 partial pressure leads to an increase of activation energy and the change of magnetic behavior from superparamagnetic to ferromagnetic ordering can be correlated to the change of activation energy.

The TACTIC telescope is a recently constructed atmospheric Cherenkov imaging telescope with the prime focus of the Kims Hopkins University Mirror Lab in Baltimore, MD. The main scientific goal of this new telescope is the imaging detection of very high energy gamma-rays with a sensitivity an order of magnitude greater than previous similar instruments. In addition, this new facility is well suited to observing the fluorescence of atmospheric trace gas compton scattering spectroscopy and measuring night-sky brightness. The performance of this telescope is briefly summarized in this abstract and a more detailed publication is in preparation. Neutron--proton scattering is one of the fundamental interactions in the universe. The low-energy parameters of the neutron--proton interaction describing low-energy effective interactions in the scattering domain are of crucial importance for various nuclear, particle, and astrophysical phenomena. These low-energy parameters are usually determined by a comparison of the phase shifts of the partial waves of the neutron--proton scattering derived in the effective-field-theory framework with the corresponding experimental data. In this paper, a procedure for determination of the neutron--proton scattering low-energy parameters on the basis of the modern experimental data from partial-wave analyses is proposed. The suggested procedure includes the following steps. First, a database of all available phase-shift data with a fit to all the data is generated. Second, all the data are divided into four energy regions. In each of the energy regions, the parameters of the two-parameter potential model are adjusted to the phase-shift data with an error estimation. Third, the sum of the squared residuals is calculated for each data set. Fourth, the obtained sums are fitted to the functional form, and the parameters of the function are adjusted. Fifth, the procedure is applied for the four energy regions considered. The proposed procedure was applied to phase-shift data on the basis of the most up-to-date partial-wave analyses by the GWU, CSFL, and IUF groups. The performed fits gave the following values of the neutron--proton scattering low-energy parameters: {C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C7, C8} = {0.0726, -0.0748, 0.0023, -0.0032, 0.0069, -0.00028, -0.00058, 0.00004} fm-3. The reliability of the obtained results was verified by performing a root-mean-square analysis and calculating the corresponding statistical characteristics of the fitted parameters. The obtained results for the low-energy parameters are in a good agreement with the current recommendations of the Nijmegen group and the latest calculations performed within the EFT framework. The performed analysis also demonstrated that the energy regions around the K- and P-wave phase shifts provide the most accurate determination of the corresponding low-energy parameters.

A sample of 62 quasars located behind a dense foreground galaxy cluster were imaged with the Hubble Space Telescope in two programs designed to test the gravitational lensing hypothesis for the mass distribution in clusters. Strong evidence is found for the lensing hypothesis for 45 of the quasars, with critical surface density consistent with that for clusters, as expected for the expected cluster mass-to-light ratio. An analysis of the optical spectra of the quasars yields a constraint on the distribution of matter in the Universe similar to that from studies of distant Type Ia supernovae. The mass distribution is consistent with a critical density universe, with no significant contribution from an additionalcomponent of dark matter. The observations are consistent with the standard ΛCDM model of structure formation, with the primordial density perturbations grown into large-scale structure by gravitational instability. The quasarareas above mean density, the clusters below, provide the most direct probe of the dark matter component of the ΛCDM model to date. The lensing hypothesis has been tested in the sample of 45 quasars with strong lensing evidence, yielding the most extensive test to date of the cluster mass-to-light ratio from strong lensing. The results are consistent with the expected cluster mass-to-light ratio, as expected from the cluster mass-to-light ratios measured from X-ray and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich surveys. The optical spectra of the quasars are used to provide a test of the critical density universe, with no significant contribution from an additional component of dark matter. The results are consistent with the standard model of structure formation in the ΛCDM model, with the primordial density perturbations grown into large-scale structure by gravitational instability. The observed quasars are generally too bright to be strongly lensed by individual galaxies in the clusters, with observed redshifts typically z≳ 2.2, corresponding to emitted rest-frame wavelengths of 1300 Angstroms. Strong lensing is most effective for clusters at lower redshift, with the sample of observed quasars thus drawn from a somewhat higher mass population of clusters than those normally studied by X-ray and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich surveys. A subsample of the observed quasars was selected for spectroscopic observations with the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) satellite. Thirty-three quasars show no absorption lines, yielding a lower limit on the neutral hydrogen fraction of around 10-6. However, if indeed a significant fraction of the matter in clusters is in the form of dark matter, which would be expected to thermalize and become statistically indistinguishable from cold dark matter on the cluster scale, then the neutral hydrogen fraction could be much lower, around 10-9, below the current sensitivity limit of FUSE. We study dynamical systems of integer sequences, which we call Diophantine systems. In particular, we focus on the case when the sequences satisfy a recurrence with a polynomial characteristic polynomial. We construct a wide class of systems with Liouville functions, which show the abundance of inhomogeneous phenomena in Diophantine systems. We apply our result to the celebrated Thue-Siegel-Roth theorem on diophantine approximation and give a new proof of this theorem. At the end, we present some possible extensions and applications of our results. Consider the following Diophantine system of recurrence relations $$ x_{n+1} = f(x_n, y_n) $$ where $f(x, y)$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients. We will refer to $x_n$ as the sequence of variables and $y_n$ as the sequence of parameters. We will call a system dynamical Diophantine (or Dio for short) if there exists a neighborhood of zero in the space of parameters, such that for every solution $(x_n, y_n)$ in this neighborhood, the ratios $x_n/y_n$ converge to a limit, which we call the Liouville function of the system. We will study the local stability of Liouville functions, looking for conditions when the linearization of a Liouville function at its unique equilibrium is similar to the identity matrix. We will also study aperiodic solutions of dynamical Diophantine systems. We will see that the abundance of aperiodic solutions is closely related to the existence of Liouville functions with a neighborhood of zero of empty linearization.

The magnetic properties of the geometrically frustrated antiferromagnet volborthite have been investigated using a combination of neutron scattering, magnetic susceptibility, and theoretical modeling. The analysis reveals that volborthite orders antiferromagnetically below TN = 34 K, with propagation vectors k = (0, 0, 1) and (1/2, 1/2, 1/2). The magnetic structure consists of ferromagnetic zigzag chains, with spins lying in the kagome plane, stacked along the c direction. The spins in each chain are weakly coupled with a G-type interaction, J1, and are essentially uncoupled along the a and b axes, with J2 approximately 0.25 J1. The large G-type interaction indicates that Heisenberg theory is a good approximation for the magnetic Hamiltonian, and the best description of volborthite is given by a classical Heisenberg model on the kagome lattice.

There has been increasing interest in using globular clusters (GCs) as cosmic clocks, in particular for investigating the assembly history of galaxies. For this purpose, the structural parameters of GCs, which include the total luminosity, effective radius, surface brightness, and color, are important. However, previous studies have obtained inconsistent results because of limited sample sizes and/or data limitations. In this Letter, I reanalyze the GC data for M31, the Milky Way and other galaxies with the advantage of the newly-released WFC3/IR imaging of the Fornax cluster from the HST Frontier Fields project. Through precise measurements of photometry in both the V and I band, for the first time, I obtain structural parameters for a sample of 56 GCs, more than doubling the number of known structural parameters for GCs in M31. The mean surface brightness and half-light radius of the GCs in M31 are consistent with previous results. The size and surface brightness of M31 GCs are also consistent with the relations for GCs in the Fornax and Milky Way, which share a similar luminosity with M31. The size-luminosity and surface brightness-luminosity relations for M31 GCs are fully consistent with the fundamental plane (FP) for elliptical galaxies. I also find that M31 GCs with the same size as GCs in the Milky Way have similar luminosity and surface brightness to those GCs, suggesting that the formation efficiency of GCs in M31 is similar to that in the Milky Way. The above results suggest that GCs are good tracers of galaxy assembly. Theoretical models have shown that the FP of galaxies is a product of two fundamental planes (FP1 and FP2), which are also valid for GCs. FP1 relates the total luminosity of the galaxy to its total mass. FP2 relates the effective radius of the galaxy to the dispersion of the galaxy’s stellar population. The FP has been widely used in studies of elliptical galaxies, although there are some recent debates on its universality. I propose that GCs might form a FP (GCP) since many of their fundamental parameters (such as total luminosity and effective radius) depend on the total mass and dispersion of the parent galaxies. The GCP can be used to investigate the formation history of galaxies in the early universe.

The Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) was a NASA mission that covered the electromagnetic spectrum from obscuration by the Earth's atmosphere to the mid-UV. GALEX performed a all-sky survey in the far-UV and sampled Galactic structure in the near-UV. The All-Sky survey provided calibrated, visible-light image data for substantial portions of the sky that had not been observed by other space or Earth-based telescopes. The survey sensitively measured how the brightness of objects in the sky varied as a function of position on the sky. It also provided a catalog of more than a million objects with statistical properties that could be used to estimate the brightness of individual objects in the All-Sky survey that were not detectable in the images. This calibration information was essential to enable precise measurement of how the brightness of celestial objects varied across the sky. The GALEX Nearby Galaxy Survey and GALEX Deep Extragalactic Survey obtained images of targeted regions of the sky that had not been observed with other telescopes and obtained spectra of many more galaxies than had been accessible before GALEX.

In the center of the nearby galaxy M82, a stellar system in the early phases of transformation into a globular cluster, reside two high mass X-ray binaries (HMXB), dubbed M82 X-1 and M82 X-4. They were first discovered by the Einstein observatory. The nature of these sources is still unknown. They were considered candidates to powered the gamma-ray emission discovered by INTEGRAL. The discovery of a strong stellar proper motion with a position angle of ~70° relative to the molecular gas in the center of M82 confirmed the previous hypothesis that M82 X-1 and M82 X-4 are experiencing a rapid orbital decay due to the emission of gravitational waves. However, this proposed explanation is challenged by the large observed X-ray luminosity of the sources, which would imply a large mass for the neutron stars at the upper end of the initial mass function, even larger than 40 solar masses, and render such objects unphysical. Alternative scenarios invoke a high-density environment where the emission of gravitational waves is enhanced.

One of the most promising avenues towards solving the hierarchy problem is to realize the effective field theory below the cut-off of the new high energy theory in terms of some higher dimensional theory with large compact internal dimensions. This ‘large volume compactification’ makes use of the observed volume of the internal space to stabilize the vacuum energy scale. This allows us to naturally explain the observed cosmological constant while keeping the gravity localized on our universe. In this paper we consider phenomenological consequences of such large volume compactifications in four dimensions. In particular we examine the signature flux fluctuations from the form fields of the stabilization lattice and comment on the stability of these fluxes. We also consider the implications of these backgrounds for cosmology and constraints from nucleosynthesis and Big Bang Nucleosyte reionization. A detailed examination of phenomenological and cosmological constraints on large volume compactifications has recently been carried out in [1]. Here we will focus on the signature flux fluctuations from the form fields of the stabilization lattice and comment on the stability of these fluxes. We will also examine the implications of these backgrounds for cosmology and constraints from nucleosynthesis and Big Bang Nucleosyte reionization. Our four dimensional effective theory below the cut-off of the new high energy theory comes with no additional symmetry. Nonetheless, we expect it to be stable due to the following reasons: 1. We expect the effective theory below the cut-off to be a non-gravitational Yang-Mills theory with gauge group $SU(N)\times SU(N)\times \cdots \times SU(N)$. Such a theory is known to be perturbatively stable. 2. In the strong coupling limit of the Yang-Mills theory, we expect the low energy effective field theory to be a strongly coupled $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity. This supergravity is known to be free of instabilities. We now present our analysis of signature flux fluctuations from the form fields of the stabilization lattice and comment on the stability of these fluxes. We begin with some general comments on flux fluctuations and their potential destabilization in the presence of background fluxes. In the large volume case we are considering, the compactification manifold $X$ has no generics, meaning that there are no topologically non-trivial cycles. All topologically non-trivial fluxes have been wrapped and become dualized into component fluxes. These are the dilaton and the volume form fluxes. We assume that the internal manifold admits a nowhere vanishing vector field $V$ whose field strength $dV$ is Poincaré dual to the elliptic fiber class characteristic of the heterotic duality. The fluxes are therefore ‘pseudo-constructed’ [2], i.e. we must perform a gauge transformation so that the fluxes are an integer multiple of $2 \pi$. The isolated spiral galaxies of the sample are fairly similar to the Magellanic Clouds in the optical appearance. They are nearly round with slightly flocculent, ocher-colored spiral arms. The flocculent appearance is similar to that of the M33 galaxy, but the isolated spirals are slightly larger. Elliptical isophotes are rare. The distance estimates range from 9 to 17 Mpc, with an average of 13 Mpc. The apparent V band magnitudes range from 15.9 to 16.4 with an average of 16.0. The absolute V band magnitude Mv ranges from -18.4 to -17.0 with an average of -16.5. The colors are fairly blue, with V-R equal to 0.6 and R-I equal to 0.7. The colors and magnitudes of these isolated spiral galaxies are very similar to the corresponding characteristics of the Magellanic Clouds. Thus these galaxies are probably satellites of the Milky Way. The similarity of the two galaxies in characteristics also suggest a close physical relationship. The isolation of the galaxies implies that they have been fairly untouched by neighboring galaxies. Thus their original shapes may have been more nearly circular than those seen today. The effect of tidal forces from the Milky Way is probably to have flattened the original shapes and formed the flocculent appearance. These galaxies have not been completely dissolved by the Milky Way's gravitational field. The estimated masses of these galaxies based on their observed rotational velocities and projected spatial extents are on the order of 10 billion times the mass of the Sun. These large masses indicate that the galaxies are in a fairly late stage of evolution. The colors and absolute magnitudes of the isolated spiral galaxies are typical of dI galaxies, whose evolution is generally thought to be caused by the gradual loss of mass to large scale structures via a process of tidal stripping. The estimated ages of the isolated spiral galaxies based on their integrated colors and based on the presence of blue stars in their cores range from 3 to 7 Gyr, with an average of 5 Gyr. These estimated ages are generally much less than the probable ages based on the number of remnants of intermediate and old age present, which range from 10 to 14 Gyr, with an average of 12 Gyr. The estimated ages based on integrated colors may be underestimated if there is significant internal reddening in the galaxies. These differences between the estimated ages based on integrated colors and the probable ages based on the numbers of old stars may be due to the galaxies having a relatively short evolutionary life span. This paper considers the problem of determining the best possible way to pack equal spheres in d dimensions, where 'best' is defined in terms of certain scalar measures of order and density. First, the optimal number of sphere packings in d dimensions is calculated; in all dimensions d greater than or equal to 8, the kissing number is 28. Second, the packing density for 3D, 6D and 8D sphere packings is computed, and it is shown that the optimal density gradually decreases with increasing dimension. Third, explicit constant-factor approximation algorithms for dense sphere packings in high dimensions are presented, with the approximation guarantee deteriorating as the dimension increases. Finally, it is shown that there does not exist an efficient algorithm to compute the densest packing of equal spheres in any dimension d < 10. The first two sections of this paper determine the best possible number of distinct sphere packings in high dimensions and the optimal density for sphere packings, respectively. The third section presents constant-factor approximation algorithms for dense sphere packings in high dimensions. The final section presents a negative result stating that it is impossible to compute the densest sphere packing in any dimension less than 10. The best possible number of distinct sphere packings in d dimensions is calculated in Theorem 1. First, it is shown that the kissing number in d dimensions is 2d, where d is the dimension. Second, it is shown that the densest sphere packing in 3 dimensions has packing density 0.75. It is conjectured that the optimal packing density in 3 dimensions is 1. However, the best packing known in 3 dimensions has density 0.9067. In higher dimensions, the best possible number of distinct sphere packings is calculated for d≥6 in Theorem 2. First, it is shown that the kissing number in d dimensions is 2d+2. Second, it is shown that the maximum possible number of sphere packings in d dimensions is Ω(d3). Third, it is shown that the ratio of the actual number of sphere packings to the maximum possible number of sphere packings is at most 1/Ω(d2). In d dimensions, the densest sphere packing has density ρd. The best possible density for sphere packings in d dimensions is computed in Theorem 3. It is shown that the density gradually decreases with increasing dimension and that the optimal density in d dimensions is ρopt=1/δ(d) where δ(d) is the kissing number in d dimensions.
