The Spitzer c2d Survey of Large, Nearby, Interstellar Clouds. IV. Lupus Observed with MIPS. We present the results from the fourth and last installment of the Spitzer c2d survey of large, nearby clouds. Lupus I, II & III were surveyed with IRAC in the 3.6, 4.5, 5.8 and 8.0 μm bands and MIPS in the 24, 70 and 160 μm bands. The resulting dataset is described in papers I, II and III. In this paper we present new low mass pre-main sequence (pre-MS) candidates in Lupus I, II, and III, and focus on one dark cloud, Lupus III-Vul, in more detail. This dark cloud was initially surveyed by Evans et al. (2009), who identified 60 new low-mass pre-MS candidates with HST/COS. We combine our Spitzer data with that of Evans et al. (2009) to obtain new submillimeter andbolometer fluxes and SEDs for 45 of the candidates. Thirty three of these objects have multiple 24 μm measurements and agree with an extinction model to haveDISK brightnesses with a median of 7.2% and a dispersion of 11.3%. These 33 objects with measured DISK brightness are considered to be good Lupus pre-MS candidates. Twenty four of the candidates do not have DISK brightness measurements due to saturation in the MIPS 24 μm measurements or 24umGALOR algorithm rejection, and are considered to be good Lupus pre-MS candidates. We perform a Bayesian analysis to combine the Spitzer and HST/COS data for the 60 new candidates to obtain median disk masses and the probability of a disk around each of these objects. We discuss new submillimeter data and analysis of MIPS data in more detail for Lupus III-Vul. We also discuss the membership for seven additional Lupus dark clouds for which we did not detect any new low mass pre-MS candidates.

A new metallicity indicator has been derived from photometry of the Galactic globular cluster M75 (NGC 6864). This cluster is especially interesting because its horizontal branch (HB) is multi-colored. The color difference between the HB and the main sequence turnoff point is found to be relatively large: δ(b-y) = 0.145 ± 0.002, that is 0.219 in the Caret Colour System. Such a color difference is due to the relatively high heavy element content of M75, and can be used to measure its metallicity. To test the applicability of M75 as a metallicity indicator we have compared its \[Fe/H\] values with published spectroscopic measurements. We find a very good agreement, with a slope of 1.009 and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.999. The derived metallicity index, (b-y)0 = 0.439, is found to be strongly insensitive to the theoretical input parameters. We use our new metallicity indicator to analyze the HB morphology of M75. We find that the distribution of stars along the HB follows the characteristic "hook" shape, in accordance with previous findings. We confirm that the HB of M75 is distinctly bluer than the rest of the cluster's population, with the most likely explanation being a large helium content in the cluster's population. We also analyze the red giant branch (RGB) morphology of M75 and confirm that it has an extended clump, which is another common signature of a high helium abundance.

A useful bound on the quantum mutual information of a quantum channel ϒ Alexandria, Virág; Plantenberg, Mark M; Renner, Prof. Dr. Renate ́ [ {max},C> } ] is derived in terms of the least solution of a certain set of inequalities. This provides a convenient and easy to verify information bound on the amount of information that ϒ transmits about its environment. Examples are given for phase- damping, depolarizing and amplitude-damping quantum channels. This paper provides a bound on the quantum mutual information of a quantum channel in terms of the least solution of a certain set of inequalities. This bound is useful in that it is straightforward to verify, and provides a convenient and easy to verify bound on the amount of information that a quantum channel transmits about its environment. We provide examples for the case of phase-damping, depolarizing and amplitude-damping quantum channels. The paper is part of a larger ongoing effort to quantify the information capacity of quantum channels. This is one of the first steps in this quantification process, and provides a lower bound on the mutual information of a quantum channel. In turn, the mutual information is an important quantity in the characterization of quantum channels, with applications in, e.g, the distillation of quantum entanglement.

Sm2IrIn8 is an interesting compound with potential applications as a thermoelectric material, since it has the best properties of any Ir-based thermoelectric material known to date (see Takimoto et al., “Unusually High ZT Composed of Rare-Earths and InverseMETAs in the triangular lattice,” phys. stat. sol. (a) 220.11 (2013): 28). Magnetic order in this material was recently discovered to be in the tricritical regime, meaning that the magnetic order undergoes a second-order phase transition at the temperature T Tr = 290 K, but the correlation length increases so rapidly at this temperature that the system appears to be “tricritical” (see Woods et al., “Metamagnetism and the tricritical regime in the ternary iron pnictide Sm2IrIn8,” J. Phys. Condens. Matter 30, 255602 (2018)). This unusual behavior is believed to be related to strong electronic correlations, but the precise relationship is not yet understood.

Arctic East Siberia is an area of the Arctic with significant summer ice (also known as Eurasian Arctic). As such it has been subject to fluctuations in ice cover during the Quaternary. The changes have had profound impact on the ecology and evolution of animal and plant species living in the region. Two major phases of glaciations can be discerned in the records of Arctic East Siberia: Younger Dryas event about 12,800 years BP; and Glesisspermia event about 900 years BP. The last glaciation phase, the Glesisspermia, was most recent. In this phase the Arctic East Siberia was periodically covered by permafrost ice, interspersed with Earth's warmer periods, that refroze each time. This made it possible for trees and shrubs, that were rarely or never before seen in this region, to take root and grow. One such plant is currently dominant in many peat bogs of this region—shepard's-broom, Genisteae. The diversity and biomass of birds and mammals changed significantly at the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries, likely caused by changing climatic conditions associated with glaciations. The study of these changes provides an insight into how the Quaternary environment and climate have affected the life in this region of the Arctic.

The Cryogenic Telescope for ELT (CRYTES) is an international scientific collaboration for the development of a large-diameter space telescope to be dedicated to the search for Extremely Low Frequency signals from Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence. The telescope consists of a 1000 m diameter antenna supported by a 20 m diameter cantilever structure. The cantilever will be placed in a Earth geostationary orbit, where the satellite will act as a large scale preamplifier for signals from outer space. The low temperature structure will be realized by a triple layer carbon-fibre composite structures, attached to a sapphire windows, for a total of three cold masses of about 200 kg. The thermal noise from the three cold masses coupled with the motion of the satellite, induce a parasitic drag, limiting the operational life-time of the telescope. In this paper, we present the results of an ongoing program to characterize the CTE-Shift of a graphite test mass, realized with a Honeywell ACTIVE probe system at LN2 temperature. The test mass was exposed to a modulated reference signal at different frequencies in the range of 1 Hz to 1000 Hz, with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 1 mHz to 200 mHz and a modulated power of 0.2 mW to 20 mW. The test mass response to the input signal was measured at different positions on the surface of the test mass, in order to evaluate the CTE-Shift performance. The frequency dependence of the CTE-Shift was measured in the range of 1 Hz to 1000 Hz, with a frequency step of 1 Hz. The measured CTE-Shift was -0.52 μm/K at 1 Hz, and it increased up to -0.93 μm/K at 1000 Hz. The increase in CTE-Shift was higher than the one predicted by the linear theory of CTE-Shift, as discussed in the paper.

Coleman and De Luccia showed that nontrivial topologies with nontrivial first homotopy group allow for Euclidean wormholes. This method of traversing the wormhole requires that the Euclidean path integral be performed across the wormhole, with the traversal switched on at the end of theColeman and De Luccia showed that nontrivial topologies with nontrivial first homotopy group allow for Euclidean wormholes. This method of traversing the wormhole requires that the Euclidean path integral be performed across the wormhole, with the traversal switched on at the end of the wormhole and switched off at the end of the Euclidean universe. Here I demonstrate that the Euclidean path integral may be performed without reference to a global Euclidean metric, but rather based on a local thermal energy density. Because the Euclidean wormhole instanton is based on local thermal energy, the traversal of the wormhole may occur at any point along the wormhole without concern for global temperature or topology, and the traversal need only be switched on at one end of the wormhole to be complete. This allows for tunneling from one topology to another without reference to a global Euclidean metric. This new version of Euclidean wormholes is also applicable to Lorentzian spacetimes, and so Euclidean wormholes with nontrivial first homotopy group may now allow for traversal from one Lorentzian universe to another without violation of the Coleman-Herman uniqueness theorem.

Neutral and charged heavy mesons are often produced near threshold in e+e- annihilation. The yield of these states is highly sensitive to their masses, which are poorly known. Experimentally, a comparison of the yields of high-statistics samples of oppositely charged pairs of these states yields a close match, leading to the conclusion that these states near threshold have spin 1. Experiments at the B factories, however, have demonstrated that, in fact, these mesons have spin 0 or 2. To reconcile these observations, it has been suggested that the isospin of these states is broken at a level sufficient to explain the observed spectrum. We report on a model-independent study of this isospin breaking, based on an exact rewriting of the spectrum in terms of Weinberg's isospin breaking parameter Ω. We find that, indeed, Ω must be positive in order to explain the observed spectrum, and we determine its value. We conclude that the spectrum of these states near threshold exhibits evidence of isospin breaking.

In this paper we consider a problem of multiple user detection and channel estimation in a dynamic environment, which refers to a situation when different users share the same time-frequency resource. We propose to solve this problem in two stages. In the first stage we identify which user has co-accessed the channel using some energy detection method. In the second stage we use data detection method to find the actual transmitted information from the identified user. We consider both non-coherent and coherent detection techniques. In the non-coherent detection case, we use a generalization of non-coherent MRC (maximum ratio combining) receiver for the multiple access channel. In the coherent detection case, we use a recently proposed algorithm for multiuser detection in the time-varying channel with cyclostationary noise, which is based on the the analog domain spread-spectrum technique. In the numerical part of this paper, we demonstrate the superiority of the proposed detection technique over conventional approaches. We also provide the results of computer simulations for other channel estimation algorithms, which were not analyzed in the paper due to the lack of space.

Aluminium-80-nickel-20 (Al-Ni-4.5 at.%) alloy is a promising structural material for fusion reactor applications due to its high strength, fracture toughness, and creep resistance at high temperatures. However, the high diffusivity of nickel in aluminiumat high temperaturespoor concerns for interaction concerns between the melt and vessel walls in fusion reactors. In this study, we present molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and experiments of Al-Ni alloys at temperatures relevant to fusion reactor conditions. We find that the self-diffusion of aluminium and interdiffusion between aluminium and nickel increase with temperature in both the simulations and experiments. At 1023 K, the self-diffusion of aluminium in the Al-Ni alloy is four times faster than that in pure aluminium, and the ratio of the diffusivities of aluminium in the Al-Ni alloy and pure aluminium is estimated to be 4.2. We also find that the atomistic configurations in the simulations and experiments at high temperature resemble each other and exhibit a network of fourfold rotationally symmetrical stringers composed of Al atoms and interspersed with vacancy-type regions. The diffusivities in the simulations and experiments are correlated in both the trends and the relative values, and the MD-predicted diffusivities are within a factor of two of the experimentally measured values. This is an encouraging result for using molecular dynamics simulations to investigate self-diffusion and interdiffusion in complex metallic systems and demonstrates the feasibility of using atomic-scale simulations to complement experiments for understanding material properties at the nanoscale. This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, Materials Sciences and Engineering Division. The computational work was performed at the Arlene Tackles Extreme Computing (ATTEC) facility at Oklahoma State University, which is supported by the Elemental Science Award number DE-FG52-09NA28438.

Relativistic fluctuation theorems are a set of equalities relating the probabilities of different outcomes for systems in thermal equilibrium. They were conjectured by Robert equilibrium in the late 1990s and proved for the first time in 2003 by Euc59lin Wang and Keiji Saito. Since then, a multitude of variants and generalisations have been proven. The original versions are only valid in the special case of thermodynamic processes in which the dynamics are Markov and the system has only first-order time-dependent dependencies. In this case the corresponding theorems are known as the classical or non-covariant fluctuation theorems. More recently it has been shown that, under less restrictive conditions, similar theorems also hold with a covariance factor which depends on the dynamics of the system. In this article we present a complete derivation of these general theorems, including all covariances. As a check, several previously proven special cases are shown to be recovered as limiting cases of the general theorem. This article is an extended and updated version of a review published in 2014.

The HELLAS2XMM survey is a wide-area (0.3 ster) X-ray survey performed with XMM-Newton of the region in the SSA 22 field covered by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SSS). Nine luminous, highly obscured (based on X-ray absorption) quasars are detected. By combining X-ray and Spitzer data, we determine their bolometric output, finding that, despite their high intrinsic power, these quasars contribute a much lower fraction of the total bolometric output of all luminous AGN (~5%) than they do of their bolometric output in X-rays (~50%). This implies that they represent a missed population of luminous, but heavily obscured, AGN. Luminous, obscured quasars are promising candidates for the seeds of galaxy growth. These quasars may be missed in surveys which only detect unobscured or mildly-obscured AGN because they contribute a relatively low fraction of the total bolometric output of all luminous AGN. Surveys which extend to higher obscurations will therefore miss an important population of active galactic nuclei (AGN). Here we present results from the HELLAS2XMM survey, which is a deep X-ray survey of a region covered by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. This region was targeted because it contains several luminous, highly obscured (NH[i] > 2 × 10[22] cm-2) quasars. Nine quasars are detected, and when combined with X-ray data from XMM-Newton, we determine their bolometric output. The total bolometric output of these quasars is ~2.5% of the total bolometric output of all AGN in the field, and they contribute a much lower fraction (~5%) of their X-ray output. This implies that these objects represent a population of heavily obscured AGN which are missed in surveys which only detect unobscured or mildly-obscured AGN. Overall, this work demonstrates the value of combining X-ray and infrared data to characterize the bolometric output of AGN and to identify potentially important sources of feedback.

EF Cha is an unique star in our solar system. It has a close solar sibling named AD Cha, but has strong stellar emissions at mid-infrared. We carried out the first spectro-astrometric observation of EF Cha and did not observe any significant motion of the warm dust around the star. We conclude that the warm dust does not orbit around EF Cha, but is instead a member of the same stellar system as EF Cha and is heated by the same UV/optical/mid-infrared emission from the young star. --- EF Cha is an unique star in our solar system. It has a close solar sibling named AD Cha, but has strong stellar emissions at mid-infrared. We carried out the first spectro-astrometric observation of EF Cha and did not observe any significant motion of the warm dust around the star. We conclude that the warm dust does not orbit around EF Cha, but is instead a member of the same stellar system as EF Cha and is heated by the same UV/optical/mid-infrared emission from the young star.

A dense equatorial structure has recently been identified in the spectrum of the cool, evolved star HD Nyrae, using high-resolution spectra obtained with the HST/STIS echelle spectrograph. The presence of this structure, at a velocity relative to the star that is consistent with membership of the Cyg X-3 system, implies a distance of around 3 kpc to HD Nyrae, and therefore age estimates of around 500-1000 years for the circumstellar structure. Using archival data from the Optical/Infrared Telescope Facility and VLT, we have obtained high-resolution spectra of 11 post-LBV Wolf-Rayet stars. The spectrum of each of these objects exhibits the absorption structure identified in HD Nyrae, providing further evidence for the existence of dense equatorial winds in this late phase of evolution for a substantial fraction of these stars. The fact that the structure is only present in stars that have recently left the LBV phase, and that it has a typical mass-loss rate of ~10-5-10-4 M⊙ yr-1, indicates that the mass-loss event that led to the formation of the dense equatorial structure was driven by a thermally-driven instability. In this regard, the recent discoveries of dense equatorial structures around HD Nyrae and other evolved LBV stars supports the link between these stars and the long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs).

The Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) is a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. It is of particular interest for studies of chemical evolution, as it has lower metallicity than the Large Magellanic Cloud. Planetary nebulae (PNe) are old stars whose atmospheres have been expelled by strong stellar winds. Their elemental abundances can be used to study the chemical evolution of a galaxy. However, very few PNe have been found in the SMC. Here we present optical spectroscopic observations of 19 PNe in the SMC. We measure their radial velocities and chemical compositions. We find that the distribution of nitrogen and the period of oxygen isotopes are similar to those in the Large Magellanic Cloud, while those of sulphur and argon are different. The similarity between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds suggests that the SMC experienced similar evolution with the LMC. However, the measured differences imply that the SMC had a different formation history from the LMC.

Magnetodielectric media with simultaneously large magneto-optical and dielectric losses support traveling waves that are simultaneously attenuated and refracted. When resonant loss features of these media are broadened by radiative processes, the resulting local-field enhancement and media degeneration can lead to significant refraction and absorption reduction. Here we demonstrate, both theoretically and experimentally, this phenomenon of negative refraction and absorption reduction in a resonant plasmon-radiative medium based on inverse Faraday rotation in a thin yttrium iron garnet film. The observed resonant refraction reduction of over 25% is greater than that of standard resummed negative-index media. The derived absorption reduction is greater than 10% in the measured frequency range, which is the largest value reported for any resonant plasmon-radiative medium. Our results indicate that radiative losses may provide a promising approach for enhanced absorption and refraction in plasmonic and magnetic media."

In this paper, we present results from new, sensitive observations of the high-mass star-forming region Orion Source I using the SiO maser transition. These observations were carried out with therecent commissioning of the Eight MIxing performed at the Arizona Radio Observatory (ARO). These observations achieve a resolution of approximately 0.02 pc and a 5-GHz RMS noise level of approximately 0.2 K across this region. These observations reveal the dynamical evolution of a high-mass star-forming region over the course of 10-100 AU scales. We find strong evidence for two concurrent star formation episodes, with the younger B0.5 and B1 stars residing within a centrally concentrated cluster of Class 0 sources, and the more evolved O7 and O9 stars spatially offset from this cluster. These results help elucidate the complicated interactions between these multiple forming regions on scales from 10s-100s of AU.

Semiclassical scalar propagators in curved backgrounds are of importance in a wide variety of situations ranging from the effective action for diffusion modes in inflationary backgrounds (relevant for studying the impact of cosmic inflation on structure formation) to quantum gravity. Previous analyses of semiclassical scalar propagators have been carried out either in certain gauge conditions or within some particular approximation, or have been restricted to geometries with certain symmetries. In this work we provide a general and detailed exposition of the requisite formalism, presenting a number of new results (including a previously unsuspected absence of Hadamard-like conditions in scalar field theory, which we highlight) as well as making precise the sense in which previously known results may be generalised. We also discuss a variety of issues which are special to scalar field theories (including some new ones which do not arise in the electromagnetic or gravity cases). We hope that this will be of use to a broad class of problems in theoretical high energy physics as well as in cosmology and quantum gravity.

Triangulations and Catalan's intervals Triangulations of the convex hulls of point sets in the plane have been studied since the 1990s. There exist eight different generic types of triangulations, depending on the number of points, the distances between the points, and their spatial disposition. In this paper, we analyze the realizers of all these generic types. The realizers of a triangulation are edge-lists of simple polytopes defining the same homology class as the original triangulation. They can be constructed algorithmically from the given topological space. The knowledge of all realizers of a given triangulation is very useful for many geometric, topological, and computational applications. We identify all possible realizers for eight generic types of triangulations. The total number of different realizer sets we find is 46. The article also provides a Java software for computing realizers of given triangulations.

Multiferroics with coupled magnetic and ferroelectric orders are interesting not only from the fundamental point of view but also for their potential applications in spintronics and magnetoelectric devices. Among these materials, B-site cationic order in multiferroic Bi2FeCrO6 has been predicted to induce a large magnetic entropy change with a large polarization as well as a magnetic field inducedferroelectric polarization. In this work, we have successfully grown bi2-aryance of bismuth (Bi), iron (Fe) and chromium (Cr) with the B-site cationic order using optimized PLD methods. Our characterization using x-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and neutron diffraction reveals that our films are epitaxial with the B-site cationic order. Our magnetization and neutron diffraction measurements confirm that our films possess a net magnetic moment and exhibit a helimagnetic phase transition at Tc = 155 K. More importantly, our broadband infrared magneto-optical measurements reveal a significant magnetic entropy change as high as |Δ S m| = 57.7 mJ/kgK, which is one of the largest magnetic entropy change values ever reported for multiferroic materials. We also performed electric polarization measurements using x-ray diffraction, which reveals a weak but nonzero ferroelectric polarization of ~0.03 μC/cm2 at room temperature. Finally, we propose a possible magnetoelectric coupling mechanism in Bi2FeCrO6 based on our experimental observations.

A long-term stable orbit about a black hole is possible in the context of standard general relativity. Such an orbit is permitted only in an annulus outside the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). Strong dissipative processes such as gravitational wave radiation will drive a test particle out of this region, unless some means to overcome the classical excitation barrier is available. Here, I show that a rotating black hole may act as a “catcher” due to resonant interactions with planewave oscillations of the particle in the test orbit. The black hole efficiently “catches” low-order Kelvin and Foust modes, transferring orbital energy to the black hole spin. The back reaction from the black hole is shown to suppress excitation of lower-order modes, allowing for efficient transport to the innermost stable circular orbit. This work presents a new channel for energy and angular momentum exchange between a black hole and an orbiting particle, which may enable more efficient extraction of energy from black holes in future gravitational wave observations and tests of general relativity.

In August 2022, a hitherto unnoticed dwarf galaxy passed near the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). Optical observations by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope, which is located on Haleakala on Maui, Hawaii, revealed a massive globular cluster, similar in colour and magnitude to the LMC, trailing behind the dwarf. Spectroscopic follow-up with the Keck I and II telescopes showed the globular cluster to be extremely metal-poor, with an average metallicity of only 5% of the solar value. The only other known object of such low metallicity is the Small Magellanic Cloud. The only possible explanation for the formation of this object is the infall of a relatively massive galaxy in the early stages of its evolution. We conclude that this object is the remains of a galaxy nucleus that has been stripped of its gas and is currently being assimilated into the LMC. This remarkable object shows that galaxies can interact with one another in unexpected ways.

The WMAP satellite has provided the most accurate measurements to date of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation, allowing studies of spatial variations in the properties of the CMB. One such study is that of morphology, which measures fluctuations in the temperature of the CMB on various angular scales. The NVSS, a total intensity map of the radio sky, has also been obtained, allowing the study of morphology on smaller scales. Using correlation techniques, these two local morphological measures have been shown to be highly correlated on small angular scales, allowing the detection of a slight deficit in large-angular scale CMB temperature variations, a detection of the so-called'Cosmic Web'. It has been argued that this deficit is due to the presence of dark energy, a supposed component of the universe causing its expansion to accelerate. This paper uses steerable wavelets to extend previous results, finding a slight deficit in the correlation of WMAP and NVSS local morphological measures on slightly smaller angular scales. This is consistent with previous results, and allows detection of the so-called 'Cosmic Web' of filaments and walls. Using steerable wavelets allows the scale of deficit to be studied as a function of position on the sky, showing slight variations in morphology with position. This can be used to constrain the presence of dark energy, finding a best-fit ofΛCDM model with dark energy equation of state w=-0.98+/-0.13 at 2 sigma confidence.

In this work, we develop a microscopic theory for toroidal moments in bulk periodic crystals. By employing a systematic, momentum-space approach, we derive the general form of the effective Hamiltonian in the presence of magnetic-anisotropy and Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions. The theory is then applied to describe the nature of toroidal moments in magnesium diboride (MgB2) and dichalcogenides with either orthorhombic (TMDC) or polar (WS2) structures. Our calculations demonstrate the coexistence of symmetric and antisymmetric toroidal moments in MgB2, whereas in TMDC and WS2 only antisymmetric toroidal moments are allowed. We show that the antisymmetric toroidal moments in MgB2 and TMDC are equivalent and induce an effective magnetic field that modifies the dispersion of surface plasmons. In WS2, we predict the emergence of a new circularly-polarized plasmon mode that is protected by symmetry and not affected by the inclusion of Coulomb interactions. These predictions could be experimentally verified by means of spectroscopic techniques such as Raman scattering and infrared optical absorption. Our work provides a solid theoretical foundation for engineering toroidal moment couplings in periodic crystals and for exploiting their emergent electromagnetic properties in plasmonics and excitonics.

A photospheric velocity field of a Supergranular cell is presented. The cell is a small-scale feature on the solar surface, with a typical area of a few square kilometers. These small-scale features are of great interest because they control the energy flux through the sun and thus influence the global weather on Earth. Supergranules are persistent, approximately spherical features on the solar surface. The Supergranule cell analyzed in this paper appears as a dark cavity in time-slice movie of the photospheric velocity field. Using the Local Correlation Function, the cell's shape has been revealed. The velocity field was obtained by the time-distance helioseismology. It has been shown that the cell's axis is almost exactly aligned with the solar rotation axis. The maximum amplitude of the solar rotation, and thus the supergranular flow, occurs near the center of the cell. The supergranular flow in the cell is directed along the cell's axis. The amplitude of the supergranular flow is 350 m/s. The radius of the supergranule flow was estimated as half the distance between the cell's edge and the maximum velocity value.

A wide-field survey around the Local Group dwarf spheroidal galaxy Leo II was conducted using the Dragonfly cluster camera on the Kueyen telescope at the ESO La Silla observatory. The goals were to map the spatial distribution of the Leo II stellar content, and of any candidate ultra-compact dwarf (UCD) galaxies, in order to better characterize the cluster environment, and to probe the possible occurrence of interactions and dwarf-dwarf mergers. The observations, covering a field of view of 8.5×8.5 degrees, were carried out over the course of four nights in November 2017, for a total of 23h of exposure time. A catalog of 1064 sources, corresponding to 583 individual stars and 167 candidate UCDs, was constructed. The corresponding spatial distribution is found to be relatively featureless, with no clear evidence of disruption or tidal interactions with neighboring systems. By means of statistical subtraction of two plausible stellar density models, it is tentatively inferred that Leo II may host an additional 20-30 unresolved UCDs, with a mass fraction in excess of 10%, within its observed extent.

New superstring isometries, including ones that generate the E8 and SO(32) symmetries and that uplift to seven and eleven dimensional supergravities, are identified. These isometries can serve as the foundation for models with large or warped hidden dimensions that are consistent with all existing experimental and observational constraints. A sample model with large hidden dimensions is presented that contains 27 moduli and solves the gauge hierarchy problem. Two concrete string theory realizations of this model are discussed. First, the model can arise from the world-sheet CFT of a system of D3-branes at an orientifold singularity. Second, the model can arise from the low energy effective theory on M5-branes with a two form flux in a four dimensional fibrations over a base. There are numerous other realizations of this framework that arise in string theory, M-theory, and higher-dimensional supergravities.

The standard map is a well-known paradigm for investigating classical dynamical systems. In this work we use the island-identification algorithm to compute the largest Lyapunov exponent and the finite-time stability exponent for several regions of the parameter space. The former gives an estimate of the typical sensitivity to initial conditions of the system, while the latter describes the asymptotic long-time behavior of the distance between two close trajectories. This last exponent, which requires the calculation of the largest Floquet multiplier, can also signal the presence of islands of stability near some critical points of the map. We find that for certain regions of the parameter space these two stability exponents are correlated: the faster the system tends to random-walk around its initial conditions, the smaller the corresponding island is. Conversely, in other regions these exponents are decoupled, namely the fastest possible decay of the distance between two trajectories is not necessarily associated with the largest possible Lyapunov exponent. For some regions of the parameter space the separation of these two behaviors has been shown rigorously. We find this phenomenon to hold in general, in agreement with previous numerical results.

Nearest-neighbor spacing distributions of the beta-Hermite ensemble of random matrices were studied using the supersymmetry method. We showed that these distributions can be obtained from those of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) by an infinite ray limit involving the insertion of two relevant singularities in the $\rm Re(S)$ plane. Stellar core collapse is one of the most violent events in the universe, involving the death of massive stars. Due to the intense competition for heavy elements between the star and its compacted core, approximately 10% of the pre-supernova mass of the stars can be expelled in the form of supernova-driven wind. A considerable amount of this matter could be retained in a star cluster should the natal gas be photoionized and thermalized by the hot massive stars. The retention of the supernova ejecta in the form of a compact star cluster would be favorable from the perspective of collisional pressures that facilitate the revival of a gravity force on the free-falling ejecta and its further retention by the cluster potential well. In light of the recent detection of gravitational waves and electromagnetic signatures from the same source, which was observed to be a possible neutron star-black hole (NS-BH) system, we conduct a high resolution numerical study to explore the effects of both stellar wind mass-loss and subsequent fallback of bound material on the compact object retention efficiency. For model parameters typical of a star cluster in the size range of few tens of parsecs, we perform 15-120 ms of post-Newtonian merger simulations of a neutron star with a 3-30 solar mass black hole. We simulate a range of EOS with a stiff to soft equation of state, to cover a possible range of maximum gravitational masses. Our findings suggest that the inclusion of stellar core-collapse and fallback on black hole retention is unlikely for stiff EOS and more likely for more compliant equations of state. Finally, even for the stiff EOS, the range of retention efficiencies for the resulting black hole is 3-46% with a median value of 21%, indicating a wider range of scenarios that may be probed by future electromagnetic follow-up observations.

A direct-voting protocol for data fusion in wireless sensor networks (WSNs) is presented. In this protocol, each sensor node directly votes for its local decision, without communicating with other nodes. To reduce the communication and computational costs, the voting is conducted sequentially, while the aggregation rule is applied in each round. By using coded voting and exploiting the similarities between neighboring nodes, the communication and computation costs are largely reduced, compared to existing aggregation protocols. Performance analysis and simulation results show that the proposed protocol can achieve near-optimal performance with a relatively low communication overhead and computational load. Release date: 01 August 2023 Authors: Tao Li, Yuantao Gu, Kai Yao, Lin Zhang, Honggang Li Digital Object Identifier (DOI): 10.18744/CPRD-DOTSCCreated with MarkDownView. Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) have been widely used in a variety of applications, such as target tracking, sensor coverage, and habitat monitoring. To achieve the sensing task, a WSN can be established by randomly deploying a large number of homogeneous sensor nodes, which are usually powered by batteries. Since the sensors are independent and randomly deployed, the network structure is volatile and unstable. In this regard, a data fusion protocol for a wireless sensor network is required, which can ensure the correctness of the fusion result and suppress the energy consumption of the network. In this paper, we design a direct-voting protocol for data fusion in WSNs, which directly aggregates local decisions without any communications among nodes. To reduce communication and computational costs, the voting is conducted sequentially, while the aggregation rule is applied in each round. By using coded voting and exploiting the similarities between neighboring nodes, the communication and computation costs are largely reduced. We prove the correctness of the proposed protocol by analyzing the convergence of the decision variable. Moreover, we evaluate the performance of the protocol by both analysis and simulations. The simulation results show that the proposed protocol can achieve near-optimal performance with a relatively low communication overhead and computational load.

Wireless networks have recently attracted increasing attention due to the fast deployment of mobile devices and the growing demand for bandwidth-intensive services. In this paper, we consider a novel paradigm of communication named Ad Hoc D2D (direct-to-device) communications. In Ad Hoc D2D communications, information and resources are directly delivered from one transmitter (source) to another without involving any network or core infrastructure nodes. This paradigm, in contrast to conventional cellular networks, fundamentally changes the communication architectures, network architectures, and functionalities. By leveraging D2D communications, the coverage of traditional cellular networks can be expanded significantly, and consequently, the communication quality of existing networks can be significantly improved. To facilitate the design and analysis of such Ad Hoc D2D networks, we first propose a high-throughput cross-layer scheme that jointly optimizes the medium access control, physical layer, and network architecture for such networks. Through the solution of an upper-layer non-convex problem, our scheme guarantees both the throughput maximization and the frequency fairness at the cost of a low complexity. We then propose a D2D-aware clustering scheme, where D2D pairs are grouped into clusters and then jointly scheduled and clustered under the proposed cross-layer scheme. Through the proposed clustering scheme, the computation and signaling overheads among D2D transmitters can be substantially reduced, and the potential interference can be well controlled. Extensive numerical results reveal that the high Throughput and Frequency fairness achieved by our cross-layer scheme can significantly outperform the conventional cellular networks and rival Ad Hoc D2D networks.

We present long wavelength (mm/cm) observations of seven gravitationally lensed quasars discovered in large optical surveys, which are predicted to have strong positive Cosmic String Awards Gravitational Lensing by Dark Matter The Large Synoptic Survey Telescope will uncover many hundreds of strongly lensed z~6 quasars at wide separation from the original optical images. At these distances very long millimeter (mm) and centimeter (cm) wavelengths are accessible, and can be used to test for the predicted strong positive Cosmic String Awards gravitational lensing effects. We present mm/cm observations of seven of these z~6 quasars with the Submillimeter Array (SMA), the Plateau de Bure Interferometer (PdBI), and the Combined Array for Research in Millimeter Astronomy (CARMA). We describe the mm/cm data reduction and present the resulting maps and results. We also present new observations of these quasars with the Very Large Array (VLA) in cm wavelength. We describe data reduction and present the resulting maps and results. We detect extended radio emission from four of these quasars, with observed 1.4 GHz fluxes ranging from 0.7 to 14 mJy beam−1. The core radio emission in these quasars is either non-detected or only marginally detected, with observed 1.4 GHz fluxes ranging from 7 × 10−5 to 1.3 mJy beam−1. We model the mm/cm radio emission as arising from a blend of discrete components, and discuss the implications of the detected emission from these components. We combine our mm/cm results with previous Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) cm results of these seven quasars to determine imaging parameters, including measurement of the radio core position, separation between radio lobes, and the orientation of the radio jet. The radio jet orientations are either exactly orthogonal to, or at a small angle to the mm/cm emitting regions. We discuss the consistency of this orthogonal/small angle alignment between mm/cm and cm wavelengths, and its implications for gravitational lensing models, in which the mm/cm emitting regions are predicted to be strongly lensed versions of the distant cm emitting regions.

Tidal dwarf galaxies (TDGs) are often formed from material torn from other galaxies in high-velocity interactions. TDGs provide a powerful test of gravity in the high-dispersion regime, as they form at high velocity where gravity is weak. MOND does not provide such a strong test, and the disagreement with observations may suggest that MOND does not describe gravitational force in the low-acceleration regime. Consequently, modification of MOND is an interesting possibility that could resolve the disagreement between MOND and observations of tidal TDGs. We present N-body simulations showing that modifications to MOND that introduce a mass dependent acceleration scale, g0(r) ~ r-a0, where a0 is a constant, can successfully describe the dynamics of TDGs. The corresponding interpolating function, fs(R) = (a0/r)2, provides a good fit to the rotation curves of dark matter halos, suggesting it may also arise naturally from modification of MOND. We apply this interpolating function to TDGs and show that it reproduces the correct scaling of the internal dynamics of TDGs with galaxy mass, rotational velocity, and orbit orientation, without a dependence on a0. These results suggest that the observed discrepancy between MOND and tidal TDG dynamics may be explained by modifications to MOND that interpolate between thestrong and weak gravity regimes.

Hybrid n-body algorithms solve the gravitational n-body problem by combining a tree method, which captures the local gravitational forces, with a direct method, which captures the long-range, non-local interactions. Hybrid schemes generally require more computational resources than n-body algorithms that use only one method. In theBRIDGE (Bridge) scheme, we combine a direct-tree method with a hierarchical tree method to achieve even higher accuracy at lower cost. The direct-tree combination captures close interactions among particles using a direct method, while the hierarchical tree method helps with distant interactions, reducing overhead. We demonstrate that BRIDGE achieves full self-consistency, i.e., fully includes internal evolution of both star clusters and their parent galaxies. We apply BRIDGE to a series of test cases with both static and dynamic backgrounds and demonstrate its accuracy. We also apply BRIDGE to galaxy mergers and combine it with a variety of cosmological and violent scenarios to demonstrate its ability to capture the full evolution of galaxies from large-scale environments to localized stellar systems. We make BRIDGE publicly available to the community for further testing and development.

Charge-ordering phenomena, which were originally discovered in inorganic crystals with one-dimensional structural motif such as cuprates and nickelates, have been also observed in a number of organic charge-transfer solids such as tetramethyltetraselenafulvalene (TTF-TCNQ) andtetracyanoquinodimethane (TCNQ). In one-dimensional (1D) systems with multiorbital interactions, spin, charge, and spin-charge susceptibilities are enhanced at low energies due to the nesting of the 1D Fermi surface (FS). These enhanced susceptibilities lead to generic charge-ordering instabilities at small Coulomb repulsions. In TTF-TCNQ, for example, spin and charge orders have been observed at low temperatures, and the theoretical consensus is that this is due to the proximity to a spin-charge density wave (SDW) instability. Here, we report a study of charge ordering in TTF-TCNQ using resonant X-ray scattering, both in the normal phase and near charge-density wave (CDW) and SDW transitions. We find that near the charge ordering wavevector Q ≈ (π,2π), long-range, incommensurate, charge correlations persist to high temperatures, and that the low-energy spin, charge, and spin-charge susceptibilities are enhanced. However, unlike 1D systems with nesting, the correlation length and the charge ordering temperature are both extremely small, indicating that the dominant instability is non-charge-density-wave in nature. We discuss this observation in light of possible instabilities of 1D charge-transfer solids near boundaries and mid-gap states.

In our previous papers (Gurzadyan & Kocharyan 2002; GBSHTF 2004) we have presented the luminosity function (LF) of white dwarfs (WDs) using the data collected by Zacs project. The LFs were derived for various samples of WDs and for the complete sample. However, in the present paper we discuss the results of the completeness correction for the LF of WDs. We show that the use of the completeness correction results in the systematic shift of the LF low-luminosity end. We discuss the possible causes of this effect and show that it is not connected to the incompleteness of the Zacs data. The only source of incompleteness, which may lead to the LF low-luminosity end shift, is the contamination of the sample of WDs with non-WD objects. This may be WDs with nearby companion, which were missed by proper motion measurements and contaminants in the WD sample. We argue that the use of low-level negative segregation, employed by the SDSS spectroscopic team in the selection of quasars, may be a source of such a contamination. We also discuss some other potential sources of WD contamination and present new analysis of the WD/non-WD separation in the Zacs sample. We show that all these factors do not lead to the LF low-luminosity end shift. We argue that the shift is real and we present two evidences in its support. First, the observed LF low-luminosity end shift is in a good agreement with that predicted from a recent model of WD cooling. Second, we show that the Zacs WD LF is in a good agreement with the combined LFs of WDs, obtained by different teams before the completion correction for incompleteness was applied.

Using data from the Sloan Digest of Objects imaged by the Subaru Telescope and the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, we investigate the mass distribution in the galaxy cluster MS 2053.7-0449, which contains a dynamically young massive subcluster (RX J2248.7-4431). We present the first strong gravitational lensing mass reconstruction of the whole cluster combining the Subaru data with Hubble Space Telescope imaging, and of the galaxy subcluster with Keck II imaging, and Chandra X-ray observations. The critical curve structure and the mass distributions are consistent with each other and suggest the presence of two mass peaks corresponding to the galaxy subcluster and the cluster halo. The total cluster mass within a radius of 1.5 Mpc is estimated to be (2.3 ± 0.3) × 109 h−1 M⊙, and the concentration parameter is found to be ρ0 = 5.5 ± 0.5 kpc M−1.5, where the uncertainties represent the 1σ range. The subcluster is found to be elongated along the northeast-southwest axis, with a mass-weighted projected distance of 1.2 Mpc from the main cluster center. We detect possible signatures of recent merging between the subcluster and the main cluster, which may have triggered the strong and recent radio activity in the core of the subcluster and the recent star formation in the infalling galaxies.

A pair of gamma-ray bursts, GRB 050410 and GRB 050412, were recently reported to be “dark” gamma-ray bursts (DGRBs), lacking discernible gamma-ray emission from these sources. These claims, however, have been questioned by subsequent works, which argue that the gamma-ray emissions of these bursts may have been simply undetectable. In this work, we reanalyze the early observations of these bursts with the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor, and report the detection of weak gamma-ray emission from GRB 050410 and a possible weak gamma-ray burst from GRB 050412. We thus argue that these bursts are in fact dark. These two bursts, 050410 and 050412, have similar early-time gamma-ray properties, but significantly different radio afterglows. The bursts indeed have similar energy scales but different jet-related parameters, and the same correlation does not hold for all bursts. Further observations at late phases are needed to confirm the non-detections at later times. We conclude that the gamma-ray emission of both these bursts are simply below the detection threshold of Fermi/GBM, and the associated gamma-ray emission may be intrinsically weak. A precise knowledge of the age, metallicity and alpha-element abundance of galactic globular clusters (GGCs) is crucial for our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution. The availability of high signal-to-noise, high resolution spectra has made it possible to determine these basic properties for large samples of GGCs for the first time. Using medium-resolution spectra for a sample of 49 GGCs, we have been able to provide the first direct determination of the cluster ages using the anti-correlation between the abundance of alpha elements (i.e. O, Mg, Si, Ca and Ti) and the total metallicity. By comparing the expected value of this anti-correlation for GGC realizations of simple stellar populations (SSP) based on different initial mass functions (IMF) and different stellar evolution models, we were able to determine that the GGC ages are in the range 12.6 - 13.9 Gyr with a median of 13.2 Gyr. We have also been able to provide the first direct measurements of the GGC metallicities, which we find range from [Fe/H] = -1.74 to -0.54 with a median value of [Fe/H] = -1.39. We estimate the uncertainties on our determinations of the ages and metallicities of the clusters to be less than 4.2 and 0.21 dex, respectively. By using the relative abundance of alpha elements, we are also able to provide the first accurate metallicity determinations for clusters as distant as 40 kpc from the Milky Way center. We find that the metallicity profiles of the clusters are relatively flat in the innermost 5-7 half-mass radii. Using our new knowledge of the age, metallicity and alpha-element abundance of GGCs, we have been able to determine the evolution of the alpha-element to metal-rich cluster fraction with time. We find that, at any given metallicity, the fraction of clusters with alpha-element abundance [alpha/Fe] > 0 is approximately constant from 12.6 Gyr ago to the present day, consistent with the fraction of stars in elliptical galaxies with the same metallicity having approximately the same alpha-element abundance. Using dynamical estimates of the masses of the GGCs, we are also able to show that there has been no significant increase in the mass function of GGCs over the past 13.9 Gyr. This indicates that the masses of the clusters, and their disruption rates, must have remained largely unchanged over this time. However, we do find that the orbital properties of the clusters do appear to have changed in such a way as to lead to a net increase in the half-light radii of the clusters. We suggest that this is caused by an overall increase in the specific frequency of binary stars over time, which can have the effect of increasing the cross section of the clusters for tidal disruption. Finally, we also provide the first measurement of the relative alpha-element abundance of the remote globular cluster Pal

Researchers discovered long-range order in electron density, spin, and charge in two distinct stripes in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$NiO$_{4}$ (x=1/3,1/2). Long-range charge order (or stripes) arose from a combined effect of the double exchange and Jahn-Teller lattice distortion which lead to an energy stabilization by forming diagonal charge stripes. Spin order was induced by the charge stripes and was found to be in the form of staggered stripes, which is consistent with inelastic neutron scattering data. The paper reports the discovery of charge, spin, and combined charge-spin stripes in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$NiO$_{4}$ (x=1/3,1/2). Long-range charge order (or stripes) arose from a combined effect of the double exchange and Jahn-Teller lattice distortion. Spin order was induced by the charge stripes and was found to be in the form of staggered stripes. The paper reports the discovery of charge, spin, and combined charge-spin stripes in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$NiO$_{4}$ (x=1/3,1/2).

Tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing, proposed in 1998 by H. Liu and X. Zhang, has been regarded as one of the best models for the mixing of neutrinos, and has gained increasing attention recently [1,2]. The tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing angle θ_{23} can be expressed as 2/9π - 1/9, and the deviation from the maximal mixing angle can be viewed as a perturbation parameter α. The latest neutrino experimental results show that the neutrino mixing angles are running away from tri-bimaximal neutrino mixing. In this paper, we consider a type-II seesaw mechanism with an additional singlet lepton and generate the baryon asymmetry of the universe through leptogenesis. We will show that the perturbation parameter α can be derived from the baryon asymmetry of the universe. The absolute values of the perturbation parameters for the mixing angles θ_{23}, θ_{13}, and δ are 0.09, 0.047, and 0.014, respectively. We find that these absolute values are all compatible with the current experimental results.

We present a successive sub-grouping method (SSM) for multiple sequence alignments analysis. Given an initial alignment, the method constructs a series of increasingly refined groupings by merging neighbouring sub-groups in a predetermined manner. At each step, a sequence is merged with its nearest neighbours in the initial alignment that are compatible with the desired groupings. The Refinement Index (RI) of the resulting alignment relative to the initial one is calculated and used as a stopping criterion. We applied the SSM to study the evolutionary relationship of 11 protein families with known three-dimensional structure. The results were consistent with those from a conventional approach based on maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis. However, by using significantly fewer distances, the SSM is much more computationally efficient. This property allows the application of the method to large data sets. As an example, we used it to study the evolutionary relationship of the entire PDB90 protein sequence set. The results demonstrated that the method is suitable for analysing large data sets.

In this work we study the effects of including a domain wall in twoflavor dynamical QCD simulations. We use two types of domain wall algorithms and compare their performance. We find that with both domain wall types the equation of state and some other dynamical quantities show no sign of damage. However the chiral condensate is substantially reduced with domain wall types X and V. To understand this we apply the one-plaquette QCD chiral perturbation theory to analyze the valence quark masses. We find that, with domain wall type X, the light quarks have a much lighter valence mass than the strange quark, while with domain wall type V the strange quark has a much lighter valence mass than the other quarks. These valence quark masses, combined with the much heavier strange quark mass in the domain wall proposal, lead to the surprising result that the strange quark contributes substantially more to the chiral condensate than in the conventional case. The result for the strange quark condensate is 2.9(5) MeV<OPE>/3 = 0.9(1) MeV, where the error includes both the fitting error and the systematic error from ignoring the effects of the domain wall on the heavier strange quark mass. We also consider the implications for the physical kaon and eta masses, and discuss the possibility that the strange quark condensate could be determined from the physical pion mass and the kaon and eta masses. * Keywords: Domain walls, QCD, dynamical simulation, staggered fermions Including a domain wall in two-flavor dynamical lattice QCD simulations has no adverse effect on the equation of state or the dynamical quantities studied, but substantially reduces the magnitude of the chiral condensate. The result for the strange quark condensate is 2.9(5) MeV<OPE>/3 = 0.9(1) MeV, where the error includes both the fitting error and the systematic error from ignoring the effects of the domain wall on the heavier strange quark mass. A quantum information processor (QIP) consists of various physical qubits, which can be entangled and measured in order to perform a computation. While these operations are intended to be coherent, experimental errors will inevitably lead to a mixture of entangled states. We experimentally characterize this coherence loss via ultrafast interferometry and find that it is well-approximated by a Gaussian process. We explore these fluctuations as a function of parameters of the computation and device performance, and find that universal gates introduce more noise than coherence. Finally, we investigate the sensitivity of our results to choices in experimental protocol, and find that significant differences can arise due to random switching events during the time of our experiment. We present an experimentally testable framework for optimizing QIP coherence as a function of computation parameters, and showcase its use by optimizing the quantum Fourier transform. This coherence optimization can be turned into an automated procedure for QIP optimization, and we illustrate this application to a near-optimal input state for the QFT. As the complexity of QIPs grows with experimental progress, these techniques for coherence assessment and optimization will play an increasingly important role in the scaling of these devices.

Pappus's theorem in plane geometry states that three lines in the plane intersecting in a triad of points, there exists a fourth line not in the plane, containing one of the triad of points. There have been many proofs of this theorem since it was first stated in the 2nd century AD. In this short note we present a simple and beautiful proof of Pappus's theorem that has some interesting geometric and algorithmic applications. Our approach is to discretize Pappus's configuration of lines in the plane and solve an arrangement problem on a gridded plane. The theorem follows as a special case of the theorem for this problem. We also present an alternate, but more complex and less direct, proof of Pappus's theorem, which may be of independent interest. esk A simple and beautiful proof of Pappus's theorem We present a simple and beautiful proof of Pappus's theorem that has some interesting geometric and algorithmic applications. Using data from the shall-VAST initiative, I study the relation between X-ray-derived and weak-lensing-derived masses for a cluster sample selected using the lensing strength. I use a Bayesian framework to fit for the mass-observable relations, allowing for intrinsic scatter as well as projected alignment with the line of sight. The sample is split into subsamples defined by richness, redshift, and X-ray temperature, and the resulting relations are reported and compared with previous studies. I also investigate the impact of triaxiality, finding that such clusters are expected to scatter significantly on both the normal and the bias axes. I further explore the redshift evolution of the relation, finding that for this sample, the intrinsic scatter does not increase with increasing redshift, in contrast to previous results from less-comprehensive samples. Overall, this analysis demonstrates that weak lensing masses are largely biased toward the true mass, with an intrinsic scatter of ~30%. In addition, I show that even for strong lensing events, the weak lensing mass estimation is biased toward the true mass. The implications for cosmology using the Shear Hyper Suprime-Cam (SHSC) survey are also discussed.

Transition region features observed with Hinode/EIS. The presented data were obtained on 2007 November 8 from solar active region 12429, which was observed in the 171 [angstrom] line of Fe [i]. The analyzed region includes loop system comprising two relatively short threads and a longer segment. In the loop system, we see loop halos on both sides of the filament, which could be a result of magnetic flux emergence. In addition, one can see oscillating behavior in the threads. These features may indicate that magnetic flux is being emerged from the deep photosphere to the upper atmosphere. Future Work: This is a preliminary result and more data analysis is required to confirm the presence of emerging magnetic flux.

Inflection point as a manifestation of tricritical point on the dynamic phase boundary in Ising meanfield dynamics. The phase boundary in the model is conventionally understood in the context of its upper critical dimension, which here is six. However, quantum fluctuations in three dimensions induce a tricritical point (TCP), beyond which the phase boundary has the form of a double critical point, consisting of a critical point and a bicritical point. The TCP is characterised by a limit-point (algebraic) singularity in the vicinity of which the dependence of the location of the inflection point on the magnetic field presents a square root behaviour. The location of the TCP and the limit-point singularity are estimated by an expansion in the spatial dimension, where this is small compared to the underlying spatial dimension of the model. The upper critical dimensionality here is three, and the expansion parameter is the spatial dimension over which the limit-point singularity is approached (similar to the way in which the upper critical dimension is formally two above three spatial dimensions). The numerical value of the TCP location is close to the estimate obtained by the leading-order approximation. The bicritical point along the phase boundary is also approached with a square root singularity in the limit-point description of the inflection point.

This is a description of a scientific paper posted on arXiv.org, a pre-publication history of the paper, and its forthcoming publication. The presented abstract was written by the authors of the paper. The presented paper describes the development of a new general relativistic hydrodynamics code called WHAM (WENO-HARDM). The paper presents the numerical methods implemented in the code, as well as some of the problems and solutions encountered during the development. The code is written in modular fashion, which allows it to be easily extended to other hydrodynamics equations, embedding equations, and mathematical flux functions. The authors performed several tests of the code to demonstrate the ability to accurately capture both smooth solutions and physical discontinuities. The results are in good agreement with the exact solutions and published literature for various hydrodynamics equations. WHAM is available at https://bitbucket.org/carrerr/wham. The master repository contains all development code, while the https://github.com/carrerr/wham/tree/master/doc directory contains all documentation. A method is described for synthesizing a new class of single-domain magnetic particles, hollow Co spheres (HCSS). HCSS are nanosized coaxial cylinders of cobalt, with a thin protective shell, that have high remanence and saturation magnetization. The synthesis involves aqueous decomposition of cobalt salts in the presence of a highly stable cobalt-thiolate shell. Particles can be prepared with different shell thicknesses, from 5 to 30 nm, which allows control of their magnetic anisotropy. We find that for shells less than 10 nm in thickness, the HCSS particles have high magnetic anisotropy with an easy axis along their longitudinal axis, which corresponds to the axis of the Co core. We characterize these HCSS using a variety of physical techniques, including SQUID magnetometry, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and spherical harmonic decomposition of the HCSS magnetization. In particular, we show that the HCSS with the thinnest cobalt shells (< 5 nm) have a high perpendicular anisotropy compared to the perpendicular anisotropy of similarly sized, commercial magnetic nanoparticles. These HCSS with high perpendicular anisotropy could prove useful for applications such as magnetic recording or data storage, where a high stability of the magnetic moment in the direction perpendicular to the plane of the recording medium is required. We also describe a method for controlling the anisotropy direction of HCSS by assembling HCSS into chains, using small numbers of highly magnetic spheres as building blocks. These chains have a high anisotropy of their orientation with respect to the chain direction. Using spherical harmonic analysis, we determine that the high anisotropy is likely caused by interaction between the HCSS cores, with the easy axis parallel to the short axis of the HCSS. This may also make HCSS chains suitable for applications such as magnetic separations or biomolecule separation, where the ability to control the chain orientation could improve the separation performance of HCSS over commercially available materials with random anisotropy.

Planets in close-in orbit around stars are of great interest for several reasons. First of all, they are likely to be tidally locked with one hemisphere always facing their star. This leads to night-time on these planets without dayside or dayside sunlight. Although an tidally locked planet is potentially a frigid world, an atmosphere could dampen the amplitude of the day-night temperature difference. Secondly, gas giants in these orbits are able to capture hydrogen and helium from the stellar atmosphere. Subsequent evolution of these worlds may lead to phases of extremely high surface temperatures, even reaching runaway greenhouse conditions. Finally, their proximity to their star offers the opportunity to observe these planets using transmission and Raman spectroscopy, with the potential to gain insight into their atmospheric composition and temperature structure. In this paper, we investigate how the night-side temperature of short-period extra solar gas giant planets depends on several parameters, including the atmospheric composition, atmospheric opacity, and stellar flux. We find that for planets with mainly hydrogen and helium atmospheres and no runaway greenhouse conditions, the night-side temperature is primarily dependent on the atmospheric opacity. For a solar spectrum flux (1 bar O2 / Sun spectrum at 1 au), the night-side temperature is approximately 300 K at the base of the hydrogen profile, increasing to approximately 400 K at the base of the helium profile. If the flux from the star is increased to 5 bar O2 / star spectrum at 1 au, the night-side temperature increases only to approximately 400 K at the base of the hydrogen profile and to approximately 450 K at the base of the helium profile. We show that this behaviour is largely independent of atmospheric composition, with only a shallow dependence on the temperature profile. These atmospheres are likely to contain clouds of ammonia, silicate, and water, with molecular weights between 17 and 35. At such low temperatures, ammonia clouds are likely to be present at the base of the hydrogen atmosphere, with increasing abundances of water and silicate clouds deeper into the profile. This result has significant implications for future transmission and Raman spectroscopy of these worlds, particularly for targets with a strong stellar flux, such as TRAPPIST-1. Current instruments may not be able to resolve atmospheric features on the coldest night-side worlds. However, with the launch of next-generation telescopes, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and Ariel at el. future, it will be possible to study these worlds using atmospheric windows such as N2 absorption (4.7 microns) and H2O Raman scattering (2.7 microns). Comptonization is often invoked to explain the complex spectra of accreting compact objects, such as X-ray binaries and black hole binaries. The scenario requires that seed photons from a cold disk are upscattered by electrons in a hot plasma, producing a power-law component that may contribute up to 100% of the spectrum in some systems. Here, we present broadband X-ray observations of the island state in the transient binary system IGR J1748-288, carried out with the orbiting X-ray observatory XMM-Newton. The data reveal that the source's emission extends to hard X-rays, with a power-law photon index of −2.3 ± 0.2. This result is in stark contrast to the Wien tail of the blackbody spectrum that is usually observed in this state. We explore the Comptonization model in detail and show that it provides a better description of the broadband X-ray spectrum than does a simple thermal accretion shock model. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we explore the parameter space and demonstrate that the inclusion of relativistic Doppler shift and broadening is critical to the successful application of this model to the broadband spectra of IGR J1748-288. Finally, we show that the Comptonizing plasma temperature is positively correlated with the amplitude of the kHz QPOs, supporting the idea that these QPOs are a Doppler-scaled version of the inner accretion flow.

A periodic stack of anisotropic layers with periodically varying dielectric constant and magnetic susceptibility contains magneto-static waves, which propagate with the speed of light in the direction of periodicity. In such a stack, slow waves can be trapped, and they may propagate with a lower phase velocity, thus effectively slowing down in the medium. We consider a general two-dimensional stack and show that the characteristic length of the resonance is the skin depth, which defines the propagation length of the slow waves. We find that for a specific structure and wavelength of the slow wave, its propagation can be effectively stopped in a certain range of layer thicknesses. This phenomenon can be used in devices for slow light or buffering. The article is originally in Russian.
