Cosmic rays, or highly energetic particles originating outside the solar system, have been studied for decades. They can tell us about the evolution of our galaxy and beyond. These studies are made using cosmic rays withparticle detectors which can detect the secondary particles produced by the interactions of these high energy particles with the atmosphere. These interaction products are called cosmic rays and are divided into several groups, each with different energies. One of these groups called gamma rays are especially interesting because they can provide information about their origin. Gamma rays are a form of electromagnetic radiation and can provide useful information about the objects where they were originated. For this reason, the detection of gamma rays originating from different parts of the universe is of great interest to astronomers and astro- physicists. Gamma rays are commonly detected using experiments with smaller facilities across the globe. Because of the great expense and difficulty of constructing these small experimental facilities, few have studied gamma rays originating from the same region of the universe. To study gamma rays originating from the same region of the universe, an international group of researchers, known as FERMI, built a satellite with a large experimental facility to detect gamma rays in the energy range of 0.5 GeV to 30 GeV. The data from this experiment has been analyzed and presented in this paper. The results of this analysis show an increase in the number of gamma rays originating from a particular region of the universe when compared to previous results. The implications of this increase are also discussed. This paper presents an analysis of data from a satellite experiment known as FERMI that studied gamma rays in the energy range of 0.5 GeV to 30 GeV. The data from this experiment has been analyzed and presented in this paper. The results of this analysis show an increase in the number of gamma rays originating from a particular region of the universe when compared to previous results. The implications of this increase are also discussed.

A massive protocluster, potentially one of the most massive structures formable in the universe given its short dynamical time, has been discovered in the S255N region. Analysis of optical and near-infrared data from multiple telescopes have revealed an overdensity of Yellow-Green (YG) stars with respect to the diffuse background population, a distribution consistent with that of a spherical Gaussian, and a projected size of 1.6 x 1.3 kpc (2.2 x 1.7 Mpc), corresponding to 0.14% of the diameter of the Orion Arm. This overdensity is at least partially corroborated by weak optical emission from dust, as measured by the *Spitzer Space Telescope, and is consistent with infrared spectroscopic surveys showing a high number density of young, hot, and massive stars. The most massive stars, with a likely initial mass of several hundred solar masses, have an implied present formation mass of several thousand solar masses if they have starved-looking disks and are considered to be in the main sequence phase. The derived mass and size are also consistent with stellar-mass-threshold predictions for formation of intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs), an expected signature of active supermassive black hole growth at the center of the cluster. The age and masses of the stellar populations are also consistent with IMBH formation via seeds from the remnants of very massive stars, although higher chance of coalescence for lower mass seeds cannot be ruled out. A peculiar velocity of the cluster with respect to the local standard of rest, measured from the motion of bright member stars, and the mass projected along the line-of-sight, both suggest the cluster may not be virialized. If a supermassive black hole is present, as suggested by its likely formation via intermediate-mass black hole seeds or very massive star remnants, the observed properties of the cluster systematically depart from those expected for a classical star cluster. This intriguing object suggests that either massive seeds for IMBHs could have formed outside of clusters, and grown via accretion, or there is more than one mode of IMBH formation. Future optical spectroscopy of cluster members, in combination with infrared studies of the dust emission and a search for an IMBH, will help determine the most likely formation channel for this enigmatic object.

Recent near-infrared surveys have identified a population of galaxies with mean redshift z~2–3 that were likely in the process of assembly many ($>$10) billion years after the Big Bang. These galaxies are prominent mechanics contributors and may reside in the critical early stages of galaxy evolution, providing vital information about the cosmic environment during the epoch of reionization (EoR). However, their identification in large volumes of the distant universe has thus far been limited by the availability of suitable optical filters, requiring these galaxies to be studied using instruments capable of near-infrared (NIR) surveys. Here, we present data from the quadruple image commissioning run of the Cosmic Assembly Near-Infrared Deep Survey (CANDELS), primarily using the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) in the near-infrared, that allows the identification of many of the most promising z~2–3 galaxies. Utilizing WFC3/IR observations of the UDS, COSMOS, and GOODS-S fields, we construct a sample of 112 candidate z~2–3 galaxies, nearly doubling the known population of such high-redshift galaxies and providing the first statistically robust sampling of this critical population during the EoR. At low redshift, we measure spectroscopic redshifts for 91 of these 112 candidates, demonstrating the high success rate of the color selection method. We measure 1.4<z<2.5 physical sizes for these candidate z~2–3 galaxies, corresponding to a median angular scale of ~0.5kpc. We compare the size distribution of the z~2–3 galaxies to the low-redshift Coma Cluster and find no significant overlap in their size distributions, suggesting the majority of z~2–3 galaxies are likely in the process of undergoing local evolution, distinct from the population of giant z~2–3 cluster galaxies. Finally, we find that these high-redshift galaxies are likely hosted by galaxies with median stellar mass of ~3.2×10$^{10}$ M⊙, with 38.0±7.3% of these galaxies located inmassive hosting halos with M~5×10^11M⊙. This Letter presents the first statistically robust assessment of a critical population of high-redshift galaxies during the epoch of reionization and highlights the power of NIR observations for such studies. We present a fully Bayesian method for determining the mass function (MF) of active black holes (BHs), the distribution of their masses at any given time. Using N = 725,543 active black holes (BHs) from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we model the mass function as a sum of two power laws and allow the normalizations and breaks of the power laws to be functions of host galaxy properties. We use a Markov Chain Monte Carlo technique to sample from the posterior distribution and determine the posterior distribution of the mass function. We find that the normalization of the heavy end of the MF is proportional to the stellar mass of the host galaxy and that the slope of the light end is approximately independent of the properties of the host galaxy. We also study how the MF varies with time and find that, once metallicity is accounted for, the total mass in young, intermediate-mass BHs decreases with time, consistent with recent estimates of the growth rate of these systems.

A recent study has provided the first predictions for the locations of triple star systems, which include a pulsar, in star clusters. These predictions will be useful for selecting target systems for refined pulsar radial velocity monitoring. We present new, comprehensive calculations for the locations of pulsars in triple systems, with and without stellar companions. These predictions have significantly more covered parameter space than those of previous studies, enabling more accurate assessments of the properties of triple systems and providing guidance for selecting systems for pulsar radial velocity monitoring. We find that the majority of pulsars in binary star systems are members of hierarchical triple systems, with typically one or both other stars being significant stellar companions. For triple star systems, the pulsar is more likely to be in a hierarchical triple system if its companion is a main-sequence star, while brown dwarfs are much more likely to be components of quadruple (four star) systems. The likelihood of a pulsar residing in a hierarchical triple or quadruple system increases with increasing companion mass. We calculate that at least 75% of binary pulsars reside in hierarchical triple systems. Approximately 25% of these pulsars are in triple star systems, while the remaining 50% are in quadruple systems. Based on our results, a pulsar is more likely to reside in a hierarchical triple or quadruple system if its companion is a main-sequence star (in terms of mass) or has a higher mass. We provide improved calculations for the locations of all three components (pulsar, companion star, and distant companion) in hierarchical triple systems. For pulsars with low companion-star mass fractions (less than ~20%), which include systems in which the companion is a white dwarf, our predictions for the locations of the three components are essentially identical to previous ones, and our calculations for these systems provide a useful update. For binary pulsars with more massive companions (greater than ~20% of the companion mass), in which the companion has a stellar core or is a neutron star or black hole, our predictions provide significantly more covered parameter space and therefore enable more accurate assessments of the properties of these systems. For triple star systems in which the pulsar does not reside in a hierarchical triple system, we also present updated predictions for the locations of the pulsar and its companion star. The pulsar is more likely to reside in such a system if its companion has a low mass (less than ~20% of the companion mass) and is a main-sequence star. Finally, we compare the new predictions for the locations of pulsars in triple star systems with the locations of observed systems and note that a fraction of the observed pulsar systems could not exist according to our new calculations. We speculate that these "discrepant systems" may represent close encounters within star clusters that have perturbed systems with initially small separation and increased the likelihood that the systems are resolvable via dynamical interactions. *[The abstract is a copy of the published paper, A Comprehensive

In quantum mechanics, the act of observing the outcome of a measurement of a physical system has been found to retroactively change the wavefunction of the system, leading to what is called the "which-way" (WW) interference effect. This phenomenon has been used to explain numerous counterintuitive quantum mechanical phenomena, such as the "Schrödinger's cat" problem and the "many worlds" interpretation of quantum mechanics, which considers the act of observation to be a branching quantum event. We herein introduce a generalization of the Born rule, which we call the "weakly generalized Born rule" (WGBR), according to which the WW effect is not considered to change the probability of potential outcomes, but instead provides a new causal explanation for the observation of those potential outcomes. Unlike previous interpretations of quantum mechanics, this new explanation does not require setting aside the many-worlds interpretation, and it also does not conflict with existing interpretations such as the Copenhagen interpretation. We test our theory on a single photon in a one-dimensional wave packet, and we observe the expected WW interference pattern in accordance with the WGBR. We also discuss potential applications of our theory to understanding quantum thermodynamics, predicting when a quantum system will respond differently to positive and negative measurement results, and formulating quantum algorithms without using explicit wavefunction evolution.

Bok Globule CB190, located in the constellation Boötes at a distance of about 21.5 light-years from the Sun, is the closest known globular cluster flyby that is not an open cluster. Spitzer observations at 24 microns cover the first half of 2013 and include two cold dust shell sources: Bok Globule CB190 and Lynga 7. Unlike Lynga 7, which is a confirmed member of the Boötes globular cluster, Bok Globule CB190 has been a controversial member of Boötes until recently, when its radial velocity was determined to be -38.2 km/s, consistent with the known Galactic standard of rest (GSR) velocity of Boötes. This reaffirmed Bok Globule CB190 as a true member of Boötes and resolved the long-standing debate about its status as a cluster or association, thereby establishing a connection between this previously unassociated stellar system and the well-known Boötes globular cluster.

The phenomenon of stochastic resonance (SR) has been observed in a great variety of nonlinear systems. The nonequilibrium-potential approach has been proposed to investigate SR in the context of the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation. In this approach, an effective potential is introduced to describe the probability distribution of the system and thus the dynamics of the system is reduced to an effective classical dynamics in the potential well. This potential is determined by the noise and the signal. When the system evolves from a low-density region to a high-density region, a resonance phenomenon occurs due to the competition between the noise-induced transitions and the signal-induced changes of the potential. In this work, we apply the nonequilibrium-potential approach to investigate SR in a few selected reaction-diffusion systems. These systems include the FitzHugh-Nagumo system, the Brusselator system, and the complexes of chemical reactions. Comparisons with existing theoretical results and numerical simulations are also presented. It is found that the nonequilibrium-potential approach is effective and efficient to describe the SR phenomenon in the considered systems.

Using a modified Nishimori transform, we study two-sublattice Spontaneous Magnetization (SPM) model with temperature-dependent shape anisotropy, that describes many soft ferromagnetic materials with in-plane magnetization. We show that the coercivity of such system exhibits a minimum near the Stoner-Wohlfarth condition, even when the anisotropy is strong enough to realize a single-domain state at zero temperature. By considering an applied magnetic field aligned with the easy axis, we derive a closed-form expression for the coercivity and show that it exhibits a maximum as a function of the applied field. The position of the maximum and the value of the coercivity at the minimum depend on the field and temperature as observed in experiments. We conclude that the microscopic mechanism behind the observation is the temperature-dependence of the anisotropy strength that creates a soft mode in the system. In the past, several studies have been conducted to understand the coercivity of soft ferromagnetic materials. However, most of them focused on the temperature dependence of the anisotropy field, while anisotropy that changes with temperature has not been considered. In this work, we study a two-sublattice Spontaneous Magnetization (SPM) model with temperature-dependent anisotropy and derive the general expression for the coercivity. The model considers many soft ferromagnetic materials such as Terbium Dysprosium Iron (TbDyFe) that are known to have temperature-dependent anisotropy. The expression for coercivity is analyzed in detail and compared to the results of micromagnetic simulations. It is shown that the temperature-dependence of anisotropy leads to two significant effects. First, the temperature dependence creates a soft mode that contributes to the minimum of coercivity. Second, it changes the position of the maximum of coercivity with respect to an applied magnetic field.

Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) are a unique feature of the universe predicted by theories of cosmological inflation. They are an absorption line in the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation left over from the earliest moments of the universe, and have a characteristic scale and dispersion. The locations and sizes of these features can be used to determine cosmological parameters with high precision. In this work, we present the first high-resolution N-body simulations of nonlinear evolution of BAO, which cover 100 $h^{-1}$Mpc (comoving) on a side. These simulations implement a high-order accurate free streaming module that includes contributions from baryonic feedback, and fully resolve the nonlinear evolution of modes with wavenumber 10$h$Mpc$^{-1}$ and smaller. We find that nonlinear evolution of BAO increases the scatter in the relation between predicted and observed distance measurements, and decreases the significance of cosmological constraints that use the BAO feature. We show that a subset of our simulation volumes can be used to accurately model the galaxy distribution in weak lensing surveys, providing a means to accurately determine cosmological parameters using the BAO feature in this way.

A muon, electron, andtau particle neutrino interaction with a nuclear target can lead to various channels. Of particular interest in neutrino oscillations experiments are the channels in which a charged current interaction produces a charged current signature lepton plus a missing transverse momentum. In this paper, we demonstrate that these channels can be reduced to a complex symplectic invariant, which we call s. The structure of this invariant allows us to predict the structure of the corresponding charged current neutrino interaction matrix in the Standard Model, namely the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix. We use experimental data for the leading order structure of the CKM matrix and demonstrate that it reduces to a good approximation to the structure predicted by the invariant. We apply our analysis to precisionglobal fits to the neutrino mixing matrix and show that the corresponding structure predicted by s is in agreement with data at the 1.7 sigma level. We also discuss the connection of this result to higher-dimensional physics and flavor symmetry.

I present a complete solution to the quantum dynamics of the Volume operator in Loop Quantum Gravity. This operator, which provides a natural'size' to the universe, has eluded a complete quantum treatment. Until now. Using techniques from the full LQG analysis, I provide a detailed operator analysis of the Volume operator, showing that it has a well-defined, discrete spectrum. I then solve the full quantum dynamics and show that the spectrum is stable under small perturbations, showing that the Volume has a well-defined, classical limit. This solves the longstanding problem of quantizing the'size' of the universe in LQG and opens the door for studying the quantum dynamics of other operators with a well-defined classical limit such as the Ashtekar variables. Note: This is a summary of my arXiv paper: [https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00288](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.00288). The full paper has additional technical details and proofs.

Wiretap channel with causal, noiseless feedback. The encoder sends a sequence of messages to the channel. The channel outputs a sequence of messages, one at a time, based on previous channel outputs and current input. The objective is to communicate from the encoder to the decoder a sequence of messages so that the decoder can decode the messages reliably, even when it does not have causal access to the channel input. This is the first result for this model, proven by El Gamal and Verdú. This work has many implications for coding and channel networks, and many open problems remain. This model considers the case where the channel is noiseless and causally accessible to the encoder. The channel output depends only on the channel input and previous channel outputs. The objective is to communicate a sequence of messages to the decoder so that the decoder can decode the messages reliably, even when it cannot access the channel input n advance. This is the first result for this model, proven by El Gamal and Verdú. This work has many implications for coding and channel networks, and many open problems remain. A related model without causal access to the encoder is the Brown and Yato model, where the channel output is a function of both the channel input and previous channel outputs as well as random noise. Ahlswede and Csiszár obtained the capacity for this model when the encoder has access to a noisy version of the channel output. Even without access to the channel output, it is possible to obtain an approximation to the capacity of this model within a small constant gap. This model is of fundamental interest. It generalizes the models with access to the channel input in both directions: both the channel and the encoder have access to a finite number of past channel inputs, or the encoder has access to an infinite number of past inputs. The case where the channel and encoder have access to a finite number of past inputs is less powerful than the case with access to an infinite number of past inputs, as demonstrated by the examples of noiseless channels with finite memory and channels with delay. It is still open whether this model with access to an infinite number of past inputs has infinite capacity in the discrete memoryless case. Ahlswede and Csiszár obtained the capacity of this model when the encoder has access to a noisy version of the channel output. Even without access to the channel output, it is possible to obtain an approximation to the capacity of this model within a small constant gap. This model with access to an infinite number of past inputs has a constant gap approximation with maximum difference of 1/32 from the capacity, which is the first constant gap approximation with non-trivial bounds on the gap for this model. Astronomical object size is one of the most basic attributes. It is measured by the apparent angular diameter, which in turn is a function of the projected physical diameter and the distance to the object. Planets, gas giants, and other large asteroids typically have visible angular diameters less than 1 arc-second, corresponding to physical diameters of a few times that of the Earth. However, when considering smaller objects in the solar system, such as comets, asteroids, and Kuiper Belt Objects (KBOs), their sizes become much more difficult to determine. For example, the typical large KBO system has a diameter of a few hundred kilometers, corresponding to less than 1 arc-second, or a few tens of kilometers, in visible light. To characterize the size and structure of these objects requires a detailed understanding of how light interacts with them. As a first step, this work determines the reflected light curves and sizes of largest object in the Kuiper Belt, dwarf planet (1480) Pluto. Using observations in the visible and infrared with the Hubble Space Telescope and the Spitzer Space Telescope, we measure the apparent diameters of Pluto and Charon as a function of phase angle, and produce the first light curves of Pluto and Charon. These observations place the size of the largest object in the Kuiper Belt at approximately 500 km x 400 km, with 3-4 components, corresponding to a physical diameter of 300-400 km. For the first time, this work presents light curves for Pluto and Charon which can be used in additional analyses of the Kuiper Belt to determine physical and chemical properties. In general, Kuiper Belt Objects (KBOs) are extremely cold, dark and distant worlds. Located beyond the orbit of Neptune, the Kuiper Belt is the third zone in the Solar System, beyond the inner main belt and the asteroid belt, and is characterized by a myriad of small icy bodies. The Kuiper Belt contains the asteroid belt's most primitive objects as well as the largest and most geologically inactive bodies in the Solar System. In spite of the fact that Pluto, the smallest and most distant known member of the Kuiper Belt, was classified as a dwarf planet in 2006, it is the only one for which no light curve was available. Thanks to observations carried out between 2014 and 2018 with Hubble and Spitzer, we were able to characterize the shape, size and structure of Pluto. This work joins a long list of Kuiper Belt Object light curve measurements that began with 1994 QB1, and which include such diverse objects as 2012 VP113, Varuna, Haumea, Makemake, Eris, and (136108) 2004 BF3. By determining Pluto's light curve, we also obtained its size. The fact that Pluto is the largest KBO with a light curve allows us to constrain the KBO size

Existence of inward motions in starless cores has long been proposed based on analysis of simple chemical models. Such motions are of great interest as they may be associated with the process of core fragmentation and subsequent star formation. Inward motions are observable by detection of optically thick, high rotation transition lines such as NH 3 ( J = 1-0) whose derived spin relaxation times are longer in regions with small velocity dispersion than would be expected from the gas temperature. We have completed a pilot study for detecting inward motions in dark clouds using the HCN J = 1-0 line. We have obtained excellent systemic pointing with this line for the region in the TMC-1KP core that includes TMC-1C, 1D, and 1E, which are well-known sites of ongoing low-mass star formation. Preliminary results from the HCN J = 1-0 line are positive for TMC-1C and TMC-1D, but not for TMC-1E; a more detailed analysis is in progress. We have also observed a reference position in the adjoining core known as TMC-1F. The TMC-1KP project is an expanded version of this work. We also seek observations of additional cores in the TMC-1 clouds and of other starless cores in this line. We use the term "pointing" to refer to a set of observations (along a chosen set of coordinates) of the same region. A pointing is considered excellent if the noise in the TMC-1KP channel maps is primarily thermal noise, the map is symmetric with respect to the chosen coordinates, and the intensity range covers at least a 5:1 intensity range and the transition line is cleanly centered on the chosen coordinates.

We present the discovery of fifteen new low-mass companions to planet host stars, using data from the squeezernigton component of the high-contrast imaging instrument GPI. These new planets raise the total count of imaged planets to thirty-eight, and the total number of planet host stars to twelve. Most of the new discoveries are super-Earth sized planets, with sizes ranging from 1.3 to 5.7 Earth radii, and masses from 2 to 20 Earth masses. Two of the planets have very high equilibrium temperatures, and may be classified as Hot Neptunes. Twelve of the new planets were detected in direct imaging, and fifteen come from high density Bonner Powell modeling of the trajectory of planets observed with GPI. We also update the orbital properties for twelve of the planets, including eight that are likely in multiple systems. We also compare the properties of planet host stars to those of similar stars without detected planets, and find that planet host stars are more likely to have a higher metallicity and exhibit smaller spin rates.

A large acceptance detector with read-out by wavelength shifting fibre has been constructed for use in searches for eta-nucleus bound states. The method of detecting eta-mesic nuclei, in which a ’bare’ nucleus of interest is coated with a layer of eta, with the underlying idea of observing the ’dressed’ nucleus via its interactions with the eta, has a recent revival due to the possibility of producing eta in substantial quantities at FAIR. The detector uses a large array of 1 inch PMTs in a cylindrical volume of 3.3 million liters of liquid scintillator located at the Surface Science Studies facility at Indiana University. The light from the PMT photocathodes is coupled into single mode fibres which then run the length of the detector inside a wavelength shifting fibre loop. Light from the eta atom in the interaction near the nucleus is thought to shift wavelength with a peak around 575 nm, well matched to the transmission spectrum of the fibre. Scintillating oil is used as the active medium providing particle identification through measurement of the magnitude and direction of the momentum vectors of charged particles produced in the nucleus-eta interaction. The apparatus has been optimised for two beam tests at the Indiana University Cyclotron facility in 2021, one with a beam of eta particles, the other with a beam of protons. For both, detectors were exposed for short times and the data was taken at low statistics, nevertheless significant evidence of eta interactions was observed. Further tests are planned during 2022.

In this paper, we study the correlation between the ratio of the coefficients of the electron dipole moment operator to that of the electric dipole moment operator, epsilon'/epsilon, and rare K decays in the Littlest Higgs Model with T-parity (LHT). We find that new contributions from the LHT model enhance the coefficient of the epsilon'np term, and suppress that of the epsilon'nt term in the kaon decays, and the correlation between epsilon'/epsilon and rare K decays in the LHT model is largely strengthened. The possible constraints on the LHT parameter space from the epsilon'nt term of kaon decays and epsilon'np/epsilon are discussed. [ Dongdong Liang, Chong S. Chau, and Tsung-MW Yan]{} epsilon'nt and epsilon'np terms in kaon decays are induced at one-loop level in the Littlest Higgs Model with T-parity. The current upper limits on epsilon'nt and epsilon'np from BaBar and Belle collaborations give severe constraints on the LHT parameter space.

Recently, non-Markovian quantum processes became a subject of great interest due to their applications in, e.g, open quantum systems and quantum information. In this context, a fruitful and powerful approach is the flow of information approach, in which the relative entropy between the evolving state and a dynamical target state quantifies the distance between the respective time-evolving flows of information. This approach has been successfully applied to out-of-time-ordered correlations, geometric quantum Fisher information, and production of quantum entropy. In this Letter, we generalize this approach by considering time-local quantum dynamical maps. Our formalism can be used to quantify the total production of quantum entropy (and hence of information) in arbitrary non-Markovian dynamics. As an example, we consider the driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard model and show that the total production of quantum entropy is a direct measure of the breaking of trace-preservation. Our framework opens the possibility of studying production and consumption of quantum information in quantum nonequilibrium steady states.

The nucleon and other baryons are vital entities in the study of nuclear physics and particle physics. For more than fifty years, numerous models have been built to explore the structure of these particles, including the Cloudy Bag Model, the Skyrme Model, chiral effective field theory, and most recently, large- N Sugamoto mesons. Each of these models has had success in describing the gross properties of baryons; however, more recent developments in the theory of String duality have led to the development of a novel, comprehensive model of the baryon as a full tower of strings. In this model, each baryon is comprised of a fundamental string and its excitations, the vector mesons. The full dynamics of the system are given by the Nambu-Goto action for the strings, and at long distances, the system reduces to the Skyrme Model with pions described by the vector mesons. The model exhibits many of the previously observed properties of baryons, and additionally predicts that the baryons are magnetic moment ferromagnets, in excellent agreement with experiments. In addition to describing the gross properties of baryons, the model also yields predictions for excited baryon masses, which may be tested in the near future with current and upcoming experiments. The model developed herein is a compelling addition to the theoretical framework of baryons, describing both their gross and subtle properties with a single, comprehensive equation.

In this work, we present the results of a spectral analysis of five Chandra observations of the Oort cloud comet (C/2001 Q4) Newburn. The spectra were analyzed in the 0.3–10 keV energy range, and the data are best described by a single component model with absorption consistent with interstellar medium values. We find a best-fit temperature of 1.2 ± 0.4 keV and measure a 21-240 keV luminosity of (6.8 ± 2.8) × 1025 erg s−1. We also consider two more complex models, a single temperature thermal emission model and a power-law model, and find that both models are statistically equivalent to the single component model, and give best-fit values of temperature of 1.0 ± 0.3 keV and 22-240 keV luminosity of (7.6 ± 3.4) × 1025 erg s−1. We find this emission to be consistent with previously reported X-ray emission from the Oort cloud comet 9P/Templar. This work demonstrates the feasibility of using X-ray emission from Oort cloud comets as a diagnostic of their size and orbit.

A boundary element method (BEM) solution of the two-dimensional Laplace’s equation in the half-plane using triangular elements is presented. Boundary conditions are applied on a part of the boundary of the half-plane. The BEM linear system is singular, which is typical for BEMs, because a Green’s function is used for representing the solution at the interior points of the domain. The BEM matrix is non-symmetric, and the use of a proper preconditioning method is required for achieving a good numerical accuracy. We propose a new technique for building the preconditioner which requires the solution of a local Helmholtz problem with a non-symmetric operator in the variational formula. We show that the proposed method provides a high accuracy solution, and that the numerical error is nearly exact, in the sense that the difference between the exact solution and the numerical solution is limited to the discretization error. The method works well even for very fine meshes with thousands of triangles. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated by several numerical examples.

Bicategories are closed general categories, with two-sided cells, sitting in four-category assemblies. These can be considered as generalizations of monoids, with two elements, and arranged in categories, whose fibers are two-category with one object. A framed bicategory is an enriched category in bicategories, with three-sided cells, sitting in six-category, and hom-bicategories of them, sitting in eight-category. These can be considered as generalizations of 2-categories, with one object, and fibers being 2-groupoids, with one 2-morphism. A monoidal fibrations between two framed bicategories are weak functors between their underlying categories, weakly satisfying some additional equations. These fibrations capture 2-cells in fibers. They also generalize crossed modules of 2-groups and strict monoidal functors of monoidal categories. Framing a bicategory with three-sided cells changes it into an enriched category, with six-category as its fibers. These fibrations capture 2-cells in fibers. They also generalize crossed modules of 2-groups and strict monoidal functors of monoidal categories. The paper studies framed bicategories, their 2-cells, and their monoidal fibrations, from various points of views, explaining main concepts and constructions. - bicategories as closed general categories - two-sided cells as generalizations of one-element sets - four-category assemblies as generalizations of two-element sets - Main concepts and constructions are explained in this framework - Framed bicategories as enriched categories - fibers as two-category - 2-cells as 2-morphisms - 2-groups as fibers of strict monoidal functors - Morita equivalence of 2-groups as isomorphism between corresponding strict monoidal functors - crossed modules of 2-groups as monoidal deformations of corresponding 2-groups - monoidal fibrations between framed bicategories - strict monoidal functors between corresponding framed bicategories - weakly satisfying some additional equations as fibrations with fibers 2-groupoids - Generalizations of these are also described - Appendices are provided with technical results.

This paper defines universal invariants for higher K-theory and higher signatures, and demonstrates their relevance by determining higher K-theory of one-point compactifications of hyperbolic groups. These universal invariants satisfy the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence for topological K-theory, a calculation of the fundamental group, and the universal coefficients theorem. In this framework, the strong Novikov conjecture, which states that the higher signatures of a closed manifold are universal among degree-one cohomology classes, is equivalent to the homotopy invariance of higher K-theory. This implies that the higher K-groups satisfy the Hirzebruch signature theorem, and, under certain hypotheses, also detect exotic elements in the stable homology of manifolds. We also establish twisted versions of these universal invariants and apply them to the Bismut intersection formula, the Borel regulator, and elliptic genera. This approach to higher K-theory and universal invariants extends to other stable homotopy theories, such as bordism and generalized cohomology. In particular, we define twisted variants of these theories and show how to compute these variants using the invariants defined here. This approach unifies the study of K-theory, bordism, generalized cohomology, and stable homotopy by viewing these theories as localizations of a single universal theory of stable derived functors. In particular, the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence for topological K-theory arises as the key element in the localization process. In addition to defining this universal theory of stable derived functors, we also calculate its rationalization. This provides a powerful way to determine the rational homology of one-point compactifications of hyperbolic groups, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we propose a framework for studying twisted stable homotopy theories in which various structures, such as vector bundles and operators, are replaced by connective coverings and corresponding universal invariants. We indicate some examples of these twisted theories and indicate how to compute their universal invariants. I thank David Giesen, Sean Tammar, and Robert Yager for their advice and support. Higher K-theory via universal invariants Higher K-theory captures key features of continuous cohomology by considering all homotopy groups at once. This is a pro-spectrum, or internal homology theory, meaning it admits a normalized complex with homology the homotopy groups of the K-theory spectrum KU. These homotopy groups may be given the structure of a ring by means of coefficients; the Hopkins-Miller theorem identifies this ring as topological cyclic homology TC, allowing K-theory to be studied via universal properties. This pro-spectrum includes a lot of information. The fundamental theorem of K-theory describes it as a collection of pieces separated by unique extensions, whose cancellation requires the Elliott invariant. The Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) is an optical multi-object spectrograph designed for the Siding Spring Observatory in New South Wales, Australia. It is capable of carrying out high signal-to-noise ratio optical spectroscopy of up to 72 objects simultaneously over a wide field of view of 8 square degrees on a ten-chip Hawaii-2RG detector. WiFeS is able to achieve these performance goals through the use of an image-tube M pixels, a MarconiÂ E2V CCD218-CF array as the science array, and an Orbit Gem Â InstrumentsiftsLight optics, with image stabilisation. Target acquisition is performed using a state-of-the-art fibre-Optic IDS, and the data are reduced using a custom pipeline written in Python and described in this document. The pipeline currently consists of bias subtraction, flat-fielding, order merging, extraction, wavelength calibration, and telluric correction. The current version of the WiFeS module also includes an Object cataloguing pipeline, which uses Source Extractor to create target lists. This is being used in the ASKAP observations and other instrumentation, and in the construction of an extensive WiFeS reference catalogue for the Australian Astronomical Observatory.| The main advantages of WiFeS over other existing multi-object spectrographs are its small size, good throughput, ability to observe up to ten objects at once, and broad wavelength coverage, spanning from 3700 to 10,000 Å. The performance of WiFeS in terms of efficiency and resolution is summarised in Table 1, where it is shown to be comparable to other instruments, and in some cases exceed them. Importantly, the data quality is consistently high, with a median signal-to-noise ratio of 110 per pixel at 5000 Å for 1.25 Å pixels. The high efficiency and performance have resulted in WiFeS being used for a wide range of programs, including the commissioning of the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP), the Sydney Outer Star Region (SOAR) program, the GAMA survey, the Hunter Region Supercomputing Initiative (HRSI) galaxy cluster survey, and several programs with the Anglo-Australian Telescope (AAT).

V2104 Cygni is a relatively bright Be star which was recently shown to be multiperiodic, with all identified modes characterized in a comprehensive analysis. In this study we report five new $f_1$, $f_2$, $f_3$, and two $p_1$ modes, as well as three newly identified $p_2$ modes. The addition of these modes increases the total number of identified modes to 31, supporting the hypothesis of variability due to non-radial pulsations. Additionally, we report a high amplitude mode with aperiod of 538s and provide an interpretation for its presence. V2104 Cygni is aBe star with a relatively bright 9.8mag apparent magnitude.It belongs to a class of highly luminous supergiants, that also includes Wolf-Rayet stars, another group of rapidly evolving, massive stars. The high luminosities and surface temperatures of these stars result from an extensive hydrogen-rich envelope, which is mostly ionised hydrogen and helium. These envelopes are thought to be generated by mass loss during the main sequence phase, probably resulting from the bifurcation of the originally slower rotating main sequence star into two objects, through MarshmiR instability. The driving mechanism of the pulsations in Be stars is not fully understood, but non-radial modes of pulsation have been suggested to be the most likely explanation. It is known that some of these stars are multiperiodic, with many different modes being identified at different times. V2104 Cygni has previously been shown to be multiperiodic, with a comprehensive analysis of all the modes identified to that time. Newly discovered multiperiodic behaviour was the focus of a companion paper. In this paper we report five new $f_1$, $f_2$, $f_3$, and two $p_1$ modes, as well as three newly identified $p_2$ modes. The addition of these modes increases the total number of identified modes to 31, supporting the hypothesis of variability due to non-radial pulsations. We also report a high amplitude mode with a period of 538s and an amplitude of 20.2mmag. The presence of this mode could not have been detected in the previous analysis, because it was below the detection limit of approximately 5mmag. We suggest that this mode represents a new type of variability not previously recognised. We provide an interpretation for its presence, based on nonlinear oscillatory modes originating from the surface of the star. The data presented in this paper were obtained by the AAVSO Rapid Eye network, as part of the international BeSS network.

We present a catalog of 98,653 discrete sources detected in the three quarters of the 5 square degrees of the Carina Nebula surveyed by the Gaia Survey in its first visit to this region of the Milky Way. We use this catalog, in combination with the much deeper catalog of sources detected in the entire Carina Nebula Survey published in a companion paper, to study global properties of the Carina Nebula and its distribution across the energy spectrum. We find that the Nebula has an energy budget of 6 - 21%, rising to 21 - 30% in its densest regions. The Nebula is most homogeneously distributed around 6% in the region surrounding the HII region Trion Nebula and most clumpy toward its south and west, in a pattern typical of sequential energy injection. We show that this clumpiness has an environmental origin, with dense gas in Carina being shielded from external influences and having a lower density than the less dense ISM in the surrounding areas.

Recent cosmological hydrodynamic simulations and revised measurements of the faint-end extrapolation of the sub-millimeter cosmic infrared background (CIB) suggest that approximately 40% of the critical density of the universe was in gaseous form at redshifts ≥ 7, corresponding to an era known as the Epoch of Reionization (EoR). Existing models of the first generations of stars predict that these Population-II stars were significantly cooler than their Population-I counterparts, and likely formed in bound clusters known as protogalaxies. The assembly of these protogalaxies into larger structures is a predicted sequence of events known as hierarchical growth. The most distant quasars provide a promising search-space for such protogalactic structures around the epoch of reionization. Yet, despite extensive searching with existing mid-infrared instrumentation, only a single plausible-but-not-confirmed detection (HUDF12-3713) has been reported to date at such high redshifts. With the assistance of the new Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) and Laser Guide Star Facility on the United Kingdom Infra- Red Telescope (UKIRT), we have recently obtained a unique and substantial improvement in sensitivity in this region of the electromagnetic spectrum, with the discovery of a second high-redshift candidate (HUDF-JD2). The HUDF-JD2 candidate is relatively bright in the mid-infrared, with a 7.5σ detection in an extremely deep, 9.6 hours of WFC3/IR imaging followed by a positive detection in both a 1.4hours of additional UKIRT/MKO imaging and 13hours of SHARP ICL imaging. The 3σ limit on the contribution from nearby galaxies to this total flux density is ~25%. We use this emission to trace significant reservoirs of obscured rest-frame ultraviolet light from the earliest generation of stars, arising from a Population II galaxy at a redshift of z = 8.3, corresponding to an age of the universe of ~250 Myr following the'minus-z' convention. If this signal is confirmed, it will represent the most distant confirmed galaxy to date and will provide strong evidence for hierarchical growth at a time coincident with the last major epoch of reionization.

An ab initio density functional theory (DFT) study of electronic and crystal structure of orthorhombic phase of barium iron oxide (BaFeO3) is presented. The most stable phase is determined using the full structural relaxation and the results are compared with previously proposed experimental data. The influence of the vdW interactions on the structural properties and the electronic structure is discussed. The calculations were performed using a high-throughput DFT library PLUMED with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) for the Raman spectra calculations. The Raman active modes in the studied compound were classified in different groups and their possible origins were suggested. The presented data suggest that the studied phase is stable and the Raman modes can be classified in the following groups: A1g (m) and B2g (m); A1g (m) and B2g (m); B2g (m) and B2g (m); B2g (m) and E2g (s); B2g (m) and E2g (s); A1g (m) and B2g (m); B2g (m) and E2g (s). First-principles DFT calculations were performed to study the structural, electronic and Raman spectra of orthorhombic phase of barium iron oxide (BaFeO3). The most stable structure obtained from the full structural relaxation is compared with previously proposed experimental data. Ab initio calculations predict the most stable structure with the space group Pnma (No. 62), which is in agreement with the previously proposed experimental data. The computed electronic structure shows that the studied phase is a metal. Ab initio calculations suggest that Raman spectra of BaFeO3 can be classified in the following groups: A1g (m) and B2g (m); A1g (m) and B2g (m); B2g (m) and B2g (m); B2g (m) and E2g (s); B2g (m) and E2g (s); A1g (m) and B2g (m); B2g (m) and E2g (s). BaFeO3 is a remarkable material with multiferroic properties that attracts attention of both academic and industrial research community. The structure, mechanical and electrical properties were investigated in detail experimentally, however electronic structure and, especially, Raman spectra of this material were studied less thoroughly. Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal lattice, is one of the most exciting two-dimensional materials. Its electronic band structure presents two points of non-dispersibility, the so-called Dirac points, which are directly related to its intriguing transport properties. Recently, this material has attracted a great deal of attention due to its response to strong magnetic fields, which is reminiscent of the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) effect. In particular, the transmission coefficient of charge carriers in graphene rings exposed to a uniform magnetic field exhibits a step-like dependence as a function of the Fermi energy, which is a characteristic signature of the AB effect. Similar behavior has also been observed in other carbon allotropes such as bilayer graphene and boron nitride. Despite its potential interest, to date, there have been few rigorous works exploring the response of graphene to a nonuniform magnetic field. In this paper, we show that a magnetic flux generated by a solenoid with a large radius, compared to the magnetic length, leads to a strongly deformed band structure in graphene, without splitting the Dirac points. Furthermore, when the radius of the solenoid is comparable to the magnetic length, new degrees of freedom, namely, the so-called topological valley, emerge. We show that the conductance spectrum is completely different from the AB effect, even in the limit of a strong magnetic field. Finally, we extend our findings to propose a realistic device that implements the AB effect in graphene.

Fractal dimension is a measure of the complexity of a self-similar structure. The spin glass phase of disordered magnetic systems is characterized by the presence of correlated local fluctuations called flips (or flipping spins), leading to a hierarchical structure. Here we study the fractal dimension of domain walls between degenerate ground states in two-dimensional random bond Ising spin glasses. We compute this dimension using probability distributions of spacings between domain walls and demonstrate that it is intimately related to the critical behaviour of the model. We compute this dimension using probability distributions of spacings between domain walls and demonstrate that it is intimately related to the critical behaviour of the model. As the temperature is decreased, the correlation length ξ of the local flips diverges in a manner consistent with the dynamical scaling hypothesis, ξ∼(T_{f}-T)^{-\nu}. The fractal dimension of domain walls also increases with decreasing temperature, approaching 3 from below. This increase can be explained by assuming that domains of different degeneracy are separated by rough domain walls with Hausdorff dimension close to 4.

Noise can drastically change the behavior of a system. For example, in a system with feedback, a weak noise can induce instability, while a strong noise can promote stability. Here we report the experimental observation of a third regime: the suppression of growth by multiplicative white noise. We demonstrate that the addition of infinitesimal amplitude noise to a damped driven nonlinear system can stabilize the system. By performing direct numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, we identify this unusual phenomenon to be associated with the parametric resonance. Our work highlights the different noise strategies that can be employed to stabilize a dynamical system and could have potential implications for the stabilization of real world systems. In this study, we experimentally observe that the addition of infinitesimal amplitude noise to a damped driven nonlinear system can stabilize the system. We demonstrate that the addition of infinitesimal amplitude noise can suppress the growth of zero-mean oscillations in a finite range of frequencies. This suppression of growth is quantified by using the mean-square amplitude of the oscillations. The addition of infinitesimal amplitude noise can stabilize the system. This unusual phenomenon is highlighted in our work by using direct numerical simulations and theoretical analysis. We study the topological and entanglement entropy of the toric code at finite temperature. The topological entropy is shown to coincide with the exponential growth or decay of the number of different energy eigenstates in the finite temperature regime. We characterize the topological entanglement entropy by considering a quantity proportional to the square of the mutual information, which we call the mutual information entanglement entropy (MIEE). We show that this MIEE also exhibits an exponential decay in the finite temperature regime. We evaluate the finite-size scaling of these topological and topological entanglement entropies using numerical exact diagonalization of small clusters. These results are used to compute the entanglement entropy of a version of the toric code at finite temperature, for comparison with experiments in photonic lattices, that could realistically simulate the model with current technology. We study the topological and entanglement entropy of the toric code at finite temperature. The topological entropy is shown to coincide with the exponential growth or decay of the number of different energy eigenstates in the finite temperature regime. We characterize the topological entanglement entropy by considering a quantity proportional to the square of the mutual information, which we call the mutual information entanglement entropy (MIEE). We show that this MIEE also exhibits an exponential decay in the finite temperature regime. We evaluate the finite-size scaling of these topological and topological entanglement entropies using numerical exact diagonalization of small clusters. These results are used to compute the entanglement entropy of a version of the toric code at finite temperature, for comparison with experiments in photonic lattices, that could realistically simulate the model with current technology. This work was primarily motivated by recent interest in the topological entropy of the toric code as a qubit noise threshold in quantum error correction. We calculate the topological entropy via the Loschmidt overlap transform, which expresses the number of distinct eigenstates as an exponential growth or decay in the number of Riemann zeros. We confirm the noise threshold by numerically evaluating the topological entropy of the toric code on small lattices. We also characterize the topological entropy via the mutual information entanglement entropy (MIEE), introduced to photonic lattice experiments recently. The MIEE is defined via a quantity proportional to the square of the mutual information, and can be estimated via the Loschmidt overlap transform. We numerically evaluate the finite-size scaling of topological entropy and MIEE for system sizes up to 15 x 15 with periodic boundary conditions. This calculation confirms that the topological entropy coincides with the exponential decay of the number of energy eigenstates in the finite temperature regime, and that the MIEE coincides with the exponential growth of this number. We also estimate the topological entropy and MIEE of the smallest non-trivial subsystem of the toric code on 15 x 15 lattices with open boundary conditions.

In this paper we present a Bayesian analysis of the low-resolution polarized 3-year WMAP sky maps. We perform likelihood-based principal component analysis (PCA) of the noise dominated full-mission WMAP data to obtain a set of basis vectors, which explain the majority of the variance in the data. We then use the maps obtained from WMAP satellite to test the validity of this approach on synchrotron, thermal dust and instrumental polarization component maps. We carry out the analysis in the direction of supercluster and obtain the principal components, which are used to forecast the various CMB temperature and polarization signals in the low resolution WMAP data. We also perform similar analysis with different cosmological models and obtain the Bayes factors, which suggest the preference of the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology over the non-standard models. The analysis is performed at three different $\ell$ ranges, namely, $\ell < 30$, $30 < \ell < 50$ and $50 < \ell < 500$ to check the robustness of the results.

In this paper, we explore the cosmological analogue of the Schwinger effect, i.e., the process by which charged fermions could attain an effective mass due to an electromagnetic-like Chern-Simons coupling. We show that even in the very early universe, when the energy density was dominated by the electromagnetic kinetic term, the Chern-Simons coupling could still lead to an effective mass for the fermions. Since this process does not require spatial variation of the coupling constant, but only initial conditions for the fermions' distribution function, we argue that this effect may be generic and could occur in a wide variety of cosmologies. We conclude by outlining some potentially observable signatures of this phenomenon, including inhomogeneities in the Cosmic Microwave Background and a vector spectral index for primordial gravitational waves.' Binary star systems provide a unique opportunity to study planetary systems in a much morecompact configuration than can be studied around single stars. A key challenge in detectingplanets around binary systems is their proximity to the host star, which increases thetechnological requirements for planet detection and characterization. This paperprovides an overview of observational techniques for planet detection inbinaries, with a particular focus on methods which have the potential to beapplied to circumbinary planet systems. Following an introduction to binary starsystems, the different methods of planet detection and their sensitivity to different systemparameters are described. For each method, examples from recent planet detection surveys arepresented. A preliminary analysis of the characteristics of the known circumbinaryplanets is also provided, and suggestions for future surveys which could extend thisanalyis to larger samples are offered. As new techniques for planet detection aredeveloped and demonstrated, these methods should also be tested on circumbinary planetsystems.

The thermal Casimir force is attracting much attention as a medium-range interaction in nanotechnology. Recently, an analytic approach to the thermal Casimir force between metal and dielectric was proposed. The method is based on the use of the so-called dielectric permittivity spectral functions, which are measurable in the time domain. A plasma model was used for modeling the dispersive metal. It was shown that the thermal Casimir force is given by the derivative of the free energy with respect to the distance between the surfaces. The general expression for the thermal Casimir free energy was obtained. This expression was used for calculating the thermal Casimir force for various combinations of metal and dielectric parameters. It was demonstrated that the thermal Casimir force is strongly modified by dispersion of the metal. The most notable example is a change in the sign of the thermal Casimir force for a metal and a dielectric at certain combination of the parameters of these two objects

The Mira variable star photometer on the 3.5-meter telescope at Las Campanas Observatory has been in operation since 2012. In this time we have achieved continuous photometric precision of 3 millimag for bright stars and 7 millimag for faint stars, and have obtained time series photometry for tens of millions of stars. With these data, we have studied the pulsation modes of Miras, the period-luminosity and the color-magnitude relations, the structure and pulsation geometry of semiregular variables, the rotation and multiplicity of pulsating stars, and the variation of these quantities with mass, luminosity, and wavelength. This paper presents a summary of our findings and discusses their implications for our understanding of these fascinating stars. We have studied the pulsation modes of Miras, the period-luminosity and the color-magnitude relations, the structure and pulsation geometry of semiregular variables, the rotation and multiplicity of pulsating stars, and the variation of these quantities with mass, luminosity, and wavelength. These findings are presented and discussed.

As an alternative to the traditional RF QC device design, which comprises a scanning function, the DAFNE baseline design incorporates an ion clearing electrode (ICE) in the feedback loop to mitigate the RF induced beam rotation and energy spread effects. Results obtained with the ICE inserted in the feedback loop demonstrate an improvement in beam energy and stability when compared to the DAFNE baseline performance without the ICE. However, the ICE induced feedback component in the focusing element generates significant beam trajectory changes, which needs to be mitigated by adjusting the wavefront sensor based feedback offset. This paper reports the results of the impact of ICE on DAFNE beam dynamics. The paper starts with an overview of DAFNE concept and design followed by the description of ICE, the effects the ICE have on the DAFNE baseline performance, different methods to mitigate the ICE effect, and the effects of different mitigation methods on the beam dynamics. The paper concludes with a discussion of the achieved beam stability and the trade-offs involved in the different mitigation methods.

In this article we consider two closely related notions of information density defined in the context of finite state automata (FSA). The first, used for instance in the Kolmogorov complexity theory, is based on the length of the shortest program needed to generate a string. This density is always greater or equal to the second density, related to Lempel-Ziv compression, and often much greater. Both definitions coincide for FSA with a unary input, but in the general case they are different and sometimes vastly so. For example, the pushdown automaton with one pushdown symbol having two internal states generating binary sequences of length 2n has bounded pushdown dimension 1, but Lempel-Ziv information density 2n. We also show that for every real number x there exists an automaton having bounded pushdown dimension 1 but Lempel-Ziv information density at most x. Overall, the relation between pushdown dimension and Lempel-Ziv information density is highly nontrivial and, as far as we are aware, has not been previously noted.

In a recent paper (Zucker et al. 2018), we presented the results of a survey for neutral hydrogen emission towards early-type stars from the ESO-POP survey. We selected a volume-limited sample of early-type stars and searched for neutral hydrogen associated with these stars. In the process, we discovered two high-velocity clouds (HVCs) with possible intergalactic origins. In this follow-up study, we present similar searches for intermediate-velocity clouds (IVCs) and high-velocity clouds (IVCs and HVCs). Using three different catalogs of early-type stars, we selected a total of 589 targets for which we obtained spectra, and report new detections of IVCs and HVCs. We also report 21 new HVCs, of which 7 may have intergalactic origins. We performed statistical analysis of our results, and found that a significant portion of the IVCs and HVCs are consistent with originating in the local environment. The large number of detections of HVCs and IVCs in our survey, combined with the clustering of detections around known high-density regions of the local Universe, provide strong evidence that these clouds have intergalactic origins. If these HVCs are from tidal disruption of dwarf galaxies, their dark matter contents could make them efficient microlenses for gamma-rays from nearby galaxies such as the Milky Way.

In this paper, we present an anatomy of Malicious Singularities. Malicious singularities are special solutions to the Einstein field equations that could form from very simple initial conditions and could explain the multitude of observed phenomena in the universe. Singularities could form from the collapse of very small density perturbations in the early universe. They could also form from the coalescence of black holes or from the collision of neutron stars. We classify the singularities that could form in the early universe into three distinct groups: 1. Type I: These are Fingers of God, where a massive object appears to be pointed at the observer. These can form from large density perturbations in the early universe. 2. Type II: These are ring-like objects, which could form from the collision of black holes. 3. Type III: These are Black Holes and neutron stars, which could form from the coalescence of smaller objects. We study the formation of these singularities in the context of elementary particles, paying particular attention to those with dark energy (quintessence) fields as this could explain the current acceleration of the universe. We find that if the quintessence equation of state parameter is less than -1, then the future singularity is a Malicious Singularity. We also identify special initial data that lead to the formation of Malicious Singularities that are solutions to the field equations with an equation of state parameter less than -1. We then consider the astrophysical implications of Malicious Singularities. We find that, under the assumption that such singularities do form, they could provide an alternative explanation for gamma-ray bursts, X-ray flashes, pulsar kicks, supermassive black holes, and dark matter. We also show that, in general relativity, Malicious Singularities could form from the merger of two black holes with various dark energy fields present, and that the kick velocity of the merged black hole could be affected by the equation of state of the dark energy. Malicious Singularities have wide-ranging implications for cosmology and astrophysics, and could explain a multitude of observed phenomena in the universe. It is an open question whether the future singularity of general relativity is a Malicious Singularity. If so, this could have significant impact on our understanding of the universe, and provide new and testable hypotheses for cosmological and astrophysical phenomena.

Correlations in the dynamical behavior of supercooled liquids emerge from the interactions of individual molecules. Their temperature dependence provides insight into the interactions between molecules. Using dielectric spectroscopy we measured the temperature dependence of the Stokes-shifted motion of carbon-13 nuclear spin pairs in ortho-terphenyl. We find that the dominant contribution to the dynamical correlation length has an inverse proportionality to temperature, inconsistent with both currently proposed dynamical correlation models. Furthermore, we observe that the temperature dependence of the dynamical correlation length is consistent with mean-field, structural models of the glass transition. In ortho-terphenyl (o-terphenyl, strong Van der Waals bonds and a relatively simple structure) we find that the Stokes-shifted relaxation time for the motion of carbon-13 nuclear spin pairs has an inverse proportionality to temperature. The inverse proportionality of the correlation length to temperature means that a plot of correlation length vs. temperature looks linear at high temperatures but breaks down at low temperatures due to the freezing of molecules into a glass. To characterize these correlations we use a simplified multi-particle versions of the Mode Coupling Theory (MCT). At high temperatures we find that the correlations are consistent with a mean-field structural transition. As the temperature is decreased correlations become longer and temperature dependence is more consistent with a glass transition.

Several scenarios for the formation of galaxies have been proposed, ranging from slow and hierarchical merging of substructure within massive dark matter halos to violent and monolithic collapses of gas at the center of dense dark matter halos. A common element of these models is the formation of a central bulge of stars, and the correlation between the properties of these bulges and their host galaxies has been well established. What has been less clear, however, is the process by which these bulges form and grow. It is thought that much of the bulge mass is formed early during the collapse of the galaxy, before significant Population II star formation or black hole growth, and that further growth comes from subsequent assembly of satellite galaxies and massive gas-rich clumps. These processes are notoriously difficult to model and are difficult to observe, since direct observational signatures from the process itself—e.g., globular clusters—are relatively scarce. This paper presents a highly simplified model of this process, based on the merger of clumps in a live dark matter halo. These clumps are evolved using smoothed particle hydrodynamic techniques and resolve gravitationally stable entities of 20 - 150 pc in size. Using initial conditions from cosmological simulations, we follow the evolution of these clumps through several key phases: tidal shocking and energy equipartitioning, radial collapse and dissipationless quiescently forming disk, strong starburst, and later phase of gas cooling, mergers, and black hole accretion. We find that the system undergoes radial collapse and forms a self-similar, rotationally supported, dispersion-supported dwarf galaxy, but that the detailed behavior depends on the temperature, density, and rotation of the halo. At late times, these systems develop a population of globular clusters that resembles those observed in the Milky Way and other local galaxies. Using a baryonic Tully-Fisher relation, we show that this globular cluster mass-to-light ratio is sufficient to form the observed relation between bulge and total galaxy mass. This strongly supports the idea that assembly via the hierarchical merger of baryons within halos is a viable mechanism for bulge growth, and provides the first detailed simulation of this process.

The chemically peculiar star nu Indi shows solar-like oscillations and demonstrates the complete observed p-mode spectrum from both the adiabatic and the helioseismic INcycle modes. In this study, I analyse the solar-like oscillations in nu Indi from two perspectives. First, I perform a helioseismic analysis of the observed modes to determine the global oscillation parameters using time-dependent modelling. Second, using seismology, I infer the sound speed structure in the outer 5 Mm of the star. I find that the observed frequencies, even though they belong to a low-degree p-mode spectrum, are best matched by an intermediate-age, 1.4 billion years, model with significant radiative transfer effects present in the upper 500 km of the star. From the observed mode lifetime and spatial sensitivity of the observed mode amplitude, I deduce the sound speed has a relatively flat profile in the upper 500 km of the star.

Statistical mechanics has been extremely successful in explaining many physical systems arising in natural, social and economic sciences. In particular, interdisciplinary approaches, bridging micro and macro levels, have led to remarkable insights, helping to understand and quantify phenomena that before were thought to be exclusive to either the micro or the macro realm. Amongst different areas of research that have benefited from such a fusion, the study of complex networks has witnessed a spectacular recent growth. One of the main reasons behind this is that recent technological advances have allowed us to generate a large amount of data on the topology, the organization, and the interconnections, not only of physical networks (such as the Internet and the World Wide Web), but also of social (friendships, collaborations), biological (such as the genetic or neural networks), and economic (trade networks, food webs) ones. In this framework, this paper develops a macroscopic, thermodynamical approach to complex networked systems, focusing on the Ising model, the paradigmatic example of a paradigm-breaking, mean-field theory that became fundamental in statistical mechanics. The paper derives, from a properly generalized, modular version of the Helmholtz free energy, a family of pseudo-free energies, each of them encoding the thermodynamics of a particular type of network modular structure. The approach is applied to several prototypical network instances, and its validity is tested in comparison with other, more standard thermodynamical frameworks.

Recent discovery of the Higgs boson with a measured mass of 125.3 ± 0.4(stat) ± 0.4(syst) GeV/c² at the CERN LHC has provided evidence in favor of the standard model (SM) of particle physics. However, the precise mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking remains a mystery. There is no guarantee that the Higgs boson is the only new particle beyond the standard model (BSM). The unparticle scenario postulates existence of a hidden sector, with exact or approximate scale invariance, and an unparticle operator that may or may not be embedded in the standard model. If the scale invariance is exact, unparticle physics emerges at the TeV scale, making it accessible at the LHC. In this scenario, the Higgs potential arises due to the coupling of the Higgs field to the unparticle operator. The Higgs boson may thus acquire mass. Moreover, the coupling of the Higgs boson to standard model fermions is generated radiatively from the unparticle operator. Model-independent searches for lepton flavor violation (LFV) processes provide an avenue for testing the unparticle scenario. In this letter, we study the LFV processes in the unparticle scenario. We show that the branching ratio of the decays processes such as radiative decays of muon and tau, corresponding to flavor changing neutral current (FCNC) interactions, can reach to the level of $10^{-15}$ for unparticle scale about $1/\lambda^{2}_{\mu\Lambda} \sim$ TeV. Our results show that the unparticle scenario can be tested at the LHC and future colliders.

In the long run, a sterile species, that is, a species whose males contribute no genetic material to the next generation, would be expected to deplete over time due to random mating and genetic diversity. However, following a quantum mechanism, it has been shown that for short enough times, the sterile species can be produced, and its depletion avoided. This occurs due to the tail of the quantum distribution function, which has been shown to be greater than zero for all times, leading to an instantaneous effect. Using the Fokker-Planck equation, the probability density function of the time to depletion is computed. It is shown that the production of a sterile species for short times can provide a way to prevent the depletion of this species for all times, and hence a method of producing a "quantum kinetics." The production of a sterile species, that is, a species whose males contribute no genetic material to the next generation, has been shown possible following a quantum mechanism. Following the example of recent work on quantum sensing, a protocol has been proposed which utilizes strong atom-field coupling in a two-level system to enact quantum kinetics. In particular, a two-level atom is irradiated with a strong, rotating magnetic field, such that a Rabi cycle is completed within the interval of interest. A Feshbach procedure is then used to render the atom incapable of influencing subsequent generations. The production of a sterile species for short enough times can provide a way to prevent the depletion of this species for all times, and hence a method of producing a "quantum kinetics." Using the Fokker-Planck equation, the probability density function of the time to depletion is computed. It is shown that the production of a sterile species for short times can provide a way to prevent the depletion of this species for all times, and hence a method of producing a "quantum kinetics." For simplicity's sake, the results are presented for the specific case of a production schedule consisting of a sequence of infinitesimal intervals. However, it has been shown that even when a finite number of steps is taken, the effect remains. Additionally, it is possible to prove, for a general production schedule, that the quantum kinetics provides a way to produce a sterile species for all times. The theory presented here can be extended to more complex production schedules, such as those in which the production of a species is incremented by some function of time, or in which the interval between production intervals is not infinitesimal. It is also possible to relax some of the conditions on the model. For example, it would be of interest to examine the effects of varying the homogeneity of the atom-field coupling, as well as the effects of changes to the atom or field energy levels. Additionally, it would also be of interest to consider the effects of variation in the Rabi cycle duration, which governs the timescale of depletion.
