An explicit description of quasicrystals as a particular type of approximant—a solid solution with periodic modulations on top of a repeating base cell—often involves a division into two different projection functions. The first, used to generate the approximant configuration, projects the modulation from the parent B2 lattice into the substrate B12 lattice; this is followed by the second projection, which maps the approximant superstructure back into the B2 lattice. The necessity of two separate projections significantly hinders theoretical understanding of quasicrystal formation and limits precise prediction of approximant properties. This paper introduces a unified projection formalism for the Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystal Xi-approximants and their metadislocations. This formalism is demonstrated to predict several key properties of these quasicrystals—such as superspace group symmetry and the corresponding three-dimensional realization—without the need for explicit determination of the first and second projection matrices. Importantly, this enables a systematic investigation of quasicrystal formation through approximant-metadislocation phase space and the direct prediction of approximant properties—such as stability and misfit energy—based on the precise location of phase space catastrophe points.

Recently, the existence of planets around the star 14 Herculis has been announced. This star is located in the constellation Hercules at a distance of 20.7 light years from the Earth. The existence of 14 Her planets make this system the seventh closest system to the Earth. Since the discovery of the planets around 14 Herculis was announced, several studies have been carried out in order to confirm their physical and orbital characteristics. 14 Her planets can be categorized into three groups according to their sizes. The planets in the inner group have semi-major axes between 0.13 and 0.36 astronomical units, the planets in the middle group have semi-major axes between 0.36 and 0.7 astronomical units, and the planets in the outer group have semi-major axes greater than 0.7 astronomical units. Planets in the inner and outer groups have minimal masses between 7 and 22 Earth masses, whereas the mass of the planets in the middle group is between 22 and 55 Earth masses. In this study, we performed numerical simulations to characterize the dynamical evolution of the 14 Her planets. We show that, because of their relatively short periods and the proximity of the outermost planet in the system to their star, the 14 Her planets might have formed in multiple blocks and were unable to move further away from the star due to planet-planet scattering. Moreover, we predict the existence of a fourth outer planet in the system with a minimal mass of 9 Earth masses. However, further precise radial velocity measurements are required in order to confirm the existence of this planet and to characterize its orbit. This study was performed as part of the Dynamical Analysis of Planetary Systems (DAPS) network, which was designed to characterize the long-term dynamical evolution of planetary systems. This is a large-scale European Research Council-funded project running from January 2015 until December 2020 (ERC Consolidator Grant Number 681627-Dynamical Analysis of Planetary Systems). Authors: Ali Naytext Teslimi and Margarita Karangelova

High energy afterglows and flares from Gamma-Ray Burst by Inverse Compton emission have been observed in the last few years by several satellites such as Fermi, Suzaku, AGILE, HAWC and Swift. The observation of such afterglows at energies higher than gamma-rays can give important information about the properties of the emitting region. In this work, we use the observed high energy flares detected by AGILE to constrain the emission region size. We also present a detailed study of the high energy emission detected by Fermi and Suzaku from the same source. The AGILE satellite, which is in routine operations since April 2009, has detected many gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and observed the emission at lower and higher energies simultaneously. The AGILE observational program is focused on the study of high energy emission from gamma-ray bursts. Thanks to the observation in the MeV-GeV range, it has been possible to detect and study the afterglow emission in the x-ray and gamma-ray energy bands. The study of the temporal and spectral properties of this emission has allowed us to obtain information about the characteristics of the particles that are accelerated and the emission region size.

A superconducting electromechanical clock (SEMCLK) with a very high quality factor (Q) has been designed, tested, and characterized. The SEMCLK employs a low loss quartz crystal resonator to provide the clock mechanism and electrical feedthroughs, and a superconducting electronic circuit as the time keeping apparatus. The Q of the clock mechanism is proportional to the ratio of the integral of the resonance curve to the peak amplitude of the resonance curve. The resonance curve of the quartz crystal is subject to unpredictable and non-linear disturbances from outside sources, which limit the clock stability and thus the Q of the clock mechanism. To improve the stability and thus the Q of the clock, a stabilization feedback circuit is implemented using a fast acting electronic analog filter to mitigate the disturbance on the resonance curve and an analog digital converter (ADC) to sample the stabilized waveform and feed it back to the clock mechanism using a digital loop filter. A fiber laser was used to act as a coherent light source to provide a stable optical feedback scheme for the stabilization feedback circuit. The design, test, and characterization results of the superconductor clocks are presented. Using a niobium nitride-based superconducting electromechanical resonator with a Q of approximately 210 million, a stabilization feedback circuit with a 48 dB improvement in the Q was achieved, resulting in a Q of greater than 6 billion for the complete clock system. Using this clock stabilization technique, a simple digital synchronization circuit was implemented and the stability of the system was verified. By using an FPGA based analog design system, the SEMCLK demonstrated the capability to synthesize arbitrary waveforms in both the analog domain and digital domain using a single clock system, and a synthesized waveform with an RMS noise level of 8.5 pm was generated and measured.

The effect of the spin-orbit interaction on the thermodynamic properties of crystals was studied by Hotta in 1922, by calculating the specific heat of bismuth. Bismuth has a simple face-centered cubic structure. The spin-orbit coupling leads to the splitting of the electron bands at the band edges. In a crystalline material, the conduction band and the valence band may not be fully separated due to the intervalley scattering. The specific heat of bismuth was measured at various temperatures and the residual specific heat v(0) was calculated. It was found that v(0) can be well explained by a calculation with a simple spin-orbit interaction Hamiltonian, excluding any additional contributions. Hotta obtained a very simple expression for the specific heat of bismuth, v(T) = a + bT^2 + v(0), where a, b, and v(0) are constants. The first term a + bT^2 corresponds to the electronic contribution from the upper and lower bands, and the second term v(0) corresponds to the Van Vleck contribution from the separated band edges. The calculation of Hotta was valid at low temperatures, where the higher bands can be neglected. The third term is a constant, since the crystal field should not change with temperature. This expression was tested by Hotta by calculating the specific heat of various materials and comparing the calculated values with the measured specific heat of bismuth. The calculation with the spin-orbit interaction was found to be good for potassium, sodium, and mercury, but not for calcium and barium. Hotta proposed that bismuth may be an ideal material to observe the effect of the spin-orbit interaction, because the residual specific heat v(0) is large and positive, and the spin-orbit interaction should be enhanced. Experiments were performed later to investigate the possible magnetic order in bismuth, but no order was found down to 2 K. The possible contribution from nuclear moments was also examined. Bismuth was found to be a good metal, and a large negative contribution to the specific heat was found below 6.5 K, which was possibly due to electron scattering by nuclear moments. The temperature dependence of the specific heat of bismuth was also examined. The measured specific heat was fitted with the functional form v(T) = a + bT + v(0), where b was close to zero. This means that the higher term v(0) can be neglected. The value of a was close to the electronic specific heat coefficient a + bT, which is also very small. This means that the electronic specific heat is dominated by the first term a + bT^2. The temperature dependence of the entropy was also examined, and the entropy should be a constant up to 7 K. The measured entropy was well fitted with a constant, which excluded any temperature dependence of the entropy up to 7 K.

In this paper we study the neutrino Majorana masses in compactified weakly coupled type I string models on $ SO(32) \times E_8 \times E_8 $ orientifold with MSSM-like spectra. This model has three copies of MSSM spectrum in 4d effective field theory description, which provides a solution to the flavor problem of the standard model (SM) by postulating a $\nu$SUSY mechanism. The model also has three identical copies of hypercharge $U(1)_Y$ and a spectator $U(1)$ gauge groups in 4d effective theory, which lead to the gauge unification in this model at the string scale. Due to the presence of three identical copies of hypercharge in the theory, the triplets of $SU(2)_L$ can not mix with the triplets of $SU(2)_R$ in 4d effective theory, which is also a desirable feature from flavor point of view. Moreover, in this model there are two sets of spinor representations of $SO(32)$ gauge group which are symmetric and antisymmetric under permutation of two $E_8$ gauge groups. In the symmetric part we can write three $\bf 16$ and $\overline{\bf 16}$ representations of $SO(32)$ which are $SU(5)$ quiralty with appropriate linear combination of right-handed neutrinos. Then by promoting these right-handed neutrinos to scalar fields in 4d effective theory, we can generate Dirac neutrino masses at one loop. On the other hand, in the antisymmetric part of spinor representations we have two $\bf 75$ and $\overline{\bf 75}$ representations of $SO(32)$, which contain two sets of spinors of $SO(10) \times SU(4)$ symmetry and can be decomposed to $\bf 10 + 45$ and $\overline{\bf 10} + \overline{\bf 45}$ of $SU(5) \times SU(4)$ and two $\bf 16 + \overline{\bf 16}$ of $SO(10) \times SU(4)$ respectively. We argue that by assigning suitable $U(1)$ charges to $\bf 10 + 45$ and $\overline{\bf 10} + \overline{\bf 45}$ under $SU(4) \times SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ to obtain $SU(5)$ invariant and $SU(4)$ invariant operators, these spinors can couple to Higgs bi-doublets and lead to the needed suppression of proton in this model. To summarize, we have an Instanton Induced Neutrino Majorana Masses (IIMNMM) model, which can explain tiny neutrino masses via $\nu$SUSY, can address the gauge coupling unification problem and have a relatively high suppression of proton decay rate.

Through UV and optical analysis of 260 galaxies from the GEMS survey and 899 galaxies from the GOODS survey we detect two distinct Hubble-type dependent tidal tail morphologies. The first, most common, morphology is a smooth, narrow, linear structure with an average width of 18.6 ± 4.6 pc (6.1 ± 1.5") in emission from $0.4L_{B}^{\star}$ to $2L_{B}^{\star}$, where $L_{B}^{\star}$ is the characteristic blue luminosity of the galaxy. The width of the smooth tail is found to be independent of galaxy luminosity and nearly independent of Hubble type. The smooth tail is comprised of hydrogen from which we are able to calculate a stellar velocity dispersion of 20-40 km/s. The smooth tail is associated with a high tidal strength of 0.8-1.3 and typically points back toward the parent galaxy. The second morphology is from $2L_{B}^{\star}$ to the detection limit of the survey. Here we observe a distinct change in the nature of the tidal tail. Instead of a smooth linear structure we now observe highly clumpy, irregular structures with an average width of 84.8 ± 26.6 pc (26.9 ± 8.6") and velocity dispersions up to 130 km/s. These irregular structures are associated with lower tidal strengths of 0.3-0.5. The smooth/starburst dichotomy in the morphology of tidal tails cannot be explained by different masses of the parent galaxies, and is likely linked to the difference in their star formation properties. Smooth tails are likely the product of late type (disk) driven encounters, while starburst tails are the result of early type (elliptical) driven encounters. The former produce more slowly moving clouds, primarily heated by the mechanical energy of the shock front caused by the passage of the perturber through the halo of the host galaxy, while the latter generates shock heated gas at higher velocity dispersions.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most violent explosions in the universe. Locally, they are detected as very bright flashes of gamma rays, with hundreds of photons detected from some bursts. They have been detected far away galaxies redshift 7.9, even to the edge of the observable universe at a redshift of 10.0. The energetics of gamma-ray bursts make them challenging to explain with current astrophysical models. The fast-moving clouds of plasma ejected by theGRBs also typically result in the production of optical and infrared afterglows, which further study of these bursts has enabled the determination of the high-redshift properties of the host galaxies. The non-local nature of GRBs has facilitated the observation of their coincident, but unrelated, gamma-ray counterparts, marking the first time that a cataclysmic event has been used as a cosmological probe. These observations have led to the hypothesis that long-duration GRBs are associated with the observation of core-collapse supernovae. However, recent observations have shown that some short-duration GRBs do not have any associated supernovae and some long GRBs do not have an associated supernova, leaving open the possibility that at least some gamma-ray bursts arise from different phenomena.

In this paper, we construct a effective action for a (super)string propagating in an arbitrary (super)gravity including higher order curvature corrections. The action consists of two parts. The first part is the worldsheet (super)gravity action. The second part is the (super)string effective action, which is constructed by the duality relation. The duality relation relates the (super)gravity and the (super)string theories. We consider the case that the (super)gravity is derived from the (super)string effective action. Thus, the (super)string effective action is constrained by the (super)gravity. We consider the vacuum of the (super)string effective action with $\hat{\cal R}^2$ and $ \hat{\cal R}^{ab}\hat{\cal R}_{ab}$ corrections. The $\hat{\cal R}^2$ term is responsible for the cosmological constant, whereas the $ \hat{\cal R}^{ab}\hat{\cal R}_{ab}$ term is related to dark energy. Then we construct the (super)string effective action with these corrections. We show that the vacuum has the desired $\hat{\cal R}^2$ and $ \hat{\cal R}^{ab}\hat{\cal R}_{ab}$ corrections and the action is stable. The dynamical dilaton appears as a natural inclusion in the model. By varying the action with respect to the metric, we obtain a (super)gravity with a dynamical dilaton field. We discuss cosmological solutions.

A new unified description of ultra-relativistic hydrodynamics and MHD in an arbitrary magnetic field is derived using a relativistic thermal Riemann solver. For the first time, we resolve the coupled hydrodynamics, special relativistic heat conduction, general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, and Maxwell's equations in a single framework. We simulate a variety of extreme flow configurations including a non-linear ultra-relativistic shock, a relativistic two-dimensionalblast wave with strong magnetic field, a relativistic two-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, and a one-dimensional vortex seeded in two dimensions. Excellent agreement is obtained between our simulation results and special relativistic hydrodynamics, general relativistic MHD, and magnetic field evolution. This is the preprint version of the paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.09318.pdf The full paper is available from the link above.

Cosmic rays with energies greater than 10^{15} eV are believed to interact with the atmosphere of our planet and their fluxes are significantly diminished as compared to the fluxes at lower energies. The so-called "knee" in the energy spectrum of these cosmic rays is defined as the energy at which the differential flux becomes approximately constant. There are two conflicting hypotheses for the nature of this "knee". One hypothesis attributes the knee to a suppression of the spectral index of the cosmic ray energies observed by the experiments flying at lower altitudes, while the other argues that the knee is an actual change of the primary cosmic ray energy spectrum. To settle this dispute, it is important to have a method to determine the energy of primary cosmic rays with an adequate precision to either detect a change or determine if a suppression of the flux is present. The GAMMA (Gamma-ray Astronomy in the Initiative Era) experiment, designed for the detection of gamma-rays produced by cosmic ray interactions in the atmosphere, can contribute to this problem because, in contrast to most other cosmic ray experiments, it is able to measure the energy of primary cosmic rays with an absolute accuracy of approximately 30%. In this work, we present spectra of primary cosmic rays measured by the GAMMA experiment for four different rigidities of the experimental setup. We found that the differential flux of primary cosmic rays decreases with energy approximately according to a power law with an index of −2.59 at rigidities greater than 10^{18.5} eV/(γ-1), where γ is the Lorentz factor of the primary cosmic ray. For rigidities between 10^{18.5} and 10^{17.5} eV/(γ-1), the energy spectrum of cosmic rays starts to slowly flatten, indicating a possible change in the energy spectrum. However, the available statistics does not allow us to determine if the change is statistically significant.

After Einstein’s remarkable success in explaining the gravity force as Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (EGB) gravity, there has been a continuous effort to generalize the Lagrangian of gravity. Recently, higher order Lovelock Lagrangians were shown to be equivalent to particular choices of EGB gravity. This suggests that there may be an infinite number of theories of gravity that are consistent with general relativity (GR) at low energies but with different answers for some observable quantities. Such generalizations not only have the potential to address current cosmic coincidences (i.e., the current Hubble rate of the universe and its damping-like dark energy, is roughly equal to the expected value from the cosmic accident), but also could lead to qualitatively new phenomena and are amenable to observational tests. In this paper, we consider two generalizations of general relativity: Einstein-Lovelock gravity and Einstein-invariants gravity. We show that, for these theories, the vacuum cosmological solutions are equivalent to $R+\Lambda$ and $\mathcal{R}+\nabla_{\lambda}(\mathcal{R}\star \mathcal{R})$, respectively, where $\Lambda$ is a cosmological constant, and $\star$ is the Kernel convolution. The corresponding Friedmann equation, for Einsteint-Lovelock gravity, takes the form $H^2=\frac{\kappa}{3}(\rho_{m} + \rho_{de})$, where $H$ is the Hubble rate, $\kappa$ is Einstein’s constant, $\rho_{m}$ is the matter density, and $\rho_{de}$ is the dark energy density. In Einstein-invariants gravity, the Friedmann equation is of the form $H^2 = \frac{\kappa}{3} \rho_{c} + \frac{\Lambda}{3}$, where $\rho_{c}$ is the critical density, and $\Lambda$ is a cosmological constant. These results show that both classes of theories have the general form $f(R) + \Lambda$ and $f(\mathcal{R}) + \nabla_{\lambda}(f \star \mathcal{R})$, respectively, with arbitrary nonlinear functions $f$ of the scalar curvature. These are completely general and very appealing gravitational theories that may be useful to do away with fine-tuning and cosmic coincidence problems, and to give rise to additional observational signatures. We also discuss the physical significance of the critical density and potential cosmic singularities that may arise in these theories. We analyze the cosmological stability of these gravity theories in the presence of scalar perturbations and show that there exist stable solutions corresponding to $\Lambda$CDM models. Finally, we point out the existence of a correspondence between Hořava-Lifshitz gravity and a particular Einstein-Lovelock gravity theory, which provides a new point of view on Hořava gravity.

Brownian particles interacting via pair potentials often display complex nonequilibrium phenomena such as phase separation and condensation. While the equilibrium dynamical properties of these systems are well understood, this understanding in limited for non-equilibrium situations, in which the fluid phase and the aggregate phase can coexist, for example. Using diagrammatic techniques, we formulate the dynamics of such systems within the framework of kinetic theory. We then apply this approach to Brownian particles with short-ranged repulsion, for which an exact solution of the corresponding kinetic equation is available. As a case study, we consider the dynamics of a binary mixture of Brownian particles with different self-diffusivities. We find a qualitative change in the decay of density fluctuations at intermediate times, with an initial power-law decay followed by a decay towards an equilibrium oscillatory state. Our results provide new perspectives for analyzing the dynamics of interacting Brownian particles and highlight the utility of diagrammatic methods in the analysis of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.' -- This paper presents a diagrammatic approach to the dynamical properties of interacting Brownian particles. Using this approach, we are able to derive dynamical evolution equations for the one-particle irreducible (1PI) Green's functions, which encode the non-local correlation functions of the system. This formulation is advantageous in that it allows one to employ diagrammatic techniques in the systematic evaluation of dynamical response and correlation functions. As an example, we apply this approach to the dynamics of a binary mixture of Brownian particles with different self-diffusivities. We find a qualitative change in the decay of density fluctuations at intermediate times, with an initial power-law decay followed by a decay towards an equilibrium oscillatory state. Our results provide new perspectives for analyzing the dynamics of interacting Brownian particles and highlight the utility of diagrammatic methods in the analysis of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

Near a superconductor–normal-state quantum phase transition, the dynamical scaling form of the finite temperature resistivity is where β and γ are non-universal metric factors, ω/T is the reduced frequency, T is the temperature, and f(x) is a universal function. For temperatures above the superconducting dome, μ(T) exhibits a minimum, which has been ascribed to quantum criticality. Here we show that the resistivity exhibits a sequence of temperature crossovers as a function of reduced temperature t=T/Tc, where Tc is the superconducting dome's critical temperature. At high t, μ(T) decreases as T2; at intermediate t, it decreases as T; and at low t, μ(T) increases as T2. At low temperature, μ(T) decreases as T4, instead of T2, as predicted by the quantum-critical theory of spin-fluctuation superconductivity. The intervening temperature crossovers cannot be explained by the theory of pair-breaking quantum criticality, which does not distinguish different regions of t. We develop an effective field theory of fermionic charge fluctuations near the quantum critical point, and show that its predictions accurately capture the resistivity over three decades in temperature. The theory establishes a firm basis for the existence of fermionic quantum criticality in cuprates and other correlated superconductors.

Relativistic collisionless shocks mediate intense bursts of energy release in extreme astrophysical sites, including Active Galactic Nuclei and Gamma-Ray Bursts. These shocks generate a complex plasma composed of thermal electrons and ions, as well as several non-thermal populations of electrons and positrons. Understanding the physical processes at work in these collisionless shocks is essential to characterizing the associated astrophysical phenomena, as well as for the development of efficient particle acceleration mechanisms. In particular, these plasmas are unstable to the trapping of magnetic fields within the shock precursor, leading to the generation of magnetic turbulence. Using first-principles plasma kinetic theory, we perform a long-termevolution study of relativistic collisionless electron-positron shocks, considering the nonlinear interactions of unstable magnetic turbulence. In contrast to previously studied magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) shocks, we find a direct scaling between the evolution of the relativistic collisionless shock and the energy injection rates of the non-linear turbulent cascade. By analytically incorporating cyclotron splitting and quantum drift effects, we are able to capture the full turbulent nonlinear dynamics. In particular, we find that the resulting electron-positron pair distribution function is well-described by a truncated Lenard-Balescu equation of motion, which we use to perform a statistical characterization of the resulting turbulent fluctuations. We also explore the nature and characteristics of the energetically important populations of trapped particles, namely the lab-frame equivalent of the Weibel-like electrostatic fluctuations produced by the nonlinear turbulence. By contrast to Weibel filaments, these fluctuations are predominantly magnetic in nature. We find that these magnetic filaments contribute significantly to the acceleration of non-thermal particles within the shock precursor, and argue that this constitutes an additional major non-MHD-diffusive mechanism in these systems. Finally, we discuss the astrophysical implications of our findings, and suggest new diagnostic signatures for the detailed study of collisionless shocks in the astrophysical context.

The serendipitous XMM-Newton survey has recently been published by@_alexander_et_al_2016. It contains 1750 X-ray sources and more than 1100 unique sources were identified in the soft (0.5-2keV) band and 500 in the hard (2-10keV) band. Motivated by their findings, we performed a comprehensive analysis of the 250 X-ray sources with off-nuclear optical spectra. We identified 31 quasars, 52 AGN, 25 massive Young Stellar Objects (YSOs), 68 galaxies, 5 radio galaxies, and 10 unclassified sources. We also report one X-ray active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) that has neither been classified as a quasar nor a galaxy, and discuss the possibility that this could be an elusive quasar. This elusive quasar is XMMXCS J1121590.4+4140253, hereafter XCS 1122, and has an optical magnitude of i=20.15 which is among the i-band brightest sources in the XMM-Newton field. We discuss the nature of this source and argue that it could be a heavily obscured quasar with a minor merger event. This would be an example of highly obscured, rapidly growing black holes and highlight the necessity to explore the properties of the XCS 1122 optical counterpart.

In this paper, we investigate the theoretical status of $B_s$-mixing and lifetimes of heavy hadrons. The latest lattice QCD calculations indicate that the branching fraction of $B_s$ meson into two mesons, $B_s \rightarrow (D^+ \pi^-, D^- \pi^+)$, is in tension with the standard model (SM) prediction by 3.5 sigma. The $B_s$-mixing phenomena can be explained by rescattering and hadronic effects with small hadronic parameters, but the uncertainties from these assumptions are not well understood. The lifetime of $B_s$ meson can be measured precisely in the decay processes $B_s \rightarrow J/\psi \phi$, which can be used to test the standard model prediction and the hadronic effect scenarios of $B_s$-mixing. We perform a global analysis of $B_s$-mixing and lifetime using the most recent data, and obtain the most precise predictions of $B_s \rightarrow (D^+ \pi^-, D^- \pi^+)$ and $B_s$ meson lifetimes. Our results show that the measurements of $B_s \rightarrow (D^+ \pi^-, D^- \pi^+)$ and $B_s$ meson lifetimes can significantly reduce the uncertainties of hadronic parameters, and can help to determine the sources of $B_s$-mixing and clarify the hadronic effects of $B_s$-mixing.

High-temperature superconductors exhibit a complex phase diagram with multiple competing orders. Theoretically, it has been difficult to reconcile various experimental observations using a single model. Here, we propose a model of high-temperature superconductivity based on the SU(4) symmetry for four components of critical fields. This model allows for a variety of experiments to be qualitatively explained, including the suppression of magnetic order by a momentum dependent pairing interaction, the appearance of d-wave symmetry of the superconducting order parameter, and a neutron scattering resonance at wavevectors connecting four rounded Fermi surfaces that are themselves composed of small warped spheres. Several theoretical predictions are directly testable with current technology. GG Tau is a nearby (d= 2.2 pc) multiple system that contains at least five infrared sources (D'Alessio et al. 2005) and has been modelled as a circumbinary ring system (White et al. 2004). Radial optical cuts of the GG Tau system show three separate rings of dust that are radially stratified, with the inner and outer rings extending from the midplane of the system to a radius of 20 and 40 AU, respectively. In this work, we investigate the possibility that the dust in the middle ring is dynamically linked to the binary system, as suggested by White et al. (2004). We use ALMA observations of the CO v = 2-1 line at a spatial resolution of 12.8 x 4.8 AU to estimate the radial velocity dispersion of the gas within the ring. We find that the dust and gas kinematics are consistent with each other within the errors, suggesting that the dust and gas in the ring are dynamically coupled. Based on the Toomre parameter and gravitational stability criteria, the observed ring radius and temperature are consistent with a population of planetesimals whose ephemeris is maintained by an external perturber. We investigate whether the outer ring is externally disturbed by calculating the mutual gravitational interaction between the two rings and find that the observed offset between the dust peaks is insufficient to maintain the observed ring structure. However, if the GG Tau system has an additional component in a nearly counter-clockwise orbit with a semi-major axis of 210 AU and a current projected separation of 20 AU, we find that the system is unstable over timescales of 100 Myr. We therefore suggest that the outer dust ring is a co-planar companion to the GG Tau circumbinary ring system, as previously proposed by Guilloteau et al. (2013).

In this paper, we consider the effect of Lorentz-violating massive gravity in the Einstein-Hilbert action coupled to a standard model Higgs field. We show that the sum of the graviton and theaxion modes describe a massive spin-2 field with Lorentz-violating interactions. We show that for a sufficiently large value of the graviton mass, these Lorentz-violating interactions become dominant and Bigravity theory emerges. We calculate the vacuum expansion rate and the effective mass of this theory and show that the latter can account for the present expansion of the universe. In this paper we report inelastic neutron scattering measurements of spin fluctuations in underdoped YBa2Cu3O6.35. We find that the spin-fluctuation self-energy exhibits a well defined dispersion in the flat region of the pseudogap with no sign of a separate mode at theAFM, or AFM. Moreover, the width of the peak in the imaginary part of the self-energy remains nearly constant from 50 meV to 200 meV, far above the energy scale of the magnetic transition at Tc. We argue that the observed behavior is consistent with a two-dimensional (2D) spin-fluctuation system, with interaction-driven spin pseudogap of magnitude 50 meV, much greater than the mean-field superconducting gap of 7 meV. The normal state of high temperature superconductors exhibits several distinct behaviors depending on the temperature vs. the doping level. At high temperature, well above the superconducting transition temperature Tc, most of the materials exhibit metallic behavior and simple Fermi liquid theory applies. At intermediate temperatures, known as the pseudogap phase, the quantum oscillations only reveal an hole-like Fermi surface, while angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) observations of the electronic structure give evidence of an electron-like Fermi surface. Moreover, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and neutron scattering experiments reveal a temperature-dependent anomalous relaxation behavior. Most interestingly, superconductivity suddenly appears at low temperature as the doping is reduced through a second order phase transition. The phase diagram is well summarized in the "Uemura plot"1: the correlation length of the fluctuating magnetic order increases rapidly with decreasing temperature until it becomes comparable to the Cu-O bond length at Tc. The system becomes superconducting, and the phase diagram becomes simple and consistent with the superconducting phase ending in a critical point at the edge of the magnetically ordered region. In contrast to this well understood behavior above Tc, the normal state behavior below Tc in the underdoped regime is not well understood and there are still many open questions. In particular, while it is well established that the nature of the low temperature phase changes abruptly across the critical doping level x* (for a review see 2), the exact behavior of the normal state below Tc in the underdoped regime remains controversial. In particular, whereas for x* < x the normal state in UD8923 is widely thought to exhibit Fermi liquid behavior characterized by well defined quasiparticles with an energy gap ( pseudogap phenomenon), for x* > x there is growing evidence that the normal state may not be well characterized by a Fermi liquid theory (see 3 and references therein). Evidence includes unusual properties of the magnetic susceptibility and NMR relaxation rate

A unified shear-thinning treatment of both film thickness and traction is presented for Oldroyd-B fluid, which is of fundamental importance to many industrial and biological systems. The proposed theory not only unifies the existing theoretical treatments for both film thickness and traction in a single theory, but also allows one to study the effect of rheology on the film dynamics, which is not possible with previous theories. Furthermore, the proposed theory is general enough to be applied to a wide range of film dynamics including viscous and capillary draining, linearly and weakly contractive films as well as viscoelastic films with or without stress relaxation. As an example, we consider a free-standing viscous film drainage on a vibrating plate, and validate the proposed theory by comparing the simulation results with the available experimental data. Furthermore, we discuss the possible relevance of the present theory in a stabilized float-Switch configuration, where a heavier film can be stabilized on a lighter liquid.

In the cut-off approximation to the BCS theory of superconductivity, the energy gap, $\Delta$, is proportional to the ultraviolet momentum cutoff, $\Lambda$. In this paper, we present a new interpretation of $\Delta$ in the cut-off approximation. In the language of Nambu formalism, the energy gap, $\Delta$, represents the energy required to break a Cooper pair into two separated fermions. The proposed interpretation of $\Delta$ differs from the existing interpretations in the literature in that it is related to the energy required to break a Cooper pair, and it does not require ultraviolet regularization. We test the proposed interpretation of $\Delta$ in the cut-off approximation by comparing the results of the numerical renormalization group calculation of the momentum dependence of the energy gap with the prediction of the cut-off approximation. The comparison shows good agreement between the two for the case where the ultraviolet cutoff is much larger than the size of the superconducting gap.

In this paper, we consider three agent games in extensive form, where the number of agents is greater than two. The first game is the classic Chicken game, in which players choose between cooperating and defecting. The second is a variant of the hawk-dove game in which players are partitioned into two groups and each group alternately chooses between protecting a shared dove or a Hawk. The third is a multiplayer prisoner's dilemma game in which each player chooses between cooperating and defecting. We present conditions for stability of mixed strategies and the existence of pure strategy Nash equilibria. We provide sufficient conditions for stability of mixed strategies, as well as necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of pure strategy Nash equilibria. Our main techniques are coupling and projective stability. We illustrate our results with examples and simulations. The analysis in this paper extends to general games with more than three players. However, to keep the discussion within the limits of this abstract, we confine our attention to the case of three players. In the first game, we show that the unique mixed strategy Nash equilibrium is pure if and only if a related matrix is diagonally dominant. Using this characterisation, we show that when the related matrix is diagonally dominant, the unique mixed strategy Nash equilibrium is pure if and only if at least one player strongly prefers the pure strategy. We present a numerical example to illustrate our main theorem. In the second game, we show that there is a pure strategy Nash equilibrium for all player partitions if and only if the related matrix is diagonally dominant. We illustrate this result by means of a numerical example. In the third game, we show that the pure strategy Nash equilibria are precisely the fixed points of an operator, which we also describe. We show that this operator is contractive and apply this result to show that the pure strategy Nash equilibria are convergence to a unique fixed point. We illustrate our results with a numerical example. Finally, we examine convergence rates for all of the above results. This work was funded by the Australian Research Council (Discovery Projects 170101319 and 170100213).

Gaussian valence bond (GVBS) states provide an alternative way of representing quantum spin chains to the famous valence bond states. Entanglement properties of the valence bond states has been investigated in many literature. However, optical realization of the Gaussian valence bond states has not been reported yet. In this letter, we propose a scheme to generate Gaussian valence bond states using linear optics and spontaneous parametric down-conversion. The proposed scheme can be realized within current technology and has the advantage of high efficiency. Entanglement distillation protocol is also proposed to improve the fidelity of the Gaussian valence bond states. The entanglement verification of the Gaussian valence bond states is performed by measuring two-mode squeezed states, which can be realized using the same optical elements as the Gaussian valence bond states. We also discuss how to perform local operations to produce Gaussian cluster states for quantum computation. The proposal is suitable for current experimental technology and has a potential to be implemented in the future.

The cluster Blanco 1, in the direction of the Chamaeleon star-forming region at a distance of 120-150 pc, was identified by Béjar et al. (2004) as a young open cluster with an estimated age of about 10-30 million years. The masses of its low-mass members have not been directly measured. In this work we estimate the masses of the 10-3 Mjup substellar members with the combination of adaptive optics imaging in the infrared and high-precision radial velocities. We derive a lower mass function of n(m) ~ m^ - 1.5, with a median value of 0.088 Mjup, i.e., 7% of the cluster mass. This is the deepest exploration to date of the substellar regime in a young cluster. The cluster Blanco 1 contains low-mass members from 30 Mjup down to the substellar domain, with a median value of 0.088 Mjup. The lower mass function is n(m) ~ m^ - 1.5.

The competition of hydrogen-like and isotropic interactions on polymer collapse is studied with a simple off-lattice model. A polymer chain in a good solvent is described by a self-avoiding walk on a lattice, with nearest neighbor interactions of both hydrogen-like (repulsive) and isotropic (neutral) kinds. It is found that there is a critical temperature below which the polymer collapses into a compact structure. This collapse is initiated by the isotropic interactions, which induce more compact structures than the hydrogen-like interactions. However, once the compact structures are formed, the hydrogen-like interactions further stabilize them against decay into separated coils. The consequences of these findings are discussed in the context of the stability of DNA in a cell. History and Motivation Since the advent of polymer physics (1949) it was realized that the entropy of a polymer chain in solution decreases with decreasing its radius of gyration, and that this decrease becomes maximal at a certain minimal value of the radius of gyration. This phenomenon was named "enthalpic stabilization" of polymer chains and it led the way to a new branch of polymer physics: thermodynamical biology. But why should a polymer chain have a finite radius of gyration at all? The entropy of a long chain (its extension being much larger than its radius of gyration) decreases with the square of its radius of gyration, because its effective linear dimension decreases like the cube of its radius of gyration. That is why the radius of gyration is a small number: the chain has to be "globular" to decrease its entropy. Therefore, a globular polymer (with a minimal value of its radius of gyration) is also called "compact" polymer. Biology Thermodynamical biology was the first attempt to use physics concepts to describe biological mechanisms. Because the early 1970s, this approach lead to a first table of correspondence between concepts in polymer physics and in biological parlance. A landmark was the so-called "Flory's hypothesis" from 1971: the so-called persistence length of a polymer is the parameter which best describe its folding, that is to say the correlation between neighbouring atoms in its primary and higher dimensional structures. The persistence length of a polymer is proportional to the inverse of its radius of gyration. This led to the conclusion that the folding of biological molecules such as DNA or proteins should be stabilized by an enthalpic mechanism: a new research field was born called "protein thermodynamics". However, at the end of the 20th century, it was realized that the persistence length is not really a folding parameter. Other parameters had to be introduced to characterize folding, and in particular a so-called " contact order ". It was also realized that the folding of proteins and nucleic acids is an entropic process, stabilized by the release of conformational heat. This "floppiness" is also due to an enthalpic stabilization: a negative non-bonded potential

Allovalency, the valency of an atom or molecule by a multisite attachment, is an important concept in chemistry, physics and biology. Aromatic molecules such as benzene only allow single attachment (bifurcated attachment is forbidden by symmetry) and consequently only allow a valency of 2. However, a multisite attachment is possible in many other molecules such as porphyrins and protein kinases. Such molecules with higher valencies exhibit non-classical reactivity. For example, haem proteins such as cytochrome c which participate in electron transfer reactions have a valency of 4. In this study, we analyze a protein kinase, casein kinase II, with a valency of 7, by treating it as a multisite attachment. Our method of analysis is based on the Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approximation which is applicable to reactions with highlyvalent molecules. First, we calculate the entropy of the multisite attachment using the Savage formula. Then, we analyse the flux term, an expression which governs the flux of electrons into the reaction from the reactants, in the WKB approximation. We find that despite a high valency, the kinase follows the common substrate-in-vesicle model for electron flow. As the entropy increase is quadratic in the valency, it can be very high in multisite reactions. Nevertheless, such reactions occur in biological systems in an ordered fashion, governed by the laws of thermodynamics.

This paper is an theoretical analysis of non-Markovian dynamics of two-mode entanglement of continuous variable systems in thermal environments. We consider both Lorentzian and non-Lorentzian noise to model the non-Markovian effect, and derive analytic solutions for two-mode entanglement under the influence of colored noise. We find that the entanglement becomes maximum at some temperature and then decreases to zero gradually when the temperature increases. In addition, we also study the sudden death and sudden birth of two-mode entanglement, and find that these processes are related to the minimum and maximum temperatures, respectively. Our results may be helpful in designing accurate detection schemes for non-Markovian environments and studying the relationships among the non-Markovian effect, temperature, and quantum entanglement award I. The model and solution for two-mode entanglement A. Consider two quantum harmonic oscillators with annihilation operators a1 and a2 and creation operators a1* and a2*. The Hamiltonian of the system is H = ω1(a1†a1 + a1a1*) + ω2(a2†a2 + a2a2*) - λ(a1†a2 + a2†a1), where λ is the coupling strength. The corresponding Heisenberg equation can be written as da1/dt = −ω1 a1 − λ a2*, da2/dt = ω2 a2 + λ a1*, where ∂/∂t = −i H. For the system initialized in the vacuum state |00> = (0, 0)^T, the time evolution of two-mode entanglement can be obtained as Sneg<--Spos, where Sneg = |N neg|2− |N pos|2, Spos = |P neg|2− |P pos|2, N(t) = cos(θ/2) a1(t) a2*(t) + sin(θ/2) a1*(t) a2(t), P(t) = sin(θ/2) a1(t) a2*(t) − cos(θ/2) a1*(t) a2(t), θ = arctan [2λ/(ω2 − ω1)], with |N(t)|2 + |P(t)|2 = 1. For Sneg>0, the time-dependent two-mode entanglement decreases to zero gradually when t→∞. B. A combined density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and cluster embedding approach is employed to study the electronic transport through a single level quantum dot (QD) with non-ideal boundaries. The transport properties of the QD are investigated as a function of the coupling between the left and right leads, the energy of the attached molecular orbitals, the level position and the degree of ploymathicity. The computed currents show good quantitative agreement with recent experiments on self-assembled InAs quantum dots. We also discuss the evolution of the underlying states as the coupling to the leads is varied. In general, we find that the nature of the Kondo state is preserved, however, a finite-bias splitting emerges between the molecular and conduction band states due to the finite-bias phase of the corresponding Kondo state. In addition, we discuss the spectral function which is computed for the open quantum system. We find that for broad and non-symmetrical coupling to the leads, resonant transport through a bound state in the continuum (BISC) occurs. Furthermore, we show that the dynamical quantum dot charge fluctuations can be extracted from the current noise spectrum.

A binary quantum search algorithm, operating on a database of size n, examines each item in the database, one at a time, until a specific item is located. The algorithm uses only elementary operations on a two-level quantum computer, requiring at most √n elementary operations total. This is optimal, up to a constant factor. Furthermore, the algorithm only makes use of the first n/2 bits of each entry in the database, requiring only one ancilla bit. Thus, it should be possible to implement the algorithm using present day technologies. It is widely believed that quantum computers with coherence times on the order of minutes are needed for this algorithm to have practical value. The algorithm, described by Bernstein and Holenstein in "A quantum speed up for the binary search", Computers and Chemistry, 31(14): 2484-2486, 2007, is as follows. Let index i be the number of items in the database that are not the target. The initial state of the database is uniform superposition { 1 / √n, − 1 / √n } n. The quantum search begins by applying Hadamard transformation to each entry in the database. The resulting state is { 1 / √n, 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, − 1 / √n } n. Next, we apply a Hadamard transformation to the ancilla bit, which in superposition gives { 1 / √n, 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, 1 / √n, 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, − 1 / √n } n. Finally, we apply the quantum search operation controlled not (CNOT) to the target bit and the database ancilla bit. The resulting state is { 1 / √n, 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, 1 / √n, 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, − 1 / √n, 1 / √n } n. Perform phase estimation on the target bit and output the estimated phase. If the target is not in the database, the estimated phase will be 0. If the target is in the database, the estimated phase will be pi. For a database of size n, this algorithm requires at most √n elementary operations. This is optimal, up to a constant factor. Furthermore, the algorithm only uses the first n/2 bits of each entry in the database, requiring only one ancilla bit. Thus, it should be possible to implement the algorithm using present day technologies.

The purpose of this short note is to introduce an equivariant cohomology theory for twisted generalized complex manifolds, which we call twisted generalized complex equivariant cohomology. We construct this theory as a homotopy quotient, constructing a homotopy elliptic defined functor from a stable model category of twisted generalized complex manifolds to spectra. We then prove that the homotopy groups of this spectrum give the desired cohomology theory. Our main result is the introduction of an equivariant version of the Deligne class, which is an element of twisted generalized complex equivariant cohomology theories. We use this Deligne class to show that the twisted generalized complex analogue of the Thom class is a universal Thom class for twisted generalized complex bundles. One can think of twisted generalized complex manifolds as complex manifolds equipped with a (complex) structure and a Borel-Serre sheaf of generalized complex structures. The Borel-Serre sheaf equips twisted generalized complex manifolds with a holomorphic volume form and thus facilitates the definition of twisted generalized complex equivariant cohomology. We construct this theory as a homotopy quotient of a version of the classical Deligne cohomology theory adapted to the generalized complex setting.

In this paper we consider the on-line shortest path problem under partial monitoring, where the process of generating the online shortest path algorithm may be observed by a remote observer, but the algorithm itself is not revealed to the observer. We propose a new dynamic programming algorithm for this problem, and prove that the algorithm generated by our algorithm is equivalent to the optimal algorithm for the case where the observer has full access to the decision process of the algorithm. We also provide experimental results that demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm on a variety of network topologies. In the full monitoring setting, where the algorithm and the decisions it makes are revealed to the observer, dynamic programming is known to be an efficient method for solving the on-line shortest path problem. However, when the decision process is hidden from the observer, it is in general not possible to obtain a clean separation between the dynamic program that generates the algorithm, and the algorithm itself. This setting is commonly referred to as the partial monitoring problem, and it has been shown to be at least as hard as approximation of MAXSNP.

In this paper we present a new method for determining the workspace of parallel manipulators. As we know, a parallel manipulator can be model as a collection of point- masses connected by virtual rods. A rotation and translation of the whole assembly, corresponds to a unique transformation of the virtual rods and point- masses. But in the workspace of a parallel manipulator, there are pairs of corresponding points, which means that for a same set of rotations and translations of the joints, there are two different configurations of the virtual rods. These pairs of corresponding points induce singularities in the workspace, which we call uniqueness domains. In this work, we present a method to detect these uniqueness domains with 6 joints, by determining the singularity of the jacobian of the virtual-rod-to-joint-configurations mapping. Then, we propose a method to reduce the number of singularity points, by merging the uniqueness domains with an appropriate geometrical operation. We also propose a method to automatically determine this geometrical operation. We present the efficiency of the presented approach with an experimental validation on a 6 joints robot.

We study the migration of star formation sites from z = 0.8 to z = 0.4 in the GALEX Arecibo SDSS LOWZ sample using restframe ultra-violet selected galaxies from the Canada-France- Hawaii Lensing Survey (CFHTLS) and the GALEX Arecibo SDSS UV Luminosity survey (GALEX Arecibo SDSS). We select galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts in the range z = 0.8-0.4 and construct spatially contiguous groups of galaxies with overlapping redshift intervals of 0.4 each. These “blocks” are used to examine the frequency of spatial groupings of star-forming galaxies at z = 0.8, 0.6, 0.4 and 0.2. We find that at z = 0.8 a quarter of all galaxies are in spatially contiguous groups with other star-forming galaxies. By z = 0.2 this fraction is only seven percent. These results suggest that much of the star formation occurring in massive galaxies in the local Universe was triggered by major mergers at higher redshifts.

A computer program AFINN (for fast non-LTE analysis of interstellar line spectra) is presented. It can compute excitation and ionization equilibria for arbitrary distributions of atoms and molecules, including the treatment of diatomic molecular species by the discrete dipole approximation. The equilibrium solutions are found by an updated Newton-Raphson procedure which preserves validity of the solution in the sense of the overall conservation of the particle number density, the total energy, and the total momentum, together with accuracy requirements for a selected set of molecular lines. The procedure is stopped when the specified accuracy is reached. The newly developed formula for the energy transfer in the lines and a simple approximation for the radiative rate distribution corrections are found to be essential for an adequate convergence of the solutions even in strongly nonequilibrium cases.
