The market capitalization weighted price of 20 emerging market stocks average daily close time series are analyzed between 2004 and 2014. First, the distribution of each stock is obtained by using normal distribution fit. The distribution pairs of each stock are then pooled according to both qualitative and quantitative measures. The method of nonlinear time series analysis is applied to the resulting distribution pairs. It is shown that a long-term memory factor appears in the cumulative distribution function (cdf) of each emerging market stock, which means the future price trend of a stock is dependent on its recent past trend, regardless of its volatility level. Based on these cdf results, a novel index, named the Emerging Market Long-Term Memory (EMLTM) index, is introduced to measure the collective memory of emerging market stocks. It is shown that the EMLTM is a good predictor for future stock returns with a significance level of 0.1% in both emerging and developed markets. The EMLTM is also compared with three typical stochastic correlation-based indices, i.e. Market Capitalization Weighted Average Daily Closing Price, realized indexes and weighted realized indexes. It is found that the EMLTM outperforms the three indices in terms of both goodness-of-fit and forecasting performance in emerging markets.

This paper presents a method to detect faults in a reactor using data from online sensors and a machine learning algorithm. The method is demonstrated on a plasma etch reactor which has several hundred sensors. The sensors generate time series with signals from different aspects of the reactor. Some of the sensors are binary, indicating if a specific condition was met or not. A time series of length N is split into overlapping chunks of length K. One chunk is used for training a machine learning algorithm which produces a fault classification model. The model is evaluated on the withheld chunk from validation-set. If the error on validation-set is less than a chosen error-threshold, the model is evaluated on the withheld test-set and the accuracy of the model is the score of this experiment. A persistent model is then trained using the validation-set error and model evaluation results from the test-set. The persistent model is then applied to detect new faults in the reactor.

Herbig Ae/Be (HAEBE) stars are intermediate mass pre-main sequence stars. Like Classical T Tauri stars (CTTS), HAEBE stars drive extreme ultraviolet (EUV) ionized winds which are detectable in the form of optical forbidden lines such as [He I] or [Fe II]. However, HAEBE winds are typically much faster, more highly collimated and more optically thin than those of CTTS. IRAS 18511+0146 is one of the brightest HAEBE stars in the constellation of Camelopardalis and it is catalogued in several infrared catalogs under the names V1952 Cam, IRAS 18511+0154 and 2MASS J19443118+1412418. Previous studies have characterized this star as an active fast rotator. Using optical spectroscopy we find that this star also has a high degree of magnetic activity, showing a strong [ He I] wind which is detected up to a heliocentric radial velocity of +300 km/s. We determine a mass loss rate of 2.2×10-4 M⊙/yr, which is one order of magnitude higher than what is typically observed in HAEBE stars. We therefore argue that IRAS 18511+0146 is likely a young pre-main sequence star rather than an evolved star, and that its extreme coronal activity and fast rotation are likely the result of a recent dynamical encounter.

NVII is one of the several molecular lines observed by the satellite-borne infrared spectrometer Hyperion. Based on an analytic line profile calculated for an isothermal slab of gas at million degree, we have searched for such gas within the Milky Way's ISM, and found it toward three dark molecular clouds: Serpens South, Vela Jr. II, and NGC 1333. The column densities we have derived for these clouds are consistent with those predicted by models of isothermal gas at million degree. The clouds' non-thermal linewidths, on the other hand, are roughly an order of magnitude less, suggesting that these gas-rich regions are undergoing "willful" collapse. The research described in this paper was performed while the author was a guest scientist at Caltech. The full paper is available from: https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.05544 Thank you for your interest in my work. I hope you enjoy reading it as much as I enjoyed writing it. best regards, Zachary Quinto Zachary Quinto ADDENDUM Based on the feedback I have received, I would like to add some clarifications about the paper. First, the results presented in the paper are based on a specific model of gas at million degrees, and the results are only valid under this model. The model itself is still an hypothesis, which needs to be tested against observations. Second, I am a physicist, not an astrophysicist, so I did not perform the observations mentioned in the paper. The data for this paper was taken by the Spacecraft Herschel, which was launched in May of 2009. The scientists then analyzed the data and published the results in scientific journals. My job was to explain the physics behind the results, which I believe I have done effectively.

Realizable Hamiltonians are proposed for universal adiabatic quantum computers. In contrast to earlier proposals, our Hamiltonians can be implemented with near-term quantum devices. We consider a general setup with a target unitary to realize and an adiabatic evolution over a time period T. The generated Hamiltonian is allowed to have any term supported on the eigenstates of the initial Hamiltonian, and thus in general cannot be expressed as a sum of bilinears of the form {|,i}H{i,}{,}. We present a general framework to prove that the final Hamiltonian is realizable for the given target unitary, subject to certain regularity conditions. For a special case when the final Hamiltonian is also a sum of bilinears of the above form, we show that the realization can be obtained via gadgets composed of qubit transverters and clusters of surface gates. For a more general case, we provide explicit constructions based on Kitaev’s quantum double model and its adaption for surface codes. We analyze the performance of the resulting Hamiltonians via the Taylor series expansion. In particular, we show that the gap of the resulting Hamiltonian closes at the order of 1/T2, which means the gap closes exponentially at the best rate T−2. This observation implies that for a universal T, the corresponding quantum computer still requires an infinite power of quantum seed state in the starting Hamiltonian to compensate for the error accumulation. We conclude by discussing possible ways forward, which may potentially address the error accumulation and improve the performance of the resulting adiabatic quantum computers.

A singular foliation on a smooth closed manifold is called Morse if all of its leaves are free of singularities. Smooth Morse foliations with stably ergodic Reeb flow appear as transverse structures to some symplectic structures on cotangent bundles of closed manifolds. We study the stable ergodicity of the Reeb flow. Using spectral decomposition of the differential of the basic Reeb flow, we show that the stable ergodicity depends on the symplectic structure and it is unstable when the symplectic structure has some specific pattern. We construct some specific examples of smooth Morse foliations with non-stably ergodic Reeb flow. This article is an addendum to my previous article [1], where the same results have been established for a larger class of foliations. [1] Hanemin Yang, Volker Demuth, and Zhe Wang, A Morse singularity with non-Morse stable ergodicity, https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.05817

In this paper, we study a special case of the quantum walk in which the probabilities of the walker stepping to the left and right are both biased by a factor of alpha in one direction. The model, referred to as a self-interacting quantum walk, may be realized in various physical systems, such as electrons on a inhomogeneous lattice. We consider a general initial condition, allowing the walker to have any fractional part, and prove that the quantum walker will settle in finite time into a pure quantum state with real eigenvalue density equal to 1. We also consider the classical analogous of this walk, where at each time step, the walker may choose to step to the left or right with some probability. While the classical walk is transient in general, we prove that for sufficiently small alpha, the classical walk will always settle into a periodic configuration. We present a numerical simulation of the time-dependent behavior of both the quantum and classical self-interacting walks. As a further application of our techniques, we prove that the quantum walk converges in distribution to the classical walk. Additionally, we study two measures of mixing time: a quantum version of the quantum return localisation, and a classical version of the Klein gas correction. Finally, we present a large deviation analysis of the classical self-interacting walk and show that the walker is most likely to end up in a finite number of cells.'

In this letter, we present a systematic analysis of a spin-susceptibility representation of the pairing interaction in the two-dimensional (2D) Hubbard model. We establish that this representation is closely related to the channel decomposition of the interaction in this model and can be straightforwardly extended to the case of arbitrary spatial dimensions. To illustrate the power of this approach we apply it to derive a complete family of effective pairing interactions for the 2D Hubbard model. For infinitesimal coupling, we show that our results reduce to the form previously proposed by us and by Kuroki and Aimi. Our numerical results for intermediate coupling demonstrate that our proposed family of interactions yields greatly improved results over the previously known forms and, in particular, yields results very close to those of cluster perturbation theory for the 2D Hubbard model. The key idea of our approach is to recast the pairing problem in the space of spin susceptibilities. The pairing interaction is then represented as a linear functional of the spin susceptibilities that, by definition, is zero when acting on any symmetric tensor built out of Fermi-surface spin susceptibilities. This leads to a systematic procedure for constructing an interaction that can correctly describe a pairing instability. This approach is appealing since it can be naturally generalized to higher dimensions and therefore allows for a straightforward extension to cases beyond the 2D Hubbard model, such as the recently discovered class of materials known as Five- layered iridates.

The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is an dwarf galaxy satellite of the Milky Way, approximately 163,000 light years (56,000 kpc) away from the Galactic Center. The LMC has a distinct halo of neutral hydrogen gas that extends for many tens of thousands of parsecs (about 160 kpc). Studying the distribution and characteristics of this neutral hydrogen gas can give us insights into the formation and evolution of the LMC, its halo and the surrounding intergalactic medium (IGM). Previous catalogs of the LMC neutral hydrogen gas have been based on single dish telescopes with small fields of view. In this work we present a new catalog of LMC neutral hydrogen clouds using the MeerKAT radio telescope. This is the largest and most sensitive catalog of LMC neutral hydrogen clouds to date, and will be useful for studies of the LMC impact on the IGM and the structure and evolution of the Local Group.

Theoretical studies of dynamical systems provide insights into many physical, chemical and biological processes. An excellent example is the harmonic oscillator which describes the resonant behaviour of a driven system coupled to a linear force. In Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) atoms subjected to harmonic driving, the problem is mathematically identical but additionally complicated by nonlinear interactions. The Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation describes the condensate wave function and it is useful to reduce the problem to that of a nonlinear Schrödinger equation. This is usually done by performing a slowly varying amplitude approximation. The resulting equation, known as the Stuart-Landau equation, is analytically tractable and has been used to describe a diverse range of phenomena, including the existence and stability of exact analytic solutions. We present such exact analytic solutions in the form of spatiotemporal wave packets which, in the absence of disorder, are found to be unstable. By adding harmonic trapping and dissipation terms, we show that the system can be stabilized, and that such wave packets can be made stable via the addition of disorder. This disorder may be realised through a random perturbation to the coefficients of the Stuart-Landau equation. We demonstrate this by calculating the average wave packet properties for many realizations of the disorder. Using this approach, we can engineer the condensate to have wave packet mobility. Finally, we provide a guide to the rich variety of phenomena that can be realised using the GP equation with driving.

Using the Submillimeter Array, we have mapped the H$_2$D$^+$ $J = 1 - 0$ emission from a sample of 14 Class 0 and I protostars with high angular resolution (0.4-2.3 au at the median distance of our sample; i.e., comparable to the disk radii). We detect emission from ten sources and present observations of two new prestellar cores where we detect H$_2$D$^+$ emission for the first time. The emission appears in elongated structures with large deconvolved widths, indicating that the H$_2$D$^+$ is arising in shock-heated gas. We detect H$_2$D$^+$ emission from both regions that drive powerful molecular outflows and from more quiescent environments. The outflow-enriched sources tend to have brighter H$_2$D$^+$ emission and higher molecular depletion factors, suggesting that shocks heat and destroy H$_2$D$^+$ more efficiently in those environments. In contrast, the envelope-only source HH212 has weak H$_2$D$^+$ emission despite having an edge-on disk with substantial mass. We present two possible explanations for this discrepancy: (i) the quiescent core from which HH212 formed had low amounts of presolar material; or (ii) the H$_2$D$^+$ emission in HH212 traces a vertically extended torus rather than a warped or disky disk. Future observations of H$_2$D$^+$ $J = 1 - 0$ and transitions with ALMA and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array will test these and other hypotheses by constraining the H$_2$D$^+$ excitation and abundance, and tracing different velocity components in the outflow-enriched sources.

We present an analytical model for the self-similar scaling relations between the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect signal and the physical properties of the astrophysical systems they are derived from. The model considers the projection effect in the spatial structure of the systems and takes into account the hydrostatic bias caused by the luminous or total mass distribution. We apply our model to interpret the SZ profiles obtained with the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and show that the ACT-derived SZ surface brightness profiles can be well fitted by the self-similar form if certain scaling relations are imposed. We also show that there are systematics in the SZ measurements due to the limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and beam-smoothing effect and propose an empirical method to reduce these systematics. We test our method on numerical simulations and show that the self-similar scaling relations can be violated if the hydrostatic bias is not properly taken into account. We apply our model to the Horizon-AGN simulation and demonstrate that the typical magnitude of the violation of the scaling relations is around 40%. We also show that the amplitude of the scaling relations can be used to measure the bias factor between the total mass and the gas mass, which can be used to calibrate the flux bias correction for SZ effect. All the scaling relations obtained with our model are independent of the cosmological model, which can be used to put robust cosmological constraints with SZ effect data.

Lattice QCD with two light dynamical quark flavors is an actively researched area of research. In this limit, the theory exhibits spontaneous breaking of the symmetry between the up and down quarks, resulting in two macroscopic masses. These light two quark flavors also make the theory susceptible to new nontrivial phenomena, such as explicit chiral symmetry breaking by the light quark masses. This is the theory of two-flavor QCD in the epsilon-regime, with epsilon = (m_u - m_d)/2 api denoting the breaking of explicit chiral symmetry. Explicit symmetry breaking is described by the HFB effective theory. The predictions of HFB and LQCD in the epsilon-regime match well in the range of |epsilon| ~ mQ, where mQ is the quark mass, and this range includes the case of zero explicit symmetry breaking, |epsilon| ~ 0. This Letter presents LQCD calculations of the two-flavor QCD epsilon-regime at three different lattice spacings and a range of light quark masses, providing strong evidence in favor of the phase transition in this theory as a second-order shift in the real part of the epsilon condensate. The results for epsilon in the range of mQ ~ 300 MeV are consistent with a chiral random matrix theory (CRMT) description, with one important correction to the effective chiral theory (AdS/QCD). The form of this correction is given in the Letter, and its implications for this theory and the resulting phenomenological applications are discussed.

Star-forming galaxies are believed to evolve along a typical sequence from warm neutral medium (WNM) to CNM to HII regions. Thus, study of their composition across these different phases will help to understand the evolutionary sequence. X-rays are extremely energetic photons and are believed to penetrate through the interstellar medium easily. Thus, they are an ideal tracer to explore the different components of a galaxy. Using Chandra data, we have studied six star-forming galaxies at various stages of the evolutionary sequence. We have detected one WNM, one CNM and two HII regions. However, no significant X-ray emitting Warm Absorber was found. We have also estimated the temperature and column density of the detected phases and compared them with the values from previous IR and radio observations. We also estimated the star formation rates (SFRs) from the HII region luminosity. Our findings suggest that the evolutionary sequence is consistent with the increasing pressure of the external environment. Futhermore, the HII region luminosity seems to correlate well with the X-ray luminosity and SFR, suggesting that the ionizing photons are able to penetrate through the gasphase and are mostly absorbed in the molecular cloud.

Two intermediate-redshift (0.6 < z < 2.2) quasars are used as pointings for themulti-slit spectroscopy mode of the Haro-3D integral-field spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope. Both targets are known to be high-luminosity, radio-quiet quasars with significant polarisation from a young, rotating black hole. The first quasar, [DES J022555.6-051024]{}, is studied in two optical data sets from 2017: one taken with the Wide Field Spectrograph on the Haleakala Observatories and one taken with the Zwicky Transient Facility in infrared. The second quasar, [DES J022856.4-032600]{}, is observed with the Kilo-Degree Survey in the optical and the Puckett Queued Telescope Observatory 2 in the near-infrared. The data are reduced and their spectra are extracted using a combination of python and idl tasks. These spectra are used to measure the line and continuum properties of the two objects, which are then used to calculate the size of the broad-line region (BLR). This calculation is performed using the virial theorem, using both the full line profile and broad Hβ as a constraint. For both quasars, a distinct BLR component is detected, whose size is calculated to be (1.4 ± 0.2) × 106 light-years for [DES J022555.6-051024]{}, and (2.2 ± 0.3) × 106 light-years for [DES J022856.4-032600]{}. The full line width is also measured for both objects, and indicates that both sources have [Mg II] as a broad line, though some extreme broadening is observed in [DES J022856.4-032600]{}. Both quasars are relatively low-redshift objects, but have higher BLR sizes than a similar sample of quasars at lower redshifts. This could be evidence of either higher black hole growth in the past (consistent with previous results on the evolution of black hole and host properties), or selection effects against finding large BLRs in high-redshift quasars with the techniques used so far.

The variable star R Aqr is classified as an Z Cam-type star, which are notorious for their sudden dramatic optical variability. R Aqr is a binary system, with a period of 7.32 days, consisting of an A0IV plus star and a weaker K0IV secondary. Because the primary is a rapid rotator, it is heavily magnetized and outflows are often seen from this star. In July 1999, R Aqr experienced a violent variation of its polarization and brightness, called a "state change". It has remained in the'very active' state for the past 14 years, making it one of the best studied Z Cam stars. We present new results from our monitoring of R Aqr with the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) between 1999.8 and 2004.0. During this time we observed regular episodes of enhanced X-ray emission lasting up to a few hundred days, separated by long periods of inactivity. These X-ray bursts have a peak luminosity of ~1037erg/s and are undetected at other wavelengths. We also review the recent multi-wavelength optical, X-ray, and radio observations of R Aqr. We suggest that these X-ray bursts are the result of the same process that causes the optical outbursts - enhanced mass transfer from the secondary star into the primary. We describe how the size of the accretion disk, estimated from the X-ray bursting period, is inversely proportional to the mass of the compact primary star. This supports the idea that the bursts are due to the direct impact of transferred matter onto the compact star. Finally, we compare our results to models of isolated magnetic neutron stars and discuss the implications for each model.

The star U Geminorum, also known as Geminorum Star,appa,rles with Mizar, is a yellow subgiant approximately 25 light-years from the Earth in the constellation Gemini. In 2016, the star displayed distinct brightness variations of approximately 5.6 magnitudes, which could be associated to orbital periods of two stars similar to the binary orbit of Uranus. In this work, analysis of nearly 9 years of U Geminorum observation using high-accuracy visual telescopes and long-slit spectroscopy revealed two orbital periods of 13.8 and 25.2 days. Radial velocity curves for both periods are well fitted by circular orbits with mid-orbital RV semi-amplitudes of about 83.2 and 112.7 m/s. The preliminary ephemerides for both periods are also provided. The results confirm the star as a potential candidates for precision studies in the future, for example, investigating the interactions of matter in the two inner planets of the Solar System.

Graph coloring is the process of using as many colors as possible so that no two adjacent vertices in the graph have the same color. The problem of graph coloring was introduced by Charles Wiener in 1946. The chromatic number of a graph is the number of colors needed to color the vertices of the graph such that no two adjacent vertices have the same color. The colorings of the vertices of a graph can be thought of as the edges of the corresponding partitioned coloring graph. Thus the problem of finding the chromatic number of a graph is equivalent to that of finding the partition number of the corresponding coloring graph. The problem is hardwired to find for graphs of large maximum degree and was proven to be APX-hard for graphs of maximum degree five. A new constant factor approximation algorithm is presented for the general case. Using statistical physics the partition number is found to be characterized by a second order phase transition. The algorithmic results are corroborated by the findings from statistical mechanics.

Near-IR spectra of red supergiants and giants are important diagnostic tools for evaluating scenarios of stellar evolution. Yet, these important classes of objects have largely been neglected in the model atmosphere community. The fundamental reason is the computational expense of radiative-transfer calculations in the near-IR, which requires high-resolution (e.g., R ≳ 100,000) and cover a large wavelength range (0.8 to 2.5 μm). Here, we present new MARCS model atmospheres for the modeling of red supergiants and giants. At solar and substantially subsolar metallicities, these models can reproduce the near-IR spectra of these objects well across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (T[eff] ∼ 10,000–30,000 K). For hot objects, we include opacity from grains, which become the dominant source of opacities above 3000 K. We also present a new set of models for cooler stars (T[eff] < 10,000 K) that include enhanced helium and metal abundances. These models are relevant for the spectroscopic analysis of bright giants in the Galactic disk. In summary, our new models allow the observation of red supergiants and giants to be put into proper astrophysical context.

Heavy baryon chiral perturbation theory (HBChPT) is the low energy effective field theory for nucleons and heavy particles bound by the forces set by the lightest particles in the Standard Model, typically called the DM candidate. In the past decade, a great deal of effort has been devoted to the next-to-leading order (NLO) calculation of chiral perturbation theory for such systems. We present a variant, called staggered heavy baryon chiral perturbation theory, in which the derivatives in the action are replaced by noise and the doubler modes are suppressed. The theory can be simulated efficiently using high temperature molecular dynamics on a lattice and we present results for the nucleon mass and residual mass in HBChPT and in the staggered theory with a cutoff of 600 MeV. The results for the staggered theory agree well with the next-to-next-to-leading order calculation in HBChPT, showing that the doubler modes are suppressed efficiently. -- Chen-Chen Pang from Peking University

A diagrammatic category for the representation theory of U_q(sl_n). This defines a compact closed structure on the equivariant K-theory of a nilpotent Hamiltonian reduction, generalising the Springer correspondence and its recent categorical extensions. Through the combinatorics of lattice paths, it allows for a uniform treatment of (a) type A, (b) type B, and (c) arbitrary quantum groups. There are several exciting applications of this in the form of conjectural categorifications of classical multiplicative preSchur functions, and generalised Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials. Applications to finite type representations, categorified combinatorics, quasihereditary modules, and quantum groups will appear in later work. The diagrammatic category in question is the path category P(N-1, N) of the symmetric Laplacian; this gives it a uniform treatment of types (a) and (b) (as well as (c) when N is a integer).

A natural broadening of the iron K alpha resonance line was observed in the X-ray spectrum of NGC 3783 for the first time. The observed width of this line is significantly larger than the instrumental resolution. Since the observed width is comparable to the velocity of the gas in the Broad Line Region, the observed broadening is most likely produced by velocity-dependent scattering in the disk of the nucleus. This scattering may be caused by small scale inhomogeneities in the gas density or by deviations from spherical symmetry in the gravitational potential of the nucleus. The redshifted iron K alpha line and the underlying continuum were also studied for the first time. The shape of the continuum is in good agreement with the results of previous studies. The equivalent width of the line was measured to be approximately 120 eV. The equivalent width of this line in the rest frame is approximately 240 eV. The observed correlation between the equivalent width and redshift of the line indicates that the line emission and fluorescence processes in the Broad Line Region are more complex than previously assumed. The variability of NGC 3783 on different time scales was also investigated. Two years of X-ray observations with Chandra revealed no significant variability of the line flux. The variability of the equivalent width was not significant at a 2-sigma level. Variability on longer time scales cannot be detected in the available data.

The dynamics of open quantum systems is often modeled by a Markovian master equation, which can be used to compute the evolution of the system's density matrix. While this dynamics is symmetric under exchange of heat with cold and heat with hot at a given temperature, we show that this exchange symmetry is broken for multiple temperatures. This is caused by the emergence of a quantum thermal gradient, which leads to a corresponding violation of Fourier's law. We establish this result by proving a new equilibrium inequality for quantum processes. We demonstrate this result by considering a generic model system consisting of a qubit that can be coupled to two thermal baths, which can exchange heat at different temperatures. We obtain explicit expressions for the evolution of the system's reduced density matrix under symmetric exchanges of heat at various combinations of temperatures. We then use this result to show that the corresponding flux of entropy exhibits non-symmetric behavior under these exchanges. Finally, we apply our results to various physically relevant thermal states and show that these can violate Fourier's law if the exchange symmetry of the quantum thermal gradient is broken.

High-harmonic generation (HHG) in diatomic molecules is reviewed. The HHG process is illustrated as the 3-step action of a free electron on an external laser field. It is shown that this simple picture can be greatly extended by quantum-orbit analyses of the laser-field wave functions. A semiclassical approach to HHG is developed in this framework. Examples of diatomic molecules, namely N2 and O2, are considered. For both molecules, the phase-space picture of HHG is completely characterized, and several new features are emphasized: the anisotropy of the electron motion, the impact of neighboring atoms, and the dependence on the two arms of the double bond. The dependence of HHG on the direction of the internuclear axis is also identified. The influence of the properties of the A-band continuum on HHG is emphasized. A qualitative description of the "window" for HHG is given, which relates the intensity and duration of the driving field to the frequency of the emitted light. The resulting phase diagram is applied to diatomic molecules with an inner shell 1s22s, such as Kr, Xe, and Rn. The onset of HHG is discussed and the large differences in HHG yield between even- and odd-mass isotopes are highlighted.

Chiral symmetry and the string description of excited hadrons. The chiral symmetry, being a symmetry of the QCD Lagrangian with massless up and down quarks, is a fundamental symmetry of the universe. The spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry, responsible for the mass of most hadrons and the familiar physical world ofGPIO, is one of the most dramatic examples of a spontaneous symmetry breaking in physics. The states generated by this chiral symmetry breaking are called pions, kaons, eta and their interactions are governed by the Chiral Perturbation Theory. On the other hand, the string theory (or strings for short), being a very successful theory for the elementary particles, also have an unbroken global symmetry, called scale or chiral symmetry, spontaneously and with a quite different spectrum from that of the QCD. There are claims in the literature that the two approaches should be compatible. Here, we demonstrate how this can be achieved, by introducing the Nambu-Goldstone bosons into the effective string theory action in a gauge invariant way, and deriving dynamically the corresponding string spectrum.

In this paper we show that certain one dimensional spin chains with short range dimer interactions, and short range forward and backward free fermion interactions, are in the same quantum phase described by a two parameter super quantum group SU(2|2). We also give a detailed description of the symmetry content and the dual Coxeter amplitudes of this quantum phase. Specifically, we show that the spin 1 XXZ chain with periodic boundary conditions and dimer interaction strength 1, the spin 1/2 Heisenberg chain with periodic boundary conditions and arbitrary spin 1/2, the super spin 1/2 XX chain with periodic boundary conditions and arbitrary coupling constant λ, and the super spin 1/2 XXZ chain with periodic boundary conditions and dimer interaction strength 1, all have the same quantum phase as a parameter p in the range 0<p<4. This phase is described by a two parameter deformation of the super quantum group SU(2|2), where the deformation is controlled by a complex parameter τ=x+iy with x<0. The precise expression for τ is (the square root of) the determinant of a particular S matrices of the model. This deformation of SU(2|2) was also found by Guruswamy (2013) in a different approach, and is called a super quantum group because it is a deformation of both the super group of quantum double s, as well as the quantum group SU(2) with a nontrivial three parameter deformation. We also show that the fermions in the spin chain map to free fermions in a1 dimension with boson order a2, where a2 is equal to 2x-y. We also give a detailed description of the symmetry content and the dual Coxeter amplitudes of this quantum phase. For the XXZ chain, these are the same as those of the XX chain, whereas for the super spin chains they are different.

The paper presents a detailed study of a quantum mechanical system consisting of a photon box open at both ends, one mirror partially reflective, and one perfectly reflective and stationary. The study includes both analytical and numerical solutions of the time-dependent wave equation for a range of starting conditions corresponding to various initial photon numbers and wavepacket configurations. The system exhibits a range of behaviors depending on the distance between the partially reflective and the stationary mirror, the energy of the incident photon, and the initial wavepacket configuration. These behaviors include reflection, transmission, and splitting into transmitted and reflected waves for various combinations of the above parameters. In general, the transmitted wavepacket exits the system to the right of the stationary mirror and the reflected wavepacket enters the system to the left of the stationary mirror. For some parameter values, all wavepacket components exit the system to the left of the stationary mirror, corresponding to perfect complementarity, i.e. all information about the initial state is perfectly preserved in the system.

Manganese and other rare earths are examples of impurities that may localize in the interstitial sites of the semiconductor host lattice. Such defects may form bound states with free carriers - usually referred to as localized charge carriers - leading to the formation of impurity bands. While for nonmagnetic impurities the dominant interaction mechanism is the so-called Hunds rule coupling, in the presence of localized magnetic moments of the impurity the Zeeman interaction has to be taken into account. If both, the localized magnetic moments as well as the carriers are deconfined at finite temperature, we encounter a magnetic impurity band that may exhibit properties characteristic for both, localized and delocalized charge carriers. In order to understand the nature of the impurity band we study for the case of diluted magnetic semiconductors (DMS) the crossover from localized to delocalized charge carriers via a systematic variation of the Coulomb attraction by the acceptor. In this context the physical concept of Wannier functions is employed to describe the spatial extent and localizability of the impurity band wave functions. The Coulomb attraction by the acceptor is modeled by a dielectric background in order to account for the screening behavior of the charge carriers in the valence band. By comparing calculated optical spectra with corresponding experiments we are able to extract the relevant material parameters. The result of this theoretical study allow to conclude that the acceptor-limited mobilities of the DMS systems can be described by the simple formula σ(cm2/V·s) = (μ0(cm2/V·s) · epsilon(0) · N(D) · N(A))½, where μ0 is the band mobility in the absence of localized charge carriers, N(D) is the acceptor density, and N(A) is the density of donors. Hence, for a fixed acceptor density, the acceptor-limited carrier mobility in diluted magnetic semiconductors is only determined by the density of donors. This fundamental relation has to be considered as a general property of all IV-VI compounds which contain both, magnetic impurities and non-magnetic acceptors.

In recent years, thanks to the early efforts in applying advanced numerical techniques to simulate lattice QCD with chemical potential, more and more attention has been paid to the connection between QCD thermodynamics and the phase structure, especially the chiral phase transition. In the current manuscript, using the P4 algorithm to simulate lattice QCD with two light flavors and opposite determinant mass, we investigate the effect of the anomaly on this chiral phase transition. We find that the anomaly decreases the critical temperature of the transition, while has no qualitative influence on the chiral transition itself. The reason is that the anomaly works to decrease the spatial size of the QCD windows, which suppresses the critical temperature coming from the deconfinement phase transition. For the determination of the transition, apart from the Polyakov loop, we also consider the chiral condensate and the dion distribution function to study the chiral order parameter, and find that the anomaly decreases the chiral transition temperature while the crossover behavior remains. Overall, the anomaly decreases the chiral transition temperature, while has no qualitative influence on the chiral transition itself.

This paper studies the theoretical properties of the L1-regularized logistic regression. First, we show that for well-chosen parameters, this estimator is uniformly consistent over a wide class of logistic regression functions, and parameter values can be exactly recovered in this large model agnostic setting. We then study the property in a more narrow framework, where only a particular (Hodge) estimator is considered. By identifying the asymptotic regime where the estimator is almost minimax, we show that the L1 regularized logistic regression is asymptotically equivalent in minimax sense to the Hodge estimator. In addition, we demonstrate that the L1 regularized logistic regression is nearly minimax, i.e, the estimator is within $o_n(1)$ factor of the minimax rate over a large class of logistic regression functions. We provide both theoretical and empirical evidence to support our claims. In particular, we establish near minimax rates of convergence for logistic regression with the Lasso and the SCAD penalty. We also provide a comprehensive empirical evaluation of the L1 regularized logistic regression over a large variety of synthetic and real datasets. Our numerical experiments strongly suggest that, in contrast to popular belief, the L1 regularized logistic regression is not only minimax over the Hodge class of logistic regression, but also uniformly consistent over the much wider range of possible logistic regression functions.

Galaxy clusters are important test beds for studying galaxy evolution. The spectra of the bright galaxies in clusters offer a unique opportunity to study the chemical and physical properties of galaxies, unobscured by dust and in a controlled environment. The spectra of galaxies in clusters show evidence of recent star formation, quasar-like emissions, and absorption line systems from the individual galaxies as well as evidence of merging and accretion through the observation of large-scale shock-heated gas structures. Brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) contain the most massive and visually brightest galaxies in the clusters and exhibit distinct spectral features that aid in their classification. BCGs are usually elliptical galaxies that are tightly bound to the cluster, and many are located at the center of the cluster potential well, feeding the halo black hole and emitting quasar-like radiation. This quasar-like radiation dominates the optical/UV spectra of the BCG and can obscure the underlying galaxy spectrum. In this paper, we present rest-frame optical spectra of 8 BCGs in the redshift range 0.03 < z < 0.07. Using data from the DEep Near Infrared Survey Facility (DEepNIRS), we measure line fluxes from the Hα,,, and Paα lines and estimate star formation rates from the Hα luminosities. We also include measurements from the original discovery paper and Gemini/SINFONI measurements of the Hα flux, as well as FIR and UV data from the * Spitzer and * HST when available. The star formation rates and gas excitation states for the sample are compared to published relations and the behavior of these correlations with cluster mass and redshift are examined. While 7/8 galaxies in our sample exhibit low levels of star formation and kinematics consistent with a static cluster potential, the spectrum of one galaxy (RXJ0152.7-1357) exhibits high levels of star formation and vigorous activity. The average Hα star formation rate of the entire sample is 2.2 M☉ yr-1, consistent with the mass-specific star formation rates of normal galaxies at similar redshifts, and the average star formation rate density of the sample is 7.3 M☉ yr-1 Mpc-3. This star formation rate density is higher than the mean in the nearby universe and decreases with increasing cluster mass, in agreement with the trends in the field. We also find tentative evidence that the star formation rate density may increase with increasing redshift in the most massive clusters, a result which may be a signature of positive feedback in the cluster growth, or potentially due to the effects of environmental quenching. We use a novel method for removing quasar-like light from the spectra of the brightest cluster galaxies, which is critical for accurate line flux measurements. We find that the equivalent width of the Hα emission line, a robust SFR indicator, is correlated with the cluster X-ray luminosity, which we interpret as indicative of strong positive feedback in the cluster core. In the propegal nebula OH 231.8+4, water vapor and silicon monoxide (SiO) were observed using the Green Bank Telescope (GBT). SiO is one of the most abundant interstellar molecules and its emission is frequently used to trace shocked material. Water vapor has also recently been found in numerous protoplanetary nebulae (PPNe). Although not common, previous detections of water vapor in PNe have been used to study the processing of water through AGB stars. Si, O, and H are the main constituents of water and SiO. In the PPN, gas is heated to millions of degrees and undergoes chemical processing. The current detection of water vapor and SiO toward the same region and the coincident detections of H2 and OH suggests that these molecules are shock-generated and not static. This work expands the number of sources where shock-generated molecules have been detected in the interstellar medium.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are among the most powerful events in the universe. The leading theory to explain their huge observed energies postulates that the energy is released through a relativistic jet, which is structured into many shocks and possibly also endowed with a magnetic field. One consequence of this model is that the afterglow emission from the electrons accelerated at these shocks should gradually decay as the blast wave slows down. Here we present a sample of 19 X-ray afterglows of long gamma-ray bursts, detected by the *CHANDRA X-Ray Telescope between 1 and 10 hours after the initial gamma-ray emission. We find that for 13 afterglows this simple model over-predicts the decay rate, by a factor of 2-10. Using a phenomenological broken power-law, we find that the difference in decay rates is significant at more than 4 sigma. We discuss several potential solutions to this discrepancy, such as variability of the blast wave, the presence of a high-density region in the jet, or an intrinsically flat decay phase in the emission. These results imply that a large amount of energy may be deposited into the ambient medium by the GRB jets, and the circum-burst medium has a density structure on scales smaller than the initial jet opening angle.' *Contribution to this conference paper published online: 21st February 2014 Author(s): Axel Weiss, Lars Pen Hertog, Catherine Gou trunc, Matteo Guan, Cheng Wang, Yi Yang, Francesca Pooley, Felipe Villaescusa, Alexander Nagumo, Anatoly Yakutski, Jens Nyland, Jules PUTTIN, Olivier LARSS, Frederic DESCHAMPS, Alberto ISENHOWER, David HAYABUSA, Jean-Pierre VERNAGE, Thomas J. The European higher education area has experienced impressive transformations over the last few decades. Universities have been encouraged to increase their internationalization, adopt prestigious internationalization strategies, and improve their attractiveness to students. Most universities in Europe have therefore enlarged their student bodies, recruited more international professors, and strengthened their research activities. This boom in science and student affairs has translated into a significant increase in scientific research at European universities. However, although universities rank first among European players in the tertiary education field, quantitative analysis of their research activities is still lacking. In this context, the European Commission, within its Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme, launched a public call for access to rich data related to European universities' research activities. The 100 largest universities in Europe (according to the enrolment size) responded to this call, furnishing detailed information about their research projects' funding, academic impact, and number of publications. Using the methodologies of extreme value analysis and fractal modeling, this work reveals a multitude of prevalent scaling rules operating at the European university level. The resulting framework can help universities to understand their scientific performance and develop their strategies to accelerate their research activities.

The evolution of orbits under the joint action of gravity and general relativity is determined by the unique combination of two effects: the time variation of the Newtonian gravitational constant G and the deferential curvature of space time caused by the planet's gravitational field. Tidal coupling between the planet and its companion results in differential acceleration of the planet and the companion. For planets with short orbital periods, relativistic contributions to the tidal acceleration are larger than Newtonian contributions and the direction of the acceleration can change, reversing the direction of the orbital inclination. We present an analytical model for the long-term evolution of orbits for Earth-mass planets in eccentric orbits in the near-resonant, two-body configurations with negligible orbital expansion due to General Relativity. We demonstrate that in these configurations the relativistic contributions to the tidal acceleration are large enough to reverse the direction of the planetary orbital inclination. We find that this situation is most likely to occur for near-resonant planets with periods of 7-15 days and, for planets near the host star, the location of the conjunction or pericentre.

A long paper abstract from arXiv.org We give a detailed exposition of the Flip algorithm and its analysis in the last two sections. The algorithm and its analysis have three parts: in the first part, we give a new proof of the Computation of nega-flip (the Inertia Theorem), using essentially the structure theory of graded modules over Weyl algebras; in the second part, we give a detailed analysis of the rounding step of the algorithm, including the proof of the Saturation and Positivity Results; in the third part, we show how to modify the algorithm to compute the BSD-representation stability of quivers, in addition to the Schofield representation stability. Let us finally mention that a similar Computation of nega-flip was given by Kramer and Wyss in a recent preprint, building on ideas of Fulton and later also of Wieland; however, our proof is different, more direct, and in fact we give a very simple and explicit generator of the radical of the relevant Bockstein, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we would like to mention that our Analysis of the rounding step of the flip algorithm also extends to several other cases, where this step was not analyzed before. These include: (1) the case of quivers with relations; (2) the case of 2-representation-finite algebras; (3) the case of (skew) symmetric algebras, also in arbitrary characteristic; and (4) the case of representation-finite Cohen-Macaulay algebras.

In astrophysics, rotating black holes (BHs) are a source of observational signatures across all length and time scales, from gamma-rays to radio to optical bands. The most readily observable manifestation of a rotating BH is the apparent ellipsoidal modulation of the light of the companion star passing behind it, as seen in an astronomical object known as an X-ray binary. Such an X-ray binary comprises a normal star that forms a close binary with a compact object, a black hole or a neutron star. This normal star is surrounded by an accretion disk that is fed by the normal star's winds and ejects the matter of the stellar envelope into space, forming an X-ray binary system. If the compact object is a rotating black hole, the surface of the black hole will be disrupted by frame dragging, resulting in a large-scale magnetic field. This magnetic field will warp the trajectories of particles in the disk, causing them to precess. The closer the companion star is to the black hole, the more powerful the magnetic field is expected to be. This allows us to potentially measure the black hole's rotation rate.

In this paper, we establish the weak convergence of the unique solutions to some new classes of linear structural error-in-variables models with explanatory variables in the domain of attraction of the normal law. These results are applied to provide central limit theorems for certain quadratic forms of the solutions. The limit distributions are expressed in terms of the Green function and a stationary version of the variance function of the solution. The limit theorems established here imply weak convergence of the quadratic forms in two different situations. One situation is for the case where the noise is non-Gaussian and a polynomially bounded domain of attractions of the normal law is assumed for the regressors; another situation is for the case where the noise is Gaussian and the domain of attraction of the normal law is assumed for the regressors. This paper is an extended version of our recent article “Central limit theorems in linear structural error-in-variables models” [arXiv:1807.08832]. Here we present the proof of Theorem 3.1 and some additional simulations.

In this part, we study the space-time symmetries and the corresponding representations of the algebra governing the free fields. We prove the invariance of the canonical commutation relations under the spatial translations, the spacetime translations and the spacetime gauge transformations. We also discuss the corresponding representations of the corresponding generators. We give the explicit expressions of the generators of the corresponding symmetries in terms of the fields and their derivatives. The MINOS Experiment at FNAL has deployed the first long-baseline neutrino oscillation appearance experiment in the NuMI beamline and has recently published its first-year results. The experiment uses a 3-detector setup, with one upstream detector at the Northern Initial Data taking site and two downstream detectors at the Soudan Underground Mine in Minnesota (NE detector) and Saints, Louisiana (SW detector). The data taking period was from 2011 to 2012, and the total exposure in the far detector was 2.2 ton-years. In this period MINOS measured muon neutrino disappearance with a significance of 5.2σ, and presented first evidence for electron neutrino appearance, with 3.6σ of significance. This first MINOS results paper presents the new data and preliminary global fit results. MINOS was developed to study muon neutrino disappearance and pion- created electron neutrinos appearance. The new dataset includes neutrino interactions in the detector during 2011 and 2012, and the global fit incorporates the full dataset, with the preliminary results presented in this paper updated to include the full dataset. The main update in the new results is the re-weighting of the event rates with the improved cross section calculations by the NNPDF collaboration. This allows for a more precise estimate of the experiment’s background and sensitivity. The experiment finds no evidence for muon neutrino disappearance and presents 3.6σ of evidence for electron neutrino appearance. The result has an element of uncertainty from our knowledge of the neutrino flux and cross sections, which is reduced with this update.

Acoustic emission (AE) mapping is a source localization technique which maps the spatial distribution of the amplitude of acoustic signals as they spread from active sources. In this paper, we present an algorithm for estimating the location of simultaneously active sources from AE mapping data, when the location of the sources is known a priori but their activity is not known a priori. The algorithm is an implementation of a recently developed acquisition scheme that enables the measurement of the (spatially filtered) cross-correlation of two AE maps. We apply this algorithm to simulated data as well as experimental data from a numerical and a physical model of a plate tearing under shear. In both sets of experiments, we show that our algorithm is able to accurately estimate the locations of simultaneously active sources, even when the active sources are closely spaced. The results are in agreement with the true locations of the sources, as determined by an assumed truth. In a companion paper, we show how this technique could be used to reduce the amount of sensor array channel data required to localize simultaneously active sources.

Early-type galaxies are important components of modern galaxy clusters and are believed to be the direct progenitors of massive elliptical galaxies. Despite this central role, the formation and evolution of these galaxies is not well understood. In particular, their star formation activity over time has not been well constrained, due to a lack of measurements of their obscured, dust-corrected, star formation rates (SFRs). Here we report new, accurate estimates of the obscured SFRs of a large sample of early-type galaxies at z = 0.4–1.0, based on the MIPSGAL 843 μm surveys of the Great Observatory Origins Deep survey (GOODS) fields. We find that at these redshifts, the SFRs of these galaxies are modest at best (mean <SFR> = 0.1–1.0 M⊙ yr−1, depending on stellar mass), much lower than previously reported values for similar galaxies, and in broad agreement with recent SFR tracers (e.g., rest-frame UV). We compare our results with past work that used an optical SFR indicator and find the new MIPS-derived SFRs are a factor of ~3–10 lower. We find that the ratios of obscured to unobscured SFR for these galaxies are consistent with those of the local universe, and rule out maximal obscuration. We explore potential interpretations of these results in light of recent models of early-type galaxy formation, finding that models with rapid early-type galaxy assembly in low mass halos are able to reproduce the new SFR measurements.

Nanocrystal synthesis is essential for technological innovation in various industries such as healthcare, energy, and national defense. To date, there are still challenges in recognizing small, similar crystals with similar chemical compositions, particularly for large data sets of generated nanocrystals. In this work, a machine-learning-based structural fingerprinting approach is introduced for rapid identification of nanocrystals with minimal human intervention. This approach can be used to identify nanocrystals across various chemical space through the construction of a unique structural fingerprint. As a proof of concept, the approach is demonstrated for silver nanocrystals, where a fingerprint model based on five structural parameters is developed to recognize crystals with up to 98% accuracy. This structural fingerprinting method provides researchers with an enhanced strategy for nanocrystal identification, and the resultant database can be used for nanocrystal screening, discovery, and classification. This approach can be readily extended to nanocrystal identification problems in other domains such as energy and healthcare.

In this paper we present a method for translating combinatorial optimization problems into systems of polynomial equations. We show that, under natural hypotheses, the presence of duality symmetries in an optimization problem allows us to express the problem as a system in which the polynomials have nonnegative coefficients. Using ideas from algebraic geometry, we prove that these systems of polynomial equations have solutions if and only if a related optimization problem has optimal value zero. We illustrate our approach with several examples, including an SDP involving totally nonnegative matrices and an integer program with a nonsmooth objective function. Our method can be applied to problems with arbitrary integer or continuous variables, and we present one such application in the form of a theorem that provides a sufficient condition for the vanishing of polynomials in several variables. The method described in this paper has several applications. First, it allows us to obtain algorithms for solving combinatorial optimization problems by interpreting the problems as manifestations of the theory of polynomial optimization. This approach has been very effective in solving integer programs with a non-negative cost function and an arbitrary number of variables (see, e.g., [1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]). Second, it allows us to express duality symmetries as transformations that change one system of polynomial equations into another. This has allowed us to obtain optimal-value results for problems that were not amenable to traditional methods based on the theory of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions (see, e.g., [5, 6, 8, 14, 15, 16, 17]). Third, it allows us to express polynomials as linear combinations of sums of squares (SOS) of other polynomials, which is a powerful technique for solving polynomial optimization problems (see, e.g., [4, 13, 14]). In principle, each of these applications could be used independently of the others. However, in most of the applications mentioned above, the use of duality symmetries has led to significant additional simplifications.

Recent X-ray observations with both ʻNewtonʼ and ʻRXTEʼ satellites revealed the presence of a soft excess above the thermal emission of the accretion disk in a significant fraction of Seyfert 1 galaxies. A popular hypothesis to explain this phenomenon is the reprocessing of hard X-rays in Compton-thick material around the central supermassive black hole. However, detailed studies of a few sources with ʻNarrow Field Instrumentsʼ failed to detect such columns of gas. We propose an alternative scenario in which the excess emission originates from electrons in the accretion flow instead of being direct from reprocessing. The electrons will inverse-Comptonize the UV/X-ray light emitted by the disk, and will be cooled through the Moliere process, producing a spectral signature significantly resembling the one observed. The model is consistent with the data from ʻXMM-Newtonʼ and ʻChandraʼ satellites and can provide a satisfactory fit to the soft excess in a large sample of objects.

High-resolution H I imaging of the local group galaxy M33, obtained with the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope (WSRT) shows extended H I emission at velocities corresponding to the host’s asymptotic velocity. A complex H I structure is seen in a tail emanating from M33, resembling features seen in similar emission towards other galaxies. These features can be explained by tidal stripping of the H I gas caused by the close encounter with M32 approximately 130 million years ago. This is the first time that an unambiguous case of tidal stripping of H I has been seen, and it suggests that M32’s tidal forces may have played a significant role in the evolution of the Local Group. The H I imaging of M33 was obtained with the Westerbork Synthesis Radio Telescope (WSRT). H I spectra are shown for selected areas of the galaxy. A very massive star ends its life as a supernova by shedding its outer layers. These removed layers produce observable light and may be discernible in remnants of the star such as a planetary nebula (PNI). We report evidence for such pre-supernova mass loss in the enigmatic Galactic supernova remnant 3C 58 using images and spectra of its planetary nebula. We measure the mass of the central star and of the layer of ejected material using stellar evolution modeling, and we find pre-supernova mass loss parameters of α = 3.2 ± 0.4% and β = 0.9 ± 0.2, where α is the fraction of the star's mass lost in the stellar wind prior to the supernova explosion and β is the fraction of the star's mass lost in a prior shell ejection prior to the core collapse event. The large measured value of α is in contrast to previous suggestions of mild or no pre-supernova mass loss and suggests that the majority of the star's mass was lost in a prior ejection event. This supports the hypothesis that the progenitor star of 3C 58 was a member of a binary system at some point prior to the supernova explosion.

The dynamical state of the galaxy cluster Abell 115 was studied using a set of 39 accurately determined red-sequence member galaxies drawn from the full catalog of members with available SZ flux measurements from the Planck Collaboration VIII. Abell 115 was shown to be dynamically relaxed based on its X-ray isomass contours and the distribution of pairwise velocities of its member galaxies. However, some signatures of substructure are detected in the optical galaxy distribution, which is also in general agreement with the X-ray isomass distribution. The galaxy cluster shows a filamentary structure in the spatial distribution and has a slightly elongated total mass distribution. The mass of the cluster within a 1.1 Mpc/$h$ radius (r_{500}) is measured to be M_{500} = (1.32 \pm 0.27) x 10^{14} h^{-1} M_{\odot}$ from the X-ray data, in excellent agreement with the mass within r_{200} = 1.06 Mpc/$h$ from the measured velocity dispersion of the cluster members. The mass distribution of Abell 115 can be well described by an NFW profile with a scale radius of r_s = 1.43 $\pm$ 0.21 Mpc/$h$ and a concentration parameter of c = 5.1 $\pm$ 1.0. The redshift-dependent diameter of the cluster is estimated to be D(z) = 2.33 $\pm$ 0.42 Mpc/$h$, corresponding to a linear scale of 1.95 $\pm$ 0.33 kpc/$h$. The large-scale coherent X-ray gas velocity is measured to be v_r = 1125 $\pm$ 38 km/s, consistent with the observed galaxy velocity dispersion. The evolution index of the cluster mass determined from the mass-scaling relations is significantly different from that measured from the dynamical measurements, implying that the so-called critical versus transitional regime may not be a useful dividing line between the two relations. However, the mass-scaled relation shows a better agreement with the dynamical state of Abell 115 than thevirialrelation.

A good portion of the solar flux is absorbed in the interstellar medium through ionisation and chemical reactions initiated by the interaction with interstellar neutral hydrogen. Due to the strong ionisation potential (IP) of these elements and the low temperature of the interstellar medium, most of the interactions occur in the form of neutral hydrogen ions. The exact kinetics of this process is still a matter of debate and is crucial for the correct modelling of some high temperature processes in the solar atmosphere. In this article, we investigate the efficiency of the neutral hydrogen interaction with Ti I and Ca II, two elements with significant abundance in the solar photosphere and play an important role in the solar chemistry. We perform complex collisions with the catalytic Evala version of the k - optimal expansion code ( klaus ) and compare the results with effective collision strengths calculated using Dirac-Fock wavefunctions and random phase approximation. We find that the Dirac-Fock evaluation yields results 4 times lower than the more expensive k-linear results. This implies that the consideration of excited configurations, even for the lightest element in the solar system, is crucial for the correct description of the interaction of Ti and Ca with neutral hydrogen.

Detection of a rapid increase in the Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) fraction in high-redshift clusters of galaxies with the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), advancing the argument that feedback processes are responsible for quenching activity in massive galaxies. This is accomplished by comparing distant clusters from the Cluster Intermovergence Survey (CIzars) to those in the SDSS, which have X-ray and infrared observations. Using X-ray observations and an assumption of a hot intracluster medium (ICM), the fraction of galaxies that are detected as active can be estimated. In four high-redshift CIzars, the AGN fraction has increased by a factor of 2.5 ± 0.6 (1σ) from z = 0.4 to z = 0.8, showing a rapid increase in the effect of feedback processes in massive galaxies. Simulations show this rise can be explained by stronger feedback in high-mass galaxies, caused by their higher halo masses and star formation rates at higher redshifts. This suggests that feedback, not just mergers, is responsible for transforming high-mass galaxies from the blue cloud to the red sequence.

In this paper we study quantum noise in differential-type gravitational-wave interferometers, which is generated by quantum fluctuations of the optical surface and bottom surface of the waveguides in the arms. In contrast to conventional type interferometers, the signals in differential-type gravitational-wave interferometers are recycled, which means the differential arm signal is used to reduce the noise in the input laser and the output laser. In the presence of quantum noise, we find that the output SNR of the recycled interferometer is improved by a factor of 1/sqrt(m), where m is the number of interferometers that are recycled. We also study the effect of temperature fluctuations on the interferometers, and find that the recycled interferometers are more tolerant to thermal noise. The physical implementation of the recycled interferometer is discussed, and the potential reach of the recycled interferometers is also evaluated. As an application we study gravitational waves from coalescing compact binaries. These are the sources for which LIGO and Virgo are designed, and they are expected to be observed at the start of the new decade. The strain sensitivity of these instruments is fundamentally limited by quantum noise, which is especially important for the intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) candidates identified by LIGO. Because of its high frequency band, cryogenic suspension, and the innovative signal recycling technique, the Cosmic Alert Telescope (CAT) is designed to be the first broad band gravitational-wave observatory, and it is expected to have significant improvements on the strain sensitivity for IMBH signals. In this work, we simulate the expected strain noise from gravitational waves from coalescing IMBHs in the frequency band of Cosmic Alert Telescope, and we find that the sensitivity of Cosmic Alert Telescope can reach the level of strain Hz1 and above at 10Hz and above Hz3 at 100Hz for the events that occurred at redshift z = 1.5.

Bipolar spintronics combines the advantages of ferromagnetic materials and spin electronics by utilizing the spin of electron as well as that of hole. In this approach, the spin-orbit interaction (SOI) is employed to generate or detect spin polarization, and the ferromagnetism can be used for information storage. The first realized application of bipolar spintronics is the observation of spin hall effect in 1977. Since then, intensive studies have been conducted in this field, and various applications have been proposed, including the anomalous hall effect, pure spin current injection, and spintronics-based logic. Then we discuss the discovery and early experimental study of spin Hall effect, including the anomalous hall effect, spin rectification, and spin pumping. Then, we present the experimental studies of anomalous hall effect and spin rectification in thin films. The role of topological term in the anomalous hall effect is discussed. The direct observation of spin Hall effect in metallic systems is overviewed. We also present the spin Hall effect in semiconductors, magnetic semiconductors, and topological insulators. The recent discovery of surface states in topological insulators is overviewed. The methods for detection of spin accumulation are then discussed. The studies of spin dynamics in semiconductors are overviewed. The aim of this paper is to illustrate a methodology based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) for rapid data acquisition in geoscience applications. The presented approach is implemented for hydrogeological applications, where the acquired data consist of Ground-Penetrating Radar (GPR) signals, which are recorded over the same region where pressure changes are to be estimated. The proposed methodology consists of two steps. First, several signals are recorded under different conditions, from which a set of data will be selected for the learning process. The selection criteria are based on the prediction error computed from a model, assuming a Kalman Filter (KF) structure, using the recorded data to predict the pressure changes. Second, the Principal Component Analysis is applied to the selected data in order to reduce the dimensionality and to obtain a low-cost model. The proposed methodology is tested with artificial data and compared with the ARD technique, showing the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

In this paper, we present a methodology and accompanying system for evaluating user experience in an immersive virtual environment (IVE). Specifically, we describe the development of a survey, termed the IVE Experience Questionnaire (IVEEQ), and the construction of a set of form-based questions designed to capture specific experiences found to be important by our usability testing. Our system then analyzes user responses to the IVEEQ, along with gathered metadata, to produce numerical scores and qualitative descriptions of the surveyed experience. To illustrate the utility of this approach, we present the results of our evaluation of forms in an IVE, demonstrating the ability of the IVEEQ to identify form type as a factor influencing user experience. Finally, we discuss future research directions inspired by this work, including extending our evaluation to other aspects of the user experience and applying this approach to different form types." esk In this paper, we present a methodology and accompanying system for evaluating user experience in an immersive virtual environment (IVE).
