Neutralinos could be a major component of the dark matter (DM) in the universe. Many well-known SUSY GUTs suggest that the lightest SUSY particle (LSP) is a good candidate for neutralino, and a DM candidate. However, such SUSY GUTs often have difficulties in matching the measured values of the gauge couplings at the GUT scale, or have to make ad hoc assumptions to explain this. We propose that these difficulties can be avoided if the SUSY is broken in a hidden sector and mediated to the observable sector through strong SUSY breaking effects mediated by scalar supersymmetric partners of standard model fields. In this framework, the SUSY GUTs with a good GUT unification prediction for the strong coupling can naturally give rise to a light neutralino as the LSP which is a good DM candidate. In addition, we show that the correct value for the weak mixing angle can also be obtained. Moreover, we provide one concrete realisation of this framework in which the lightest scalar partner of the standard model Higgs field is the LSP and therefore also a good candidate for DM. This provides a very predictive DM framework which can be tested in the near future both at colliders and at indirect detection experiments such as Cherenkov telescopes.

Single crystals of PbZr0.52Ti0.48O3 (PZT) undergo a phase transition from a higher to a lower symmetry phase at around 600 °C. This structural phase transition is accompanied by a large change in electrical conductivity. It has been shown that the conductivity change can be explained by a change in carrier concentration caused by thermal excitation of deep trapping states. It has further been suggested that in order to describe the change in conductivity correctly, the distribution of activation energies of the deep trapping states has to be considered. The traditional method to obtain this distribution is the quasiequilibrium approximation (QEA), which is an assumption about the thermal evolution of the carrier concentration and requires a full description of the carrier diffusion. Here, we propose a method that relaxes the quasiequilibrium assumption and solves the coupled heat diffusion and drift-diffusion equations with the finite-element method. The obtained conductivity-temperature-relaxation-time-distribution function is in agreement with the quasiequilibrium approximation results for lattice temperatures below around 700 °C. For higher temperatures, however, the difference between the two approaches is considerable and increases with temperature. We argue that this is due to an approximation inherent to the quasiequilibrium approximation and suggest a different approximation that yields results in good agreement with our new method.

In dynamical systems theory, the Generalized Alignment Index (GALI) is a new dynamical measure of local numerical order able to detect also weak interactions between chaotic trajectories. In this work, we study the basic properties of GALI: its definition, its stability to changes of coordinates, and its saturation behavior. We also discuss its main geometric characteristics, including its singularities and limit sets. We illustrate the different features and applications of GALI with several examples, including the calculation of the geometrical factors affecting the stability of different types of periodic orbits, the estimation of the thresholds of global instability of dynamical systems, and the analysis of the route to separatrices of perturbed homoclinic and homoclinic bifurcations. We also apply GALI to the detection of multiple synchronization, with illustrative examples, and to the analysis of the stability of synchronous regimes in coupled maps of different dimensions.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most luminous explosive events in the universe. Despite intensive study for over four decades, the nature of the progenitors and the identity of the elusive central engine that powers them remain unknown. The leading physical scenarios involve mergers of two neutron stars (NS-NS), or a NS-NS merger followed by the birth of a rapidly-rotating magnetar. After merger, a hypernova or a long-duration gamma-ray burst is expected to form as the ejected material travels through the universe. A promising model to explain the broadband emission of GRBs involves synchrotron radiation from electrons accelerated by a returning shock and/or curvature radiation from accelerated electrons. These interactions may occur in the vicinity of a central engine (or a series of engines) and thus may be detectable in other wavelength band(s). In this paper, we show that, for reasonable parameters of the central engine, the prompt emission of GRBs in the GeV-TeV band can be produced by pp, pn and $\pi^{+}\pi^{-}$ interactions in the surrounding baryonic material, resulting from the jets from the central engine. As an example, we consider a long-duration GRB with typical parameters and show that the emission in GeV-TeV is within the sensitivity of current and future telescopes.

Hankel determinants are ubiquitous in mathematics and physics. One way to estimate their behavior is to look at their almost-product evaluation, i.e., to study how they change under small deformations of the matrix. The well-known Wigner semicircle law states that for an ensemble of random matrices with independent identically distributed entries with mean zero and variance one, the logarithm of the ratio of two consecutive Hankel determinants converges in distribution to the Tracy-Widom distribution. Using the joint distribution of the entries, we can also predict the almost-product evaluation of Hankel determinants. We prove that almost all Hankel determinants evaluated at points that are linearly independent over the complex field are constant with probability one. Finally, we explain how to compute the almost-product evaluation of Hankel determinants for matrices with nonnegative entries.' !--more-- We study the almost-product evaluation of Hankel determinants. Consider an $n \times n$ Hankel matrix $H$ with kernel $h$. For $n \times m$ matrices $X$ and $Y$ with $H = [x_{i+j}]_{i,j=0}^{n-1}$, we define $H(t) = [x_{i+j}+th]_{i,j=0}^{n-1}$. We say that $H(t)$ almost-product evaluates to $c$ if for all $1 \le i_1 < i_2 \le n$ and all $t$ we have $$\lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{\left|H(t)[i_1,i_1+k]\right| \cdot \left|H(t)[i_2,i_2+k]\right|}{\left|H[i_1+k,i_2+k]\right|} = c$$ Using the joint distribution of the entries of the matrices, we show that almost all Hankel determinants evaluate to a constant. In particular, for $n$ large, we show that $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{2n^2} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \log \left|H[i,j]\right| = - \frac{1}{8} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \log(1-x^2) d\rho(x)$$ where $\rho$ is the semicircle distribution. For matrices with nonnegative entries, we show that the logarithm of the ratio of two consecutive Hankel determinants almost-product evaluates to the Gaussian free field on the Hermitian discrete plane. In this case, the equality above still holds almost surely.' !--read--

The Feynman-Weinberg quantum gravity (FW QG) is a hybrid quantum-classical theory of gravity based on renormalizable Effective Field Theory (EFT) obtained from the cutting edge of quantum gravity research. It provides a candidate theory of everything (TOE) to unify all known interactions including gravity. The FW QG is an EFT valid up to thePlanck scale, The FW QG extends the standard model (SM) of particle physics to include not just the currently observed fields but also those to higher energies as per the EFT principle. The FW QG is the first theory to incorporate quantum gravity into a relativistic quantum field theory. To date it has passed all known empirical tests: gravitational physics, the weak force, and the strong and electromagnetic forces with its remaining parameters calculated using the EFT approach. Its extension to include the full Standard Model and additional terms to close the missing equations (Planck scale detection/interactions) remains a priority for future research. The FW QG is thus a fully renormalizable, empirically consistent, and self-consistent TOE.

Intercalation of potassium in graphite represents a promising approach to develop an efficient next-generation energy storage device. However, it remains challenging to achieve both high storage capacities and practical electrode potentials. Here we perform a comprehensive first-principles study of the structural, electronic, and dynamical properties of potassium intercalation in graphite. Our main findings are as follows: (i) The graphite intercalation compound (GIC) forms via one-pot synthesis and chemical vapor deposition, in which potassium atoms adsorb onto defective graphene layers between two graphite sheets. (ii) Intercalation occurs without significant changes to the graphene structure or lattice parameters, but induces a sharp increase in the C—C bond length by as much as 0.39 Å. (iii) Potassium incorporation leads to a large decrease in the conduction band minimum of graphite, but only causes a small and highly dispersive increase in the valence band maximum. (iv) The dynamical stability of potassium intercalated graphite is significantly improved by eliminating interactions between potassium and the defective graphene layers. Our findings provide new design strategies for potassium-graphite intercalation batteries, and promote the development of novel two-dimensional materials for energy storage.

In this paper we provide Belyi-type theorems for the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers, written as a pro-finite group, acting on the components of the moduli space of surfaces. We use Galois cohomology with compact support in order to control the geometric part of the étale cohomology of the moduli spaces. By combining our results with previous work of Kevin Hutchinson, we deduce that the absolute Galois group acts faithfully on the components of the moduli space of surfaces. Our work has implications for the rigidity of the Absolute Galois group, namely that it is semisimple. In particular, we deduce that the topological fundamental group of the number field of defnition is trivial. We hope that our work will have further applications to the moduli problems of surfaces. For example, we use our results to deduce that the Hodge bundle on the moduli space of surfaces is nef and big, and so gives rise to a semi-stable family of curves. Our main tool is nonabelian cohomology, in particular the use of compact supports. We also use work of Kevin Hutchinson on the Frobenius morphism on the moduli space of curves. Finally, we also mention that our results confirm a prediction of Yau's generalized sndp conjecture. Authors: Yuri Proshina, Elena A. Matveeva, Victor M. Braito, Alexander A. Golubov, and Sergey Y. Shustov Title: Point-contact spectroscopy of the antiferromagnetic superconductor HoNi2B2C in the normal and superconducting state. Abstract: We study the point-contact spectra of the antiferromagnetic superconductor HoNi2B2C in the normal and superconducting state. In the normal state the observed spectra are typical for an antiferromagnet with small spin-orbit coupling: the effective spin value is 1.3 and a low-temperature dependence of the density of states (DoS) at the Fermi level can be well fitted by the two-dimensional $\sqrt{T}$ law. The spectrum in the superconducting state has a more complex structure. The zero-bias peak and the coherence peak are observed. A low-temperature dependence of the DoS at the Fermi level can be well fitted by the two-dimensional $T^3_2$ law, with the $T^3_2$ coefficient equal to 1.2 times the value for an ordinary superconductor with s-wave order parameter. This fact can be used to distinguish between d-wave and s-wave superconductivity in this material.

In the paper “Are constant loop widths an artifact of the background and the spatial resolution?” Andreas Madsen, Mads Trolle, and Jesper Thygesen challenge the current methodology of loop shaping, a commonly used VASIMR campaign planning procedure. They claim that, because current VASIMR designs assume a steady magnetic equilibrium, the width of the plasma channels that guide the magnetic field lines will be constant even during disruptions in the equilibrium. They show by comparison to data from the Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) stellarator that, in fact, the channel width does not remain constant but rather varies by up to 30%, and that this variation is sufficiently large to cause the ion flow pattern to deviate significantly from idealvacuum and interfere with mission operations. The implication is that current disruption mitigation strategies are not sufficient to fully protect VASIMR architectures from unintended excursions from equilibrium. The article argues that a more robust stabilization strategy based on an examination of the ion flow pattern may be required.

The phase behavior of a fluid with competing attractive and repulsive interactions was studied by means of Monte Carlo simulations in two and three dimensions. A moderate strength repulsion was sufficient to establish the competition between a fluid and a crystalline solid phases. In the two-dimensional case, there exist two continuous phase transitions: a fluid-crystal transition and a fluid-fluid transition. In contrast, in three dimensions, only a single phase transition was observed. The critical behavior of the fluid-fluid transition was found to be consistent with that of the three-dimensional Ising model. The present work is a numerical study of a fluid with competing interactions in two and three dimensions. It has previously been established that a fluid with purely attractive interactions exhibits a first-order fluid-fluid transition. It was hypothesized that the addition of a small amount of repulsive interactions would yield a continuous fluid-fluid transition. Such a fluid with competing interactions could, in principle, be realized in certain mixture systems with negative fluid-phase interaction and positive colloidal stability. The Monte Carlo simulations reported in this work were conducted to test this hypothesis. The results are in excellent agreement with the theoretical predictions and provide further evidence in support of this newly discovered fluid-fluid transition.

We present a detailed study of 47 clusters of galaxies which have signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10 and which lie within cz < 5000 km/s of the DR4 spectroscopic sample. We measured the global cluster properties, namely the X-ray temperature, the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect temperature, the luminosity and the radius, the velocity dispersion, the mass and the temperature from the spectroscopy and Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect data. In addition, we measured the intra-cluster gas mass from the X-ray data. The global properties were derived using both the projected parameterizations and the three dimensional model and compared. We also estimated the total mass from the velocity dispersion assuming that the clusters are relaxed systems. The velocity dispersion were calculated using both the photometric (optical) members and the spectroscopy members. We compared the total mass derived from both the X-ray and the velocity dispersion. The global properties of these clusters were studied using X-ray, Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect and optical data. All of these results are summarized in this paper.

On September 20, 2015, a X8.2-class solar flare occurred in active region NOAA 11497, which was located on the solar disk with P9 solar class visibility. The accompanying gamma-ray and hard X-ray emissions showed a rapid onset and dramatic initial decay, which has been commonly attributed to the impact of accelerated electrons into cold target atoms. Here we report the radio observations of the flare by the New Solar Telescope (NST) at Big Bear Solar Observatory (BBSO). The high-cadence, high-resolution dynamic spectra show that the initial HXR burst is associated with the rapid increase of nonthermal radio emission at multiple wavelengths, while the subsequent decline is due to the decreasing and self-absorption of the nonthermal electrons. Compared to the standardimpulsive model of flare acceleration, the radio data favor a highly rarefied plasmascheme, in which the electrons are accelerated by the first-order Fermi process at the low-energy cutoff, and then continuously cooled by the radiation loss, which naturally produces the observed non-thermal emission with slowly-decaying light curves and short lifetimes of ~10 minutes. Such a slow radiative loss also allows these electrons to reach very high energies, which is consistent with the very-high-energy gamma-ray emission detected by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on board the Solar Dynamic Observatory (SDO) and the extensive observations of coronal electron beam at late times. This study provides new observational constraints on the electron acceleration and transport in the solar atmosphere and the subsequent broadband emissions. The continuous observations at different acceleration sites and different timescales reveal the energy and spatial dynamics of the accelerated electrons and challenge current flare models.

Generalised Mirror Symmetry conjectures that certain quantum phases of QFTs are equivalent as ribbon-based?uchsheets, despite not having a classical description in common. Particular examples of such quantum phases include Chern-Simons theory with group G, and two-dimensional twisted?insulators (with certain conditions on the twisted boundary conditions). A remarkable conjecture in Generalised Mirror Symmetry, due to Abouzaid, Auroux, and Katzarkov-Kontsevich, states that the 'classical mirror' of a twisted?insulator is a?uicket phase of QFTs, whose gauge symmetry is generated by certain twisted de Rham complexes. In this paper, we provide evidence for this conjecture by proving the Abouzaid-Katzarkov-Kontsevich theorem for the special case of two-dimensional twisted?insulators, and thereby establishing twisted Generalised Mirror Symmetry in this case. We then generalise this proof strategy to establish twisted Generalised Mirror Symmetry in the two-dimensional setting for any two-dimensional twisted?insulator. As a consequence, we recover and significantly generalise previous twisted Generalised Mirror Symmetry predictions for the classical mirrors of some well-known two-dimensional twisted?insulators, such as the A-model for the Chiral de Rham Complex, or A-model for the?uicket phase constructed by Kapustin, Li and Naqvi. In particular, we provide the first example of twisted Generalised Mirror Symmetry between two-dimensional QFTs and curved target spaces, and establish the existence of an A-model for a wide range of two-dimensional twisted?insulators.

Iron abundances of B-type post-Asymptotic Giant Branch stars in globular clusters: Barnard 29 in M 13 and ROA 5701 in omega Cen. Iron (Fe) is one of the most abundant elements in the universe, and is ubiquitous in the cosmos. This work presents the first large survey of iron abundances in globular clusters (GCs). Spectroscopic observations were obtained for 26 B-type post-Asymptotic Giant Branch (B-PAGB) stars in M 13 and 28 B-PAGB stars in omega Cen. The iron abundances were derived from equivalent widths of absorption lines in high-resolution spectra. Our results show that iron is deficient with respect to the scaled solar mixture at the 2-3σ level in all GCs with measured abundances. We also find a number of individual stars with enhanced iron abundances, which could be the results of internal pollution from fast-rotating massive stars. This work demonstrates the feasibility of large-scale spectroscopic analyses of GC B-PAGB stars and provides important new constraints for models of GC formation.

The leading order behavior of the Friedmann equations in modified gravity theories is typically modified by an additional function of the curvature invariants. In particular, for f(R) models this function typically diverges at points in field space where the model exhibits equation of state (EOS) singularities. These EOS singularities correspond to infinite values for the density, pressure, or both. In this work, we explore the phenomenological implications of these EOS singularities, focusing on the specific case of finite-time singularities. We explore the model parameter space for which EOS singularities render the universe non-physical, formulating the question as an exclusion plot in the plane of model parameters. We show that such an exclusion plot is significantly restricted by existing data from SNIa, baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) and direct detection experiments, allowing for only a small region of this parameter space. We present a new EOS formulation that is well-behaved across all parameter space and show that this significantly expands the viable model space. In addition to validating the existing results, this demonstrates the ability of existing data to rule out non-physical models. Finally, we show that EOS singularities cause regions of field space to become ghosts—unitary theories that have propagating degrees of freedom with negative energy. Such regions of field space can be ruled out by local gravity constraints from tests of the equivalence principle. We show that these constraints are more than sufficient to rule out all regions of ghostly parameter space, further strengthening the case for f(R) models as the standard gravity theory.

The stationary state of the asymmetric target process is found. This process is a multi-type birth and death process with local reactions. It may be viewed as a specific variant of the partially asymmetric exclusion process. This model is relevant to the DNA transcription mechanism, in which a RNA polymerase transcribes a DNA template into an RNA molecule. The RNA may then be translated into a protein by the cellular machinery. The RNA molecule may also be damaged, in which case it is sent to the RNA degradation machinery for destruction. The degradation machinery may also be saturated, in which case a portion of unscathed RNA may be repaired into DNA for subsequent transcription. The model has two types of particles: P-particles and C-particles. A particle of type i denotes a particle that is intersted in reaction i. A particle of type i is born with rate rPib(1) into the neighborhood of a P-particle of type i. The neighboring P-particles of type i move as a cluster with migration rate a. A particle of type i dies with rate rCdc(1) into the neighborhood of a C-particle of type i. The C-particles of type i move as a cluster with migration rate a. The asymmetric model is defined differently from the symmetric model. In the symmetric model, P-particles and C-particles have the same parameters, whereas in the asymmetric model, the rates of the reactions may differ. In the steady state, the density of P-particles is equal to the density of C-particles. The structure of the steady state is encoded in the generating functions of the two densities. The algebraic equations that must be satisfied by the two generating functions are the stationary equations of the model. In the special case of symmetric dynamics, these equations were found by Schütz and others in 1998. The exact solution of the stationary equations is possible only for a special set of rates, called kinasich limit. In this limit, the densities depend only on the local density of C-particles. This density-dependent solution can be expanded into a perturbative series in a parameter which is the ratio of the rates. The first-order approximation, which is also sufficient to determine the structure of the solution, is presented here. This approximation is valid when the local density of C-particles is low, which corresponds to a high density of P-particles. The solution has a phase transition at a critical value of the asymmetry. When the asymmetry is below the critical value, there is no stable cluster of C-particles. When the asymmetry is above the critical value, there is a stable cluster of C-particles of any size. The present solution is limited to the kinasich limit, but the same method can be used to obtain the expansion for any set of rates. This should yield new information about the behavior of the asymmetric model away

The vibrational spectrum of nitrous oxide has been studied in solution, for the first time, using an infrared (IR) laser as the source of vibration. The OH and NH2 anti-solvent refrigeration technique was used to produce samples of nitrous oxide in diethyl ether solution. A range of data analysis methods were used to analyse the spectra, and it was found that the global minimum nitrous oxide conformer in solution has a gamma-proton resonance as a single hydrogen bond and a symmetric CH2O hydrogen bond between the two molecules. This is in contrast to the vapour, where the global minimum has two strong NH...O hydrogen bonds, leading to the resonance form. The reorganisation energy of the gamma-proton resonance in solution is 18 cm-1, very close to the value in the gas phase. The calculated am1g-frequencies for the two strongest NH...O and gamma-proton hydrogen bonds are 3650 and 3300 cm-1 respectively, and are found in the infrared spectrum at 3520 and 3220 cm-1 respectively. The calculated lifetime of the gamma-proton hydrogen bond in solution is 44 ps, and is found from the linewidth of the frequency range corresponding to this hydrogen bond, which is 10 cm-1. The linewidth is used to calculate the vibrational lifetime of the nitrous oxide solution molecules. The nitrous oxide solution has a weaker gamma-proton hydrogen bond than in the gas phase or other solution conformers, and this has been proposed to be one of the causes of the strong inversion, general anaesthesia, produced by inhalation of the solution. The gamma-proton hydrogen bond in solution has a lifetime which is less than that in the gas phase or other solution conformers, and this has implications for the theory of general anaesthesia produced by inhalation of nitrous oxide solution. The nitrous oxide spectrum in solution has been found to be in good agreement with previous gas phase studies, with a combination of methods for analysing IR spectra. The global minimum nitrous oxide solution conformer has a much lower energy than the observed gamma-proton resonance form in the gas phase, and this may be one of the reasons why general anaesthesia is only produced by inhalation of the gas form. The results could be relevant to understanding nitrous oxide general anaesthesia, and the differences could be used to characterise solvents and correlate with trends in anaesthetic potency.

A short abstract of a scientific paper from arXiv.org. The article explores the X-ray properties of V2301 Oph, a binary system composed of a late-type main-sequence star and an unseen, highly magnetized hot-Jupiter exoplanet in a highly eccentric orbit. The X-rays are generated in the stellar magnetosphere, which is distorted by the planet's gravity. The distortion causes cyclotron resonance scattering of X-rays in the planet's magnetosphere, resulting in the appearance of a dark spot on the visible hemisphere and a bright spot on the other hemisphere of the planet. The observations were carried out in 2013 using the XMM-Newton observatory. The results confirm that the planet possesses a massive and highly magnetized magnetosphere, and that the global atmosphere of the planet is strongly dominated by molecular hydrogen. The article is accompanied by 8 high resolution figures and 1 table. The figures show the temporal and spatial variability of the X-ray flux, as well as distribution of elemental abundances. The table provides planet and star parameters, and a summary of the results.

In this paper, we construct equilibrium measures for the family of Boutroux curves with external field and analyze their properties. These measures do not minimize a energy, but rather belong to a natural space of measures. In the case where the external field is constant, these measures are related to certain orthogonal polynomials. For general external fields, the behavior of these measures is more complex. We characterize their equilibrium potential, which is the unique Hölder continuous function with zero force. We then determine the associated diffuse measure, which is purely singular. We also prove convergence of the corresponding densities and we compute an expansion at the points of maximum external field. Finally, we give formulas for the transversemeasure and the full topological measure, which allow us to compute explicitly theSzego kernel, as well as correlation functions. This paper presents a construction of equilibrium measures for the Boutroux curves with external field. These measures do not minimize a classical energy, but rather belong to a natural space of measures. In the case where the external field is constant, these measures are related to certain orthogonal polynomials. For general external fields, the behavior of these measures is more complex. We characterize their equilibrium potential, which is the unique Hölder continuous function with zero force. We then determine the associated diffuse measure, which is purely singular. We also prove convergence of the corresponding densities and we compute an expansion at the points of maximum external field. Finally, we give formulas for the transversemeasure and the full topological measure, which allow us to compute explicitly the Szego kernel, as well as correlation functions.

Neurons in the central nervous system transmit information by propagating action potentials, also known as “spikes”. These spikes initiate at the axon of a neuron, and then propagate along the axon to the terminal bulb, where they cause a change in membrane potential. This change in membrane potential subsequently leads to a change in membrane conductance, which causes a post-synaptic potential in target cells. This post-synaptic potential may then lead to a new spike in the target cell. This positive feedback loop is often called the neuron’s “wave”. Positive feedback is necessary for neurons to fire at high rates. However, not all neurons exhibit oscillatory behavior. For these neurons, the axon may ultimately repolarize below the threshold for spike initiation, leading to the cessation of the post-synaptic potential and the cessation of the spike. This type of negative feedback is known as “repolarization feedback”. Repolarization feedback has been observed in a variety of preparations, including locust giant Kenyon cell dendrites, lamprey spinal interneurons, and mammalian neocortical pyramidal neurons. Repolarization feedback has been shown to play a critical role in regulating the firing rates of neurons.

In quantum physics, effective potentials are frequently used to describe the effective interaction between particles, e.g. in molecules or in neutron scattering. Usually, the effective potential depends on the spatial coordinates, the temperature, etc. Therefore, the exact form of the effective potential is unknown and has to be determined from experiments or theories. An exact effective potential can only be determined up to a functional, i.e. an arbitrary constant. A famous example is the Debye model of the solid state, where the exact pair potential is approximated by an inverse-square potential. A more complex case is the Heisenberg model for ferromagnets, where the spin direction is represented by a 3D vector. In this model, the exact pair potential contains two cosines with different wave vectors. Since all these models are just approximations, they are usually called effective potentials. However, if the spatial dependence and the frequency dependence are separated, the exact effective potential can be determined in a unique manner. It is the solution of the Wetterich equation, which is based on the properties of the Renormalization Group (RG). This effective potential is called the Wilson effective potential. Although it can be determined in a unique manner, it is not very suitable for applications, because it contains high-order derivatives. In this paper, an approximate solution of the Wetterich equation is proposed. It separates the spatial dependence from the frequency dependence and therefore is easier to apply. For this, an operator product expansion is used, which is well known in critical phenomena. This approximation is compared with the exact solution of the Wetterich equation and with the Debye model. As a consequence, the new approximation is better than the Debye model only in a region far away from boundaries and anisotropies, where the three models coincide. But the new approximation is much simpler than the exact solution and therefore more convenient for applications.

Excitons in single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are strongly influenced by the nanotube’s environment. In this paper, we investigate dielectric screening of the SWCNT’s environment on exciton transition energies. We find that the screening effect is significant in some cases, and it can induce spectral redshifts of several hundred meV. Moreover, the screening effect varies significantly among different exciton transitions, and it can alter the exciton symmetry. These findings provide new mechanisms for environment-induced dispersion of exciton energies and new ways to manipulate exciton properties via dielectric environment modification. Two dimensional lattice systems with short range interactions and correlated random perturbations typically exhibit a second order phase transition at zero temperature from a disordered phase to an ordered phase in which spontaneously formed domains have a uniform average orientation. Systems with quenched random anisotropy in the spin-spin coupling usually display a first order transition between high and low temperature phases in which the direction of alignment is either randomly distributed or uniformly aligned with respect to a fixed direction in the anisotropic plane. Systems in two dimensions with uniaxial spatially correlated anisotropies typically exhibit a multicritical point at which three critical lines of first order transitions between high and low temperature phases meet. We study a model of coupled two dimensional XY systems with spatial anisotropy using high precision computer simulations and conclude that the multicritical point is in fact a lower-dimensional boundary and that the true critical behavior is that of the abelian universality class. In particular, we demonstrate that the low temperature phase is perfectly aligned and that the magnetization has power law dependencies on system size and temperature with different exponents along different directions in the anisotropic plane.

This survey is aimed at optically bright X-ray sources selected from the XMM-Newton survey of hard X-ray sources [1]. It is part of the XMM-SSC survey, which is intended as an annual survey of the XMM-Newton survey area performed with the XMM-Newton soft-stateCA (SSC) instrument in the 0.2-12 keV energy band. The sample is constructed from the list of sources with count rates in the HECS1 and/or BECS1 detector more than 3 sigmas from the mean count rate, derived from the exposure map for the survey interval. Optical counterparts are sought for from the optical monitor on XMM-Newton and accurate positions are obtained from the XMM-Newton slew survey. Subsequent optical spectroscopy is performed at the Calar Alto and ESO 2.2 m telescopes. Here we present the analysis of the first part of the survey, comprising data taken in 2011. A total of 371 such sources were identified in the XMM-Newton survey area, of which 102 were located in the ESO region. Of these, 93 had secure optical IDs: 45 are known quasars, 39 are galaxies and 9 are stars. The remainder are unclassified. This leaves a total of 87 potential new quasars in the ESO region. The catalogue is available in electronic form at the CDS and Table 2 is presented here. A total of 48 sources are in the final catalogue of XMM-SSC survey, presented in a subsequent paper.

In this paper, we study the wetting transition on a one-dimensional random medium with a quenching nature. We use the simple Landau-Ginzburg effective Hamiltonian to describe the interface between two phases. The quenched medium is inhomogeneous and the variation of the environment changes gradually from one region to another. The randomness of medium presents local defects which can take different positions and have different strengths. For convenience, we call the system with monotonic variation of the local environment as smooth medium, and the system with non-monotonic variation as rough medium. In the case of smooth medium, the wetting transition is first order. While in the case of rough medium, it is of the second order. Our simulation shows that the roughening of the medium promotes the wetting transition from first order to second order. Here, we use a modified Landau-Ginzburg theory to discuss the wetting behavior on the random medium. We use the effective interface Hamiltonian to represent the interface between two phases. In the case of smooth medium, the interface is described by the Ising model. While in the rough medium, we use the effective interface Hamiltonian with double-well potential to represent the interface. The Gaussianrandomness of medium presents local defects which can take different positions and have different strengths. The roughness of the medium promotes the symmetry-breaking of the interface and makes the interface state become polarized. Our simulation shows that the roughening of the medium promotes the wetting transition from first order to second order.

A survey of molecular gas in and around the supergiant HII region NGC 604 has been carried out using the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT). The JCMT is an innovative facilities instrument, operating as a dedicated mission in the submillimetre wavelength range. This allows the study of cold gas, an important phase of the ISM, in extreme environments such as those present in the NGC 604 region. Two areas of distinct complexity have been observed: the ring-like structure, often called the bow shock, associated with the fast moving cluster of young stars central cluster; and a broader arc-like distribution of high CO(J=3-2)/CO(J=1-0) ratio gas surrounding the central star cluster. The arc is highly unusual given its small size (a few parsecs) and extremely high brightness temperature (Tb ~ 105 K). The most plausible explanations for this extreme emission are extremely high densities (n(H) ~ 1023 cm-3) and extremely low temperatures (T < 10K), either due to high volume densities and low volume temperatures (i.e. very high energy densities), or far-ultraviolet radiation from the central cluster.

In this paper, we propose a novel method to calculate the critical nucleus and the surface tension in systems with first order phase transition. This method is based on an expansion of the free energy around the tricritical point and the integration of the radius of the critical nucleus. We also present a correction of the radius of the critical nucleus using the Ginzburg–Landau approximation. This method can be used to calculate the critical nucleus in various systems, such as liquid–vapor phase transition in water, vapor–liquid phase transition in systems with different fractions of vapor and liquid, equilibrium stages of two-phase saturation in van der Waals fluid, etc. The results were verified by Monte Carlo simulations. We also used this method to calculate the surface tension and obtained good agreement with the results of the previous works. The source code of this method can be found in the supplementary materials of this paper.

NGC 5466 is an extended globular cluster lying at a distance of 27 kpc from the Sun in the southern constellation of Grus. Its apparent magnitude is 10.7, which means it is barely visible to the naked eye. The composition of the cluster has been studied extensively, with many studies focusing on the variability of its red giants. NGC 5466 has a metallicity of -1.6, making it more similar to the halo population than to most globular clusters. As a result, it has been hypothesized that a significant fraction of its population are not actual members of the cluster, but rather escaped, shredded primordials. The photometric study of NGC 5466 presented here focuses on the detection of red giants in two datasets: V and I band photometry from the Victor M. Hayes Telescope at Lowell Observatory, and g'r'i'z' photometry from the Gaia satellite. Analysis of these datasets has found 65 red giant members in V, 62 in I, and 51 in g'r'i'z'. The V-band half-light radius of the cluster is 13.0 arcmin, while its distance is known with high precision thanks to Hydra ESA mission measurements of the gravitational pull of a large number of cluster stars. Analysis of the number of red giants compared to the half-light radius and distance to the cluster indicates the presence of a significant number of escaped, shredded primordials. Additionally, the presence of blue stragglers has been found through analysis of the V and I bands. These consist of bloated stars created through binary evolution, rather than shredding primordials. Blue stragglers were not found in the g'r'i'z' dataset, suggesting they may absorb blue light at g'r'i' but not at g' and r'. Overall, this study supports the hypothesis that a significant fraction of the population of NGC 5466 are escaped primordials. Future studies of their spectra may allow further differentiation between these two populations, as well as additional insight into the nature of shredded primordials.

We have obtained the first imaging observation of transient brightenings in the cores of galaxies. These X-ray transients were discovered with the Chandra satellite when it observed the central regions of the galaxies NGC 4874 and 6052 during 2002 and 2003. X-ray luminosities comparable to those of classical novae were observed, as well as apparent motions corresponding to massive outflows from the nuclei of the galaxies. The X-ray emitting regions are restricted to 10 - 15 parsecs in diameter, much smaller than the gravitational radii of the galaxies' central black holes. Together, these observations indicate that the galaxies' central black holes are endowed with significant populations of hypercompact X-ray binaries. Because these X-ray binaries can be as massive as early type stars, they may play a key role in fueling the central black holes and furthering the transformation of their host galaxies from normal to quasar phases.

In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical approach for dependability analysis of a commercial cache-based RAID storage architecture. The proposed approach combines fault detection and isolation techniques with Markov Chain analysis and Bayesian network analysis to evaluate the impact of different types of faults on the availability and response time of the system. The effectiveness of the approach is illustrated using a set of real-world experiments on a high-availability production cluster involving over 2000 virtual machines and hundreds of file transactions. The results show that a large number of faults can occur without any adverse impact on the availability of the cluster. Furthermore, the response times of the system are also unaffected by many of the faults that occur. However, a large number of faults do affect the response time of the system and this can have a significant impact on the overall user experience. Using the proposed approach, we are able to identify and quantify these faults and their impact on the dependability of the cluster.

In this work, the first study of the gluon-quark-antiquark static potential in SU(3) lattice QCD is presented. The potential is calculated using Wilson loops with temporal extent of $T$ = 5 and 7. The calculations were performed on $32^3 \times 64$ and $24^3 \times 48$ lattices with five values of the renormalization group invariant momentum scale, $\mu$, corresponding to quark masses, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 and 0.7 GeV. The results are presented both in the laboratory frame and in the quarkonium rest frame. It is found that at short separations the interaction is linear in all frames. In the limit of zero separation the string tension is computed to be $\sigma$ = (0.437 $\pm$ 0.002) GeV/fm. This study was performed using improved Wilson glue and quark actions. The quarkonium masses range from approximately 2.2-3.2 GeV, corresponding to a pion mass of approximately 430-600 MeV, and a renormalization scale of 0.40-0.70 GeV.

A method for fast and effective production of large area films of aligned single-walled carbon nanotubes is described. The method uses Langmuir-Blodgett assembly to deposit densely packed nanotube films from a noncovalently stabilized suspension in alcohol. The resulting films are shown by optical and atomic force microscopy to be highly aligned and to consist of individual nanotubes as well as small bundles. The films have excellent mechanical properties and retain this functionality after exposure to air. This approach provides a simple and effective way to make large area films of aligned single-walled nanotubes for use in various devices and applications. In this paper, we show that off-shell N = 8, D = 4 supergravity can be formulated in a self-dual (14+14) representation, by interpreting the graviton as a conformal spin-2 field together with its dual. The theory is coupled to a single, massless, scalar hyper-multiplet, which can be used to fix the local Weyl invariance of the action. The supersymmetry transformation laws and the explicitly gauge-fixed action are then obtained. The theory admits a unique Minkowski solution with an additional electrically gauged u(1) isometry. By studying BPS solutions, we show that this happens to be the whole interpolating orbit of Minkowski solutions. We also consider the case of an abelian hyper-gauge group, discussing the solvable structure of the local symmetry group. Finally, we show that twistor theory on $P^{3,3,1}$ naturally arises as the space of orbits of the local Weyl group.

Galaxy clusters are complex environments where galaxies, dark matter and hot plasma from surrounding material congregate. As the largest virialized structures in the universe, they can reveal important insights into how structures form and influence each other. X-ray observations of clusters can identify the hot plasma (plasma is the fourth state of matter) and galaxies, and study the distribution of these components within the cluster. Flashes from galaxy clusters are rare, but an analysis of the Chandra archive has identified four galaxy clusters with unusually bright filaments of galaxies. A2744, located in the constellation Coma Berenices, is one of these clusters. At a distance of approximately 100 million light years, A2744 is one of the most distant clusters observable by Chandra. The cluster has a strong peak in the X-ray emission and X-ray observations show that the cluster has an unusually bright filament of approximately 20 million light years in length, extending between galaxy groups to the north and south of the cluster. Optical and infrared observations have shown that many of the galaxies along this filament are extremely bright, indicating that the filament is lit up by very energetic source. The authors propose three potential explanations for this phenomenon; a chance alignment of very bright galaxies, a region of the cluster where galaxy groups have recently collided, or indication of unexpected amounts of hot, low-mass material in the cluster. Further X-ray observations of the region, optical and infrared observations of the galaxies and detailed analysis of the distribution of dark matter in the region will help determine the cause of this unusually bright region of the cluster.

Modern online services, such as image and video hosting services, have gained a lot of popularity in recent years. These services often allow users to tag images with keyword or category labels. Such keyword or category labels are often expensive to acquire and very skewed. For example, most images contain people and outdoor scenes, and the category “people” and “outdoor” respectively have many highly-used tags. It is desirable to infer the likely categories of unlabeled images from the keyword or category tags already assigned to them. This problem of tag auto-labeling has many important applications. For example, a service could suggest labels to unlabeled images based on their metadata and content. Moreover, users could contribute more meaningful labels to images that they judge contain specific categories. Existing approaches to this problem of tag auto-labeling mainly exploit the local label semantics. However, the inferred semantics often do not match the global label semantics. For example, images of people often contain backgrounds with trees or buildings, and these global semantics are often unrelated to the local “people” category. These methods often resort to spectral clustering or other local optimization techniques that can only handle relatively small tag vocabularies. They often need large amounts of training data and suffers from data sparsity. In this paper, we analyze the global attentional shift of users while browsing image tags. By measuring global attentional shift, we can use computer vision techniques to automatically infer the global label semantics, and this global inference can alleviate the problems caused by local label semantics. More importantly, the inferred global label semantics often match the human semantics, which further justifies the effectiveness of our proposed approach. Our algorithm has two stages. The first stage tracks the global attentional shift of users based on tracking clicks on the server. We first estimate the bounding boxes of the user heads and record the clicks on tags within these boxes. Next, we identify the regions of interest (ROIs) by grouping the clicked boxes with a relatively high density. We then determine the global attentional shift by measuring the density of the boxes in the ROIs. The second stage infers the label semantics from the global attentional shift. For each image, we first find the most similar images in the training set using a deep network based on the learned representations. By combining the global attentional shift and local semantic information, we can infer the global label semantics. We finally use a straightforward optimization algorithm to learn the global label semantics. Our algorithm tracks both local and global attentional shift. It can accurately identify the regions of user interests and can also model the global attentional shift between different regions. By combining both local and global information, we can accurately infer the label semantics and thus automatically auto-label unlabeled images. Experiments show that our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art method in terms of both tagging accuracy and efficiency. Our algorithm has two stages. The first stage tracks the global attentional shift of users

A new model of gravity which overcomes the singularities and other problems of the Standard model of Einstein is proposed. This new model is called'repulsive gravity' and it is built around the theory of discrete/holographic dimensions. The small extra spatial dimensions, dark energy and dark matter are explained by the effects of the volume increase due to the compression of the physical dimensions in the presence of mass/energy. The new model is tested against the available cosmological and solar system data, and is shown to provide a good fit without the need of dark energy or dark matter. The new model also naturally explains the anomalous perihelion shift of Mercury without the need of non-standard gravitational parameters or other contrary to expectations effects. Introduction The Standard Model of Einstein gravity is the best current model of gravity. This model assumes that the Universe has three spatial dimensions, and one time dimension. The theory has passed a number of tests, and there is no experimental evidence to reject it. However, the Standard Model has some serious problems. It cannot explain the small size of the extra spatial dimensions. This leads to the existence of large numbers of dark energy particles and a universe with negative pressure. In order to resolve this problem, a lower energy scale than the Planck scale is assumed, which makes the theory incomplete. Also, there are many additional problems with the Standard Model of gravity such as the existence of black holes with severely negative binding energy, or naked singularities. The new theory of'repulsive gravity' proposed here overcomes these problems. In the new model, the spatial dimensions are assumed to be discrete, with the smallest physical length being 'holographic' in origin. The existence of these small dimensions explains the need for a lower energy scale, as well as the large numbers of dark energy particles. The small extra dimensions also give a natural explanation for the anomalous perihelion shift of Mercury without the need for non-standard gravitational parameters. A large number of theoretical arguments exist in favor of the existence of small spatial dimensions, so the new model is theoretically well motivated. However, there is currently no experimental evidence to support these assumptions. The discrete/holographic nature of the dimensions makes the new model essentially indistinguishable from the Standard Model of gravity at low energies. However, when probing the gravitational field at high energies, the new model becomes dramatically different from the Standard Model. This is because the new model assumes the existence of multiple disconnected space-time manifolds, whereas the Standard Model assumes the validity of Riemannian geometry. As a result, the effect of mass becomes anisotropic, as the physical dimensions compress in the direction of the mass, while expanding in the dimensions transverse to the mass.

The formation of spiral arms and rings in barred galaxies is a long-standing problem in astrophysics and cosmology. While leading theories have been proposed in the past two decades, our current understanding of this process is still incomplete. In this paper, we present high-resolution cosmological simulations, which follow the formation of stars, dark matter and active galactic nuclei in a self-consistent way, that resolve both the gravitational instability and feedback processes in detail. We find that during the bar formation, density waves are excited in the disk, and the star formation is dramatically enhanced in the regions of trailing arms. As a result, most of the stars are formed in the trailing arms, and some fraction of the gas is also converted into stars and settle into the rings. The pattern of the formed spiral structure and rings is closely related to the morphology of the host galaxy, in particular the bar strength and pattern speed. When the bar strength is moderate and the pattern speed is low, the resulting spiral pattern and rings are dominated by two arms. When the bar becomes stronger, the inner disk is severely depleted and a two-armed bulge pattern is formed. This pattern is also associated with the two rings. When the pattern speed is very high, the stellar rings become loosely wound spirals with large pitch angles. The distribution of the gas in these cases is rather irregular, with some additional stellar rings. The distribution and kinematics of the stars in these systems are very complicated. These numerical results are in good agreement with previous observational studies and theoretical works.

In this work we investigate the presence of selection effects in the observations of Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) with their associated cosmology implications. Current GRB brightnesses distributions (in various light curves parameters) are inconsistent with being only due to observational selection effects. We provide evidence for the existence of a third population of bursts with peak energies above the sensitivity band of current instruments and that could therefore be responsible for the “false positives” found in the current sample. The proposed model is in agreement with current findings about GRBs host galaxy population and be able to reproduce the current redshifts distribution. The detection method is based on the comparison of the signal to noise in different energy bands and is very general and could be applied to other transient sources for which there are not enough photons in the raw data to properly infer their redshift. WZ Sge was first identified as a strongly interacting binary system consisting of a K-type donor and a white dwarf secondary. Using very recent data, WZ Sge still stands as an unique example of a dwarf nova with extremely fast outbursts. Its giant outbursts reached a magnitude of 5.5 in 1957, 1957, 1964, 1966, 1967, 1969, 1970, 1971, 1973, 1975, 1976, 1977, 1978, 1981, 1982, 1983, 1984, 1985, 1986, 1988, 1990, 1991, 1992, 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999, 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016. The 2017 outburst was only recently caught by ASAS-SN. WZ Sge is the longest recognized outburst interval of a dwarf nova. Here we report the results of a long-term photometric and spectroscopic monitoring of WZ Sge since 2010. Our data set covers 19 outbursts of WZ Sge, one normal outburst and several normal non-outburst intervals. We describe the method and data analysis in the Appendix. Our results show that the WZ Sge system has undergone a long-term behaviour evolution that can be described by a variation of the mass ratio q=K3secondary/Kdonor=0.068±0.002 ranging from 0.068 to 0.078.

Applicability of layered sine-Gordon models to layered superconductors: II. The case of magnetic coupling. We extend our analysis of coupled layered sine-Gordon models to the case of magnetic coupling. First, we note that, in general, a spatially varyingLondon magnetization interacts with the charge density wave order parameter in a layered superconductor. We demonstrate, through a simple 1D Ginzburg-Landau analysis, that the magnetic coupling between the two order parameters competes with their conventional charge density wave (CDW) coupling. Depending on material parameters, such a magnetic coupling may either destroy or stabilize the charge density wave order. We verify our analytical results by carrying out a complete numerical study of the two coupled SG models using a gradient energy regularization scheme. Our numerical results suggest that in some systems the magnetic coupling may even stabilize the charge density wave order. asquarters The applicability of coupled layered sine-Gordon models to layered superconductors is analyzed in [1]. Magnetic coupling between the charge density wave order parameter and spatially varying London magnetization is analyzed. Depending on material parameters this coupling may either destroy or stabilize charge density wave order. Results of numerical study of two coupled sine-Gordon models are presented. Verification of analytical results is done using gradient energy regularization.

The Primordial density distribution of our universe is commonly modeled as a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric, with finite size, but infinite expansion. This model is consistent with recent observations of the cosmic microwave background if the universe has a low matter density (ρM < 0.5ρc, where ρc is the critical density) and is comprised of 75% radiopures photons and 25% compact hyper-massive objects (HomoSol). This, combined with the smoothness assumption, yields a density distribution of the form ρ ∝ (1 + ax2) − 3. Despite its mathematical equivalence to the matter distribution, the Friedmann model has no physical motivation. In an Einstein gravity theory with a minimally coupled scalar field, this implies a beginning without a cosmological singularity. We show that for this to happen, the universe must had a period of asymptotic anti-de Sitter (AdS) expansion at early times, with a scale factor a(t) ∝ t-1/2. This initial condition is consistent with current observations of cosmological structure if the AdS period begins at some finite epoch t 0, with |t 0| < 10-6 s. This is but one of an infinite number of homogeneous and isotropic solutions to the Einstein equations with a positive cosmological constant. These solutions are saddlepoints of the Einstein action and thus correspond to degenerate ground states. A geodesically complete universe with this asymptotic structure necessarily has a period of hyperbolic expansion at early times, with a scale factor a(t) ∝ tp, for some p < 1. For a(t) to begin at a finite value a0, the AdS period must end at some finite value aF, where a(aF) = a0. We show that for this to happen, the universe must have had a period of de Sitter expansion earlier in its history, with a scale factor a(t) ∝ e(Ht + κ), for some constants κ and H. Since a(t) is increasing on each of these intervals, the universe obeys the energy condition and is necessarily spatially infinite. However, the smoothness assumption is incompatible with the presence of a strong curvature regime, and the universe necessarily ends in a curvature singularity. Finally, we comment on extensions to this model. In particular, we consider the effects of coupling the scalar field to ordinary matter, curvature, and a self-interacting potential. The matter coupling allows for a period of smooth evolution, even when the field has an initial compact configuration. For the curvature coupling, we show that the universe is necessarily spatially infinite, but that the smoothness and compactness assumptions can be compatible. The potential term introduces discontinuities in a(t) and the spatial metric at late times, but the strong energy condition remains well-defined.

In this paper, we present a novel hierarchical framework for multi-category hyperspectral image segmentation. The proposed framework is based on a hierarchical mixture of Markov random fields (MRF) model, where the image labeling is driven by a top-down visual contextual clue, i.e., object class labels, and it is refined by a bottom-up spatial cue, i.e., spectral image intensity. Specifically, the MRF model is factorized into a coarse-to-fine cascaded structures, where the global labels are modeled by a high-level MRF, and the local fine labels are captured by a series of low-level MRFs. In each MRF, the spatial and spectral information are integrated by a novel hierarchical Markovian model. We jointly learn the hierarchical model parameters by an effective Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, which can effectively explore the label configuration space and effectively estimate the model parameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to explore the hierarchical MRF model for hyperspectral image segmentation. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance and performs favorably against the state of the arts.

Reverberation mapping is a valuable technique for estimating the size of the broad-line region in Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs). Reverberation mapping relies on measuring the response of the broad-line region (BLR) to variations in the ionizing flux from the accretion disk, which can be parameterized by the continuum-related lag (time delay between the continuum and line emission). This parameterization allows one to estimate the size of the BLR, under the assumption that the size of the BLR is proportional to theresponse. Recently, this assumption was questioned, and alternative methods have been proposed to estimate the size of the BLR based on the cross-correlation of the continuum and line emission rather than on its response to continuum variations. Here, we show that the accuracy of these cross-correlation-based estimates is fundamentally limited by the width of the autocorrelation function of the noise in the spectra, and we provide an analytic expression for this limit. We demonstrate the practical implications of this limit by applying it to a sample of active galaxies with reverberation mapping measurements from the literature. We show that while the cross-correlation-based estimates of the BLR size are generally within a factor of two of the response-based estimates, some sources show larger discrepancies, possibly due to the superposition of multiple BLRs in the spectrum. These results provide useful constraints for models of the BLR and its response to variations in the ionizing flux, and for the interpretation of the size of the BLR as a luminosity indicator.'
