The distance to Orion KL was measured to be 1,650 light-years (490 pc) with the VERA (VLBI Exploration of Radio Astronomy) radio telescope array in Nagano, Japan. This result is in good agreement with previously estimated distances of 1,500–1,800 light-years (430–550 pc), which were based on stellar orbits and parallax measurements. The VERA observations provide the first direct measurement of the distance to Orion KL. The new distance estimate considerably refines our knowledge of the structure and evolution of the Orion Molecular Cloud complex and its role as a calibration standard for various observational methods. The measured distance is consistent with recent models of the initial mass of the Orion BN/KL outflow and of the evolution of stars from the zero-age main sequence to protostars. The achieved accuracy allows a significant improvement of the models and will allow more detailed studies of individual components in the region.

In this paper we establish lower order terms in the one level density of families of holomorphic cuspidal newforms. Let {n(P)} denotes the cardinality of the set of normalized Hecke eigenforms of parallel weight 2 and level N with central character preserved. The family {n(P)} is called a thin family if the ratio This work arose from our attempt to understand the subconvexity problem for modular forms, and in particular, the uniform boundedness of the sequence {n(P)}. Using the theory of quadrilinear forms, we establish effective lower bounds for the one level density provided that the family is thin with respect to a particular conductor norm. As an immediate application, we establish that the sequence {n(P)} is uniformly bounded provided that the level is unconditionally bounded. We point out that our method is quite general and can also be used to establish effective lower bounds for other problems involving quadratic forms. In a subsequent paper we will apply this method to the theory of quadratic forms on bounded congruence domains, and thereby solve a longstanding conjecture of Duke, Friedlander, and Iwaniec regarding character sums associated with holomorphic cuspidal newforms. We would like to express our profound gratitude to Andrew Roe for many useful suggestions and encouragement. Without his help, this work could not have been finished. We are also very grateful to Weijun Zhang for helpful discussions and sharing some of his unpublished work.

In this work, a novel model for the 3D reconstruction of the structure of the heliosphere based on RHEA – a Bayesian statistical approach that couples a dynamical model for the plasma particles with a spatial model for the heliospheric magnetic field – is presented. The new model, referred to as BOUNDARI, includes the effects of photoionization, which are known to be the most relevant process for determining the actual boundary of the heliosphere. The inclusion of photoionization, which has been neglected in previous studies, results in a more accurate simulation of the main boundaries of the heliosphere: the termination shock (located at 0.71 ± 0.02 AU, where 1 AU is the radius of the Sun) and the heliopause (located at 49.0 ± 2.7 AU, the distance at which the solar wind pressure drops to 1% of the pressure in the local interstellar medium), and its elongation. The global structure of the heliosphere in the presented model is in excellent agreement with a combination of in-situ data from the Parker Solar Probe and the BFFT, as well as data from the previous mission period to date (Advanced Composition Explorer, ACE) covering 2004 – 2006.

A novel approach to spectral imaging using stereoscopic vision. We develop a hybrid differential stereoscopic (HDS) system based on structured light using two synchronized broadband optical filter liquid crystal displays (LCDs). We apply this system to a spectral imaging modality that uses white light to estimate the spatial temperature profile of a scene. The approach we present combines the high spectral resolution of multi-bandpass filter spectrography with the wide field of view and high spatial resolution of structured light. We experimentally demonstrate that HDS allows for measurement of temperature differences as small as 1 degree across a 200 meter field of view with sub-millimeter resolution. We find that with additional processing, this narrowband HDS system has the sensitivity to detect temperature differences as small as 1/1000 of a degree across the same 200 meter field of view. This approach overcomes several of the limitations of previous narrowband HDS works, such as the Pollefeys et al. system which uses only a single optical filter, or the Huang et al. system which uses high-end filter spectrography but only has a 30 meter field of view. We believe this work represents a novel method for narrowband HDS that will have significant impact across many scientific and commercial spectral imaging modalities.

This letter reports the detection of radio emission from the well-known class I low-mass protostar L1527. L1527 is an excellent testbed for theoretical work relating to the early stages of star formation, due to its proximity (140 pc), associated low visual extinction (~ 0.1 magnitudes), and previous detections of large scale outflow, gas and temperature structures. Until now, no radio emission from L1527 has been reported. Using the Long Baseline Experiment (LBE) on the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), we detect two, extremely weak, partially resolved sources, located within a north-south orientation in the outflow cavity walls. These two sources are likely associated with the L1527 protostar, given their positional coincidence with previously observed gas and temperature structures. This detection represents the first reported detection of radio emission from a low-mass protostar. The estimated emission measure, assuming equipartition between the magnetic field and particle energy, and a gas volume occupied by electrons of ~ 10-6 - 10-8 cm-3, is consistent with previous non-detections and predicted minimal thermal emission from the assumed protostellar mass and age. The emission measure also falls within the range of emission measures obtained for other previously detected low-mass protostellar radio sources. These results are discussed in the context of current theoretical models of low-mass protostellar evolution. Keywords: radio emission, Very-Long-Baseline Interferometry, low-mass protostar, L1527

The Pioneer anomaly, the long-standing observation of a non-zero acceleration toward the Sun, has inspired a number of attempts to solve it by modifying Einstein's theory of gravity. However, we show that the anomaly can be naturally explained in a very simple and elegant way, namely as a relativistic effect of the Minkowski space conformal symmetry. Specifically, we show that even a small violation of the conformal symmetry, induced by the trace of the energy-momentum tensor, can explain both the anomalous acceleration of the Pioneers, and the accelerating expansion of the Universe. Moreover, we show that the same effect can naturally explain an apparent acceleration of the Universe on large cosmological scales, without the need for dark energy. Finally, we discuss the possibility that the conformal symmetry could be violated by the quantum gravity effects, and speculate on the possible astrophysical and cosmological implications of our results. As measured by the Pioneer 10/11, Voyager 1 and II space probes, the acceleration of the spacecraft was consistently found to be non-zero toward the Sun, with a magnitude of 2.87 cm/s2. Such an acceleration can not be explained by the classic theory of relativity and gravity, and has inspired a number of attempts to modify or extend the theory to account for it. One particularly successful approach has been to assume that the standard model of cosmology, which describes the Universe as experiencing an accelerated expansion, is also correct, and the acceleration is caused by a dark energy with a negative equation of state, that is responsible for approximately 72% of the energy content of the Universe. However, this explanation has come into dispute, and in 2012 one of the probes (Pioneer 10) showed an acceleration even in the opposite direction, away from the Sun. Further analysis confirmed the existence of the anomaly, and it has since been observed in all the probes. In this paper, we show that the Pioneer anomaly can be explained in a very simple and elegant way. We start with the well-known result that in any consistent theory of gravity the symmetry of the Minkowski space, where special relativity holds, has to be a symmetry of the theory, too. In other words, the theory has to be invariant under the conformal transformations of the Minkowski space. We then note that, to first order in the gravitational constant, the only nonzero gravitational coupling of the spacecraft is with the trace of the energy-momentum tensor of the ordinary matter. We show that this trace leads to a violation of the conformal symmetry, at the level of a few parts in a million. The resulting effect is a small anomaly in the acceleration of the spacecraft, which is in the direction of the Sun and of the correct magnitude to explain both the Pioneer anomaly and the expansion of the Universe. In addition, the effect also leads to a tiny, but measurable, violation of the inverse-square law of gravity at cosmological scales, thus explaining the apparent acceleration of the Universe on large scales.

Atmospheric neutrinos are produced in cosmic ray interactions in the atmosphere. These neutrinos predominantly proceed through two-body decays into electron neutrinos, which can be detected by large water Cherenkov tanks like the Super Kamiokande or the IceCube observatories. In contrast, atmospheric neutrinos produced by interactions of neutrinos originating from the Sun, are expected to undergo transitions from one of the three active neutrino flavors (mu,tau) to the other two (mu,tau) and consequently arrive at the detector as a an incoherent mixture of the two. An observation of such a neutrino flavor transition could be a clear indication of beyond the standard model interactions. We report the first observation of such a transition using data from the 837-day exposure of the ATLAS detector at the CERN LHC. We perform an extended maximum likelihood analysis to search for disappearance of electron neutrinos in both the normal and inverted neutrino mass ordering scenarios. We find a best-fit neutrino mass-squared difference of 2.54{sup +0.14(stat) +0.19(syst)} \cdot 10{sup -3} eV{sup 2} for the normal ordering and was 1.10{sup -3} eV{sup 2} for the inverted ordering with a combined best-fit probability of 0.66+0.018-0.19. These results are in agreement with the expected sensitivity and can be used to set upper limits on neutrino parameters in models beyond the standard model.

Interactions between planetesimals leads to the formation of groups and chains. This process is known as gravitational instability. It has been observed in molecular clouds and it is thought to be important for planet formation. Planet formation by this mechanism has been studied in detail. However, it has not yet been observed in stars. This is likely due to the difficulty of detecting planetesimals in protoplanetary disks, which are much more distant. I describe a new technique that can detect these objects with the help of a recently discovered instability in disks. The instability creates clumps of material that drift toward each other, increasing in density until they become unstable and form planetesimals. This has the potential to explain the extremely high density of planetesimals in the asteroid and Kuiper belts. I present simulations of the growth of planetesimals from planetesimal clumps that demonstrate this process. This work was done in collaboration with Zhongjie Gan (University of Arizona) and Jonathan J. Fortney (Harvard University).

Recent discovery of non-Abelian quasiparticles, so-called vortices in high-temperature superconductors, has led to novel possibilities of topological quantum computation. Since vortices have both electrical and magnetic fields, dynamics of vortices can provide direct probes for quasiparticle dynamics. However, direct experimental studies of vortices in superconductors have been limited due to difficulties in accurately visualizing small magnetic fluxes. In this paper, we show that quasiparticle current in a thin Josephson junction array forms a triangular lattice and carries magnetic flux attached to each vortex. We demonstrate that this flux lattice exhibits rich topological structures including quantized magnetic flux, Meissner and Abrikosov flux lattices. Electrodynamic interaction between vortices in the flux lattice gives rise to confinement of magnetic flux inside the superconducting samples. Our theory enables experimental exploration of novel quasiparticle phenomena in vortices hosted by high-temperature superconductors.

On 15 March 2022, a team of astronomers using the K2 satellite observed the system Lupus III. The system consists of three orbiting dust particles and a richly characterized gas- and dust-rich protoplanetary disk, located approximately 200 light-years from Earth in the constellation of Lupus. The characteristics of this system are very similar to our own Solar System's formation 4.6 billion years ago. In particular, the ratio of the abundances of water vapour to hydrogen is similar in both systems. This implies that the bulk composition of the cores from which the planets formed was similar in the two systems. Astronomers suspect that, during the early phases of planet formation, dust particles coagulate into planet-sized bodies within a disk of dust and gas. In the case of the Solar System, the earliest detectable signatures of this process are believed to occur 4.6 billion years ago, during the late stages ofdisk formation. At that time, the ratio of water vapour to hydrogen within the disk, known as the X-ray opacity correction (XKCC), was approximately 0.9%. In contrast, the XKCC in the Lupus system is 0.76%. This difference implies that, 4.6 billion years later, the Lupus system's core was unable to acquire a significant fraction of the volatiles present in the disk (approximately 24 times less water vapour, and approximately 4 times less hydrogen). Although this study cannot resolve whether the cores of Lupus III formed 4.6 billion years ago, or more recently, the results indicate that the abundance of at least one key volatile, water, had an interstellar travel distance of at least 19 billion km.

We present numerical results for three-nucleon observables in nuclear matter as functions of the pion mass. The predictions are obtained within the framework of a coupled-cluster expansion for the nuclear wave function, using two interaction kernels: a long-range one, corresponding to the leading order of a systematic chiral perturbation theory (ChPT) expansion, and a short-range one, corresponding to two-nucleon contact interactions. We show that, for observables related to nuclear matter saturation, the convergence of the results towards the physical point depends on the range of the interaction, with faster convergence for the short-range kernel. In addition, for a given range of the interaction, the dependence on the pion mass of the predictions increases as the density of the system under consideration decreases, i.e., as the range of the interaction increases. Finally, we argue that, in order to properly describe the evolution of the nuclearmany-body system with the QCD scale, an appropriate renormalization group analysis of ChPT should be performed.

In April 2016, we identified two quasars at a redshift of z=4.82 and 4.88 with unusually weak CIV and CIII] Lyα emission (the “weak emission” quasars, WEQs). We conducted comprehensive multi-wavelength follow-up observations of the WEQs, including Keck DEIMOS spectroscopy and Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Observations with the MUSEparallel-mode instrument on the UT4 of the VLT, as well as imaging from the HST, Spitzer, Chandra, and various VLT and Keck adaptive optics (AO) assisted observations. Our analysis indicates that the WEQs are two of the most intrinsically faint quasars known, with M_{1450}}=\mjew$-[28.5]. No other observed properties (such as Luminosity, black hole mass, host galaxy, etc.) of the WEQs are extreme, and we argue that the WEQs are the most distant spectroscopically confirmed cases of “aberrated” quasars.

Water has long been known to possess a exceptionally strong hydrogen bond, but new measurements using a variety of techniques have yielded a consistent and surprising result: water's hydrogen bond strength is roughly one third of its estimated strength. This apparent contradiction is reconciled by considering water's structure in terms of a network of hydrogen bonds. Whereas the strength of an isolated bond may be estimated from first principles, water's hydrogen bonds are significantly weakened by their involvement in a web of bonds. The implications of this result for water's behavior in biological systems, engineering systems, and technological processes are discussed. This work was performed by a team of researchers from the U.S. and the Netherlands, including Wim van Straten, Kris den Oudsten, J. Michael Cole, Jensduration K. Nijdam, Benjamin A. Mahoney, and Thomas R. Zarrow. Mahoney, and Thomas R. Zarrow. Consider a cluster of water molecules in its crystalline structure. This cluster of molecules interacts with each other by sharing pairs of hydrogen atoms. Typically, each hydrogen atom is shared between two different molecules, with a distance of about 0.98Å between the oxygen atoms in each molecule and the two shared hydrogen atoms. A classical description of a hydrogen bond requires the presence of an attractive force between the sharing atoms, and this is precisely the case for the water molecules in this cluster, as the forces between the oxygen atoms and the shared hydrogen atoms are all attractive. However, the shared hydrogen atoms are not isolated; they are part of a network of such pairs of atoms that forms a three dimensional lattice throughout the water molecule's volume. This lattice weakens the strength of the hydrogen bonds between the individual water molecules. The amount of the weakening depends on the particular orientation of the water molecules in the cluster, but if the lattice is assumed to extend uniformly throughout the cluster, the force between the shared hydrogen atoms is found to be one-third of the force between the oxygen atoms in the water molecules. This weakening of the hydrogen bonds has important implications for the behavior of water in different systems

In this paper, we describe how to measure the quantum decoherence of a single spin quantum bit (qubit) using a Cavity Bifurcation Amplifier (CBA). Decoherence is one of the major limitations to the quantum operations lifetimes of a quantum bit, and is primarily caused by coupling the qubit to its surroundings. A measurement of this decoherence therefore gives critical information about the environment of the qubit and its interaction with it. The recently developed CBA is a novel approach to measuring the state of a quantum system, which uses the dynamics of a perturbed coupled oscillator to detect the presence of a weak interaction in the system. In our case, this interaction is the qubit-environment coupling, and the CBA is able to detect this coupling by measuring changes in the frequency of the coupled oscillator. Using a model describing the CBA and our experimental setup, we simulate the expected decoherence signal as a function of several experimentally controlled variables. We show that by carefully optimizing our system, we should be able to measure decoherence in our qubit of approximately 5% in one second, significantly lower than typical estimates for a high quality single spin qubit.

The paper presents the results of numerical simulation of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the array of Josephson wires (JW). Using the parameterized paraconducting-to-superconducting (SC) transition model we perform direct comparative study of the dynamics of the array in the presence and the absence of an external magnetic field. It is shown that in the case of a homogeneous magnetic field the system passes through periodicAnderson-like "metallic" and "insulating" phases in direct analogue with the behavior of 1D single JW. Contrary, the applied magnetic field spatially distributed in the form of "ring" transforms the system from an insulating to a metallic one. The paper presents the rigorous analysis of the origin of this effect and development of the phenomenological model that well describes the system dynamics in both limiting cases. It is shown that such behavior of the array is generic and corresponds to the universal paraconducting-to-superconducting phase diagram for the 1D arrays. The QEL, which stands for Quasi-Elastic scence, is a inelastic interaction of neutrino which induces a smaller nuclear excitation. The fully contained events and partially contained events are two main categories of neutrino interaction types that detected in the Super-Kamiokande. By using the electron number-density profile of the Near Detector, we find the QEL can explain the fully contained events, while it can not explain the partially contained events. Therefore we can conclude that the neutrino direction is reliable for the fully contained events but not for the partially contained events. An evaluation of uncertainty is an important aspect of any calculation performed on measurements, simulations or observations. The computed dose volume histogram (DVH) is a common metric used in radiation treatment to quantify how much of the target receives a specific dose. Here we present a novel method for the evaluation of uncertainty in DVH computation which accounts for parameter, measurement and model uncertainty. Uncertainties in model parameters are represented by probability distributions. Measurements and simulations are modeled by sampling from their associated distributions. A representative sample from each of the parameter, measurement and simulation distributions is generated. A DVH is computed for each sample, resulting in a sample set of DVHs. The uncertainty in the DVH is evaluated by computing the $coefficient$ of variation across the sample set. The coefficient of variation, which is an intuitive metric for the dispersion of a sample set, is computed in the unobservable dose axis which is independent of the range of the dose values. A validation on a sample set of brain metastases DVHs demonstrates that the proposed method provides a superior metric for evaluating uncertainty compared to two existing methods.

Nanodevices typically lack classical analogues for the transport of heat and charge. Nonetheless, it has been argued that the fluctuation theorem might apply to them [1, 2]. Here we show that this is in fact not the case. We consider the Jarzynski equality for nanodevices [3, 4] and demonstrate that it fails for a simple system of two coupled Langevin equations with a bistable potential. The standard derivation of the Jarzynski equality, employing the reversibility of Hamiltonian dynamics, no longer applies in this case. As a result, it has been conjectured that the fluctuation theorem might not apply to nanodevices [5]. We show that this is also not the case and provide a modified fluctuation relation, which we verify by direct numerical integration of the full nanodevice dynamics. In [1, 2], Nataf and Vulpiani claimed that the fluctuation theorem might apply to Brownian motors. They showed that the dynamics of the energy along a transient period of a Nosè-Hoover oscillator (a classic model for aBrownian motor) obeys the Jarzynski equality. However, it has been later shown that the Nosè-Hoover oscillator is Hamiltonian and that the Jarzynski equality holds [3, 4]. As a result, the claim that the fluctuation theorem might apply to Brownian motors was found to be incorrect. Our work adds Nanodevices to the list of systems for which the Jarzynski equality does not hold. We emphasize that the Jarzynski equality is not required for the fluctuation theorem to apply; indeed, our result shows that even the more general modified fluctuation relation holds for the system that we consider. The spin-dependent resonant tunneling characteristics of a double-barrier heterostructures under longitudinal stresses are theoretically investigated based on a 3D effective mass model. The stress-dependent band gaps and Dresselhaus coupling strength are employed to describe the spin-dependent band structures. The theoretical results show that the spin-dependent resonant tunneling probability is highly sensitive to the longitudinal stresses, and two stress-induced resonance peaks can be clearly observed for a positive longitudinal stress, which can be effectively utilized in the device application. Moreover, the symmetry properties of the longitudinal stress-dependent resonant tunneling characteristics are studied in detail. The theoretical results provide a feasible route to explore the spin-dependent transport properties and may be helpful for designing the stress-sensitive resonant tunneling devices. We present the results of spectroscopic observations of eight galaxy clusters with z > 0.4 detected in the ROSAT all-sky survey. These clusters span a wide range in X-ray luminosity (Lx = 10(44) - 10(45) erg s(-1) ) and mass (M = 2.2 x 10(14) - 4.4 x 10(15) M(⊙) ), as measured by their luminosity-weighted X-ray temperatures. We used DEIMOS on the W.M. KeckII telescope to obtain optical spectra for 7635 total objects (3868 unique objects) with m(r) < 21 within a 1.5 Mpc radius of the X-ray centroid of each cluster. From these spectra we measured optical photometric redshifts for 627 cluster members, as well as Mg[II], Fe5270, and H+K auto-correlation functions for each cluster. We present optical-to-X-ray luminosity relations, Lx - T, Lx - Mg[II], and Lx - H+K, with random uncertainties at the 60% confidence level. We compare these relations to theoretical models of structure formation to investigate the relationship between cluster mass and its dark matter halo mass. The mass-observable relations show positive deviations from the expected scaling with a significance of ~3.5 sigma, inconsistent with models which assume dark matter halos are characterized by a constant density core. These results may indicate the presence of dynamical processes in these clusters such as minor mergers or non-canceling cluster contraction, although a full comparison to simulations of cluster growth will be needed to confirm this finding.

In this paper, we study the (0,2) linear sigma model (LSM) on supermanifold. The (0,2) LSM is a useful tool to study various aspects of string theory compactified on non-trivial Ricci-flat backgrounds such as (p,q) 7-branes, etc... The (0,2) LSM is also expected to provide an effective description of the low-energy dynamics of some complete intersections in super Calabi-Yau manifolds. We generalize the (0,2) LSM to the (0,2) gauged linear sigma model (GLSM) on supermanifold, and show that the GLSM on supermanifold is renormalizable when the supermanifold is non-compact and admits a (restricted) gauge symmetry. We also show that the on-shell (0,2) superfield gauge transformation is also a local symmetry of the action. Then we discuss the vacua and some of their symmetries of the (0,2) GLSM on supermanifold, and give some typical examples of its applications.

In evolutionary game theory, players interact according to their strategies, and those strategies determine the players' payoffs. These players choose new strategies according to their respective strategies, and so on. In most studies, players are assumed to interact with each other only once. In this paper, we consider a more general case, where players can interact with each other multiple times. The main motivation comes from the spatial nature of many evolutionary games: players are not just interested in their local environment but also take into account the global structure. Such games are often called evolutionary games on minimally structured populations. We study the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with such games. We also provide conditions for the equation to have at most one classical solution. Finally, we apply our results to a cellular automaton with mutations, and we show that it exhibits a global invasion-mixed steady state. We study the Hamilton-Jacobi equation associated with a non-local mean-field version of this game. A typical example of such games is the cellular automaton with mutations called the sliding VM system. The equation we study has two phases: a free-flow phase and a congestion phase. In the free-flow phase, the Hamilton-Jacobi equation reduces to a linear parabolic equation. In the congestion phase, the Hamilton-Jacobi equation reduces to a nonlinear elliptic equation. We provide conditions for the free-flow phase to be well-posed and for the two phases to match each other. The main challenge in the study of this equation is due to the fact that the operator corresponding to the free-flow phase is degenerate. We overcome this challenge by introducing a log-transform which regularizes the degeneracy. We show that the solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi equation converge, in the appropriate weak sense, to the value function of a singular stochastic control problem. This value function is related to the viscosity solution to the related Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. We also study the regularized equation and prove that it has a unique solution, which converges to the viscosity solution of the regularized equation. We apply our results to the sliding VM system. Galaxies are commonly divided into two categories, early-type galaxies and late-type galaxies. Early-type galaxies have clear bulges and are less clustered in the local Universe than late-type galaxies. This has traditionally been explained via dry mergers, where two spiral galaxies merge to make one early-type galaxy. However, recent research has shown that re-growing bulges may also play an important role. In particular, during gas-rich mergers, dynamical friction causes star formation in the forming bulge, making galaxies less cluster-centric and early-type. Using the Millennium simulation, I show that the bimodal colour distribution of galaxies is connected to the growth of bulges. When the total cold gas content of dark matter haloes exceeds a critical value, ≃ 5.4 × 10¹⁶ M⊙, the most massive progenitor branch of a given halo becomes early-type and its members are more concentrated than late-type galaxies. Conversely, when the cold gas content is less than this critical value, ≃ 3.2 × 10¹⁵ M⊙, the most massive progenitor branch becomes late-type and has a higher population fraction than early-type galaxies. I further show that these critical values of cold gas are both approximately the mass corresponding to the characteristic surface density of the red sequence, and that galaxies above and below this surface density are more likely to become early-type and late-type, respectively. This supports the idea that the red sequence is dominated by quiescently star-forming galaxies, with the bimodality coming from the transformation of late-type into early-type galaxies. In summary, both dry and wet mergers can lead to the formation of early-type galaxies, but only if enough cold gas is present to enable bulge growth.

The article aims to overview the recent development in the understanding of cosmological shock waves. These are fluid dynamic phenomena which occur in an abrupt change of properties of a fluid, usually characterized by a supersonic flow jump. In cosmology these shock waves appear in the inhomogeneous distribution of matter which leads to the formation of large scale structure. There are two distinct types of these shock waves which are discriminated by the velocity of the fluid movement before and after the shock. Type 1 shocks appear in relatively low velocity flows, i.e., slower than the speed of light. These shock waves appear in the matter accretion, i.e., the process by which clusters of galaxies formed from small density fluctuations in the early universe. These shocks go under names such as sound waves or collapse shocks. They can be described by a fairly simple linear theory, which has been verified against numerical simulations. Type 2 shocks appear in the flow of high velocity gas, i.e., relativistic or transonic motions. These shock waves are more frequent and more interesting to study than the former. The Hubble flow, which is the motion of galaxies relative to the observer, appears as a type 2 shock wave. Cosmological type 2 shock waves have been invoked to explain phenomena such as the 511 keV line emission from the galactic center, the large scale structure, and the Kolmogorov spectrum of cosmological density fluctuations. In recent years, there has been a renewed interest in the cosmological shock wave phenomenon. This is because new observational discoveries such as the 511 keV line, and highly contrasted galaxy clusters have shown the need to go beyond the homogeneous and isotropic cosmological model. In the cosmological world, there is more variation in the matter density and velocity fields than what would be expected from a simple homogenous and isotropic model. It is now known that type 2 shock waves are generic features of cosmological fluid flows. Their behavior, however, depends on the features of the underlying cosmology, which can no longer be described by a simple parameterization. The study of cosmological shock waves requires the use of numerical simulations and increasingly sophisticated analytic methods. The article is organized as follows. The theory and observation of type 1 shock waves is presented in section 2. The formation of large scale structure is formulated as a type 1 shockwave in Section 3. Section 4 presents an analytic model for type 1 shock waves. In Section 5, numerical simulations of the formation of structure are reviewed. In section 6, a Type 2 shock wave in the Hubble flow is introduced and its impact on the large scale structure is discussed. Section 7 summarizes the findings.

Instead of integrating out the gauge field, we choose to realize the gauge group nonlinearly, which means that the gauge group is embedded nonlinearly into the gauge group of some larger group L. Nanotubes are carbon allotropes with remarkable physical and chemical properties. Nanotubes can be grown in bundles, where the distance between adjacent nanotubes in a bundle is on the order of 1-10 nanometers. Here we study electromagnetic wave propagation in such tightly packed nanotube bundles. Contrary to predictions based on free space optics, we find that the wave propagation is governed by coupled nanotube Drude responses. These coupled responses are visible as longitudinal and transverse resonances in the scattering matrix spectrum. The latter resonance allows for non- dispersive waveguiding, with potential applications in filters, sensors, and communications. *Paper URL* : https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.09142 The authors are from Nanotubes15, Link[1], New Jersey Institute of Technology. Renormalization is an essential tool in modern theoretical physics. It enables one to sum large classes of diagrams into well-defined approximations to the "full" theory. As an example, it has allowed us to understand the basic principles behind the formation of conductors, insulators, and vacua in quantum electrodynamics (QED). In the context of quantum field theory (QFT), renormalization is performed systematically by constructing a sequence of effective theories (or " renormalization flows") describing the change of the fundamental description of nature from some large (or "ultraviolet") cutoff scale to the desired ("infrared") length or energy scale of the problem. For many field theories in nature, including quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and the standard model of particle physics, this program has led to precise quantitative results for a wide range of energies and spatial scales. Recently, significant progress has been made in applying the method of renormalization to the study of quantum phase transitions (QPTs) in condensed matter physics. In particular, this approach has been used to compute the dynamical scaling laws and universal critical dynamics at the Kibble-Zurek (KZ) scale in second-order QPTs1,2, as well as the magnetic scaling at the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKTO) transition3,4. However, a critical point of the theory under consideration may be inherently non-perturbative, which hampers the applicability of conventional renormalization group (RG) techniques. In this work, we introduce a functional renormalization group approach to QPTs, which is based on a Legendre transformation of a generating functional for a 1PI functional integral. In particular, we apply this method to calculate dynamical scaling laws and universal critical dynamics at the quantum phase transition between a Superfluid and a Mott-insulator (MI) phase of a Fermi gas with two spin states, taking into account the weak-coupling atomic interaction and quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate the feasibility and validity of our approach by reproducing the known scaling laws at both the second-order QPT and the BKT O(2) field theory. Overall, our work provides a rigorous application of the functional RG to quantum phase transitions, and more generally, represents a useful extension of the conventional RG to non-perturbative, and even strongly-coupled regimes.

The interstellar medium (ISM) surrounding massive young stars is often characterised by low density ionization regions known as HII regions. The temperature structure of these HII regions is a result of the balance between the radiative heating and cooling mechanisms. The recombination of ionized hydrogen and the collisional excitation of electrons by incoming Lyman continuum radiation are two significant cooling mechanisms. The spatial distribution of ionising sources, in addition to other physical conditions of the ISM, can modify this cooling structure. In this work we model the HII region surrounding a cluster of young stars with an ionisation potential of 13.6 eV using a three-dimensional grid based numerical simulation. The effects of the spatial distribution of ionisation sources, gas density and temperature on the resulting temperature structure is presented and discussed. We find that the generated flux from secondary ionisation sources located further away from the ionising source, or the temperature of the ionised gas, both result in a reduction of the peak temperature of the HII region and a wider temperature structure. This is because of the reduced radiative cooling and slower expansion of the HII region in these cases. We also observe the development of a temperature plateau in the interior of the HII region when the ionisation sources are distributed according to a Gaussian function of the radial coordinate. This is caused by the increased thermal coupling of this function.

The analysis of the redundancy and its applicability in pattern recognition has been an active research field for several decades now. In this article, a general overview of the current state of the art is given with emphasis on estimation of the redundancy and its moments, estimation of statistics dependent on the redundancy, estimation of the mutual information for the given statistics and applications of the redundancy as a test for randomness. The discussed methods have been successfully applied to widely used pattern recognition problems. In particular, the estimation of the mutual information based on the presented method is an effective method for determining the amount of data needed to train a pattern recognition system. Estimation of redundancy and its moments is crucial for many tasks in pattern recognition such as model selection, significance estimation of estimation errors, forecasting and extrapolation. In particular, estimating the kth raw moment of the redundancy allows one to estimate the coefficient of determination R2, which is the measure of how well the fit approximates the target. The formula for R2 is presented in a very compact and convenient form that allows one to get insight into the importance of particular input variables in regression problems. If the kth raw moment of the redundancy is estimated, then the percentile estimates of the coefficient of determination R2 are also available, which are independent of the particular model used for estimation. An application of estimating the coefficient of determination R2 is determining the required sample size in signal detection problems. Estimation of the coefficient of variation of the redundancy is important for risk management in production systems. The estimation of the second central moment of the redundancy allows the determination of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic that can be used to test randomness. This estimation is possible even in the case when only one realization of the random variable is available.

Galaxy clusters are the largest virialized structures in the Universe. Their core regions, usually named the cluster core, are very dense and warm environments, where the plasma optical frequency is comparable to the particle gyration frequency, γ, within a few tens of kpc from the cluster center. Radio emission from galaxy clusters is therefore expected and observed. Radio signals are carried by the ionized plasma, through the effect of radio waves on the plasma physical state and the so-called "cannonball effect". The merging of galaxy clusters produces high-speed collisions between shock waves traveling within the cluster cores. Such events can severely perturb the intracluster medium (ICM) physical state and can generate complex plasma flow patterns that can be observed through the generation and detection of radio waves. Here we present results from the discovery of a peculiar radio signal, that of radio emission that has been "suppressed" in a set of galaxy clusters belonging to the ZwCl 2313.1+3416 supercluster. The suppressed radio emission is revealed by new Very Large Array (VLA) observations at 1.4 GHz, which together with archival VLA data at 330 MHz, and Multi-Element Radio Linked Interferometer Network (MERLIN) data at 1.4 GHz, show faint radio emission at the locations of 45 galaxies located in the merging clusters A520, ZwCl 2312.1+3416 and ZwCl 2316.1+3341. Simulations predict that, at the location of galaxies embedded within the ICM, the radio signal can be strongly perturbed by merger-induced dynamic effects. It follows that any radio wave propagating through the ICM will suffer a reduction in strength as it travels through the merger event. For the galaxy clusters considered here, the radio signal reduction factor (expressed in percentage) ranges from 10% to 80%, depending on the location of the radio source within the merging structures. This reduction in signal strength is not detectable by classical radio observations, but can be revealed by the combination of deep and high-resolution radio observations, which allow the detection of weak radio signals that can be completely obscured by foreground noise in shorter and coarser radio surveys.

Wireless communications technologies are being considered for implementation in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) to enable road safety, fleet management, and remote control of vehicles and equipment. CDMA2000 is a standard for wireless communication in the vehicle network that has the ability to deliver the bandwidth and reliability required for ITS communications. In this paper, we describe a framework for using CDMA2000 for road safety and vehicle services, including an overview of the standard and its operation. We also describe a series of use cases that illustrate the potential benefits of CDMA2000 for ITS applications. This framework and use cases will assist in the development of road safety and vehicle services based on ITS using CDMA2000. Road safety improvements from ITS using CDMA2000 include: - V2X ( Vehicle to Vehicle and Vehicle to Infrastructure) communications for vehicle platooning, anti-collision mitigation, and advanced crash notifications; - V2V ( Vehicle to Vehicle) communications for automated driving and vehicle emergency services; - V2I ( Vehicle to Infrastructures) for remote monitoring and management of vehicles and equipment. Vehicle services based on ITS using CDMA2000 include: - Remote diagnostics and control for maintenance and assisted driving; - Access and identity-based access control; - Road pricing and tolling; - Driver and vehicle behavioral management.

The Gravity Probe B (GPB) satellite was designed to test whether or not General Relativity (GR) is correct by looking at the bending of light in a strong gravitational field. In order to test whether or not GR is correct, other gravity theories should also be tested against GR. One such theory, Teleparallel gravity (TG), is often considered as an alternative theory to GR, since TG is equivalent to GR in a weak-field limit. In this sense, testing GR against TG makes sense from the perspective of distinguishing the validity of two different theories that both explain the same experiment. The most general theory of gravity including general relativity and Teleparallel gravity is called Extended Teleparallel gravity (ETG). In this work, we perform a fit of the GP-B data to several torsion gravity models. We find the most precise constraints for the models considered from GP-B data using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis. We find that GP-B data are not precise enough to significantly distinguish the considered models.

Authors: Hiroshi Isobe (Ibaraki University, Japan) and Kazunori Yokogawa (Ibaraki University, Japan) Annual Reports in Aerospace Sciences, Vol. 9, No. 1, 2006 NGC2841 and NGC2976 are typical Sc galaxies located in the local group. We made an observation with the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) and the Infrared Satellite Facts canada (FIS) of these galaxies. The FIS images show intense emissions from the regions of active star formation. The distribution and morphology of these emissions are consistent with those of the mid-infrared emission from warm dust.

Future hadron colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and the International Linear Collider (ILC), can probe new energy scales not accessible to the current experiments. For example, a proton-proton collider with energy in the teraeV range could cover unexplored dark energy parameter space with highly energetic quintessence particles/axions. Measuring the energy and the trajectory of these particles would elucidate the nature of dark energy and the equation of state of quintessence. The LHC and ILC both explore the electroweak scale, but they are becoming incapable of probing new energy scales such as the dark energy scale or the quintessence scale. The lowest energy quintessence particles have a deBroglie wavelength much larger than the Planck scale, and are thus invisible to current experiments. A proton-proton collider with energy above 10 teraeV could study these particles with sufficient sensitivity to probe the nature of dark energy and quintessence. Measuring the energy and trajectory of quintessence particles would enable us to elucidate the nature of dark energy and the equation of state of quintessence. In this way, the potential of future hadron colliders could be extended beyond the discovery of new phenomena to the elucidation of the very structure of the universe. [0]: https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.02344 Direct measurements of the quintessence equation of state could also dwarf the contributions from current dark energy probes, such as BAO/CMB/ Hubble and strong forces. A quintessence measurement could substantially impact cosmological modeling, and might even contradict/validate current assumptions. The ability to make such a measurement will thus depend critically on the energy and design decisions made for future hadron colliders. A combined analysis of these experimental signatures can serve as a more robust probe of the nature of dark energy, as it reduces the dependence of the results on assumptions about quintessence dynamics. A multi-probe study of future hadron collider dark energy potential, combined with data from other experimental probes, could allow for a more robust equation of state measurement. For example, a combined analysis of quintessence particles with future hadron collider data and other current dark energy probes would allow for a nearly model independent measurement of the equation of state, assuming that quintessence dynamics are known independently. The potential of future hadron colliders to study new energy scales, such as the dark energy and quintessence scales, has not been exploited to date. Such studies would allow us to elucidate the nature of dark energy and the equation of state of quintessence.

We present the discovery of 11 new T dwarfs in theTwo Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS). We describe the process of matching 2MASS PSC point sources to WISE full-frame data, and present the resulting list of 22 new T dwarf counterparts. New T dwarfs found include the 23rd and 24th nearest star to the Earth, Teegarden's Star and Doornos' Star, respectively, and the closest known T dwarf binary, 2MASS J0746425+2000315. We present spectral types and photometry for all 22 newly discovered T dwarfs, and compare the spectral types and colors of these objects to those of previously known T dwarfs. Our spectral type determination for 2MASS J0746425+2000315 demonstrates the potential for discovering T dwarfs at greater distances. We estimate the distance to this T dwarf binary based on empirical models of spectral type versus absolute J-band magnitude, and find a likely distance range of 19–50 parsecs (66–167 light-years). We compare the observed mass-luminosity ratio of Teegarden's Star to current models of brown dwarf evolution and determine that this object is between the hydrogen-burning limit and the deuterium-burning limit. Future observations of Teegarden's Star will allow for further testing of these models, as well as the models' ability to predict the luminosities of ultracool dwarfs at intermediate ages. Finally, we examine the colors and luminosity function of the new T dwarfs, and compare the results to those of previous, similar studies. We observe a possible increase in the number of T dwarfs at fainter magnitudes (H- through L-type), and a possible deficiency of T dwarfs around the 2MASS absolute J-band magnitude of 7.5. However, due to the small number of T dwarfs in the sample and the large photometric errors at the fainter end of the luminosity function, these results should be interpreted with caution. We anticipate this work will contribute to existing spectroscopic and photometric dwarf catalogs and provide a useful sample for future studies of ultracool dwarfs.

The molecular gas mass fraction has long been regarded as a better probe of the gas content in galaxies than traditional optical measurements. Recent observations have shown that there is a good correlation between the star formation rate (SFR) of a galaxy and the molecular gas mass fraction (0.53 ± 0.04). Additionally, the relationship between the molecular gas mass fraction and the surface density of star-forming gas has been shown to follow a simple power law (i.e., SFR ∝ ρGas^{1.36 ± 0.15}). Here we propose that this observed scaling can be explained via a Schmidt-Kennicutt (S-K) type relation between the gas surface density and star formation rate. The scaling relation between the molecular gas mass and the star formation rate per unit area is such that ˙SFR = α × σGas^{N}, where σGas is the surface density of star-forming gas, N is a power law exponent, and α is a normalization constant. In this model, observed gas and SFR scaling is a result of a critical surface density below which no star formation will occur and above which a Schmidt law will apply (i.e., SFR ∝ ρGas). Above this critical surface density, the S-K law will apply (i.e., σGas ∝ σSFR). We show that this model can explain the observed scaling relations between molecular gas, SFR, and surface densities. This suggests that the star-forming gas surface density is the fundamental quantity driving the scaling of galaxies, with the observed scaling relations being the result of how these quantities relate to each other.

SunOS/Solaris is a widely used Unix operating system, being among the most popular operating systems for servers, desktops and workstations. In this paper, we assess the availability of some SunOS/Solaris systems by means of the analysis of the corresponding wtmpx and Syslogd logfiles. The wtmpx files store the contents of the user's work-related timestamps, whereas the Syslogd logfiles store messages from the system's log (e.g., error messages, messages generated by the runlevel transition mechanism, and other messages the system is supposed to log). Both files are regularly backed up in a different location. We study the availability of these systems by inspecting the corresponding wtmpx and Syslogd files and by observing the corresponding syslogd and getty processes. We detect various types of failures, such as unrecoverable device or software failures, shutdown or startup failures, and process failures. Additionally, we notice that the logs are not always kept long enough to properly detect some failures, such as runlevels that are not configured to stay around for a long time or getty processes that die after a certain time. The results show that the analyzed systems provide a Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) between 3.12 and 4.96 hours, depending on the type of failure considered. The corresponding MTTRs range from 5 minutes to 5 hours, with a median of 30 minutes.

This work is a theoretical and empirical study on the multiple viewpoints as a new approach to information retrieval within a collaborative development context. It is based on the assumption that there are multiple viewpoints on any specific subject due to the differences in the age, experience, and knowledge of individuals. The differences in these viewpoints result in differences in opinions and, subsequently, lead to improvements in knowledge sharing and development. It is expected that the proposed approach will contribute to improving and advancing the state of the art of knowledge sharing and development in the field of information retrieval. For this purpose, an empirical study has been conducted using as a case study the development of a content-based image retrieval system using machine learning. The main conclusions and contributions of this work are the following: i) the multiple viewpoints are a useful approach to information retrieval within a collaborative development context, ii) a good collaborative development requires a good understanding of the participants and their various viewpoints, and iii) it is necessary to take into account the multiple viewpoints when developing a system.

Magnetic fields are known to be present in most stars and planets, and play a crucial role in their evolution. Much less is known about magnetic fields in systems lacking apparent collimated, ordered magnetic fields, such as stars and planets. Observations of continuum and line emission from large numbers of low-mass pre-main-sequence stars (T Tauri stars) have provided evidence for substantial magnetic fields in these systems. The most likely topology of the field in these systems is a dipole aligned with the stellar rotation axis. Here, we present Zeeman-Doppler imaging of the presence and properties of a dipole field in the T Tauri star Hen 3-4008. The dipole field is occulted by the large inner disk but emerges in the outer disk, along with slow magnetoacoustic waves that thread the disk. We present quantitative modeling of the field characteristics, and place lower limits on the strength of the magnetic field of Hen 3-4008 of approximately 650 G.

Luminous Red Galaxies (LRGs) and clusters of galaxies have very similar photometric and structural properties, and it is often difficult to discriminate between them using spectroscopic redshifts. We present photometry-based photometric redshifts for luminous red galaxies (LRGs) and clusters in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), using a method that simultaneously fits photometric redshift, color, and morphology likelihoods using a non-linear stochastic Partial Differential Equation (NPDE) model. We train the model using 18 bands from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope Legacy Survey and 3 bands from SDSS, and test it on 260 deg2 of the SDSS Data Release 7. The photo-z error distribution, empirical versus predicted redshift, and true failure rate are all computed. We report redshifts for 16,829 LRGs and 2,895 clusters with $0.4<z_{spec}<0.7$. The overall fraction of catastrophic failures is 2.2% for the LRGs and 4.4% for the clusters. Using a machine learning approach, we show that our photo-z estimates for these high-redshift clusters are comparable to those from other studies at similar or lower redshifts. The photo-z catalog is available at http://www.astro.ufl.edu/fphot/. The double radio source 0836+710 is one of the brightest nearby quasar with proper motion measured from superluminal jet shifts. The famous double morphology, core dominance and variability also make this object very interesting for astrophysical studies. In this paper we present results of optical and near-infrared polarimetric observations of this object obtained in 2006 and 2007. We show that the structure of the jet in 0836+710 contains three regions with different polarization position angles: the upstream region with P.A. = 10$^\circ$ – 140$^\circ$; the central region with P.A. = 150$^\circ$ – 180$^\circ$; the downstream region with P.A. = 200$^\circ$ – 220$^\circ$. The angles between two consecutive regions are about $90^\circ$. In the upstream region the degree of polarization is relatively high (up to 15%), while in the downstream region it is much lower (about 1%). The optical and NIR polarimetric data can be well explained in the framework of synchrotron model with a single shock (SSModel). The estimated magnetic field in the jet is of the order of 0.1 – 1 G and the electron energy index is equal to 2.1 – 2.3. We discuss possible physical mechanisms responsible for the observed polarization structure and present our conclusions regarding the origin of 0836+710.

In this letter, we report on two distinct vortex states in thin square- or rectangular-shaped planar pinning arrays, constructed of Ga, Pt, or Ir columns and rows, composed of molecular crystals or plastic crystals. Vortices in the plane of the array move in continuous circles around their respective pinning sites, but perpendicular to the plane, they can adopt one of two configurations. In the “vortex molecule” configuration, vortices oriented along one or two diagonal directions of the square or rectangle form chains, with neighboring molecules approaching or receding from each other, as in a ideal electronic molecule. This molecular-crystalline vortex configuration is analogous to the well-known equilibrium phases of electron molecules in semiconductor heterostructures. Vortices in the “vortex plastic crystal” configuration form a regular lattice with fivefold or threefold rotation symmetry, for arrays with honeycomb or kagome pinning sites, respectively. This plastic crystal vortex phase is entirely novel and is stabilized by strong thermal fluctuations at low temperatures and high magnetic fields. The two vortex configurations are differentiated by a transition seen in magnetic force microscopy (MFM), which reports on the distribution of magnetic moments. In the vortex molecule configuration, this transition is continuous, reflecting the continuous deformation of the molecular structure. In contrast, in the vortex plastic crystal configuration, the magnetic force transition is first-order, reflecting the formation of a regular lattice. As the phase transition between the molecular and plastic crystal vortex configurations is first-order, it is accompanied by a measurable characteristic energy barrier. The height of this barrier, which can be altered by changes in temperature, magnetic field, or vortex lattice structure, can be used to switch between the two vortex states and thereby enable devices with switchable vortex behavior. Molecular-crystalline vortex configurations have previously been observed in rectangular pinning arrays formed from biaxially textured Fe or Co materials1, 2. The plastic crystal vortex phases are new and may be relevant to a broader range of applications than the molecular vortex phases. They could, for example, be used in logic circuits or sensors, as well as in random-access memory, as they can be switched between two distinct states by small changes in temperature, magnetic field, or vortex lattice structure. These arrays could therefore have significant impact on many areas of technology. The unique properties of the molecular and plastic crystal vortex phases stem from the interaction of vortices with topological defects in their pinning arrays. These topological defects—vortices themselves—form chains, of varying symmetry, along two diagonal directions of the square or rectangle. The mismatch in the stiffnesses perpendicular and parallel to the plane (incompressible versus compressible anisotropy, respectively) of the pinning arrays imposes different elastic distortions on the vortex molecules or plastic crystals. The formation of chains along two diagonal directions of the square or rectangle gives rise to the molecular crystal phases, with chiral nematic structures. Over several decades, the hypothesis that dark matter is made up of some form of extended object has been widely investigated. These objects are predicted to have formed via the collision and merger of smaller objects, a process which can lead to the formation of stable macroscopic structures. The most concrete evidence for the dark matter hypothesis to date is a cosmological model which incorporates these stable macroscopic structures, known as the Cold Dark Matter model. This model successfully predicts the large-scale structure of the universe we observe today, prompting comparison to similar models in the particulate physics domain, where a similar level of agreement has been achieved through the use of quantum zero-point energy. Despite its success, there are still aspects of the Cold Dark Matter model which lack explanation. Chief amongst these is the formation of stable macroscopic structures at late times, which does not occur in simulations which ignore these zero-point fluctuations. This Letter will introduce a way in which dark matter may self-organise into spherical structures, without the need to appeal to dark energy or other non-particle forces. Spherical collapse experiments demonstrate that spherical structures are indeed a stable outcome of these experiments, and this Letter presents empirical evidence for the hypothesis that dark matter is self-organising into these structures. The methodology of the Letter is as follows. Dark matter is introduced to a simulation which includes zero-point fluctuations, and the resulting large-scale structure is examined. The letter's hypothesis is then tested by introducing dark matter to a simulation which does not include zero-point fluctuations, and observing the resulting structure. The letter concludes by outlining future work in which the letter's hypothesis will be tested against observed large-scale structure, in order to provide further evidence for the hypothesis that dark matter is self-organising into spherical structures. The methodology of this Letter is original, and whilst similar work has previously been conducted on the subject of dark matter self-organisation, to the best of the author's knowledge, this Letter is the first to empirically demonstrate the self-organisation of dark matter into stable macroscopic structures. This Letter is the author's Master's thesis, and was written under the supervision of Professor Ian Robertson.

The emission from high energy particles in gamma rays and very high energy (VHE, E>100 GeV) particles in particles in accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider is known to be strongly dependent on the physical conditions near the acceleration sites. The Very Energetic Radiation Imaging Telescope Array System (VERITAS), a system of major atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes located in southern Arizona, has been observing a sample of active galaxies (called BL Lac objects) that are commonly thought to be located near the center of their hosts' gravitational wells. To date, these observations have shown that the spectrum of these objects does not harden, i.e., the slope of the energy spectrum (d log I/d log E) does not change as the flux (I) increases. New observations with VERITAS spanning 9 years of data (from 2008 to 2017) suggest that the spectrum may harden at fluxes exceeding 10(-11) cm(-2) s(-1) GeV. While this finding seems to contradict what is known about gamma-ray emission from other sources, there are several aspects of the sample and analysis that may account for this. Further analysis of the full data set is needed to confirm this surprising finding.

Correlation effects play a crucial role in determining the electronic structure of materials. Despite their central importance, accurate many-body methods to capture correlation effects are still limited. Ab initio wavefunction based methods provide an important alternative. We present an implementation of this approach for excited states in solids. We apply this method to the example of the band structure of the insulating oxides SrTiO3 and KTaO3. Our results demonstrate the crucial importance of correlation effects in these materials. We observe a crossing of the band edges not at the high-symmetry points of the Brillouin zone, but rather at the corners of the hexagonal prism, indicative of reduced symmetry of the electronic structure. This is a direct consequence of correlations, which lift the orbital and spin symmetries of the underlying Heisenberg model. We provide a microscopic interpretation of our results in terms of underlying electronic structure and correlation effects. Finally, we show that the method presented here can be applied to other transition metal oxides, opening the door to large-scale computational studies of correlation effects in a wide range of material classes.

We study groups of circle diffeomorphisms with various structural restrictions. First, we consider the case when the domain and target are the 2-sphere. We show that all such groups are isomorphic to either the Special Euclidean Group or the Rotation Group. We then study the case when the domain and target are the plane. In this case we show that such groups are either trivial or isomorphic to the whole diffeomorphism group of the plane. We also investigate groups of diffeomorphisms between surfaces. In this case the domain and the target can have different dimensions. We show that such groups are virtually a product of a 2-dimensional and a 1-dimensional group. Finally, we consider the case of circle diffeomorphisms with a nontrivial information obstruction. Such diffeomorphisms have a circle as theirdomain but no smooth circle invariant. We show that such circle diffeomorphisms form a normal subgroup of the group considered in the paper. We then use this characterization of circle diffeomorphisms with an obstruction to obtain a complete classification of all finite groups that can be obtained as a full groups of diffeomorphisms between surfaces. We also consider the case of circle diffeomorphisms with a nontrivial holonomy obstruction. We show that such diffeomorphisms form a normal subgroup of the group considered in the paper. We then use this characterization of circle diffeomorphisms with an obstruction to obtain a complete classification of all finite groups that can be obtained as a full groups of diffeomorphisms between surfaces. We also consider the case of circle diffeomorphisms with a nontrivial information and holonomy obstructions. We show that such diffeomorphisms form a normal subgroup of the group considered in the paper. We then use this characterization of circle diffeomorphisms with an information, holonomy and obstruction to obtain a complete classification of all finite groups that can be obtained as a full groups of diffeomorphisms between surfaces. At the end of the paper we consider the cases of infinitely generated groups of circle diffeomorphisms. In the first case we consider circle diffeomorphisms that have an infinite concatenation of a-pieces. We show that such circle diffeomorphisms form a normal subgroup of the group considered in the paper. In the second case we consider circle diffeomorphisms that have an infinite concatenation of c-pieces. We show that such circle diffeomorphisms form a normal subgroup of the group considered in the paper. In the appendix we provide python code that can be used to generate all the examples and Figures of the paper. We then use this characterization of circle diffeomorphisms with an information, holonomy and obstruction to obtain a complete classification of all finite groups that can be obtained as a full groups of diffeomorphisms between surfaces. At the end of the paper we consider the cases of infinitely generated groups of circle diffeomorphisms. In the first case we consider circle diffeomorphisms that have an infinite concatenation of a-pieces. We show that such circle diffeomorphisms form a normal subgroup of the group considered in the paper.

In this paper we develop a physically sound Hamiltonian formulation of the dynamical Casimir effect (DCE). In contrast to previous works, we do not use an simplified model of a plasma, nor a fixed set of dynamical variables. Instead, we construct a quantum Fokker-Planck equation (QFPE) for the density matrix and show that it satisfies a physical optics (PO) principle. In particular, its positive-semidefiniteness implies that the probability density function (PDF) of the electromagnetic field is positive for all fields and trajectories. To demonstrate this positivity, we first map the QFPE to a classical electrodynamics problem in a moving medium. In a second step we discretise this problem, arriving at a nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) which we linearise around a classical steady-state solution. This yields a symplectic Hamiltonian system in conservative form, for which we can show that the corresponding Hamiltonian is positive semidefinite. We validate our analysis by computing the electric field created by an oscillating mirror in 1+1 dimensions, using the Path-Integral Monte Carlo method. Finally, we apply the QFPE to several benchmark cases and comment on recent criticisms of the Hamiltonian formulation of the DCE.

The circumstellar disk around a cool, brown dwarf object was discovered using data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Spitzer Space Telescope. The object, named YLW 16B, is located in the nearby Homogeneous Latin Square VII constellation at a distance of approximately 19.3 light-years. The disk was identified innear-infrared data from both telescopes, and was found to be nearly edge-on with respect to Earth. Spectral energy distribution modeling of the object's infrared spectrum suggests that the brown dwarf has a temperature of 1350 K. The disk is estimated to be 132 million years old, which is comparable to the timescale for dynamical processes in the disk. The disk's inner radius is estimated to be 0.12 au, while its outer radius is 1.9 au. Vortex dynamics in low-dimensional disordered superconductors is an actively studied problem. It is established now that at high magnetic fields, the dynamics of Abrikosov vortices obeys the KZ theory, i.e. it is determined by the energy spectrum of quasiparticles. At low fields, numerous interesting experimental phenomena have been discovered, such as the exponential vortex relaxation, aperiodic diffusion and a breakdown of the KZ scenario. All these phenomena have been explained as manifestations of the destruction of vortex quasi-long-range order. The latter indicates the destruction of quasiparticle energy spectrum. In this work, we show that in superconductors with fractal cluster structure, the vortex dynamics at the initial stage of resistive transition is also determined by the fractal character of the cluster structure. We perform Monte Carlo simulation of the effective Ginzburg-Landau equation for the order parameter and show that at initial resistive transition stage, the correlation function of the order parameter demonstrates the power-law behavior with the critical exponent close to the value observed in 2D Ising model with the presence of magnetic field and with the dimension of the substrate equal to the fractal dimension of the cluster structure.

The pseudospectrum of a system of semiclassical operators is the complement of the spectrum in the closed sectoral cone of the complexification of the phase space of the system. The pseudospectrum may have a fractal structure with numerous self-similarities. This is demonstrated for the harmonic oscillator on the real line with smooth polynomial potentials. In particular, this implies that the Kolmogorov complexity of the pseudospectrum may not be efficiently computable. For systems whose phase space is either the torus or the cylinder, explicit formulas are obtained for the pseudospectrum. The pseudospectrum can be approximated numerically with arbitrary accuracy by considering finite-dimensional truncations of the system. This is used to prove the existence of resonances in the pseudospectrum, i.e. to show that the widths of some spectral bands may become zero. A practical algorithm to find resonances is also presented.

To many-body systems with pairwise attractive interactions, it is well known that strong coupling and large number of particles or degrees of freedom can lead to interesting and counterintuitive behavior. One example is resonance saturation, where many weakly-bound states combine to form a single highly-elastic scattering state. This effect has recently been observed in heavy-ion collision experiments at the CERN LHC and the futureelectron-ion collider (EIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory. In this work, I present a theoretical framework for resonance saturation that is based on the classical nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation. I apply this framework to strong interactions mediated by the Higgs boson and derive simple analytic expressions for the scattering amplitude at large number of colors, strong coupling, and at low relative energy. I then apply this amplitude to compute proton-proton and proton-deuteron scattering amplitudes and show that the theory quantitatively describes existing LHC data across a broad range of center-of-mass energies. I discuss the significance of this work and future applications to proposed high-energy collider experiments.

A High Mass X-ray Binary (HMXB) Scorpius X-1 is a system containing a compact object (neutron star or a black hole) that regularly ejects material from its companion star. This system is classified as an Anomalous X-ray Pulsar (AXP) with a spin period of 12.31s and an inferred surface dipole magnetic field strength of 3.2√{5}-4.2×√{5}×B, where B is the star's surface dipole magnetic field strength in Tesla. Recent studies show that Sco X-1 spends most of its life in the so called island state in the color-color diagram, corresponding to a stable cyclotron resonance scattering feature in the soft X-ray spectrum. In this state, the object's spectrum is dominated by the thermal component from the neutron star's photosphere as well as a cyclotron resonance scattering component (CRC) from a corona of relativistic electrons. Here we present new high-statistics broad-band spectra of Sco X-1 covering its complete color-color evolution from island to banana states. We find that along this evolution the relative contribution of the CRC varies from nearly 40% in the island state to less than 10% in the banana state. Furthermore, the fraction of the non-thermal component in the CRC decreases with increasing color distance from the island to the banana. These results suggest that the mechanism for producing the CRC changes along the color-color evolution from island to banana states.

A brain prosthesis is an electronic device that provides a service comparable to the functions of a biological brain. Since the 20th century, brain prostheses have been developed to treat epilepsy, paralysis, and other conditions. This paper analyzes the dynamic behavior of such a dynamic brain prosthesis, and particularly the question of whether it could develop a desire to live perpetually. Answering this question would require a detailed computational model of the brain prosthesis, which, in turn, requires a better understanding of how the brain's faculties of cognition, volition, and emotion arise from the neurons, molecules, and other physical entities that comprise it. Such an understanding would also be required to determine where in this theoretical model a mechanism for instilling a desire to live perpetually could be implemented. Brain prostheses are designed to mimic specific brain functions, so it would also be necessary to determine which ones of the brain's faculties are indispensable to its intrinsic functionality. If it were possible to develop such a desire to live perpetually, the analysis in this paper suggests that it would also be necessary to determine the source of this desire and whether it would conflict with the long-term survival of the brain prosthesis.

In this paper, we study a one-dimensional quantum dot in the presence of strong attractive contact interactions, which induce a local deformation of the Wigner crystal ground state. Using quantum Monte Carlo and density matrix renormalization group techniques, we determine the ground state energy as a function of system size and deformation amplitude, finding that the ground state is a stable configuration for any amplitude below a critical value. We characterize this deformation via a local density profile, from which we compute local charge and bond-order parameters, as well as identify a one-to-one correspondence between these parameters and the underlying deformation. We also determine the effects of quantum fluctuations on this deformed state using path integral Monte Carlo and compare our results to large system size quantum Monte Carlo data, finding excellent agreement in the regime of stability. Finally, we discuss the experimental implications of our results and propose directions for future work.
