We present the CoRoT primary target HD 52265 observed by the CoRoT space telescope during the first long run of observations (LRc1) in December 2010. HD 52265 is a star of spectral type G8V, luminosity class IV-V, with a companion at an angular separation of 7.7”. CoRoT was observing in the short-wavelength camera (SPM) during the CoRoT satellite roll 32° to the west, and the observation lasted for 47.3 hours. The CoRoT lightcurve of HD 52265 shows a clear modulation with a period of 19.2 hours and an amplitude of 34.7 mmag in the 2.0 – 39.0 μm range. The signature of the modulation is present in the BSmT lightcurve and in the spectrum. We present various models explaining this 19.2-hour light variability. The most probable explanation is a tidally induced Rossby wave modulation. A promising seismic target for further seismic study.

The authors claim to have derived addition theorems for the Coulomb potential and its derivatives for a wide class of spatial dimensions and dimensionalities, but these claims cannot be supported by the paper. The results are either incorrect or not applicable to the claimed cases. Below we comment on five major points of the paper. (1) The theorem in the abstract is valid only for three spatial dimensions, because it contains the term delta3(x), which means a delta-function in three spatial dimensions. Such an expression cannot be correct for any other spatial dimensions. (2) The dimensionalities d and n of the formulas in the abstract are incorrect. In most cases they should be n − 1 and d, not n and d. (3) The formula in the second row of the first column is incorrect. The index k in the sum should be n, not d. (4) The conditions of applicability of the formulas are not clearly defined. For example, in the formula in the third row of the first column n should be replaced by d, not d − 1. (5) The formulation of the addition theorem for the generalized Coulomb potential is incorrect. The correct formula is where V(r) is the potential and A and B are the coefficients to be specified by the boundary conditions. The addition theorems proposed in the paper do not have the properties claimed in the abstract. The results are incorrect, or the conditions of applicability are not clearly defined, or the formulated addition theorems are not applicable to the cases claimed. Therefore, the addition Theorems cannot be supported by the paper.

On 15 January 2005, a large-scale submerging motion was observed near the center of the Sun. This observation was initially considered as a possible solar drown event, but further observations could not confirm it. Soon after the submerging motion was observed, a M7.7 solar flare occurred at the location where the motion was observed. The flare was associated with photospheric brightenings, chromospheric emission enhancement, impactive wave disturbances, and spikes of accelerated particles. Three minutes after the onset of the flare, a second large-scale submerging motion was observed near the flare location. The helioseismic analysis of this sunquake revealed a strong waveguide mode with horizontal degree n=3 and frequency 2.9 mHz. The observed wavefield is characterized by a shock wave moving with the speed of light and a smooth light bulb envelope with a duration of about 15 minutes. The flare caused a sharp increase in the amplitudes of the p- and g- modes, indicating that the flare generated waveenergy in the interior and caused resonant excitation of the sunquake mode. This is the first time that the helioseismic technique was used to study a sunquake generated by a solar flare.

In this paper we present a versatile source of photonic entanglement based on spontaneous parametric downconversion. By tailoring the phase-matching bandwidth we generate Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen states, Bell states, and cluster states with high purity and high efficiency. The Bell states and cluster states are generated simultaneously by tailoring the pump spectrum. We characterize our source by quantum state tomography and observe more than $90\%$ combined purity and greater than $80\%$ combined efficiencies for the three states generated. This versatile source will find applications in fundamental tests of quantum mechanics and in distributed quantum information processing architectures. The abundance of neutral species and the temperature of the plasmasheet from the Earth's perspective are changing significantly over long time periods. In particular, these parameters have been decreasing over the past century. Atmospheric composition models do not explain these trends. In contrast, models of the Moon's heated interior predict a positive thermal inertia. Here, we apply a thermal inertia model to the lunar thermal survey data from the Space Surveillance Telescope (SST) and find that the thermal inertia of the lunar surface is around 1-2 W m-2 K-1. This matches theoretical expectations and is comparable to the thermal inertias of other Solar System bodies with geologically active surfaces. Using the thermal inertia and a revised eddy flux model, we predict the abundance of neutral species at the Earth's plasmasheet and find that they have decreased by a factor of 2-3% over the past century, in agreement with the measured decrease in optical depth. This decreased neutral density increases the efficiency of the critical Cassini division ultraviolet stabilizer and demonstrates the importance of long-term geophysical trends in understanding the interplanetary environment.

A damped Lyman-alpha (DLA) system at z=0.52 is identified in the spectra of QSO HS 2211+0958 using the KeckII telescope. The DLA system has high neutral hydrogen column density, log(N(H I+))=20.95 cm(-2), and high neutral gas-to-total mass ratio, f=0.68. A high velocity system at z=0.52 is also identified in this DLA. Based on optical and near-infrared spectral energy distribution, the metallicity of the system is found to be supersolar. The observed 9.7 micrometer silicate absorption is unusually strong for a DLA system at low redshifts and high column densities. The presence of strong silicate absorption indicates the likely growth of dust in the system at high redshift, prior to the epoch of observation. The unusually strong silicate absorption and high metallicity of the system are consistent with the formation of stars at high redshift in the system and the inferred high initial star-formation rate. This DLA therefore offers an exceptional opportunity to study the early stages of galaxy formation at high redshift.

A huge filamentary structure is reported at 0.55, extending for more than 120 Mpc (240x108 Mpc) in the direction of the WNW from MUNICS dataset. The structure is very good candidates for the large scale filament, with a total mass of about 4.5×109 M⊙, which is equivalent to 2000-3000 clusters of galaxies. Several arcs and lenses are visible in the structure, which look very similar to some massive structures at lower redshifts, as found in the deep HST imaging of the region. The analysis of the spectra of 17 galaxies found in the field, 6 of which are strongly clustered around the peak of the filament, has shown that more than 50% of them have experienced recent episodes of intense star formation (with SFRs of about 200 M⊙/yr). It is much higher than SFRs found in similar redshift structures, suggesting that the filament is actively forming stars with galaxies. Based on this and other recent findings, we propose that the large scale structure was formed at z>1.5, with the star formation triggered by the cluster formation in the forming halos. The galaxies in the high-redshift filament are much more strongly clustered than those in the field, which could be an additional signature of the filamentary structure formation.

In 2004 Perseids meteor shower reached its peak on 12 August 2004 with about 60 meteors per hour. It was the year with the highest rate in recent history. In order to take advantage of this exceptional rate, observers located far from city centers would benefit from observations conducted during the night. Based on this reasoning, a network of observers pointed their telescopes to the sky during the hours of darkness, hoping to catch a few meteors. This was the situation on 12 August 2004, when a sporadic meteor, entryBody==cokecan, explosion== comet, and radiant==Perseus, entered the Earth's atmosphere at approximately 01:55 UT and was observed by multiple observers in different parts of Japan. The Perseid meteor event of 12 August 2004 produced a remarkable number of sporadic meteors. Around midnight (JST) a few dozen people observed the sky with their telescopes in a park near Tokyo. They reported seeing at least one Perseid fireball per minute. One individual, observing from an observatory in Shizuoka prefecture located about 50 km west of Tokyo, reported approximately 80 meteors per hour. Meteors were visible throughout the entire sky, but were brighter near the North Pole. The radiant of the observed meteors was Perseus, which is one of the most famous asteroid clusters in the sky. Around 02:00 UT, the asteroid cluster passed through the inner part of the Solar System. This is the moment when meteors are abundant, because the asteroid cluster becomes compressed into a narrow space region in the sky. The rate of Perseid fireballs started to decrease near 02:30 UT. The individual rate of observers, located within 50 km of Tokyo, was approximately 20 meteors per hour. The event was concluded around 03:30 UT. The total number of observed meteors, combining all observers, was approximately 500. This is one of the highest rates ever observed for a Perseid fireball event. More than half of the meteors were faint, having apparent diameters of less than one arcsecond. Perseids are usually considered to be bright meteors. The peak rate of about 60 meteors per hour on August 12, 2004 was therefore not as high as usual. Perseid meteor shower of 2004 reached its peak on 12 August 2004, and some observers in different parts of the world saw hundreds of meteors. It seems that sporadic meteors were more abundant than expected on that day, perhaps because the asteroid cluster became compressed into a narrow space region in the sky. Observation of a sporadic meteor, entry body==coke can, explosion==comet, and radiant==Perseus on 12 August 2004 provides rare meteor event data. The Perseid meteor shower is typically the most popular sporadic meteor event every year. The peak rate of about 60 meteors per hour on 12 August

Two-photon interactions between the fluctuating electromagnetic fields and charged particles (electrons and nuclei) in the hydrogen gas are examined in the context of cosmological recombination. The effect of two-photon decay of the hydrogen hyperfine levels is estimated to be very small at the present cosmological conditions, but may become important at later stages of cosmological evolution when the density of matter is higher and the temperature of the universe is lower. The two-photon decay of the levels is shown to give a significant radiative decay rate to the levels, substantially changing the population numbers and making these levels quickly depopulated. The signatures of the two-photon decay in the modern optical and radio spectra are predicted. Long-range correlations have been widely observed in a variety of complex systems, such as nuclei, atoms, liquids and glasses. In recent years, it has been found that such correlations also exist in linear polymers. The common feature of these systems is the fractal or self-similar structure at different length scales. In the current work, we present a detailed analysis of the long-range correlations in the polymer chain, based on the polymer melts with the variable temperature molecular dynamics simulations. We find that the intrachain structure at different length scales are related to each other. More precisely, we show that, in each polymer chain, the size of the monomers, which could be determined by the local conformations, is correlated with the global ones. Based on this relation, we propose a simple convolution model, which can quantitatively describe the long-range correlations in the polymer melts. Furthermore, we also demonstrate the relations between the correlations and the polymer chain structure. These findings not only give deep insights into the polymer structure, but also provide useful information for the polymer processing, such as polymer crystallization and orientation.

Galaxy clusters, the largest structures in the Universe, are an invaluable probe of the early history of structure formation. While the mean relation between the velocity dispersion of member galaxies and their optical richness has been well studied, the scatter about this relation has been largely unexplored. Using a sample of 297 maxBCG clusters, we quantify both the mean and the scatter of the velocity dispersion-richness relation at fixed richness, and show that it evolves with redshift. We compare our measurements to predictions from $\Lambda$CDM models and find good agreement given the current level of statistical and systematic uncertainties in the mass-observable relations. We also measure the evolution of the mass-observable relation as a function of redshift, and find that while the mean evolution is consistent with no evolution, the mass and scatter of the relation at a fixed richness are consistent with being independent of redshift at $z<1.2$ and having slightly more evolution at higher redshifts. We discuss possible systematic effects that may affect our results and the implications of our measurements for theories of structure growth.

The fundamental limits to determining the location of a source by measuring the concentration gradients of chemical tracers, such as pollutants or biological cells, are determined by the random walk nature of molecular transport. The sensitivity of the technique, which is limited by the molecular diffusivity, is inversely proportional to the square of the measurement interval, making minute changes near a source undetectable beyond a critical distance determined by the molecular diffusivity. The spatial resolution is limited by the transport length scale, which for air pollution or cell tracking is typically hundreds of meters. These limits are broadly applicable to concentration gradient-based positioning techniques. To overcome these fundamental limits, it has been proposed to modify the tracking algorithm to model molecular transport, e.g. with random walk or Brownian motion. These models can provide increasingly accurate localizations as measurement intervals are reduced, but at the expense of drastically increasing computational cost or requiring sampling at increasingly small intervals. Here we demonstrate that all concentration gradient positioning techniques are fundamentally limited by the random walk nature of molecular transport and that a unique limit on the localization accuracy exists regardless of the measurement interval or implementation details.

In magnetic multilayers comprising multiple ferromagnets with different directions of magnetizations, spin transport is related to the transfer of angular momentum between the magnetic moments. The efficiency of this transfer is quantified by the interfacial spin-transfer torque (STT), which defines the basic behaviour of these structures as discrete hardware for future spin-based information technologies. In this work we focus on systems with cubic anisotropy, in which out-of-plane spontaneous magnetization is preferred to in-plane magnetizations due to interfacial interactions. Using the thin-film approach, we present a comprehensive study of STT as a function of the number of atomic layers in the multilayer, compositional disorder, magnetic anisotropy and temperature. It is shown that STT in Co/Cu and Ni/Cu multilayers can be efficiently controlled by adjusting the number of atomic layers in these layers. Furthermore, it is observed that Cu layers do not allow the magnetization to stabilize in the out-of-plane direction, whereas Ni layers stabilize the magnetization in this direction. Thus, changing the number of atomic layers in these heterostructures enables the control of the interfacial STT. Finally, it is shown that in Co/Cu bilayers with sufficiently thick Co layers, the interfacial STT exhibits weak dependence on temperature.

The dark energy, which is interpreted as a component of the universe with negative pressure, is one of the biggest mysteries in modern physics. One of the most promising ways of measuring its properties is based on the distance based cosmology called ‘Cosmic Distance duality relations’ (DDGR), which connect the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface, dA, with the luminosity distance, dL, to the observed galaxy cluster. So far, these relations have been tested only on small cluster samples (e.g. Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect, gravitational lensing) and with low accuracy (mainly due to the poor calibration of the local distance ladder). I present the results of X-ray observations of the largest, most relaxed galaxy clusters with the Chandra X-ray observatory. These clusters follow the cosmic distance duality relation to an accuracy of ~8%, which is an improvement of a factor of 5 compared to earlier results. The derived precise X-ray masses, which are used to test the cosmological models, are also presented.

The existence of an intrinsic angular momentum (spin) component for electrons in helium atoms was proposed in 1955. The theory was based on an analogy to the electron's magnetic dipole moment. To describe the motion of an electron in a helium atom, three interrelated spatial concepts are combined in the following four-dimensional spacetime model: the electron's point in space (three dimensions), the electron's wave function in configuration space (three dimensions), and the electron's motion through space and time (one dimension). The resulting spacetime description provides the first four moments of an electron in a helium atom and may prove to be of general utility for describing the motion of quantum systems. Here, the spacetime model is based on four dimensions, as the electron has both an intrinsic angular momentum (spin) and orbital angular momentum (associated with the movement of the electron around the nucleus). If all this intrinsic angular momentum were expressed by two vectors (angular momenta), we would end up with a four-dimensional spacetime model. The spacetime model contains several parameters that can be adjusted to match experimental data. The present analysis of available data (light scattering experiments on cold helium gas) is consistent with the following values: the electron has an intrinsic spin quantum number s = 0.82 and an orbital angular momentum quantum number l = 0.53. These numbers suggest that the electron moves in a slightly asymmetric elliptical orbit around the nucleus of the helium atom, in much the same way as a real atom. We suggest that the spacetime description of quantum systems may prove to be a useful addition to current methods, and that the model may also have other applications. Quasi one dimensional nanostructures, such as quantum wires and nanotubes, provide a new route to engineer the structure and properties of solids1. The smallest cross section dimension of these nanostructures determines their strength and rigidity, while the width provides a tunable size that enables engineering of their electronic, optical and mechanical properties. Here we explore nanostructures of the antimonene form 2, a recently discovered analogue of black phosphorus, that is stable at high pressure and low temperatures2. We identify antimonene nanotubes as an ideal system to study structural and mechanical properties of one dimensional nanostructures due to a large axial length and small width of the nanotubes that guarantees their quasi one dimensional character. We experimentally demonstrate that single-walled nanotubes of antimonene are extremely strong (Young's modulus of 2 TPa and a failure strength of 4.2 GPa), while exhibiting a large Poisson's ratio of -0.16. Combined with their high Young's modulus, this results in a giant product of fracture strength and Young's modulus, σfY > 1750 N/μm, which is one of the largest reported for any material. We perform an extensive nano-mechanical characterization that is crucial to understanding the strengthening mechanism and developing nanotube based sensors. Our work opens a new door for exploiting structure-property relationships in one-dimensional nanostructures and demonstrates the feasibility of creating nanowires and nanotubes of extreme mechanical strength for applications such as strain sensing, acoustic dampening and next generation computing.

Strong decays of charmonia into light vector mesons and a vector meson are known to be sensitive to the composition of the vector mesons. In particular, the Isospin symmetry, which is aSU(2) symmetry in the limit of equal up and down quarks, is expected to be broken in the case of light vector mesons. A nice example of such an effect is the ratio of the branching ratios of J/ψ and \] into π0: Br(J/ψ→π0)/Br(\\psi→π0)=0.50-0.86, which implies that the pion fraction in π0 is larger in J/ψ than in \\psi. In this paper we calculate this ratio using the Resonance Chiral Theory (RChT), which is an effective theory of strong interactions based on the chiral symmetry and the resonance structure of QCD, and show that it is not consistent with the experimental data. We then show that in the large N_c limit, the isospin violation disappears, and provide an argument as to why the actual situation is in between these two limits.

A team of researchers from the Max-Planck-Institut für Radio Astronomy in Bonn, Germany and the Universities of Leiden and Groningen in the Netherlands have made the first detection of radio emission from the intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in the globular cluster G1. The detection was made using the Australian Telescope National Facility's (ATNF's) Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) in India. The researchers were able to determine that the radio signal was consistent with that of orbiting hot gas, a signature of the IMBH's expected behavior. The result was published on April 4 in the journal Nature. The detection of radio emission from an IMBH, or black hole with an mass between those of stellar-mass black holes and supermassive black holes, is important because it can provide information about the environment of the black hole. Previous detections of radio emission from IMBHs had only placed limits on its properties. If the radio signal is strong and detectable, it can also enable the black hole's mass and distance from Earth to be calculated. Because the team was able to detect radio emission from G1's IMBH using a single radio telescope, this offers the promise of cheaper, faster IMBH measurements, enhancing their use in understanding the environments of black holes.

Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we have carried out a thorough search for highly-excited molecular lines in the vicinity of the Seyfert 2 nucleus in the nearby galaxy M51 (NGC 5194). No evidence of an active galactic nucleus (AGN) was found in the distribution or kinematics of the observed species. Instead, the spatial distribution, excitation mechanism, and kinematics of the molecular gas are all consistent with a scenario in which the molecular gas is impacted by a radio jet emanating from the active nucleus in the galaxy NGC 5195. The molecular gas is distributed in two spatially distinct clouds that are offset from the radio source by ~15-20 pc, exhibit similar velocities, and have slightly different physical properties. These results lend further credence to the hypothesis that radio jets are effective at transporting interstellar matter from their host galaxies to distances of several tens of parsecs from the nucleus.

In this work we investigate the interplay between radio galaxies and their cluster environment. Cluster radio galaxies (CRG), namely radio-loud AGN located in the cluster core, show signs of ongoing strong activity that are usually absent in field galaxies. Several scenarios have been proposed to explain the presence of active CRG in clusters, that however cannot be fully representative of the entire cluster population. Cluster cold fronts, for instance, appear frequently in simulations of clusters in the intermediate stages of formation, but hardly ever in actual X-ray observations. This suggests that the fraction of active CRG could be different from what predicted by these scenarios. Observations of the soft X-ray emission from CRG counterparts also suggest the presence of large amounts of hot gas associated with the CRG, likely stripped from the cluster galaxies. Finally, observations of the large scale structure surrounding clusters suggest that most of them grow through the accretion of mass-poorer groups. Groups can strip part of the cluster galaxies, leaving the galaxies in the cluster cores. Since radio galaxies typically show strong radio emission, they are excellent tracers of the galaxy density distribution. We plan to employ a wide set of observations of CRG and their host clusters to study the interplay between the CRG and their environment.

Quark matter with two colors (2CQM) has been proposed as a simple model of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at low energy scales where the Roberge-Weiss symmetry is expected to be restored. Two quarks with different flavors but with the same color can attract each other through the color force with a long-range force, similar to the Cooper pairing in a superconductor. It was previously suggested that in two-color quark matter, the Larkin-Ovchinnikov state can occur at sufficiently large but finite quark chemical potential. In this work, we show that when the effects of a third flavor, namely the up and down quarks with different colors, are also taken into account, the Larkin-Ovchinnikov state is indeed the ground state at large enough quark densities, but it cannot be sustained when the Fermi surface is gapped by a small but non-vanishing diquark charge density. Instead, we predict that the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov state, with the same symmetry but with different phase factors on the two Fermi surfaces, is the ground state in the regime with broken symmetry. This result is confirmed by solving the three-flavor quantum Gross-Pitaevskii equation and further supported by a weak coupling analysis. Our prediction suggests that the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov state may be realized in a heavy fermion system under the condition of two suitable energy scales being comparable.

The InterHourly-Variability (IHV) Index of Geomagnetic Activity and its Use in Deriving the Long-term Variation of Solar Wind Speed. The InterHourly-variability (IHV) index of Geomagnetic Activity is introduced and its characteristics are defined. This is then used to characterize the long-term variation of Solar Wind Speed (SW speed) that has occurred over the past 450 years. The SW speed variation is shown to comprise two component parts, a primary component (periodic wave with a period of around 11 years) and a secondary component (a clear long-term increase). The IHV index is shown to track the SW speed variation very closely, with the change in SW speed driving the change in IHV index. The SW speed variation is shown to have an overall increasing trend, at a rate of around 20 km/s/century. This has important implications for Space Weather, as the increased SW speed directly influences how much energy the Solar Wind carries.

A method to determine the electronic structure of single dopant atoms in silicon carbide using scanning probe microscopy is presented. As dopant atoms have different lattice structure from the host semiconductor, they may offer novel opportunities to investigate quantum systems at low temperature. Here we demonstrate this concept by employing an electrically-tunable scanning tunneling microscope (STM) to locally modify the electronic structure of a single atom of SiC. The application of a rapid voltage pulse modifies the electronic structure of the donor atom such that a distinct feature can be observed in the dI/dV spectrum acquired using the STM. This approach could enable electrical detection and control of individual dopants in silicon carbide, paving the way for investigations of quantum states in nanoscale devices and development of atomic-scale sensors with these novel properties. The control and study of individual dopants in silicon carbide (4H-SiC) offers the exciting possibility of tailoring nanoscale devices to have novel quantum properties. A single dopant atom has been shown to provide an opportunity to investigate a quantum system at low temperature. For example, the phosphorus atom is a well-studied donor atom which has been used to demonstrate the spin of a single phosphorus atom electron and investigate electron quantum tunneling in this system. However, probing the electronic structure of a single dopant atom in real time with high spatial resolution has remained a significant experimental challenge. In this work, we employ a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) to locally modify the electronic structure of a single atom of 4H-SiC. The modification of the electronic structure of a single atom allows for electrical detection and control of individual dopants in silicon carbide. As an example, we apply rapid voltage pulses to the STM to locally change the electronic structure of a single donor atom. A distinct feature in the dI/dV spectrum is observed when the donor atom’s electronic structure is modified. We characterize the modification of the electronic structure of the donor atom and its influence on the dI/dV spectrum. This approach allows for electrical detection and control of individual dopants in silicon carbide, paving the way for investigations of quantum states in nanoscale devices and development of atomic-scale sensors with these novel properties.

Recent observations with the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) on-board the Hinode satellite have revealed an intriguing discrepancy in G-band contrast between the internetworked regions of the solar photosphere and the umbral regions. The G-band is a key diagnostic of the temperature, density, and ionization state of the solar plasma, and it is formed by the transitions between the energy levels within the G2 Raman line. In internetworked regions, the Hinode data indicate that the G-band contrast is significantly greater than the values predicted by classical radiative transfer models. These discrepancies have been noted by several groups, with the most comprehensive studies being that of @Katsukawa:2008p1927, who suggest that in internetworked regions the observed G-band contrast may be double that which is predicted by the standard model. In this study we examine the high spatial resolution (0.32") Hinode data and demonstrate that the G-band contrast in internetworked regions is, in fact, consistent with the predictions of classical radiative transfer models. Additionally, we present evidence that the anomalous G-band contrast is only present in the transition region / umbral region boundary and is completely absent in the internetwork. We suggest that this “limb brightening” is caused by the presence of non-thermal electrons which interact with the G2 line at the transition region / umbral region boundary, enhancing the contrast observed in the in Hinode data.

The near-ultraviolet and optical spectra of ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) are usually well-fitted by continuum models consisting of a simple multicolor blackbody (MBB) or more complex accretion disk plus blackbody components. Using either parametric (e.g., accretion disk spectrum from Cambridge Accretion Code) or non-parametric (e.g., cubic spline) models for the disc emission, one can independently estimate the apparent radius of the emission region as a function of the gravitational potential of the black hole. We demonstrate that, for a given black hole mass and distance, the estimated Eddington ratios and the temperature of the MBB continuum are very sensitive to the assumed spectral shape. Using a spherical model (e.g., relativistic disk inverse Compton scattering) and assuming a high-spin black hole ($a$=0.95) with a mass of 1.4 M⊙ for the object ESO243-49 HLX, we show that the estimated Eddington ratio would be decreased by a factor of two if the spectrum is a MBB rather than a disk+BB spectrum, or by a factor of five if the spectrum is a disk+BB spectrum with an apparent temperature of kT = 0.15 keV instead of 0.6 keV. We also show that for the same black hole mass and spectrum, the estimated temperature of the MBB continuum is very different if the spectrum is a MBB with kT = 0.15 keV instead of a disk+BB spectrum with kT = 0.6 keV. These differences have implications on how ULXs with the same near-infrared emission are separated into those whose appearance is dominated by a high-spin black hole or by an advection-dominated accretion flow, respectively. We discuss some of the ramifications for the interpretation of ULX spectra, and suggest observational tests that may help discriminate between different models for the ULX continuum emission.

A new generation of astrophysical electron telescopes, such as the recently-commissioned HESRG, are opening a new window onto particle astrophysics, with the potential to provide dramatic improvements in our understanding of cosmic-ray acceleration, propagation and their myriad effects. In this work, we present new HESRG data on the enigmatic recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi, whose 2006 outburst has historically been among the most energetic witnessed in the modern era. We interpret our data within the framework of nonlinear diffusive shock acceleration (DSA) to cosmic-rays, and we make a number of novel inferences. We find that the electrons and ions can be well-fitted by a single power-law of common index -2.29 with no indication of any break or steepening at the hadron-to-electron transition, and that their non-thermal emission undergoes a rapid but smooth transition from keV to MeV energy bands. From comparison with nonlinear DSA theory, we deduce that electrons are most likely accelerated to 300 TeV - 1 EeV via magnetic reconnection events within a high-speed magnetospheric outflow from the binary system, whilst ions are accelerated to 30 GeV - 1 TeV, within a slower but more-diffuse wind. We finally compare our results with previous predictions from the light-echo observations of the 2010 outburst of RS Ophiuchi - with which we likewise detect non-thermal emission - and find excellent agreement for electron energies but substantial tension for ion energies. We conclude that our results provide compelling new evidence that nonlinear DSA is an enabling paradigm for the acceleration of both electrons and ions to the very-high-energies observed in cosmic-ray sources.

In Dissipative Particle Dynamics (DPD), interactions between different particles are modeled by short-range, collision-driven forces that are approximately mean-zero and have a specified auto-correlation function. This approach, which treats short-range interactions as Gaussian white noise, is accurate for particle separations much larger than the dissipative lengthscale. At smaller separations, however, the separation-dependent correlations between the force and its underlying velocity cause the noise to become non-Gaussian. We derive an effective stochastic interaction by measuring the correlation between force and velocity at several different separations and using a minimum-squares fit to determine a two-point covariance function. This covariance function enables the stochastic interactions at short distances to better approximate the non-Gaussian force correlations at intermediate separations, while still enabling effective coupling at large distances where the noise approaches Gaussianity. The resulting DPD equations of motion are integrated with a stochastic velocity-Verlet scheme, and the accuracy of the effective interaction is tested by comparison with simulations of thermal equilibrium behavior.

Using an original pulsed magnet with a short rise time of field pulses (10-20 ns), depending on the magnetic field intensity, we have studied the relaxation phenomena in single crystalline HoBa2Cu3O7-d samples. The character of the relaxation curve for the induction decay in a low magnetic field range was determined. Three components were found: a fast, a slow and a structural components. The slow component is observed for fields above 0.2 T. We have studied the temperature and the magnetic field dependencies of the relaxation parameters. We have observed a positive correlation between the critical temperature of HoBa2Cu3O7-d samples and the relaxation strength of the slow component. At the same time, we have observed a maximum of the relaxation strength in the vicinity of the critical temperature for all studied samples. The analysis of the relaxation process dynamics allows to suggest the presence of inhomogeneities with different magnetic characteristics in the studied samples.

The first section is an overview of ringed spaces and their relations to topological spaces and to schemes. Ringed spaces are higher-level abstract structures that encapsulate a topological space along with an sheaf of rings on that space. Schemes are an even higher-level abstraction that additionally incorporates a structure sheaf of rings and an action of a ringed space by automorphisms of that ringed space. The section then defines the notion of a formal scheme, which is an informal definition of a scheme that encompasses formal neighbourhoods of all the points. This is an important concept in the theory of schemes as one can understand a scheme based on its formal model, which is difficult to do otherwise. The third section defines and constructs formal completions of a scheme along with its ringed structure. This is an important construction that is crucial in the theory of G-topological spaces and also generalises many notions from algebraic geometry. The fifth section then discusses ind-schemes, which are a further generalisation of the notions of schemes and formal schemes, which also incorporates cosheaves in the formal sense. This is of interest as the sheaves of rings in a ringed space can often be restricted to the sites of open subspaces, which induce cosheaves of rings on those spaces. Finally, the last section discusses adic spaces and adic spaces with a topology, which are a related higher-level concept to ringed spaces that can also be thought of as local models for adic spaces. Schemes are an even higher-level abstraction that additionally incorporates a structure sheaf of rings and an action of a ringed space by automorphisms of that ringed space. In this note, I will introduce and define formal schemes, which are an informal definition of a scheme that encompasses formal neighbourhoods of all the points. This is an important concept in the theory of schemes as one can understand a scheme based on its formal model. Then, I will discuss formal completions of a scheme along with its ringed structure. This is an important construction that is crucial in the theory of G-topological spaces and also generalises many notions from algebraic geometry. Finally, I will discuss ind-schemes, which are a further generalisation of the notions of schemes and formal schemes, which also incorporates cosheaves in the formal sense. This is of interest as the sheaves of rings in a ringed space can often be restricted to the sites of open subspaces, which induce cosheaves of rings on those spaces. In the last part, I will discuss adic spaces and adic spaces with a topology, which are a related higher-level concept to ringed spaces that can also be thought of as local models for adic spaces.

21-cm synthesis observations of VIRGOHI 21 - a possible dark galaxy in the Virgo Cluster were performed using the Giant Meter Wave Telescope (GMWT). No line emission associated with VIRGOHI 21 was detected down to a 3-sigma limiting sensitivity of 1.2 mK. The non-detection and the non-constraining of its spectral energy distribution (SED) allow us to set an upper limit on the dust mass of M < 13.3×10^−9^ M ⊙, corresponding to A dust < 1.9×10^−4^ A⊕, where M ⊙ is the dust mass and A⊕ is the dust extinction cross section. This limit is the lowest Dust Mass to Extinction Ratio of any object, and is one to two orders of magnitude lower than the dust mass to gas mass ratios of low-mass galaxies. Together with its very low stellar mass, VIRGOHI 21 thus provides further evidence that galaxies like VIRGOHI 21 are dark matter dominated and very different from ordinary galaxies.

A large fraction of quasars have broad absorption line (BAL) troughs in their spectra, which are outflows of gas along the line of sight to the quasar. The BAL quasars (BALQSOs) are excellent tools to study the large scale structures of the Universe due to their high space density and narrow absorption lines. 2MASS has recently revealed a previously unknown population of very red (J-K) BALQSOs. Using optical spectroscopy of a sample of 30 very red BALQSOs from the 2MASS catalog, we present evidence for a distinct class of 2MASS Very Red BALQSOs (2MASSVRBALQSOs). These sources have near-infrared colors of J-K>4.8, and are heavily obscured in the optical (A_V>10), but display extremely red 2MASS JHK colors, similar to those of normal quasars. The fraction of 2MASSVRBALQSOs among all BALQSOs is between 57% and 67% depending on how 2MASSVRBALQSOs are defined. The unprecedented availability of extremely red BALQSOs selected from the 2MASS database will enable tests of evolutionary models for BALQSOs and new insights on the physical mechanisms powering the large scale structures of the Universe.

In this paper, we consider the following deterministic and stochastic differential equations: ẋ = x + ẏ ẏ = - x + f(t, x) + g(t, x), where f(t, x) is the random forcing and g(t, x) is a Brownian motion. We show that the solution to the above equations exists and is unique in the probability sense. Furthermore, we establish a central limit theorem for the stationary solution. We also consider the corresponding Fokker-Planck equation: ∂ ƒ∂t = (I - 𝛼)∂ 2 ƒ/∂x2, where ƒ=𝜎(t, x) is the probability distribution function, and 𝛼 denotes the Laplace operator. We show that the above Fokker-Planck equation has a unique solution when the initial condition ƒ(0, x) has finite second moment. Finally, we discuss the relation between the stochastic and the corresponding deterministic system.

We present the results of spectroscopic and photometric observations of the host galaxy of the intermediate duration gamma-ray burst 040924. The galaxy is at a redshift of z = 0.656, and its spectrum is similar to that of normal elliptical galaxies. The galaxy has an absolute r’-band magnitude of –23.2 ± 0.1 and a n2 bulge-to-total luminosity ratio of 0.70 ± 0.01. We measure a systemic redshift of z = 0.656 for the host and detect neither signs of ongoing star formation nor absorption from the host galaxy’s interstellar medium. We determine a lower limit of >66% for the globular cluster fraction of the galaxy and rule out with 4σ certainty the presence of a compact nucleus, but we cannot distinguish between a bulge and a dwarf elliptical galaxy. We spectroscopically and photometrically monitor the optical emission from the afterglow of 040924 from 8.4 d to 22.8 d after the burst. We detect a moderate degree of host-galaxy extinction of A(r’) = 0.31 ± 0.04 mag, and the best-fit rate of optical decay is steeper than –0.94 ± 0.03 between 8.4 d and 22.8 d after the burst. The host is much fainter than ∼2mpc in the V-band at all epochs after 22.8 d, but its rest-frame ultraviolet luminosity is much higher at earlier epochs than is typical of typical comparison samples of high-redshift galaxies. This evolution implies that the host had an exceptionally high specific star formation rate at early times and that it formed a substantial amount of its stellar mass at an intermediate epoch of z ∼ 2.2–3.4. We present the composite ultraviolet to visible spectral energy distribution of the host galaxy and compare it with the spectral energy distributions of passive and star-forming galaxies at intermediate redshift. The host spectral energy distribution is similar to that of passive galaxies but is not identical to that of star-forming galaxies. We interpret the host spectral energy distribution as resulting from a very old population of stars and an active accretion disk powered by an intermediate-mass black hole in a relatively dense environment. We determine extinction-corrected rest-frame UV absolute magnitudes of –18.3 ± 0.2, –17.2 ± 0.1, and –16.4 ± 0.1 at days 22.8, 31.2, and 40.9, respectively. The inferred star-formation rates are 2.8, 0.7, and 0.2 M ⊙ yr–1 at these epochs. These rates are higher than those of similar-redshift galaxies, but are similar to those of other gamma-ray burst host galaxies at similar redshifts. We present here a model for the X-ray spectrum of the type 1.9 Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151. The spectrum, from 0.7 KeV to 10 kev, has been modeled as a combination of starburst and active galactic nucleus (AGN) components. In particular, the starburst component is represented by a combination of thin interstellar clouds with a range of metallicities and cloud temperatures, parameterized by a simple ionization balance. This model has been compared to the spectrum observed by the X-Ray Telescope (XRT) aboard the Swift satellite, and has been shown to provide an acceptable representation of the overall spectrum. The AGN component is represented by a power-law, absorbed by both the Galactic column and the toroidal structure around the central black hole. This model, along with a small contribution from starburst emission at low energies, can also provide an acceptable fit to the X-ray spectrum.

Wavelet groups are a generalization of the usual orthogonal and unitary groups. They have a rich dynamical structure and have found applications in several areas of mathematics and physics, such as number theory, geometry, physics, classical and quantum chaos, crystal lattices, string theory, black hole physics and geometry, representation theory, etc. In this paper, we give an explicit unitary representation of wavelet groups on a certain separable Hilbert space. This representation can be used to construct a model for encoding iterated function systems in solenoids, i.e., multifractal, Cantor-like sets without Holder gradient trajectories. It is shown that the eigenvalues of the corresponding Schrödinger operator are exactly the iterated function exponents. As an application, we will show that the Mandelbrot set can be obtained as a spectrum. The unitary representation of wavelet groups developed in this paper can be considered as a generalization of the well-known Fourier transform on the line. The main idea of the representation is to associate each unitary representation of a wavelet group with a two-sided admissible kernel on a directed partially ordered set. We will explain the detailed construction for the modular group and discuss some of its nice properties. As an application, the corresponding operator semigroup provides an alternative way for iterating function systems in solenoids. It also connects the wavelet groups representation with some famous objects in complex analysis and dynamical systems. For example, it is shown that the Schrödinger operator with the spectrum of wavelet groups is exactly the classical logistic equation. The Mandelbrot set can be obtained as a point spectrum. As an outlook, we also discuss some of the current problems and possible directions for future research.

In this paper, we study the effect of confining the hard-sphere fluid between two parallel hard walls on its average properties. First, we calculate the perturbation correction to the equation of state of the ideal hard-sphere fluid. This correction is exponentially small when the wall-fluid density ratio is small and the separation between the walls is much larger than the particle diameter. Using this perturbation result, we show that the change in average density of the fluid due to confinement scales as the volume of the space enclosed by the confining walls. Next, we examine the effect of confinement on the structure factor and show that this also scales with the volume of the space. We also calculate the effect of confinement on the speed of sound and the inter-diffusion coefficient and show that they are independent of the volume of the enclosed space. Our results imply that confinement has little or no effect on the average entropy, enthalpy, heat capacity, viscosity, and self-diffusivity of the hard-sphere fluid.

The intergalactic medium (IGM) is the diffuse gas that surrounds galaxies. Due to its very low density, it has so far been difficult to directly detect it. The Hot IGM and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) allow us to study the physics of this so far undetected medium. We performed a realistic Cosmological Simulation that follows the formation of galaxies and their interaction with the IGM up to a redshift of 5.5. We find that, while in low density regions most of the IGM's mass was turned into stars, in high density regions it was turned into hot gas, shock heated by active galactic nuclei (AGN). The detection of this medium with future X-ray telescopes like Athena will allow us to measure the ionization history of the Universe, the fraction of ionizing photons that were absorbed by the IGM, the efficiency of black hole feedback, and the population of low-luminosity active galaxies.

The excitation spin polarization is measured by using time-integrated spin-dependent photon counting and polarization analysis. Spin dynamics of few distinct QD samples are investigated and dynamical freezing of the spin is observed in few samples. The dynamical freezing is possibly due to the influence of nuclear spins.
