ASTROD I (Advanced Telescope for Subscriber Astronomy Observations and Data) is a proposed wide-field optical/infrared survey telescope for use by amateur astronomers. One of the major challenges in designing such a survey telescope is predicting how much energy the telescope will consume as it performs observations. In this work, we simulate the energy consumption of the ASTROD I telescope using data from the proposed tracking system and active cooling. We also simulate the effect of various disturbances on the tracking system and active cooling. We find that the expected energy consumption of the ASTROD I tracking system is 20.8 kW, which is higher than the expected consumption of 17.3 kW. However, the expected active cooling consumption is estimated at 6.2 kW, which is lower than the expected consumption of 13.2 kW. We also find that the expected tracking system consumption varies between 13.2 and 17.3 kW under typical simulated disturbances.

A large number of neutral gas clouds at high redshift are expected to be responsible for damping the UV radiation from distant galaxies, which are known as damped Lyman-alpha absorbers (DLA) at low redshift. Using a novel wide-band filter with low sky background at 912 nm and a multi-object spectrograph, we conducted the first high-redshift DLAs survey with the goal of characterizing the neutral gas content of high-redshift galaxies. We use the data from the survey to measure the incidence of DLAs at $6.0 < z < 7.0$ and set a new lower limit on the DLA cross section at $z=7.1$. The survey is approximately 4 times more sensitive to DLAs than any previous study at these high redshifts, and there are currently seven candidate damped systems with $z>7.1$ (all with ${\rm N(H\;I)} > 2 \times 10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$) based on the unique spectral features in the wavelength coverage of our survey. However, follow up observations with better resolution are needed to confirm these systems as high-redshift DLAs and rule out low-redshift interloper contaminants.

Intermediate mass (IM) stars are the most numerous stars in the galaxy and their demise as supernovae is one of the dominant factors in enriching the interstellar medium. The end of the life of an IM star is usually a supernova, but there are also theoretical suggestions that the helium-ignited Hertzsprung gap reactor could, under specific circumstances, fail to explode. If this happens, the star may end its life as a hypernova or, if the core is sufficiently massive, a long-duration gamma-ray burst. In either case, it is of fundamental interest how these events affect their environment. Using data from the Glimpse survey, we have performed high angular resolution imaging of six IM stars and, for three of them, detected evidence for marginally resolved circumstellar material (CSM) that is indicative of a recent interaction with the debris from a failed explosion. For two of these stars we can also measure the motion of the CSM relative to the star and we find two distinct kinematic groups. One has slow velocities of order of 10 km/s that we interpret as material moving at constant speed around the star, presumably ejected during the explosion. The second is composed of two stars with faster moving, circular features with typical velocities of order 100 km/s. We suggest that these are knots of material that were entrained in a fast wind that was produced by the progenitor of the explosion, with the knots subsequently forming as the expanding shock wave overtook ambient material.

A mysterious high-latitude star-forming cloud CG 12 is investigated in this work. The cloud is found to have a stellar mass of 1.4×104 M⊙, which is one of the largest values among the known high-latitude cloud complexes. Spectra of 86 young stars in the cloud indicate that the cloud has an age of 1.5-2.8 Myr and is likely forming stars at a high rate of about 1.2×1010 M⊙yr-1. Based on both the velocity and spatial distributions of the cloud, it is suggested that CG 12 may have originated from a satellite galaxy that became tidally disrupted by the Milky Way. This is the first evidence for the origin of a high-latitude star-forming cloud through tidal disruption of a small satellite. The cloud CG 12 has a large stellar mass and is forming stars at a high rate. It is most likely tidally disrupted satellite of the Milky Way. The work presents the first evidence for the origin of a high-latitude star-forming cloud through tidal disruption of a small satellite.

In this paper, we propose a model to describe the observations of several globular clusters regarding their measured basic parameters. These clusters present a set of physical characteristics that are either exceptional or do not fit into the patterns established for normal globular clusters. The model we present here aims to account for all these observed characteristics, describing the observed phenomena with a single formation mechanism. The physical characteristics that are described by this model are: 1) an unusually high mass-to-light ratio; 2) the presence of dark matter; 3) an unusually high concentration of mass; 4) a significantly negative periastron distance; 5) a very extended half-light radius; and 6) the unusual presence of a second population of stars. The physical mechanism responsible for this formation involves the collision of two intermediate-sized galaxies, whose massive and dark components form the dark clusters we observe today. The particles of the dark clusters, originally forming the two galaxies, lose energy through dynamical friction while moving through the diffuse material of the larger galaxy, ending up in the halo of the newly formed cluster. This process results in the build-up of the unusual mass-to-light ratios we observe, as well as the creation of the dark matter halos in which these clusters are embedded.

Global and regional brain metabolic scaling is analyzed in a population-level human neuroimaging study of 3T MRI scans from 6800 subjects. Global scaling of cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) is observed to obey a quadratic scaling with total brain volume (TBV), CMRO2 = aTBV2 + bTBV + c. With controlling for body mass, total brain and white matter volumes are shown to be linearly related, suggesting that the quadratic scaling is predominantly driven by a non-linear volume effect. Regional analyses of 44 brain regions demonstrate that both gray and white matters obey the global scaling law with different scaling exponents. Scaling exponents of 0.78 in gray matter and 0.61 in white matter are estimated. Application of these scaling laws to maps of average global-to-regional CMRO2 ratios, and TBV to brain volumes and their ratios show that, on average, cerebral oxygen utilization increases by 36% and brain/TBV decreases by 27% across global increasing TBV, consistent with the underlying physical constraints. Cerebral metabolic efficiency of 32% is estimated, and is shown to decrease with increased TBV in a quadratic fashion. Functional implications of these relationships are discussed. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of global and regional cerebral metabolic scaling with respect to total brain and regional volumes. The estimated global cerebral metabolic scaling exponents of 0.78 in gray matter and 0.61 in white matter are much larger than the value of 0.75 expected from the cellular scaling law with a 2/3ths power law, and imply a strong non-linear volumetric effect. The observed non-linear scaling relationship between average global CMRO2 and TBV implies that, on average, cerebral oxygen utilization increases by 36% across global increasing TBV, consistent with physical constraints. Furthermore, average cerebral metabolic efficiency of 32% is estimated, and decreases with increased TBV in a quadratic fashion. Functional implications of these relationships are discussed.

Perfect matchings and permanents of bounded treewidth matrices can represent several notions of expressivity. In this paper, we investigate the expressive power of the former, first showing that it is $\mathrm{AC}^0$-reducible to the latter (and in fact, even computing matchings is $\mathrm{AC}^0$-reducible to computing permanents of matrices of bounded treewidth). This reduction gives us a sense of what level of expressivity is achievable via matchings. We then show that while matchings are expressively powerful, they fail to capture two other natural notions of expressivity, matching topological sort and generalized assignment. In particular, we exhibit matrices of treewidth two that have a matching but do not have any generalized assignments, and vice-versa. We then characterize the level of expressiveness achieved by matchings and permanents of matrices of bounded treewidth. We show that they are either equivalent to the class of planar graphs, or are captures by the existence of certain topological subgraphs of planar graphs. We also give a characterization of when a graph has a matching, or a corresponding perfect matching matrix of bounded treewidth, that captures matching topological sort. We conclude by discussing some open questions, including whether planar matchings are equivalent to planar perfect matchings, and whether planar matchings of bounded treewidth can capture generalized assignment."

We report the results of the second half of our LuckyCam survey for very low mass binaries (VLMBs), performed with the 5.1m Magellan/Baade Telescope at Las Campanas Observatory, Chile. In the new part of the survey, we observed 22.7 sq. degrees of the southern constellation of Scorpius with $i'$ and $z'$ filters, with total exposure times of 10.4 and 5.6 hours, respectively. We used a trapezoidal selection function to detect L/T transition brown dwarfs, where L and T are the low and high-temperature components of the L/T transition. The equatorial coordinates, $J$, $H$, and $K_s$ 2MASS photometry, and optical and near-infrared colors of the 13 confirmed binaries are presented. Spectroscopy is underway to confirm the physical nature of the candidates and to measure radial velocities. We also discuss the effects of large Poisson errors and crowding on our results, and we show that the observed spatial density of VLMBs is consistent with previous catalogs.

Exoplanet transits provide information about a planet's radius, and thus bulk composition, by determining the star's dimming in accordance with the planet's size. Transit spectroscopy can additionally determine the planet's atmospheric composition by studying the star's spectrum during the planet's transit. Although current missions, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, will enable atmospheric characterization of many transiting exoplanets, understanding how signals from different layers in the atmosphere are separated will require a more fundamental understanding of the planet's atmosphere itself, as well as a method for determining the planet's rotation rate from its transit light curve. We demonstrate a model for transit light curve synthesis that simultaneously determines the planet's rotational period, radius, and other system parameters, as well as the relative height of signals from different atmospheric layers. We apply this model to observations of the transiting exoplanets 55 Cancri e and c, for which we independently measure the respective heights of the Roche lobe and hydrogen envelopes, as well as the rotation period. Our results demonstrate the ability to characterize atmospheric dynamics and composition with transit spectroscopy, and to provide precise constraints on planetary physical and atmospheric properties for future transmission spectroscopy measurements.' Link to the paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.08479

This paper analyzes various statistical properties of the final iterate of the gradient algorithm for minimizing a real-valued function. The first part of the analysis is a characterization of the global minima as the only critical points with smallest descend value. From this we are able to obtain sharp bounds on the second and third moments of the final iterate. These moments tend to the corresponding population values as the number of iterations tend to infinity. In the second part of the analysis, we study the evolution of the gradient method, obtaining sharp bounds on the fourth and fifth moments of the iterates. Again, the moments of the final iterate converge to the corresponding population values. We also establish convergence rate results for the iterates and the final iterate. All results are established under only very weak technical assumptions on the real-valued function and on the stepsize. Numerical simulations corroborate the analysis and provide additional empirical evidence in support of the conjectured convergence rates.

The genus-one Gromov-Witten invariants of a Calabi-Yau hypersurface are expressed in terms of lower-genus invariants, theeta invariants, and some intersection numbers of the virtual fundamental class withclasses of codimension two. The result applies to complete intersections of codimension greater than three as well as hypersurfaces. The proof uses localization, genus-zero and oneader to reduce the problem to the case of a linear system with a base locus of lower dimension, and an Euler characteristic argument. This can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10486 This study begins by considering the Gromov-Witten invariants of Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces. The topological string, defined by Dijkgraaf, Verlinde, and Verlinde, offers a prediction for the genus-one Gromov-Witten invariants of a Calabi-Yau hypersurface in terms of lower-genus invariants, eta invariants, and some intersection numbers of the virtual fundamental class with classes of codimension two. We express the result for complete intersections of codimension greater than three as well as hypersurfaces. The proof uses localization, genus-zero and one-dimensional ancestor results to reduce the problem to the case of a linear system with a base locus of lower dimension, and an Euler characteristic argument.

Galois theory, which was originally introduced as an arithmetic theory of correspondences, has recently attracted considerable attention in dynamical system theory. In this work, we generalize Galois theory to the setting of iterated endomorphisms. We introduce the notion of a Galois correspondence for iterated endomorphisms and prove its many properties analogous to those of the classical Galois theory. As a concrete example, we apply our general results to iterated rational maps and study the field of exponents of these maps. We also consider topological entropy in this context and relate it to the topological Bogoliubov theorem. For more than a century, the field of exponents of a rational map has been a challenging open problem, with recent progress mostly coming from ergodic theory. We prove this field of exponents is algebraically closed. As an application, we solve a problem of Osel Economic about the closure of the field of complex analytic functions under taking roots. We also apply our results to iterated polynomials and prove some Silver-Mapp conjecture. Our results can be applied to solving open problems in number theory, such as Bhargava’s twelve number problem and its generalizations, and the explicit Brauer-Siegel theorem. More broadly, our results can be used in investigating the structure of endomorphism rings and the local-global principle for endomorphism rings and fields of functions of non-Archimedean places. Our results provide powerful techniques for understanding dynamics of rational and real maps. I believe that our work will have great impact and influence in complex dynamics, arithmetic dynamics, and dynamics of rational and real functions. Our techniques combine tools from algebra, combinatorics, geometry, and dynamical systems. This work is joint work with Tong Zhang and Shengwen Wang.

H-deficient post-AGB tracks are a recently discovered population of pulsating stars, located on the cooler side of the AGBhypological phase. It was predicted that these stars pulsate in the same modes as solar-type asteroseismology but with much higher pulsation amplitudes due to the strong H-deficient composition profile at the surface. In this work, we study the variability of two exemplary H-deficient post-AGBtracks, i.e. PG1716+426 and SDSSJ105751.77+010112.9. Despite high-quality optical photometry, only in the case of PG1716+426 did we manage to detect periodic variations. Furthermore, the detected period is relatively long (~1 h) and does not correspond with any of the predicted unstable modes. We conclude that the detected variability may be due to stochastic oscillations rather than pulsations. We also investigate the SDSSJ105751.77+010112.9 and find only very small variations, far below the detection threshold. We conclude that this object may not be a pulsator but rather an anomalous Cepheid. The main finding of this paper is the non-detection of pulsations from H-deficient post-AGBtracks, which we interpret as the low-massive evolutionary state of these stars resulting in low amplitude oscillations. We discuss the implications of this result for asteroseismology studies of similar objects, i.e. Hot DQ stars and other post-AGB stars with thin hydrogen-deficient envelopes.'

Stars with initial masses greater than about 2.5-3 M⊙ evolve into carbon-rich asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars when they have lost most of their initial hydrogen and helium envelopes. We find that the electron-capture s-process occurs in the oxygen-rich AGB stars with initial masses less than about 4 M⊙. As a result, these stars eject large amounts of oxygen-rich material into the interstellar medium (ISM). The oxygen-rich AGB stars with initial masses in the range of 4-7 M⊙ develop degenerate carbon-oxygen cores during the asymptotic giant branch phase and are susceptible to undergoing electron-capture supernovae if their cores exceed the Chandrasekhar mass limit. Consequently, they have little time to expel the material before collapsing to neutron stars. In this study, we simulate the evolution of oxygen-rich AGB stars with initial masses of 2.5, 3, 4, 5, and 6 M⊙. We find that the amount of oxygen-rich material expelled from the stars increases with decreasing initial mass, and the stars with an initial mass of 2.5 M⊙ do not develop degenerate carbon-oxygen cores. Massive stars lose most of their mass during their lifetimes as a result of both stellar evolution and strong stellar winds. It is well-known that asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars are excellent producers of carbon dust in the Universe. Thus, one might expect that the more massive an AGB star is, the more likely it is to develop a carbon dust shell. It has been shown that the mass-loss rate correlates with the luminosity and the temperature of the AGB star [i.e., the greater the mass-loss rate, the lower the luminosity and the effective temperature; e.g., @vanB88; @vdH01; @woo13]. These correlations are well-approximated by a linear relation: where ΔMLR is the change in the AGB mass-loss rate and L, T are the luminosity and effective temperature of the AGB star, respectively. The value of the constant a depends on whether one is interested in the total AGB mass-loss or just the increase in the mass-loss rate. However, we would like to point out that both L and T are not constant throughout the evolution of an AGB star. In particular, these two parameters show a noticeable decrease toward the end of the AGB evolution. Thus, it is not surprising that there is a linear correlation between ΔMLR and L–T. Some researchers have investigated this correlation in theoretical studies [e.g., @woo13; @mar13; @pan13]. These studies show that there is a weak correlation between ΔMLR and the pulsation period of the AGB star. In a linear fit, the correlation coefficient is approximately 0.4 for Δ

We present high frequency (43.7-111.4 GHz) linear and circular polarization observations of fifteen AGNs from the BL Lac object frame, consisting of six quasars, six BL Lacertae objects, and three galaxies. Five of the sources were observed to have correlated linear and circular polarization on time scales ranging from tens of minutes to over an hour, while no linear polarization was detected on time scales longer than a few minutes. The observed polarization variability in these sources is best explained by jet rotation occurring in a helical magnetic field, rather than by spatial variation of intrinsic polarization as in orientable AGN models, or fluctuation in magnetic field strength as in stochastic magnetic field models. These results are consistent with a magnetic field structure that is dominated by a helical component. We also present nine-epoch imaging polarimetry at 22 GHz of the core of 3C84. During each epoch, the 22 GHz core became fainter, but the linear polarization remained constant at approximately 3% linearly and 1.5% circularly. This indicates that the polarization position angle remained constant within the measurement uncertainties.

The problem of a classical point particle moving in a potential under the influence of a force whose magnitude is a function of the particle's position has a long history in classical mechanics. The trajectories of such a particle are the solutions to a second order differential equation, the so-called Hamiltonian equation. Since the equation is second order, the initial conditions determine a unique trajectory through phase space, allowing the solution to be written as a function of time only. However, it is well-known that when the potential is rapidly oscillatory (meaning that the velocity of the fastest changing feature of the potential is much smaller than the speed of light), the evolution of a wavepacket is well-approximated by the evolution of its mean position and momentum, the so-called slowly varying envelope approximation (SVEA). In this case the Hamiltonian equation reduces to a first order differential equation whose solution is only dependent on the initial conditions. Although this fails to capture the full evolution of a wavepacket, it is widely used in theoretical treatments of such systems. The question then arises: how sensitive is the evolution of a wavepacket to the initial phase of the potential? In this work it is shown that for an initial Gaussian wavepacket the mean position of the packet will correctly track the time-varying minimum of the potential for a range of initial phases. However, when the initial phase corresponds to the position of one of the potential’s local maxima, the mean position diverges from the time-varying maximum. As the initial phase is moved away from this value, the mean position converges to the time-varying maximum. Ultimately, for an initial phase corresponding to a local minimum, the mean position and time-varying minimum become equal. It is also shown that this behaviour is reproduced by a simple classical equivalent, the wave equation.

In this paper we present a new approximation algorithm for the traveling salesman problem on graphs with edge weights, which we call the Hamiltonian graphs approach. Given a graph, the idea is to first compute its Hamiltonian graph, i.e., a graph in which each vertex represents a distinct cluster and there is an edge between two vertices if and only if the corresponding clusters can be joined by a series of edges with minimal weight. Our approximation algorithm then constructs a TSP tour on the Hamiltonian graph by letting the cluster representatives travel along the edges of the graph in a round-robin fashion, visiting each cluster exactly once and minimizing the total weight of the edges used. To ensure a good approximation ratio, we make sure that the cluster representatives cover all vertices of the input graph, which allows to bound the weight of the TSP tour locally. We analyze the approximation guarantee of our approach and give several generalizations and applications, including a fixed-parameter approximation algorithm for thetraveling salesman problem.

A coronagraphic observation of the T Tauri binary system UY Aur is presented. UY Aur A is a Herbig Ae/Be star, and UY Aur B is a young stellar object (YSO) in the system with an orbital period of 3.9 days. The YSO UY Aur B is likely causing disc perturbations that affect the wind dynamics from the Herbig Ae/Be star. UY Aur B is occulted by a coronagraph, and many previously unseen features are visible in the dataset. A dark point within the UY Aur B atmosphere is detected for the first time at the anticipated position of UY Aur B. Additionally, two bright spot-like features are observed within the UY Aur A disc, one on each side of the companion. These features are indicative of heating from the UY Aur B magnetic field, either from near-L2 orbit crossing by UY Aur B, or from the tidal effects of the companion. Future analysis of the dark point and the bright spot features will help to better understand the tidal effects and wind-disc interactions in this binary system.

In this work, we propose a solution of the following fractional reaction-diffusion equation involving the Riesz potential: \begin{equation} D_{t}^{\beta }u\left( x,t\right) +u\left( x,t\right) \ast u\left( x,t\right) =0, \qquad 0<\beta<1, \quad x\in \Omega, \quad t\in (0,T], \end{equation} where $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ is a bounded domain with a smooth boundary $\partial \Omega $, $T>0$ is a given real number, $*$ denotes the Riesz potential, $D_t^{\beta }$ is the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative of order $\beta \in (0,1)$, and $\dot{H}^{s,\beta}(\Omega)$ is the fractional Sobolev space with norm $\| \cdot \|_{\dot{H}^{s,\beta}(\Omega)} $ and the inner product $(\cdot, \cdot)_{\dot{H}^{s,\beta}(\Omega)} $. We express the solution in terms of the H-function, which represents an entire function of both the frequency $\omega $ and the time $t$.

Masses of the quarks play an important role in the theory of the fundamental interactions, Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). They form matrixes that describe their interactions. Measurable properties of this matrices can put bounds on the possible values of the matrix elements. The strongest bounds on these matrix elements are obtained by comparing the calculated with the measured values of the masses and properties of the particles described by these matrixes. The authors present a calculation of the bounds on the matrix elements of the up and down quark mass matrices, resulting from present knowledge of the angles of the Unitary mixing matrix and the masses of the up, charm and down quarks. Masses of the quarks form matrixes that describe their interactions. Measurable properties of these matrixes can put bounds on the possible values of the matrix elements. The strongest bounds on these matrix elements are obtained by comparing the calculated with the measured values of the masses and properties of the particles described by these matrixes. The presented calculation shows that the matrix elements of the up and down quark mass matrices can have their values with 10% accuracy estimated only by the measured masses of the up, charm and down quarks. This calculation takes into account the present knowledge of the angles of the Unitary mixing matrix.

gamma-ray sources are extremely high-energy cosmic gamma-ray emitters and they are of great interest to astrophysicists. One such source, TeV J2032+4130, was discovered by the ground-based Atmospheric Gamma-ray Emitter (AGER) telescope system and the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA) during observations by the H.E.S.S., Fermi, and AGILE gamma-ray observatories. Since its discovery, there has been some disagreement over the source identity. Recent observations by the X-Ray Telescope (XRT) onboard the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory suggest that this source is probably an active galaxy located at a distance of 1.3 billion light years from Earth, making it one of the farthest objects ever observed in the universe. The surprisingly large distance and high luminosity, however, suggest that this source may be a new discovery of enormous scientific importance.

Flory's model of polymerisation in dilute solution assumed that the radius of the new monomer shell does not depend on the number of subunits in the cluster. This is at odds with the original model of Smoluchowski and Marcus-Lushnikov, which included this effect. In this work we derive the Smoluchowski and Marcus-Lushnikov models from the Flory model with both excluded-volume and density-dependent interactions. Both exact treatment and mean-field theory are considered. In the mean-field theory, the correlation functions are expressed through the pair correlation function, which is obtained from simulations. It is found that the Flory model with excluded-volume interactions, but without the density-dependent term, can be used to describe the Smoluchowski model, whereas the Flory model with both excluded-volume and density-dependent interactions can be used to describe the Marcus-Lushnikov model. As a check, we simulate the Marcus-Lushnikov model and find good agreement with the exact solution.

In this paper, we describe the Wang-Landau molecular dynamics (WL-MD) technique to search for low-energy conformational space of proteins. WL-MD has been shown to be very efficient in searching the high-dimensional energy landscape of flexible molecular systems. The method is used to search for low-energy configurations of a small protein, Azurin, by assuming different theoretical probability distributions on the configuration space. For the first time, a high-dimensional global energy surface is sampled for this protein, and several metastable states that had not been observed in previous molecular dynamics simulations are identified. The transitions between these metastable states have large energy barriers and could be very relevant to protein folding and functional dynamics. Wang-Landau molecular dynamics technique is very efficient in searching the conformational space of flexible molecular systems such as proteins. Using this method, we identified several metastable states of Azurin protein that had not been observed before. Such states usually exhibit large energy barriers that might be relevant to protein folding and functional dynamics.

Turbulent flows are often characterized by the assumption of locality, where the kinematics and dynamics are largely separable in space and time. In this paradigm, fluid motion is decomposed into characteristic modes, or eddies, often arranged into quasi-regular structures such as shears, jets, and fronts. As an example, in compressible turbulence, these eddies often exhibit a hierarchical arrangement with large-scale structures such as filaments and clusters forming out of the eddies at smaller scales. This process is often characterized by a power-law scaling, where the size, velocity, density, and temperature of eddies at each scale are related to those at the next smaller scale through a characteristic scale factor. This phenomenon, known as multiscaling, implies a self-similar structure and has been observed to varying degrees of rigor in a range of physical systems. In this work, we present direct numerical simulations of compressible turbulence at high resolution, focusing specifically on the nature of multiscaling in the scaling regime. We find that multiscaling is not as evident as in comparable experimental and Eulerian grid-based simulations, but is clearly present for a range of flow conditions. We posit that this is due to the evolution of multiscaling over time in compressible turbulence, where scaling relationships gradually break down as modes gradually separate through an increasing characteristic time scale. This process, known as intermittency, implies a negative scaling exponent and correspondingly flatter multiscaling exponents. We validate this hypothesis through the construction of a multifractal model, and demonstrate that the predicted intermittency leads to a breakdown of multiscaling as the flow transitions from steady to unsteady. This provides a useful framework for interpreting observations of multiscaling in turbulent flows, and has important implications for the dynamics of clusters in highly compressible turbulent flows such as those arising in the atmosphere and fusion plasma simulations.

Single-walled carbon nanotube forests with thicknesses up to a millimeter were grown by chemical vapor deposition using ferrocene and dioctylsulfoxide as catalyst and carbon source, respectively. The forests exhibit a unique growth window that requires a high-temperature anneal prior to growth that results in oriented growth along the CVD-fed direction. Simulations indicate that the growth window corresponds to nanotube forests containing only semiconducting nanotubes and the oriented growth is semiconducting nanotube segment alignment along the CVD-fed direction. The observed millimeter-thick forests are of interest for several applications that require large-volume, high-concentration nanotube dispersions. We are currently exploring several methods for separating the forests from their growth substrate, including supercritical fluid separation, wet chemical treatment of the forests for dissolving the growth substrate, and direct solvent exfoliating the forests for regrowing on other growth substrates.

Nova Geminorum 1912 was the first observed gravitational lens, making it the first known example of strong gravitational lensing. Many scientists and science-fiction writers have postulated that strong gravitational lenses could be used for technological interference and military purposes, leading to the development of observational programs to find strong gravitational lenses and study their implications. In this paper, we examine the scientific and cultural significance of Nova Geminorum 1912 and the development of the field of gravitational lensing. We begin by providing a brief overview of gravitational lensing, including a discussion of critical curves and caustics. Next, we describe how strong gravitational lensing was observed for the first time, and how the observation of Nova Geminorum 1912 led to the discovery and study of gravitational lensing as a distinct phenomenon. We also examine how the observational discovery of Nova Geminorum 1912 led to the development of super-gravity and the wider science fiction genre's interest in strong gravitational lensing as a weapon. Finally, we discuss how subsequent observations of gravitational lenses have led to new understandings of the phenomenon, including the first observations of gravitational waves and the determination of Hubble's constant.

The geometry and dynamics of microtubules is crucial for the function of the eukaryotic cell. Microtubules are dynamic intracellular fibers composed of tubulin monomers that are assembled into a right-handed helix. Several cancer cells have been shown to have shorter and more malformed microtubules when compared to normal cells. This deformation has been suggested to be a factor in the development of various cancers. In order to maintain cellular structure and function, the cell has many factors that keep microtubule dynamics in check. One way this is accomplished is through the introduction of motor proteins into the cellular medium that serve as a factor in microtubule dynamics. Through the use of magnetic tweezers, we have shown that the force generated by the molecular motor kinesin and the phenomena of rescue continue to act on microtubules even when the polymerization force has been suppressed. We also propose a simple Brownian ratchet model to explain the measured results. This work shows that the interaction between motor proteins and microtubules requires further exploration to fully understand the dynamics of the microtubule lattice.

Achieving network scale immunity while facilitating adaptivity and efficiency is a major challenge for next generation wireless networks. In this regard, the use of multiple input, multiple output (MIMO) techniques coupled with network coding has the potential to revolutionize the wireless access infrastructure by enabling high capacity, high adaptivity, and low energy consumption. Unfortunately, MIMO-based wireless networks are vulnerable to large scale (i.e., the number of nodes in the network)missort errors, which stem from the high degree of feedback required to generate optimized multicast beams over large-scale networks. In this regard, this paper develops a two-layer cross-layer approach to optimizing MIMO-based wireless networks over large-scale multi-hop topologies. In the first layer, we develop a transmit beamformer that adaptively modulates network coding beams over a flat fading channel. In the second layer, we develop an affine-optimal multicast beamformer that adaptively constructs multicast beams over the large-scale, complex, and possibly non-convex interference map. We develop a low-complexity distributed algorithm that efficiently implements the two-layer cross-layer approach. We show that our two-layer approach can significantly reduce multicast missort error probability (MSEP) compared to the conventional single-layer beamformer approach. We also show that the two-layer approach yields improved system throughput and dynamic spectrum usage (DUS) compared to the single-layer approach. Our results suggest that the two-layer approach can facilitate significant gains in network capacity, adaptivity, and efficiency over existing approaches.

This paper presents a procedure to quantify the cosmological parameters allowed by current observations. Using the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT), South Pole Telescope (SPT), and the low-resolution detector on the Planck satellite, we find that the standard $\Lambda$CDM model is in tension at the 2.3 sigma level with the local geometry of the universe, as parametrized by the comoving sound horizon at radiation drag epoch, $r_s$. Adding minimal modifications to $\Lambda$CDM, e.g. curvature or dark radiation, improves the agreement with data at the 2.1 sigma and 1.4 sigma levels, respectively. In this model, the sound horizon is given by $r_s=154.1\pm5.2$ Mpc. Fitting for the neutrino mass using the Ly-$\alpha$ data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) gives $\sum m_\nu<0.23$ eV at the 1.8 sigma level, or $\sum m_\nu<0.36$ eV at the 2.3 sigma level if the tension with the Planck baseline is explained by a neutrino mass model with $\Lambda$CDM extensions.

In the galactic center, Sgr A* is the supermassive black hole (SMBH) located in the center of the galaxy cluster comprising of several thousands of galaxies. Stars with high velocity dispersion (up to few hundreds of km/s) escape the galactic center due to unknown mechanism and travel along the hyperbolic orbit towards the outer region. We discovered that some of these hypervelocities stars has path perpendicular to the Sgr A*’s jet. This discovery indicates that there may be an high-density and relatively young population of stars in the region beyond 0.01 pc from Sgr A* with age less than 1 Myr. This young population may have been formed through tidal disruption of stars by Sgr A* or through collisions between stars in the SMBH’s cluster. Our result indicates that the stellar environment around Sgr A* is less relaxed than we previously thought and it can provide an effective place for the star capture and collision for creating black holes binaries. The authors are Taotao Fang, Xue-Ning Bao, and Lin Cheng, from IHEP, CAS. The article is “Hypervelocity Stars and the Environment of Sgr A*” (arXiv.org 1811.09776v1)

Genetic networks describe the relationship between genes and the phenotypic effects of perturbations on the gene expression. Inferring these networks from expression data is challenging due to the high dimensionality, statistical noise, and regulatory complexity. We use a novel algorithm to identify network modules and their regulators from expression data. The algorithm assumes that genes in the same module are co-regulated and that the regulators of this module affect the expression of this module primarily through a small number of key regulators. Using this assumption, the algorithm first estimates the regulators of each network module, and then infers the network structure by optimizing a balance between the number of links in the network and the sum of squared errors. This algorithm not only finds meaningful sub-networks, but also discovers key regulators that explain the expression patterns in the modules. We applied this algorithm to a simulated data set and three expression datasets of Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis and identified network modules that represent known biological pathways as well as novel pathways. We also validated the predicted links by comparing with curated networks. We provide the code to implement the method. Here is an example of an abstract of a paper published by this authors: Inferring dynamic genetic networks with low order independencies Recently, there has been increased interest in understanding the gene regulatory networks that control cellular behaviors such as differentiation and development. Inferring these networks from gene expression data is challenging due to the high dimensionality, statistical noise, and combinatorial complexity. Here we use a novel algorithm to identify network modules and their regulators from expression data. The algorithm assumes that genes in the same module are co-regulated and that the regulators of this module affect the expression of this module primarily through a small number of key regulators. Using this assumption, the algorithm first estimates the regulators of each network module, and then infers the network structure by optimizing a balance between the number of links in the network and the sum of squared errors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the method on simulated data as well as expression data from Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis. We also validate the predicted links by comparing with curated networks.

The Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) and the Multi-band Imaging Photometer (MIPS) were mounted on the Spitzer Space Telescope to study the physical properties of galaxies by observing their spectral energy distributions (SEDs). The data obtained by these telescopes can be used to study the Star Formation Rate (SFR) of galaxies by using different algorithms to measure their Mid-Infrared (MIR) SEDs. In this work, the calibration of these algorithms for the MIR SFR indicators is presented. The data used in this study was obtained from the Hi-GAL, GAMA and PACSplus surveys. A Large Sample Study (LSS) of these data was performed to find the SFR Indicators with the highest reliability. The data was analysed using three methods: 1) the neural network of the Random Forest algorithm, 2) the Bayesian Photometric Penalisation and 3) the Mean T Y Model. The results obtained show that the reliability of the measurements of the SFR Indicators using the MIPS 24 μm filter is better than that of the MIR SFR Indicators derived using the IRAC Channels 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the MIPS 24 μm filter. Furthermore, the best pair of indicators is IRAC 3 (8 μm) / MIPS 24 μm with a reliability of 0.84, followed by IRAC 4 (11 μm) / MIPS 24 μm with a reliability of 0.82. The reliability of the measurements of the SFR Indicators using the MIPS 70 μm filter is lower than that of the SFR Indicators derived using the IRAC Channels 1, 2, 3 and 4 and the MIPS 24 μm filter. Finally, a comparison between the SFR Indicators derived using these data and the SFR calculated using data from the ultraviolet (FUV) and far-infrared (60 μm) is performed. The SFR derived using the MIR SFR Indicators is consistent with the SFR calculated using the FUV and 60 μm data.

Fast particles flowing into a medium may interact with it partially or fully via various processes, such as synchrotron or adiabatic expansion losses, reflection or bremsstrahlung, which lead to a decrease in their energy. When the particle velocity difference across a shock front is large enough, such processes become inefficient and the particle energy is preserved. Such relativistic streaming is a natural outcome of diffusive processes. Here, we show that in the presence of a magnetic field, cosmic rays can strongly interact with the medium surrounding SNRs via the process of magnetic reconnection – acting as a source of magnetic turbulence – at least within the shock radius. We carry out 1D PIC simulations of a moving cosmic ray permeating a magnetized plasma and show that magnetic reconnection occurs and efficiently injects plasma waves into the upstream region of the shock, resulting in the turbulence formation. We also show that the efficiency of cosmic-ray acceleration increases as the level of turbulence increases, which further supports the idea of magnetic reconnection as a mean for efficient cosmic-ray production in SNRs.

The Millennium simulation is a large cosmological box which was carried out by the Virgo Consortium between 2000 and 2005. One of its outputs is a catalog of galaxy clusters, which was made public in 2008. I identify 21 red sequences in this catalog, using a technique that matches cluster galaxies’ colours to the location of the most massive member of the cluster. The scatter in the red sequence is 0.17 magnitudes, much lower than previously found, and is only statistically significant in the most dense regions of the clusters. I also show that the observed scatter is consistent with the observed colour-magnitude relation of the member galaxies, suggesting that galaxy evolution may be responsible. The colour-magnitude relation has also been seen in other observational samples, so this may be a more generally applicable explanation for the scatter on the red sequence. Complex networks have been identified in a variety of fields, ranging from natural systems to man-made engineering, to model these networks. In the last decade, significant effort has been put into understanding the topological properties of these networks, especially those scale-free networks have been identified to be highly popular. A plethora of real-world complex networks exhibit this property, such as the Internet, the cellular network, the metabolic network, and many social and biological networks. Scale-free network topologies have been interpreted as an advantage in many fields, from spreading of pathogens to information dissemination. However, it has been recently shown that the small-world property of scale-free networks is at odds with the definition of network architectures that exhibit efficient spreading of information. The small-world property allows the fast spreading of information, but at the same time enhances the vulnerability of the networks to failures and attacks. In this work, we show that the previously identified scale-free properties are in fact the disadvantages of these networks, and that the architectural principles of small-world and scale-free networks might be contradictory.

The theory of protein folding was first suggested in 1946 by Bijvoet and his colleagues. It took more than six decades for the field to catch up with Bijvoet’s proposal, with the development of computational power and simulation methods. Protein folding is the process by which a linear chain of amino acids (the protein’s ‘building blocks’) folds into a three-dimensional structure that exposes, protects or carries out biological functions. Many proteins assume stable, rigid three-dimensional structures, but some, known as ‘flexible’ or ‘conformational’ proteins, remain malleable. The recent advances in experimental and computational structural biology have given a fresh impetus to the field of protein folding. The new understanding of the experimental techniques and molecular dynamics simulations have allowed scientists to track the process of protein folding in unprecedented detail. In addition, this new knowledge has inspired the development of new methods to predict protein folding. The field of protein folding has traditionally been dominated by researchers using experimental and computational techniques that were far too expensive to be of any real use to protein scientists. However, in the past two decades, protein folding has entered the realm of protein science, as scientists have built tools that can predict the three-dimensional structures of proteins from their sequences, using computation. Today, several methods that allow a protein sequence to be used to determine its three-dimensional structure exist. The oldest and most common is the ‘protein folding funnel’ approach, which relies on the fact that amino acid sequences typically encode for three-dimensional structures with similar neighborhoods of low energy. The difficulty in predicting the three-dimensional structure from the amino acid sequence has slowed the adoption of such methods by protein scientists. However, recent advances in the field have shifted the balance in favor of the methods that can predict protein three-dimensional structures from sequence information. In this article, I provide an introduction to protein folding for the general reader, and review the key recent discoveries in the field.

In this paper, we construct some new supersymmetric vector multiplets in non-adjoint representations of SO(N). We obtain these vector multiplets by dimensional reduction from eleven-dimensional supergravity. We construct these multiplets in two steps. At first, we construct some special hyper-special symplectic representations of SO(12) and use these special representations to build some vector multiplets in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime. In second step, using these four-dimensional vector multiplets, we construct some vector multiplets in eleven-dimensional supergravity. We consider a special case and obtain some special non-adjoint representations of SO(6). We demonstrate that the new vector multiplets we constructed admit an unbroken eight-dimensional local N=1 supersymmetry, where the R-symmetry is gauged. This research was partially supported by grant 1142852 of the Fonds de la Recherche Scientifique -FNRS, and by the Interuniversity Attraction Poles Program, initiated by the Belgian Science Policy Office. As a novelty, we would like to construct some new supersymmetric vector multiplets in non-adjoint representations of SO(N). We obtain these vector multiplets by dimensional reduction from eleven-dimensional supergravity. We consider a special case and obtain some special non-adjoint representations of SO(6). We demonstrate that the new vector multiplets we constructed admit an unbroken eight-dimensional local N=1 supersymmetry, where the R-symmetry is gauged.

Law of gravity can be viewed as a smooth function f: A vector of physical parameters x → R, where A is the dimensionality of x. Existence of continuous derivative of f on an open set U ⊂ R implies that f can be represented as a smooth function of x. This approach is applied to modeling physical laws. As an example, exponential decay can be described by y = Ae −bx. Application to more complicated processes (e.g. first-order linear ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients and given initial conditions) is also presented. Complex data from real world often include more than one physical law. Therefore, a nonparametric method for simultaneous identification of several laws from data is developed. The method is based on Bayesian statistical inference. The prior distribution of the model is defined by the maximum entropy. The posterior distribution is approximated using Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. Example using real data of carbon emission is presented.

The 74MHz system ( 74MHz ) was deployed on the very large array ( VLA ) in 2012, and has since detected hundreds of radio sources including pulsars, planets, and synchrotron radiation from our own galaxy. The 74MHz system is comprised of 24 independent 225kHz wide channels, and covers a total frequency range of 11.2-74.1MHz. The entire band is divided into two 75.6MHz-wide polarizations which are Nyquist-sampled at 1.2875MHz sample rate. Each baseband channel is 25.6kHz wide, providing a velocity resolution of 22.1km/s and a temperature sensitivity of -82.6dBm in a single beam. The 74MHz system has been used to measure redshifts in bright galaxies up to redshift 7.5, investigate the Epoch of Reionization, and conduct experiments on gravitational waves. The data from the 74MHz system are made available to the public through the F.C. Williams antenna record.

We study the relaxation dynamics of an Edwards-Wilkinson elastic line in a random medium, i.e. a one-dimensional string, submitted to a constant force. The configuration of the string evolves in time according to a continuity equation with no noise term and with a nonlinear drift. For initial conditions with zero average velocity, the system relaxes to a steady state characterized by a non-zero average velocity. The long time behavior of the system is given by a Gaussian distribution of the position with non-zero average velocity. The associated equation of evolution, obtained by means of the Kramers-Moyal expansion, is the damped linear Schrödinger equation with a random potential. We evaluate the ground state of the potential and compute the anomalous exponent governing the long time decay of the average velocity. This work was done in collaboration with Nicolas Rougerie, Alain Guitter and Jean-Michel Raimbault Reference: Jean-Michel Raimbault, Nicolas Rougerie, Alain Guitter, and Denis Bartolo, "Out-of-equilibrium relaxation of the Edwards-Wilkinson elastic line", arxiv.org preprint arXiv:1711.02216 (2017).

The Galactic Center (GC), the region near the supermassive black hole (Sgr A*) at the center of the Galaxy, is of great importance to studies of black holes, galaxies, and fundamental physics. The Galactic Center Lobe (GCL), a massive cloud of cold gas and dust, is one of the most intriguing structures in the central parsec of the Galaxy. Using data from the Submillimeter Common User Bolometer Array (SCUBA) camera at the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT), and the 22 cm line of Molecular Hydrogen emission from the Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA), we have constructed the first map of the GCL at sub-millimeter wavelengths. We describe our observations and data reduction techniques, and discuss results for the mass, temperature, velocity, and volume of the GCL. We find that the GCL has a lower mass than previously estimated, with an inferred upper limit of 1,150,000 M_{\odot} within a radius of 0.2 parsec from Sgr A*. The temperature of the GCL is low, estimated at 6.5 K, and has a large range, from 14.7 K within 0.14 parsec to 1.1 K within 0.6 parsec. The total molecular hydrogen mass of the GCL is at least 4.5 x 10^5 M_{\odot}, and the GCL contains at least 1,350,000 M_{\odot} of molecular hydrogen. While the GCL may have initially been inspired by an impulsive event, this molecular hydrogen is relatively cool and would have taken longer to form via gas dynamics. We also rule out the possibility that the GCL was produced by the recent tidal disruption of a satellite, and present a new hypothesis for its origin. We suggest that the GCL may be a remnant from a recent major merger of two gas-rich galaxies, and that it is in the process of dispersing molecular hydrogen for the first time.

The standard model of particle physics is an extremely successful model that describes the fundamental interactions between nearly all known particles. One of its most intriguing features is that it is generally believed to be a Lorentz-invariant theory: its interactions adhere to the symmetry between observers, who may each accelerate in a unique reference frame. However, there are numerous scenarios for which the standard model is an effective theory—it must be completed by other physics at some higher scale. One such scenario is the spontaneous Lorentz violation (SLV) paradigm, which posits that the standard model is an effective field theory that lacks a consistent UV completion. In this case, Lorentz symmetry is broken at some high energy scale, giving rise to SLV at low energy. We show that this SLV can induce non-Abelian interactions, and we present the first example of this type of SLV: a fermion that transforms non-trivially under the non-Abelian group SU(2) ⋯ {\mathrm{Lorentz}} ⋯ SU(2). We show that this SLV leads to unique phenomenology—it predicts the existence of a massless SU(2) triplet gauge field, as well as a massive SU(2) doublet gauge field. We perform a phenomenological study of these unique massless and massive vectors, and we show that they can have important experimental consequences. For instance, they may couple to standard model fermions, allowing for tests of this SLV scenario at the LHC. Furthermore, the massive vectors can induce nuclearites, cosmic strings, and neutron stars with unusual spins.

The min-sum decoding algorithm is widely used for forward error correction (FEC) in various coding schemes, such as the low-density parity-check (LDPC) and the convolutional code. Its decoding performance is very sensitive to the initial message passed in the algorithm. A good initialization is essential for the algorithm to converge, but the initialization schemes proposed in the literature are usually suboptimal. In this paper, we investigate the degree optimization and stability condition for the min-sum decoding algorithm. We first consider the block error probability of the min-sum algorithm for the binary-input memoryless channels. The error probability is found to be a sum of probabilities of error events in a region around the first nontrivial fixed point. We then find the region of interest in the probability expression, and show that the error exponent is a convex function of the channel normalized degrees. We then propose a method to calculate the channel normalized degrees by solving a system of equations, which can be used as the stability condition for the min-sum algorithm. Finally, we show through both numerical examples and explicit formula for general LDPC codes that the stability condition is almost always satisfied, and is tight for some codes.

Synaptic transmission is subject to ongoing fluctuations, often termed "background noise". This background noise profoundly alters the way in which incoming synaptic currents are represented in the postsynaptic cell, which may, in turn, affect neural processing and behavior. We used whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings from cortical layer 2/3 neurons in a brain slice to characterize the noise present at individual excitatory and inhibitory synaptic contacts. We found that the power spectrum of synaptic current fluctuations was typically very low-pass, with a corner frequency that varied between synapses but was frequently in the tens of hertz. We next constructed a computational model of a layer 2/3 neuron with approximately 5,000 synapses and incorporated empirically-derived estimates of the amplitude and corner frequency of synaptic current fluctuations. We then used a numerical technique known as dynamic mesh simulation to predict the voltage response of the neuron to arbitrary synaptic current inputs. We found that synaptic current fluctuations tended to broaden and reduce the amplitude of postsynaptic voltage responses to step changes in current input, but also introduced significant fluctuations in the time it took the voltage response to reach its peak value. The former effect likely diminished the efficacy of synaptic transmission, whereas the latter may have broad physiological implications, potentially contributing to noise-induced decorrelation of postsynaptic spike times.

Symmetric Heavy-Light Ansatz (SHLA) is a relativistic effective field theory (EFT) for systems composed of both heavy and light particles. SHLA assumes that the light particle moves at speed $v$ and that the total momentum and angular momentum of the system are both proportional to the light's velocity, $p^i = - m \, v \, \Delta^{ij} \, p_j$ and $S^i = m \, v \, \Delta^{ij} \, S_j$, where $\Delta^{ij} = g^{ik} \, \eta_{kl} \, \Delta^{lj}$ is the convenient projectors, with $g$ being the spacetime metric, and $\eta$ the metric in the light-particle's local rest frame (LRF). The SHLA provides a simple and intuitive way of including the light particle's motion in the system's dynamics.

Epitaxial multiferroic thin films represent a class of unique material systems combining the properties of ferroic order (such as magnetic ordering) and ferroelectricity in the same phase. This property allows for the control of magnetic order by applying an electric field and the control of electric polarization by applying a magnetic field. Since multiferroic films typically have large spontaneous ferroelectric polarization ( P s) and small Born effective charges, these materials are expected to exhibit significant electro-mechanical coupling and high dielectric constants. Dielectric spectroscopy is therefore a powerful technique to study the ferroelectric properties of multiferroic materials. However, conventional dielectric spectroscopy techniques require a significant sample mass (>100 mg) and are time-consuming, making them impractical for screening large numbers of potential multiferroic materials. Here, we develop a piezoelectric sampling method to perform dielectric spectroscopy on a much smaller sample mass (as low as 3 mg), comparable to that of an individualdomain particle. As an example application, we measure the dielectric constant of epitaxial (RexWO~4~) thin films using this method and find that these materials can achieve high dielectric constants on par with organic ferroelectrics and inorganic perovskite oxides. Keywords: multiferroics, dielectric spectroscopy, RexWO4, sampling method

The multiferroic BiFeO$_3$ exhibits both ferromagnetic and ferroelectric orders, giving rise to intriguing electric and magnetic properties. Among the latter, electric field control of magnetization is highly attractive for potential applications. Early models of this magnetic ferroelectric considered the origin of magnetoelectric behavior in a model incorporating a direct coupling between electric and magnetic order parameters. We demonstrate, via a combination of neutron scattering, reciprocal space mapping, and first-principles calculations, that in BiFeO$_3$ this coupling is in fact considerably weaker than expected, with no evidence of long-range magnetic order in magnetic fields as high as 16 T. These findings indicate that the observed magnetoelectric response is more likely mediated by modifications of magnetic exchange interactions induced by electric polarization. BiFeO$_3$ exhibits both ferromagnetic and ferroelectric orders at low temperatures, giving rise to both electric and magnetic properties that are intriguing. Among the latter, electric field control of magnetization is highly attractive for potential applications. Early models of this magnetic ferroelectric considered the origin of magnetoelectric behavior in a model incorporating a direct coupling between electric and magnetic order parameters. We demonstrate, via a combination of neutron scattering, reciprocal space mapping, and first-principles calculations, that in BiFeO$_3$ this coupling is in fact considerably weaker than expected, with no evidence of long-range magnetic order in magnetic fields as high as 16 T. These findings indicate that the observed magnetoelectric response is more likely mediated by modifications of magnetic exchange interactions induced by electric polarization.

Triangular galaxy M33 (the Southern Pinwheel) is an intriguing object. It is an older system, with the oldest stars lying in a ring around the midplane, and no evidence of recent star formation. This is unusual in galaxies of its apparent mass, which are typically not quiescent systems but are usually star-forming, even at radii as distant from the center as the galaxy’s disk. An exception is M33 itself, but this is often ascribed to unusual environmental conditions, such as the presence of the Milky Way, or even just the Local Group, which seems to inhibit M33’s normal mode of star formation. However, there is another strange aspect of M33: its apparent companion M32. It too is an older system, with only a small fraction of the mass of its companion. It also shows no sign of star formation. While the pair may be physically interacting, their current separation is large enough to not cause significant gravitational tidal forces. A broader perspective reveals a similarly odd behavior in the distribution of dark matter within M31 and M33. At large radii, the dark matter distribution follows the light, supporting the notion that M31 and M33 are gravitationally bound. But at smaller radii, the distribution of dark matter peaks sharply towards the centers of both galaxies. This ‘central peak’ is a property of simulated dark matter halos that form through the aggregation of many smaller galaxies, and which is commonly interpreted as evidence for galaxy formation through merging. In this paradigm, M33 is the remnant of a smaller galaxy that has cannibalized M31’s dark matter halo. In the process, it acquired M31’s halo’s central peak, which may explain why M33 appears so quiescent despite its proximity to M31. This perspective provides an alternate view of M33 and its companions in the Local Group, and provides a framework for considering the properties of galaxies more generally. This article is based on a number of previous papers, the latest of which is J. I. Read et al. 2020, MNRAS, 491, 2933 It uses observational data from several telescopes and cosmological simulations to present a new perspective on how galaxies in the Local Group were formed. It is plausible that this alternate view of M33 and its companions is more generally applicable to galaxies throughout the observable Universe, and so this article presents a new paradigm for galaxy formation in action. While this article presents a novel interpretation of the data, it also draws upon results from a series of other works, and so shares the significant conceptual components of the conventional paradigm for galaxy formation through hierarchical aggregation. M33’s status as the remnant of a cannibalized satellite galaxy, and its apparent similarity to other galaxies of similar mass, are consistent with its position within the broader context of galaxy formation.
