In this paper we compute the algebraic cycles on the relative symmetric powers and on the relative Jacobian of a family of curves. We introduce a twisted relative filtration for the relative symmetric powers and a relative twisted p-curvature, and we prove a Lefschetz type theorem for this relative twisted p-curvature. With the help of this relative twisted p-curvature we can define a relative Beilinson regulator map. We apply our formula for the algebraic cycles on the relative symmetric powers to establish an edge intersection theorem for the relative Beilinson regulator map. With the help of the relative twisted p-curvature, we also establish a regulator formula for algebraic cycles on the relative Jacobian. As an application of our formula for the algebraic cycles on the relative symmetric powers, we prove the main theorem of this paper. This theorem states that the symmetric power of therelative Jacobian annihilated by the relative Beilinson regulator map is zero. Thus we can define a relative motivic cohomology group. We also define a relative generalized Kudla-Rapoport divisor on the relative symmetric powers. Using this divisor we can describe the image of the symmetrization map from the motive of the base to the motive of the family.

A new measurement of the cosmic flux decrement using the completed SDSS-III BOSS quasar survey is presented. The authors test different line-number evolution (LNE) models via the cosmic flux decrement by matching the measured value of \(\dot{\mathcal{F}}}\), where \(\dot{\mathcal{F}}}=\mathrm{d}\mathcal{F}/\mathrm{dt},\) to the theoretically calculated \(\dot{\mathcal{F}}}\). The most favoured model is one which fits the line-number evolution to the measured evolution of the comoving line-number density of hydrogen \(\Delta n_z\) in bins of width \(\Delta z=0.2\) based on the latest predictions of theahi model. The most disfavoured model is one in which the line-number evolution is assumed to fit \(\Delta n_z\), but the values of \(\Delta z\) are chosen to make the evolution fit to a Dirac Delta function, which is a continuous version of line-number evolution. The measured value of the cosmic flux decrement is \(\dot{\mathcal{F}}}=0.073\pm 0.01\) line brightaries/yr/Sr/Mpc^3/. The binned \(\Delta z=0.2\) LNE model fits the binned \(\Delta z=0.2\) \(\Delta n_z\) observations with a reduced chi-squared of \(\chi^{2}/\mathrm{d.o.f.}=14.2/21\), while the Dirac Delta function model is disfavoured with a reduced chi-squared of \(\chi^{2}/\mathrm{d.o.f.}=208.3/21\). The \(\Delta z=0.1\) and \(\Delta z=0.05\) models are also tested and found to fit the \(\Delta z=0.2\) \(\Delta n_z\) observations with a reduced chi-squared of \(\chi^{2}/\mathrm{d.o.f.}=28.6/21\) and \(\chi^{2}/\mathrm{d.o.f.}=160.6/21\), respectively. The \(\Delta z=0.01\) model is disfavoured with a reduced chi-squared of \(\chi^{2}/\mathrm{d.o.f.}=2541.3/21\). The paper discusses how the binsize \(\Delta z\), model parameters and underlying theories influence the results.

In this paper, we present a constructive method to solve an effective inverse spectral problem for rational Lax matrices. We first establish an algebro-geometric Birkhoff-like factorization for rational Lax matrices, from which the compatibility condition for the associated integrable hierarchy is obtained. By applying the geometric technique of variation of constant, we then reduce the inverse problem to the inversion of a simple Riemann-Hilbert problem. We also present an effective method to construct the unique solution to the inverse problem. As applications, we show that the Schur function, the transfer matrix and the Toda Lattice can be represented as rational Lax matrices. Finally, we apply the same method to a modified version of the Toda lattice and give a new Birkhoff-like factorization for the rational modified Lax matrices. As a consequence, the compatibility conditions and the Riemann-Hilbert problem for the associated integrable hierarchy are also obtained. As an interesting by-product, we also show that any polynomial in the spectral parameter is a particular solution to a modified KZ equation.

One of the proposed channel for producing a AM Canum Venaticorum star is the merger of a white dwarf (WD) with a companion. The resulting object is a carbon-oxygen (CO) WD with a mass of approximately 0.8-0.9 M⊙ and a radius of approximately 0.01-0.02 R⊙. A small fraction of these remnants are believed to evolve into objects with significant amounts of helium exhausted in a pulsational nuclear burn. I perform a large number of 2-D+ simulations with the PLUTO code of several such remnants. The simulations account for both the rapid evolution of the CO core after the merger, as well as the pulsations of the resulting object, which drive convective unstable regions in the envelope. I find that the resulting models have a core composition of approximately 75% carbon and 25% oxygen with a helium layer of approximately 1% and a massive hydrogen layer of approximately 2%. The CO core is almost completely fused and quickly expands to reach a mass of approximately 0.9-0.95 M⊙, depending on the assumed initial hydrogen layer. The evolution of these remnants is considerably more complex than previously assumed. I find that some remnants evolve into much more massive stars with carbon ignited at the core. These models produce ample carbonaceous material and potential sources of short-hard gamma-ray bursts.

A sample of protostellar jets from data obtained with Spitzer is presented. The data show that many pre-main-sequence stars with ages of a few million years are active, showing rotation rates up to 0.4 days and coronal temperatures above 4,000 K. A few stars show much faster rotation, up to 3.2 days, suggesting the presence of fossil magnetic fields. The presence of angular momentum is often not correlated with accretion rates. One protostar, L1527 IRS, exhibits both low accretion and slow rotation, suggesting that it has nearly fallen into the starhood. Two similar objects, L1535 IRS and TMC1A, exhibit much faster rotation, consistent with their earlier status as potential stars. Another interesting object, the Classical T Tauri star RY Tau, shows variability in its inferred magnetic field orientation. This could imply that accretion and rotation are variable on short time scales. The data suggest that most protostars accrete gas at a relatively constant rate, but about one-third spin up significantly due to disk-averting winds or mergers with other prestellar cores.

Understanding quantum fluids is important for diverse applicatons, such as superfluid helium and the rarefied gas flows in galaxies and cosmology. During the past decade, direct experimental exploration of Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) in dilute gases of alkali atoms has evolved into a highly successful method for producing quantum fluids. In this article, we review the theoretical foundations of the BEC, from the ideal Bose gas to the weakly and strongly interacting Bose gas. Our emphasis is on explaining, in pedagogical fashion, the mathematical techniques used in theoretical BEC, with emphasis on their historical development. This discussion is organized by considering the main effects that make the gas “quantum”: interactions among the atoms, thermal agitation, and quantum statistics (zero-point fluctuations). We also discuss ground-state phenomena, including the depletion and formation of BEC, as well as excitations. We conclude with a discussion of future directions in BEC research, including the appearance of vortices in both single and multi-component condensates.

Resistivity of SrRuO3 shows quadratic temperature dependence down to the lowest measured temperature, 150 mK, consistent with a non-Fermi liquid. A corresponding coherence peak in the specific heat is observed, with no peak or divergence in the spin fluctuation spectrum. These results are consistent with a marginal Fermi liquid state due to enhanced ferromagnetic quantum fluctuations. Indistinguishable non-Fermi-Liquid behaviour is observed in several other heavy fermion systems, most notably in planar antiferromagnets such as URu2Si2. The enhancement of ferromagnetic quantum fluctuations in the Kondo lattice scenario provides a unifying explanation for the diversity of non-Fermi-Liquid behaviour observed in these systems. The observed behaviour is consistent with previous theoretical work on a Kondo lattice with fully isotropic interactions but with strong ferromagnetic fluctuations. The present results provide additional experimental support for the Ising-like (planar) scenario for the unconventional magnetic properties of the Kondo lattice. The paper provides evidence for a novel non-Fermi-Liquid state in the Kondo lattice, which may be realized in SrRuO3, URu2Si2, or possibly other systems with similar low-temperature behaviour.

This paper is concerned with the derivation of hyperbolic - second-order parabolic formulations of general relativity that are equivalent to the standard - second formulation. In the hyperbolic - second-order parabolic (HSP) formulation, one directly estimates the strain (or possibly higher-order derivatives of the metric and its derivatives) and takes advantage of the local in time character of the principal part of the hyperbolic equations to simplify the right-hand-side (RHS) of the equations. The resulting numerical evaluation is more robust and efficient than simulations carried out using the standard - second formulation, especially at strong gravity (where velocities and spacetime distortion are large). Convergence tests carried out in an companion paper (Babiuc et al., arXiv:1811.11802) demonstrate that, for a range of physically interesting problems, the HSP formulation significantly outperforms the standard - second formulation. The HSP formulation is also significantly more expensive to solve since, in addition to the strain estimates, one must also solve for second-order time derivatives (this additional unknown is called the jerk). The present work develops an equivalent hyperbolic - second-order parabolic formulation that, in addition to the estimates of strain and jerk mentioned above, also estimates a dynamical variable known as the Delta-freescala or (in plain English) the differencing invariant (or differential invariants) of the Riemann tensor. The RHS of the resulting equations is expressed in terms of these differential invariants and the dynamical variables already present in the equivalent HSP formulation. The resulting formulation is a combination of - second-order hyperbolic and parabolic equations for the dynamical variables strain, jerk, and Delta-freescala. We demonstrate that the proposed equivalent formulation is equivalent to the original HSP formulation in the sense that the equations of each formulation are (formally) identical. We also carry out a series of numerical tests which illustrate that the two formulations are equivalent in the sense that the solutions obtained using each formulation are in exact agreement. Finally, this paper provides extensive details on the derivation of the proposed formulation. As a prerequisite, we first provide a comprehensive review of hyperbolic systems and their properties, particularly the geometric classification of these systems. We also consider several notational issues relating to the abstract derivations of systems of conservation laws.

In this work, we present a generic approach for building decision trees using relational views. Decision tree models are frequently used to support classification and regression tasks in data mining applications. They are abstract models that represent the relationship between the response (dependent variable) and one or more predictor variables. Construction of decision trees requires the elimination of data points that are not useful for splitting the classification nodes. One of the major challenges in building decision trees is the explosion of tree size with increased data dimensionality, leading to a bad classification performance and high computational costs. We present a generic algorithm that combines concept and instance representations in a decision tree model to reduce the number of leaves and avoid the explosion of tree size. The algorithm uses view expressions to perform relational algebra operations on the original data to efficiently identify and prune the redundant instances. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated on both real-world and synthetic datasets and results are promising, with an improvement of at least 1.3x compared to related state-of-the-art approaches in terms of memory consumption and computational time.

In this paper I present an investigation of the proper motions in the Galactic bulge, using microlensing effects in the Galactic bulge as a tool. In particular, I investigate a new potential Galactic bulge tracer: proper motions. Unlike most other potential bulge tracers, proper motions could be measured for a number of sources in the Galactic bulge fields of the MOA, OGLE and Wise projects, due to the sufficiently long timescales of the microlensing events. I use data from the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) and the Calan/Tuc collaboration, and show that Plaut's window, which is a potential structure in the Galactic bulge is moving with respect to the rest of the bulge at a rate of 12.1 +/- 1.4 km/s toward the southwest and -11.8 +/- 1.4 km/s toward the northwest, consistent with previously measured components of the total Galactic rotation velocity for the bulge. I compare this to models of the Galactic bar and find that the sum of the rotation velocities for the bulge and bar are able to reproduce the observed motions. Finally, I estimate the required sample size for further proper motion measurements in this region, and show that with data from ongoing and future Galactic bulge microlensing projects, proper motions could be measured for approximately 10 million sources in the Galactic bulge, sufficient to map the mass and pattern of the inner Galaxy.

The 2D Ising model with strong square coupling in the limit of zero aspect ratio of the system exhibits a continuous transition at temperature Tc between a low temperature phase in which the interfaces are pinned by the Gaussian disorder and a high temperature phase in which they are unpinned. Using Monte Carlo simulations we estimate the critical exponent associated with the order of the transition as o = 1.23(2) which is consistent with the theoretical prediction of o = 4/11 = 0.3622.... We propose an efficient dynamic renormalization group (DRG) approximation to the problem. The DRG flows for the effective interface tension and Gaussian disorder strength are shown to be inconsistent with the two-sided free field fixed point. This indicates that the transition is indeed continuous. The predicted critical exponents are o = 1.25(5) and y = 0.38(1). Our DRG results were checked against the strong coupling expansion of [1] and excellent quantitative agreement was found for T < Tc. Beyond Tc our DRG flows fail to converge and a new fixed point with nontrivial field content must be sought for. [1] B. Nienhuis, J. Phys. A: Math. A phononic bandgap (PBG) structure for microwave solids was proposed recently [1]. It consists of a one-dimensional (1D) PC channel with a defect and coated by a surface plasma layer (SPL). The PBG structure provides a possibility to achieve a high phononic quality factor (Q) in a compact size. We designed, fabricated, and experimentally investigated such a PBG resonator. The resonant frequency was found to be 19.35 GHz with a spectral width of 0.5 GHz. The measurement results of the linewidth and the Q factor are in a good agreement with the numerical results. It is also shown that the nonautonomous phaser dynamics within the PBG resonator is modeled well by the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The nonautonomous terms in the equation are induced by the SPL. Such nonautonomous terms provide an additional nonlinearity that can stimulate optical wave break up. Indeed, it is demonstrated that, under the critical power of the external pump, optical wave break up occurs in the experiment. The timing of the break up is in good agreement with the numerical results. The underlying mechanism for this phenomenon is discussed.

In this paper we study harmonic sections of the sphere bundles over the effective cycles in the following cohomological round of the theINDEXF=INDEX0 of algebraic varieties. The effective cycles are given by reduced effective representatives, which are typically constructed using loxodromic approximations. Given an effective cycle, we construct a so-called normal neighborhood, which is a semianalytic subset of a flat family of weighted projective spaces. We use the theory of harmonic sections to prove the existence of a nonvanishing section, and hence the semianalyticity. As an application, we deduce the existence of smooth harmonic sections on the entire normal neighborhood. We also consider the special case of hypersurface reductions, where the normal neighborhood is of the simplest possible kind. In this case, we obtain differentiable harmonic sections on the entire reduction locus, with its small canonical model, as follows from a recent result of Ohsawa. Finally, we use harmonic sections on the normal neighborhoods to construct instanton moduli spaces on certain definite $4$-manifolds, such as K3 surface bundles.

In this work, we propose a novel method to gain analytic control over parton showers (PS). Shower evolution is typically described using differential equations, which in the case of PS requires a solution near the singular region. While next-to-leading order (NLO) PS solutions are available, they are complicated and difficult to use for precision physics applications. Instead, we propose to use an expansion around a singular solution, constructed from a series of leading order events. This series converges exponentially, and thus allows for the use of NLO solutions without the computational overhead. This also extends to multiple PS algorithms, such as dipole shower Monte Carlos. We demonstrate the validity of this approach using Z+jet and W+jet production as examples. Furthermore, we show that this technique is also applicable to the resummation of fixed-order Coulomb corrections. We thus achieve both analytic control over PS and also resum large logarithms in the case of Coulomb corrections. As a by-product of this approach, all orders in $\alpha_s$ are accessible, allowing for a more physical description of the evolution.

Recently a lot of interest has been devoted to stochastic interacting particle systems out of equilibrium, where the particles interact through complicated nonlocal interactions and the dynamics is driven by noisy forcing. Depending on the nature of these interactions, these systems can exhibit different phases. For hard-core interactions, such systems have been shown to be amenable to a hydrodynamic limit, provided that the interaction has short range and the number of particles goes to infinity with the radius of interaction. When the latter condition is not met, a more refined multi-scale analysis is needed, which allows to identify, in a large parameter regime, an intermediate scale on which the microscopic dynamics converges to a Markov dynamics. Finally, when all these conditions are met, it has been proved that the macroscopic behavior of the system is described by a nonlinear Mckean-Vlasov equation, coupling a transport term to a nonlocal reaction term. The results reviewed above have been established for systems in which the number of particles $N$ is infinite. Although many of these results have been later extended to the case of a large but finite $N$, much less is known in this case. In particular, it is still an open problem to establish a hydrodynamical limit in the case of hard-core interactions and without short-range assumption on the interaction. Even in the case of periodic boundary conditions and with short-range interactions, rigorous results are known only in one dimension and for very specific interaction kernels. In this work, we review what is currently known in the case of infinite number of particles, and we discuss several challenging open problems. We also provide a self-contained introduction to the model, starting from the precise definition of the interaction kernel, the noise terms, and finally the hydrodynamic equation. The model we study is defined as follows. For each integer $N \geq 1$, we consider $N$ interacting Brownian particles, each one characterized by its position $\left( X^{i,N}(t), i=1,\cdots,N \right)$, and its velocity $\left( V^{i,N}(t), i=1,\cdots,N \right)$, defined on a suitable probability space $\left( \Omega^N, {\mathcal{F}}^N, P^N \right)$, where ${\mathcal{F}}^N$ is the $\sigma$-field generated by the $N$ particles' trajectories and $P^N$ is the associated probability distribution. In this paper, we consider an Abelian two-Higgs model with a strongly correlated electron field. This model is motivated by the effective theory of strongly correlated electrons. We assume that this electron field is compact U(1) gauge field with a critical Higgs-Coulomb interaction. The resulting theory is known to have a separation of energy scales. At low energies one finds conventional Fermi liquid of conduction electrons with a weakly screened long-range (or dynamical) Coulomb interaction. At high energies one finds compact U(1) sector with a short-range (or statical) interaction. Between these two regimes, there are intermediate scales, where the correlation length of electrons becomes comparable with the lattice spacing. In this paper, we show that, in addition to this separation of scales, the theory has a separation of degrees of freedom. In particular, we show that at high energies, which is close to the separation scale, the compact U(1) sector decouples and we obtain an Abelian Higgs model with strongly interacting fermions. We show that this model has a strengthening of the known phase transition. Finally, we apply the results of this paper to the case of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at finite baryon density. We assume that the low energy theory, which is Fermi liquid, has a static quarks at large distances. This theory has the conventional BCS instability of the Fermi liquid at low temperatures and high densities, which leads to a formation of diquark condensates. We argue that in addition to this BCS instability, the strongly interacting electrons, which we find at high energies, may also lead to a formation of Bose condensation of excitons. We show that in the mean field approach this leads to a qualitative change in the behavior of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for diquark condensate and, therefore, to a first order phase transition to the superconductive state with diquark condensate. We also argue that the QCD pion condensate and, possibly, kaon condensate may change the second order phase transition to the superconductive state to a first order one.

Perturbation theory is one of the most important techniques in physics. It provides a framework to describe the low energy dynamics of a system using the interactions between its various components or scales. Examples of such interactions include Coulomb force between electrons in atoms, or the gravity between planets. In quantum mechanics, the basic theory of almost all particles, perturbation theory is applied to motion of electrons in atoms. When these interactions are weak, perturbation theory provides a good approximation to the dynamics of the system. Despite its success, perturbation theory only considers the first order changes in variables as a function of another variable. For example, if I sit in a chair and ask you how I am related to the height of the chair, you would only need to consider my height and the height of the floor to accurately answer how I am related to the height of the chair. You would not need to consider my weight, or the weight of the Earth, as these are said to be higher order corrections. Parametric Perturbation Theory (PT) allows us to consider higher order changes in variables when calculating the response of a system to changes in another variable. For example, I can sit on a chair and calculate how my weight relates to the height of the chair, as well as the changes in height of the floor and the weight of the Earth. In this way, PT extends the limits of how we can consider changes in variables, or corrections, in systems and their dynamics.

In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), scalar quarks and scalar quarks are nearly mass-degenerate with the corresponding scalar gluinos, and their mixing angles are typically very small, so that the decays of these superpartners are nearly entirely hadronic. However, such a constrained spectrum is rarely observed in nature, so that non-minimal flavour violation (NMFV) is an effective theoretical framework for MSSM spectra. In this work, we study the squark and gaugino production and decays in the NMFV framework. We perform a detailed study of the parameters' dependence of the leading and next-to-leading order (NLO) production cross sections and decay branching ratios in this framework. We find that the gluino and squark productions are enhanced relative to the MSSM ones, especially for the first two generations, and the scalar bottom and stop can be as light as around 200 GeV even for a 1 TeV gluino, which is within the reach of the 14 TeV LHC. The gluinos and squarks could be the predominantly bino or wino LSP, leading to bino- or wino-like NLSP, respectively. These NLSP decays could give various distinct final states, including missing energy, same-sign dilepton plus jets, multi-lepton plus jets, and multilepton plus disappearing energy. We provide detailed signal scenarios for several well-motivated parameter sets.

We present a study of the chemical composition of the circumstellar envelopes (CSOs) of yellow hypergiants (YHGs), which are evolved stars with extremely thick winds. We obtained near-infrared high-resolution spectroscopy of 22 YHGs with the APOGEE and GTC instruments. We determined CSO composition using a nearest-neighbor retrieval algorithm, finding that the most abundant elements are C, O, and Ca in most cases, with strong enhancements of neutron-rich elements such as Na and Al. The results provide support for recent simulations suggesting that the dramatic mass loss that characterizes YHG evolution is initiated via a radiation-induced phenomena known as nucleosynthesis-driven mass loss. The rapid evolution of YHGs during the first few hundred thousand years of the post-main-sequence phase has made them valuable indicators of both nucleosynthetic processes operating during extreme evolutionary phases and dynamical processes active in the early stages of compact star formation.

We present rotation measures (RMs) of extragalactic sources behind the southern galactic plane. We analyzed 605 frequency channels of the RM Synthesis images of these sources acquired with the multichannel Correlation Improvement Telescope (CIGALE) on the Purple Mountain Observatory (PMO) 13.7-meter telescope. We detect RMs from almost all regions along the LOS, extending from 23.5 pc cm−1/rad s^−1^ in the north to −69.0 pc cm−1/rad s^−1^ in the south, with a rotation measure zero point of about −600 pc cm−1/rad s^−1^. The RMs gradually change along the LOS, and the rotation measures of almost all sources are enhanced at low Galactic longitudes. We perform simulations to show that these large-scale features are unlikely to be produced by the effects of the anomalous dispersion and the traditional Faraday screen models are not sufficient. We suggest that these features could be the results of large-scale structures of the magnetic field in the inner Milky Way. We also explore the correlation between RMs of the same sources at different frequencies and find that most of them are negatively correlated, which may be related to the random interstellar variations. This work is based on observations obtained with the PMO 13.7-meter CIGALE Telescope, which is operated by the PMO node of theChinese Academy of Sciences and the Sternberg Astronomical Institute, Moscow University.

In our recent work (Carroll et al. 2012, hereafter Paper I), we presented evidence for an active star formation event in the ultracompact H ii region, NGC7538, in the Perseus spiral arm using Spitzer and IRAS data. IRAS determined that 70% of NGC7538’s luminosity was coming from this small region, and Spitzer identified 12 infrared point sources with spectral types of B3 or later. These results, along with our multiwavelength analysis of the region, suggested that this region was likely forming stars at a high rate. In this work, we examine this formation event further through the use of new molecular outflow data obtained with the Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA). We combine our new observations with existing near-infrared and mid-infrared data to further examine the processes acting in NGC7538. We utilize the CLOUDY photodissociation region (PDR) modeling code (cloudy) to create a physical-based scenario for the molecular outflows in NGC7538. This analysis implies that the region is likely producing stars at a high rate through ambipolar diffusion, and not gravitational collapse.

In loop quantum cosmology, the isotropic models are obtained as a special case of the anisotropic models. The stability of the isotropic models in the classical regime has been proved assuming the validity of the classical Hamiltonian and the absence of matter sources. Here we show that the same assumption leads to unstable solutions in the quantum theory, unless the lattice is refined substantially. In the refined lattice, there are no normalizable solutions in the classical regime and the spectrum of the dynamical algebra is unbounded from below. This conclusion holds for the critical values of the anisotropic parameters. If the parameters take values inside the stable region, then the solutions in the quantum theory coincide with those in the classical theory. The presented results apply to thegowdy model with the spatial sections of the form T^3×S3. They could be generalized to other models, but the implementation of the refined lattice and the stability analysis become considerably more complicated.

The globular clusters (GCs) and planetary nebulae (PNe) in the galaxy NGC 5128 (Centaurus A) are analyzed in a comprehensive way for the first time. Kinematics and dynamics of the stellar systems in this huge galaxy provide crucial information on the formation and evolution of the parent galaxy and its dark matter halo. The distance of NGC 5128 is 13.7 Mpc which, given the scale of 1 kpc = 1 pc, corresponds to a spatial resolution of about 40 pc. This is the first time that such an analysis is presented for this object. In the present work we have performed a wide analysis of the GC and PNe systems in this galaxy, obtaining the following results: •Ages of the GCs and PNe are similar, being the mean age of PNe 2.2 ± 0.1 billion years and of GCs 4.3 ± 0.3 billion years. •The mass of the parent galaxy calculated from the GCs using the virial theorem is (2.1 ± 0.6) × 10^11 M⊙. The enclosed mass at the radius where the GC velocity curve starts is 1.1 ± 0.2 × 10^11 M⊙. This gives a mass-to-light ratio of the galaxy of 2.8 ± 0.7. •The mass of the dark matter halo obtained from the PNe is 4.2 ± 0.7 × 10^11 M⊙. The corresponding enclosed mass is 1.2 ± 0.2 × 10^11 M⊙. This gives a dark matter mass-to-light ratio of the galaxy of 6.2 ± 1.5. The PNe rotation curve shows the presence of a dark matter halo, while the GC rotation curve is not described by a rigid body model but by a flat core and a large amount of dispersion. Such different behaviors are explained by the interaction of the GC system with its parent galaxy, while the PNe belong to the galaxy itself.

Recent developments in understanding the dynamics of galaxies in the absence of standard dark matter lead to the conclusion that the observed dynamics of galaxies requires a modification of the Newtonian force law of the form g=g(v/v_{0}), with v being the typical velocity of the particles under consideration. This is usually referred to as a modification of Newton’s law of gravity or MOND (modifiedNewton’s law of gravity). The most popular form of MOND is the so-called ‘triple gravity’: the two Newtonian forces, gravity and an additional, exotic force, which describes the dynamics at small accelerations, have identical strength, but the latter has a different power-law dependence on velocity. Furthermore, it has been realized that MOND can also be described by relativistic theories of gravity which depend on a scalar field (scalar-modified Newtonian dynamics, or ‘smn-like’ gravity). This has opened the way for comparison with and testing of MOND models against observations. In this paper, we present a comparison of several such field-theoretical MOND-like gravity theories, including the popular ‘triple gravity’ and ‘smn’-like gravity. For most of these theories, there is no fully satisfactory realization in terms of a single, generally covariant action. We compare them in the context of weak gravitational fields in the post-Newtonian approximation. We find that ‘triple gravity’ and ‘smn’-like gravity can be discriminated with high confidence, given future experiments, since they give rise to very different post-Newtonian predictions. We also comment on some implications of MOND for dark matter experiments and cosmology.

Recently it has been realized that certain holographic theories, originally formulated in asymptotically Anti-de-Sitter (AdS) space times, can be generalized to include dual descriptions of systems that exhibit instead Bjorken boost invariance in time, rather than radial boost invariance. In this work we construct the first gravity dual of a system exhibiting Bjorken boost invariance in space as well as time. This solution is obtained by Lifshitz transforming the usual AdS black hole, allowing for both the existence of non-trivial spatial gradients, and for the existence of normalizable bulk solutions with arbitrary energy density. Remarkably, in the regime of late time, appropriate decay of the boundary energy momentum tensor is precisely equivalent to that of a relativistic fluid with pressure, density and velocity described by a Bjorken flow at some initial time. This duality is explored in detail in the companion paper [1]. The main focus of this work is the development of the bulk theory needed to describe such solutions. In particular we examine the presence of terms in the dual gravitational action that encode both spatial gradients, and the establishment of thermal equilibrium for the dual field theory. Remarkably, the inclusion of such terms enables one to reproduce the scaling form of the energy momentum tensor for Bjorken boost-invariant flow even in the absence of spatial translation symmetry. This work extends and develops the results of [1], where analogous actions were introduced that reproduced the scaling form of the energy momentum tensor for Bjorken boost-invariant flow in the absence of spatial translation symmetry. In this work we show that such actions can also be generalized to allow for the establishment of thermal equilibrium in the dual field theory. The consequences of such a generalization are explored. Finally we present evidence, based on holographic conservation laws, that the dual field theory exhibits Bjorken boost invariance at late times. We work in units where the AdS radius and the speed of light are set to 1, and use a system of coordinates where the Bjorken flow is defined in the x direction. We consider a field theory consisting of an admixture of free fields in 2+1 dimensions. We will consider two different actions; the first with a general function of the Kretschmann invariant (containing only terms that are at most quadratic in derivatives of the metric) and a specific choice of parameters, allows for the emergence of Bjorken flow in the far field (at times early compared to the initial energy density, but late compared to the speed of sound) with perfect fluid symmetry. We then present numerical evidence based on holographic conservation laws, that the dual field theory exhibits Bjorken flow with late time scaling symmetry. Diffusive radiation in Langmuir turbulence produced by jet shocks has been observed and measured in experiments. This phenomenon is the result of resonant wave–particle interactions mediated by the ion plasma frequency. The resulting energy diffusion coefficient depends on the wave phase and energy flux, as well as the plasma density and temperature. These effects can be explained using a simple analytical theory. The theory describes the nonlinear stage of wave evolution as well as the experimentally observed anisotropy. The above-mentioned physical effect was observed and measured for the first time by an ITER team in the tokamak Test Blanket Facility (TBF) Using a rotating Langmuir probe, it was possible to continuously measure the flux of energy carried by Langmuir waves throughout the entire plasma profile. The turbulence energy reached a maximum at the shock front. The distance between the shock front and the maxima of energy flux corresponds to the thickness of the diffusion zone, as calculated from the theory.

First order phase transitions are observed in classical lattice gas models of interacting spins. At a given temperature, a first order transition separates a high-temperature phase with coexistence of two phases from a low-temperature phase with different ordered and non-ordered states. Existence of metastable states leads to an analytic first order transition with thermal singularities. These singularities cause difficulties in the numerical analysis of first order transitions and result in a large hysteresis and multistability in thermodynamic functions. The models studied here are the famous Ising, Potts and Lenz spin models. These singularities are rounded in the mean field theory and mean field models have second order transitions. In this paper, the existence of first order transitions in the Ising, Potts and Lenz spin models are shown to be a lower bound on the value of the coupling constant below which the mean field theory models have first order transitions.

A dedicated article describing the design, physics capabilities and initial performance of a proposed $2\times250$ GeV CLIC $\gamma\gamma$ collider based on its drive beam FEL is presented. The proposed CLIC $\gamma\gamma$ collider will have a significant improvement in $\gamma\gamma$ luminosity over current colliders, and its initial performance shows that it is feasible to explore the CLIC $hh$ parameter space with enough events for discovery and studying the nature of new phenomena. The new $\gamma\gamma$ collider will be based on the CLIC $e^+e^-$ linear collider drive beam facility, and use the CLIC 1.04 km drive beam parameter as the start-of-train energy and luminosity. The main structures of the collider are as follows. First, the new $\gamma\gamma$ collider will use two250 GeV CLIC $\gamma$s to drive a FEL to produce two photons which collide to produce two 250 GeV photons, and the collision energy will be transferred by two sextupole magnets. Next, the photons will enter the former CLIC pick-up point and make two CLIC $\pi^0$s by Compton back-scattering. The CLIC $\pi^0$s will be cooled by two cooling linacs and exit the collider, forming the collider $\gamma\gamma$s. Finally, the beam will run through a double-focusing final focus scanner to form a stable circulating beam with two250 GeV $\gamma\gamma$s. The physics potential of the CLIC $\gamma\gamma$ collider is analyzed. The precision measurements of the standard model (SM) particles, such as the Higgs and gauge bosons, and searches for new phenomena will be performed using the high luminosity and high energy $\gamma\gamma$ collider. In addition, the potential of the $\gamma\gamma$ collider to study SM BSM models will also be shown. The excellent event rates and stable circulating beam of the CLIC $\gamma\gamma$ collider will make it an ideal machine to discover new phenomena and study the nature of new phenomena. This study shows that the CLIC $\gamma\gamma$ collider is feasible with a current 250 GeV drive beam FEL, and the collaboration between CLIC and FEL field should be considered seriously.

Much attention has been devoted to understanding the spin decoherence in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs). Several theories based on different concepts have been developed to describe this phenomenon. In this paper, we reexamine this issue within an equation-of-motion approach and provide a unified description for all the currently available data. Our results show that, for the central QD charge-steered spin resonance (CSSR) and the interdot charge-shift spin resonance (CSSR-Inters), the spin dephasing times are respectively 21 and 11 ns, which are comparable to the recent experimental results. For the pure QD spin resonance (QD SR), our calculation gives a dephasing time of 21 ns at zero magnetic field and 12 ns at a field of 8 T, which is also in qualitative agreement with the recent experimental results. We also predict the complete spin depolarization at finite fields for the CSSR and QD SR, but an asymptotic behavior of spin polarization for the CSSR-Inters.

Intersection bodies are generalizations of different convex sets. They were introduced by by L. Lovász and M. Simonovits as a tool for studying the complexity of convex bodies. The first intersection bodies were defined as the sets of vertices of the convex hulls of kissing polytopes. We define generalized cosine transforms and show that they map generalized intersection bodies to generalized intersection bodies. We also define a variant of generalized cosine transforms and show that they map generalized log-concave bodies to generalized log-concave bodies. Finally, we apply our results to the problem of bounding the radius of convex bodies with a small intersection body. We obtain the bound in the case of even Radon transform and in the case of intersection body generated by a centrally symmetric body and odd Radon transform. We conclude with open problems and conjectures.

Two-dimensional defect modes in optically induced photonic lattices. Using an interferometric technique, we create periodic lattices with arbitrary real structures in two dimensions. We demonstrate the formation of defect modes localized in distinct square regions of the lattice, and show that these modes are protected by a symmetry-based continuous translational symmetry. Using numerical simulations, we further demonstrate the creation of topological interface modes localized between two square lattices. The existence of these modes is confirmed by observing connection lines in k-space that originate from the lattice's discrete translational symmetry. By engineering these photonic structures in two dimensions, we demonstrate a complete platform for studying a broad spectrum of wave phenomena and developing techniques for defect mode isolation and routing. Recently, carbon-based materials have gained increasing attention due to their potential for application in electronics. A carbon allotrope with large opto-electronic gap is fullerenes, including C$_{60}$ and C$_{70}$ family. Other allotropes, including graphynes and carbopines, are also being studied. However, all of these materials have finite dimensions, and thus electronic properties are also affected by edges and defects. By using density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory, we show that it is possible to design a two-dimensional atomic carbon sheet that exhibits large optical bandgap and nearly perfect flatness. The bandgap can be tuned by bond-lengths and arrangement of the atomic sites. The calculated spin-orbit coupling is significantly enhanced compared to graphene and other two-dimensional atomic carbon allotropes. The electronic properties of this material make it an attractive platform for applications in spintronics and quantum electrodynamics.

Magnetic field generation by turbulent flow has been known for long. With the first experimental confirmation of magnetic Prandtl number, Pm, less than one a few decades ago, it was assumed to be a limitation due to molecular conductivity. However, the advent of improved simulation and analysis methods has provided evidence of this process at low Pm in the limit of magnetic diffusion dominating. This paper details turbulent induction as a mechanism for generating magnetic field at low Pm. An improved phenomenological model, wherein induction and diffusion are treated as coupled partial differential equations and the resulting model equations solved numerically, is used to demonstrate this process. The importance of non-zero magnetic diffusion in maintaining dynamo action is shown to be a result of induction leading to a statistical spatial bahaviour of the field even in the limit of zero magnetic diffusivity. raviva Cisehatta and Scott McFatter, authors of the paper discussed, are both scientists at National Renewable Energy Lab in Golden, CO, USA.

Using data from the X-ray monitoring of Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a constant spectral index of 0.88±0.14 has been derived during the X-ray and infrared intensity variations. The variability of the slope is most likely associated with changes in the electron density and/or height of the emitting region, although other explanations cannot be ruled out. The obtained value of the spectral index is consistent with other observations of the spectrum of Sgr A* in the mm/sub-mm wavelength range, where it has been found to be constant within a factor of 2, in contrast to the predictions of some models of the sublimation region around a black hole. A constant spectral index for Sgr A* has not been reported before. This is the first time such a low variability of the spectral index has been obtained for such a compact object as a black hole.

Wireless data networks often employ sophisticated schemes for bandwidth allocation to support interference-limited transmission. In this regard, non-cooperative games have recently emerged as an attractive framework for the efficient enforcement of network-wide policies, including throughput efficiency, spectrum occupancy, interference avoidance and energy conservation. In this paper, we develop new variational game models for the radio resource allocation in wireless networks. In particular, we formulate three distinct network objectives - spectral efficiency, energy efficiency, and fairness - into non-cooperative games, and propose distributed algorithms to attain NEs through a primal-dual iteration. To enable the implementation of the proposed algorithms, we further develop an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm, which decomposes the complicated non-convex optimization problem into easy-to-solve SDP and convex optimization subproblems. The proposed solution approach is demonstrated to achieve significant performance gains over existing schemes, including very-low-complexity clustering-based solutions.

Flicker noise is the noise associated with the variation of light caused by rapidly turning the light on and off. The origin of flicker noise has been a topic of study for many years, with a large body of research dedicated to understanding it in resistive electrical conductors. Here we report direct detection of flicker noise in superconductors. We detect noise down to 6 parts per million (ppm), and find the flicker noise spectra can be well fitted by the broken power law with 1/f^α characteristics. Our observations are consistent with expectations for a single electron charge hop between localized states in a resistive environment. We observe significantly different noise spectra at different places on the sample, with the noise at the surface of the samples following the 1/f spectrum expected for a purely resistive environment, while the bulk noise is closer to the 1/f^3 characteristic expected in a pure crystalline environment. We speculate that the difference in the spectra arises from quantum interference between different potential fluctuations, modeled in 1/f and 1/f^3 forms.

A new temperature analysis of the brown dwarf 2MASS J05352184-0546085, which orbits closely enough to its companion to be tidally synchronized, yields an unexpectedly low surface temperature of 20.8 ± 0.2 K. This is more than 500 K below what would be expected based on the observed near-infrared flux. Surprisingly, inclusion of J05352184-0546085’s blackbody emission alone is not sufficient to explain the observed fluxes. Instead, a secondary component at a higher temperature must also be present, with temperatures of 47.2 ± 1.0 K and 66.5 ± 1.2 K for its blackbody and Rayleigh-Jeans components, respectively. The component at 66.5 K is likely a spiral arm of the Milky Way, and this source may be an anomalous Extremely Red Object. The secondary component may be a consequence of an eccentric orbit, with the closer approach in the past when the system was both cooler and brighter allowing for a greater contribution of this component to the observed fluxes. As 2MASS J05352184-0546085 approaches its companion further, the magnitude of this effect will decrease.

A research-based curriculum for teaching the photoelectric effect was developed and evaluated with 31 students at a large, mid-western university. The curriculum was informed by input from experts in the field, existing textbooks, and student interviews. Students demonstrated improvement on exams and instructor evaluations, and many students suggested additional topics they would like to learn about. These results suggest that this curriculum may be a useful tool for instructors teaching the photoelectric effect. ingham A research-based curriculum for teaching the photoelectric effect was developed and evaluated with 31 students at a large, mid-western university. The curriculum was informed by input from experts in the field, existing textbooks, and student interviews. Students demonstrated improvement on exams and instructor evaluations, and many students suggested additional topics they would like to learn about. These results suggest that this curriculum may be a useful tool for instructors teaching the photoelectric effect. The photoelectric effect (Maxwell's famous experiment) is among the most well-known and well-understood phenomena in physics. Yet, many students report difficulty learning and understanding this topic, in large part due to the complexity of the equations involved. We developed a four-week curriculum to teach the photoelectric effect that was informed by input from experts in the field, existing textbooks, and student interviews. Students took pre- and post- assessment tests and instructors evaluated students both pre- and post-assessment. Both the pre- and post-test consisted of multiple-choice questions, constructed-response questions, and short essay questions. All students showed significant improvement on the pre-test, on average, and most showed significant improvement on the post-test. Instructors evaluated the curriculum as being successful overall and suggested areas for improvement. In response to student requests, we plan to develop additional modules that address lessons learned from this curriculum.

A light-cone QCD approach to study distribution amplitudes of axial-vector mesons is presented. Using a collective representation of light-cone distributions amplitude, we obtain the following: (1) The famous first few Gegenbauer polynomials/coefficients for three flavor light-cone DAs of axial-vector mesons have been reproduced; (2) Two more Gegenbauer polynomials/coefficients for the leading twist 2 distribution amplitude (DA) of axial-vector mesons are computed; (3) Three asymptotic DAs are studied in details: Chernyak-Zhitnitsky DA, its vertical version and the positive-parity version of more usual Lambert W DA; (4) several desirable properties of axial-vector DAs are studied and explained in the language of light-cone QCD; (5) The recent CLAS12 data for pion transition form factors are well described.

The Leavitt law was discovered by Isaac Arthur Leavitt in 1908. It states that the luminosity of a Cepheid variable is approximately proportional to the square of its pulsation period. In other words, the steeper the Cepheid’s period-luminosity (P-L) relation, the brighter it is. Since then, many investigations have been made about the P-L relations of classical Cepheids. The non-linear P-L relations were firstly found in 1977 by E. Evans and K. Maddox. The non-linearity means that brighter Cepheids have longer pulsation periods. In this paper, by using Monte-Carlo simulations, we explore the P-L relation of low-mass Cepheids in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) using the OGLE III dataset. The non-linear P-L relation was discovered and confirmed with Testimator, which is a Bayesian non-linear regression model. We also apply Schwarz Information Criterion (SIC) to the non-linear P-L relation. The results show that the P-L relation is highly statistically significant with P-L = 3.82(-0.37)(+0.40)logP + 5.18 where P is the pulsation period in days and SIC and Testimator give the same result. The linear P-L relation is not statistically significant. Our results also show that the P-L relation is not a simple linear function but a highly non-linear one. We discuss the physical implications of the non-linearity and the reason for the difference between the theoretical P-L relation and the observed one.

In this paper, we present new results from the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) on the emission of polarized microwave background radiation from the Universe some thirteen billion years ago. The amplitude and frequency spectra of the gravitational waves present in the primordial F polarization were investigated using both map-based and template methods. We found that the data are consistent with the WMAP5 best-fit cosmology and power spectrum, with no statistically significant detection of B-mode polarization at the levels predicted by standard inflation. However, we did detect a large-scale E-mode polarization pattern that is consistent with the standard inflation prediction within the statistical errors. When the WMAP K-band data were included in the analysis, the detection of E-mode polarization was almost entirely accounted for by the BOOMERanG and MAXIMA experiments. Our best-fit polarization power spectrum suggests a tensor-to-scalar ratio, r, of 0.31% at the 95% confidence level. We also re-examined the previously analyzed WMAP FEE and B-mode maps, adding the K-band data and improved calibration for the 2005 data. We again found no significant detection of B-mode polarization. However, we did detect a large-scale E-mode polarization pattern that is consistent with the standard inflation prediction within the statistical errors. When the WMAP K-band data were included in the analysis, the detection of E-mode polarization was almost entirely accounted for by the BOOMERanG and MAXIMA experiments. Our best-fit polarization power spectrum suggests a tensor-to-scalar ratio, r, of 0.31% at the 95% confidence level. Finally, we discuss the constraints on the gravitational waves B-mode polarization amplitude from WMAP combined with information on the E-mode polarization power spectrum. If future experiments do detect B-mode polarization, this will rule out many versions of inflation and indicate the need for new ideas in explaining the initial state of the Universe. If B-mode polarization is not detected in future experiments, our constraints will improve, but then only by a relatively small amount.

In quantum field theories with spontaneous symmetry breaking, the particle spectrum and the interaction strength are influenced by the existence of Gribov copies, which are equivalent but non-identical local minima of the Yang-Mills action. In this work, we show that these copies also appear in the spectrum of bound states of color-singlet clusters of static quarks in the Coulomb gauge, up to an overall multiplicative constant. Using lattice Monte Carlo simulations at various values of the coupling and the number of colors, we find that the potential governing the chromoelectric interactions between color charges has a minimum, with an equilibrium separation given by the screened lengthscale e2/(4π√αNc), where Nc is the number of colors. This is consistent with previous calculations in the Feynman gauge, where the Coulomb and Feynman potentials differ by a pure constant. We argue that this potential has a unique absolute minimum, which corresponds to a stable spectrum of color-singlet bound states.

The work function is the energy required to remove an electron from a material surface. The work function is an important physical property of a material, since it influences the efficiency of electron emission and deposition, the electric field needed to remove electrons from a surface, and the stability of a surface. The work function is not itself an observable, but it may be computed from density functional theory (DFT) or related calculations. In the case of metals, the work function is generally thought to be related to the band structure of the material near the Fermi level. The determination of work functions is often part of the characterization of electronic materials. It is well known that the work function of a metal strongly depends on the crystalline orientation of the material. However, it was not clear how the work function is affected by the chemical composition of the material, or how it compares to the band structure of the material. Here, we report a new method to calculate the work function of crystalline materials from first principles. Our method, developed for the particular case of photoemission experiments, is based on the effective-mass approximation and relies on the calculation of the average electrostatic potential at the surface of the material. We demonstrate the applicability of this method to a broad range of materials, and find that the work function can be up to 1.5 times larger than the band structure-derived approximation. We discuss physical implications of our results and suggest possible improvements to the current methods for calculating the work function."

On Jan. 24, 2019, the ASAS-SN team announced the discovery of an isolated compact object (CCO) in the Galaxy. ASASSN-19pg is a little over 2 solar masses and has a high proper motion of approximately 400 km/s. Using data from the All-Sky Automated Survey (ASAS) and Gattini simulations, we determine that ASASSN-19pg is a very unlikely high-magnification event with an estimated probability of 0.0013%. With only 3 observations taken over 7 years, ASASSN-19pg was likely discovered as a result of regular single-object follow-up observations with large telescopes. Given ASASSN-19pg's proximity to the Galactic plane (b = -4.1 ± 0.2º) and distance of 720 ± 110 pc, we propose that it is likely an old star that has traveled a long distance from its birthplace via Galactic evolution.

Finite covers of 3-manifolds are often far from free: in particular, every prime subdividing a cover must also divide the cover. Nevertheless, it is rare for a cover to be free or almost free. In this short note, we provide a condition for when such a cover is almost free: the covering group must be almost-free. This condition is easily satisfied, for example by suitable Schottky groups, and we apply it to give many examples of almost-free finite covers of $S^3$. Finite covers of 3-manifolds are a powerful tool in 3-manifold topology, thanks to their use in the Wirtinger inequality, the characterization of hyperbolic 3-manifolds as those with no non-trivial finite covers, and their relations to 3-manifold group theory. Furthermore, the problem of understanding finite covers of 3-manifolds is an important problem in itself, as it has interesting connection to classical group theory and finite permutation groups. By a theorem of W.B.R. Lickorish, every closed orientable 3-manifold admits a finite cover, whose first Betti number is the rank of the first homology group of the 3-manifold. In general, given a subgroup H of the mapping class group (the group of isotopy classes of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of the surface), it is always possible to construct a finite cover whose covering group is isomorphic to H; if we instead consider subgroups of the extended mapping class group, whose elements also fix a base point, then it is possible to obtain finite covers whose covering groups are abstract groups. In particular, a finite cover whose covering group is a non-abelian simple group is of great interest. This note is concerned with almost-free covers. Given a subgroup H of the mapping class group, the degree of the cover and the ratio of the index of H in the mapping class group to the order of H are important invariants of the cover. We say the cover is almost free if these invariants satisfy deg(cover) (ind H) / |H| = 1 + o(1) as H approaches the identity in the Teichmüller space. We show this is a general condition that often holds. For example, we show that if the surface has genus at least 2, and any simple closed curve has nonzero genus, then any finite subgroup of the mapping class group is almost free. As a consequence, we apply this to give many examples of almost-free covers of the 3-sphere. These include all finite simple groups, certain Schottky groups, groups arising as finite quotients of surface mapping class groups, and the alternating group A6. We describe how to produce infinite families of almost-free covers, and in particular show that any sufficiently large alternating group is almost free.

A microscopic theory of quantum dot interactions with quantum light is presented. Quantum light is elementary excitations in the quantum electrodynamics (QED) theory. The formalism is based on the effective action for the photon field, including both the field and its quantized excitations. The theory includes also QDs and their interactions, which are modelled as additional degrees of freedom that couple to the photon field. The theory is applied to calculate the quantum dot luminescence spectrum, including the radiative and non-radiative recombination processes. It is shown that the dependence of the spectra on the photon field amplitude, polarization, and propagation direction have unique features, determined by the photon field state and quantum dot properties. These features allow to identify the photon field and QD states, in particular, in experiment. The proposed theory can be used for analysis of recent experimental data for photoluminescence (PL) lineshape and intensity in InAs/GaAs quantum dots (QDs) induced by a pump laser field, which contain a strongNon-Kramer's vibronic sideband (nKSVSB) and a weak vibronic sideband (KSVSB). The theory explains the origin of the nKSVSB and gives reasonable explanation of the KSVSB intensity and positions. The nKSVSB is explained as a result of the photon field self-interaction, produced by the field quantization in the QD, which leads to the level anticrossing that modifies the Rabi splitting.

A halo coronal mass ejection (CME) was observed on 2015 April 15 at 19:15 UT by the Large Angle and Spectrometric COloro Observer (LASCO) on the Sun-Earth line. The CME was associated with an M9.0 flare which produced radio emission with a frequency of 0.16, 0.22, 2.25, and 10.0 GHz for the following four regions of interest (ROI): longitudinally separated radial antennas, circular polarized antennas, total power and linearly polarized antennas, respectively. The total intensity of the radio emission observed at each of these frequencies follows a similar trend over the time period of the radio observations. The flare was located near the center of the LASCO CME field of view (FOV) so observations of the radio emission are confined to a localized ROI. The spectrum of the source emitting the radio emission is relatively straight over the four frequencies observed, indicating that the emission is dominated by plasma at a single temperature. A simple emission model based on a simple, isothermal, relativistic Maxwellian distribution fits the total intensity of the observed radio emission well for each frequency. However, a two-component model composed of an isothermal component and a non-isothermal component provides a significantly better fit to the total intensity of the observed radio emission. The best-fit model has a hot component with a peak temperature of 10,000 K, a cool component with a peak temperature of 1,000 K, and an initial minimum velocity of 330 km s−1. The non-isothermal component best fits the enhancement in the total intensity in the later time periods of the radio observations, which is likely related to the observed Mach stem and shockwave associated with the CME.

Microring optical resonators in lithium niobate are electro-optically tunable via7 84-MHz-wide optical carrier waves. Tunability ranges from 1528 to 1553 nm, with a total ring volume of approximately 3.2 pm3, and a tuning efficiency of >20,000 dB/mm. Using this capability, a 19-nm wide resonance is observed to have an extinction ratio of approximately 30 dB when wavelength-locked to a slave laser, and rapid, broadband (<250 kHz) tuning has been observed with resistance changes of up to 6.6%. Tunability of this order is expected to enable quantum state control of neutral atoms and linear optics using a common resonant cavity. In this paper, we experimentally demonstrate a surface mounted LiNbO3 microring resonator electro-optically tunable via an 84 MHz wide optical carrier wave. Tunability ranges from 1528 to 1553 nm with a total ring volume of approximately 3.2 pm3. We observe a 19 nm wide resonance to have an extinction ratio of approximately 30 dB when wavelength-locked to a slave laser, and rapid, broadband (<250 kHz) tuning has been observed with resistance changes of up to 6.6%.

For inelastic, viscosity-dominated flows, there is a well-known inviscid ideal limit, where the viscous stresses can be expressed in terms of the strain rate. In this limit, the Fourier and linearized Euler fluid dynamics equations take the form of a hyperbolic conservation law, with a right-hand side that is a quadratic function of the gradient of the fluid velocity. If the material parameters of this equation are chosen so that this right-hand side is manifestly positive semi-definite, then the existence of a unique, smooth solution to the fluid dynamics equations is guaranteed. Conversely, if one relaxes this requirement and allows the material parameters to depend on the shear rate (and in general, on the fluid configuration and history), then there exist Riemann problems that lead to finite-amplitude, oscillatory solutions. For two-dimensional flows, it is possible to show that these oscillations have a single frequency. The goal of this work is to compute the transport coefficients in the limit where the shear rate is a relevant parameter, but where the range of shear rates is finite. We find that while some coefficients remain positive definite, others become negative, signaling a possible instability.

A fundamental problem in machine learning is to cluster data such that the within-cluster data points are similar to each other and the between-cluster data points are as different as possible. Correlation clustering (CC) is one of the most popular and successful methods for this task, which can be efficiently solved by convex relaxations and proven to recover the optimal solution under certain conditions. However, these conditions are difficult to satisfy in practice, leading to a rapid growing literature to understand the relationship between convergence rate and parameters, and the pervasiveness of correlation clustering in a variety of domains. In this paper, we argue that correlation clustering is inapproximable within any constant factor, based on the observation that it can easily get stuck in local optima and the problem's correlated nature. This inapproximability result holds for a large family of differentiable relaxations, and we present a specific algorithm to capture the core difficulty of the problem. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on benchmark data sets, and the results confirm our analysis, strongly suggesting that correlation clustering is indeed an NP-hard problem.

In this paper we present an analytic result for the one-loop massless triangle Feynman diagram. The triangle integral is of the type B0 and has three space-time dimensions. It cannot be evaluated by standard Feynman parameter or Mellin Barnes solutions. We present an analytic result for this integral and also for the corresponding dual diagram, which is obtained by crossing two lines of the triangle. This is the first known analytic result for this class of diagrams. Our result is based on a combination of Schwinger parameterization and Euler parametrization of the three propagators, a suitable regularization, use of the DR or $D$ function regularization of the triangle integral, and finally the uniqueness of the result up to a holomorphic function. We believe that the result presented in this paper will be useful in understanding various properties of triangle diagrams in general, and in particular in the field of perturbative quantum field theories.

Zero-temperature phase of the XY spin glass in two dimensions: Genetic embedded matching heuristic April 20, 2023 In two dimensions, we find a zero-temperature phase of the two-dimensional (2D) XY spin glass that exhibits a spontaneous rotational symmetry breaking and concomitant long-range order in the chirality degree of freedom, namely, the direction of the net chiralities of the spins in each small volume of the system. This zero-temperature phase is characterized by a non-zero value of the chirality Edwards-Anderson order parameter θ_{EA}, as well as a non-zero amplitude A_{chiral} of the chiral spiraling correlations, which decay algebraically with distance. Both θ_{EA} and A_{chiral} are computed via efficient genetic algorithms, embedded within the standard replica-exchange Monte Carlo algorithm. Our findings suggest the possible existence of a discontinuous phase transition to a disorder-dominated phase at nonzero temperature. The direct calculation of θ_{EA} and A_{chiral} has not been possible so far in two dimensions, owing to the extreme computational cost of existing exact techniques. Our genetic algorithms yield the first estimates of θ_{EA} and A_{chiral}, and of the chiral glass exponent z=2.21(4). We expect that similar techniques will allow us to prove the existence of this phase and of its associated critical exponents, as well as of its continuum limit, in the general case of d dimensions and general lattice models of correlated electrons. The chirality is a discrete, global degree of freedom that has not been taken into account so far in spin glass models. It is a (net) rotation angle of the spin structure (e.g. left or right spin). As the spins are coupled in pairs in the standard XY model, it is natural to consider the chirality of each spin separately. Chirality appears as a local order parameter in models with discrete degrees of freedom. In equilibrium statistical physics, the chirality is a useful tool to detect spin glass order. For classical spin glasses, the chirality behaves in many ways as an ordinary spin (in a random Ising magnet, the chirality only distinguishes up and down spins). The XY spin glass is a classical, random spin model. The chirality can also be seen as a discrete, global order parameter in XY models. In continuum models, its detection via usual equilibrium tools (e.g. correlation functions) is impossible because of the critical character of the transition: long range order is absent at criticality. However, we found that, in the XY model on a lattice, chirality spontaneously appears at zero temperature, with very good accuracy. It would be interesting to prove this zero temperature chirality in the continuum limit. The chirality degree of freedom appears also in certain low temperature phases of higher dimensions and different lattice models (e.g. Heisenberg and Potts models). The

The characterisation of the dark matter (DM) component in clusters of galaxies is important for our understanding of the Universe on the largest scales. While observational signatures of DM are sought by many methods, one of the most direct is the measurement of the velocity anisotropy of the DM particles as a function of their position within the cluster. We describe a method for measuring the DM velocity anisotropy, using optical observations of the cluster galaxies and strong gravitational lensing of background galaxies. We apply this method to the galaxy cluster MACS J0429.6-0253, combining our measurements of the projected mass distribution with strong lensing observations from the Subaru telescope. We find strong evidence for an axisymmetric DM velocity anisotropy in this cluster, with the amplitude of the anisotropy dependent on radius. Our results show that dark matter is not fully collisional, but instead retains some of its velocity memory from earlier times. The methods described in this paper can be applied to other galaxy clusters, as well as other large scale structures in the Universe, allowing further tests of the nature of DM and its dynamical evolution.

In this paper we develop a Bayesian approach for the reconstruction of the cosmological large-scale structure of the universe from CMB and LSS measurements. The reconstruction is formulated as an inverse problem, and we present a highly efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to sample from the posterior distribution. The likelihood for the cosmological observations is computed by convolving the Gaussian primordial perturbation and the nonlinear matter power spectrum, and includes precise modeling of the nonlinear galaxy bias. For the prior on the initial density field we adopt a scale-independent log-normal distribution, which can efficiently represent both Gaussian and non-Gaussian initial density fields. We show that a correct treatment of the nonlinear evolution of density fluctuations is essential for the accurate reconstruction. We apply our method to an N-body simulation and demonstrate that our reconstruction recovers the input cosmology correctly, even on large scales ($> 10 h^{-1}$Mpc) inaccessible to the N-body simulations. Finally, we point out some potential systematics in our method and how to avoid them in the future.
