We report on a new flaring of an ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX) in the nearby edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 1365. The X-ray luminosity increased from L_X=7.5×10^{39} erg s-1 to L_X=1.2×10^{40} erg s-1 in about 2.2 hours, and the spectrum became hard with a photon index of ≈1.8. The size of the X-ray source remained constant at ≈20,000 km s-1. This large increase in flux was observed over multiple flaring episodes, separated by ≈16 hours. We argue that the new flaring episode is related to the previous outburst, since its timing and spectral properties are similar. A comparison with predictions of disc evaporation and direct collision models are discussed. This new flare of ULX NGC 1365 L1 was observed by the XMM-Newton and INTEGRAL satellites. The XMM-Newton data were analyzed in 2011. New observations with INTEGRAL separated by 16 hours and timing analysis confirm the previous claim that this ULX is variable. The spectrum became hard and the size of the X-ray emission region remained constant. This supports a model of this source as a colliding stellar system - the size and spectrum variations can be explained by the changes in the distance between the donor star and the compact object - a white dwarf.

A sample of quasars from the Palomar survey whose emission line spectra show multiple broad absorption line systems at high redshift are examined for evidence of polarized optical continuum radiation. In all cases but one, sufficient polarized flux is present to account for the total observed reddening, if the continuum source is larger than the size of theBroad Absorption Line System. This indicates that the source of the polarized flux is within a few light-days of the continuum source, or less in all cases but one. In one object, 1H 0323+342, polarized flux is observed only on two nights, and it is unclear if this object is more variable than those for which polarized flux was observed continuously for a week or more. From these data, we are unable to determine if the Broad Absorption Line systems are intrinsic to the quasar, a foreground system, or a superposition of both. If the polarized flux originates within a few light-days of the continuum source, as is the case in most objects, the emission regions are smaller than the event horizon of the mass absorber in all but one object. If the polarized flux is emitted from a region near the putative black hole, then General Relativity must be incorrect in these objects. Either general relativity must be supplemented by some mechanism for creating an horizon, or the emission regions of these quasars are larger than previously thought.

Galaxy positions within dark matter (DM) halos reveal signatures of different alignments. These are dubbed as types I, II, and III depending on the strength of their DM halo major axes. We show that the different types of alignments are also observed in the properties of satellite galaxies, and their cross-correlations with DM halos. The three alignments are related to the depth of DM potential well, the structure of satellite galaxies, and the distribution of DM halos, respectively. Our results suggest that the morphology-density relationship and alignments of galaxies are two aspects of the same cosmic structure, and the specific alignment reflects the hierarchical growth of large-scale structure. In the concordance cosmology, structure formation in the universe is driven by dark matter (DM) and dark energy. Galaxy morphology is closely related to its surrounding environment, which is formed by the underlying DM structures. Based on the distribution of satellite galaxies in and around large clusters, three types of alignments between galaxy major axes and the three coordinate axes (azimuthal, polar and projected) are observed. From weak to strong, these three alignments are Type I, II and III, respectively. These alignments also appear in the distributions of corresponding DM halos. We propose that these alignments are related to the hierarchical growth of large-scale structure, where the formation of galaxies are along the deepest DM potential well, along the DM major axes and along the plane of DM halos. The morphology-density relationship is the observed connection between the distribution of galaxies and the environment they reside in. This relation is usually presented in a diagram showing the fraction of spheroidal (elliptical and spiral) galaxies as a function of the density of the environment. Our work provides another angle to this morphology-density relationship. We find that these three alignments are connected to the hierarchical growth of large-scale structure. This connection should also exist in other large structures such as superclusters and filaments. We use observations of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) data and Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) data, as well as results from cosmological numerical simulations including the Millennium Simulation, the MultiDark Run and the Bolshoi simulation. These samples are divided into six mass ranges and six environments. We find these three alignments in each of the six mass ranges. We also study the relationship between these three alignments and the satellite galaxy properties such as color, luminosity and spectral type, as well as DM halo properties such as mass and large scale structure (LSS) orientation. These alignments are observed in three dimensions: the azimuthal alignment is along the spin vector of DM halos, the polar alignment is along the major axes of DM halos, and the projected alignment is along the planes of DM halos. Radiative transfer effects are ubiquitous in interstellar clouds and are known to be important in the evolution of newly formed stars. In the past, the treatment of radiative transfer in both isolated star simulations and in large-scale cosmological simulations has been complicated by the need to resolve the spatial scales of interest to radiation transport. This has restricted the use of radiation in such simulations to large, coarse cells, with parameters designed to capture the bulk properties of the gas but not its detailed local behavior. In recent work, we have coupled a modified-Lagrangian criterion for Schmidt decomposition with a photon-conserving discretization of the Eddington tensor to evolve the radiative transfer equations in the adaptive mesh refinement code Enzo. This allows the treatment of very strong stellar sources, which drive local cooling and enable radiation to play a role on spatial scales resolvable by the simulation. We illustrate the implementation in the context of a large-scale, cosmological simulation, exploring the role of radiative transfer feedback on the interstellar medium and on the condensation of baryons into stars. We find that while the local escape of radiation does not affect the global thermal evolution of the ISM, it does reduce the overall star formation efficiency of the simulation, due to the reduced available gas pressure support.

Early-type galaxies are believed to be very old and passively evolving systems, hence their structure and composition can reveal details about the early formation and growth of their parent structures. We use data from thezilla project to measure the stellar masses, dark matter masses, and the baryon mass fractions of 333 early-type galaxies, selected by using rest-frame optical color and morphology to isolate galaxies at z > 0.2. We find that early-type galaxies have a mean stellar mass of ξ M* = 7.6 × 10 13 h-2. For the subset of massive early-types ( M* ≥ 2.2 × 10 12 h-2 ), we also measure the hot gas fractions and find that, on average, they are lower than the stellar masses by a factor of 3.8: M* = 1.7 × 10 13 h-2. At fixed stellar mass, we find a strong relation between baryon fraction and galaxy mass, with more massive early-types having smaller baryon fractions. At fixed galaxy mass, we do not find a strong relation between the dark matter fraction and color, luminosity, or environment. However, the most dense environments contain a population of early-type galaxies with the highest baryon fractions and the most slowly growing total mass-to-light ratios. We discuss a few different possibilities to produce such a tension between the baryon fraction and the total mass-to-light ratio, as well as future work that will extend these results to lower masses and higher redshifts.

In the landscape paradigm of eternal inflation, the multiverse is understood as the sum of all consistent vacuum states. Yet, perturbative quantum gravity fails to specify the state of the universe at non-planckian energies, and so the sum must be understood as an integral over all such states. An entropy-weighted sum over these non-perturbative vacua yields a measure density of vol(M) = (0.78 ± 0.15)ħ ∼ (0.67 ± 0.13)cm³ on our universe, which agrees with the measured density of matter. Conversely, the existence of non-perturbative vacua with a density equal to the matter density implies that the measure is nontrivial, contradicting a long-standing assumption of spacetime selection. This implies the multiverse is fundamentally non-classical, and may provide a new arena for quantum gravity. -- Authors: Gregory S. Asgari, Diego A. Valiveiro, Soroush Dalal, Vlatko Vedral ArXiv link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.03239 --

The top-quark is a unique particle whose large mass renders it susceptible to strong interaction effects, making it especially important in theories of electroweak symmetry breaking. The mass of the top-quark can be measured through a characteristic energy release in the scattering of its anti-quark partner from the rest mass of the top-quark. This so-called missing transverse energy plus jets signature can be produced at the Tevatron proton-antiproton collider. CDF has performed the first experimental measurement of the top-quark mass using this signature, analyzing a sample of 13.0 fb$^{-1}$ of Run II data. The measured top-quark mass is $m_t = 173.3 \pm 0.6 ({\rm stat}) \pm 1.2 ({\rm syst})$ GeV, corresponding to a relative precision of 1.2% and indicating that the top-quark mass is very nearly its nominal mass of 172.5 GeV.

A two-user wireless link with Rayleigh fading and with both users knowing only one of the channels is considered. Cooperation is achieved by using dirty paper coding (DPC) at the transmitter, and multi-user detection (MUD) at the receivers. For the case when only the better channel of the two is known at the transmitter and receiver, it is shown that Cooperation gain of 2 with channel symmetry can be achieved. When both channels are known, it is shown that Cooperation gain of 3 is possible under favorable conditions. The case with only one channel known at the transmitter and receiver, is studied in [1]. In this case, the capacity gain from cooperation is 2. The case with both channels known, is studied in this paper. It is shown that when the channels are symmetric, cooperation gain of 3 is possible under favorable conditions. For a noetherian scheme $X$ over a field $k$ of characteristic $0$, let $D^b_-(X)$ be the bounded derived category of the constructible derived category $D_c(X)$. This paper develops the relationships between the abelian category of weight structures on $D^b_-(X)$, the abelian categories of weight filtrations on the $\under chance $ categories of motives over $k$, the two sphere vanishing and Beilinson motives over $k$ and weight spectral sequences and complexes. As an application, we calculate the weight structures and the weight spectral sequences and complexes on the perverse Tate motives with coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}$ over any noetherian scheme. We also compare our results with the existing work of Hadian and Pour Several Attacks on Formal Motives (PAFM) and check that they agree. In particular, we prove that there is a unique weight structure for every choice of weight filtration on the cohomology ring of the spectrum of formal log motives, and a unique weight filtration on the cohomology ring of the étale homotopy category of finite correspondences. For any weight filtration on the cohomology ring of the formal log motives, we construct the corresponding weight spectral sequence. We also construct weight complex and filtration for the étale homotopy category of finite correspondences without assuming the existence of weight structure, and we prove that they are equivalent. We also compare our results with the existing work of Hadian and Pour Several Attacks on Formal Motives (PAFM) and check that they agree.

The position eigenvectors are unitary eigenvectors of the position operator, i.e. they are eigenvectors of the translation group. We demonstrate that these position eigenvectors have a simple expression in terms of plane wave eigenfunctions of the free Maxwell field, i.e. they are photon wave mechanics (PWM) position eigenvectors. Hence position is an observable in PWM, in which the translation group is a fundamental symmetry. We show that this implies that the standard proof of the equivalence of PWM and Maxwell theory, due to Holland and Burnett, is actually a proof that Maxwell theory is a position eigen theory, and we propose a new derivation of the Maxwell Lagrangian from PWM. This paper addresses the question of position in quantum mechanics, specifically the question of whether position has a meaningful precise meaning at the quantum level. There are many reasons to think that it does not. One is that it is not possible to localize a quantum wavefunction, since a localized wavefunction is an eigenstate of the position operator, and the position operator is not self-adjoint. Hence there is no self-adjoint position and localization is not a precise meaning. However, this does not answer the question of whether position is an observable in some more precise sense. In this regard the existence of a symmetry analogous to translation invariance, the so-called Galilei invariance, has a remarkable property. This is that the generators of Galilei transformations form a Lie algebra, which implies that position is an observable in the sense that its eigenvectors can be position wave functions. This was noticed by Newton and Wigner. A second problem with position as an observable is that although there are position eigenvectors they do not have a simple explicit form. They do not form a natural basis in terms of which other observables in the theory can be expressed. The position eigenfunctions of PWM do have an explicit form and they form a natural basis of wave functions which is especially well suited for the study of a variety of problems in quantum mechanics. These basis wave functions are eigenfunctions of a remarkable set of operators, which includes the kinetic energy operator and the position operator. Therefore, in the present paper, we answer the question of whether position has a precise meaning at the quantum level in the affirmative. We show that position is an observable in the precise sense, namely as a symmetry of the theory. It is an observable which has eigenvectors which have an explicit simple form. Henceforth, we will call this position eigencv. We will call the position eigenfunctions of PWM photon wave mechanics (PWM) position eigenvectors.

The most general Lagrangian describing the decay of the Z^0 particle into two photons has been studied. The corresponding partial widths have been calculated and compared with the values measured by the ALEPH, DELPHI, L3 and OPAL collaborations. It is found that this standard model process can only take place through a twisted coproduct structure of the Poincar'{e} group. This leads to a modification of the parity and time reversal transformation properties of the photons. This is a finding of potentially great significance, as nontwistcoproduct theories have been shown to arise naturally in the low energy limit of certain types of string theory. Note: this work was done in collaboration with Peter Schupp and Joseph Schmidt.

We present the results of spectroscopic observations of the quiescent state of the intermediate polar EX Hydrae, conducted with the Low Resolution Spectrograph on the HET and the X-shooter spectrograph on the VLT. We find that the spectrum of EX Hydrae in quiescence is best fit by an absorbed blackbody + flared-disk spectrum model, with a temperature of 12,000 K and a distance-independent radius of 0.2 R☉. We discuss the implications of these results for the EX Hydrae system and for compact object astrophysics in general. We present the results of spectroscopic observations of the quiescent state of the intermediate polar EX Hydrae, conducted with the Low Resolution Spectrograph on the HET and the X-shooter spectrograph on the VLT. We find that the spectrum of EX Hydrae in quiescence is best fit by an absorbed blackbody + flared-disk spectrum model, with a temperature of 12,000 K and a distance-independent radius of 0.2 R☉. The spectrum of EX Hydrae can be explained by emission from a warm, massive degenerate star, likely in the process of losing rotational energy to gravitational wave emission. The system parameters are highly constrained, and the system cannot be modeled simply as a blackbody with a temperature of 12,000 K. In particular, the radius and distance are tightly constrained by the data, and the data are consistent with EX Hydrae having the same radius as the Roche radius of its components. The large radius suggests that the compact object is a neutron star. These observations of EX Hydrae provide strong evidence in favor of the hypothesis that the most rapid rotation rates in compact binary systems are reached by way of evolutionary shrinkage of white dwarf components. This conclusion has significant implications for our understanding of the evolution of close binaries, for the production of gravitational wave sources, and for the population of neutron stars and black holes.

Stellar-mass black holes (BHs) are ubiquitous in globular clusters (GCs), yet their influence on the dynamics of cluster stars is not well constrained. Here we show that the presence of an intermediate-mass BH in a GC modifies the equilibrium structure of the cluster, with an overall expansion of the stellar distribution. In contrast with earlier studies, we show that the presence of a black hole hardly alters the structural properties of young GCs, and is only significant for older clusters. We perform N-body simulations with varied particle numbers and show that our findings are consistent with the presence of a central intermediate-mass black hole, of a mass above ~20% of the total cluster mass, having been formed via runaway mergers of individual stars and stellar remnants. This implies that BHs of high masses could have formed in GCs via processes occurring at low efficiencies during their early dynamical evolution. This provides a novel means for the formation of massive stellar-mass BHs, and may help to resolve an apparent contradiction between observations of stellar-mass BHs and the predictions of standard GC evolution.

A paper by Anna Duamant A short overview of the history and importance of non-commutative geometry, and the theory of the non-commutative sphere.In non-commutative geometry, instead of the usual manifold structure, sets are given by a quadruple (A, {\mathfrak}{H}, D, J), where A is a C*-algebra, {\mathfrak}{H} is a Hilbert space on which A is represented as multiplication operators, D is a derivation (i.e. a generalized version of a Lie algebra element), and J is a complex structure, imposing certain conditions on the commutator of A. The sphere is the only example of a non-commutative manifold, studied in particular in connection with the encyclopedia of manifolds, [15]. In the seminal paper on the non-commutative sphere, [8], Curran, Edwards, and Gull proved that the sphere (A, [|x|=1], D, J), with A the C* algebra of complex, continuous functions on the unit sphere in Cn and J the complex structure given by multiplication by i, satisfies all the axioms for a non-commutative manifold.

A measurement of the production of charged pions by protons on a tantalum target is presented. The data were obtained with the activation method using a 12.5 cm diameter tantalum target and a 1359 g/cm^2 54.6 MeV proton beam from the CERN SPS. Channels with positive and negative pion production are separated using a 9.2 cm thick precision air core magnetic shield. The protons incident on the tantalum target range in depth from -10.6 to -1.3 cm, with a mean value of -5.8 cm. For negatively charged pions, the measured cross section is sigma(proton + tantalum → pi^- + X) = 21.2 \pm 1.7 (stat) ± 4.0 (syst) nb, and for positively charged pions it is sigma(proton + tantalum → pi^+ + X) = 16.7 \pm 1.7 (stat) ± 4.0 (syst) nb. These are the first cross sections for individual pi production channels measured with a tantalum target and a 1359 g/cm^2 proton beam. The values are compared to recent nuclear model predictions.

The Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) has allowed the observation of the lowest lying energy levels of many molecular species in the solar chromosphere for the first time. These observations reveal how the atmospheric levels of some species are very dynamic, with clear signatures of cooling and downflows. ALMA also provides the first clear view of how these dynamics couple to magnetic flux elements at the photospheric level. These observations offer fresh insight into how the chromosphere is both coupled to and affected by the solar surface. Potential energy minima of (H2O)n clusters on graphite are located using genetic algorithm techniques. The clusters are identified as global energy minima for n≤5 and low values of n on graphite. These minima are found to be depending on the number of molecules n and the number of water molecules in the first hydration layer. The stability of these global minima is discussed in terms of interaction energy and dihedral angle restraints. The analysis of the most stable clusters shows that the molecules are embedded in a dense, hydrogen-bonded water network. Clusters of n=3 and 5 molecules are suggested to be interesting structures for vapor deposition experiments. In this paper, we propose a concise theoretical framework to understand various physical phenomena observed in chiral lipid membranes. First, the membrane can have a macroscopic amount of nonchiral defects such as proteins or nanoparticles, which lead to a net chirality in the membrane. This could explain how chirality can self-assemble in vivo at low energy and lead to various phenomena such as the segregation of left- and right-handed molecules or the anchoring of proteins to a particular side of the membrane. Second, even in the absence of such microscopic defects, the membrane can still have a macroscopic amount of microscopic handedness, which could arise from the fact that water and dissolved compounds are typically not fully nonracemic but have a small amount of residual enantiomeric imbalance. The spontaneous breaking of inversion symmetry in water means that right-handed water tries to prefer one enantiomeric form of a compound, and this preference will partially mirror that of the membrane. This residual microscopic handedness leads to several physical phenomena such as the unique properties of waterPCs, which could lead to applications in asymmetric catalysis or DNA separation. The theory also suggests new experiments, such as probing microscopic handedness in vivo by measuring the sign of surface magnetization of the membrane.

The value of the cosmological constant is very tiny from the point of view of theoretical physics. The reason for this has so far been a mystery to researchers. In this paper, we propose a novel explanation for this phenomenon. We show that the cosmological constant, α, appears in the action in the form of a term which penalizes the volume of spacetime. While this term is apparently a consequence of the field equations of classical General Relativity, it is apparently of fourth order in α and hence has the effect of cancelling its contribution to the action. We show this explicitly for a classical, time-independent Robertson-Walker universe and argue that this cancellation must still be exact to a high degree of precision at the quantum level. Consequently, we argue that the cosmological constant must be exactly zero and certainly much much closer to zero than any actual positive value. This explanation can potentially apply to any form of gravity which derives its equations of motion from an action, and so may have wide applicability beyond classical General Relativity. This explanation is entirely theoretical and no direct experimental tests are proposed. However, we note that if this cancellation is exact to a high degree of precision, then quantum corrections to α could still give it a small but non-zero value. We briefly comment on the possible implications of this.

Modern wireless systems often operate in the finite resolution limit, where the signal bandwidth is smaller than the minimal spatial scales of the underlying environment or channel. In such scenarios, the channel response cannot be represented by a (possibly high-dimensional) vector, but instead lies in a low-dimensional manifold. This paper establishes the Gaussian- Quantization Bound (GQB) and the Max-Information Processing Bound (MIPB) on Grassmann manifolds of arbitrary dimensions. On top of establishing fundamental limits on communication, these results enable simple signaling algorithms that significantly outperform existing techniques in practice, especially in high-dimensional, low-resolution models. Moreover, we present a novel MIMO transceiver architecture that efficiently exploits these results, allowing to approach the capacity limits of the MIMO channels in the finite-resolution limit. In the finite-resolution regime, the transceiver design for MIMO systems has largely focused on the singular value decomposition (SVD) based waterfilling. However, this policy has been shown to be suboptimal even in low-dimensional models. In this work, we develop simple alternating and closed-form Max-Ratio-Max-Min (MRMM) transceiver algorithms that significantly outperform both SVD- and waterfilling-based approaches. In particular, we show that on Grassmann manifolds of arbitrary dimensions, the GQB and the MIPB can be tightly approximated by the $\log \det$ and the nuclear norm, respectively. These results, along with the MRMM algorithm, enable linear transceiver algorithms with near-optimal performance, even in high-dimensional, low-resolution models. Finally, we extend our results to the MIMO CSI feedback case, and establish the MIMO GQB and CSI MIPB. These results enable CSI acquisition via simple quantization algorithms that significantly outperform CSI averaging/refreshment.

The analysis of Hubble constant measurement from Hubble Space Telescope (HST) yields a value of 72.5 km/s/Mpc which corresponds to a distance modulus of 31.5 if we adopt the $\Lambda$CDM model with the current values of the cosmological and astrophysical parameters. However, if we assume the presence of a time-dependent, positive cosmological constant, the expansion of the universe would be self-accelerating and would lead to a distance modulus of 30.3 for the same values of the cosmological and astrophysical parameters. Alternatively, if we adopt the framework of a dark energy with a varying equation of state, we find a minimal reasonable value of -1 for the equation of state parameter and the distance modulus of 31.2 is reproduced for the same cosmological and astrophysical parameters as before. It is clear that the measurement of the Hubble constant could discriminate between these three possibilities and strongly favour a dark energy with a varying equation of state.

In this paper we study theoretically electron transmission through a strongly modulated one-dimensional spin-split quantum wire with local Rashba interaction. By using non-equilibrium Green's function method, we find that the transmitted spin-flipped electron spin current is strongly modulated by the wave vector of the electron spin precession in the Rashba interaction region. Due to the destructive interference between the spin-up and spin-down transmission amplitudes, the total spin current becomes nearly zero. However, we also show that the Fano factor, defined as the ratio of the zero-current noise to the mean current, is not suppressed even for strong modulation. In contrast, the zero-frequency noise, which is an indicator of the long-range correlations between the transmitted particles, remains finite even in the deep subband limit. Our results reveal the different roles of the real and momentum scattering in the spin transport of a spin-split quantum wire with Rashba interaction. The authors are gratefully acknowledged for helpful discussions with Yafis Barlas, Massoud Mobed Sayad, Matthias B[ä]{}ttig and Andreas Knorr. This work was supported by the DFG (research group 18 returned to service), by the Research Fund of the University of Hasselt, and by the Flemish supercomputing centre TIM Quinque and the Hercules Foundation (HERMES project).

The Milky Way (MW) accreted tens of satellite galaxies over its lifetime, some of which may have survived to the present day. These satellites, which can have masses ranging from 10s to 1000s of times that of the MW, can leave a coherent signal in the form of the stellar halo. Until now, such a signal has not been detected. Here I present a set of N-body simulations that demonstrate that satellite galaxies with the right properties can leave such a signal even after being completely disrupted. These simulations, which include the full response of the host halo and satellite to their interactions, are shown to match the properties of the stellar halo observed today. The accretion of such galaxies can therefore explain the stellar halo of the MW, a constraint which was previously thought difficult to satisfy. This is possible because the disruption of satellite galaxies leaves both dark and stellar haloes in the MW, and this stellar halo can be detected in current data. This work highlights the utility of galaxy haloes in exoplanet detection efforts, as many of the nearest bright stars are surrounded by faint stellar haloes that should be detectable with current instrumentation.

SNO+ is a next-generation Nobel Prize-winning solar neutrino observatory that will study the mysteries of the solar neutrinos by complementing the precision of the SNO experiment with a large far detectors and combining it with the detailed particle physics measurements provided by SNO+ solar beam. SNO+ will use the latest developments in scintillator technology to build the largest ever liquid mineral neutrino detectors, with megaton masses in the shallow underground Lake Baikal in Russia. SNO+ will study the incoming neutrinos, producing information about their emission properties, the inner workings of the Sun, and the consistency of the Standard Solar Model. These solar studies will help to better understand the stability of our climate system, the variability of which is critical to human survival. The wide spectrum of solar neutrinos provides a powerful tool to study the solar interior and resolve long-standing questions about the Sun. While studying the physics of the neutrinos will help us understand the workings of the Sun, the Sun’s energy output is needed to predict the neutrino flux. The Standard Solar Model uses the physical laws of quantum mechanics, special relativity, nuclear physics and much else, to model the structure and thermodynamics of the Sun. This model gives a close prediction of the total solar luminosity, but with a wide uncertainty. These uncertainties propagate to the predicted neutrino flux, and limit the ability of experimenters to probe new physics with solar neutrinos. New, precise measurements of the total solar luminosity could be made with a space-based solar radiometer, ACRIMSAT, which is now in operation. Alternatively, it has been proposed to use a neutrino beam created by targeting proton beam of an accelerator with an alloy target to create a neutrino beam at a lower cost. The near-term version of this idea, dubbed “SNO+”, would study solar neutrinos in the beamline at Boulby, United Kingdom, in order to determine the flux to an accuracy of 20%. This would provide a key calibration of the total solar luminosity and reduce the uncertainty on the prediction of the solar neutrino flux, and so provide the best opportunity for new physics to be discovered.

Single point mutations (SPMs) in protein sequences have long been of interest to biologists and engineers, due to their capability to affect protein stability and function. Historically, SPMs have been characterized with binary classification approaches, whereby proteins are classified as either stable or unstable based on some SPM-specific stability metric. While this metric-based approach has been useful, it has several limitations, including: i) the metric must be pre-calculated for the SPM of interest; ii) the metric typically analyzes the entire protein sequence rather than individual sites of the protein, and therefore loses site-specific information; and iii) the metric is based on an abstract protein representation, making the interpretation of stability changes difficult. Recently, a new SPM characterization paradigm has emerged, known as "energy decomposition analysis". In essence, this method first characterizes the wild-type protein with a high-level method like molecular mechanics energy decomposition analysis (MM-EDA). For each SPM, the method then decomposes the total energy difference between the wild-type and mutant proteins into residue-level contributions. This method allows us to capture site-specific contributions of the mutant and wild-type proteins, and therefore may be a better tool for understanding the stability impacts of SPMs. We tested this paradigm on the recently published CO-BRASS data set (1). In this dataset, the authors experimentally characterized the effects of 402 alanine mutations in flavodoxin (a 7.3 kD protein). Each mutation was examined in both the oxidizing (oxidized) and non-oxidizing (reduced) states. The authors determined that 220 mutations resulted in significant stability changes. Using the energy decomposition method, we were able to accurately predict whether a SPM would impact stability (i.e. be positive or negative). As shown in Table 1, we were able to achieve 91% accuracy on the test set. Although not particularly impressive, this level of performance is significant given that no feature engineering was done, and no additional data (e.g. structural information) was utilized. Here we present a Keck/DEIMOS spectroscopic survey of 28 candidate satellite galaxies of the Milky Way (MW) within 20 kpc of the galaxy center, based on data from the SDSS and Pan-STARRS1 surveys. We selected candidates using photometric positions and metallicities, and found that our survey is 80% complete to a limiting stellar mass of 1.2 x 10^8M⊙. We detect six new dwarf galaxies, the least massive of which has a likely mass of 8.1 x 10^7M⊙, or approximately one tenth of the mass of the least massive classical dwarf spheroidal (dSph). We compare our observations to predictions from the cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, Eris, and find that at the 95% confidence level Eris predicts that no galaxies with stellar masses less than 10% of that of the least massive detected galaxy should exist. Using this constraint, we calculate that Eris contains at most 1.2 x 10^8M⊙ of stellar mass, or 2.5% of the expected stellar mass of the least massive detected galaxy. We conclude that either the theoretical predictions of the number of low-mass galaxies in the Local Volume are in error by at least 2.5%– possibly up to five times more– or the earliest dwarf galaxies had much lower mass fractions of dark matter than the current paradigm assumes. We examine several possible explanations for the high predicted mass-to-light ratios of Eris, including that the stellar Initial Mass Function is top-heavy, that feedback processes in the simulation suppress star formation, or that the simulation includes too many baryonic components and does not faithfully reproduce the effects of Dark Matter. Future surveys with better volume and stellar mass completeness may be able to distinguish between these scenarios.

A system in thermal equilibrium displays fluctuations around its mean thermodynamic state. These fluctuations, or fluctuations around equilibrium, are quantified by the mean square deviations from the mean. The second order structure function is defined as the variance of these fluctuations. Its scaling behavior is described by the spectral density. In this paper we consider the case of an isolated quantum system which undergoes a unitary time evolution. We evaluate the fluctuations of the energy and show that the second order structure function exhibits activated behavior at low temperatures. This result is in agreement with recent experimental data. This article is based on a Master's thesis submitted to École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) in 2009 by STUART ALDISS under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Werner Krauth. The spectrum of a system at equilibrium displays an activated behavior at low energies. This result is shown to apply to the second order structure function of the energy for an isolated quantum system which undergoes a unitary time evolution. The contribution of this work is the evaluation of the fluctuations of the energy for an isolated quantum system, and the derivation of its second order structure function. This is a prerequisite to study its spectrum. In this article we consider the case of a quantum harmonic oscillator with canonical variables defined by the position and the momentum, and we evaluate the fluctuations of the energy for a general initial quantum state. The expression of the second order structure function is then deduced. This result is used to compare the contribution of the energy fluctuations to that of the partition function. The analysis is extended to the evaluation of the energy and the partition function for different thermodynamic states. These results allow the study of the spectrum by means of the dynamical structure function. The article concludes with a discussion of the possible implications of this result for recent experimental results which suggest the applicability of statistical mechanics to biological systems.

In the context of high-level, declarative programming languages, linear tabling is a strategy for computing definite integrals that has been known for more than a century. Despite recent algorithmic improvements, the implementation of linear tabling for high-performance computing platforms has been lacking, with the notable exceptions of VNCast and the UK SciPy Marching Cubes. In this work, we present a tabling implementation in the open-source Kepler code base, which allows for high-performance computing platforms to benefit from linear tabling. In particular, we describe a novel algorithm for eliminating the costly residual computation in the backward substitution step, as well as a hybrid method that combines backward substitution with a novel predictor-corrector strategy. We provide experimental results on a state-of-the-art HPC system using both MPI and OpenMP parallelism, showing that our implementation yields substantial performance improvements in the context of common scientific computing use cases.

In many scientific applications, especially those utilizing parallel architectures, the problem data is often distributed non-uniformly in memory, leading to inefficient use of local memory and parallel hardware. Multidimensional Data Redistribution (MDR) has been developed to address this problem. MDR allows the computation to access any portion of the data without requiring a shuffle. Unfortunately, existing MDR implementations suffer from excessive memory traffic and low efficiency on commodity clusters. We present the Earliest Vexed Exit (EVE), an optimization to MDR that reduces the memory traffic while maintaining high efficiency. EVE exploits the spatial locality of processes’ intermediate data to overlap computation with data redistribution. We evaluate EVE on a topology-independent benchmark and a model application and demonstrate up to a 4.7x speedup over the state-of-the-art MDR implementation on a 64-node Summit cluster with 24 CPUs.

This paper continues the study of fall of Quantum Vacuum Energy (QVE) begun in the preceding paper. In that paper it was shown that although in vacuum state the Quantum Vacuum Energy (QVE) falls as 1/r2 its apparent weight increases as 1/r1.5. In this paper we show that this increase is caused by the dynamical nature of the vacuum, the rate of change of which determines the rate of QVE fall. In the standard model quantum field theory QVE is determined by quantum fields fluctuations. Our results show that the dynamical nature of the vacuum ensures that the gravitational acceleration of the QVE fall is not constant but it varies in time in a way that depends on frequency of QVE oscillations. As a result, the apparent weight of the QVE increases with the square of the frequency of oscillations. The highest weight is observed at zero frequency. In the standard model QFT it equals zero for obvious reasons but in some extensions of the standard model it can have non-zero values. We discuss possible extensions that can provide non-zero QFT weight of Gravitational Constant. Acknowledgments. A stacked analysis of the deepest ISO-SWS and Spitzer MIPS 24um observations of the ESO/Sculptor Deep Field and SSA24 field are presented. A subsample of galaxies that satisfy the diagnostic of a robust detection at both 12um and 24um is selected, revealing a surprisingly bright median level of (1.5 +/- 0.2) x 1032 erg s-1 Hz-1 sr-1 Mpc-3 at 24um. Such a bright 24um background signal cannot be reconciled with a simple model of the evolution of normal galaxies, nor with the model of cold dark matter galaxy formation, even when allowing for a factor of 10 uncertainty in the amplitude of the redshift evolution. This 24um background signal is readily reconciled with the combined emission of normal galaxies, starburst galaxies, and powerful active galactic nuclei (AGN), but these terms are interpreted in a new fashion. Rather than normal galaxies, starburst galaxies, and powerful AGN, these galaxies are interpreted to be a new category of extremely dusty, rapidly evolving, massive ellipticals. Such extreme star formation activity in the most massive and dusty systems at the peak of galaxy formation is required to re-distribute mass and metals to the epoch at which they are observed, with a corresponding decrease in the star formation and AGN activity in less massive systems. Coupled with the previous work using the 12um data and updated methodology, this allows for a unifying model of the evolution of galaxies through cosmic time, in which galaxy formation is dominated by the evolution of a small number of high-redshift, extremely massive, rapidly evolving, dusty galaxies, with normal, starburst, and AGN galaxies arising as secondary populations from the merging/interaction of these dusty galaxies, which become the most massive systems in the local universe. Such a model is consistent with many galaxy evolution studies at other wavelengths, while providing new insights into the nature of the most extreme star-forming, dusty galaxies in the distant universe, and their link to the most massive and rapidly evolving massive galaxies at the peak of galaxy formation.

Penumbral filaments are observed in sunspots by spectrographs such as the Solar Dynamics Observatory's (SDO) Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI). They appear dark at continuum wavelengths but have bright roofs at coronal wavelengths (e.g., 171 A does not show penumbral filaments at all). Most explanations of these filaments focus on simple cool, dark, inversions, with three novel aspects. First, the period of the dominant signal increases from the inside to the outside of the filament. This is opposite of cool, dark inversions, which are expected to have a shorter period near the surface. Second, the period increases more rapidly near the edges of the filaments than in the interior. This is also unexpected from inversions, but may be explained by a model involving evaporation at the edges into a rarefied corona. Third, the frequency of the signal and the periodicity in the signal are the same up to the edge of the filament, but beyond this point the signal is multiples of the signal. These properties may all be explained by a model of magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) waves that become localized around sharp boundaries (for example, around field concentrations) due to a breaking mechanism. This model can also explain the spatially unresolved brightenings visible in other spectrographs such as Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on SDO.

Orbital-Free Density Functional Theory (OF-DFT) is an approach to electronic structure theory that combines the advantages of local density and wavefunction-based theories. The theory is formally obtained from conventional Density Functional Theory (DFT) by partitioning the total energy into a linear combination of local energy functionals, each depending on the density and one additional parameter. The parameters, called potentials, are determined by solving a constrained minimization problem. Thus, in contrast to DFT, the orbital-free OF-DFT does not assume a single-electron wavefunction and can therefore directly handle molecules and solids. We provide an implementation of the theory based on a numerical implementation of the Schrödinger equation in Lagrangian form. The theory is validated on molecules and solids and shown to give excellent results for several test cases. Finally, we present a case study of graphene on Au(111), where we find that interaction-induced physis and chemisn plays a significant role in determining the structures.

At ultra-relativistic energies, the survival of fragments produced by nuclear fragmentation depends on their atomic number Z. Larger fragments may survive the explosion, but are more likely to be completely destroyed in the shock front. Kr is a light, stable isotope that is often used in experiments studying nuclear fragmentation. We present here the fragmentation of this isotope at 64 MeV/nucleon, studying the properties of the produced fragments and their dependence on the distance between the source and the observer. We observe complete, charge-symmetric fragmentation for the first time in 64 MeV/nucleon fission-type reaction. This phenomenon is very different from the usually observed single-chondron evaporation-multiplicity-reduction type of fragmentation at lower energies. We also observe the onset of fission at much lower energies (~50 MeV/nucleon) than previously reported, which we attribute to the larger sample of nuclei produced by the new experimental setup. Our results will be compared with theoretical models, to increase understanding of the extreme conditions experienced by fission fragments at ultra-relativistic energies.

We consider Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms for sampling from probability distributions over graphs that are Bernoulli- randomized (. Mrg), dependent on some vector of random variables Θ. Such distributions are often intractable to sample from directly, even using dynamic programming. We present Gibbs sampling, a family of algorithms that alternates between sampling from the graph distribution and performing conditional draws of the underlying variables given the graph. We analyze the mixing time of Gibbs sampling on a broad class of sparse random graphs. On average, our graph distributions lie in a high-dimensional parameter space and have “RDP” (rich get richer) nodes, allowing us to characterize the mixing time in terms of a strong form of the neighborhood growth theorem. In particular, we show that the spectral gap of the transition kernel of the graph walk increases geometrically in sample size. As an immediate consequence, we obtain convergence rates independent of the number of nodes, uniformly over all graph topologies, as well as for the number of iterations required for the method to produce a given probability of acceptance. We provide numerical experiments supporting our theory and demonstrating the effectiveness of our method on real data.

(65489) Ceto/Phorcys: A tidally-evolved binary Centaur is a target of interest for the next OSIRIS-REx mission, which is designed to gather samples for analysis on Earth. Ceto/Phorcys has a size of 16.2 km x 19.1 km and an albedo of ~0.5. If its density is comparable to that of water (nine kilograms per cubic meter), then Ceto/Phorcys has a radius of approximately 12 km. Given these dimensions and the currently-known orbital parameters, it will make several close approaches to Earth in the next few centuries, including a nominal approach with a distance of <0.15 AU in the year 2195. Masses, composition, and other physical characteristics will be discussed for Ceto and Phorcys, as well as their binary nature and evolution.

A concise technique to create efficient numerical stable implementations of factorials is presented. The technique is particularly well suited for fixed-point hardware such as FPGAs and ASICs. As a generic example, we present a fixed-point 16.16 (16 bits signed and 16 bits integer) factorial implementation that runs approximately six times faster than the standard Booth algorithm on a 8th generation Intel Core i7 processor while maintaining numerical stability. Additionally, we present a fixed-point 16.16 512 byte multiplier that is six times faster than the current best fixed-point 16.16 multiplier and 10 times smaller than the IEEE 754-2008 binary multiplier. Background The calculation of factorials has a long history in computer hardware, with efficient implementations relying on a combination of fixed point, polynomial and series expansions. Recently, we presented a concise technique, termed "Multiple Integer-Width Adders", which can be used to efficiently compute arbitrary integer factorials. Multiple Integer-Width Adders The Multiple Integer-Width Adders (MIA) technique computes an integer factorial N! using a network of adders, each computing the factorial of a small factor. These intermediate results are then added sequentially to the product of the two smaller factorials, with carry propagation across the network. The final result is obtained by discarding the high-order bits of each addend, resulting in a numerical scheme that is immune to accumulation of rounding error. Example Consider the factorial of 8! (8 factorial). We break this computation up into 7 multi-adder networks, each computing the factorial of 2, 4, or 6. These results are shown below as 2! 4! 6! (factors of 2, 4, and 6). These intermediate results are added sequentially, with carry propagation from left to right. Finally, the high-order bits are dropped, resulting in 8! (factorial of 8). N! = 2! * 4! * 6! + 2! * 4! * 6! + 2! * 4! * 6! The MIA technique can be applied to any mathematical function that can be computed using a network of adders. By combining the flexibility of custom networks with the simplicity of a fixed-point adder abstraction, the MIA technique has the potential to increase the performance of a wide range of fixed-point hardware accelerator designs. Hardware Implementation We present the design, circuit synthesis, and testing of two MIA multipliers and a shifter. The first multiplier uses a dedicated circuit to implement the MIA addition stages, whereas the second multiplier uses a generic multiplier circuit and performs custom back-propagation and carry generation. Both multiplier designs achieve more than 6 times faster multiply-with-factorial operations than the best Booth-based multiply-with-factorial implementation, while maintaining numerical stability. The KATRIN experiment at FZK has finished taking data for the beta decay spectrum on |$q$| = 0.75 eV/c and aims to determine the neutrino mass hierarchy. KATRIN uses a totally dark room with sub-ppm levels of background radiation to measure the beta spectrum. The experiment is expected to reach a sensitivity to the neutrino mass of 0.35-0.9 eV at the 1 σ level, depending on the neutrino hierarchy, and to right-handed currents in the neutrino sector with a sensitivity of 10-35%. The experiment uses an array of 18 metallic wires (katrodes) with an inner diameter of 3 mm that are actuated relative to one another to reduce the motion noise of a micro-manipulator that sits on top of the wires. The wire axial motion is read out with a reflection hybrid, and the phase of the reflection signal is used to determine the time of flight. For high precision determination of the endpoint, a high speed digitizer with 0.5 ns timing is used to record the spectra.

We study theoretically spin-dependent transport properties of superconducting single-electron transistors (SSETs) connected in parallel to normal-metal electrodes. The conductance of each SSET as well as the total conductance of the structure depend on the relative orientation of the magnetic moments of the two SSETs and the spin polarization of the terminals. We analyze the influence of the phase differences between the superconductor leads on the magnetoconductance oscillations. We show that the structure exhibits a new kind of nonequilibrium magnetic response, which is based on the difference between the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic arrangements of the magnetic moments. The phenomenon is analogous to the exchange enhancement of magnetoresistance in magnetic heterostructures. We observe oscillations of the total conductance related to the flux quantum through the SSETs' Josephson junctions. The position and the amplitude of the peaks in the magnetic response as well as the period of the flux quantum oscillations depend on the phase differences between the superconductors. These results could be used to develop sensors based on magnetic superinductances using hybrid structures with SSETs.'

In this paper, we consider the problem of non-parametric field estimation using a large number of independent, randomly deployed binary sensors. Each sensor is capable of sensing an entire field, but only senses a small, local region of the field. We assume that each sensor makes a Bernoulli observation, indicating that a field element is in its sensing region with probability p, and otherwise indicates that the field element is not in its sensing region. We assume a fixed sensing radius and a fixed density of deployed sensors. We propose a non-parametric field estimation algorithm which, given sufficiently many observations, produces an estimate of the field that minimizes a cost function which quantifies the bias and variance of the estimate. The algorithm is inspired by recent results in compressed sensing, and provides a theoretical performance guarantee when the sensing radius is sufficiently small. We also present extensive simulation results which demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm in practice, both for a synthetic field and for a dataset describing magnetic field measurements in a fusion reactor.' Link to Paper: [https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.09435](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.09435)

The classical distance scale to galaxies is based on the Cepheid variable stars in the Milky Way and in host galaxies with accurate distances measured via trigonometric parallax. In order to calibrate this relation, it is useful to have methods that measure the distances to galaxies outside of our own. In this Letter we present an alternative method based on the properties of stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The LMC is our closest satellite galaxy and is a excellent calibration point as its distance is well established via measurement of its Hubble flow velocity. We use the fact that stars in the LMC are mostly red clump stars. The properties of red clump stars are well understood and can be used to measure their distances via multi-variable polynomial fits. We find the median distance to the LMC measured via this method is 18.1 kpc, with an estimated observational uncertainty of 0.4 kpc. We measure the distance to five populous star clusters in the LMC and apply the same technique to these clusters and find they are also around 18 kpc with a small range in distance of 0.1 kpc. We conclude that the precision of this method for determining the distance to the LMC is 0.4 kpc.

A 520 MeV/nucleon proton beam from the CERN SPS was used to study matter stopping in U+U collisions. The measurement of the projectile fragmentation produced in the interaction was used to infer the properties of the created system. Results on stopping in U+U collisions are presented and compared to the expectations of a simple sum of individual nucleons. The results suggest that in these collisions primary fragments interact strongly before they stop in the collision volume. The CERN SPS has recently restarted operations with a stable beam of 520 MeV/nucleon. These beams have been used to study matter stopping in U+U collisions. This measurement was performed using the detection of secondary fragmentation particles produced in the interaction. These secondary particles are typically emitted in the later stages of the interaction between the projectile and target when most of the stopped material has already been ejected from the collision volume. The results suggest that in U+U collisions primary fragments interact strongly before they stop in the collision volume. This study was presented at the 45th International Nuclear Physics Conference (November 10-16, 2016, Chicago). Reference: J. Chen et al. Optical Probe Diffusion (OPD) is a non-invasive and non-destructive analysis technique used to determine the distribution of molecular sizes in a solution. This technique is based on the random movement of particles in a fluid, which is called "Brownian motion". OPD uses a Laser Point Source and an Oil Spreading Plate to measure the displacement of particles within the fluid. Within the oil, the intensity of the Light Point Source is higher on one side than the other. The distribution of the particles in the fluid is related to the strength of the Brownian motion. Smaller particles travel more than larger particles. By analyzing the Light Intensity variation on the Spreading Plate it is possible to determine the size distribution. Polymer solutions are used in different applications and their molecular weight can be changed during processing. This variation can affect the mechanical and optical properties. In this work, we present an Optical Probe Diffusion analysis of polymer solutions and how this can be used to follow their molecular weight during processing. Our findings show that it is possible to follow the variation of molecular weight using this non-destructive technique with high repeatability.

Planetary microlensing events are commonly observed for 3-4 weeks following the peak time in order to search for a debris cloud near the planet host star, but the detectability of the cloud depends on the event properties as well as the distances to the lens and the observer. Therefore, we propose a method to select the optimal target events for the follow-up observation from a pool of candidates given a set of resources such as the telescope time and the amount of resource. As a case study, we applied this method to the follow-up observation of OGLE-2017-nom27, one of the two microlensing events toward the nearby star catalog in the bulge region of the Milky Way. We selected bumper events with similar properties to OGLE-2017-nom27 as the follow-up candidate events and found that the simulated detectability of the bumper event was similar to that of OGLE-2017-nom27. In particular, we found that the detectability of the event was not necessarily high when the lens or the source object had large proper motion. This suggests that the follow-up observation of the microlensing events toward the bulge region can be efficiently conducted by selecting the follow-up candidate events based on the properties of the original event.

We present a detailed study of the physical properties of a sample of 50 MgII absorbers at z = 2.5 (1+z = 2.5), selected from the SSA22 field based on visual and model fits to their spectra, and observed with the FMOS and GES at the Subaru Telescope. By fitting the Mg II and metal lines in the quasar spectra with synthetic spectra we measure their physical properties: gas phase metal abundances, velocity widths and internal gas pressures, the latter of which we utilize in combination with the Mg II column densities to calculate the total mass of the gas halos. We compare our measurements to predictions from high-resolution, large N-body/hydrodynamical simulations, and find good agreement for the ensemble properties of the sample, and weak to no evolution in the individual absorber properties with redshift. However, we find that the absorbers have an effective radius of b(eff) = 1.2 ± 0.3 physical kpc at z = 2.5, an order of magnitude smaller than predicted from recent results for the relationship between Mg II absorber properties and dark matter halo masses. We argue that this discrepancy may be reconciled by taking into account the effect of feedback and galactic feedback in the simulations, which can significantly reduce the extent of the galaxy halo dark matter envelopes.' We also present weak lensing measurements of the mass distribution in the same field using optical imaging from the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) survey. We find no significant correlations between absorber properties and the positions of individual galaxies, nor of the dark matter halos themselves, nor of the HSC-inferred dark matter distribution. However, we do find that the effective radius of the gas halos measured from absorption are weakly but significantly correlated with the mass of the corresponding dark matter halos; this correlation has been observed previously in simulation, and is consistent with theories of hydrodynamical instability induced by cold, low-density gas accretion onto dark matter halos. Overall, we find good agreement between absorption-based and lensing-based halo mass measurements, suggesting that observed Mg II absorbers likely trace the most highly biased regions of the underlying dark matter distribution, and that further studies of these objects can be used to study structure formation and the circum-galactic medium.

Using state-of-the-art galaxy formation models, this study compares the predicted evolution of the rest-frame optical luminosity function (LF) with that observed in the Cosmic Assembly Near-Infrared Deep Extragalactic Survey (CANDELS) UltraDeep field at 2.0<z<3.3. The models considered span a wide range of assumptions, including the formation history of dark matter halos, the efficiency with which galaxies grow their baryons, the mechanisms by which outflowing gas is heated and cooled, and the spectral energy distribution of galaxies. Despite the considerable parametric freedom, the models are able to capture many of the observed features of the high-redshift LF, most notably the bright-end cut-off. The simulated LFs do, however, under-predict the number of galaxies at the faint-end and in particular at the very-low-luminosity end. A better match to the observed number density of low-luminosity galaxies can be obtained by introducing explicit episodes of “delayed" galaxy feedback, but such models are still unable to reproduce the fraction of galaxies that are quiescently star-forming at fixed luminosity. The failure of current models to reproduce the faint-end slope of the high-redshift LF might suggest that feedback processes have been over-efficient at preventing the cooling of gas at high redshift, or that the active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback mode is not particularly efficient at expelling gas from low-accretion rate galaxies. Additional processes such as energy re-distribution by radiation and/or effective viscosity in the gas disk or merger-induced starbursts might also play a role in suppressing cooling and driving gas out of galaxies. Redshift range: 2.0<z<3.3 Galaxy formation models have developed dramatically in recent years, incorporating more physics and a wider parameter range. With a dedicated calibration to low-redshift observations, such models can now predict the evolution of the galaxy population to high redshifts. By using the Great Observatories Origins Survey (GOODS) Ultra Deep Field (CDF-UDF), this study directly compares the predictions of seven such models with that of the observed evolution of the rest-frame optical luminosity function (LF) at 2.0<z<3.3. Despite the considerable parametric freedom, the models are able to capture many of the observed features of the high-redshift LF, most notably the bright-end cut-off. The simulated LFs do, however, under-predict the number of galaxies at the faint-end and in particular at the very-low-luminosity end. A better match to the observed number density of low-luminosity galaxies can be obtained by introducing explicit episodes of “delayed" galaxy feedback, but such models are still unable to reproduce the fraction of galaxies that are quiescently star-forming at fixed luminosity.
