Spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) is one of the most remarkable phenomena in physics. SSB usually occurs in ordered phases, and is usually associated with the long-range orders. However, spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) can also occur in the absence of long-range order. Here we report a novel type of SSB in spin systems, which occurs in the disordered phase and does not require any conservation law. We demonstrate this phenomenon in the spin-1/2 XXZ chain with spatial anisotropy and frustration, where the homogeneous ground state spontaneously breaks the translational and rotational symmetries. We call this type of SSB “spontaneous translational SSB” (STSSS). We obtain the wave functions of the elementary excitations and discuss the stability of the SSB against small perturbations. Finally, we discuss the experimental realization of the model and the relation to experiments on Na2V3O7.

In this paper we prove a general version of the Kalman--Yakubovich--Popov (KYP) inequality for discrete-time passive systems described by linear difference equations. We provide a simple and unified approach to the classical KYP inequality, including results for discrete-time LTI systems, discrete-time linear time-varying (LTV) systems, and continuous-time LTV systems. We also extend the KYP inequality to the case of partial measurements. Finally, we show that the classical KYP inequality for LTI systems with input constraints is a consequence of our more general result. The classical KYP inequality, valid for LTI systems, states that the difference between the observability and controllability Gramian matrices is a semi-positive definite quadratic form with respect to the input matrix. This result has been extended to LTI systems with input constraints (i.e., with zero inputs) by various authors. In contrast, here we provide a simple and unified treatment for discrete-time passive systems described by linear difference equations. More specifically, we show that the observability, controllability and total-squared-root-norm matrices of the discrete-time passive system have symmetric positive semidefinite quadratic forms with respect to the input matrix. As a consequence, we obtain a general version of the KYP inequality for discrete-time passive systems. We provide a simple approach to the classical KYP inequality based on a formula for the input-output map of a discrete-time passive system in terms of its transition matrix. In this way we obtain a new proof of this result for discrete-time LTI systems, discrete-time LTV systems and continuous-time LTV systems. As an example, we also prove the classical KYP inequality for LTI systems with input constraints. Finally, we apply our results to design an observer for a linear time-invariant system with bounded gain, based on the discrete-time output error, and to establish a discrete-time analogue of the Continuous-time LQR Theorem for discrete-time passive systems.

Novel technique for monitoring the performance of the LAT instrument on board the GLAST satellite J. R. Leon, V. Reglero, G. B. Hobbs, R. E. Ransome, A. A. Aguilar-Torres LAT, also known as the Large Area Telescope, is a Gamma Ray Telescope with a large surface area (about 4% of a sphere) and fine angular resolution (about 10 degrees half-power diameter) designed to detect gamma rays from a large region of the sky and perform gamma-ray bursts or air showers. To enable the detection of astrophysical gamma-rays of energies as low as 20 MeV, the detector's response is calibrated using a radioactive source inserted into a small canister attached to the outside of the LAT. This calibration, however, can only be performed periodically, since repeated insertions of the canister could change the performance of the LAT. We present a novel technique to monitor the performance of the LAT without re-insertion of the radioactive source canister. The technique makes use of the regular cargo satellite Chang'e 3, which carries an identical canister with a radioactive source, to perform a similar calibration maneuver but on a regular basis. We show that the agreement between the response measured using the radioactive source on Chang'e 3 and the one measured using a similar canister on the LAT is within 10% for all energies between 20 MeV and 100 GeV. This article is a recommended reading for the PHYSICS OF GAMMA RAYS II (December 2017)

The complexity of model checking higher-order logic has been a long-standing open problem. Since the 1980s, model checking has been reduced to decision problems for several fragments of higher-order logic. However, in the worst case, checking whether a given formula is satisfied by all fixpoints of a fixpoint logic formula requires solving a Picard iteration, an optimal fixpoint algorithm, for every projection of the logic formula. Thus, even when the logic formula is over a small set of variables, model checking Higher-Order Fixpoint Logic (HOF logic) is np-hard. We study HOF logic in the parameterized complexity framework, where the complexity of a problem is bound by a function of the size of the formula. We give two parameterizations: tree decomposition, and block decomposition. We show that model checking HOF logic with respect to tree decompositions is FPT, and we prove that model checking HOF logic with respect to block decompositions is not FPT. Our parameterizations leave plenty of room for further parameterizations. We also give a 3d-Printable structure, a width-bounded syntactic abstraction, that preserves FPT parameterized complexity.

Extreme High Energy (EHE) peaked BL Lacs (HBLs), knowns as the Third Frequency, are largely unobservable at optical wavelengths due to their high Doppler-shifted equivalent widths. Here we report on optical spectroscopy of 32 EHE HBLs performed with the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory (NGSOM) spectrograph. This is the largest homogeneous sample of EHE HBLs with optical spectroscopy to date. We observe compelling connections between EHE HBLs and low Doppler-shifted optical magnitudes in a complex web of correlations among equivalent width, full width at half-maximum, continuum spectral slope, redshift, and synchrotron peak frequency. Higher equivalent widths, higher full width at half-maximum, steeper spectral slopes, and higher redshifts are all associated with the presence of low Doppler-shifted optical components. Conversely, lower equivalent widths, lower full width at half-maximum, flatter spectral slopes, and lower redshifts are associated with the absence of optical components at or near the host galaxy systemic redshift. We measure the highest equivalent widths and full widths at half-maximum yet observed in the optical band from EHE HBLs. The results of this work have profound implications for EHE HBL central engines, trigger models, and EBL re-processing.

Neel surface anisotropy (NSA) is a novel magnetic anisotropy which has been proposed as an effective way to stabilize magnetic nanoparticle (MNPs) structures. In this study, the effective anisotropies and energy barriers of NSA, tetrahedral and cube anisotropy types are derived and compared. It is shown that the NSA can stabilize various MNP geometries such as cube, octahedron, decahedron and octapod, in addition to the usual capped and hollow triangles. Moreover, it is observed that NSA has the ability to induce high effective anisotropies in very small particle sizes. Finally, it is demonstrated that NSA can provide higher anisotropy barriers than tetrahedral anisotropy for some particles with very thin diameters A. Hamza et al., Effect of Neel Surface Anisotropy on the structural and magnetic properties of cubic, octahedral and decahedral Co nanoparticles, Applied Sciences: Journal of University of Sciencies, 12(1), February 2018, Pages: 136-144. https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.01696

Dewetting is an important micro-machining technique for nanometer-scale feature fabrication in a wide range of materials, including metals, semiconductors and dielectrics. The process relies on the removal of a thin layer of material from one substrate to produce a thin film of the material on another substrate. Dewetting is initiated by selectively reducing the temperature of one or more regions of the substrate material, which can be thermal, chemical or mechanical patterning. One typical dewetting scenario is the removal of a thin layer of material from a bulk semi-conductor to produce a thin film of the material on another substrate. This generally results in the formation of one or more holes, which can have sharp edges and possess a high energy surface in the form of a free-air interface. A significant problem in this scenario is the ability of the edge of the hole to relax towards equilibrium, which requires the provision of sufficient edge energy to overcome surface tension forces. In this work, we perform a full-scale hydrodynamic calculation of the relaxation of an initially circular dewetting hole, which is constrained at its edges and is free to move in two dimensions. We compare the evolution of the hole shape and energy with both circular and elliptic equilibrium solutions, and examine the importance of various physical mechanisms for relaxation, including bulk diffusion, convection and surface tension.

Cosmic rays play a key role in the evolution of dense molecular clouds. They induce ionization and chemical reactions and trigger the formation of star clusters. In this work, we show that high-energy particles produced by pulsars and active galaxies can have a significant effect on the formation of the first stars and galaxies. We performed detailed calculations of the formation of Population III (Pop III) stars in minihalos subject to the combined effect of the photoelectric effect and ionization, as well as the pair production and photon pressure exerted by high-energy particles. We find that the mean free path of low-energy particles is much larger than the size of the minihalos, and thus the effect of cosmic rays is to induce local variations in the density and temperature but has no global effect. We also estimate the effect of cosmic rays on the formation of the first low-mass galaxies. At the end of the simulations, we calculate the expected fraction of metals produced by Pop III stars. We find that the presence of cosmic rays can increase this fraction by up to one order of magnitude in the most favorable conditions. We discuss the conditions under which this process can lead to the early transition from Pop III to Pop II star formation.

The origin of the light elements Li, Be and B in X-ray binaries is a long-standing question, but its answer is still debated. It is now possible to study this issue via the detection and measurement of the 6Li/7Li isotopic ratio in the light elements lithium and beryllium, which exhibits a different behaviour in these two scenarios. In particular, a 6Li/7Li isotopic ratio below 10-11 can only be reproduced if the light elements are of extragalactic origin, whereas a ratio below 10-12 indicates the presence of Li synthesized in the interior of stars, such as our Sun. We report new measurements of the 6Li/7Li isotopic ratio in the metal-rich giant Cen X-4, which reveals a ratio of 7.3(3) x 10-12, consistent with the presence of Li formed in the interior of stars. We also report the first upper limit on 6Li/7Li in another metal-rich giant, h Per, which exhibit a ratio above 10-11, consistent with the presence of Li formed in the interiors of stars. We discuss the implications of these results for the formation channel of Li in X-ray binaries and future directions.

Space elevators have been proposed to enable low-cost access to LEO. The proposed Space Elevator consists of an electrodynamic tethered shaft that augments the capacity of low-Earth orbit (LEO) by counteracting orbital decay and enabling elevator cars to access higher speeds. Electrostatic space elevators have been shown to enable additional capacity over electrodynamic elevators. However, previous work has not examined the optimal configuration of an electrostatic space elevator, nor has it incorporated actual fabrication considerations. In this paper we develop a framework for optimal design of electrostatic space elevators based on the concept of virtual work. We demonstrate that a toroidal ring structure is optimal, in that it achieves the greatest total torque about the Earth's center. The total structural height of the optimal ring, as well as the radius of the ring, is determined by the length of the tether and the strength of the background magnetic field. We evaluate the performance of the optimal ring design against several criteria: total energy cost, maximum structural height, and power consumption. The optimal electrostatic space elevator has a structural height of 16,875 km, which is over 62% greater than the Electrodynamic elevator proposed in the 2004 Space Elevator Act. The total cost of the optimal space elevator is $2.3T, where T is a specified operational lifetime, compared to $3.7T for the electrodynamic space elevator. Thus, even with a much longer operational lifetime, the total cost of the optimal space elevator is approximately 20% less than the electrodynamic design.

A large family of type ${\rm II_1}$ factors with property (T) are constructed via an approximation procedure using sequence of uniform type ${\rm II_1}$ factors with countably infinite fundamental group. This allows us to obtain type ${\rm II_1}$ factors with any countable fundamental group. As an application, it is shown that the free group of countably many generators has Property (T) as a group relative to its boundary at infinity. 2 In this paper, we develop a method to construct type ${\rm II_1}$ factors with prescribed countable fundamental group. The main idea is to approximate a given type ${\rm II_1}$ factor $M$ with property (T) by a sequence of uniform type ${\rm II_1}$ factors $M_n$ with countably infinite fundamental group. By Takesaki's duality, we can identify the dual of $M_n$ with $M$. Using this identification, we can formulate the dual action of $M$ on its unique separable infinite dimensional subalgebra $\overline{M}_n\subset M_n$ through the normalizer of the uniform MASA. We then apply Elliott's classification theorem to $\overline{M}_n$ to obtain a (unique) type ${\rm II_1}$ factor $N$ with countable fundamental group such that $M_n$ is continuously orbit equivalent to $N\ast\mathbb{Z}$. This allows us to obtain type ${\rm II_1}$ factors with any countable fundamental group. As an application, it is shown that the free group of countably many generators has Property (T) as a group relative to its boundary at infinity.

This paper describes the results of a search for sterile neutrinos using an exposure of 21.7 cm³·years at the Double Chooz nuclear reactor. We search for spectral shape distortions in the electron anti-neutrino spectrum produced by a point-like nuclear reactor, by the mixing of at least one sterile neutrino with the three active neutrinos. We perform a precision profile-based analysis using six observables from the Double Chooz near and far detectors and three parameters describing the three active-sterile neutrino oscillation scenarios. We find no evidence for the sterile neutrinos and set an upper limit of 0.29 at the 95% confidence level (CL) on the mixing parameter, Ω sterile. This is the first search for sterile neutrinos using an exposure of 21.7 cm³·years at the Double Chooz nuclear reactor. We also perform a global sensitivity study that includes previous reactor antineutrino experiments. For the first time, we find a positive sterile neutrino parameter space region at more than 3 standard deviations from the expected value for all scenarios that can explain the reported 3.5 standard deviation excesses found in previous short-baseline experiments.

Long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most violent explosions in the universe. However, their study is complicated by their unpredictable, randomly directed beams, making it difficult to precisely localize them. Short-lived and beamed Gamma-Ray Bursts with known cosmological redshifts provide a crucial opportunity for studying the nature of the universe and its structure. A majority of long GRBs have been observed with the Swift satellite, which provides not only rapid localization but also a wealth of multi-wavelength data. We have examined the spectral evolution of 57 Swift long GRBs with known redshifts, finding that three distinctly different regimes exist. The first regime is characterized by a cooling break followed by a simple power law. Between two and four dissipation slopes are observed in this regime. The second regime, seen in 17 bursts, is characterized by an initial thermal component with a blackbody function or a non-thermal tail, followed by a single power law. In the third and final regime, seen in 30 bursts, no identifiable spectral break is present and the spectra are well fit by a single power law. The cosmological models that best describe the observed burst data are curveduploads and a finite universe, with a probability of 68.3% and 95.7% respectively. This result is surprising because standard candle models assume that all bursts have the same intrinsic luminosity, which would result in a single power law across all regimes. This work was supported in part by a NASA Swift Award No. 1223370 to the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

A single transverse-spin asymmetry (TSA) is observed in the production of two hadrons with back-to-back jets in proton proton collisions at sqrt[s]=13 TeV. The TSA is measured as a function the difference in the absolute value of the transverse momentum of the two hadrons, |Δ|tp, and the absolute value of the sine of thehadron polar scattering angle in the azimuthal plane, |Δ|sinc. A significant TSA is observed for hadron-pair transverse momenta of 50-450 GeV and |Δ|tp |>&mu|Ms + 20 |, where Ms is the mass of the strange quark. The TSA is compared to models based on global parton distributions, collineation-based parton distributions, fragmentation functions, and scalar and axial-vector diquark production. None of these models is found to give a good description of the TSA over the whole measured region. Some of these models are found to give a reasonable description of the TSA over specific regions of the measured parameter space.

Deconstructing dwarf galaxies: a Suprime-Cam survey of Andromeda II [...] This paper presents the first results of an exploratory program designed to characterize the structures of nearby faint galaxies using deep imaging obtained with the Subaru Prime-Focus Camera (Suprime-Cam). Our survey, of the small, faint Andromeda II (M31N) system, probes primarily the system's diffuse light, and it is 100% orbit-based, avoiding the well-known problems of bright-center incubation and particle-hole problems associated with galaxy-sensitive wide-field imagers. From images obtained in June and July 2005, we detect an unprecedented number of resolved stars in M31N, and use these to precisely measure the galaxy's structural parameters and velocity dispersion. The luminosity-specific stellar mass-to-light ratio is high (M/L˜300–500 M⊙/L⊙), consistent with previously-observed Local Group dwarfs, and the structural parameters are similar to those of other Local Group dSph galaxies with little evidence for dark matter. We use these observations to examine several scenarios for the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies. In the closest system to our Milky Way, we find compelling evidence that M31N is a low luminosity post-merger remnant of a collision between two dwarfs. If so, this represents the first direct evidence for the hierarchical clustering paradigm of large-scale structure formation. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Brian Maxwel Harrington (1936–2004).

The angular momentum is removed from the gas by magnetic winds and the gravitational torque of the forming planets. The characteristic scale of the transitional disk is about a few tenth of au, which is small enough for the gravitational torque to remove the angular momentum sufficiently fast. We perform 3D MHD simulations with planet on orbits of 100, 500 and 2000 au, and find that the inner disks are fully cleared within 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 orbital periods, respectively. For the 2000-au-wide disk, the mm-sized grains are also depleted by the direct gravitational drag in a shorter time scale of a few tens of orbits. Our results show that the transitional disks inside-out evacuate via the magnetic wind and the planet induced gravitational torque. In this paper, we propose a new geometric flow, called the nonholonomic Ricci flow, for non-symmetric metrics on manifolds. The nonholonomic Ricci flow preserves the nonholonomic structure and it reduces to the corresponding geometric flow on symmetric spaces. We study examples of nonholonomic manifolds that solve the nonholonomic Ricci flow, including some physically important examples, such as Einstein spaces, commutative or noncommutative Hyperkähler manifolds and certain Lagrange spaces. We also discuss the case of non-positive horizontal curvature and applications to algebraic and symplectic geometry. We show that the flow between two nonholonomic metrics with non-trivial distinguished structure is completely defined by the Hamiltonian function on the dual 1-form and Hamilton-Cartan canonical equations. Using the method of conservation laws and choosing an appropriate density, we find solutions of the nonholonomic Ricci flow for non-commutative Hyperkähler manifolds and some commutative and noncommutative examples. The Ricci flow can be considered as an example of the large class of geometric flows that involve nonholonomic constraints. In particular, for certain types of nonholonomic distributions and constraints it allows to prove long-time solutions and study singular limits. We prove that for nonholonomic manifolds with Killing and hyper-Killing structures the flow provides derivatives of the solution that are determined by the initial metric and certain non-linear functionals that can be expressed in terms of flows on symmetric spaces. Our results provide a unified approach to geometric flow solvers on nonholonomic manifolds and prove that the nonholonomic Ricci flow and certain singular limits have very good properties, such as long-time solutions, smooth singular limits and property to reduce to the geometric flow on symmetric spaces. In this paper we study algebraically closed real geodesics on n-dimensional ellipsoids. We prove that algebraically closed real geodesic loops on ellipsoids are dense in the space of all free loops provided the algebraically closed field is sufficiently large and the loop is sufficiently non-constant. We also study relations of algebraically closed real geodesics on ellipsoids to hyperelliptic tangential coverings of the projective plane and to real Jacobi varieties. The presented results have many applications, in particular in the theory of integrable systems, Klein geometry and mirror symmetry. For example, we show that algebraically closed real geodesic loops on ellipsoids correspond to multiple covers of the projective plane with branch loci being real curves of minimal genus. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 1 we give some necessary definitions and present some preliminary facts. In Section 2 we study algebraically closed real geodesics on ellipsoids. In Section 3 we discuss relations between algebraically closed real geodesics on ellipsoids and tangential coverings of the projective plane. In Section 4 we present consequences of our study for real Jacobi varieties.

Tumour development involves the growth of mutant cells which arise due to DNA mutations. These mutant cells can vary in number within a clonal population in a way that appears to be genetically programed. We characterized the growth dynamics of a clonal population of tumour cells from a long-term in vitro evolution experiment. We found that the population grew exponentially for most of the period of observation, but there were periods of time where the population grew sub-exponentially and periods of time where the population grew exponentially but at a different rate than the median. We developed a model to describe this growth variability, which includes the effects of intrinsic noise and cell density-dependent signalling. This model captures the qualitative features of the data and can explain the period of exponential growth followed by transitions to sub-exponential and linear growth. These results quantitatively describe a genetically driven form of population variability and should be of broad interest to those studying developmental dynamics and evolution of clonal populations.

Anisotropic exchange interaction between the nearest neighbors in quantum spin systems generates a spontaneous DM vector that determines the chirality of the system. If this DM vector is perpendicular to thechain, the qubits in the chain get entangled by an antisymmetric part of the anisotropic interaction. This work reports an experimental implementation of such a chain with $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ atoms in an optical lattice. By measuring the entanglement of the pair of atoms at the edges of the chain we have shown that the entanglement survives for a long time. We have observed a logarithmic scaling of the life-time with the length of the chain which is in agreement with the theoretical expectation. Low surface brightness (SB) galaxies are dark matter dominated structures whose physical extent is difficult to study in detail using traditional optical techniques due to their low luminosities. Fortunately, they emit most of their light beyond IR wavelengths, which makes them easier to study with optical/NIR observations coupled with mid/far-IR observations. Although low SB galaxies emit most of their light in the infrared, relatively few such systems have been studied in the infrared due to difficulties in observing them and low sensitivity of existing infrared telescopes. Recently, the *Wide Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) has begun to make deep infrared maps of the whole sky, thus opening a new window to explore SB galaxies in the infrared. In this work, we carry out a cross-correlation study of the WISE and Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) optical data for a sample of low SB galaxies selected using infrared criteria, and perform an analysis of the properties of the resulting infrared-selected systems. We find that IR-selected galaxies cover a wide range of masses (10<$log(M_{star}/M_{\odot})$<12) and redshifts (0.05<z<0.5), and we study their spatial distribution, star formation rates, and stellar populations, as well as the dependence of these properties on various galaxy parameters, such as optical SB and size. We find that IR-selected galaxies tend to be more concentrated and compact than similar optical-SB systems, have older stellar populations, and have suppressed star formation rates. We also study the properties of the high SB SDSS galaxies in the sample and find that some of them appear to be massive spiral galaxies seen at an angle which causes them to appear as low surface brightness galaxies in optical imaging. However, the majority of our IR-selected systems have low masses and appear to be massive Ellipticals or S0 galaxies. Therefore, the sample demonstrates the limitations of the current optical techniques used to select high SB galaxies and the need for multi-wavelength studies to characterize the galaxies fully.**

Objective: To understand the evolution of the infrared (IR) SEDs of quasars and active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Approach: The Spitzer Space Telescope was employed to observe 24 Palomar-Green (PG) quasars and 7 ULIRGs at 4.5 and 8.0 μm between 2005 and 2009 as part of the QUEST program. Results: The IR SEDs of PG quasars and ULIRGs were modeled with a dual-component dust model. The cold dust component traces the stellar mass, while the warm dust component traces the growth of the dust and the AGN activity. The dual-component dust model provides an adequate description of the data with the least $\chi^{2}$ values. The peak of the cold dust component shifts from a characteristic wavelength of 120 μm for PG quasars to 30-40 μm for the most advanced stage of ULIRGs. For PG quasars, the mid-IR emission is dominated by the cold dust, which reprocesses the UV-optical light from the central engine into IR; this component also represents the bulk of the total IR luminosity. In contrast, for ULIRGs the warm dust is the dominant component, which reprocesses the accretion-related light from the cold dust into IR. The warm dust component increases significantly with the merger stage from PG quasars to ULIRGs. The IR SEDs of PG quasars and ULIRGs are separated with a 2nd-order polynomial function. The 4.5-μm fractional variability amplitude increases with wavelength for PG quasars and decreases for ULIRGs. The 4.5-μm fractional variability is larger for PG quasars than ULIRGs at all stages. The cold and warm dust temperatures were modeled as a function of the 1.7 μm luminosity for PG quasars and ULIRGs. For PG quasars, the warm dust temperature increases with 1.7 μm luminosity. In contrast, for ULIRGs, the dust temperatures of both components are not correlated with 1.7 μm luminosity. For PG quasars, the 12 μm luminosity is correlated with the accretion rate estimated from the optical/UV luminosity. However, this is not the case for ULIRGs. For PG quasars, the 2-1000 × 10(38) Hz luminosity is correlated with the accretion rate estimated from the 1.7 μm luminosity. For ULIRGs, there is no correlation between the 2-1000 × 10(38) Hz luminosity and the accretion rate. The accretion rate is estimated from the 12 μm luminosity for PG quasars and the 1.7 μm luminosity for ULIRGs. The accretion rate estimated from the 12 μm luminosity is consistent with that from the 1.7 μm luminosity for PG quasars. The evolution of the V4334 Sgr system from its formation approximately 675Myr ago has been followed using computer models. The evolutionary pathways considered include mergers of white dwarf and helium star sequences, a possible electron-capture supernova and a double helium white dwarf sequence. The most recent modelling indicates that a merger of a helium star and a white dwarf of approximately 1.1+0.8M⊙ produced a unstable evolutionary path and lead to a common envelope event about 675Myr ago. The system is likely to have subsequently undergone a gravitational wave induced spiral-in event and the final merger may have been observed as the recurrent nova T Pyxidis. The progenitor system for V4334 Sgr had a initial separation of approximately 8.2×10^{12} cm at the time of the spiral-in. If the earlier merger models are correct, it is likely that the total mass ejected in the spiral-in event was sufficient to reduce the mass of the residual core to the levels observed today, with the final envelope ejected in a series of hydrogen rich superoutbursts.

Nonlinear methods for analyzing complex systems have been successfully applied to investigate the properties of atomic nuclei. In this work fractal and recurrence quantification analyses have been applied in order to characterize the complexity of the energy spectra of several atomic nuclei. Fractal dimensions and correlation dimensions were calculated for these nuclei and results show that they have complex dynamics and a high degree of self-similarity. Furthermore, the possibility of predicting the spectral dimensions was also tested and it was found that it is possible to predict the correlation dimensions of these systems with high accuracy. These findings can be used to improve the models for predicting the properties of atomic nuclei. Nonlinear methods have been used to investigate the properties of atomic nuclei. Several techniques have been used and the most important are described below. First, the energy spectrum of several atomic nuclei was calculated using the Berggren ensemble and the correlation dimension was calculated. It was found that the nuclei under investigation had high complexity and this showed that these systems had self-similarity. Second, the fluctuation spectrum was calculated using singular value decomposition and the correlation dimension was also calculated. It was found that the nuclei had high complexity and this showed that they had self-similarity. Third, a surrogate data analysis was used in order to investigate the degree of determinism of the energy spectra. Fourth, the wavelet transform was used and the largest Lyapunov exponent was calculated. It was found that this nucleus had a low degree of determinism. These techniques have been used to characterize the complexity of the energy spectra of several atomic nuclei. Fractal and recurrence quantification analyses have been applied to these data and the results show that the nuclei under investigation had high complexity and this had not been discovered before. The possibility of predicting the spectral dimensions was also tested and it was found that it was possible to predict the correlation dimensions of these systems with high accuracy. These findings can be used to improve the models for predicting the properties of atomic nuclei. It is important to mention that the Berggren ensemble was used to calculate the energy spectra of the nuclei under investigation. This method is more accurate than the conventional methods and it was used to calculate the properties of these systems. The results showed that these nuclei had high complexity and this had not been discovered before.

In this paper, we study the properties of premixed laminar flames of methane doped with two unsaturated hydrocarbons, allene and propyne. Flames of natural gas are used as a reference since they are notoriously difficult to study. We first establish that, in contrast to flames of methane alone, these flames can support propagation with a constant speed, without thermal runaway, which makes them highly suitable for detailed studies. We next study these flames under conditions similar to an operating conditions of gas turbines. We find that the flames behave as expected and we compare the measured properties with the predictions of 1D hydrostatic models. This first part of the study focuses on allene; the second part will focus on propyne. methane doped with two unsaturated hydrocarbons, allene and propyne. Flames of natural gas are used as a reference since they are notoriously difficult to study. We first establish that, in contrast to flames of methane alone, these flames can support propagation with a constant speed, without thermal runaway, which makes them highly suitable for detailed studies. We next study these flames under conditions similar to an operating conditions of gas turbines. We find that the flames behave as expected and we compare the measured properties with the predictions of 1D hydrostatic models. We first show that a simple 1D model based on a non-local radiative transport equation (RTE) with an equilibrium mixing ratio accurately predicts the flame front speeds for allene and propyne in pure methane flames. We then apply this model to the study of premixed laminar flames of methane doped with allene and propyne. We find that the addition of the two unsaturated hydrocarbons has a complex effect on the flame front speed: it decreases for low levels of doping and increases for higher levels of doping. This non-monotonic behaviour can be explained by a change in the thermal capacity of the mixture. We then apply this model to the study of premixed laminar flames of methane doped with allene. We find that the addition of the allene has a complex effect on the flame front speed: it decreases for low levels of doping and increases for higher levels of doping. This non-monotonic behaviour can be explained by a change in the thermal capacity of the mixture.

Barium titanate, BaTiO3, is an interesting material with a wide variety of electrical, optical and mechanical properties. In this work, the electronic structure of BaTiO3 has been calculated within the density functional theory (DFT) using the projector augmented wave (PAW) method. The calculations have been performed using the VASP and ABINIT codes with the PBE parametrization of the exchange-correlation functional and a plane-wave energy cutoff of 550 eV. The calculations have been done for various cell parameters corresponding to the cubic phase as well as tetragonal and orthorhombic phases. The obtained results show a metallic behaviour for all the phases with the tetragonal and orthorhombic phases being semiconducting. BaTiO3 has a complex bonding mechanism. In this material, the TiO6 units are connected via the Ba atoms along the edges of the regular octahedra. The Ti-O bonds within each octahedron are quite short with an magnitude of around 1.9 Å, whereas the Ba-O bonds have a longer length of around 2.5 Å. These different bond lengths result in a weak coupling between the TiO6 octahedra which causes the high variability of the crystal phases. In the cubic phase, the TiO6 units are tightly connected leading to a metallic behaviour. Once the symmetry is reduced to tetragonal or orthorhombic, the coupling between the units becomes less effective which is reflected by a decreasing metal-insulator transition temperature as shown by experiments.

A few hours before solar activity increased rapidly with the appearance of two regions of strong magnetic field rotation, with peripheral disappearance, located near the central part of the Sun (observed by the Heliospheric imager on board the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, SOHO). These two regions of strong magnetic field rotation are considered as magnetic active regions. These regions are rotated with respect to each other by approximately 90 degrees in the course of four days. It is characteristic of some active regions that they produce, apparently temporarily, regions of strong magnetic field rotation, which are called flares. It was observed that these active regions, between June 14 and June 17, 2002, produced two flares of magnitude X10 and X8, respectively, recorded by the X-ray emission of the solar atmosphere. These active regions are observed to have two regions of peripheral disappearance of the magnetic field, one in each hemisphere, as well as two regions of strong magnetic field rotation, with peripheral appearance, in the central part of the Sun. Thus, it can be seen that these active regions generated, apparently temporarily, two regions of strong magnetic field rotation, which, as it was mentioned, are considered as magnetic active regions. These regions are rotated with respect to each other by approximately 90 degrees in the course of four days.

The WMAP satellite has detected a cold spot in the polarized sky with a smaller but statistically significant brightness temperature of 1.3 K compared to the region away from the cold spot with a mean temperature of 2.2 K. The absence of corresponding structures in the unpolarized and in the table maps leads to several hypotheses for the nature of this cold spot. One hypothesis is that it is the result of a systematic effect in the WMAP data. Such systematic effects have been observed in the past, and the WMAP team is conducting an extensive investigation of possible residual thermal noise and contamination sources. Another hypothesis is that the cold spot is a sign of a yet undiscovered type of structure in the universe. If this is the case, it would have significant implications for the cosmology and the very early universe. We have performed a detailed analysis of temperature and polarization data of 84 extragalactic radio sources from the WMAP data to search for signatures of the reported cold spot. We do not find any such features and therefore conclude that the reported low temperature region is not a systematic effect in the WMAP data but rather signifies a real feature in the Universe.

In this work, we introduce a new standard for disk stability simulations of planetary mass objects (PMOs) based on 3D radiative hydrodynamics (3D RHD). We demonstrate the impact of our new testing standard on the hydrodynamics and the radiative transfer by presenting new 3D RHD results for the hydrodynamics and the thermal spectrum for a specific case. The new testing standard for disk stability simulations defines the following criteria: 1) the height of the maximum optical depth of the atmospheric region must be at least 10 pressure scale heights, 2) the optical depth at 10 bar must be at least 1000, and 3) the entropy of the atmospheric region must be greater than 0.5 log(p/p0) + 5, with p0 being the pressure at the bottom of the atmospheric region. The presented 3D RHD results pass all these criteria and show the impact of the new testing standard on the hydrodynamics and radiative transfer. First, we find that a resolved scale height in the atmospheric region has a significant influence on the entropy profile of the atmosphere and the strength of the L1 point, the point where the lowest point on the disk coincides with the secondary's orbit. Second, we find that the optically thin limits of the Rosseland and Planck mean opacity have a significant effect on the strength of the bow shock forming around the primary. Third, we show that the cooling rate in the atmospheric region plays a critical role in setting the thermal wind of the planet. In summary, the presented 3D RHD results confirm the influence of our new testing standard on the hydrodynamics and radiative transfer. We propose the use of the 3D RHD results presented in this work as a new testing standard for disk stability simulations of PMOs. We demonstrate its use by comparing the 3D RHD results to previous 2D RHD results from the literature and to a case from the dynamical cooling lunar simulation (DCLS) code[1], which is currently the state-of-the-art in 3D RHD disk stability simulations. The presented 3D RHD results pass all the testing standards proposed in the new testing standard for disk stability simulations. In addition, the presented 3D RHD results are of sufficient quality to be compared to other 3D RHD disk stability simulations, which cannot yet fully confirm or refute the influence of the new testing standard on the hydrodynamics and radiative transfer.

Galactic subhalos retain information about their formation history. This paper presents a statistically significant shape, orientation, and alignment analysis of the three-dimensional shapes, orientations, and alignments of subhalos in the Mill simulation, a large dark matter only simulation of the Local Group. Subhalos have axes of intermediate to low linear resolution (a few to tens of kiloparsecs) and bound masses of approximately 102 to 103 particles. The shapes of subhalos are prolate, with axis ratios of ~1:1.2:1.5, consistent with triaxial logarithmic distributions with slopes of −1.0, −0.8, and −0.6 for densities of 0.5, 1, and 5 times the background density, respectively. The distribution of orientations is nearly uniform in three-dimensional space, with a slight preference for intermediate-to-major axis alignment. The major axes of subhalos are predominantly oriented along the intermediate axis of the three-dimensional triaxial logarithmic distribution with a population excess along ±45∘. Major axis alignment is significant at the 5% level. The distributions of three-dimensional alignment angles are non-uniform, with a preference for zero alignment and significant values near ±90∘ and 0. These results support the hierarchical scenario of structure formation, in which major mergers explain the shapes of subhalos, while orbital dynamics dominate their orientations. While these results support cold dark matter as the dominant component of the Universe, they also imply that the inner structure of dark matter halos is imprinted at very early times. These results have important implications for many areas of cosmology, such as the statistics of large-scale structure, the orientation distributions of galactic satellites, and the initial conditions for structure formation.

Recent advances in technologies for measuring molecular parameters have enabled direct experimental access to quantities that were previously thought to be robustly constant, such as electrostatic interactions. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for extracting such constant parameters from molecular simulation data, using a treatment of statistical inference as a form of statistical mechanics. We apply this framework to the problem of electrostatic interaction extraction, where a natural measure of the interaction strength between molecules is given by their Boltzmann factor, the logarithm of the ratio of the respective interaction and kinetic energies. This ratio is typically observed to be constant, but we show that its fluctuations are an order of magnitude smaller than previously assumed. Using a crude model of interaction sampling, we find that these fluctuations could lead to a 5-20% systematic error in electrostatic interaction extraction. We demonstrate that by using more complex models of interaction sampling, this error can be reduced to the level of statistical uncertainty, opening up the possibility of computationally efficient fixed-point iterations for electrostatic interaction extraction. We further demonstrate the broader applicability of our approach by applying it to the estimation of three other constant parameterizations: the forcefield-specific parameters that define the strengths of covalent bonds, angular bonds, and non-bonded interactions; and simulation-specific parameters that define the bin size and range of the LJ potential.

A long-time evolution of the vortex lattice in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) is simulated using the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation. An initial configuration, which is simply prepared from a single symmetric lattice, is perturbed through application of a spiral wavefront pattern which triggers a dynamical instability of the lattice flow. The resulting wave packet leads to the formation of several new periodic lattice states which differ in orientation and spatial symmetries. The wave nature of the lattice soliton is confirmed by direct numerical simulation of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The vortex lattice dynamics is also understood within a classical analogy with a system of self-gravitating particles in a periodic potential. The evolution of the vortex lattice in a trapped condensate exposed to far-from-equilibrium dynamics through application of a spiral wavefront pattern leads to the formation of several new periodic lattice states which differ in orientation and spatial symmetries. The lattice soliton character is confirmed by direct numerical simulation of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the vortex lattice dynamics is also understood within a classical analogy with a system of self-gravitating particles in a periodic potential. In the GP simulation, the spiral wavefront pattern triggers a dynamical instability of the lattice flow and the resulting wave packet leads to the formation of several new periodic lattice states. The most common states are the rectangular, rhombic and face-centered cubic (FCC) crystals, however, all observed symmetries with corresponding multiple states are displayed. The characteristic time of lattice evolution depends on the initial density of lattice nodes and lattice degeneracy. In the case of a large density mismatch between the initial and final states, which occurs in the considered system, the observed period of lattice evolution is equal to two. The dynamical symmetry breaking process is a nonlinear phenomenon and leads to a nontrivial, non-isotropic quasilinear dispersive equation for the soliton describing a localized wave packet in the lattice potential. In the classical analogy, the system of self-gravitating particles in a periodic potential can be understood as a bi-harmonic approximation to the hydrodynamic model of the ideal quantum Bose gas with a polynomial energy functional that includes the mean-field interparticle interaction, the Thomas-Fermi depletion correction, the energy of excited modes, and the lattice potential. The system admits soliton solutions of the static Holzwarth equations, which are also valid for the moving lattice with a small but definite mismatch between the local soliton velocity and the velocity of the wave packet. For small lattice mismatch, the evolution of the lattice is dominated by the interaction between solitons, while for high mismatch the quasilinear dispersive model becomes applicable. The presented simulation and analysis of the Bose-Einstein condensate's vortex lattice evolution suggest a way to design dynamical lattice transformations in potentials with degenerate symmetry and to control the lattice evolution. The unique feature of the dynamically induced lattice transformations is the substantial reduction of the simulation time in comparison with the classical analogue.

Nucleobases are molecules essential for life. It is hypothesized that nucleobases first interacted with graphite in early organic synthesis, prior to polymerization to form nucleotides. However, graphene, a one-atom-thick planar sheet of carbon, has received little attention as a nucleobase capture substrate. Here we show that nucleobases are strongly physisorbed to graphene, with binding energies on the order of megajoules per mole. We observed isolated purine and pyrimidine nucleobases as well as nucleobase dimers, in both neutral and protonated forms, with binding occurring both atop and at defect sites. This work suggests a plausible route for nucleobase capture in prebiotic chemistry and molecular fossilization, and provides a new system for studying physisorption, a crucial process in organic chemistry and nanotechnology. This research investigates the interaction of nucleobases (the molecular building blocks of life) with a one-atom-thick planar sheet of carbon, graphene. Despite graphene's recent and extensive study, nucleobases have received little attention as potential substrates. Given the hypothesized role of graphite in prebiotic organic synthesis and the diverse chemistries nucleobases undergo on graphite, it was hypothesized nucleobases may also bind to graphene. Indeed, nucleobases are strongly physisorbed to graphene, with binding energies on the order of megajoules per mole. Furthermore, we observed nucleobases both intact and in protonated forms, with binding occurring both atop and at defect sites. This work suggests a plausible route for nucleobase capture in prebiotic chemistry and molecular fossilization, and provides a new system for studying physisorption, a crucial process in organic chemistry and nanotechnology. Keywords: prebiotic chemistry, graphene, physisorption

Here we report on afterglow observations of three bright gamma-ray burst (GRB) events, 060218, 070306, and 080319, conducted with theNeil Gehrels Swift Observatory (tentatively designated SWIFT 110320b, 110330, and 110601, respectively) as well as the X-Ray Telescope (XRT) on board the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. These events were chosen because they all exhibited extended X-ray afterglow emission that, in two cases, could be fit with a broken power law, a characterization often taken to imply a structured circumburst medium (CBM). Additionally, 060218 exhibited a thermal component in its early X-ray afterglow, a behavior not commonly seen. We fit our data to a model consisting of a constant isotropic-equivalent gamma-ray burst energy release and a power-law distribution of interstellar medium (ISM) clouds with a mean free path of the kinetic energy release greater than the radius of the afterglow emission region. This leads to a density profile p(r) ∝ r−2, where r is the distance from the central engine. For two of the events, 060218 and 070306, we find that the density profile is best fit by an r−2 profile with no density gradient (∝ 0), while for the third event, 080319, a weak gradient of p(r) ∝ r−3 was required at the 3.5σ level. For 060218, the density profile could be equally well fit by either an r−2 or r−2 with a gradient. This is the first time that such weak (3.5σ) gradients in the density profile have been reported for an afterglow for a gamma-ray burst with extended X-ray afterglow emission. This behavior is potentially intriguing, as it is not consistent with a wind profile, which would predict a gradient ∝ r−1. We discuss these findings in the context of existing theoretical work on circumburst medium density profiles as well as physical implications of these results for explosion mechanisms and wind profiles. To date, approximately 4/5 of gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows with extended X-ray afterglow emission have exhibited broken power-law decay light curves, a characterization that has sometimes been taken to imply a CBM consisting of a mixture of high and low density regions. Here, we report that this is not a clear-cut signature, as some events with evidence of a CBM also exhibit a thermal component in their early X-ray afterglows. In particular, 060218 exhibited such a component, which faded in a manner that could be fit with a broken power law.
