We introduce the dynamical discrete web, a framework that formalizes the idea that interactions between objects can be modeled as a web, where nodes represent objects and links model interactions between objects. We apply this framework to the study of networks of interacting items. We show how the discrete web, a discrete dynamical system, can be used to analyze networks of interacting items. We study random discrete webs and characterize their spectral properties. We apply spectral analysis to the study of various real world networks. We then study how local modifications to a discrete web can induce global dynamics on the underlying network. We define and analyze the local resonance and globalization principles. We conclude with a discussion of some open problems. The dynamical discrete web (DDW) framework formalizes the idea that interactions between objects can be modeled as a web, where nodes represent objects and links model interactions between objects. We apply this framework to the study of networks of interacting items. We study random discrete webs and characterize their spectral properties. We apply spectral analysis to the study of various real world networks. We then study how local modifications to a discrete web can induce global dynamics on the underlying network. We define and analyze the local resonance and globalization principles. We conclude with a discussion of some open problems. Some open problems for the DDW framework: 1. Develop effective algorithms to find/construct low dimensional discrete webs. 2. Develop efficient numerical algorithms to simulate discrete dynamical systems. 3. Develop and analyze conserved quantities for discrete dynamical systems. 4. Develop and analyze the global resonance and globalization principles. 5. Develop and analyze stochastic versions of the discrete web framework. 6. Develop and analyze effective methods to cluster and separate discrete webs. We define and analyze the local resonance and globalization principles. We show that local modifications that conserve local resonances are globalization mechanisms. We conclude with a discussion of some open problems for the DDW framework. Many networks of interacting items arise in physical, biological and social systems. These networks range in size from the web of human sexual contacts, the network of scientific collaborations, protein interaction networks, neural networks, food webs, ecological networks, word networks, power grids and many others. Recent developments in network science and complex systems have provided new insights into these networks. A fundamental framework for studying these networks is the complex network framework, where nodes represent objects and links model interactions between objects. This framework has been applied to study networks of scientific collaborations, protein interaction networks and neural networks. The dynamical systems point of view of networks has also proven to be powerful. In this framework, nodes and links are represented by dynamical systems. Links represent the interactions between the dynamical systems represented by the nodes. The interactions between links induce dynamics on the networks. We can study the local and global dynamics on networks from this point of view. This dynamical systems point of view has been used to study networks of human sexual contacts,

Nucleon density and momentum distributions in nuclei provide unique information on the spatial distribution of nucleonic momenta and currents in atomic nuclei. In the standard analysis, the center-of-mass (c.m.) correction is applied sequentially after the removal of the nucleon resolution function. Here, we present a method that combines these two corrections in one step, thus termed simultaneous center-of-mass (s.c.m.). The s.c.m. correction improves the agreement of theoretical predictions with experimental data for a wide range of nuclei and distributions. The accuracy of the new method is illustrated by a simultaneous description of the deuteron and W(d,2p) distributions. The method can be readily applied to other nuclear reactions and extends the applicability of nuclear reaction theory to regions of current interest, such as the studies of spin-isospin excitations of nuclei and structure changes during the evolution of nuclear systems in collisions. The method can be downloaded from https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.09044.

Here we present a comprehensive model for the physical and chemical evolution of a cloud at very low metallicity. This is of particular interest for the early Universe at redshifts above 6, where the density was once below 10−4 times the value at Earth. We explore the effects of reduced metallicity on H2 molecule formation, enabling the formation of stars at lower densities and potentially higher redshifts than previously thought possible. We show that the presence or absence of molecular hydrogen is the main factor determining the thermal and dynamic evolution of the gas, with the absence of H2 at low metallicities causing an increase in the thermal pressure of the gas. We also find that the reduction in the efficiency of H2 molecule formation means that the Jeans mass is higher than previously thought, and is thus a possible solution to the problem of producing dwarf galaxies at very high redshift. Finally, we show that the spin temperature of the 21 cm transition is also significantly altered by the low metallicity, with higher neutral fractions and thus potential applications to next generation 21 cm telescopes.

One of the main goals of the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is the exploration of the mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking (EWSB). A crucial part of this study will be the investigation of the role of Supersymmetry (SUSY), a hypothetical symmetry that extends the symmetries of the known interactions between particles to include those fermions whose masses enable them to propagate in either a spin-0 or spin-1 representation of the symmetry group. One of the most popular models that has enjoyed great success in reproducing the observed particle spectrum is the Minimal Supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model (MSSM). In this model, SUSY must be broken, and the breaking mechanism, which has profound implications for the scale of EWSB and the character of physical Higgs bosons, is among the major targets of experimental study at the LHC. The MSSM Higgs sector comprises two CP-even Higgs bosons, h and H, one CP-odd Higgs boson A, and two charged Higgs bosons, Hplus and Hminus. A crucial test of this model is the determination of the spin and parity quantum numbers of the observed Higgs bosons. The large sparticle masses predicted by the mSUGRA model motivate a particular benchmark region known as the focus point region, which exhibits relatively light Higgs bosons, in particular a 126 GeV Higgs boson. The observation of a Higgs boson with these characteristics would be a strong indication of supersymmetry and would greatly strengthen the case for this mysterious energy scale. In this letter, we present the prospects for the detection and measurement of this 126 GeV Higgs boson at the 14 TeV LHC, including both direct reconstruction in the di-Higgs plus final state and more prosaic measurements based on the observation of its decay products. We examine bothgg production via gluon fusion and VBF, the t-, W-, and Z-associated production modes, and the associated production with bottom quarks or gluons. We focus on analyses performed by the ATLAS experiment and make use of 13 TeV data with an expected 15-20 fb-1 of total LHC luminosity. The reach of this study is strongly dependent on the decay mode of the 126 GeV Higgs boson. If this Higgs boson is a SM-like Higgs boson, it will be challenging to observe, particularly in the gluon fusion production mode. However, if the 126 GeV Higgs boson has either a large amount of decay to bottom quarks or it has a high proportion of decay totau lepton pairs, then this study will have good sensitivity to these scenarios, and the ATLAS experiment, with its excellent di-tau trigger, will be well-positioned to make the discovery of such a Higgs boson.

In this paper, we present a method for the detection of periodic orbits in chaotic dynamical systems based on time series decomposition. We use the Broomhead–King–Plus (BKP) spectrum to separate the continuous component of a time series from its periodic component. The periodic component is further decomposed into sine and cosine components using the discrete Fourier transform. We then calculate the maximum likelihood estimate of the fundamental period of the time series and use it to fold the continuous and periodic components of the time series at the fundamental period. This results in a new time series, which contains all the periodic components of the original time series that have periods less than the fundamental period. We employ a genetic algorithm to determine the best fitting cyclic pattern to this new time series and use it to decompose the original time series into a series of periodic orbits. Finally, we apply a series of tests to the periodic orbits to eliminate those that are unlikely to correspond to periodic orbits. The method is tested on several low-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems and is shown to be capable of detecting all the periodic orbits that have periods between one and ten times the length of the time series under consideration.

In this work we consider a generalization of classical repeated games, called asynchronous games. In an asynchronous game, there is no requirement that the players observe the history of past actions, but rather each player’s action only depends on the current state and the current action of the player. Asynchronous games allow for more general interactive strategies than their classical synchronous counterparts. One setting that has been studied extensively is that of mixed-motive, or Hawk-Dove, games. Here, one player (the Hawk) can choose to do nothing, and the other player (the Dove) must decide between two actions. In this case, it has been established that mixed strategies are optimal for the Dove, i.e. the Always Defect policy is a Nash equilibrium. Here we introduce a game in which there is only a single player, and the player can choose to do nothing, participate in the game, or switch between these two actions infinitely often. We show that such a player has an almost sure optimal strategy, i.e. that they will play a best-response against any strategy that the opposite player may employ. We also show that there is an initial profile for which the payoff of the first-player is strictly less than that of the second-player. In particular, this implies that the first-player has an optimal almost-sure strategy in this initial profile. We believe this example to be of independent interest, as it shows that a.s. optimality can be achieved without the requirement of alternation of plays.

Peierls-Nabarro (PN) models assume that dislocations interact with each other via an elastic potential involving long-range interactions. Despite its simplicity, the PN model is able to describe qualitatively many dislocation dynamics, such as creep and fast dislocation dynamics in many crystals. The present study provides a detailed theoretical explanation for recent high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) observations of dislocation interactions in FCC metals. Dislocations moving in glide direction (DS) may jump over climb dislocations (BC), which are immobilized in their conventional sense. BC start to move in the opposite direction, which leads to an elastic interaction with DS. The observed BC annihilation and annihilation barriers are calculated theoretically and found to be in excellent agreement with the observed dislocation interactions. This observed dislocation interaction is unexpected in the conventional sense of BC immobilization, because there is no Peierls stress, which would act as an external force driving the BC/DS interaction. However, according to our numerical calculations, the BC start to move when the shear modulus in the direction perpendicular to the dislocation line is smaller than the diagonal critical value, determined by the compatibility of BC and DS displacement patterns. In metals with a sufficiently large lattice parameter, this condition is always fulfilled, leading to BC motion. The PN model, which has been successfully applied to many other systems, is able to describe qualitatively dislocation dynamics in FCC metals.

The Large Area Telescope (LAT) on the Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST), when operating in the Diffuse Sciences mode, will study the isotropic gamma-ray emission of our Milky Way galaxy. This emission results from the high-energy interactions of Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) with the interstellar gas and radiation fields. An adequate modeling of this component is needed in order to accurately study gamma-ray sources in our galaxy and perform comparisons with models of the Galactic diffuse emission. In this work we present the development of a GCR simulation that will be used to build the Galactic diffuse emission model for the GLAST. The simulation was developed using the GEANT4 toolkit, and includes a model for the gas and radiation field components, and for primary and secondary GCRs. We describe the simulation setup, the simulation results, the data analysis steps performed to build the GCR simulation output into 3D spatial maps of the spectrum, spatial distribution and time variation of the primary and secondary gamma-rays fluxes, and we discuss future improvements that we are considering to develop a complete GLAST Galactic diffuse emission model.

Recently, various anomalies have been found in the WMAP data, such as the alignments between the regions of high (positive) and low (negative) signed intensities and the directions of the solar wind, and the correlations between the temperature and the components of the WMAP data in the KQ75 orientated dataset. These anomalies have been widely interpreted as indirect signatures of the presence of electromagnetic interference and/or possible contamination from Solar System dust. In this paper, we report the discovery of several other alignment and intensity anomalies in the WMAP data that have not been reported previously and are more difficult to explain. We also provide a plausible physical explanation for these anomalies, which are due to interference from man-made radio signals. We demonstrate that the same interference is also responsible for the recently observed anomalies in the signed-intensity and cross-power spectra. The interference we report here probably comes from man-made radio signals in the frequency bands 128 - 137 MHz, 143 - 149 MHz, and 333 - 349 MHz. The radio waves from these sources would have propagated from North America into the northern hemisphere of the sky (where the WMAP spacecraft were located) in the period from May 2003 to November 2003.

This paper describes the data processing and calibration issues encountered during the execution of the AMBER (Advanced MBERoletz telescope for the Elongation). The VLTI consists of three main components - the AMBER, the PIONIER and the CVI]{}. The AMBER usesu 430 Hz laser light to create a image of the object via wavefront sensing. The data are recorded on three different instruments, which were configured differently. In particular, the data volumes and formats were different between the instruments, resulting in different levels of data quality. To unify the data from the different instruments, a number of pre-processing tasks were carried out, including filtering, different kinds of data re-sampling and table generation. Several of the calibration tasks are also described, including atmospheric dispersion correction, instrumental polarization correction, coherent integration and P2P]{} communications. The data were also affected by software bugs, of which the most serious caused a reduction in the visibility of the first and last few cm of the standard star, [$\mathrm{VYL\_ceos}'$]{}. These calibration and data processing issues meant that some of the results had to be flagged, and the final sensitivitiy was reduced by around 5%. The calibration and data processing issues detailed in this paper are not unique to AMBER, but will affect any long-baseline interferometry project that uses distinct data processing and analysis pipelines for each instrument. The lessons learned from this work will be valuable for future long baseline interferometry projects, and in particular for the GRAVITY instrument, for which AMBER provided the calibration setup.

The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is an extremely successful theory. In particular, its elegant symmetry structure,arks of to which it converges along the Electroweak Symmetry Breaking (EWSB) funnel, make it a fine-tuned result of Nature. From the first moment of its invention, physicists have been striving to unify the description of the fundamental particles into a larger framework, supersymmetry (SUSY). Since SUSY at low energy requires superpartners for every Standard Model (SM) particle, the hunt is on for candidates for such a framework. The current observational evidence for the SM Higgs boson is weak, and will likely be met with disappointment at the coming LHC runs. If discovered at the 14 TeV run, a heavier SM Higgs will be pushed lower than the reach of the LHC, leaving room for other candidate theories of EWSB. A prominent example is a scenario with General Gauge Mediation (GGM), where supersymmetry is typically realised as a local symmetry. In this scenario, the lightest SUSY particle (LSP) is a natural candidate for dark matter, and the superpartners of the known Standard Model particles provide the gauge couplings of the SM at the GUT scale. The running between these two scales is mediated by the interactions of the SM fields with the scalar component of the supersymmetry breaking superpartners, which are massless at the GUT scale, leading to a description of the Electroweak Symmetry Breaking (EWSB) in this framework of weakly-coupled dynamics. These successful predictions of the SUSY GGM scenario motivate the study of the landscape of string theory compactifications, with the goal of realising an effective field theory with these properties. One of the simplest such scenarios is that of Type IIB string theory compactified on an orientifold of ${\cal M}$ with Z_6' symmetry, where the resulting particle spectrum consists of the Standard Model states plus their superpartners, with the D- and F-terms of the underlying string theory yielding the local SUSY of the GGM scenario. The application of the efficient computational techniques of the LGET method to this class of models has resulted in a new benchmark point with 126 GeV mass for the lightest Higgs boson, in agreement with the LHC Run 2 searches. This result is quite robust, as different Monte Carlo sampling techniques applied to the LGET result yield similar features.

A first-principles model of early evolution: Emergence of gene families, species and preferred protein folds By Adam Woolf and Jason Eberle ABSTRACT A first-principles model of early evolution: Emergence of gene families, species and preferred protein folds Early life was likely a slow, gradual process that was facilitated by chemical mutations that slightly increased the stability of key biomolecules. One such chemical mutation was the emergence of stable proteins with stable secondary and tertiary structures. The selective advantage of these novel proteins was reduced complexity of the environment and increased replication rate of the cell. Over time, variants of these proteins with further enhanced stability emerged, which in turn promoted the emergence of protein families and eventually cellular life forms. We implement a spatially explicit, molecular dynamics model of early Earth with simple amino acid chemistry to demonstrate the emergence of key protein structure classes in the earliest stages of life's history. These experiments show that the combination of gradually increasing protein stability and concentration, and the simultaneous emergence of RNA-like molecules with the ability to capture and transmit information, is sufficient for the rapid emergence of more complex molecular species with the ability to self-replicate. This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is managed by UT-Battelle for the U.S. Department of Energy. This work was supported by the Assistant Secretary for Science of HHS/USDHHS (ARRA) under contract HHSN272200900057C. The authors acknowledge funding from the Laboratory Directed Research and Development Program at ORNL, as well as high performance computing resources at ORNL and Drexel University.

In this work, we develop an inverse kinetic approach for the solution of the incompressible Navier-Stokes (INS) equations. The dynamics of the INS equations are encoded in a distribution function, whose evolution is governed by the Boltzmann equation. A popular discretization of the Boltzmann equation is the Lattice Boltzmann method, whereby the distribution function is represented as a set of particle distribution functions, which evolve according to a discretized version of the continuous Boltzmann equation. While in recent years, a number of well-established approaches have emerged for the solution of the Boltzmann equation, analogous advances for the Lattice Boltzmann equation have been less pronounced. Here, we develop an inverse kinetic approach for the solution of the INS equations. The dynamics of the INS equations are recovered from a mapping between the spatial velocity vectors and discrete tracer fields, which evolve according to a variational principle. The enforcement of incompressibility in the mapping yields the INS equations. We provide a detailed description of the numerical method and report its stability and convergence properties. We present two test problems, the Poiseuille flow and the channel flow, to demonstrate the ability of the method to capture fundamental solutions to the INS equations. The channel flow case is used to assess the ability of the method to capture the dynamics of variously initialized fluid flows.

The presence of an Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) in the nearby late-type galaxy NGC 3621 was discovered by Spitzer spectroscopy. The spectrum of the nucleus is highly polarized, has broad optical emission lines, and very little dust extinction. The optical spectrum is similar to that of Seyfert 1 galaxies, but the infrared spectrum is better described by that of a Seyfert 2 nucleus. This unusual combination of features is most readily explained by the presence of a completely obscuring dust torus surrounding the engine in NGC 3621. This is the first clear detection of an AGN in a late-type galaxy, and it is an example of an extreme version of the AGN unification model. The nucleus of the nearby late-type galaxy NGC 3621 (NGC 3621) was discovered by Spitzer spectroscopy. The spectrum of the nucleus is highly polarized, has broad optical emission lines, and very little dust extinction. The optical spectrum is similar to that of Seyfert 1 galaxies, but the infrared spectrum is better described by that of a Seyfert 2 nucleus. This unusual combination of features is most readily explained by the presence of a completely obscuring dust torus surrounding the engine in NGC 3621. This is the first clear detection of an AGN in a late-type galaxy, and it is an example of an extreme version of the AGN unification model. NGC 3621 is a member of the Ursa Major cluster, located at a distance of about 23 megaparsecs (73 million kilometers).1 Its low inclination (only 7 degrees) makes it suitable for optical studies. Although originally classified as an S0 galaxy, subsequent studies have shown it to be a late-type galaxy.2 Its nuclear spectrum resembles that of an S0 galaxy, with weak H and K lines and strong optical emission lines of hydrogen and other metals.3–5 The nucleus has been classified as a Seyfert 2 nucleus on the basis of the weakness or absence of the stellar H and K lines, and strong optical emission lines with a narrow component and a broad component with FWHM greater than 1000 km s−1.5, 6, 7 However, there are several arguments against this classification. First, the optical spectrum has similar features to an S0 nucleus, not a Seyfert 2 nucleus. Second, the infrared spectrum shows strong dust extinction, which is not typical of Seyfert 2 nuclei. Third, the equivalent width of the broad lines is small, and there is very little reddening of the emission lines. Finally, the strong optical emission lines require a high density of gas (about 109 atoms cm−3) and a very low ionization parameter (less than 10−4).6 Spitzer spectroscopy resolves some of these problems.8 In the infrared spectrum, NGC 3621 shows clear evidence for very strong dust extinction, with a steep far-infrared to blue optical flux slope of about 7.2.9 The infrared spectrum is very similar to that of a Sey

The Linear Collider (LC) is an ideal machine to probe new physics beyond the standard model (BSM). Within the framework of the minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM), it is possible to extract precise measurements of SUSY parameters by studying the process pp e^- \+ SUSY particles + e^+, which is known as susy reconstruction. The supersymmetric partners of the charged fermions, such as the chargino, are usually good candidates to be observed at the LC. However, in generic BMSSMs, the leptonic flavour violation, LFV, can occur at one-loop level and can influence the predicted parameters from the MSSM. In this work, we perform a detailed analysis of the LFV effects on the CMSSM-like scenarios, where we vary only one trilinear coupling among the three possible ones. The trilinear term a_mu, is included in the analysis due to its relevance in the LFV phenomena. After the analyses, it is possible to determine how the LFV parameters influence the constrained scenarios, and we also present the correlations among the parameters. In conclusion, we show that the LFV phenomena can have a relevant influence on the chargino production at the LC, motivating the need of a precise determination of these parameters in order to achieve the susy reconstruction with a precision that can be reached at the LC.

In this paper, we propose the nonperiodic anyon model to describe the quantum Hall effect (QHE) in terms of elementary excitations. This model shares a lot of the same mathematical symmetries as those used in the theory of the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE), but the anyons are nonperiodic and live in a larger global symmetry group, the Morita equivalence class of the gauge group of the standard model (SM) formulation of the FQHE. We calculate the electromagnetic (EM) scattering matrix in this model and show that it gives the correct scattering and interference patterns for the FQHE, with the same FQHE conductance factors. The QHE without Landau levels is explained as the condensation of nonperiodic electrons, which carry the EM current. We also speculate about possible cosmological implications of our model, particularly with regard to the Majorana zero modes that may arise from the vacuum expectation value of a particular nonperiodic electron field.

A recent Galactic Globular Cluster NGC 6791 exhibits extended red giant branch (RGB) populated by helium-4 stars, which are likely the descendents of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars. Due to inefficient removal of stellar mass by stellar winds, many of these stars cross the RGB Tip and ignite hydrogen in their cores as helium stars, evolving into carbon-Nitrogen-O-type (CNO) stars. A small number of these stars have already shed most of their hydrogen-rich envelopes and evolve into very thin hydrogen-burning shells, called naked helium stars. The remainder of helium stars still retaining their hydrogen-rich envelopes merge into low-mass white dwarfs (MWDs) after cooling V > 5000 km/s. Such a prolonged RGB is not seen in the other Galactic GCs. We suggest that similar evolution can account for the nature of two faintest stars in the cluster, which have effective temperatures of < 4,000 K and could be MWDs stripped of their hydrogen-rich envelopes. This provides evidence for mass loss on the RGB and supports the possible connection between the existence of MWDs and RGB mass loss in old, metal-poor stellar populations.

Si and Ge nanocrystals (NCs) have potential applications in optoelectronics and photovoltaics because of their localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR), high refractive index and facile synthetic approaches. However, pure nanocrystals are not suitable for photovoltaic devices due to inefficient carrier separation and charge collection. To enhance light absorption of nanocrystal-based solar cells, localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPC) of NCs can be coupled with solar radiation in the optical regime. In this study, the authors used first-principles density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the absorption spectra of Si and Ge NCs embedded in a wide band-gap lattice. It was shown that interband, intraband and excited-state direct photon absorption can occur in this system. Therefore, it is expected that these findings can be utilized to engineer NC-based broadband optical absorbers.

The infrared Ca II triplet (CaT) is a powerful and well-established abundance indicator. This work investigates its potential to be extended to the metallicity measurement, a task that has been so far elusive. By employing a large dataset of three dimensional chemodynamical models of galaxies we show that the CaT parameter can be converted into a quantitative estimator of the metagalactic ionizing radiation field normalization, an indirect indicator of the interstellar medium (ISM) metallicity. Moreover, we provide the calibration for this conversion, both as a function of spatial resolution and signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio of the observations. We demonstrate that such calibration can be used to determine the gas-phase metallicity with a precision of 0.3-0.5 dex in regions of low S/N (S/N<10) with a spatial resolution of 1 kpc, and of 0.2 dex in regions of high S/N (S/N>20) with a spatial resolution of 10 kpc. We provide example applications to specific systems, for which the metallicity can be recovered with such precision. In particular, we estimate the gas-phase metallicity of the local group member galaxies: M33, M31, and the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). We find evidence of a decrease of the metallicity of the LMC over time, as predicted by the models. Finally, we discuss caveats of the method, its limitation and potential improvements.

We study the power allocation in multi-user scenarios with delay-limited fading channels. The general case where both the number of users and the number of channel uses are more than one is considered. We propose a low-complexity water-filling-like algorithm with closed-form expressions for the per-user water levels. We show that the proposed algorithm maximizes the average sum-rate of the system under total power constraints on the users’ transmission powers. Moreover, the proposed algorithm is shown to outperform existing algorithms in the low-to-moderate SNR regime. VI statements, initiated by A. In this paper, we present a theoretical investigation of non-adiabatic transport through a quantum dot turnstile device coupled to source and drain leads. We focus on nanoscale systems for which the quantization of energy levels of the quantum dot molecule is significantly less than the electronic temperature. We examine a wide range of parameter space to explore the transition from sequential to resonant transmission regimes as the quantum dot level positioning is modified relative to the Fermi levels of the source and drain leads. We show how the correlated sequential and resonant transmission modes present different characteristics in the dot population and real time current statistics. In particular, the resonant transmission mode characteristics are strongly time-dependent throughout the turnstile cycle. This non-adiabaticity has a significant effect on the quantum statistics of the transmitted electrons.

In this paper, we present a small set of analytic gravitational lens models that can reproduce the characteristic features of the lens potentials induced by galaxies and clusters of galaxies. These models are able to simultaneously match multiple observational constraints including the positions and fluxes of multiple images, and the strong and weak shear positions and strengths. These analytic models can be used as inputs into numerical simulations of strong gravitational lensing, potentially enabling faster simulations that require less compute time. Additionally, the analytic potentials can be used as an additional discriminant between competing lens models. Finally, the models presented here can be used to estimate approximate locations of critical curves, defined as the points where the lensing susceptibility, defined as the second derivative of the lensing potential with respect to the source position, is zero, which can aid in rapid lens mapping using software such as GLAlPHA. The models presented here were generated using a recently developed analytic lens modeling method that generates a large set of lens models by sampling the uncertainty of the lensing mass distribution. The lensing mass distribution is fit to observed galaxy light distributions using a Bayesian parameter estimation technique, which accounts for observational uncertainties as well as uncertainties in the input physics of the galaxies' dark matter and stellar components. This method generates a probability distribution function (PDF) over the lensing mass distribution, which we use as the basis of our lens model. For each modeled lens configuration, we solve the lens equation numerically using the method of characteristics, allowing us to explicitly associate models with specific lens configurations. To produce sample models, we consider two different galaxy types: Early-type galaxies (ETGs) and disk galaxies. The surface brightness profiles of ETGs are modeled with a Sérsic profile, while disk galaxies are modeled with an exponential profile. We also consider cluster-scale lenses, which are modeled as dual Einstein rings, with the inner ring made up of all ETGs and the outer ring made up of all disk galaxies. We generate parameter sets for each lens configuration by drawing from a prescribed probability distribution based on cosmological simulations. We compare the resulting model lens configurations to observational data from strong gravitational lensing systems, finding excellent agreement between the models and the data.

Here we present an Economical Polymer Optical Fiber Demultiplexer (EPoFDM), consisting of a small low-cost polymer optical fiber (POF) loop mirror in conjunction with a large regular POF and two inexpensive interferometers. The POF has a nonlinear refractive index (NRI) that can be precisely controlled by thermal or optical means. This NRI can be used to achieve an amplitude mask to control the reflected powers from different demultiplexing channels, and thus minimize the inter-channel crosstalk. The two interferometers can be accurately aligned by minimizing the differential group delay between the channels. Simulations show that, with our proposed design, the insertion losses of the demultiplexing channels are less than 2.1 dB with a total demultiplexing budget of 12.6 dB. The total cost of our EPoFDM is approximately 10% of the commercial silica-based Mach-Zehnder Interferometers (MZIs). It may find potential applications in low-cost POF sensors or networks.

Infrared high-resolution spectroscopy of post-AGB circumstellar disks has so far been performed on a limited number of objects. The origin of the observed IR emission is still a matter of debate. The presence of a fast, collimated, wind in the post-AGB phase had been suggested to be one of the reasons explaining the presence of a IR excess, although the role of a slow, equatorial wind is still a matter of discussion. Here, we present a new, high-resolution (R=600,000), mid-IR spectrum of the post-AGB object HR 4049. The spectrum was recorded in November 2014 with the 10.4-meter GTC telescope. The presence of strong emission lines suggests that the post-AGB object is undergoing extreme mass-loss. We identify a fast, collimated wind, corresponding to a few percent of the speed of light, which contributes the bulk of the mid-IR flux. We also detect the previously reported slow, equatorial wind, with an extension to low velocities. The observed IR emission is consistent with a model in which the post-AGB star is losing mass through a fast, polar wind, which drives a slow, equatorial mass-loss via interaction with the fast polar wind. This is the first time that such a configuration has been observed in an evolved star.

Air showers producing detectable levels of microwave emission typically generate large amplitude signals at radio frequencies as well. The emission at these wavelengths is composed of discrete pulses, each reflecting the nature and behavior of the underlying particle shower. Detection of the microwave emission provides a means of identifying air showers occurring in the atmosphere and allows for accurate measurement of various properties of the primary particle, including its energy. This paper presents observations of microwave emission from air showers recorded by the COn-Tiqqe experiment at several facilities around the world. The sensitivity of the observations to the primary energy and zenith angle are also presented. The presented data were acquired between the years 2011 and 2016. The data show the presence of microwave emission from several air showers, with a clear statistical distinction between normal and anomalous events. The primary energy and zenith angle of these anomalous showers are also reliably determined. The observations reported in this paper were acquired using a number of complementary experimental approaches. An array of radio antennas was used to measure the radio pulses emanating from the air showers. A dedicated set of receivers operating at frequencies ranging from 78 to 116 GHz was deployed at various sites. Data were also acquired at the COn-Tiqqe site using a network of receivers that did not include a dedicated antenna. In this case, the data were digitized and analyzed using a network of computers interfaced to a central data collection system. Finally, extensive background monitoring was performed using a network of ambient noise monitoring stations. All of these systems detected anomalous signals from air shower events, though with varying levels of confidence.

Exact and Adaptive Algorithms for the Determinant of a Rational Matrix The determinant of a rational matrix is the function that maps a matrix to its coefficient of the multiplicative monomial 1 x 1. This is a widely used notion in linear algebra, and it is interesting in its own right because of its ubiquity and several applications. Over the years, several algorithms have been developed to compute the determinant. On the exact algorithm side, the first-order-subresultant algorithm is an exact algorithm to compute the determinant. On the adaptive algorithm side, the first-order-partial-resultant algorithm is an adaptive algorithm to compute the determinant with work proportional to the cube of the matrix size. The first-order-partial-resultant algorithm has to perform multiple algebra computations and divisions, and it has a per-matrix overhead that grows with the matrix size. In this paper we present a new adaptive algorithm to compute the determinant. The core of the algorithm is the computation of the first-order-complete-resultant. The complete resultant is a generalization of the determinant that includes more information than the determinant. In particular, the complete resultant encodes the total Galois group of the polynomial that defines the rational matrix. The first-order-complete-resultant algorithm has the same complexity as the first-order-partial-resultant algorithm, and it has a much lower per-matrix overhead. It is an exact algorithm to compute the determinant. We give a new implementation of the complete resultant that is faster than the existing implementations. We test our new algorithm on several matrices arising from geometry and numerical linear algebra, and we demonstrate that the new algorithm is orders of magnitude faster than the previous algorithms in some cases.

AM1934-563 is a polar ring galaxy, a unique type of galaxy exhibiting a polar ring of stars, enshrouded by a large halo of ejected material, orbiting around a central elliptical galaxy. It was observed in 1822 for the first time by Karl Ludwig Philippovich Shapovalova (Shapovalova, K.P.) who used the name 'AM1934-56'. The ring-like structure of this galaxy was noted for the first time in 1974 by Davies, Warin &$_-$Williams (1974). The name 'polar ring galaxy' was coined by Schweizer (1980). The interesting and unusual morphology of AM1934-563 attracted the attention of many scientists worldwide, and more than a dozen papers were published regarding the ring galaxy, until 1983 when it was finally classified as a polar ring galaxy. A rich environment of AM1934-563 was noticed by Len Oulpout, a talented amateur astronomer, in 2011 with the use of telescopes. The galaxy shows a clear bridge of material connecting the polar ring to the elliptical host. The bridge becomes denser the closer one gets to the host galaxy and a very interesting morphology is observed. The dark matter halo of the elliptical host galaxy is not able to interact with the polar ring and it is likely that the ring is made of stars from the disrupted galaxies.

In recent years several experiments searching for the neutrinoless double beta decay have been conducted. In particular, two experiments using scintillating emulsion: NEST and DEAP set new upper limits on the neutrino double beta decay half-life. The obtained results are controversial and cause a discussion on whether the double beta decay really exists or not. It seems that the reason for this difference is a presence or absence of an interference term in the considered processes. The interference term appears due to simultaneous absorption and emission of two photons by a particle. The first experimental search for the neutrino double beta decay with the detection of the interference term had some drawbacks that could not find this interference. It is shown that this could be caused by an inadequate modelling of the Theta+ component in the studied data sample. A possible explanation why the Theta+ is seen in some experiments and not in others is proposed.

In general relativity (GR), one of the principal methods of analyzing weak solutions to Einstein's field equations is the method of nonlinear perturbations, whereby a solution to the equations is analyzed in a perturbative sense around a more simple spacetime. Since the discovery of the Exact Solutions to the Einstein's field equations, a great deal of effort has been made to generalizations of the class of solutions to the nearly-flat and empty-universe variants of the theory. One of the assumptions in the derivation of the solvability conditions for the linearized field equations is that the background geometry is flat. Recently, two of the current authors (JSS and DSR) proposed a framework for analyzing weak solutions to the field equations that include generalizations of the nearly-flat and empty-universe solutions. The central idea in this framework is to relax the assumption of a flat background geometry to one of a curved background geometry. As a result, in addition to the equations satisfied by the perturbation(s) about the curved background, a global constraint on the perturbation is obtained. This constraint, which is a variant of the well-known Bel-Robinson vector field, guarantees that the curvature of the background geometry is propagated by the perturbation(s). In this paper, we provide a detailed exposition of these results for general relativity, general relativity with a negative cosmological constant, and generalizations of these two theories in the presence of a general matter content. We demonstrate the derivation of the perturbed field equations for each of these three theories, as well as the derivation of the global constraint, in both abstract index notation and in the language of tangent frames. This exposition is meant to serve as a tutorial for those not well-versed in general relativity and its applications, as well as as a detailed exposition for those versed in the subject. Furthermore, we have provided multiple appendices with details not central to the exposition.

Granular media is a fascinating area of research, with a great deal of both fundamental and applied relevance. Here, we experimentally study the dynamics of a bidimensional granular medium at large scale, with controlled volume fraction, realized as a cylinder of 1 mm diameter plastic balls. We observe that upon increasing the volume fraction, the medium gradually changes from fluid-like, with a smooth density field, to solid-like, with an increasingly disordered structure. We observe a sudden, first-order-like, jamming/rigidity transition at around ϕ = 0.64, that is not accompanied by any pronounced change in the dynamics. At and above the transition, the dynamics of the medium is diffusive, with a somewhat anomalous, super-diffusive behavior appearing at low Reynolds numbers. Our observations are successfully captured by a dynamical phase transition scenario, where a continuous dynamical phase changes into a discontinuous one. At the transition point itself, we observe a scaling behavior in the dynamics that is similar to what is found in thermodynamic phase transitions. This work presents a complete experimental study of the dynamics of a two-dimensional, bi-dispersed, cylindrical granular medium, spanning nearly two decades in length and time scales. With this work we provide a solid, experimentally grounded, dynamical explanation of the fascinating phenomenon of rigidity-induced super-diffusion.

The evolution of the atmospheric chemical composition of substellar objects plays a key role in determining their spectra, observable characteristics, and eventual fate. However, the chemical evolution of atmospheres is rarely considered in the context of thermochemical equilibrium, despite this being a reasonable assumption for most atmospheric chemistries. Here, we present the first comprehensive study of departures from thermochemical equilibrium on a system-wide scale for a wide range of both stellar parameter and atmospheric composition. By simultaneously modeling each spectrum as the sum of in-situ formation and photochemical products, we demonstrate the ubiquitous nature of non-equilibrium chemistry on brown dwarfs and characterize the chemical evolution of a series of "supercomets," resulting from rapid release of non-condensable gases at high altitudes. We find the strongest supercomet signatures in the presence of strong downward cloud transport, consistent with recent observations of a supercomet at Comet Lovejoy. Furthermore, we identify several processes that control the composition and yield of supercomets. These results indicate that the atmospheric chemical composition of substellar objects is not fully constrained by thermochemical equilibrium, and that deviations from this assumption should be considered in future analyses of observed spectra and phenomenology.

A newly fabricated Al_2O3_film with ultra low friction against water and a dynamic testing result under elevated hydrostatic pressure and temperature are presented. The friction force measurement is conducted on a customized friction testing apparatus, where the tested surface is a sphere with a 2 mm diameter. The experiment is conducted at 200 °C with a pressure of up to 20 MPa. For the negative control experiment, a bare sphere sliding on water shows a friction force of 2.1 μN. In contrast, the Al_2O3_film yields a friction force of only 0.1 μN at an extremely low pressure of 0.2 MPa. The normalized friction force is less than 0.01 in the negative control and extremely low traction region. The motion track of the sphere is visualized to show that the sphere barely moves after 18 h of constant motion. A large-scale numerical simulation is conducted to study the friction and traction behavior of the sphere-water system. The calculated friction and traction coefficients are respectively 0.005 and 0.9E-7, which are in excellent agreement with the experimental results. The physics behind the ultra low friction and traction properties are interpreted and attributed to the coexistence of hydrodynamic lubrication and boundary lubrication. For lubrication to occur, the pressure ( Laplace pressure) of water between the sphere and the Al_2O3_film needs to be higher than the applied pressure. High pressure and temperature in combination yield synergistic effects, which significantly reduce the friction and traction forces. The Al_2O3_film can sustain an extremely low traction of 9.8E-8 N/m and an extremely low friction of 0.3 μN under 20 MPa and 200 °C.

Stellar clusters are environments in which low-mass stars are born and grow. The stars in a given cluster thus have the same age and are linked by a common history. Understanding the processes that govern the formation and evolution of star clusters is important for a wide range of astrophysical applications. Realistic simulations that capture the full physics of star formation are an essential tool for learning how clusters form. In this work, we use the Illustris simulation to quantify the spatial and mass distributions of star clusters. The Illustris simulation models the formation of galaxies in the universe down to the resolution of individual clouds of gas and dust. The simulation includes a comprehensive treatment of the thermodynamics and chemistry of the gas, self-consistent models of the evolution of thesupermassive black holes, and radiative transfer effects from the CMB and bright sources such as stars and quasars. We find that the fractional mass of the most massive cluster core (${M_{\mathrm{c}}}\\geq{}10^5\,{M_{\odot}}}$) is 0.16 within a 1 Mpc volume around each host halo at $z=0$. The average number of clusters more massive than $10^5\,{M_{\odot}}}$ within this volume is 17. The same volume at higher redshift has lower but non-zero mass fractions of the most massive cluster core. We use these results to show that the comoving volume contained in a given mass range is approximately fixed at high redshifts and increases with time at low redshifts. We find that 50-90% of the total cluster population is in clusters with ${M_{\mathrm{c}}}}\geq{}10^5\,{M_{\odot}}}$ at any given time in the simulation. This population changes due to continuous mass infall and mergers, such that more than half of the clusters more massive than $10^5\,{M_{\odot}}}$ have disappeared by $z=0$. We show that the ratio of cluster numbers in different mass ranges tracks the universal dark matter halo mass function in both time and in simulations that predict no cluster formation. We conclude that the relationship between clusters and their hosts is largely preserved over time, as predicted in hierarchical structure formation models.

In this paper, we present an overview and current status of Japanese detectors used in various research fields. In this work, we investigate the relationship between contractions, deformations, and curvature of surfaces with the motivation of developing a deeper understanding of the behavior of surfaces under varying conditions. Our study investigates the problem of understanding how the curvature of a surface changes under deformations and contractions, and how different contractions affect the curvature. We are interested in understanding concavities and convexities that arise in surfaces and how they are affected by contractions.

Our methodology involves modeling different surfaces and using analytical tools such as the Hessian Matrix to investigate their behavior under deformation and contraction. We apply these methods to a variety of shapes and curves and compare the results to gain insights into how different shapes lead to different behaviors. Our results show that certain contractions can lead to changes in curvature in certain regions, while remaining constant in others. We also demonstrate that the shape of the surface plays a critical role in the magnitude and direction of the change of curvature.

Our findings have potential applications in various fields such as mathematics, physics, and engineering, where surfaces play an important role. Our work contributes to the ongoing efforts to better understand the behavior of surfaces under various conditions and provides an important foundation for future research in this area.

In this work, we investigate the role of adiabatic index in the equation of state of relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, specifically in relation to its variability versus constancy. Adiabatic index is a fundamental parameter representing the thermodynamic properties of a fluid, and its value can have a considerable impact on equation of state and the resulting physical behavior. This study aims to address the discrepancy between varying adiabatic indices in magnetohydrodynamic simulations and the observation of more constant values in astrophysical plasmas. 

Our analysis involves the derivation and implementation of a variable adiabatic index equation of state in a 2D relativistic MHD code, followed by numerical experiments exploring the effects of different adiabatic index models on the resulting dynamics of plasma. Our simulations demonstrate that using a constant adiabatic index in MHD calculations produces inaccurate results in relativistic systems with evolving thermodynamic parameters. On the other hand, implementing a variable adiabatic index results in more accurate representation of physical processes in magnetohydrodynamic simulations and offers a better representation of real-life astrophysical plasmas. 

The methodology utilized in this research primarily focuses on theoretical analysis of the equation of state, a numerical simulation of relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, and the comparison of results obtained with respect to varying adiabatic index models. Our findings hold significant implications in modeling the dynamics of astrophysical processes such as Gamma-Ray Bursts, supernovae explosions, and astrophysical jets.

In this work, we investigate the role of zero-point radiation in the Big Bang model of cosmology. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that zero-point radiation was ubiquitous throughout the early universe and played a crucial role in shaping its evolution. Despite its importance, the exact nature and consequences of this radiation remain poorly understood. Our work attempts to address this gap in knowledge and shed light on the role of zero-point radiation in the early universe.

To achieve this goal, we draw upon both theoretical and observational methods. We begin by developing a mathematical framework for describing the evolution of zero-point radiation in the context of the expanding universe. Using this framework, we then analyze observational data to test our predictions and refine our understanding of the behavior and properties of this radiation. 

In particular, we focus on the impact of zero-point radiation on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), which is a key observational probe of the early universe. Our analysis reveals that zero-point radiation played a significant role in generating the large-scale structure of the CMB and can provide insights into the physics of the early universe. Overall, our work advances our understanding of the early universe and sheds light on the role of zero-point radiation in its evolution.

In this paper, we present a study on the design of a Slide-o-Cam Transmission, which aims to provide a solution to the problem of limited torque control in traditional transmissions. Our key idea in this work is to combine the benefits of a variable mechanical advantage system with a cam mechanism to create a transmission capable of achieving a significant range of gear ratios in a compact and efficient package.

The methodology employed in this study involved a combination of theoretical analysis, experimental testing, and computer simulations. We first derived the equations of motion for the sliding components of the transmission and used them to generate force and displacement profiles for different operating conditions. We then built a prototype transmission and tested it under various loads and speeds to validate the theoretical predictions and identify areas for improvement. Finally, we developed a simulation model of the transmission using Matlab/Simulink to allow for more detailed analysis of the system performance.

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the Slide-o-Cam Transmission in achieving high torque control in a compact, lightweight package. The transmission was found to have a wide range of gear ratios, high efficiency, and excellent load-carrying capacity, making it suitable for use in a variety of applications. The study also provides insights into the design considerations for implementing such a transmission, including the need for careful selection of materials and optimization of the cam profile. Overall, our work contributes to the body of knowledge in the area of mechanical engineering and has practical applications in the development of innovative transmission systems.

The Leo Elliptical NGC 3379: A Metal-Poor Halo Emerges is a study that aims to investigate the metallicity of a previously discovered, metal-poor halo within the Leo elliptical NGC 3379. The key idea behind this research is to use the Multiple Mirror Telescope (MMT) and Hubble Space Telescope (HST) to analyze the metallicities of stars located within the halo of NGC 3379.

The methodology employed in this study involves the analysis of spectroscopic data obtained using the HST and imaging data obtained using the MMT. The results obtained indicate the presence of a metal-poor halo surrounding NGC 3379, with a metallicity that is significantly lower than that of the main body of the galaxy. Furthermore, the study reveals the presence of a metallicity gradient within the halo, with stars located closer to the center of the galaxy having higher metallicities.

The motivation for this research lies in understanding how and when galaxies form their halos and in gaining insight into the chemical evolution of galaxies. The results presented in this study contribute significantly to our understanding of the metallicity distribution within galaxies and provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxy halos.

In conclusion, the study of the metal-poor halo surrounding NGC 3379 using the MMT and HST has led to significant findings that provide insight into the chemical evolution of galaxies. The results obtained from this study are a significant contribution to the field of astronomy and will inform future research on galaxy halos and their formation.

We present the results of the XMM-SSC survey of hard-spectrum XMM-Newton sources, focusing on optically bright sources. Our aim is to identify and study a significant population of extragalactic X-ray sources, particularly those with hard spectra, that have been missed by previous surveys. We rely on multi-wavelength data to identify a sample of 148 sources, of which 120 have been spectroscopically identified. Our results show that the majority of the sources are AGN, with a significant fraction classified as blazars, high-redshift quasars, and narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. We investigate the X-ray spectral properties of the sources and find that their spectra are typically hard, with photon indices below 1.5, and many have iron lines and Compton reflection features. We also examine the optical properties of the sources and find a significant number of sources with peculiar optical spectra, including broad-line AGN with very low accretion rates. Our study provides a valuable contribution to the understanding of the high-energy universe, helping to identify and characterize a population of X-ray sources that has been largely overlooked in previous surveys.

In our work, we investigate turbulent mixing in the surface layers of accreting neutron stars. The motivation for this research stems from the growing interest in the dynamics of accreting neutron stars, which are known to be extreme environments for fluid dynamics phenomena. Our research aims to understand the dynamics of turbulent mixing in the surface layers of these objects, and to identify the underlying physical mechanisms driving this process. 

The problem we address is the lack of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of turbulent mixing in these complex systems. While previous work has explored the basic features of turbulent mixing, they have not taken into account the unique conditions present in accreting neutron stars. Our work attempts to solve this problem by developing a new theoretical framework that accounts for the relevant physics involved in the turbulent mixing of accreting neutron stars.

Our key ideas and methodology involve the development of a new mathematical model that incorporates the fundamental physics involved in turbulent mixing in accreting neutron stars. We use a combination of numerical simulations and analytical methods to investigate the behavior of the turbulent mixing process, and compare our results with observations of real-world accreting neutron stars. By providing a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of turbulent mixing in these extreme environments, our work will contribute to a better understanding of the evolution of accreting neutron stars and their associated phenomena.

In this study, we report on observations of the temperature drop of carbon monoxide (CO) gas inside the dense core of L1544, a pre-stellar object located in the Taurus molecular cloud. With high-angular resolution data obtained using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we found that the gas temperature drops significantly towards the center of the core, reaching a minimum value of about 6 K at the peak density position. This temperature profile indicates that the thermal energy of the CO gas is being dissipated as the gas is squeezed by the gravitational pull of the core. In addition, we observed that the line widths of the CO (J=2-1) and N2H+ (J=1-0) emissions also drop towards the core center, implying that the turbulence in the gas is reduced by the increasing gravitational force. These results provide insights into the physical processes that occur in the earliest phase of star formation, where dense cores are formed before collapsing into protostars. Our study contributes to a better understanding of the initial conditions that shape the formation of stars and planetary systems.

In this study, we investigate the alignment properties of galaxies within dark matter halos using numerical simulations. Specifically, we focus on three different types of galaxy alignment: radial, parallel, and perpendicular. Our results show that radial alignment, where galaxies align with the direction towards their host halo center, is the dominant alignment signal for satellite galaxies. Contrarily, central galaxies exhibit preferentially parallel alignment - where galaxies tend to align with the orientation of their host halo's major axis. Furthermore, our analysis found that perpendicular alignment, in which galaxies align perpendicular to the direction of the host halo's major axis, is weak for both central and satellite galaxies. 

To investigate these different alignment types, we analyzed the large-scale dark matter structure, identified and classified halos as central or satellite, and compared their orientation with their respective galaxies. Our methodology used a high-resolution N-body simulation of cosmic structure formation that spans 100 mega parsecs. We also employed a halo-finding algorithm to identify and classify halos of different types. 

Our motivation lay in exploring the various mechanisms that drive galaxy alignment, which are still not well understood. Investigating the alignment properties of galaxies within dark matter halos can provide insight into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the universe. Our results can help shape current models and theories used to understand the evolution of galaxies in a cosmic context.

In this study, we developed a Finite Element (FE) framework for the computation of protein normal modes and their corresponding mechanical response. Our motivation for this research emerged from the need for more accurate and efficient methods to predict the mechanical properties of proteins, as they play a crucial role in their function and interactions with other molecules. 

The basic idea of our FE framework is to use a continuum mechanics approach to describe the mechanical behavior of proteins and exploit the analogy with structural mechanics. The 3D protein structure is divided into a set of finite elements, which represent the local deformation and movements of the protein in response to external forces. By solving the eigenproblem of the stiffness matrix of the protein, we obtain the protein's normal modes and their associated frequencies and damping factors, which describe the protein's most probable collective motions. 

The methodology is based on the principle of energy minimization, and we use the minimization of the potential energy of the protein as an objective function for the eigenvalue problem. We test the accuracy and efficiency of our FE framework on several different proteins and compare our results with those obtained from experimental data and other computational methods.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the need for a more efficient and versatile method for the computation of protein normal modes and mechanical response. Our FE framework provides a viable alternative to existing approaches and has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of the mechanical properties of proteins.

In this study, we investigate the presence of submilliJansky (submJy) transients in archival radio observations. The importance of identifying such low-flux sources lies in the potential to gain insights into the early universe, as submJy sources are likely to be at high redshift. It is challenging to detect these transients due to the faintness of the sources and high levels of noise in the data. Hence, we develop a sensitive image processing method to better detect submJy transients in archival data from the Janskys Very Large Array (VLA). Our work attempts to solve the problem of low signal-to-noise ratios in archival data, which could potentially cause the exclusion of these crucial sources in previous surveys. 

The results show that our method improves the detection and characterization of submJy transients in archival VLA data. We find multiple new submJy transients that were previously undetected in the images. By comparing the newly detected sources with those from optical and X-ray catalogs, we find evidence of associations between some submJy transients and active galactic nuclei, whereas others are likely to be star-forming galaxies. Our study demonstrates the successful application of a novel and sensitive image processing method to archival radio data, providing a new window to explore the early universe.

The protoplanetary disk that surrounded the early Sun was a crucial environment where planet formation took place. Jupiter and Saturn were the most massive planets in the disk that affected the dynamics of the gas and the dust in the environment. This study aimed to understand the role of Jupiter and Saturn in shaping the protoplanetary disk and the implications of their dynamics on planet formation. 

We used numerical simulations to model the interactions between Jupiter, Saturn, and the disk of gas and dust. The simulations were based on the hydrodynamic equations and the physical properties of the disk, such as viscosity, temperature, and pressure. Our simulations revealed that Jupiter and Saturn had a significant impact on the disk's structure, affecting its density, temperature, and flow patterns. Additionally, Jupiter and Saturn also influenced the formation of planetesimals, which are the building blocks of planets. 

Our findings shed light on the early stages of planet formation and the mechanisms that shaped the Solar System. Specifically, Jupiter's and Saturn's positions and their migration had an essential role in the formation of the terrestrial planets and the asteroid belt. Our study provides a fundamental insight into the dynamics of protoplanetary disks and planet formation that could be applied to other star systems.

In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of bimodality in both Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) and galaxies. AGNs are often classified based on their X-ray and optical properties as either "hard" or "soft" AGNs, while galaxies are classified based on their morphology as either "elliptical" or "spiral". However, recent studies have shown that there is a bimodality in both categories. In this work, we aim to explore the relationship between bimodal AGNs and bimodal galaxies. 

We used data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) to analyze a sample of X-ray selected AGNs in galaxies with varying morphologies. Our results show that bimodal AGNs are more commonly found in bimodal galaxies, with the majority of hard AGNs found in elliptical galaxies and the majority of soft AGNs found in spiral galaxies. Furthermore, we found evidence for a correlation between the mass of the central supermassive black hole and the morphology of the host galaxy.

Our methodology involved crossmatching data from different surveys and using statistical analyses to identify correlations and trends. These findings suggest that the coevolution of black hole growth and galaxy morphology is more complex than previously thought, with bimodal AGNs and galaxies playing an important role. Understanding the relationship between these two bimodalities sheds new light on the origins and evolution of galaxies and AGNs.

In this work, we present the second part of the ACS Survey of Galactic Globular Clusters. The study focuses on the stellar evolution tracks, isochrones, luminosity functions, and synthetic horizontal-branch (HB) models. Our main objective is to understand the basic stellar population properties of globular clusters (GCs) and to construct a set of theoretical models that can reproduce most of the observational data. The study makes use of high-resolution images from the Hubble Space Telescope Advanced Camera for Surveys to obtain magnitudes and colors of stars in 45 GCs in the Milky Way. 
  
We start by constructing a set of theoretical isochrones and HB models based on the stellar evolution tracks of the Yale-Yonsei group, which we then compare against the observations. We then adjust the models to obtain a better fit to observations by tuning some of the free parameters, such as the helium abundance and the mass-loss rate. Our results reveal that the cluster-to-cluster variation of the HB morphology is due to the variations in the helium abundance. Moreover, we find that the helium abundance can explain the discrepancy between the observed and theoretical luminosity functions of the horizontal branch. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive set of theoretical models that can serve as a benchmark for future studies of GCs.

In this work, we propose a new method for generating optimal cache-oblivious mesh layouts that can greatly improve the performance of algorithms that operate on meshes. The motivation for this research is the fact that cache-oblivious algorithms can provide significant performance gains over traditional algorithms by minimizing the number of cache misses. However, achieving optimal performance requires careful management of the memory hierarchy, which can be difficult and time-consuming. Our approach leverages the properties of cache-oblivious algorithms to automatically optimize mesh layouts for maximum performance without the need for manual tuning.

To achieve this, we use a combination of graph-based representations of meshes and mathematical optimization techniques to find layouts that minimize the number of cache misses for a given memory hierarchy. We evaluate our approach using both synthetic and real-world meshes and show that it consistently outperforms existing approaches to cache-oblivious mesh layout generation. Our results demonstrate that our method can provide significant performance improvements for a variety of mesh-based algorithms, including finite element simulations, surface reconstructions, and ray-tracing applications.

Overall, our work represents an important step towards the development of more efficient and effective cache-oblivious algorithms for mesh-based computations. By automating the process of mesh layout generation, we believe that our approach can help researchers and practitioners to quickly and easily optimize their algorithms for specific hardware architectures, without sacrificing performance or efficiency.

In this work, we investigate the coherent lattice vibrations in superconductors and its relation to the superconductivity mechanism in these materials. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of comprehensive understanding of the role of lattice vibrations in the formation and maintenance of superconductivity in these materials. The motivation for our research is the potential breakthrough in the development of superconducting materials for various applications, including energy generation, transportation, and medical devices.

Our key idea is to study the phonon-mediated electron pairing, which is a widely accepted theory for superconductivity, and its dependence on the lattice vibrations in the superconducting material. We use the density functional theory combined with dynamical matrix calculations and electron-phonon coupling calculations for our methodology. The lattice dynamic properties and electron-phonon coupling strength are calculated using first-principles methods, and the coherence of lattice vibrations is quantified by coherence factors.

We find that the coherence of lattice vibrations in superconductors plays a crucial role in determining the electron-phonon coupling strength and, hence, the critical temperature for superconductivity. Our results show that highly coherent lattice vibrations favor stronger electron-phonon coupling and higher critical temperatures. Our findings provide a fundamental understanding of how lattice vibrations contribute to superconductivity and could help design new materials with higher critical temperatures for practical applications.

In this work, we present a theoretical framework for studying capillary-induced interactions that extends beyond the common superposition approximation. The motivation for this research arises from the fact that capillary forces play a crucial role in many natural as well as technological processes, ranging from cell adhesion to the behavior of nanoparticles in liquid suspensions. In order to understand these phenomena more accurately, it is necessary to go beyond the traditional assumption of linear superposition of capillary forces.

Our approach is based on the concept of non-additive interfacial energies, which takes into account the interaction between the liquid menisci. We develop an analytical model that incorporates both the capillary interactions and the elasticity of the interfacial film, taking into account spatial non-uniformities in the curvature of the liquid-solid interface. We use this model to explore different geometries and material properties, with the goal of predicting and quantifying the interactions between small particles or structures immersed in a liquid.

Our results show that capillary-induced interactions can be strongly non-additive, and that this effect becomes increasingly pronounced as the liquid menisci become more curved. We demonstrate the importance of including higher-order terms in the interfacial energy expansion, and highlight different regimes of interaction that can arise depending on the relative size of the particles or structures. Overall, our work provides a more accurate and versatile framework for understanding and predicting capillary forces, and has implications for a broad range of fields.

In this work, we explore the current problems and experimental approaches related to photon-induced nucleosynthesis. We aim to understand the process of light element production in the universe through photon-induced reactions, which play a crucial role in the evolution of galaxies. Despite extensive research in this area, these reactions remain poorly understood, and many discrepancies exist between observational data and theoretical models. The main problem this work attempts to solve is to provide an improved understanding of the mechanisms of photon-induced nucleosynthesis.

We employ various experimental approaches, such as measuring reaction cross-sections and studying the energetics of nuclear reactions, to identify and quantify the contributions of these reactions to the production of light elements in the universe. Our work highlights the importance of experimental data in constraining theoretical models and developing a comprehensive understanding of nuclear reactions. Furthermore, we highlight the fundamental role played by photon-induced nucleosynthesis in the formation of stars and galaxies across the universe. The key ideas and methodology presented in this work contribute to an important area of astrophysics research and open up new avenues for future studies.

We present a high-resolution survey of O VI absorption lines in the spectra of 36 low-redshift QSOs. The primary objective of this work is to characterize the physical conditions and statistical properties of O VI absorbers found in the intergalactic medium (IGM). The study aims at addressing the important question of the origin of O VI absorbers - whether they arise solely from photoionization or from a combination of photoionization and collisional ionization. 

Our analysis of the O VI absorbers reveals a complex interplay between various physical processes that shape the properties of the absorbers. We find that the O VI absorbers have a low Doppler parameter and a wide range of ionization fractions, indicative of a mixed origin. We also find that the O VI absorbers are more prevalent in denser environments and that the metallicity of the absorbers is closely linked to the gas density. The findings of this study suggest that the physical conditions of the IGM are highly complex and that the ionization state of the gas cannot be explained solely by photoionization. These results have important implications for understanding the nature of the IGM and its role in shaping the evolution of galaxies.

In this study, we investigate the contribution of BL Lac objects to the extragalactic gamma-ray background (EGB) using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope.
