Through our analysis, we aim to shed light on the mechanisms that drive these processes and provide a more complete understanding of the physical conditions within these stars.

In this paper, we present the results of our study aiming to obtain empirical photometric redshifts of luminous red galaxies and clusters in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The problem we tackle is the identification of galaxies and clusters at high redshifts, which is essential for understanding the properties and evolution of the universe. However, spectroscopic redshift measurements for a large sample of galaxies and clusters are time-consuming and expensive. Hence, we use photometric redshifts, which are derived from the spectral energy distributions of galaxies and clusters. 

Our motivation for this study is to develop an accurate photometric redshift technique that can be applied to a large sample size. We use luminous red galaxies and clusters as they are more massive and found to be better tracers of large-scale structure at higher redshifts. We train and test our method on a sample of 1,000 SDSS DR7 galaxies, which have available spectroscopic redshifts. We evaluate our results using various statistical measures, including the root mean square error,  scatter, and outlier fraction.

Our results show that our empirical photometric redshift technique achieves a scatter of 0.063, with an average outlier fraction of 5.6%. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on samples of luminous red galaxies and galaxy clusters at higher redshifts. In conclusion, our study provides a reliable and efficient technique for obtaining photometric redshifts for large-scale surveys.

In this paper, we aim to establish the equivalence between the Linear Programming (LP) relaxation and Max-Product for solving the problem of weighted matching in general graphs. The primary motivation for this research is the need for efficient methods of solving combinatorial optimization problems. The weighted matching problem is a fundamental problem in graph theory and has many real-world applications, such as matching patients to organ donors in the field of medical science and matching tutors with students in educational domains.

Our work shows that the Max-Product and LP relaxation algorithms are equivalent for the weighted matching problem in general graphs. The proof we present is based on the duality theory of Linear Programming and exhibits the gap between the two approaches. The equivalence we establish between the LP relaxation and Max-Product algorithms is significant for the theoretical aspects of combinatorial optimization and contributes to the existing literature in this field.

The problem we attempt to solve is to find a more efficient algorithm for solving the weighted matching problem. Our research provides insights into the optimality of the Max-Product algorithm and demonstrates the effectiveness of LP relaxation in solving this problem. Therefore, our work is useful for researchers and practitioners working in the field of combinatorial optimization, algorithm design, and graph theory.

In this study, we examined the temperature and frequency dependent impedance of an electroceramic functional oxide thermistor. Our motivation for conducting this research was to gain a deeper understanding of the impedance behavior of this thermistor and explore its potential applications in various electronic circuits. 

To achieve our research goals, we employed a series of measurements and analyses. First, we conducted a series of temperature-dependent impedance spectroscopy experiments to investigate the thermistor's impedance characteristics at different temperatures. Secondly, we performed a frequency sweep experiment to explore the frequency-dependent impedance behavior of the thermistor. Finally, we used the Cole-Cole plot to analyze the relaxation behavior of the thermistor impedance.

The results of our study revealed that the electroceramic functional oxide thermistor has a strong temperature dependence, exhibiting a typical negative temperature coefficient behavior. We also found that the impedance modulus of the thermistor decreased with increasing frequency. Furthermore, the Cole-Cole plot analysis showed that the thermistor exhibits a Debye-type relaxation behavior.

Overall, our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the temperature and frequency-dependent impedance behavior of the electroceramic functional oxide thermistor, which can serve as a foundation for future research on the development and application of this type of thermistor in electronic circuits and devices.

In this study, we investigate the diffusion of optical probes in polymer solutions using fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS). Our goal is to understand the mechanisms governing the interaction between the probes and the polymer matrix, and to explore the effects of polymer concentration, temperature, and probe size and charge on diffusivity. 

Our results show that the diffusion of probes is hindered by the crowded and viscoelastic polymer environment, resulting in slowed-down and anomalous diffusion behaviors. We found that the increase in polymer concentration leads to the reduction in the hydrodynamic radius of the probe due to entanglement effects, and that the presence of charges on the probes enhances their interactions with the polymer chains, reducing their mobility. 

Our study provides insights into the dynamic behavior of polymer solutions at the microscopic level and the effects of probe-polymer interactions on diffusivity, which have implications for a wide range of applications such as drug delivery, sensing, and biomaterials engineering. The methodology we used involves combining FCS with theories of diffusion in complex media and simulations, enabling us to obtain a deeper understanding of the key processes involved. Our work contributes to the ongoing efforts in the polymer research community to design novel materials with tailored properties by providing a fundamental understanding of diffusion dynamics under complex conditions.

In this study, we analyze a spatially extended phytoplankton-zooplankton system, subject to additive noise and periodic forces, in order to understand the resonance and frequency-locking phenomena within the system. Our motivation for this research is to gain insight into the possible response of plankton dynamics to environmental disturbances, including climate change and human activity. 

Our analysis combines the use of bifurcation theory, numerical simulations, and statistical measures to explore the collective behavior of the system. Our results show that the resonance and frequency-locking phenomena can arise in the spatially extended system under certain conditions, including the addition of noise and periodic forces. In particular, we observe the presence of synchronized oscillations between the plankton species, as well as the emergence of spatial patterns in the phytoplankton population. 

Our study provides novel insights into the complex dynamics of plankton systems and highlights the importance of including noise and periodic forces in models that seek to explain the behavior of these systems under real-world conditions. Our findings have important implications for the management of marine ecosystems and the development of effective strategies for mitigating the impact of environmental disturbances on plankton populations.

In this article, we present a branch and cut algorithm for the Halfspace Depth Problem. Our motivation for this research stems from the desire to provide an efficient solution to the problem of finding the deepest subspace containing a given point in high-dimensional data analysis.

The algorithm starts with an initial solution and iteratively divides the solution space into smaller partitions until a valid solution is found. Our approach uses the LP relaxation of the problem to strengthen the lower bounds and a cutting plane technique to improve the upper bounds.

We have tested our algorithm on several datasets and compared its performance with other state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm performs significantly better than the other approaches, both in terms of solution quality and computation time.

The key ideas and methodology of our approach involve formulating the problem using mixed integer linear programming, developing efficient branching techniques, and using a cutting plane method to generate valid inequalities. Our approach also considers problem-specific heuristics to improve the initial guess and speed up convergence.

Overall, our work provides an efficient and effective algorithm for the Halfspace Depth Problem, which can be applied in a wide range of research fields, including statistics, machine learning, and data mining.

We present a study on quantum quenches in extended systems. The problem we attempt to solve is to understand the dynamics of such systems after they undergo a sudden change in their parameters. In particular, we investigate the behavior of the entanglement entropy between two regions of the system, which is a measure of the amount of correlations between them. We focus on one-dimensional spin chains, which are paradigmatic models of quantum many-body systems. 

Our key idea is to use a combination of theoretical and numerical methods to analyze the dynamics of the entanglement entropy after a quench. We employ the powerful framework of conformal field theory, which allows us to obtain analytical predictions for the behavior of the entropy in the long-time limit. We also use numerical simulations based on matrix-product-state methods, which allow us to study the entanglement entropy in finite-sized systems.

Our results show that the dynamics of the entanglement entropy after a quench can be quite complex and sensitive to the parameters of the system. We observe different regimes of behavior, ranging from ballistic to diffusive to logarithmic growth of the entropy, depending on the nature of the quench and the properties of the system. Our study provides insights into the behavior of quantum many-body systems far from equilibrium, which are relevant for a variety of physical phenomena, including quantum computing and condensed matter physics.

In this paper, we present our predictions based on non-trivial quark-lepton complementarity (QTLC), a hypothesis that has emerged from the study of quark and lepton mixing matrices. We are motivated by the observation that the quark and lepton mixing matrices have strikingly similar structures despite the vast differences in their masses and charges, leading us to speculate that the two sectors may be related in a fundamental way. 

Our work attempts to solve the puzzle of why the quark and lepton mixing matrices have such similar structures by proposing a new framework that unifies the two sectors. Specifically, we propose that there is a symmetry that underlies both quark and lepton mixing. We introduce a generalization of the democratic ansatz that is manifestly invariant under this symmetry, and demonstrate its ability to reproduce the observed mixing patterns of both quarks and leptons with high accuracy. 

The key ideas in this work are the identification of a new symmetry that relates quark and lepton mixing, and the use of a modified democratic ansatz that respects this symmetry. The methodology involves developing a mathematical framework to express this idea and test it against existing experimental data. Our results provide strong evidence for the existence of a fundamental connection between the quark and lepton sectors, and open up new avenues for exploring physics beyond the standard model.

We present a white paper highlighting the importance of finding solar system analogs using astrometric measurements from the Space Interferometry Mission (SIM) and the Hipparcos mission. The aim of this paper is to guide the ExoPlanet Task Force in identifying and prioritizing potential targets for future missions. We believe that understanding the physical and chemical properties of other solar systems is crucial in order to decipher the origins and evolution of our own solar system. Our strategy revolves around first identifying stars that have properties similar to the Sun, such as mass, age, and metallicity. We then use SIM and Hipparcos data to measure these stars' astrometric signatures, which are indicators of the presence of planets in their orbits. Using this method, we identify stars with planets in the habitable zone, as well as those with planetary companions in different regions of potential habitability. With the ultimate goal of characterizing the atmosphere and habitability of exoplanets, finding analogs to our solar system is a crucial step forward. We recommend the ExoPlanet Task Force to consider the use of SIM and Hipparcos data to prioritize future exoplanet missions, thereby laying the foundation for continued exploration of the cosmos.

In this research, we investigate the origin of the molecular emission surrounding the southern hemisphere Re 4 IRS - HH 188 region. This region encompasses young-formed stars, and it is well-known for its massive stellar outflow, which exhibits a highly complex morphology. Our research aims at understanding the physical processes that cause the molecular emission around the region by analyzing the spatial and kinematic structure of the molecular gas.

To achieve this aim, we used data obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). We combined different molecular tracers to obtain a complete mapping of the molecular environment surrounding the region. By analyzing the spatial and kinematic structure of the molecular gas, we have identified a complex kinematic pattern, which suggests the presence of a rotating disk-like structure.

The key idea behind our research is to understand better the molecular gas's role in the formation and evolution of young stars. Our results provide new insights into the physical processes that occur in the Re 4 IRS-HH 188 region, and we believe that they will help us to understand better the formation mechanism of young stars and their associated outflows. Ultimately, our research aims to advance our understanding of the physical processes that govern the formation and evolution of stars in our galaxy.

In this study, we present the surface brightness profiles of a sample of Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC), and Fornax galaxy globular clusters. The motivation behind this research is to understand the properties of globular clusters in these galaxies, which are important tracers of their formation and evolution history.

Our key idea is to use high-quality photometric data obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope to derive accurate surface brightness profiles for a sample of globular clusters in these galaxies. We employ a combination of rigorous data reduction techniques and state-of-the-art image modeling tools to extract these profiles. 

The methodology involves fitting a series of analytical models to the observed data and quantifying the best-fit parameters using minimization algorithms. We evaluate the accuracy and robustness of our approach by comparing our results with those obtained from other independent techniques.

The main problem our work attempts to solve is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the structural properties of globular clusters in LMC, SMC, and Fornax galaxies, which is crucial to understand their formation and evolution processes. Our results reveal a wide range of structural parameters, indicating that the globular clusters in these galaxies have complex and diverse origins. The importance of this study lies in its contribution to our understanding of the properties of globular clusters and their role in galaxy formation and evolution.

Our research delves into Conservation Laws, specifically the Generation of Physical Fields and Principles of Field Theories. The primary motivation behind this work was to understand the fundamental principles of field theories and the laws governing the conservation of physical fields. Our approach involved analyzing a variety of examples from classical physics to modern field theories. Our study revealed that conservation laws are fundamental principles that govern physical fields, making them an essential concept in the study of physical phenomena.

Furthermore, our work proposed a new theoretical framework that allows for a better understanding of field theories and conservation laws. Our methodology involved a combination of theoretical analysis, experimentation, and numerical simulation. Through this approach, we succeed in developing a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying principles governing physical fields. The practical implications of this work extend to multiple fields, including quantum physics, astrophysics, and materials science.

Overall, this work contributes to the existing literature by providing a deeper understanding of conservation laws and physical fields. Our findings have significant potential for further exploration and practical applications in various fields. This study confirms that understanding the fundamental principles of field theories and the laws governing physical fields is critical to advancing our knowledge of the physical world.

In our work, we explore Markov properties when observations are noisy. We seek to understand how to uncover the underlying structure of a system when the observations we collect are not perfectly accurate. To do this, we develop a theoretical framework that allows us to model how measurement noise affects the variables being tracked. Our approach provides new insights into how we can infer the state of a system in the presence of measurement error. 

Our motivation for this research comes from the fact that in many practical settings, measurement noise is an inevitable challenge. Whether we are monitoring a chemical reaction or tracking the movement of a flock of birds, there will always be some degree of measurement error. The goal of our work is to provide a deeper understanding of how this noise affects the Markov properties of a system so that we can better infer its underlying structure.

To achieve this, we approach the problem by formulating a framework based on the Bayesian belief network and Hidden Markov Models. These methods allow us to model the system in a way that integrates the effects of measurement noise into the Markovian context. We conduct experiments to validate our approach, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

In summary, our work provides an insight into the Markov property in the presence of measurement noise. We offer a novel framework for modeling this phenomenon, which can enhance performance and accuracy in various real-world settings.

In this study, we present the results of our analysis of solar-like oscillations in the metal-poor subgiant nu Indi, with a focus on the acoustic spectrum and mode lifetime. Our aim was to provide further insights into the physical properties of nu Indi and its internal structure.

To achieve this, we used high-precision time-series photometry data collected by the TESS space telescope, and applied various data analysis techniques including power spectral density and autocorrelation function analysis to extract mode frequencies and lifetimes.

Our results reveal the presence of numerous low-degree, high-radial-order p-mode oscillations with a frequency range of 0.5-2.5 mHz and mode lifetimes of 1-5 days. The acoustic spectrum exhibits a clear frequency pattern consistent with the mode trapping phenomenon, and we find evidence of rotation in the form of frequency splittings.

Overall, our study provides valuable information on the internal properties of nu Indi and sheds light on the behavior of metal-poor subgiants in general. The findings have important implications for our understanding of stellar evolution and the fundamental laws of physics that govern the behavior of stars.

In this work, we investigate the mean-field magnetohydrodynamics of accretion disks. Our study aims to understand the role of magnetic fields in shaping the dynamics of accretion disks and their associated astrophysical phenomena such as the accretion of matter onto a central object, jet formation, and the emission of radiation. We employ a theoretical approach that combines hydrodynamic and magnetic field equations describing turbulence and angular momentum transport in disks. Our methodology involves deriving a set of magnetohydrodynamic equations from first principles and using numerical simulations to solve them under different physical conditions. 

The motivation for our research stems from the fact that accretion disks are ubiquitous in astrophysics and play a fundamental role in the formation and evolution of various cosmic structures, including planets, stars, and galaxies. It is known that magnetic fields can have a profound influence on the dynamics of these disks and is therefore essential to include them in any comprehensive model of accretion disks. Our simulations show that magnetic fields can significantly affect the rate of accretion, the formation of jets, and the radiative output of disks. The results of our study provide insights into the physical mechanisms that drive accretion disk dynamics and offer useful predictions for observations of astronomical phenomena.

We present a new approach to derive irreducible metric variations of the action terms associated with the sixth-order gravity theory. Our method aims to obtain the approximated stress-energy tensor of the theory by using the metric variations. 

We start by constructing the most general polynomial action of sixth-order gravity that respects the field equations and has a well-defined variational principle. We then consider variations of the action with respect to the metric and obtain a set of equations that need to be solved to determine the irreducible components of the metric variations. We use a decomposition of the metric that naturally emerges from the analysis of the field equations to simplify the computations. 

Our approach differs from previous works in that we obtain a closed-form expression for the metric variations, which allows us to derive the approximated stress-energy tensor of the theory without resorting to numerical simulations. This result represents a significant advancement towards the understanding of the properties of sixth-order gravity and its connection with the classical theories of gravitation. 

Our motivation for this work is to shed light on the properties of higher-order gravity and to provide a tool for the analysis of astrophysical systems that are subject to strong gravitational fields. The method presented here can be applied to study a variety of problems in gravitational physics, such as black hole thermodynamics and the dynamics of compact stars.

In this work, we investigate quantum fields on the Groenewold-Moyal (GM) plane, focusing on charge conjugation (C), parity (P), time reversal (T), and their combination CPT. Our goal is to understand the implications of noncommutativity for these symmetries, which play a crucial role in particle physics. Noncommutativity is a fundamental feature of the GM plane, which allows for a deformation of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. 

We show that CPT is conserved for free fields on the GM plane, as it is in commutative spacetimes. However, for interacting fields, we find that CPT is violated, even in the absence of CP or T violation. This implies that the CPT theorem, a cornerstone of relativistic quantum field theory, does not hold in noncommutative spacetimes. We argue that this is a consequence of the non-locality introduced by noncommutativity, which disrupts the delicate balance between quantum mechanics and special relativity.

Our methodology is based on a rigorous treatment of quantum field theory on the GM plane, using the Wigner transformation to map noncommutative fields to commutative ones. We use this approach to derive the CPT transformations for noncommutative fields, and to study their properties for various classes of interactions. Our results provide important insights into the interplay between noncommutativity and fundamental symmetries, with potential applications to theories beyond the standard model.

In this study, we investigated the high-energy threshold reaction rates on a 0.8 GeV proton-irradiated thick Pb-target. The motivation for this research was to understand the interaction between high-energy protons and thick Pb-targets, which is important for many applications in nuclear science and technology. However, previous studies have focused mainly on thin targets, and there is limited information on the reaction rates in thick targets. Therefore, our work attempts to fill this knowledge gap by performing experiments with a thick Pb-target and measuring the reaction rates using a gamma spectrometer. 

Our results showed that the reaction rates were much lower in the thick Pb-target compared to the thin target, due to the decrease in proton energy as it penetrates the material. We also observed some new gamma ray lines which have not been previously reported, indicating a possible reaction pathway in the thick target. Our findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of high-energy protons in thick materials, which can be used to improve the design of radiation shielding for nuclear reactors and accelerators. Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of the fundamental physics of nuclear reactions and has practical implications for nuclear safety and radiation protection.

In this work, we present GEMS, a publicly available catalog of galaxy fitting parameters obtained by testing a suite of parametric fitting codes on simulated data. The aim of this study is to provide a benchmark for galaxy fitting codes that will enable astronomers to select the code best suited to their scientific aims.

To achieve this goal, we generated simulated galaxies with varying morphological characteristics and then fit them using five widely-used parametric fitting codes: GALFIT, GIM2D, SExtractor, ACS GALFIT, and the Fitting and Assessment of Synthetic Templates code (FAST; a new code developed for this study). We tested the codes on realism, completeness, and repeatability and found that all codes perform well on bright galaxies with simple morphologies. However, faint and complex galaxies pose significant challenges for all codes, with GALFIT and ACS GALFIT performing best overall.

The GEMS catalog contains fitting parameters for 173 object simulations generated with 9 morphological templates, covering a range of magnitude, flux, and galaxy sizes and inclination angles. These simulated galaxies represent diverse galaxy populations from local to high-redshift universe and different signal-to-noise ratios. GEMS also provides data on the corresponding input parameters for each simulated galaxy, including total magnitudes and half-light radii, enabling validation of the accuracy of the outputs of galaxy fitting codes.

Overall, GEMS provides a unique resource for those interested in comparing and improving existing parametric fitting codes, as well as for those developing new algorithms suitable for galaxy fitting. This work contributes to enhancing the accuracy of photometric measurements and demonstrating their reliability.

In this study, we present the results of near-infrared polarimetric observations of the bipolar nebula IRAS 19312+1950 using the NAOS/CONICA instrument on the very large telescope. The motivation for this research was to understand the physical and morphological properties of this bipolar nebula, which appears to be a very young bipolar planetary nebula. We aimed to investigate the geometry and alignment of dust grains within this nebula through the analysis of polarization data.

Our results show a clear indication of polarization in the bipolar nebula, suggesting the presence of elongated dust grains aligned with the outflow axis. We found that the polarization degree decreases with increasing wavelength, which is consistent with the theoretical predictions for light scattering by non-spherical particles. There is also a strong variation of the polarization degree across the nebula, likely due to the complex geometry and dusty environment of this object. Our study provides important insights into the physical processes and properties of bipolar nebulae, and highlights the usefulness of near-infrared polarimetry in probing the structure of these objects.

The key methodology of this work involved the collection of high-quality polarimetric data of IRAS 19312+1950, and the subsequent analysis of this data through techniques such as aperture photometry, Stokes parameters, and polarization degree calculations. Our study demonstrates the power of near-infrared polarimetry in understanding the morphology and physical properties of bipolar nebulae, and opens the door for further investigations in this exciting area of research.

In this study, we report the results of our work on infrared (IR) observations of the galaxy cluster MS 1054-03. Our research has focused on exploring the star formation and its evolution in rich galaxy clusters, which is a crucial area of study in astrophysics. Our primary motivation for this research was to understand the physical processes that govern star formation in such environments.

Our observations of MS 1054-03 revealed three distinct subpopulations of galaxies, separated by their IR luminosities. The first subpopulation exhibited only a mild enhancement in IR luminosities, whereas the second subpopulation showed a significantly higher increase in IR luminosities than the first. The third subpopulation, which consisted of the brightest and most massive galaxies in the cluster, showed the highest increase in IR luminosities.

By comparing the observed distributions of these subpopulations with theoretical models of galaxy evolution, we found that the observed IR luminosity enhancement in each subpopulation can be explained by different physical mechanisms. Our work thus provides new insights into the interplay between star formation and the overall evolution of galaxies in rich galaxy clusters.

In summary, this study represents a significant step towards understanding the complex processes governing star formation and galaxy evolution in rich galaxy clusters. Our findings provide crucial constraints for theoretical models of galaxy evolution in such environments.

We aim to investigate the average kinetic energy of the heavy quark in the $\Lambda_b$ baryon using the Bethe-Salpeter Equation Approach. Our motivation for this research stems from the gaps in our understanding of the internal structure of hadrons, which are composite particles made up of quarks and gluons. The $\Lambda_b$ baryon, in particular, contains a heavy b-quark that plays a crucial role in the dynamics of the hadron. The average kinetic energy of this heavy quark provides essential information about its motion inside the baryon.

Our work involves utilizing the Bethe-Salpeter Equation approach, which considers the interaction between two particles and takes into account the effects of relativity and quantum mechanics. By solving this equation, we are able to find the wave function of the $\Lambda_b$ baryon and extract the average kinetic energy of the heavy b-quark. This method provides a more accurate and comprehensive approach to understanding the internal structure of hadrons.

Our research has the potential to contribute significantly to the understanding of the dynamics of hadrons, which is essential to many areas of particle physics, including nuclear physics and high-energy physics. By elucidating the average kinetic energy of the heavy quark in the $\Lambda_b$ baryon, our work helps to deepen our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter and its interactions.

We present the results of our high-resolution spectroscopic analysis of the post-Asymptotic Giant Branch (post-AGB) star, HR 4049. Our observations, obtained with the CRyogenic InfraRed Echelle Spectrograph (CRIRES) instrument on the Very Large Telescope (VLT), reveal several spectral lines in the near-infrared region that are associated with the circumstellar disk around the star. We have analyzed these lines using radiative transfer models to infer the physical properties of the disk, such as its density, temperature, and velocity structure. Our results suggest the presence of a fast, collimated outflow in the disk, possibly caused by the interaction between the stellar wind and the disk material. This outflow may be responsible for the observed depletion of refractory elements in the stellar photosphere, known as the "winnowing effect". Our observations and analysis offer important insights into the formation and evolution of post-AGB circumstellar disks and their role in the chemical enrichment of the interstellar medium. Our methodology provides a framework for future studies of similar systems, and our findings contribute to a better understanding of the late stages of stellar evolution.

In this paper, we investigate the instabilities that arise in the time-dependent neutrino disc in Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs). GRBs are high energy astronomical events that occur when a massive star collapses, producing a jet of particles that emits intense bursts of gamma rays. The presence of neutrinos in the jet plays a key role in the energy transport and emission mechanism of GRBs. However, since the neutrinos interact weakly with matter, their dynamics are affected by a range of micro-physical dissipation processes.

Our work aims at characterizing the dynamics of the neutrino disc in the presence of these micro-physical instabilities using high-fidelity numerical simulations. Specifically, we investigate the effects of the neutrino cooling, the generation of turbulence due to the convective instability, and the impact of neutrino oscillations on the evolution of the disc. Our analysis demonstrates that these instabilities can significantly affect the energy transport properties of the neutrino disc and have important implications for understanding the emission mechanism of GRBs.

Overall, our research provides crucial insights into the micro-physical processes that govern the behavior of the neutrino disc in GRBs. These findings may help to shed light on the underlying physics of these enigmatic astrophysical objects, informing future observational and theoretical studies.

In this work, we investigate the Nonperiodic Anyon Model (NAM), which is a generalization of the Periodic Anyon Model (PAM) used to describe the Fractional Quantum Hall Effect (FQHE). The NAM relaxes the periodicity assumption of the PAM, allowing for non-periodic boundary conditions. Our study focuses on the mutual statistics of the quasi-particle excitations in the NAM, which is in contrast to previous studies of the PAM that explored the topological properties of the ground state. We propose to use an effective field theory approach to describe the anyonic quasi-particles in the NAM. Moreover, we use Sugawara's construction to derive the algebraic fusion rules and to identify the anyonic Hilbert spaces of the NAM.

Our main result is the computation of the quasiparticle self-statistics. This quantity is shown to exhibit unusual dependence on the topological angle θ0 characterizing the nonperiodic boundary conditions. When θ0 is zero, the model breaks translational symmetry, and the quasiparticles have completely free statistics. As θ0 increases, the self-statistics become increasingly constrained, going through the rational numbers and eventually becoming periodic.

Our work provides insights into how quasi-particles behave in the FQHE, with potential applications in topological quantum computing. Our results also provide a basis for further exploration of the NAM and its connections to other anyon models and topological phases of matter.

Galaxy Evolution and Environment is a study that aims to explore the relationship between the evolution of galaxies and their environment. The leading problem the research attempts to solve is how the evolution and structure of galaxies are influenced by their environment. Our motivation behind conducting this research is to understand the interplay between galaxies and their surrounding environment, which is crucial for predicting the behavior of galaxies and stargazing.

The research involved analyzing a sample of galaxies at different distances from clusters using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The results demonstrate that interactions between galaxies and their environment, such as mergers, tidal forces, and gas stripping, play a significant role in shaping the evolution and structure of galaxies. We further found that the environmental impact on galaxy evolution depends on various factors such as galaxy mass, distance from the galaxy cluster, and the distribution of matter in the cluster.

Our findings suggest that the environment plays a critical role in shaping the evolution of galaxies. This research offers insights into the growth and formation of galaxies in different environments, making it a vital contribution to our understanding of the universe. Understanding the complex relationship between galaxies and their environment is the key to unlocking the mysteries of the universe.

In this work, we present a detailed investigation of the nonlocal excitation spectra in the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model. The motivation behind this research is to understand the nature of the electronic excitations that give rise to the phenomenon of high-temperature superconductivity. Using the Lanczos exact diagonalization technique, we obtain the spectral functions of the doped Hubbard model for various doping levels and interaction strengths. 

We find that the excitation spectra show distinct features at different dopings, particularly in the vicinity of the Fermi energy. The spectral weight is primarily concentrated below the Fermi energy for low doping and moves to above the Fermi energy with increasing doping. Moreover, the Hubbard interaction strength significantly alters the spectral weight distribution as well. 

Our work sheds light on the interplay between doping level and interaction strength in shaping the nonlocal excitation spectra of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model. It contributes to a better understanding of the microscopic mechanisms underlying high-temperature superconductivity, which is essential for designing new materials with enhanced superconducting properties. Our study may also have implications for other strongly correlated systems where the Hubbard model is applicable.

In this study, we explore the absorption spectroscopy of individual single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) as a method to understand their electronic and optical properties. Absorption spectra of SWCNTs can provide critical information on their electronic band structure and exciton binding energy, essential parameters for developing nanotube-based electronics and optoelectronic devices. However, the presence of multiple chiralities and diameters in typical SWCNT samples complicates analysis of their absorption spectra. To overcome this hurdle, we used a customized spectroscopy system with submillisecond acquisition times to measure absorption spectra of individual SWCNTs with high spectral resolution. By calculating the absorption peak position and intensity, we identified the chiral indices and diameter of individual SWCNTs, revealing a dependence of exciton binding energy on their diameter. Furthermore, we characterized the excitonic transitions of a single SWCNT, which exhibited highly asymmetric absorption lineshapes beyond simple Lorentzian functions, indicating the presence of strong electron-electron interaction. Our results provide key insights for understanding the optical and electronic properties of SWCNTs and for designing nanotube-based devices with new functionalities.

We present a study of the behavior of spinons and triplons in spatially anisotropic frustrated antiferromagnets. Our motivation for this research is to understand the complex behavior of magnetism in materials with competing interactions. Such systems can display a range of exotic phenomena, including fractional excitations like spinons and triplons. These excitations behave much like particles, each carrying fractional quantum numbers of the spin and charge. 

We employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods to investigate the properties of spinons and triplons in an Ising model with bilinear and biquadratic interactions on a two-dimensional square lattice. We find that the anisotropy of the interactions leads to a rich phase diagram, with distinct regimes of behavior for spinons and triplons. In particular, we observe a critical point at which the spinon gap closes, indicating the onset of an unconventional phase. Moreover, we find that triplons are only weakly affected by the anisotropy and retain their spin and charge properties over a broad range of parameter space.

Our results shed light on the role of anisotropy in frustrated antiferromagnets and provide important insights into the behavior of fractional excitations in these systems. Our methodology lays the groundwork for further investigations of other models and materials with competing interactions.

In this study, we present a successive sub-grouping method for multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) as an efficient tool to analyze sequence data. MSAs are widely used in various research fields, including evolutionary biology, comparative genomics, and structural biology. However, accurate analysis of MSAs remains challenging because of their size and complexity. In particular, MSAs can contain large numbers of sequences with varying lengths, structures, and similarities, which makes it difficult to apply existing methods to optimize the alignment.

Our proposed method involves iteratively removing sequences that have minimal similarities with the remaining sequences in the alignment until all sequences have been clustered into subgroups with a pre-defined similarity threshold. The key idea of our method is rooted in the observation that the accuracy of MSAs generally improves when sequences with low similarity are separated from highly similar ones. Profiling the sequence alignment this way improves computational efficiency, increases the accuracy of multiple sequence alignment, and makes the method applicable to a wide range of sequence datasets.

We tested our successive sub-grouping algorithm on various sequence datasets and compared the results to existing multiple sequence alignment algorithms, demonstrating that our method generates highly accurate MSAs in a fraction of the time compared to other methods. Consequently, our method offers an efficient tool for analyzing large and complex sequence datasets in a variety of research fields.

In this work, we measure the spin-transfer-torque (STT) vector in magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) by employing a spin-torque ferromagnetic resonance (ST-FMR) technique. The STT effect refers to the transfer of spin angular momentum from one layer to another via a spin-polarized electric current, leading to a torque on the magnetization. The STT vector, which describes the directional dependence of the STT effect, is a crucial parameter for optimizing STT-based devices for spintronics and information processing applications. Our motivation for this research is to provide a robust and accurate measurement method for the STT vector, which remains a challenging experimental task due to the complex interplay between the STT effect and the magnetic anisotropy, damping, and resonance modes.

We present experimental results for CoFeB/MgO MTJs showing pronounced variation in the STT vector with the applied magnetic field direction. By quantifying the angle dependence of the STT vector, we extract the effective spin polarization, spin diffusion length, and Gilbert damping parameter of the CoFeB layer. Our key innovation is the use of an optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) technique that allows us to measure the current-induced magnetization dynamics of the MTJ with high sensitivity and spatial resolution. This work contributes to a better understanding of the fundamental mechanisms underlying STT-based devices and provides a valuable tool for their optimization and characterization.

In this work, we aim to characterize the properties of the low-redshift intergalactic medium (IGM) towards the quasar PKS1302-102, which is at a redshift of z ≈ 0.278. The IGM is a crucial component in our understanding of the large-scale structure and evolution of the universe since it is the medium through which most of the baryonic matter in the universe travels. 
We use a combination of high-resolution spectra obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope and multi-wavelength data obtained from ground-based telescopes to study the IGM absorption properties. We analyze the column densities and the Doppler parameters of the gas, and also study its metallicity and ionization state. 
Our motivation for this work is to gain a deeper understanding of the physical conditions of the IGM at low redshifts, which can provide vital input for models of galaxy formation and evolution. We find that the IGM towards PKS1302-102 has a low ionization state, a high metallicity, and a narrow range of Doppler parameters. We also observe signatures of a warm-hot component and an excess of low-ionization absorption. These results have implications for models of the low-redshift IGM and its role in galaxy evolution.

In this study, we investigated the habitability of super-Earths in Gliese 581, a planetary system located approximately 20.3 light years away from Earth. The problem we attempted to solve was whether super-Earths in Gliese 581 could support life as we know it. We obtained our results by analyzing data collected from the Habitable Exoplanet Catalogue and simulations from the Habitable Zone Gallery. Our key ideas and methodology involved examining the distance of each super-Earth in the planetary system from its host star, its orbiting period, its mass, and the presence of water. 

Our findings revealed that one of the super-Earths, Gliese 581g, had the potential to be habitable. It was located within the habitable zone of the planetary system, which is defined as the range of distances from a star where an orbiting planet could maintain surface water. Additionally, it had a mass similar to that of Earth, and the possibility of water on its surface. Furthermore, our analysis provided evidence to suggest the existence of a second habitable planet within the system, although further research is needed to confirm this.

Overall, our study contributes to the ongoing exploration of exoplanets and their potential habitability. The findings bring us closer to understanding the conditions needed to sustain life beyond our own planet Earth.

In this review, we delve into the topic of bipolar spintronics and investigate its potential for developing spin-controlled logic devices. The central idea of this field is to utilize the magnetic properties of electrons, known as spin, for manipulating the flow of currents in electronic systems. This approach offers a promising solution for improving the efficiency and performance of modern electronic devices. 
We highlight the key methodologies that have been employed in bipolar spintronics research, including spin injection, spin transport, and spin detection. We discuss how researchers are integrating these methodologies with traditional electronic circuitry, resulting in a hybrid system that integrates electronic and magnetic functionalities. 
This review focuses particularly on the challenges posed by bipolar spintronics in terms of realizing spin-controlled logic. We discuss the current limitations of spintronic devices, including their sensitivity to temperature and the need for high magnetic fields for operation. Additionally, we examine various experimental approaches that researchers have used to address these challenges.
Our motivation for this research is to offer a comprehensive overview of the field of bipolar spintronics, including its potential for developing spin-controlled logic devices. We hope that this review can serve as a foundation for future research in the field and inspire researchers to continue exploring the possibilities of spintronics in developing novel and efficient electronic devices.

We present a study on the effects of selection and covariance on X-ray scaling relations of galaxy clusters. X-ray scaling relations are well-established empirical correlations between different observable properties of galaxy clusters, such as their X-ray luminosity and temperature. These relations are important tools for galaxy cluster studies, as they allow us to infer various physical quantities that are otherwise difficult to measure directly, such as the total cluster mass. 

Our work aims to quantify the potential biases in these scaling relations that arise due to selection effects, particularly those that result from the limitations of current X-ray observations. We also investigate the effects of covariance between X-ray observables, which has recently been shown to have a significant impact on the inferred scaling relations. We use a combination of simulated and observed X-ray data to model the selection and covariance effects on scaling relations, and compare our results to theoretical predictions. 

The motivation for our study is to improve the accuracy and precision of cluster mass estimates, which are crucial for understanding the evolution of large-scale structure in the universe, as well as testing cosmological models. Our work attempts to solve the problem of potential biases in X-ray scaling relations, which threaten the reliability of cluster mass estimates. Our results have important implications for future X-ray surveys, as they provide insight into the potential limitations of these observations, and may inform the development of new observational techniques.

In this study, we investigate the relation between the equivalence principle and the electromagnetic field in the context of its effects on birefringence, dilaton, and axion. The motivation is rooted in a correlated understanding of these phenomena and their dependence on the equivalence principle, which says that gravity exhibits an acceleration-effect equivalent to all other forces. 

Our key idea is to consider how the equivalence principle influences the polarization state of electromagnetic waves in a gravitational field beyond the usual treatments of general relativity. We examine the propagation of linearly polarized waves in an electromagnetic field subject to gravity and show that the equivalence principle constrains these waves through the elimination of birefringence – the dependence of light's refractive index on polarization orientation, which contributes to significant deviations from the principles of special relativity and the equivalence principle.

Through mathematical and numerical analysis, we demonstrate that the absence of birefringence can also lead to the absence of dilaton and axion fields, which are scalar fields controlled by the string theory of gravitation. We conclude that the equivalence principle is a fundamental principle of modern physics, governing a wide range of phenomena across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays. Our results have significant implications for the interpretation of gravitational waves and the study of high-energy physics.

The Output Stream of Binding Neuron with Feedback is an attempt to solve the problem of understanding how binding neurons in the brain function. The motivation of our research project is to explore the mechanisms that underlie the ability of binding neurons to identify and link perceptual features with a specific object or location. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to gaining deeper insights into how the brain processes sensory information, and how it creates integrated representations of the external world.

To tackle this problem, we used a computational approach that involves simulating the activity of a binding neuron with feedback. Our key idea was to model how the binding neuron's output stream is shaped by its input and feedback signals, and how it can be used to infer the properties of the target object or location.

Our methodology involved building a neural network model that incorporates biologically realistic features of the binding neuron. We conducted extensive simulations to explore the range of conditions under which the output stream of the binding neuron could successfully identify a target object or location.

Overall, our findings suggest that the output stream of binding neurons with feedback plays a critical role in linking sensory features with complete representations of objects or locations. Our work has important implications for ongoing efforts to understand how the brain processes and integrates sensory information.

In this work, we present the second part of our census of the Carina Nebula, focusing on the energy budget and global properties of the nebulosity. The Carina Nebula is a massive star-forming region located in our Milky Way Galaxy, which provides an excellent natural laboratory to study the physics of massive star formation and the resulting feedback on the surrounding interstellar medium. 

Using multi-wavelength imaging and spectroscopy data from the Hubble Space Telescope, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and ground-based telescopes, we obtained a complete picture of the energy budget in the Carina Nebula, from the ionizing radiation of massive stars to the heating of dust grains by ultraviolet photons and cosmic rays. We also derived global properties of the nebulosity, such as its size, mass, and gas metallicity. 

Our results show that the energy input from ionizing radiation is the dominant mechanism of energy injection in the Carina Nebula and that the nebulosity is in a state of expansion, driven by feedback from massive stars. We also found evidence of a complex interplay between ionizing radiation and magnetic fields, which may play a role in shaping the structure and dynamics of the nebulosity. 

Our study provides crucial information for understanding the formation and evolution of massive stars and their impact on the interstellar medium.

In this work, we present a microscopic model for the neutron dynamic structure factor of solid methane in phase II. Our study seeks to understand the behavior of the collective excitations of methane molecules in a high-pressure environment. The neutron dynamic structure factor is a tool that provides important information about the atomic and molecular motions within a material. Despite extensive experimental studies of the neutron dynamic structure factor of solid methane, there is still a lack of understanding regarding the underlying mechanisms that drive the excitation dynamics in this material. 

To address this problem, we developed a microscopic model based on first-principles calculations of the intermolecular potentials and the molecular dynamics simulations. Our calculations show that the excitation frequency of the collective excitations in solid methane is highly sensitive to the intermolecular potential and the density of the material. Furthermore, we found that the neutron dynamic structure factor of solid methane in phase II can be described by a superposition of oscillatory modes and a low-frequency background, which arises due to the strong interactions between the methane molecules. 

Overall, this study provides a deeper understanding of the nature of the collective excitations in solid methane and lays the groundwork for future studies of neutron scattering in high-pressure materials. Our results demonstrate the key role of intermolecular interactions and density-induced effects in the neutron scattering properties of materials.

In our study, we investigate the optimal stimulus and noise distributions for information transmission via suprathreshold stochastic resonance. Our research objective is to determine the optimal parameters of a noisy system that can effectively transmit and detect weak signals in both the sub- and suprathreshold regimes. The motivation for this research stems from the challenges involved in reliably transmitting weak signals while suppressing random noise sources.

To achieve our research objectives, we utilize a noise-induced resonance model in which a weak periodic signal is transmitted through a nonlinear threshold system with added noise. We optimize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the output signal by optimizing the stimulus amplitude and noise strength. Our analysis quantifies the optimal SNR improvement achieved by a multi-noise distribution strategy and determines the corresponding optimal signal and noise strengths.

Our results demonstrate that the optimal stimulus and noise distributions for subthreshold and suprathreshold stochastic resonance are fundamentally different. In the subthreshold regime, the optimal stimulus amplitude is at the detection threshold, while in the suprathreshold regime, it is above the threshold. Our optimization approach reveals that the combined use of multi-noise distributions can yield a significantly improved SNR for weak signal transmission. These findings provide new insights into the mechanisms of stochastic resonance and have potential applications in signal detection, communication systems, and biomedical imaging.

In this paper, we present bounds on the elements of the quark mass matrices that arise from the measured properties of the mixing matrix and the present values of the quark masses. The bounds are derived using a model-independent approach and are valid for any new physics scenario beyond the Standard Model that preserves the minimal flavor violation hypothesis. 

Our methodology consists of combining the unitarity of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) mixing matrix with the quark mass ratios and and current experimental bounds on the CKM elements from muon decay and other precision measurements. We take into account higher-order corrections due to quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and electroweak interactions at next-to-leading order where applicable. 

Our results show that the bounds on the quark mass matrix elements are in good agreement with the current experimental values. We find that the heaviest quark, the top quark, plays the dominant role in constraining the mass matrix elements, followed by the charm quark. Interestingly, our results also show that the strange quark mass is more tightly constrained than the up quark mass, in contrast to the standard assumption of flavor symmetry.

Our motivation for this research is to provide constraints on the fundamental parameters of the Standard Model and to search for new physics beyond it. These bounds can guide future experimental searches for deviations from the Standard Model and inform experimentalists on areas of parameter space that need to be explored to discover new physics.

In this personal historical perspective, we reflect on the mass loss and evolution of stars and star clusters, influenced by our own research experiences and collaborations with experts in the field. The exploration covers the key ideas and methodologies that have guided the study of stars’ evolution, beginning with the seminal work by Edwin Salpeter. We describe how, during the 1970s and 1980s, a shift occurred towards the inclusion of mass loss as one of the key drivers of stellar evolution, leading ultimately to the newer perspective of clusters as the natural crucibles for star formation. 

Our work has resulted in several key findings that help contribute to the ongoing discourse in this field. We document the evolution of stars up to more massive endpoints and explore how highly massive AC-stellar systems could become the source of gamma-ray bursts, among other things. Additionally, we examine the role of binary stars governed by mass-transfer in the context of star cluster evolution. Finally, we reflect on some of the remaining enigmas in the field, perhaps most notably the stunted formation of massive stars and its intersections with observed star clusters. This work aims to delineate a complete picture of the interwoven mechanics of star evolution.

In this study, we present a new multiphilic descriptor that can be used to predict the reactivity and selectivity of chemical compounds. The motivation for this research comes from the need to develop a reliable and accurate method for predicting the behavior of chemical molecules in various reactions and environments. Current methods for predicting reactivity and selectivity are often limited in their ability to incorporate multiple factors that can influence the behavior of chemical compounds. Our multiphilic descriptor is based on the concept of integration, which allows for the incorporation of multiple chemical properties into a single descriptor.

To test the utility of our new descriptor, we applied it to a diverse set of chemical reactions and found that it was able to accurately predict the reactivity and selectivity of the compounds involved. Our results demonstrate that our multiphilic descriptor is a valuable tool for chemists and researchers working in the field of chemical synthesis and design. We believe that our descriptor has the potential to accelerate the discovery of new chemical compounds with desired properties and can help to reduce the time and cost associated with traditional trial-and-error-based methods.

Overall, our study presents a novel approach to predicting reactivity and selectivity in chemical compounds and has the potential to significantly impact the field of chemical synthesis and design. Our work highlights the importance of incorporating multiple chemical properties into predictive models and demonstrates the potential for multiphilic descriptors to be used as powerful tools for chemical discovery.

Our research aims to investigate the spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems. The key idea of spectrum pooling is to allow multiple unlicensed users to share the same spectrum band simultaneously, by dynamically assigning available spectrum resources. Our methodology involves mathematical analysis and simulations to evaluate the impact of various parameters on the spectral efficiency. These parameters include the user density, the channel fading, the interference level, and the channel allocation scheme.

The main motivation for this research is the increasing demand for wireless data traffic, which poses a serious challenge to the existing spectrum allocation mechanisms. Spectrum pooling has been recognized as a promising solution to improve the utilization of scarce spectrum resources, but its performance under various conditions needs to be investigated thoroughly. Our research sheds light on the factors that affect the spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems, and provides insights for designing efficient spectrum allocation policies.

Our results show that the spectral efficiency of spectrum pooling systems can be significantly improved by optimizing the channel allocation scheme based on the user density and the interference level. However, this improvement comes at the cost of higher complexity of the allocation algorithm. Our study highlights the trade-off between complexity and performance, and suggests potential directions for future research on spectrum pooling systems.

In this work, we investigate the G-convergence and homogenization of viscoelastic flows in order to understand how these complex fluids behave in different conditions. Our research is motivated by the fact that the behavior of these fluids is fundamentally different from that of Newtonian fluids under certain conditions, and understanding their behavior is crucial for applications ranging from biomedical engineering to industrial processing.

Specifically, we examine the case of viscoelastic fluids flowing through a porous medium with periodically varying microstructure, using a combination of asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations. Through our analysis, we demonstrate the convergence of the solutions of the viscoelastic flows to those of a simpler, homogenized system governed by an effective equation.

Our results show that both the G-convergence and homogenization of viscoelastic flows play a key role in explaining the behavior of these fluids in porous media. Our work provides a solid foundation for future studies of viscoelastic flows in complex environments, and highlights the importance of understanding and modeling the behavior of these fluids in a variety of different applications.

In this work, we investigate the Parametrized Post-Newtonian (PPN) expansion of Chern-Simons (CS) gravity, which is a modification of General Relativity involving a topological term. Our main motivation for this research is to explore the implications of this modified theory of gravity on the motion of bodies in the Solar System and its observational tests using experiments. To accomplish this task, we develop a systematic approach to derive the PPN parameters for CS gravity to the first post-Newtonian order. Our methodology involves the use of the harmonic gauge condition and the iterative process, which allows us to obtain the PPN expansion of the metric, the Christoffel symbols, and the Riemann and Ricci tensors. 

Our main results show that the PPN parameters for CS gravity are different from those of General Relativity, which suggests that the modification of the theory has observable effects on the Solar System dynamics. In particular, our calculations show that the CS term introduces a new parameter that can be constrained using the existing observations of the Earth-Moon system. In summary, this work contributes to the ongoing efforts to test the validity of General Relativity and its modifications and provides a framework for future studies on the implications of CS gravity in cosmology and astrophysics.

In this paper, we explore the phenomenon of spontaneous Lorentz violation through the lens of non-Abelian gauge fields as pseudo-Goldstone vector bosons. The key idea behind our work is that the breaking of Lorentz symmetry can be manifested in the effective dynamics of gauge fields which undergo spontaneous symmetry breaking.

We use a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to demonstrate how the non-Abelian gauge fields can arise as a result of spontaneous Lorentz violation. Specifically, we rely on the so-called Stückelberg mechanism, which allows for the introduction of additional degrees of freedom in the theory.

Our motivation for this research comes from the fact that spontaneous Lorentz violation is a fascinating and relatively unexplored area of theoretical physics. By introducing non-Abelian gauge fields into the picture, we add another layer of complexity to the problem, which leads to novel effects and potentially new observables. Furthermore, our work contributes to a broader effort of understanding how symmetries can emerge or be broken in physical systems.

Overall, our results provide a compelling case for the importance of studying spontaneous Lorentz violation and its implications for theoretical physics. We hope that our work will stimulate further research in this area and lead to a deeper understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe.

In our work titled "Evolution of Supermassive Black Hole Binary and Acceleration of Jet Precession in Galactic Nuclei", we investigate the dynamics of supermassive black hole binaries and their influence on the precession of jets in galactic nuclei. We propose a new mechanism for the acceleration of jet precession in binary black hole systems by considering the interaction between the binary and a surrounding circumbinary disk.

To study the dynamic evolution of the binary system, we perform hydrodynamic simulations using state-of-the-art numerical methods. Our simulations show that as the two black holes orbit each other, they create a tidal deformation in the surrounding disk. This deformation, in turn, generates gravitational torques on the binary, leading to a precession of the black hole orbits. This precession results in the observed jet precession in galactic nuclei.

Our work also demonstrates that the black hole binary, coupled with its surrounding circumbinary disk, can significantly affect the jet dynamics, leading to a more complex and diverse observational behavior. This study fills in a crucial gap in our understanding of the formation and evolution of binary black hole systems and their impact on jet dynamics.

By demonstrating how the unique dynamics of black hole binaries can contribute to the complex behavior of jets in galactic nuclei, this study sheds light on the origin of the observed diversity of extragalactic jets. Our findings provide a new insight into the role of supermassive black hole binaries in shaping the universe's evolution and its structures.

The Santa Fe Light Cone Simulation Project aims to provide a better understanding of the nature and distribution of baryonic matter in our universe. In this paper, we focus on the issue of confusion - the inability to differentiate between high-redshift clusters and the Warm-Hot Intergalactic Medium (WHIM) - and explore its impact on upcoming Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect surveys. To address this problem, we have developed a new simulation pipeline that combines dark matter simulations and hydrodynamical simulations, allowing us to accurately reproduce the density and temperature distribution of cosmic gas.

Our methodology involves a series of tests to assess the validity of our simulations and confirm their ability to reproduce the expected physical properties of the universe. We then use these simulations to generate synthetic SZ effect maps that mimic the observations expected from upcoming telescopes such as CCAT-prime and CMB-S4. Our results indicate that confusion can lead to an overestimation of the WHIM contribution to the SZ signal, potentially up to 50% in some cases. Furthermore, we find that the effect of confusion is highly dependent on the instrumental sensitivity and survey depth. 

In conclusion, our study has shown that confusion is a significant source of error in upcoming SZ effect surveys, and should be carefully considered when interpreting their results. The new simulation pipeline we have developed provides a valuable tool for predicting and mitigating such errors, and will help pave the way towards more accurate measurements of the WHIM and the large-scale structure of the universe.

In recent years, the study of Josephson junction arrays has attracted significant attention due to their potential applications as qubits in quantum computation. In this work, we investigate the superconductor-insulator duality for an array of Josephson wires. The motivation for this research is to understand the fundamental properties of the system, including the possible existence of a quantum phase transition between a superconducting phase and an insulating phase. 

We consider an array of Josephson wires coupled via tunneling junctions and investigate the system’s behavior using a renormalization group method. Our analysis suggests that the superconductor-insulator duality holds in the low-energy regime, with the superconducting phase corresponding to a fixed point of the renormalization group flow. We also find that the insulating phase is associated with a different fixed point.

Our results demonstrate the existence of a quantum phase transition between the superconducting and insulating phases of the Josephson wire array. The critical behavior at this transition point is found to be characterized by universal scaling exponents, providing insight into the critical behavior of more complex systems. Our investigation contributes to the understanding of the Josephson effect in condensed matter physics and sheds light on the possible application of Josephson junction arrays in quantum computation.

In this work, we present a new approach to understand the energy distribution in gravitational systems. We study the energy content of an axially symmetric solution in the teleparallel theory, which is equivalent to General Relativity. The methodology consists of starting from the teleparallel version of Einstein-Hilbert action, computing the field equations, and obtaining the gravitational potential and the energy conditions. We then obtain the energy-momentum complex and the energy density of a charged axially symmetric solution in teleparallel theory, which is a well-known family of exact solutions. This solution can describe the gravitational field outside and inside a highly compact, charged object, such as a black hole or a neutron star. The motivation for this research is to provide a new framework to understand the energy distribution in strongly gravitating objects, which is important for astrophysical applications. The result obtained shows that the energy density is positive everywhere outside the object, which means that the energy is indeed localized around the compact object. Our result can provide useful information for the interpretation of astrophysical observations and for the development of new models to study exotic objects such as black holes and neutron stars.

In this work, we investigate the impact of the rotational r-mode instability on the spin evolution of accreting neutron stars. Neutron stars are compact objects that exhibit a wide range of astrophysical phenomena, such as X-ray bursts and pulsations. One of the most important observables of these objects is their spin rate, which can change during accretion processes. The r-mode instability arises due to the curvature of spacetime and affects the dynamics of rotating stars through the emission of gravitational radiation. 

Our approach involves a theoretical model that incorporates the nonlinear aspects of the r-mode instability, using numerical simulations to study the evolution of the system under different external conditions. We have focused on accreting neutron stars that are undergoing mass transfer from a companion star, which affects the r-mode instability and can lead to significant spin changes. Our results reveal a complex interplay between the accretion torque and the r-mode instability, which leads to intricate spin evolution scenarios. 

Our work provides insights into the astrophysical implications of the r-mode instability in neutron star systems and highlights the need for further investigations on the topic. The methodology of our study can be extended to other types of accreting compact objects, such as black holes and white dwarfs. The theoretical model developed in our work has the potential to improve our understanding of the fundamental physics of neutron stars and their observational properties.

In this study, we investigate the two-way coupling of FENE dumbbells with a turbulent shear flow. This work is motivated by the need to better understand the behavior of polymer solutions in turbulent flows, which has important implications for a wide range of industrial and engineering applications. To that end, we attempt to solve the problem of predicting the dynamics of FENE dumbbell suspensions in turbulent shear flows.

Our approach involves using direct numerical simulations (DNS) to model the flow field and the dynamics of the suspended FENE dumbbells. The key ideas underlying our work include the use of a generalized FENE dumbbell model that accounts for the effects of finite extensibility, and the use of DNS to accurately capture the turbulent flow field. With these ideas in mind, we develop a numerical scheme that integrates the FENE dumbbell equations of motion with the Navier-Stokes equations that describe the turbulent fluid flow.

Our results show that the presence of FENE dumbbells has a significant impact on the turbulent flow field, leading to changes in the vorticity and strain rate distributions. As a result, the dynamics of the FENE dumbbells themselves are also affected, with increased stretching and deformation. In conclusion, our work provides important new insights into the complex physics of FENE dumbbell suspensions in turbulent flows, and may lead to improved predictive models for industrial and engineering applications.

In this paper, we present the analysis of the optical and ultraviolet (UV) spectra of PHL 1811, an intrinsically X-ray weak quasar. Our study aims to understand the nature of this system, which exhibits a unique quasar-like spectral shape but with unusually weak X-ray emission. We obtained optical and UV spectra of PHL 1811 using the GALEX, Swift, and SDSS telescopes, with a total coverage from 1300 to 6200 Å. The analysis was performed by fitting the continuum and emission lines using various models, such as the power-law plus blackbody model. We also measured the equivalent widths of the emission lines and compared them to those of typical quasars. Our results show that PHL 1811 has a relatively low accretion rate and low black hole mass, which explains its weak X-ray emission. Additionally, we found evidence of intrinsic absorption of the ionizing continuum, which could be due to the presence of a dusty torus. Our study sheds light on the physics of low-luminosity AGN and provides new insight into the relationship between X-ray and UV/optical emission in quasars.

In this work, we present the use of colour pairs as a tool to constrain the age and metallicity of stellar populations. The motivation of this research lies in the need to improve our understanding of the history and evolution of galaxies, which can only be achieved by accurately determining the age and metallicity of their constituent stars.

Our key idea is to utilise colour pairs, defined as the difference in magnitudes between two filters, to obtain a more reliable measure of age and metallicity. We employ this methodology on synthetic spectra from a grid of models, covering a variety of stellar ages and metallicities. By comparing the resulting colours with observational data from a sample of real galaxies, we are able to calibrate the colour pairs to accurately predict the age and metallicity of stars within these galaxies.

Our results show that the use of colour pairs can significantly improve the accuracy of age and metallicity determinations, reducing the potential biases caused by differences in dust extinction and star formation histories. Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of this technique, showing that it can be applied to a wide range of galaxies with varying properties.

Overall, our use of colour pairs provides a valuable tool for constraining stellar ages and metallicities, while also improving our understanding of galaxy evolution.

In this work, we explore the properties of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) in one dimension at a nonzero chemical potential and attempt to solve the problem of understanding the phase diagram of this system. Our motivation for this research is to better understand the behavior of QCD in extreme conditions such as those present in heavy-ion collisions.
