The problem that this work attempts to solve is the identification of the equilibrium points of a three agent game and the various strategies employed by the players to reach those points. Through an iterative process that simulates the interactions of players, we investigate how the behavior of one agent affects the strategies of the other agents and how this interaction influences the overall outcome of the game.

We are motivated to study this problem because of the growing interest in multi-agent systems, which have become an important area of research in artificial intelligence and game theory. Moreover, understanding the dynamics of multi-agent systems can reveal insights into real-world situations, such as market competition, political negotiations, and social interactions.

Our results demonstrate that the dynamics of three agent games can be complex and unpredictable, with different players exhibiting different behaviors and strategies. Additionally, we find that the equilibrium points of the game can shift depending on the initial strategies of the players, and that certain strategies may be more effective in achieving equilibrium than others. Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of the dynamics of three agent games and can provide insights into more complex multi-agent systems.

Our work aims to improve the precision of astrometry data obtained from the Very Large Telescope (VLT)/Focal Reducer and Low Dispersion Spectrograph (FORS1) instrument at short time scales. Astrometry data plays a crucial role in fields such as astronomy, astrophysics, and geodesy to measure distances, orbital parameters, and movement of celestial objects. However, the limitations of instrumental and atmospheric effects can affect the accuracy of astrometry measurements. In response, we implemented a high-precision astrometry calibration method using a reference star catalog. The calibration method was applied to short time scale data sets obtained from observations of a nearby star cluster. To assess the accuracy of our method, we compared our results with astrometry data obtained from the Gaia mission. Our analysis showed an improvement of up to 10 times in the astrometry precision compared to the raw data from the VLT/FORS1 instrument. The improved precision of the astrometry data has the potential to broaden our understanding of stellar dynamics, binary star systems, and the detection of exoplanets, among others. Our work addresses a critical aspect of astrometry data analysis and demonstrates the potential of our method to improve the precision of astrometry measurements in future observations.

In this paper, we provide a critical review of the statistical analysis presented in "A new experimental limit for the stability of the electron" by H.V. Klapdor-Kleingrothaus, I.V. Krivosheina, and I.V. Titkova. The authors aim to test the hypothesis that the electron, a fundamental particle in physics, is stable over long periods of time. The methodology used involves conducting an experiment to search for evidence of electron decay and performing a statistical analysis of the collected data. 

Our analysis highlights potential issues with the methodology used in the study, including the lack of a clear statistical model and the failure to account for multiple testing. Additionally, we note that the study's results are highly dependent on the choice of prior probability distributions, which may introduce bias. We suggest that future studies investigating the stability of the electron should address these issues to ensure the reliability of their results. 

Overall, this work attempts to contribute to the rigorous evaluation of experimental findings in physics research. By identifying potential pitfalls in statistical analysis, we hope to encourage researchers to carefully consider their methods and interpretations to advance our understanding of the fundamental laws of nature.

In this study, we investigate the crossover from impurity states to the valence band in diluted magnetic semiconductors, and how Coulomb attraction by acceptor ions plays a role. The motivation behind this research is the ultimate goal of developing novel spin-based electronics utilizing magnetic impurities in semiconductors. We utilize computational methods based on density functional theory to model impurity states in Cd1-xMnxTe, a prototypical diluted magnetic semiconductor. Our key idea is to analyze the wave functions and energy levels of impurity states under a varying range of acceptor Coulomb potential strengths. We found that by increasing the Coulomb attraction of the acceptor ions, the impurity states gradually shift towards the valence band. Our methodology involves a comprehensive analysis of the electronic structure of Cd1-xMnxTe, using advanced techniques in density functional theory and first-principles calculations. Our main result is a clear demonstration of how the Coulomb attraction by acceptor ions plays a pivotal role in the crossover from impurity to valence band states, with important implications for future research in spin-based electronics.

In this work, we model the spectral energy distribution (SED) and variability of 3C 66A during the Whole Earth Blazar Telescope (WEBT) campaign of 2003 -- 2004. The main problem that we aim to solve is the understanding of the nature of variability of 3C 66A. This source has been studied extensively in the past, but the nature of its variability is still not completely understood. The motivation for our research is to provide a more complete understanding of this source, which will aid in the development of models for other similar objects.

Our methodology involves collecting data from various ground-based and space-based telescopes, which are fitted with a variety of instruments, including photometers, spectrometers, and polarimeters. We construct the SED using the data obtained from these instruments and use it to model the variability of 3C 66A. We also use a statistical analysis to determine the significance of the variability detected in the source. Our key idea involves the use of multiple instruments to obtain a complete dataset and the construction of SED models that are capable of representing the variability in the source.

In conclusion, our work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the variability of 3C 66A as observed during the WEBT campaign. The combination of our multi-instrument approach and statistical analysis provides a robust and rigorous methodology for studying the variability of blazars, which will aid in the development of models for these sources.

In this work, we explore the Landau-Lifshitz (LL) sigma-models and their relation to the AdS/CFT correspondence. We focus on the inclusion of fermionic fields in the LL sigma-models, and analyze their impact on the AdS/CFT correspondence. Our methodology consisted of a comprehensive literature review and a mathematical analysis of the LL sigma-models and the AdS/CFT correspondence. 

Our motivation for this research was to gain a better understanding of the relationship between LL sigma-models, fermions, and the AdS/CFT correspondence. This is important as these models are ubiquitous in the study of condensed matter physics and string theory. The inclusion of fermions in LL sigma-models is particularly relevant since these models are often used to describe magnetic systems, which are inherently spin systems.

Our results show that the inclusion of fermionic fields in LL sigma-models leads to novel behavior in the AdS/CFT correspondence. We demonstrate that the AdS/CFT correspondence can be used to map out the behavior of fermionic fields in LL sigma-models, which provides a useful tool for studying magnetic systems. Moreover, we show that the AdS/CFT correspondence can be used to derive exact results for certain observables in LL sigma-models that are difficult to calculate otherwise. Altogether, our work presents a concrete example of the interplay between two fundamental theories in physics.

In this research work, we investigate the origin of the major solar event that occurred on 2006 December 13. Our study focuses on the interaction between a fast-rotating sunspot and ephemeral regions, which are small-scale magnetic regions that are short-lived on the Sun's surface. The study aims to understand the conditions under which such interactions occur and the impact they have on the solar atmosphere.

The motivation for this research was to gain a better understanding of the underlying physical processes involved in the formation and evolution of such solar events. This is critical given the significant impact that solar events can have on our technological infrastructure, including communication and navigation systems.

Our analysis, which incorporates high-resolution observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, suggests that the interaction between the fast-rotating sunspot and the ephemeral region led to the emergence of a large magnetic structure on the Sun's surface. This structure then underwent a series of magnetic reconnections, ultimately resulting in the eruption of a coronal mass ejection.

The findings of our study provide new insights into the origin of solar events and highlight the importance of monitoring and understanding the complex dynamics of the Sun's magnetic fields.

This paper aims to investigate the role of geometry and topology in relativistic cosmology. We utilize the fundamental principles of general relativity and topology to understand the structure and evolution of the universe at a large scale. We propose that the topology of the universe plays a critical role in determining its geometry.

Our methodology involves both analytical and numerical techniques to obtain accurate results. We start by employing the standard cosmological model, which assumes that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales. We then explore the implications of different topologies, including flat, open, and closed universes, in determining the geometry of the universe.

Furthermore, we investigate the fundamental properties of cosmic strings and their impact on the topology of the universe. We analyze both the observational and theoretical evidence for the existence of cosmic strings and the implications for the topology of the universe.

The results obtained indicate that the topology of the universe has a significant impact on its geometry and evolution. The cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation provides observational evidence that supports the idea of a flat universe with a topology that is consistent with the standard cosmological model. However, our analysis also suggests that the existence of cosmic strings could lead to a non-trivial topology, which would have important implications for the evolution of the universe.

Overall, this work contributes to our understanding of the interplay between geometry and topology in relativistic cosmology and highlights the importance of topology in determining the properties and evolution of the universe.

In this study, we investigate the occurrence of H$_2$D$^+$ line emission in proto-planetary disks, which are sites for planet formation. The motivation behind our research stems from the fact that H$_2$D$^+$ can function as a marker for cold and dense gas, which is essential for the formation of planetesimals and ultimately planets. By analyzing data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we identified H$_2$D$^+$ line emission signatures in three proto-planetary disks, namely, AS 209, Elias 32, and IRS 63. This suggests that the disks contain cold gas reservoirs at temperatures below the typical CO freeze-out temperature.

Our results also indicate that H$_2$D$^+$ emission is correlated with the morphology of the disks, with the sharper edge disks exhibiting the strongest H$_2$D$^+$ detections. This observation reinforces the notion that H$_2$D$^+$ can be a useful tracer for the study of planet formation and disk structure. The problem our work attempts to solve is the lack of a suitable tracer for the identification of cold and dense gas in proto-planetary disks. Previous research has shown that CO, a commonly used tracer, can become depleted in disks, thereby rendering it unsuitable for the detection of cold gas. Our findings suggest that H$_2$D$^+$ can provide a complementary tool for the study of proto-planetary disks and the processes driving planet formation.

In our work, we attempt to solve the problem of applying quantum mechanics principles to macroscopic configurations through the concept of a quantum-like representation. This is motivated by the growing need to understand how the principles of quantum mechanics can be extended to larger scales than ever before. We propose a mathematical framework to represent macroscopic configurations as quantum-like states, which can be manipulated using quantum mechanics formalism. 

The key ideas of our work involve treating the degrees of freedom of macroscopic configurations as corresponding to quantum observables. We develop a set of transformation rules for these observables and establish a mathematical structure that mimics the mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics. We apply our framework to several examples of classical physical systems, including a pendulum and a diatomic molecule, and show how our quantum-like representation allows for a more unified approach to studying these systems.

Our methodology involves using a combination of mathematical rigor and physical intuition. We utilize concepts from both classical mechanics and quantum mechanics to develop our framework. We also make use of mathematical tools from linear algebra and analysis, which are necessary for defining and manipulating quantum-like states. Through this work, we hope to provide a foundation for a new field of study that can bridge the gap between classical and quantum mechanics, and ultimately lead to new and exciting discoveries in the world of physics.

In this work, we investigate the structural parameters of globular clusters (GCs) in M31, aiming to generalize these findings to the larger "fundamental plane" of GCs. Our methodology involves analyzing deep Hubble Space Telescope imaging of 49 GCs in M31, measuring their half-light radii and ellipticities to derive their structural properties. We also collect and analyze data on GCs in other galaxies, including the Milky Way and M87, to compare and draw conclusions about GC structural properties at large.

This work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the physical processes and drivers that govern GC formation and evolution, which in turn are important indicators of the evolutionary history and formation mechanisms of their host galaxies. Furthermore, by exploring the fundamental plane of GCs, we aim to uncover potential correlations or relationships between their structural properties and other galactic-scale physical parameters such as stellar mass and metallicity. This may provide insight into the formation mechanisms and evolutionary pathways of galaxies, from the smallest dwarf galaxies to massive galaxy clusters.

Our motivation for this research is grounded in a desire to expand our understanding of the cosmic story, and to uncover the physical processes that shape the universe we observe today. By elucidating the structural properties of GCs in M31 and other galaxies, we hope to contribute to the broader field of galaxy evolution and formation, and deepen our insights into the underlying physical mechanisms that drive these processes.

In this work, we investigate the relationship between the weighted complexity and the determinant functions of graphs. Our motivation stems from the fact that the study of spectral graph theory has become increasingly relevant in fields such as computer science, physics, and chemistry. Furthermore, the weighted complexity of a graph measures the amount of information contained in its adjacency matrix, which is a foundational object in spectral graph theory. Our objective is to exemplify the importance of the weighted complexity by establishing a connection between this parameter and the determinant function of the graph. 

To achieve our goal, we first introduce the definition of the weighted complexity and study its properties. Next, we provide a thorough discussion of the determinant function, including its definition, properties, and various known bounds and estimations. We then present our main results, which include formulas that relate the weighted complexity of a graph to the values and moments of the determinant function. Our findings not only exhibit the utility of the weighted complexity, but also provide new insights into the determinant function, which is a central object in graph theory and beyond.

Our work aims to investigate the geochemistry of uranium (U) and thorium (Th) and how they have influenced the origin and evolution of the Earth's crust and biological evolution. We employed various analytical techniques to study the distribution and concentration of U and Th in rocks from different geological settings, as well as their isotopic composition. Our research indicates that U and Th have played a crucial role in the formation of the Earth's crust and the evolution of life on our planet.

The origin and differentiation of the Earth's crust have been attributed to several factors, including the distribution and mobility of U and Th. Our study supports the notion that these elements have played a significant role in the formation of continental crust, and their distribution helped shape the chemical and physical properties of the crust. Furthermore, the decay of U and Th isotopes has also been a primary source of heat that drives geological activities on Earth.

Apart from their geological significance, U and Th have also influenced the biological evolution of life on Earth. Their isotopes are used as chronometers by geologists and paleontologists to determine the age of fossils and rocks. This technique has been fundamental in understanding the timeline of the evolution of different species.

To sum up, our research highlights the role of U and Th in the origin and evolution of the Earth's crust and biological evolution. Our findings provide insights to better understand the processes that have shaped our planet over billions of years.

We present a theoretical study on two-photon interactions with broadband down-converted light and entangled photons. Our approach is based on the second quantization formalism and involves a comprehensive analysis of the relevant quantum field operators. We derive the general expressions for the two-photon amplitude and calculate the corresponding cross-sections for different photon states.

Our results show that broadband down-converted light and entangled photons can be utilized to enhance the two-photon process significantly. Furthermore, the spectral and polarization properties of the photon states play a crucial role in determining the efficiency and feasibility of the process.

This work contributes to the development of quantum optics and photonics with a fundamental understanding of two-photon interactions. The theoretical framework presented in this work is poised for further extensions and applications in quantum information and technology.

The main problem we aim to solve is to understand the effect of broadband down-converted light and entangled photons on two-photon interactions. The key ideas in our methodology are to utilize the formalism of quantum field theory to develop the theory and generalize the results for different photon states. We believe our work presents a significant step towards developing new techniques for manipulating photon states.

In this paper, we investigate the multifractal statistics of the local order parameter at random critical points, with a focus on its application to wetting transitions with disorder. The main problem we attempt to solve is the characterization of the critical behavior of the wetting transition in the presence of disorder, which has remained a challenging topic in statistical physics. 

Using extensive simulations, we provide evidence that the multifractal analysis of the order parameter provides a reliable method for characterizing wetting transitions with disorder. Our results indicate the existence of a universal scaling behavior for the multifractal spectrum of the order parameter, which is independent of the specific details of the disorder that affects the system. We also observe that the critical exponents associated with the wetting transition depend on the type of disorder present. 

Our approach involves the systematic computation of the moments of the local order parameter and the construction of the corresponding multifractal spectrum. We also use the finite-size scaling theory to extract the critical exponents of the wetting transition from the simulation data. Our findings suggest that the multifractal analysis of local order parameters can be a powerful tool for studying critical phenomena in the presence of disorder.

In this paper, we explore the BBGKY hierarchy for spatially inhomogeneous systems of Hamiltonian and Brownian particles with long-range interactions. This work is part of a series of research aimed at understanding the behavior of physical systems with long-range interactions. The key idea of our approach is to formulate the BBGKY hierarchy in terms of the Fourier decomposition of the density and correlation functions. This allows us to obtain a set of coupled equations for the Fourier modes, which can be solved numerically for arbitrary inhomogeneities.

We present numerical results for two specific models: a Hamiltonian system of particles interacting via a power-law potential, and a Brownian system of particles with a long-range diffusion. For the Hamiltonian model, we show that the Fourier modes approach a self-similar scaling form in the long-time limit, characterized by the power-law exponent of the potential and the degree of inhomogeneity. For the Brownian model, we observe a complex interplay between the diffusion and the long-range correlations, which lead to non-trivial stationary states and anomalous diffusion regimes.

Our results shed light on the fundamental properties of long-range interactions in physical systems, and provide a framework for studying more complex and realistic models. The methodology we develop here can be extended to other types of interactions and geometries, and is expected to have broad applications in fields ranging from condensed matter physics to astrophysics and cosmology.

We present an analysis of diffuse HI disks in a sample of 50 isolated galaxies drawn from the ALFALFA survey. Our goal is to study the properties of these disks and their potential impact on galaxy evolution. We performed a detailed study of the HI data and examined the distribution and kinematics of the gas. Our results show that a significant fraction of the galaxies in our sample have extended and often asymmetric HI disks. We also found that these disks can play a crucial role in redistributing gas within galaxies and triggering star formation. Our methodology included analyzing the HI data using a combination of tools such as velocity field modeling and surface density profile fitting. The motivation for this research is to better understand the role that gas dynamics play in shaping the evolution of galaxies. By studying isolated galaxies, we can isolate the processes that are intrinsic to galaxies, rather than those that are the result of environmental factors. Our work contributes to the current efforts to build an accurate understanding of the gas dynamics in galaxies and their role in galaxy evolution.

In this study, our team aimed to search for Earth analogues around the nearest stars by characterizing the disk age-metallicity relation and the age distribution in the Solar Neighbourhood. The motivation for this research stems from the importance of Earth analogues in the search for habitable planets outside of our Solar System. By investigating the age-metallicity relation and age distribution of stars in our neighbourhood, we can identify the stars that are most likely to host Earth-like planets.

To accomplish our goal, we obtained data on a sample of stars within 100 parsecs of the Sun. We measured the elemental abundances of these stars and applied a Bayesian statistical framework to determine their ages. Our results show a clear age-metallicity relation, with older stars generally having higher metallicities. Additionally, we found that the age distribution of stars in the Solar Neighbourhood is complex, with a significant number of young stars.

Overall, this study provides valuable insights into the age-metallicity relation and age distribution of stars in our neighbourhood. Our findings can inform future searches for Earth analogues and contribute to our understanding of the formation and evolution of planetary systems.

We report on the discovery of two extremely low luminosity globular clusters (GCs) in the Milky Way. The motivation behind our research is to investigate the possibility of finding more low luminosity GCs, which could provide us with a better understanding of the formation and evolution of our galaxy. The problem that our work attempts to solve is identifying GCs that are previously undiscovered due to their low luminosity. 

Our research uses deep imaging data obtained through the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) mounted on the Blanco 4m telescope in Chile. The data was processed and analyzed using standard techniques to identify the two GCs, designated J0926+4427 and J1124+4535. Their characteristics, including their metallicity and distances, were determined using spectroscopic observations obtained through the Keck-II telescope in Hawaii. 

We found that both GCs are extremely faint, with absolute magnitudes of -4.2 and -5.0, respectively, making them among the least luminous GCs known in the Milky Way. They are also very metal-poor, with metallicities significantly lower than the average value for Milky Way GCs. The discovery of these two low luminosity GCs provides new insights into the formation and evolution of the Milky Way, and highlights the potential of deep imaging surveys to uncover more low luminosity clusters.

In this work, we present multi-color photometry of the Galactic globular cluster M75 = NGC 6864 using data collected with the 2.6-m Shajn telescope at the Crimean Astrophysical Observatory. The metallicity estimation for M75 is challenging due to its peculiar chemical composition and high reddening. We introduce a new sensitive metallicity indicator based on the differences between the (U-V) and (V-I) colors, which is calibrated using high-resolution spectroscopic data. Additionally, we investigate the position of the horizontal branch (HB) in the ultraviolet (UV) portion of the spectrum using the (U-B) vs. (B-V) color-color diagram. The HB morphology and the presence of a spread in the main sequence turnoff region are discussed. 

Our methodology includes applying color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) to the multi-band data in order to identify different stellar populations within the cluster. We use both theoretical isochrones and empirical calibrations of the RGB stellar parameters to derive the age and distance of M75 and confirm that it is a relatively old and distant globular cluster. The correlation between photometric and spectroscopic metallicities is examined to validate our proposed metallicity indicator. 

The motivation for this research stems from the need to accurately determine the properties and evolution of globular clusters, which are crucial for our understanding of the Galaxy's formation and evolution. Our results contribute to the study of M75 and provide new insights into the metallicity and HB properties of this cluster.

In this study, we investigate the dust temperatures of prestellar cores within the rho Oph main cloud and other star-forming regions and explore the implications for the core mass function. Prestellar cores are dense, collapsing structures that form protostars and ultimately, young stellar objects. Understanding their properties and distribution is crucial for advancing our knowledge of star formation. We use infrared observations from the Herschel Space Observatory to estimate the dust temperatures of prestellar cores and compare them to theoretical predictions. Our analysis reveals that the dust temperatures of prestellar cores in the rho Oph main cloud are colder than those in other star-forming regions. We show that this has important consequences for the inferred properties of these structures, particularly their masses. Specifically, colder cores have higher masses than previously estimated, leading to a shift in the shape of the core mass function towards higher masses. Our findings have implications for our understanding of star formation and the origin of the initial mass function of stars.

In this work, we present the results of our MOST photometry and Dominion Astrophysical Observatory spectroscopy of the eclipsing (white dwarf + red dwarf) binary V471 Tau. Our motivation for this research was to study the orbital and intrinsic properties of this system, which is a prototype for a class of binaries that are useful for testing models of stellar structure and evolution. Specifically, we aimed to determine accurate physical parameters of the white dwarf, such as its mass, radius, and cooling rate, which are important for understanding the mechanisms that govern the evolution of such objects.

Our analysis of the photometric and spectroscopic data revealed a number of interesting features, including the presence of periodic brightness variations due to the mutual eclipses of the two stars, as well as spectral signatures of the white dwarf's photosphere and accretion disk. We also derived precise values for the masses, radii, and temperatures of the two stars, which we compared to theoretical models of low-mass stars and white dwarfs.

Overall, our work represents a significant step forward in our understanding of the V471 Tau system and provides valuable constraints on the physical processes that govern the evolution of white dwarfs and red dwarfs in close binary systems. By using a combination of advanced observational techniques and sophisticated modeling tools, we hope to continue making progress in this exciting field of astrophysics.

In this work, we investigate the catalytic effect of black hole motion on the resonant dynamics of planetary systems. Resonances between planet orbits play a significant role in shaping the long-term evolution of planetary systems and have important implications for habitability. However, understanding the mechanisms that drive resonance capture and evolution remains a challenge in this field. 

We propose that black hole motion can act as a trigger for resonance capture by stretching and compressing the orbits of the planets, destabilizing some and stabilizing others. We use N-body simulations to test this hypothesis and confirm that the resonance capture probability increases significantly when a black hole is present in the system. Moreover, we find that black holes can also drive resonance jumps, causing significant changes in the semi-major axes of the planets. 

Our findings suggest that black hole motion should be considered as an important factor in the dynamical evolution of planetary systems. This work opens up new avenues for research into the formation and evolution of planetary systems in galactic environments. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of multi-scale studies that incorporate black holes in the context of planet formation and evolution, and broader astrophysical applications.

In this work, we investigate the UV star formation rates in the local universe. The problem we aim to solve is the lack of understanding of the physical processes that trigger star formation in galaxies and the correlation between these processes and the resulting observed UV radiation. This research is motivated by the fundamental importance of star formation in shaping the structure and evolution of galaxies, as well as the crucial role played by UV radiation in shaping the interstellar medium and regulating the formation of new generations of stars. 

Our key idea is to use multi-wavelength observations from a large sample of local galaxies to explore the link between star formation and UV radiation. We employ a robust, data-driven approach to quantify the UV emission from galaxies, while taking into account the contribution from other sources such as dust, extinction, and background radiation. We also employ sophisticated statistical tools to identify and quantify the relationships between star formation and other galaxy properties, such as morphology, environment, and metallicity. 

Our methodology involves the collection and analysis of data from large surveys such as GALEX, SDSS, and WISE, as well as the development of novel tools to extract and interpret information from these data. Our results provide new insights into the physical mechanisms driving star formation in galaxies and have important implications for our understanding of the evolution of galaxies and the interstellar medium.

In this study, we investigated the consistency of the thick brane model with recent astronomical observations. The motivation for this research is to examine the possibility of explaining dark matter and dark energy as effects of modifications to standard gravity. The thick brane model is a modification of the standard cosmological model, which proposes that the universe consists of a four-dimensional spacetime and a higher-dimensional space. This model can predict modifications to the standard gravity, which can explain some of the observed astronomical phenomena, including the accelerated expansion of the universe.

To evaluate the consistency of the thick brane model with observations, we compared its predictions with the recent observations of dark matter and dark energy. Our methodology involved investigating the modified gravity solutions in the thick brane model and comparing them with the observed mass density of galaxies and cosmic microwave background radiation measurements.

Our results show that, while the thick brane model can describe the modified gravity, it struggles to provide a consistent explanation for the observed dark matter and dark energy phenomena. Additionally, the model struggles to explain the cosmic microwave background radiation temperature fluctuations. Therefore, while the thick brane model is an interesting modification of the standard cosmological model, significant modifications or extensions are required to provide a consistent explanation of the observed universe.

In this study, we investigate the anisotropic ac dissipation at the surface of mesoscopic superconductors, in order to better understand the dissipation mechanisms that occur in these materials. We focus specifically on the impact of surface roughness and the orientation of the ac current with respect to the surface.

To achieve our goals, we use a combination of numerical simulations and micromagnetic theory. Our simulations are performed using the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equations, which describe the behavior of the superconducting order parameter. These equations are solved numerically using a finite element method.

Our results show that both surface roughness and the orientation of the ac current have a significant effect on the dissipation properties of mesoscopic superconductors. In particular, we find that the dissipation is highly anisotropic, with larger dissipation occurring when the ac current is oriented perpendicular to the surface. Additionally, we find that the dissipation is strongly influenced by the magnetic vortices that form in the superconductor.

Our findings have important implications for the design and optimization of superconducting devices, as well as for the development of new materials with improved performance characteristics. Overall, this study contributes to a better understanding of the fundamental physics of mesoscopic superconductors and their behavior under different conditions.

In this paper, we present the discovery of multiperiodicity in the newly discovered mid-late Be star V2104 Cygni. The motivation for this work stems from the fact that Be stars have long been known to exhibit complex variability, both in terms of their spectral lines and their photometric light curves. However, until recently, few tools were available to systematically detect and characterize such variability, particularly in the case of mid-late Be stars. Our work addresses this issue by utilizing Fourier analysis techniques to identify and quantify periodic variations in the spectral lines and photometry of V2104 Cygni.

Our results reveal the presence of multiple periodicities in both the photometry and spectral lines of V2104 Cygni. Specifically, we find two dominant frequencies in the photometry, along with two additional frequencies that are weaker. Similarly, spectral line variations show three dominant frequencies. Our analysis also reveals a possible connection between the spectral line and photometric variability, which is consistent with the idea of a pulsation-driven disk instability as the mechanism behind Be star variability.

In conclusion, the work presented here provides evidence for multiperiodicity in a newly discovered mid-late Be star, which has implications for our understanding of the physical mechanisms that drive variability in these objects. We hope that our results will help pave the way for future studies of Be stars and their complex variability.

We examine the relationship between daemons and Dark Matter Annihilation (DAMA) and their connections in celestial mechanics. Our research explores how these entities interrelate and affect the cosmos on a larger scale. Using analytical and numerical techniques, we investigate the effects of daemons and DAMA on the galaxy, taking account of the different types of interactions and feedbacks they exert on the surrounding matter. Our study serves to bridge a gap in the understanding of the effects of dark matter on various scales. We aim to establish the impact of these cosmological phenomena on the formation and evolution of galaxies, tracing the role of daemons and DAMA in the early Universe. The focus here, is on exploring the relationship between theory and observation and providing insight into how the universe has evolved over time. Ultimately, our work serves as a stepping stone for future discoveries in the field of astrophysics, laying the foundation for new research and emerging theories.

In this work, we provide some comments concerning the examples that were proposed in counterargument to the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture. The motivation for this research is due to the importance of the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture in algebraic geometry and the fact that the counterexamples have led to some confusion and doubts regarding the conjecture's validity.

We start by reviewing the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture and its statement. Next, we outline the counterexamples proposed by certain authors and analyze why they fail to refute the conjecture. We then provide some new insights into the original conjecture by presenting a more detailed description of its geometric interpretation and the associated commutative algebraic background.

Our results indicate that the proposed counterexamples have been misleading and incomplete. We demonstrate that the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture is still a valid result and a fundamental tool in algebraic geometry. Our methodology involves a rigorous analysis of the existing literature, a thorough exploration of the counterexamples, and a detailed exposition of the main ideas behind the conjecture.

In conclusion, our work sheds light on the validity of the Generalized Jacobian Conjecture and provides a better understanding of its geometric and algebraic properties. We hope that this research will stimulate further investigation into this important topic and contribute to the ongoing development of algebraic geometry.

In this paper, we derive a hypercontractive inequality for matrix-valued functions and apply it to problems in quantum computing and locally decodable codes (LDCs). The hypercontractive inequality we derive generalizes the well-known hypercontractivity theorem for real-valued functions, which states that the L2 norm of a function raised to a power is greater than or equal to the Lp norm of the function for p strictly between 1 and 2. Our hypercontractive inequality for matrix-valued functions provides a similar bound in terms of the operator norm of the function and an exponent that is again strictly between 1 and 2. 

The main motivation for this research comes from the fact that matrix-valued functions arise naturally in many quantum computing and LDC problems. For example, in quantum computing, the unitary operators that implement quantum gates are matrix-valued functions. In LDCs, the decoding algorithms involve evaluating matrix-valued functions at various points in the code. By establishing a hypercontractive inequality for matrix-valued functions, we can obtain new results and bounds for these problems that were not previously possible with the real-valued hypercontractivity theorem.

Overall, our work contributes to the growing body of research in harmonic analysis and its applications to quantum computing and coding theory. The hypercontractive inequality we derive provides a powerful tool for analyzing complex functions and systems, and we believe it will have many future applications in a variety of fields.

In this study, we analyze three-particle correlations in Au+Au collisions at √sNN=200 GeV, using data collected by the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy-Ion Collider. The key idea behind this work is to search for evidence of long-range collective effects in the azimuthal distribution of particles produced in these collisions.

Our analysis begins by identifying triplets of particles with the same charge sign, and calculating the corresponding correlation functions for different combinations of the three particles' angular separations. We then compare these correlation functions to results from a Monte Carlo simulation which includes contributions from both jet fragmentation and hydrodynamic flow.

The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the underlying dynamics of heavy-ion collisions at RHIC energies. By examining three-particle correlations, we can gain insights into the interplay between jet quenching and collective phenomena such as the formation of a quark-gluon plasma.

Our results show that the observed three-particle correlations are largely consistent with the expected contributions from jet fragmentation and collective flow. However, we observe some significant deviations from the Monte Carlo simulation, particularly in the region of small angular separations. These deviations may be due to additional effects such as magnetic fields or non-linear hydrodynamic modes. Further studies are needed to fully understand the observed three-particle correlations and their implications for our understanding of heavy-ion collisions.

In this work, we investigate the impact of reparametrization invariance on the extraction of the CKM angle $\alpha$ from $B\to\pi\pi$ decays. This extraction has been a topic of controversy in the past, as it relies on theoretical assumptions regarding the form of the decay amplitudes. We show that reparametrization invariance poses a significant challenge to these assumptions, which can lead to incorrect determinations of $\alpha$ and possibly obscure the presence of New Physics. 

Our methodology involves a systematic study of the impact of reparametrization on the extraction of $\alpha$, using both analytical and numerical techniques. We introduce a new approach based on the use of angular correlations, which allows us to isolate the effects of reparametrization and extract $\alpha$ without making strong assumptions about the underlying dynamics. Our results demonstrate that reparametrization invariance plays a crucial role in the extraction of $\alpha$, and that neglecting this effect can lead to biased or incorrect determinations. 

Overall, our work highlights the importance of reparametrization invariance in the search for New Physics in $B$ decays, and provides a new tool for the extraction of $\alpha$ that is both theoretically robust and experimentally accessible. We anticipate that our findings will have a significant impact on the interpretation of future $B$-factory data, and on the ongoing effort to unravel the mysteries of CP violation in the Standard Model and beyond.

In this work, we explore the impact of surface brightness on the rotational widths used to calculate the Tully-Fisher relation. The Tully-Fisher relation is a powerful tool in extragalactic astronomy that relates the luminosity of a galaxy to its rotational velocity. While the relation is well established, different methods for determining rotational velocities can lead to systematic errors that impact the precision of the relation. Our work aims to quantify the impact of surface brightness on these errors. 

To do this, we used a sample of galaxies with high-quality rotation curves and surface brightness measurements. We then fit these rotation curves with analytical models, accounting for both the rotation and dispersion components of the velocity field. We found that surface brightness does have an impact on the rotational widths measured for these galaxies, with low surface brightness galaxies having systematically lower widths for a given luminosity. 

This work has important implications for the use of the Tully-Fisher relation in cosmological studies. By quantifying the impact of surface brightness, we can improve the precision of the relation and better understand the underlying physics of galaxy formation and evolution.

In this study, we investigate the measurement of dark energy through the use of gamma-ray bursts and other cosmological probes. Dark energy is a hypothetical form of energy that is thought to be responsible for the accelerating expansion of the universe. The study of dark energy is one of the biggest challenges in modern cosmology, and this work attempts to provide a new and innovative approach to measure this mysterious force.

Our methodology involves the use of observational data collected from gamma-ray bursts and other cosmological probes, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, supernovae, and baryon acoustic oscillations. These observations provide insight into the behavior of the universe at different points in its history, and allow us to measure the effect of dark energy on the expansion of the universe.

The results obtained suggest that our approach is a promising avenue for measuring dark energy. In particular, we find that the use of gamma-ray bursts as a cosmological probe is a valuable tool for constraining the behavior of dark energy. However, this work also highlights the need for further study and refinement of our methods in order to obtain more precise measurements.

Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of dark energy and provides a new approach to measuring it. By continuing to refine our methods and collect more observational data, we can gain a better understanding of this mysterious force and its role in the evolution of the universe.

In this work, we analyzed the phenomena of jet-breaks in the X-ray light-curves of Swift GRB afterglows. Our goal was to determine the physical properties of these jet-breaks, including the jet opening angle and Lorentz factor, and how they relate to the broader properties of the GRB event. To achieve this, we compiled a sample of 78 Swift GRB afterglows with X-ray observations covering at least 10 days post-burst. We then fit the X-ray light-curve data to a model that incorporated the jet-break, and calculated the key properties using Bayesian methods. 

Our results revealed that the jet opening angles are broadly distributed, with a median value of ~0.1 radians, and that they are weakly correlated with the isotropic gamma-ray energy released during the GRB. We also found that the jet-break timescale is strongly correlated with the observed X-ray flux decay rate, suggesting that a physical change in the afterglow emission mechanism is responsible for the break. Finally, we showed that the slope of the X-ray light-curve before the jet-break is steeper than that predicted by standard afterglow models, indicating that the energy injection from the central engine may play a role in shaping the early X-ray emission.

Our work provides a comprehensive analysis of jet-breaks in Swift GRB afterglows, demonstrating how these events can be used to probe the physics of relativistic jets and the broader properties of GRBs. This research has significant implications for understanding the properties of violent cosmic events and their consequences.

In this work, we investigate the systematic uncertainties of hadron parameters obtained with QCD sum rules. The motivation for this research lies in the fact that QCD sum rules have been used to calculate various properties of hadrons, such as masses, decay constants, and form factors. However, there are several sources of systematic uncertainties associated with these calculations, which need to be understood in order to obtain reliable results.

We perform a detailed analysis of the uncertainties arising from the choice of the operator product expansion (OPE) region, the number of terms included in the OPE, the choice of the renormalization scale, and the quark and gluon condensates, which are the key parameters in QCD sum rules.

Our results show that the uncertainties due to the OPE region and the number of terms in the OPE are typically larger than those arising from the choice of the renormalization scale and the condensates. We also find that the uncertainties increase with the complexity of the hadron under consideration, and that different hadrons have different sensitivity to the various sources of uncertainties.

This work contributes to the ongoing effort to improve the accuracy and reliability of hadron parameters obtained with QCD sum rules, and provides useful insights for future calculations.

In this work, we present the determination of the spectral gap in the Kac model for physical momentum and energy conserving collisions. The Kac model is a classical kinetic theory model used to study the behavior of a dilute gas consisting of hard spheres interacting inelastically. Spectral gap is a mathematical concept that measures the decay of correlations in a system. It is an important parameter that characterizes the dynamical behavior of the system and has been extensively studied in the context of many physical systems.

Our motivation for this research is to understand the impact of conserving physical momentum and energy on the spectral gap of the Kac model. Previous studies have shown that the spectral gap of this model is inversely proportional to the temperature of the system. However, our work shows that the spectral gap is no longer inversely proportional to the temperature when physical momentum and energy are conserved. Specifically, we find that the spectral gap is proportional to the inverse of the logarithm of the temperature squared.

Our results have important implications for the study of inelastic collisions in kinetic theory and are relevant to a wide range of physical systems, including granular materials and molecular gases. The techniques and methods developed in this work can also be extended to other models in statistical mechanics and beyond.

We present observations of the 658 GHz water maser transition toward two star-forming regions, W3(OH) and Orion-KL, using the Submillimeter Array. These observations represent the highest frequency detection of water masers to date and are the first detection of vibrationally-excited water masers in Orion-KL. The key idea behind this work is to study the physical conditions and dynamics of the molecular material in these regions through the use of masers, which are bright and compact amplifiers of emission from molecular line transitions. The methodology used consists of interferometric imaging at high angular resolution, allowing us to observe both the spatial distribution of the masers and their kinematics. Our results show that the maser emission from both sources is concentrated in compact regions, and in the case of Orion-KL, the masers are aligned with the more massive molecular gas. Additionally, we observe variations in the maser emission over time, implying a dynamic environment with time-dependent energy injection. The work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the physical processes responsible for the maser emission and their relationship to the broader molecular environment, shedding light on the complex interplay between star formation, high-energy phenomena, and molecular gas.

We present atomic data for Ca II, which is a highly abundant element in the universe, obtained from the latest calculations from the Iron Project. The aim of this work is to determine and provide efficient and reliable data that can be used in theoretical models and astrophysical calculations. We have calculated radiative transition rates and collision strengths for the first 286 levels, which were generated using the multiconfiguration Hartree-Fock and relativistic methods. For the first time, allowed and forbidden transitions are considered to account for their importance in various astrophysical environments. We have also compared our results with previous calculations and experimentally measured values where available. The theoretical approach used in our calculations is based on both relativistic and quantum mechanical models which enable us to account for various electronic and relativistic effects, important for precise calculations of atomic parameters. The data obtained in this study will be useful in models of stellar atmospheres, stellar spectra, and photoionization processes in astrophysics. Overall, our results are important for understanding the basic physics of the Ca II atom, which is ubiquitous in the universe, and also for providing realistic simulations of astrophysical environments.

In this study, we explore the scaling laws of cognitive networks and aim to identify the key factors that impact the performance of cognitive networks. The current problem that cognitive networks face is the difficulty in designing and implementing networks that can operate efficiently and effectively over a wide range of scales and sizes. We use a theoretical framework to investigate the network's performance as it scales up or down, and we show that the network's performance can be explained by the relationship between the number of nodes and the network's connectivity.

We found that cognitive networks display a nonlinear scaling behavior, and that their performance depends on the balance between two different types of scaling. We also proposed a new methodology that uses the power-law scaling to study the cognitive network's behavior. Our work suggests that the performance of cognitive networks can be optimized by controlling the network's connectivity and adapting to the changing demands of the network.

In conclusion, our study provides important insights into the understanding of cognitive networks by demonstrating that the network's topology and connectivity play a crucial role in the network's performance as it scales up or down. The proposed methodology can aid the design and optimization of cognitive networks and offer new opportunities for research on the scaling laws of other complex systems.

In this work, we report the discovery of two spectroscopically peculiar, low-luminosity quasars at a redshift of z~4. The detection of these objects is relevant to the study of the early Universe, as quasars are thought to play a crucial role in the ionization of the intergalactic medium in the first billion years after the Big Bang. However, previous surveys have mostly focused on high-luminosity quasars, which may not be representative of the overall population. The aim of this work was therefore to identify low-luminosity quasars that would be missed by traditional selection methods.

We used several techniques to identify the two objects, including the detection of broad emission lines and the measurement of the UV continuum slope. Both spectra show peculiar features compared to typical quasars, such as a softer ionizing spectrum and weaker high-ionization lines. This suggests that the objects may be part of a more diverse population of quasars than previously thought.

The discovery of these low-luminosity quasars has important implications for our understanding of the early Universe and the role of quasars in it. The methodology used in this study can be applied to future surveys to better understand the diversity of quasar populations and their contribution to the evolution of the Universe.

In this work, we investigated the dynamical status of the galaxy cluster Abell 115. Our study aims to provide insights into the mass distribution and gravitational interactions among the galaxies in the cluster. We used optical spectroscopy data obtained from the Arizona Cluster Redshift Survey and applied the virial theorem to estimate the cluster's mass and velocity dispersion. We also analyzed the spatial distribution of the cluster members and their relative radial velocities. Our findings suggest that Abell 115 is a dynamically old cluster in a post-collapse phase, with a high concentration of dark matter at its core. The excess in the central velocity dispersion is consistent with the presence of substructures, possibly merging groups, within the cluster. The cluster's velocity dispersion profile appears to be nearly isothermal, indicating that the enclosed mass distribution is close to spherically symmetric. Our results provide evidence of the complex dynamics and rich internal structure of Abell 115. This research advances our knowledge of galaxy clusters' physical properties and their evolutionary history, which can contribute to understanding the large-scale structure of the Universe.

In this work, we investigate the collective states of odd-mass nuclei within the framework of the Interacting Vector Boson Model (IVBM). Our motivation for this research lies in the fact that odd-mass nuclei are essential to the study of nuclear structure and are important for understanding nuclear phenomena like nuclear reactions and radioactive decay.

We use the IVBM to investigate the properties of odd-mass nuclei and study their excitation spectra and electromagnetic transition rates. The IVBM considers a nucleon as a composite system that can interact with other nucleons within the nucleus via the exchange of vector bosons. This model is particularly useful for the description of nuclear collective states, such as rotational bands and vibrations.

Our methodology involves using computer simulations based on the IVBM to study the properties of odd-mass nuclei. We examine several isotones and isotopes of different elements and analyze the spectra and transition rates of these nuclei.

Our results show that the IVBM is capable of describing the collective states of odd-mass nuclei with reasonable accuracy. We find that the electromagnetic transition rates and excitation energies of these states are consistent with experimental data, indicating that the IVBM can provide a useful framework for understanding the properties of odd-mass nuclei. Overall, our study contributes to the ongoing efforts to understand the structure of atomic nuclei and the properties of the strong nuclear force.

In this work, we study the impact of network structure on switch integration in complex dynamical systems. Specifically, we focus on systems with loops, which can create challenges for effective switch integration due to the potential for feedback loops and complex interactions. Our goal is to better understand the ways in which network structure can be utilized to facilitate switch integration and mitigate these challenges.

To achieve this goal, we use a combination of analytical and computational methods to study the behavior of dynamical systems with varying network topologies and switch configurations. We analyze the impact of loop structure on system behavior and explore different strategies for switch placement and integration. Through our simulations, we are able to identify optimal switch configurations and network structures that promote effective switch integration and robust system behavior.

The work presented here has important implications for a range of applications, from engineering and robotics to biological systems and ecology. By understanding the ways in which network structure impacts switch integration, we can design more effective and robust systems that are better able to adapt to changing environments and demands. Moreover, our work sheds light on the broader role of network structure in complex systems, highlighting the importance of understanding the complex interplay between structure and dynamics.

In this study, we analyzed the transient X-ray emission from normal galactic nuclei in order to understand the nature of the observed short-term variability. We aim to solve the puzzle of whether the variability is intrinsic or extrinsic to the source. Using archival data from Chandra and XMM-Newton observations, we analyzed more than 200 galactic nuclei over a span of 10 years. Our analysis revealed the presence of short-term flares lasting less than an hour in about 26% of the observed sources. The peak photon flux during these flares exceeded that of the source in quiescence by a factor of 4-10.

Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that the variability is intrinsic to the source rather than due to changing absorption. We propose that the flares arise from the accretion disk's innermost regions, possibly associated with magnetic reconnection events. This hypothesis is supported by the short timescales and high peak fluxes observed.

Our methodology involved extracting, processing, and analyzing data from multiple X-ray observatories using widely accepted analysis techniques. Overall, our study provides important insights into the physical processes that are occurring in galactic nuclei and may guide future investigations in the field.

In this study, we aim to investigate the accretion process of neutron stars in Low-Mass X-Ray Binary (LMXB) systems. These systems consist of a low-mass star and a neutron star that are closely orbiting each other, with the neutron star accreting material from its companion. The accretion process can result in X-ray emission, providing insight into the physical properties of the neutron star and its environment.

The motivation for our research is to understand the complex interactions between the neutron star and its companion star, which are crucial for our understanding of astrophysical phenomena such as X-ray bursts and gravitational wave emission. The key idea behind our work is to use numerical simulations to model the accretion flow onto the neutron star and study the resulting X-ray emission. Our methodology involves solving the equations that govern the behavior of the accreting material and the X-ray emission using advanced computational techniques.

The primary goal of this research is to gain a better understanding of the accretion process and its associated X-ray emission. By studying how the physical properties of the neutron star and its companion star affect this process, we hope to shed light on the underlying physical mechanisms that govern these systems. Ultimately, this work will contribute to our broader understanding of the behavior of compact objects in the Universe, and will have implications for a wide range of astrophysical phenomena.

We present an investigation of the infrared spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of a sample of z~0.7 star-forming galaxies. Our work is motivated by the fact that the SEDs of galaxies are a powerful probe of their physical properties, including their star formation rates, dust content, and stellar populations. Despite the importance of understanding the physical processes driving galaxy evolution, the connection between the SED of galaxies and their underlying physical properties is not yet fully understood.

To address this knowledge gap, we assembled a sample of 184 star-forming galaxies at z~0.7 from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) data. We used available multiwavelength data from the UV to the far-infrared to construct their SEDs. We analyzed the SEDs using star-forming and dust models, parameterized by stellar mass, star formation rate, and other physical properties. The resulting fits allowed us to constrain the physical parameters of our sample of galaxies.

Our work attempts to solve the challenge of understanding the physical properties of galaxies through their SEDs. By providing insights into the physical processes driving galaxy evolution, our study advances our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution in the early Universe. Overall, our results provide a significant contribution to the field of galaxy evolution and will serve as a valuable reference for future studies.

In this work, we investigate the impact of unbalanced seesaws on massive and massless neutrinos. Despite the discovery of neutrino oscillations, the nature of neutrinos remains one of the great mysteries in physics. The seesaw mechanism is a widely accepted theory that allows for the introduction of massive neutrinos. However, the presence of the massless state complicates the theory and necessitates the use of unbalanced seesaws.

Our methodology involves solving a set of coupled differential equations derived from the seesaw mechanism. These equations describe the behavior of the neutrinos and allow us to investigate the effects of different seesaw parameters on the neutrino masses and mixing angles. We also explore how the presence of massive and massless neutrinos affects the cosmological implications of the unbalanced seesaw.

Our results show that the unbalanced seesaw can successfully explain the observed neutrino masses and mixing angles. We find that the mass hierarchy of the neutrinos plays a crucial role in determining the impact of the massless neutrino on the seesaw mechanism. Additionally, including both massive and massless neutrinos in the theory leads to new possibilities for explaining the origin of dark matter.

Overall, our work provides a deeper understanding of the seesaw mechanism and opens up new avenues for exploring the nature of neutrinos and their role in the universe.

In this study, we aimed to characterize the remnants of open clusters. Open clusters are groups of stars that formed together and are scattered throughout our galaxy, but over time, they dissolve through various processes. These remnants are important to study as they can provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies. However, identifying and characterizing them is a challenging task due to their diffuse nature and low contrast against the background stars. 

To achieve our goal, we used photometric and kinematic data from the Gaia mission and cross-matched it with data from previous surveys to identify open cluster remnants. We then analyzed the photometric and kinematic properties of the identified remnants to determine their ages and distances. Our results show that some of these remnants are significantly older than previously thought, indicating that they may have formed much earlier in the Galactic history.

Our study also revealed that some open cluster remnants exhibit significant velocity dispersions, which may be due to the interaction with the Galactic disk and/or other clusters. Additionally, we found that the remnants located at higher Galactic latitudes tend to have lower velocity dispersions compared to those at lower latitudes, suggesting a possible correlation with the Galactic structure.

In conclusion, our study provided a detailed characterization of open cluster remnants, shedding light on their formation and evolution within the Milky Way. Our results not only contribute to the understanding of galactic dynamics but also have important implications for future studies of star formation and evolution.

In this study, we investigate the post-oligarchic evolution of protoplanetary embryos and its impact on the stability of planetary systems. Our research aims to solve the problem of understanding the formation and evolution of planetary systems, which are complex and dynamic systems that involve the interactions between small bodies, massive planets, and their host stars. Specifically, we focus on the late stages of the formation process, after the oligarchic growth phase, when the embryos are dynamically excited due to mutual gravitational interactions.

We use N-body simulations that include both the gravitational interactions and the physical collisions between embryos. Our results show that the post-oligarchic evolution leads to significant changes in the size and eccentricity distributions of the embryos, as well as their mutual inclinations. These changes can have a profound impact on the final architecture of the planetary system, including the distribution of planets in different orbits and the presence or absence of gaps in the disc.

Our motivation for this research is to better understand the formation and evolution of planetary systems, which is one of the most fundamental questions in astronomy and astrophysics. The results of this study can have important implications for the search for habitable planets and the understanding of the diversity of planetary systems in the Universe.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of vortices in superconductors with fractal cluster structures at the initial stage of resistive transition. The problem we attempt to solve is the understanding of how complex structures, such as fractals, affect the onset of resistance in superconductors. Fractal structures have been found in various systems, including superconducting materials, and have been shown to affect their physical properties. Our research aims to uncover the dynamics of vortex matter in such systems to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the behavior of superconductors with fractal structures. 

We employ a numerical simulation approach using the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau equation to study the vortex dynamics. We consider the behavior of vortex matter under the influence of magnetic fields at various temperatures, exploring the transition from the superconducting state to the resistive state. Our findings indicate that the fractal cluster structure affects the dynamics of vortices, leading to a more complex transition from the superconducting to the resistive state. 

Overall, our study provides insight into the role of fractal cluster structures in the physical properties of superconductors, which may have implications for the design and development of high-performance superconducting materials.

In this study, we investigate the topology of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) through the use of position-position-velocity (PPV) data cubes. The motivation behind our research is the importance of understanding the three-dimensional structure of these gas clouds as they are key to the formation of stars and galaxies. Our work attempts to address the problem of characterizing the topology of the HI gas in the LMC, which is crucial for providing a deeper understanding of the physical processes involved in star formation. 

To achieve this objective, we employ computational techniques such as contouring, extracting filamentary structures, and topology-based analysis. Specifically, we utilize the Morse-Smale complex, a topological method for analyzing scalar and vector fields, to identify and classify critical points, ridges, and holes. Our analysis reveals a rich and complex topology of the HI gas in the LMC, consisting of filaments, loops, and voids, which interact in intricate ways. 

In conclusion, this work provides valuable insights into the structure and morphology of the HI gas in the LMC and helps to shed light on the physical mechanisms involved in star formation. Our methodology and results hold significant implications for future studies of the LMC and other galaxies, as well as the broader field of astrophysics.

Our study aims to investigate the global Wolf-Rayet content of NGC300, an irregular galaxy located approximately 6.1 million light-years away from us. In particular, we focus on determining the optical counterpart of the NGC300 X-1, an X-ray binary system consisting of a black hole and a Wolf-Rayet star. This study is motivated by the need to deepen our understanding of the evolution and formation of black holes and their associated stars.

To achieve these objectives, we used VLT/MUSE observations to conduct a detailed spectroscopic analysis of NGC300's central region, where the X-1 system is located. Our analysis allowed us to identify the optical counterpart of the X-1 system and accurately measure its radial velocity. Furthermore, our spectroscopic data allowed us to identify and classify hundreds of Wolf-Rayet stars in the galaxy, which gave us insight into the global Wolf-Rayet content of NGC300.

In conclusion, our study represents a significant contribution to the understanding of black hole and Wolf-Rayet star formation and evolution. Through our use of advanced observational techniques and spectroscopic analysis, we provide new insights into the global content and evolutionary processes of Wolf-Rayet stars in NGC300.

The Millennium Galaxy Catalogue (MGC) has been a valuable resource for galaxy studies, providing comprehensive data on over a million galaxies. In this work, we investigate the relationship between close galaxy pairs and asymmetry in the MGC, with implications for the galaxy merger rate. The problem of understanding the mechanisms driving galaxy evolution is a fundamental one in astrophysics, and galaxy mergers are a key process in this context. The rate of galaxy mergers and their impact on galaxy morphology and star formation rates is still a matter of debate. Our goal is to shed light on this issue by investigating the link between close pairs and asymmetry, a common indicator of merger activity. 

We have found a clear correlation between pair separation and asymmetry, with closer pairs showing higher levels of asymmetry. This suggests that galaxy interactions are indeed a main driver of galaxy asymmetry. Furthermore, we have used mock catalogs generated from simulations to estimate the galaxy merger rate implied by our measurements. We find that our results are consistent with previous estimates based on other methods, supporting the notion that mergers are indeed a key process in galaxy evolution. Our work provides new insights into the mechanisms driving galaxy evolution and lays the groundwork for future studies using the MGC.

In this study, we investigate the viscous torque and dissipation in the inner region of a thin accretion disk surrounding a black hole, and we explore how this can be used to measure the spin of the black hole. Our motivation for this research is the fact that the black hole spin is a fundamental parameter of the system that carries important information about its formation, evolution, and dynamics. However, measuring this parameter is challenging, and it requires sophisticated theoretical models and observational techniques.

Our key idea is that the viscous torque and dissipation in the inner region of the disk depend strongly on the black hole spin, and by modeling these effects and comparing them to observations, we can infer the value of the spin. To accomplish this, we use a combination of analytical calculations and numerical simulations, which allow us to explore the complex dynamics of the disk and track the behavior of the gas as it spirals towards the black hole.

Our main result is that the viscous torque and dissipation in the innermost region of the disk are sensitive to the black hole spin, and they can be used to constrain its value with high accuracy. Moreover, we find that the thermal and non-thermal emission from the disk also depend on the spin, providing additional probes for this fundamental parameter. Our work sheds light on the complex physics of accretion disks and offers new insights into the study of black hole spin.

In this study, we examined the polarization states of primordial gravitational waves via Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies. The investigation was motivated by the fact that such gravitational waves are produced in the early universe and provide crucial insight into the universe’s early expansion. As such, they are a critical aspect of modern cosmology and fundamental physics.

Using numerical simulations and CMB observations, we generated a likelihood analysis of the polarization states of the primordial gravitational waves. Our results showed that CMB observations are more sensitive to the tensor-to-scalar ratio (r) which profoundly influences the detection of the polarization of gravitational waves. These findings are significant in that they offer an improved understanding of the early universe and the overall expansion of the cosmos.

This research was conducted to contribute to the progress of measuring the gravitational waves, augment our knowledge of the early universe's dynamics, and offer insight into the cosmic inflation era. Our study provides significant contributions to the investigation of the origins of the universe, encourages future research on gravitational waves, and provides a path toward the development of next-generation experiments, which can more accurately measure gravitational waves.

In this work, we present a novel method to obtain zero-variance and zero-bias estimators of the spherically and system-averaged pair density based on quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations. The pair density is a fundamental quantity in statistical mechanics and is related to the thermodynamic properties of the system. It is challenging to calculate pair densities accurately from first principles due to the high dimensional nature of the problem, but QMC methods offer a promising avenue to obtain accurate estimates. 

The main contribution of our work is the derivation of zero-variance and zero-bias estimators for the pair density that eliminate statistical errors and systematic biases, respectively. We show that these estimators can be obtained by taking suitable ratios of QMC estimators for the two-body correlation function. We test the performance of our method on a model system of interacting particles in three dimensions and show that it yields accurate and reliable results. 

Our approach has the potential to be extended to other quantities related to the pair density and can be applied to a wide range of systems, including molecules, solids, and liquids.
