The zero-variance and zero-bias estimators derived in this work are particularly useful in bridging the gap between theory and experiment, as they provide a way to benchmark and validate experimental measurements based on first-principles calculations.

The study presented herein is motivated by the need to better understand the origin of orbital quantum structures found within the nucleon. These structures have significant implications for our understanding of subatomic physics and the manner in which fundamental laws hold. Our approach involves examining chiral mechanisms as they contribute to the formation of these anomalous structures.

Our research has led to some interesting and promising results. Specifically, we have identified the exact nature of the interplay between chiral symmetry breaking and orbital angular momentum, highlighting the critical role played by the quark-gluon vacuum. Furthermore, we have developed a theoretical model that predicts the appearance and interactions of these structures at the level of individual quarks.

Overall, the present study can be seen as an attempt to solve a deep and fundamental problem in the field of subatomic physics. We hope that our work will serve as a starting point for further exploration and investigation into the strange and wondrous workings of the universe at its most fundamental level. By providing greater insight into the mechanisms leading to orbital quantum structures in the nucleon, we believe that our research will help contribute to a broader understanding of the nature of matter and the laws governing our universe.

In this study, we investigated intrinsic ripples in graphene, which are believed to play a crucial role in the material's mechanical and electronic properties. Our motivation for this research was to gain a better understanding of graphene's behavior at the nanoscale, a crucial step towards optimizing its applications in fields such as electronics and energy storage. Using atomic force microscopy, we measured the topography of graphene samples with varying degrees of doping and analyzed the resulting scan data. Our findings suggest that intrinsic ripples occur more frequently in doped graphene and that their amplitude and wavelength decrease with increasing doping concentration. Moreover, we observed that additional ripples appear in the vicinity of impurities and defects in the material. This behavior is believed to stem from the interplay between lattice vibrations, electron-phonon interactions, and disorder-induced localization effects. Overall, our study sheds light on the role of intrinsic ripples in graphene's functional properties and sets the stage for further investigation of their influence in real-world applications.

In this study, we explore the merger potential of Abell 576, a galaxy cluster comprising over 400 galaxies. We examine the anomalous distribution of dark matter and X-ray gas, which appear to separate from each other, and investigate whether Abell 576 could be a line-of-sight projection of a Bullet Cluster. The Bullet Cluster is a well-known example of two galaxy clusters that have recently passed through each other. Using data from a combination of Chandra and VLA observations, we construct a dynamical model to simulate the collision of two clusters, and use it to evaluate the merger scenario.

Our findings suggest that Abell 576 is not a line-of-sight Bullet Cluster, but rather a result of a complex merger with an infalling sub-cluster. Our dynamical model provides a plausible explanation for the anomalous distribution of dark matter and gas. Our simulation indicates that Abell 576 is undergoing a complex merger with a sub-cluster between 0.2 and 0.4 of its mass, and that the sub-cluster has partially stalled in the halo of the main cluster. Our results have demonstrated the need for careful modeling of the merger processes in galaxy clusters, and highlighted the potential of Abell 576 to deliver important insights into the physics of cluster mergers.

In this study, we investigate the damage propagation at the interface localization-delocalization transition of the confined Ising model. The Ising model is a well-known statistical model to describe the behavior of magnetic materials. The localization-delocalization transition is an interesting phenomenon that occurs when the system goes from being in a disordered state to a ordered one. 

Our methodology involves using Monte Carlo simulations to simulate the system and analyze it. We introduce a new method to measure the damage propagation using the Green's function. Our results indicate that the damage propagates differently depending on the temperature range where the transition occurs. Furthermore, we observe that the damage does not propagate when the transition occurs at a temperature range where the system is in a ordered state.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is to understand the dynamics of damage propagation at the transition between different phases of the Ising model. This can help provide insights into the mechanisms governing the localization-delocalization transition and guide the design of future materials with potential applications in spintronics and other fields.

The motivation for this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the behavior of magnetic materials and explore new ways to control their properties. This study has the potential to contribute to the development of new technologies that rely on spin dynamics.

In this paper, we investigate the shapes of molecular cloud cores in the Orion Molecular Cloud Complex. Our main motivation is to understand the physical processes that contribute to the morphology of these structures. We use archival data from the Herschel Space Observatory to study the dust emission from the cloud cores and derive their morphologies using the astrodendro package. Our analysis reveals that the shapes of the molecular cloud cores in Orion are highly diverse, ranging from nearly spherical to highly elongated and irregular. We find that the dendrogram-based classification of the cloud cores is a useful method for quantifying their shapes and for identifying substructures within them. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the shapes of the cloud cores and their physical properties, such as their masses and temperatures. Our results suggest that the morphology of molecular cloud cores is influenced by a combination of factors, such as turbulence, magnetic fields, and protostellar feedback. Overall, this work provides important insights into the formation and evolution of molecular cloud cores in the Orion region, and it contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the processes that shape the interstellar medium.

In this work, we investigate the Burgers turbulence by studying the dissipation dynamics of energy. The Burgers equation is a simplified form of the Navier-Stokes equation that can capture the essential features of turbulent flows. We aim to understand the mechanism of energy transfer from large to small scales and its ultimate dissipation due to viscosity. 

Our methodology is based on direct numerical simulations of the Burgers equation in one and two dimensions using a pseudospectral method. We observe that the dissipation rate of energy has a power-law dependence on the Reynolds number in the inertial range. Additionally, the probability distribution of energy dissipation exhibits a clear deviation from a Gaussian distribution and displays heavy tails. These findings suggest that bursts of energy dissipation events are common in turbulent flows. 

Our motivation for this research is to gain insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying turbulence. Understanding turbulence is essential in various fields such as fluid dynamics, atmospheric sciences and oceanography. Our study contributes to the ongoing effort of developing models that can accurately predict the dynamics of turbulent flows. The findings also provide a deeper understanding of the statistical properties of turbulence, which could lead to more efficient engineering design and control of turbulent flows.

We report on the development and implementation of a new 60-cm radio survey telescope equipped with a sideband-separating superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) receiver for the 200 GHz band. This project was motivated by the need to study the high-frequency component of the radio spectrum, where many astronomical phenomena occur, such as star formation and the early universe's evolution. The 200 GHz band, in particular, is a window into the molecular universe where probing the gas content of galaxies is possible. The installation of a sensitive and high-resolution telescope, specifically optimized for this band, is a significant contribution to the current state of observational radio astronomy.

The primary problem this project aimed to solve was the lack of suitable telescopes within the 200 GHz band. The previous instruments had either limited sensitivity or poor spectral resolution, thereby making it hard to study faint and small-scale features. In contrast, the new telescope we developed has achieved high sensitivity and excellent spectral resolution, enabling us to study various astronomical objects in unprecedented detail.

We present the initial commissioning results of the telescope, including pointing accuracy, beam profile, and system temperature measurements. The telescope's sensitivity and spectral resolution are qualitatively shown by observations of a nearby molecular cloud and a Galactic star-forming region. The 60-cm Radio Survey Telescope with Sideband-Separating SIS receiver for the 200 GHz Band is now open for regular observing programs and will undoubtedly yield a wealth of science.

In this work, we investigate the effects of galactic winds on the metallicity distribution of dwarf spheroidal galaxies. These galaxies are known to be dominated by dark matter and have lower metallicity compared to the Milky Way. We aim to study how the galactic winds affect the metallicity distribution in these galaxies, which will help us understand the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies.

To achieve this goal, we conducted numerical simulations using a cosmological hydrodynamical code. Our simulations incorporated the effects of stellar feedback and galactic winds on the formation and evolution of dwarf spheroidal galaxies. We considered a range of different wind strengths and found that stronger winds lead to a more uniform metallicity distribution across the galaxy. This result suggests that the observed metallicity distribution of dwarf spheroidal galaxies can be partly explained by the effects of galactic winds.

Our study helps to constrain the complex interplay between the various astrophysical processes that influence the evolution of dwarf spheroidal galaxies. This work highlights the importance of considering feedback and galactic winds in models of galaxy formation, and provides insights into the metallicity distribution of these systems. Overall, our results contribute to a broader understanding of the formation and evolution of galaxies in the universe.

In this work, we present the results of optical BVI imaging and HI synthesis observations of the dwarf irregular galaxy ESO 364-G 029. Our primary objective was to understand the structural properties and evolutionary stage of this galaxy by analyzing its morphology, star-forming regions, and gas content. We utilized the Wide Field Imager (WFI) at the ESO 2.2-m telescope in La Silla and the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) to carry out the optical and radio observations, respectively. Our optical analysis revealed that ESO 364-G 029 has a highly complex star-forming activity, consisting of multiple, distinct regions of intense star formation within its main body. The HI synthesis observations revealed rich structure in the gas content, with a number of regions of varying densities and velocities present in the galaxy. Our study also estimated the total gas content, implying that this galaxy is moderately gas-rich when compared to other dwarf irregular galaxies. Our results provide valuable insights into the evolutionary history of ESO 364-G 029 and contribute to our understanding of dwarf galaxies in general.

In our study, we investigate the microscopic features of the superconducting quantum critical point (QCP) and the finite temperature crossovers in transport near a pair-breaking QCP. We carry out a thorough analysis of experimental data to reveal the key features of the system, which include unconventional critical exponents and unusual spectral functions. Our work attempts to address the problem of understanding the microscopic origin of the pair-breaking QCP, which is of significant interest in modern condensed matter physics. 

We employ state-of-the-art experimental techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/STS) measurements, which allow us to image the electronic properties of the sample with nanometer resolution, as well as inelastic neutron scattering (INS), which probes the collective excitations. Our analysis is supported by theoretical calculations that provide a framework to interpret and understand the experimental data. 

Our findings demonstrate that the superconducting quantum critical point is characterized by specific signatures in the electronic properties of the system, and the associated crossover regime is distinct from other quantum phase transitions. Our work sheds new light on the mechanisms that underlie the unusual behavior of the pair-breaking QCP, which is essential in the exploration of new superconducting materials and high-temperature superconductivity.

In this paper, we investigate the future projections of the local large-scale structure of the universe, with an emphasis on the roles of dark matter and dark energy. The motivation behind this research is to explore the current state and potential evolution of the local universe in light of recent observational and theoretical advancements. Specifically, we aim to provide insights into the fate of our local group of galaxies, which is the Milky Way, Andromeda, and Triangulum galaxies. 

The problem this work attempts to solve is the lack of knowledge about the ultimate fate of the local large-scale structure and how it is influenced by dark matter and dark energy. To address this problem, we analyze data from large cosmological simulations and examine the effects of gravitational interactions between galaxies, dark matter, and dark energy on the evolution of the structure.

The key ideas of our work are first, that the gravitational dynamics of dark matter and galaxies play a crucial role in shaping the large-scale structure of the universe. Second, dark energy has a repulsive effect that acts against gravity. Thus, the combination of dark matter and dark energy determines the ultimate fate of the universe on larger scales. Our methodology involves running simulations with advanced computational techniques to model the evolution of the local universe over billions of years.

In conclusion, our work provides a comprehensive perspective on the future of the local large-scale structure of the universe, with an emphasis on the roles of dark matter and dark energy. The integration of theoretical advances and observational data provides unique insights into the complex interplay between dark matter, galaxies, and dark energy, shedding light on the ultimate fate of our local universe.

In this work, we explore the higher-order angular galaxy correlations in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and investigate the redshift and color dependence of non-linear bias. We aim to understand the physical mechanisms that underlie the clustering of galaxies in the SDSS and to improve our knowledge of the structure formation processes.

To achieve this goal, we use a theoretical framework based on perturbation theory and halo models to calculate the power spectra and bispectra of the galaxy distributions. We then compare our theoretical predictions with the observational data from the SDSS. 

Our results show that the non-linear bias term is sensitive to both the redshift and color of the galaxies, with a stronger dependence on the former. We also find clear evidence of a non-zero bispectrum signal, which is a signature of non-Gaussianity in the distribution of galaxies. These findings have important implications for understanding the formation and evolution of large-scale structures in the universe.

Overall, our work presents a novel approach to studying the higher-order correlations of galaxies and provides new insights into the non-linear bias and the clustering properties of galaxies in the SDSS. Our research contributes to the broader scientific effort to understand the physical processes driving the evolution of the universe.

We present our recent work on CKM and tri-bimaximal MNS matrices in a SU(5) x (d)T Model. Our research is motivated by the need to better understand the flavor puzzle in particle physics. The flavor puzzle is related to the mysterious patterns observed in the quark and neutrino masses and mixing angles, which remain unexplained within the Standard Model framework. Our approach is based on a grand unified theory, which unifies the strong, weak, and electromagnetic interactions at high energy scales. We extend the minimal supersymmetric standard model to include a gauge singlet field that couples to the matter fields and a discrete symmetry (d)T that breaks the gauge symmetry at a lower scale. We show that the CKM and tri-bimaximal MNS matrices can be naturally obtained in this model, providing a possible explanation for the observed patterns. We use the renormalization group equations to study the evolution of these matrices from high to low energies. Our results suggest that the CKM matrix is consistent with the current experimental measurements, while the tri-bimaximal MNS matrix predicts a non-zero contribution to the reactor angle. Our work provides a promising direction for future studies of the flavor puzzle in particle physics.

In this work, we present a novel deterministic framework for characterizing the behavior of stochastic genetic circuits. We propose a methodology based on moment closure techniques that allow us to obtain a system of deterministic differential equations that captures the dynamics of the circuit at a macroscopic level. Our approach is based on making approximations to the probability distribution of the state of the system, allowing us to obtain a closed system. Our results show that this analytical framework provides us with a precise characterization of the steady-state behavior of genetic circuits. We provide a detailed analysis of the model and show that the accuracy of the deterministic model improves as the number of molecules in the system increases. Furthermore, our framework allows us to investigate the effect of circuit parameters on the circuit behavior.

The motivation for this research lies in the growing interest in the dynamic behavior of genetic circuits and the need for mathematical tools to analyze their behavior. Although stochastic models have been widely used to study genetic circuits, they are computationally intensive and often lack the ability to provide a clear understanding of circuit dynamics at a macroscopic level. Thus, deterministic models remain critical in guiding the design and engineering of genetic circuits. Our work provides a useful alternative framework for characterizing the behavior of genetic circuits, complementing the existing stochastic models.

In this work, we investigate the S-parameter in Holographic Technicolor Models (HTCs) as an important quantity that can constrain the electroweak symmetry breaking dynamics. The traditional HTCs with fundamental fermions are based on the 5D gauge-gravity duality, where the strongly-coupled gauge theory on the boundary corresponds to a weakly-coupled gravity theory in the bulk. However, these models have faced several theoretical issues, such as the mass hierarchy problem.

More recently, lattice simulations of the underlying gauge theory have led to the development of the AdS/QCD correspondence, which is expected to provide a better description of realistic QCD dynamics. Motivated by this, we consider a specific AdS/QCD-inspired model where the gauge group is broken via a scalar field in the bulk. We calculate the S-parameter in this model by using the gauge field propagators, which are obtained from the five-dimensional gauge fields.

Our key idea is to show that the S-parameter in this scalar-HTC model can be smaller than that in the traditional fermionic-HTCs. By using the technique of holographic renormalization, we also derive the renormalization group equation for the S-parameter. Our methodology involves a careful analysis of the AdS/QCD formalism and a comparison with experimental bounds on the S-parameter.

The significance of our work lies in its potential to improve our understanding of the underlying electroweak symmetry breaking dynamics and its possible connections to the QCD confinement mechanism. By investigating the S-parameter within the context of AdS/QCD-inspired models, we hope to pave the way for future experimental and theoretical studies in this area.

In this work, we investigate the connection between star-forming galaxies, AGN host galaxies, and early-type galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). Our research attempts to understand the relationship between these three different types of galaxies and how they evolve over time. The problem we aim to solve is understanding the role AGN host galaxies have in the evolution of galaxies and their potential impact on star formation.

Our methodology involves analyzing a large sample of SDSS galaxies using publicly available data. We examine different properties of each galaxy, including its morphology, stellar mass, gas content, and level of star formation. We also investigate the presence of AGN activity in these galaxies.

Our key results indicate that AGN host galaxies exhibit different properties compared to both star-forming and early-type galaxies. Specifically, AGN host galaxies tend to have higher stellar masses and lower levels of star formation than star-forming galaxies. However, they also show a higher gas content than early-type galaxies, indicating their potential for future star formation.

In conclusion, our work sheds light on the complex relationship between star-forming galaxies, AGN host galaxies, and early-type galaxies. The results obtained from this analysis provide new insights into the evolution of galaxies and the role of AGN in this process.

In this study, we propose a generic mechanism for adaptive growth rate regulation. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a mechanism that can effectively regulate growth rate in response to changes in the environment. To address this problem, we propose an adaptive feedback mechanism that employs both intrinsic and extrinsic signals to regulate growth. Our key idea is to use a control system to sense changes in environmental conditions and adjust the growth rate accordingly. The methodology involves the use of mathematical modeling techniques and simulations to study the behavior of the proposed mechanism. 

The results obtained suggest that our approach can effectively regulate growth rate in response to changes in the environment. Specifically, our simulations show that the mechanism can maintain a constant growth rate in response to fluctuating environmental conditions. Moreover, the mechanism is able to adjust the growth rate to different environmental conditions, allowing organisms to achieve optimal growth under different conditions. In conclusion, our proposed mechanism provides a promising avenue for the development of adaptive growth regulation systems that can enhance the fitness of organisms in changing environments.

In this work, we present an efficient method for detecting periodic orbits in chaotic maps and flows. Chaos theory has been extensively researched over the years, and it has practical applications in several fields, such as physics, biology, and engineering. However, in many cases, chaotic systems display recurrent behaviour, which can be represented by periodic orbits. Detecting these periodic orbits is essential for understanding the dynamics of a chaotic system and predicting its behaviour. However, identifying such orbits can be a challenging computational task, especially for high-dimensional systems. 

To address this problem, we propose a technique that combines the benefits of symbolic dynamics and clustering analysis. This approach allows us to convert the time series of a chaotic system into a symbolic sequence, reducing its dimensionality and identifying recurring patterns. Subsequently, we use a clustering algorithm to group the symbolic sequences, each representing a possible periodic orbit. We validate the effectiveness of our method with several examples, including the Lorenz system, Henon map, and Rössler system. Our approach can detect periodic orbits with high accuracy, even for very high-dimensional systems, and it can be applied to a broad range of chaotic systems. The proposed method has the potential to be a valuable tool for scientists and engineers working with chaotic systems.

In this article, we present a novel approach for exploring the geometry of regular shear-free null geodesic congruences and CR functions, and their application to the flat-space Maxwell equations. Our work addresses a significant challenge in theoretical physics: the need to understand the geometrical and topological properties of null geodesic congruences in order to develop a deeper understanding of fundamental physical processes such as electromagnetic radiation. 

Our approach utilizes a combination of complex analysis, differential geometry, and CR geometry to develop a unified framework for explorations of null geodesic congruences, CR functions, and the Maxwell equations. Our results highlight a number of key geometric and analytic properties of regular shear-free null geodesic congruences, including their associated CR structures, which play a critical role in understanding the behavior of electromagnetic waves in flat-space Maxwell theory. 

We demonstrate the power of our approach through a number of concrete examples and applications, including a detailed analysis of the geometric properties of a canonical shear-free null geodesic congruence, and the application of our techniques to the study of the polarization properties of electromagnetic waves. These findings offer new insights into the geometric and topological nature of fundamental physical phenomena, and provide a roadmap for further explorations of null geodesic congruences and their associated structures.

In this work, we present a Bayesian analysis applied to the low-resolution polarized sky maps derived from the three-year data of the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP). Our goal is to infer statistical properties of the polarization field at large angular scales, taking into account uncertainties arising from instrumental noise and cosmic variance. Our approach relies on modeling the polarization field as a Gaussian random process, parameterized in terms of power spectra and correlation functions. We use Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to sample the posterior distribution of the parameters of interest. We find that our results are consistent with the best-fit cosmological model favored by the analysis of the temperature anisotropy maps. In particular, we obtain constraints on the amplitude and shape of the polarization power spectra that are consistent with theoretical predictions based on the inflationary paradigm. We also investigate the level of non-Gaussianity in the polarization patterns, and find no evidence for significant deviations from Gaussianity. Our work provides a systematic and rigorous method for testing cosmological models using polarization data, and lays the groundwork for future analyses that will take into account the full sky coverage and higher resolution of data from future experiments.

In this work, we explore the Ramsey interferometry protocol applied to a two-level Tonks-Girardeau gas. Our motivation lies in the interest of studying the effects of quantum statistics on the interference patterns of the system. To investigate this phenomenon, we apply a sudden displacement of one of the well-separated components of the gas, following a Ramsey excitation scheme. We calculated the time evolution of the probability of finding the gas in the excited state as a function of the displacement and showed that the interference signal strongly depends on the interaction and statistics regimes of the system. Our results reveal that the two-level Tonks-Girardeau gas presents striking interference patterns that can be analyzed to infer relevant information on the dynamics of strongly correlated systems. Additionally, we provide an analytical approximation of the probability of finding the system in the excited state in the large-displacement limit, which agrees with our numerical simulation, ascertaining the validity of our approach. This work offers a novel perspective on how the investigation of quantum correlations can enlighten the interferometry of strongly interacting two-level systems.

In this study, we investigate the connection between mass loss and the evolution of carbon-rich Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars. To achieve this, we performed a detailed analysis of 22 AGB stars using the hydrodynamical code MESA, coupled with s-process nucleosynthesis calculations. The key idea behind our research was to understand the mechanisms that lead to the formation of carbon stars and the enrichment of elements. The methodology employed was to simulate the evolution of AGB stars that undergo mass loss via stellar winds and dust formation.

Our results reveal that the mass loss rate has a significant influence on the evolution of carbon stars, as it affects the nucleosynthesis process inside the stars. We found that AGB stars with high mass loss rates have lower surface carbon-to-oxygen ratios compared to stars with low mass loss rates. In addition, we discovered that mass loss can lead to the production of heavy elements with atomic masses greater than 60.

Our motivation for this research was to broaden our understanding of the stellar evolution of carbon-rich AGB stars and their role in the chemical evolution of galaxies. This has important implications for our understanding of the origins of elements in the universe and the evolution of galaxies.

In this study, we investigate the clustering properties of restframe UV selected galaxies and their evolution with cosmic time. We utilize the multi-wavelength data from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) and Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope Legacy Survey (CFHTLS) to construct a sample of over 40,000 UV-selected galaxies at redshifts 0.5 to 1.5. The key idea of this study is to examine the migration of star formation sites within these galaxies as they evolve over time. To achieve this, we utilize the Bayesian Photometric Redshift (BPZ) code to estimate the redshifts and stellar masses of these galaxies, and then employ the Voronoi Delaunay Method (VDM) to determine the clustering properties of the sample. 

Our results show that the clustering strength of restframe UV-selected galaxies increases with cosmic time, suggesting that these galaxies become more clustered as they evolve. We also find that there is a clear migration of star formation sites within galaxies, with star formation being more concentrated towards the central regions of galaxies at higher redshifts. This trend is most notable for the youngest and most star-forming galaxies in our sample. The methodology applied in this study provides insights into the properties and evolution of star-forming galaxies and can pave the way for further investigation into the physical processes that drive the observed migration of star formation sites.

In this research work, we investigate some aspects of measurement error in linear regression of astronomical data. The motivation for this research stems from the prevalence of measurement error in observational data, which can lead to misleading conclusions and inaccurate results. Our work aims to address this issue by examining the impact of measurement error on the regression coefficients and standard errors in linear regression models. 

We begin by conducting a simulation study, where we generate data with varying levels of measurement error and examine the resulting regression coefficients and standard errors. We also investigate the effect of sample size and signal-to-noise ratio on the accuracy of the regression results. In addition, we apply our methods to a real-world astronomical data set and compare the results to those obtained from traditional regression techniques. 

Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for measurement error in linear regression analysis of astronomical data. We demonstrate that ignoring measurement error can lead to biased estimates and incorrect inference, and that our proposed methods can improve the accuracy and reliability of regression results. Our work contributes to the development of statistical methods for handling measurement error in observational data, with potential applications in a wide range of scientific fields.

In this work, we present a new understanding of special Finsler manifolds using a global approach to their theory. The problem we aim to solve is the lack of a comprehensive theoretical framework that encompasses the various types of special Finsler manifolds, thus hindering the development of applications and computations using these structures. We propose a generalization of the classical notion of Berwald manifolds, incorporating different types of special Finsler structures, such as Randers and Kropina manifolds, under a single framework. 

Our approach is based on the observation that special Finsler metrics arise as specific solutions to a set of algebraic constraints on Finsler metrics. We use a global differential geometric approach to prove the existence of a corresponding special Finsler metric over any given Finsler manifold and provide explicit formulas for its fundamental tensor fields. We also show how our framework leads to a characterization of geodesics and curvature properties for the special Finsler manifolds, as well as relationships among different types of special Finsler metrics.

The motivation behind this research stems from the increasing demand for a mathematical structure that can model a wide range of physical phenomena, including the study of black holes, quantum gravity, and dark energy. Our results offer a new perspective on the theory of special Finsler manifolds that supports the development of diverse applications in geometry and physics.

In this work, we investigate the dynamics of Fuzzballs with internal excitations in the context of string theory. Fuzzballs are hypothesized to be the non-perturbative objects that replace the notion of black holes in the string theory framework. They are composed of a collection of strings and D-branes, and are characterized by their horizonless structures. However, the precise details and properties of fuzzballs remain largely unknown.

We focus on the issue of internal excitations within fuzzballs, which arise due to the multiple string winding modes around compactified extra dimensions. We demonstrate that these excitations lead to interesting dynamics and novel features in the behavior of fuzzballs. In particular, we show that the internal modes give rise to collective phenomena that are reminiscent of quasi-particle excitations of conventional condensed matter systems.

Our work contributes to the growing body of research aiming to unravel the mysteries of fuzzballs and their implications for black hole physics and the holographic principle. Our main motivation for this work is to shed light on the nature of the fundamental building blocks of the universe, and to advance our understanding of the fundamental laws that govern the behavior of matter and spacetime.

In this work, we investigate the holographic confinement/deconfinement phase transitions of AdS/QCD in curved spaces. Our study is motivated by the possibility that the interaction between gravity and QCD, the theory of strong nuclear interactions, will play a crucial role in the understanding of the behavior of strong interactions at low energies. To achieve this, we focus on a holographic description of QCD in which the confinement/deconfinement phase transitions take place in the context of an AdS geometry.

Our study reveals that the confinement/deconfinement phase transition is sensitive to the geometry of the AdS space. We use the gauge/gravity duality to map QCD to the classical gravitational theory and investigate the behavior of the AdS/QCD system in a black hole geometry background. Our findings suggest that the confinement phase can be suppressed in certain regions of the parameter space. In particular, a high temperature black hole geometry can cause a transition from the confined phase to a deconfined phase.

The key idea behind this work is to investigate the effect of curved spaces on the confinement/deconfinement phase transitions of AdS/QCD. Our research employs a combination of theoretical and numerical techniques, such as the holographic renormalization procedure and the computation of the free energy. Our study addresses the problem of understanding the behavior of strong interactions at low energies in the context of gravitational theories and provides a new framework for investigating the AdS/QCD system in curved backgrounds.

In this work, we present the recent results of the STAR high-energy polarized proton-proton program at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL). The goal of this research program is to study the spin structure of the proton and the strong interactions between its constituents, quarks and gluons. The spin of the proton is an essential aspect of its structure, and understanding it requires experimental investigations at high energies and with polarized beams.

The key methodology of the STAR program involves measuring the spin-dependent asymmetries in proton-proton collisions. Using polarized proton beams, we can study the polarization of different quark flavors in the proton and their contribution to the overall proton spin. Additionally, by measuring the differential cross-sections for different kinematic variables, such as transverse momentum and rapidity, we can study the dynamics of the strong interactions inside the proton.

The motivation for this research program comes from the desire to understand the fundamental properties of matter and the strong force that binds quarks and gluons together. By studying high-energy proton-proton collisions, we can probe the structure of the proton and test our theoretical understanding of the strong force. The recent results from the STAR program show intriguing effects in the polarization asymmetries, challenging our current understanding of the proton spin puzzle. These findings pave the way for new investigations into the nature of the strong force and the internal structure of the proton.

In this work, we investigate the emergence of Neel order in square and triangular lattice Heisenberg models. The motivation for this research stems from the importance of understanding the behavior of magnetic materials at low temperatures, as well as the fundamental interest in studying the quantum properties of interacting spin systems in condensed matter physics.

Using Monte Carlo simulations, we find that the square lattice model exhibits Neel order at low temperatures, in agreement with theoretical predictions. However, the triangular lattice model does not exhibit Neel order even at the lowest temperatures studied. Instead, we find evidence of two sub-lattices showing different magnetic behaviors, leading to a non-uniform magnetic pattern.

Our results contribute to a better understanding of the magnetic behavior of two-dimensional Heisenberg models and provide insights into the differences between the square and triangular lattice systems. The methodology employed in this work involves the use of a stochastic simulation method, which enables us to model the behavior of complex physical systems with a large number of interacting variables.

In conclusion, our work sheds light on the rich diversity of magnetic order observed in Heisenberg models and provides a valuable platform for investigating the behavior of other complex quantum systems in condensed matter physics.

In this study, we investigate the age distribution of star clusters in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) and explore its interpretation. The significance of this research is two-fold: first, the SMC is an ideal target for analyzing star clusters, being a low-metallicity galaxy having a wide range of ages and located at a known distance from Earth. Second, interpreting the age distribution of star clusters can provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies.

Using archival Hubble Space Telescope (HST) data, we selected a sample of 56 star clusters in the SMC and measured their ages via color-magnitude diagram fitting. Comparing the age distribution of star clusters in the SMC with that of a Milky Way globular cluster catalog, we found that the former has a broader and flatter distribution, suggesting that different mechanisms might be at play for forming star clusters in the two galaxies.

Furthermore, we compared our results with theoretical models of cluster formation and found that the power-law exponent of the age distribution is more consistent with the predictions of the turbulent cloud model rather than the competitive accretion model. Our findings confirm that the age distribution of star clusters in the SMC can provide crucial constraints on current theories of cluster formation.

We present a study on logarithmic corrections and soft photon phenomenology in the multipole model of the nucleon form factors. The motivation for this research lies in the need to improve our understanding of the internal structure of the nucleon, which is crucial in the interpretation of high-energy experiments. Our work attempts to solve the discrepancy between the experimental measurements of the nucleon form factors and their theoretical predictions, by considering the effects of soft photon radiation.

The key idea behind our research is to incorporate logarithmic corrections, which arise from the summation of infrared divergences in radiative corrections, into the multipole model. We develop a systematic theoretical framework to calculate these corrections and apply it to the proton and neutron form factors. Moreover, we investigate the role of soft photons in the form factor measurements by studying the radiative corrections to the unpolarized and polarized electron-proton scattering cross sections.

Our methodology involves using a combination of analytic and numerical techniques to compute the logarithmic corrections and soft photon radiation effects. We demonstrate that our results account for a significant part of the discrepancy between theory and experiment for the proton form factors, with prospects for further improvement. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the nucleon's internal structure and paves the way for more accurate predictions of nucleon properties from first principles.

In our work, we present a first-principles model of early evolution that aims to unravel the origins of gene families, species, and preferred protein folds. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a holistic and comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms that enabled life to emerge and persist in the early stages of evolution. While previous studies have shed light on individual aspects of early evolution, such as the emergence of simple replicators or the evolution of functional proteins, they often fail to capture the complex interplay between various evolutionary processes and the constraints imposed by the physical and chemical environment of the early Earth.

Our motivation for this research is to develop a more unified and predictive framework that can explain the emergence of key biological features such as gene duplication, speciation, and protein folding. Leveraging the power of computational modeling and statistical physics, we construct a self-consistent model that simulates the replication, mutation, and selection of genetic sequences and their corresponding protein products. We explore the role of different evolutionary forces such as drift, selection, and recombination in shaping the diversity of gene families and the emergence of novel protein folds. In particular, we find that gene duplication followed by subfunctionalization and neofunctionalization can lead to the rapid diversification of gene families, and that the selective pressure for efficient folding can drive the emergence of stable and robust protein structures.

Our results provide new insights into the early stages of biological evolution, and our model can serve as a valuable tool for testing hypotheses and predicting the behavior of evolving systems.

In this paper, we present our results on the investigation of the possible annual modulation of the source J1128+5925. This object is a gamma-ray emitting blazar located at a redshift of 1.5 and belonging to the Fermi-LAT catalog. Our motivation for this work is twofold. Firstly, annual modulations on astrophysical sources are believed to be a signature of the interaction between dark matter particles and the galactic halo. Therefore, detecting such modulations can provide information on the nature of dark matter. Secondly, gamma-ray blazars are known to vary with time, and their flux modulation can be described in terms of a periodic function with a period of one year. Therefore, investigating the possible annual modulation of J1128+5925 can shed light on the physical processes occurring in these sources. 

We analyzed 11 years of Fermi-LAT data and performed a Lomb-Scargle periodogram analysis and a Bayesian block method to search for a possible periodic modulation. Our results showed evidence of a periodic signal with a period of one year and a confidence level of 96.7%. However, further investigation is needed to confirm the significance of the signal and rule out other sources of variability. 

The method presented here can be applied to other gamma-ray sources to search for annual modulations and understand the variability of blazars. Furthermore, the existence of annual modulations can help improve our understanding of the distribution and nature of dark matter in the Milky Way halo.

In this study, we present new evidence of recent feedback energy release in the cores of two elliptical galaxies based on Spitzer observations of the transient, extended dust. The key ideas behind our research are to investigate the mechanisms powering the high-energy processes in the nuclei of early-type galaxies and to understand their impact on the interstellar medium (ISM). The methodology employed in this work involves the analysis of imaging and spectroscopic data obtained with the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) instrument on board the Spitzer Space Telescope. We detect extended dust features in the nuclei of NGC 5419 and IC 4296 that are spatially associated with outflows of hot gas and X-ray emission, indicative of an active galactic nucleus (AGN). Furthermore, we find that these dust structures have properties consistent with the presence of newly formed dust grains that have been heated by the AGN. The motivation for this study is to better understand the interplay between the AGN and the ISM in early-type galaxies, as this relationship has significant implications for galaxy evolution and the growth of supermassive black holes. Overall, our work represents a step forward in our understanding of feedback processes in galaxy cores, and sheds light on the physical conditions under which dust can be created and destroyed in these environments.

In this work, we investigate the dynamic phase transition in the two-dimensional kinetic Ising model using the conjugate field and fluctuation-dissipation relation. The motivation for our research is to understand the behavior of the dynamic phase transition in the Ising model, which is a paradigmatic model for statistical physics. The problem that our work attempts to solve is how to describe the behavior of the system near the critical point, where the correlation length becomes infinite.

To achieve this goal, we use the conjugate field method to derive the equation of motion for the order parameter and the fluctuation-dissipation relation to compute the critical exponents. We find that the behavior of the order parameter is governed by a non-linear diffusion equation, which exhibits both stationary and travelling wave solutions. We also find that the critical exponents can be obtained from the scaling behavior of the order parameter near the critical point.

Our methodology involves analytical calculations and numerical simulations of the Ising model using Monte Carlo methods. Our key idea is to use the conjugate field method to derive the equation of motion and the fluctuation-dissipation relation to compute the critical exponents. Our results provide insight into the behavior of the dynamic phase transition in the Ising model and can be used to understand other systems with similar behavior.

We present a detailed analysis of the properties of (65489) Ceto/Phorcys, a binary Centaur orbiting in the outer Solar System. Our study aims to determine the orbit, mass, size, albedo, and density of the system using a combination of observational data and numerical simulations. The motivation for this research lies in the need to understand the physical properties and evolutionary history of Centaurs, a population of small bodies that have been dynamically scattered into their current orbits from the Kuiper belt by the giant planets.

We use observations from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based facilities to calculate the system's orbit, while numerical simulations are used to model the binary's tidal evolution and estimate its properties. Our results suggest that (65489) Ceto/Phorcys has a mass of 188±19 km, a size of 168±8 km, and a density of 1.14±0.12 g/cm³. The albedo of the system is found to be 0.059±0.011, consistent with the values found for other Centaurs.

This work provides new insights into the properties of Centaurs, such as the tidal evolution of binary systems and the physical characteristics of these primitive Solar System bodies. Our study demonstrates the importance of combining observational data and numerical simulations to understand the formation and evolution of small celestial bodies in the outer Solar System.

We present results from imaging the cosmic matter distribution using gravitational lensing of pregaltic HI. Our motivation for this research stems from the need for a better understanding of the large-scale structure of the universe and the properties of dark matter. The problem that we attempt to solve in this work is to develop a technique for imaging the cosmic matter density distribution, which is crucial for understanding both the formation and evolution of cosmic structures and the nature of dark matter. 

Our study involves analyzing data from the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), a futuristic radio telescope that promises to revolutionize the field of astronomy. Using the SKA, we have constructed a map of the gravitational lensing effect of pregaltic HI over a wide area of the sky. Our analysis shows that the pregaltic HI provides a unique tracer of the matter distribution in the early universe, and that the lensing signal is sensitive to the underlying matter density distribution. We have compared our results with simulations of the universe, finding a good agreement between the two. 

Our imaging technique has important implications for future studies of cosmic evolution and the nature of dark matter. It provides a powerful tool for mapping the distribution of cosmic matter on large scales, which can reveal key insights into the nature of the universe and help resolve longstanding cosmological puzzles.

In this work, we explore the use of free additive convolution for regularization in both the square and rectangular cases. The motivation for this research arises from the need for effective regularization techniques in signal and image processing, where data may be noisy or undersampled. Our results demonstrate that free additive convolution is an effective method for regularization in both cases, enabling accurate reconstructions of signals and images even in the presence of noise or incomplete data. 

Our approach involves using free additive convolution to impose a regularity prior on the data, effectively reducing the dimensionality of the problem and allowing for more accurate reconstruction. This regularization scheme is implemented using iterative algorithms, such as proximal gradient descent, which allows for efficient computation and scalability to large datasets. 

Key idea behind our approach is to exploit the independence structure of the additive convolution to incorporate prior knowledge about the underlying data distribution. This approach enables regularization without the need for explicit assumptions about the noise or data distribution, which makes it a powerful tool in a wide range of applications including MRI, CT scans, and audio signal processing. 

Overall, this work suggests that free additive convolution can be an effective regularization technique in a range of settings, providing insight into the benefits of incorporating prior knowledge in signal and image processing.

In our study, we investigate Charge Polarization Effects and Hole Spectra Characteristics in Alxgai-xN/Gan Superlattices. The problem we aim to solve is the limited understanding of the influence of charge polarization on hole spectra in nitride semiconductor materials. Our motivation for this research is the potential applications of Alxgai-xN/Gan superlattices in optoelectronic devices. Therefore, we carried out a theoretical analysis of the effect of charge polarization on hole spectra in Alxgai-xN/Gan superlattices.

We used the finite-element method to calculate the valence band structure, four-band k · p Hamiltonian to calculate the hole subbands, and the density functional theory to calculate the polarization effects of superlattices. By analyzing the bandgap, effective hole mass, and hole subbands, we discovered that charge polarization presents a significant effect on the hole spectra in Alxgai-xN/Gan superlattices.

Our results demonstrate that charge polarization contributes to the blue shifts of the valence band and reduces the hole effective masses, which leads to an improvement in the hole mobility. This study provides useful insights for the design and optimization of Alxgai-xN/Gan superlattice-based optoelectronic devices. Our findings are also relevant to other quantum heterostructures, and the methods we used can be applied to exploring polarization effects on other materials.

In this study, we report on the search for pulsation among suspected A-type binaries and the discovery of a new multiperiodic Delta Scuti star, HD217860. The motivation for this research stems from the fundamental astrophysical questions related to binary star systems and the pulsational properties of Delta Scuti stars. Our key idea was to identify and analyze potential pulsating stars within known binary systems, which can provide insight into the interaction between the components and the underlying physical mechanisms of variability. 

We used photometric observations from the TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) mission and ground-based data to conduct a frequency analysis of the light curves. Our methodology involved pre-whitening the data to remove the orbital signal of the binary system and identify the pulsation frequencies. We successfully identified multiperiodic pulsations in HD217860, a previously unknown Delta Scuti star, with up to six detected frequencies. While no significant pulsations were found in the suspected A-type binaries, the results provide valuable constraints on the presence or absence of variability and can inform future studies of these systems.

Overall, our findings contribute to the ongoing efforts to improve our understanding of binary systems and the properties of Delta Scuti stars, which are crucial to advancing our knowledge of stellar evolution and fundamental astrophysical processes.

In this paper, we present a new model for the Galactic diffuse emission observed by the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on the Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST). This model is based on the observations of the LAT during the first few years of operation and is intended to provide a more accurate prediction of the Galactic diffuse emission than the previous models. The motivation for this work stems from the need to have a more accurate model of the Galactic diffuse emission in order to improve the sensitivity of the LAT to gamma-ray sources.

Our approach involves fitting the LAT data to a model that includes both the Galactic diffuse emission and the residual cosmic-ray background. The model parameters are then optimized using a maximum likelihood method, which ensures that the model provides the best fit to the data. The results obtained show that our new model provides a significant improvement over the previous models in terms of its accuracy and reliability.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the need for a more accurate model of the Galactic diffuse emission, which is crucial for the detection and analysis of gamma-ray sources. This work provides an important contribution to the field of gamma-ray astronomy and is likely to have a significant impact on future observations and analyses of the LAT data.

In this work, we propose a new testing standard for 3D radiative hydrodynamics simulations of disks, a key tool for understanding disk stability, accretion processes, and planet formation. We discuss the challenges and limitations of current models and present new results obtained with our improved approach. 

Our methodology incorporates an innovative combination of radiation transport and hydrodynamics algorithms, allowing us to accurately capture the physical properties of disks, including the effects of radiation pressure, heating and cooling, and dust opacity. With our new testing standard, we benchmark different numerical methods and assess their reliability, consistency, and accuracy in modeling disk instabilities. 

Using this standard, we carry out a set of simulations that explore the role of radiation feedback in shaping disk dynamics and fragmenting structures. Our findings indicate that radiation significantly affects the disk temperature and pressure profiles, leading to the formation of clumps and spiral arms, which can potentially trigger planetesimal formation. We further analyze the sensitivity of our results to different physical and numerical parameters and discuss possible implications for disk observations. 

Our work represents a significant step towards a comprehensive and standardized framework for modeling disk instabilities with 3D radiative hydrodynamics, and sheds light on the complex interactions between radiation and hydrodynamics in protoplanetary disks.

In this study, we investigate the electromagnetic wave propagation in an almost circular bundle of closely packed, metallic, carbon nanotubes (CNTs). The key idea behind this research is to understand the behavior of electromagnetic waves in CNTs, which possess remarkable mechanical and electrical properties. The motivation behind this study is to explore the potential of CNTs for various applications in electronics and photonics. 

To conduct this research, we developed an analytical model based on the partial wave expansion technique. The model considers the interactions between the CNTs as well as the electromagnetic properties of the surrounding medium. We examined the effect of the radius and number of CNTs on the transmission and reflection coefficients of the bundle. Our results indicate that the wave propagation is strongly influenced by the geometrical parameters of the CNT bundle. 

The problem this work attempts to solve is the lack of understanding of the electromagnetic wave propagation in CNTs, which hinders the potential applications of these materials in advanced electronics and photonics devices. The outcomes of this study provide useful insights into the design and optimization of CNT-based devices for various applications such as nanoscale sensors and antennas.

Our work titled "The First Survey of X-ray Flares from Gamma Ray Bursts Observed by Swift: Spectral Properties and Energetics" presents an analysis of high-energy emission from Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) using data from the Swift satellite. Our aim is to characterize X-ray flares emitted by GRBs and investigate the associated spectral properties and energetics.

We utilized Swift's Burst Alert Telescope (BAT) to identify 90 GRBs and their corresponding afterglows, and analyzed their X-ray flares with Swift's X-Ray Telescope (XRT). From our results, we find that X-ray flares in GRBs can be divided into two types based on their spectral properties: hard and soft flares. Additionally, we calculate the energetics of the flares and find that they contribute a significant fraction of the total energy released by the GRBs.

Our study aims to solve the problem of understanding the physical mechanisms that drive X-ray flares in GRBs, which have remained a mystery since their discovery. Our results suggest that X-ray flares are produced by internal shocks within the GRB outflow, and provide insight into the amount of energy released during these processes.

Overall, our study represents the first comprehensive survey of X-ray flares from GRBs using Swift data, and lays the foundation for future studies in this field.

In this work, we focused on testing the radiative neutrino mass generation mechanism at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We proposed a novel methodology, which allowed us to investigate the impact of a heavy neutrino and a charged scalar in the generation of radiative neutrino masses at the LHC. Our simulations involved heavy neutrino's decay into a lighter neutrino and the charged scalar, which subsequently decayed into a neutrino and a photon. We then investigated the modulation of the invariant mass of the photon-neutrino system, which provided us with a conclusive signature of the radiative neutrino mass generation mechanism. 

Our results showed that the proposed methodology was efficient in testing the mechanism at higher energies than previous experiments, which were carried out at the electroweak scale. We found that the presence of a heavy neutrino enhanced the significance of the signature, allowing us to increase the sensitivity to the mass of the radiative neutrino. Additionally, we demonstrated that the proposed methodology was complementary to other experimental approaches, such as the direct search for heavy neutrinos.

Overall, our work aimed to solve the longstanding problem of testing the radiative neutrino mass generation mechanism at higher energies than previous experiments. We believe that the proposed methodology could pave the way for new studies at the LHC, allowing us to further explore the electroweak sector of the Standard Model.

In this work, we aim to solve the problem of efficiently updating finite element models (FEMs) using a Response Surface Method (RSM). FEMs are widely used in engineering to simulate and analyze complex systems, but their accuracy heavily relies on the input parameters and assumptions. Thus, updating the models to fit with experimental data is essential for obtaining accurate predictions. However, traditional methods for updating FEMs require time-consuming iterations between simulations and experiments, making them impractical for large-scale problems.

The motivation for this research stems from the need for efficient and accurate model updating methods for real-world engineering problems. RSM is a statistical optimization technique that enables surrogate modeling between variables, reducing the number of simulations required for model updating. In this study, we propose an efficient FEM updating method by integrating RSM with FEM. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a numerical example and compare the accuracy and efficiency with traditional methods. Our results show that the RSM-based approach can achieve higher accuracy with fewer simulations, reducing the computational time and cost of model updating.

In conclusion, this work offers an effective and efficient method for updating FEMs using RSM, which can benefit a wide range of engineering applications.

We present an analysis of the outer jet X-ray and radio emission in R Aquarii from 1999.8 to 2004.0 using Chandra X-ray Observatory and Multi-Element Radio-Linked Interferometer Network (MERLIN) data. R Aquarii is a symbiotic star system consisting of a red giant and a white dwarf in a binary system. It is known for its extended bipolar jet that manifests in both X-ray and radio frequencies. Our work aims to study the temporal variability of the outer jet emission over five years and understand the interplay between different physical mechanisms responsible for the observed emission. 

The motivation for this research is to gain insights into the physical processes involved in the formation and evolution of the R Aquarii jet and study the effects of the interaction between the jet and ambient medium. We use spectral and imaging analyses to characterize the jet emission and investigate the effects of shocks and synchrotron radiation in the jet. The methodology adopted involves analyzing X-ray and radio light curves, spectra, images, and comparing the results with state-of-the-art models. 

Our study shows a complex temporal behavior of the outer jet emission that is attributed to the interaction between the jet and the surrounding medium. The spectral analysis indicates that the jet is powered by a combination of thermal and non-thermal mechanisms, and synchrotron radiation is a dominant contributor to the radio emission. Further, the imaging analysis reveals a limb-brightened outer jet morphology with evidence of shocks and precessional motion. Overall, our work provides valuable insights into the physics of the jet in R Aquarii and highlights the importance of multiwavelength studies to understand the nature of astrophysical jets.

In our work titled "Measuring the dark matter velocity anisotropy in galaxy clusters," we explore the dark matter distribution and its velocity anisotropy in galaxy clusters. Galaxy clusters are ideal laboratories for studying dark matter since they are the most massive gravitationally bound systems in the universe. Using numerical simulations and high-resolution spectroscopy data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we find that there is a strong velocity anisotropy of dark matter in galaxy clusters. The dark matter has a higher velocity dispersion in the radial direction than in the tangential direction, indicating that it is elongated along the line of sight. Furthermore, we find that there is a correlation between dark matter velocity anisotropy and cluster mass, with more massive clusters having a stronger anisotropy.

Our research is motivated by the need to better understand dark matter, a form of matter that constitutes around 85% of the total matter in the universe but cannot be directly observed. Measuring the dark matter velocity anisotropy in galaxy clusters can provide important insights into the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter, its nature, and its interactions with other matter. Our work attempts to solve the problem of accurately quantifying the dark matter velocity anisotropy in galaxy clusters, which is essential for constraining the properties of dark matter and testing theories of its formation and evolution.

In this study, we investigate the regularity of the minimal probability of ruin in a game of stopping and control, which is a mathematical model used to analyze financial risk management decisions. Our research aims to provide a better understanding of this probabilistic quantity and establish its regularity properties. 

Based on a stochastic control approach, we establish a set-valued partial differential equation, which characterizes the optimal value function of the game. We establish the Lipschitz continuity of the value function and use this result to prove the upper semicontinuity of the minimal probability of ruin. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the minimal probability of ruin is a concave function of the initial reserve level. 

Our results provide significant insights into the fundamental properties of the minimal probability of ruin in the game of stopping and control. The key idea of the study is to use the theory of stochastic calculus to obtain analytical results for this probabilistic quantity. The methodology combines analytical techniques with numerical simulations to validate the obtained results. 

The motivation for our research is to contribute to the development of robust and reliable models for financial risk management. The regularity properties established in this study can be used to design optimal risk-control strategies for investors and insurers. Overall, our work sheds light on a fundamental aspect of financial risk management and contributes to the ongoing research in this area.

In this work, we present a study of neutral hydrogen absorption toward XTE J1810-197, a radio-emitting magnetar located in the Galactic plane. The aim of this research is to determine the distance to the source using the absorption features seen in the spectra. We have used the Green Bank Telescope to obtain high-resolution and high-sensitivity absorption spectra at 21-cm wavelength.

Our analysis shows that the absorption features are consistent with cold gas in the foreground of XTE J1810-197. Based on the properties of the absorbing gas, and by comparing our data with previous studies, we constrain the distance to the source to be 3.5 ± 0.2 kpc.

The distance measurement is crucial for studying the physical properties of XTE J1810-197, such as its magnetic field and age. One of our key findings is that the absorption features suggest that the magnetar is located beyond the Carina-Sagittarius spiral arm, which is in agreement with previous studies.

Our methodology involves a careful analysis of the spectral data, including modeling of the continuum emission and fitting of the absorption features. This study highlights the importance of neutral hydrogen absorption as a tool for Galactic distance measurements and provides a valuable constraint for understanding the properties of radio-emitting magnetars.

In this work, we explore the magnetic focusing of charge carriers in spin-split bands using the semiclassical framework of the Zitterbewegung effect. The main objective of the study is to understand the mechanisms and principles underlying the magnetic focusing of spin-polarized electrons and holes in semiconductor heterostructures. Our approach involves solving the semiclassical equations of motion of the Bloch wavepacket, which describes the spatiotemporal evolution of the charge carriers in the presence of an external magnetic field. 

We show that the magnetic focusing effect depends critically on the interplay between the spin and orbital degrees of freedom of the charge carriers. Specifically, we find that the Zitterbewegung-induced motion of the Bloch wavepacket leads to a separation of the spin-up and spin-down components, which are then focused to different locations in the sample. We also find that the focusing efficiency can be enhanced by tuning the strength and direction of the magnetic field, as well as by controlling the initial spin polarization of the carriers. 

Our study provides new insights into the fundamental physics of spintronics and may have important implications for the design of spin-based electronic devices. The methodology we employ combines theoretical calculations with analytical insights, paving the way for future studies of magnetic focusing of charge carriers in other types of semiconductor systems.

In this work, we investigate the production of TeV gamma-radiation in the vicinity of the supermassive black hole in the giant radiogalaxy M87. The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the processes involved in the launch of relativistic jets from the centers of active galaxies, as well as to explore the potential of gamma-ray observations as a tool for probing black hole physics. Using data from the H.E.S.S. telescopes, we find evidence for TeV gamma-ray emission from the center of M87, consistent with the location of the supermassive black hole. We model the emission as arising from inverse Compton scattering of low-energy photons by relativistic electrons in a jet, and infer the properties of the jet and the electrons. Our results suggest that the jet in M87 is dominated by leptonic processes, and that the electrons in the jet have a power-law energy spectrum with an index of approximately 2.2. Our work contributes to the understanding of the physical processes operating in the vicinity of supermassive black holes, and highlights the potential of TeV gamma-ray observations as a probe of black hole environments.

In this study, we present a large scale extinction map of the Galactic Anticenter from 2MASS. The aim of this research is to understand the distribution of interstellar dust and evaluate its impact on observations in the near-infrared regime. The Galactic Anticenter has been a region of interest for astrophysical studies given its proximity to the Galactic plane and the presence of obscured star formation regions. However, the identification of these regions, as well as the interpretation of their properties, are hampered by the presence of dust, which absorbs and scatters the light.

Our approach to generating the extinction map is based on the observation of background stars that pass through the dusty regions. We use their color excess information to estimate the amount of foreground dust extinction along their path. The method is based on the combination of photometric data from the Two Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) and the Quasar Equatorial Survey Team (QUEST), and it covers an area of approximately 100 degrees in Galactic longitude and 30 degrees in Galactic latitude. 

The resulting extinction map shows significant variations across the surveyed region, with values ranging from a few 10ths to several magnitudes. The map is a valuable tool for identifying and characterizing obscured regions such as molecular clouds, star-forming regions, and dust lanes, and for improving the interpretation of observations in the near-infrared regime.

In this work, we investigated topological insulators beyond the Brillouin zone using Chern parity. Our research is motivated by the need to develop a theoretical framework that accurately describes topological insulators, which are materials that exhibit unique electronic properties due to their topology. The key idea behind our approach is to extend the concept of Chern parity, which is a topological invariant, to study systems that are outside the conventional Brillouin zone. To achieve this, we developed a generalization of the Hamiltonians that describe topological insulators by using a non-commutative algebra. With this framework, we were able to analyze the emergence of nontrivial topological phases in a system in some regions of the parameter space. Our methodology involved numerical simulations using a tight-binding model, which confirmed the emergence of topological phases and their robustness against perturbations. We also established the role of edge states in the topological characterization of the system. Our work shows that Chern parity can be employed as a powerful tool to explore topological insulators beyond the conventional Brillouin zone. These results have implications for the design and engineering of materials with tailored electronic properties, which could have applications in electronic devices.

In this paper, we present a study of GLSM's for partial flag manifolds. The partial flag variety is a class of algebraic varieties that plays a central role in algebraic geometry and representation theory. Our goal is to develop a framework for constructing gauge theories that live on these manifolds using the tools of Geometric Langlands-Siegel Modularity (GLSM) theories. The main advantage of GLSM's is that they provide a way to relate geometry and representation theory through modular forms.  

To achieve our goal, we first describe the geometry of partial flag manifolds and review the theory of GLSM's. We then develop a general method to construct GLSM's for partial flag manifolds using a combination of representation theory, algebraic geometry, and modular forms. Our methodology involves studying the moduli space of stable sheaves on the partial flag manifold and constructing a Hilbert scheme for it. The Hilbert scheme is a moduli space of subschemes of the partial flag manifold that takes into account the stability condition of the sheaves.

One of the key ideas behind our work is that the modularity of GLSM's can be used to study the geometry of partial flag manifolds. This has important implications in representation theory and mathematical physics. Our motivation for this research lies in the desire to further understand the relationship between algebraic geometry, representation theory, and modular forms, and to develop new tools for studying moduli spaces and gauge theories.

In this work, we present our findings on the extended envelopes around two Galactic Cepheids, Y Oph and alpha Per, using near-infrared interferometry with CHARA/FLUOR. Our key idea revolves around studying these extended envelopes, which have been previously detected via photometry, and analyzing their properties to better understand the physics of Cepheid variables.

Our approach involved utilizing high-precision CHARA/FLUOR interferometry with a spatial resolution of 0.5 milli-arcseconds to measure the extension of the envelope around Y Oph and alpha Per. By combining these measurements with previously obtained photometric data, we could estimate the physical parameters of the envelopes, such as their temperature and density.

Our motivation for this research stems from the desire to gain a better understanding of the physical processes driving Cepheid variability. We also aim to contribute to the larger body of research on Cepheids, which has implications for areas such as galaxy evolution and the cosmic distance ladder.

The problem we attempt to solve in this work is to accurately measure the properties of the extended envelopes around Cepheids. By doing so, we can improve our understanding of the physical processes driving Cepheid variability and contribute to our overall understanding of these important variables.
