We also found strong molecular hydrogen emission in the nuclear region, indicating an interaction-induced shock. We estimate a high star formation rate (∼60 M/yr) and a substantial AGN contribution to the IR luminosity (∼30%).

Our study demonstrates the power of high-resolution mid-IR spectroscopy in understanding the physical processes that shape luminous infrared galaxies.

In this work, we present a study on non-standard neutrino interactions (NSI) using neutrinos emitted by core-collapse supernovae. These interactions, beyond the standard model, can alter the neutrino oscillation parameters and affect the supernova's explosion mechanism. Therefore, it is imperative to investigate these interactions and their potential implications. 

To probe NSI, we use a three-flavor neutrino propagation simulation in which we vary the NSI parameters. We simulate the expected neutrino signals from a distant supernova and compare them to the standard neutrino oscillation scenario. We also investigate the degeneracy of some NSI parameters to better understand their effect on the expected signals. 

The problem this work attempts to solve is to quantify the impact of NSI on the neutrino signal from a core-collapse supernova. Our results show that NSI can significantly impact the neutrino signals, leading to deviations from the standard oscillation scenario. Furthermore, we found that these deviations can be used to place constraints on non-standard neutrino interactions. 

In conclusion, our work demonstrates the importance of considering non-standard neutrino interactions in supernova neutrinos and provides a framework to probe these interactions and place constraints on their parameters.

The Infrared Cloud Monitor for the MAGNUM Robotic Telescope at Haleakala aims to address the challenges posed by atmospheric conditions in astronomical observations. Infrared observations are particularly sensitive to atmospheric moisture and cloud cover, which can significantly impair data quality. To mitigate this problem, we developed a cloud monitoring system that utilizes the thermal infrared emissions of the atmosphere to track the presence and extent of cloud cover. The system comprises a customized thermal camera and a software suite that processes the camera feeds in real time to determine cloud cover metrics, which are then transmitted to the telescope control software. 

Preliminary testing of the system has yielded promising results, with accurate and timely detection of cloud cover under a range of atmospheric conditions. The system has been fully integrated into the MAGNUM Robotic Telescope at Haleakala and is now fully operational. The motivation for developing this system is to increase the efficiency and quality of astronomical observations under variable atmospheric conditions. We believe that this innovation will enhance the scientific yield of the telescope and enable more reliable and accurate observations of celestial objects in the infrared spectrum. The Infrared Cloud Monitor for the MAGNUM Robotic Telescope represents an example of how technology can be used to overcome challenges inherent to astronomical observations, improving our understanding of the universe.

In this work, we present a study on the equivalence of three-dimensional spacetimes. The main problem that we aim to solve is to understand the relationship between different spacetime models and to identify when they are equivalent. Our motivation for conducting this research is the need to create a consistent framework for discussing gravitational physics in three-dimensional spacetimes.

We show that two-dimensional groups are useful in describing three-dimensional spacetimes, and identify the conditions under which a three-dimensional spacetime can be decomposed into a Cartesian product of two-dimensional spacetimes. We also establish the equivalence between different three-dimensional models, such as the warped-product model and the diagonal metric product model.

Our results provide a deeper understanding of the structure of three-dimensional spacetimes, particularly in relation to gravitational physics. They also have important implications for fields that use three-dimensional spacetimes as a tool for modeling physical systems, such as string theory and coset models.

Overall, our work contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying structure of spacetime, which is essential for studying fundamental principles of physics such as gravity. We hope that our findings will be useful to researchers working in this area and will inspire further exploration of this important topic.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the electronic properties of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) through a combination of density functional theory (DFT) and the empirical pi-bond model. The motivation behind this research is the potential of CNTs to revolutionize the field of electronics due to their unique structural and electronic properties. However, the properties of CNTs are not yet fully understood, and thus, we sought to explore this area further. 

Our work attempted to solve the problem of accurately predicting the electronic properties of CNTs, which is critical for their practical applications in electronic devices. Specifically, we investigated the bandgap, electronic structure, and charge transfer between metallic and semiconducting CNTs using our computational approach. 

Our results show that the pi-bond model accurately predicts the bandgap of semiconducting CNTs, while DFT is suitable for predicting the electronic structure of metallic CNTs. Moreover, we found that the charge transfer in CNTs is highly dependent on the chirality and diameter of the tube, as well as the surrounding environment. 

In conclusion, our study provides valuable insight into the electronic properties of CNTs and sheds light on their potential applications in nanoelectronics. Our findings suggest that a combination of DFT and empirical models is necessary for accurate prediction of the properties of CNTs. Our results will contribute to the ongoing efforts to unlock the full potential of these materials for practical applications in electronics and other fields.

In this study, we investigate the role of elastic stresses in leaf venation morphogenesis. Understanding the mechanisms underlying leaf venation development is essential for predicting the consequences of environmental perturbations and for identifying strategies to increase crop yields. Previous studies have focused on genetic and hormonal determinants, with little attention given to mechanical forces. We hypothesize that elastic stresses play a crucial role in guiding the formation and patterning of veins during leaf development.

To test our hypothesis, we used a combination of computational simulations and experimental measurements. Our simulation results show that elastic stresses can induce the formation of complex vein patterns from a simple initial state. We found that these patterns are robust and insensitive to changes in external conditions such as nutrient availability and light intensity.

Our experimental data support the simulation results and show that changes in mechanical properties affect the development of veins. The results suggest that mechanical stimuli play a crucial role in determining the final architecture of the leaf vasculature.

Our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying leaf venation development and highlights the importance of considering mechanical forces in plant morphogenesis. These findings can inform efforts to engineer crops with improved efficiency and resilience, enhancing food security and sustainable agriculture.

In this work, we investigate the potential of transit surveys in star clusters by analyzing the impact of correlated noise and radial velocity follow-up. The main objective of this study is to provide insights into the feasibility of using transit surveys to detect exoplanets in star clusters and to determine the optimal observational strategies for this purpose.

We performed a set of simulations to investigate the effects of correlated noise on transit detection efficiency. Our results show that the presence of correlated noise can significantly reduce the detection efficiency of transit surveys, particularly for small planets and short periods. However, we demonstrate that the inclusion of radial velocity follow-up can significantly improve the detection efficiency of transit surveys in star clusters.

Our analyses also revealed that the optimal observational strategy for transit surveys in star clusters is to focus on clusters with a high central concentration and to observe in the infrared wavelength range. We also found that the choice of the transit detection algorithm has a significant impact on the detection efficiency of transit surveys in star clusters.

In conclusion, our study showcases the potential of transit surveys in star clusters and provides important insights into the impact of correlated noise and radial velocity follow-up on their detection efficiency. Further studies are needed to explore the optimal observational strategies and to assess the potential of transit surveys in detecting exoplanets in star clusters.

In this work, we investigate the fluctuation behavior of competitive random sequential adsorption (RSA) from a binary mixture. Specifically, we examine the partial filling factors of the two components in the mixture, and explore how they vary due to the competitive nature of the adsorption process. To achieve this, we utilize a numerical simulation approach based on a previously established algorithm. 

Our work tackles the critical problem of understanding the effects of competitive adsorption, which is relevant in a wide range of practical applications such as catalysis, chromatography, and purification processes. We demonstrate that fluctuations of the partial filling factors can be attributed to the competition between the two components, as they attempt to occupy the available sites on the surface. Furthermore, we show that the exact nature of these fluctuations depends on various parameters such as the surface coverage and the size ratio of the different components.

Our results point to the importance of considering the dynamics of competitive adsorption when designing efficient and optimized surface coatings. The methods and insights presented in this work pave the way for further research in this area, and contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex behavior of adsorption in binary mixtures.

In this study, we investigate the photospheric environment of a solar pore with a light bridge. The motivation for this research is to understand the characteristics of the magnetic fields that create and maintain these structures on the solar surface. Pores are dark and compact regions on the photosphere that are associated with weak magnetic fields. The presence of a light bridge, however, implies that there is a stronger magnetic field in the surrounding region. The problem this work attempts to solve is to understand how these two kinds of magnetic fields interact with one another in the formation and evolution of these structures.

Using high-resolution observations taken with the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we analyze the photospheric magnetic field in and around a pore with a light bridge. We use the magnetic field information to compute various parameters that characterize the photospheric environment, such as magnetic flux, magnetic inclination, and magnetic shear. Our results indicate that the magnetic field in the region of the light bridge is more complex than the magnetic field in the surrounding pore, with multiple magnetic polarities and a higher degree of magnetic shear. These findings imply that the light bridge is a site of magnetic reconnection, where the magnetic fields of opposite polarities interact and release magnetic energy. Our work provides valuable insights into the physical processes that govern the generation and evolution of solar magnetic structures.

In this study, we employ ab initio density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the electronic structure of barium titanate (BaTiO3), a material with significant technological relevance in electronic and optical applications. The motivation for this research is to understand the underlying electronic properties that govern the behavior of BaTiO3, providing fundamental insights that can aid in the development of advanced devices and technology.

Our results show that BaTiO3 is characterized by a significant band gap, with a value of 3.2 eV, which is in good agreement with experimental data. We further identify that the electronic structure of BaTiO3 is highly anisotropic, with different regions of the material exhibiting distinct electronic states. This anisotropy is found to be strongly correlated with the crystal symmetry of the material, with regions of high symmetry exhibiting a greater electronic uniformity.

Overall, this work aims to solve the problem of understanding the complex electronic properties of BaTiO3, which are essential for the development of advanced electronic and optical technologies. With the insights gained from our study, we have identified key features of the electronic structure of BaTiO3 that can be used in the design of novel materials and devices with enhanced performance.

This study investigates the isospin asymmetry in the continuum of the A=14 mirror nuclei, namely, 14C and 14O. The primary objective of the research is to address the disparity between mirror nuclei and understand the fundamental properties of nuclear reaction dynamics. The theoretical framework is based on the mathematical formulation of the shell-model approach incorporating the isospin degree of freedom. The experiments were performed using a magnetic spectrograph and the Beverly-Wheeling data analysis method.

Our project findings reveal that 14C has a smaller isospin asymmetry than 14O in the continuum due to the energy needed to break the nuclear bond. Moreover, the work sheds light on the subtle correlation between nuclear forces and the isospin degree of freedom. The study emphasizes the importance of understanding the isotopic properties of atomic nuclei to develop a comprehensive theoretical understanding of nuclear structure and properties.

The approach implemented in this research is fundamental in nature and opens up new avenues for future research projects, which could significantly impact the field of nuclear physics. The methodology employed in the research focuses on studying the nuclear force in different systems, including those not accessible by other experimental techniques. The findings of this work are relevant to other scientific fields, including astrophysics and particle physics.

In this paper, we present a detailed study of the stability of magnetized spine-sheath relativistic jets in the context of General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) and Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations. The problem we are attempting to solve is the understanding of how jet collimation and energy dissipation is maintained in the presence of internal instabilities that can disrupt the flow. In particular, we focus on the interaction between the magnetized plasma in the jet spine and the surrounding sheath, which are believed to play a crucial role in determining the jet structure and dynamics.

The motivation for this research stems from the fact that relativistic jets are ubiquitous astronomical phenomena, observed in a wide range of cosmic scales, from microquasars in our Milky Way to active galactic nuclei (AGN) in distant galaxies. However, the physics of jet acceleration and collimation is still largely unknown, and a better understanding of the underlying mechanisms is crucial for our comprehension of astrophysical processes on a cosmological scale.

To address this problem, we performed three-dimensional numerical simulations of magnetized jets using the GRMHD and RMHD equations, which describe the dynamical behavior of the plasma in a strong gravitational field and the relativistic regime. We analyzed the results in terms of jet stability and the evolution of different instability modes, such as Kelvin-Helmholtz, current-driven, and sausage modes. Our findings suggest that the spine-sheath configuration can indeed enhance the jet stability, suppressing the growth of internal instabilities and promoting efficient energy dissipation through magnetic reconnection.

In this study, we present a novel method for generating minimally coupled Einstein-scalar field solutions from vacuum solutions with an arbitrary cosmological constant. The key idea of our approach involves considering the scalar field as a perturbation of a given vacuum solution, and solving the resulting coupled system of equations. Our methodology is based on a perturbative expansion scheme, in which the scalar field is assumed to be small compared to the vacuum energy density. Using this approach, we derive a set of first-order equations for the perturbation variables, which are then solved numerically using standard numerical integration techniques. We illustrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to several well-known vacuum solutions with both positive and negative cosmological constant. Our results show that our method produces viable Einstein-scalar field solutions that exhibit interesting features such as hair, scalar charge, and non-trivial dynamics. Importantly, we find that our solutions are stable under small perturbations, thus suggesting that our approach is a reliable tool for studying the role of scalar fields in shaping the dynamics of the universe. Overall, our research is motivated by the need to develop new methods for exploring the rich and complex physics of scalar-tensor gravity, which plays a crucial role in many areas of modern cosmology and astrophysics.

In this study, we present the discovery and characterization of 33 new nearby white dwarf systems as part of The Solar Neighborhood XIX. Our motivation was to expand upon the known population of nearby white dwarfs and improve our understanding of their distribution, formation, and evolution. White dwarfs are the end product of low-mass stars similar to our Sun and, as such, offer a unique opportunity to study the late stages of stellar evolution.

Our work attempts to solve the problem of an incomplete census of nearby white dwarf systems. Despite efforts in the past to identify such systems, a significant fraction had remained undetected due to various observational biases. Our methodology involved utilising data from the SuperCOSMOS Sky Survey, targeting regions that were previously undersampled, and using proper motions and photometry to identify white dwarf candidates. We then followed up on these candidates using spectroscopy to confirm their nature and characterise their properties.

Our results reveal a diverse population of white dwarf systems that includes single white dwarfs, binary systems, and systems with debris disks. Our discoveries push the completeness of the nearby white dwarf population to 95%, providing valuable insight into the history and demographics of our Galactic neighbourhood.

In this work, we present a dynamical analysis of the 14 Her planetary system, which consists of a hot Jupiter and a distant giant planet. The motivation for this research, is to understand the origin and stability of this system, as well as to improve our understanding of the dynamics of hot Jupiter systems. Our study is based on a numerical simulation of the system's dynamical evolution over a period of 10 million years, which takes into account the planets' gravitational interactions, as well as the effects of General Relativity and tidal dissipation. 

Our results show that the 14 Her system is in a dynamically stable configuration, with the two planets maintaining their orbits for the entire simulation period. The hot Jupiter undergoes significant eccentricity oscillations on a time scale of a few thousand years, but its orbit remains within a safe distance from the star. The distant planet, on the other hand, is shown to be in a long-term stable orbit with a moderate eccentricity. 

Our study concludes that the 14 Her system is a rare example of a dynamically stable hot Jupiter system, and may provide important insights into the formation and evolution of such systems. The methods and techniques used in this work can also be applied to other exoplanetary systems, providing key insights into the dynamical processes that shape planetary systems.

In this study, we investigate the gravitational acceleration of quantum vacuum energy, specifically the Casimir energy. While there have been previous studies on the Casimir energy, there has been little exploration of how it falls under the influence of gravity. We focus on analyzing the behavior of a perfect conductor plate system under different gravitational conditions using the Dirac equation. We observe that the Casimir energy falls with gravitational acceleration, contrary to the usual behavior of energy in free fall where there is no clear direction.

Our motivation for this research stems from the theoretical implications of understanding the behavior of energy in the strong gravitational field. Moreover, this study further aids in developing our understanding of the Casimir effect, which has a range of practical applications, from efficient energy harvesting to building nanoscale machines. By studying the interaction between the Casimir energy and gravity, we can also gain insight into the more fundamental mechanisms behind gravity and possibly develop a better understanding of the gravitational force.

Our results indicate that there is indeed a gravitational acceleration of the Casimir energy, and this effect can be understood through the behavior of the solutions to the Dirac equation in a gravitational field. This study provides new and important insights into both the behavior of quantum vacuum energy in the presence of gravity and the more fundamental mechanisms behind the laws of gravitation.

In this study, we investigate the influence of oxygen partial pressure on the structural, transport, and magnetic properties of Co-doped TiO2 films. The motivation for this research stems from the increasing demand for materials with multifunctional properties, particularly those with the potential to exhibit both magnetic and semiconducting behaviors. Understanding the underlying factors that affect the magnetic and transport properties of Co-doped TiO2 films is critical for engineering new materials for use in spintronic and magnetic sensing applications.

To achieve this, we grew Co-doped TiO2 films under varying oxygen partial pressures using pulsed laser deposition. We then conducted a thorough characterization of the samples’ structural, transport, and magnetic properties. Our results indicate that the oxygen partial pressure strongly influences the structural properties of the films, with a transition from an anatase to rutile structure observed at lower oxygen partial pressures. Moreover, we find that the oxygen partial pressure also influences the magnetic and transport properties of the Co-doped TiO2 films, with a significant improvement in both properties observed at higher oxygen partial pressures.

In summary, our work demonstrates the potential for manipulating the oxygen partial pressure during the growth of Co-doped TiO2 films to engineer materials with tailored magnetic and transport properties for use in spintronic and magnetic sensing applications.

In this work, we investigate cuspidal representations of general linear groups over discrete valuation rings. Our motivation for this research is to deepen our understanding of these representations and their connections to other areas of mathematics. Specifically, we seek to shed light on the Langlands correspondence, a deep and far-reaching conjecture which links automorphic forms to Galois representations. Our work attempts to contribute to this ongoing endeavor by providing a more complete picture of cuspidal representations.

One of our main results is a classification of irreducible cuspidal representations of GLn over a discrete valuation ring of finite residue field. In addition, we establish a connection between these cuspidal representations and certain classes of modular forms. We also investigate the behavior of cuspidal representations under certain operations, such as twisting and parabolic induction.

Our findings are based on a thorough analysis of the underlying algebraic structures and the use of powerful mathematical techniques, including representation theory and algebraic geometry. The insights gained from this work have the potential to inform other areas of mathematics and contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the Langlands correspondence.

In this paper, we study the actions of J-class operators and their relation to hypercyclicity in Banach spaces. The main objective of this work is to provide a careful analysis of the hypercyclicity properties of J-class operators and to obtain some new results in this area. Specifically, we aim to examine when an operator in the J-class is hypercyclic or when it can be used to construct hypercyclic operators. 

Our study provides several new insights into the hypercyclicity theory of J-class operators. We show that the existence of a hypercyclic operator in the J-class is closely related to the existence of certain non-zero coefficients in the power series expansion of the operator. Furthermore, we also prove that some restrictions on the coefficients can lead to the absence of hypercyclic J-class operators. 

The key ideas and methodology employed in this work involve a careful analysis of the action of J-class operators on certain sequences and the use of several well-known techniques from hypercyclic theory, such as the Birkhoff transitivity theorem and large deviation estimates. We also utilize some recent results from the theory of composition operators to establish our main findings. 

Overall, our study provides a deeper understanding of the interplay between J-class operators and hypercyclicity, and sheds new light on the properties of these important classes of operators in Banach spaces.

In this paper, we investigate the complexity of approximating entangled games. Entangled games are a generalization of the well-known concept of non-local games, which are commonly used in the study of quantum computing and communication complexity. The motivation for this research arises from the fact that entangled games are a key tool for understanding the limits of quantum computation and communication, and for developing new quantum algorithms and protocols. 

Our main result is that entangled games are hard to approximate within a certain range of values, under plausible complexity assumptions. Specifically, we show that it is NP-hard to approximate the value of entangled games within a constant factor, and that it is unlikely that such approximations can be efficiently computed unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. Our proof relies on a reduction from the problem of approximating the permanent of a matrix, which is known to be #P-hard.

To obtain our results, we build on recent advances in the study of non-local games and their connections to computational complexity theory. Our proof technique involves using the concept of low-degree testing to analyze the structure of entangled games and derive lower bounds on their approximability. 

Overall, our work sheds new light on the complexity of entangled games and provides insights into the fundamental limits of quantum computation and communication. These results have implications for the design of future quantum algorithms and the development of new approaches to quantum information processing.

In this research, we report on the observation of quantum-measurement backaction with an ultracold atomic gas. Our work focuses on the fundamental principle of quantum mechanics that measurement necessarily disturbs the system being measured. This idea has been extensively studied in quantum optics using light, but less so using ultracold atoms.

Our experimental methodology involves using a cloud of ultracold atoms in a trap and applying a weak measurement via a probe laser beam. We analyze the recoil of the atoms due to the measurement and observe a deviation from the expected trajectory caused by quantum backaction. We show that this effect is stronger for larger measurement strength and longer measurement times, and we demonstrate that it can be explained using a model that incorporates the effects of decoherence and measurement noise.

The motivation for our research is to better understand the behavior of quantum systems and the limitations of measurement in quantum mechanics. This work also has potential applications in quantum metrology and sensing.

Our work attempts to solve the problem of experimental characterization of quantum backaction in ultracold atomic gases. By demonstrating this effect, we contribute to the development of quantum technologies and advance our understanding of the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

In this work, we investigate the stability of isentropic viscous shock profiles in the high-Mach number limit. The motivation for this research lies in the fact that such shocks are ubiquitous in gas dynamics, and they play a key role in various engineering applications, such as supersonic combustion and high-speed flight. However, high-Mach number shocks are notoriously difficult to analyze due to the nonlinear nature of the governing equations and the resulting lack of closed-form solutions. Thus, it is important to develop a deeper understanding of the stability properties of such shocks.

To this end, we use a combination of asymptotic analysis and numerical simulations to study the linear and nonlinear stability of isentropic viscous shock profiles. Our key idea is to exploit the large-Mach number limit, which allows us to simplify the governing equations and isolate the dominant physical effects. We then apply a rigorous theoretical framework based on the Evans function method to analyze the linear stability of the shock profiles. Additionally, we perform numerical simulations using a high-resolution shock-capturing scheme to investigate the nonlinear evolution of perturbed shocks.

Our main result is that isentropic viscous shock profiles are generically unstable in the high-Mach number limit, both in the linear and nonlinear regimes. We show that the instability arises from a destabilizing effect of the viscous dissipation, which leads to the formation of vortices and shear layers inside the shock structure. Our findings have important implications for the design and optimization of high-speed engineering systems, and they suggest that additional measures, such as active flow control, may be needed to enhance the stability and performance of isentropic viscous shocks.

Our research investigated the gamma rays emanating from the galactic center, and aimed to understand their source and properties. The motivation behind this study is to gain insight into the high-energy processes within the Milky Way's central region. This study is based on data obtained from the Large Area Telescope (LAT) on board the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope, which has been observing the sky at high energies since its launch in 2008.

Our results reveal a complex gamma-ray source structure with contributions from both point-like and extended sources. We found that the spectral properties of the sources are consistent with the emission from a population of rapidly spinning neutron stars known as pulsars. We discovered the presence of several new sources, highlighting the importance of characterizing the gamma-ray sky at high energies.

This work presents a significant step towards understanding the nature of the gamma-ray sources in the galactic center region. Our findings provide valuable information on the high-energy processes in the central region of the Milky Way and have important implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of massive black holes. Further study of these gamma-ray sources is critical in comprehending the fundamental properties of the universe.

In this study, we present the discovery of a planetary system around HD 155358, the lowest metallicity planet host star ever found. Metallicity is a crucial parameter for planet formation and evolution, and studying planets around low-metallicity stars provides a unique opportunity to probe the role of metallicity in planetary systems. 

Our goal in this research is to understand the formation and evolution of planets in low-metallicity environments and explore how the properties of such planets differ from those orbiting more metal-rich stars. We used the radial velocity method to detect two planets around HD 155358 with masses of approximately 1.3 and 2.3 times that of Jupiter and orbits with periods of about 33 and 133 days, respectively. The orbital parameters of the two planets reveal a dynamically stable system and suggest that they formed further out and migrated inward as the protoplanetary disk dissipated.

The discovery of this planetary system adds to the growing collection of planets orbiting low-metallicity stars and provides an opportunity to investigate the role of metallicity in planet formation and evolution. Our study demonstrates that low-metallicity environments can also host planetary systems with diverse characteristics and highlights the importance of exploring different planetary systems to understand the overall picture of planet formation and evolution.

In this work, we investigate the structure of phylogenetic mixtures, a type of tree that incorporates multiple phylogenetic models into a single structure. The problem we attempt to solve arises from the need to combine trees from different sources and infer a consensus tree. This is a common task in evolutionary biology, where multiple phylogenetic trees are often used to represent different aspects of the same evolutionary history. However, these trees may differ in their underlying assumptions, and constructing a consensus tree that captures all relevant information can be challenging.

We introduce a formal definition of phylogenetic mixtures and develop algorithms to analyze their structure. Our results show that mixtures can be decomposed into a set of core trees, each representing a distinct set of shared relationships among the taxa. We also demonstrate how this decomposition can be used to construct consensus trees that capture all relevant information from the input trees.

Our motivation for this research stems from the need to better understand the structure of phylogenetic mixtures and develop methods for analyzing them. We believe that our results will be of interest to biologists working in fields such as systematics, phylogenetics, and evolutionary biology, as well as to computer scientists interested in algorithms for tree processing and analysis. Overall, our work provides a new perspective on the problem of combining phylogenetic trees and offers a promising direction for further research.

In this study, we propose a yield design formulation for porous media under the effect of flow, using an approximate pressure field. The motivation for this research is to understand the complex behaviour of porous materials, such as soils and rocks, under the influence of water movement. This understanding is crucial for various engineering applications, including environmental protection, geotechnical engineering, and petroleum engineering.

The methodology involves a kinematic approach to yield design, which considers the deformation of the porous medium under different flow conditions. We use the concept of "equivalent strain" to describe deformation in a more practical manner than traditional plasticity theory. We also introduce an approximate pressure field to account for the influence of pore pressure on the deformation.

Our results show that the proposed methodology accurately captures the behaviour of porous media under different flow conditions. The key ideas of the study include the identification of the dominant mechanism of deformation during yield, the calculation of the effective stresses, and the incorporation of an approximate pressure field to capture the effect of pore pressure.

In conclusion, the proposed yield design formulation under flow provides a more accurate and practical understanding of the behaviour of porous media. The study highlights the importance of considering the effect of pore pressure in geotechnical analysis and design.

In our study titled "Theory of Macroscopic Quantum Tunneling in High-T_c c-Axis Josephson Junctions," we investigated the phenomenon of macroscopic quantum tunneling in high-T_c superconducting c-axis Josephson junctions. Our primary objective was to develop a theoretical understanding of this process and its dependence on various environmental factors such as temperature and applied magnetic field.

Our research employed the concept of the phase difference between the superconducting wave functions present on either side of the junction. We derived analytical expressions for the tunneling current and explored the effects of applied magnetic fields on the escape rate of the superconducting phase difference.

Our results show that when the temperature and magnetic field were very low, the macroscopic quantum tunneling of the phase difference increased by several orders of magnitude. We also discovered that the tunneling process can be enhanced or suppressed based on the parameters used, indicating that external factors can control the tunneling of the phase difference.

Overall, our study provides an understanding of the tunneling mechanism in high-T_c c-axis Josephson junctions that can aid in the development of future quantum computing technologies. We hope that our research provides valuable insights into this exciting field that can be useful for further investigation.

In this study, we aim to extend the concepts of coherence and phase synchronization to pairs of multivariate time series while simultaneously eliminating the zero-lag contributions. Our motivation for this research is to develop a method that can efficiently identify and quantify the synchronization between multiple time series, which is an essential task in numerous scientific domains, ranging from neuroscience to climate science. We propose a new measure called Generalized Coherence Phase Synchronization (GCPS) that estimates the coherence and phase synchronization between each pair of multivariate time series without the need for pairwise comparisons. GCPS provides a comprehensive measure of the degree of coherence and phase synchronization between multiple time series with desired statistical properties and is not susceptible to the spurious synchronization that often occurs at zero lag times. 

We validate GCPS on simulated datasets, showing its superiority over established methods in multivariate synchronization analysis. Furthermore, we apply GCPS on real-world EEG data and demonstrate the detection of previously confirmed synchronization patterns. Overall, our results indicate that GCPS is a promising tool for studying synchronization between multivariate time series in diverse fields.

In this work, we present the results of a multi-transition molecular line study of 10 candidate massive young stellar objects (MYSOs) associated with methanol masers. The observations were carried out using the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) in the 3 mm and 7 mm wavelength ranges. The main goal of this study is to constrain the physical properties of the MYSOs and investigate the kinematics of the gas surrounding them.

We detected a total of 32 molecular transitions, including high-excitation lines of HCN, HCO+, and CH3CN, which allowed us to estimate the gas temperature and density, as well as to investigate the chemistry and dynamical structure of the sources. We found that the majority of our sources are likely to be massive and young, with gas densities on the order of 10^6 cm^-3 and kinetic temperatures around 50 - 100 K. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the molecular emission from the MYSOs is dominated by dense and compact gas structures, indicative of ongoing accretion.

The methodology employed in this study involves using multiple transitions to model the physical conditions of the molecular gas surrounding MYSOs. This analysis allowed us to constrain the properties of the sources, including their masses and ages, and to reveal the kinematics of the gas surrounding them. Our work provides critical insights into the earliest stages of massive star formation and reinforces the importance of methanol masers as signposts for these objects.

In this work, we investigate the dynamics of localization phenomena for hardcore bosons in optical lattices. We study the behavior of these systems under the effect of disorder and an external potential and examine how the interplay between these two factors affects the localization properties of the bosons.

Our methodology involves the use of analytical and numerical techniques to investigate the properties of the hardcore bosons in the optical lattices. We explore the phase diagrams of the system and identify the critical points where the localization phenomena occur. Furthermore, we utilize the concept of entanglement entropy to characterize the properties of the states and examine how entanglement properties evolve in the presence of disorder.

The motivation for this research stems from the recent advancements in the experimental techniques for controlling and manipulating ultracold atoms in optical lattices. In particular, we are interested in understanding the properties of hardcore bosons, which are a model system for the strong interactions between particles.

The problem this work attempts to solve is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the localization phenomena for hardcore bosons in optical lattices under the effect of external potential and disorder. This study may have implications for the design and control of quantum systems and may contribute to the development of new technologies based on ultracold atoms.

In our work, we investigate the quantum spin liquid states in the two-dimensional kagome antiferromagnets, ZnxCu4-x(OD)6Cl2. The kagome lattice is a highly debated system in condensed matter physics, which is gaining prominence due to its interesting and complex behavior. Kagome antiferromagnets have been previously shown to possess strong frustration, leading to various exotic states of matter. Our aim is to study the quantum spin liquid behavior in these materials as we believe that this can help us gain a better understanding of the underlying physics of the system.

Our research has been motivated by the fact that despite extensive studies on kagome antiferromagnets, the nature of the ground state and the possible existence of a quantum spin liquid state remain elusive. We utilized neutron scattering measurements and performed extensive theoretical analysis, which helped us to unveil various features of these materials' quantum behavior. We discovered that we had observed the most conclusive evidence of a quantum spin liquid in ZnxCu4-x(OD)6Cl2 compounds to date.

Our results show that there is a profound and exciting relationship between the magnetic properties and structural changes in these materials. This research marks a significant step towards further understanding quantum spin liquids and their associated behavior in highly complex systems. The insights offered by our work are likely to play a vital role in the development of future spin-based technologies, with possible applications in quantum computing.

In this study, we investigate the impact of trehalose, maltose, and sucrose on the structural and dynamical properties of lysozyme using molecular dynamics simulations. The objective of the research is to gain insight into how these three disaccharides interact with lysozyme, a well-known antibacterial enzyme. The study aims to contribute to a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the stabilization effects of disaccharides on proteins.

We used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to study lysozyme in the presence of trehalose, maltose, and sucrose molecules. The conformational stability, hydrogen bonding pattern, and flexibility of lysozyme were analyzed in the presence and absence of the three disaccharides.

Our results show that trehalose and sucrose form stronger hydrogen bonds with lysozyme than maltose. Additionally, the presence of trehalose and sucrose increases the conformational stability of lysozyme, while the flexibility of lysozyme decreases. On the other hand, maltose does not affect the structural stability of lysozyme, indicating a weaker interaction.

Our findings provide valuable insights into the stabilizing effects of trehalose, maltose, and sucrose on lysozyme and how they potentially enhance protein stability. This research can serve as a basis for designing novel protein stabilizers and therapeutic agents that exploit the stabilizing effects of disaccharides on biomolecules.

In this work, we investigate the two-stage inflationary scenario that arises when considering hybrid inflation followed by modular inflation. The main motivation behind our research is to provide a consistent and comprehensive framework, in line with current observational data, for the early universe. To achieve this goal, we consider how these two inflationary models can naturally arise in the context of string theory and analyze their combination in detail.

We employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods to study the dynamics of our model in the presence of a non-minimal coupling to gravity. In particular, we focus on the generation of primordial gravitational waves, which remains a crucial probe of the inflationary epoch.

Our results demonstrate that our hybrid-modular inflationary scenario can potentially reproduce the current observational constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio and other cosmological parameters. We find that such a scenario can leave detectable signatures in the cosmic microwave background, which could be measured in future experiments.

Overall, we propose a novel approach to inflationary cosmology that can provide a unified and consistent picture of the early universe, bridging the gap between different inflationary models and their connection to underlying fundamental physics.

In this work, we investigate a massive, filamentary structure at redshift z=0.55 and the star formation histories of galaxies at lower redshifts. We employed the data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to identify and study the filamentary structure, measuring its mass and luminosity through the use of spectral analysis tools. Additionally, we analyzed the star formation histories of galaxies at redshifts below z=1, using data from the Cosmic Assembly Near-infrared Deep Extragalactic Legacy Survey. We applied a Bayesian spectral fitting methodology to derive the star formation rates of these galaxies.

The motivation for this research stems from the desire to better understand the large-scale structure of the universe and the processes driving galaxy evolution. The filamentary structure we studied is of particular interest, as it is among the most massive known structures in the universe. Additionally, investigating the star formation histories of galaxies can provide insights into the mechanisms that drive the formation of new stars in galaxies.

The problem we aim to address in this work is to broaden our understanding of the physical processes that shape the formation and evolution of galaxies. By studying these massive structures and the star formation histories of galaxies, we can gain insights into the interactions between galaxies and their environment, the role of gas accretion in galaxy formation, and the influence of mergers and collisions on the evolution of galaxies. Overall, this work contributes to our knowledge about the formation and evolution of galaxies and the structure of the universe at large.

In this research, we analyze the presence of compact starbursts in the central regions of Seyfert galaxies. These active galactic nuclei emit intense radiation caused by accretion of matter onto a supermassive black hole. However, the mechanisms responsible for their star formation activity are still not fully understood. Our motivation for this study was to investigate the possible role of compact starbursts in enhancing the star formation rate in these regions. To achieve this, we used a multi-wavelength approach, combining optical, near-infrared, and radio data from different surveys. We analyzed the spectral energy distributions and the morphology of the galaxies, and identified a sample of Seyfert galaxies with significant compact starburst activity. Our results reveal that these starbursts are contributing significantly to the total star formation rate in the central regions of Seyfert galaxies. Moreover, we find that the star formation efficiency is higher in galaxies with stronger nuclear radiation, suggesting a tight relation between the starburst and active galactic nucleus activity. Overall, our study provides new insights into the complex interplay between nuclear activity and star formation in Seyfert galaxies.

In this study, we investigated the Critical Casimir Effect (CCE) in superfluid wetting films. We aimed to understand how the confinement of superfluids influences the CCE, which is an important phenomenon that arises near critical points in fluids. To achieve this, we used Monte Carlo simulations to analyse the behaviour of superfluid films near a wetting transition point. Our results show that the critical behaviour of the CCE strongly depends on the thickness of the film and the properties of the wall confining the fluid. We found that thicker films exhibit a stronger influence of the wall confinement on the CCE, and that this confinement effect dominates over the effects of long-range forces in the vicinity of the critical point. Our findings highlight the complexity of the interplay between confinement and critical phenomena in superfluid films, and provide insight into the fundamental mechanisms underlying the CCE. This research contributes to a broader understanding of critical phenomena in confined systems, and could have important applications in the design of novel materials and devices.

In this work, we investigate the theory of norm and numerical peak holomorphic functions on Banach spaces. The research seeks to extend the existing theory in the domain of complex analysis by analyzing two classes of holomorphic functions. The central problem this work attempts to solve is the characterization of the structure of the set of norm and numerical peak functions for a given Banach space. 

Our results show that the set of norm peak functions is always convex and has an extreme point which is a norm peak function that cannot be written as the convex linear combination of any other norm peak functions. We also establish that the set of numerical peak functions is pre-compact, and if the space has a Schauder basis, then the numerical peak functions are dense in the space of holomorphic functions. 

The work furthers the understanding of peak functions on Banach spaces, and represents a step towards understanding peak theory in the broad setting of infinite-dimensional complex analysis. We are motivated by the desire to extend the reach of peak theory by exploring the intrinsic connection between peak sets and the theory of Banach spaces. The results of this paper may have important implications for the study of holomorphic functions on infinite-dimensional spaces in fields such as functional analysis, harmonic analysis, and operator theory.

In this work, we investigate the scaling laws governing the angular momentum transport in accretion disks driven by MRI-induced turbulence. We hypothesize that the relationship between the accretion stresses and the turbulent magnetic fields should follow a universal power law that can be expressed by a single scaling parameter. To test our hypothesis, we use numerical simulations of turbulent accretion disks and measure the accretion stress and the turbulent magnetic field strength at different radii. Our simulations cover a wide range of disk parameters, including various levels of turbulence, magnetic field strengths, and disk densities.

Our results indicate that the angular momentum transport efficiency in MRI-driven turbulence can indeed be characterized by a single scaling parameter. We find that the scaling parameter is related to the ratio of the thermal and magnetic pressures in the disk, as well as the strength of the MRI-induced turbulence. Interestingly, we also find that the scaling parameter is remarkably robust and insensitive to the details of the numerical simulations.

The motivation for this research stems from the importance of understanding the physical processes that govern accretion disks, which are key components in a wide range of astrophysical systems, including protoplanetary disks, active galactic nuclei, and X-ray binaries. By elucidating the scaling laws of angular momentum transport in these disks, we hope to contribute to a better understanding of their dynamics and evolution. In particular, our work sheds light on the relationship between the magnetic fields and the turbulence in accretion disks, which is a crucial factor in determining the accretion rate and the energy output of these systems.

In our work, we explore the new functionalities of microlasers and optoelectronic components through the creation and study of photonic molecules made of matched and mismatched microcavities. Our motivation lies in the potential to achieve enhanced control over light-matter interactions, leading to greater design flexibility and increased device performance. 

Our approach involves using semiconductor-based microlasers and microcavities, with a variety of shapes and sizes, to construct larger structures with novel optical properties. By carefully controlling the spacing and coupling between the individual microcavities, we form photonic molecules that exhibit novel resonance effects, including anticrossing and supermode splitting. 

Through experimental and theoretical analysis, we aim to understand the underlying physics of these new structures and the mechanisms that give rise to their unique optical behavior. Furthermore, we investigate the potential applications of these photonic molecules, such as ultra-compact sensors, integrated photonic circuits, and advanced optical signal processing. 

Our work represents a significant step towards the development of highly functional and efficient optoelectronic devices, with potential uses ranging from telecommunications to medical imaging. By leveraging the power of photonic molecules, we unlock new possibilities for manipulating light at the nanoscale.

In our research, we explore the wave mechanics of photons and analyze the position eigenvectors. Our work is motivated by the need to understand the fundamental characteristics of quantum mechanics and improve our understanding of photon behavior. Our research focuses on addressing a key problem in photon wave mechanics, which involves the limitations of existing models in describing photon behavior in complex systems.

Our work attempts to solve this problem through the development of a novel approach that uses position eigenvectors to model the behavior of photons. Our approach is based on the premise that a photon can be described as a wave packet that contains position information. Furthermore, we integrate this position information with quantum mechanics principles to model the behavior of photons in complex systems.

Our key ideas and methodology involve the development of a mathematical framework for describing photon behavior using position eigenvectors. Our approach makes use of Schrödinger's equation to model the behavior of photons in complex systems, and we test our approach using computer simulations. Our findings suggest that our approach is more accurate and provides a better understanding of photon behavior than existing models. Overall, our work has important implications for the development of more advanced technologies that rely on photon behavior, such as quantum computing and communication systems.

In this work, we present a local approximation approach to solve the problem of superconductivity in a magnetic field. Superconductivity is a phenomenon in which a material exhibits zero electrical resistance and perfect diamagnetism, and it is suppressed in a magnetic field. The problem we seek to solve is to understand the behavior of superconductivity in the presence of a magnetic field, taking into account the local variations of the field.

Our key idea is to use the Ginzburg-Landau theory to describe the superconductor, and to treat the magnetic field as a perturbation around the superconductor. We then develop a local approximation approach to solve the Ginzburg-Landau equations in the presence of the magnetic field, taking into account the local variations of the field.

We apply our approach to different configurations of the magnetic field, including uniform and non-uniform fields. Our results show that the superconducting properties of the material depend critically on the local variations of the magnetic field. We also find that the local approximation approach is computationally efficient, making it a promising tool to study superconductivity under more complex magnetic fields.

In conclusion, our work presents a new approach to study superconductivity in a magnetic field, taking into account the local variations of the field. Our results shed new light on the behavior of superconducting materials under different magnetic field configurations, and pave the way for future studies in this exciting field.

In our work titled "CP Violation From Standard Model to Strings", we delve deep into the concept of CP violation and their origins in the Standard Model of particle physics. The motivation behind our research stems from the fact that CP violation is crucial in understanding the asymmetry between matter and antimatter in the universe. The study of CP violation has been a significant topic of research since its initial discovery in the 60s, and it continues to remain a crucial issue in particle physics. Our research aims to provide a comprehensive overview of CP violation and the role it plays in the Standard Model of particle physics. 

We present a detailed analysis of several theoretical models, including the Kobayashi-Maskawa theory, which explains CP violation in the weak interaction of elementary particles. Additionally, we explore the possibility of explaining CP violation through string theory, which offers a broader framework of theoretical models. We have obtained several results that provide a new perspective on the origins and mechanisms of CP violation. Our work highlights the importance of exploring various theoretical models to understand the fundamental aspects of the universe. The methodology we employed involves a detailed analysis of existing literature and theoretical models to present a comprehensive overview of CP violation and its mechanisms. Our work contributes to the ongoing efforts in the field of particle physics in understanding the fundamental nature of the universe.

In this work, we present the results of millimeter and radio observations of four z~6 quasars, J1148+5251, J1048+4637, J2315+0304, and J0338+0021. These observations were carried out using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) to study the properties of the quasar host galaxies and their environments. 
Our motivation for this research was to investigate the properties of the early Universe, particularly during the epoch of reionization. Quasars are believed to be powered by supermassive black holes and can provide clues about the physical conditions of the early Universe. The millimeter observations allowed us to study the cold gas reservoirs in the host galaxies, while the radio observations provided information on the radio jets and the interstellar medium of the surrounding environment. 
We found that all four quasars had prominent dust emission, particularly J1148+5251 which showed a clumpy disk-like structure. We also detected radio emission from all four quasars, which suggests the presence of powerful radio jets. Our results provide new insights into the formation and evolution of quasars in the early Universe and contribute to our understanding of the epoch of reionization.

In this study, we investigate the outer disk of the Triangulum Spiral Galaxy M33 using Keck spectroscopy and Spitzer Space Telescope data. Our motivation for this research is to gain a better understanding of the properties of the outer regions of spiral galaxies, which are important for determining the formation and evolution of galaxies. We aim to analyze the structure and composition of M33's outer disk in order to shed light on its kinematics and star formation history.

Our analysis reveals that the outer disk of M33 exhibits a clear rotation pattern, which is consistent with previous studies. However, we also found evidence of a warp in the disk, which suggests that the outer disk may have been influenced by interactions with neighboring galaxies. By analyzing the star formation history of the outer disk, we found that it has been forming stars at a relatively constant rate over the past 2 billion years. Additionally, we identified several regions of enhanced star formation activity, which may indicate the presence of gas-rich regions within the outer disk.

Our methodology involved using Keck spectroscopy to obtain kinematic data, and Spitzer Space Telescope data to provide information on the stellar populations and dust extinction in the outer disk. Our results provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics and star formation history of M33's outer disk, which may have implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of spiral galaxies as a whole.

In this work, we introduce a novel methodology for decoding the top flavor violation (TFV) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) with B factories. TFV is a rare phenomenon in the standard model of particle physics and can only occur through the exchange of a Higgs boson. Its detection will provide insights into the Higgs sector and potential extensions to the standard model. However, its rarity makes its detection challenging, which is why the LHC and B factories are used together to increase the chances of detection.

Our methodology is based on combining the differential decay rates of top quarks with heavy quarks at the LHC and B factories. Using a kinematic analysis, we show that this approach increases sensitivity to TFV processes and reduces uncertainties. Our methodology provides a powerful tool for discriminating between different models of new physics that predict TFV, such as two-Higgs-doublet models and models with extra dimensions.

The motivation behind this research is to identify new physics beyond the standard model and to shed light on the Higgs sector. The successful detection of TFV will provide clear evidence of new physics, and our methodology will enable researchers to make more precise predictions and distinguish between different models. This work represents a significant step forward in our understanding of the standard model, and we believe it will have important implications for future high-energy physics experiments.

We present the second part of our work on multidimensional supernova simulations with approximative neutrino transport. In this study, we focus on the role of convection and the advective-acoustic cycle in the supernova core. Our main motivation is to investigate the impact of these physical processes on the supernova explosion mechanism and compare the results with previous studies. 

To achieve this goal, we have developed a state-of-the-art hydrodynamic code that includes approximative neutrino transport and simulates the dynamics of the supernova core in two and three dimensions. We use a realistic equation of state, neutrino heating and cooling, and a roughly parameterized neutrino transport scheme. We perform a series of simulations varying the initial conditions and the assumptions of the transport scheme to explore the range of possible outcomes. 

Our main result is that the convection and the advection-acoustic cycle, which are triggered by the neutrino-driven convection instability, play a crucial role in the development of the supernova explosion. In particular, the advection of nuclear burning products by convective motions and their subsequent combustion enhances the neutrino heating and triggers the explosion. Moreover, the acoustic waves generated by the interaction of the convective motions and the shock wave modify the shock structure and influence the spectrum of neutrinos emitted from the core. Our simulations provide a comprehensive picture of these processes and offer insights into the complex mechanisms that govern the supernova explosion.

In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the transfer matrix of superintegrable Chiral Potts Model (CPM) and its relation with the Q-operator of Root-of-unity XXZ chain with cyclic representation of $U_q(sl_2)$. The key idea behind the work is to establish the equivalence between these two seemingly different mathematical objects, thereby providing an alternative and more simplified approach to analyzing the CPM. 

Our methodology involves a detailed investigation of the algebraic structures of these two models, followed by a comparison of their defining properties. We derive an explicit expression for the transfer matrix of the CPM in terms of the Q-operator and establish the equivalence between their spectra and eigenfunctions. Our work thus sheds light on the underlying mathematical unity between the CPM and the XXZ chain with cyclic representation of $U_q(sl_2)$.

The results of our study are significant, as they provide a deeper understanding of the CPM and its properties. Our findings also shed light on the broader field of integrable models and quantum integrability. The motivation for this research is to further advance the understanding of theoretical physics and to uncover new insights into the interplay between distinct mathematical models. Overall, our approach contributes towards a more unified and comprehensive view of integrable models in theoretical physics.

In this work, we report on the properties of a one-dimensional quantum dot containing a deformed Wigner crystal. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the interplay between Coulomb repulsion, confinement, and the geometrical asymmetry of a quantum dot. The motivation for this research stems from the complexity of analyzing properties of a Wigner crystal in a confined environment. Our work aims to address this issue by introducing deformations in the shape of the quantum dot.

To accomplish this, we solved the Schrodinger equation via numerical integration for various geometrical parameters. Our findings show that when the confinement potential is modeled as a harmonic potential, the dot remains symmetric. However, as the potential deviations increase, the dot takes on a deformed shape, and consequently, changes the electronic properties of the dot. Furthermore, we also observed an unconventional splitting of the lowest-energy state in the deformed dot, indicating a quantum phase transition.

In conclusion, our work provides insights into the behavior of deformed Wigner crystals in a confined quantum dot. Our methodology outlines a general approach for analyzing this intricate system. The findings of our research have strong implications for unconventional computing models and quantum phase transitions in low-dimensional systems.

In this paper, we present Dynamical Masses for Pre-Main Sequence Stars: A Preliminary Physical Orbit for V773 Tau A, with the aim of addressing the discrepancies existing in the current literature on the masses of pre-main sequence (PMS) stars. The problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of reliable mass estimates for these stars, which are essential for understanding their evolution and formation. The motivation for this research stems from the need to improve the accuracy of these estimates, which is currently limited by uncertainties in the various methods used to derive them. 

To accomplish this goal, we analyzed high-resolution astrometric and spectroscopic observations of the V773 Tau A binary system. Using the OrbFit software and a Monte Carlo approach, we derived the dynamical masses of the stars, which are independent of assumptions on the age, composition, or binarity of the system. Our results show that the primary star has a mass of 1.22+/-0.11 solar masses, while the secondary star has a mass of 0.36+/-0.03 solar masses. 

These values are consistent with previous estimates based on evolutionary models, but with smaller uncertainties. Furthermore, our analysis allowed us to establish the orbit parameters and improve the knowledge of the system parameters, contributing to a better understanding of PMS star formation and evolution. Our preliminary physical orbit for V773 Tau A provides a benchmark for future studies on PMS stars and their properties.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for temporal runtime verification using Monadic Difference Logic (MDL). Our approach offers a solution for verifying temporal properties of software systems in real-time, by utilizing the power of MDL to reason about the changes between consecutive system states.

The key idea behind our approach is to model temporal properties of a system as constraints in MDL, which is a powerful formal language for expressing and reasoning about changes between system states. We further develop an algorithmic framework for checking the satisfaction of these constraints in real-time, by transforming MDL formulas into Boolean formulas and optimizing the verification process using SAT/SMT solvers.

The results of our experimental evaluation demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of our approach for temporal runtime verification, with significant speedups compared to other state-of-the-art approaches. We also provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the computational complexity of our approach, proving its polynomial-time complexity in most cases.

Our work addresses the problem of verifying temporal properties of software systems in real-time, which is critical for ensuring the correctness and reliability of modern software systems. Our approach offers a promising solution for this problem, with formal correctness guarantees and efficient execution times.

In this paper, we explore the geometry of parallelizable manifolds in the context of generalized Lagrange spaces. The motivation for the research arises from the need to understand the interplay between parallelizable manifolds and the symplectic geometry of Lagrange spaces. The study of parallelizable manifolds has applications in many fields, including physics and engineering.

We develop a methodology that exploits the structure of generalized Lagrange spaces to study parallelizable manifolds. In particular, we show that the existence of certain specific forms on the Lagrange spaces yields additional constraints on the geometry of parallelizable manifolds. Using this methodology, we prove new and interesting results about the geometry of parallelizable manifolds, including the existence of a canonical almost complex structure and the non-existence of certain classes of parallelizable manifolds.

Our approach is rigorously mathematical and makes use of various tools from differential geometry and symplectic geometry. Our results extend and generalize existing results in the field, making contributions to the theory of parallelizable manifolds and of generalized Lagrange spaces.

Overall, our work sheds new light on the interplay between parallelizable manifolds and symplectic geometry, and provides a foundation for future studies in this area.

In this study, we investigate X-ray flares in low mass stars located in the Orion star-forming region. Our primary motivation is to better understand the complex physics behind these powerful events and their impact on the surrounding environment. X-ray flares are intense bursts of high energy radiation that only occur in stars with magnetic activity. These bursts can have a significant impact on both the star's own atmosphere and any nearby planetary systems. 

The problem we attempt to solve in this study is to establish the correlation between X-ray emission and stellar activity, as well as to understand the underlying mechanisms behind the X-ray flares in low mass stars. To achieve this goal, we analyze data collected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and match it with optical and infrared observations made with ground-based telescopes. 

Our results show that X-ray flares occur much more frequently in low mass stars than previously thought. Additionally, we found a positive correlation between the X-ray brightness and the magnitude of the optical or infrared emission. This indicates that the X-ray flares arise from the same magnetic activity that causes the visible light from the star. Our findings suggest that X-ray flares are a common occurrence in low mass stars and may play an important role in shaping planetary systems. These results offer significant insights into the magnetic activity of stars and their impacts on their surrounding environments.

In this paper, we present our investigation on the role of GRB 031203 in clarifying the astrophysical scenario of Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs). We used a comprehensive approach combining observational data, data analysis techniques and modeling to address key issues surrounding this celestial event. Our results show that GRB 031203 is a unique discovery that has given us vital information about the nature of GRBs and their associated phenomena. We demonstrate that the spectral index of this GRB is consistent with the curvature effect model providing further validation of this physical model of Gamma Ray Bursts. 

Additionally, our study provides evidence that the X-ray radiation from this event supports the importance of reverse shock emission in the overall emission mechanism of GRBs. Crucially, we highlight the potential of GRB 031203 as a diagnostic tool for studying the structure of the progenitor star and binary system. Our work seeks to address persistent scientific concerns around the nature of GRBs, their environment, and their association with astrophysical systems. This study lays a solid foundation for further research that can provide more insight into the complex phenomenon of GRBs.

In this paper, we propose a novel spacetime concept to describe the electronic motion within a helium atom. The problem we attempt to solve is the limitation of the traditional quantum mechanics frameworks in explaining the complex behavior of atomic systems. The key idea of our approach is to introduce a geometric interpretation of the electron's motion that unifies time and space dimensions and provides a rigorous understanding of the electron's path and momentum.

Our methodology is based on a modified version of the Schrödinger equation that introduces a new variable, the velocity vector, to the time-dependent wavefunction. This approach allows for the determination of the electron's position and velocity at any given time and provides a more complete and dynamic picture of the system's behavior.

The results obtained from our analysis indicate a significant improvement in the accuracy and reliability of atomic models. Our new framework provides a consistent and intuitive interpretation of the electron's behavior and allows for more precise predictions of atomic properties and behavior. Moreover, the introduction of the velocity vector concept offers a new perspective on particle-wave duality and represents an important step towards a more unified description of matter and energy.

In conclusion, our novel spacetime concept represents a significant contribution to the field of atomic physics and paves the way for further advancements in the understanding of complex physical phenomena.

In this work, we aim to gauge the hidden symmetries in two-dimensional systems. The problem we attempt to solve is to reveal previously unobserved symmetries in physical systems by introducing a new method of analysis. Our approach utilizes the concept of topological invariants, which are measures of symmetry that are insensitive to local changes in the system. These invariants allow us to identify the presence of hidden symmetries that may not be readily apparent in the system's physical properties.

Through our research, we have developed a new algorithm that can calculate topological invariants without requiring detailed knowledge of the system's properties. Using this algorithm, we have been able to demonstrate the presence of additional symmetries in a wide range of systems, including electronic wave functions, geometric patterns, and biological systems.

Our research is motivated by the desire to gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental principles that underlie the behavior of complex systems. By uncovering hidden symmetries, we aim to shed light on the underlying structure of these systems and open up new avenues for scientific inquiry. In addition, our work has practical applications in fields such as materials science, where the discovery of new symmetries can lead to the development of novel materials with unique properties.

In this study, we present a photoionization model that can accurately predict the soft X-ray spectrum of the Seyfert 1 galaxy NGC 4151. The difficulty in modeling this spectrum arises from the presence of complex atomic structures that yield multiple lines and absorption edges. Furthermore, the X-ray emission from this galaxy is thought to originate from various physical regions, including the active galactic nucleus (AGN) and the surrounding warm absorber. We aim to develop a model that can simultaneously reproduce the observed spectrum and provide insights into the physical properties of these regions.

Our key idea is to use the photoionization code CLOUDY to simulate the ionization state and emission properties of the gas surrounding the AGN. The model includes parameters such as the density, column density, and ionization parameter of the gas. Additionally, we introduce a second absorber to account for the X-ray emission from the warm absorber.

Our results indicate that our model can accurately reproduce the observed spectrum of NGC 4151. The inclusion of the warm absorber leads to a better fit of some of the absorption edges in the spectrum. Additionally, we find that the absorber has a column density of ~10^22 cm^-2, which is consistent with previous estimates. Our model provides a useful tool for studying the physical properties of AGNs and their surrounding gas.
