We leverage the coding gain from the adaptive refinement process to improve the performance while reducing the requirements for the channel coding resources. By applying Gaussian Layered Broadcast Coding to the channel coding, we encode information in multiple layers, where each receiver extracts the maximum number of layers possible with their channel quality.

Our work aims to address the problem of distortion caused by channel heterogeneity in conventional broadcast coding and provide a practical solution to minimize it. The proposed method achieves significant reduction in the distortion with the same transmission power and time, compared to other state-of-the-art approaches. Our contributions offer significant potential for practical improvements in wireless communication systems.

In this work, we investigate the way in which language networks interact and influence the creative process in the production of a language learning resource. Our motivation for this research stems from the desire to understand how creativity can be facilitated through networks, and how these networks can be enhanced to facilitate creativity. At the core of our inquiry is the production of Mykyta the Fox, which was created as a comic book language resource for young adults. We examine the key ideas that contribute to the design strategy of the comic book and reveal the relationship between effective language teaching and the creative process in Mykyta the Fox.

The methodology employed in this study allowed us to identify the main features of the language network that contributed to the success of the comic. This methodology combined network analysis and corpus linguistics to explore the patterns of dialogue between the characters in the story. It enabled us to examine the interconnectedness of dialogue and the way in which this interaction led to the production of complex and engaging language structures.

Our findings suggest that by introducing a network of creative professionals, such as writers and illustrators, into the language learning resource development process, we can enhance the creativity of the resource and improve its efficacy. Moreover, our approach highlights how network analysis can be used to explore the relationship between language use and creativity, opening up new avenues of research in the field of language acquisition and creative processing.

In this paper, we present Truecluster matching, a novel approach to estimate similarity among high-dimensional datasets, particularly those with structure and clustering patterns. Our method is based on a clustering-based distance metric that can detect similarities and dissimilarities between two datasets more efficiently and accurately than traditional methods. We propose a novel mapping procedure that aligns the two datasets based on their true structure, resulting in a more accurate similarity estimate among them. We test our method on various synthetic and real-world datasets, including gene expressions and image datasets, and compare it with other state-of-the-art methods. Our results show that Truecluster matching can achieve better performance in estimating similarity and detecting clustering patterns among datasets, particularly when the datasets have overlapping or noisy features and structures. 

Our motivation for this research is to improve the accuracy and efficiency of matching high-dimensional datasets and to provide more reliable tools for analyzing complex and large-scale data. Our contribution is to propose a novel clustering-based distance metric and mapping procedure that can capture the true structure of datasets and align them more accurately. We believe that Truecluster matching can have a wide range of applications in data mining, pattern recognition, image analysis, and bioinformatics. Our future work will focus on extending our method to handle more complex and diverse data types and exploring its potential applications in various domains.

In this study, we present the results of our investigation on the outflows associated with young stellar objects (YSOs) in the Perseus molecular cloud complex. Our main motivation for this research is to understand the role of outflows in the star formation process, which is still not well understood. We used data from the Submillimeter Array (SMA) and the Combined Array for Millimeter-wave Astronomy (CARMA) to map the CO(2-1) emission of the outflows and the 1.3 mm continuum emission of the YSOs, respectively. 

We detected 39 outflows associated with 31 YSOs. The outflow properties such as outflow mass, momentum, and kinetic energy show a correlation with the YSO properties such as mass and luminosity, indicating that the outflows are intimately related to the YSOs' accretion processes. Additionally, the outflow orientations show a preferential alignment with the magnetic field, suggesting that the magnetic field plays a crucial role in shaping the outflows. We also found evidence of multiple outflows associated with some YSOs and complex outflow geometries, which highlights the complex nature of the star formation process. Our study contributes to the growing body of literature on outflows and their role in the star formation process and emphasizes the need for multi-wavelength and multi-tracer observations to fully understand the complexities of star formation.

In this work, we present new methods for determining the mass loss rates of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars based on radio data. AGB stars are crucial in the chemical enrichment of galaxies, and determining their mass loss rates is essential for understanding their evolution. However, accurately determining these rates has proven to be challenging due to the complex nature of AGB winds. 

We propose two new methods based on radio observations: the first uses spectral indices to estimate mass loss rates, while the second utilizes radio light curves to directly measure the mass loss rates. We validate our methods using observational data of AGB stars. Our results demonstrate the feasibility and accuracy of these methods, providing a valuable tool for future studies of AGB stars and their winds. 

Our work seeks to address the challenge of accurately determining mass loss rates of AGB stars. Our proposed methods are innovative and add to the current techniques used in the field. We believe that our methods can be used in conjunction with existing methods to further constrain the mass loss rates of AGB stars. This work showcases the potential of radio observations in improving our understanding of AGB stars, and we hope it will inspire future work in this area.

In this work, we present a comprehensive catalog of Swift Gamma Ray Burst (GRB) spectra and durations gathered from a carefully selected sample of GRBs observed by Swift satellite. Our aim is to address the long-standing debate in the community regarding the physical origin of pre-Swift high-energy correlations. Traditionally, researchers believed that the gamma-ray emission came from the internal shocks produced by a relativistic jet expanding to larger and larger radii, until the scatterers were no longer tightly coupled through magnetic fields. This leads to a prediction of strong correlations between the prompt gamma-ray emission and various afterglow properties; however, our results conclusively show no such correlations exist in Swift data. 

Our catalog includes a total of 98 GRBs, out of which 72 have measured redshifts. For these GRBs, we compute the so-called "isotropic equivalent" gamma-ray energy and peak photon energy. We find that there is a wide range of observed isotropic equivalent gamma-ray energies and peak photon energies for the GRBs in our sample, with no significant correlation between them. Furthermore, we demonstrate that no correlation exists between these quantities and any afterglow properties, such as the burst duration or the temporal and spectral evolution of the afterglow. These findings suggest that the traditional model of internal shocks may no longer be valid for understanding the prompt gamma-ray emission. Our complete catalog of Swift GRB spectra and durations is thus a valuable resource for understanding the physical mechanisms responsible for GRBs.

In this study, we present the discovery of two new basaltic asteroids, which may provide insight into the formation and evolution of the Outer Main Belt (OMB). These asteroids, named 2020 NX and 2020 NW, were identified through observations made using the Infrared Camera and Spectrograph (IRCS) on the Subaru Telescope in Hawaii. 

The discovery of basaltic asteroids in the OMB is significant, as they are believed to be remnants of the early Solar System and can provide information about the conditions and processes involved in the formation of the rocky planets. However, finding these asteroids can be challenging due to their small size and dark surfaces.

To determine the composition of the observed asteroids, we used spectroscopic analysis of their reflectance spectra, which revealed a basaltic mineralogy similar to that of Vesta, the second-largest asteroid in our Solar System. This suggests that the parent body of these new asteroids may have undergone a significant impact event that produced the basaltic material.

Our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge about the composition and evolution of the OMB, and may help further our understanding of the early Solar System. Further studies are required to determine the exact formation and evolutionary processes of these asteroids and their parent body.

In this work, we investigate the particle-vibration coupling within the theoretical framework of covariant density functional theory (CDFT). CDFT is an effective model to study the nuclear structure and dynamics by treating the nucleons (protons and neutrons) as independent particles governed by a mean-field potential. Moreover, the CDFT also introduces collective excitations such as vibrations, rotations, and shape deformations, which are essential for providing a complete picture of the nuclear ground and excited states. 

In our study, we propose a new approach for treating the particle-vibration coupling based on the theory of quasiparticle random-phase approximation (QRPA). Specifically, we extend the QRPA framework to include both the particle mean-field and the residual interaction beyond the second order. By applying this method to various isotopes, we obtain a comprehensive understanding of the coupling mechanism and its impact on nuclear properties, such as excitation energies, transition strengths, and deformation patterns. 

Our results demonstrate that particle-vibration coupling plays a crucial role in shaping the nuclear structure, especially in the low-lying energy region. Moreover, our theoretical approach provides a systematic way to handle the complex many-body problem in the CDFT framework, which is crucial for predicting the properties of exotic nuclei that are difficult to access experimentally. Therefore, this study contributes to our understanding of the fundamental physics of nuclei and opens up new avenues for exploring the role of collective excitations in nuclear dynamics.

In this study, we address the issue of quantile and probability curves crossing each other, which can lead to erroneous statistical conclusions. The main objective of our work is to propose a novel approach that ensures the monotonicity of both curves, without crossing. 

The motivation behind this work is to provide a solution to the inconsistencies that arise when quantile and probability curves cross each other. These curves are used in various fields, such as finance, healthcare, and environmental studies, to evaluate the distribution of data and estimate probabilities. However, the crossing of these curves can lead to biased estimates and incorrect inferences.

To achieve our goal, we introduce a constrained optimization problem that takes into account the statistical properties of both curves. We show that the proposed method preserves the order of the data and results in smoother and more accurate curves compared to existing methods.

Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective in solving the problem of crossing quantile and probability curves. The smoothed curves obtained using our technique have better goodness-of-fit statistics compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient and can be applied to large datasets.

Overall, our study provides a robust method for generating quantile and probability curves that do not cross, providing more accurate and reliable estimates for statistical analysis.

In this work, we investigate the influence of the maximum Planckian momentum on the cosmological Casimir effect in the context of an accelerating universe. Casimir effect describes the attraction between two parallel plates due to the vacuum fluctuations of the quantized fields trapped between them. When this effect is considered at cosmological scales, it is called the cosmological Casimir effect. Our aim is to study the effect of the maximum momentum allowed by the quantum nature of spacetime on this phenomenon.

To achieve our goal, we use a modified version of the DeWitt-Schwinger technique which takes into account the maximum momentum. We find that this restriction changes the behavior of the vacuum fluctuations and thus the Casimir effect, specifically its magnitude and sign. We also show that the accelerating universe enhances the Casimir force, and that the observable effects are related to the geometry of the universe.

The problem we attempt to solve is the effect of the maximum momentum on the cosmological Casimir effect, which has been largely overlooked in previous studies. This research can provide a deeper understanding of the Casimir effect in an expanding universe and contribute to the development of a consistent and comprehensive quantum theory of gravity. Our motivation stems from the fundamental importance of understanding the quantum nature of spacetime and its implications on cosmology.

In this work, we present a prediction derived from string phenomenology that suggests the existence of extra matter at low energy. The motivation behind our research is to study the fundamental properties of string theory, one of the most promising candidates for a theory of everything. The prediction we propose arises from the fact that string theory predicts new symmetries related to the presence of extra dimensions, which could result in the emergence of extra matter fields. 

Our study is based on a mathematical framework that combines string theory with field theory to generate a set of predictions that can be tested through experimental observation. We find that the extra matter fields could have distinct implications for the behavior of particles at low-energy scales, including interactions with the Higgs field and other known particles. Moreover, the presence of this extra matter could help address some longstanding problems with the standard model, such as the hierarchy problem and the nature of dark matter. 

Our methodology consists of applying advanced mathematical techniques to extract predictions from string theory. Specifically, we analyze the properties of the compactified extra dimensions of the theory to evaluate the implications for particle physics. Overall, our study offers a novel perspective on the relationship between string theory and low-energy physics, and could motivate future experiments and theoretical developments in this area.

In our work, entitled "Plasma Modes Along the Open Field Lines of a Neutron Star", we investigate the behavior of plasma modes along the open field lines of a neutron star. The study is motivated by the fact that neutron stars are astrophysical objects with strong magnetic fields that can extract energy from the plasma they interact with, and this energy transfer is mediated through various plasma modes. We used a combination of analytical and numerical methods to investigate the dispersion relation and growth rate of the plasma modes in the presence of a strong magnetic field.

Our results show that in the presence of a strong magnetic field, the plasma modes can undergo a Landau damping, which leads to a significant decrease in their amplitude. We also found that the plasma modes along the open field lines are more susceptible to growth than those along the closed field lines. Specifically, the Kelvin-Helmholtz mode near the Alfvén resonant surface can grow exponentially due to the plasma instability, which has important implications for the energy transfer from the neutron star to the plasma.

Our work aims to contribute to the understanding of astrophysical plasma behavior in extreme environments, and specifically, to provide insights into the energy transfer mechanisms between neutron stars and their surrounding plasma.

Our research is focused on developing a general approach to statistical modeling of physical laws using nonparametric regression. The motivation behind our work is to enhance the accuracy and predictive power of physical models by incorporating statistical methods. We believe that this approach can lead to better understanding of physical processes, more accurate predictions, and more informed decision-making. 

To achieve these goals, we utilized a flexible and powerful nonparametric regression technique, which allows us to model complex relationships without limiting the number of parameters. Unlike traditional parametric models, which rely on pre-specified functional forms, nonparametric models can adapt to the data and capture any nonlinearities and interactions. Our method is based on the use of modern statistical tools, such as Bayesian inference, cross-validation, and regularization techniques, to ensure optimal model selection and robustness. 

Our results illustrate the potential of this approach by demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling diverse physical phenomena, including heat transfer, fluid dynamics, and quantum mechanics. Our findings show that nonparametric regression can provide accurate predictions and reveal intricate structures that may not be captured by linear models. 

In conclusion, our work represents a significant step towards developing a general framework for statistical modeling of physical laws using nonparametric regression. We believe that our approach has the potential to revolutionize the way physical models are constructed and utilized, ultimately leading to better understanding and management of complex systems.

In this work, we investigate the properties of supersymmetric vector multiplets in non-adjoint representations of SO(N) symmetry. Our research aims to elucidate the behavior of such multiplets under supersymmetry transformations. We employ theoretical methods of gauge, group and supersymmetry theory in our analysis. 

The motivation behind this research arises from the need to understand the dynamics of particle physics beyond the standard model. Non-adjoint representations of SO(N) have been shown to be crucial in the construction of various grand unified theories. Vector multiplets are also important in the feature of supersymmetry and the breaking of electroweak symmetry in the standard model. Thus, our research provides an insight into the interplay between these two crucial concepts in theoretical particle physics.

The problem this work attempts to solve is to explore the supersymmetry algebra in theories with non-adjoint representations of SO(N) which has not been fully investigated. The study of the properties of supersymmetric vector multiplets in non-adjoint representations is crucial to the construction of viable theories of particle physics beyond the standard model. 

Our results show that supersymmetry is broken by the non-adjoint representation, and we observe additional effects due to the non-abelian nature of SO(N). This research sets a foundation for the exploration of new avenues in building theoretical models for particle physics, that incorporate the elements of non-adjoint representations of SO(N) and super-symmetric vector multiplets.

In this work, we investigate the prompt emission of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) from high-energy protons, muons and electron-positron pairs. Our results indicate that high-energy protons play a crucial role in the GRB emission, particularly in the GeV-TeV energy range. Specifically, we show that the energy released by the protons through their interaction with the surrounding medium produces a significant fraction of the observed GRB radiation.

Our work aims to address the long-standing problem of the origin of prompt emission in GRBs, which has been a topic of intense debate for many years. Our results provide a new insight into the physics of GRB emission and highlight the importance of considering the interactions of high-energy protons with the ambient medium.

The motivation for our research comes from the fact that GRBs are among the most energetic phenomena in the universe, and understanding their emission mechanisms is crucial for elucidating the fundamental physics of the universe. By studying the role of high-energy protons, muons and electron-positron pairs in GRB emission, we hope to contribute to a deeper understanding of these enigmatic and fascinating astrophysical phenomena.

In conclusion, our work represents a significant step forward in our understanding of the prompt emission of GRBs and the role played by high-energy particles in this process. These results have important implications for future studies of GRBs and the physics of high-energy astrophysical phenomena.

In this work, we investigated the internal states of model isotropic granular packings. Our study aimed to understand the relationship between the assembling process, the geometry of the packing, and the contact network formed between the grains. We used a discrete element method in numerical simulations to assemble an isotropic granular packing from an initially random distribution of particles. From these simulations, we analyzed the geometry of the packing, the coordination number, and the contact force distribution of the grains within the network. 

Our results demonstrate that the assembling process significantly affects the internal states of the packing, resulting in variations in the packing geometry and the number of contacts formed between the grains. Furthermore, we observe that the contact networks of the isotropic granular packings exhibit spatial patterns, with regions of different contact force clusters present in the packing. 

This work aims to contribute to the understanding of the inner workings of granular materials, which are widely utilized in various industrial processes. Our findings provide insight into the complex behavior of grains in isotropic granular packings and offer key perspectives for the design and optimization of engineering applications utilizing granular materials.

In this work, we present a systematic analysis of a spin-susceptibility representation of the pairing interaction in the 2D Hubbard model. The Hubbard model is a standard model used to study phenomena in condensed matter physics and is considered a prototype of strongly correlated electron systems. The pairing interaction and its role in the model have been the focus of much research due to its significance in superconductivity.

Our goal is to explore the spin-susceptibility representation of the pairing interaction and its physical implications. We use a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, including perturbation theory and exact diagonalization, to calculate the pairing interaction strength, the critical temperature for superconductivity, and the energy gap. Our analysis reveals that the spin-susceptibility representation provides an intuitive interpretation of the superconducting transition and allows for a systematic exploration of its physical properties.

Our work sheds light on the mechanisms underlying superconductivity in the Hubbard model by providing a comprehensive analysis of the pairing interaction. Our results contribute to the understanding of superconductivity in strongly correlated electron systems and highlight the usefulness of the spin-susceptibility representation for understanding the underlying physics.

In this work, we present a physical investigation of the potentially hazardous asteroid (144898) 2004 VD17. Our primary objective is to provide a comprehensive analysis of its physical properties, including size, shape, rotation period, and spectral characteristics. We conducted optical observations and analyzed photometric and spectroscopic data obtained from different telescopes. We used various numerical tools such as light curve inversion and thermophysical models to derive the asteroid's physical properties. Our results show that 2004 VD17 is an elongated object with a size of about 600 meters, a rotation period of 4.7 hours, and an albedo of 0.15±0.01. Spectral analysis reveals that this asteroid belongs to the Sq spectral class, consistent with the implication that it is of stony composition. Our study also highlights the importance of investigating potentially hazardous asteroids such as 2004 VD17 to understand their physical characteristics and potential threat to Earth. Our findings provide new insights into the properties of this potentially hazardous asteroid and its potential impact on Earth, contributing to the overall understanding of the characteristics and risks posed by Near-Earth Objects.

In this study, we present the direct diameter measurement of the semi-detached binary SS Leporis, filling its Roche lobe. Precise measurements of the star and its envelope are crucial for understanding the structure and evolution of such systems. Our motivation for this research was to obtain accurate measurements of the binary system to better understand its formation and evolution.

The Roche lobe is the theoretical boundary around a star, beyond which material is gravitationally lost to its companion star. By measuring the diameter of the star filling its Roche lobe directly, we can infer the size and shape of the Roche lobe and determine the mass transfer and evolution of the binary system. We used the VINCI/VLTI interferometer to spatially resolve the system and obtain precise measurements of the star's diameter.

Our results show that the diameter of the primary star is 2.365 ± 0.05 milliarcseconds, corresponding to a physical radius of 3.16 ± 0.03 solar radii. This measurement is consistent with theoretical models of semi-detached binaries, supporting the validity of such models.

Overall, our study demonstrates the importance and feasibility of direct diameter measurements of stars in binary systems and provides insight into the formation and evolution of these systems.

In this work, we present the results obtained from the Pulse-Shape Discrimination (PSD) technique implemented at the Counting Test Facility (CTF) of the University of West Virginia. PSD is a crucial tool applied in various scientific and industrial applications, particularly in gamma and neutron detection systems, as it can differentiate between multiple types of radiation and background noise. The primary objective of this research was to develop and enhance the PSD technique to improve the detection performance of the CTF radiation detection system.

Our approach involved the use of an unbiased digital signal processing algorithm based on the shape of the pulses from radiation detectors. We observed that the PSD technique enhanced the signal-to-noise ratio, which increased the probability of correctly identifying the type of radiation detected.

Our results showed that our PSD algorithm enhanced the CTF’s ability to distinguish between neutron and gamma radiation sources in various environments. Moreover, we observed that our PSD algorithm increased the time resolution of the detection system, which is a critical factor in reducing background fluctuations and improving detection efficiency.

The motivation for this research was to enhance the capability of radiation detection systems used in nuclear power plants, security, medical, and industrial applications, among others. The PSD technique’s optimization has significant implications, reducing the false detections and enabling a more robust and accurate identification of radiation sources.

In this work, we explore the concept of discrete thermodynamics in lasers. Our methodology involves a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental observation to investigate the thermodynamic properties of lasers at the quantum level. The aim of our research is to uncover the fundamental principles that govern the behavior of lasers, with the ultimate goal of developing more efficient and effective laser technologies.

The key idea behind our work is that lasers operate according to a discrete thermodynamic cycle, rather than a continuous one. This means that energy is transferred in discrete packets, or quanta, rather than continuously flowing. By studying the thermodynamics of lasers in this way, we can better understand how they work and optimize their performance.

One of the main challenges our work attempts to solve is the efficiency problem associated with traditional laser technologies. By taking a discrete thermodynamic approach, we believe we can develop more energy-efficient laser systems that are better suited for a range of applications, from communications to medical procedures.

The motivation for our research is driven by the need for more effective laser systems in a rapidly changing technological landscape. By developing a deeper understanding of the thermodynamics of lasers, we hope to contribute to the development of new, innovative laser technologies that can address real-world challenges.

In this research, we focused on the merging activity of galaxy clusters and its impact on the kinetic polarization of the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) signal. The motivation behind this research was to better understand the underlying physical mechanisms that govern the galaxy cluster formation and evolution, which is crucial for studying the large-scale structure of the universe.

Using high-fidelity hydrodynamical simulations, we investigated the effects of merging on the SZ signal polarization. Our results showed that the merging of galaxy clusters can induce significant changes in the polarization profile of the SZ signal, increasing its amplitude and altering its shape and orientation. We found that this effect is most prominent in the post-merger phase, where multiple clusters are coalescing and the gas dynamics is highly complex.

Our work attempts to solve a fundamental problem in modern cosmology, which is to accurately model and predict the observable properties of galaxy clusters, including the SZ signal polarization. By providing a more accurate and comprehensive picture of the merging activity and its influence on the SZ signal, our research can help improve the theoretical models and observational strategies for studying galaxy clusters, as well as shed light on the mysteries of the universe's evolution.

In this study, our aim was to investigate the interplay between electron-phonon coupling and strain coupling in manganites. Our research is motivated by the fact that while both coupling types are known to be important factors in various physical phenomena, the relationship between them is not yet well understood. We carried out a series of density functional theory calculations on magnanites with different compositions and structures. Our results indicate that for certain materials, the electron-phonon coupling is very weak, while the strain coupling is strong. This suggests that for these materials, strain coupling may play a more significant role than electron-phonon coupling in determining their physical properties. We also found that the strength of the electron-phonon coupling depends not only on the composition of the material, but also on the specific phonon mode involved. Our methodology involved a careful analysis of the electronic structure, as well as a detailed study of the lattice dynamics. Our work sheds new light on the complex interplay between electron-phonon coupling and strain coupling, and provides a basis for future investigations in this area.

In this study, we analyzed the transversal structure of the jet in the quasar 0836+710, aiming to reveal its physical properties and gain insight into the mechanisms behind the jet formation and evolution. We obtained data from multi-frequency VLBI observations carried out with the European VLBI Network at seven epochs between 2011 and 2018. Using these data, we constructed maps of the jet at different epochs, and performed quantitative analyses on the jet morphology and kinematics. 

Our results showed that the jet in 0836+710 displays a complex transversal structure, consisting of bright ridges and fainter filamentary features. The ridges are found to be associated with higher brightness temperatures and faster apparent speeds, and show signs of synchrotron self-absorption. The filamentary features, on the other hand, exhibit slower speeds and lower brightness temperatures, suggesting that they are associated with lower-energy particles within the jet. 

Our study provides new insights into the physical properties of the jet in 0836+710, and sheds light on the mechanisms that power the jet and shape its morphology. Understanding these properties is crucial for elucidating the physical principles behind jet formation and evolution, and for advancing our knowledge of high-energy astrophysics.

In this paper, we present a data-driven approach to identify structural damage in civil engineering structures utilizing Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD) techniques. The primary objective of this work is to extract statistical features from the input signal and determine the most relevant ones for damage identification.

PCA is used as a feature extraction technique to reduce the dimensionality of the input data, while ARD is utilized to enhance the efficiency and reliability of the damage detection process. These methods are applied to a simulated data set of a beam structure and a real-world data set of a cantilever beam.

The results obtained show that the proposed method can accurately identify the location and severity of the damage with high accuracy. This approach outperforms the traditional technique, which is based solely on the frequency domain analysis and relies on expert knowledge.

The study attempts to solve a critical issue in structural health monitoring, which is to develop an automated approach to detect and locate structural damage. The proposed method provides a promising foundation for future research in the area of damage detection and health monitoring of civil engineering structures.

This study aimed to search for the radiative decays of Upsilon(1S) into eta and eta' using the data collected at the Belle experiment. The motivation behind this research was to investigate the potential of these decays in shedding light on the discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental observations in the physics of mesons. The methodology involved analyzing large amounts of experimental data collected in the Belle detector at the KEK-B electron-positron collider in Japan. The main challenge was identifying the signal from the background and filtering out the noise using a range of techniques tailored for this particular study. The results obtained revealed no clear evidence of radiative decays of Upsilon(1S) into eta and eta' and, therefore, placed stringent limits on their branching ratios. Additionally, the results were compared to theoretical predictions, and further interpretations and implications of this new experimental analysis were discussed. In conclusion, the study provides a valuable contribution to the physics of mesons and highlights the importance of experimental tests for refining and advancing theoretical models.

The problem of the origin of the early-type R stars has plagued astrophysicists for over a century. It has been speculated that these stars may have evolved from a single massive star or through some sort of binary interaction. In our work, we consider the latter possibility and explore the feasibility of a binary-merger origin for these stars. We have used state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations to model the evolution of massive binary stars and subsequent stellar mergers. Our simulations demonstrate that the merger of two massive helium-core stars can lead to the formation of an R-type star, which explains the observed properties of these stars, including their peculiar abundance patterns and high rotational velocities. We have also calculated evolutionary tracks and synthetic spectra of these merger products and found them to be in excellent agreement with observed early-type R stars. Our results suggest that the binary-merger scenario can indeed solve the long-standing mystery of the origin of these stars. This work has important implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of massive stars and binary systems.

In this work, we consider the Interval Conjectures for level Hilbert functions, which aim to provide a way to analyze the levels of homogenization of a given ideal. The problem we tackle is to generalize the conjectures for arbitrary ideals, which have so far been only proven for monomial ideals. Our results show that the Interval Conjectures hold for all radical ideals, which is a significant extension of the previously known results, and provide a way to compute the levels of a given ideal in a simple and straightforward manner. 

To achieve these results, we use combinatorial and algebraic techniques, such as the theory of Gröbner bases and the combinatorial description of level Hilbert functions. We also introduce a new concept, called the associated graded module of an ideal, which allows us to simplify the computations and relate the Interval Conjectures to other important concepts in commutative algebra, such as the depths of an ideal. 

Our work contributes to the understanding of the levels of homogenization of ideals, which is a fundamental concept in algebraic geometry and computational algebra. Our results have potential applications in various fields, such as cryptography, coding theory, and optimization, where algebraic techniques are used to solve complex problems.

In this work, we investigate the properties of generic black holes in de Sitter spaces, emphasizing the existence of anomalies and de Sitter radiation. Our main motivation lies in understanding the implications of these phenomena for black hole thermodynamics and the fate of black holes in the universe. We approach the problem by considering a semiclassical treatment of gravity, which takes into account the quantum effects of matter fields in the vicinity of the black hole. 

Our analysis reveals the presence of several types of anomalies associated with the conformal symmetry of the de Sitter metric. These anomalies lead to violations of the conservation laws for energy and momentum, and may have important consequences for the stability and evolution of black holes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a de Sitter radiation flux emanating from the black hole, which is determined by the Hawking temperature as modified by the de Sitter cosmological constant. 

Our research provides a new perspective on the behavior of black holes in de Sitter spaces, and sheds light on the fundamental properties of quantum gravity. The findings are relevant for a wide range of physical phenomena, including the early universe, cosmology, and the dynamics of black hole mergers.

In our research, we have developed a k-dependent SU(4) model of high-temperature superconductivity and explored its coherent-state solutions. Our motivation was to extend the scope of current theories of superconductivity and to address the outstanding questions of strongly correlated electron systems. The key idea behind this model is to include SU(4) symmetry, which describes the coupling of the charge and spin degrees of freedom of electrons in a non-perturbative way. This allows us to investigate the interplay between charge and spin degrees of freedom, which is crucial for understanding high-temperature superconductivity.

Using a numerical mean-field approach, we have studied the magnetic and superconducting properties of the SU(4) model. Our main results show that the model naturally gives rise to unconventional superconductivity with an extended s-wave pairing symmetry, consistent with experimental observations in high-temperature cuprate superconductors. Moreover, we find that the model predicts the existence of a novel magnetic phase near the superconducting dome, with exotic spin textures and topological properties.

Overall, our k-dependent SU(4) model provides a novel and comprehensive framework for understanding high-temperature superconductivity. It sheds light on the fundamental physics of strongly correlated electron systems and opens up new possibilities for designing and engineering novel superconducting materials with enhanced functionality.

In this work, we present a novel approach for measuring energy-dependent polarization in soft gamma-rays. The proposed method implements Compton scattering in the PoGOLite instrument, which has been designed specifically for measuring hard X-rays and soft gamma-rays. The measurement of polarization is a crucial aspect of astrophysics as it provides valuable insights on the underlying physics of cosmic sources. Despite the significance of polarization measurement, it still remains an underexplored research area in the field of gamma-ray astronomy. Our work attempts to address this gap in understanding by formulating a method that can measure energy-dependent polarization.

The key idea behind the method is to measure the azimuthal modulation of the scattered photon, and then use this information to calculate the polarization of the incident Soft gamma rays. Our methodology involves experimental data analysis and Monte Carlo simulations to validate the measurement technique. PoGOLite has an advantage in detecting soft gamma-rays, hence, provides a feasible platform for such measurements.

The motivation for this study is driven by the need for better understanding of gamma-ray sources, including black-holes, pulsars, and Supernova remnants. Our measurement technique can provide new insights in understanding the geometry, composition and evolution of these astrophysical sources, leading to advancements in both astrophysics and fundamental physics.

In our research, we attempt to provide an accurate description of optical precursors and their relation to weak-field coherent optical transients. Optical precursors refer to fast and intense electromagnetic fields that precede the arrival of a main pulse in a dispersive medium. These precursors play a critical role in the temporal dynamics of light-matter interactions, leading to the development of new optical technologies and applications in quantum information processing, sensing, and imaging.

The motivation for our work is to enhance our understanding of the fundamental physics behind optical precursors and to explore potential applications of weak-field coherent optical transients. We also aim to develop efficient techniques for controlling and manipulating these precursors in order to improve the performance of optical devices and systems.

Our research results suggest that optical precursors can be effectively generated and controlled through the use of femtosecond laser pulses and waveguide structures. We also find that the spectral and temporal properties of these precursors can be tailored by modifying the dispersion properties of the medium. These findings have significant implications for the design and optimization of optical devices and systems, and pave the way for future research on the development of novel optical technologies and applications.

In this study, we investigate whether the gamma-ray spectrum of blazars becomes harder as the flux increases. To accomplish this, we analyze nine years of EGRET data from 66 blazars. Our main motivation for undertaking this research is to better understand the emission processes in these sources and to test the validity of the standard leptonic model for gamma-ray production.

We apply a variety of statistical tests to the data to determine if there is a correlation between the photon spectral index and the flux. Additionally, we investigate whether any trends persist after accounting for redshift. Our results indicate that there is a significant correlation between the photon spectral index and flux at the 99% confidence level. However, after accounting for redshift, this trend becomes weaker and may not be statistically significant.

Our findings have important implications for our understanding of the production mechanisms in blazars, demonstrating that the standard leptonic model may not fully explain the observed gamma-ray spectrum. These results also have implications for future observations with instruments such as CTA, as understanding the mechanisms behind blazar emission will be critical in interpreting the data.

In this work, we investigate the concept of algebraic charge liquids and present our findings on the theory of algebraic entropy. The central problem we attempt to solve is the classification of charged liquids and their phase transitions. Our research is motivated by the need for a deeper understanding of the behavior of charge-carrying fluids, which have significant implications in various fields of physics, including condensed matter, high-energy physics, and cosmology.

First, we introduce the concept of algebraic charge liquids, which are fluids composed of electrically charged particles with an algebraic symmetry. We then study their properties, including the relationship between the charge and entropy of the system. We find that the algebraic entropy of a charge liquid is a unique quantity that describes the macroscopic behavior of the system. We also demonstrate that the phase transition of a charge liquid can be characterized by the change in the algebraic entropy.

Our results provide a new perspective on the thermodynamics of charged fluids. The theory of algebraic entropy provides a framework to study the behavior of these complex systems and opens avenues for further research. We anticipate our work will have implications for the understanding of various phenomena in the fields of high-energy physics, condensed matter, and cosmology.

In this work, we present the development of a room temperature spin polarized magnetic semiconductor. The key idea is to enhance and control the spin polarization effect in semiconductor materials, which is crucial for the advancement of spintronic devices. This semiconductor is fabricated using a hybrid approach, where a ferromagnetic material is deposited on a semiconductor surface, followed by a heat treatment process. We investigate the structural, magnetic, and electronic properties of the resulting material using various experimental techniques, including X-ray diffraction, magneto-optical Kerr effect, and Hall effect measurements. 

The problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of efficient and reliable techniques for spin injection and detection in semiconductors, which is a significant hurdle for the practical implementation of spintronics. Our approach provides a feasible technique for obtaining room temperature spin-polarized semiconductor materials, which can be used as a platform for developing various spintronic devices. 

Our results showcase the successful development of a room temperature spin-polarized magnetic semiconductor, with a significant enhancement in the spin polarization effect. We observe a clear indication of spin injection and detection using non-local measurements, demonstrating the potential of this material for spintronic applications. The hybrid technique used in this work is promising for further exploration of other magnetic materials as well as alternative semiconductor substrates. Overall, these findings provide a significant step towards the realization of practical and efficient spintronic devices based on semiconductor materials.

In this paper, we present the first part of a comprehensive study of catalogued nearby galaxy clusters from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 4 (SDSS-DR4). The motivation behind this research is to advance our understanding of galaxy clusters as fundamental building blocks of the universe, and to unveil their global properties like richness, velocity dispersion, luminosity, and projected size. To achieve these goals, we follow a systematic approach to construct a large cluster catalogue from the SDSS-DR4 using the well-established red-sequence method combined with the adaptive matched filter technique. We perform a careful visual inspection and manual refinement of each cluster candidate to eliminate false positives, resulting in the identification of a sample of 1978 clusters in the redshift range of 0.05 < z < 0.2. We then study the statistical distributions of their global properties, as well as their scaling relations with each other, using various analytical tools including the likelihood ratio test and the Pearson correlation analysis. Our results provide a comprehensive and detailed characterization of the SDSS-DR4 cluster sample and extend our knowledge of the large-scale structure of the universe. They also lay the groundwork for the second part of this study, which will explore the internal properties of individual clusters and their implications for galaxy evolution.

We present a study of the sparticle spectra and LHC signatures for large volume string compactifications. The aim of this work is to investigate the possibility of observing supersymmetry at the LHC, assuming low-energy supersymmetry breaking arises from gravity-mediated mechanisms in string theory.

Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that supersymmetry is an attractive candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, which could explain a range of problems such as the hierarchy problem and the unification of gauge couplings. Moreover, string theory offers a unified framework for gravity and the other three fundamental forces of nature, providing a natural setting for supersymmetry.

We employ the Large Volume Scenario (LVS) as a framework for our study. We use the MSSM spectrum generator SUSY-HIT to calculate the spectrum of sparticles that arise in this scenario, including the lightest neutralino and the Higgs bosons, among others. We then analyze the LHC signatures of these sparticles, including the production cross-sections, decay channels, and kinematic distributions.

Our results show that the sparticle masses in the LVS scenario are typically in the multi-TeV range, making them difficult to produce at the LHC. However, we find that certain LHC signatures, such as monojet and displaced vertices, could potentially probe this scenario in the next few years of LHC running. We conclude that the LVS scenario represents a viable and testable framework for studying supersymmetry in string theory.

Protoplanetary disks around millisecond pulsars have garnered much interest in the scientific community due to their potential to shed light on the formation and evolution of planets in highly compact stellar systems. The PSR 1257 +12 system is a particularly interesting case study, as it boasts three planets orbiting a pulsar with a period of only 6 milliseconds. In this study, we investigate the evolution of protoplanetary disks around millisecond pulsars, specifically in the context of the PSR 1257 +12 system.

Our findings reveal that the protoplanetary disk around the PSR 1257 +12 system is likely to have been significantly impacted by the pulsar's radiation. By modeling the radiation pressure exerted on the disk, we demonstrate that the disk would have been truncated at a radius of about 0.1 AU, possibly explaining the relatively compact orbits of the three planets in the system. Additionally, we find that the disk is likely to have been affected by viscous spreading, with a characteristic timescale of around 10,000 years.

The motivation for this research stems from the desire to better understand the formation and evolution of planets in highly compact stellar systems. By studying protoplanetary disks around millisecond pulsars such as the PSR 1257 +12 system, we gain insight into the physical processes that govern the formation and migration of planets in such environments. Furthermore, our findings contribute to the broader effort of understanding the diversity of exoplanetary systems and the conditions that give rise to them.

In this work, we investigate the evolution of the Carter constant for inspirals into a black hole, specifically examining the effect of the black hole quadrupole. The Carter constant is a fundamental quantity that characterizes the angular momentum of a particle orbiting a black hole, and it plays a crucial role in understanding the dynamics of gravitational waves emitted during the inspiral phase.

Our work builds on previous research that focused on the effect of the black hole spin on the Carter constant. Using numerical simulations, we study the evolution of the Carter constant for a range of black hole quadrupole moments and initial conditions. Our methodology involves solving the geodesic equations of motion for a test particle in the background of a Kerr black hole with a quadrupole moment.

Our research is motivated by the fact that understanding the effect of the black hole quadrupole is important for the detection of gravitational waves by ground-based detectors such as LIGO and VIRGO. The work attempts to solve the problem of accurately predicting the gravitational wave signal from inspirals into a black hole with non-zero quadrupole moment, which has practical implications for the interpretation of future observations.

In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the dynamics of inspirals into a black hole with non-zero quadrupole moment and highlights the importance of including this effect in the analysis of gravitational wave observations.

In this work, we investigate the renormalization of Quantum Yang-Mills fields in curved spacetime. Our primary objective is to extend the renormalization program for flat spacetime to the realm of curved spacetime, where there is no translational symmetry. We develop an approach based on an effective action that includes all non-trivial divergent contributions to the stress-energy tensor. The renormalization of gauge couplings is also studied, and we show that the usual methods are well-defined in curved spacetime.

Our key idea is to use the background field method, in which the metric tensor is treated as a classical field, and the quantum fields are perturbations around this background. This allows us to compute the stress-energy tensor using the Schwinger-DeWitt expansion. The divergent terms are then extracted, and a counterterm Lagrangian is introduced to cancel these divergences.

To test our methodology, we apply our framework to various toy models in curved spacetime, including the two-sphere, the hyperbolic space, and the de Sitter space. We find that our approach leads to finite results and is consistent with the standard results in flat spacetime.

This work attempts to solve the problem of the renormalization of quantum fields in curved spacetime, which has challenged physicists for decades. By developing a new approach based on the effective action and the background field method, we are able to show that the renormalization program can be extended to curved spacetime, opening up new avenues for research in quantum field theory and cosmology.

In this study, we present the first results on the clustering of Luminous Red Galaxies (LRGs) at z~0.7 using the AAOmega spectrograph on the Anglo-Australian Telescope. The motivation for this research is to understand the processes involved in the formation and evolution of LRGs in the context of large-scale structures. The problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of accurate measurements of LRG clustering at intermediate redshifts, and the subsequent uncertainty in constraining cosmological parameters and galaxy formation models.

By analyzing spectra from a sample of ~6700 LRGs over a wide area of the sky, we measured their spatial correlation function, which provides information on the clustering strength and scale. Our findings show that LRGs at z~0.7 are highly clustered, with a correlation length of r0=8.4±0.3 h-1Mpc and a slope of γ=1.9±0.1, consistent with previous measurements at lower and higher redshifts. In addition, we investigate the dependence of LRG clustering on galaxy properties such as luminosity and color.

Our methodology involves measuring the two-point correlation function using the Landy-Szalay estimator, and performing extensive tests to account for various sources of systematic errors. Our results support the current paradigm of hierarchical structure formation, where larger structures grow through the merging of smaller ones. The precise measurements of LRG clustering obtained from this work will be an important input for future cosmological analyses and theoretical studies of galaxy formation and evolution.

In this work, we present new calibration techniques for spectrometers based on optical frequency combs. Our research is motivated by the need for more accurate calibration methods for spectrometers, which are widely used in chemistry, physics, and other scientific fields. By using an optical frequency comb, we are able to accurately measure the frequency of light emitted by a spectrometer, which allows us to calibrate the instrument with much greater precision than traditional methods. 

Using this new technique, we were able to achieve a significant improvement in the accuracy of our spectrometer measurements. We also found that our technique is more efficient and time-saving compared to traditional calibration methods. 

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the lack of accurate calibration methods for spectrometers. Inaccurate calibration can lead to significant errors in scientific measurements, which can impact the validity of research findings. Our new calibration technique provides a solution to this problem, allowing for more precise and reliable measurements. 

In summary, our research presents a significant advancement in the field of spectrometer calibration. We anticipate that our new technique will be widely adopted in scientific research, leading to more accurate and impactful findings.

In this work, we present a detailed analysis of the technical issues involved in the numerical propagation of high energy cosmic rays in the Galaxy. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that high energy cosmic rays are an important source of information about the origin and evolution of the universe. However, accurately simulating the propagation of these cosmic rays has proven to be a challenging task due to the complex nature of the galactic magnetic field and interactions with plasma and radiation fields.

Our computational framework is based on the Green's function method, which allows us to accurately simulate cosmic ray propagation in a broad range of astrophysical environments. We present a detailed evaluation of the numerical accuracy and stability of our method, including discussions on grid resolution, time stepping schemes, and boundary conditions.

Our results show that our method is capable of accurately simulating high energy cosmic ray propagation in a variety of astrophysical environments. We also identify several technical issues that need to be addressed in future work, such as improving the accuracy of the numerical integration and the selection of appropriate boundary conditions.

In summary, this work aims to provide a solid foundation for future numerical studies of high energy cosmic ray propagation in the Galaxy. We believe that our method will be an important tool for investigating the origin and evolution of cosmic rays and their relevance to astrophysical phenomena.

Our work on "Enhanced Half-Metallicity in Edge-Oxidized Zigzag Graphene Nanoribbons" aims to investigate the effects of edge oxidation on half-metallicity in graphene nanoribbons (GNRs). Half-metallicity, a property where only electrons with one spin orientation are allowed to flow, is crucial for spintronic devices. However, GNRs do not exhibit ideal half-metallicity due to edge irregularities and defects. 

We used density functional theory calculations to study the electronic structure of zigzag GNRs with different degrees of edge oxidation. Our results indicate that edge oxidation enhances half-metallicity in zigzag GNRs. In particular, when oxygen atoms attach to the edges of the GNRs, the defect states near the Fermi level disappear and the magnetic moments become more stable, leading to a more efficient half-metallicity.

The key idea behind our work is that edge oxidation can improve the quality of GNRs and enhance their half-metallicity, making them promising candidates for spintronic devices. We hope that our work will stimulate further research on edge oxidation in GNRs and pave the way for developing efficient spintronic devices.

In conclusion, our work provides a fundamental understanding of the effect of edge oxidation on the half-metallicity of zigzag GNRs. Our methodology involves density functional theory calculations, and our results highlight the potential for edge oxidation to enhance the half-metallicity of GNRs, which is critical for the development of efficient spintronic devices.

In this paper, we present a study on the high energy emission of GRO J1655-40 during its 2005 outburst through INTEGRAL spectroscopy. We analyzed the source's spectrum through broad energy ranges, establishing its soft X-ray and hard X-ray properties. Our analysis allowed us to separate the source's high and low energy components and assess their relative contributions. We also studied the source's spectral variability to gain a better understanding of its underlying physics.

Our main motivation for this research was to study the properties of the black hole X-ray binary GRO J1655-40, which is known to be an essential laboratory for studying the properties of accretion flows onto black holes. By studying the high energy emission of this object, we aimed to understand its accretion mechanisms, as the high energy properties of the source are directly related to the conditions of accretion and black hole properties.

Our research tries to solve the issue of understanding the high energy emission properties of GRO J1655-40 and the mechanisms that drive them. Our findings offer new insights into the accretion processes onto black holes and the mechanisms that fuel the X-ray emissions of accreting black hole systems. Our study contributes to the understanding of black hole X-ray binaries and provides future directions for research on accreting black hole systems.

In this study, we investigate the discrepancy in G-band contrast between quiet Sun and network regions. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that our understanding of the fundamental processes occurring in the solar atmosphere still suffers from significant uncertainties. Specifically, G-band contrast is a key observable of the solar photosphere that is related to the magnetic field concentration. However, its behavior in quiet Sun regions has been shown to differ significantly from what is observed in the network regions. 

We use high-resolution images from the Swedish Solar Telescope to analyze the properties of the quiet Sun regions. Our findings show that the discrepancy in G-band contrast is linked to the presence of unresolved magnetic elements in the quiet Sun. These unresolved elements are responsible for the enhanced G-band contrast observed in network regions. Furthermore, we find that the size distribution of the magnetic elements is log-normal, regardless of the type of region.

Our work emphasizes the need to properly account for unresolved magnetic elements when studying the properties of the quiet Sun. This is critical for understanding fundamental processes such as the generation of the solar magnetic field and its influence on the solar atmosphere. Our results will help advance our understanding of the Sun as a whole, providing information that can be used to improve current models and simulations.

In this paper, we present a detailed modeling analysis of the Photon Dominated Region (PDR) of the Barnard 68 molecular cloud. With this study, we aim to investigate the chemistry and physical structure of the PDR in the dark cloud, which is believed to be a crucial region for star formation. We performed a series of simulations using the Meudon PDR code, which included various model parameters such as the elemental abundances, radiation field, and gas temperature. Our study revealed that the Barnard 68 cloud is characterized by a thin PDR layer of 1-2 × 10^15 cm in thickness, with a total hydrogen column density of 7.6×10^21 cm^-2. Furthermore, we observed an increase in the fractional abundance of CO in the PDR layer, suggesting that CO photodissociation is the significant mechanism in the PDR. Therefore, we can conclude that the main source of energy influencing the chemical and physical structure of the Barnard 68 cloud is the ultraviolet (UV) radiation field. Our study highlights the importance of detailed modeling analysis of PDR in star-forming regions and will serve as a fundamental baseline for future investigations in this field.

We present a study in which we investigate the use of close galaxy pairs as proxies for galaxy cluster mergers. The motivation of our research is to develop efficient techniques for identifying galaxy cluster mergers, which are important events in the evolution of galaxies and clusters. However, detecting these mergers is not an easy task, as they often involve significant dynamics and complex gravitational interactions. Our approach here is to use the proximity of galaxies as an indicator of gravitational perturbations in the cluster environment, which could be evidence of an ongoing merger. Specifically, we analyze a sample of galaxy clusters from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and search for pairs of galaxies separated by distances smaller than a given threshold. We then compare the properties of these pairs with those of clusters identified as mergers by other means. Our results indicate that galaxy pairs can indeed serve as useful proxies for cluster mergers, with pairs in merging clusters showing distinctive properties such as higher galaxy masses and larger velocity dispersions. We also find that the effectiveness of our method depends on the choice of pair distance threshold and the dynamical state of the clusters. This study provides an alternative and complementary method for identifying galaxy cluster mergers, with potential implications for a wide range of astrophysical research.

In this study, we investigate the origin of the work function by analyzing the electronic structure of metallic surfaces. The work function is an essential parameter in studying the physics and chemistry of surfaces, and it characterizes the energy required to remove an electron from the material. Despite its importance, the fundamental origins of the work function are not yet fully understood. 

In our work, we attempt to solve this problem by developing an analytical model based on first-principles calculations. Our approach is based on a combination of density functional theory and thermodynamic principles to explore the electronic structure of metallic surfaces and their corresponding work functions. 

We find that the work function is related to the surface dipole moment and the electronegativity of the atoms involved. Furthermore, we observe that the electronic density near the surface is significantly different from the bulk, leading to the work function’s sensitivity to surface perturbations. 

Overall, our theoretical analysis provides new insights into the mechanisms behind the work function and sheds light on how we can engineer surfaces with specific electronic properties. Our results contribute to the fundamental understanding of surface chemistry and provide valuable guidance for designing surface-based technologies.

In this work, we investigate the phenomenon of superradiance and stimulated scattering in SNR 1987A. Our main motivation for this study is to understand the fundamental principles behind the interaction of photons with matter in astrophysical systems. Superradiance is a collective behavior of a large ensemble of quantum emitters, resulting in the cooperative emission of radiation, while stimulated scattering is the process of photon amplification through the interaction with an ensemble of particles. We explore the manifestation of these two phenomena in the context of the supernova remnant of SN 1987A. 

By analyzing the observational data from the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA), we find that the emission of the remnant exhibits clear signatures of superradiance and stimulated scattering. The key idea behind this observation is that the dense and compact cloud of particles in the remnant provides an ideal environment for these phenomena to occur. 

Our methodology involves performing a detailed analysis of the ALMA data and simulating the emission using numerical models. We fit the observations to the simulations to extract the relevant parameters and understand the physical processes at play. Our results provide valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms that govern the interaction of photons with matter in astrophysical systems, highlighting the importance of collective behaviors and ensemble effects.

In our work on network statistics on early English syntax, we sought to shed light on syntactic structures in Old English by identifying key structural criteria that could be used to construct networks of syntactic relationships. Our motivation for this research was the recognition that previous work on Old English syntax had been largely based on manual analysis of individual texts, which made it difficult to identify broader patterns and trends in the language. Furthermore, the use of network statistics allowed us to examine how different syntactic structures were interconnected and how these networks evolved over time.

To achieve these goals, we used a corpus of Old English texts spanning from the 7th to the 11th century and applied network-based clustering techniques to identify nodes and edges representing syntactic relationships. We also examined various metrics, including degree centrality and betweenness, to identify important nodes in the network. Our results showed that certain syntactic categories, such as prepositions, tended to be highly central in the network, while other categories, such as adjectives, were less central. We also found evidence of evolution in the syntactic network over time, with earlier texts being characterized by more complex, hierarchical structures than later texts.

Overall, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the syntactic structures of Old English and provides a methodological framework that could be applied to other historical languages and linguistic phenomena.

In this work, we tackle the problem of multiple-antenna beamforming with imperfect knowledge of the channel state information at the transmitter (CSIT), where the goal is to improve the error performance of the system while maintaining or increasing spectral efficiency. We propose a new scheme, which we call bit-interleaved coded multiple beamforming (BICMBF), that combines channel coding, bit interleaving, and beamforming to achieve this objective. 

The motivation for this research stems from the fact that in practical systems, the channel information available to the transmitter is often inaccurate or outdated due to channel estimation errors, feedback delays, or fast channel variations. Such imperfections can severely degrade the performance of beamforming systems, especially at high data rates, and therefore need to be addressed. 

The key ideas and methodology behind BICMBF involve jointly optimizing the coding rate, beamforming weights, and bit interleaving pattern to minimize the bit error rate (BER) under imperfect CSIT. We leverage tools from information theory, optimization theory, and communication theory to derive analytical expressions for the BER and spectral efficiency of the BICMBF scheme, as well as to develop efficient algorithms for practical implementation. 

Our simulation results show that BICMBF outperforms existing coded beamforming schemes for various channel conditions and SNR regimes, and can achieve substantial gains in BER while maintaining high spectral efficiency. Thus, our work contributes to the development of practical and robust multiple-antenna systems for future wireless networks.

In this work, we investigate the multicritical behavior of the (2+1)-dimensional gonihedric model as a realization of the (d,m)=(3,2) Lifshitz point. The gonihedric model is a lattice gauge theory that was initially introduced to study quantum gravity and has found several applications in condensed matter physics. We employ a combination of numerical simulations and analytical techniques to explore the critical properties of the model in the presence of a background scalar field. Our main findings reveal the existence of a multicritical point in the phase diagram, characterized by scaling exponents that differ from those of the standard Ising model. Moreover, we obtain evidence that supports the validity of a recent conjecture linking the gonihedric model with the three-state Potts model. The identification of the (d,m)=(3,2) Lifshitz point in the gonihedric model is an essential contribution to the understanding of critical phenomena in systems with anisotropic scaling. Our research is motivated by the interest in developing new theoretical frameworks to describe complex phases of matter and their phase transitions. By providing a detailed analysis of the gonihedric model, we contribute to the ongoing quest for a more profound understanding of critical phenomena in geometrical lattice models.

In this work, we investigate the chemical and dynamical properties of the stellar halo. The motivation behind this study is to better understand the origin and evolution of the Milky Way Galaxy. The stellar halo is a low-density region surrounding the galactic disk, consisting of ancient stars that are typically metal poor. Therefore, studying the halo provides us with a glimpse of the early stages of the galaxy's formation and history.

To probe the chemical properties of the halo, we use spectroscopic observations of halo stars to measure their metallicity, which is a measure of their abundance of heavy elements. We also use simulations to model the dynamical evolution of the halo stars, which allows us to infer how they became distributed in the Milky Way's halo.

The main problem that this work attempts to solve is how the stellar halo formed and evolved over time. Our key idea is to combine chemical and dynamical information to better understand the halo's formation history. By doing so, we hope to shed light on the origins of the Milky Way Galaxy and the processes that contributed to its early evolution.

The Hamiltonian formalism has proven to be a powerful tool for studying the dynamics of physical systems, including those in cosmology. In this work, we apply the Hamiltonian approach to the Friedmann cosmology model, which describes the large-scale evolution of the universe. Our goal is to obtain a Hamiltonian formulation of the model and investigate its quantization. 

The motivation for this research is twofold. Firstly, it allows us to study the quantum properties of the universe, providing a theoretical framework for understanding phenomena such as the cosmic microwave background or the formation of galaxies. Secondly, it allows us to test the validity of fundamental physical theories, such as general relativity, in the high-energy regime where they are expected to break down.

The key ideas of our approach involve identifying the canonical variables of the Friedmann model, constructing the corresponding Hamiltonian, and imposing appropriate quantization conditions. Our methodology involves combining analytical calculations with numerical simulations, such as solving the Schrodinger equation for the system's wave function.

Our main results include the derivation of a Hamiltonian formalism for the Friedmann model, as well as preliminary calculations for its quantum properties. We discuss the implications of our findings for the broader field of cosmology, highlighting the potential for future research in this area.

Our research aims to investigate the behaviour of superconducting material MgB2 when confined to magnetic field tuned cylinders by means of critical fluctuations. The motivation for this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the behaviour of superconducting materials under confinement, which can have significant implications for the design and construction of superconducting devices.

Our methodology involves preparing MgB2 samples and confining them to magnetic field-tuned cylinders. We will then measure the critical temperature and critical current density, which are critical parameters that describe the behaviour of superconducting materials. We will use these measurements to study the critical fluctuations that occur in the superconducting material under confinement.

By probing the superconductivity of MgB2 in this way, we hope to shed light on the effects of confinement on the superconducting properties of materials, and to gain a better understanding of the underlying physics. This research has the potential to contribute significant insights into the fundamental behaviour of superconducting materials under confinement. Knowing how to manipulate and control superconductors could eventually lead to the development of more efficient and advanced technologies, which could benefit society in many ways.

In this work, we study a general $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{EM}$ sigma model with external sources, dynamical breaking, and spontaneous vacuum symmetry breaking. The motivation for this research lies in understanding the dynamics of strong interactions and the underlying symmetries that govern them. The standard model of particle physics is based on the local gauge symmetry $SU(3)_C\times SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y$, which describes the strong, weak, and electromagnetic interactions. However, the strong interaction sector of the standard model is not yet completely understood, and there is a need to study alternative models to gain insights into its dynamics.

We approach this problem by considering a general $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{EM}$ sigma model, which is a nonlinear realization of chiral symmetry. We introduce external sources and study their effects on the model dynamics. We also consider spontaneous vacuum symmetry breaking, where the vacuum expectation value of the scalar field is nonzero, breaking the chiral symmetry.
