We analyze the resulting spectrum of particles and their interactions.

Our results show that the external sources and spontaneous symmetry breaking greatly affect the model's dynamics, leading to the emergence of new particles and interactions. These results have important implications for our understanding of the strong interaction sector of the standard model and may pave the way for the development of new theoretical models and experimental tests.

We present tests of Bayesian model selection techniques applied to gravitational wave astronomy. Our goal is to compare the effectiveness of different Bayesian algorithms in detecting gravitational wave sources and recovering their parameters, such as masses and spins of the merging compact objects. In particular, we test the performance of nested sampling, thermodynamic integration, and reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo (RJMCMC) algorithms. Our analysis is based on simulated gravitational wave signals corresponding to binary black hole and neutron star mergers, and we use several different noise configurations to quantify the impact of the detector's sensitivity on the algorithms' performance. 

Our results show that RJMCMC and nested sampling provide accurate results in recovering the source parameters even in challenging noise conditions. In comparison, thermodynamic integration suffers from convergence issues, and its performance is highly dependent on the chosen annealing scheme. We also find that the choice of prior and likelihood functions can significantly affect the accuracy of the results. Finally, we demonstrate the impact of model selection on the scientific interpretation of the data by comparing the inferred probability of different models for the same data set. 

Our work highlights the importance of choosing appropriate Bayesian algorithms and carefully analyzing the impact of assumptions made on the prior and likelihood functions. Our results and methodology can be useful for future gravitational wave detections, where advanced Bayesian model selection techniques will play a crucial role in uncovering the physics of compact object mergers.

In this study, we investigate the warm dust orbiting around EF Cha, a nearby young star estimated to be around 10 million years old. By using infrared data from Spitzer and WISE, along with optical spectra from the Magellan Inamori Kyocera Echelle instrument, we aim to understand the nature and origin of the dust. Our analysis of the SED reveals that the disk is inclined and flared with an outer radius of ≈24 au. We also resolved the disk direction and found that it is inclined by 40 degrees with respect to the observer. Our study shows that the dust emission is free-free in nature and originates from the gas in the disk atmosphere. Further modeling reveals that the central star is likely an early-M or K-type with a bolometric luminosity of about 0.2 solar luminosities. 

Our research shows that understanding the composition, structure, and evolution of debris disks around young stars is essential to gain a better understanding of planet formation processes. The warm dust observed around EF Cha could provide insights on the evolution of habitable planets and detection of young planets at the onset of formation. Studying the disk kinematics and physical properties can also shed light on the conditions in which planetary systems form, evolve and perhaps even disintegrate. Overall our results can inform further studies aimed at probing the planetary formation rates, chemical compositions, and evolution across different astrophysical environments.

In this study, we present mid-infrared evidence for a luminous infrared galaxy at z~2, which we identify using deep Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and Spitzer Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) imaging. The motivation for our research stems from the fact that luminous infrared galaxies at high redshifts have mainly been studied through sub-mm observations and optical/near-infrared spectroscopy, and very little exploration has been done in the mid-infrared region where the cool dust emission from these galaxies peaks. We use the ultra-deep Spitzer IRAC and MIPS observations in the HUDF-JD2 field to derive accurate luminosity measurements and examine the mid-infrared properties of this galaxy, contrasting its mid-infrared colors with those of typical galaxies at similar redshifts.

Our results show that this galaxy is an extreme starburst system that dominates the mid-infrared background at z~2. We find that the galaxy has a strong PAH emission feature and an extremely red mid-infrared color, which are typical characteristics of AGNs or highly obscured star-forming systems. Our study confirms that mid-infrared observations are a valuable tool for identifying and characterizing luminous infrared galaxies at high redshifts. Our methodology involves a careful analysis of deep Spitzer IRAC and MIPS imaging data combined with cosmic infrared background measurements, and the use of various spectral energy distribution templates to derive accurate properties of the target galaxy.

In this work, we present laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations of dielectronic recombination (DR) of Fe XV forming Fe XIV. The motivation for this research stems from its importance in modeling various astrophysical plasmas such as those found in the solar corona and some X-ray emitting astrophysical objects. The precise knowledge of the DR rate coefficient enables accurate calculation of Fe XIV population and ionization fraction in these environments.

The experimental measurements were carried out utilizing an Electron Beam Ion Trap (EBIT) coupled with an X-ray detector. The DR rate coefficients were obtained by measuring the 1s2s$^3$S$_1$ - 1s2p$^3$P$_2$ dielectronic recombination resonance (DRR) energy position and strength. Our theoretical calculations were performed using the non-perturbative R-matrix method, where we have included 95 fine-structure levels within the $n=2$ shell.

Our experimental measurements of the DRR energies and strengths for Fe XV show excellent agreement with our R-matrix calculations. We obtained the DR rate coefficient for Fe XV forming Fe XIV over a temperature range of log$_{10}$T[K] 6.0-7.0 with uncertainties less than 10%. Our results can be used to improve calculations of optical and X-ray line intensities in astrophysical sources as well as to promote future astrophysical observations.

In this study, we investigate the statistical properties of the far-infrared (FIR) emission from interstellar dust in order to better understand the properties and evolution of the interstellar medium (ISM). The FIR emission from dust is one of the most important probes of the ISM and its properties, such as dust temperature and emissivity, are crucial for our understanding of the ISM's physical conditions and processes. This study attempts to address the lack of a systematic study of the statistical properties of the FIR emission of dust in the literature. 

We analyze the FIR emission from a sample of over 1000 galaxies observed by the Herschel Space Observatory, and quantify the relationships between dust luminosity and several key parameters, including stellar mass, star formation rate, and metallicity. Our results suggest that the FIR emission from dust is closely linked to the star formation activity and the chemical composition of the ISM. We also investigate the dust temperature and emissivity properties across the sample and find that they are highly variable. 

The key ideas involved in this study are the use of statistical techniques to examine the properties of dust emission and the close relationship between the dust properties and the ISM conditions. The methodology we employ involves the use of multi-wavelength data and statistical analysis techniques to derive the principal physical parameters and statistical relationships. Our study sheds new light on the statistical properties of dust FIR emission and provides valuable insights into the evolution and properties of the ISM.

In this study, we explore the survival of millimeter to centimeter-sized grains in protoplanetary disks. The problem we aim to solve pertains to the seemingly contradictory observations of grain growth and limited grain retention in such disks. While protoplanetary disks are known to be the birthplaces of planets, it remains unclear how the growth of dust grains from micron to millimeter sizes occurs and how these grains are ultimately retained or lost from their natal disks. Our motivation for this research is to gain a better understanding of the formation of planets and planetary systems, which is vital in understanding our own solar system and its history. 

To achieve this, we utilize a high-resolution numerical model to simulate dust dynamics in protoplanetary disks. This allows us to investigate the growth and survival of grain populations of different sizes under varying conditions. We find that while larger grains are more likely to be retained, the survival of smaller grains is imperative for the growth of larger grains. Our key finding is that turbulence plays a crucial role in both the evolution of dust and the retention of grains. Our methodology involves a combination of numerical simulations, analytical calculations, and comparison with observational data. Our results have significant implications for the formation and evolution of planets and contribute to our understanding of the processes that shape protoplanetary disks.

In this work, we present results from a multiwavelength study of young massive star forming regions, focusing on the dust environment. Our study aims to investigate the properties of the dust and gas in the densest regions of these star forming regions and explore how these properties relate to the formation of massive stars. We use data from the Herschel infrared space telescope and the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment (APEX) telescope to probe the dust properties at different wavelengths between 70µm and 870µm. We find that the dust temperatures and luminosities in these regions are higher than those in other star forming regions, indicating that they are characterized by higher mass accretion rates. We also find evidence for high gas-to-dust ratios, suggesting that the gas is less processed and therefore more pristine in these regions. 

Our results shed light on the intricate interplay between stars, the gas, and the dust in star forming regions and provide insights into the conditions required for the formation of massive stars. This work contributes to a larger effort in understanding the fundamental physical processes driving star formation and the role of these massive stars in shaping the structure and evolution of galaxies. The methodology employed in this study can be extended to other star forming regions and can be used to uncover the underlying physical processes governing the formation of stars in the universe.

In this work, we focus on exploring the phenomenon of spin-orbit coupling in non-Abelian hydrodynamics. The motivation behind this research is the growing relevance of spintronics in the field of computing and information technology. Spin transport mediated by spin-orbit coupling is a promising area of study for creating next-generation information processing devices. However, the understanding of spin transport in non-Abelian systems, where particles exchange both spin and charge, is still incomplete due to the complex nature of the interactions.

Using a combination of theoretical and computational methods, we introduce a framework to study the spin flow in non-Abelian hydrodynamics. We derive a set of equations that describe the dynamics of spin flow under the influence of various factors such as magnetic fields and boundary conditions. We also study the effect of non-Abelian topological structures on spin flow.

Our results reveal the emergence of novel transport phenomena in non-Abelian systems, such as spin vortices and spin textures. Additionally, we find that the character of the spin transport is significantly altered by the non-Abelian topology, leading to surprising behavior not observed in Abelian systems.

In conclusion, this work sheds light on the interplay of non-Abelian hydrodynamics and spin transport, opening doors for innovative ideas in the field of spintronics.

We present a study focused on the infrared (IR) extinction law of a dark cloud core at extreme depth. Our motivation for this research arises from the need to explore the underlying physical nature of the extinction law, particularly concerning the central regions of dark clouds. To achieve this, we used publicly available IR data from the Spitzer Space Telescope and applied Monte Carlo radiative transfer modeling to a selected dark cloud core.

Our key methodology included spectral energy distribution fitting of the core, using a two-component model consisting of a central protostar surrounded by a dusty envelope. We then examined the ratio of the visual over IR extinction, known as the selective extinction ratio (Rv), as a function of the line of sight depth. Our results demonstrate a trend of Rv decreasing with increasing depth into the cloud core, indicative of grain growth in the central dense regions of the core.

Our study provides crucial insights into the physical processes driving the dust properties in the central regions of dark cloud cores. The research highlights the essential role of grain growth and its impact on thermal emission and dust properties. Our findings have significant implications for the understanding of the evolution of dense cores and protostars in the early stages of star formation. Overall, our study highlights the importance and suitability of IR observations for probing the physical properties of dark cloud cores.

In this study, we present a spectrophotometric model that has been applied to the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (WINGS) dataset of cluster galaxies. The motivation for this research was to investigate the physical properties that govern the evolution of galaxies in clusters, including their star formation histories, chemical enrichment, and mass assembly. By analyzing the spectroscopic data from the WINGS survey, we aimed to identify key correlations between these properties and determine their underlying physical drivers.

Our model is based on a Bayesian approach, which allows us to quantify the uncertainties associated with our results and provides a robust statistical framework for comparing different models. Using this method, we found that the star formation histories of galaxies in clusters are complex and exhibit a wide range of timescales and amplitudes of star formation activity. We also observed that the chemical enrichment histories of these galaxies are strongly influenced by their stellar masses, with more massive galaxies showing higher metallicity.

Overall, our results support the hypothesis that the evolution of galaxies in clusters is driven by a combination of internal processes, such as star formation and chemical enrichment, as well as external processes, such as tidal interactions and gas stripping. Our spectrophotometric model provides a powerful tool for understanding these complex mechanisms and sheds new light on the fundamental processes that shape the evolution of galaxies in the universe.

In this work, we investigate the distribution of the very first PopIII stars and their correlation with bright z~6 quasars. The motivation for this research arises from the fact that the first stars are crucial in shaping the evolution of the early universe and that the quasars at z~6 represent the most luminous objects in the universe, which can help us understand the formation of galaxies and black holes. We employ numerical simulations and analyze their outputs to trace the formation and evolution of the first stars and their spatial distribution with respect to bright quasars. Our main result is that PopIII stars appear to have formed in the highest density regions of the universe, where the first bright quasars are observed. Furthermore, we find that the feedback from these stars and quasars leads to the heating and ionization of gas in their vicinity, which sets the stage for the formation of the first galaxies. This work provides insights into the early universe, shedding light on the mechanisms that governed the formation of the first sources of light and their relation to the most luminous objects we observe today.

In this study, we investigate the age constraints in the double pulsar system J0737-3039. By analyzing the system's orbital evolution, we aimed to determine the minimum and maximum ages of the pulsars. Through this, we seek to address the problem of constraining the ages of binary pulsars, as accurate age estimations are essential for understanding the physics of these systems.

Using timing observations from radio telescopes, we fit orbital models to the pulsar data and derive the system's age. By considering various model uncertainties, we calculated the maximum and minimum ages of the pulsars. Our study reveals that the binary system had a minimum age of 85 million years and a maximum age of 210 million years. These results are consistent with previous age estimations for both pulsars.

Our study's key idea is that age constraints placed on binary pulsars provide valuable insight into the binary's formation and evolution, as well as their resultant gravitational wave emission. These determinations aid in understanding pulsar evolution and the fundamental physics of neutron stars.

In conclusion, our work places constraints on the ages of the double pulsar system J0737-3039, with implications for our understanding of binary pulsar formation and evolution. Overall, these age estimates provide insight into the complex dynamics of these fascinating systems.

In this study, we propose an adaptive strategy for the classification of G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), which represent a vital class of transmembrane proteins that play an essential role in diverse physiological processes. Upon activation by an extracellular ligand, GPCRs activate intracellular signaling pathways mediated by G-proteins, which in turn, regulate various cellular functions. Due to their significant role in cellular signaling, GPCRs present potential targets for drug development. However, the vast number of GPCRs, coupled with their high structural diversity, pose a significant challenge in predicting their biological functions and designing drugs. 

Our work attempts to solve the problem of accurately classifying GPCRs based on their primary amino acid sequences. We used a combination of feature extraction techniques and machine learning algorithms to create an adaptive classifier capable of accommodating newly discovered GPCRs and ever-increasing sequence data. Our results show that our adaptive classifier outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity while requiring less computational resources. Overall, our adaptive strategy represents a valuable framework for the classification of GPCRs, which may lead to a better understanding of their biological functions and facilitate drug discovery efforts.

In our work, we investigate the families of holomorphic bundles, with a strong motivation to develop a better understanding of the geometric behavior of such bundles. In particular, we aim to investigate the role of the curvature of the bundle connection in relation to its holomorphic symmetry, as well as to study the relationship between deformation classes of these bundles and the space of their holomorphic sections. 

Our work addresses a significant problem in the field of algebraic geometry and topology, which is the lack of a comprehensive understanding of how the curvature of the connection behaves in families of complex bundles. Our approach is to use a combination of analytical and geometric techniques, building on the foundations of the theory of deformation quantization and the concept of torus actions on vector bundles. 

Our results suggest that the curvature of the connection plays a crucial role in the deformation theory of holomorphic bundles. Specifically, we can see that there is a close relationship between the curvature and the deformation classes of the bundle, as well as between the curvature and the space of holomorphic sections. Our findings are a significant contribution to the field and could lead to a better understanding of the geometry of complex vector bundles.

We present a theoretical study of the electronic properties of a C$_{20}$ molecule using the extended Hubbard model. The Hubbard model considers the interplay between the kinetic energy and Coulomb interaction of electrons in a lattice, which leads to the formation of strongly correlated electron-electron pairs. However, this model is limited in its ability to capture the effects of long-range interactions and excitonic effects. The extended Hubbard model overcomes this limitation by including an additional interaction term that includes long-range Coulomb interactions.

Our aim is to study the effects of long-range interactions on the electronic properties of the C$_{20}$ molecule. Previous studies have shown the presence of excitonic states, which are formed due to the strong electron-electron interactions in the system. We investigate how the inclusion of long-range interactions affects the formation and stability of these excitonic states.

We employ a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to solve the extended Hubbard model. We use density functional theory (DFT) to obtain the physical parameters required for the model, such as the hopping integral and on-site Coulomb interaction. We then solve the extended Hubbard model using Monte Carlo simulations to obtain the thermodynamic properties of the system.

Our work aims to provide a deeper understanding of the electronic properties of C$_{20}$ and the effects of long-range interactions on strongly correlated electron systems. It also sheds light on the efficacy of the extended Hubbard model in describing such systems.

In this study, we report on the precise timing of X-ray pulsar 1E 1207.4-5209, which is a neutron star that was weakly magnetized at birth and has remained relatively steady throughout its life. The main goal of this work is to improve our understanding of the physics underlying neutron stars and their magnetic fields.

To achieve this goal, we carried out detailed observations of 1E 1207.4-5209 using the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories. We analyzed the resulting data using state-of-the-art modeling techniques, including the use of Bayesian statistical methods to estimate the parameters of the pulsar's timing model.

Our results show that the pulsar's rotation is extremely stable, with a period that is virtually constant over time. This implies that the pulsar's magnetic field, which is thought to be responsible for its spin-down, is also relatively stable and weak.

Overall, our study confirms previous findings that 1E 1207.4-5209 is a rare and interesting neutron star, and sheds new light on the physical processes that govern its behavior. These results have important implications for our understanding of neutron stars in general, and may help to constrain models of their formation and evolution.

In this work, we explore the prospects of making precision measurements of atomic helium using direct frequency comb spectroscopy. The problem we aim to solve is the lack of high-precision measurements of atomic helium, despite its fundamental importance in both atomic physics and quantum mechanics. Despite decades of experimental efforts, most measurements of helium's atomic structure and spectra are still based on theoretical calculations due to the lack of accurate experimental data. 

Our research is motivated by the need to better understand the fundamental properties of atomic helium. By advancing our knowledge of this simple, two-electron system, we can improve our understanding of more complex atoms and molecules. 

To achieve our goal, we employ direct frequency comb spectroscopy, which is a powerful tool for measuring the spectra of atoms and molecules with unprecedented precision. The key idea behind our work is to use the frequency comb technique to directly measure the energy levels of the helium atom, thus enabling accurate determination of fundamental atomic properties. 

In our methodology, we first use the frequency comb to measure helium's atomic spectra to an accuracy of a few parts in 10^10. We then use these measurements to extract new values for the ionization energy of helium, enabling us to better understand the properties of this important atom. Our work holds great promise for improving our understanding of the fundamental properties of atoms and molecules.

In this work, we investigate the initial conditions of star formation in the Ophiuchus main cloud by studying the kinematics of protocluster condensations. We identify ten protocluster condensations based on molecular line observations with the Nobeyama 45 m telescope. By analyzing the kinematics of the condensations, we find that they are gravitationally bound and have supersonic internal motions. These findings suggest that the protocluster condensations are the sites of future star formation in the Ophiuchus main cloud. 

The motivation for this research lies in the importance of understanding the early stages of star formation, which are poorly understood. Protocluster condensations are thought to be the precursors to star clusters, which are common objects in the universe. Studying the properties of protocluster condensations, such as their kinematics, can provide insight into the processes that lead to the formation of star clusters. Additionally, the Ophiuchus main cloud is a nearby star-forming region that has been extensively studied, making it an ideal target for understanding the initial conditions of star formation. 

This work attempts to solve the problem of determining the initial conditions of star formation in the Ophiuchus main cloud by studying the kinematics of protocluster condensations. Our results provide important information about the properties of protocluster condensations and suggest that they are the sites of future star formation in this region. The identification of these protocluster condensations also provides targets for future observations, which can help to further our understanding of the early stages of star formation.

In this work, we investigate the properties of isolated horizons in higher-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity. The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the behavior of black holes in higher dimensions, which are an essential aspect of theories such as superstring theory and braneworld scenarios. To achieve this, we extend the isolated horizon framework to dimensions beyond four and explore its implications in the context of the Gauss-Bonnet (GB) term of the Einstein-Hilbert action.

We first establish the formalism for isolated horizons in the higher-dimensional context and elucidate their key properties, such as the surface gravity, angular momentum, and electric charge. We then demonstrate that the presence of the GB term modifies the horizon conditions and introduces new effects, such as the possibility of non-trivial topologies and higher-dimensional Gauss-Bonnet charges. We also investigate the thermodynamics of these horizons and show that the inclusion of the GB term changes the behavior of the thermodynamic quantities.

Our methodology involves a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, in which we use the Hamiltonian framework to derive the evolution equations and then solve them numerically for black hole examples in various dimensions. Our results shed light on the behavior of higher-dimensional black holes and enhance our understanding of the role of the GB term in their properties and dynamics.

Searching for the missing baryons at low redshift is an ongoing problem in astrophysics. Through our research, we aim to find the missing matter in the Universe, which is unaccounted for by the observed baryonic matter. We utilized the cosmic web, which is a lattice-like structure of galaxies and gas in the Universe, to track the missing baryons. We computed the density of gas in filaments, which connect the galaxy clusters, by using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS).

Our results show that, at low redshift, the baryon fraction in filaments is up to 50% higher than what is observed in galaxy clusters, indicating a significant reservoir of baryonic matter in the cosmic web. Our findings are consistent with previous work, which suggests the presence of diffuse gas outside galaxy clusters. However, the baryonic matter's distribution remains elusive, leading us to conclude that dedicated surveys are needed to locate the hot and cold components of the intergalactic medium.

The study's motivation is to address the discrepancy between the observed and predicted baryon fraction in the Universe, as the discrepancy could indicate a gap in our physical understanding of the Universe. Our research offers insight into the baryonic matter's distribution in the cosmic web, and the observed baryonic fraction can be incorporated into future simulations to reconcile the discrepancy between observations and predictions. Our results will contribute to a more coherent and complete understanding of the structure and evolution of the Universe.

In this work, we present a new method of integrating stochastic differential equations on Lie groups using stochastic Lie group integrators. Our method is motivated by the difficulty of numerically solving stochastic differential equations on non-Euclidean manifolds such as Lie groups, which arise frequently in applications such as robotics and control theory. Current approaches using the Euler-Maruyama scheme suffer from the fact that they do not preserve the geometric structure of the Lie group, leading to numerical errors that accumulate over time.

Our method overcomes this issue by constructing stochastic integrators that are exactly geometric, allowing us to simulate stochastic processes on Lie groups with high accuracy and long-term stability. We provide a theoretical analysis of our method and show that it possesses desirable properties such as strong convergence. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to practical problems such as simulating the motion of a rigid body in a viscous fluid.

Our results show that the stochastic Lie group integrators offer a practical and efficient method for simulating stochastic differential equations on Lie groups. The numerical experiments conducted revealed that our approach provides more accurate approximations than existing methods, with lower computational costs. This work provides a valuable contribution to the field of stochastic analysis on manifolds and opens up new avenues for applications in areas such as control theory, robotics, and machine learning.

In this paper, we tackle the problem of scheduling directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) under uncertainty. The uncertainty in the DAGs is due to possible changes in the processing times of the tasks or the availability of the resources. We formulate the problem as a stochastic optimization problem, where the objective is to minimize the expected makespan of the schedule, which is the maximum completion time of any task in the DAGs. We propose an optimization algorithm based on the decomposition of the problem into subproblems, each of which is solved by a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver. We also propose several heuristics to reduce the computational time of the algorithm without sacrificing the quality of the solutions. We evaluate the proposed algorithm on various types of random DAGs and compare it with several state-of-the-art algorithms. The results show that our algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of the solution quality and the computational time. The motivation for this research is to provide an efficient and effective algorithm for scheduling DAGs in several practical applications, such as task scheduling in cloud computing, project management, and production planning.

In this study, we investigate multidimensional fluid motions with planar waves and explore the mathematical framework and computational techniques to understand and predict these complex phenomena.  Our aim is to unravel the intricate dynamics of fluids and waves by combining analytical and numerical methods. The study focuses on the evolution of fluids under the influence of planar waves, which are periodic disturbances that move along a single direction. 

We start by developing a mathematical model that incorporates the key physical and geometric factors that are relevant to the problem. This model describes the fluid motion as a system of partial differential equations that capture the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy of the fluid. Using the model, we derive the equations that govern the evolution of fluid properties, such as pressure, velocity, and density, under the influence of planar waves.

To solve the equations, we use numerical methods based on finite difference and finite element methods, which offer accurate and efficient solutions for complex problems. We validate our results using numerical simulations and compare them with analytical solutions where possible.

Our study provides significant insights into the dynamics of fluids with planar waves, which are relevant to many real-world applications, such as ocean engineering, coastal structures, and fluid mechanics. The results of this study could aid design and planning of systems affected by these phenomena.

In this work, we present a study on the ongoing galactic accretion, which is a crucial process in galaxy formation and evolution. Understanding this process is necessary to comprehend how galaxies grow and how they acquire new material to fuel the star formation. We approach this problem with simulations and observations of condensed gas in hot halos, which are reservoirs of gas surrounding galaxies. Our simulations reveal that condensed gas in halos may originate from several sources, including gas cooling, inflow, and merger events. Additionally, we find that the amount of condensed gas is significantly affected by various parameters such as halo mass, accretion rate, and AGN feedback. 

Furthermore, we carry out observational studies on several nearby galaxies using the Hubble Space Telescope. Our observations show that the hot halos contain cooler filaments of gas, which could be the condensed gas predicted by our simulations. These results can help us better understand how galaxies acquire new material, and ultimately, how they grow and evolve over time. Our work sheds new light on the complex process of galactic accretion and emphasizes the need for further observations and simulations to improve our understanding of it.

In this work, we investigate the low energy cut-offs and hard X-ray spectra in high-z radio-loud quasars, with a particular focus on the Suzaku view of RBS315. Our goal is to provide a deeper understanding of the physical processes that occur in the high energy regime of these objects, and to contribute to the growing body of research on the properties of distant, active galactic nuclei (AGN).

To achieve this, we used data from the Suzaku satellite to perform a detailed analysis of the X-ray spectra of RBS315, which is known to be a powerful radio-loud quasar at a redshift of z=0.11. Our methodology consisted of fitting the X-ray spectrum with a combination of models, including a power-law component to describe the hard X-ray emission, and a thermal component to account for the soft X-ray emission.

Our results show that the hard X-ray spectrum of RBS315 is quite steep, with a spectral index of Γ~2.  This is consistent with previous studies of high-z radio-loud quasars, and supports the idea that these objects are powered by accretion onto supermassive black holes. Moreover, we find evidence for a low energy cut-off in the X-ray spectrum of RBS315, which suggests the presence of thermal emission from a corona surrounding the accretion disk.

Overall, our study provides new insights into the X-ray emission properties of high-z radio-loud quasars, and highlights the importance of systematic studies of these objects to further our understanding of AGN physics.

We present a research work on Relativistic X-ray Lines from the Inner Accretion Disks Around Black Holes. The study investigates the X-ray spectral features observed from near the horizon of a black hole, and the associated physical processes that generate these features. The key idea behind this research is to understand the geometry of the inner accretion disk around black holes, and the physical mechanisms that produce the observed spectral features. The methodology employed includes the use of analytical models and numerical simulations to explore the properties of the accretion disk and its radiation.

The primary problem that this work seeks to solve is the need to understand the nature and origin of the relativistic X-ray spectral lines that have been observed in the vicinity of black holes. These spectral features are thought to originate from the innermost regions of the accretion disk, where the strong gravitational field of the black hole affects the motion of matter and radiation. Our research aims to shed light on the processes that result in these spectral lines, so as to provide insights into the dynamics of the accretion disk and the nature of the black hole.

Our results obtained show that the relativistic X-ray lines are indeed a consequence of the matter motion around a black hole, with the strong gravitational field being the primary driver of the spectral features. The findings also highlight the importance of the relativistic effects in the innermost regions of the accretion disk, and provide a new understanding of the physical processes that shape the X-ray spectra of black holes. The work offers a significant contribution to our understanding of astrophysical phenomena and provides a new perspective for future research on black holes.

In this research, we investigate the predictability of the solar cycle using mean-field models, a popular tool in the field of solar physics. Our motivation for this investigation is to improve our understanding of the solar cycle and to make accurate predictions of its activity. To achieve this goal, we first propose a new approach that combines mean-field models with the Bayesian framework. This method allows the incorporation of new observations over time and provides us with a constantly updated estimate of the solar activity levels. We then apply this approach to the observed solar cycle data and compare our predictions with the actual observations. Our analysis shows that our new method outperforms the traditional mean-field models and provides more accurate predictions of the solar cycle. Furthermore, we use our approach to make predictions for the next solar cycle, which is expected to peak around 2025. Our results suggest that the activity levels during the next solar cycle will be similar to the current cycle, with a peak in activity around 2025. Our findings have important implications for predicting the effects of solar activity on Earth's climate and for forecasting space weather events.

In this study, we present the results of high resolution mid-infrared spectroscopy of ultraluminous infrared galaxies (ULIRGs). ULIRGs are galaxies that emit an extremely large amount of infrared radiation, and are thought to be powered by intense star formation and/or active galactic nuclei. These galaxies are crucial to our understanding of galaxy evolution and the role of feedback mechanisms that regulate star formation in galaxies. However, the nature of the dominant energy source in ULIRGs remains unclear.

Through our observations using the Infrared Spectrograph on board the Spitzer Space Telescope, we seek to identify the dominant energy source in ULIRGs through the detection of mid-infrared spectral features that are indicative of active galactic nuclei or star formation. We also aim to obtain measurements of the physical properties of the gas and dust in these galaxies.

Our results show that the mid-infrared spectra of most ULIRGs are dominated by emission from star formation, and we detect only a few sources that show clear signs of active galactic nuclei activity. We also find evidence for variations in the properties of the gas and dust in different regions of the galaxies, which may be linked to differences in the energetics of star formation and feedback mechanisms.

Our study highlights the importance of mid-infrared spectroscopy in understanding the energy sources and physical properties of galaxies in the early universe, and provides new insights into the complex interplay between star formation and active galactic nuclei in ULIRGs.

In this paper, we aim to refute a recent attack on the REESSE1+ cryptosystem that was published in the academic literature. The motivation behind our research is premised on the need to enhance the security of cryptosystems used in various applications, including banking and military communication systems. 

The problem we seek to solve is to establish the soundness of the REESSE1+ cryptosystem in the face of an attack that purported to expose its vulnerabilities. We adopt a rigorous and comprehensive approach to studying the REESSE1+ cryptosystem and the claimed attack on it. 

Our research is based on an intensive analysis of the algorithm and mathematical foundations of the REESSE1+ cryptosystem. We also conduct a series of computer simulations and experiments to test the theoretical assumptions and algorithms that underlie the system. 

Our results show that the attack on the REESSE1+ cryptosystem is trivial and does not pose a serious security threat to the system. Our study thus provides valuable insights and contributions to the field of cryptography by refuting a potentially damaging attack on a vital cryptosystem. This paper is, therefore, a must-read for security experts, researchers and practitioners interested in the resilience and efficacy of cryptosystems.

In this study, we investigate the charmless three-body decays of B mesons, which is a complex decay process that has been poorly understood. We attempt to identify the key decay modes and decay amplitudes by analyzing the decay products of B mesons, which consist of two lighter mesons and one light neutral meson. Our methodology involves computing the decay amplitudes using perturbative QCD and chiral perturbation theory combined with experimental data to constrain the parameters. The study is motivated by the fact that charmless three-body decays play a crucial role in determining the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix elements and provide new and independent tests of the Standard Model. Moreover, it gives insight into the strong dynamics of the hadronic sector and represents an essential tool to explore physics beyond the Standard Model. Finally, the knowledge of the charmless three-body decays of B mesons is crucial for the analysis of LHCb data, which aims to measure the CP violation and other rare decays. This study will contribute to the understanding of the charmless three-body decays of B mesons and will help to uncover the underlying physics of these processes.

In this research project, we examined the effect of magnetic field on spontaneous Fermi surface symmetry breaking. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that symmetry breaking in condensed matter physics has been a topic of considerable interest over the years, and understanding how magnetic fields affect this phenomenon is essential for developing novel materials for next-generation technology. 

Our work aimed to solve the problem of how magnetic fields influence the broken symmetry of the Fermi surface in different materials. We employed a theoretical framework based on Landau's theory of spontaneous symmetry breaking and a phenomenological model for the Fermi surface. The model was then used to derive the magnetic field dependence of the order parameter and related thermodynamic properties of the system.

Our results revealed that magnetic fields can significantly modify the symmetry of the Fermi surface to either a complete or partial suppression of the order parameter of the system. Furthermore, the changes in the symmetry of the Fermi surface caused by magnetic fields may lead to a plethora of exotic phenomena, including small-angle quasielastic magnetic neutron scattering.

In conclusion, our work provides new insights into the effect of magnetic fields on spontaneous Fermi surface symmetry breaking, which can aid researchers in developing new materials for advanced technological applications and improve our understanding of fundamental condensed matter physics.

In this work, we present the results of spectroscopy and multiband photometry of the afterglow of intermediate duration gamma-ray burst 040924 and its host galaxy. Our main motivation for conducting this research was to understand the physical properties of these transient events and their host galaxies. Gamma-ray bursts are one of the most energetic events that occur in the universe. They are also important probes of the early universe as they are detectable out to high redshifts. Our aim was to investigate the nature of these events in the context of their host galaxies.

We obtained spectroscopic observations of the host galaxy using the Keck telescope and multiband photometry using several telescopes including Swift, TNG and RATIR. Our key idea was to use the afterglow observations to derive the physical properties of the afterglow shock. This allowed us to study the properties of the host galaxy and compare them with those of other host galaxies.

Our analysis of the data revealed several interesting results. We found that the host galaxy of 040924 is a low-metallicity star-forming galaxy. Moreover, the origin of the gamma-ray burst is likely to be related to the core-collapse of a massive star. Our work provides important insights into the physical properties of intermediate duration gamma-ray bursts and their host galaxies.

In this study, we investigate the oscillation thresholds for "striking outwards" reeds that are coupled to a resonator. We explore the dynamics of the coupled system and their dependence on the physical parameters of the individual elements. The motivation for this research stems from the desire to better understand the fundamental principles underlying the operation of musical instruments such as the clarinet, saxophone, and oboe, which rely on the interplay between the reed and the resonator for generating sound.

Our approach involves analyzing the system using a combination of analytical methods and numerical simulations. We consider both linear and nonlinear models and investigate the dependence of the oscillation thresholds on the stiffness and damping of the reed, the geometry of the resonator, and the strength of the coupling between them. 

Our results demonstrate that the oscillation thresholds are highly sensitive to these parameters, and that small changes in the system can lead to dramatic changes in the amplitude and frequency of the oscillations. We also find that the nonlinear effects play a significant role in the dynamics of the system, leading to the generation of complex, multi-harmonic waveforms. Our findings have important implications for the design and optimization of musical instruments, as well as for the understanding of the general principles governing oscillatory systems.

In this paper, we investigate regular homogeneous T-models with vacuum dark fluid. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that cosmological models incorporating dark energy continue to be a topic of great interest in current cosmology. We aim to explore the physical consequences of vacuum dark fluid in a T-model, which is a particular class of cosmological models characterized by homogeneity and isotropy. 

By integrating the field equations for T-models with dark fluid, we obtain exact solutions that describe the dynamics of the universe at different epochs. Our main results show that vacuum dark fluid can generate accelerated expansion in T-models, which is consistent with recent observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation and large-scale structure surveys. We also observe that the presence of dark fluid affects the evolution of the cosmic scale factor, which can be used to constrain the properties of dark energy.

Our key ideas and methodology focus on the mathematical formalism of T-models and the physical interpretation of the solutions obtained. We adopt a formal academic and scientific writing voice and use the first plural person to convey our collaborative effort in this research. We use active voice to clearly express our findings and their implications in the context of current cosmology research. In conclusion, our study sheds light on the potential role of vacuum dark fluid in the evolution of T-models and provides new insights into the nature of dark energy in the universe.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of the local stellar velocity field via vector spherical harmonics. The problem that this work attempts to solve is the characterization of the kinematical properties of stars in the Galactic neighborhood. The motivation for this research stems from the need to obtain a better understanding of the dynamical structure and evolution of the Milky Way, including the distribution of dark matter.

We analyzed the data from the Gaia-ESO survey and applied a vector spherical harmonics decomposition to the velocity field in the Solar neighborhood. Our approach allowed us to separate the velocity field into its radial, azimuthal, and polar components and study their properties. We found that the velocity field exhibits both coherent motion and random fluctuations, with clear signatures of bulk rotation and possible streaming motions on smaller scales. The amplitudes of the modes of the vector harmonics are in agreement with expectations from theoretical models.

Our results provide new insights into the kinematical properties of stars in the Galactic neighborhood and contribute to our understanding of the large-scale structure and evolution of the Milky Way. This work demonstrates the powerful tools that can be applied to study the velocity field of nearby stars and paves the way for future studies of Galactic dynamics using vector spherical harmonics.

In this work, we investigate the coherence dynamics of non-equilibrium states in one-dimensional Bose gases. The study of coherence dynamics is crucial in understanding the properties of these systems and their interaction with the environment. Our research was motivated by the recent experimental advances in the manipulation of Bose gases, which have allowed for the creation of non-equilibrium states that exhibit interesting coherence properties. 

Using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we developed a theoretical framework to investigate the coherence dynamics of Bose gases in non-equilibrium states. We found that the coherence properties of these states are strongly dependent on the non-equilibrium parameters such as the time-dependent potential and driving frequency. Our results also showed that non-equilibrium states display novel coherence properties that can be used for quantum information processing.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the lack of understanding of the coherence dynamics in non-equilibrium states of one-dimensional Bose gases. Our research provides insights into the coherence properties of these states, which can be used to develop new techniques for manipulating quantum systems. Our findings have broad implications for the study of non-equilibrium states in general and provide a roadmap for the continued investigation of coherence dynamics in condensed matter systems.

In this study, we examine the velocity structure of moving magnetic feature pairs around sunspots by investigating supporting evidence for the U-loop model. The U-loop model suggests that submerged magnetic fields in sunspots exhibit a twisted and helical configuration, creating two moving magnetic feature (MMF) pairs running in opposite directions. Our aim is to explore the dynamics of these MMF pairs, particularly the velocity structure, to ascertain the validity of the U-loop model.

Using time-series data obtained from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we analyze the velocity profiles of MMF pairs located around sunspots. Our results show that MMF pairs exhibit a distinct velocity pattern, characterized by an initial inward motion, followed by an outward motion at a faster speed, while displaying a notable asymmetry in their velocity profiles. Importantly, these results corroborate the predictions of the U-loop model, which attributes these features to the motion of the Sun's twisted magnetic fields.

Our analysis thus provides strong evidence for the U-loop model, backed up by empirical data. The implications of these findings could have significant implications for our understanding of sunspot dynamics, as well as the role of magnetic fields in the Sun's interior.

In this work, we investigate the dynamical heterogeneities of water molecules and their role in breaking the Stokes-Einstein and Stokes-Einstein-Debye (SED) relations through molecular dynamics simulations. The SED relations connect the diffusion coefficient of a particle to its friction and the temperature of the solvent, and have been widely used to describe the transport properties of simple liquids such as water. However, recent experiments and simulations have shown that the SED relations break down in complex liquids such as supercooled water, and their underlying assumptions do not hold.

Our results show that the breakdown of the SED relations in water can be attributed to the dynamical heterogeneities of the liquid, where some regions of the liquid are more mobile than others. We find that the diffusion of water molecules in these heterogeneous regions is faster than in the bulk, leading to a non-linear relationship between the diffusion coefficient, viscosity, and temperature. Moreover, we observe a decoupling between the rotational and translational motion of water molecules, suggesting that the rotational and translation relaxation times depend on different factors.

Our study is motivated by the need for a better understanding of the transport properties of complex liquids such as water, and our work sheds light on the role of dynamical heterogeneities in breaking the SED relations. We adopt a molecular dynamics simulation approach with state-of-the-art force fields and statistical analysis to investigate the dynamical properties of water on a microscopic level.

In this study, we analyze the spatial characteristics of joint application networks in Japanese patents. Our key motivation is to investigate the spatial patterns that emerge when firms cooperate in patent applications. We aim to understand how geographic proximity and inter-organizational relationships influence joint application networks in Japan. 

To achieve our objective, we first extract co-applicants from Japanese patents granted between 2000 and 2018. We then construct joint application networks by connecting co-applicants who have filed for a patent together. The networks are analyzed using spatial statistical techniques, including measures of network density, centrality, and clustering. 

Our findings reveal that the majority of joint application networks cluster in urban areas of Japan, consistent with the notion of an innovation cluster. Additionally, our results show that firms cooperate more often with geographically proximate partners. However, we also find that established inter-organizational relationships, such as joint ventures and technology licensing, do not necessarily lead to frequent patenting together. 

This study contributes to the literature on joint patents, innovation clusters, and inter-organizational relationships by providing unique insights into the spatial characteristics of joint application networks in Japan. Our research offers important implications for policy-makers seeking to promote innovation and regional development through cross-sectoral collaborations.

We present a novel approach to calculate the luminosity function of binary X-ray sources using the Scenario Machine. Our work aims to solve the problem of predicting the number of X-ray sources in a given volume of space to better understand the origin and evolution of X-ray binaries. Our methodology consists of integrating the Scenario Machine with X-ray luminosity functions, which are functions that describe the distribution of the luminosity of X-ray sources. The Scenario Machine is a powerful computational tool that allows us to generate a large number of possible scenarios for the formation and evolution of X-ray binaries, considering several physical mechanisms.

Our results show that the predicted number of X-ray binaries is highly dependent on the assumed population synthesis model and the input physics. The use of the Scenario Machine allows us to explore a wide range of physical parameters, providing a more realistic range of possible luminosity functions for binary X-ray sources. We found that the predicted number of bright X-ray sources is particularly sensitive to the assumed mass-transfer rate, indicating the importance of including more accurate physics in population synthesis models.

Overall, our work provides a valuable tool for understanding the observations of X-ray binaries and their contributions to the overall X-ray emission of galaxies. Our approach can be extended to other astrophysical populations and can be used to explore physical parameter space in a robust and efficient way.

In this paper, we present a study focused on the understanding of transients from initial conditions in N-body simulations using Lagrangian perturbation theory. N-body simulations are one of the primary tools in cosmology to explore the evolution of large-scale structures in the Universe. However, the precise reproduction of observed galaxy clustering statistics remains a challenge. A major source of systematic errors comes from the initial conditions, which are typically generated using linear perturbation theory assumptions. We propose a novel approach that employs Lagrangian perturbation theory to compute the initial conditions for the simulations, thereby accounting for non-linear effects that can have a significant impact on the final clustering statistics. Our proposal is based on the idea that high-order corrections can be systematically included and give rise to non-Gaussianities in the initial conditions. The methodology is tested on a set of numerical experiments, where we demonstrate that our approach leads to improved results in the clustering statistics even on large scales. Our work aims to contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable simulation tools that can be used to test cosmological models and explore the fundamental properties of the Universe.

In this work, we investigate the Dbar-N interaction using both meson-exchange and quark-gluon dynamics. The Dbar-N interaction is of great importance, as it is fundamental in understanding the properties of Dbar-mesons, which are believed to play a significant role in heavy-ion collisions. 

We use two formalisms to describe the Dbar-N interaction: meson-exchange and quark-gluon dynamics. The meson-exchange formalism involves the exchange of mesons between Dbar and N nucleons, while quark-gluon dynamics considers the Dbar-N interaction in terms of the interactions between quarks and gluons. Our methodology consists of predicting the meson-exchange and quark-gluon contributions individually, and also combining them to understand their combined effect.

The motivation behind our research is to uncover the nature of the interactions involved in the Dbar-N interaction and to highlight the most influential forces at play. Throughout the research, we have found that the quark-gluon interactions are more significant than the meson-exchange interactions, unlike previously thought. Furthermore, we found that both the meson-exchange and quark-gluon interactions are of importance in the Dbar-N interaction, and their combined effect can lead to a deeper knowledge of the heavy ion collisions. 

Overall, our work provides a better understanding of the Dbar-N interaction with the help of both meson-exchange and quark-gluon dynamics, highlighting the important role of quark-gluon interactions and the combined effect of both the interactions in heavy-ion collisions.

In this work, we aimed to derive the temperature, mass, and age of evolved stars from high-resolution spectra, using the open cluster IC 4651 and field stars as case studies. Our motivation for this research is grounded in the need to estimate stellar fundamental parameters with high precision and accuracy. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a clear method for determining temperatures, masses, and ages of evolved stars, which are essential for understanding the stellar evolution history. 

We utilized the SME spectral synthesis code and made use of the H𝛽 line for temperature estimates, the Ca II K line for surface gravity, and Fe I and Fe II spectral lines for metallicity determinations. Our results reveal that the derived parameters for IC 4651 field stars are consistent with previous determinations, while the derived cluster parameters show improvement in accuracy. Our age estimation for the cluster is 1.7±0.1 Gyr, which is in agreement with previous studies. 

In conclusion, our approach of using high-resolution spectra and the SME code proved to be effective in deriving stellar fundamental parameters for evolved stars. This study provides vital information for understanding the evolution of stars and can be extended to other types of stars in the future.

In this study, we investigate the effects of thermal micropulses on oscillatory secular modes. Oscillatory secular modes are periodic variations in a star’s pulsation frequency that are believed to be caused by the effects of stellar evolution and convection zone boundaries. These modes play a key role in determining the structure and evolution of stars. However, the physical mechanisms that cause these modes are still not well understood. 

We aim to shed light on this problem by exploring the role of thermal micropulses in inducing oscillatory secular modes. Our simulations show that thermal micropulses can indeed trigger these modes, with their frequency and amplitude depending on the properties of the micropulses. We find that the presence of thermal micropulses can explain some previously unexplained features in observed oscillatory secular modes. Our work thus provides new insights into the underlying mechanisms of these modes and paves the way for future studies in this field.

The motivation for this research stems from the importance of understanding the physical processes that govern stellar evolution. Oscillatory secular modes are a key aspect of this evolution, and understanding their properties and behavior helps us to understand the evolution of stars over time. By investigating the effects of thermal micropulses on these modes, we gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physics and hope to improve our ability to model and predict stellar evolution.

In our research, we investigate the scalar radius of the pion and zeros present in the pion's form factor. The pion is an essential part of the Standard Model of particle physics, and as such, understanding its properties is crucial. The scalar radius of the pion is a measure of the distribution of its mass, while the form factor describes the probability of the pion being scattered at a certain momentum transfer. We approached this problem by using chiral perturbation theory and a dispersive approach, which allowed us to obtain accurate results.

Our investigation revealed that the scalar radius of the pion is not equal to zero, as previously thought. Furthermore, we found evidence of a zero in the pion's form factor at low momentum transfer. This zero is unexpected, as it is not present in the vector form factor and requires the presence of a pion pole in the scattering amplitude.

Our work aims to solve the problem of the scalar radius of the pion and the apparent zero in its form factor. This problem has implications for the understanding of strong interaction physics, and our results contribute to the ongoing discussion about the fundamental properties of the pion. Overall, our methodology and results provide valuable insight into the nature of the pion and its role in modern particle physics.

In this study, we investigate the closed bosonic string field theory at quintic order II, focusing on marginal deformations and effective potential. Our research aims to address the limitations in existing string theories by developing a deeper understanding of the dynamics of the closed bosonic string field. 

The motivation for our study is the need for a comprehensive and unified framework for studying all string theories. Although string theory has become the leading candidate for a unified fundamental theory of physics, it faces significant conceptual and technical challenges, such as the existence of different string theories and the identification of a vacuum state. We believe that understanding the dynamics of the closed bosonic string field theory can contribute to a better understanding of string theory in general.

Our results show that the effective potential of the closed bosonic string field is invariant under marginal deformations, which is a novel finding. We also demonstrate that the effects of marginal deformations can be captured through the variation of the effective potential. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the existence of a duality symmetry that relates two different marginal deformations. These findings contribute to our understanding of the closed bosonic string field theory and may have implications for other areas of physics.

Overall, our research provides a deeper insight into the dynamics of the closed bosonic string field theory, which may contribute to a broader understanding of string theory.

In this paper, we present a novel approach to ensemble learning that leverages the power of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to automatically generate diverse ensembles. Ensemble learning is a popular technique in machine learning, which combines multiple classifiers to improve the overall prediction accuracy of a given task. The traditional approaches to ensemble learning involve manually selecting and combining the member classifiers, which can be time-consuming and requires expert knowledge. Our proposed approach enables the automatic generation of diverse ensembles with minimal human intervention.

Our key idea is to apply EAs to evolve the ensemble composition, aiming to maximize the ensemble's accuracy on a given task. We frame the problem of ensemble composition as a multi-objective optimization problem, with the objectives of maximizing the ensemble's accuracy and minimizing its complexity. We then use a specialized EA, the NSGA-II algorithm, to explore the ensemble's solution space and generate diverse ensembles.

Our approach is evaluated on several benchmark datasets, and the results show that our evolved ensembles outperform or match the performances of traditional ensembles, which require more human intervention. Moreover, our approach generates diverse ensembles that are not available in the literature, which can be useful for improving the understanding of the ensemble's performance and the role of the individual classifiers in the ensemble.

In summary, our work proposes a novel approach to ensemble learning with EAs, which reduces the human intervention required in traditional approaches and generates diverse ensembles with improved accuracy.

Our work focuses on the development and implementation of an online repository for Swift/XRT light curves of Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs). The repository is hosted by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) and contains over 2000 light curves of GRBs observed by the Swift/XRT telescope. Our objective was to provide a user-friendly interface for researchers to access and analyze the data, enhancing collaboration and knowledge-sharing within the scientific community. 

The methodology involved the construction of a web-based interface that includes a search engine, data visualization tools, and access to auxiliary information. Our approach allows users to search for specific GRBs by name, date, or sky coordinates, and to select their preferred data format. The light curves can be presented in different graphical representations and users can perform basic analysis tasks such as measurements of peak flux and fluence. The inclusion of auxiliary information such as redshift, classification, and other spectroscopic data facilitates research on specific GRBs.

The results of our work have been highly satisfying, as researchers in the field can now easily access and analyze a vast quantity of data available in one centralized location. The repository has been and continues to be a valuable resource for researchers worldwide, promoting the scientific investigation of GRBs and collaborations between researchers. This project is motivated by the potential for future discoveries and technological advancements in the field, and the importance of facilitating access to scientific data for researchers.

We present a comprehensive analysis of degree optimization and stability conditions for the min-sum decoder. Our motivation behind this research is to enhance the decoding performance of the min-sum algorithm in low-density parity-check codes.

In the past, there have been several attempts to optimize the degree distribution of codes as well as to ensure the stability condition is satisfied. However, none of them have provided a thorough analysis of how degree optimization affects the stability condition and decoding performance of the min-sum decoder. Therefore, we sought to investigate the relationship between degree optimization and stability condition with respect to the min-sum decoding algorithm.

Our analysis reveals that in the absence of the stability condition, degree optimization can lead to suboptimal decoding performance, as the min-sum algorithm tends to converge to a suboptimal solution. We provide a novel stability condition that guarantees optimal decoding performance when used with carefully optimized degree distributions.

Furthermore, we demonstrate our results using simulations on various codes, and the results obtained show improvements in both the error rate and decoding performance. This research provides important insights for further development of the min-sum decoder, as we now know that degree optimization alone is insufficient for ensuring optimal decoding performance.

In this work, we present a novel method to model transcription factor binding events to DNA using a random walker/jumper representation on a 1D/2D lattice with different affinity sites. We propose a general mathematical framework for the simulation of the binding process and develop two types of models, one with a 1D lattice and the other with a 2D lattice, to demonstrate the flexibility and versatility of our approach. Our method is capable of simulating a broad range of experimental scenarios and can capture subtleties such as correlations between binding events.

To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we present simulation results for different affinity sites in the lattice. We observe that the effective binding rate decreases as the affinity of the sites increases, which is consistent with the experimental results reported in the literature. Additionally, we perform a sensitivity analysis of our model parameters and observe that the performance of our method is robust to changes in the parameters.

Our work provides a new perspective on modeling transcription factor binding events and can serve as a powerful tool for understanding the underlying mechanisms that govern gene regulation and expression. Our method can also be extended to other biological processes where molecular diffusion is involved, such as protein-protein binding, RNA folding, and enzyme catalysis.

In this study, we investigate the formation and collapse of quiescent cloud cores induced by dynamic compressions. The motivation for our research is to better understand the key physical processes that trigger the formation and collapse of quiescent cloud cores. These cores are crucial in the formation of stars, planets, and other astronomical objects. Identifying the factors that contribute to the formation and collapse of these cloud cores, as well as understanding the dynamics of their evolution, will ultimately improve our understanding of the universe and how it has evolved over time.

Our key approach in this work involves numerical simulations, which allow us to investigate the behavior of cloud cores under dynamic compression conditions. We employ a three-dimensional, magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation model to study the effect of compressing a pre-existing cloud core. Our simulation setup includes a hydrostatic initial equilibrium cloud that is subjected to a pulse-driven shock compression. By tracking the evolution of the cloud core under these conditions, we are able to analyze the mechanisms that drive its formation and collapse.

The problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of a comprehensive understanding of the physical processes that govern the formation and collapse of quiescent cloud cores. By studying these processes within the framework of our simulation model, we aim to develop a more detailed understanding of these phenomena and their role in the formation of astronomical objects. Our findings will be relevant to researchers studying the evolution of the universe and the conditions that led to the formation of stars and other celestial bodies.

In this study, we investigate the transient behavior of surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) that are scattered at a subwavelength groove using a theoretical method based on a finite element analysis. The results show that the scattering behavior of the SPPs strongly depends on the position of the groove and the direction of the incident SPPs. Moreover, we found that the scattering amplitude of the SPPs is significantly enhanced when the width of the groove matches the wavelength of the SPPs. This enhancement is attributed to the excitation of Fabry-Perot resonances between the SPPs and the groove.

The motivation for this research stems from the fact that SPPs have attracted considerable interest due to their unique properties, which make them suitable for a wide range of applications such as sensing devices, nonlinear optics, and plasmonic waveguides. The control and manipulation of SPPs can be achieved by designing subwavelength structures such as grooves and gratings, which can scatter and couple SPPs. Therefore, understanding the behavior of SPPs scattered by subwavelength structures is essential for designing and optimizing plasmonic devices.

In conclusion, our research provides important insights into the transient behavior of SPPs scattered by subwavelength grooves. Our results reveal the potential for enhancing the scattering amplitude of SPPs by tuning the width of the groove with respect to the wavelength of the SPPs. This study contributes to the advancement of plasmonic devices and opens new avenues for designing and optimizing plasmonic applications.

In this work, we present our analysis of the B->D \pi decays with a focus on CP violation, using the Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) approach. The primary goal of our work is to identify the sources of CP violation in these decays and to determine whether they agree with the Standard Model predictions. 

To achieve this, we use the QCD factorization method, which allows us to factorize the decay amplitude into two parts: a hard-scattering kernel and a set of soft hadronic matrix elements. We calculate these matrix elements using non-perturbative techniques, such as lattice QCD simulations and light-cone sum rules. 

We then perform a phenomenological analysis of the B->D \pi decays using these QCD factorization calculations. Our results indicate that the CP violating observables are sensitive to the strong phases of the hadronic matrix elements, which can lead to new physics contributions. We find that the Standard Model predictions for CP asymmetries in these decays are consistent with our calculations, within the current experimental uncertainties. 

Overall, our work offers a comprehensive QCD-based analysis of the B->D \pi decays and provides a valuable tool to understand CP violation in these processes. We hope that our findings will stimulate further experimental studies of these decays, to provide a more accurate determination of CP violation parameters and to search for new physics beyond the Standard Model.

In this work, we present accurate X-ray observations and multiwavelength observations of the isolated neutron star RBS 1774. The main problem that we try to address is the lack of high-precision X-ray positions for RBS 1774, which makes it difficult to accurately study its properties. The motivation for this research is to understand the physical properties of neutron stars, which are remnants of massive stars that have undergone supernova explosions. Neutron stars are the most dense objects known in the universe, and their properties are still poorly understood. Accurate observations of isolated neutron stars, such as RBS 1774, can provide important insights into their properties.

Our key idea is to use X-ray observations taken with the Chandra X-ray Observatory to obtain accurate positions of RBS 1774. We also obtained multiwavelength observations to study the neutron star's properties in other wavelengths. We analyzed the X-ray data to obtain improved positions and determined the neutron star's X-ray spectrum. We also analyzed the optical and near-infrared data to place constraints on the neutron star's properties such as its age and magnetic field.

Our results provide the most accurate X-ray position to date for RBS 1774 and improve our understanding of its properties. This work will help guide future studies of this and other isolated neutron stars.

In this work, we explore central limit theorems for linear structural error-in-variables models with explanatory variables in the domain of attraction of the normal law. The motivation for this research lies in the fact that the theory of central limit theorems is an important tool for analyzing statistical models. Specifically, we are interested in understanding how the limiting distribution of model parameters changes as the sample size grows larger. This is important for practitioners in fields such as economics, finance, and engineering, where modeling errors and measurement errors are often present.
