With this in mind, we employ various theoretical models and numerical simulations to study the dynamics and properties of the first supernovae.

Our results suggest that the first supernova explosions were driven by rapidly rotating massive stars that had lost most of their hydrogen envelopes. These explosions were likely highly energetic, releasing large amounts of radiation and ejecting significant amounts of matter. Furthermore, our simulations indicate that these explosions had a significant impact on the surrounding medium, altering its physical and chemical properties and triggering the formation of subsequent generations of stars.

The key ideas in this work are focused on the role of the earliest supernovae in shaping the history of the universe. Specifically, we emphasize the energetic feedback and chemical enrichment that occurred as a result of these events, shaping the evolution of the first galaxies. The methodology employed in this study combines numerical simulations with analytical modeling, allowing for a more detailed and comprehensive understanding of the physics involved.

Overall, this work provides new insights into the energetics, feedback, and chemical enrichment of the first supernova explosions. By studying these events, we can better understand the mechanisms that drive stellar evolution, the formation of the first stars and galaxies, and the evolution of the universe as a whole.

In this study, we investigate the disordering transitions and peak effect in polydisperse particle systems. Our primary aim is to understand how particle size distribution affects the collective behavior of disordered particle assemblies. We begin by discussing the key ideas and methodology employed in our experiments. Specifically, we use a combination of differential scanning calorimetry and ac susceptibility measurements to study the particle size distribution in a variety of systems. 

Our study reveals several interesting results. Firstly, we find that the degree of polydispersity plays an important role in determining the disordering transition temperature of the system. Furthermore, we observe a peak effect in the ac susceptibility, which we attribute to collective ordering of the particles. Our findings suggest that the peak effect is highly sensitive to the particle size distribution, and that there is a critical range of polydispersity that leads to the largest peak effect. 

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the lack of understanding of how particle size distribution affects the collective behavior of disordered particle systems. Our results contribute to a growing body of literature on the subject, and may have significant implications for the development of new materials with tailored properties.

In this paper, we investigate the geometry of generalized Gaussian distributions. Our work aims to understand how these distributions can be fully described by their geometric properties, which are determined by their covariance matrix. Specifically, we examine how the curvature of the space containing these distributions changes as we vary their shape parameters. We then analyze a novel class of generalized Gaussian distributions, which we call \emph{skew-symmetric}, that can model asymmetric data.

To achieve our goals, we use differential geometry techniques to study the geometry of the space of covariance matrices. We derive new expressions for quantities such as the curvature and volume element of this space, which allow us to characterize the shape of generalized Gaussian distributions. We also study the geometry of the space of skew-symmetric covariance matrices and identify a connection with the Lie algebra of skew-symmetric matrices.

Our main motivation for this research is the observation that many real-world data sets have non-Gaussian distributions that exhibit asymmetry and heavy tails. Understanding the geometry of these distributions can help us develop more accurate generative models and estimation algorithms. Additionally, our work has implications for fields such as signal processing, machine learning, and statistics.

In this work, we investigate the phase structure of an Abelian two-Higgs model of strongly correlated electrons in the context of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) at finite density. The main problem we seek to address is the phenomenon of confinement-deconfinement phase transition in strongly correlated electron systems. Through intensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the inclusion of an additional Higgs field in the standard model of particle physics leads to a significant strengthening of the confinement-deconfinement phase transition, resulting in a rich and complex phase diagram. Furthermore, we establish a direct link between QCD at finite density and the topological properties of the Higgs fields, demonstrating the pivotal role played by bosonic excitations in the system. Our key contribution lies in the development of a novel theoretical and numerical framework that allows us to investigate the intricate interplay between the electromagnetic and strong interactions in a unified formalism, shedding new light on the fundamental nature of confinement in strongly correlated electron systems. These results have implications for the design of new materials with tunable topological properties, and provide a novel perspective for the study of complex quantum systems beyond the standard model of particle physics.

In this paper, we present a novel technique to deconstruct functions on quadratic surfaces into their respective multipole components. The problem that our work attempts to solve is the inability to obtain a clear understanding of the underlying physical or mathematical reasons that govern the behavior of the functions on the quadratic surfaces. We demonstrate that by understanding the individual contributions of each multipole component, one can more easily comprehend the behavior of functions on curved surfaces.

The motivation for our research stems from the lack of efficient methods to analyze the complex behavior of functions on curved surfaces. The inability to discern the contribution and impact of individual components on the overall behavior of the function hinders both scientific and engineering endeavors. Our approach resolves this issue by breaking down the functions into their component parts, providing a clear understanding of the function's behavior.

Our results show that the technique presented in this paper allows us to gain deeper insights into the behavior of functions on quadratic surfaces. With the multipole decomposition approach, we show that a clear understanding of the behavior of the individual components of the function allows one to better predict the impact of perturbations in the function. Overall, the approach presented in this paper could have significant implications for areas such as materials science, engineering, and physics.

In this work, we present an analysis of the decoherence of a quantronium qubit using a cavity bifurcation amplifier. We employed a standard semi-classical model of the amplifier and an experiment involving a qubit coupled to the cavity. Our focus was on the dephasing induced by the cavity on the qubit. By analyzing the time evolution of the population of the qubit, we were able to determine the decoherence time.

Our results indicate that the decoherence time varies with the detuning between the qubit and the cavity. We also found that the decoherence time decreases with the coupling strength between the qubit and the cavity, as expected. Moreover, we determined that the decoherence time could be extended by optimizing the detuning between the qubit and cavity.

The problem we aim to solve with this work is to provide a new method to measure the decoherence of a quantronium qubit. Decoherence is a major obstacle in the development of quantum computing and, thus, extending the decoherence time would increase the feasibility of constructing a quantum computer.

In conclusion, our study provides an insight into the relationship between the decoherence time and the system parameters, indicating that cavity bifurcation amplifiers can be useful in the characterization of qubit decoherence. This novel method for measuring decoherence could facilitate the development of error-correcting codes and improve the accuracy and reliability of quantum computing systems.

In this study, we present the results of an extensive survey of massive stars in the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds using the VLT-FLAMES instrument. Our focus was on investigating the evolution of surface N abundances and effective temperature scales in these galaxies. Massive stars play a crucial role in the evolution of galaxies and have a significant impact on the cosmic enrichment of chemical elements, such as nitrogen. The complex interplay of physical processes that govern the evolution of massive stars and the chemical enrichment of their surroundings make them vital objects of study. In this regard, the VLT-FLAMES survey is particularly relevant, as it provides a large sample of massive stars with high-quality data, allowing us to make statistically significant conclusions.

Our analysis reveals a robust correlation between surface N abundance and effective temperature, indicating that N enrichment is tied to the late stages of stellar evolution. We also found clear differences in the N abundance and effective temperature distributions between the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds, highlighting the importance of environment in shaping the properties of massive stars. These results provide essential insights into the mechanisms of chemical enrichment and the evolution of massive stars, shedding light on the broader aspects of galactic evolution.

Our work, titled "The Magnetic Field of the Solar Corona from Pulsar Observations", aims to address a longstanding problem in solar physics: the lack of direct measurements of the magnetic field in the Sun's corona. This is a critical issue because the corona is the outermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere and plays a crucial role in driving the solar wind, which impacts the Earth's space environment. However, the corona is extremely difficult to observe directly due to its faintness and proximity to the bright solar disk.

To overcome this challenge, we turn to pulsar observations. Pulsars are highly magnetized neutron stars that emit regular pulses of radiation and are extremely precise natural clocks. As the pulses travel through the corona, they experience a delay due to the magnetic field of the corona, which we can measure with high precision.

In our study, we analyze data from multiple pulsars to obtain a global view of the magnetic field in the solar corona. Our results reveal a complex and dynamic magnetic field that varies in strength and direction on spatial scales ranging from a few thousand kilometers to the size of the entire corona. This is a significant advance in our understanding of the Sun's magnetic field and provides important insights into the mechanisms driving the solar wind.

In this paper, we present a dynamical computation of the coefficients of electroweak chiral Lagrangian (EWCL) in the context of one-doublet and topcolor-assisted technicolor (TC2) models. We use the operator product expansion (OPE) to evaluate the coefficients in terms of the vacuum expectation values (VEVs) of the composite operators. Our approach combines chiral perturbation theory (ChPT) for the low-energy dynamics and heavy quark effective theory (HQET) for the heavy quark contributions. We calculate the leading-order contributions and work with the two-loop level in ChPT. We also take into account the mass splittings between the top quark and the other quarks. Our results show that the EWCL coefficients are sensitive to the composite operator VEVs, and they can provide information about the dynamics of the strongly interacting sector. 

The motivation for this study is to explore the properties of the electroweak symmetry breaking sector and its relationship with the strong interaction sector in the standard model. In particular, we investigate the validity of the one-doublet and topcolor-assisted technicolor models and their predictions for the electroweak chiral Lagrangian coefficients. Our approach provides a rigorous method for evaluating the coefficients and can be extended to other models with similar composite operators. Our results demonstrate the importance of the EWCL coefficients as probes of the underlying dynamics of the electroweak symmetry breaking sector.

In this paper, we explore the phenomenon of CP violation and penguin effects through the decay of $B^0_d \to D^+D^-$ and $B^0_s \to D^+_sD^-_s$. CP violation is a fundamental aspect of particle physics and refers to the breakdown of CP symmetry. The penguin diagram is a higher-order diagram in the weak interaction that contributes to CP violation. This decay is a rare process that occurs through the weak interaction and can provide insight into these theoretical concepts.

Our methodology involves the use of data obtained from the Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) experiment. We conduct a detailed analysis of the decay in order to study the penguin contributions and CP violation in the decay. We use statistical techniques to extract the magnitude and phase of the penguin contributions and CP asymmetry parameters. 

Our results demonstrate strong penguin contributions and significant CP violation in both decays. The CP asymmetry parameters obtained are in agreement with the standard model of particle physics, which is a crucial test of the theory. Our work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the fundamental processes of particle physics. Through this analysis, we gain a better understanding of the behavior of these processes, which can inform and guide future research in the field.

In this work, we investigate the intersection of post-Newtonian and numerical-relativity waveforms in the context of gravitational waves. We demonstrate that these seemingly disparate approaches can be combined to produce accurate and efficient waveform models for the most extreme astrophysical events, such as the merger of black holes or neutron stars.

We employ a methodology that involves comparing and calibrating post-Newtonian and numerical-relativity waveforms using a set of hybrid waveforms. These hybrid waveforms are constructed by patching together post-Newtonian and numerical-relativity waveforms, ensuring that the overlapping regions are consistent with each other.

Our results show that the hybrid waveforms accurately reproduce the full numerical-relativity waveform, while also capturing the essential features of the post-Newtonian waveforms. Moreover, we identify specific regimes where one approach is more appropriate than the other, providing a framework for the development and calibration of waveform models for future gravitational-wave observations.

This work contributes to the ongoing effort to enhance the accuracy and computational efficiency of gravitational-wave data analysis, ultimately aiming to extract valuable astrophysical information from these elusive signals. By combining the strengths of post-Newtonian and numerical-relativity waveforms, we bring a new level of precision to the gravitational-wave modeling field, opening up exciting new avenues of research.

In this study, we investigate the modified p-modes observed in penumbral filaments of sunspots, utilizing a combination of theoretical and observational methods. We first introduce the key concepts underlying our research, specifically the nature of penumbral filaments and the characteristic p-mode oscillations that occur in these structures. We then describe the methodology used to analyze observational data obtained from the Hinode satellite to investigate the possibility of modified p-modes in these filaments. Our findings suggest that modified p-modes may indeed be present in these structures, and we discuss the implications of this result for our understanding of the physical processes at work in sunspots.

The motivation behind this research stems from the importance of sunspots in the study of solar physics, and the potential insights that can be gained by investigating the properties of oscillations within these structures. Additionally, the observation of modified p-modes in penumbral filaments could provide important information about the structure and dynamics of the magnetic field in these regions, which is a key area of interest in solar physics.

Overall, our work aims to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the behavior of oscillations in penumbral filaments, and to shed light on the complex processes that govern the physical properties of sunspots. By utilizing both theoretical and observational approaches, we hope to provide a more complete picture of the underlying physics of these fascinating structures.

Looking beyond the horizon is a study that delves into the phenomenon of foresight, exploring the means by which individuals can envision and anticipate the future. Our investigation was motivated by the recognition that many people harbor a natural curiosity about what lies ahead, but few have a clear understanding of how to develop this skill and apply it to their lives. To address this gap, we engaged in a multi-method research process that included review of the literature, interviews with experts, and analysis of real-world case studies.

Our findings suggest that foresight is a complex skill that can be developed over time through a combination of cognitive and behavioral strategies. These strategies include active imagination, systematic thinking, strategic planning, and through collaboration. We also identified key personal traits that are associated with effective foresight, such as curiosity, optimism, and openness to change. Critically, we found that foresight can be an essential tool in navigating uncertainty and achieving desired outcomes in business, personal, and social contexts.

Overall, this work advances understanding of the psychological and practical issues surrounding foresight and makes a valuable contribution to the growing field of future studies. It is our hope that our results will help individuals and organizations alike to “look beyond the horizon” and prepare for the opportunities and challenges that await them.

In this work, we present a novel approach to the computation of Faithful Effective-One-Body (EOB) waveforms of small-mass-ratio coalescing black-hole binaries. The key idea is to use the fact that the gravitational-wave (GW) signal from such binaries is dominated by the dominant modes of the GW emission, and to compute the EOB waveform by a combination of analytical and numerical methods that allows to accurately track these modes. 

Our methodology is based on a combination of analytic calculations of the dominant modes of the GW signal and numerical solutions of the EOB equations of motion with a high accuracy. We validate our approach by comparing our EOB waveforms with accurate numerical simulations of binary black-hole mergers, and find excellent agreement. 

Our results show that the Faithful EOB waveforms we obtain are accurate enough to be used for data analysis of GW signals from small-mass-ratio binaries with current and future GW detectors, such as LIGO, Virgo, and the planned LISA mission. Moreover, our approach allows for a faster computation of EOB waveforms than current techniques, thus enabling the analysis of a larger number of waveforms and the extraction of more information about the astrophysical properties of black-hole binaries.

The motivation for this research is to provide accurate and computationally efficient methods for the analysis of GW signals from small-mass-ratio binary black-hole mergers, which are expected to be detected with increasing sensitivity in the near future. Our approach may lead to new discoveries about the nature and properties of black holes and their astrophysical environments.

In this work, we explore Poincare Duality Pairs (PDPs) in dimension three, which are algebraic structures that relate the topology and geometry of a space. The key idea of PDP is that the compact non-orientable spaces can be oriented if they have a duality pair. Our goal in this research is to better understand how these structures work and how they can be applied to solve more complex problems in topology.

Our approach is based on a series of theorems and proofs that help us understand how PDPs are defined, their properties, and their role in establishing duality between chains and cochains. We also analyze different families of PDPs, such as Davidson–Freed, Pemantle–Wilson, and Cycle Decomposability, and study their interrelations and how they can inform each other.

The motivation for this research is to further the development of algebraic topology and provide new ways to analyze and represent complex spaces. The application of PDPs has potential for use in fields such as physics, biology, and computer science, where understanding the topology of a space can help solve problems related to the behavior of complex systems. By better understanding the structure of PDPs in dimension three, we can create a more comprehensive framework for algebraic topology and its applications, ultimately leading to more efficient and accurate solutions for real-world problems.

In this work, we present a novel approach to solve the problem of Bayesian inference in astronomy. Multimodal nested sampling is proposed as an efficient and robust alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for data analysis. Nested sampling is a Monte Carlo algorithm that has proven useful in a range of problems, from estimating parameter uncertainties to model selection. However, in its original form, it struggles to sample multimodal distributions, which are common in astronomy and many other fields.

Our solution is to incorporate multimodality into nested sampling by rejecting samples from regions with low prior probability. This involves pruning the existing set of live points and replacing them with new samples drawn from high-prior-probability regions. We demonstrate the superiority of our method in comparison to both conventional and state-of-the-art MCMC techniques in a series of experiments on real and simulated data. We use a number of performance metrics, including efficiency, accuracy, and robustness to initialization, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

This work addresses a major challenge faced by astronomers and other researchers faced with large and complex datasets, namely the need to perform Bayesian inference on multimodal distributions. Our results show that multimodal nested sampling is a valuable tool for data analysis in these situations, providing fast, accurate and robust estimates for quantities of interest.

Our study focuses on the anticenter open cluster NGC 1883 and aims to investigate its radial velocity and metallicity. We utilized multi-object spectroscopy for 45 targets in the cluster region using the 6.5-m telescope at Xinglong Station, NAOC. Radial velocities of cluster members were obtained by cross-correlating with template stars, highlighting the high membership probability of stars with consistent radial velocities. In addition, calcium triplet line strengths were measured to determine cluster metallicity. Using a high-resolution spectroscopic template, we found that the cluster has a metallicity of [Fe/H]=-0.41 ± 0.06 dex, indicating a relatively metal-poor system.

Our results provide important contributions to the current database of open clusters in the Galactic anticenter direction. NGC 1883 is a significant target for study due to its crucial role in understanding the Galactic disk dynamics and chemical evolution. We aim to develop a more comprehensive view of the cluster's properties and identify its origin, evolutionary stage, and possible connection with nearby structures. Our research provides insights into the interplay between the Galactic evolution and the formation of open clusters. This study also sets the stage for future research on this and other Galactic open clusters.

In this work, we investigate the hadroproduction and decays of squarks and gauginos in a non-minimal flavour violating supersymmetric scenario. The motivation for this research lies in the fact that a minimal supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model cannot account for certain experimentally observed phenomena, such as neutrino masses and mixing, and requires flavour blind interactions between squarks and quarks. Non-minimal flavour violating scenarios, on the other hand, allow for squark flavour mixing and interactions that can potentially explain these phenomena. 

We employ a Monte Carlo simulation to generate events that involve the production and decay of squarks and gauginos, and study the effects of flavour violation on various kinematic variables. Our results indicate that the presence of flavour violation can lead to significant deviations from the predictions of a minimal supersymmetric scenario, particularly in the distributions of invariant masses and transverse momenta. Furthermore, we explore the implications of our findings for the collider search strategies for supersymmetry. 

Overall, our work sheds light on the potential consequences of non-minimal flavour violating supersymmetry and emphasises the need for experimental searches that take into account such scenarios. Our methodology and analysis can also be extended to other supersymmetric models or beyond the scope of the Standard Model, making it relevant for future research in the field of particle physics.

In this work, we investigate the dependence of the estimated luminosities of Ultra-Luminous X-ray sources (ULXs) on spectral models. ULXs are point sources with X-ray luminosities that exceed the Eddington limit for a neutron star. The estimation of their luminosities is a crucial task for evaluating their physical properties, such as their black hole masses and the accretion rates. However, the luminosity estimation is significantly affected by the choice of spectral models. The primary objective of this work is to understand and quantify the impact of different spectral models on the luminosity estimation of ULXs.

We use a large sample of ULXs from the Chandra and XMM-Newton archives and analyze their spectra using different spectral models, including power-law, thermal, and Comptonization models. We employ a Bayesian framework to compare the goodness-of-fit of the spectral models and estimate the uncertainties of the luminosity measurements. Our results indicate that the choice of spectral models has a significant impact on the estimation of the luminosity of ULXs. We find that thermal models tend to overestimate the luminosity, while power-law models tend to underestimate it. We show that a Comptonization model provides a better fit to the data and yields a more accurate luminosity estimation.

The implications of our work are important as it contributes to a better understanding of the nature and physical properties of ULXs, which can have a significant impact on the field of high-energy astrophysics research.

In this work, we investigate the emergence of nonstationary patterns in unsynchronizable complex networks. Our motivation for the research is rooted in the observation that many real-world networks, such as social networks and biological systems, are inherently nonstationary and exhibit time-varying dynamics. However, existing studies of synchronization in complex networks have primarily focused on stationary patterns, which pose limitations in understanding and modeling nonstationary behaviors in real-world networks.

To address this gap, we propose a novel framework that incorporates nonstationary effects into the dynamics of unsynchronizable complex networks. We validate our model through numerical simulations and provide theoretical analysis to demonstrate the emergence of nonstationary patterns in the network. Our results show that nonstationary behaviors can arise due to the interplay between network structure and the dynamics of individual nodes.

The key idea behind our approach is to use adaptive algorithms that adjust the dynamics of nodes in response to changes in the environment. We also explore the impact of different types of coupling between nodes and how they can impact the emergence of nonstationary patterns. Our methodology integrates both analytical and empirical techniques to provide a comprehensive understanding of nonstationary behaviors in complex networks.

Overall, our research contributes to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying nonstationary patterns in complex networks. By providing a more complete picture of network dynamics, our work can help guide the development of more accurate models and algorithms for analyzing and predicting complex network behaviors.

In this work, we investigate the phonon-mediated decay of an atom that is trapped in a surface-induced potential. This research is highly motivated by the need to better understand how atoms interact with their surrounding environment, particularly in nanoscale systems. Specifically, we aim to address the challenge of phonon-induced decay, which is a key obstacle in the development of quantum computing and other advanced technologies that rely on the precise control of single atoms.

To tackle this problem, we employ a combination of theoretical and numerical methods, including quantum master equations and Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis reveals that, in the presence of a surface-induced potential, the phonon-mediated decay rate of the trapped atom can be significantly reduced by tuning the potential parameters. This result is of great significance for the development of quantum information processing devices, as it provides a potential means of mitigating the effects of phonon-induced decoherence and improving quantum efficiency.

Overall, our work sheds new light on the fundamental mechanisms underlying phonon-mediated decay in nanoscale systems and provides useful insights for the engineering of quantum devices. As such, our findings represent an important contribution to the field of quantum information science and have significant implications for the future of quantum computing and other quantum technologies.

In this work, we present an approach for improving intrinsic decoherence in multi-quantum-dot charge qubits. Decoherence is a major obstacle for realizing quantum information processing. Multi-quantum-dot qubits, composed of a few electrons in several quantum dots, show promise for quantum computing, but are prone to decoherence. In this work, we focus on intrinsic decoherence that is induced by the inherent interactions between the system and its environment. We demonstrate that an optimized voltage pulse sequence can enhance coherence by suppressing intrinsic decoherence mechanisms. We develop a numerical model of the physical system based on the density matrix formalism, and show that decoherence is caused by the inter-dot hopping and the spin interaction between the electrons. We use optimal control theory to design a voltage pulse sequence that counteracts these sources of decoherence. We find that the optimized pulses preserve coherence for a longer time than standard fixed-voltage pulses. Our findings contribute to the development of scalable quantum computing architectures, and provide a viable approach for suppressing intrinsic decoherence in multi-quantum-dot charge qubits.

In this work, we aim to investigate the distribution and properties of dark matter in the Milky Way galaxy through the use of HI gas as a tracer of the gravitational potential. The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the nature and distribution of dark matter, which constitutes most of the matter in the Universe. While its presence is inferred from astrophysical observations, its nature and properties are still mostly unknown, hence the need for studies such as this.

Our specific problem is to determine the shape and size of the dark matter halo surrounding the Milky Way based on the distribution and kinematics of HI gas. We utilize radio interferometric observations from the THINGS survey and combine them with measurements of the galaxy's rotation curve to model the mass distribution of the Milky Way. Using Bayesian statistics, we compare different dark matter density profiles to infer the most probable shape and size of the halo.

Our key finding is that a cored profile with a scale radius of around 20 kpc provides the best fit to the data, suggesting the Milky Way's dark matter halo may be less concentrated than previously thought. This work contributes to our understanding of the properties of dark matter and has implications for the formation and evolution of galaxies in the Universe.

In this work, we present a new approach to obtain analytic control over parton showers in Monte Carlo simulations. Our methodology is based on the recently developed UNBiased Inclusive multi-Parton Shower (UNI-IPS) algorithm, which implements a color covariance formalism that assigns each event a weight proportional to the probability of its occurrence. By combining the UNI-IPS with a recursive method to compute tree-level kinematics, we demonstrate the possibility of resummation of logarithmic Sudakov factors to arbitrary orders, while keeping the shower emission probabilities under analytic control. 

Motivated by the need to achieve higher accuracy in the description of complex final states and to incorporate next-to-leading logarithmic corrections, our work provides a powerful tool to improve high-energy physics simulations. We illustrate our results by comparing the output of our algorithm with that obtained through current state-of-the-art Monte Carlo simulations, finding a significant improvement in the accuracy of the predictions. 

Our approach represents a significant step forward towards achieving a complete understanding of the underlying physics in high-energy scattering processes, and it will have important implications in the analysis of data from current and future collider experiments. Ultimately, it will allow us to precisely investigate and identify new physics phenomena and shed light on some of the most pressing questions in particle physics today.

In this paper, we investigate the decoherence of highly mixed macroscopic quantum superpositions, which is a crucial step towards understanding the boundary between the classical and the quantum worlds. The main idea behind our work is to analyze the behavior of entanglement and purity in a system consisting of two macroscopic objects that are initially prepared in a highly mixed quantum superposition state. We use a novel approach based on quantum trajectory theory to investigate the evolution of the system under the influence of environmental noise. Our results demonstrate that, despite the highly mixed nature of the initial state, the system exhibits rapid decoherence and loses its quantum coherence in a very short time. In particular, we find that the entanglement decays faster than the purity, indicating that entanglement is more sensitive to decoherence than purity in this system. Our work aims to shed light on the fundamental problem of how macroscopic objects can lose their quantum coherence in a noisy environment, which is one of the central challenges in the field of quantum mechanics. Our findings might have important implications for the development of quantum technologies, such as quantum computing and communication, which rely on the control of highly mixed quantum states.

In this study, we aim to unveil the broad band X-ray continuum and iron line complex in Mkr 841. The motivation for our research stems from the fact that Mkr 841 has been identified as a Compton-thick Seyfert 2 galaxy, displaying a heavily obscured nucleus. Previous observations in the X-ray continuum have been limited, and a thorough understanding of the spectral features of the nucleus is crucial for a better understanding of its physical properties. 

To achieve our objective, we used data from the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) and Suzaku. We performed detailed spectral analysis to investigate the spectral properties of the X-ray continuum and the iron line complex. Our findings reveal that the X-ray continuum of Mkr 841 displays a prominent Compton hump, which is characteristic of Compton-thick environments. We also detected a strong iron K-alpha line, indicating that iron is highly concentrated in the nucleus. 

Our results provide significant insights into the physical properties of Mkr 841. Our study offers new findings on the spectral properties of a highly obscured Seyfert 2 galaxy and enhances our understanding of the Compton-thick environment. This research has important implications for advancing our knowledge of active galactic nuclei and how they evolve over time.

We present a study on the possible progenitors of long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). These enigmatic phenomena are thought to be associated with the collapse of massive stars and the formation of black holes. However, the exact mechanism of long GRB formation remains elusive, as does the identification of the underlying stellar progenitor. In this work, we investigate the potential link between long GRBs and the mass-loss history of their progenitors.

Our study involves a detailed analysis of the properties of the host galaxies of a sample of long GRBs, including their star-forming rates and metallicity. We also consider the effects of binary interactions on the evolution of massive stars and their ultimate fate. Our methodology consists of computing a grid of stellar evolutionary models that take into account different mass-loss prescriptions and binary evolution scenarios.

Our results reveal that low-metallicity and rapidly rotating stars are the most likely progenitors of long GRBs. In addition, binary interactions can significantly enhance the mass-loss rates of massive stars, thereby increasing the likelihood of GRB formation. These findings provide important insights into the origins of these powerful cosmic explosions and shed light on the crucial role of massive stars in shaping the universe as we know it.

In this work, we explore the boundary conditions of the heliosphere through photoionization models. The motivation for this research lies in the need to better understand the interactions between the solar wind and the interstellar medium. The heliosphere acts as a protective shield for our solar system, and its structure depends on the solar wind's properties along with interstellar conditions. Our study aims to constrain the photoionization models through the comparison of both interstellar and in situ data. 

Our methodology consists of using the latest available interstellar data and in situ measurements from NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft. We compared our results with previous ionization models to assess the accuracy of our approach. We applied the models to study the ionization rates and relative abundances of different chemical species in the heliosphere's boundary regions. The results of these simulations allowed us to gain insight into the properties and structure of the heliosphere. 

Our analysis reveals that a model that includes multiple ionization sources, such as the interstellar radiation field and charge exchange collisions, provides a better fit to interstellar and in situ data than models with only one ionization source. Our study provides a new perspective on the boundary conditions of the heliosphere and offers valuable insights for future studies.

In this study, we present the results of a spectral analysis of the Chandra Comet Survey (CCS). The CCS is a long-term project aimed at characterizing comets through X-ray observations. Our analysis focused on the spectral properties of the seven comets included in the survey. We applied both phenomenological and physical models to extract information on the plasma composition, temperature, and emission mechanisms.

The motivation for this research is twofold: first, understanding the X-ray emission of comets is crucial for the interpretation of X-ray observations of other Solar System bodies and exoplanets; second, the CCS represents an unprecedented dataset with a high potential for discoveries. Our work attempts to address the puzzle of the X-ray emission from comets, which has been known for over two decades but is still not fully understood. The widely accepted scenario involves solar wind particles interacting with the coma gas, but the exact mechanisms at play are still the subject of debate.

Our analysis reveals that the cometary X-ray spectra are complex and can be best explained by a hybrid model that includes thermal and non-thermal components. This finding suggests that multiple processes are involved in producing the X-ray emission, and that the traditional scenario might not be sufficient to capture the full complexity of the problem. We discuss possible interpretations of our results and the implications for the understanding of the plasma environment around comets.

Overall, our work contributes to advancing the field of cometary X-ray astronomy and provides new insights into the physics of these enigmatic objects.

The active black hole mass function in the local universe is crucial for understanding the evolution of galaxies and their central supermassive black holes. We present a comprehensive study of the active black hole mass function over a wide range of black hole masses in the local universe. Our analysis is based on a sample of 615 active galaxies selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) with robust black hole mass estimates available in the literature. We used the virial method to estimate black hole masses from the broad emission lines observed in the SDSS spectra. Our results demonstrate that the active black hole mass function shows a power-law shape with a slope of -1.5 at low masses, which flattens to -0.75 at high masses, suggesting a change in black hole growth mechanisms. Additionally, we investigate the role of galaxy properties on the active black hole mass function, such as the host galaxy mass, star formation rate, and morphology. We find that the black holes hosted by more massive galaxies tend to have higher masses, which illustrates the importance of black hole-galaxy co-evolution. This study provides essential insights into the growth and assembly of supermassive black holes in the local universe and their connection to galaxy evolution.

In this work, we present a unified projection formalism for describing the Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystal and its Xi-approximants with metadislocations. Our aim is to address the challenge of understanding the structural properties of quasicrystals, which exhibit long-range order without periodicity. The complexity and lack of symmetry in quasicrystal structures make it difficult to describe them using conventional crystallographic methods. 
The key idea in our proposed formalism is to project the quasicrystal onto a higher-dimensional space and represent it as a regular crystal with a higher symmetry than the original system. Metadislocations, which are a characteristic feature of quasicrystals and play an important role in their mechanical properties, are also included in this formalism. 
The methodology involves constructing a mathematical model that incorporates the projection of the quasicrystal, the representation of its symmetry in the higher-dimensional space, and the description of metadislocations using topological methods. 
The motivation for this research is twofold. Firstly, it contributes to the fundamental understanding of the Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystalline system, which has been of interest in both materials science and solid-state physics. Secondly, our formalism has practical applications in the design and engineering of quasicrystalline materials, particularly in the development of new alloys with enhanced mechanical properties. Overall, our approach provides a powerful and unified framework for describing quasicrystal structures, opening up avenues for future research in this field.

In this paper, we study the emergence and resilience of cooperation in the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma via a reward mechanism. The Prisoner's Dilemma is a well-known game theory problem that has been used to model situations in which individuals make choices that impact not only their own payoff but also that of others. In the spatial version of the game, individuals are located on a grid and interact only with their nearest neighbors. Cooperation can be beneficial for all participants, but defection is the dominant strategy.

Our motivation for this research lies in the importance of cooperation for many social and economic systems. We aim to understand how reward mechanisms can foster cooperation in situations where defection is the dominant strategy. To do so, we use agent-based modeling and simulations to study the behavior of individuals in the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma. Specifically, we explore how reward mechanisms that incentivize cooperation can lead to the emergence of cooperation and increase its resilience in the face of defection.

Our key findings demonstrate that a reward mechanism can indeed foster cooperation, even in the presence of defectors. However, the effectiveness of the reward mechanism depends on the population size, the intensity of the reward, and the topology of the interaction network. These results have important implications for understanding how reward mechanisms can promote social cooperation in complex systems. Overall, our research contributes to the growing literature on the role of incentives in promoting cooperation and provides insight into the conditions under which cooperation can emerge and persist in the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma.

In this study, we investigate a unique solar flare that features a lack of associated X-ray emission but has a clear radio signature. We aim to understand the plasma heating and electron acceleration mechanisms that are responsible for this atypical behavior. We employ multiwavelength observations and modeling techniques to reconstruct the radiative properties of the solar atmosphere at different stages of the flare. 

Our results reveal that the flare is characterized by a gradual rise and a rapid decay in the radio flux density. Furthermore, the radio spectral emission exhibits a hardening trend with time. We propose that the observed behavior can be explained by the rapid heating and subsequent cooling of the coronal plasma, which leads to a nonthermal electron distribution with a power-law index of around 4. 

Our findings not only help to uncover the physical processes taking place in this particular flare, but also contribute to the understanding of plasma heating and electron acceleration in general. The lack of X-ray emission in this event challenges the traditional paradigm of flare energy release mechanisms and highlights the importance of radio observations as a complementary tool for investigating solar eruptive events.

In this paper, we present a detailed analysis of GRB 060912A, a gamma ray burst (GRB) that has been classified as a long GRB despite its relatively short duration. We investigate whether this classification is accurate and what this might tell us about the long-short GRB divide, a fundamental and still unresolved issue in the study of GRBs.

Using a combination of data from both the Swift and Fermi satellites, we find that GRB 060912A exhibits several characteristics typically associated with short GRBs, such as a lack of extended emission and a relatively hard spectrum. However, we also find evidence that it may be associated with a supernova, a hallmark of long GRBs. Based on these results, we suggest that GRB 060912A may represent a new type of GRB that blurs the lines between long and short.

Our work contributes to the ongoing debate over the nature of the long-short GRB divide and highlights the need for more nuanced classifications of these events. We employ a rigorous and thorough methodology, including detailed analysis of both temporal and spectral data, to arrive at our conclusions. Overall, we hope that this case study will serve as a valuable contribution to the field and support further investigation into the diverse and complex phenomena associated with GRBs.

In this work, we aimed to test the accuracy of synthetic stellar libraries used in spectroscopic analysis. These libraries are widely employed in astronomers' studies due to their convenience and speed in obtaining stellar parameters. However, it is crucial to verify their reliability, given their synthetic nature. The problem we attempted to solve is the overall uncertainty in determining stellar parameters using synthetic libraries. 

Our methodology involved using observed spectra from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and comparing them to synthetic spectra generated from different libraries. We calculated the goodness-of-fit and root mean square deviation (RMSD) between the observed and synthetic spectra. Then we tested the dependence of synthetic spectra accuracy on different atmospheric parameters such as gravity, temperature, and metallicity. 

The motivation for this research is to improve the accuracy of physical parameter estimation and reduce systematic errors in spectroscopic analyses. Our findings revealed that synthetic libraries can accurately estimate stellar parameters, although large RMSDs and high uncertainties occur when fitting poor-quality spectra. Our results are significant in validating the reliability of synthetic libraries in interpreting observed spectra and can assist in optimizing the future generation of synthetic libraries.

In this work, we present the results of our search for transiting exoplanets around the M dwarf debris disk host, AU Microscopii. We observed the star for 14 days with the MUSCAT instrument, installed on the Himalayan Chandra Telescope. Our main aim was to detect small exoplanets transiting the star, aiming at better understanding the population of planets around this type of star. 

We used differential photometry to detect the transit signals in the light curve of AU Mic. After analyzing the folded transit curves, we found no significant transit signals in the data. From the obtained results, we were able to place upper mass limits of about 1.6, 2.9, and 4.6 Earth masses (at 68% confidence level) on transiting planets with orbital periods of 1, 5, and 10 days, respectively. 

Our work aims to contribute to the ongoing efforts for planet hunting around M dwarf stars. The detection of transiting exoplanets around an M dwarf debris disk host, like AU Microscopii, would provide valuable information on the properties and formation of exoplanets. Our negative results will help to set constraints on the abundance and properties of planets that can be hosted by AU Mic, such as the maximum radius and mass of potentially transiting planets.

In this study, we present a Boolean network model to predict the cell cycle sequence of fission yeast. The motivation for this research is to better understand the complex behavior of the cell cycle and to identify potential targets for anti-cancer drugs. Fission yeast is a model organism with a well-characterized cell cycle that can be easily studied in the laboratory. Our key idea is to use Boolean networks, a mathematical tool that can simulate the switching behavior of genes, to model the progression of the cell cycle. 

To construct the model, we first identified a set of genes known to be involved in the fission yeast cell cycle. We then defined logical rules to describe the interactions between these genes and used the resulting Boolean network to simulate the progression of the cell cycle. Our results show that the Boolean network model accurately predicts the cell cycle sequence of fission yeast, including the timing of cell cycle events such as DNA replication and cell division.

This work attempts to solve the problem of predicting complex cellular behaviors using a mathematical model. Boolean networks provide a simple and intuitive framework for modeling gene regulatory networks, and our study demonstrates their usefulness in predicting the sequence of cell cycle events. Our approach could be applied to other complex biological systems to uncover fundamental principles of cellular behavior.

In this research, we explore the discrete dipole approximation (DDA) for the simulation of light scattering by particles that are much larger than the wavelength. The motivation for this work stems from the need to better understand light interaction with complex particles in a variety of natural and man-made settings, such as atmospheric science, environmental science, and materials science. Such understanding can provide critical insights into the behavior and properties of these systems, which are important for applications ranging from remote sensing to biomedical imaging.

To achieve our goal, we first review the theoretical basis of DDA, which is a numerical method for solving the Maxwell equations for the interaction of light with particles. We then demonstrate the implementation of DDA in practical simulations of light scattering, including several examples of particles that are much larger than the wavelength of the incident light. Our results show good agreement with previous experimental and theoretical studies, indicating that DDA is a promising tool for studying light scattering by complex particles.

Overall, our work addresses the problem of simulating light scattering by particles that are much larger than the wavelength, which is a challenging problem in many scientific and engineering fields. We hope that our findings will contribute to the development of new applications and understanding in these areas.

In this work, we investigate the feasibility of sending a charged dust ball through the Reissner--Nordstr\"{o}m (RN) wormhole. Our aim is to shed light on the nature of these exotic tunnels in spacetime and their potential applications as shortcuts in interstellar travel. The central problem we address is the identification of the physical conditions under which a charged particle can cross the RN wormhole without violating the laws of physics. To this end, we develop a theoretical framework that combines classical electrodynamics with general relativity, taking into account the self-gravity and electromagnetic interactions of the dust ball and the wormhole. The key idea behind our methodology is to solve the coupled system of Einstein--Maxwell equations that governs this scenario, using numerical simulations and analytical approximations to explore the parameter space of the problem. Our main motivation for this research is to advance our understanding of the fundamental physics of gravity and electromagnetism in the presence of wormholes, and to explore the practical implications of such solutions for faster-than-light travel and other exotic phenomena. Our preliminary results suggest that charged dust balls can indeed traverse the RN wormhole under certain conditions, opening up new avenues for future investigations in this field.

In this work, we present a 3D velocity field of a Supergranular cell's photosphere. Supergranulation, which is the largest observed pattern of convective motion on the solar surface, is known to play a crucial role in the transport of heat and magnetic fields in the Sun's photosphere. However, it remains a challenging task to accurately determine the fundamental characteristics of Supergranular flows, such as their size, lifetime, and origin. 

To address this problem, we made use of a series of high-resolution full-disk Dopplergrams acquired by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory, spanning over three consecutive days. Specifically, we applied a local correlation tracking technique to derive the horizontal velocity fields from the Dopplergrams, which were then used to reconstruct a 3D map of the Supergranular cell's velocity field.

We found that the flow structure of the Supergranular cell is characterized by a large-scale cyclonic circulation in its interior, as well as smaller-scale convective cells near its boundaries. Moreover, the average flow speed in the cell is found to be around 400 m s-1, consistent with previous studies. Our results provide important insights into the dynamics of Supergranulation and demonstrate the potential of 3D velocity field analysis for studying the Sun's photosphere.

In this work, we investigate the relationship between dimer models, free fermions, and super quantum mechanics. Dimer models are a type of statistical mechanics model that describe the formation of dimers on a lattice, while free fermions are particles that obey Fermi-Dirac statistics and can move freely in a lattice. Super quantum mechanics, on the other hand, is a generalization of quantum mechanics that incorporates supersymmetry. We aim to understand how these three concepts are related and use this understanding to gain insights into the behavior of physical systems.

To achieve this, we begin by introducing the mathematical framework for dimer models, free fermions, and super quantum mechanics. We then explore how these frameworks interact, focusing on the mathematics that underline their relationship. Our key idea is that certain dimer models have a hidden supersymmetry that emerges when they are described using free fermions. We formalize this relationship using mathematical tools, including complex analysis and representation theory.

Our results show that understanding the relationship between dimer models, free fermions, and super quantum mechanics provides a new perspective on the behavior of physical systems. We demonstrate this by using our insights to address several open problems in statistical mechanics and condensed matter physics. Specifically, we use our understanding of supersymmetry in dimer models to predict the existence of certain phase transitions in materials science. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our work, including its potential applications in fields such as quantum computing and high-energy physics.

We present the results of our investigation on the growth behavior of millimeter-thick single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) forests and possible growth mechanisms that give rise to the unique characteristics of these structures. Our motivation for this study stems from the potential of these forests to have large surface areas and high conductivity, which make them ideal for various applications including electrochemical energy storage, sensing, and electronic devices.

Our work involves optimizing the growth parameters to obtain uniform and dense SWCNT forests that are several millimeters thick. We investigate the growth window, which refers to the range of growth conditions that enable the formation of the desired structure, as well as the role of the catalyst and gas flow rates in achieving the desired growth behavior. Furthermore, we propose a possible growth mechanism based on the saturation of reactive sites and kinetic limitations that explain the dependence of forest thickness on the growth time.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the lack of understanding of the growth behavior of millimeter-thick SWCNT forests, which hinders their widespread adoption in practical applications. Our study provides insights into the factors that affect the growth of these structures and a possible mechanism that can be used to rationally design and tailor their properties for specific applications.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of vortical and wave modes in 3D rotating stratified flows that experience random large-scale forcing. Our aim is to better understand the complex interplay between these two modes of motion, and how they interact with external perturbations. This is an important problem to solve because it represents a fundamental challenge in the study of fluid dynamics, with numerous applications in geophysical and astrophysical contexts.

Our key ideas and methodology involve using numerical simulations to model the behavior of fluids undergoing random large-scale forcing. Specifically, we employ direct numerical simulations, using high-performance computing to resolve the complex details of the flow. We focus on parameter regimes that are relevant to geophysical and astrophysical scenarios, such as ocean currents and atmospheric dynamics.

The motivation for this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physics behind rotating stratified flows, which are an essential component of many natural systems. By studying how vortical and wave modes interact with each other and with external perturbations, we can improve our ability to predict and control these flows, with potential applications in climate modeling, oceanography, and astrophysics.

Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing effort to better understand the complexities of fluid dynamics, with the ultimate goal of improving our ability to model and predict the behavior of natural systems.

In this work, we investigate the pair production of doubly-charged scalars at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), with a focus on their implications for neutrino mass. Doubly-charged scalars arise in various extensions of the Standard Model, including models with lepton number violation, and can be probed at the LHC through their decay into same-sign dileptons. We perform a comprehensive study of the production and decay of these scalars, including higher-order QCD and electroweak corrections, and investigate their impact on neutrino mass. We use the seesaw mechanism to relate the mass scale of the doubly-charged scalars to the neutrino masses, and find that a sizable fraction of the parameter space is already excluded by existing LHC searches. However, there remain interesting scenarios in which the doubly-charged scalars can contribute to neutrino mass while evading existing constraints. We provide detailed predictions for the LHC signatures of these scenarios, which can be used to guide future searches. Our work highlights the important interplay between high-energy collider physics and the properties of neutrinos, which remain one of the most intriguing and puzzling aspects of the Standard Model.

In this work, we present the results obtained from the observation of the South-West extension of the hard X-ray emission from the Coma cluster. The motivation for this research was to study the non-thermal processes associated with the large-scale structure of the Coma cluster, which is one of the largest known clusters of galaxies in the local Universe. The emission mechanism of this non-thermal X-ray radiation has been attributed to the inverse Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background photons by relativistic electrons in the intracluster medium (ICM). 

By analyzing the X-ray data obtained by the INTEGRAL satellite, we discovered a significant extension of the hard X-ray emission of the Coma cluster towards the South-West direction. We found that the spatial distribution of the emission aligned well with the radio relics, which suggests that the same population of relativistic electrons that produce the radio emission are also responsible for the X-ray emission. Additionally, we found that the X-ray spectrum of the extension was significantly harder than the spectra of the other X-ray features in the cluster.

Our results shed light on the physics of the intracluster medium, the origin of the relativistic electrons, and the mechanisms of injection, acceleration, and propagation of high-energy particles in the Coma cluster. This work attempts to solve the problem of the origin of the hard X-ray emission in the Coma cluster, which has been poorly understood so far.

In this paper, we present the results on axion physics from the CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) Experiment. Our study aims to search for the hypothetical particle axion, which is a promising candidate for dark matter. The key ideas behind this research stem from the discrepancies between the observed gravitational effects on astrophysical scales and the predictions of the Standard Model. The axion is a light, weakly interacting particle that could provide a plausible explanation for these discrepancies.

Our methodology involves using the CAST experiment to detect axions produced in the core of the sun. The experiment works by converting axions into detectable photons through a magnetic field. Our data analysis includes the statistical treatment of the measured signal and the development of an axion-photon interaction model.

The results of our study show no evidence of axions, providing new limits on their properties and interaction strengths. Our findings rule out the existence of a broad range of axion masses and strengthen the constraints on the axion-photon interaction, thus improving our understanding of dark matter. This research highlights the importance of continually exploring new avenues of research to expand our knowledge of the universe.

In this paper, we investigate the algebraic cycles on the relative symmetric powers and on the relative Jacobian of a family of curves. The main goal of this research is to explore the relationship between these two objects and to derive explicit formulas for their intersection numbers. We offer a new perspective on these algebraic cycles that allows us to derive fundamental results that were previously overlooked.

Our motivation for this work stems from the overarching goal of understanding the geometry of moduli spaces of curves. These moduli spaces are objects of interest in algebraic geometry and have important applications in many areas of mathematics. However, their study is notoriously difficult due to the complicated structure of their algebraic cycles. One of the main contributions of this paper is to provide new tools that can be used to better understand the geometry of these spaces and to obtain more precise results.

The key ideas and methodology involved in this research rely on the study of the cohomology of families of curves using relative symmetric powers and relative Jacobians. We make use of several algebraic techniques, including intersection theory and the theory of Chow groups, to derive our results. Our main theorem establishes explicit formulas for the intersection numbers of algebraic cycles on the relative symmetric powers and the relative Jacobian. Overall, this work contributes significantly to our understanding of algebraic cycles on moduli spaces of curves, and may have important applications in many areas of mathematics.

In this work, we investigate the role of non-coding DNA in the process of biological adaptation and the possible existence of a universal law governing this process. Non-coding DNA constitutes a major portion of the genome and has long been considered “junk DNA” with no functional role. However, recent studies have revealed that non-coding DNA may play critical roles in gene regulation, development, and other important biological processes.

Our work attempts to explore the hypothesis that non-coding DNA contains programs that express adaptation in response to environmental changes. To this end, we analyze the non-coding DNA of several organisms that have adapted to various environments and compare them to non-adapted organisms. We find that the non-coding DNA of adapted organisms shows a significant difference in its sequence and expression patterns, indicating its involvement in adaptation.

Furthermore, we propose the existence of a universal law of adaptation based on our findings. This law suggests that the non-coding DNA programs enable organisms to adapt to their environments by modifying protein expression and other cellular processes. Our findings and proposed law have important implications for understanding the evolution of life on Earth and may also have practical applications in fields such as biotechnology and pharmacology. Overall, our research provides insight into the functional role and importance of non-coding DNA in the process of biological adaptation.

In our study, we aimed to investigate the role of calcium in the synaptic dynamics underlying reverberatory activity in neuronal networks. The reverberatory activity is defined as the persistence of neuronal activity in the absence of ongoing inputs and has been proposed to underlie short-term memory and pattern recognition. The problem that we attempt to solve is to understand the mechanisms underlying this phenomenon and how it can be modulated to enhance cognitive function. 
Using electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological manipulations, we found that calcium influx through NMDA receptors is necessary for the maintenance of reverberatory activity in the hippocampal network. Additionally, we identified a specific calcium-sensitive potassium channel, BK, which plays a crucial role in regulating the duration and strength of the reverberatory activity. By modulating the activity of this channel, we were able to selectively enhance or decrease the reverberatory activity in the network. 
Our results provide insight into the mechanisms underlying the regulation of reverberatory activity and suggest potential targets for therapeutic interventions in cognitive disorders. By understanding the role of calcium and potassium channels in controlling synaptic dynamics in neuronal networks, we may develop novel approaches for enhancing cognitive function in aging and neurodegenerative disorders.

In this work, we present analytic models of plausible gravitational lens potentials that aim to solve the problem of accurately predicting the gravitational lensing phenomenon. The gravitational lensing phenomenon, where light from a distant object is bent and magnified by an intervening massive object, is one of the striking predictions of Einstein's theory of general relativity. It has become a powerful tool for testing cosmological models and probing the nature of dark matter. However, modeling the gravitational potential of the lensing object accurately remains a challenging problem in astrophysics. 

Motivated by the need for more accurate models, we developed a new framework for creating analytic models of plausible gravitational lens potentials. We focused on mass distributions that are observationally viable and physically motivated. Our method allows us to reconstruct the mass profile of a lensing object from the observed lensing signal and estimate the statistical uncertainties in our model. 

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in modeling a wide range of gravitational lens potentials. Our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We also provided insights into the degeneracies and biases in gravitational lens modeling and highlighted the importance of careful model selection. Overall, the analytic models presented in this work can aid in the interpretation of current lensing data and guide future observations.

We present a study on low-dimensional supersymmetric lattice models, motivated by the search for new phenomena in strongly correlated systems. Our investigation is founded on the fact that supersymmetry, a powerful concept in theoretical physics, provides a technique to solve certain statistical mechanics problems. We exploit this strategy to design models that describe an interplay between bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom. Remarkably, we demonstrate that the supercharges of these systems generate transformations that map the space of physically relevant states to auxiliary sectors of lower energy. This property known as the exact supersymmetry enables us to compute correlation functions and thermal properties in a rigorous way. Our numerical simulations, based on Monte Carlo methods, allow us to go beyond analytic calculations and probe the strong coupling regime for various lattices. We observe a tendency towards the formation of ordered phases at low temperatures, and we analyze the nature of the corresponding order parameters. We also identify the presence of topological excitations, such as instantons, which modify the scaling behavior of the models. Our results contribute to the understanding of low-dimensional supersymmetric models and provide a framework for further investigations in this field.

In this paper, we present a methodology to search for dark matter candidates in the framework of the nuMSM. This model extends the Standard Model (SM) and provides a natural explanation for the smallness of the neutrino masses, while also explaining dark matter and the baryon asymmetry of the universe. In the nuMSM, neutral leptons, called sterile neutrinos, are possible dark matter candidates. The search for these leptons is motivated by the fact that, if they exist, they would contribute to the total dark matter density of the universe. Our methodology is based on the analysis of the production and decay of sterile neutrinos at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We have used data from the ATLAS experiment to set new limits on the parameters of the nuMSM and on the mass range of the sterile neutrinos. Our results show that the nuMSM is consistent with experimental data and that sterile neutrinos of masses below 60 GeV are excluded at 95% confidence level. The results obtained contribute to the ongoing search for dark matter and the understanding of the nuMSM, providing useful information for future experimental research.

In this work, we investigate the stability of viscous shock waves in isentropic gas dynamics. The motivation for this research originates from the scientific interest in understanding the behavior of shock waves, a phenomenon widely observed in nature and engineering applications. While the existence of shock waves has been known for some time, the dynamics of their stability are not well understood. In this study, we focus on isentropic gas dynamics, where the thermodynamic process of the gas is characterized by constant entropy.

Our approach combines analytical and numerical methodologies to study the stability of viscous shock waves. Specifically, we use the linearized stability analysis to investigate the behavior of small perturbations around the steady-state shock structure. Additionally, we perform numerical simulations using a high-resolution shock-capturing method to validate the theoretical results and study the stability of nonlinear shock waves.

Our main contribution is the elucidation of a new instability mechanism that arises due to the presence of viscous effects. We show that the viscous terms can destabilize the shock structure, leading to the formation of a new type of instability, which we term "viscous roll-up." This mechanism is characterized by the development of small-scale, high-frequency oscillations that are not present in the purely inviscid case.

In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the stability of viscous shocks in isentropic gas dynamics and highlights the importance of viscous effects in understanding the behavior of shock waves.

In this study, we investigate the magnetic properties of uranium-based multilayer thin films in order to gain a deeper understanding of their potential applications in spintronic devices. Our methodology involves the fabrication of multilayers composed of uranium and a transition metal, where we vary the thickness of each layer to obtain different properties. Magnetization measurements were conducted using a Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect (MOKE) system to determine the magnetic anisotropy and coercive fields of the multilayers.

Our results indicate that the magnetic properties of these films strongly depend on the thickness of the transition metal layer and the annealing temperature. In particular, a decrease in the thickness of the transition metal layer leads to an increase in coercive field, which could be advantageous for spintronic applications. Additionally, we observed a high magnetic anisotropy in certain films, suggesting that they may exhibit strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy. These findings provide valuable insights into the design and fabrication of uranium-based multilayers with tailored magnetic properties.

This work attempts to solve the problem of developing new materials with desirable magnetic properties for spintronic applications. By studying the magnetic properties of uranium-based multilayers, we hope to unlock their potential as a versatile and efficient material in these devices. The results of this study have potential implications for the development of next-generation computer technologies, which could benefit from the unique properties of these materials.

In this work, we examine the vacuum energy associated with a quantum field theory on the edge of a system in two dimensions. Specifically, we investigate the effects of the renormalization process on the vacuum energy in the presence of a boundary. The problem we aim to solve is to understand how the renormalization process modifies the vacuum energy in a system with a boundary. In particular, we focus on how the quantum fluctuations near the boundary influence the vacuum energy.

Our calculations show that the presence of the boundary leads to a modification of the renormalization procedure, which in turn modifies the vacuum energy. This modification arises because the boundary conditions at the edge of the system introduce a new length scale. As a result, the vacuum energy near the boundary becomes more sensitive to the cutoff length scale.

Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that the vacuum energy is a fundamental quantity in quantum field theory and has important implications for a wide range of fields, including cosmology and condensed matter physics. Understanding the vacuum energy on the edge of a system is essential for describing the behavior of real systems such as quantum Hall systems and topological insulators, where the edge plays a crucial role. Our results provide new insights into the connection between boundary conditions, renormalization, and vacuum energy and contribute to the ongoing effort to understand the role of boundaries in quantum field theories.

In this work, we investigate the spatial distribution of high CO(J=3-2)/CO(J=1-0) ratio gas surrounding the central star cluster of the supergiant HII region NGC 604. The central cluster in this region is young and massive, and its interaction with the surrounding gas is likely to play a major role in the evolution of the region. We use new observations obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) to map the CO(J=3-2) and CO(J=1-0) emission in NGC 604 with high angular resolution. We find that the high CO(J=3-2)/CO(J=1-0) ratio gas is distributed in an arc-like structure around the central cluster, suggesting that the dense gas may have been swept up and compressed by the stellar winds and radiation from the massive stars within the cluster. Our results provide new insights into the feedback processes occurring in young and massive star clusters and the effects of these processes on their immediate environments.
