Our methodology combines analytical calculations, numerical simulations, and statistical analysis of the resulting trajectories. We further explore the implications of our findings for the study of exoplanetary systems and the search for habitable worlds. Our results highlight the importance of considering the dynamics of multiple interacting bodies in celestial mechanics and provide a new perspective on the organization of co-orbital configurations.

In this work, we present an analysis of the X-ray spectra obtained from the central regions of the Seyfert 1 galaxy NGC 4593, observed with the XMM-Newton telescope. Our main goal is to investigate the physical properties of the emitting plasma and the structure of the central engine of this active galactic nucleus (AGN). We used a model that accounts for different physical processes such as photoelectric absorption, scattered continuum, emission lines, and Compton reflection. We also performed a variability analysis to explore the temporal behavior of the source.

Our motivation for this research is to contribute to the ongoing efforts to understand the physics of AGNs, and specifically to characterize the diversity of their X-ray properties. NGC 4593 is a particularly interesting object due to its strong X-ray variability and complex spectral features.

Our results show that the X-ray spectrum of NGC 4593 can be explained by a combination of an absorbed power-law and a narrow Gaussian emission line. We also found evidence for a significant reflection component that increases with energy, indicating the presence of a highly-ionized accretion disk. The variability analysis revealed that the source undergoes flux changes by a factor of two on timescales of hours, suggesting a compact, rapidly variable central engine.

In summary, our X-ray spectral analysis of NGC 4593 provides new insights into the nature of the central engine of this AGN, shedding light on the physical processes that drive its emission and variability.

In this paper, we present our assessment of the Accretion vs Colliding Wind (AVCW) models for the gamma-ray binary LS I +61 303, which has been a topic of controversy among the astrophysical community. The motivation behind our research was the need to clarify the origin of the gamma-ray emission in this binary. Our methodology involved the use of non-LTE radiative transfer simulation to construct synthetic spectra, which were then compared with the observed data. We also made use of Chandra and HST observations to study the X-ray and optical emission, respectively.

Our results suggest that the colliding wind scenario is favored over the accretion scenario since it better reproduces the observed gamma-ray spectrum of LS I +61 303. Furthermore, the colliding wind model is able to explain the observed behavior of the binary on larger timescales. This result is consistent with previous studies that have suggested that colliding wind interactions between high mass stars can produce non-thermal gamma-ray emission.

In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the nature of gamma-ray emission in LS I +61 303, and adds to the growing body of evidence that suggests colliding wind models are a viable mechanism for producing non-thermal radiation in high-mass binary systems.

We present a study on the nonlinear dynamics of infectious diseases transfer, with possible applications for the case of tubercular infection. Our work is motivated by the problem of understanding the spread and persistence of infectious diseases in populations, which is a fundamental issue of public health. The key idea of our approach is based on the use of mathematical models that capture the dynamics of the host-pathogen interactions, taking into account the effects of demographic and environmental factors.

We propose a compartmental model that accounts for the transmission of tuberculosis infection, including the possible reactivation of latent infections and the impact of drug therapy. We obtain analytical expressions for the basic reproduction number, which is a key threshold parameter that determines the conditions for the disease to persist in the population. We also perform numerical simulations of the model, which allow us to analyze the effects of different interventions strategies, such as vaccination and quarantine.

Our results show that the dynamics of tuberculosis infection is highly nonlinear, exhibiting a rich variety of patterns, including periodic oscillations, complex attractors, and chaotic behavior. We discuss the implications of these findings for the control of the disease, and the development of new therapies and vaccines. Our work contributes to the growing field of mathematical epidemiology, providing insights into the complex dynamics of infectious diseases transfer.

In this work, we explore the perspectives for the detection and measurement of supersymmetry (SUSY) in the focus point region of mSUGRA models with the ATLAS detector at LHC. The main motivation for our research lies in the fact that SUSY, a theoretical extension of the Standard Model of particle physics, provides a solution for several limitations of the latter, including the hierarchy and dark matter problems. Despite the promising nature of SUSY, no experimental evidence has been found so far to support its existence.

Our work attempts to solve this problem by analyzing the focus point region of mSUGRA models, which predicts a high SUSY mass that makes detection challenging. By using the ATLAS detector at LHC, we investigate the potential sensitivity of the detector to the SUSY particles produced in this region. We apply a series of cuts to the data to reduce the background noise and increase the signal-to-noise ratio. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we determine the potential for statistical significance of our results.

Our results show that the focus point region of mSUGRA models may still be detectable by the ATLAS detector at LHC, depending on the specific values of the model parameters. Our research opens the possibility of exploring these models further and of shedding further light on the existence of SUSY.

In our work, we present an Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) study of thick lamellar stacks of phospholipid bilayers. The purpose of this research was to characterize the morphology and mechanical properties of thick lipid layers and to evaluate the suitability of AFM for analyzing them. In addition, we aimed to gain insights into the structural features of lipid bilayers, such as their thickness, roughness, and interlayer spacing.

Using AFM imaging, we were able to observe the shape and topography of the multi-layered phospholipid stacks with high resolution, and to accurately determine the thickness and layer-to-layer distance of the bilayers. Our results showed that the thickness of the bilayers were consistent within the same stack, with an average thickness of ~4.7 nm. Furthermore, we found that the roughness and spacing between the layers increase with an increase in the number of layers.

The motivation for this study arises from the need for a better understanding of the structural properties of lipid bilayers, which play important roles in various biological processes. Our results provide important insights into the structure of thick lipid bilayer stacks, thereby contributing to the development of new models of lipid bilayer membranes with potential applications in drug delivery and biomimetic materials. In conclusion, our AFM study represents a valuable tool for investigating complex lipid systems, with promising prospects for future research on the nanoscale characterization of biological and soft matter samples.

In this study, we present the results of our comprehensive survey in the centre of the sigma Orionis star formation region using near-infrared (NIR), optical, and X-ray imaging. Our primary objective was to explore the physical and environmental properties of young stars and their circumstellar disks in this region. We used data from both archival and newly obtained observations to identify 602 candidate young stellar objects (YSOs). By analyzing their NIR colors and spectral energy distributions (SEDs), we classified the YSOs into Class I, II, and III, with 88% of them being Class II. We also find evidence for the presence of transitional disks, which are disks with inner depleted cavities, around 26% of the YSOs. 
Furthermore, we correlated the NIR and optical data with the X-ray properties of the YSOs to investigate their relationship with the disk evolution and disk locking mechanism. We found that the X-ray emission correlates with the disk fraction and surface density. Our results suggest that disk evolution in sigma Orionis is likely regulated by the interplay between magnetic fields, accretion, and X-ray ionization. Overall, our survey provides valuable insights into the physical processes governing star and disk formation in this region, which could help us to better understand the early stages of star formation and the diversity of planetary systems.

In this research work, we report on the discovery of two candidate pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) in the very-high-energy gamma ray band. These PWNe are potential sources for high-energy astrophysical phenomena that are thought to be powered by the intense magnetic fields and relativistic particles in the vicinity of young, rapidly rotating neutron stars – pulsars.

Our research methodology involved analyzing the deep observations of the gamma-ray sky with the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.), which is an array of Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes located in the Khomas Highland of Namibia. By carefully examining the spatial distribution of the emission detected from the region around two gamma-ray sources, we identified extended emission that could be associated with the emission from a PWNe.

The results obtained from this study suggest that the newly discovered PWNe could be key sources for investigation of pulsar phenomena, such as the interaction of fast-moving pulsar winds with the ambient medium. The discovery of these candidate PWNe opens up new opportunities for the study of the high-energy astrophysical processes in the universe, and provides insights into the mechanisms that drive the emission of very high-energy gamma rays.

In this paper, we present our work on the kinetic theory of two dimensional point vortices, which has been motivated by the need to understand the behavior of such vortices in various fluid dynamics applications. To this end, we have developed a BBGKY-like hierarchy for the point vortices system, and derived the kinetic equation for the one particle distribution function. In order to obtain this result, we have used a well-known technique in the field of plasma physics, where we have treated the velocity of each point vortex as a random variable. 

Our results show that the kinetic equation for the one particle distribution function corresponds to the kinetic equation for a two-dimensional ideal gas. By analyzing the moments of this equation, we have also derived the evolution equations for the moments of the vorticity field. We have further used the formalism of the kinetic theory to derive the equation for the energy spectrum of the point vortices, which shows that the energy cascades from the large scales to small scales similar to the enstrophy cascade in two-dimensional turbulence. 

Overall, our work provides an analytical foundation for understanding the dynamics of point vortices in two-dimensional systems, which has implications for a wide range of applications in fluid dynamics and geophysics.

We present a comprehensive analysis of full-wave electromagnetic cloaking, a subject of great interest in the field of metamaterials and invisibility. The problem we attempt to solve is that of designing an electromagnetic cloak that can make an object invisible to electromagnetic waves in the time domain. Our approach is based on a rigorous time-domain analysis of the cloaking mechanism, which involves solving the Maxwell's equations for a cloak of arbitrary shape and refractive index profile. 

The key idea behind our work is to use a numerical simulation technique called finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) to model the propagation of electromagnetic waves through the cloak and the background medium. Our methodology involves designing and optimizing a cloak with a specific refractive index profile that can satisfy the necessary boundary conditions for wave cloaking. We show that our approach can lead to the creation of a cloak that can make an object invisible to electromagnetic waves, even in the presence of a background medium. 

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the cloak in hiding a perfectly conducting cylinder and a metal sphere from electromagnetic waves in a wide frequency range. Our analysis also reveals the limitations of the cloak's performance, such as the sensitivity to the geometry of the background medium. Our work provides an important contribution to the field of metamaterials and invisibility, and it can pave the way for the development of practical applications in areas such as stealth technology and electromagnetic protection.

In this work, we investigate the finite temperature corrections and embedded strings in noncommutative geometry and the standard model with neutrino mixing. The motivation for this research stems from the need to develop a deeper understanding of the theoretical framework underlying the unification of the standard model with gravity. This unification can only be achieved if the effects of quantum gravity at high energy scales are taken into account. Noncommutative geometry has been proposed as a potential approach to incorporate these effects at a fundamental level.

To study this framework, we introduce the notion of embedded strings in noncommutative geometry and study their properties. We then compute the finite temperature corrections to the partition function of the standard model with neutrino mixing using the path-integral formalism. Our methodology involves the use of perturbative techniques, such as the heat-kernel expansion method, to compute the trace of the operator involved. Our methods allow us to explore the effects of thermal fluctuations on the dynamics of the system.

We find that the partition function exhibits non-trivial behavior that can be attributed to the presence of embedded strings. These results contribute to the ongoing efforts to understand the microscopic origin of gravity and may provide new directions for future research.

In this study, we investigate the evolutionary dynamics of the most populated genotype on rugged fitness landscapes. The motivation for our research stems from the longstanding question of how populations adapt to complex environments that pose challenging fitness landscapes. We aim to explore the behavior of the most common genotype and understand whether it is adaptive under such conditions.

We use a computational approach to investigate the evolutionary dynamics of the most populated genotype on rugged fitness landscapes. Our results reveal that this genotype can jump between different fitness peaks, which is a critical property for populations to adapt to complex environments. This switch of peaks is facilitated by genetic drift or through mutations in the genotype. We show that the frequency of these transitions depends on the ruggedness of the fitness landscape.

Our work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the adaptability of populations to complex environments and advancing our knowledge of evolutionary dynamics. Our study sheds light on how the most prevalent genotype behaves on rugged fitness landscapes and provides insight into the potential for adaptive evolution in such environments. Our findings have implications for understanding the evolution of complex traits and the mechanisms that underlie population adaptation.

In this work, we propose a novel logic for formalizing the notion of reachable patterns in linked data-structures. Our logic encompasses the ability to represent complex relationships among the nodes of a linked data-structure, enabling us to reason about their properties and behavior. The ability to define and reason about these relationships is crucial in various applications, such as program analysis, model checking, and cryptography. 

The goal of our work is to provide a coherent and expressive framework for defining and reasoning about linked data-structures and their properties, while remaining amenable to automated reasoning. We approach this problem as a generalization of first-order logic by adding a new quantifier that captures the notion of reachability. We show that our logic is sound and complete with respect to a natural semantics, which we define as a first-order theory over a rich class of graph structures. 

We illustrate the power and applicability of our logic through a variety of examples, including a toy implementation of a security protocol, and a proof of correctness for a variant of Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm. Our methodology draws on concepts and techniques from graph theory, automata theory, and mathematical logic. Overall, we believe that our work represents a significant advance in the formalization and analysis of linked data-structures with complex relationships.

In this work, we investigate profinite complexes of curves and their automorphisms, with a focus on anabelian properties of moduli stacks of curves. The motivation for this research comes from the desire to understand the geometry of curves, both in terms of their algebraic structure and their moduli spaces. Our key ideas are centered around the concept of profinite completion, which provides a way to capture the global structure of curves by studying their automorphisms in a topological framework. We also explore how this relates to anabelian geometry, a branch of algebraic geometry that seeks to understand the structure of algebraic varieties by studying their fundamental groups. 

Our methodology involves a combination of algebraic and geometric techniques, including the use of profinite group theory, étale cohomology, and the theory of algebraic stacks. We focus on the study of moduli stacks of curves, which provide a natural framework for organizing families of curves over arbitrary base schemes. By studying the automorphisms of these moduli stacks, we hope to gain a deeper understanding of how the geometry of curves can be encoded in their algebraic structure.

Overall, our work seeks to shed light on the connections between algebraic geometry, topology, and arithmetic, with the goal of providing new insights into the geometry of moduli spaces of curves. Our ultimate aim is to use this understanding to develop new techniques for studying families of algebraic varieties more generally, and to explore the deeper connections between algebraic geometry and number theory.

In this work, we present a CCD BV survey of 42 open clusters with the aim of identifying their basic physical properties such as age, distance, and color magnitude diagrams. We obtained the data from small telescopes and CCD cameras at different locations, and we astrometrically calibrated them using Gaia DR2 data. We then constructed color magnitude diagrams, isochrones, and mass functions to infer the clusters' ages, distances, and masses. 

Our survey aims to solve the problem of incomplete, inconsistent, and inaccurate open cluster databases with the latest astrometric calibration and photometric measurement techniques. We expect these determinations to improve knowledge of the structure, evolution, and Galactic distribution of open clusters. 

Our results show that the majority of the surveyed clusters are young, with ages ranging from 10 to 500 million years. The distances range from 570 to 9830 pc, with uncertainties of about 5-10%. The masses range from 11 to 700 solar masses, with a median value of 100 solar masses. We also identified a significant number of unresolved binary systems and the presence of mass segregation in some clusters. These results will serve as a resource for further studies of open clusters and their parent molecular clouds.

In this paper, we investigate the Stokes phenomenon that arises in the confluence of the hypergeometric differential equation using the Riccati equation. Our research seeks to provide a deeper understanding of the Stokes phenomenon and explore a new method for studying it. 

The motivation for this research stems from the fact that the Stokes phenomenon is an important concept in the study of differential equations and has numerous applications in physics and engineering. However, its occurrence in the confluence of the hypergeometric equation is particularly challenging to analyze. 

To address this issue, we employ the Riccati equation as a tool for studying the Stokes phenomenon. Our methodology involves transforming the hypergeometric equation into a Riccati equation, which provides us with a more accessible equation to work with. From there, we apply the theory of G-functions to obtain asymptotic solutions and analyze the Stokes phenomenon. 

Our results demonstrate that the Riccati equation provides a useful framework for studying the Stokes phenomenon in the confluence of the hypergeometric equation. We obtain explicit formulas for the Stokes matrices and show that they exhibit the expected behavior. Additionally, we investigate the case where the confluence parameter approaches infinity and provide asymptotic expansions for the coefficients of the Stokes matrices. Overall, this research contributes to the understanding of the Stokes phenomenon and provides a new method for analyzing it.

We present our analysis of multiepoch radial velocity observations of L dwarfs, which aim to address the challenge of accurately measuring the masses of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs. Accurate mass measurements are essential for understanding the fundamental properties and evolution of these objects, and precise radial velocity measurements are an important tool for determining masses. However, L dwarfs are challenging targets for radial velocity measurements due to their low luminosity and weak spectral features. 

To overcome these challenges, we conducted a precision radial velocity survey of a sample of L dwarfs over multiple epochs using the Keck II telescope and the High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES). Our observations spanned a period of 10 years and allowed us to accurately track the radial velocity variations of these objects, yielding more precise mass estimates. We combined our radial velocity measurements with published parallax measurements to determine the masses of our sample of L dwarfs with unprecedented accuracy. 

Our results show that multiepoch radial velocity measurements are a powerful tool for determining precise masses of L dwarfs, which will be critical for improving our understanding of these objects. This work highlights the importance of continued radial velocity monitoring of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs, and the need for more powerful telescopes and instruments to meet these challenges.

In this paper, we present a methodology for exploiting social annotation to assist automatic resource discovery. Our motivation for this research was to address the ongoing challenge of effectively managing the vast amount of digital information available today. The key idea of our approach is to use social annotation, which involves human-generated metadata, to supplement traditional metadata in enhancing resource discovery. To achieve this, we developed a system that collects and analyzes social annotations from various social media platforms, such as Reddit and Twitter. Our methodology involves using machine learning algorithms to extract relevant information from the collected annotations and use it to create personalized resource recommendations. We evaluated our approach by conducting a user study involving 30 participants who were asked to search for resources related to various topics using our system. Our results show that social annotation can significantly improve resource discovery, particularly in cases where traditional metadata is limited or lacking. Moreover, our methodology was able to provide personalized recommendations to each user, making the search process more efficient and tailored to their needs. Overall, our research provides insights into how social annotation can be effectively utilized for automatic resource discovery, contributing to the development of smarter and more effective information management systems.

In this work, we have reported the fabrication of half metallic ferromagnetic metal via an innovative approach. The half metallic materials demonstrate remarkable magnetic properties with huge magnetoresistance which make them highly appealing for spintronics applications. However, the development of such materials has been challenging due to several issues. The conventional methods have limitations and fail to produce half metallicity with high precision and reproducibility. Therefore, an alternative method is required to overcome these challenges.

In this work, we have utilized a unique approach based on the well-established technique of thin-film deposition, controlled annealing and ion implantation. A ferromagnetic metal thin film is deposited, and the half metallic state is induced through the introduction of precise amounts of impurities using ion implantation. We have performed an extensive characterization of the half-metallic thin films using various analytical techniques, including magnetometry and X-ray diffraction.

Our results show that under appropriate experimental conditions, the half metallic state can be achieved reproducibly with highly controlled magnetic and transport properties. The fabricated materials have shown excellent half metallic characteristics, which have been verified theoretically and experimentally. Our innovative technique thus provides a promising approach for the fabrication of half metallic materials, with potential applications in spintronics and other related fields.

In this paper, we present a method for generating 2D path solutions using a single layer excitable CNN model. The motivation for this research is rooted in the need to produce a realistic simulation of an excitable system that could be applied to various scientific and practical fields such as image processing, pattern recognition, and neural computation. The problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of an efficient algorithm that could generate 2D path solutions that could accurately represent the complex behavior of excitable systems.

Our proposed methodology utilizes a single layer excitable CNN model to generate 2D path solutions. The model consists of a grid of excitable units arranged in a regular pattern. Each excitable unit is capable of transitioning from a refractory state to a propagating state, which creates a wave-like behavior in the CNN. By applying appropriate boundary conditions and initial conditions, we are able to create paths that follow the wavefront of the excited cells.

Our key idea is to exploit the wave-like behavior of excitable systems to generate 2D paths. We achieve this by computing a vector field that directs the propagation of the wavefront. This vector field is then integrated to produce a path that smoothly follows the wavefront. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating complex and intricate 2D paths that accurately represent the behavior of excitable systems, which could be applied in various scientific and practical scenarios.

In this work, we present an application of the generator coordinate method (GCM) in time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) for simulating complex electronic systems that require the inclusion of memory effects. Our main goal is to simplify memory-dependent calculations in TDDFT by reducing memory functions to a set of independent coordinates. The resulting framework is an extension of the widely-used adiabatic approximation, with the added advantage of being able to incorporate memory effects in a computationally manageable way without losing accuracy.

We first demonstrate the validity of our approach by applying it to a model system of two electrons in an external potential. The results show good agreement with exact solutions, and we compare our method to other memory-dependent methods in TDDFT. We then apply our approach to the calculation of excitation energies in molecular systems, where we find that our method offers a significant reduction in computational cost compared to other memory-dependent methods.

Overall, our method offers a promising avenue for accurately simulating complex electronic systems that require the inclusion of memory effects in TDDFT. Our motivation for this research is to provide an efficient and accurate way to study such systems that are currently computationally prohibitive.

In this work, we present a high-throughput cross-layer scheme for distributed wireless ad hoc networks. The motivation for this research stems from the growing demand for efficient wireless communication systems as well as the increasing prevalence of ad hoc networks. However, these networks often suffer from limited network capacity, low data rates, and high packet error rates. To address these issues, we propose a cross-layer design that optimizes the performance of the physical, MAC, and network layers jointly. Our scheme utilizes multi-channel transmission, hierarchical channel access, adaptive modulation, and power control to increase network throughput, reduce packet loss, and prolong network lifetime. We evaluate the performance of our approach through simulations and compare it with existing methods like CSMA/CA and EDCF. Results show that our scheme outperforms both in terms of network throughput, packet delivery ratio, and energy consumption. Our design also performs well in dense and highly dynamic scenarios, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. Overall, our research contributes to the development of efficient wireless communication systems and provides a practical solution to the challenges faced by ad hoc networks.

In this work, we present a theoretical study of vortices in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). Our aim is to understand the formation, dynamics, and properties of vortex structures in these systems, which are of interest both from a fundamental perspective and for potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum metrology. We begin by reviewing the basic physics of BECs, including their mathematical description in terms of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. We then discuss the formation of vortices in BECs and the properties of the resulting vortex structures, including their quantized core with a well-defined angular momentum. We analyze the dynamics of vortices, including their motion and interactions, both in the presence of external potentials and in homogeneous systems. Our results show that the dynamics of vortices are highly nonlinear and can lead to interesting and complex behavior, such as vortex reconnections and the formation of vortex lattices. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of vortex structures in BECs, including the generation of entangled states of atoms and the production of high-precision rotation sensors. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive theoretical treatment of vortices in BECs and sheds light on the fundamental physics of these fascinating quantum systems.

In this work, we investigate the behavior of nonhomogeneous magnetization and its effect on superconductivity in superconductor-ferromagnet structures. Our motivation for this research stems from the need to understand and control spin-polarized transport in superconducting devices, which has important implications for spintronics and quantum computing applications. 

Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we have studied the interplay between ferromagnetic and superconducting order parameters, taking into account the spatial variation of the magnetization within the ferromagnet. Our key finding is the emergence of nonhomogeneous magnetization profiles that can induce a spatially varying pairing potential in the adjacent superconductor, leading to nonuniform suppression of the superconducting order parameter. 

Additionally, we have found that the behavior of the superconductor-ferromagnet structure depends crucially on the orientation of the magnetization relative to the interface, with different magnetization configurations inducing distinct spatial patterns of superconducting suppression. Our results shed light on the complex interplay between magnetism and superconductivity in hybrid structures and provide guidance for the design of new spintronic devices.

In this study, we investigate the applicability of layered sine-Gordon models to the case of magnetic coupling in layered superconductors. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that layered superconductors are complex systems composed of alternating superconducting and non-superconducting layers, with unconventional properties that depend on the number, thickness, and coupling strength of the layers. These properties are of great interest for both fundamental and applied research, as they can be used to tune and control the superconducting state and its response to external fields.

The problem we attempt to solve is to develop a theoretical framework that can capture the essential physics of magnetic coupling in layered superconductors, by extending the well-established sine-Gordon model to the case of layered systems. We use a perturbative approach that takes into account the interaction between the in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields and the order parameter of each layer. We also compare our model predictions with experimental data from several layered superconductors, including cuprates, iron pnictides, and organic crystals.

Our results show that the layered sine-Gordon model can be a powerful tool to study the behavior of layered superconductors under magnetic fields, provided that the coupling between the layers is weak enough to be treated perturbatively. We find that the model can reproduce several key features of the experimental data, such as the anisotropic response of the critical current and the formation of flux lattices with different symmetries. Our work sheds light on the role of coupling in determining the properties of layered superconductors and paves the way for further theoretical and experimental investigations.

In this work, we investigate the conserved charges associated with spacetimes that are asymptotically flat or anti-de Sitter and have a wide range of dimensions. These charges are important in understanding the global properties of solutions to Einstein’s equations and are well established in most cases. However, there are some subtleties that arise when considering spacetimes in arbitrary dimensions that have not been fully explored. 

Our motivation for this research is to broaden our understanding of these conserved charges and to establish their validity in the aforementioned cases. In particular, we aim to explore the underlying geometrical structures that give rise to the conserved charges and to understand how these charges are related to other quantities, such as the asymptotic behavior of the spacetime and its boundary conditions. This work also aims to clarify some of the open questions and misunderstandings in the literature concerning the asymptotic charges in higher dimensions. 

To accomplish this, we examine some key ideas and methods related to the construction of conserved charges, such as the Hamiltonian approach, the use of variational principles, and the conservation laws of symmetries. Our analysis involves a careful treatment of the asymptotic behavior of the metric and the corresponding boundary conditions needed to ensure the validity of the charges. Our results provide a better understanding of the conserved charges in asymptotically flat and anti-de Sitter spaces and highlight the importance of their proper definitions and physical interpretation.

In this work, we investigate the third-order cosmological perturbations of zero-pressure multi-component fluids in the context of pure general relativistic nonlinear effects. Our aim is to gain a deeper understanding of the dynamics of the Universe by studying the nonlinear effects which arise due to the interaction of various components that make up the cosmic fluid. To this end, we derive the governing equations for the perturbations and analyze their behavior in different scenarios. 

Using a combination of analytical and numerical techniques, we explore the evolution of the perturbations and investigate their impact on the large-scale structure of the Universe. We find that the third-order perturbations can have a significant effect on the cosmic clustering of matter, leading to possible deviations from the standard predictions of linear perturbation theory. Moreover, we demonstrate that our results can be used to test the validity of various cosmological models and improve our understanding of the origins of cosmic structures. 

Overall, our work represents a significant step towards a more comprehensive understanding of the nonlinear dynamics of the Universe. The key idea of our study is to incorporate higher-order perturbations and nonlinearity into our cosmological framework, which provides a more accurate representation of the actual behavior of the cosmic fluid. Our methodology involves a combination of analytical derivation and numerical simulation, which allows us to explore the behavior of the system in different scenarios and to validate our results. The problem our work attempts to solve is the lack of a complete understanding of the nonlinear effects that arise due to the interactions between different components of the cosmic fluid. Our study provides new insights into this problem and brings us closer to a more comprehensive understanding of the Universe.

Our work investigates the possible evolution of dim radio quiet neutron star 1E 1207.4-5209 in the context of a beta-decay model. The motivation for our research lies in the fact that dim radio quiet neutron stars evolve differently from those that shine brightly in the form of pulsars. Our work attempts to solve the problem of understanding the astrophysical mechanisms behind the evolution of dim neutron stars. 

We conducted numerical simulations based on a beta-decay model, which assumes that neutron stars contain a small fraction of free neutrons that can decay into protons, electrons, and antineutrinos. The results show that the decay of free neutrons is responsible for generating heat in the core of the neutron star, which prolongs the cooling timescale of the star. Our simulations also suggest that the beta-decay model can explain the observed dimness of neutron star 1E 1207.4-5209 and its unique X-ray spectrum.

In conclusion, our work sheds light on the possible evolution of dim radio quiet neutron stars such as 1E 1207.4-5209 and provides a framework for future studies in this field. Our results are important for understanding the complex astrophysical processes that govern neutron stars and for advancing our knowledge of the overall universe.

In this study, we explore the Laplacian instability of planar streamer ionization fronts through the lens of pulled front analysis. The problem we seek to solve is the understanding of the mechanism behind the instability of planar streamer ionization fronts which has been observed recently in experiments. To accomplish this task, we use the pulled front framework, which is well suited to describe the dynamics of propagating curved fronts. 

Our key idea is to provide a rigorous framework for the understanding of the Laplacian instability of streamer fronts, which is in many ways similar to the Mullins-Sekerka instability of crystal growth. We use a combination of analytical and numerical tools to investigate the behavior of pulled fronts, starting from their linearized dynamics and leading to the full nonlinear regime. 

Our results demonstrate the existence of a bifurcation behavior as the Laplacian instability parameter is increased, leading to the appearance of multiple branches of solutions. Furthermore, we identify the role of the various physical parameters, such as the surface tension and the conductivity, on the formation of these bifurcations. Overall, our work sheds new light on the complex dynamics of planar streamer ionization fronts, providing a starting point for future experimental and theoretical studies.

In this study, we investigate the formation of galactic disc warps due to intergalactic accretion flows onto the disc. Our methodology involves running high-resolution simulations of isolated discs and comparing them to simulations including an accretion flow. We use a gas-dynamical code and consider different parameters, such as the strength of the gravity of the accreted material and the angle of incidence on the galactic disc.

Our main objective is to understand the origin and evolution of warps in galactic discs. These warps have been observed in several nearby galaxies and are believed to be caused by interactions with nearby galaxies or intergalactic gas streams. However, the role of intergalactic accretion flows in causing disc warps has not been fully explored.

Our results show that intergalactic accretion flows can indeed induce disc warps, with the angle of incidence and the strength of the gravity of the accreted material being the key factors in determining the severity and longevity of the warp. Our findings suggest that accretion flows should be taken into account when studying the evolution of galactic discs and may explain some of the observed warps that cannot be explained by interactions with nearby galaxies. Overall, our research sheds light on the complex interplay between galaxies and their surroundings and provides a new perspective on the formation of galactic disc warps.

We present the results of a search for gravitational radiation from binary black hole MACHOs (Massive Astrophysical Compact Halo Objects) in the Galactic Halo, using data from the LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) detectors. The motivation for this research stems from the possibility that a significant fraction of dark matter in our Galaxy is made up of MACHOs, including black holes, which can form binary systems. These systems can potentially emit gravitational waves as they orbit and merge, providing a unique opportunity to probe the dark matter content of our Galaxy and test gravitational wave physics.

We analyzed more than two years of LIGO data, searching for signals consistent with binary black hole mergers in the Galactic Halo. We found no evidence for such signals, placing upper limits on the rate of compact binary mergers in the Galactic Halo. Our results are compared with theoretical predictions for the merger rate of binary black hole MACHOs in the Galactic Halo, and placed constraints on the fraction of dark matter made up of MACHOs.

This work contributes to the growing field of gravitational wave astronomy, expanding our understanding of the Universe and its composition. We demonstrate the importance of using gravitational wave observations to explore the nature of dark matter. Our results provide valuable insights into the search for black hole MACHOs, while also highlighting the challenges faced in detecting them. Further studies are needed to fully understand the composition of dark matter and the Universe at large.

We present a study on the energy transfer between throats in the context of 10 dimensions. Our motivation is to deepen the understanding of how energy flows between different regions of space and to develop a more comprehensive model for energy transfer. Our key idea is to use the AdS/CFT correspondence to describe the energy transfer between throats in terms of the gauge theory living on the brane. In order to study this, we first construct a model that involves two parallel AdS black holes connected by a throat. Then, we calculate the energy flux between the two throats by identifying the modes of the gauge theory on the brane. Our results reveal that the energy flux is directly proportional to the temperature of the black holes indicating that hotter black holes allow for more efficient exchange of energy between throats. These findings provide important insights into the dynamics of energy transfer in higher dimensions and could have implications for the understanding of black hole thermodynamics.

In this paper, we present a thorough analysis of the universal features of dimensional reduction schemes arising from breaking general covariance. Our motivation for this work was to develop a deeper understanding of how such reductions can be used to identify the fundamental degrees of freedom governing a system's dynamics. We approached this task by examining a wide range of covariant systems, including scalar, electromagnetic, and gravitational, that have been reduced to lower dimensions. In doing so, we identified several key ideas, including the crucial role of gauge symmetries, the importance of geometric structures, and the emergence of boundary conditions. To elucidate these concepts, we utilized a variety of mathematical techniques, ranging from perturbation theory to differential geometry. Our main objective was to provide a comprehensive framework for studying dimensional reductions that could serve as a basis for future investigations into the nature of fundamental physics. Overall, we believe that our work sheds new light on the problem of determining the appropriate dimensionality of a physical system and represents a significant contribution to the field of general covariance breaking.

In this study, we analyze the mass-to-light ratio of Ly-alpha emitters at redshifts z=5.7, 6.5, 7, and 8.8 and the implications of Ly-alpha surveys. Our primary aim is to address the critical issue of the formation and evolution of galaxies in the early universe. Using  lenses to magnify the light from galaxies, we analyze the shapes of galaxies and their offset from the dark matter halo. We find that the mass-to-light ratios of typical Ly-alpha galaxies at z=5.7 and 6.5 are higher than those of nearby galaxies, indicating that these early galaxies are less evolved. At redshifts z=7 and 8.8, however, the mass-to-light ratio is lower than expected, indicating that these galaxies may have already completed their star-forming process. We also show that the results of Ly-alpha surveys may be affected by galactic winds and ionizing radiation. This study provides insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies in the early universe and emphasizes the importance of multifaceted studies, including simulations and observations, to understand this complex process.

In this study, we present a continuous microscale magnetophoretic separation technique for isolating blood cells from plasma by using a microfluidic approach. We developed a microfluidic device that consists of a magnetized nickel nanowire array, which can selectively capture magnetic particles while allowing non-magnetic components to pass through. The microdevice was designed to effectively separate white blood cells (WBCs) and red blood cells (RBCs) from human plasma in a highly efficient and continuous manner.

The objective of this research was to offer an alternative approach for blood separation that is fast, efficient and could potentially be utilized in clinical and diagnostic applications. The results obtained demonstrate the effectiveness of the microfluidic system in separating blood components based on their magnetic properties. Our method is capable of separating plasma from human blood samples with a recovery rate of approximately 90%. Furthermore, we have shown separation efficacy of 85.5% for WBCs and 76.9% for RBCs, respectively.

Overall, the microfluidic separation technique presented in this study has demonstrated substantial potential for simplifying the separation of blood cells from plasma in a continuous, efficient, and robust manner. The results obtained provide a promising platform for next-generation point-of-care diagnostic applications that are more sensitive and accurate than current diagnostic platforms.

The SSS phase of RS Ophiuchi observed with Chandra and XMM-Newton I: Data and preliminary Modeling is a research article that presents observational data and preliminary modeling of the super-soft X-ray (SSS) phase of the recurrent nova RS Ophiuchi. The motivation behind this work is to understand the physics behind the SSS phase, which is the most luminous and longest-lasting phase of recurrent novae. This phase is characterized by high temperatures and long-lasting X-ray emission, which is believed to come from the collision of material ejected by the nova explosion with a white dwarf. 

The article describes the observation of RS Ophiuchi with the Chandra and XMM-Newton X-ray observatories during the SSS phase in 2018. The analysis of the data revealed that the X-ray spectrum of RS Ophiuchi during the SSS phase is much harder than expected, and it has a complex structure indicating the presence of multiple emission components. 

Preliminary modeling of the data using synthetic spectra modeling software also revealed that the observed emission can be explained by a multi-temperature plasma with a range of ionization states. The current work aims to improve the understanding of the physics of the SSS phase in recurrent novae and to help explain the observed X-ray spectra. 

In conclusion, this work provides important new observational data and preliminary modeling of the SSS phase of RS Ophiuchi, which will aid in improving our understanding of the underlying physics of this important phase of recurrent novae.

In our research, we investigate the Non-zero trilinear parameter in the minimal supergravity (mSUGRA) model and its implications for the detection of dark matter and collider signals at both Tevatron and LHC. Our motivation comes from the need to better understand the properties of dark matter and its interactions with other particles. The mSUGRA model is a Supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model of Particle Physics, which predicts the existence of a stable, weakly interacting, massive particle that could account for dark matter. 

We focus on the trilinear Higgs-squark-squark coupling, which plays a significant role in the neutralino annihilation cross-section, particle spectrum, and the relic abundance of dark matter. We study the impact of this coupling on various observables, such as the spin-independent and spin-dependent scattering cross-section, the branching ratios of the Higgs boson, and the production of supersymmetric particles at Tevatron and LHC. 

Our results show that a non-zero trilinear parameter can significantly enhance the direct detection rates of dark matter and lead to a richer signal of supersymmetry at colliders. In particular, a sizable coupling can significantly alter the upper bounds on the spin-independent scattering cross-section and lead to observable deviations in the Higgs branching ratios. Our findings emphasize the importance of considering the trilinear parameter in the mSUGRA model when searching for supersymmetric dark matter and collider signals.

In this work, we explore the Stochastic Loewner Evolution (SLE), a family of random processes that originates from the study of conformal maps. The key idea behind SLE is to use a special family of curves called SLE curves to describe the boundary evolution of a simply connected domain under a conformal map. The methodology behind SLE involves defining a continuous family of probability distributions on curves by specifying the probability of a curve being used to describe the evolution of a domain boundary. This approach allows us to study the statistical properties of conformal maps, which have proven useful in many fields, including mathematical physics, probability theory, and complex analysis.

The motivation for this research is rooted in the desire to understand the behavior of a wide range of natural phenomena, including the behavior of phase transitions, critical phenomena, and the scaling limits of random processes. In particular, SLE has been shown to provide a natural framework for understanding the scaling limits of a wide range of physical systems. We aim to provide a comprehensive account of the SLE theory, including its rigorous mathematical foundations and its applications to various fields of physics and probability theory.

This work attempts to solve the problem of describing the scaling limits of random processes in a rigorous and mathematically sound way, while also providing a useful tool for understanding the behavior of physical systems. Specifically, we seek to study the statistical properties of conformal maps in order to gain insight into the scaling limits of critical models in statistical physics. By providing a comprehensive account of the SLE theory, we hope to contribute to a better understanding of these phenomena, both in theory and in practice.

In this work, we present a simulation of single reed instruments oscillations based on modal decomposition of bore and reed dynamics. We introduce a new method that allows for the generation of realistic sound from single-reed instruments. Our methodology is based on the modal decomposition of the instrument's internal dynamics, which provides a model for the acoustic pressure response of the bore and the motion of the reed. 

Our work focuses on clarinets and saxophones as representative examples of single-reed instruments. First, we analyze the acoustic response of the bore and reed and use data from experiments to construct a finite element model. Then, we decompose the model into a combination of modes using a modal analysis method. Once the modal coefficients are determined, we use them to simulate the reed vibrations and the sound production process. 

The results of our research are promising, as we are able to generate realistic sounds for varying playing conditions. Our methodology can be used for the optimization of single-reed instrument design and in the development of sound synthesis software. 

The motivation for this work lies in the need for a more accurate and cost-effective method of instrument sound modeling. The simulation of single-reed instruments' dynamics is an intricate and challenging problem due to the nonlinear nature of the response. Our work presents a unique solution by employing modal decomposition to achieve a more realistic representation of the instrument's internal dynamics.

In this study, we investigate the line emission of the Brightest Cluster Galaxies (BCGs) in the NOAO Fundamental Plane and Sloan Digital Sky Surveys (SDSS). This investigation aims to unravel the role of BCGs in feeding and quenching the overall star formation in galaxy clusters. We obtained and analyzed spectral lines using a sample of 943 BCGs, selecting the most prominent emission lines to obtain their fluxes and equivalent widths. We compare our results with a control sample of non-BCG galaxies.

Our analysis reveals that BCGs display strong line emission, particularly [O II] and [O III], which are indicators of the presence of ionized gas and ongoing star formation. We find that BCGs have higher line emission than non-BCGs, suggesting that BCGs have a more active quenching phase compared to non-BCGs. Furthermore, our study shows that BCGs with significant line emission tend to have lower velocity dispersions and are located closer to the cluster center.

Our findings suggest that BCGs efficiently quench star formation in their surroundings, possibly due to their proximity to the cluster center and their high velocity dispersions. Our results also emphasize the importance of studying the line emission of BCGs in cluster environments and their role in quenching star formation in neighboring galaxies.

In this work, we focus on multivariable generalizations of the Schur class, which are characterized through positive kernel functions. Our main motivation is to develop a framework for the study of systems with multiple inputs and outputs that is more general than classical theories such as the transfer function representation. We adopt a function-theoretic approach based on the theory of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) to study multivariable Schur functions and their properties. 

Our key methodology involves studying the positive kernel representations of multivariable Schur functions, which lead to a rich set of results and applications. We develop a notion of transfer function realization based on these kernel representations, which gives a new perspective on the representation of multivariable systems. In particular, we show that the kernel representations provide a natural setting for the study of algebraic and analytic properties of multivariable Schur functions.

Our main result is a generalization of the classical factorization theorem for scalar Schur functions to the multivariable case. Specifically, we prove that any multivariable Schur function can be factored into a product of an analytic function and its transpose, where the analytic function is characterized by its positive-definite kernel representation. This factorization result has important implications for the study of multivariable systems, including the design and analysis of control systems.

Overall, our work provides a new perspective on the theory of multivariable Schur functions and their applications to systems theory. We expect our results to have broad implications for the study of multivariable systems in a wide range of applications, including control, signal processing, and communications.

In this study, we present multiwavelength imaging and modeling of the debris disk around AU Microscopii (AU Mic), a nearby M-dwarf star. The debris disk is believed to be the result of collisions of planetesimals and represents a unique window into the formation and evolution of planetary systems. 

We conducted high-resolution scattered light imaging of the disk using Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and Gemini Planet Imager (GPI) in the optical and near-infrared, respectively. We also used archival data from Spitzer Space Telescope (Infrared Array Camera and Multiband Imaging Photometer) and Herschel Space Observatory (Photodetector Array Camera and Spectrometer) to probe the thermal emission from the dust in the disk at mid and far-infrared wavelengths. 

Our analysis of the data reveals a complex morphology of the disk, with radial variations in brightness and morphology. We compare the multiwavelength images to a suite of theoretical models, including both planetesimal belts and exocomets. We find that no single model can fully explain the observed features, highlighting the need for more sophisticated models that can incorporate the dynamical effects of planets and small bodies on the disk structure and evolution. 

The study sheds light on the origin and evolution of planetary systems, demonstrating the power of multiwavelength imaging and modeling to decipher the complex structures of debris disks.

In this paper, we explore the generation of graph states using noisy mirror-inverting spin chains and investigate the effects of noise on their fidelity. Graph states are important for quantum computing, as they enable efficient quantum error correction and measurement-based quantum computing. However, due to the inherent difficulty of generating and maintaining entangled states, it is crucial to study the fidelity of graph states subject to noise. 

Our work demonstrates that noisy mirror-inverting spin chains can generate high-fidelity graph states, even in the presence of decoherence. We present a theoretical analysis of the spin chain model, highlighting the importance of robustness against noise. Additionally, we employ numerical simulations to validate our analysis and examine the impact of various noise sources on the quality of the generated graph states. 

Our methodology involves maximizing the fidelity of the generated graph state by optimizing the spin chain parameters and identifying the most robust state against noise. We also investigate the effect of different types of noise on the spin chain model, including external noise and imperfections in the control pulses that generate the spin chain.

This research is motivated by the need for reliable methods to generate and maintain entangled states, which are crucial for the development of quantum technologies. Our findings provide insights and tools to improve the fidelity of graph state generation, potentially advancing the use of quantum computing in a practical setting.

We present a study of the stratified dust distribution in the GG Tau circumbinary ring based on ALMA observations. Our results show that the dust distribution in the ring is largely influenced by the binary stars and the large-scale pressure gradients caused by the stellar illumination. We find that the dust particles in the inner and outer regions of the ring have different vertical structures due to the different heating sources from the binary stars. We also investigate the impact of the dust dynamics on the ring evolution and find that the dust particles are subject to radial drift, which could lead to the accumulation of planetesimals and the formation of planets. 

The study attempts to solve the open question of the dust evolution in the GG Tau circumbinary ring. Previous models have not fully accounted for the stratification and dynamics of the dust particles, leading to discrepancies between observations and simulations. Our work fills this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of the dust distribution and dynamics using high-resolution ALMA observations. 

The motivation for this research stems from the unique properties of the GG Tau system, which contains multiple protoplanetary disks and potential sites for planet formation. Understanding the dust evolution in the circumbinary ring is fundamental for constraining the mechanisms of planet formation and the formation history of planetesimal belts. Our findings have implications for the wider study of binary star systems and their role in shaping the architecture and diversity of exoplanetary systems.

In this study, we present the results of a wide-field survey around the Local Group dwarf spheroidal galaxy Leo II, focusing on the spatial distribution of its stellar content. The motivation for this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the nature and evolution of dwarf galaxies, which are believed to be the building blocks of larger galaxies in the universe.

The problem we attempt to solve is to identify the spatial distribution of stars in Leo II and assess whether there are any correlations with the dwarf galaxy's properties. We aim to determine if there are any asymmetries or new substructures that may have been missed in previous studies and provide new insights into the origin of dwarf galaxies.

To achieve our objectives, we use deep imaging data from the Subaru telescope and perform a comprehensive analysis of different magnitudes and colors of stars across a wide field around Leo II. We use a statistical approach to map the density distribution of stars and identify possible asymmetries or substructures. Additionally, we investigate the spatial distributions of different stellar populations, such as blue/young and red/old stars, and compare them to theoretical predictions.

Our findings reveal the presence of a new substructure in the outer region of Leo II, which had not been previously detected. The substructure's shape and orientation suggest that it may have formed through a tidal dwarf galaxy process. Our results also suggest the occurrence of a significant event that disrupted Leo II in the past and reshaped its inner region.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the charge injection capability of the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) onboard the Suzaku satellite. The XIS camera, which consists of four detectors with different spectral responses, is widely used for observing celestial objects in the X-ray energy range. However, in recent years, a gradual degradation of its detection capabilities has been reported due to the accumulation of unwanted charges in the device. To mitigate this effect, Charge Injection (CI) has been proposed as a useful technique that allows to remove these charges by injecting fabricated signals into the detectors. 

We conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the efficiency of the CI method and to optimize the injection parameters. With our procedures, we found that the optimal CI frequency was dependent on various factors such as the detector gain and intensity of X-ray sources. In addition, we confirmed that the CI technique showed significant improvement in the performance of both the spectral resolution and energy droop of the XIS. 

Our research was motivated by the concern raised by the scientific communities that the degradation of the XIS's performance would limit the quality and scope of the X-ray observations. Therefore, improving the charge injection capability of the XIS is essential to retain its functionality and ensure the quality and accuracy of future X-ray observations. This research aims to contribute to the resolution of a significant problem in the field of X-ray astronomy through effective techniques and measurements.

In this study, we investigate the dynamics of horizon-penetrating transonic accretion disks around rotating black holes. We aim to understand the physical mechanisms controlling the structure and evolution of these disks and their role in the production of high-energy radiation. Our work is motivated by the fact that accretion disks around black holes are an essential component of a wide range of astronomical objects, including active galactic nuclei and X-ray binaries. These systems produce some of the most energetic phenomena in the universe and provide unique insights into the physics of strong gravity and plasma astrophysics.

We employ numerical simulations to study the hydrodynamic flow and radiative properties of accretion disks around rotating black holes. Our findings reveal that the inner parts of the disk exhibit strong shocks, resulting in significant dissipation and energy release. We also demonstrate that the presence of strong magnetic fields can modify the dynamics of the disk and enhance its ability to produce high-energy radiation. Moreover, we show that the observed spectra of accreting black holes can provide valuable information about the properties of the disk and the black hole.

Our work provides critical insights into the physics of accretion disks and their role in the production of high-energy radiation in astrophysical systems. The results of our study can inform future observations and theoretical models of black hole accretion disks in a number of astrophysical contexts.

In this work, we present a detailed discussion on particle number and quantum indistinguishability in the context of many-body quantum systems. The problem we attempt to solve is to shed light on the effects of particle exchange and quantum statistics on the properties of such systems. In particular, we explore the implications of quantum indistinguishability which leads to a fundamental limitation on our ability to count the number of identical particles within a given volume. 

Our analysis reveals that the particle number in a quantum system is an emergent property that depends on the statistics of the particles and the symmetry constraints imposed by the system. This result challenges the classical notion of counting discrete objects and highlights the importance of considering the quantum nature of the system.

We employ a theoretical approach based on the use of the second quantization formalism and Green's function techniques. We show that these methods provide a powerful framework for addressing the problem of particle number and quantum indistinguishability.

Our findings have implications for a wide range of many-body systems, including quantum gases, solids, and plasmas. Furthermore, our work provides a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties of quantum systems, which has implications for the development of new quantum technologies.

In our research, we conducted polarimetric studies of Comet Hale-Bopp to investigate the physical and chemical properties of this highly active comet. The motivation for our research was to unravel the mysteries surrounding Comet Hale-Bopp, which is regarded as one of the most significant cometary events of the last century. Since its discovery in 1995, Comet Hale-Bopp has been a fascinating subject for astronomers, given its bright coma and extensive dust and gas emissions. 

Key ideas of our research include determining the polarization characteristics of the comet's coma, coma dust, and gas emissions to understand the size distribution of dust particles and the nature of the gas species. Additionally, we aimed to explore the rotational properties of the nucleus and the distribution of coma emissions. To achieve this, we used polarimetric observations obtained from several ground-based telescopes in different parts of the world.

Our methodology involved analyzing data from the observations to obtain polarization phase curves, which we then used to investigate the scattering properties of the comet. Our work's primary problem was to determine the comet's physical and chemical properties to provide insights into the early stages of the solar system's formation. We hope that our study will contribute to advances in cometary science and add to the knowledge of comets' origins and evolution.

In our work titled, "Excluded Volume, Local Structural Cooperativity, and the Polymer Physics of Protein Folding Rates," we seek to understand the relationship between protein structure and the dynamics of folding. Specifically, we investigate how the excluded volume, or steric hindrance, of a protein's amino acid residues affects the folding process and the cooperativity of local structural changes. This work attempts to solve a fundamental problem in the field of protein folding: understanding the factors that determine the rates at which proteins adopt their native conformations.

To address this problem, we use computer simulations of a minimalist protein model that captures the essential features of the folding process. Our results show that the excluded volume of residues plays a crucial role in both the cooperativity and the rate of structural transitions during folding. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the relationship between excluded volume and folding rate is non-linear, highlighting the importance of considering cooperative effects in protein folding.

The motivation behind this research lies in the need to bridge the gap between protein sequence and structure, as understanding the factors that drive protein folding has implications for drug design, biotechnology, and understanding the origins of life. Through this work, we provide insight into the basic physics of protein folding and lay the groundwork for future research in this field.

In this paper, we investigate the environmental dielectric screening effect on the exciton transition energies of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs). The motivation for this research stems from the desire to understand the fundamental electronic properties of SWCNTs and their potential applications in optoelectronic devices. We use a dielectric continuum theory to model the effect of the surrounding environment on the electronic structure of SWCNTs. Our key idea is that the exciton transition energies are affected by the dielectric constant of the surrounding material, which may be different from that of the nanotube itself. To test our model, we perform electronic structure calculations using density functional theory (DFT) and the GW method.

Our results demonstrate that the exciton transition energies of SWCNTs are significantly influenced by the dielectric screening effect of the surrounding environment. We find that the exciton binding energy decreases with increasing dielectric constant of the surrounding material, which leads to redshifts in the optical absorption spectra of SWCNTs. Furthermore, our results show that the dielectric screening effect is stronger for semiconducting SWCNTs than for metallic ones. Overall, our research sheds light on the electronic properties of SWCNTs and provides insights for the design and optimization of SWCNT-based optoelectronic devices.

In our research, we explored the invariance, attractivity, and control of quantum Markovian subsystems. The motivation for this work is rooted in the desire to understand the behavior and dynamics of quantum systems under the influence of environmental noise or disturbances. The problem that we attempt to solve is to characterize the properties of a quantum Markovian subsystem and to find ways to control and manipulate its evolution. 

We developed a novel framework that enables the analysis of the invariance and attractivity of quantum Markovian subsystems. Specifically, we defined the notions of steady-state attractivity and global attractivity, and provided criteria for their determination. Moreover, we demonstrated that controllability of quantum Markovian subsystems can be achieved using simple local operators. 

Furthermore, we proved that the existence of an invariant subspace can ensure the persistence of coherence in open quantum systems, providing a key insight for the development of practical applications in quantum information and computation. Our model serves as a valuable tool for the analysis, design, and optimization of quantum systems, with potential implications for the advancement of quantum technologies. 

In conclusion, our work contributes to the understanding of the fundamental properties of quantum Markovian subsystems and provides a practical means to control and manipulate their behavior.

In this work, we aim to directly calculate interfacial tensions from computer simulations with a focus on tangent hard sphere chains. Interfacial tensions are important for understanding the behavior of materials and are difficult to measure experimentally. Our study seeks to provide a more accurate and efficient method for calculating interfacial tensions. 
To achieve this, we utilized simulations of freely jointed tangent hard sphere chains in order to obtain the density profiles and corresponding pressures at the interface. We then applied a thermodynamic integration method to calculate the interfacial tensions. Our results reveal that the interfacial tensions increase with the length of the chain and have a stronger dependence on temperature. Additionally, we find that the interfacial tensions for tangent hard sphere chains are lower than those for linear chains of the same length.
The key idea behind our study is to provide a direct and reliable method for calculating interfacial tensions. The methodology involves simulation, data analysis, and a thermodynamic integration approach. Our findings have important implications for the development of new materials and the understanding of interfacial properties.

In this paper, we investigate the inapproximability of correlation clustering. Correlation clustering is a well-known clustering problem wherein the goal is to partition a given dataset into clusters in such a way that the clusters correspond to strongly correlated elements. Despite its practical applications in various fields, we show that the problem is in fact NP-hard to approximate within any non-trivial factor. 

Our work builds on existing literature on the correlation clustering problem and its inapproximability. We employ a combination of reduction techniques and hardness results to prove our main findings. Specifically, we rely on the long-standing results on the inapproximability of the unique games problem, a standard tool in computational complexity theory.

Our results have important implications for the design of approximation algorithms for correlation clustering. We show that any approximation algorithm for correlation clustering is doomed to fail in achieving good approximations, and thus, new techniques beyond standard approximation algorithms must be considered. Our work highlights the importance of finding new approaches and polynomial time approximation schemes for this problem in future research. 

Overall, our paper contributes to the growing body of literature on the intractability of clustering problems, and emphasizes the need for more effective algorithms for solving such problems.

In this study, we explore the possibility of detecting coronal radio emission from protostars using Very-Long-Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that our understanding of the coronal properties of protostars is limited, and observations in the radio band can provide valuable insights into the nature of the plasma in these regions. 

We conducted VLBI observations of four protostars, including three Class 0 protostars and one Class I protostar, using the European VLBI Network (EVN) at 5.0 GHz. Our analysis revealed no detection of coronal radio emission from any of the protostars. We used these non-detections to place upper limits on the coronal flux densities for each source. 

Our methodology involved careful calibration of the VLBI data and analysis of the visibilities and spectra at each observing epoch. We also performed simulations to estimate the expected coronal flux densities for the protostars and compared these predictions to our observational results. 

Our key idea was to use VLBI observations to provide high angular resolution imaging of the coronal emission from protostars and to search for potentially detectable signatures of plasma emission. 

Overall, our results indicate that while coronal radio emission from protostars is challenging to detect using VLBI, future observations at higher radio frequencies and with deeper sensitivity may reveal new insights into the coronal properties of young stellar systems.

Our research contribution entitled “The interplay between radio galaxies and cluster environment” seeks to explore the complex relationship between the radio galaxies and their host clusters. The existence of radio sources has been shown to correlate with the presence of dense environments, such as clusters, but the nature of their interaction with the surrounding medium is still unclear.

Using multi-wavelength data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Very Large Array (VLA), we investigate the influence of the cluster environment on 20 radio galaxies. Our work attempts to solve the problem of how the cluster affects the radio emission of these sources and how the energy exchange between the radio jet and the intercluster medium occurs.

Our results show that, in most cases, radio galaxies tend to reside in the denser regions of the cluster, suggesting that cluster merging could trigger the radio activity. Furthermore, we also found that the radio galaxies located in the peripheral regions of the cluster tend to have less powerful radio jets compared to those residing at the center.
