The key ideas of this project are the calculation of various atomic properties for ions in the francium isoelectronic sequence, including oscillator strengths, transition probabilities, and lifetimes. 

The methodology employed in this study involves the Relativistic Many-Body Perturbation Theory (RMBPT) approach within the framework of the Dirac-Coulomb-Breit (DCB) Hamiltonian. We have utilized a highly accurate numerical method called the Multiconfiguration Dirac-Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) method to obtain the atomic wave functions. 

The results obtained in this work show that the electron correlation and relativistic effects have a profound influence on the atomic properties of ions in the francium isoelectronic sequence. Our calculations provide amplified information and a more comprehensive understanding of the atomic structure and properties of the francium isoelectronic sequence, which can aid experimentalists in the knowledge development of the atomic and plasma physics field.

In this work, we present a novel quasi-quadratic point counting algorithm based on p-adic arithmetic. Our approach aims to efficiently determine the number of points on an elliptic curve over finite fields with large prime orders. The motivation for our research stems from the importance of point counting in cryptographic applications, where the security of many schemes relies on the number of points in the elliptic curve.

Our algorithm improves upon previous methods by using a combination of basic p-adic techniques and techniques derived from Mahler's inequality. The key idea behind our approach is to convert the problem of point counting to a discrete logarithm problem in the p-adic field. By doing so, we are able to reduce the complexity of the calculation and improve runtime. Our algorithm exhibits quasi-quadratic complexity in terms of the input size, which significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods.

To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we present experimental results showing that our algorithm is faster than existing methods for large prime orders. Our work has potential implications for the development of faster and more efficient cryptographic algorithms relying on elliptic curve point counting. The proposed approach can also be applied to other mathematical problems that involve point counting.

In this study, we aimed to determine the polarizabilities of intermediate sized lithium clusters using Density-Functional Theory (DFT). The motivation for our research stems from the increasing interest in lithium clusters due to their unique physical and chemical properties. These characteristics make them ideal candidates for a wide range of applications including energy storage, catalysis, and cluster-ion beam lithography. However, there is still a lack of understanding about the polarizabilities of these clusters, which is crucial for interpreting their response to external fields. We carried out DFT calculations to systematically investigate the size-dependent behavior of the polarizabilities of Lithium clusters comprising up to 21 atoms.
Our key idea was to model the clusters as a set of point charges, and test the response of these charges to the external electric field. Our methodology involved the use of DFT with the B3LYP functional, combined with the 6-311++G(3df, 3pd) basis set, to model the clusters. Our results show that the polarizabilities of the clusters increase with cluster size, following a clear trend. This size-dependent behavior is consistent with the classical dipole model, which is expected to apply in the larger clusters. Overall, our study provides a valuable insight into the polarization response of intermediate sized lithium clusters, with important implications for a range of applications in nanotechnology and materials science.

In this work, we present a precision measurement of the Casimir-Lifshitz force in a fluid. The Casimir-Lifshitz force arises due to quantum fluctuations in the electromagnetic field and is pervasive in many areas of physics, including nanotechnology and condensed matter. However, its measurement in a fluid is extremely challenging due to the complex interactions between the fluid molecules and the metal surfaces. 

We overcome these challenges by designing a novel experiment where we place a thin metal-coated sphere in a fluid-filled chamber and measure the force between the sphere and a flat metal surface using a highly sensitive force sensor. We carefully control the temperature and concentration of the fluid and measure the force as a function of separation between the sphere and the surface. 

Our results show agreement with theoretical predictions for the Casimir-Lifshitz force and provide new insights into the role of fluid dynamics in this phenomenon. Furthermore, our measurements demonstrate the potential for using the Casimir-Lifshitz force as a precise tool for probing the properties of fluids at the nanoscale. 

Overall, our work addresses a long-standing problem in the field of Casimir-Lifshitz physics and opens up new avenues for research and technological applications in fluid systems.

In this study, we present the results of our investigation into the high-frequency radio continuum emission from 13 massive young stellar objects (MYSOs). The motivation for our research stems from the desire to gain a better understanding of the physical processes that lead to the formation and evolution of massive stars. MYSOs are important targets for studying these processes due to their high luminosity and mass, which makes them rare and challenging to observe. 

We used the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array to observe MYSOs at a range of frequencies between 21 and 37 GHz. Our analysis revealed that the radio continuum emission of MYSOs is dominated by free-free emission from ionized gas associated with outflows and expanding HII regions. We also detected compact, non-thermal emission that may be associated with synchrotron radiation from shock fronts. 

Our study contributes to a better understanding of the processes involved in massive star formation and provides important insights into the physical properties of MYSOs. The work attempts to solve a problem in astrophysics by providing new insights into the high-frequency radio continuum emission associated with massive stars, which has important implications for the study of the early stages of stellar evolution.

In this work, we explore the connection between algebraic K-theory and partition functions in Conformal Field Theory (CFT). The motivation behind our research stems from the fundamental question of how algebraic structures manifest themselves in physics. The main idea is to utilize the well-established machinery of K-theory to study modular invariance and duality properties of partition functions arising in CFT. The methodology involves formulating a mathematical model that bridges the gap between the two subjects. Specifically, we define an algebraic object associated to a given CFT partition function, known as the K-theory spectrum of the CFT. We then study its key properties and relate them to physical properties of the CFT, such as modular invariance and duality. 

Our main result is a classification of K-theory spectra associated to rational CFTs. Additionally, we elucidate the connection between K-theory and physical spectra, leading to a deeper understanding of the structure of CFT partition functions. One of the most interesting implications of our work is the emergence of algebraic structures in physics that were not anticipated in previous studies. Our findings have the potential to significantly impact the fields of algebraic topology and theoretical physics. By uncovering the rich and unexplored interplay between algebraic K-theory and CFT partition functions, we hope to inspire further research in this area and pave the way for new discoveries in both mathematics and physics.

Our research explores the development of an electrostatic climber for a space elevator and launcher. The motivation behind this study is to overcome the current limitations posed by conventional launch systems, which require vast energy and resources to take off into space. This work aims to solve the problem of high energy and cost utilization by introducing an innovative approach to space launch and transportation.

Our key idea involves designing an electrostatic climber capable of moving at high speeds along a conductive track, powered by static electricity. The climber will generate an electric charge that will facilitate smooth movement along the tracks, resulting in a cost-efficient means of launching payloads into space. The methodology entails constructing and testing a prototype electrostatic climber on a small-scale model track to demonstrate its feasibility and capabilities.

The proposed electrostatic climber has the potential to revolutionize the space industry by providing a new way to navigate space and launch payloads. This innovative technology requires minimal energy and resources to transport payloads, offering significant cost savings in the long-term. Our research contributes to the ongoing advancement of space engineering technology and may offer a more sustainable approach for space travel and exploration.

In this paper, we present an analysis of the end-to-end distortion (EED) for a buffered transmission over fading channels. Our work attempts to provide a comprehensive understanding of the effect of fading channels on the distortion caused by buffering, and to identify the optimal buffer size that minimizes the EED. 

To achieve this, we employ a theoretical framework in which we model a buffered transmission system as a discrete-time stochastic process. We assume that the system operates in a time-varying fading channel, where the channel gain evolves according to a Ricean model. We then derive expressions for the mean square error (MSE) and the distortion as functions of the buffer size, the channel parameters, and the signal characteristics.

Our results show that the EED for a buffered transmission over a fading channel increases with the buffer size, the channel fading severity, and the signal correlation. Moreover, we demonstrate that for a given buffer size, there exists an optimal signal-to-noise ratio that minimizes the EED. We also highlight the effect of the channel correlation on the EED behavior.

Overall, our work contributes to the understanding of the fundamental tradeoff between buffering and channel fading, which has a wide range of applications in wireless communications and multimedia systems.

We present our investigation of the rotational braking and magnetic field strength in three components of the late-M multiple system LHS 1070. Our motive is to gain insight into the relationship between the rotational evolution and the magnetic properties of each component in the presence of strong magnetic fields and chromospheric activity. For this purpose, we carried out a study combining high-resolution spectroscopy, the Zeeman-Doppler Imaging technique, and photometry. Our analyses suggest that the spectral type-dependent rotational braking is indeed present in LHS 1070, and that it is most effective in the earliest-type, most massive star of the system. Additionally, we observed strong surface magnetic fluxes in all components, believed to be the main agents responsible for the braking of rotation in each star. Our results indicate that the rotational evolution and magnetic activity in the three components of LHS 1070 are indeed the manifestations of the interaction between the stellar spin, magnetic fields, and magnetic cycles. Furthermore, our study emphasizes the importance of multi-component systems in the study of late-M stars and their magnetic properties.

In this study, we investigate the dynamic condensation of water at crack tips in fused silica glass. Our motivation stems from the fact that water plays a crucial role in the behavior of cracks in materials and can often promote their growth and failure. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we show that water molecules condense spontaneously at the surface of silica glass as the temperature drops below the dew point, forming a thin liquid layer that can significantly affect the mechanical behavior of the material. We further investigate the influence of surface tension and contact angle on the water condensation process and find that these factors strongly affect the morphology and stability of the liquid layer. Our results also show that the presence of water can alter the critical stress intensity factor required for crack propagation in fused silica glass by up to 20%, highlighting the importance of considering water effects in fracture mechanics studies. Overall, our findings shed new light on the behavior of water at crack tips in silica glass and provide important insights into the design and optimization of materials for diverse applications.

In this review, we explore the concept of dynamical 3-space, its key ideas, and methodology. At its core, dynamical 3-space aims to unify Einstein's theory of relativity with quantum mechanics by positing that a third spatial dimension exists, which is dynamic and constantly changing. We evaluate the theoretical framework underlying this idea, reviewing its implications for key physical phenomena, such as gravity, and explore its potential applications for understanding fundamental aspects of the universe, including dark matter and dark energy.

The motivation for this research lies in the fact that our current understanding of the universe's physical laws remains incomplete, particularly in the context of the fundamental forces of nature and their relationship with space and time. There are important problems such as the issue of quantum gravity that continues to elude physicists. The dynamical 3-space conception offers a promising framework that may help bridge some of these gaps and provide a more coherent, fundamental theoretical picture of the universe.

We evaluate various proponents of dynamical 3-space, examining their methodological approaches and presenting their key insights. Additionally, we highlight the challenges and limitations associated with this framework, such as the difficulties in constructing accurate predictive models or experimental tests. Nonetheless, we argue that dynamical 3-space remains an intriguing and important avenue for further research, with the potential to expand our understanding of the universe's fundamental nature in exciting and meaningful ways.

In this work, we investigate the anisotropic distribution of satellite galaxies around their isolated central galaxies. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that the orientation of these satellite galaxies can provide insights into the formation and evolution of their host galaxies, which in turn can lead to a better understanding of the larger scale structures of the universe. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that the satellites' orientations are preferentially aligned with the central galaxy's major axis. 

To investigate this hypothesis, we construct a sample of central galaxies taken from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and select their surrounding satellites. We then measure the alignment between the major axis of each central galaxy and the axes of its surrounding satellites. We find that, on average, satellite galaxies are preferentially oriented along a plane perpendicular to the direction of the central galaxy’s major axis, which suggests that the central galaxy's effect on its surrounding environment is stronger than previously thought. Moreover, we find that this anisotropic distribution is more prominent for high-mass central galaxies than for low-mass ones. These results shed light on the intricate interplay between central galaxies and their satellite galaxies, emphasizing the importance of their mutual interactions in shaping the universe's large-scale structures.

In this work, we explore the topic of symmetries in differential geometry through a computational approach to prolongations. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that symmetries play a crucial role in many areas of mathematical physics and mechanics, with applications ranging from fluid dynamics and elasticity to relativistic mechanics and quantum field theory. Our main goal is to develop a computational framework for computing the prolongations of Lie symmetries of a given differential equation, which essentially amounts to determining the highest-order derivatives that can be expressed in terms of the dependent and independent variables and their lower-order derivatives. 

Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed computational approach, which is based on the use of symbolic manipulation software and Lie symmetry algorithms. We show that this approach can be applied to a wide range of differential equations, from simple linear equations to highly nonlinear systems. Moreover, our approach allows us to obtain explicit formulas for the prolongations of Lie symmetries, which can be used to determine the Lie point symmetries of the equation. This, in turn, provides valuable insight into the underlying symmetry structure of the equation and its physical implications. Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of the role of symmetries in differential geometry, and provides a powerful computational tool for investigating these structures in various contexts.

Our research investigates the accretion process in low mass stars and brown dwarfs situated in the Lambda Orionis Cluster using Spitzer data. Our motivation for this study is to understand the formation and evolution of low mass stars and brown dwarfs in the early stages of their lives. Accretion is a fundamental process in the evolution of these astronomical objects.

We found that the accretion rate is positively correlated with the mass of the central source. Additionally, the accretion rate distribution of the brown dwarfs in the cluster is consistent with those of known brown dwarfs in other regions, indicating universal accretion mechanisms.

Our work aims to solve the problem of understanding the accretion process in low mass stars and brown dwarfs in the early stages of their formation. Accretion is vital in determining the mass of the central object, which affects its evolution and eventual fate. By analyzing Spitzer data, our research provides insight into the physical processes governing the observed system. This information is crucial in advancing our understanding of star and brown dwarf formation and provides a stepping stone towards a complete understanding of the universe.

In this paper, we present our work on Finite Euler Products and the Riemann Hypothesis. Our study aims to provide a rigorous analysis of the relationship between the zeroes of the Riemann zeta function and certain special functions known as Euler products. The Riemann Hypothesis, one of the fundamental unsolved problems in mathematics, states that all non-trivial zeroes of the zeta function lie on the critical line of the complex plane. Our research attempts to establish a connection between the presence of zeroes of certain finite Euler products and the distribution of zeroes of the Riemann zeta function.

We have derived new results that establish the existence of unexpected zero-free regions for finite Euler products. We have demonstrated that certain algebraic expressions, referred to as approximate functional identities, can yield information on the number of zeroes of the Riemann zeta function within certain rectangles in the complex plane. Our methodology involves techniques from complex analysis, number theory, and representation theory.

Overall, our findings provide new insights into the relationship between the Riemann Hypothesis and Euler products and have potential implications for related problems in number theory.

In this paper, we introduce needlet algorithms for estimation in inverse problems. We address the problem of estimating an unknown signal x_0 from indirect and noisy observations. We assume that the signal x_0 can be represented in a suitable known basis and aim to recover this representation in a stable and efficient manner. The proposed method involves reconstructing the signal in a sparse representation by projecting it onto the space of needlets, which allows for an adaptive and multiscale analysis of the data. The methodology relies on a two-step approach that first estimates the needlet coefficients by convex optimization and then reconstructs the signal by inverting the needlet transform. The performance of the proposed algorithms is illustrated through numerical experiments on a range of inverse problems, including compressed sensing, deconvolution, and image denoising. Our results demonstrate that needlet algorithms can achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Overall, this work contributes to the development of robust and scalable algorithms for solving a wide range of inverse problems in various applications.

In this paper, we investigate the occurrence of difermion condensates in vacuum in 2-4D four-fermion interaction models. We introduce the concept of a non-local four-fermion interaction in 2-4D spacetime, which allows us to study the formation of condensates in the vacuum state. Our methodology involves the use of a mean field approximation and numerical simulations to analyze the relevant parameters and their effects. Our main goal is to understand the role of the four-fermion interaction in the emergence of difermion condensates in vacuum, as well as to explore the dynamics of these condensates.

Our work builds upon previous studies in the field, but focuses specifically on the effects of the four-fermion interaction, which has not been extensively studied in this context. Our approach allows us to make predictions about the behavior of difermion condensates under different conditions and to identify the key factors that influence their formation and dynamics. Through our simulations, we demonstrate the emergence of stable difermion condensates in 2-4D vacuum space, and analyze their properties in detail.

Our results suggest that the formation of difermion condensates in vacuum is a robust phenomenon, which can occur in a wide range of conditions and is strongly influenced by the strength of the four-fermion interaction. Our work contributes to the understanding of the dynamics of these condensates and may have implications for the study of particle physics and cosmology.

In this study, we present the results from three-year observations of the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) in the context of foreground polarization. Our main objective was to develop an understanding of the polarized synchrotron and dust emission that contaminate the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMB) maps. We employed the maximum likelihood estimation method to characterize the polarized Galactic foregrounds in five frequency bands between 23 and 94 GHz. 

Our work shows that the observed polarization patterns can be attributed to both synchrotron and thermal dust emission, depending on the frequency region. We find that the polarized synchrotron radiation is strongest at high Galactic latitudes, whereas the polarized dust emission is predominantly concentrated in the Galactic plane. The emission from polarized dust presents challenges for forthcoming CMB experiments, as it can mimic the polarization signal from the primordial gravitational waves in the early universe.

Our investigation provides insight into the origin and characteristics of Galactic foreground polarization, which is crucial for improving the accuracy of cosmological analyses. This work underscores the need for a comprehensive study of polarized foregrounds, given their impact on the precision of future CMB measurements.

In this work, we aimed to investigate the robustness of cortical networks against lesions. Lesions, caused by diseases or injuries, can disrupt the connectivity of the brain and lead to functional impairments. To address this problem, we utilized a simulation approach to examine the network performance under different lesion conditions. Specifically, we considered two types of lesions - targeted attack and random damage - and evaluated the impact on network efficiency, connectivity and modularity. Our findings indicate that the cortical network is capable of maintaining high efficiency and strong connectivity despite the presence of lesions. Moreover, we observed that modular structures in the network play a crucial role in preserving functionality following lesions. Our results provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of brain plasticity and offer potential applications for diagnosing and treating neurological disorders. The key idea of our methodology is to use a realistic computational model of cortical networks and simulate different types of lesion scenarios. We also used graph theory analysis to quantify the network metrics. This work contributes to the understanding of the resilience of cortical networks and offers a foundation for further research on the development of therapeutic interventions for brain lesions.

In this work, we present a methodology for causal inference in longitudinal studies through the use of history-restricted marginal structural models (HMSMs). The motivation for this research stems from the need to control confounding factors effectively, which is crucial for accurate causal inference. Existing methods for causal inference often fall short in this regard, as they are unable to account for time-varying confounding variables that can arise in longitudinal studies. By incorporating time-varying confounding factors into our framework, we can overcome this limitation and obtain more robust estimates of causal effects.

The key idea of our methodology is to modify marginal structural models (MSMs) to a history-restricted setting. In contrast to traditional MSMs, which assume that the history of exposure and confounding variables does not influence future outcomes, HMSMs allow us to account for past events that may influence both past and present exposures and confounding variables. This modification enables us to effectively control confounding bias while maintaining the benefits of MSMs for causal inference.

Our approach represents a major step forward in the analysis of longitudinal data, offering a powerful tool for identifying causal relationships and drawing more accurate conclusions. Through simulation studies and real data analyses, we demonstrate the utility of our methodology in a variety of settings. Overall, we believe our work represents a significant contribution to the field of causal inference and has important implications for research in a range of disciplines, including epidemiology, psychology, and sociology.

We present a novel approach to the study of brain prostheses as a dynamic system, exploring the potential for immortality of the human brain through integration with technology. Our research is motivated by the limitations of current brain-computer interfaces that suffer from signal degradation and loss over time, leading to unreliable performance. In contrast, our approach seeks to understand brain prostheses as a constantly evolving, adaptive system that can learn and improve with time.

Using a combination of physiological modeling and machine learning techniques, we demonstrate that brain prostheses can be effectively integrated with human neural networks to create a dynamic, self-improving system. Our simulations suggest that such a system has the potential to achieve near-immortality, as its ability to learn and adapt would enable it to compensate for neural degeneration and loss over time.

Our work addresses the problem of limited lifespan of existing brain-computer interfaces and explores the potential of brain prostheses as a dynamic, self-adaptive system. Our findings suggest that such a system could not only provide a solution to the problem of degeneration over time but also open up new opportunities for enhancing human capabilities and achieving immortality of the human mind.

We investigate the sensitivity of low-degree oscillations to the change in solar abundances, motivated by the need to understand the impact of solar variability on our planet's climate. Solar variability is caused by changes in the amount and distribution of energy emitted by the Sun, which can have significant impacts on our planet's atmosphere and climate patterns. To better understand this variability, we explore how changes in the abundance of elements in the Sun's outer layers affect the frequencies of low-degree solar oscillations. 

We apply a combination of theoretical modeling and observational data analysis to explore the sensitivity of these oscillations to changes in the abundances of select elements, including helium and carbon. Our results suggest that the frequencies of low-degree oscillations are sensitive to changes in these elements, with the magnitude of the effect varying depending on the specific element in question and the mode of oscillation. These findings could have important implications for our understanding of the Sun's variability and its impact on Earth's climate. 

Our methodology includes numerical simulations of the Sun's outer layers and analysis of oscillation data collected by the Solar Dynamics Observatory. By applying a data-driven approach and integrating these results with theoretical models, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex processes driving solar variability. This work thus provides an important contribution to the ongoing effort to better understand the Sun's behavior and its impacts on our planet.

In this work, we present the results of our multicolor observations of the afterglow of the short/hard GRB 050724. Our motivation for this research is to better understand the physical mechanisms responsible for the prompt emission and afterglow of short/hard gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and their associated host environments. Short/hard GRBs are brief, intense bursts of gamma-ray radiation with durations of less than two seconds. Unlike long-duration GRBs, they are not associated with supernova explosions and are believed to be produced by mergers of compact objects such as neutron stars or black holes. 

Our observations were carried out using the 2.2-m telescope at Calar Alto Observatory in Spain and the 8.2-m Subaru Telescope in Hawaii. We obtained multicolor photometric data over several epochs spanning a few hours to several days following the GRB. We used these data to construct the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the afterglow, which allowed us to derive its physical properties such as the electron energy distribution and the density of the surrounding medium. 

Our analysis showed that the afterglow of GRB 050724 had a steep spectral slope, indicating that the electron energy distribution was particularly steep. This is in contrast to what is typically observed for long-duration GRBs. Our observations also revealed a possible break in the afterglow light curve, which could be due to either a jet break or the injection of fresh energy into the blast wave. Our study provides valuable insights into the physics of short/hard GRBs and their associated host environments.

In this research, we showcase new object classification techniques for difference imaging that will help find more supernovae with less work. Difference imaging technology uses the subtraction technique to locate objects that exhibit variations in brightness between two images of the same region of the sky taken at different times. Supernovae are among these objects. However, the process of manually scanning through large amounts of image data to distinguish and identify supernovae from other objects can be limiting, time-consuming, and potentially error-prone.

Our research aims to address this limitation by presenting an automated object classification technique designed to enhance the identification of supernovae in difference imaging images. Specifically, we propose a combination of machine learning algorithms and image feature extraction techniques to simplify the object classification procedure. We carried out evaluations on various datasets using different classification algorithms to determine the suitability of our approach. 

The motivation behind this research is to develop a more efficient and accurate technique to identify supernovae in astronomical observations, which can potentially lead to deeper insights into their origins and properties. Our results show that the proposed object classification technique enhances the accuracy and efficiency of supernova identification, demonstrating its potential for use in large-scale astronomical surveys and the broader scientific community.

In this work, we develop a novel approach to multiresolution analysis and pseudo-differential operators in the $p$-adic setting. Our goal is to provide a framework to study functions on non-Archimedean fields, which are important in number theory and theoretical physics. Specifically, we propose a construction of $p$-adic Haar wavelets and we define their corresponding scaling functions, which generate a multiresolution analysis. We prove that our wavelets satisfy the properties of orthogonality, completeness, and vanishing moments. Then, we adapt the concept of pseudo-differential operators to the $p$-adic context, defining the action of these operators on the spaces generated by the multiresolution analysis.

The core methodology involves applying abstract harmonic analysis and operator theory techniques in the context of $p$-adic analysis. We use the properties of Haar measure and $p$-adic exponentiation to construct the Haar wavelets. We build on insights from previous research on $p$-adic multiresolution analysis, but add a new perspective with our approach to pseudo-differential operators.

Our main theoretical results include the construction of the $p$-adic Haar wavelets and the proof of their properties. We also define a class of pseudo-differential operators and we show that they are bounded on the spaces generated by the multiresolution analysis. Our work is an important contribution to the study of $p$-adic analysis and it opens up new avenues for research in non-Archimedean harmonic analysis.

In this work, we present an advanced method for determining the equation of state of atomic systems beyond s-wave in the limit of large scattering lengths. The motivation for this research stems from the fundamental question of understanding the nature of strongly interacting atomic gases. The low energy scattering properties of such systems are determined by universal physics that is independent of the details of the atomic interactions. This universality is described by a set of integral equations called the renormalization group (RG) equations. However, solving the RG equations is computationally demanding and often requires sophisticated numerical techniques. 

We introduce a lowest order constrained variational (LOCV) method that provides an efficient and accurate alternative to solving the RG equations. Our method involves solving a simplified version of the RG equations subject to a set of constraints. By varying the constraints, we can obtain the equation of state as well as other properties of the system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by computing the equation of state for several model systems and comparing our results with those obtained using other techniques. 

Overall, our work addresses a significant problem in the field of atomic physics and provides a powerful tool for understanding the behavior of strongly interacting atomic gases. The LOC-V method presented here is a rigorous and practical approach for the study of atomic systems beyond s-wave and will enable new insights into the universal physics of these fascinating systems.

We report on the self-assembly of a multicellular organism that replicates the behavior of the Dictyostelium slime molds. Dictyostelium is a genus of social amoeba that exhibits a remarkable ability to form complex multicellular structures during their life cycle, which involves transitioning from a unicellular to a multicellular state. Inspired by this natural process, we developed a simplified model of a multicellular organism that resembles the behavior of Dictyostelium. 

The experimental setup consisted of a suspension of microbeads that could interact with each other through a tunable attraction force. We were able to control the behavior of the microbeads by modulating the interaction potential between them. By tuning the attraction force, we could induce the formation of multicellular structures that resemble Dictyostelium slugs. Moreover, the relationship between the attraction force and the size of the multicellular structures was found to be in good agreement with theoretical simulations. 

The motivation for this study is to advance our understanding of self-assembly phenomena in complex systems and to explore the potential of simple models for bio-inspired design. The successful construction of a Dictyostelium-inspired multicellular organism demonstrates the potential of our approach for advancing the field of synthetic biology. Our work may have implications for the design of novel nanomaterials, bio-inspired robotics, and even regenerative medicine.

In this paper, we continue our work on the classification of finite-dimensional complex filiform Leibniz algebras. We build upon the results of our previous paper and provide a complete classification of these algebras of dimensions six and seven. Our methodology involves a thorough analysis of the structure of these algebras through a combination of algebraic, computational, and geometric techniques.

The main motivation for this research is the practical application of Leibniz algebras in fields such as physics and engineering. These algebras provide a powerful framework for modeling and analyzing complex systems, and a better understanding of their properties can lead to more efficient and accurate models.

The problem we attempt to solve in this paper is the classification of filiform Leibniz algebras of low dimensions. The classification of these algebras is particularly challenging due to their nontrivial structure and the large number of isomorphism classes. However, our results show that a complete classification is possible, providing new insights into the algebraic and geometric properties of these structures.

In conclusion, our work contributes to the ongoing development of the theory of Leibniz algebras and demonstrates the potential of these structures in practical applications. Our methodology and results may also be useful in other areas of algebraic research and provide a foundation for future work on these intriguing and complex algebraic structures.

In this work, we investigate the critical scaling and heterogeneous superdiffusion across the jamming/rigidity transition of a granular glass. The problem we attempt to solve is the understanding of the jamming process and the transition from fluid-like to solid-like behavior in granular systems. This transition is known as the jamming/rigidity transition and is a fundamental concept in condensed matter physics. Motivated by the numerous practical applications of granular materials in industry, we aim to shed light on the underlying physical principles that govern such systems.

We find that the jamming/rigidity transition is associated with a critical scaling behavior of the relaxation time, which diverges as a power-law as the jamming point is approached. Furthermore, we show that the system exhibits heterogeneous superdiffusion across this transition, characterized by a non-Gaussian probability distribution function of displacements. Our methodology consists of numerical simulations of a model granular glass and a careful analysis of its dynamical properties.

In summary, our work provides new insights into the jamming/rigidity transition of granular glasses, which are relevant to the understanding of many natural and industrial processes. The critical scaling and heterogeneous superdiffusion we observe are important characteristics of granular materials that can inform the design of new materials and technologies.

Nuclear physics is one of the fascinating fields of study, carrying a lot of promise for the betterment of our technological society. In particular, the study of nuclei's properties is an essential aspect of nuclear physics. In this paper, we present our research on the simultaneous center-of-mass correction of nucleon density and momentum distributions in nuclei. 

Our research aims to achieve an accurate measurement of the structure of nuclei, which is crucial in understanding phenomena such as nuclear fission, fusion, and energy production. To that end, we utilized the nuclear shell model to simulate the nucleon density and momentum distributions of several isotopes of helium, carbon, and oxygen. We applied a novel method that conserves the total energy of the system while correcting the center-of-mass motion. 

Our simulations revealed that the previous center-of-mass corrections provided only a partial correction and resulted in misleading measurements of nuclear properties. The simultaneous center-of-mass correction presented in this work provides a robust framework for accurately measuring the nucleon density and momentum distributions of nuclei. Our work highlights the importance of taking into account the center-of-mass motion in accurately determining nuclear properties. Our findings will aid in furthering the research in nuclear physics and have important implications for developing new energy sources and medical applications.

We present a comprehensive review of the major findings from the BABAR experiment, focusing on the hottest topics that have emerged in the past decade. Our analysis is based on a vast amount of data collected by this ultraprecise detector system, located at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center. The key ideas of our work are to identify and explore the most challenging issues in particle physics, such as CP violation, rare decays, and tests of the Standard Model. To achieve this, we utilize advanced statistical techniques and machine learning algorithms to extract the signal from the background in our high-dimensional data sets.

Our results show that we have made significant progress in understanding the fundamental nature of matter and its interactions. We have discovered new particles, measured their properties, and confirmed the predictions of the Standard Model to a high degree of precision. The BABAR experiment has also revealed a plethora of unexpected phenomena, such as the violation of CP symmetry, that have challenged our understanding of the universe at its most fundamental level.

Ultimately, our work attempts to solve the problem of unraveling the mysteries of the subatomic world. By providing insights into the nature of particles and how they behave, we hope to shed light on some of the most fundamental questions in physics, such as the origin of mass, the nature of dark matter, and the ultimate fate of the universe.

In our work titled "Generalized Brjuno Functions Associated to $\alpha$-continued Fractions", we investigate the behavior of certain functions arising from the study of continued fractions. Specifically, given a real number $\alpha$, we consider the Brjuno function $\beta_\alpha(x)$, which encodes the Diophantine properties of the continued fraction expansion of $\alpha$. We extend this function to a more general setting, where $\alpha$ is replaced by a certain class of complex numbers with modulus one. We call these functions generalized Brjuno functions and study their properties.

Our main result shows that these functions exhibit a "jump discontinuity" phenomenon, providing a connection to complex dynamics and the theory of renormalization. This is in contrast to the behavior of the classical Brjuno function, which is continuous everywhere. We also highlight the connections of these functions to the study of small denominators, which arise in the analysis of differential equations.

The key idea behind our methodology is to study the continued fraction expansion of complex numbers with modulus one, and to use tools from complex analysis and dynamical systems to study the properties of the generalized Brjuno functions. Our work contributes to the ongoing study of the complex behavior of continued fractions and could have further applications in the study of small denominators and dynamical systems.

In this study, we investigate the minimal size of a barchan dune, which is a characteristic type of sand dune found in arid regions. Barchan dunes are crescent-shaped, with horns facing downwind and a gently sloping slip face on their lee side. They form as a result of wind action on loose sand particles and can have a significant impact on local ecosystems. Here, we use a combination of field observations and numerical simulations to analyze the minimum size required for barchan dunes to form. Our methodology involved collecting data on existing barchan dunes in various locations and running simulations using computational fluid dynamics models to study the wind flow in relation to sand particle movement. We aim to understand the problem of the physical mechanisms that govern the formation of barchan dunes and determine the critical conditions that must be met to sustain stable dune shapes. Our results indicate that barchan dunes can form under a range of wind velocities and sand granularities, but the minimum size required for stable formation depends on several factors, including wind speed, grain size, and vegetation cover. Our findings suggest that understanding the minimal size of barchan dunes is crucial for predicting sand dune formation in desert environments and could have implications for environmental management and conservation efforts in arid regions worldwide.

In our work, we present a detailed analysis of the afterglow of the gamma-ray burst (GRB) 050802 as observed by the Swift satellite. This GRB was particularly interesting due to its two-component afterglow, which had never been seen before in such detail. We used photometric and spectroscopic data obtained from Swift's Ultraviolet and Optical Telescope and X-ray Telescope to study the temporal and spectral evolution of the afterglow.

Our analysis revealed that the early-time afterglow emission was dominated by a narrow component while the later-time emission was dominated by a broad component, each with its own spectral index and decay rate. We proposed several possible explanations for this behavior, including a structured jet and the contribution of reverse shock emission. Our results provide insight into the complex physics of GRB afterglows and may shed light on the underlying physical processes responsible for the observed variability in these events.

One of the main problems that our work attempts to solve is to understand the origin of the two-component afterglow in GRB 050802. We address this problem by carrying out a comprehensive analysis of the available data and proposing several possible explanations for the observed behavior. Through this work, we hope to contribute to a better understanding of the physics of GRBs and their afterglows.

In this article, we present our research on scalability and optimisation of a committee of agents using genetic algorithm. The problem that we attempt to solve is the challenge of designing multi-agent systems that are scalable and capable of providing optimal solutions. Our work is motivated by the fact that multi-agent systems are becoming increasingly common in a wide range of application domains, including transportation, finance, and healthcare. 

We propose a novel approach that utilises genetic algorithms to optimise a committee of agents. Our approach entails evolving the population of candidate committees using genetic operators such as selection, crossover, and mutation. We then evaluate these committees using a fitness function to identify the most effective committee. Our results show that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing algorithms in terms of scalability and optimisation. 

Our research has significant implications for the design and development of multi-agent systems. By providing a scalable and optimised framework for committees of agents, we enable the deployment of large-scale systems that can provide optimal solutions to complex problems. Our work provides a valuable contribution to the field of multi-agent systems and highlights the potential of genetic algorithms in solving real-world problems.

In this work, we investigate the propagation of travelling waves in sub-excitable systems driven by noise and periodic forcing. The main motivation for this study is to understand the dynamics of excitable media such as cardiac tissue or neural networks, where travelling waves play a crucial role in the generation and propagation of electrical signals.

We employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods to study the effects of noise and periodic forcing on the propagation of waves in sub-excitable systems. Specifically, we consider the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, which is a paradigmatic model for excitable media, and we explore the conditions under which travelling waves can be sustained under noisy and periodic conditions.

Our study reveals that the interplay between noise and periodic forcing can lead to rich dynamics, such as the emergence of complex spatiotemporal patterns and the destabilization of stationary solutions. Furthermore, we find that the propagation speed of the waves is strongly influenced by the amplitude and frequency of the periodic forcing.

Overall, our work contributes to the understanding of the role of noise and periodic forcing in the propagation of travelling waves in sub-excitable systems, which has important implications for the design of interventions to modulate the dynamics of excitable media.

In this work, we investigate the spin effects in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and its connection with recurrence lattices with multi-site exchanges. QCD is a theory that describes the interactions between quarks and gluons, which are the building blocks of matter. The spin of these particles is an important property that can affect the way they interact with each other. However, the study of spin effects in QCD is a challenging problem due to the complex nature of the theory.

To address this problem, we develop a new approach based on the concept of recurrence lattices with multi-site exchanges. Our methodology involves using lattice QCD simulations to compute the relevant observables and analyzing the data using a statistical technique known as Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Our results show that the spin effects in QCD can be explained in terms of the recurrence properties of the lattice, and that multi-site exchanges play a crucial role in this process.

The key ideas behind our work are rooted in the general principles of QCD and the mathematical properties of recurrence lattices. The methodology we employ is based on a combination of numerical simulations and statistical analysis, which allows us to explore complex phenomena in a rigorous and quantitative way. Our results shed new light on the spin effects in QCD and provide a deeper understanding of the underlying physics.

In this study, we focus on understanding the behavior of very massive stars (VMS) in high-redshift galaxies. The aim of this research is to shed light on the mechanisms of formation and evolution of these stars, which are believed to play a crucial role in the early Universe's history. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of observational evidence that can confirm the existence of such stars in high-redshift galaxies. Our motivation for this research stems from the desire to better understand the early Universe, a period that is still shrouded in mystery.

The key idea behind this research is to create a set of models that simulate the behavior of VMS in high-redshift galaxies. We base these models on the currently accepted formation and evolution theories and incorporate the latest astrophysical data. We then use our models to predict the properties of these stars, such as their mass, luminosity, and spectral signature, and compare them with the available data. Our methodology involves developing and utilizing high-performance computing simulations to create these models.

The findings of this study will broaden our knowledge of the formation and evolution of VMS and help us understand how they impact the evolution of high-redshift galaxies. Moreover, the results from this research will provide the groundwork for future observational studies, potentially leading to the discovery of VMS in high-redshift galaxies. This study's broader implications will impact our understanding of not only the early Universe's evolution but also the overall evolution of galaxies.

In this study, we investigate the switching mechanism of photochromic diarylethene derivatives molecular junctions. Our motivation for this research arises from the potential applications of photochromic materials in optoelectronic devices, such as molecular switches and memory devices. However, a complete understanding of the molecular-level properties of these materials is crucial for the development of such devices, and many questions regarding their switching mechanism remain unanswered.

To address these questions, we performed molecular dynamics simulations of the diarylethene derivatives in open and closed states, using density-functional theory and non-equilibrium Green’s function formalism. Our key ideas include exploring the effects of molecular geometry and the contact with metal electrodes on the switching mechanism and understanding the role of electron transfer in photo-induced processes.

Our results confirmed that the switching mechanism is strongly influenced by the orientation of the molecular dipole moment and the chemical nature of the metal electrodes. We also observed that photo-induced electron transfer plays an essential role in the switching process, mitigating hysteresis effects and improving the overall performance of the molecular devices.

Overall, our study contributes to a better understanding of the fundamental properties of photochromic materials and their potential applications in optoelectronic devices, aiding the development of more efficient and reliable molecular switches and memory elements.

In this study, we investigate the presence of exoplanets orbiting retired A stars and their companions, specifically focusing on three intermediate-mass subgiants: HD 120084, HD 96127, and HD 81817. Our motivation for this research stems from the importance of understanding the relationship between a star and its planetary system, as well as the role of intermediate-mass subgiants in the evolution of stars and their planets. 

Using radial velocity measurements obtained from the HARPS-N spectrograph, we perform a detailed analysis to detect potential exoplanets in these systems. Through careful analysis of the data, we are able to confirm the presence of exoplanets orbiting HD 120084 and HD 81817, with HD 120084b being a gas giant planet and HD 81817c being a low-mass Neptune-like planet. We also find a strong hint of a planetary companion orbiting HD 96127. 

Our results provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of planetary systems, as well as the behavior of intermediate-mass subgiants. We utilize our methodology, consisting of precise radial velocity measurements and rigorous data analysis techniques, to accurately detect planets in these systems, contributing to the growing body of research on exoplanetary systems. The implications of our findings are significant, underscoring the need for continued exploration of planetary systems in order to fully understand the dynamic relationship between a star and its planets.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the structural properties of uranium-based multilayers. The motivation for this research stems from the importance of uranium in various fields, including nuclear energy and medical applications. Furthermore, the fabrication and characterisation of uranium-based multilayers are crucial for the advancement of nanotechnology and material science. 

To achieve our objectives, we used a methodology that included the deposition of uranium-based thin films via magnetron sputtering. The structural characterisation of the multilayers was carried out using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy. The obtained results demonstrated an excellent uniformity and adhesion of the thin films on the substrates. Also, the multilayers showed a preferred orientation along the (111) plane of face-centered cubic uranium, which indicates that the films possess a high degree of crystallinity. 

In summary, this study provides vital insights into the fabrication and structural characterisation of uranium-based multilayers. These findings are expected to contribute significantly to the development of advanced materials for various applications, particularly in nuclear-related fields.

In this research, we aim to provide a Bayesian approach to reconstruct the large-scale structure of the Universe based on observational data. The motivation behind this work is the necessity to accurately trace the large-scale distribution of matter, which is presently unavailable through direct observation due to its complexity, inhomogeneity, and distance. Our method solves this problem by employing statistical methods and numerical optimization techniques to predict and reconstruct the underlying large-scale structure. 
The key idea behind our approach is to use a combination of data sets, including Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation, and baryonic acoustic oscillations (BAO), to identify the large-scale distribution of matter. We propose to use a statistical model based on a combination of Bayesian inference and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques. Moreover, we introduce a novel approach by employing an inverse algorithm to identify the three-dimensional distribution of matter from two-dimensional sky maps. 
We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our method by applying it to real observational data and comparing the resulting reconstructions to state-of-the-art methods. Our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and precision and can provide new insights into the formation and evolution of cosmic structures.

In this research paper, we present a novel approach to solving the hierarchy problem in physics through the use of black holes and Large N species. The hierarchy problem refers to the large discrepancy between the weak and gravitational forces, which mathematicians have long sought to reconcile.

Our research incorporates string theory to address this problem, suggesting that black holes can be used to bridge this gap. By considering an N-dimensional theory with Large N species, we show that the effective gravitational field strength from the black hole scales with the number of species. Specifically, this results in a cancellation effect where the hierarchy problem is eliminated.

Our research has been conducted using a rigorous mathematical framework, backed by extensive simulation data. This approach represents a significant breakthrough in the field, which has long been seeking an effective solution to the hierarchy problem. Specifically, our research provides a new method for addressing the problem that goes beyond traditional approaches, such as the Standard Model of Particle Physics.

Our work is motivated by a desire to push the boundaries of current physics and find innovative solutions to long-standing problems. Through our modeling and simulations, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of using black holes and Large N species to address the hierarchy problem, and we hope this new approach will inspire future research in this area.

In this work, we investigate the spheroidal and torsional modes of quasistatic shear oscillations in solid globe models of nuclear physics and pulsar astrophysics. The main goal of this research is to expand our understanding of the seismic properties of compact stars. Specifically, we aim to shed light on how differences in the internal structure and composition of such stars might impact their observed oscillation patterns.

To achieve this, we employ a combination of analytical techniques and numerical simulations. Our analysis is grounded in the equations governing linearized perturbations of the fluid and solid components of the star, which we solve using appropriate boundary conditions. In particular, we explore the effects of different density profiles, equation of state models, and geometries on the excitation and damping of these oscillations.

Our findings suggest that the presence of a solid crust, as well as variations in the core composition, can significantly affect the evolution of spheroidal and torsional modes in compact stars. These results have far-reaching implications for our ability to accurately infer the properties of pulsars and other compact objects based on their observed oscillations. Overall, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the rich dynamical behavior of compact stars and their possible astrophysical origins.

In this study, we investigate the aromatic emission from the ionised mane of the Horsehead nebula, a well-known and extensively studied astronomical object located in the Orion molecular cloud complex. The problem we aim to solve concerns the nature of the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the carriers of the strong and ubiquitous mid-infrared emission features in galactic and extragalactic environments. In particular, we attempt to shed light on the origin and destruction mechanisms of these molecules in harsh interstellar conditions.

To achieve our goal, we used the Spectro-Polarimetric High-contrast Exoplanet Research (SPHERE) instrument at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile. Our observations allowed us to map the spatial distribution of the PAH emission and identify possible variations in intensity and morphology across the Horsehead nebula.

The motivation for this research stems from the fundamental role of PAHs as a tracer of the interstellar medium's physical and chemical properties. By investigating the aromatic emission from the ionised mane of the Horsehead nebula, we contribute to our understanding of the complex interaction between radiation, gas, and dust in star-forming regions. Our results have implications for the interpretation of PAH emission in other environments and the modelling of interstellar chemistry and evolution.

In this study, we investigate the possible association between extragalactic radio sources and the WMAP cold spot, a puzzling feature in the cosmic microwave background radiation. The motivation for this research stems from the desire to better understand the origin of the WMAP cold spot, which is inconsistent with the standard cosmological model and could potentially challenge our current understanding of the universe. 

To address this problem, we conducted a statistical analysis of the positions of extragalactic radio sources and compared them with the location of the WMAP cold spot. Our results reveal a significant excess of radio sources at the position of the cold spot, indicating a possible connection between these two phenomena. 

Furthermore, we performed a detailed analysis of the properties of the identified radio sources, including their brightness and redshift, and found that the excess is mostly driven by a population of faint radio sources at high redshifts. These results suggest that the WMAP cold spot might be caused by large-scale structures in the universe, such as cosmic voids or supervoids, which can produce a lack of hot gas and hence a deficit in the CMB temperature.

Overall, our study provides new insights into the origin of the WMAP cold spot and highlights the potential of extragalactic radio sources as a valuable tracer of large-scale structures in the universe.

In this study, we have investigated the luminous infrared composite Seyfert 2 galaxy NGC 7679 through the [O III] 5007 emission line. Our main aim was to gain insight into the physical properties of this galaxy's ionized gas and its origin. To achieve this, we used a combination of spectroscopic and imaging data obtained from the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph Integral Field Unit (GMOS-IFU) and the Hubble Space Telescope. 

Our analysis revealed that the ionized gas in NGC 7679 is likely to be powered by the active galactic nucleus (AGN), with a strong contribution from star formation in the galaxy. We found that the [O III] emission is highly concentrated in the nucleus, with evidence of outflows and shock-heated gas in the inner region. This suggests that the AGN is driving gas out of the galaxy, which has important implications for galaxy evolution.

Overall, our study provides new insights into the complex interplay between AGNs, star formation, and gas kinematics in NGC 7679. By using cutting-edge observational techniques and analytical methods, we have advanced our understanding of this galaxy's physical properties, which will be valuable for future studies of AGN-host galaxy co-evolution.

In this work, we explore the exciting possibility of vector mesons in the context of AdS technicolor (TC) and their connection to the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our research aims to address the long-standing problem of the origin of mass in electroweak symmetry breaking (EWSB) in a theoretical framework based on strong dynamics.

We start by introducing the AdS/TC model, which merges the AdS/CFT correspondence and TC technology to provide a holographic description of EWSB. We then turn our attention to the vector mesons, which play a crucial role in this framework, and their properties, such as their masses and decay constants. We also discuss the scalar resonance, which is a crucial ingredient for generating the masses of the electroweak gauge bosons.

Next, we investigate the phenomenology of vector mesons at the LHC. We study the production and decay of resonances such as ρ, ω, φ, and J/ψ, and their potential for discovery or exclusion.

Our motivation for this study is twofold. Firstly, we aim to contribute to the field of EWSB and its connection to strong dynamics. Secondly, we seek to provide a theoretical framework that can be tested at current or future collider experiments, thus bringing us closer to understanding the fundamental nature of matter and its interactions.

In this work, we investigate the helical, angular, and radial ordering of a linear chain polymer across varying pore sizes of narrow capillaries. The research aims to provide insight into the unique effects of confinement on the molecular conformation of confined polymers, which have implications for a range of fields, including materials science and biotechnology.

Our simulations show that in the smallest capillaries, the polymers exhibit a helical structure due to the geometric constraints of the pore dimensions. As the pore size increases, the angular and radial ordering of the polymers becomes more pronounced. These results suggest that helical structures are favored in extreme confinement and support recent experimental findings.

The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the behavior of confined molecules in nanoscale environments. The properties of polymers in nanoconfinement are not well understood and investigating the ordering mechanisms provides critical insights for designing novel materials with tailored properties.

Overall, our work highlights a fundamental understanding of molecular organization in nanoscale environments and can provide guidance for designing new materials for specific applications.

In this work, we investigate the MiniBooNE experiment results and explore various neutrino schemes with two sterile neutrinos to understand the possible mass orderings and observables related to neutrino masses. The lack of knowledge about the neutrino masses and their mixing patterns has been a longstanding issue in particle physics that can have a profound impact on our understanding of the universe. 

The problem with neutrino masses arises from the fact that the neutrinos are massless in the standard model, which assumes that the neutrinos have no mass. However, various experiments, including the MiniBooNE experiment, have provided evidence that the neutrinos do have mass. Therefore, it is necessary to develop new theories and models to explain this phenomenon. 

We found that there are different possibilities for mass orderings and observables in neutrino schemes with two sterile neutrinos. Our research shows that the mass ordering and observables in such schemes depend on the exact values of the mixing angles and the masses of the neutrinos. 

The motivation for this research is to gain a better understanding of the neutrino masses and the mysteries of their mixing patterns. The results obtained from this work can guide future experiments to understand the nature of the neutrinos and their mass. Overall, this study provides a crucial contribution to the field of particle physics and can have implications for our knowledge of the universe.

In this work, we investigate the diameters of random scale-free graphs generated by preferential attachment models. We explore the effect of the preferential attachment mechanism on the growth of diameters and show that diameters can increase logarithmically with the number of nodes in the network. More specifically, we examine several well-known preferential attachment models, including the Barabási–Albert model, and develop new models that generalize the preferential attachment approach. Our theoretical analyses are based on probabilistic arguments and numerical simulations of the models. We show that our new models can produce networks with shorter diameters than those generated by existing models.

The motivation for our research is rooted in the practical need to understand how diameters scale with the size of complex networks. Diameters are relevant to many problems in network science and have implications for algorithms that rely on global properties of networks, such as search algorithms and routing protocols. Our work attempts to solve the problem of how to model the growth of diameters in random scale-free networks.

Overall, our findings provide insights into the growth of scale-free networks and suggest new avenues for understanding the underlying mechanisms that generate these types of networks. Our work has implications for a broad range of scientists and engineers who study complex networks and rely on their global properties for designing efficient algorithms and optimizing network performance.

In this work, we aim to investigate the properties of binary microlensing light curves beyond caustic crossings. Binary microlensing is an important tool to detect and study planetary systems around other stars. However, the interpretation of binary microlensing light curves is very complicated due to the presence of multiple lenses and complex light paths. Previous studies have focused on the behavior of binary microlensing light curves near caustic crossings, which occur when the source passes close to the lens system. However, the behavior of binary microlensing light curves away from caustic crossings has not been well studied.

We use a Monte Carlo simulation to generate a large sample of binary microlensing events, and we analyze the properties of the resulting light curves. Our simulation includes a range of lens masses, separations, and orientations. We find that the behavior of binary microlensing light curves depends strongly on the mass ratio of the lenses and the separation between them.

Our results show that binary microlensing light curves away from caustic crossings can provide valuable information about the lens system. In particular, we find that the shape and duration of the light curve can be used to constrain the masses and separations of the lenses. Our work provides a framework for interpreting binary microlensing light curves in a more comprehensive way, which is essential for understanding the properties of planetary systems around other stars.

In this work, we present the results of non-resonant and resonant X-ray scattering studies on the multiferroic compound, TbMn2O5. The motivation for this research was to investigate the coupling between magnetism and ferroelectricity in this material, and to understand the origin of the multiferroic behavior.

The key idea behind our work is to use X-ray scattering as a probe of the atomic and magnetic structure of TbMn2O5. Non-resonant X-ray scattering measurements were performed at room temperature, while resonant scattering measurements were performed at the Tb L3 edge to probe the magnetic ordering of the Tb ions. Our methodology involved growing single crystals of TbMn2O5, performing X-ray scattering experiments at various temperatures, and analyzing the scattering data using advanced data analysis techniques.

Our results reveal a complex magnetic ordering pattern of the Tb ions that is strongly coupled to the ferroelectric polarization of the material. We also observe a temperature-dependent deviation of the magnetic Bragg peaks from ideal positions, which is indicative of coupling between the magnetic and lattice degrees of freedom in TbMn2O5. Overall, our work provides new insights into the coupling between magnetism and ferroelectricity in multiferroic materials, and helps to advance our understanding of the underlying physics.

In this study, we investigate the possibility that massive black holes in galactic centers can be enhanced in their activity through the capture of stars, and the subsequent formation of a self-gravitating accretion disc. Our research focuses on the mechanisms that drive the accretion of captured stars, and how the accretion disc feedbacks on the black hole's activity. To achieve this, we carry out detailed numerical simulations of the stars' dynamics when they are captured by the black hole's gravity, and follow the evolution of the accretion disc as it forms and feeds the black hole. 

The work attempts to solve the long-standing question of how black holes in galactic centers can become active, despite having relatively low levels of gas available to them. Our results suggest that, under certain conditions, the capture of stars can fuel intense accretion events that boost the black hole's activity to much higher levels than expected. We also explore the implications of these findings for our current understanding of black hole growth and evolution. 

Our research has important implications for a wide range of astrophysical topics, including the formation and evolution of galaxies, the chemical enrichment of the universe, and the production of gravitational waves. Understanding how black holes in galactic centers can be enhanced in their activity is crucial to advancing our knowledge of the universe's most mysterious and energetic phenomena.

In this work, we propose a novel approach for analysing the structure of graph patterns using clustering with lattices. The key idea behind our method is to transform the original graph into a lattice structure which captures the underlying relationships between the nodes. We then apply traditional clustering algorithms, such as k-means or hierarchical clustering, to this lattice representation of the graph.

Our approach is motivated by the fact that existing graph clustering methods can be computationally expensive, especially when dealing with large and complex graphs. Moreover, such methods often fail to preserve the structural properties of the graph, which can be crucial for certain applications such as social network analysis or protein interaction networks. By using lattices as a representation for graphs, we can exploit their inherent regularity and reduce the complexity of the clustering task.

Our experiments on a variety of graph datasets have demonstrated that our method is not only computationally efficient but also achieves high clustering performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, our method is robust against noise and can handle graphs with different sizes and topologies. Overall, our proposed approach of clustering with lattices offers a promising new direction for analysing graph patterns and has the potential to impact a range of disciplines from biology to computer science.

In our work, we investigate a brane world scenario in an arbitrary number of dimensions without the Z_2 symmetry. The motivation for this research is to explore the effects of a broken Z_2 symmetry on the properties and behavior of a brane world scenario. In particular, we aim to address the question of whether or not a non-zero cosmological constant can emerge in such a scenario. To achieve this goal, we extend the standard Randall-Sundrum two-brane model by including more than two branes and by allowing for a non-zero bulk cosmological constant. 

The problem that our work attempts to solve is the understanding of the role of the Z_2 symmetry in brane world scenarios. The Z_2 symmetry is a well-known symmetry in brane world scenarios, and it has been extensively studied in the literature. However, the effects of a broken Z_2 symmetry on the properties and behavior of brane world scenarios are still not well understood. 

Our results show that a non-zero cosmological constant can indeed emerge in a brane world scenario without the Z_2 symmetry. We find that the presence of the non-zero bulk cosmological constant leads to significant modifications in the behavior of the matter fields living on the branes. These modifications are due to the fact that the bulk geometry is no longer symmetric under Z_2 transformations. Our work sheds new light on the role of the Z_2 symmetry in brane world scenarios and opens up new avenues for further investigation.

In our work on "Two-dimensional defect modes in optically induced photonic lattices," we propose a novel theoretical framework for studying the complex behavior of light propagation in the two-dimensional lattices formed by optically induced interference patterns. The novel method includes the creation of a defect in an otherwise periodic structure as a means to explore the optical properties of these lattices. Our objective was to understand the mechanism underlying the enhancement of the intensity of the light field over the structural defect by the interference of multiple waves that constructively interfere, leading to increased coherence and stronger light confinement. 

Our research was motivated by the insistent demand for new applications of photonic crystals to enhance solar cells' efficiency, high-power lasers, and quantum optical systems. We report the discovery of spatially dispersive photonic localization, identified via the tight localization, enhanced transmission, and high Q-factors of the two-dimensional defect modes, which are all optimal characteristics for boosting the efficiency of photonic devices.
