We perform a statistical analysis of solar and KamLAND neutrino data using a global fit to the experimental results. Our results indicate that non-standard decoherence can have a significant impact on the determination of oscillation parameters. In particular, we find that non-standard decoherence suppresses the solar neutrino flux below the expected level and increases the disappearance probability of KamLAND neutrinos. We analyze the sensitivity of future experiments to non-standard decoherence and discuss the implications of our findings for the upcoming generation of neutrino experiments.

In this work, we present simulations and theoretical predictions of one- and two-component bottle-brush polymers. We explore the effects of both polymer segment length and volume fraction on the structure and self-assembly behavior of these complex macromolecules. Our approach is based on molecular dynamics simulations combined with theoretical methods such as self-consistent field theory. We find that the self-assembly behavior of one-component bottle-brush polymers is strongly influenced by the segment length, and we observe both disordered and ordered phases. In contrast, for two-component bottle-brush polymers, we observe the formation of alternating phases with well-defined interfaces. Our simulations are in good agreement with theoretical predictions, and we discuss the underlying physical mechanisms that govern the self-assembly behavior of these systems.

Our research is motivated by the potential applications of bottle-brush polymers in various fields such as nanotechnology and materials science. These polymers have unique properties due to their high molecular weight and complex architecture. However, their behavior is not fully understood, and our simulations and theoretical predictions provide new insights into the structure and self-assembly behavior of these fascinating macromolecules. Overall, this work contributes to the understanding of bottle-brush polymers and lays the foundation for future design and synthesis of functional materials based on these polymers.

In this work, we present a study of cosmological models with $(1+z)^6$ corrections that encapsulate the effects of modification to the standard cosmological model arising from a possible spatial variation of the fine-structure constant. The problem we attempt to address is the selection of the most compatible model with observational constraints. In order to solve this problem, we employ the Supernova Legacy Survey 3-year dataset, the baryon acoustic oscillation data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 and the cosmic microwave background observations from the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe 7-year dataset. 

Our key idea is to employ the Felizola-Cunha-Silva parametrization of the $(1+z)^6$ correction and to test the models by comparing their theoretical predictions to the observational data. The methodology we use is based on a Bayesian analysis that takes into account the systematic and statistical uncertainties of the data. Our main findings reveal that the data favors models with the $(1+z)^6$ correction that are consistent with a spatial dependence of the fine-structure constant. 

The motivation for our research is the growing evidence of the possible variation of fundamental constants in the Universe. Our work provides a practical way to test and select cosmological models that accommodate such a variation. This study contributes not only to the understanding of the present-day Universe but also to the interpretation of the fundamental physical laws that govern its dynamics.

In this study, we present the development and implementation of MCHIT, a Monte Carlo model for proton and heavy-ion therapy. Our motivation was to address the challenges associated with accurately modelling the complex interactions of charged particles with biological tissues for the purpose of predictive modelling of proton and heavy-ion therapy. We aimed to create a model that accurately simulates the physical and biological interactions of charged particles with human biological tissues, incorporating sophisticated treatment planning and beam delivery models.

Our findings demonstrate that MCHIT is capable of reproducing the physical and biological effects of proton and heavy-ion therapy, with high fidelity and accuracy. The model shows an excellent agreement with experimental data and provides reliable predictions of relative biological effectiveness (RBE), dose distribution and cellular damage. In addition, MCHIT provides an array of user-friendly tools for treatment planning and optimization, making it a valuable asset for clinicians and researchers in the field of proton and heavy-ion therapy.

In conclusion, MCHIT represents a significant improvement over existing models, providing a robust and accurate tool for simulating charged particles' interactions with biological tissues. Our model offers a powerful research tool for further understanding of the biological and physical properties of proton and heavy-ion therapy, and provides a powerful tool for developing new treatment strategies.

In this research work, we present the measurement of the aerosol phase function using the fluorescence detector of the Pierre Auger Observatory. The main objective of this study was to improve our understanding of the atmosphere's optical properties and to characterize the aerosol scattering properties, which directly impact the reliability and accuracy of the fluorescence technique.

Our methodology involved collecting fluorescence data from atmospheric nitrogen molecules excited by cosmic ray showers. We analyzed the spectral dependency of the fluorescence light intensity for different zenith angles, and using that information, we extracted the aerosol phase function. Our measurement of the aerosol phase function was found to be consistent with the modified Gamma distribution model within the confidence intervals, and we computed the aerosol optical depth as well.

Our findings offer valuable insights into the aerosol scattering properties for the fluorescence technique used in the Pierre Auger Observatory, which will help in understanding and reducing the systematic uncertainties in the energy estimation of ultra-high energy cosmic ray events detected by the observatory. This research thus makes a significant contribution towards improving the accuracy and reliability of cosmic ray measurements, ultimately advancing our understanding of the universe.

In this work, we investigate the magnetic properties of volborthite, a material that exhibits the Heisenberg antiferromagnet with anisotropic exchange on the Kagome lattice. The Kagome lattice is known for its frustration, making it a particularly interesting system to study. Using a combination of experimental techniques including neutron scattering, magnetization, and specific heat measurements, we obtain a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic ordering in volborthite. Our results indicate that it exhibits long-range magnetic order with an interesting spin structure that deviates from the traditional Neel order.

The motivation for this research is twofold. Firstly, understanding the properties of magnetic systems on the Kagome lattice is important for fundamental research in condensed matter physics. Secondly, volborthite has been proposed as a potential candidate for quantum computation, making it important from a technological perspective.

Our key idea is to investigate the anisotropic exchange interactions in volborthite, which have not been thoroughly studied before. To do this, we use a combination of experimental techniques and theoretical modeling. Through this work, we have determined the critical temperature of volborthite and obtained key insights into the magnetic properties of this material. Furthermore, our results have implications for other systems with similar magnetic properties on the Kagome lattice.

In this work, we investigate the fluctuations of finite-time stability exponents in the standard map and their utility in detecting small islands. The standard map is a widely used model in physics and applied mathematics for the study of dynamical systems. However, the presence of small islands in the phase space of the model can complicate the understanding of the dynamical behavior of the system. Hence, it is of great interest to develop effective methods for the detection of small islands.

We propose a novel approach for the identification of small islands using fluctuations of finite-time stability exponents. Specifically, we analyze finite-time stability exponents from numerical simulations of the standard map with a varying noise level. We observe that the fluctuations of these exponents exhibit distinct features in the presence of small islands, allowing us to distinguish them from the background behavior.

Our method provides a promising new avenue for the detection of small islands in dynamical systems. The key idea is to leverage the fundamental properties of the finite-time stability exponents and the smooth varying of the underlying system. By using this method, we can obtain insights into the stable and unstable regions of a dynamical system and thereby inform its overall behavior. Overall, the proposed approach can find a range of applications in physics and applied mathematics.

In this work, we investigate the complex marginal deformations of D3-brane geometries, their Penrose limits and giant gravitons. The main goal of our research is to gain a better understanding of the holographic correspondence between string theory and gauge theory, which provides a powerful tool for studying the dynamics of strongly coupled gauge theories. 

We use a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to study the Penrose limits of complex marginal deformations of D3-brane geometries. We found that the Penrose limit is determined by the behavior of the metric near the boundary of the space, and that it is possible to construct giant gravitons in these backgrounds. These giant gravitons are solitonic solutions in the higher-dimensional space that are naturally interpreted as dual to certain gauge theory operators. 

Our findings suggest that complex marginal deformations of D3-brane geometries provide a rich landscape for studying the holographic correspondence between string theory and gauge theory. We have demonstrated the utility of our methodology in analyzing the Penrose limit of these geometries, which can shed light on the dynamics of strongly coupled gauge theories. Our work provides a solid foundation for future research in this area.

In our work titled "Oscillation Effects and Time Variation of the Supernova Neutrino Signal", we investigate the time and oscillation variations of the neutrino signal arising from a core collapse supernova. Neutrinos are instrumental in providing information about the dynamics of supernovae and the possible formation of neutron stars and black holes. We employ a detailed numerical model of the core-collapse and neutrino emission processes to simulate an expected neutrino signal.

Our analysis incorporates the complex interplay between the neutrino production rate and the propagation of the neutrinos through the dense and varying environment of the supernova core. We demonstrate that the observed neutrino signal can vary by as much as 40% over a period of tens of milliseconds due to these effects. Additionally, we show that neutrino oscillations can lead to a substantial deformation of the neutrino spectra and, at certain epochs, even a total suppression of certain neutrino flavors.

The results show that the time variation of the neutrino signal is linked to the dynamics of the supernova and can be used to probe the structure of the supernova core which is not accessible to other means. Our work provides valuable insights for future neutrino detections from core-collapse supernovae, which will aid in deciphering the astrophysical and particle physics properties of these fascinating events.

In this work, we present a comprehensive review of Hartree-Fock Self-Consistent Field (HF-SCF) methods in Quantum Chemistry from a mathematical and computational perspective. The main objective of this work is to shed light on the theory, methodology and numerical implementation of HF-SCF, which is widely used in modeling molecular systems. To achieve this aim, we first provide a general overview of the theoretical foundations of Hartree-Fock theory and the HF-SCF approach, focusing on the fundamental principles, mathematical equations, and computational algorithms involved. We then delve into the mathematical and computational aspects of HF-SCF, addressing crucial issues such as convergence, basis sets, electron correlation, and multi-reference problems. 

The results obtained from this work provide a deeper understanding of the underlying theory of HF-SCF methods, as well as the limitations and challenges associated with their numerical implementation. Our analysis highlights the importance of using appropriate numerical techniques to overcome the computational bottlenecks encountered in solving the complex equations involved in HF-SCF calculations. Overall, this study emphasizes the necessity of continuously developing novel and improved computational methods for solving molecular quantum chemistry problems.

In this work, we investigate the wetting transition phenomenon on a one-dimensional disorder. The wetting transition has been a subject of interest for physicists for several decades, as it plays a role in various fields such as fluid mechanics and materials science. In the present study, we simulate a one-dimensional disordered substrate using Monte Carlo simulations and observe the wetting transition of a fluid droplet on it. Our methodology involves studying the adsorption-desorption behavior of a fluid droplet on the substrate as a function of temperature and chemical potential. 

Our results show that the wetting transition is strongly influenced by the one-dimensional disorder, and that the transition temperature shifts towards higher values as the disorder strength increases. Additionally, we observe that the wetting and dewetting behavior of the droplet is strongly dependent on the substrate disorder. Our findings shed light on how the wetting transition is affected in disordered systems and provide insight into how disordered substrates can be used to manipulate the behavior of fluids at interfaces. 

This study aims to contribute to the ongoing effort to understand the wetting transition phenomenon and its role in various fields. Through our simulations, we attempt to solve the problem of lack of understanding regarding the effect of one-dimensional disorder on the wetting transition. Our work will be useful for researchers working on fluid dynamics, materials science, and related fields to formulate new theories and design novel applications based on the behavior of fluids at solid-liquid interfaces.

In this work, we investigate the advantages of considering four-dimensional composite Higgs models over the commonly studied three-dimensional ones. The key idea is to assume that the Higgs particle is a composite object, which has been formed as a bound state of a fundamental particle and a new strong interaction. Composite Higgs models are a promising alternative to the Standard Model, and they can account for the origin of the Higgs mass without introducing additional particles. 

Our methodology consists of a detailed analysis of the effects of introducing an extra dimension, which can modify the properties of the heavy spin-1 particles, called vector resonances, that appear in composite Higgs models. We show that the inclusion of a fourth dimension can result in a richer phenomenology, with the possibility of new resonance structures and different coupling patterns among the particles. Additionally, we study the consequence of these additional resonances on the Higgs production and their potential to be observed in the Large Hadron Collider.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is to improve the predictive power of composite Higgs models while maintaining their simplicity and elegance. Our motivation for the research is to search for potential signals of new physics beyond the Standard Model that can be observed in present and future experiments. Overall, our work suggests that four-dimensional composite Higgs models offer a fascinating perspective on the nature of the Higgs boson and can have a broad impact on particle physics.

In this study, we challenge the theoretical framework of the cosmological constant, which posits that empty space is pervaded by a constant energy density. We argue that this framework presents significant problems, as the predicted energy density is far greater than what has been observed in experiments.

To address this issue, we propose a modification to the cosmological constant, in which the energy density is allowed to vary with time and space. This approach is based on the idea that the vacuum energy density is influenced by the presence of matter and radiation in the universe, and therefore should not be constant.

To test our hypothesis, we analyze the observed large-scale structure of the universe, as well as the cosmic microwave background radiation. Our analysis shows that our modified cosmological constant framework provides a much better fit to these observations than the conventional framework.

Our study offers a new perspective on the nature of vacuum energy and its role in shaping the evolution of the universe. We hope that our work will inform the ongoing attempts to reconcile the theoretical predictions with the observed properties of the universe, and ultimately contribute to a deeper understanding of the fundamental laws of physics.

In this paper, we investigate the cycling operation in braid groups. One of the main motivations for this research stems from the need to understand the structure of braid groups better. Braid groups have been widely studied and applied in various fields such as algebraic geometry, topology, and physics. As such, understanding the cycling operation in braid groups can help in the development of algorithms for computing braid group representations and in solving problems in knot theory and topological quantum field theory.

In this work, we explore the properties of the cycling operation in braid groups and its relation to various group structures. We show that the cycling operation is a well-defined map that preserves the order of the braid group, and we study its effect on different types of braids. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the cycling operation and the conjugation action on braid groups. We also provide examples of how the cycling operation can be used to compute braid group representations.

Our research aims to contribute to the development of a better understanding of braid groups and their properties. We hope that our results will pave the way for further research in this area and inspire new applications of braid groups in the different fields where they have been proven useful.

In this study, we analyze the stellar mass assembly history of galaxies over the last 8 billion years using data from the VIMOS VLT Deep Survey. Our main objective is to understand the growth and evolution of galaxies as a function of their stellar mass and cosmic time. We use a sample of more than 20,000 galaxies with stellar masses greater than 10^10 solar masses extracted from the survey. The mass growth of these galaxies is traced through their cumulative stellar mass density profiles as a function of cosmic time.

Our results show that the stellar mass assembly history of galaxies is strongly dependent on their initial mass. We find that the most massive galaxies (>10^11 solar masses) have already assembled a significant fraction of their mass at high redshifts (z>2), while smaller galaxies continue to grow in mass until the present day. We also find that the rate of mass growth decreases with increasing redshift, indicating that the assembly of galaxies has slowed down over time.

Our methodology involves the analysis of galaxy number counts, cumulative stellar mass density profiles, and the use of the stellar mass-halo mass relation to infer the evolution of dark matter halos. Our research seeks to shed light on the physical mechanisms responsible for the observed growth of galaxies over cosmic time.

Overall, our study provides a critical insight into the formation and evolution of galaxies and provides a foundation for future research in this field.

In this work, we investigate the behavior of self-dual critical Z(N) spin systems in the presence of the spontaneously broken Z(2) symmetry, commonly known as spontaneous symmetry breaking. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that this type of symmetry breaking is a fundamental phenomenon in many physical systems, including magnetism, superconductivity, and particle physics. Using the powerful tools of Conformal Field Theory (CFT), we derive and analyze the critical exponents of the Singular Limit of Entanglement (SLE) curves in these systems. Specifically, we focus on the critical behavior of the so-called restricted solid-on-solid (RSOS) model and its connection to the self-dual criticality of the 3-state Potts model.

Through a detailed analysis of the SLE curves, we obtain precise CFT predictions for the anomalous dimensions, the central charge, and the conformal blocks of the RSOS model. Our results provide strong evidence for the universality of the self-dual criticality and shed new light on the critical behavior of the Z(N) spin systems. The methodology we use involves a combination of numerical simulations, CFT calculations, and analytical techniques such as the Coulomb gas formalism and the conformal bootstrap equations. Our findings pave the way for future research on the critical properties of self-dual Z(N) spin systems and their applications in condensed matter physics, statistical mechanics, and quantum field theory.

We present an innovative framework for asset pricing in the context of information-based models. Our work addresses the critical issue of how to incorporate economic fundamentals within an information-based framework, which has emerged as an increasingly prominent tool in modeling financial markets. We focus on a vast array of information sources, including public news, private reports, and social media, and use them to estimate the underlying state variables and the corresponding values of assets. 

Our methodological approach aims to resolve the challenges associated with the standard modeling strategy, which assumes that all investors have identical expectations and access to the same information. Instead, we employ machine learning techniques to capture the heterogeneity of investor beliefs and derive more accurate pricing relationships. 

Our empirical results demonstrate that our framework outperforms the standard benchmark models in explaining the existing cross-sectional and time-series anomalies. Moreover, we observe that our model generates a higher out-of-sample predictability of asset prices and better matches the observed higher moments of asset returns.

In conclusion, our work makes a significant contribution to the literature on information-based asset pricing by proposing a novel methodological approach that captures the complexity of information sources and the heterogeneity of investor beliefs.

We present the second installment of the Spitzer c2d survey of weak-line T Tauri stars, concentrating on characterizing the infrared spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for a sample of 105 objects. Our aim is to gain insight into the timescale and mechanisms of planet formation in these young stars. We find that 80% of the sources in our sample display excess emission longward of 4.5 μm, indicating the presence of circumstellar disks. We use radiative transfer models to fit the SEDs and estimate the disk properties, such as the inner edge radius and masses. We find that our sample of disks appear to have relatively little mass in the inner disk, which suggest that rupured inner disks may be relatively common. Finally, we perform a statistical analysis to set upper limits on the occurrence of Jupiter-mass planets in our disk sample. Our results suggest that fewer than 10% of circumstellar disks produce Jupiter-mass planets within three astronomical units, consistent with other surveys of young stars. Our findings thus provide important constraints for theories of planet formation.

In this work, we explore the long-term evolution of magnetic turbulence in relativistic collisionless shocks in electron-positron plasmas. The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the mechanisms underlying the dissipation of kinetic energy and the acceleration of particles in such extreme environments. We utilize state-of-the-art numerical simulations that self-consistently evolve the plasma and magnetic fields. Using these simulations, we demonstrate that the amplification of magnetic turbulence is sustained over long periods of time, leading to the efficient acceleration of particles to very high energies.

Our results reveal that the magnetic turbulence is generated through the Weibel instability, which occurs due to the counter-streaming of particles in the plasma. This instability leads to the growth of strong magnetic fields, which in turn scatter the particles and accelerate them through a process called Fermi acceleration. We find that this process is very efficient in electron-positron plasmas, and can account for the production of high-energy cosmic rays observed in astrophysical settings.

Overall, this work provides new insights into the physics of relativistic collisionless shocks, and sheds light on the mechanisms responsible for the acceleration of particles in such environments. Our research contributes to the broader efforts to understand the origin and nature of high-energy cosmic rays, and has implications for a wide range of astrophysical phenomena.

In this work, we investigate the possibility that galactic dark matter can be explained as a bulk effect on the brane. The key idea is that dark matter, which seems to dominate the universe, may be a consequence of gravitational interactions between the visible matter and a hidden bulk space. This theory is motivated by the observation that the visible matter on the brane seems to be inadequate to generate the observed gravitational dynamics within galaxies and other astrophysical systems.

To test this theory, we use the Randers-Finsler geometry approach, which builds on a hybrid of the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms, in order to derive an effective equation of motion. We then solve this equation of motion for dark matter particles in the presence of a gravitational potential generated from the visible matter. Our results show that dark matter can indeed be interpreted as a bulk effect, as its observed distribution and clustering properties can be reproduced at the observed scales of galactic rotatioin curves.

Overall, our work provides a promising avenue for explaining dark matter, one of the key outstanding problems in astrophysics and cosmology today. By developing a new and testable theoretical paradigm that links dark matter to the properties of the bulk space, we hope to provide a foundation for future work to refine and develop these ideas even further.

In this paper, we investigate the orbital magnetization and its effects in spin-chiral ferromagnetic Kagome lattice. Our study focuses on understanding the influence of the orbital magnetization on the electronic and magnetic properties of the Kagome lattice via the spin-orbit coupling. The Kagome lattice is a two-dimensional material composed of interconnected triangles, with the ability to exhibit exotic electronic states.

We employ the tight-binding model and the Green's function formalism to analyze the electronic band structures of the Kagome lattice. Our study revealed that the orbital magnetization leads to a shift in the electronic bands and the appearance of band gaps. The appearance of the gaps is attributed to the destruction of the chiral symmetry of the Kagome lattice due to the spin-orbit coupling. We also observed that the orbital magnetization has a significant effect on the electronic and magnetic properties of spin-chiral Kagome ferromagnet. The applied magnetic field results in the changes of the magnetic moment, spin polarization, and the orbital angular momentum.

Our research aims to provide a better understanding of the effects of the orbital magnetization in spin-chiral ferromagnetic Kagome lattices. The study is motivated by the potential applications of these materials in next-generation electronic and magnetic devices.

In this study, we investigate the concept of complementarity in the Bohr-Einstein photon box. Our work aims to explore the fundamental limits of our ability to predict the behavior of quantum systems. In particular, we focus on the complementary nature of wave-like and particle-like behavior in light. This work is motivated by the fact that understanding complementarity is key to developing a better understanding of the fundamental nature of quantum mechanics. 

The results of our study show that the Bohr-Einstein photon box can provide important insights into complementarity. We find that there are certain conditions under which the wave and particle-like behavior of photons are mutually exclusive. However, when certain constraints are relaxed, both wave and particle-like behaviors can be observed simultaneously. 

In terms of methodology, we utilize a theoretical framework that describes the behavior of light in the presence of boundary conditions. Our approach involves using mathematical models to describe the behavior of photons and the constraints that act on them in the Bohr-Einstein photon box. 

Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the nature of complementarity in quantum mechanics, and provide important insights into the behavior of photons in constrained environments. The findings of this study have implications for the development of quantum technologies, which rely on a nuanced understanding of the behavior of quantum systems.

In this paper, we present a hydrodynamical simulation of detonations in superbursts. The motivation for this research is to enhance our understanding of superbursts, which are unusually intense and energetic stellar explosions that occur on the surface of neutron stars. These explosions release large amounts of energy and light, which can potentially help astronomers better understand the nature of matter in the extreme conditions present in neutron stars.

Our simulation employs a high-resolution numerical method for solving the equations of ideal gas hydrodynamics. We also use a specialized algorithm that allows us to properly resolve the detonation front and track its propagation in time and space. The preliminary one-dimensional results we obtained suggest that the detonation propagation consists of two phases: a slower deflagration phase followed by a faster detonation phase. The detonation velocities we obtain are consistent with observational data for superbursts.

The problem this work attempts to solve is the lack of a comprehensive theoretical model for superbursts. Our simulation provides a valuable tool for exploring the physics of superbursts and obtaining insights into the mechanisms responsible for their occurrence. The results obtained can guide future observational studies and help to better understand the properties of neutron stars.

In this work, we investigate the magnetic sensitivity of the Ba II D1 and D2 lines of the Fraunhofer spectrum with the aim of improving our understanding of the magnetic fields in the Sun and other stellar objects. The problem we attempt to solve is the need for a more accurate and reliable method of measuring magnetic fields in the atmosphere of the Sun and other stars.

The key ideas and methodology behind this study involve the use of Zeeman splitting and the application of a magnetic field to the Ba II D1 and D2 lines. We use spectroscopic observations of the Sun's photosphere and laboratory experiments to measure the changes in the spectral line profiles due to the presence of a magnetic field.

Our motivation for this research is to contribute to the field of solar physics and the study of other stars by improving our ability to measure magnetic fields and understand their effects on stellar atmospheres. We believe that our findings will help further our understanding of the Sun's magnetic activity and its impact on the Earth's climate.

In summary, our work aims to contribute to the advancement of solar physics and the study of other stars by improving our ability to accurately measure magnetic fields. We use Zeeman splitting and spectroscopic observations to investigate the magnetic sensitivity of the Ba II D1 and D2 lines of the Fraunhofer spectrum.

In this study, we investigate the remote Galactic globular cluster NGC 2419. Using data from the Hubble Space Telescope, we analyze the cluster's color-magnitude diagram and study its stellar populations. Our primary objective is to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the cluster's properties, including its age, metallicity, and distance. We apply isochrone fitting techniques to estimate these parameters and find that NGC 2419 is a rather old and metal-poor cluster, located at a large distance from the Galactic center. Our results provide valuable insight into the formation and evolution of globular clusters and their relation to the Milky Way's formation. Additionally, we examine the possibility of NGC 2419 being a disrupted dwarf galaxy and find only weak evidence supporting this hypothesis. Our work contributes to the ongoing efforts to understand the properties and origins of globular clusters and provides a detailed analysis of one of the most remote and fascinating clusters in the Milky Way. The motivation for this research is to deepen our understanding of the dynamics of globular clusters and provide critical information for future studies of the formation and evolution of the Milky Way.

In this work, we investigate the dynamics of a class of hypersurfaces under the width and mean curvature flows. The study is motivated by the fact that these two flows are rich geometric structures that have been widely employed in mathematical models in natural sciences, such as in materials science and biology. However, there are still many open questions regarding their behavior, even in simple cases.

The main problem that this research aims to address is to determine the long-term behavior of hypersurfaces under these flows. Specifically, we seek to identify the conditions under which the flow converges to a stable manifold. We construct a formal mathematical framework to study the width and mean curvature flows, establish the well-posedness of their evolution equations, and explore their properties in detail. 

Our results show that our proposed framework leads to a sharp characterization of the global behavior of the flows. In particular, we establish conditions for the flows to converge to a stable manifold and prove the uniqueness of the solution. This work provides new insights into the behavior of hypersurfaces under these important geometric structures, which are expected to have significant implications in various fields of natural sciences and mathematics.

In this work, we present the results of modelling and seismic testing of the CoRoT primary target HD 52265. The motivation for our research stems from the need to improve our understanding of the internal structure of stars and their evolution. HD 52265 is an ideal target for this study as it is a main sequence star with a mass of 1.5 solar masses and a radius of 1.6 solar radii. We constructed a grid of stellar models with a range of input parameters including different chemical compositions, which we fitted to the observed properties of HD 52265. We then calculated the frequencies of acoustic oscillations of these models and compared them to the frequencies observed by the CoRoT satellite. By matching the observed and theoretical frequencies, we were able to determine the internal properties of HD 52265 to a high degree of accuracy.

Our seismic tests allowed us to infer the rotation rate and the extent of core mixing in HD 52265, as well as to constrain the age and the extent of hydrogen and helium burning. Our results show that HD 52265 is a relatively young star with a core that rotates faster than its envelope and that the extent of core mixing is less than suggested by previous theoretical studies. We demonstrated that the combination of modelling and seismic testing is a powerful tool to constrain the fundamental properties of stars.

The formation of vortex structures by merging of multiple trapped Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) is investigated in this study. Our motivation for this research is to understand the dynamics and complexity of the vortex structures formed by the merging of BECs. The problem we attempt to solve is the explanation of the observed vortex structures formed by the interference and merging of multiple BECs. 

Using numerical simulations and experimental observations, we demonstrate that the merging of BECs leads to the emergence of different types of vortex structures, including vortex rings and linked vortex chains. We show that the final vortex structure obtained depends on the number of merging BECs, their initial relative positions, and the strength of the interatomic interactions. Our results also reveal that the formation of vortex structures is a dynamical process that can be controlled by adjusting the magnetic trapping potentials.

In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive characterization of the vortex structures formed by merging multiple trapped BECs. Our results can contribute to the development of new methods for controlling the dynamics and complexity of vortex structures with potential applications in quantum simulations and information processing.

In this work, we investigate nucleon-nucleon (NN) scattering using a model-independent approach known as effective field theory. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that NN scattering is essential to understanding the properties of atomic nuclei and how they interact with each other. Additionally, the study of NN scattering plays an important role in probing the dynamics of the strong nuclear force and the underlying theory of quantum chromodynamics.

The key idea behind our work is the decomposition of the NN scattering amplitude into irreducible partial waves. We then use a systematic expansion in the ratio of the momentum transfer to the typical nucleon mass to calculate the low-energy scattering amplitude up to a certain order. This approach allows us to explore the previously unknown connections between the observables of different partial waves in NN scattering and provides a way to test the limits of effective field theory.

Our methodology involves applying the principles of effective field theory to NN scattering data from previous experiments. Our work aims to address the long-standing problem of reconciling the different scattering data sets measured at low energies. Specifically, our approach aims to provide a unified framework for interpreting the scattering data, which will ultimately lead to a better understanding of the strong nuclear force and contribute to the ongoing effort to develop a complete theory of the fundamental forces of nature.

In this study, we validate the performance of module network learning algorithms using simulated data in order to provide a reliable framework for analyzing complex biological systems. The key idea is to accurately detect modules or subnetworks of closely interacting genes that are perturbed in specific biological conditions. We utilized two different types of simulated data: i) a realistic model with gene expression levels curated from publicly available microarray data in order to reflect the true biological complexity, and ii) a simplified model that more explicitly highlights the signal to noise ratio in the data. We employed two prevalent module detection algorithms (WGCNA and ARACNE) and evaluated their performance under various levels of noise and module size. Our results demonstrate that both algorithms exhibit excellent precision in detecting modules, but ARACNE outperforms WGCNA in terms of sensitivity, especially for smaller modules. Furthermore, our analysis of the simplified model reaffirms the importance of having a large enough sample size to accurately detect modules. The motivation for our research stems from the need for reliable module detection algorithms that can accurately predict gene behavior in diverse biological conditions to advance our understanding of complex biological systems. By validating module network learning algorithms using simulated data, we provide a valuable tool for the analysis and interpretation of gene expression data in biological systems.

In this article, we aim to explore the concept of continuous tensegrities and its applications in engineering and architecture. The motivation behind our research stems from the need to develop structures with enhanced stability and flexibility, while also minimizing material usage. To this end, we seek to investigate the properties of continuous tensegrities and explore their potential as structural components. 

One of the main problems that our work attempts to solve is the challenge of designing structures that can withstand dynamic loads and deformations. Conventional rigid structures are often limited in their ability to adjust to changing external conditions, whereas tensegrities can adapt and respond to different loads and forces. Our research investigates the ways in which continuous tensegrities can be used as modular building blocks for the construction of complex and adaptable structures.

The key ideas and methodology for our research include a review of the existing literature on tensegrities, the use of computational simulations to explore different designs, and physical experiments to test the structural properties of the tensegrities. We will also consider the potential applications of continuous tensegrities in various fields, including robotics, aerospace engineering, and construction.

Overall, our research aims to contribute to the development of innovative and sustainable building practices, by exploring the potential of continuous tensegrities as a versatile and adaptive structural system.

In this research, we investigated the competition between hydrogen-like and isotropic interactions on polymer collapse. We aimed to understand the driving forces behind the collapse of polymer chains in various solvents and to determine the dominance of each interaction type on this process. To achieve this goal, we employed theoretical calculations and simulations based on a coarse-grained model of polymers. 

Our findings suggest that the strength and orientation of both hydrogen-like and isotropic interactions can significantly affect the collapse behavior of a polymer chain. In particular, we found that hydrogen-like interactions can enhance the collapse, while isotropic interactions can either stabilize or destabilize the collapsed state, depending on their strength and orientation relative to the polymer backbone. 

The importance of this work lies in providing a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics of polymer collapse and in providing a theoretical basis for designing polymer-based materials with desired properties. Our results can also shed light on the behavior of biological macromolecules, such as proteins and nucleic acids, which are strongly affected by hydrogen-like and isotropic interactions in their native environments.

In this study, we investigate the radio emission from the intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in the globular cluster G1. Our aim is to understand the nature of the accretion process onto the IMBH, as well as to estimate its mass and spin.

The existence of IMBHs is still a topic of debate in astrophysics. However, some recent studies suggest that globular clusters may host such objects. Therefore, we seek to provide observational evidence supporting the presence of an IMBH in G1.

We collected archival data from the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) telescope for a total of eight hours of observation. We found strong radio emission coming from the center of the cluster, which we attribute to an accretion disk around the IMBH. Our modeling suggests a black hole mass of about 2,200 solar masses and a high spin parameter.

These results provide key insights into the properties of IMBHs and their host environments. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential of radio observations to probe the existence and properties of these elusive objects.

In this work, we present a multiscale model to understand the electronic behavior and localization of dry DNA under strain. A thorough analysis of DNA electronic behavior and localization is crucial in understanding various biological mechanisms and can have implications in biotechnology and medical sciences. We aim to address this problem by studying DNA stretching as a means of inducing changes in its electronic properties. Our model employs a combination of classical molecular dynamics and density functional theory to simulate the dynamics of DNA under strain and its corresponding electronic behavior. We investigate the effects of stretching on the structural and electronic properties of DNA, including band gap reduction and electron localization, with the latter being of particular relevance to DNA damage and repair. Our findings suggest that under beyond-yield strain, DNA undergoes significant structural deformation, resulting in an exponential reduction in its band gap. The localization of electrons also experiences significant alterations, providing crucial insights into the mechanism of DNA damage and repair under strain. Overall, this work provides a platform for further research on DNA electronic properties for better understanding various biological processes.

We present the design and implementation of a circulating hydrogen ultra-high purity system utilized for the MuCap experiment for the measurement of the singlet capture rate in hydrogen. The purpose of this study is to improve the current measurement by reducing the background and systematic uncertainties. The MuCap experiment aims to measure the capture rate of negative muons in hydrogen by trapping the muon in hydrogen atoms, where it eventually forms a bound state with the neutron. The detection of this state relies on the utilization of detectors with high spatial and time resolution. The ultra-high purity system used in this work allows for the removal of residual gases, impurities, and moisture that can contribute to unwanted background signals, consequently improving the experiment's overall sensitivity and reducing systematic uncertainties. 
   
The implementation of the circulating hydrogen system enabled a reliable and stable purification process, which resulted in a significant reduction of interfering signals, providing a cleaner environment and increased data quality for the MuCap experiment. The system achieved a hydrogen purity level of over 99.999%, which meets the MuCap experiment's requirements and has enabled the achievement of the most precise measurement of the singlet capture rate to date. Our results establish the critical role of the ultra-high purity system in facilitating a clean and stable experimental setup, providing a substantial contribution to the improvement of the overall sensitivity and accuracy of the measurement.

In this work, we investigate the influence of dust covering factor on silicate emission and star formation in luminous quasars (QSOs). We found that the dust covering factor has a significant impact on the observed silicate emission. The silicate emission flux is reduced in the presence of higher dust covering factors due to absorption by dust grains, which is consistent with the theory of dust attenuation. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the dust covering factor and the star formation rate (SFR) of the QSO's host galaxy. Luminous QSOs with higher dust covering factors tend to have lower SFRs. Our study suggests that the dust covering factor is an essential factor to consider when studying the dusty properties of QSOs. To carry out this investigation, we analyzed a sample of 119 luminous QSOs from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and utilized a variety of statistical techniques to determine the relationships between dust covering factor, silicate emission, and SFR. The work aims to solve the problem of understanding the relationship between dust and star formation in QSOs, which is critical for understanding the evolution of galaxies and the role of QSOs in the process.

We present the report of the US Long Baseline Neutrino Experiment Study, which is aimed at advancing the knowledge of neutrino physics and understanding of the universe. The motivation for this research stems from a long-standing gap in our understanding of neutrinos. Despite their prevalence, these subatomic particles remain mysterious, and their properties are not well understood. The study aimed to address this problem by designing and building a neutrino beamline and two multi-ton detectors to observe neutrinos produced at Fermilab.

The results obtained from this study have been groundbreaking. A total of 1754 neutrino interactions were observed, leading to the measurement of several properties of neutrinos. Most notably, the observation of oscillation between neutrinos of different flavors and precise measurements of neutrino masses.

The research solves several problems, including understanding the hierarchy and nature of neutrino masses, detailed measurements of charge-parity violation in the lepton sector, and searching for new physics beyond the standard model. Several future experiments are proposed to improve the precision of the measurements and provide spectral information on neutrinos produced in the beamline.

In conclusion, the Long Baseline Neutrino Experiment study has made fundamental contributions to the field of neutrino physics and has opened up new opportunities to better understand the universe.

In this study, we investigate the ionization fraction of the molecular cloud Barnard 68 (B68) using measurements obtained at the Caltech Submillimeter Observatory (CSO). Our aim is to examine the role that the ionization fraction plays in the process of star and planet formation in this cloud. We utilized the molecular lines CO, N2H+, and HCO+ to probe the conditions inside the cloud and the level of ionization. Our results indicate a low ionization fraction in B68, which is consistent with its low temperature and lack of star formation. We also compared our findings to other molecular clouds and found that compared to other clouds with active star formation, B68 has a significantly lower ionization fraction. Our study showcases the implications of ionization fraction in cloud dynamics and mass-to-charge ratios, thus providing essential information for understanding star and planet formation processes in molecular clouds. In summary, our research highlights the importance of analyzing the ionization fraction of molecular clouds for our fundamental understanding of star and planet formation.

In this study, we aim to investigate the luminous red galaxy (LRG) population in clusters at redshifts $0.2\leq z \leq 0.6$. The motivation behind this research stems from the need to understand the evolution of galaxy populations in clusters over cosmic time. LRGs are a particularly interesting subset of galaxies given their high stellar masses and strong clustering bias. By understanding the properties and behavior of LRGs in clusters at different redshifts, we can gain insight into how the cluster environment affects galaxy evolution. 

We used data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) to identify galaxy clusters in the target redshift range and to select samples of LRGs and other galaxies in these clusters. We then analyzed the clustering properties of these samples, using a two-point correlation function. 

Our results indicate that LRGs in clusters at $0.2\leq z\leq 0.6$ are more strongly clustered than other galaxy types in the same clusters. This finding is consistent with previous studies and suggests that LRGs are more likely to reside in the centers of clusters. However, we also find that the clustering bias of LRGs in these clusters is weaker than that of LRGs in nearby clusters. This may be due to environmental effects on the evolution of LRGs in cluster environments at different redshifts. 

Overall, our study provides insight into the evolution of LRG populations in clusters over cosmic time and highlights the importance of investigating the clustering properties of galaxy populations in different environments.

In this study, we present an approach to decision tree modeling with relational views. Traditionally, decision tree algorithms have been developed to work with flat data, but this approach falls short when dealing with data that is better represented in a relational format. Our methodology leverages the power of relational databases to structure complex data and build more informative decision trees. 

Our approach was tested on several datasets, including one from a real-life application in the healthcare industry. The results show that decision tree modeling with relational views outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and interpretability. Our methodology produced decision trees that led to a better understanding of the data and insights that were not previously apparent. 

We were motivated to develop this approach by the need to make sense of complex, interrelated data and situations. In many domains, data cannot be represented as a flat table, and traditional decision tree methods are not adequate. Our methodology offers a solution that takes into account the power of relational databases and the structure of data. 

Overall, our work aims to solve the problem of building decision trees with relational views. We offer a methodology that improves the accuracy and interpretability of the results, providing valuable insights for decision makers.

In this study, we investigate the general relativistic flux modulations that arise from disk instabilities in Sagittarius A*. Our key goal was to understand how these instabilities affect the accretion processes in the vicinity of Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy. To achieve this, we structured our research around a series of numerical simulations, informed by observations of the accreting gas in the Galactic center. 

Our methodology involved modeling the magnetic field and radiation transfer in the accretion disk and simulating its behavior near the black hole. We then analyzed the resultant flux distribution and its modulations to understand how disk instabilities can lead to the observed variability in the X-ray spectra in post-flare periods.

Our results point towards significant general relativistic flux modulations that arise from disk instabilities and demonstrate that these modulations can provide a critical means of understanding the turbulent and dynamic accretion behavior in the vicinity of the black hole. Moreover, our simulations draw on observations of the accretion flow from the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and our findings can inform future research and observations on black hole accretion behavior.

Overall, our study provides a critical step forward in understanding the complex physical processes surrounding Sagittarius A* and the black hole accretion behavior, advancing our understanding of the fundamental nature of gravity and some of the most extreme objects in the universe.

In this work, we investigate the resonant spin polarization in a two-dimensional hole gas (2DHG) taking into account the interplay among Luttinger term, structural inversion asymmetry, and Zeeman splitting. Spin-orbit interaction is known to give rise to a large range of interesting spintronic phenomena in semiconductors, which can be used for efficient information manipulation, storage, and transport in spin-based devices. However, the spin relaxation due to various spin-orbit coupling terms is a major bottleneck in realizing such devices. Here, we aim to understand the effect of the competing Luttinger term, structural inversion asymmetry, and Zeeman splitting on the resonant spin polarization of a 2DHG. Our theoretical analysis based on a model Hamiltonian and the Green’s function formalism shows that the Luttinger term and structural inversion asymmetry play crucial roles in the spin dynamics. We find that the resonance condition can be tuned by asymmetric doping, thus providing a way to control the spin relaxation time and degree of spin polarization. The results of this work have implications for the design and optimization of spin-based electronic and optoelectronic devices.

In this work, we present a curvature-inspired cosmological scenario that attempts to provide a viable explanation for the observed accelerated expansion of the universe. We aim to explore the possibility that the universe's curvature is not negligible, contrary to the current cosmological paradigm assumptions. The underlying problem that this work attempts to solve is the problem of dark energy and dark matter, which have been postulated to explain the apparent discrepancy between observed and predicted cosmic acceleration.

Our scenario is based on a new geometrical approach, where we assume that the universe's spatial section has a non-zero constant curvature. We formulate our model using the modified Einstein's field equations, and we show that our scenario naturally leads to the cosmic acceleration observed in recent cosmological observations. We also demonstrate how our model can account for the observed fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background radiation.

Our key idea is that the curvature of the universe plays a crucial role in the overall dynamics of the cosmos, and our methodology involves a rigorous mathematical analysis of the modified Einstein's field equations. Our results show that our curvature-inspired cosmological scenario is consistent with observational data and can offer a viable alternative to current models based on the dark-energy hypothesis. Our findings may contribute to a better understanding of the universe's large-scale structure and provide a new perspective on the fundamental nature of gravity.

Our work focuses on analyzing the mode stability in delta Scuti stars through comparing the linear analysis results with the observations in open clusters. The main motivation behind our research is to develop better understanding and explain the discrepancies between theoretical models and observed data. Studying delta Scuti stars has become more relevant due to their significance as key objects for understanding stellar evolution and asteroseismology.

Our study examines the mode stability of delta Scuti stars using data obtained from open clusters. We compared theoretical models of these stars with the observed ones, using the linear analysis method. Our results demonstrated that for delta Scuti stars in open clusters, linear analysis predicts mode stability well. However, we also found that discrepancies exist between the observed data and theoretical predictions as the non-linear effects are not accounted for in the theoretical models. We discuss how this problem could be addressed with new theoretical models that take into account the non-linear behavior of these stars.

Overall, our study contributes to the advancement in our understanding of delta Scuti stars and provides insights for future studies focusing on developing better theoretical models. Our work serves as crucial groundwork for further investigation into these stars, which offers significant opportunities for future studies focusing on the understanding of stellar evolution and asteroseismology.

In this work, we examine the problem of retaining black holes with very large recoil velocities. Astrophysical scenarios, such as the merger of two black holes with unequal masses, often result in the ejection of the resulting black hole from the galaxy where it formed. These ejected black holes can reach velocities of thousands of kilometers per second, making it difficult to retain them in the galactic nucleus. Retaining these ejected black holes is crucial for understanding galaxy evolution and testing the predictions of general relativity.

We utilize numerical simulations to investigate the possibility of retaining a black hole with a recoil velocity of up to 5000 km/s via the dynamical friction effect. Our results show that the presence of stars can significantly enhance the dynamical friction, allowing for the retention of a significant fraction of the ejected black hole population. This result is particularly significant considering the potential for the upcoming LISA and Pulsar Timing Array experiments to detect gravitational waves from merged black holes.

The motivation for this research was to better understand the dynamics of black holes, their role in galaxy evolution and the implications for gravitational wave astronomy. Our findings suggest that the presence of stars can play a crucial role in the retention of ejected black holes and motivate further studies to explore the impact of different stellar populations.

In this work, we investigate the effects of non-Gaussianity and early dark energy on the cluster abundances and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (S-Z) power spectra. Non-Gaussianity is a deviation from the Gaussian distribution assumption that is made in many cosmological models. Early dark energy is a hypothetical form of energy that can affect the evolution of the universe in the very early stages of its history. We use numerical simulations to study the impact of these two factors on the cluster abundances and S-Z power spectra.

Our results show that non-Gaussianity can significantly alter the cluster abundance and S-Z power spectrum. In particular, the amplitude of the S-Z power spectrum is increased in non-Gaussian scenarios. Our results also demonstrate that early dark energy can affect the cluster abundance and S-Z power spectrum, but the effect is less significant than that of non-Gaussianity.

The key idea behind this work is to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the impact of non-Gaussianity and early dark energy on the cluster abundances and S-Z power spectra. The methodology involves running numerical simulations and analyzing the resulting data.

The problem that this work attempts to solve is to gain a better understanding of the factors that can affect the cluster abundances and S-Z power spectra. This work has important implications for cosmology, as it can help refine our understanding of the initial conditions of the universe and the nature of dark energy.

In this work we present a re-analysis of the direct $J/\psi$ production at the Fermilab Tevatron. This process has been extensively studied in the past and is an important benchmark for understanding heavy-quark production and hadronization. However, discrepancies in measurements between different experiments and theoretical predictions have persisted, making a closer inspection necessary. Our goal is to revisit the data and perform a refined analysis, with the aim of clarifying the situation and providing a more precise measurement of the direct $J/\psi$ cross section.

The key idea behind our work is to use a different theoretical framework to calculate the signal and background contributions in the data. Specifically, we use the Color-Evaporation Model to describe the production of $J/\psi$ mesons. This model has been shown to be successful in describing a wide range of data in different energy regimes, and has the advantage of being able to account for non-prompt $J/\psi$ contributions. Additionally, we employ a sophisticated fit procedure, which allows us to accurately model the background contribution and separate it from the signal.

The methodology of our analysis involves selecting a clean sample of events with a $J/\psi$ meson produced directly, rather than from the decay of a heavier particle. We use both prompt and non-prompt $J/\psi$ events in our final analysis, and we compare our results with previous measurements as well as with theoretical predictions. Our main result is a measurement of the direct $J/\psi$ differential cross section as a function of the transverse momentum ($p_T$) in the rapidity range $|y|<1$. We demonstrate that our measurement is in good agreement with theoretical predictions and previous measurements, providing additional confidence in the standard model of particle physics.

In this paper, we investigate the expressive power of planar perfect matching and permanents of bounded treewidth matrices. The motivation for our research comes from the fact that these combinatorial objects are ubiquitous in computer science and mathematics, and they play a crucial role in many applications, including circuit theory and network optimization.

Our main result is a complexity classification of the expressive power of planar perfect matching and permanents of bounded treewidth matrices in terms of the Circuit Value Problem (CVP). Specifically, we show that planar perfect matching and permanents of bounded treewidth matrices are equivalent to small-depth circuits with threshold gates. Moreover, we prove that the expressive power of these combinatorial objects is strictly weaker than that of arbitrary polynomial-size arithmetic circuits.

Our work attempts to solve a long-standing problem of characterizing the expressive power of planar perfect matching and permanents of bounded treewidth matrices. Prior to our research, it was not clear whether these combinatorial objects could compute functions that are beyond small-depth circuits with threshold gates. Our results provide a comprehensive understanding of the expressive power of these objects and their relationship to the CVP and circuit complexity. Overall, our findings contribute more knowledge to the field of computer science and combinatorics and open up new research opportunities for the design and analysis of algorithms based on these objects.

We present our work entitled "A Massive Yang-Mills Theory based on the Nonlinearly Realized Gauge Group". The main motivation behind this research is to develop a theory that describes the behavior of gauge particles in a non-linear way. Such a theory is critical in understanding the dynamics of the strong nuclear force, which is mediated by gauge particles known as gluons.

Our work attempts to solve the problem of the absence of a consistent theory that can describe the properties of these gluons in a non-linear way. In this paper, we have presented a comprehensive study of a massive Yang-Mills theory based on a non-linearly realized gauge group. We have utilized mathematical techniques such as Goldstone's Theorem, the Higgs mechanism, and non-linear sigma models to derive the equations for the theory.

Our results show that the theory has important features such as confinement, the existence of massive gluons, and the screening of static charges, which are all consistent with observations in experiments. It is important to note that this theory is a significant breakthrough in the field of particle physics and has important implications for our understanding of the strong nuclear force.

In conclusion, our work provides a framework for a more comprehensive theory of gauge particles that can be tested through experiments. The non-linearly realized gauge group is a critical component in understanding the dynamics of the strong nuclear force and may lead to the development of new technologies in high-energy physics.

The Cornell Caltech Atacama Telescope (CCAT) is a state-of-the-art millimeter-wave telescope that aims to explore the universe's mysteries by capturing images of galaxies, stars, and interstellar gas. The instrument is located at one of the world's highest and driest observatory sites, in the Atacama Desert of Chile, presenting extraordinary possibilities for deep sky surveys. The CCAT is a collaboration between Cornell University and Caltech, which has proven effective for the development of exemplary instrumentation for astronomy. The primary goal of this research is to present the design of the telescope and its features, operational capabilities, and performance measurement techniques. 

The CCAT is a comprehensive observatory that uses the latest innovations and technologies to detect and study cosmic phenomena. This study aims to address the significant challenges associated with simulating telescopes. The team used advanced software to model the telescope and then used validated simulations to verify how multiple operational configurations of the CCAT would perform. In addition, the team performed sensitivity studies to investigate the optimal observing configurations. 

The research has resulted in a detailed analysis of the CCAT telescope's functionality and potential use of simulating telescopes. The team has shown that the CCAT will have outstanding performance in achieving the science goals outlined in this research. The CCAT is anticipated to transform the study of astronomy significantly and lead to a better understanding of the current cosmological model. The collaborative work done on the CCAT telescope by Cornell University and Caltech marks an exciting phase in astronomical research.

In this work, we investigated the Marcus-Lushnikov process and its relation to Smoluchowski's and Flory's models. The Marcus-Lushnikov process describes the diffusion-limited reactions between particles in solution, while Smoluchowski's and Flory's models are used to describe the behavior of polymers in solution and the formation of aggregates in colloidal systems, respectively. Our motivation for this research was to understand the relationships between these models and to uncover potential new applications of these concepts in chemical and materials science.

Using a combination of analytical techniques, simulations, and numerical calculations, we found that the Marcus-Lushnikov process can be used to model the aggregation of polymers in solution. This result provides a new understanding of the aggregation behavior of polymers, which is important for developing new materials with desired properties. Additionally, we determined that the Flory model can be used to describe the diffusion-limited reactions between particles in solution. This finding has implications for developing new methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and other small-scale materials.

Overall, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex behavior of particles and polymers in solution, and provides new insight into the applications of these concepts in materials science.

In this study, we present the results of our X-ray detection of the substellar twin 2MASS J11011926-7732383 AB. The motivation for the research was the need to better understand the properties of substellar objects, which are objects that are too small to become stars but too large to be considered planets. Our observations were carried out using the X-ray Multi-Mirror (XMM-Newton) Space Telescope, which allowed us to accurately measure the X-ray activity of the substellar object.

Our observations revealed that 2MASS J11011926-7732383 AB is a highly active source of X-rays, which suggests the presence of a strong magnetic field and a hot, magnetically heated corona. This is particularly interesting as it challenges our understanding of the evolution and magnetic activity of substellar objects, since such activity is observed typically in stars with masses similar to or higher than that of the Sun.

The key methodology used in this study involved observing the target with the XMM-Newton telescope and analyzing the obtained X-ray data using standard software and techniques. Our work provides new insights into the physical properties of substellar objects and further demonstrates the power of X-ray observations in studying them. These observations also have implications for the detection and characterization of such objects, as well as for our understanding of the evolution of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs.

In this study, we investigate the entanglement dynamics and the effects of DM antisymmetric anisotropic exchange interaction on a two-qubit $XYZ$ magnetic chain. Our work aims to provide a deeper understanding of the interaction between DM and exchange interactions and how these interactions impact entanglement properties. To achieve this aim, we adopted a numerical approach based on time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) simulations. 

Our results show that the antisymmetric exchange interaction in the $XYZ$ magnetic chain with DM can significantly enhance the entanglement between two qubits and change the entanglement dynamics compared to the conventional exchange interaction. In particular, we find that the DM interaction can induce the emergence of a multipartite entanglement structure in the two-qubit system, leading to a critical entanglement behavior like sudden death and revival of entanglement. Furthermore, we show that the entanglement dynamics can be controlled by manipulating the external magnetic field strength or tuning the DM interaction. 

Our findings have significant implications in the development of quantum computation, communication, and information processing. Our methodology and analytical framework provide a basis for future theoretical and experimental studies on quantum information processing and quantum technologies more broadly.

In this study, we conduct a multi-wavelength analysis of 18um-selected galaxies in the AKARI/IRC monitor field towards the North Ecliptic Pole. The motivation behind our research is to study the role of infrared (IR) luminous galaxies in galaxy formation and evolution. Our methodology involved cross-matching the AKARI/IRC 18um-selected galaxy sample with the Herschel/PACS and SPIRE maps, as well as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) database. We performed a spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting to derive the physical parameters of the galaxies, such as star formation rate, dust temperature, and luminosity. 

Our results show that the majority of the galaxies were classified as infrared-luminous, with high star formation rates and dust temperatures. We also found that these galaxies have higher dust obscuration than the average SDSS galaxy. Furthermore, we observed a trend between the IR luminosity and dust temperature, suggesting a link between dust heating and star formation activity. Finally, we compared our sample with previous studies and found that our selection criteria have successfully identified a substantial number of IR-luminous galaxies at high redshifts.

In conclusion, our multi-wavelength analysis has allowed us to gain a better understanding of the physical properties and evolution of IR-luminous galaxies. Our study is relevant to the ongoing efforts to explore the formation and evolution of galaxies in the era of cosmic reionization.

In this work, we explore the (0,2) Gauged Linear Sigma Model (GLSM) on Supermanifold. Our goal is to understand the mathematical structure of this model and its physical implications. One of the main challenges in this area is the lack of a well-established framework for studying GLSMs. Our research attempts to address this issue by introducing an algebraic approach that allows us to describe the theory in a more systematic and rigorous way.

The motivation for our study comes from the fact that (0,2) GLSMs have been extensively used in string theory to describe supersymmetric vacua. However, many important questions remain open, such as the existence of a non-perturbative definition, the computation of correlation functions, and the understanding of their symmetries. By investigating the (0,2) GLSM on Supermanifold, we hope to shed light on some of these fundamental issues.

Our key results include the derivation of the equivariant cohomology ring for the (0,2) GLSM on Supermanifold with a torus gauge group. We also provide explicit formulas for the Betti numbers and the Hodge numbers of this theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a topological twist that relates the (0,2) GLSM on Supermanifold to a Landau-Ginzburg model. Our analysis shows that this twist preserves important aspects of the theory, such as supersymmetry and the flavor symmetry. Overall, our work provides a valuable contribution to the understanding of (0,2) GLSMs and opens up new avenues for future research.

In this work, we report on the detection of very high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray emission from Cygnus X-1, the first stellar-mass black hole discovered. This result was obtained using the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov (MAGIC) telescopes, which provide very good sensitivity to gamma-rays in the TeV energy range. The observation campaign lasted for almost 6 years, from 2006 to 2012, and a total of 200 hours of data were collected.

The VHE emission from Cygnus X-1 was detected with a statistical significance of 5.6 standard deviations, which makes it the first black hole to be detected in this energy range. The photon spectrum of the VHE emission was measured in the energy range of 0.15 TeV to 1.4 TeV. It appears to be very hard, with a spectral index of 1.5±0.2.

The motivation for this research was to test the hypothesis that black holes accelerate particles to very high energies and release them in the form of VHE gamma-rays. This is a key question in high-energy astrophysics, and the observation of VHE gamma-rays from Cygnus X-1 provides evidence that black holes are indeed capable of producing such particles.

Our methodology involved the use of the MAGIC telescopes, which are sensitive to gamma-rays in the 100 GeV to 50 TeV energy range. We observed Cygnus X-1 for a total of 200 hours and analyzed the data using a maximum likelihood method. The result obtained confirms the presence of a VHE emission from Cygnus X-1 and opens up new perspectives in the study of the high-energy processes occurring around black holes.

In this work, we investigate the role of supernova remnants (SNRs) in the context of gamma-ray astronomy, using data obtained from the Gamma-Ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST). We focus on the question of how SNRs contribute to the overall gamma-ray emission observed in our galaxy, and explore the potential of GLAST to provide new insights into this phenomenon.

Our methodology involves a careful analysis of GLAST observations of known SNRs, in order to identify any significant gamma-ray emission associated with these objects. We also use multiwavelength data from radio to X-ray wavelengths to investigate the properties of the SNRs, such as their age, size, and environment, that may affect their gamma-ray emission.
