In this paper, we present an investigation of the signatures of incoherence in a quantum information processor. Our aim is to understand the effects of decoherence in quantum information processing and to determine how best to mitigate it. We study a model composed of two qubits in a quantum dynamical system and examine its coherence properties using a set of coherence measures.

Our investigation reveals that the coherence properties of the quantum system are strongly influenced by the initial state and the coupling strength between the two qubits. Specifically, we observe a rapid decay of coherence at time scales proportional to the degree of coupling between the qubits, which indicates the presence of incoherent effects in the system. We also show that the coherence of the system can be enhanced by introducing an external driving field that drives the system toward a particular target state.

Our study has significant implications for the development of practical quantum information processing devices. By understanding the signatures of incoherence, we can design better quantum systems with improved coherence properties. Moreover, our results suggest that the application of external fields can be an effective approach to mitigate the effects of incoherence in quantum systems. Overall, our research advances the understanding of coherence in quantum systems and offers new avenues for the development of practical quantum information processing devices.

In this work, we present the results of optical spectroscopy observations of a sample of Extreme High Energy Peaked BL Lac objects (EHBLs). EHBLs are a class of blazars that exhibit exceedingly high synchrotron peak frequencies, which make them particularly interesting targets for multi-wavelength studies. Our goal is to study their properties and determine their redshifts in order to understand their physical nature and the mechanisms that produce such high-energy emission. We used the 6.5m Magellan/Baade telescope located in Chile to observe 8 EHBLs, resulting in successful spectroscopic redshift measurements for 5 of them, with values ranging from z=0.07 to z=0.55. These new redshift measurements can help constrain models of EHBLs' formation and evolution. Furthermore, we confirm previous reports of the presence of broad emission lines in EHBLs, suggesting the presence of an accretion disk. Our study highlights the importance of multi-wavelength observations to better understand the nature of EHBLs, and the potential for upcoming facilities like the Cherenkov Telescope Array to provide important new insights in this field.

In this work, we present the XMM-Newton X-ray observations of the Wolf-Rayet binary system WR 147, which is located in the star-forming region of Cygnus OB2 association. Our observations aim to investigate the X-ray emission from the colliding stellar winds of the binary system. 

To achieve this, we performed data reduction and analysis on the XMM-Newton observations using the Science Analysis Software package and XSPEC software. We extracted the spectrum of the binary system and fitted it with a two-temperature plasma model. 

Our results reveal that the colliding wind region of WR 147 produces a significant amount of X-ray emission. The fitted model suggests the presence of two plasma components with temperatures of 0.8 keV and 5.1 keV, respectively. The derived X-ray flux for WR 147 is 4.4 × 10−13 erg cm−2 s−1. 

Our analysis also reveals that the X-ray emission from WR 147 is variable on short timescales, likely due to instabilities in the colliding wind region. Overall, our study provides crucial insights into the high-energy processes occurring in the colliding wind region of Wolf-Rayet binary systems and highlights the importance of X-ray observations in understanding these complex astrophysical environments.

In this paper, we investigate the (an)isotropy of the Hubble diagram by comparing different hemispheres. The Hubble diagram is a plot of the apparent magnitude of an object on the y-axis against its redshift on the x-axis. It is a fundamental tool in modern cosmology, providing valuable insight into the expansion of the universe. However, recent research suggests that the Hubble diagram may exhibit anisotropy, meaning that it looks different depending on the direction in which we observe the universe. This could have significant implications for our understanding of the structure and dynamics of the cosmos.

To investigate this, we compare the Hubble diagrams of two hemisphere maps using different statistical tools and tests. We use the Union2.1 compilation of supernovae type Ia observations for this purpose. Our results suggest that the Hubble diagram exhibits slight anisotropy when comparing hemispheres in terms of the mean of absolute magnitudes or the residuals of the fits. However, we also found some agreement with the null hypothesis of no difference between hemispheres, and this implies that more work needs to be done to confirm the anisotropy findings.

Overall, this work contributes to the ongoing efforts to understand the fundamental properties of the universe, and it suggests that further research is necessary to clarify the (an)isotropy of the Hubble diagram.

In this work, we investigate the Casimir effect in a 6D warped flux compactification model with a priori different compactification radii. Our aim is to extend the known results on the Casimir effect in 5D spacetimes to a nontrivial 6D spacetime with a nonzero flux parameter. The Casimir effect is a fascinating quantum phenomenon that arises as a consequence of the field fluctuations in the presence of boundaries or boundaries-like conditions. It has been extensively studied in the past few decades due to its importance in quantum field theory and its potential applications in nanotechnology and cosmology. However, most of the previous works have focused on simple 5D spacetimes with smooth compactifications, and very few investigations have been done in more complex 6D spacetimes with nontrivial boundary conditions. To this end, we use the zeta-function regularization method and the mode summation method to compute the Casimir energy density and the corresponding pressure in our model. We show that the Casimir energy density and pressure depend crucially on the compactification radii and the flux parameter, and their values may diverge or vanish in different limits. Our results reveal new insights into the Casimir effect in nontrivial 6D spacetimes and provide a foundation to explore various cosmological implications of the Casimir effect.

In this work, we develop a method to extract the spatial trajectories of particles in a quantum system governed by an entangled wavefunction. Specifically, we apply the de Broglie-Bohm theory to a two-particle system with spin degrees of freedom. The wavefunction of this system is a superposition of two entangled states with different relative phases. By solving the corresponding Schrödinger equation, we obtain the probability density and the phase of the wavefunction, from which we calculate the Bohmian trajectories of the particles. Our approach is based on the interpretation of the phase of the wavefunction as a potential that guides the particles' motion. This method enables us to visualize the effects of entanglement on the trajectories of the particles in a simple quantum system.

We present numerical simulations for different initial states and demonstrate that the entangled state leads to non-trivial interference patterns in the probability density and the trajectories of the particles. Specifically, we show that the particles can be steered by the entanglement to follow different paths compared to the non-entangled case. Our results highlight the importance of considering the entanglement of particles in the microscopic world, and provide insights into the intriguing phenomena of quantum interference and non-locality.

In summary, our work aims to elucidate the role of entanglement on the behavior of particles in a quantum system, and offers a novel method to explore the non-local properties of wavefunctions.

In this work, we investigate the rotational periods and phase functions of dwarf Plutonian planets and other large Kuiper Belt Objects. Our main objective is to determine their absolute magnitudes, which can provide insight into the objects' physical parameters and surface properties. To achieve this, we obtained light curve data from various sources, including ground-based observations and space-based missions such as New Horizons and Kepler. 

Our results indicate that most of the studied objects have rotation periods ranging from 5 to 20 hours, with the exception of Haumea, which has a period of only 3.9 hours. We also found significant variability in the phase functions, which reveals variations in albedo and surface composition. By combining the absolute magnitudes with other data, we estimate the sizes and densities of the objects. 

One key aspect of our methodology is the use of statistical modeling to generate a large number of synthetic light curves, which allows us to compare the observed data with a range of possible rotational and phase parameters. This approach helps us to better constrain the physical properties of the objects and reduce the uncertainties in our results. 

Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of the rotation and surface properties of dwarf Plutonian planets and other large Kuiper Belt Objects, and has important implications for future missions and observations of these fascinating bodies.

In our work on Network tomography based on 1-D projections, we aim to tackle the issue of accurately diagnosing and localizing faults on large scale computer networks. The motivation for this research lies in the fact that failures in computer networks can cause significant financial losses and have far-reaching consequences. While traditional fault diagnosis methods involve analyzing packet loss and delays, they frequently fall short in providing a complete picture of the problem.

Our study proposes a novel approach to the problem by leveraging 1-D projections of network measurements, which allows us to capture more nuanced information about the network. To achieve this, we develop a neural network model that takes in network data and generates accurate 1-D projections. We then use these projections alongside machine learning techniques to reconstruct the topology of the network and pinpoint the location of faults with higher precision and accuracy than previously possible.

The results of our study demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency, making it a promising solution to the problem of fault diagnosis in large-scale computer networks. This work has the potential to significantly improve the reliability and performance of complex network systems, benefitting organizations and individuals alike.

In our study, "Clustered Star Formation in the Small Magellanic Cloud. A Spitzer/IRAC View of the Star-Forming Region NGC 602/N 90", we aimed to investigate the process of clustered star formation within this specific region. Our motivation for conducting this research was to gain a better understanding of the formation of massive star clusters and how they evolve within galaxies, in particular the Small Magellanic Cloud.

Using data from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we identified 865 young stellar objects within NGC 602/N 90. We observed that the majority of star formation occurs in dense environments, suggesting hierarchical structures in which smaller stellar groups gather to form larger star clusters. Additionally, we found evidence of sequential star formation, in which younger star clusters form in close proximity to older, more evolved clusters.

Our study attempts to solve the problem of understanding the mechanisms behind massive star cluster formation and the way in which they evolve over time. The results of our research provide new insights into the hierarchical nature of star formation and the dynamics of star clusters in the Small Magellanic Cloud. Our findings also have implications for our understanding of star formation within other galaxies and for the larger field of astrophysics.

In this study, we investigate the production of high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos from semi-relativistic hypernovae. The existence of cosmic rays with energies up to 10^20 eV and the recent discovery of high-energy neutrinos have been a long-standing mystery in astrophysics. Several theoretical models have been proposed to explain the origin of these phenomena, including supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and hypernovae. However, the origin of these cosmic rays and neutrinos is still unclear, which motivates our research. 

Our work aims to model the production of cosmic rays and neutrinos from semi-relativistic hypernovae. We apply a Monte Carlo approach to simulate the interaction between cosmic rays and the hypernova ejecta. In addition, we calculate the neutrino flux emitted from the hypernova using a time-dependent diffusion equation. Our calculation takes into account the effects of magnetic fields, shock acceleration, and neutrino oscillation. 

Our findings suggest that semi-relativistic hypernovae are a viable source of high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos. We find that the cosmic ray spectrum is consistent with observations and that the predicted neutrino flux is within the sensitivity of current and future detectors. Therefore, our research provides a new insight into the origin of high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos, which can help to improve our understanding of the universe.

In this study, our team conducted experimental investigations to explore the phenomenon of vacancy-induced ferromagnetism in undoped TiO2. This research is motivated by the need to clarify and understand the underlying mechanisms that drive ferromagnetic behavior in non-magnetic materials. The problem that our work attempts to tackle is the scarce knowledge of the origin and characteristics of ferromagnetic ordering in TiO2, which could have potential applications in various fields like spintronics and catalysis. 

We employed various experimental techniques, namely thermoluminescence measurements, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, to investigate the properties of TiO2 samples under varying conditions. Our study confirmed that the presence of oxygen vacancies in TiO2 induces ferromagnetism in the system, which is attributed to the exchange interaction between the localized electrons at the vacancy sites. Furthermore, we observed that the magnetization of TiO2 samples improved with increasing irradiation dose, temperature, and annealing time.

In conclusion, our experimental findings provide essential insights into the origin and nature of vacancy-induced ferromagnetism in TiO2. Such knowledge could pave the way for the development of new approaches for engineering the magnetic properties of non-magnetic materials, bringing significant advancements in various scientific and industrial applications.

In this paper, we present a study of the magnetic field properties in the nearby spiral galaxy NGC 6946. Our main motivation is to explore the mechanisms responsible for the formation and evolution of magnetic arms and the depolarization rings observed in this galaxy. Additionally, we investigate the dynamo modes operating within the interstellar medium and the helical fields present in the galaxy.

Our research is based on Faraday rotation and polarimetric measurements obtained from multi-frequency radio observations of NGC 6946. We use a combination of statistical and spectral analyses to evaluate the magnetic field properties at different spatial scales within the galaxy. We find that the magnetic arms are associated with the spiral arms, while the depolarization rings are traced by magnetic field reversals in the disk. We observe strong evidence for a turbulent dynamo mode operating within the interstellar medium, leading to the amplification of magnetic fields in the disk. Moreover, we find significant helical fields in the outer disk regions, possibly related to galactic shear or dynamical instabilities.

Our study provides valuable insights into the complex nature of magnetic fields in spiral galaxies and advances our understanding of their origin and evolution.

In this study, we investigate the cascading behavior in large blog graphs, aiming to understand how information diffusion occurs in such systems. The motivation for this research stems from the significant role that blogs play in shaping the public discourse and influencing the opinions of their readers. Through the analysis of a real-world blog dataset, we observe that cascades in blog graphs exhibit distinct characteristics from those in other social media platforms. Specifically, we find that blogs tend to have fewer but more influential cascades, with a longer cascade duration and a higher probability of reaching a large audience. 

Our study contributes to the growing body of literature on information diffusion in complex networks and presents novel insights into the dynamics of blog-based communication. Moreover, we propose a framework for quantifying the cascading behavior of blog graphs, which can facilitate further research and help in developing more effective strategies for spreading information on these platforms. The problem that this work attempts to solve is the lack of a comprehensive understanding of how information spreads through blog networks and how different factors such as content, network topology, and user behavior influence this process. By shedding light on these issues, our study fills an important gap in the current literature and provides a valuable resource for social scientists, communication experts, and policymakers.

In this paper, we explore the concept of nontrivial geometries and their implications for the curvature of the universe. We investigate the possibility of a universe with a non-zero curvature and its consequences for our understanding of spacetime. 

Our work attempts to solve the problem of determining the upper and lower bounds for the curvature of the universe. We examine the theoretical limits predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity, as well as observational data gathered from cosmic microwave background radiation measurements and other astrophysical observations. 

The key ideas underlying our methodology involve the use of mathematical tools, including differential geometry and topology, to analyze the possible geometries of the universe. We develop mathematical models to describe the curvature of spacetime and apply them to observational data to determine whether the universe is flat, positively curved, or negatively curved. 

Our results show that the curvature of the universe is likely to be very close to zero, consistent with the flatness prediction of inflationary cosmology. However, our analysis also reveals that a non-zero curvature cannot be ruled out entirely, and we provide upper and lower bounds on the curvature based on our analysis. Our work has important implications for our understanding of the universe's evolution and the development of future cosmological theories.

In this study, we present our analysis of RXTE and INTEGRAL data of the X-ray binary system 4U 0115+63, focusing on the pulse profile and cyclotron line energy. Our motivation for this research was to gain a better understanding of this complex system and its unique high magnetic field, known to influence its accretion onto the compact object. 

Using RXTE PCA and HEXTE data, in combination with INTEGRAL IBIS/ISGRI and JEM-X data, we studied the pulse profile and discovered a multi-peaked structure with a complex harmonic content. We also studied the evolution of the pulse profile as a function of energy and found distinct changes in the profile shape with increasing energy. 

A cyclotron line was detected at 19 keV with a measured width indicating that it is produced in a region close to the compact object. We also observed a correlation between the cyclotron line energy and the luminosity, providing important insights into the accretion mechanism.

Our results offer a new perspective on the dynamics of the 4U 0115+63 system and provide important constraints for theoretical models of accretion onto magnetized compact objects. These findings highlight the power of multi-mission observations and showcase the potential for future studies with advanced X-ray imaging instruments.

In this study, we investigate the correlations between the peak color and the peak metallicity of old metal-rich globular cluster populations and the mass of their host spheroids. We analyze a sample of 25 galactic and extragalactic spheroids with known globular cluster populations to examine how the properties of the host spheroids influence the chemical evolution of their globular cluster systems.

Our analysis reveals that there is a direct correlation between the peak color of the globular cluster system and the mass of the host spheroid, with more massive spheroids having redder peak colors. In contrast, the peak metallicity of the globular cluster system shows no significant correlation with the host spheroid mass. These results suggest that the color evolution of the globular cluster system is primarily driven by the metallicity evolution of the host spheroid at early times.

The motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the formation and evolution of globular cluster systems, which provide important insights into the formation histories of galaxies. Our findings shed light on the interplay between the globular cluster system and its host spheroid, which is crucial for constraining theoretical models of galaxy formation.

We employ a combination of empirical and theoretical methods to analyze the dataset, including photometric and spectroscopic measurements, as well as computer simulations. Our study provides new insights into the chemical evolution of globular cluster systems in the context of their host galaxies.

Our research aims to provide a comprehensive approach to conformational analysis of peptide and protein structures using NMR spectroscopy and molecular mechanics simulations. The motivation for this work is the increasing importance of understanding the details of protein conformational changes for the design of drugs and therapeutic interventions. An important aspect of this issue is the role of side chain rotational isomers in dictating protein stability and function, and their impact on drug binding and selectivity.

The challenge addressed in this work is the quantification of individual side chain rotational isomers in peptides and proteins. We present a novel method that combines NMR spectroscopy and molecular mechanics simulations to accurately determine the population of each isomer. The method is validated using several peptides of different sizes and amino acid sequences.

The results indicate that our method provides a highly accurate and sensitive approach to quantify the population of side chain rotational isomers in peptides and proteins. Importantly, we demonstrate that the method can detect subtle differences in peptide conformational preferences induced by changes in solvent or in the presence of ligands. Our approach provides a basis for a broader understanding of the structural dynamics of peptides and proteins in solution, which is an essential factor in drug design and therapeutic intervention.

In this work, we present an analysis of the bolometric output of luminous obscured quasars using data from the Spitzer Space Telescope. The study is part of the HELLAS2XMM survey, which aims to identify and characterize the properties of high-energy sources in the X-ray sky. To derive the bolometric luminosities of the targets, we combine Spitzer mid-infrared data with X-ray and optical/UV fluxes from XMM-Newton and ground-based instruments. Our sample consists of 25 obscured quasars at redshifts between 0.9 and 3.1, with X-ray luminosities in the range 10^44-10^46 erg/s. We find that the majority of the sources have bolometric luminosities in the range 10^45-10^47 erg/s, with a median value of ~10^46.4 erg/s. We also investigate the correlation between the bolometric and X-ray luminosities, and find that it is well-described by a power-law with an index of ~0.8. Our results provide insights into the energetics and accretion processes in the most luminous active galactic nuclei, and offer valuable information for theoretical models of quasar evolution.

In this work, we investigate the Horava-Witten theory on a compact complex hyperbolic threefold to explore the potential existence of TeV-scale gravity. Our aim is to establish connections between string theory and particle physics. The key idea is to examine the relationship between TeV-scale physics and the topology of extra dimensions. We employ the supergravity approximation and the AdS/CFT correspondence to analyze the behavior of the theory in high energy regimes.

Our study shows that the compact complex hyperbolic threefold can provide a promising candidate for the scale of gravity as it preserves supersymmetry and has a negative curvature. Furthermore, we show that a consistent fine-tuning of the moduli space, represented by the shape of the threefold, may lead to an enhanced gauge symmetry and the emergence of the Standard Model gauge group.

We also evaluate the cosmological implications of our findings, and suggest that this approach may shed light on the nature of dark matter and the unification of the fundamental forces of nature. Our work attempts to address the problem of reconciling gravity with the other fundamental forces in the context of string theory, and we believe it represents an important step towards a more complete understanding of the fundamental physics underlying our universe.

In this work, we investigate the photometric redshift (photo-z) accuracy required for weak lensing tomography from space missions. We focus on the role of optical and near-IR photometry in obtaining accurate photo-z for weak lensing tomography. Specifically, we use the Euclid-like simulations to explore the impact of different observational parameters, such as depth and filter configuration, on photo-z performance.

Our results suggest that a combination of optical and near-IR photometry significantly enhances photo-z precision for weak lensing tomography. For instance, we find that adding near-IR photometry typically improves the photo-z performance by 5-20%. Our analysis also indicates that the choice of filter configuration and depth plays a crucial role in photo-z precision. For Euclid-like observations, we recommend using Y and J filters to achieve the best photo-z performance.

Overall, this work demonstrates the importance of accurate photo-z for weak lensing tomography and highlights the critical role of near-IR photometry. Our findings are valuable for future space missions such as Euclid and WFIRST, which aim to utilize weak lensing tomography to investigate the nature of dark matter and dark energy in the Universe.

In this work, we explore the connection between Dirichlet sigma models and mean curvature flow. Our goal is to gain a better understanding of the behavior of these models and to develop new methods for analyzing them. The motivation for our research comes from the fact that these models are important in various areas of physics and mathematics, including particle physics, string theory, and differential geometry.

Our approach is based on the use of geometric analysis, which allows us to obtain a deeper understanding of the properties of these models. Specifically, we focus on the mean curvature flow, which is a powerful tool for studying geometric objects. We use various techniques from geometric analysis to analyze the behavior of the Dirichlet sigma models under this flow.

Our results provide new insights into the properties of these models and shed light on their behavior in various contexts. In particular, we derive new estimates for the solutions of these models and show how they evolve under the mean curvature flow. Our work also lays the groundwork for future research in this area, as we suggest several other possible directions for future investigation.

Overall, our work represents an important contribution to the study of Dirichlet sigma models and mean curvature flow. It provides new insights into the behavior of these models and opens up new avenues for further research in this area.

In this study, we investigated the effect of the spin-orbit interaction on the thermodynamic properties of bismuth via the specific heat of single crystals. Our motivation stems from the fact that bismuth is a semi-metal with a peculiar electronic structure that leads to a large spin-orbit coupling. This coupling affects the spin and orbital angular momenta of the electrons, which in turn influences the magnetic, transport, and thermodynamic properties of the material. However, the specific heat, which provides valuable information about the phonon and electronic contributions to the entropy, has not been explored in detail.

To address this gap, we measured the specific heat of high-quality bismuth single crystals from 2 to 300 K and under magnetic fields up to 5 T. We found that the specific heat of bismuth shows a dominant phonon contribution at low temperatures, but a significant electronic contribution emerges at high temperatures. Particularly, the electronic contribution increases with applied magnetic field due to a weak antiferromagnetic interaction between the spins. 

Our results suggest that the spin-orbit interaction plays a crucial role in the thermodynamic properties of bismuth, and highlights the importance of investigating this interaction in other materials. This study provides a useful guide for theoretical models of bismuth and other spin-orbit coupled systems.

In this paper, we explore the potential of using quantum mechanics in designing auctions, which we call quantum auctions. The motivation for our research is to consider how quantum information can drastically enhance the efficiency and security of auctions. Traditional auctions, used in various settings, are plagued by problems such as sealed bids being compromised, trust issues between the participants, and often resulting in less-than-optimal outcomes. By using the principles of quantum mechanics, we aim to tackle these issues by designing innovative approaches to information processing and security.

To achieve our goal, we apply the principles of quantum information theory to design new auction mechanisms, such as quantum private-bidding protocols and quantum key distribution methods. We propose a quantum auction that allows participants to bid secretly and prove the correctness of their bids using quantum states, which increases security and reduces the chance of fraudulent activities.

Our methodology includes constructing a theoretical framework to describe the workings of quantum auctions, applying game theory to analyze the behavior of participants and evaluating the efficiency of our proposed auction algorithms. We argue that quantum auctions could provide a better alternative to classical auctions and could be more suitable for future technologies. This work offers an exciting and novel direction for future research in quantum information science.

In this research, we present a detailed model to track the long-term trends in lunar exposure to the Earth's plasmasheet. The objective is to understand the effects of the plasmasheet on the lunar environment and to develop a forecasting tool for future missions. The work uses imaging data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LEND instrument, solar wind parameters from ACE satellite, and measurements from the WIND and THEMIS missions. The key idea of the paper is to model the plasmasheet's expansion and contraction using a simple analytical function that depends on the solar wind dynamic pressure. We then use this function to scale the measured energetic electron fluxes at the lunar orbit to estimate the average flux levels at the surface. The methodology includes a comparison of different data sources and careful selection of the input parameters. Our results show that the plasmasheet's intensity is relatively stable on the long-term scale, but there are significant variations on the seasonal and solar cycle time scales. We also find that the plasmasheet shows a systematic drift towards the dawn side of the Moon, which could have important implications for the design of future lunar missions. Overall, our work provides a useful tool for predicting and understanding the effects of the Earth's plasmasheet on the lunar surface and the surrounding environment.

In this study, we present our findings on the magnetorotational instability (MRI) in a shearing box with zero net flux through magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. Our motivation for this research is to understand the behavior of accretion disks in astrophysical systems, where the MRI is believed to be a crucial mechanism for the transfer of angular momentum in the disk. The shearing box model is commonly used in astrophysical simulations as it allows for the study of local phenomena within the disk, while also being a computationally efficient model. However, the issue of convergence in MHD simulations of the MRI has been a longstanding challenge.

Using a numerical code based on the Athena framework, we performed a set of simulations with varying spatial resolution and domain size to investigate the convergence behavior of the MRI in a zero-net-flux shearing box. Our results show that a sufficiently high resolution is needed to capture the small-scale turbulence that arises from the MRI and its resulting effect on the transport of angular momentum. Additionally, we find that the convergence behavior depends on the specific parameters of the simulation, underscoring the importance of performing a convergence study for each specific case. Our study provides insights into the numerical requirements for MHD simulations of the MRI in astrophysical settings and serves as a stepping stone for future studies in this area.

In this study, we investigate the alignment patterns of the spins of galaxies with the real-space tidal field using data from the Two Mass Redshift Survey. By analyzing the orientations of galaxies with respect to their local environment, we aim to better understand the formation and evolution of galaxies within the cosmic web. Our results reveal a strong correlation between the spin of a galaxy and the tidal field, suggesting that the alignment of galaxies is a consequence of the way in which they formed within their environment.

Our work attempts to solve the long-standing mystery of galaxy alignments and the physical mechanisms that drive them. Understanding these alignment patterns is fundamental to our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution in the Universe. Our research is motivated by the need to better understand the relationship between the large-scale structure of the Universe and the formation of galaxies within it. 

Overall, our study provides new insight into the relationship between cosmic structures and the properties of galaxies, which has important implications for our understanding of the cosmic web and its formation. Our findings provide important constraints for theoretical models of galaxy formation and evolution and will pave the way for future studies in this field.

In this work, we investigate the impact of gravity-like potential in photonic crystal fibers on the propagation of ultrashort pulses. The primary problem this work attempts to solve is the stretching of supercontinuum, which is crucial in many applications of optical pulse generation, frequency conversion, and sensing. 
Our motivation is to understand the underlying physical mechanism of the gravity-like potential, which involves a gradual increase in the refractive index, leading to a slowing down of the group velocity. This mechanism is important in applications where light confinement and manipulation are necessary, such as for optical waveguides and trapping of microparticles. 
We demonstrate that by tailoring the shape and strength of the gravity-like potential, we can control the spectral broadening and distribution of the supercontinuum, without significant pulse broadening. Moreover, we show that by combining the gravity-like potential with other dispersion-manipulating techniques, such as dispersion tailoring and nonlinear effects, we can further enhance the spectral control and light confinement. 
Our results offer new insights into the application of gravity-like potential in photonic crystal fibers and provide a promising platform for controlling the propagation and manipulation of ultrashort pulses in fibers.

In this work, we present an analytic result for the one-loop massless triangle Feynman diagram, which is an important building block in perturbative calculations of quantum field theories. Our motivation for this research is to improve the accuracy of theoretical predictions for high-energy particle physics experiments, such as those performed at the Large Hadron Collider. The key idea of our approach is to use a combination of mathematical techniques, including complex analysis and dimensional regularization, to compute the integral associated with the Feynman diagram. Our methodology involves applying the Feynman parameterization and carrying out a series of algebraic and trigonometric manipulations to simplify the integrand into a form that can be evaluated analytically. We obtain a closed-form expression for the integral, which is expressed in terms of logarithmic and polylogarithmic functions of the relevant momentum and coupling parameters. Our mathematical result can be used to calculate the corresponding contribution to any physical observable that involves the one-loop massless triangle diagram, such as the scattering amplitudes of elementary particles. Our work contributes to the ongoing efforts to advance the precision of theoretical predictions in high-energy physics and establishes a new benchmark for future calculations.

In this work, we investigate the stringy E-functions of hypersurfaces and of Brieskorn singularities. Our aim is to provide a geometric interpretation and proof of the additivity theorem for the stringy E-function of a complete intersection. The key idea is to use toric geometry and the theory of Ehrhart polynomials to compute the stringy E-function of a hypersurface. We extend this computation to Brieskorn singularities using the theory of equivariant Ehrhart polynomials. 

We obtain explicit formulas for the stringy E-functions of certain types of hypersurfaces and Brieskorn singularities. In particular, we obtain the complete stringy E-function of the Brieskorn-Pham singularities. Our results have applications in mirror symmetry, degeneration techniques, and tropical geometry. 

The problem we attempt to solve is the one of characterizing the spectrum of the stringy E-function of a hypersurface. Our methodology is a combination of geometric and combinatorial techniques. We use toric geometry and the theory of Ehrhart polynomials in a novel way to obtain a new proof of the additivity theorem. The contribution of this work is a better understanding of the relationship between the geometry of a hypersurface or Brieskorn singularity and its stringy E-function.

In this work, we present a study of the opposite magnetic polarity observed in two photospheric lines detected in a single spectrum of the quiet Sun. Our motivation behind this research is to understand the polarity inversion lines (PILs) present in the Sun's magnetic field and their role in the dynamics of the solar atmosphere.

Using observations acquired with the Interferometric Bidimensional Spectrometer (IBIS) at the Dunn Solar Telescope, we found a clear opposite magnetic polarity signature in two spectral lines, Fe I 6301 Å and Ca II 8542 Å. We performed a detailed analysis of the magnetic field strength and inclination using the spectral line inversion code SPINOR, which provided us with valuable information on the magnetic field topology and its evolution over time.

Our study reveals the existence of opposite polarity regions in close proximity to each other, which suggests the presence of small-scale magnetic loops that could contribute to the heating of the solar atmosphere and the formation of coronal structures. This work addresses the problem of understanding the mechanisms that drive the dynamics of the quiet Sun, which is essential for developing accurate solar models and predicting the behavior of the Sun.

In our work, we presented a large acceptance scintillator detector with wavelength shifting fibre read-out, which was specifically designed for the search of eta-nucleus bound states. The detection of these bound states can provide valuable information about the interaction between mesons and nuclei, which is of great interest in the field of nuclear physics.

The main idea behind our detector was to provide a high-efficiency and low-background detection system for eta mesons, which have a short lifetime and are often difficult to distinguish from background signals. The detector had a large active area of 1 m², which made it possible to detect multiple particles simultaneously and to better discriminate signals from backgrounds.

The key methodology we used was the combination of scintillation and wavelength shifting fibre technology, which allowed the detection of both charged and neutral particles. The scintillation material provided the initial energy deposition, while the wavelength shifting fibre read-out system allowed for efficient light collection and signal transmission.

Our results showed that the detector had a high detection efficiency, particularly for low-energy eta mesons, and a low background rate. The detector also had a good spatial resolution, which allowed for the identification of the origin of particles in the detector.

Overall, our work provides a valuable contribution to the search for eta-nucleus bound states and highlights the potential of large acceptance scintillator detectors with wavelength shifting fibre read-out for nuclear physics research.

In this work, we investigate the mid-infrared phase variations of hot Jupiters, with the aim of understanding the physical processes that lead to these variations. Specifically, we use a combination of observations and modeling to study the infrared brightness variations of several hot Jupiters over a range of phase angles. Our main objective is to understand the underlying atmospheric mechanisms that give rise to the observed phase variations and how they vary with temperature.

The motivation for this research is rooted in the fact that hot Jupiters are among the most promising targets for exoplanet characterization via direct imaging and spectroscopy. However, detailed knowledge of their atmospheric properties is necessary for interpreting such observations, and phase variations provide a unique probe of atmospheric processes. In addition, phase variations can yield information on the atmospheric dynamics, such as the presence of wind patterns or atmospheric waves.

Our results show that the phase variations of hot Jupiters can be quite complex, with both temperature and circulation patterns playing a role. We demonstrate that detailed modeling of the phase variations can yield important information on the vertical and horizontal temperature structure of the atmosphere, as well as on the atmospheric dynamics. Overall, our work provides important insights into the atmospheric properties of hot Jupiters and their potential for future exoplanet characterization efforts.

In this work, we investigate the evolution of a neutral $K$ or $B$ meson from an incoherent to a coherent state, aiming to understand the fundamental properties of CP violation and the nature of arrows of time. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that the CP violation phenomenon, which refers to the violation of the combined symmetry of charge conjugation and parity, is one of the most intriguing puzzles in modern particle physics. Moreover, the arrow of time concept, which refers to the fact that physical processes are irreversible and always flow from the past to the future, is also a fundamental characteristic of our universe that remains mostly unexplained.

To tackle these complex concepts, we employ a quantum mechanical framework that uses time-dependent Schrödinger equations to model meson evolution. We then analyze the resulting oscillations and compare with experimental data to extract valuable insights into the physics at play. Our methodology is based on extensive numerical simulations and statistical analysis to obtain robust results that can shed light on the nature of time and CP violation.

Overall, our work contributes to the ongoing effort to unravel some of the mysteries of particle physics and the fundamental properties of the universe, providing a solid foundation for future research into these intriguing phenomena.

In this work, we investigate the potential of unparticle physics to explain the observed anomalies in neutrino data. Specifically, we consider neutrino decays and neutrino-electron elastic scattering within the framework of unparticle physics. The motivation for our research arises from the well-known limitations of the Standard Model of particle physics in accounting for various phenomena in the universe. Recent evidence of non-standard interactions in neutrino experiments provides impetus to explore alternative explanations.

We find that the existence of unparticle fields can give rise to well-defined branching ratios for neutrino decays, which can be distinguished from the predictions of the Standard Model. We also study the effect of unparticle exchange on neutrino-electron elastic scattering and find that it can lead to deviations in the differential cross-section that are detectable in current and future experiments. Our work shows that unparticle physics offers a viable explanation for the observed anomalies while also providing a route towards new physics beyond the Standard Model.

Overall, this study explores the potential of unparticle physics to address long-standing questions in particle physics. Our results suggest that further study in this area may yield valuable insights into the fundamental properties of neutrinos and their interactions.

In this study, we report the direct imaging of the lateral movements of AMPA receptors within synapses. The steady-state availability of AMPA receptors within the synaptic cleft is a critical determinant of synaptic strength and, ultimately, synaptic plasticity. However, the mechanisms underlying the movement of AMPA receptors within the synaptic membrane remain poorly understood, which limits our comprehensive understanding of synapse function.

To investigate this phenomenon, we employed high-resolution imaging techniques, including total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy and single-particle tracking. By imaging fluorescently tagged AMPA receptors in live hippocampal neurons, we achieved a direct visualization of their movement at high temporal and spatial resolution. Our data reveal that a significant fraction of AMPA receptors diffuse laterally within the synaptic membrane and that this lateral diffusion is regulated by the synaptic actin cytoskeleton.

Our findings provide novel insights into the mechanisms governing AMPA receptor movement at synapses and shed light on how this movement modulates synaptic function. By understanding the dynamic behavior of AMPA receptors, we can elucidate the fundamental processes regulating synaptic transmission and long-term synaptic plasticity, thereby informing the development of novel therapeutic interventions for neurological disorders that disrupt synaptic transmission.

In this work, we present a study on standard forms and entanglement engineering of multimode Gaussian states under local operations. Gaussian states are of interest due to their importance in quantum information and communication protocols. Our goal is to find a standard form for multimode Gaussian states that facilitates their characterization and the implementation of local operations, as well as to develop techniques for enhancing their entanglement properties. 

We focus on the use of symplectic transformations to transform arbitrary multimode Gaussian states to a standard form. We introduce a novel method for entanglement engineering that employs a combination of local squeezing and beam-splitting operations. Through numerical simulations, we show that this technique can enhance the entanglement of multimode Gaussian states by several orders of magnitude. 

Our approach offers a systematic and scalable toolkit for the manipulation of multimode Gaussian states, making it useful for the implementation of quantum protocols that rely on the properties of these states. Our results provide a novel framework for the study of different measures of entanglement in Gaussian states and provide insights into how to optimize the entanglement of a given Gaussian state for a certain application.

In our work titled "Second-Order Type Isomorphisms Through Game Semantics," we aim to explore the possibility of representing second-order type isomorphisms using game semantics. Our motivation for this research stems from the fact that the representation of type isomorphisms through game semantics can offer a better understanding of the relationship between these types. This is a crucial aspect in programming languages, as second-order types enable the creation of complex data structures that can be reused across various parts of the program.

Our research investigates the problem of representing second-order type isomorphisms using game semantics. While this problem has been approached through category theory, our work provides a novel perspective using game semantics. We introduce a game model for second-order functions and use it to define a notion of second-order type isomorphism based on the synchronous and clone games. Additionally, we show that there is a correspondence between second-order type isomorphisms and a particular class of functions and games.

Our key ideas build on the foundation of game semantics and extend it to the representation of second-order type isomorphisms. We utilize the relationship between functions, games, and types to define a new model of games that can express the properties of second-order types. Our methodology involves a rigorous analysis of functions and games to understand their compositional properties.

In summary, our research provides a new insight into the representation of second-order type isomorphisms through game semantics. With the potential to simplify and improve programming languages, this approach could have significant implications for the future of software engineering.

We introduce a novel, cyclic voltammetry-based method, named EC-FORC, for observing phase changes and predicting equilibrium points. The motivation for this research was to address the limitations of existing methods, such as differential scanning calorimetry and X-ray diffraction, which can be time-consuming and yield insufficient data. In contrast, EC-FORC is rapid, simple and cost-effective, and can provide a comprehensive view of the thermodynamic behavior of a system. 
This method involves cycling the potential of an electrochemical cell over a range of values, from which the current response is recorded and analyzed to reveal transitions in phase. The technique then applies an external force, or “field”, to the system in question to map the phase transition path, from which equilibrium points can be inferred. We demonstrate the utility of EC-FORC using a battery model, examining the phase transitions during discharge and recharge cycles. The results obtained show that EC-FORC accurately predicts the equilibrium potentials of each phase, providing key insights into the behavior of the system.
In summary, EC-FORC represents a valuable new tool for studying phase transitions, allowing for rapid and detailed characterization of systems and enabling accurate prediction of equilibrium points.

In our work, we develop an invariance principle for semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions in domains with piecewise smooth boundaries. The key idea behind our research is to extend the existing results on semimartingale reflecting Brownian motions to domains with piecewise smooth boundaries, which arise naturally in many applications.

The methodology we use involves combining techniques from stochastic analysis with tools from differential geometry, specifically the theory of singularities of vector fields. We apply our approach to a broad class of domains that includes polygonal domains, Y-shaped domains, and domains with cusps.

Our motivation for undertaking this research comes from the observation that many important real-world systems exhibit boundary features that are piecewise smooth, such as interfaces in materials science, or obstacles in fluid mechanics. Understanding the behavior of stochastic processes in these systems is crucial for developing accurate mathematical models and making predictions about the system's behavior.

Our main results show that under suitable assumptions, the trajectories of a semimartingale reflecting Brownian motion converge, in probability, to a limit process that satisfies a stochastic differential equation with reflecting boundary conditions. This result provides a powerful tool for analyzing the long-term behavior of stochastic processes in domains with piecewise smooth boundaries, and can be applied to a wide range of physical and mathematical problems.

In this paper, we propose a unified approach to power control in large CDMA systems that is energy efficient. We are motivated to conduct this research because power control is a crucial aspect of wireless communication systems, and optimizing power consumption is necessary to reduce energy costs and environmental impact. 

The primary problem this work attempts to solve is how to reduce the energy consumed by wireless communication systems without sacrificing system performance. Therefore, we propose a new energy-efficient power control approach that considers the trade-off between energy consumption and system performance.

Our key idea is to design a power control algorithm that adjusts the transmission power based on the channel state information. Specifically, we utilize a game-theoretic framework that enables robust power control and network-wide cooperation among users. Furthermore, we incorporate a power-based pricing scheme to incentivize energy-saving behavior among users. 

To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we carry out extensive numerical simulations, and the results show that our algorithm achieves significant energy savings while maintaining a high throughput and low error rate. In summary, our unified approach provides a practical solution for energy-efficient power control in large CDMA systems by simultaneously taking into account the performance and energy consumption aspects of wireless communication.

In this study, we compare the particle production in quark and gluon fragmentation at sqrt s ~ 10 GeV. The motivation behind this research is to shed light on the fundamental differences between quarks and gluons and their behavior during fragmentation. Understanding particle production in quark and gluon fragmentation is a crucial aspect of modern physics, as it helps us to better comprehend the nature of strong interactions. 

Using the Monte-Carlo simulation technique, we generate events of quark and gluon fragmentation to study the characteristics of the particles produced. We analyze the distributions of particles based on their transverse momentum and pseudorapidity, and compare the results obtained from quark and gluon fragmentation. Our findings indicate that the number of particles produced in gluon fragmentation is higher compared to quark fragmentation, and the distributions are wider. Moreover, we observe that the ratio of charged and neutral particles is not the same for quark and gluon fragmentation.

The problem this work attempts to solve is to understand the particle production process in quark and gluon fragmentation. The results obtained from this research can aid in the development of new models and theories that better explain the nature of strong interactions in particle physics. This study also provides useful insights for the design of the experiments at current and future colliders, such as the Large Hadron Collider.

In this work, we explore the intriguing possibility that dark matter could form a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). This hypothesis has gained increasing attention in recent years, motivated by the fact that BECs offer an elegant explanation for some of the strange properties of dark matter. We examine the key ideas behind this hypothesis, which rests on the notion that dark matter particles could behave as bosons, and therefore condense into a single macroscopic state at low temperatures.

To test this hypothesis, we consider a range of theoretical models and observational constraints. Our analysis involves numerical simulations of the formation and evolution of BEC dark matter halos, as well as comparisons with existing data from cosmological observations such as the cosmic microwave background radiation and large-scale structure surveys. We also investigate the implications of BEC dark matter for the formation and properties of galaxies and other structures in the universe.

Our work aims to address a fundamental puzzle in modern astrophysics: what is the nature of dark matter? By exploring the possibility of a BEC dark matter scenario, we hope to shed new light on this elusive and intriguing component of the universe.

In this work, we aimed to investigate the effects of changes in reaction rates on simulations of nova explosions. Novae, nuclear explosions that occur on the surfaces of white dwarf stars, are known to be a significant source of chemical elements in the universe. We attempted to determine the impact of variations in the rates of nuclear reactions involved in the nova process on the simulation results. 

To achieve this, we employed a state-of-the-art code for simulating novae, which included updates to reaction rates based on the latest measurements from experimental studies. We performed a series of numerical experiments by varying the reaction rates of several key elements that play a role in the nova explosion. We carefully analyzed the extent of these changes on the overall simulation and compared the results to earlier models.

Our results indicate that even small variations in reaction rates can significantly alter the evolution of the explosion and its resulting chemical composition. We observed that, in certain cases, changing the reaction rates could lead to significant deviations from earlier models’ predictions. Overall, our findings suggest that accurate measurements of reaction rates are critical for predicting the behavior of novae and understanding the production of chemical elements in the universe. The present work provides much-needed insight into the impact of reaction rate uncertainties on simulations of novae and the implications for our understanding of the universe's chemical evolution.

In this work, we investigate the polarization anomaly observed in $B\to\phi K^*$ decays, where the polarization of the vector meson $K^*$ appears to be in contradiction with theoretical expectations. We aim to test different explanations for this puzzle, in order to shed light on the underlying physics of this decay mechanism. 

We employ a model-independent analysis method, which aims to extract the polarization observables from experimental data. We then compare the results with several theoretical predictions, including factorization-based and color-suppressed models. Our analysis performed on LHCb data, reveals that the polarization anomaly is present, and that all theoretical models predict it, with varying degrees of agreement with the data. We demonstrate that none of these models alone can fully describe the observed polarization. 

Our work attempts to solve the puzzling discrepancy between experimental data and theoretical predictions in $B\to\phi K^*$ decays. We demonstrate that the polarization anomaly is indeed a real effect, and that the current theoretical explanations are insufficient to explain the observation. Our results highlight the need for further theoretical developments in order to fully understand the mechanisms driving this decay.

In this study, we present a new AB-Thermonuclear reactor that has been designed for aerospace applications. The main objective of the research is to develop a new kind of energy source that can provide a high level of energy density, high power output, and long operational life in space missions. The methodology used in this work is based on the principles of nuclear physics and engineering, which involve the design of a fusion reactor that can produce a high-energy plasma. 

The results obtained show the potential of the AB-Thermonuclear reactor as a viable energy source for aerospace applications. The structure of the reactor is based on a toroidal geometry, which allows for a high plasma stability. The key features of the reactor include a high energy conversion efficiency, compact design, and autonomous operation. 

The motivation for this research stems from the need for advanced energy systems that can support long-term space missions. Conventional power systems, such as solar panels and batteries, are limited in their energy density and lifespan, which makes them unsuitable for long-range missions. The AB-Thermonuclear reactor is a promising alternative that can provide a continuous and reliable power source for space exploration. 

In conclusion, this study presents a new AB-Thermonuclear reactor for aerospace applications, which offers significant advantages over conventional power systems. The results obtained demonstrate the feasibility of this technology and its potential for future space missions. This research contributes to the development of advanced energy technologies that are essential for the success of future space exploration programs.

In this work, we present a quantum simulation of interacting high-dimensional systems and analyze their behavior in the presence of noise. Our aim is to investigate the role of noise in the performance of quantum simulations and explore the strategies to overcome its adverse effects. High-dimensional systems pose a significant challenge for numerical simulations due to the exponential increase in the number of parameters as the dimensionality increases. Quantum simulation is a promising approach to study these systems, using quantum devices as simulators. However, such simulations are prone to errors induced by noise, which can lead to incorrect results. 

To mitigate the effect of noise, we apply different error mitigation techniques such as noise filtering and error correction codes. We use a tensor network-based algorithm to simulate the dynamics of interacting high-dimensional systems and quantify the effects of noise. Our simulations reveal that error mitigation techniques can significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of quantum simulations, even in the presence of noise.

Our results demonstrate the importance of developing noise-tolerant quantum algorithms for simulations of high-dimensional systems. Our study opens up new avenues for exploring quantum simulations of complex systems and has broader implications for the design of experiments in quantum computing.

Our multiwavelength study investigated the star formation and galaxy growth of massive galaxies at z~2. This project is motivated by the need to understand the evolution of galaxies in the early universe and the underlying mechanisms that drive their growth. Using a combination of space-based and ground-based telescopes, we analyzed the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of a sample of massive galaxies at z~2. We derived their SFRs, stellar masses, and specific SFRs using a Bayesian modeling technique. In addition, we applied a novel method of measuring the dust attenuation and metallicity of individual galaxies by analyzing their UV emission line ratios. We found a strong correlation between the SFR and specific SFRs with stellar mass, indicating that massive galaxies at z~2 are still actively forming stars and growing significantly at this epoch. The high dust attenuation levels and low metallicities of these galaxies suggest that they are still undergoing rapid chemical enrichment and that their dust is primarily produced by supernovae explosions. Our multiwavelength approach provides a comprehensive understanding of the star formation and galaxy growth of massive galaxies in the early universe.

In this study, we investigate the selection effects that play a crucial role in shaping the Gamma Ray Burst (GRB) redshift distributions. GRBs are some of the most powerful and enigmatic electromagnetic explosions in the Universe, making them an exceptional tool for studying the early Universe and the cosmic evolution of galaxies. However, the observed redshift distributions are not a complete representation of the true ones; rather, they are affected by selection biases, such as the detection threshold and host galaxy properties. 

To tackle this problem, we use a Monte Carlo simulation technique, which enables us to reproduce mock GRB samples and accurately quantify the selection effects. Our results show that the observed redshift distributions of GRBs are significantly biased towards lower redshifts, due to the sensitivity limits of current detectors and the way GRBs are detected. Furthermore, we find that the host galaxy properties have a strong effect on the GRB redshift distribution, with metal-poor galaxies being more likely to host high-redshift GRBs compared to metal-rich galaxies. 

Overall, our study sheds light on the crucial role of selection effects in shaping the observed properties of GRBs and can provide a valuable tool for constraining the properties of the early Universe and galaxy evolution.

In this work, we investigate the rounding of first-order phase transitions and its effect on optimal cooperation in scale-free networks. We present a model where individuals interact in a network and can choose to cooperate or defect in a public goods game. We observe that the critical point, where cooperation becomes less prevalent, shifts for small networks due to fluctuations, but is rounded off for large networks due to the presence of hubs. We determine the optimal level of cooperation in both cases and show that rounded transitions lead to more cooperative outcomes.

Our work seeks to address the issue of phase transitions in complex networks with heterogeneous connectivity. We aim to clarify the implications of network structure on the order of phase transitions in social dilemmas and highlight the effect of large hubs as stabilizers of the system. Additionally, we explore the role of roundings in network dynamics and cooperation from a game-theoretical perspective.

Our methodology involves the use of computer simulations and analytical calculations to determine the critical behavior of the model and analyze its associated cooperative behavior. To this end, we focus on the study of the scaling properties of the network and perform numerical experiments to validate our results.

Our findings provide new insights into the behavior of complex networks and its effects on cooperative behavior. By studying the rounding of critical transitions in scale-free networks, we deepen our understanding of the underlying mechanisms that govern cooperation in social dilemmas.

In this work, we investigate the dependence of local reionization history on halo mass and environment. Specifically, we explore whether the Virgo constellation played a key role in the reionization of the Local Group. The cosmic reionization phase is crucial to the evolution of the Universe since it marks the transformation of the dark ages to the universe lit by stars and ionizing radiation. The precise contributors of cosmic reionization are still being debated, with some arguing that massive individual regions were responsible, while others propose a more uniform contribution from many sources. To understand this, we use a galaxy formation model (MUFASA) to investigate the relationship between halo mass and the reionization history in the Local Group. We found that smaller scale haloes tend to reionize earlier, and the haloes that reionize earliest depend on the specific environment of the Local Group. Our results suggest that Virgo likely contributed to the reionization of the Milky Way and its surrounding halo. These findings provide new insights about the reionization epoch and contribute to a better understanding of how astrophysical sources affected the early evolution of the Universe.

In this work, we present a study on the observations and modeling of line asymmetries in chromospheric flares. Our aim was to understand the cause and nature of the line asymmetries in such flares, and determine whether they could provide useful diagnostic information on the physical processes driving these events. 

To achieve our goal, we analyzed high-resolution spectra of the Ca II 8542 Å line obtained from the Swedish 1-meter Solar Telescope. We found that the line profiles of this line exhibit significant asymmetries during flaring events in the chromosphere, with enhanced emission on one side of the line compared to the other. We then used a radiative transfer code to simulate the observed line asymmetries under different physical conditions.

Our results indicate that the line asymmetries can be produced by the combination of various processes, including optically thin emission, opacity effects, and the Doppler shift due to the motion of the flaring material. Moreover, we show that the line asymmetries can be used as a diagnostic tool to probe the magnetic field strength and the temperature of the flaring plasma.

By providing new insights into the origin of line asymmetries in chromospheric flares and their potential diagnostic value, our study contributes to the ongoing efforts to understand the physics of these complex events.

In this work, we present a refined asymptotic analysis for generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) equations near solitons. Specifically, we extend the classical asymptotic analysis around solitons to a higher-order, more accurate analysis. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that solitons, as stable, solitary waves that propagate without changing shape, play a crucial role in various physical phenomena, ranging from water waves to nonlinear optics. As such, precise understanding of soliton dynamics is of fundamental interest, both theoretically and practically.

To tackle this problem, we employ a combination of analytical techniques (such as perturbation theory and multiple-scale expansions) and numerical simulations. Our main result is a detailed characterization of the dynamics of solutions around solitons, including the computation of higher-order corrections to the soliton's amplitude, width, and phase. We also derive an explicit formula for the leading correction to the soliton's velocity, which determines its stability or instability.

Overall, our work provides a new level of precision in understanding soliton dynamics in gKdV equations, which has important implications for a variety of applications in physics and engineering. In addition, our approach can potentially be applied to other types of nonlinear wave equations, further enhancing our understanding of the fundamental properties of nonlinear waves and their interactions.

We report on a ground-based observational campaign to search for thermal emission from the exoplanet TrES-1. Our goal was to constrain the planet's atmospheric properties by measuring the difference in brightness between the planet and its host star in the thermal infrared. We used the FLIR SC645 thermal camera to observe TrES-1 during primary transit and secondary eclipse events at 8.0 microns, 9.2 microns and 10.3 microns.

A significant challenge in our work was achieving high-precision thermal photometry in the presence of strong atmospheric variability due to changing cloud cover. Therefore, alongside our observations, we carried out extensive meteorological monitoring to identify any effects that could potentially impact the measurements. We also utilized a custom-made shelter to protect the camera, as well as additional equipment to enhance stability and control the background emission.

Analysis of our data revealed no significant thermal emission from the planet. Our findings indicate that TrES-1 does not possess a significant atmosphere capable of producing detectable thermal emission at the wavelengths we observed in. This result helps constrain the planet's atmospheric properties and facilitates future studies of exoplanet atmospheres using ground-based observations.

In this paper, we tackle the online shortest path problem under partial monitoring, motivated by the growing need for efficient path planning and routing in dynamic environments. The problem entails determining the shortest path between two nodes in a graph while receiving partial feedback regarding the distance between the current node and the target. We aim to develop a robust algorithm that efficiently and adaptively determines the optimal path given incomplete information about the network.

To address this problem, we introduce a novel framework based on the online learning paradigm, which allows us to propagate partial feedback to guide the decision-making process and progressively converge to the optimal path. Our approach incorporates a dynamic programming formulation that enables us to compute the shortest path for each round while leveraging the feedback received from previous rounds.

We evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm using both synthetic and real-world networks and show that our technique outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and running time. Our findings suggest that our approach can be a valuable tool in various applications, including transportation routing, telecommunication networks, and logistics planning.

Overall, this work presents a significant contribution to the field of online optimization under partial monitoring, offering a promising technique for solving critical path planning problems in dynamic environments.

In this study, we aim to understand the potential connection between Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and the supernova SN 1987A based on the observations collected by various telescopes. One of the main scientific inquiries in this research is to explain the origin of GRBs, which are exceedingly powerful bursts of gamma radiation that originate from seemingly random areas in the sky. Our hypothesis is that GRBs are produced by some kind of cosmic explosion, such as a supernova. By studying the data and behavior of SN 1987A, which was a relatively nearby supernova that occurred in 1987, we hope to confirm or deny the potential correlation between the two phenomena. 

Our analysis of the gamma-ray properties of SN 1987A revealed a flux enhancement, which may provide insight into the observable properties of GRBs. Additionally, we observed a significant increase in the optical light curve, suggesting the possible presence of a pulsar or magnetar within the supernova. Furthermore, we conclude that the gamma-ray burst could have originated from the supernova ejecta interacting with the surrounding gas or from the interaction of the ejecta and a central compact object. 

Our methodology involved the collection and analysis of observational data from multiple telescopes, including Chandra, Hubble, and Swift. We employed various statistical and computational techniques to analyze the data and draw conclusions from the results. The findings of this study could potentially have major implications in our understanding of high-energy astrophysics and the formation of these fascinating events.

In our study, Selection Bias in Observing the Cosmological Evolution of the Mbh-sigma and Mbh-L Relationships, we aimed to address the issue of selection bias when observing the cosmological evolution of black holes in galaxies. The problem arises because the black holes that we observe are not necessarily representative of the entire black hole population due to limitations in our observational capabilities. Specifically, we analyzed the relationship between the mass of black holes and the properties of their host galaxies, such as velocity dispersion (sigma) and luminosity (L).

To address this problem, we used a statistical method known as survival analysis, which allowed us to account for the selection bias and estimate the true distribution of black hole masses. We found that the previously observed correlation between black hole mass and sigma was weakened when selection bias was accounted for, suggesting that this relationship may be affected by observational limitations. In contrast, the relationship between black hole mass and L was found to be robust to selection bias.

Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for selection bias when interpreting observations of black holes in galaxies. By doing so, we can obtain a more accurate picture of the cosmological evolution of black holes and their host galaxies. Our study provides a valuable framework for future analyses of observational data in this field.

The Deformation principle is a unifying concept in several fields of physics, including the theory of integrable systems, quantum field theory, and statistical thermodynamics. In recent years, this principle has been extensively studied as a tool to further geometrize these areas. Our work aims to contribute to this ongoing research by investigating the deformation principle and its application in the geometrization of physical systems.

Our motivation for this research comes from the need to develop a framework that can systematically unify various branches of physics based on their underlying geometric structures. In particular, we aim to explore the potential of the deformation principle to provide deeper insights into the geometrization of physics and help establish a comprehensive theory of quantum gravity.

Our approach involves a combination of algebraic, geometric and topological methods, including homological algebra, Poisson geometry, and higher category theory. We will apply these techniques to analyze the deformation principle and its relation to various physical systems, such as integrable models and conformal field theories.

The key idea driving this research is that physical systems can be understood as geometric structures that deform under certain conditions. By exploiting this geometrization, we aim to unveil new insights and connections between various areas of physics.
