The motivation for this research stems from the fact that black hole evaporation is one of the most intriguing and poorly understood phenomena in physics. By studying this process in the context of an expanding universe, we hope to gain insights into the nature of gravity and the structure of spacetime itself.

The problem that our work attempts to solve is how black holes interact with the expanding universe, and how this affects their evolution over time. This research has important implications for our understanding of the universe, and may shed light on some of the most fundamental questions in modern physics.

In this study, we investigate evidence for a new planetary companion around the young star AU Mic. The problem that we attempt to solve is the detection of more planetary systems around nearby stars, which will help us understand the formation and evolution of planetary systems. AU Mic is a well-studied young star that is thought to be a prime candidate for harboring a planetary system, and a new planetary companion would confirm this hypothesis. 

Using high-precision radial velocity measurements with the HARPS spectrograph and radial velocity subtraction techniques, we have detected a signal that is consistent with a planetary companion with a minimum mass of 0.27 Jupiter masses and an orbital period of 8.47 days. We have also analyzed the stellar activity of AU Mic, and we find that the newly discovered signal is not caused by stellar spots or other activity. 

The motivation for this research is to contribute to the ongoing search for exoplanets, as well as to increase our understanding of the formation and dynamics of planetary systems. Our results provide evidence for the existence of a planetary companion around AU Mic and add to the growing body of knowledge about exoplanetary systems.

In this paper, we present some notes on Liouville theory with central charge c ≤ 1. The problem that we attempt to solve is to understand the behavior of the theory near the boundary of the moduli space, where the conformal factor becomes infinite. Specifically, we focus on the study of the so-called degenerate field configurations, which correspond to certain singular points in the moduli space.

We start by reviewing some basic concepts and results on Liouville theory, including the definition of the theory, its classical and quantum properties, and some known results on the moduli space and the degenerate fields. Then, we introduce a novel approach to the theory based on the use of non-local observables, which allows us to obtain new insights into the structure of the theory and its relation to other conformal field theories.

Our main results include a detailed analysis of the degenerate fields and their properties, including their conformal weights, fusion rules, and correlation functions. We also find some unexpected connections with other conformal field theories and mathematical structures, which shed new light on the nature of Liouville theory and its applications to various fields of physics and mathematics.

The motivation for our research comes from the fact that Liouville theory is a fundamental concept in modern theoretical physics, with applications to fields such as string theory, condensed matter physics, and mathematical physics. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of the theory and its connections to other areas of physics and mathematics, and may have implications for the development of new theoretical tools and techniques.

In this study, we present the results of the LuckyCam survey for very low mass binaries. Our work aims to identify and characterize M4.5-M6.0 binaries using high-resolution imaging techniques in the near-infrared and optical bands. The primary motivation of our research is to increase the sample size of known low mass binaries and improve our understanding of their properties and formation.

Thirteen new M4.5-M6.0 binaries were identified from our survey, with separations ranging from 28 to 365 AU. We found that the majority of our sample had mass ratios close to unity, indicating they were formed through fragmentation of a single cloud core. The distribution of our sample on the color-magnitude diagram suggests they are older than previously detected binaries with similar spectral types. We also analyzed the spatial distribution of our sample and found they are more likely to be found in crowded environments such as star-forming regions and clusters.

Our results contribute to the growing body of knowledge on low mass binaries and the mechanisms by which they form. The increased sample size provided by our survey allows for a more comprehensive analysis of their properties and evolution. Future studies building on our work will further probe the formation and evolution of low mass binaries.

In our study, we investigated the statistical mechanics of complex networks. Our motivation for this research was to understand how the properties of networks emerge from their constituent parts and how these properties can be quantified and modeled. The problem we aimed to solve is to develop a framework for analyzing and predicting the behavior of complex networks using statistical mechanics.

Using tools from statistical mechanics, we developed a theoretical framework for modeling the behavior of complex networks. Specifically, we focused on networks with nested and modular structures, which are common in biological, social, and technological systems. We derived equations describing the thermodynamic properties of these networks, such as their entropy and free energy, and used these equations to explore how the structure of a network affects its behavior.

Our analysis showed that the modular and nested structure of a network can strongly influence its behavior. We found that networks with nested modularity are robust to damage and can exhibit a phase transition between a disordered state and an ordered state. Additionally, we showed how our theoretical framework can be used to predict the behavior of networks in realistic scenarios.

In conclusion, our work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the behavior of complex networks using statistical mechanics. By understanding the principles underlying the behavior of complex networks, we hope to develop more accurate models and predictions for a wide range of real-world systems.

In this work, we explore the evolution of dust in the early universe and its implications for the galaxy SDSS J1148+5251. The presence of dust in the early universe presents a significant challenge to our understanding of the origin and evolution of galaxies. Furthermore, the high redshift of the galaxy SDSS J1148+5251 makes it an ideal testbed for studying the early universe. 

Our work aims to address the problem of understanding the evolution of dust in the early universe and its impact on the formation of galaxies. To this end, we utilize a combination of theoretical models and observational data to investigate the role of dust in the formation and evolution of SDSS J1148+5251. 

We develop a theoretical model that incorporates the effects of grain growth, grain destruction, and gas-phase metallicity on the evolution of dust in the early universe. We then compare our model predictions to observations of SDSS J1148+5251, including its spectral energy distribution and metallicity measurements. 

Overall, our results suggest that the evolution of dust in the early universe played a critical role in the formation and evolution of galaxies like SDSS J1148+5251. Our work highlights the need for more comprehensive theoretical models that incorporate the complex interplay between dust and gas-phase metallicity in the early universe.

In this work, we present a Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO) scheme for studying the growth of ionized regions during the reionization epoch. The motivation for this research comes from the need to accurately predict the formation and evolution of cosmic structures at a crucial epoch in the history of the universe. Our key idea is to develop a numerical algorithm that accurately and efficiently models the complex ionization processes that occur during reionization.

Our methodology involves three main steps. First, we derive a set of governing equations that describe the ionization and recombination processes. Second, we implement a WENO scheme to solve these equations on a numerical grid. Third, we validate our method by comparing results with existing simulation data and analytic solutions. 

Our results show that our WENO algorithm accurately captures the complex ionization processes during reionization, including the formation of ionized bubbles, the growth of ionized regions, and the effects of clumping and scattering. Additionally, our method is computationally efficient, making it a valuable tool for studying large-scale structures in the early universe. 

In conclusion, our work presents a novel WENO algorithm for simulating the growth of ionized regions during the reionization epoch. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for studying the important astrophysical processes that occur during reionization, and we believe that our method will be a valuable tool for future cosmological studies.

In this research paper, we work on the Lagrangian quantum field theory (LQFT) in the momentum picture with a focus on the commutation relations for free fields. The central problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a clear understanding of the operators that describe the quantum fields and their properties. This paper provides insight into the way these operators behave and their interrelations with each other.

To investigate these properties, we use the framework of the LQFT and adopt the Fourier transformation of the fields. We then obtain the commutation relations among the annihilation and creation operators using the Hamiltonian and the field equations. We analyze the commutators in different regions of the momentum space, including a detailed study of the ultraviolet and infrared regimes, and the limit of coinciding points.

The results obtained are significant for understanding quantum field theories, especially in relation to the behavior of free fields. Our findings indicate that the operators that describe the fields obey the fundamental commutation rules, which are crucial in quantum mechanics. These results provide a firm mathematical foundation for further research on the LQFT and related subjects. Moreover, our work provides valuable guidance for practitioners to avoid interpretational contradictions in the quantization of fields.

In this paper, we present a comparison of the two-dimensional (2D) stellar and gaseous kinematics in the central kiloparsec of Seyfert and inactive host galaxies. The aim of this work is to investigate whether Seyfert galaxies exhibit different kinematic properties compared to inactive galaxies and to decipher the nature of the galactic mechanisms responsible for the observed gas and stars motion.

Our motivation for this research is driven by the fact that Seyfert galaxies, being luminous and active, play a crucial role in understanding the active galactic nuclei (AGN) phenomenology and their connection to the host galaxy. Therefore, a comparison of Seyfert and inactive host galaxies provides insights into the physical processes that govern the gas and stars kinematics in galaxies hosting AGN.

Our results indicate that Seyfert galaxies have distinct kinematic properties compared to inactive host galaxies in terms of both stellar and gaseous kinematics. Seyfert galaxies exhibit higher velocity dispersion and lower rotational velocities than inactive galaxies, suggesting that AGN feedback may play a role in shaping the kinematics of the host galaxy's central kiloparsec. Furthermore, we find that the gaseous kinematics are more strongly affected by the AGN feedback than the stellar kinematics, providing evidence for an AGN-driven feedback mechanism in the central regions of Seyfert galaxies.

Overall, our findings highlight the importance of considering both stellar and gaseous kinematics in understanding the impact of AGN feedback on the host galaxy's central region.

In this study, we present a Stern-Volmer model to investigate the steady-state energy transfer between dilute, freely diffusing membrane-bound fluorophores using fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET). Our goal is to explore the mechanisms involved in FRET and better understand the physical characteristics of the fluorophores, which is essential for designing biosensors, studying molecular interactions, and monitoring biological processes. 

To accomplish this, we measured the change in the fluorescence intensity ratio of donor and acceptor fluorophores under different experimental conditions, such as varying donor and acceptor concentrations, excitation wavelength, and membrane environments. We then applied the Stern-Volmer equation to the data to obtain key parameters, such as the donor-acceptor distance and the rate of energy transfer. 

Our results demonstrated that the Stern-Volmer model is effective in describing the FRET process in dilute, freely diffusing membrane-bound fluorophores. Furthermore, we found that the rate of energy transfer increases as the donor-acceptor distance decreases, which is consistent with previous FRET studies. Additionally, we observed that the membrane environment significantly affects the FRET efficiency, highlighting the importance of considering biological contexts when designing FRET-based biosensors. 

Overall, our study provides insights into the mechanisms of FRET and offers a valuable tool for the quantitative analysis of biomolecular interactions.

In this paper, we investigate the purely transmitting defects in the context of affine Toda field theory, and present a detailed analysis of the underlying mathematical structure. Our project is motivated by the desire to gain a deeper understanding of the phenomenon of defect transmission, which occurs when a defect in a physical system propagates through space. The key idea behind our work is to use a combination of theoretical and computational techniques to probe the characteristics of these defects, and to model their transmission across different regions of space.

To achieve this goal, we utilize a range of analytical tools derived from the framework of integrable systems, including the theory of solitons, the Yang-Baxter equation, and the Bethe ansatz. We also employ numerical simulations to test our theoretical predictions and explore the dynamics of defect propagation in different settings.

Our research has yielded significant insights into the behavior of purely transmitting defects in affine Toda field theory. Specifically, we have uncovered new mathematical relationships between the properties of these defects and the underlying structure of the Toda field equations. We have also demonstrated that our theoretical predictions can be tested and validated through numerical simulations, which provide strong evidence of the validity and relevance of our findings. Overall, our work represents an important contribution to the study of integrable systems, and has important implications for many areas of physics and mathematics.

In this article, we present our research on tracking user attention in collaborative tagging communities. Our aim is to identify the factors that influence user participation and engagement in these communities. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of user behavior in two popular online tagging platforms, del.icio.us and BibSonomy. Our research covers a three-year period, from 2015 to 2018, and involves tracking the activities of over 500 users.

The key idea behind our research is that understanding user behavior in collaborative tagging communities is crucial for improving their effectiveness and sustainability. We focused on two aspects of user behavior: the number of tags created and the number of collaborations established. Our analysis reveals that users tend to show a preference for creating tags that are relevant to their personal interests and that they tend to collaborate more with other users who share similar interests.

To conduct our research, we used a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, including statistical analysis, network analysis, and content analysis. Our findings suggest that the factors that influence user participation and engagement in collaborative tagging communities are complex and interrelated. However, our study provides some insights that can help platform designers and administrators to develop more effective and engaging tagging systems.

In this work, we investigate the existence of independent transversals in locally sparse graphs. Specifically, we consider the problem of finding a set of vertices that intersects every maximum matching in the graph, without containing any edges. This problem has important applications in combinatorial optimization, algorithmic game theory, and computer science, among others. 

Our approach is based on a novel notion of sparsity that captures the local structure of the graph. We show that certain classes of locally sparse graphs have independent transversals of size at least half the size of the maximum matching. To prove our main result, we develop a new probabilistic method for finding large independent sets in locally sparse graphs, which relies on a unique analysis of the degree distribution of the graph. 

Overall, our work improves upon previous results by providing a more fine-grained understanding of the relationship between sparsity and the existence of independent transversals. Our results are applicable to a wide range of important graph structures, including regular graphs, random graphs, and graphs with bounded maximum degree. We believe that our techniques and results provide valuable insights into the structure of locally sparse graphs, and will spur further research in this area.

In this study, we investigate the role of resonances in Generalized Randall-Sundrum (GRS)-inspired braneworlds with synergistic gravity. The motivation for our research lies in the need for a deeper understanding of the behavior of gravitational waves in braneworld models. The problem we attempt to solve is the lack of a systematic approach to calculate the spectrum of gravitational waves in braneworld models.

We propose a method to calculate the spectrum of gravitational waves in the presence of resonances in a GRS-inspired model with synergistic gravity. We analyze the dynamics of radion and gravitational waves by using a perturbative approach. Our key idea is to couple the gravitational wave equation to the equation of motion of the radion field, leading to the emergence of resonances.

Our methodology involves solving the equations of motion for the perturbations of the radion and the tensor fields. We use a technique that allows us to separate the radial and angular dependencies of the perturbations. We then solve the radial part of the equations by using the WKB approximation and match them smoothly to the asymptotic solutions.

Our results show that the spectrum of gravitational waves exhibits resonances when the radion field is excited. The resonances are due to the coupling between the radion and the tensor fields. Our findings have important implications for the detection of gravitational waves in braneworld models and provide a better understanding of the behavior of gravitational waves in these models.

In this work, we study the high-energy emission properties of jets and blazars in the context of the Extragalactic Background Light (EBL) using data from the upcoming Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST) and Energetic X-ray Imaging Survey Telescope (EXIST). The EBL is a diffuse radiation field that pervades the universe and can interact with gamma rays, leading to gamma-ray attenuation and absorption. Jets and blazars, on the other hand, are astrophysical sources that release highly energetic particles along their axes. They are known to emit gamma rays up to tens of TeV, and their emission properties can be influenced by the EBL. Our main motivation is to understand the interplay between these two astrophysical phenomena.

We employ a multi-wavelength observational approach to study the spectral and temporal behavior of jets and blazars across different energy bands. Additionally, we carry out theoretical modeling to interpret our observations and extract physical information about the sources. Our results suggest that the EBL has a significant impact on the gamma-ray emission from blazars, which can be used to infer the EBL density. We also find evidence for spectral variability and flaring activity in several sources, which can provide insights into the acceleration and emission mechanisms of high-energy particles in jets and blazars. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for future surveys with GLAST and other high-energy observatories.

In this work, we revisit the plasma diagnostics of He-like X-ray emission lines. We aim to improve the accuracy of plasma diagnostics by examining the emission lines of He-like ions in a variety of astrophysical sources, such as supernova remnants and active galactic nuclei. We use a state-of-the-art plasma code to model the spectral lines and to generate synthetic spectra, with varying plasma conditions, such as temperature and density. By comparing the synthetic spectra with the observed spectra from Chandra or XMM-Newton, we extract the plasma parameters and investigate their uncertainty. Our key idea is to understand the influence of various systematic and statistical uncertainties and how their consideration will impact our measurement of the plasma parameters. We present new diagnostics ratios that are more robust against the systematic uncertainties and allow more accurate determination of the plasma conditions. We also examine the validity of using the traditional He-like diagnostic ratio. Our methodology comprises a systematic analysis of the diagnostic ratios, the uncertainties, and their dependence on the plasma conditions to improve the accuracy of plasma diagnostics in astrophysics. Our results can enable more accurate measurements and enhance our understanding of the physical processes underlying the ionised plasma emission in astrophysical sources.

Our work aimed to extract physical laws from joint experimental data using a novel approach based on machine learning techniques. The motivation for our research lies in the fact that physical phenomena are governed by fundamental laws which are difficult to directly measure due to their complexity or inaccessibility. Therefore, we sought to find a way to extract these laws from observed data. 

This problem has been addressed previously by analytical or numerical methods. However, these methods require data to follow specific mathematical forms and are limited to simple models. Our approach, on the other hand, uses machine learning to extract physical laws from experimental data without prior knowledge of the underlying mathematical relationship. To validate our approach, we used different experimental datasets and compared the derived physical laws to those obtained by analytical models. 

Our results demonstrate that our approach is effective in extracting physical laws and can achieve better accuracy than analytical models in some cases. Furthermore, our approach is more flexible and can handle complex and nonlinear relationships among variables. Thus, we believe that our work provides a promising direction for physics research, where data-driven methods are becoming increasingly important for understanding complex physical phenomena.

In this study, we investigate the impact of short-range attractions on the structural order, self-diffusivity, and viscosity of a fluid. We explore this phenomenon by performing molecular dynamics simulations on a coarse-grained model system of a binary mixture of particles with different interaction ranges. Our main motivation for this research is to better understand the underlying mechanisms that govern the behavior of complex fluids, such as colloidal suspensions, which exhibit rich and diverse phase behaviors due to the interplay between attractive and repulsive interactions.

Our results show that short-range attractions significantly alter the structural order of the fluid, inducing the formation of clusters and increasing the degree of structural heterogeneity. Furthermore, these attractive interactions lead to a decrease in the self-diffusivity of the particles, as the formation of clusters restricts their mobility. We also observe that the viscosity of the system is strongly influenced by the interplay between short-range attractions and repulsive interactions, with the viscosity decreasing initially as the strength of the attractions increases, before eventually leveling off and then increasing again due to the formation of larger clusters.

Overall, our study provides insights into how short-range attractions affect the macroscopic properties of a fluid and could have implications for the design of materials with desired rheological properties.

In this paper, we propose a minimum expected distortion (MED) optimization framework for Gaussian layered broadcast coding with successive refinement (SR). Our framework considers a layered coding scheme, where the source message is partitioned into multiple layers with different priorities, and different levels of distortion tolerance. The coded layers are broadcasted over multiple parallel channels with different channel qualities. We aim to minimize the expected distortion at the receiver in a joint coding and broadcasting design approach. 

We adopt a two-stage optimization strategy: first, we optimize the layered coding scheme to achieve the SR capacity region subject to distinct distortion constraints for each layer; then, we optimize the power allocation and channel assignment to minimize the MED subject to user fairness constraints. We prove that our approach achieves the global MED optimal solution in polynomial complexity. 

Through numerical simulations, we show that our proposed MED optimization framework outperforms the conventional SR scheme in terms of expected distortion, especially at high channel quality gaps and for delay-sensitive applications. We also observe that the proposed rolling-JPEG (R-JPEG) algorithm, in conjunction with our MED optimization framework, is highly effective in reducing the expected distortion and enhancing the user experience of multicast video streaming.

In this paper, we investigate the unitary representations of wavelet groups and their applicability in encoding iterated function systems in solenoids. Our approach to finding these representations follows the framework pioneered by Kari and Nekrashevych. We first construct a contracting auto-homeomorphism that generates the wavelet group, and then use this to generate a family of unitary representations. Using these representations, we show that it is possible to define a measurable encoding of the iterated function systems of self-similar sets in solenoids.

The motivation for this research comes from the need to better understand the structure of wavelet groups and their relationship to fractal geometry. Specifically, we are interested in the properties of the wavelet group that make it an efficient tool for encoding iterated function systems. Our work attempts to solve the problem of finding a suitable encoding for these systems in solenoids. 

The methodology we employ involves a careful analysis of the wavelet group, including its automorphism group and the properties of its associated unitary representations. We also use the theory of solenoids to provide a geometric interpretation of the encoding we develop. Ultimately, our work provides a new way of understanding the relationship between wavelet groups and fractal geometry, and may have implications for the development of new compression algorithms and other applications.

In this study, we present an improved chemical analysis of the black hole binary Nova Scorpii 1994 (GRO J1655-40) to uncover the elemental composition of this celestial object. Our primary motivation for carrying out this research was to shed more light on the origin and evolution of black hole binaries and gain a better understanding of their physical properties.

The black hole binary Nova Scorpii 1994 is a fascinating object that has a rich history of observations and studies. Our work attempts to solve the problem of incomplete knowledge of the elemental composition of this celestial object. By providing an improved chemical analysis, we aim to address this critical gap in our understanding of black hole binaries.

Our key ideas and methodology involve performing a detailed spectral analysis of the object's radiation. We used high-resolution spectroscopy to measure the absorption lines of various elements in the system. The data obtained from these measurements were compared with the expected absorption profiles for the different elements to determine the most likely elemental composition.

Our study provides new insights into the chemical composition of black hole binaries, which has important implications for our understanding of the evolution of these objects. The results obtained from our improved chemical analysis can be used to develop more refined models to describe the properties and behavior of black hole binaries in our universe.

In this study, we investigate the distribution of water vapour and hydrogen in the inner regions of protoplanetary disks, where terrestrial planets form. Our motivation for this research stems from the need to understand the process of planet formation, which is a fundamental question in astronomy. Water is a crucial ingredient for life as we know it, and determining its abundance and distribution during the planet formation process can provide insights into the likelihood of habitable planets in the universe.

To achieve our goals, we use numerical simulations to model the dynamics and chemistry of the protoplanetary disk. Our results show that the distribution of water vapour and hydrogen varies depending on the location within the disk and the presence of turbulence. In particular, we find that water vapour is more abundant in the innermost regions of the disk, where temperatures are higher. The presence of turbulence disrupts the formation of water molecules, leading to a decrease in water abundance.

Overall, our study sheds light on the mechanisms that govern the formation of terrestrial planets, and provides insights into the conditions required for the formation of habitable worlds. Our findings have implications for future studies of exoplanets and the search for life beyond our solar system.

In this paper, we investigate magnetization oscillations induced by a spin-polarized current in a point-contact geometry. The aim of our work is to understand the mode hopping and non-linear damping effects that occur in such a system. This is an important problem to solve because magnetization dynamics are at the heart of many technological applications, ranging from magnetic data storage to spintronics devices. Moreover, the point-contact geometry is a promising candidate for investigating spin-wave propagation with high spatial resolution, which may lead to new insights on the physics of magnetization dynamics.

To address this problem, we use a combination of analytical and numerical techniques. First, we derive a set of equations describing the dynamics of magnetization in a point-contact geometry. Then, we use numerical simulations to study the behavior of the system as a function of various parameters, such as the current density and the contact size. Our results show that the mode hopping phenomenon occurs when the frequency of the spin waves matches the frequency of a high-order resonant mode of the point-contact geometry. We also find that the non-linear damping effect arises from the interplay between the spin-polarized current and the magnetization dynamics.

In conclusion, our work sheds light on the complex behavior of magnetization oscillations induced by a spin-polarized current in a point-contact geometry, with potential implications for the design of future spin-based devices.

In this study, we investigate the radial distribution of plasma pressure in the inner magnetosphere during a geomagnetic storm that occurred from March 1 to 8, 1982. The main goal of our research is to better understand the behavior of the plasma pressure during a storm and its effects on Earth's environment. The study also highlights the importance of accurate measurements of plasma pressure at different altitudes and distances from Earth.

To achieve this, we utilized low-altitude satellite data to obtain measurements of the plasma pressure across different distances from Earth during the storm period. The key idea behind this approach is to study the variations in plasma pressure with proximity to Earth's surface, which can reveal important insights into the behavior of the inner magnetosphere plasma during a storm.

Our results show a clear dependence of plasma pressure on distance from Earth during the storm period. Specifically, we observed a peak in plasma pressure at radial distances of 5 to 6 Earth radii. These findings are consistent with previous studies and support the notion that the inner magnetosphere plasma pressure is affected by geomagnetic storms.

In conclusion, the findings of this study contribute to our understanding of the inner magnetosphere dynamics during geomagnetic storms and provide valuable insights for future space weather forecasting and modeling efforts.

In this study, we investigate the origin of the galaxy mass-metallicity relation and its implications for Galactic outflows. Our research challenges the conventional hierarchical galaxy formation model with  analytical models and hydrodynamical simulations. We found that the galaxy mass-metallicity relation can be explained by the balance between inflow, outflow, and star formation. Stellar-driven winds and supernova feedback also play an important role in regulating the mass-metallicity relation.

Our methodology involves running hydrodynamical simulations with different initial conditions and feedback prescriptions. We then compare the results with analytical models derived from the continuity equation and chemical evolution theory. We focus on reproducing the observed galaxy mass-metallicity relation and its variation with redshift and local environment.

By understanding the origin of the galaxy mass-metallicity relation, we can also better understand the nature of Galactic outflows. Our work suggests that outflows are efficient at removing metals from star-forming regions and enriching the surrounding intergalactic medium. However, the mass-loading factor of the outflows is highly dependent on the galaxy potential well and feedback efficiency. Therefore, the interplay between inflow, outflow, and feedback is crucial in shaping the chemical evolution of galaxies.

Overall, our study provides key implications for future observational and theoretical studies of galaxy evolution and star formation.

Our study investigates the structure of high galactic latitude interstellar neutral hydrogen (HI) and its association with high frequency continuum emission data collected by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP). The motivation behind this research lies in the understanding of the physical and chemical processes that govern the formation and evolution of the interstellar medium (ISM) in the Milky Way galaxy.

Previous studies have observed a peculiar pattern of structures in the high-latitude HI distribution called "supershells." These structures are believed to have originated from massive supernova explosions and star forming regions. Our work aims to explore how these supershells influence the distribution and properties of the high-frequency continuum emission detected by the WMAP.

We used a combination of observational data and numerical simulations to investigate the properties and distribution of the HI supershells. The simulations were based on the observational properties of the Milky Way's ISM and the energy output from massive supernova explosions. The results indicate that the observed structure in the HI distribution is consistent with the formation and evolution of supershells. Additionally, we found a strong correlation between the continuum emission data and the distribution of HI supershells.

Our research provides new insights into the nature of the ISM and its complex physical processes. The results of this study have important implications for future research in astrophysics, particularly in the understanding of the interplay between supernova explosions, star formation, and galactic evolution.

Our study focused on investigating the electron-phonon coupling in doped graphene by investigating the impact of an electronic singularity. The motivation for this research stems from the unique properties of graphene including high electrical conductivity, mechanical strength, and large surface area, leading to its potential applications in various fields such as electronics, energy storage, and biomedical applications. However, the electron-phonon coupling in graphene has been a topic of interest due to its importance in determining the electrical and thermal properties of the material. 

Our research found that the presence of an electronic singularity in doped graphene massively enhances the electron-phonon coupling, leading to a significant increase in the electron energy relaxation rate. This effect was demonstrated through first-principles calculations using density functional theory. The results obtained from this study highlight the potential use of electronic singularities in enhancing the electron-phonon coupling and thus manipulating the electrical and thermal properties of graphene. 

The problem we aimed to solve through this research was the identification of an efficient method to enhance electron-phonon coupling in doped graphene. This study provides a promising direction towards the development of graphene-based materials with enhanced performance, thereby contributing to the advancement of materials science.

In this study, we investigated the formation and evolution of protostellar clusters in intermediate-mass (IM) star forming regions. The problem that our work attempts to solve is the lack of understanding regarding the physical mechanisms that govern the formation of protostellar clusters and their evolution in these regions. This lack of knowledge has hindered our ability to map the formation of star clusters and the subsequent development of their member stars.

To address this problem, we developed a methodology that allowed us to analyze the star formation process in IM star forming regions. We used data obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope and the Herschel Space Observatory to map the star formation in two protostellar clusters. Our results suggest that protostellar clusters in IM star forming regions form through gravitational fragmentation of dense molecular clouds. We observed several stages of evolution, including the formation of protostars, the growth of clusters, and the emergence of OB stars and their impact on the surrounding interstellar medium.

In conclusion, our study sheds light on the formation and evolution of protostellar clusters in IM star forming regions. It highlights the key ideas and methodology that can be used to map the evolution of star clusters and study the physical processes that determine their characteristics. Our work has important implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of stars and galaxies.

Our research aims to explore the Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) of qubits, with the motivation of enhancing the capabilities of quantum computing and communication systems. In our study, we observed the behavior of a qubit in a superconducting circuit in the presence of a applied electromagnetic field. We found that the behavior of a qubit can be modeled as a simple forced oscillator system, which experiences Rabi oscillations when driven by a microwave field. Furthermore, we identified that the qubit exhibits both coherent and incoherent behavior, which is attributed to the qubit environment’s temperature and the strength of the applied field.

Our work attempts to solve the existing problem in the field, one of which includes understanding the interaction of qubits with electromagnetic field and its impact on the qubit’s behavior. The study of QED is essential for understanding quantum coherent behavior and harvesting its potential for computation and communication technology. Our findings offer essential insights into the dynamics of qubits in the presence of a driving field and are crucial for designing efficient and error-free quantum computing and communication systems.

Thus, our work on Quantum Electrodynamics of qubits demonstrates the significance of exploring the dynamics of qubits in a complex environment, which can be applied to the design and development of advanced quantum technology.

In this work, we investigate the influence of the Dirac sea on pion propagation in asymmetric nuclear matter. Aiming to better understand pion dynamics in dense nuclear environments, we consider a self-consistent chiral model incorporating the Dirac sea, which is known to play a fundamental role in describing the properties of the nucleon in nuclear matter. Our results show that the Dirac sea significantly contributes to the pion dispersion relation in asymmetric nuclear matter, leading to a considerable increase in the pion effective mass, especially in the presence of large isospin asymmetries. We find that the pion velocity decreases in the presence of the Dirac sea for all values of isospin asymmetry. Our study also reveals the crucial role of the isovector part of the pion-nucleon interaction in modulating the effective mass and velocity of the pion in nuclear matter.

The motivation for our research lies in the importance of understanding the behavior of pions in dense nuclear matter, which has important implications for the dynamics of many astrophysical phenomena, such as supernova explosions and neutron star mergers. Our work provides a novel theoretical framework that incorporates the effects of the Dirac sea on pion propagation, which may have previously been neglected in many theoretical models. To achieve our results, we use a self-consistent chiral model and apply various numerical techniques to solve the model equations. Our study offers insights into the role of the Dirac sea in pion-nucleon interactions and contributes to a better understanding of the properties of hadrons in dense nuclear environments.

In this work, we investigate the evolutionary history of the blue sequence in field galaxies up to a redshift of z~3. The primary goal of our research is to understand the formation and evolution of galaxies over time and to determine the key mechanisms that are responsible for their growth and development. The study aims to address a critical gap in our knowledge of galaxy formation and evolution by investigating the color magnitude distribution of field galaxies and modeling their evolution over time.

Our research is motivated by the need to understand the origin of the blue sequence in galaxies, which is a prominent feature of the galaxy population. The blue sequence refers to the tight correlation between the UV-optical color and the stellar mass of galaxies. Our work interrogates this correlation at different redshifts with the goal of developing a coherent understanding of the mechanisms that lead to the formation and evolution of the blue sequence.

To achieve our research objectives, we use a combination of data-driven analysis of galaxy photometry and modeling methods. We construct a large sample of field galaxies drawn from optical and near-infrared spectroscopic surveys and use spectral energy distribution modeling to determine their physical properties such as stellar mass, star formation rate, and dust content. We use these properties to construct a theoretical framework for the evolution of the blue sequence in field galaxies, integrating models that account for the dominant physical processes such as gravity, gas accretion, star formation, and feedback mechanisms.

Our work provides critical insights into the evolutionary history of field galaxies and establishes a benchmark for future theoretical and observational studies of galaxy formation and evolution.

In this study, we investigate the crystalline silicates and dust processing in protoplanetary disks of the Taurus young cluster in order to better understand the formation of our own solar system. The motivation for this research stems from the fact that silicates are key building blocks in the formation of planets, and the crystalline nature of these silicates plays a crucial role in determining the chemical and physical properties of the dust. Using observations from the Infrared Spectrograph on the Spitzer Space Telescope, we analyze the spectra of 53 young stars and determine the mineralogical composition of the disks. Our results show a clear correlation between the spectral features of crystalline silicates and the stellar age, with younger disks having a higher percentage of crystalline silicates than older disks. We also observe that processed dust grains are present in the inner regions of the disks but are absent in the outer regions. This suggests that the dust processing occurs early on in the disk evolution and highlights the importance of understanding the role of dust processing in planet formation. Overall, our study provides valuable insight into the formation of protoplanetary disks and their evolution.

We present a detailed analysis of the Origin of the Magellanic Stream and its Leading Arm. To understand the formation of these structures, we used a cosmological simulation that traced the evolution of the Milky Way and its satellite galaxies, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. Our simulations showed that the Magellanic Clouds have been interacting with the Milky Way for the past several billion years. These interactions have stripped gas from the Magellanic Clouds, forming the Magellanic Stream and its Leading Arm.

Our work advances previous studies by providing a quantitative analysis of the stripping process, identifying the accretion of gas to the Milky Way, and analyzing the properties of the resulting structures. To obtain these results, we used a suite of analysis tools that provided a detailed understanding of the evolution of the Milky Way and its satellite galaxies.

The Magellanic Stream and its Leading Arm are important features of the Milky Way's gaseous halo, and understanding their origins provides critical insights into the past and future evolution of the Milky Way. Our research addresses an important problem in astrophysics and has motivated future studies to investigate the formation and evolution of galaxy-galaxy interactions.

Our team explores the mechanism of converting genetic network oscillations into somite spatial pattern. The somites, a critical structure for vertebrates, have been formed as repetitions within the paraxial mesoderm. Currently, the question of how genetic oscillations could translate into somite spatial pattern remains challenging. Our study is aiming to find the answer and bring light to the process of somitogenesis.

Our methodology follows a computational model built on the previous experimental findings in the gene expression level of zebrafish somite pattern. We use the differential equation to model the intercellular communication through the Notch signaling pathway and Hes7. Mathematical analyses are conducted to demonstrate the relationships between the spatiotemporal gene expression and the morphogenesis of somites.

The motivation of our research comes from the desire to understand the fundamental process of somitogenesis, which will benefit developmental biology, regenerative medicine, and clinical research. Our work tries to solve the issue of how the periodic genetic oscillations could be transformed into a stable and regular pattern that is critical to the body plan of vertebrates.

In conclusion, we present a computational model that bridges the gap between the genetic network oscillations and somite spatial pattern. Our findings provide mechanistic insights and inspire future experiments to investigate somitogenesis.

In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the Pleiades star cluster using deep infrared data obtained from the UK Infrared Deep Sky Survey (UKIDSS). Our aim is to constrain the substellar binary fraction and the low-mass initial mass function (IMF) in this cluster. The Pleiades is an ideal target for such analyses due to its youth and well-known distance. 

Our observations cover a wide field of view and extend to very faint magnitudes, allowing us to detect very low-mass objects, down to the planetary-mass regime. We identify a total of 82 candidate cluster members, including 17 new objects, and find evidence for a higher fraction of binary systems among the brown dwarfs than among the higher-mass stars. Our results suggest that the binary fraction decreases with decreasing masses, in agreement with theoretical predictions. 

We also compare our observations with theoretical models of the low-mass IMF, finding good agreement for masses above 0.03 solar masses, but a significant deficiency of objects at lower masses. We discuss possible explanations for this discrepancy, including incomplete detection of substellar objects and the need for revision of the underlying theoretical models.

Our study provides new insights into the formation and evolution of low-mass objects in the Pleiades, and highlights the importance of deep infrared observations for constraining the substellar binary fraction and the low-mass IMF in star-forming regions.

In this work, we explore the magnetorotational collapse of very massive stars to black holes using a fully relativistic approach. Our methodology involves numerical simulations in full general relativity, incorporating the effects of magnetohydrodynamics and general relativity. We seek to address the long-standing problem of understanding the formation of supermassive black holes, and the role that magnetic fields play in their formation. 

Our simulations reveal that the magnetorotational collapse of very massive stars can lead to the formation of supermassive black holes with masses ranging from 10^4 to 10^6 times that of the sun. We find that the magnetic field strengths play a crucial role in the dynamics of the collapse, with stronger fields leading to more violent and extended accretion onto the central object. Additionally, we observe the formation of jets and outflows from the accretion disk, which may explain the observed phenomena in active galactic nuclei. 

Our work provides unique insights into the role of magnetic fields in the formation of supermassive black holes and facilitates the exploration of fundamental astrophysical phenomena. This offers an essential step forward in the understanding of the universe's evolution, as massive black holes are believed to play a central role in the formation and growth of galaxies.

In this paper, we present the findings of our research into the application of complexity theory to innovation and breakthroughs. Our motivation for this research stemmed from the need for better understanding the underlying mechanisms that drive these breakthroughs, in order to foster them in various fields.

To explore this topic, we employed a mixed-methods approach, drawing on both qualitative and quantitative data. Our study utilized case studies, interviews with innovators, and statistical analysis of patent data to identify the patterns and factors that lead to breakthroughs.

Our results indicate that breakthroughs are often the result of a particular combination of factors, including diverse perspectives, interdisciplinary collaborations, experimentation, and an environment that allows for failure. Moreover, our research identifies a number of key strategies that organizations and individuals can employ to facilitate these factors and foster innovation.

In conclusion, by applying complexity theory to the study of breakthroughs, our research provides valuable insights for those seeking to innovate in various fields. Our findings suggest that fostering breakthroughs requires a deep understanding of the complex, systemic factors that underpin innovation, and that by cultivating certain conditions, it is possible to nurture these outcomes and drive transformative change in a wide range of domains.

In this work, we present a language-based approach for improving the robustness of network application protocol implementations. We believe that network protocols are essential building blocks of modern communication systems and any issues with their robustness can lead to severe consequences. The motivation for this research work lies in the observation that protocol implementations suffer from errors which often manifest at run-time. Existing works in this domain have shown that the errors often originate from subtle inconsistencies in the specification language used. 
Our approach is language-based, and it involves developing a type system that enforces stronger invariants on the specification and implementation of the protocol. We evaluate our approach through a case study on the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) and demonstrate that it yields considerable benefits in terms of fewer run-time errors and thus improved robustness.
The approach we propose can be used for other network protocol implementations. Our approach is an essential step towards ensuring that network protocol implementations are more robust. We envisage that this work will contribute to safer and more reliable network communication systems.

In this work, we investigate the effects of lepton flavour violation (LFV) on chargino production at the linear collider. The Standard Model (SM) predicts that LFV is highly suppressed, and thus is not observable in current experiments. However, it is possible that new physics beyond the SM may introduce LFV. Chargino production is a key process for discovering new physics, as it is sensitive to the properties of both the chargino and neutralino sectors.

Using a simplified model framework, we study the impact of LFV on the chargino production cross section and kinematic distributions. We find that LFV can significantly alter the chargino production rates and distributions, with deviations from the SM expectations reaching up to a factor of three. We also examine the sensitivity of the study to the input parameters of the model, and demonstrate that the results are robust within reasonable variations of the parameters.

Our work contributes to the broader field of searches for new physics at colliders, by investigating the potential implications of LFV on chargino production. This study sheds light on the importance of considering potentially beyond-the-SM processes in experimental analyses. Overall, the results presented here highlight the potential of future linear collider experiments to probe the LFV and chargino sectors, and provide valuable input for future experimental design and data analyses.

In our work titled "On Gene Duplication Models for Evolving Regulatory Networks," we aim to address a fundamental question in evolutionary biology: how do complex regulatory networks evolve from simple ones? The duplication and divergence of genes and their regulatory regions is a key mechanism by which new functions can arise and drive evolutionary innovation. However, the precise evolutionary trajectories and dynamics of these processes are still not well understood, and many open questions remain.

To tackle this problem, we explore various gene duplication models in the context of evolving regulatory networks using computer simulations and statistical analyses. We focus on the role of gene duplication in the evolution of transcriptional regulatory networks, which play important roles in controlling gene expression and cell differentiation.

Our approach allows us to investigate the effects of various parameters such as gene dosage, the topology of the network, and the strength of regulatory interactions. By comparing and contrasting different models, we aim to shed light on the underlying mechanisms and constraints that shape the evolution of regulatory networks.

Overall, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between gene duplication and regulatory evolution, and may have important implications for fields ranging from evolutionary biology to biotechnology and synthetic biology.

In this work, we present a group-finding algorithm and a catalogue of groups of galaxies in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 5. Our aim is to identify and characterize groups of galaxies to better understand the large-scale structure of the universe.

The group-finder algorithm is based on the Friends-of-Friends (FoF) algorithm, with modifications to optimize the grouping of galaxies across a range of separation scales. We apply the algorithm to a sample of galaxies from the SDSS DR5 and generate a catalogue of groups containing at least three members.

Our catalogue contains 79,991 groups of galaxies, with a median group size of 16 members and a maximum size of over 500 members. We also provide information on the properties of each group, including the distribution of galaxy luminosities, velocities, and colors.

The motivation for this research is to improve our understanding of the nature and evolution of galaxies by studying groups as a whole, rather than as individual objects. The grouping of galaxies can reveal important information about the large-scale structure and dynamics of the universe, such as the clustering of galaxies and the formation of galaxy clusters.

Overall, our work provides a valuable resource for future studies on the properties and evolution of galaxy groups, and helps to shed light on the mysteries of the universe.

In this work, we investigate the complex Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix in the context of spontaneous CP violation and generalized $\mu$-$\tau$ symmetry. The CKM matrix describes the mixing of the three generations of quarks in the Standard Model of particle physics and plays a crucial role in the description of CP violation phenomena. While the CKM matrix is usually taken to be a unitary matrix, it can be shown that the presence of spontaneous CP violation allows for the CKM matrix to have complex elements. 

We explore the consequences of such a complex CKM matrix in the case of generalized $\mu$-$\tau$ symmetry, which relates the second- and third-generation leptons. This symmetry has recently gained attention due to its potential to explain certain neutrino oscillation data. We find that the presence of a complex CKM matrix allows for additional sources of CP violation beyond the usual phases, and that these sources can have important implications for neutrino physics.

Our results provide a new perspective on CP violation in the context of the CKM matrix and broaden the potential implications of generalized $\mu$-$\tau$ symmetry. By considering a complex CKM matrix and its effects on neutrino physics, we contribute to the ongoing effort to understand the fundamental mechanisms underlying the properties of matter and the universe.
command-xlarge-nightly: We present a method to search archival radio observations for transients with sensitivity below one Jansky. We show that archival Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations can be searched with a sensitivity of  ∼ 1 μJansky with a signal-to-noise ratio of  ∼ 5, without any special processing. We present a catalog of 13 new transient sources found in archival VLBI observations, including three sources with fluxes above 10 μJansky. These transients are correlated with previously known transient sources in the Galactic plane, supporting the hypothesis that the transient population is tightly coupled to the Galactic magnetic field. We find that the observed transient distribution has a power law dependence on Galactic longitude  ∼ -0.35, which is consistent with a simple model in which the transient distribution is controlled by the local magnetic field configuration. Our results imply that the population of transient sources in the Galactic plane is several orders of magnitude larger than previously thought on the basis of optical observations.

The SN 1987A Link to Gamma-Ray Bursts

We present a model for the origin of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) based on the analysis of a large number of observations of the SN 1987A supernova. Our model requires that the GRBs are due to the interaction of the shock wave from the supernova with the circumstellar matter. We show that the observed correlation between the optical light curve and the time evolution of the circumburst emission in gamma rays is consistent with this model, provided that the bursty emission has a simple power law decay with an exponential cut-off. We show that the observed correlation is inconsistent with the idea that the bursty gamma rays are due to the interaction of the shock wave with the ISM (interstellar medium) or with a large scale magnetic field. We show that our model can explain several aspects of the GRB phenomenon not previously explained, such as the relation between the burst rate and the ambient magnetic field, the observations of 'soft' gamma rays in some bursts, the relation between the energy of the burst and the energy of the optical light curve of the supernova, and the presence of a spectral peak at about 1 keV in some bursts. Our model predicts that bursts should occur preferentially in binaries with a large ratio between the mass of the donor star and the mass of the compact object, which is consistent with observations. We show that the energy released in a burst is on the order of 10^36 erg, which is about a factor 10^2 larger than the energy released in the subsequent supernova explosion. We discuss the physical mechanism that can produce this extraordinary energy release, and the relation with the general theory of relativity.

We present a statistical analysis of the hardness of the spectrum of low-power blazars in the 9 years of EGRET data. We find that the hardest portions of the blazar spectra are the most variable on timescales from weeks to years, consistent with thermal stratification of the accretion flow. The most energetic photons tend to come from the hardest spectrum portions. We find that the spectral index, defined as the ratio of the count rate in the hardest M15 and hardest M20 energy bands, is well described by a power law with an index of -1.91 +- 0.09 and a significance level of 4sigma. This index is nearly constant (at the 1sigma level) for all but the very highest power law galaxies, and does not harden with flux. We find that the count rate in the M15 and M20 energy bands is described by a single power law with an index of -2.35 +- 0.1 and a significance level of 3sigma. We find that the difference between the count rates in the two energy bands is described by a power law with an index of -1.06 +- 0.08 and a significance level of 4sigma. We discuss these results in the context of models of the blazar accretion flow, and find that they are consistent with a simple model in which the accretion flow is optically thick, and the observed hardness is due only to radiative cooling and not to other effects such as electron thermal conduction or the presence of a harder seed spectrum.

We investigate the effect of imposing symmetry on the structure of vortices in a hexagonal honeycomb lattice and a kagome-lattice-based pinning array. We show that the presence of a six-fold symmetry in the honeycombs or a three-fold symmetry in the kagomes introduces a rotation-symmetric state with a single vortex core. We term this state the vortex molecular crystal state. For both lattices, this state is a strictly-ordered state with a constant number of vortices, and it is one of the few examples of a quasi-molecular crystal state in a vortex system. We also show that the imposition of a four-fold symmetry in the honeycombs or a two-fold symmetry in the kagomes introduces a symmetry-broken state with a vortex core at the center of each symmetry-imposing unit cell, and we term this state the vortex plastic crystal state. The analysis of these states is facilitated by a detailed mapping of the two- vortex system onto a honeycombed or Kagome-lattice-based pinning array, which enables an application of the exactly-soluble combinatorial theory of an expanding symmetric pattern. The application of this theory allows for the determination of the number of vortex rings in the outermost regions of the systems, in terms of the basis states of the vortex system.

We give a simple mechanical proof of the second law of thermodynamics based on volume entropy. We show that the evolution of a mechanical system under the action of an external field can be viewed as an evolution of the volume entropy of a material particle. This approach allows one to give a simple proof of the second law without using the thermodynamic formalism. The proof is based only on the definition of entropy and the laws of motion. We show further that the volume entropy can be used to describe the statistical ensemble of a mechanical system in the thermodynamic limit. The statistical ensemble has the property that its total volume is constant. This has important consequences for the statistical theory of mechanics. We show that the mechanical work done by an external field on a mechanical system can be viewed as a contribution to the total change of the volume entropy of the system. This approach can be used to generalize the statistical theory of mechanics to an arbitrary number of degrees of freedom and to continuously deformable mechanical systems.

We present an experimental test of non-local realism, based on the idea that if a quantum system is prepared in a state in which the values of certain properties are non-commuting, then a measurement of one of these properties will have an impact on the value of the other property, even when this second property is measured at a distance from the first one. To this end, we prepare an entangled state of two spatially separated qutrits, and perform a joint measurement of their respective amplitudes in a particular basis. We show that the outcome of this measurement has an immediate impact on the value of the quantum state of the other qutrit, in spite of the fact that there is no communication between the two qutrits, nor between the two measurement apparatuses. Our result implies that, even when a quantum system is prepared in a state in which non-local commutativity is guaranteed by the laws of quantum mechanics, this state nevertheless has a well-defined value for the non-commuting properties, and that this value is not affected by a distant measurement of one of these properties. We also analyze a possible experimental realization of this scenario, using current technology, and find that such a realization is within the reach of current experimental capabilities.

We present a formalism for the deterministic characterization of stochastic genetic circuits. We define a stochastic protocol using only Markovian logic and elementary stochastic operations. This protocol characterizes the probabilistic behavior of genetic circuits in terms of logic-based description. The protocol is based on the identification of a suitable class of Genetic Grammars that is able to express any stochastic genetic circuit. The class is defined by extending the Genetic Algorithm in a way that allows to combine Markovian logic with stochastic operations. The characterization is achieved by means of an interpreter that takes as input a Genetic Grammar and outputs the corresponding stochastic protocol. We show how to use the interpreter to perform a formal verification of the dynamics of a genetic circuit against a specification in the form of a stochastic protocol. As an example, we apply our framework to the characterization of a stochastic genetic circuit that is involved in the evolution of modularity in bacterial gene expression.

Dynamical 3-Space: A Review

We introduce the notion of a dynamical 3-space, which is an extension of the concept of a 3-space to the setting of dynamical systems. We review the theory of dynamical 3-spaces and discuss some of their applications, such as to the representation theory of Lie groups and to the analysis of oscillatory and chaotic dynamical systems.

The theory of 3-spaces has its roots in the representation theory of finite dimensional Lie algebras. For any Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, there is a unique representation $\pi: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{B}^{n}$, where $\mathfrak{B}$ is the Lie algebra of trace class operators on $\mathfrak{g}$ and $n$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{B}$. This representation is given by the $n$-by-$n$ matrix representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ on the space of square-integrable complex valued functions $\mathfrak{B}^{n}$.

For a generalization of the notion of a 3-space to the setting of dynamical systems, one can define the notion of a dynamical 3-space as a space of functions on a system which are invariant under a finite set of affine transformations of the phase space of the system. The space is typically taken to be the space of square-integrable functions on the phase space, although this is not necessary.

We review the theory of dynamical 3-spaces, including the basic results on the structure of such spaces and the theory of 3-annihilators. We also discuss some of the applications of dynamical 3-spaces, such as to the representation theory of Lie groups and to the analysis of oscillatory and chaotic dynamical systems.

We present a morphological study of galaxies in the A901/902 supercluster from the COMBO-17 survey. A total of 570 galaxies with photometric redshifts in the range 0.155 < z_phot < 1.046 are visually classified by three independent classifiers to M_V=-18. These morphological classifications are compared to local galaxy density, distance from the nearest cluster centre, local surface brightness and photometric classification. At high local galaxy densities, log(Sigma_10 / Mpc^2) > 1.5, a classical morphology-density relation is found. A correlation is also found between morphology and local surface brightness, with the log(Sigma_10 / arcsec^2) > 1.5 relation previously found in the local group. A correlation is found between morphology and distance from the nearest cluster, with a clear tendency for galaxies to be more irregular close to a cluster. A similar correlation is found for photometric classification, with a tendency for galaxies to be more irregular or late-type galaxies close to a cluster. We also find a morphological difference between galaxies in the A901/902 supercluster and in the local group: in the local group, late-type galaxies are more common in high-density environments, while in the A901/902 supercluster the trend is reversed, with irregular galaxies being more common in high-density environments. We discuss these results in the context of recent theoretical models.

We present far-infrared spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of galaxies in the z~0.7 Universe, selected from the Halfway Galaxy survey, in order to investigate the evolution of the dust content of galaxies in the reionization era. We find a large diversity in the SEDs, with most galaxies showing a clear trend of increasing dust temperature with wavelength, but with several exceptions. The most notable result is a group of eight galaxies in which the dust temperature is below the value expected from an optically thick dust cloud at the given observed wavelength. We discuss several physical mechanisms that may be responsible for this effect, including the important role of AGN feedback. In addition, we find that the dust temperature trend is correlated with the stellar mass, but not with the gas mass, the star formation rate, or the redshift. We also find a correlation between the observed dust temperature and the dust mass, suggesting that the dust is more efficiently heated in massive galaxies. Our results are consistent with the idea that galaxies are able to preserve their dust content despite the harsh conditions of the reionization era, but at the same time they suggest that dust may be removed more efficiently in massive galaxies.

We have carried out a detailed study of the energy distribution of the cosmic rays produced in supernova remnants. Our analysis includes both the absolute intensity and the relative intensity as a function of energy. The energy distribution of the cosmic rays in supernova remnants is found to be described by a power law with a cut-off at the MeV energies. This cut-off energy is found to be in the range 0.6-1.5 MeV, with a mean value of 1.1 MeV. This is consistent with the production of cosmic rays by thermal runaway in the shock wave and with the subsequent decay of the radioisotopes produced in this process. The results are consistent with the assumption that the relative intensity of the cosmic rays produced in a supernova remnant is inversely proportional to the supernova remnant's age. Our findings are consistent with a single, universal curve describing the energy distribution of the cosmic rays produced in all supernova remnants, regardless of the type of the supernova or the nature of the interstellar medium through which the rays have propagated. The energy distribution of the cosmic rays in the supernova remnant SN 1987A is found to be described by a power law with a cut-off at the MeV energies, in agreement with our model. The present observations do not allow us to determine the absolute intensity of the cosmic rays in the supernova remnant SN 1987A, but we estimate that it is in the range 0.08-0.25 erg cm-2 s-1. The present observations also do not allow us to place an upper limit on the energy distribution of the cosmic rays in the supernova remnant SN 1987A.

We present photometric and spectroscopic data for a large sample of F and G dwarf stars in the solar neighbourhood, with the aim of investigating the relation between the properties of these stars and their evolutionary status. Our sample consists of 92 F and G dwarfs with known orbital elements and absolute photometric magnitudes, which we combine with broadband photometry and high-resolution spectroscopy from the UVES and FIES spectrographs on the ESO VLT. We find that the kinematic properties of these stars are consistent with two different prescriptions: (i) a spherically symmetric potential field with a radial distribution of masses according to the thin disc approximation, and (ii) a potential field created by the migration of massive bodies from the parent molecular cloud. In both cases, the velocity field is well described by a single set of parameters, which we determine from the analysis of the data. The derived parameters are consistent with the predictions of both the thin disc and the migration models, although the latter is able to provide a slightly better description of the data. We discuss the evolutionary status of our sample stars in the light of our results, and we draw conclusions on the mechanisms that regulate the dynamical evolution of the Galactic disc.

We propose and analyze a model of a statistical ensemble of dimers which has a continuum of discrete states. The model is studied in the limit of a large number of dimers. We show that the model is exactly solvable and we calculate the probability distribution of the occupation of the continuum of states. The results are consistent with the statistical mechanics prediction of a Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution. The special case of a dimer model with free fermions is also analyzed. We show that in this case the model is not exactly solvable, but that a probabilistic approach can be used to determine the occupation of the continuum of states. The results are consistent with the statistical mechanics prediction of a Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution. We also analyze a model of a statistical ensemble of free fermions. We show that the model is exactly solvable and we calculate the probability distribution of the occupation of the continuum of states. The results are consistent with the statistical mechanics prediction of a Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution. We also analyze a model of a statistical ensemble of "super-quantum" particles. We show that the model is exactly solvable and we calculate the probability distribution of the occupation of the continuum of states. The results are consistent with the statistical mechanics prediction of a Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution.

We investigate the effects of planetesimal formation and growth on the retention of different size grains in protoplanetary disks. We employ a hybrid algorithm combining Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations to follow the collisional evolution of grains and planetesimals. We find that planetesimal formation and growth is most efficient near the snow line, where a large number of small planetesimals can grow into large bodies by colliding with pebbles and staying in the disk. We show that this efficient planetesimal retention due to multiple growth events can explain the preference for large planetesimals over the distance of the disk, without the need for a radial dependence of the planetesimal formation efficiency. Within our model, planetesimals grow efficiently as long as their size is larger than a threshold of about 1 cm. Below this threshold, the number of planetesimals is in general too small to explain the large number of planetesimals larger than 1 km observed in exoplanet systems. We discuss how this threshold may have been reached in the disk by planetesimal formation and evolution. Our model implies that planetesimals grow efficiently as long as the disk has a turbulence intensity above a certain threshold, which is about log(Ω/L) ∼ -1.5, where Ω is the typicality length and L is the disk's radial extent. We show that this turbulence level is typical for the solar nebula and many other protoplanetary disks, and is therefore sufficient to explain the rapid growth of planetesimals observed in the disk.

We investigate the structure of collective states of the odd-mass nuclei within the framework of the Interacting Vector Boson Model. The main goal of the work is to determine the nature of the single-particle basis of the collective states and to establish the connection between the properties of these states and the structure of the original Hamiltonian. We show that the collective states can be constructed as a linear combination of single-particle states with certain properties. The masses and the widths of the collective states can be evaluated by using the single-particle basis and the structure of the original Hamiltonian in a simple and straightforward way. Our results are consistent with the odd-mass nucleus being in a collective state with two different width contributions, one of which is close to the width of the fundamental state and the other is close to the width of the first excited state.
